seo.title: Karmic tail 12 10 16 compatibility: Hanged Man, Wheel and Tower
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 10 16 compatibility: the Hanged Man, the Wheel and the Tower, and why this couple decides long before it speaks, as the Arabian Nights show.

items.title: Karmic tail 12-10-16 in compatibility: a thousand and one nights for two
items.short: The Hanged Man, the Wheel of Fortune and the Tower form a tail that only a couple can have: in a personal destiny matrix the road to the Tower as the main task never begins with the Hanged Man. The answer to the riddle fits into one sentence: this couple makes its main decision long before it says it out loud. The two hold on to each other through a deferred "to be continued", live in circles where the same scene comes back again and again, and learn the hardest thing of all: to take apart the old fortress each of them once built out of pain, while it still stands between them.

sections.h2: "I will not slay her until I have heard the rest of her tale"
paragraphs: The story begins with two betrayals. Two kings, the brothers Shahryar and Shah Zaman, discover that their wives are unfaithful and leave their palaces to wander the world. By the sea they meet an Ifrit who carries a captive woman with him. She describes for herself how he keeps her: he "put me into a casket and set the casket in a coffer and to the coffer he affixed seven strong padlocks of steel and deposited me on the deep bottom of the sea that raves" (here and below the Nights are quoted in Richard Burton's translation). While the Ifrit sleeps, the captive takes the brothers' seal rings and shows them a string on which five hundred and seventy rings already hang. She draws the moral herself: "whatso woman willeth the same she fulfilleth however man nilleth".

The brothers take comfort: "there hath happened to him a greater mishap than that which befel us", and they go home. Shahryar has his wife put to death and sets up a routine: a new bride every night, an execution every morning. Three years pass this way, until the Wazir who carries out the sentences can find no more girls in the city.

Then the Wazir's elder daughter, Shahrazad, who "had perused the books, annals and legends of preceding Kings", asks to be given to the King. She explains her reckoning to her father in one sentence: "either I shall live or I shall be a ransom for the virgin daughters of Moslems". She tells her younger sister, Dunyazad, to ask for a story during the night. The sister asks, and Shahrazad begins the tale of the Trader and the Jinni.

At dawn the tale breaks off mid-sentence, and for the first time the book uses a formula it will repeat about a thousand times: "And Shahrazad perceived the dawn of day and ceased to say her permitted say." Her sister praises the story, and Shahrazad answers: "What is this to that I could tell thee on the coming night, were I to live and the King would spare me?" And the King says to himself: "By Allah, I will not slay her, until I shall have heard the rest of her tale."

Then comes a morning worth reading slowly. The King goes to his audience hall, "and the Wazir went up with his daughter's shroud under his arm". The father has brought a shroud for his daughter. Until evening the King "promoted this and deposed that" and told the Wazir nothing.

That single day and night already holds the whole of the 12-10-16 tail. The night belongs to the Hanged Man: the sentence hangs but is not carried out. The day belongs to the Wheel: someone is raised, someone is brought down, and in the evening it all starts again. Behind both stands the thing nobody touches: the King's vow, a fortress built after the betrayal. That is the Tower, the main task, and it is the reason the wheel keeps turning.

The tale hands out its roles by sex; the tail does not. In a real couple either partner can be the storyteller, and either can have a vow of their own. More often each has half of both: one keeps the interest alive, the other keeps the door shut, and in another situation they swap places.

sections.h2: Clues in the numbers: a tail no single person has
paragraphs: The first clue is an impossibility. In a personal matrix the entry to the tail equals the main task plus the centre of the chart. If the main task is the Tower, 16, the entry can never be 12, whatever the centre. A person can have the Tower as the main task in only one tail, 21-10-16, and the centre of such a chart is always the Hierophant.

Lay the two tails side by side and the secret shows through. A 12-10-16 couple gets the same Wheel and the same Tower as a person with the 21-10-16 tail, and the same Hierophant in the centre. Only the entry changes: instead of the World, where everything comes at once and whole, there is the Hanged Man, where everything comes later. For one person this plot starts from fullness. For two it starts from a pause.

The second clue is what stands between the Hanged Man and the Tower. In couples it is almost always the Wheel: the 12-19-16 triple, with the Sun in the Wheel's place, is twenty times rarer, 0.058% of couples against 1.13%.

The third clue is the make-up of the tail. 12-10-16 occurs in roughly one couple in 89 (1.13%, 32nd of the 97 couple tails), and it is nearly always assembled from the same two personal tails. In 98% of these couples one partner has the personal tail 18-6-6 (The Moon, The Lovers, The Lovers) and the other has 21-4-10 (The World, The Emperor, The Wheel of Fortune). Another 2% come from the personal tails 3-13-10 and 9-15-6. Two 6-14-8 tails can also produce it, but so rarely that the share rounds down to zero.

Here is how it works for the dates 14.10.1975 and 04.07.1975. For the first date the day is 14, the month 10, the year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. The main task is 14 + 10 + 22 = 46 → 4 + 6 = 10, the centre 14 + 10 + 22 + 10 = 56 → 11, the entry 10 + 11 = 21, the middle 21 + 10 = 31 → 4: the personal tail 21-4-10. For the second date we have 4, 7 and 22, the main task 33 → 6, the centre 39 → 12, the entry 6 + 12 = 18, the middle 18 + 6 = 24 → 6: the personal tail 18-6-6. Each point of the couple is the sum of the same points in the two personal matrices:

The couple's middle is not recalculated from the two outer numbers: it is the sum of the personal middles, 4 + 6. For these dates the couple's centre is 11 + 12 = 23 → 5, the Hierophant, and the couple's values card is 15, the Devil.
What each card is made of is a clue in itself.

ul: **The Hanged Man** of the couple is, in 98% of cases, the sum of the World and the Moon, 21 + 18. A whole world told at night: there is no more exact description of what Shahrazad does. The same card also sits on the "Common language" point in the "Relationship and common language" sphere, so it appears twice in the couple's reading.
**The Wheel** is the sum of the personal middles, and in 98% of cases these are the Emperor of one partner and the Lovers of the other, 4 + 6. Power and choice, added together, begin to turn.
**The Tower** is always the exact sum of the two personal main tasks, and almost always these are the Wheel of Fortune of one partner and the Lovers of the other, 10 + 6.

**The Hierophant** in the centre is assembled, in 98% of these couples, from the centres of the personal charts: Strength in one and the Hanged Man in the other, 11 + 12 = 23 → 5. So the Hanged Man already lives inside one of the two, in that person's comfort zone.

sections.h2: Entry to the task, The Hanged Man: a knife stopped by the dawn
paragraphs: Shahrazad does not break off her first night just anywhere. Her first tale is about a trader who ate some dates and threw away the stones, and a stone killed the son of a Jinni. The Jinni raises his sword; the trader asks for a delay until the head of the new year so that he can settle his debts, and a year later he comes back of his own accord: he "took his shroud under his arm and bade farewell to his people, his neighbours and all his kith and kin, and went forth despite his own nose". Three old men buy his life. Each tells the Jinni a story, and for a marvellous story the Jinni promises "a third of his blood". The very first tale of the book is the frame in miniature: time is bought by delay, and life is bought by a story.

Dawn finds Shahrazad in the middle of the first old man's story. His wife, a sorceress, has turned his son into a calf, and on "the Great Festival of Allah" he must slaughter the finest beast. The night's last words are: "I went up to the calf, knife in hand". In a footnote Burton explains that the Great Festival is the Id al-Kabir, the "Festival of the Kurbán" (sacrifice). It is kept in memory of Abraham's knife, stopped above his son. The first night of the book ends with a knife raised over a son on the feast of sacrifice, and the dawn stops it just as it stops the sword above the storyteller herself.

Among Waite's divinatory meanings for the Hanged Man is the word "sacrifice", and he sums up the card in the formula "life in suspension, but life and not death". The thousand nights are built exactly that way: the execution is not cancelled, it is postponed, and inside the postponement life goes on: conversations, children, three years of marriage.

The entry to the task is what the couple wants together, its common language. Here that language is strikingly shared. The King wants to hear the end. Shahrazad wants to see the morning. It is one wish seen from two ends: that the story should go on. The Hanged Man looks at the world upside down, and the couple sees the same pause from opposite sides: for one it is curiosity, for the other it is rescue.

In a real couple this language is easy to recognise. The important conversation is always "let's talk tomorrow". The decision about moving, about the wedding, about children, about what really happened three years ago, hangs in the air, and it hangs gently, without quarrels, because that feels kinder. The evening is built like a series: we'll finish watching, we'll finish talking, the main thing can wait. Lisovskaya writes of the Hanged Man in a couple that such people take a long time to enter a relationship and need a push from outside to take the decisive step. In the tale that push sits at the foot of the couch, and her name is Dunyazad. Every night the conversation is opened not by Shahrazad and not by the King but by the third: "Allah upon thee, O my sister, recite to us some new story, delightsome and delectable, wherewith to while away the waking hours of our latter night." A real couple has its own Dunyazad, a friend, a shared project, a circumstance, who asks the question the two do not ask each other.

Lisovskaya describes the minus side of the Hanged Man as the path of sacrifice: everything for the other, nothing for oneself, one partner holding the relationship together with all their strength and unable to leave. That is Shahrazad at the moment the tale stops being a game: every night she has to be interesting again, or in the morning there is the shroud. In a couple it looks peaceful. One partner keeps trying, inventing, entertaining, reading the other's mood, while the other takes it for granted and keeps the decision to themselves.

This point has a reverse side too: it stands on the line of tasks, so the couple's wish easily turns into its resistance. As long as there is another episode, there is no need to write the ending. The pause that saved the two on the first night becomes, by the hundredth, a way of not speaking.

And yet the Hanged Man holds what leads out of this circle. Benebell Wen writes: "There is a component of grace to the card. The Seeker must show grace to his or her condemners." Shahrazad does not argue with the King about his vow and does not accuse him. She comes not with a verdict on his verdict but with a story. That is the strength of a 12-10-16 couple: the ability not to storm the other's fortress head-on.

sections.h2: Middle of the task, The Wheel of Fortune: a morning with a shroud under the arm
paragraphs: The strangest thing in the Thousand and One Nights is not the jinn but the repetition. The same formula, the dawn, the "permitted say", the sister's praise, "were I to live", the King's decision to wait, comes back night after night. A thousand and one nights is almost two years and nine months. Before Shahrazad the King had been killing for three years. Her stories lasted three years as well: at the end, in Burton's text, the King tells his brother what had befallen him with Shahrazad "during the past three years". The Wheel makes a full turn: the same span of time, the same king, the same bedchamber, only now there are stories instead of executions.

By day the wheel turns quite literally: the King "promoted this and deposed that". For the courtiers this is the Wheel of Fortune in its purest form: raised today, brought down tomorrow. And at night the same man finds himself inside someone else's wheel, held by a plot that does not belong to him.

Shahrazad knew the law of the wheel in advance. Her first words in the book are a verse with which she comforts her father: "Tell whoso hath sorrow / Grief never shall last: / E'en as joy hath no morrow / So woe shall go past." Waite says the Wheel stands "for the perpetual motion of a fluidic universe and for the flux of human life". Wen compares it to "the mathematical concept of the unit circle", to sine and cosine, "revealing the philosophy of oscillations between zeniths and nadirs", and calls the wheel "the mandala of the tarot, encompassing the whole of the teachings in the Major Arcana". Both descriptions fit the book literally: the frame holds all the tales, and life inside it runs as a sine wave, danger peaking at dawn, relief in the evening, and round again.

The middle of the task is how the couple travels from its shared wish to its main task. For 12-10-16 that path is not straight but circular. Lisovskaya sees cyclicity in the couple's Wheel: rises and crises follow one another, and what has to be accepted is the change itself, rather than fighting it. She describes the minus side as a swing between silence and conflict, and the feeling that it is hard to be together and yet something holds them. In the tale that something has a name: an unfinished story.

In a real couple the wheel shows in repetitions. The same quarrel at the same time of year. The same evening in which one waits and the other tells. Every reconciliation is like a new night: relief, tenderness, the promise to talk tomorrow. The Wheel gives the couple rhythm and a sense of destiny, which is its plus side; Lisovskaya writes of the feeling of a fated meeting. But the rhythm has a price: every turn is bought with fresh effort, and the wheel makes no decisions.

In a footnote to the ending Burton keeps a spare turn of the wheel. In the French version of Trébutien the King replies at the end: "C'est assez; qu'on lui coupe la tête, car ces dernières histoires surtout m'ont causé un ennui mortel" ("Enough; off with her head, for these last stories above all have bored me to death"), and Burton adds that "this reading is found in some of the MSS." It sounds like a joke, but it is accurate: a union held together only by suspense will one day run into boredom. The Wheel turns both ways.

The numbers show what drives this wheel. The couple's middle is the sum of the personal middles, and almost always these are the Emperor of one partner and the Lovers of the other. Power and choice. While power postpones the decision and the choice is not made, both forces go into spinning.

sections.h2: Main task, The Tower: a fortress built on one sentence
paragraphs: Behind all this turning stands a structure that no one touches for a thousand nights. In Burton's translation its foundation is fully visible. On his return Shahryar swears to marry a new wife every night and put her to death the next morning "to make sure of his honour": "For," said he, "there never was nor is there one chaste woman upon the face of earth."

The whole tower rests on one sentence. And the King drew that sentence not from his own life but from someone else's: from the Ifrit's captive and her rings. The brothers look at the Ifrit's misfortune and take comfort that he is worse off. Someone else's catastrophe becomes, for the King, a law about everyone. Wen describes exactly this kind of Tower in its reversed position: "the Seeker relied on false impressions made by others, and as a result will now feel a jolt."

The main task of a couple is the point Lisovskaya reads mostly through its minus side: what the couple fails at and what it has to learn. Among the Tower's tasks she puts first the collapse of an invented image of the partner. In a 12-10-16 couple this image is invented before they meet. Each brings a tower from the past: "everyone leaves", "nobody can be trusted", "I am loved as long as I am interesting". The partner has done nothing yet, but the sentence has already been passed, and every morning it is postponed again.

Waite calls the Tower "a card in particular of unforeseen catastrophe". This couple foresees its catastrophe every morning, and it never comes. Something else falls: the fortress itself, and it falls quietly.

At the end Shahrazad has three sons. She brings them to the King, "one walking, one crawling and one sucking", and asks him to lift the sentence for the children's sake. The King weeps, strains the boys to his bosom and answers: "By Allah, O Shahrazad, I pardoned thee before the coming of these children, for that I found thee chaste, pure, ingenuous and pious!" (Burton's translation).

Here is the answer to the riddle of the tail. "There never was nor is there one chaste woman" collapses under "I found thee chaste". That is the collapse of the invented image: not a lightning bolt but an admission. And the main thing is this: the Tower fell long before the ending. The King had pardoned her earlier, the book does not say when, but until the last night nobody said so. The wheel kept turning by inertia, the sentence kept hanging, and the storyteller kept earning her morning every night.

A 12-10-16 couple makes its main decision before it says it out loud. One partner stopped testing long ago, the other stopped being afraid long ago, yet both live as if the exam were still going on. The task of the Tower is not to wait for the blow but to say aloud: the fortress is no longer needed.

Shahrazad's last words in the book also strike at the foundation of the tower. She reminds the King that the Kings of the Chosroës before him suffered worse mishaps, "and in this is all sufficient warning for the man of wits". The very argument with which the brothers once consoled themselves by the sea, that others have had it worse, she turns the other way round. From someone else's misfortune you can derive a law about everyone, or you can understand that your misfortune is not the only one and that no law follows from it.

Music remembers this Tower too. The finale of Rimsky-Korsakov's suite "Scheherazade" was at first titled "Festival at Baghdad. The Sea. The Ship Breaks against a Cliff Surmounted by a Bronze Horseman"; later the composer removed the titles of the movements. The ship breaks up, yet the suite ends not with the wreck but with the storyteller's quiet violin.

The numbers add a final clue. The couple's Tower is almost always made of the Wheel of Fortune of one partner and the Lovers of the other, their personal main tasks. In their own lives one is learning to accept the turns of fate, the other to choose. Together they bring down what neither turning nor choosing could touch alone.

sections.h2: The atmosphere inside the couple, The Hierophant: marriage, captivity and mercy
paragraphs: The centre of a 12-10-16 couple is the Hierophant in every case without exception. This is not a coincidence but arithmetic: when the couple's main task is the Tower, the centre can only be the Hierophant or Temperance. In 3-10-16 couples it is almost always Temperance; in 12-10-16 couples it is only the Hierophant.

Waite's list of divinatory meanings for the Hierophant reads like a summary of the Thousand and One Nights: "Marriage, alliance, captivity, servitude; by another account, mercy and goodness". In the book these words come almost in order. First a marriage that is in fact captivity and servitude. Then mercy. And only after mercy comes alliance: at the end, in Burton's text, the King sends for "the Kazis and Olema", the judges and the scholars of the law, who marry the couples, and "the contracts were written out". For three years the two have lived as husband and wife, yet only now does Burton call Shahrazad the King's "betrothed", "i.e. whom he intended to marry with regal ceremony".

The atmosphere is what happens between the partners and is not put on show. Here it is the rules of speech. "Permitted say" is in Arabic "Kalám al-mubáh", and Burton explains it as speech "allowed or permitted to her by the King, her husband". Mubāḥ is a term of Islamic law: it names what is permissible, neither commanded nor forbidden. For a thousand nights the two live by a statute: at night one may tell stories, in the morning one must fall silent; the tales may be spoken of, the vow may not.

In a real couple this is recognisable at once. The two have an unspoken list: we don't talk about this in front of the family, this only on holiday, the past never. The rules hold the household together the way they held Shahryar's bedchamber. Lisovskaya sees both sides in the couple's Hierophant. On the plus side these are two people who are also friends: they can trust each other, and their conversation never runs dry. On the minus side the same conversation turns into upbringing: one keeps explaining to the other how things should be done, and the house echoes with an endless "it's all wrong".

Wen says the Hierophant "is about the pedagogy of wisdom and divine knowledge", and the Thousand and One Nights is perhaps the longest lesson in literature. Shahrazad had read the annals and legends of kings; at the end, in Burton's text, she herself calls her stories "admonitory instances of the men of yore". Even the first story in the book is a lesson, and it is not she who tells it. Her father, trying to talk her out of her plan, tells her the Tale of the Bull and the Ass to keep her away from the King. One parable forbids; the thousand that follow set free.

That is the danger of this centre. Shahrazad remade her partner, but she did not preach at him: her lessons are always about others, about traders, fishermen and kings. A 12-10-16 couple loses that lightness when the tale turns into a lecture, when one partner brings up the other in plain words and waits for them to improve.

Wen has a thought about the Hierophant that might have been written for the Ifrit and his coffer: "a person should never assume he or she knows better than another and therefore try to 'protect' or shield someone else from knowledge. We are not the keeper of others." The Ifrit locked up his captive so that she would remain chaste. The King put his wives to death to make sure of his honour. Both keepers lost. A couple's rules work as long as they are an agreement and not a lock.

sections.h2: The couple's values: a chain or a choice
paragraphs: The couple's values are the point that records what the union exists for. For the 12-10-16 tail there is a fork here, split almost exactly in half: 50.9% of these couples have the Devil, 49.1% the Lovers.

Among Waite's meanings for the Devil is "that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil". The value of these couples is a bond both partners feel as fate: it holds more strongly than any argument. Its shadow shows in the same scene at the end. Shahrazad asks for mercy for the children's sake, which means she holds the King with something stronger than a story. Among the Devil's tasks Lisovskaya names the wish to hold a partner with something stronger than feeling, a child, money, position, and her main thought about the Devil in a couple is that nobody belongs to anybody. The Ifrit with his seven padlocks learned that the hard way.

Waite gives the Lovers as "Attraction, love, beauty, trials overcome". The value of these couples is a choice made freely. The King's answer is about exactly that: the children were not needed, the decision had been made earlier, and it was made from who he had come to know she was. A chain or a choice: one tail gives two answers to the question "why are we together", and the couple's reading shows which of them the two have drawn.

sections.h2: How a 12-10-16 couple steps out of the circle
paragraphs: The tail predicts neither a break-up nor a happy ending. It shows where the two keep their key. The plot is changed not by magic but by speech.

ul: **Say out loud what has already been decided.** The main question for this couple is not "what happens next?" but "what did we decide long ago and never say?". A pardon that nobody mentions goes on working like a sentence.

**Name the vows.** Each partner has a sentence of their own in the "there never was nor is" mould: "nobody can be trusted", "I'll be left", "I'm needed as long as I'm useful". It is worth asking whether it was said about the present partner or about someone they never even saw.

**Allow the series to end.** The one who tells the stories can, for once, stop trying, and find that the morning comes anyway. The one who listens can stop "promoting this and deposing that" and say that the story has already convinced them.

**Tell a lesson from a tale.** The Hierophant in the centre gives the couple plenty to talk about; the talk goes sour when it turns into upbringing. Each speaks about themselves instead of teaching the other through other people's examples.
**Rewrite the statute.** Go through the unspoken list of "we don't talk about that" together: what in it protects the home, and what merely stands guard.

**Make the agreement afterwards, not under the sword.** In the book the marriage contract is written after the pardon. Agreements made out of fear hold like a lock; agreements made afterwards hold like a union.

paragraphs: The tale is a metaphor, even though the King in it really does put people to death. If, in a real relationship, one partner threatens the other, this is not a task of the tail and not a reason to endure for the sake of "to be continued": it is danger, and the right step is to call a local emergency number and seek help from people close by and from a psychologist.

In its strong version a 12-10-16 couple can do what few manage: wait without pressing, and change each other without preaching. The wheel does not vanish after the ending: in Burton's text the two brother kings abide "each ruling a day in turn", but now it is a rota, not a sentence. And Shahryar's last command in the book is to summon scribes and copyists and have them write down all that had befallen him with his wife, "first and last". It came to thirty volumes. A thousand and one nights lived as a postponement become a book with an ending, and that is its happiness.

intro: Three cards, three roles in the couple's task:

ul: **Entry to the task: 12, The Hanged Man.** What the couple wants together and the language it speaks: to wait, not to put a full stop, to leave the important thing for tomorrow. This wish holds the two together, and the same wish resists the ending.
**Middle of the task: 10, The Wheel of Fortune.** How the couple walks the path: in circles. Rise and fall, alarm and relief, and a scene played a year ago comes back almost word for word.
**Main task: 16, The Tower.** What the couple has to learn: to dismantle false supports, the vows of "never again" and a ready-made image of the partner, invented before the two even met.
**The atmosphere inside the couple: 5, The Hierophant, in every such couple without exception.** Rules, lessons, "the proper way" and an unspoken list of what may be talked about.

intro: There is a book in which this tail is played out from the first night to the last. Everyone who has heard the words "The Thousand and One Nights" knows how it begins. Few read the ending, and that is exactly where the answer lies.

faq.q: Is the 12-10-16 tail a sign of bad compatibility?
faq.a: No. The couple's matrix gives no percentages and passes no verdicts. The tail describes a task: how the two enter it, how they live through it and what they learn. For a 12-10-16 couple the task is to turn a postponement into a decision and to take apart the vows each of them brought from the past.

faq.q: Does the Tower as the main task predict a break-up?
faq.a: No. Here the Tower is a task, not an event and not a date. The main task is read through what the couple fails at: clinging to an invented image of the partner and to old vows of "never again". The plot of the tail shows that a fortress can fall quietly, from an admission spoken aloud.

faq.q: Why do all couples with this tail have the Hierophant in the centre?
faq.a: That is how the couple's arithmetic works. When the couple's main task is the Tower, the centre can only be the Hierophant or Temperance, and with the Hanged Man at the entry only the Hierophant ever comes up. So the atmosphere of every such couple is the same: rules, lessons and an unspoken list of what may be talked about.

faq.q: Do the tails 16-10-12 or 10-12-16 exist?
faq.a: No. The first number of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, so 16-10-12 and 10-12-16 never occur, and the engine finds no pair of dates that gives 12-16-10: these three numbers combine only in the order 12-10-16. There are other tails with the Tower as the main task, 3-10-16, 21-10-16 and 12-19-16, but those are different couples with different plots.

faq.q: What does it mean if one of us has the personal tail 18-6-6 and the other 21-4-10?
faq.a: That is the most common road to the 12-10-16 tail: 98% of these couples are built this way. The couple's entry is made of the World and the Moon, the middle of the Emperor and the Lovers, the main task of the Wheel of Fortune and the Lovers. Personal tails are read on their own terms: texts about a personal tail are not carried over to the couple's tail.

faq.q: Who is Shahrazad and who is the King in such a couple?
faq.a: The tail belongs to the couple, not to one person, and its roles do not depend on sex. Usually each partner has both: one guards the interest and fears the morning, the other holds the decision and a vow of their own, and in another situation they swap places.

And behind them the Tower: the King's vow, which nobody touches.
The answer lies in the book's last night, but it can be stated at once: **a 12-10-16 couple makes its main decision long before it says it out loud.**

report.h3: One wish seen from two ends

report: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together, its common language. Here that language is shared. The King wants to hear the end. Shahrazad wants to see the morning. It is one wish seen from two ends: that the story should go on.

In a real couple this language is easy to recognise. The important conversation is always "let's talk tomorrow". Decisions about moving, about the wedding, about what really happened long ago hang in the air, gently and without quarrels, because that feels kinder. One partner keeps trying: inventing, entertaining, reading the other's mood. The other takes it for granted and keeps the decision to themselves. The roles do not depend on sex, and the two swap them. But this point stands on the line of tasks, and the couple's wish easily turns into its resistance: **as long as there is another episode, there is no need to write the ending.**

report.h3: A wheel that turns instead of a decision

report: The middle of the task is the Wheel of Fortune, and in the book it shows as repetition. The same formula, the dawn, the "permitted say", "were I to live", the King's decision to wait, comes back about a thousand times. Before Shahrazad the King had been killing for three years; her stories lasted three years as well. The same span of time, the same bedchamber, only now there are stories instead of executions.

In a real couple the wheel shows in scenes that repeat. The same quarrel at the same time of year. A reconciliation like a new night: relief, tenderness, the promise to talk tomorrow. The Wheel gives the couple rhythm and a sense of destiny, but every turn is bought with fresh effort, and the wheel makes no decisions.

In a footnote Burton keeps a spare turn of the wheel. In the French version of Trébutien the King replies at the end: "Enough; off with her head, for these last stories above all have bored me to death", and this reading is found in some manuscripts. It sounds like a joke, but it is accurate: a union held together only by suspense will one day run into boredom.

report.h3: A fortress built on one sentence

report: Behind the wheel stands a structure that no one touches for a thousand nights. Returning home after the betrayal, the King swears to marry a new wife every night and put her to death the next morning: "For," said he, "there never was nor is there one chaste woman upon the face of earth." He drew this from someone else's misfortune: from the Ifrit's captive, kept in a casket inside a coffer under seven steel padlocks on the bottom of the sea, who still gathered 570 strangers' rings. Someone else's catastrophe became a law about everyone.

The couple's main task is the Tower, and above all it is the collapse of an invented image of the partner. In a 12-10-16 couple this image is invented before they meet. Each brings a tower from the past: "everyone leaves", "nobody can be trusted", "I am loved as long as I am interesting". The partner has done nothing yet, but the sentence has already been passed, and every morning it is postponed again.

At the end Shahrazad has three sons, and she asks the King to lift the sentence for the children's sake. The King weeps and answers: "By Allah, O Shahrazad, I pardoned thee before the coming of these children, for that I found thee chaste, pure, ingenuous and pious!" "There never was nor is there one chaste woman" collapses under "I found thee chaste". **The Tower falls not to lightning but to an admission**, and it fell long before the ending. Until the last night, nobody said so.

report.h3: After the pardon, not under the sword

report: At the centre of every such couple stands the Hierophant, and Waite's list of its divinatory meanings reads like a summary of the book: "Marriage, alliance, captivity, servitude; by another account, mercy and goodness". First a marriage that is in fact captivity. Then mercy. And only after mercy comes alliance: at the end the judges and scholars of the law are summoned and the marriage contracts are written out. Even the "permitted say" is, in the original, "Kalám al-mubáh", a term of Islamic law for what is permissible. The couple has a statute of its own as well: what may be said, what may not, and the past never. It holds the home together as long as it stays an agreement and not a lock.
What changes this plot:

ul: **saying out loud what has already been decided**: the couple's main question is not "what happens next?" but "what did we decide long ago and never say?";
naming the vows and checking whether they were made about the present partner or about someone from the past;
for the one who tells the stories, for once not trying; for the one who listens, saying that the story has already convinced them;
making agreements after the fear, not under it.

report: The tale is a metaphor, even though the King in it really does put people to death. If, in a real relationship, one partner threatens the other, this is not a task of the tail but danger: call a local emergency number or crisis line and seek help from people close by and from a psychologist.

In its strong version a 12-10-16 couple can do what few manage: wait without pressing, and change each other without preaching. The King's last command in the book is to have everything that had befallen him with his wife written down, "first and last". A thousand and one nights lived as a postponement become a book with an ending.

seo.title: Karmic tail 12 10 7 compatibility: who holds the reins
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 10 7 compatibility: the couple enters its task by yielding, lives through turns of fortune and learns to drive together, read through Persuasion.

items.title: The couple's karmic tail 12-10-7: The Hanged Man, The Wheel of Fortune and The Chariot in compatibility
items.short: A man hanging upside down who does not move. A wheel that turns by itself. A chariot that someone drives. The three cards of the couple's karmic tail 12-10-7 are three ways of standing still and travelling, and in this order they make a plot: the couple enters its task by yielding and waiting, goes through it by way of turns that come from outside, and the main task is to take the reins and drive on together, leaving the road neither to chance nor to one of the two.

sections.h2: A novel written to these three cards
paragraphs: In 1806 Anne Elliot, nineteen, becomes engaged to a young naval officer, Frederick Wentworth. He has no fortune and no connections, only the certainty that everything will come. Lady Russell, who has taken the place of Anne's mother, persuades her to break the engagement, and Anne gives way. Wentworth goes to sea. Eight years later he comes back a captain and a rich man, while Anne's father, having run through his money, lets the family estate — to Wentworth's sister and her husband, an admiral. The two sit in the same drawing room again, and neither can speak first.

This is the last novel Jane Austen finished, Persuasion; Russian readers know it as Dovody rassudka ("The Arguments of Reason"), in Elena Surits's translation. Austen completed it in the summer of 1816, and the book came out after her death, in December 1817. The title was given by her brother Henry; she herself, by family tradition, called the novel The Elliots. The word left on the cover means both "being talked round" and "conviction", and it describes the first card of the tail. Austen is quoted here in her own English.

In the fourth chapter there is a sentence in which the three cards stand side by side. Anne, at twenty-seven, thinks how eloquent she could now be on the side of "early warm attachment, and a cheerful confidence in futurity, against that over-anxious caution which seems to insult exertion and distrust Providence". The caution that does not move is The Hanged Man. The Providence it distrusts is The Wheel: Waite writes that behind its turns stands Providence, not chance. The exertion it insults is The Chariot.

The next sentence is a portrait of The Hanged Man: **"She had been forced into prudence in her youth, she learned romance as she grew older: the natural sequel of an unnatural beginning."** A life turned upside down: first the caution that suits old age, then the daring that suits youth.

The whole novel runs in the order of the tail. First the persuasion and eight years of standing still. Then the wheel of fortune, which lifts one and lowers the other. At the end, the question of who will take the reins. Austen answers it twice: with a gig in which another couple is driving, and with a letter the hero writes himself.

In the novel the woman gives way and the man holds out: that was the choice of the age and of the author. In a couple with the tail 12-10-7 the roles are not tied to sex and easily change places, and often both live in one person.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: a sacrifice nobody asked for
paragraphs: Point M in the couple's matrix is the "Entry to the task": what the two want together and the language in which they come to terms. On the couple's chart the same point also stands in the sphere "Relationship and common language". The Hanged Man here is a shared wish to protect each other at the cost of one's own step: to wait, to give way, not to drag the other into risk. This wish brings the couple into the task, and it also becomes the resistance.

Anne does not break off the engagement out of calculation. "The belief of being prudent, and self-denying, principally for his advantage, was her chief consolation." The key word is "his". A decision about two was taken by one, out of love, and handed to the other as a finished fact. Wentworth answers with what Anne did not expect: he does not forgive. She had, he thinks, "shewn a feebleness of character in doing so, which his own decided, confident temper could not endure. She had given him up to oblige others."

The striking thing is that Wentworth speaks the same language. On principle he takes no women aboard his ship, "from feeling how impossible it is, with all one's efforts, and all one's sacrifices, to make the accommodations on board such as women ought to have". His sister cuts him short: "All idle refinement!" The two say the same thing in different words: protect the other by keeping them off the road. This is the common language of a couple with The Hanged Man at the entry.

And then both of them hang. Anne refuses another suitor, Charles Musgrove, though Lady Russell would have been glad of the match. Wentworth returns to England in 1808 with a few thousand pounds and does not write to her. Later he admits: "I was proud, too proud to ask again." His letter will give the exact term — "eight years and a half". Nobody leaves, and nobody comes forward. A pause for two that nobody announced.

Waite argues with the prudent reading of The Hanged Man too. This card, he writes, "is supposed to represent Prudence", and he rejects that reading along with martyrdom and duty. His divinatory list for the card gives "Wisdom, circumspection, discernment, trials, sacrifice". Anne's prudence did indeed turn out to be not wisdom but a life in suspension: she plays the pianoforte so that others can dance, and "desired nothing in return but to be unobserved".

In Lisovskaya's book on compatibility The Hanged Man in the plus means tact, attention, a readiness to give way. The partners sense each other at a distance, take a long time to enter a relationship, and need a push from outside to marry. In a couple today it looks like this. One keeps quiet about a job offer in another city, "so as not to make her choose". The other puts off her studies "because now is not the time". Both wait until it is convenient and live for years inside the pause. The minus of the same entry: decisions taken "because that is how it has to be", a glance over the shoulder at what the family will say, and the weariness of the one who holds the relationship together with all their strength and gets reproaches in return.

The Hanged Man also has a way of speaking. In the novel the most important words are almost always said to a third person. Anne sits by a hedgerow and hears Wentworth explaining to Louisa Musgrove what firmness is. Later it is he who listens while Anne talks about constancy with his friend. A couple with this tail also slips easily into a language of hints, errands and "I thought you'd understand without being told".

sections.h2: Middle of the task: a wheel that moves the two around
paragraphs: Point N is the "Middle of the task". In Lisovskaya it has no meaning of its own, only adding to the main task; in our reading it shows how the couple lives the road from the entry to the goal. The Wheel of Fortune in the middle means the road runs through turns that come from outside and each time change where the two stand.

In English, fortune means both luck and wealth, and Austen plays on the word throughout the novel. In 1806 "Captain Wentworth had no fortune." But "he had always been lucky; he knew he should be so still." The war with Napoleon brings prize money: by the end of the novel he has twenty-five thousand pounds. Meanwhile Anne's father, the baronet Sir Walter, lives beyond his means and has to let the estate — to Admiral Croft, a sailor made rich by the same war. Sir Walter complains that the navy is "raising men to honours which their fathers and grandfathers never dreamt of". It is a complaint against the Wheel itself.

Waite's list for The Wheel reads like Wentworth's service record: "Destiny, fortune, success, elevation, luck, felicity." Even The Wheel reversed is not failure for Waite but "Increase, abundance, superfluity": superfluity is what ruined Sir Walter.

Wen adds one more face to The Wheel: force majeure, "an 'act of god,' chance occurrence, unavoidable accident, or matter beyond the Seeker's control", which changes the outcome. In the novel it happens at Lyme. On the stone breakwater Louisa Musgrove runs back up the steps so that Wentworth can catch her jump once more. He advises against it, she answers "I am determined I will", jumps half a second before he can catch her — "too precipitate by half a second" — and falls senseless on the stones. Louisa will recover, but it is this fall that rearranges events. While she slowly comes round, another captain, Benwick, is at hand, and Louisa marries him. Austen explains the match in one sentence: "It had been in situation." Wentworth is free — not because he decided it himself.

The same turn has a second side: it shows who is who. Over Louisa, Wentworth cries, "Is there no one to help me?" — and it is Anne, the one who always gave way, who starts giving orders. Charles Musgrove keeps repeating, "Anne, Anne, what is to be done next?", and "both seemed to look to her for directions". At the turn of the wheel the yielding partner takes the reins. Among Lisovskaya's examples for this energy are couples in which one pulled the other out of a crisis.

Anne herself, at the end of the novel, states the law of The Wheel. Lady Russell's advice, she says, was "one of those cases in which advice is good or bad only as the event decides". A decision is taken in one position of the wheel and judged in another. Hence the minus of the middle. The couple blames fate and each other after the fact: "if only you had…". The swing of "silence, then a row" begins; it is hard together, yet something holds them. The plus is a feeling of a fated meeting and the ability to accept the partner in any position. The wheel turns for everyone; it is just that for this couple the turns stand right on the road to the task: one partner's promotion and the other's redundancy, a move, the birth of a child, the parents' decision to sell the country house. Every turn asks again who is on top now and who is driving.

sections.h2: Main task: firmness or self-will
paragraphs: Point D is the "Main task": the couple's chief trials, read above all through the minus. The Chariot is direction and will, movement towards where you have decided to go. A couple with this tail is learning not decisiveness in general but decisiveness for two.

Wentworth at the start of the novel is The Chariot in the minus. He resents "a feebleness of character" and looks for its opposite. In that scene by the hedgerow he tells Louisa: "It is the worst evil of too yielding and indecisive a character, that no influence over it can be depended on… Let those who would be happy be firm." He picks a nut from a bough, one that "has outlived all the storms of autumn", and holds it up as an example. Two chapters later firm Louisa jumps from the steps because she has decided to.

Wentworth draws the lesson himself, and Austen records it in a sentence that could serve as the definition of this tail's main task: at Lyme **"he had learnt to distinguish between the steadiness of principle and the obstinacy of self-will, between the darings of heedlessness and the resolution of a collected mind"**.

Waite calls the charioteer "above all things triumph in the mind", yet his divinatory list for The Chariot does not begin with victory. The first words are "Succour, providence", and only then "war, triumph, presumption, vengeance, trouble". Wentworth has both halves. When Anne's little nephew hangs on her neck, Wentworth silently lifts the boy off and walks away without waiting for thanks. When Anne tires on a walk, he puts her into his sister's gig, and she feels "that his will and his hands had done it". And the same man nurses a grievance for eight years and writes of himself honestly in his letter: "weak and resentful I have been".

Lisovskaya finds the trials of The Chariot in a couple where the two share the reins. In 1806 Anne and Wentworth ran into all of them at once: his career or their marriage, her family or his road — and the question of who would sacrifice whom was settled by one of them. Today the same trials look ordinary. One partner is offered work abroad, and the question "shall we go?" is talked over for so long that the deadline for an answer decides for both. One expects the other to drop their studies or their business because his or her own goal is "more important for the family". The two plan a holiday, a renovation or a child, and the quarrel over who is in charge flares up out of nothing. Or the reverse: nobody drives, and the couple rolls wherever the road happens to tilt. Lisovskaya's advice for this energy is to name the status of the relationship and the roles clearly, leaving nothing unsaid, and not to hurry the partner.

sections.h2: The Crofts' gig: a task solved before the novel begins
paragraphs: In the novel there is a couple whose main task in this tail is already solved — Admiral Croft and his wife Sophy, Wentworth's sister. Austen shows them in the very gig into which Wentworth has put the tired Anne.

On the way the Admiral recalls his own courtship: "How many days was it, my dear, between the first time of my seeing you and our sitting down together in our lodgings at North Yarmouth?" Mrs Croft replies that they had better not talk about it: if Miss Elliot heard how soon they came to an understanding, "she would never be persuaded that we could be happy together". The same word again, this time with a smile.

And then the gig nearly runs into a post. "My dear Admiral, that post! we shall certainly take that post." Austen goes on: "But by coolly giving the reins a better direction herself they happily passed the danger; and by once afterwards judiciously putting out her hand they neither fell into a rut, nor ran foul of a dung-cart; **and Anne, with some amusement at their style of driving, which she imagined no bad representation of the general guidance of their affairs, found herself safely deposited by them at the Cottage.**" This is not a tarot reader talking but Austen herself: the gig is a portrait of a marriage.

The Chariot of a couple in the plus looks exactly like this. The reins are with one, but the other sits alongside, watches the road and calmly corrects. Nobody is a passenger, nobody is in command for all occasions. Mrs Croft has sailed with her husband for fifteen years, has "crossed the Atlantic four times", and tells her brother: "I hate to hear you talking so like a fine gentleman, and as if women were all fine ladies, instead of rational creatures. We none of us expect to be in smooth water all our days." There will be no smooth water, because The Wheel sits in the middle of the tail. The task is not to stop it but to ride it together.

In Bath Anne sees the Crofts in every street. They walk "in happy independence", and Mrs Croft stands in a knot of naval officers "looking as intelligent and keen as any of the officers around her". This matches how Lisovskaya describes The Chariot of a couple in the plus: more a team and friends than a couple, active, ready to set off, deciding together and fast.

sections.h2: A letter instead of an errand: how Austen rewrote the ending
paragraphs: In the summer of 1816 Austen finished the novel with a different scene. Admiral Croft drags Anne into his lodgings, leaves her alone with Wentworth, and behind the door demands that his brother-in-law find out from her whether it is true she is to marry her cousin. "I hate to be at an uncertainty. I must know at once," says the Admiral. "If you will not speak, I will stop and speak myself." Wentworth does speak, but, in his own words, "speaking only for another, and speaking by necessity". The explanation happens, the couple is united — by a push from outside, the very push without which, in Lisovskaya, The Hanged Man finds it hard to reach marriage.

Austen was not satisfied with the scene. Her nephew James Edward Austen-Leigh writes in his Memoir of Jane Austen that his aunt "thought it tame and flat", went to bed one night in low spirits, and in the morning cancelled the chapter and wrote two new ones in its place. The rejected chapter survived in manuscript and was later printed, so it can be set beside the final one.

In the new ending there is no push. At the inn Anne argues with Captain Harville about who loves more constantly, men or women, and says: "All the privilege I claim for my own sex (it is not a very enviable one; you need not covet it), is that of loving longest, when existence or when hope is gone." At the next table Wentworth is writing what everyone takes for a letter to Benwick. He leaves without a look at Anne, comes back "for his gloves", draws another letter from under the papers and places it before her. "I can listen no longer in silence. I must speak to you by such means as are within my reach. You pierce my soul. I am half agony, half hope… Unjust I may have been, weak and resentful I have been, but never inconstant."

The Hanged Man is still there: the letter is written, not spoken, and the pretext is a pair of forgotten gloves. But the errand is gone; he has taken the reins himself. Anne, holding the letter, feels that "anything might be defied rather than suspense". Austen rewrote the ending exactly the way this tail rewrites a couple: from a push from outside to a step of one's own.

Then the two walk along a quiet gravel path, "as they slowly paced the gradual ascent", and Austen sums up: they are now "more fixed in a knowledge of each other's character" and **"more equal to act, more justified in acting"**. Each owns their part. Anne does not disown the past: giving way to Lady Russell, she says, was right, or her conscience would have tormented her. Wentworth admits that his worst enemy was himself. He asks whether she would have answered if he had written to her in the year eight. "Would I!" — and nothing more is needed. His last words in that chapter are The Chariot finally coming to terms with The Wheel: "I have been used to the gratification of believing myself to earn every blessing that I enjoyed… I must endeavour to subdue my mind to my fortune. I must learn to brook being happier than I deserve."

sections.h2: Waite and Wen: the three cards pass the baton
paragraphs: Books on tarot know nothing of matrix tails, yet in them these three cards are linked in the same order.

Wen ends The Hanged Man reversed like this: "It is not for the Seeker to administer judgment, vengeance, or penance. **Let the Wheel of Fortune turn on its own accord.**" The card of the entry names the card of the middle itself. The Wheel reversed, for Wen, describes "a person who cannot rely on predetermined or external forces to sweep in and help support him or her", a message "to exert greater willpower". And The Chariot, in her words, "indicates great control over one's willpower". The Hanged Man lets The Wheel go, The Wheel demands will, and will is the essence of The Chariot.

Waite links the middle and the task with a single word. Of The Wheel he writes that behind it "there lies the denial of chance" and that its letters are there "to shew that Providence is implied through all". His divinatory list for The Chariot opens with "Succour, providence". The charioteer does not argue with The Wheel; he carries it on with his own hands. Austen said the same: the caution that would "distrust Providence" also "insults exertion".

On Waite's cards there is also a shared beast. At the top of his Wheel sits a sphinx with a sword, and Waite explains: "The Sphinx is the equilibrium therein", "stability amidst movement". Waite's Chariot is drawn by two sphinxes, because the charioteer "has thus replied to the sphinx". The riddle that sits on top of The Wheel is harnessed to The Chariot and pulls it. The cards of our deck are drawn differently; this detail belongs to Waite's deck.

Of The Hanged Man Waite reminds us that "the tree of sacrifice is living wood", and that the figure "suggests life in suspension, but life and not death". Anne's eight years are exactly that kind of life. She did not die to love; she hung.

sections.h2: The numbers of tail 12-10-7: what is written in the couple's cards
paragraphs: The tail 12-10-7 occurs in roughly one couple in 122 (0.822%) and ranks 45th of the 97 couple tails — almost the middle of the list. No other couple tail is made of these three numbers: not 7-10-12, not 10-12-7, no other order. This plot reads in one direction only.

Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22: if the sum is larger, its digits are added. The couple's middle is added up from the partners' middles, not from the two outer numbers. That is why 12-10-7 occurs only in a couple. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail equals the entry plus the task: 12 + 7 = 19, The Sun, and that personal tail, 12-19-7, exists. So one person goes from The Hanged Man to The Chariot through The Sun, through being seen and through a clear day of their own. Two people take the same road through The Wheel.

The couple's Hanged Man never comes from either partner's personal entry. It is made of other cards: The Moon and The World (18 + 21 = 39 → 12) in 41.1% of such couples, The Empress and The Hermit (3 + 9) in 37.5%, two Lovers (6 + 6) in 21.3%. In one couple in five The Hanged Man is put together by two people who each enter their own tail through The Lovers, that is, through choice. Two choices made towards each other produce suspension: so it was with Anne and Wentworth in 1806.

The Wheel in the couple's middle is also always the sum of two personal middles, and neither partner has a Wheel of their own there. In 34% of such couples one of the two terms is The Chariot: one partner has their own will, their own drive, in the middle of their personal tail, and together with the other's Empress it turns into The Wheel. One person's will becomes, for the two of them, a turn of fate. Wentworth's career was The Chariot for him and a wheel of fortune for Anne: first it took her fiancé away, then it brought him back rich.

The tail belongs to the couple as a whole. The Hanged Man stands in the personal tail of at least one partner in only 14.8% of such couples, The Wheel in 26.3%, The Chariot in 34%. In 39.7% of couples none of the three cards appears in either partner's personal tail: neither brought this plot along; it is born between them.

sections.h2: Atmosphere and values: Temperance, The Hierophant, The Lovers, The Devil
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's chart is the shared atmosphere, what lies between the two and is not on show. In 88.7% of 12-10-7 couples the centre holds Temperance. In the plus these are quarrels settled by talking and compromise, and the ability to wait for the right moment — the good version of The Hanged Man. In the minus Lisovskaya describes Temperance in one phrase that fits the first half of the novel: one always gives way, and the other never even thinks about it. Her advice for this energy — not to jump to conclusions about the partner — Wentworth broke after their very first meeting, deciding that Anne was "so altered that he should not have known her again".

In 11.3% of couples the centre holds The Hierophant. In its minus Lisovskaya names the family's interference, up to the choice of a partner — the part played by Lady Russell, who had towards Anne "almost a mother's love, and mother's rights". Only with The Hierophant does the couple's entry follow the personal formula, task plus centre: 7 + 5 = 12.

"The couple's values" are what the union exists for. In 58.4% of 12-10-7 couples they are The Lovers, in 41.6% The Devil. Our reading: The Lovers are a choice that has to be made a second time, as adults and in another position of the wheel, like Anne's "Would I!". The Devil is an attachment that does not let go for eight years, and the question of whether the couple is held by free choice or by a chain of other people's opinions and their own pride. Lisovskaya sums this energy up in the words "no one belongs to anyone".

sections.h2: How to work out the couple's tail: example 05.12.1975 and 07.01.1976
paragraphs: The partner born on 05.12.1975 has the personal tail 18-3-12, the partner born on 07.01.1976 has 21-7-13. The points are added pair by pair:

This example shows how the tail is assembled from other cards. For the first partner The Hanged Man is the personal main task, but in the couple's tail it becomes one of the terms and, together with the second partner's Death, gives The Chariot (12 + 13). For the second partner The Chariot stands in the middle of the personal tail, and in the couple, together with the first partner's Empress, it turns into The Wheel (3 + 7).

This couple's centre is Temperance (6 + 8 = 14), and "The couple's values" hold The Devil. The Hanged Man repeats on the "Image of the couple": from outside, too, the two are seen as people who give way and look after each other, which happens in 6.4% of couples with this tail. The Chariot repeats on the point "What fills", which happens in 6.6% of such couples. This couple's main task is also its fuel: Lisovskaya writes that The Chariot fills a union with the road, with a move to a place chosen together and with the partner's successes, when the two walk side by side but each on their own path.

sections.h2: What changes the script
paragraphs: The tail does not predict how many years the pause will last or whether there will be a "Lyme". It shows where the couple usually keeps the wheel and who lets go of it. Here is what the novel and the cards suggest.

ul: **Offer the sacrifice, do not make it.** If one partner has decided to step back "for the other's good", ask the other first. Anne decided for two, Wentworth decided for every woman on his ship, and both made the same mistake.

**Speak for yourselves, not through a go-between.** Austen struck out the ending in which the Admiral speaks for the hero. Hints, errands and "you should have known" are the language of The Hanged Man; the task of The Chariot is a plain sentence.

**Do not judge a past decision by the wheel's present position.** Advice is good or bad "only as the event decides". The reproach "if only you had…" is an argument with The Wheel, not with the partner.
**In a crisis, watch who keeps a cool head.** A turn often changes the roles: the one who always gave way suddenly takes charge. That change is worth noticing and not taking away.
**Test the firmness.** "Steadiness of principle or obstinacy of self-will?" is a question worth asking oneself before every "I am determined I will".
**Name the route out loud.** Where are we going, who is driving now, when do we change over. A move, a job, a child, a big purchase are decisions for two, not concessions by one.
**Take each other along rather than shield each other from the road.** "We none of us expect to be in smooth water all our days."

paragraphs: The Chariot in the minus can also be heavy: control over every step, bans, threats. That is no longer a lesson of the tail to be endured but a reason to seek help — a psychologist, a crisis line, and in danger the local emergency number.

The strong version of the tail 12-10-7 is the Crofts in their gig. The two know how to wait and how to give way, but no longer mistake this for standing still. The Wheel turns, and the reins are shared.

ul: **M · Entry to the task — The Hanged Man (12).** The couple's common language is to give way, to wait it out, to give up one's own move for the other's sake. With this wish the couple enters the task, and the same wish holds it back.

**N · Middle of the task — The Wheel of Fortune (10).** The road runs through changes the two do not control: money, work, other people's decisions, chance. The Wheel moves the partners around, and each time they meet in a new position.

**D · Main task — The Chariot (7).** To decide and to go together: to name the direction, to agree on who is driving now, and to tell firmness from stubbornness. In the minus, the two either stand still or each pulls the reins their own way.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 12-10-7 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the task of a couple that begins with yielding and waiting (The Hanged Man at the entry), goes through turns of circumstance (The Wheel of Fortune in the middle) and learns to choose the direction together and drive together (The Chariot as the main task). The main trial is to tell firmness from stubbornness and not to decide for the other.

faq.q: Why does the tail 12-10-7 occur only in a couple?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail equals the entry plus the main task: with 12 and 7 it would be 19, The Sun. In a couple the middle is added up from the two partners' middles, which is why it comes out as 10 here. The tail 12-10-7 does not occur in a personal matrix.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. Among the 97 couple tails, the cards 12, 10 and 7 make only the order 12-10-7. The engine gives no other permutation, such as 7-10-12, for any pair of dates.

faq.q: Does this tail mean the couple is bound to wait a long time or to part?
faq.a: No. The tail describes a task, not events or dates. It shows the language in which the couple is used to giving way, how it lives through change and what it has to learn in shared decisions. How long the pause lasts and how the turn ends is up to the two of them.

faq.q: How common is the tail 12-10-7?
faq.a: It occurs in roughly one couple in 122, which is 0.822% of all couples and 45th place of the 97 couple tails. Most often it forms between partners with the personal tails 18-6-15 and 21-4-10, 3-7-22 and 9-3-21, 3-22-19 and 9-15-6.

report: The three cards of the couple's karmic tail 12-10-7 stand side by side in a single sentence by Jane Austen. In Persuasion, Anne Elliot thinks of "that over-anxious caution which seems to insult exertion and distrust Providence". The caution that does not move is The Hanged Man at the entry to the task. The Providence it distrusts is The Wheel of Fortune in the middle. The exertion it insults is The Chariot, the couple's main task.

The plot of the novel runs in the same order. In 1806 Anne, nineteen, becomes engaged to a sailor, Frederick Wentworth, who has neither fortune nor connections. Lady Russell, who has taken the place of her mother, persuades her to break it off, and Anne gives way. Eight years later he comes back a captain and a rich man, while her father lets the family estate to his sister. The two sit in the same drawing room, and neither can speak first. In the novel the woman gives way and the man holds out; in a couple with this tail the roles are not tied to sex.

report.h3: A sacrifice nobody asked for

report: The Hanged Man at the entry is the couple's common language: protecting each other at the cost of one's own step. Anne did not break the engagement out of calculation: she believed she had been prudent and self-denying, "principally for his advantage". A decision about two was taken by one, out of love, and handed to the other as a finished fact.

Wentworth speaks the same language. He takes no women aboard his ship, "from feeling how impossible it is, with all one's efforts, and all one's sacrifices, to make the accommodations on board such as women ought to have". **Protect the other by keeping them off the road** — on this the two understand each other without words. And then both of them hang: Anne refuses another suitor, Wentworth returns to England with money and does not write to her. "I was proud, too proud to ask again." The pause lasts eight and a half years, and nobody announced it.

Austen describes it as a life turned upside down: "She had been forced into prudence in her youth, she learned romance as she grew older: the natural sequel of an unnatural beginning." The Hanged Man hangs head down, and in a couple with this tail caution and daring easily swap places too. Such a couple gets used to speaking through third parties: the most important words in the novel are almost always said to someone else, and "I thought you'd understand without being told" stands in for a plain sentence.

report.h3: A wheel that moves the two around

report: The middle of the tail is The Wheel of Fortune: the road runs through turns that come from outside. In English, fortune means both luck and wealth. The war makes Wentworth rich, Anne's father is ruined, and a sailor moves into his estate. Every turn puts the two in a new position.

A turn also shows who is who. When Louisa Musgrove falls on the stone breakwater, Wentworth cries, "Is there no one to help me?" — and it is Anne, the one who always gave way, who starts giving orders. **At the turn of the wheel the yielding partner takes the reins.** Anne herself later states the law of this card: Lady Russell's advice was "one of those cases in which advice is good or bad only as the event decides". A decision is taken in one position of the wheel and judged in another. Hence the minus of the middle: "if only…", the swing between silence and rows, resentment against fate and against each other.

Benebell Wen links these cards almost on purpose. She ends The Hanged Man reversed with the words "Let the Wheel of Fortune turn on its own accord", and her Wheel reversed calls on the Seeker "to exert greater willpower". Will is the essence of The Chariot.

report.h3: Steadiness of principle or obstinacy of self-will

report: The main task is The Chariot: to decide and to go together. At first Wentworth mistakes it for stubbornness. He has not forgiven Anne "a feebleness of character" and lectures Louisa: "Let those who would be happy be firm." Two chapters later firm Louisa jumps from the steps because she has decided to. After that, Austen writes, **"he had learnt to distinguish between the steadiness of principle and the obstinacy of self-will, between the darings of heedlessness and the resolution of a collected mind"**. This sentence holds the whole main task of the tail 12-10-7. In the minus the two either stand still or each pulls the reins their own way: whose work matters more, whether to move together, who decides about the renovation and the child.

Austen shows the task solved in another couple, Admiral Croft and his wife. They are driving a gig; she spots a post, coolly gives the reins a better direction herself and takes them past the danger. Anne thinks their style of driving is "no bad representation of the general guidance of their affairs". Mrs Croft has crossed the Atlantic four times with her husband and tells her brother: "We none of us expect to be in smooth water all our days." The reins are with one, the other sits alongside and calmly corrects, and nobody is a passenger.

report.h3: The ending Austen rewrote

report: The first ending of the novel rested on a push from outside: the Admiral makes Wentworth speak up, and Wentworth does so "speaking only for another, and speaking by necessity". Austen thought the scene "tame and flat" and rewrote it. In the new one Wentworth writes the letter himself: **"I must speak to you by such means as are within my reach."** This is how the tail rewrites a couple too: from someone else's push to a step of one's own.

What changes the script: offering the sacrifice rather than making it; speaking for oneself, without go-betweens; not judging a past decision by the wheel's present position; naming the route out loud — where the two are going, who is driving now, when they change over. Control over every step, bans and threats are no longer a lesson of the tail but a reason to seek help: a psychologist, a crisis line, and in danger a local emergency number.

The strong version of the tail is the one in which the two know how to wait and to give way but no longer mistake it for standing still. At the end Wentworth admits he must "endeavour to subdue my mind to my fortune". The Wheel turns, and the reins belong to both.
