seo.title: Karmic tail 12 13 19 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 13 19 compatibility: The Hanged Man, Death and The Sun in a couple's destiny matrix, read through the Book of Tobit, with a worked example.

items.title: The 12-13-19 karmic tail in compatibility: The Hanged Man, Death and The Sun
items.short: The couple's tail 12-13-19 sounds like the opening of a grim fairy tale: first The Hanged Man, then Death, and only at the very end The Sun. There is less to fear in it than it seems. This is the tail of a couple who enter their union with a habit of putting their own lives on hold for other people's peace, who pass through the end of an old form, and who learn the main thing — to live in daylight: to see each other rather than old fears, and to hide neither joy nor trouble.

sections.h2: The 12-13-19 tail as a story: the Book of Tobit
paragraphs: The Book of Tobit is more than two thousand years old. Fragments of it in Aramaic and Hebrew turned up among the Dead Sea Scrolls; Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include it, and the 1611 King James Version printed it among the Apocrypha. It is a family story about two houses in two cities.

In Nineveh lives old Tobit, a righteous man who buries his murdered kinsmen even though he could be killed for it himself. "My neighbours mocked me," he says. One night, back from a burial, he lies down to sleep by the wall of his courtyard, and droppings from the birds fall into his open eyes: "a whiteness came in mine eyes". With him are his wife Anna and his son Tobias. In Ecbatana lives Sara, the only daughter of Raguel. She has been given in marriage seven times, and seven times the bridegroom died on the first night — the story blames the evil spirit Asmodeus. Her father's maids throw it in her face: "thou hast had already seven husbands, neither wast thou named after any of them."

On one and the same day both of them ask God for death: a blind old man in one city and a bride of seven weddings in the other. The story says that both prayers are heard at once and that the answer to both is the same — not death, but a road. Tobit sends his son Tobias to fetch silver once left with a kinsman. A young man who calls himself Azarias is hired as his companion; the reader knows he is the angel Raphael. The road leads across the river Tigris, to Raguel's house where Sara waits, and back again — to a father who cannot see.

Lay the story out chapter by chapter and all three cards of the tail are there, in the same order. Two lives put on hold, and the fear of coming close. A wedding night on which the bride's father digs a grave. A blind man to whom the light comes back. And next to the tail, in the matrix of such couples, stand Judgement, The Lovers or The Devil — and each of these cards has its own scene in the book. The story proves nothing about living people. But as a mirror it is accurate to the smallest detail.

sections.h2: Entry to the task, 12: The Hanged Man — two people who say the same sentence
paragraphs: The entry to the task, point M, is what the couple wants together, its common language. In the couple's reading the same point sits in the sphere "Relationship and common language" and is labelled "Common language". For couples with the 12-13-19 tail, that language is The Hanged Man: a life put on hold for the sake of others.

In the Book of Tobit it can be heard word for word. Sara and Tobias have never seen each other, yet they say one and the same sentence. Sara, who had resolved to end her life, stops herself with the thought of her father: "I am the only daughter of my father… and I shall bring his old age with sorrow unto the grave." Tobias, told about the seven dead bridegrooms, answers the angel: "I am the only son of my father, and I am afraid, lest, if I go in unto her, I die, as the other before" — and so "bring my father's and my mother's life because of me to the grave with sorrow". Later Raguel describes them more precisely than anyone: "two that were the only begotten children of their fathers". Two only children with one and the same fear — of grieving their parents.

There it is, the common language of The Hanged Man: my wish can wait, as long as the people close to me are not hurt. In a living couple it sounds ordinary. "Let's not do it now, Mum is having a hard enough time." The move is put off because Dad won't manage on his own. The wedding is postponed because it would be awkward in front of the family. Each one gives way, and gives way sincerely. Yuliana Lisovskaya describes such couples as a union where one partner is ready to do nothing for themselves and everything for the other, where people take a long time to enter the relationship, and where a decisive step needs a push from outside. In the story the push comes from an angel. In life it comes from a friend who asks "how much longer are you going to wait?", from a job in another city, from a sudden clarity after a long pause.

This language has real strength. The two notice each other's tiredness before a word is said, hear each other out to the end and give way without scenes. They sense each other at a distance: Tobias, the story says, fell in love with Sara before they met, from the angel's words alone — "and his heart was effectually joined to her." The Hanged Man is not just patience: it is the ability to stop and look at life from the other side.

But the entry point stands on the line of tasks, and the wish of the entry easily turns into resistance. Suspension becomes a habit. The two are so busy with other people's peace that their own decision is put off for years. In her prayer Sara asks not for happiness but for quiet: "that I may hear no more the reproach." What matters most becomes what people will say — the maids, the neighbours, the relatives. And the one who keeps giving way starts, one day, to wait in silence for the debt to be repaid.

And there is one detail that holds the whole tail together. By the Tigris, while Tobias is washing, "a fish leaped out of the river, and would have devoured him." The angel does not say "run". He says: "Take the fish," and then: "Open the fish, and take the heart and the liver and the gall, and put them up safely." The fear of the entry is not thrown away: it is hauled onto the bank and kept. The heart and the liver will be needed on the wedding night, the gall at the very end. One fish for three cards. What the two feared at the start later becomes what sets them free and gives them back their sight.

sections.h2: Middle of the task, 13: Death — a grave dug on the wedding night
paragraphs: The middle of the task, point N, is what the couple goes through on the way from the wish of the entry to the main task. Death stands here. In Arthur Edward Waite's old list of divinatory meanings this card has, among other things, the line "for a maid, failure of marriage projects". Sara's seven weddings read like an illustration of it.

The eighth wedding is held that same evening. The bride's father is honest: "I will declare unto thee the truth" — and he tells him about the seven. Tobias lays the heart and liver of the fish on the incense, and the spirit, the story says, flees to Egypt. Then the bridegroom rises and says: "Sister, arise, and let us pray." He asks: "mercifully ordain that we may become aged together." — "And she said with him, Amen."

Then comes the quietest and most frightening scene in the book: "So they slept both that night. And Raguel arose, and went and made a grave, Saying, I fear lest he also be dead." He sends a maid to look and has already decided what will happen: "if he be not, that we may bury him, and no man know it." The maid "found them both asleep". Raguel blesses God and bids "his servants to fill the grave".

The grave is not dug by an enemy. It is dug by a loving father whom the past has taught to expect the end. In the middle of this tail it is not the union that dies but the expectation that it will end like the ones before. Among the difficulties of Death in a couple Lisovskaya names carrying the traits of former partners over onto the present one. In the story the bride's father does it; in life anyone can — relatives, friends, the partners themselves. The suitcase that, after the last break-up, was never quite unpacked. Mum's "let's see how long this one lasts". The habit of checking whether the other will leave or not. The attempt to brace in advance for the blow so that it will hurt less later. Nothing wicked — only fear, digging a pit at night while the two of them sleep.

The second half of Death is leaving. Raguel holds his son-in-law for a fourteen-day feast and binds him by an oath that "he should not depart". Tobias asks: "Let me go, for my father and my mother look no more to see me." Letting them go, Raguel hands over half his goods and tells his daughter: "Honour thy father and thy mother in law, which are now thy parents." Benebell Wen writes that "traditionally, Key 13 is related to death and birth, property and inheritance, society and family". The middle of the tail runs through exactly these places: home, inheritance, parents. What dies is the role of the "only begotten children". The two stop being first of all somebody's son and daughter and become a couple.

Meanwhile, in Nineveh, a mother is mourning a living son. "My son is dead," says Anna, and she "went out every day into the way which they went". Two families in two cities are ready to bury a man who is alive and married. This is how the middle of this tail looks from outside: to the people close by it seems that something is dying — and that is true, the old order is dying. Waite distinguished natural death from "mystical death", which he called "a change in the form of consciousness" while still in this life. For a couple it is a change in the form of the union: who belongs to whom, whose home comes first, with whom the holidays are spent.

In the positive, Lisovskaya sees in a couple's Death living proof that life goes on after hard times: the two accept each other's past and move on, and take changes in each other easily. In the negative, there are so many changes that the other has nothing left to lean on, or one partner hurries the other to change before they are ready. The middle of this tail asks not for speed but for an honest farewell to the old.

sections.h2: Main task, 19: The Sun — the whiteness, the kid and the secret of a king
paragraphs: The main task, point D, is read by Lisovskaya mainly through its negative: what does not work for the couple and what it has to learn. The Sun stands here. In the Book of Tobit its negative is shown not on the young couple but on the older one — on Tobit and Anna.

When the kinsman who has been feeding the blind Tobit goes away, Anna keeps the house: she takes in women's work, spinning wool for the rich. One day her employers give her a kid on top of her wages. The kid bleats, and her husband asks: "From whence is this kid? is it not stolen?" Anna answers: "It was given for a gift more than the wages." "Howbeit I did not believe her," Tobit admits, and orders her to give it back. Then Anna says the words after which he prays for death: "Where are thine alms and thy righteous deeds? behold, thou and all thy works are known." Rembrandt painted this quarrel in 1626, at the age of twenty; "Tobit and Anna with the Kid" is in the Rijksmuseum.

This is The Sun in the negative: one partner does not see the light the other has brought into the house. The partner's success is met with an interrogation, righteousness turns into suspicion, suspicion into a barbed reply. Among the tasks of The Sun Lisovskaya names both harsh criticism and the failure to let the partner's victory be the partner's own. In the story all of it fits into one scene with a kid. Either of the two can be the suspicious one: gender decides nothing here. In a living couple the kid is the bonus one of them mentions over dinner while the other asks: "For what, exactly?" The present from colleagues met with a jealous "why all of a sudden?" The praise nobody repeats in front of the family so as not to look boastful.

Anna has a second line too, spoken on the day her son sets off: "Be not greedy to add money to money: but let it be as refuse in respect of our child." She calls her son "the staff of our hand". One scene holds both edges of The Sun's negative: the pursuit of money and position at the family's expense — and an attachment to a loved one so strong that they are not allowed to leave for a life of their own.

The Sun comes back bitter. The angel tells Tobias to anoint his father's eyes with the fish's gall. "And when his eyes began to smart, he rubbed them; And the whiteness pilled away from the corners of his eyes." The first thing the man who can see again says is: "behold, I see my son Tobias." Not "I see the light" — "I see my son". That is the main task of a couple with the 12-13-19 tail: to see the person, not one's own fear about them. And it stings. The truth that removes the whiteness burns at first, like gall.

Then Tobit walks to the gate of Nineveh to meet his daughter-in-law — in front of everyone, "rejoicing", and "they which saw him go marvelled, because he had received his sight." The Sun is not hidden. In the positive, Lisovskaya's Sun is a couple whose house is warm and full of people, where each succeeds in their own work and pulls the other up, and where their well-being shows from outside. Waite's old divinatory vocabulary raises a smile here: for Death it has "failure of marriage projects", for The Sun "fortunate marriage". These are words from a list of fortune-telling meanings, not a promise. But this couple's road runs exactly between two lines of the same vocabulary.

At the end the companion gives his name — "I am Raphael" — and leaves the family a rule that sounds like a formula for the main task: "It is good to keep close the secret of a king, but it is honourable to reveal the works of God." And a last instruction: "write all things which are done in a book." In this story everything began in secret: burials after sundown, a companion's borrowed name, a grave that "no man know it". Everything ends told in daylight. Other people's secrets the couple keeps. Its own — joy, gratitude, the good things that have happened to the two of them — it says out loud.

sections.h2: What the numbers record: a tail that is born only between two people
paragraphs: The 12-13-19 tail occurs in roughly one couple in 57 (1.739%) — 19th place among the 97 couple tails. Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. And here the numbers reveal something that a single card cannot show.

**The Hanged Man of the entry is shared.** The tail is made from only three combinations of personal tails: 18-9-9 and 21-4-10 (88% of such couples), 18-6-6 and 21-7-13 (11%), 18-3-12 and 21-10-7 (2%). One partner's personal tail always begins with The Moon, the other's with The World: 18 + 21 = 39 → 3 + 9 = 12. The suspension at the entry is a joint invention, not a trait of one person: in 88% of such couples neither of the two personal tails contains 12, 13 or 19. The Sun is in none of the six personal tails: this couple's main task is born only from the sum.

**The middle breaks the rule of a single person.** In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is the entry plus the main task. If the couple were one person, it would come out as 12 + 19 = 31 → 4, The Emperor. But the couple's middle is added up from the partners' middles: 9 + 4, 6 + 7 or 3 + 10 — and the result is 13. That is why 12-13-19 is impossible as a personal tail. Everything else in this triple is built "as in one person": the couple's entry, just as in a personal matrix, equals the main task plus the centre, 19 + 20 = 39 → 12. Only the middle breaks. And it breaks in a curious way: 1 + 3 = 4. Where one person would hold the form, like The Emperor, two people get the same four, but unreduced — as Death, which changes the form. This is our reading of the arithmetic, not a rule of the method.

**The centre of every such couple is 20, Judgement.** The centre of a couple's matrix is the atmosphere inside the union, what is not on show. For Lisovskaya, Judgement in a couple is above all kin and family: the parents' voice sounds in the couple's home even when they are not around. The whole Book of Tobit stands on this: the marriage is made "after the law of Moses", because "thou art her cousin, and she is thine", the bride's father himself writes "an instrument of covenants, and sealed it", and Sara's "right of inheritance doth rather appertain to thee than to any other." In the positive, Judgement in the centre gives a couple whom the relatives accept, where mistakes are forgiven and the two support each other even when one of them is wrong. In the negative, a union held together by the elders' approval, and a partner who decides nothing without their parents. For a couple whose common language is the fear of grieving father and mother, this is the main place where the Hanged Man of the entry can get stuck.

**The couple's values are The Lovers or The Devil.** "The couple's values", the spiritual purpose, are 6, The Lovers, in 77.3% of such couples and 15, The Devil, in 22.7%. Both cards are present on Tobias's wedding night. His prayer begins with the first human couple: "Thou madest Adam, and gavest him Eve his wife for an helper and stay". He says: "I take not this my sister for lust, but uprightly" — the choice of The Lovers, made consciously and out loud. And the Devil of this book is Asmodeus, of whom Tobias says: "a wicked spirit loveth her, which hurteth no body, but those which come unto her". A love that kills anyone who comes near the beloved is an exact image of The Devil in a couple: attachment that has turned into ownership. Lisovskaya's final thought about the fifteenth energy: nobody belongs to anybody.

sections.h2: Worked example: 14.09.1975 and 14.10.1975
paragraphs: Two people were born on 14.09.1975 and 14.10.1975. The first one's personal tail is 18-9-9, the second one's is 21-4-10: the most common combination for 12-13-19. The points of the couple's tail add up like this:

The couple's centre is 9 + 11 = 20, Judgement, as in every couple with this tail. The values of these two are 15, The Devil: they belong to the smaller group. If the middle were counted by the personal formula, it would come out as 12 + 19 = 31 → 4, but the couple has its own — the sum of the personal middles, 9 + 4. And The Sun also appears for this couple in the sphere "Why you met", at the point "What to create together": the sum of the birth months, 9 + 10 = 19.

sections.h2: Waite and Wen: one white horse for Death and The Sun
paragraphs: This section is about the Waite–Smith deck and the texts of Waite and Wen; the cards on this site are drawn in their own way. In the books themselves the three cards of the tail hold on to one another.

Waite ends his description of The Hanged Man with a sentence that already contains the next two cards: "He who can understand that the story of his higher nature is imbedded in this symbolism will receive intimations concerning a great awakening that is possible, and will know that after the sacred Mystery of Death there is a glorious Mystery of Resurrection." Suspension, then Death, then light — the order of the 12-13-19 tail is written by Waite into one sentence about the twelfth card.

Death and The Sun are linked by a horse. Wen describes the rider of the thirteenth card as "an armored skeleton" who "waves a black flag bearing the Rosicrucian Rose" and "rides a white steed". The child of the nineteenth card, in her own words, is also "riding a white steed, waving a red banner"; in Waite he is "mounted on a white horse". The horse is the same. What changes is the rider — the skeleton becomes a child — and the colour of the banner. For a couple it is an exact image: the road and the union stay the same; what changes is who holds the reins — fear or simplicity. The sun that on Death still stands on the horizon rises overhead on the nineteenth card.

And in older decks, Waite writes, The Sun was a card of two: it showed "a wall suggesting an enclosure—as it might be, a walled garden—wherein are two children, either naked or lightly clothed, facing a water, and gambolling, or running hand in hand." In the old picture the couple's main task is two people in one light.

There are clues too in the cards that stand beside the tail. On Judgement, the centre of all such couples, "the dead are rising from their tombs—a woman on the right, a man on the left hand, and between them their child" — like the family in Nineveh, where the son had already been mourned. The summons from above, Waite says, "is heard and answered from within." Waite describes The Lovers "as if Adam and Eve when they first occupied the paradise of the earthly body", and The Devil with the same two, but now "as if Adam and Eve after the Fall", in chains. The values of couples with this tail are one and the same first human couple: free in 77% and chained in 23%.

sections.h2: How a couple with the 12-13-19 tail changes the script
paragraphs: The tail neither condemns nor promises. It shows where the couple's familiar circle lies and where the way out of it is. In the story the miracles are the angel's work, but every step is taken by people: they take the fish, rise and pray together, fill the grave, leave the father-in-law's house, anoint a father's eyes, walk out to the gate.

ul: **Name the shared fear.** Say out loud that both are afraid of grieving their parents, and agree whose grief the couple is ready to carry and whose it is not. Suspension lives on silence.

**Keep the fish.** The fear of the beginning is no reason to run and no reason to stay silent. Take it apart together: what exactly each one fears. Then it becomes knowledge about each other rather than a wall.
**Fill the grave.** Do not measure the partner by past stories — one's own or other people's. Finish unpacking the "spare suitcase" and stop checking whether this one will leave too.
**Leave the parents without leaving them.** A home of one's own, holidays of one's own, an order of one's own — and gratitude to the elders without reporting to them.
**Don't ask where the kid came from.** Accept the partner's success, gift and praise without an interrogation, and be glad for them in front of other people.

**Keep what is others', reveal what is one's own.** Guard other people's secrets, but speak to each other directly about one's own joy and one's own trouble before they turn into whiteness over the eyes.

**Entry to the task — 12, The Hanged Man.** The couple's common language: to wait, to give way, to sacrifice themselves so that the people close to them are not hurt. Hence tact and tenderness — and a long suspension, when two people take years to make their own move.

**Middle of the task — 13, Death.** The road runs through an ending. What dies is not the union but an old form: the role of obedient children, earlier stories, the expectation that this union will end the way the previous ones did.
**Main task — 19, The Sun.** To learn to see the partner as they are, to be glad of their success without suspicion, to say difficult things out loud and not to hide happiness.

intro: None of the three cards predicts events: Death in the middle is not a break-up, and The Sun at the end is not a promise. This is a picture of how a couple lives through its task. And the picture has a very old double — a story in which the three cards come in exactly this order.

faq.q: What does the 12-13-19 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail where the entry to the task is 12, The Hanged Man, the middle is 13, Death, and the main task is 19, The Sun. The two enter the union with a common language of sacrifice and waiting, pass through the end of an old form — the roles of "obedient children", earlier stories and fears — and learn to live in daylight: to see each other without suspicion, to talk about difficult things and not to hide joy.

faq.q: Does Death in the middle of a couple's tail mean a break-up?
faq.a: No. The numbers of the matrix do not predict events. Death in the middle of the tail means that the couple's road runs through the end of an old order: old expectations, familiar roles, life under the parents' roof. In the Book of Tobit a grave is dug on the wedding night, but by morning it is filled in: what dies is not the union but the fear that it will end.

faq.q: Why does a couple have the 12-13-19 tail when the partners' personal tails usually lack these numbers?
faq.a: The couple's points are added up from the matching points of two personal matrices. The entry 12 always comes from one partner's Moon and the other's World (18 + 21 = 39 → 12), the middle 13 from the personal middles, the main task 19 from the personal main tasks. In 88% of such couples neither personal tail contains 12, 13 or 19, and nobody has The Sun: this task is born only between two people.

faq.q: Why is the middle of the tail 13 and not 12 + 19?
faq.a: The middle of a couple's tail is not recalculated from the two outer numbers; it is added up from the partners' middles. By the personal formula it would come out as 12 + 19 = 31 → 4, The Emperor. That is why 12-13-19 never occurs as a personal tail: this order exists only in a couple's matrix.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. The Hanged Man, Death and The Sun form a couple's tail only in the order 12-13-19: entry to the task 12, middle 13, main task 19. No other arrangement of these three numbers appears among the 97 couple tails.

report: On the wedding night the bride's father got up, went out and dug the bridegroom a grave. "I fear lest he also be dead," he said. His daughter's seven earlier weddings had ended with the bridegroom's death; this was the eighth. The maid sent to look found the young couple asleep, and by morning the grave had been filled. This scene from the Book of Tobit is the key to the couple's tail 12-13-19. The Hanged Man, Death and The Sun come in the ancient story in the same order, and what dies in it is not the union but the expectation that it will end like the ones before.

report.h3: Two people who say the same sentence

report: Sara and Tobias have never seen each other, yet they say the same thing. She: "I am the only daughter of my father… and I shall bring his old age with sorrow unto the grave." He: "I am the only son of my father, and I am afraid, lest, if I go in unto her, I die, as the other before" — and so "bring my father's and my mother's life because of me to the grave with sorrow". Two only children with one fear — of grieving their parents.

This is the couple's common language at the entry to the task. The Hanged Man here is a life put on hold for the sake of others: **my wish can wait, as long as the people close to me are not hurt.** In a living couple it sounds ordinary. "Let's not do it now, Mum is having a hard enough time." The move is put off because Dad won't manage on his own. The wedding is postponed because it would be awkward in front of the family. Each gives way sincerely; both are tactful and alert, noticing each other's tiredness before a word is said. But suspension becomes a habit, what people will say becomes what matters most, and the one who keeps giving way starts, one day, to wait in silence for the debt to be repaid. A couple like this often needs a push from outside to take a decisive step. In the story the push comes from an angel.

On the road, by the Tigris, "a fish leaped out of the river, and would have devoured him." The angel does not say "run". He says: "Take the fish" — and has the heart, the liver and the gall put away safely. The heart and the liver will be needed on the wedding night, the gall at the very end. **One fish for three cards:** what the two feared at the start later sets them free and gives them back their sight.

report.h3: The grave is not dug by an enemy

report: The middle of the task is Death. Waite ended his description of The Hanged Man with the words that "after the sacred Mystery of Death there is a glorious Mystery of Resurrection": suspension, an ending and light stand in one sentence. In the story this Death is a grave dug by a loving father whom the past has taught to expect disaster. This is what carrying old stories over onto a new union looks like. The suitcase that, after the last break-up, was never unpacked. Mum's "let's see how long this one lasts". The habit of checking whether the other will leave or not. Nothing wicked — only fear, digging a pit at night while the two of them sleep.

The second half of Death is leaving. The father-in-law holds the couple for fourteen days and binds the bridegroom by an oath that "he should not depart". Tobias asks: "Let me go." In farewell the father tells his daughter about her husband's parents: they "are now thy parents". And in another city a mother is already mourning a living son: "My son is dead." **The old order dies** — the role of the "only begotten children", whose home comes first, with whom the holidays are spent. The two stop being first of all somebody's son and daughter and become a couple. This middle asks not for speed but for an honest farewell to the old.

report.h3: The kid nobody believed in

report: The main task is The Sun, and in the story its negative is shown on the older couple. The blind Tobit is kept by his wife, who spins wool for the rich. One day she is given a kid on top of her wages. "From whence is this kid? is it not stolen?" her husband asks. "It was given for a gift more than the wages," Anna answers. "Howbeit I did not believe her," Tobit admits. And he hears in reply: "Where are thine alms and thy righteous deeds? behold, thou and all thy works are known."

This is The Sun in the negative: one partner does not see the light the other has brought into the house. The partner's success is met with an interrogation, suspicion with a barbed reply. In a living couple the kid is the bonus one of them mentions over dinner while the other asks: "For what, exactly?" The present from colleagues met with a jealous "why all of a sudden?" The praise nobody repeats in front of the family. Either of the two can be the suspicious one — gender decides nothing here.

report.h3: A light that burns at first

report: The Sun comes back bitter. The father's eyes are anointed with the fish's gall: "And when his eyes began to smart, he rubbed them; And the whiteness pilled away from the corners of his eyes." The first thing he says is: "behold, I see my son Tobias." Not "I see the light" — "I see my son". **The couple's task is to see the person, not one's own fear about them.** The truth that removes the whiteness burns at first, like gall.

Then the man who can see again walks to the city gate to meet his daughter-in-law, in front of everyone and rejoicing. The Sun is not hidden. Leaving, the companion gives his name and leaves a rule: "It is good to keep close the secret of a king, but it is honourable to reveal the works of God." **The couple keeps other people's secrets and says its own good things out loud.** The story began in secret — burials after sundown, a borrowed name, a grave that "no man know it" — and ended told in daylight.

What changes the script can be seen in the story too: every step in it is taken by people. Name the shared fear out loud and agree whose grief the couple is ready to carry. Stop measuring the partner by past stories and unpack the "spare suitcase". Live in a home of one's own while staying grateful to the elders. Accept the other's success and gifts without an interrogation and be glad for them in front of other people.

unit.title: The grave filled by morning

captions.M: Put your own life on hold so loved ones aren't hurt
captions.N: Say goodbye to the old order and the fear of an end
captions.D: See each other, not your fears, and rejoice out loud

unit.meaning: Your task: see each other without old fears, accept your partner's success without interrogation and say good things aloud.

seo.title: Karmic tail 12 16 13 compatibility: The Hanged Man, The Tower, Death
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 16 13 compatibility: why The Hanged Man, The Tower and Death speak not of disaster but of a couple's past, read through Joyce's “The Dead”.

items.title: Karmic tail 12-16-13 in compatibility: the night the past spoke up
items.short: In compatibility, karmic tail 12-16-13 is built from three cards people are taught to fear: The Hanged Man, The Tower, Death. Its best double in literature is James Joyce's story “The Dead”, in which nobody dies all evening. This tail is not about disaster but about the past two people bring into their union: first the couple lives in a shared “not yet”, then one day the past is spoken aloud and breaks the familiar order, and the main task is to let what came before truly end and to go on together.

sections.h2: A story in which nobody dies
paragraphs: “The Dead” is the last and longest story in Joyce's collection “Dubliners”. He wrote it in Trieste in 1907; the book came out in 1914. All of it fits into one snowy night. Two elderly sisters, the Misses Morkan, give their annual dance. Their favourite nephew, Gabriel Conroy, carves the goose, makes the after-dinner speech and sees that everything goes as it should. His wife Gretta is with him.

Near the end of the evening someone upstairs sings an old Irish song. Gretta stands still on the stairs and listens. That night, in a hotel room, she tells her husband something he had not known in all their years of marriage. As a girl in Galway she was loved by a boy, Michael Furey, who used to sing that song. The night before she left, already ill, he came through the rain into the garden below her window, and a week later he died — he was seventeen. Gretta falls asleep in tears, and Gabriel lies awake watching the snow fall outside.

The title promises death, yet nobody dies all evening. The dead here are the remembered: the boy from Galway, Gabriel's late mother, an old aunt who he thinks will soon be “a shade”. Death in the couple's tail 12-16-13 works the same way. It stands as the main task not as an event that has to happen, but as a way of relating to what has already ended.

The story runs in the order of the cards. First the pause: a husband who has looked after his wife for years, put off the important words and waited for the right moment — The Hanged Man. Then a song the tenor refused to sing all evening, and one sentence after which the night cannot be undone — The Tower. At the end an old version of the marriage quietly ends: jealousy of the dead boy goes, and for the first time Gabriel sees his wife whole, past included — Death. Joyce is quoted in the original.

sections.h2: The Hanged Man at the entry: “No, it was not the moment yet”
paragraphs: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together, their shared wishes and common language. The point sits on the line of tasks, so the same wish can also become resistance. For a 12-16-13 couple the entry is The Hanged Man, and their common language is the pause.

Gabriel has taken a room at the Gresham for one night so as not to travel home to Monkstown after the dance. At the hotel door he feels that he and his wife “had escaped from their lives and duties, escaped from home and friends” and run away to a new adventure. There it is, this couple's shared wish, though nobody says it aloud: to break out of the round of duties together. In the room Gretta walks towards him along the shaft of light from the street lamp, her face serious and weary, and the words will not pass his lips: “No, it was not the moment yet.” He talks about something else and thinks: “If she would only turn to him or come to him of her own accord!” Two people love each other and hang in suspense, each waiting for the other to take the first step.

The pause has an everyday face — care. Gabriel forces his daughter to eat her stirabout, gets green shades for his son's eyes at night and buys his wife goloshes, and his solicitude has long been a standing joke in the family. In Lisovskaya's description, The Hanged Man in a couple looks exactly like this: one does everything for the other and almost nothing for themselves. The card has a shadow too: what people will say, and what parents will say, matters more. Gabriel's mother opposed his marriage and once called Gretta “country cute”. Yet it was Gretta who nursed her mother-in-law to the very end, in their house at Monkstown. A silent sacrifice on one side, a slight remembered for years on the other.

The truest scene of The Hanged Man is the staircase. Gabriel stands in the dark hall and looks up at his wife, who has stopped at the banisters to listen. He asks himself what “a woman standing on the stairs in the shadow, listening to distant music” is a symbol of. If he were a painter he would paint her in that attitude and call the picture “Distant Music”. The Hanged Man is the card of another angle of view. Here two people look at the same evening from different sides, each suspended at their own point. He invents a title for her instead of asking what she hears.

The numbers explain where this pause comes from. The couple's entry 12 is made from the entries of two people: The Moon (18) of one and The World (21) of the other, 18 + 21 = 39 → 3 + 9 = 12. Waite calls The Moon “life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit”. In his list of meanings for The World stand “voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place”. One brings night memory into the couple, the other a habit of leaving. In Joyce you can see it literally. Gretta has Galway, rain and a song. Gabriel has the continent: every year he goes on a cycling tour to France, Belgium or Germany, and when someone at the dance reproaches him for not knowing his own country, he snaps: “I'm sick of my own country, sick of it!” The common language of such a couple is made of two “not here”s. In the story The Moon belongs to the wife and The World to the husband; in a living couple it can be the other way round — gender decides nothing here.

sections.h2: The Tower in the middle: a song nobody meant to sing
paragraphs: The middle of the task is how the couple travels from the shared wish to the main task (this is our reading: Lisovskaya gives the point no meaning of its own, it only adds to the main one). For a 12-16-13 couple the middle is The Tower, and it is made from The Lovers (6) of one partner and The Wheel of Fortune (10) of the other. The Lovers is the card of choice. The Wheel is a turn no one controls. The Tower is born where an old choice meets a turn of the wheel.

In Joyce the old choice is a night in her grandmother's garden, when Gretta implored a sick boy to go home and he said he did not want to live. The turn of the wheel is the tenor Bartell D'Arcy. All evening he refused to sing because of a cold — “I'm as hoarse as a crow” — and he sang only when the guests were already leaving, uncertain both of his words and of his voice. The song is “The Lass of Aughrim”, an Irish form of an old ballad that stands as number 76 in Francis Child's collection. In it a woman with a baby stands in the rain at her lover's door, and his mother will not let her in: “O, the rain falls on my heavy locks / And the dew wets my skin, / My babe lies cold…” It looks like chance. But Waite writes that behind the symbol of the Wheel lies “the denial of chance”. For the couple this means the chance song turns out to be an old choice coming back.

After that The Tower works fast. Gabriel expects tenderness and hears: “O, I am thinking about that song.” A few lines later comes the sentence after which the evening cannot be undone: “I think he died for me.” On his way to the bed Gabriel passes the cheval-glass and sees himself in full length. “While he had been full of memories of their secret life together, full of tenderness and joy and desire, she had been comparing him in her mind with another.” He sees himself as “a ludicrous figure”: a pennyboy for his aunts, a nervous, well-meaning sentimentalist orating to vulgarians — “the pitiable fatuous fellow he had caught a glimpse of in the mirror”.

Joyce himself gave such moments a name. In his draft novel “Stephen Hero” the hero calls an epiphany “a sudden spiritual manifestation”, whether in the vulgarity of speech or of gesture or in a memorable phase of the mind itself. Benebell Wen, describing The Tower's lightning, uses the same word: the card promises “a sudden epiphany, realization”. This couple's Tower is not a catastrophe but an epiphany: the minute when the past is spoken aloud and the picture each of them kept in their head stops working. Lisovskaya's tasks for The Tower include both “the collapse of an invented image of the partner” and the habit of “looking in different directions” at a hard moment. Joyce says it in almost the same words: Gretta looks away “along the shaft of light towards the window”, and Gabriel turns his back to the light lest she see the shame burning on his forehead.

In ordinary life such an evening is rarely loud. An old song in a taxi, a photograph from a box, a letter found during a move, a name dropped at the table. And suddenly one of the two realises that all this time they have lived beside a person with a separate story, and in that story they are not the hero. The first impulse is to cross-examine. Gabriel starts just like that: “Perhaps that was why you wanted to go to Galway with that Ivors girl?” Joyce calls the tone “cold interrogation”. Yet in Lisovskaya the same Tower, in its strong form, means firm support and calm in an unexpected blow. And Gabriel changes the course of the night with one decision: “He did not question her again for he felt that she would tell him of herself.” He strokes her hand and listens.

There is a clue in the numbers too. If the couple lived by the personal formula, the middle would come from the ends: 12 + 13 = 25 → 7, The Chariot. Waite calls The Chariot “above all things triumph in the mind”. Gabriel was waiting for a triumph: Joyce writes that a vague terror seized him “at that hour when he had hoped to triumph”. But the couple's middle is made not from its ends but from the middles of the two people. Instead of The Chariot's triumph, the couple has The Tower.

sections.h2: Death as the main task: the journey westward
paragraphs: A couple's main task is read mostly through its minus: what the couple cannot manage and what it has to learn. For tail 12-16-13 it is Death. It is made from The Lovers (6) of one partner and The Chariot (7) of the other: a choice plus a movement that cannot be turned back. In Lisovskaya, Death's tasks in a couple are to help each other separate from parents and move house, to accept a partner utterly unlike the previous one, to live through partings and distance, to see one's own mistakes and not only the other's. “The Dead” shows these tasks as scenes.

Separating from the parental home. As a girl, Gretta left her grandmother's house on Nuns' Island for the convent in Dublin. That very night, while packing, she heard gravel thrown against the window. Gabriel still carries his late mother's phrase and the role of the favourite nephew, the one whose presence makes Aunt Kate “always feel easier in my mind”.

Accepting a partner unlike the previous one. Michael Furey is a boy from the gasworks who sang and stood in the rain by the wall “where there was a tree”. Gabriel is a teacher and reviewer with gilt-rimmed glasses and goloshes, carrying a quotation from Browning he is afraid to use in case it is “above the heads of his hearers”. At first Gabriel tries to beat the difference with irony: “What was he?” — “He was in the gasworks.” The irony fails and he feels humiliated.

Seeing one's own mistakes. The mirror does this work for Gabriel before he has time to blame his wife. And then the main thing happens. “It hardly pained him now to think how poor a part he, her husband, had played in her life.” He watches Gretta asleep “as though he and she had never lived together as man and wife”, and “a strange, friendly pity for her entered his soul”. “He had never felt like that himself towards any woman but he knew that such a feeling must be love.”

What dies that night is not a person but the old Gabriel: “His own identity was fading out into a grey impalpable world.” A version of the marriage dies in which the wife had no past and the husband was the only hero of her story. Wen writes of Death as the end of one stage and the beginning of a new one, and of how people resist change. Waite calls it “change, transformation and passage from lower to higher”.

Before supper Gretta had begged: “O, do go, Gabriel. I'd love to see Galway again.” He answered coldly: “You can go if you like.” The last paragraph of the story says: “The time had come for him to set out on his journey westward.” Readers have argued for over a century about what that journey means — death, reconciliation with Ireland, or simply the trip he turned down at the dance. For the couple the meaning is simpler. The main task of tail 12-16-13 is a journey to where the partner came from: to their town, their people, their past. Not erasing that past and not competing with it, but visiting it. In the final lines the snow falls equally “upon all the living and the dead”: past and present end up under one sky and stop fighting for room.

Death as a main task has a minus too, and Joyce gave it an exact word. In a letter to his publisher Grant Richards of 5 May 1906 he explained that he had chosen Dublin as the scene of the book because the city seemed to him “the centre of paralysis”. The Misses Morkan's dance, the story says in its opening lines, had never once “fallen flat”: the same guests every year, the same goose, the same speech. Death's minus is not an ending but the impossibility of one. The couple lives in the same scene for years, and the past in it does not die but stands beside them like a third person. Jealousy of someone who is gone, comparison with those who came before, projecting their features onto the present partner — all of these are ways of not letting the past end.

sections.h2: Justice at the centre: scales between two people
paragraphs: The couple's centre is the shared atmosphere, what happens between two people away from view. Every couple with tail 12-16-13 has Justice (8) at the centre. This is not statistics but arithmetic: the partner with tail 18-6-6 always has The Hanged Man (12) at the personal centre, the partner with tail 21-10-7 always has Temperance (14), and 12 + 14 = 26 → 8. Wen tells these cards apart like this: “The theme of Justice is external balance”, while Temperance “indicates internal balance”. The couple's atmosphere is made from one partner's pause and the other's inner measure, and scales appear in it.

In Lisovskaya, Justice in a couple means honesty, faithfulness, “a cool head and a warm heart”, duties fairly shared. In its minus it is the habit of measuring everything by oneself, idealising the partner, responsibility that turns into control. Its tasks are to admit one's own fault instead of blaming, and to forgive.

In Joyce even the first kiss in the room starts with a fair account. Gabriel tells her that Freddy Malins has paid back the sovereign he lent him, though he never expected it, and Gretta kisses her husband: “You are a very generous person, Gabriel.” Half an hour later the scales tip. It turns out she had been “comparing him in her mind with another”, and he himself starts weighing what part he has played in her life. And at the end the same word, generous, comes back, this time about himself: “Generous tears filled Gabriel's eyes.” Justice at the centre of the couple begins with keeping accounts and can end in generosity.

In his after-dinner speech Gabriel jokes: “I will not attempt to play tonight the part that Paris played on another occasion. I will not attempt to choose between them.” He is speaking of the three hostesses of the dance, but he means the mythical judge who gave the apple to one of three goddesses, which began the Trojan War. At the table Gabriel refuses to judge. That same night he becomes both judge and accused.

In describing Justice, Waite separates two kinds of justice. The first is the moral principle “which deals unto every man according to his works”. The second is like the gifts of the poet: “we have them or have not”, and their presence is as much a mystery as their absence. Gabriel can show his works: care, a hotel room, goloshes. Michael Furey showed one thing: he stood in the rain. This couple's scales learn to tell what can be weighed from what cannot. The Roman jurist Ulpian defined justice as the constant will “to render to each his due”. That includes the partner's past.

sections.h2: Clues in Waite's pictures
paragraphs: The cards on our site have their own designs. This section is about the Rider–Waite–Smith deck that Waite and Wen wrote about, and in it the partners' cards literally show through the couple's cards.

ul: **The Moon on Death's horizon.** Waite writes that on the Death card, between two pillars on the verge of the horizon, “there shines the sun of immortality”. Wen specifies that these are the two pillars from The Moon. The Moon is one partner's entry (18). Their night memory stands on the horizon of the couple's main task, and the sun rises exactly there.

**The World in The Hanged Man's legs.** Wen notes that The Hanged Man's crossed legs reappear on The World and concludes: “it is the hanged man who shall attain the fulfillment of the World card”. The World is the other partner's entry (21). The couple's shared entry, The Hanged Man, carries that partner's gesture.

**The serpent on The Lovers and on the Wheel.** Waite himself describes the serpent twining round the Tree of Knowledge behind the woman on The Lovers, and Typhon in his serpent form on The Wheel of Fortune. Wen brings the two cards together: the serpent warns of “an unanticipated turn of events”, of “how quickly bliss can become tragedy”. The couple's Tower is made from one partner's Lovers and the other's Wheel.

**The living tree.** Waite's Hanged Man hangs on “living wood, with leaves thereon”. Michael Furey, in Gretta's story, stands “at the end of the wall where there was a tree”, and in Gabriel's last vision he is “a young man standing under a dripping tree”. The sacrifice Gretta speaks of stands under a tree, like The Hanged Man.

sections.h2: The couple's values: a choice made again
paragraphs: “The couple's values” is what the union exists for. In 93.5% of couples with tail 12-16-13 that place holds The Lovers (6), in 6.5% The Devil (15). The Lovers also appear in one partner's personal tail, and twice: 18-6-6. The card of choice that one person carries in their own tail almost always rises into the couple's values.

Waite recalls that the old Lovers card showed married life and was called Simulacrum fidei, “the symbol of conjugal faith”. Wen insists that “in every traditional interpretation of The Lovers, the card is about a moral choice”, not mere romance. For a 12-16-13 couple choice is not a “yes” said once. Gretta once chose to leave Galway and stay in Dublin. That night Gabriel chooses his wife together with her past. Faithfulness here means not pretending the past does not exist. For couples with The Devil in their values the same question is harsher: what holds the union together — a choice, or an attachment neither can step away from.

sections.h2: Nora and Jim: a story Joyce knew from inside
paragraphs: Joyce did not invent Michael Furey. His wife, Nora Barnacle, came from Galway. Before she met Joyce, two young men she had loved died there. Michael Feeney died as a teenager. Michael “Sonny” Bodkin died of consumption in February 1900 and is buried in Rahoon cemetery outside Galway. Biographers see both of them in Furey.

Joyce met Nora in Dublin on 10 June 1904, and their first walk out together fell on 16 June — the very day into which “Ulysses” would later be packed. In the autumn of 1904 they left Ireland together, unmarried. They lived as husband and wife for twenty-seven years and married only on 4 July 1931, at the Kensington register office in London — in the words biographers quote, “for testamentary reasons”: so that their children's right to inherit would be beyond dispute. Lisovskaya writes of The Hanged Man in a couple that such couples enter a relationship slowly and need a push from outside to marry. For the Joyces the push was the law — Justice, which stands at the centre of every 12-16-13 couple.

In 1912 Nora took her husband to Bodkin's grave. A year later, in Trieste, Joyce wrote the poem “She Weeps over Rahoon” in the voice of a woman weeping over the grave of “my dark lover”: “Rain on Rahoon falls softly, softly falling…” It almost exactly repeats the rhythm of the ending of “The Dead”, where the snow is “softly falling”. A husband lent his own voice to his wife's dead love. Death as a main task, lived in its plus, looks exactly like this: someone else's past is neither erased nor defeated; it is given a place.

sections.h2: How tail 12-16-13 is built: an example with 04.07.1975 and 18.12.1975
paragraphs: Each point of the couple's matrix is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices; if the sum is greater than 22, its digits are added. The middle of the couple's tail is not recalculated from the two outer numbers; it is the sum of the partners' middles.

For a person born on 04.07.1975: day 4, month 7, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Main task 4 + 7 + 22 = 33 → 6, centre 4 + 7 + 22 + 6 = 39 → 12, entry 6 + 12 = 18, middle 6 + 18 = 24 → 6. Personal tail 18-6-6.
For a person born on 18.12.1975: day 18, month 12, year 22. Main task 18 + 12 + 22 = 52 → 7, centre 18 + 12 + 22 + 7 = 59 → 14, entry 7 + 14 = 21, middle 7 + 21 = 28 → 10. Personal tail 21-10-7.
The couple's centre: 12 + 14 = 26 → 8, Justice. The couple's values for these two dates are The Lovers (6).
What else a search through all dates shows:

ul: **Rarity.** Tail 12-16-13 occurs in about one couple in 2,367 (0.042%): 91st place out of 97 couple tails.
**One road.** It comes from only one meeting of personal tails: 18-6-6 and 21-10-7, in 100% of such couples. That is why all of them have Justice at the centre.
**Born in the couple.** Neither The Tower nor Death appears in either partner's tail or centre: these two cards arise only through the sum.

**Never in one person.** In a personal matrix the entry equals the main task plus the centre, and with a main task of 13 an entry of 12 is impossible with any centre. Besides, by the personal formula the middle would be 12 + 13 → 7, while the couple has 16.
**No twins.** There are no other couple tails made of 12, 16 and 13: these three cards meet only in this order.

sections.h2: What changes the script
paragraphs: A tail shows a task, not a fate. Here is what moves a 12-16-13 couple from minus to plus.

ul: **Say the pause out loud.** “Not yet” works for one evening, not for many years. A wish each is waiting for the other to guess is better named by the one who has it.
**Ask, don't cross-examine.** When the past is spoken, the first impulse is irony and keeping score. Gabriel's night changes when he falls silent and lets his wife tell her story.
**Don't compete with someone who is gone.** A partner's past has no future, so it is no rival. It is easy to lose to it and impossible to win.
**Separate parents' voices from your own.** “Country cute” is the mother's phrase, not the husband's. In this couple other people's judgements live longer than they should.
**Go west.** Literally — to where the partner comes from, to their people and places. And figuratively — into their past, without jealousy.
**Keep the scales honest.** Justice at the centre is not about counting who gave more, but about everyone receiving their due, the past included.

paragraphs: The strong version of tail 12-16-13 is a couple that has already lived through its night after the dance. It knows how to wait but does not hide in waiting. It knows each of them had a life before they met and is not afraid to talk about it. Its evenings do not repeat one script year after year. The past in such a couple lies, like Joyce's snow, on everyone equally — and keeps no one from going on.

ul: **12 · The Hanged Man — entry to the task.** The couple's common language is the pause: looking after each other, putting off the important words and waiting for the other to come of their own accord.
**16 · The Tower — middle of the task.** One day the past of one of the two is spoken aloud — in a song, a letter, a phrase at the table — and an evening that seemed familiar collapses in a minute.
**13 · Death — main task.** Not a loss but an ending: letting go of jealousy towards what came before, separating from parents' voices and accepting that the partner had a life before they met.

faq.q: Is karmic tail 12-16-13 a bad sign for a couple's compatibility?
faq.a: No. The Hanged Man, The Tower and Death sound frightening, but a couple's tail shows the tasks of the union, not its outcome. The numbers predict nothing: no break-ups, no misfortunes, no dates. They describe where the couple gets stuck — in the pause, in keeping score, in jealousy of the past — and where it can grow.

faq.q: Does Death as the main task mean one partner will leave?
faq.a: No. In a couple's tail Death is the end of an old form, not an event involving people: separating from parents, moving house, accepting the partner's past, letting go of an old image of the union. As in Joyce's “The Dead”, where nobody dies all evening and only an old version of a marriage comes to an end.

faq.q: Why does tail 12-16-13 never occur in a personal matrix?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and with a main task of 13 an entry of 12 is impossible with any centre. The couple's middle is built differently too: it is the sum of the partners' middles (6 + 10 = 16), not of the ends, which would give 12 + 13 → 7.

faq.q: How can you tell whether a couple has tail 12-16-13?
faq.a: It occurs only when one partner has personal tail 18-6-6 and the other 21-10-7. Then the couple's entry is 18 + 21 → 12, the middle 6 + 10 = 16, the main task 6 + 7 = 13, and Justice is always at the centre. Example: the dates 04.07.1975 and 18.12.1975; for your own dates the compatibility calculator does the sum.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. Among the 97 couple tails, 12, 16 and 13 come together only in the order 12-16-13: The Hanged Man at the entry, The Tower in the middle and Death as the main task. No other sequence of these three cards occurs in compatibility.

report: The Hanged Man, The Tower and Death in a row read like a verdict. But tail 12-16-13 has a double in literature — James Joyce's story “The Dead”, in which nobody dies all evening. The dead there are the remembered. This tail works the same way: it is not about disaster but about the past two people bring into their union.

The plot fits into one snowy night in Dublin. Gabriel Conroy and his wife Gretta are at his aunts' annual dance. Near the end of the evening someone upstairs sings an old song, Gretta stands still on the stairs, and that night in the hotel she tells her husband something he had not known in all their years of marriage: as a girl in Galway she was loved by a boy who used to sing that song and died at seventeen. The story runs exactly in the order of the cards: a pause, a blow, an ending. Joyce is quoted in the original.

report.h3: “No, it was not the moment yet”

report: The entry to the task is the couple's common language, what the two want together. For a couple with this tail the entry is The Hanged Man, and their common language is the pause. Gabriel has taken a room for one night, and at the hotel door he feels that he and his wife “had escaped from their lives and duties”. But when Gretta comes towards him, the words will not come: **“No, it was not the moment yet.”** He talks about something else and thinks: “If she would only turn to him or come to him of her own accord!” Two people love each other and hang in suspense, each waiting for the other to take the first step.

The pause has an everyday face — care. Gabriel forces his daughter to eat her stirabout and buys his wife goloshes, and the whole family laughs at his solicitude. It has a shadow too: the parents' voice. Gabriel's mother opposed the marriage and called Gretta “country cute”, yet it was Gretta who nursed her to the very end. The truest scene is the staircase. Gabriel looks up at his wife, standing still, and thinks he would call such a picture “Distant Music”. He invents a title for her instead of asking what she hears.

This couple's entry is made from one partner's Moon and the other's World. Waite calls The Moon “life of the imagination”; among the meanings of The World he lists “voyage, emigration, flight”. Gretta has Galway, rain and a song; Gabriel has cycling tours on the continent and “I'm sick of my own country!”. Their common language is made of two “not here”s.

report.h3: A song the tenor never meant to sing

report: The Tower in the middle comes from one partner's Lovers and the other's Wheel of Fortune: an old choice meets a turn of the wheel. The old choice is the night Gretta implored a sick boy to go home out of the rain. The turn of the wheel is a tenor who refused to sing all evening because of a cold and sang only when the guests were already leaving. It looks like chance. But in Waite, behind the Wheel lies **“the denial of chance”**: the chance song turns out to be an old choice coming back.

After that one sentence decides everything: “I think he died for me.” Gabriel passes the mirror, sees himself in full length and understands that while he was full of tenderness, “she had been comparing him in her mind with another”. Joyce called such moments an epiphany — “a sudden spiritual manifestation”. Wen, describing The Tower's lightning, uses the same word. This couple's Tower is not a catastrophe but an epiphany: the past is spoken aloud, and the picture each of them kept in their head stops working.

The first impulse is to cross-examine. “Perhaps that was why you wanted to go to Galway?” Gabriel asks, in a tone Joyce calls “cold interrogation”. Then he changes the course of the night with one decision: **“He did not question her again for he felt that she would tell him of herself.”**

report.h3: Scales at the centre

report: At the centre of such a couple stands Justice — scales. Even the first kiss in the room begins with a fair account: Gabriel says an acquaintance has paid back a loan, and Gretta tells him: “You are a very generous person.” Half an hour later the scales tip, and he starts weighing what part he has played in her life. Waite separates the justice that “deals unto every man according to his works” from gifts that “we have them or have not”. Gabriel can show his works: care, a hotel room, goloshes. The boy from Galway showed one thing: he stood in the rain. This couple's scales learn to tell what can be weighed from what cannot.

report.h3: The journey westward

report: The main task is Death, and it is an ending, not a loss. What dies is not a person but the old Gabriel and an old version of the marriage, in which the wife had no past. “It hardly pained him now to think how poor a part he, her husband, had played in her life.” At the end the word heard at the kiss comes back to him: **“Generous tears filled Gabriel's eyes.”**

At the dance Gretta begged him to go to Galway, and he answered coldly: “You can go if you like.” The story's last paragraph: “The time had come for him to set out on his journey westward.” For a couple with this tail that is the main task: a journey to where the partner came from — to their town, their people, their past. Not erasing that past and not competing with it, but visiting it. Separating parents' voices from one's own. No longer measuring oneself against someone who is gone: the past has no future, it is easy to lose to it and impossible to win.

Joyce named this Death's minus too. Dublin seemed to him **“the centre of paralysis”**, and the aunts' dance had, year after year, never once “fallen flat”: the same guests, the same goose, the same speech. The danger of this tail is not an ending but the impossibility of one, when the past does not die and stands beside the couple like a third person.

Joyce himself lived this tail in its plus. His wife Nora was also from Galway, and there, before she met him, a young man she had loved died. Nora took her husband to his grave, and a year later Joyce wrote a poem in her voice: “Rain on Rahoon falls softly…” Someone else's past is neither erased nor defeated — it is given a place. The snow at the end of “The Dead” falls equally “upon all the living and the dead”, and keeps no one from going on.
