seo.title: Karmic tail 12 16 22 compatibility: Hanged Man, Tower and Fool
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 16 22 compatibility exists only for a couple: no single birth date can produce it. What The Hanged Man, The Tower and The Fool say about two people.

items.title: Karmic tail 12-16-22 in compatibility: two people after the flood
items.short: No single birth date can produce the triple 12-16-22. For this tail to be personal, The Star would have to sit in the centre of the chart, and The Star never appears in the centre of a personal destiny matrix. This tail and this Star exist only for two people — and they tell how a couple waits things out together, goes through a collapse together and learns together to start from nothing.

sections.h2: Two people on Parnassus: the story of the 12-16-22 tail
paragraphs: Ovid finished the Metamorphoses around 8 AD. The first book begins with the creation of the world and almost at once drowns it. Quotations follow Henry T. Riley's literal prose translation of 1851.

Jupiter, disguised as a man, walks the earth and enters the house of Lycaon, king of Arcadia. Lycaon decides to test his guest: "I will make trial, by a plain proof, whether this is a God, or whether he is a mortal." The test turns out to be a trap, and the answer to it is lightning: "I, with avenging flames, overthrew the house upon the household Gods, worthy of their master." Lycaon flees to the fields and becomes a wolf.

One house is not enough for Jupiter: "Thus fell one house; but one house alone did not deserve to perish." He is ready to scatter his thunderbolts over the whole earth, but fears setting the sky on fire, lays them aside and chooses water. Ovid's flood is a world turned upside down. A man "catches a fish on the top of an elm-tree", an anchor is fastened in a green meadow, dolphins get into the woods, the wolf swims among the sheep, and "the towers tottered, overwhelmed beneath the stream". In the end "everything now was ocean; and to that ocean shores were wanting".

One mountain stays above the water: "a lofty mountain rises towards the stars, with two tops, by name Parnassus". Here Deucalion comes to rest, "borne in a little ship, with the partner of his couch". Jupiter sees that of so many thousands one man and one woman are left, "both guiltless, and both worshippers of the Gods", and stops the flood.

Then begins the part a couple should read this myth for. Deucalion looks at the empty earth and weeps: "O sister, O wife, O thou, the only woman surviving… we two are the whole people of the earth, whatever both the East and the West behold." The two go to the river, sprinkle themselves with its water and ask the goddess Themis for advice. The answer is a riddle: "cover your heads, and loosen the garments girt around you, and throw behind your backs the bones of your great mother." Pyrrha refuses: she is afraid to offend her mother's shade. Deucalion finds another reading: the great mother is the earth, her bones are stones. Neither of them is sure. "But what harm will it do to try?" The two throw stones behind their backs, and slowly the stones become people.

The order of the cards is the order of their own path. The entry is a boat over an upturned world, where the two have nothing but each other (12). The middle is the land where everything has fallen, and a word that must not be taken literally (16). The main task is a step with no safety net, taken with covered heads (22).

sections.h2: The Hanged Man — entry to the task: "we two are the whole people of the earth"
paragraphs: In Yuliana Lisovskaya's book on compatibility, point M is what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, a "common language". It stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish can also become resistance. For the 12-16-22 couple, the common language is the language of The Hanged Man.

It is heard best in Deucalion's speech on the empty earth. It is a declaration of love made through sacrifice: "What would now have been thy feelings, if without me thou hadst been rescued from destruction, O thou deserving of compassion? In what manner couldst thou have been able alone to support this terror? With whom for a consoler, to endure these sorrows? For I, believe me, my wife, if the sea had only carried thee off, should have followed thee, and the sea should have carried me off as well." In Waite's list of meanings for The Hanged Man, "wisdom, circumspection" stand next to "trials, sacrifice". Deucalion speaks this language: I am with you, even if it means death.

In a living couple, this entry shows in small things. The two give up their own plans for each other with ease: one does not go where they have long wanted to go, so as not to leave the other alone. They are happy together, away from people, and they sense each other at a distance. Big decisions wait "for better times". Lisovskaya writes that such a couple needs a push from outside even to marry. Ovid's push is the strongest one possible: the rest of the world has gone under water.

The Hanged Man is the card of the inverted view, and Ovid turns the whole world upside down: a fish in the treetop, an anchor in the grass, sea-calves where goats used to graze. The couple enters its task in a world where everything familiar stands on its head, and the two hold on to each other because there is nothing else to hold. In Apollodorus (Library, I.7.2) the boat is a chest built on Prometheus's advice, and the two spend "nine days and as many nights" floating in it over the sea. That is The Hanged Man: life suspended, but life.
Benebell Wen assigns The Hanged Man to the element of Water. In this couple's myth, the entry to the task is literally water.

paragraphs.h3: Where the pause becomes resistance

paragraphs: The flood is over, yet Deucalion is still afraid: "And even now there is no certain assurance of our lives; even yet do the clouds terrify my mind." The danger has passed; the waiting has stayed. This is the minus of entry 12: a couple who came through something together keeps waiting long after there is nothing left to wait for.

There is a second minus too — someone else's voice inside the couple. Pyrrha refuses to follow the goddess's advice: she "dreads to offend the shades of her mother by casting her bones". Among the minuses of The Hanged Man, Lisovskaya lists parents' power over the couple, decisions made "because that's how it's done" and worry about what people will say. Deucalion, without noticing, adds one more weight: "Thus it has seemed good to the Gods, and we remain as mere samples of mankind." A model couple has to be a proper couple — and it finds it hardest of all to say aloud what each of the two wants.

paragraphs.h3: The Moon and The World in one entry

paragraphs: In every 12-16-22 couple the entry is built the same way: one partner's personal tail begins with The Moon (18), the other's with The World (21), and 18 + 21 = 39 → 12. There is no other way to get this tail. Read with this hint, Deucalion's speech holds both cards: The World — "whatever both the East and the West behold"; The Moon — the clouds that "terrify my mind". A whole world and a night fear, added together, make a pause. This is our reading, not a rule of the method.
Among Waite's reversed meanings of The Hanged Man is "the crowd". In Latin, Deucalion says "nos duo turba sumus" — literally "we two are the crowd", the whole population of the earth.

sections.h2: The Tower — middle of the task: a house under lightning and towers under water
paragraphs: If 12-16-22 were a personal tail, its middle would come from its ends: 12 + 22 = 34 → 7, The Chariot. A couple's middle is the sum of the two partners' middles, and here it comes to 16 — The Tower. The Chariot is a vehicle steered by its own driver. The 12-16-22 couple gets no vehicle of its own: the road from wish to task runs through a collapse. In Ovid the two do not steer either — their boat is carried to the mountain.

The first Tower in the flood story is Lycaon's house, struck by lightning. Under that roof a guest was tested with a trap — that is, with deceit. "Deception" and "ruin" are in Waite's list of meanings for The Tower, and Waite himself calls the card the ruin of a "House of Falsehood". After Lycaon's house everything else goes under water, and Ovid names the drowned towers separately.

paragraphs.h3: It is not the couple's house that falls, but the world around it

paragraphs: Deucalion and Pyrrha built nothing on deceit, and it is not their house that falls. They walk across a land where the old order has ended: the temple of Themis still stands, but its roof "was defiled with foul moss", and its "altars were standing without fires". This is what the middle of this tail looks like. The couple makes its way through the ruins of a way of life that existed before it and without it: parents' rules, other people's expectations, plans once made for both of them. And the image formed at the start falls too — Lisovskaya lists the collapse of an invented image of the partner among the tasks of The Tower.

Lisovskaya's key to The Tower in a couple is that trials passed together make the union stronger. Among its minuses she notes that in hard times the partners look in different directions. Deucalion and Pyrrha look at the same empty land, and Ovid gives it a single line: "He thus spoke, and they wept." Deucalion says the same in his own words: "the marriage tie has united to me, and… now dangers themselves unite to me". The Tower in the middle of the tail is not the end of the union but a new knot.

paragraphs.h3: The letter that has to fall

paragraphs: The subtlest Tower in this story is the oracle. To "throw behind your backs the bones of your great mother", taken literally, means to desecrate a grave. Pyrrha hears the letter of it and freezes. Deucalion looks for a second meaning and finds it: "The earth is the great mother; I suspect that the stones in the body of the earth are the bones meant." To move on, the couple needs the literal reading of an old rule to collapse.

In the myth the roles are divided this way; in a living couple they change places: today one holds on to the letter, tomorrow the other. The difference in outlook that Lisovskaya puts among The Tower's minuses works as a plus here: without the second reading, the two would still be standing at the temple.

paragraphs.h3: Lightning, water and wind

paragraphs: Wen assigns Water to The Hanged Man, Fire to The Tower and Air to The Fool. In Ovid's first book the world goes through all three elements in a single episode: the fire of the lightning over Lycaon's house, the water of the flood, and the north wind Aquilo, which Jupiter sends to drive away the clouds. The fourth element, earth, ends up in the couple's hands — as stones.
In Wen's reversed Tower there are these words as well: "Not all will be destroyed. There will be mercy and some will be saved." In Ovid, two are saved.

sections.h2: The Fool — main task: "But what harm will it do to try?"
paragraphs: Point D is the couple's main task, and Lisovskaya reads it mostly through its minus: what the two cannot manage and what they need to learn. Her key to The Fool is freedom: in the plus it is the trust that gives freedom, in the minus it is a lack of boundaries and responsibility.

Here is Ovid's most Fool-like line: "Although she, descended from Titan, is moved by this interpretation of her husband, still her hope is involved in doubt; so much do they both distrust the advice of heaven; but what harm will it do to try?" No knowledge, no promise, no certainty that the reading is right — only the decision to try. And at once: "They go down, and they veil their heads, and ungird their garments, and cast stones, as ordered, behind their footsteps." The heads are covered — the two cannot see what will come of it. The belts are loosened — what held them tight is slack. The stones fly behind their backs, and looking round is not allowed.

paragraphs.h3: Testing the other, or trying it themselves

paragraphs: This book has two experiments. Lycaon enjoys "this mode of testing the truth": he tests his guest with a trap, and his house falls. Deucalion and Pyrrha try for themselves, with their own hands, and the world comes back. In the Latin, Lycaon says "experiar", "I will test", and the last line of the episode calls the people born from the stones — that is, all of us — "experiens laborum", tried in labours. Waite writes of The Fool: "He is the spirit in search of experience." The main task of the 12-16-22 couple is to choose the second kind of experiment.

This bears directly on The Fool's minus in a couple. Lisovskaya describes control and jealousy from someone who does not keep their own rules, and advises giving the partner freedom without checks. In Ovid, checking up on the other stands at the start of the collapse. Trust that is stronger than doubt stands at the start of a new world.

paragraphs.h3: An easy start and a serious step

paragraphs: The Fool is good at beginnings. After any collapse, a 12-16-22 couple can pack everything into one bag and leave, change everything, start on bare ground — Lisovskaya counts this as a plus: they start from zero with ease. The minus sits in the same place: the start is easy, and the serious step gets put off. In words everything is settled, yet a shared address, a shared account or a shared "we" never arrives. Each lives their own life, and the couple comes to resemble two neighbours.

In Ovid the serious step is taken, but not at once: first a refusal, then a long silence, then a word of doubt, and only then the throw. Ovid notes: "they reconsider the words of the response given, but involved in dark obscurity, and they ponder them among themselves." The couple's task is neither to leap over this doubt nor to drown in it, but to get as far as the throw.

paragraphs.h3: Who are we to each other now

paragraphs: Deucalion addresses Pyrrha by three names at once — sister (a cousin, in fact), wife, the only woman left in the world — and lists three bonds: shared blood, marriage, and now danger. The old words are not enough after the flood, so he adds a new one. Among The Fool's minuses, Lisovskaya lists an undefined status of the relationship. After The Tower, the old names for a 12-16-22 couple's bond may stop fitting — and the main task includes a simple thing: to say aloud who the two are to each other now.

paragraphs.h3: Not by his father's art

paragraphs: Deucalion dreams of doing what his father once did: "Oh that I could replace the people that are lost by the arts of my father, and infuse the soul into the moulded earth!" Prometheus moulded people from earth. That way is closed to his son, and the new world comes about differently — by the throw of two people, not by the craft of one master. The Fool does not inherit a method; he finds his own. The 12-16-22 couple builds its life not by its parents' recipe, however good.

And one more detail. The stones do not become people at once: they "began to lay aside their hardness and their stiffness, and by degrees to become soft", and then they look "as if from the marble commenced to be wrought, not sufficiently distinct, and very like to rough statues". What this couple starts is rough and unfinished at first, and that is normal. "There is no delay," Ovid says of the people themselves, while it is the stones that change slowly. The Hanged Man's pause does not vanish; it passes from the people into the work.

sections.h2: The Star in the centre: a hope that neither of the two has
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's chart is its shared atmosphere: what happens between the two when nobody is watching. In couples with the 12-16-22 tail, the centre always holds 17, The Star. No birth date gives 17 in the centre of a personal chart, so this hope belongs to neither partner. It appears only when there are two.

paragraphs.h3: Why The Fool and The Star make The Hanged Man

paragraphs: In a personal chart, the entry to the tail equals the main task plus the centre. This couple keeps the rule: 22 + 17 = 39 → 12. The Fool plus The Star is The Hanged Man. Read as a hint, the equation says this couple's pause is made not of fear but of its freedom and its hope. The two wait not because they are afraid to step, but because there is something inside them worth waiting for the right moment. This is our reading of the arithmetic. The weak version of the same equation is a waiting in which freedom and hope never turn into a step.

paragraphs.h3: Two summits of one mountain

paragraphs: The couple's Star is made of two personal centres, the way Parnassus is made of two summits — "a lofty mountain rises towards the stars, with two tops". Neither summit reaches the stars alone. In 56% of these couples it is Justice (8) and The Hermit (9), in 42% The Hanged Man (12) and The Hierophant (5), in 2% The Empress (3) and Temperance (14). Curiously, Ovid begins his portrait of the two with justice: "No man was there more upright than he, nor a greater lover of justice", and the advice they receive comes from Themis, the goddess of justice. This is a coincidence of images, not a law of the method.

paragraphs.h3: Hope inside the jar

paragraphs: According to Apollodorus, Pyrrha is "the daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora, the first woman fashioned by the gods". In Hesiod's Works and Days, Pandora opens the jar and troubles scatter over the world. "Only Hope remained there in an unbreakable home within under the rim of the great jar, and did not fly out at the door" (translated by Hugh G. Evelyn-White). Inside, in an unbreakable home — while houses fall all over the earth. The centre of the chart is exactly that inside: the couple's Star lives where the collapse of the middle card cannot reach.

At the decisive moment Ovid names the two after their fathers: "the son of Prometheus soothes the daughter of Epimetheus with these gentle words". In Greek, Prometheus means "forethought" and Epimetheus "afterthought"; in Hesiod, Epimetheus "took the gift, and afterwards, when the evil thing was already his, he understood." The 12-16-22 tail follows the same path: from The Hanged Man, whose list in Waite includes "circumspection", to The Fool, who steps first and understands later. The couple needs both kinds.

Waite gives The Star two upright lists at once: "Loss, theft, privation, abandonment" — and "hope and bright prospects". The empty earth after the flood is both lists at the same time. And Ovid promises no more than there is: "still her hope is involved in doubt". The Star in the centre does not promise an outcome; it is simply there.

paragraphs.h3: Water in measure

paragraphs: The first thing the two do after the flood is take a little of the very water that destroyed the world and sprinkle it on their heads and clothes: "they have sprinkled the waters poured on their clothes and their heads". Ovid's flood is "the boundless range of the sea". Waite describes The Star as the Great Mother who passes her riches to the spheres below "in the measure that they can receive her influx". Water without measure drowns; water in measure brings life. The atmosphere inside a couple with this Star needs the same distinction: support in the amount the other can take in.

Wen links the reversed Star with tears, and its message is comfort: "There, there, don't cry." Deucalion begins his speech in tears, and his first thought is who would comfort Pyrrha if he were not there. Comfort here is the first form of hope. Lisovskaya describes The Star in a couple this way: often it is only together that people understand who they want to be. In Ovid the two understand it literally: humankind begins with the two of them.

sections.h2: What Waite saw: four cards of the Waite–Smith deck
paragraphs: The cards on the site have their own artwork. This section is about the Waite–Smith deck (1909) and how Waite himself described it.

ul: **The Hanged Man.** The tree the figure hangs from is "living wood, with leaves thereon"; in the section on older versions of the card Waite writes that "the arms are bound behind him". The oracle tells the couple to do the opposite: to loosen their belts and throw stones behind their backs with their own hands.

**The Tower.** Lightning strikes the tower, the crown flies off, two figures fall. Waite explains them as "the literal word made void and the other its false interpretation" — exactly what falls at the temple of Themis. Among the card's old names he lists "God's House and the Tower of Babel".

**The Star.** A naked woman pours "Water of Life from two great ewers, irrigating sea and land". "Her left knee is on the land and her right foot upon the water." After a flood in which "to that ocean shores were wanting", this figure separates water and land again — and she does it with two vessels.

**The Fool.** A young man at the edge of a precipice looks not down but at "its expanse of sky rather than the prospect below". Waite writes: "His countenance is full of intelligence and expectant dream." Not carelessness, but expectation.

sections.h2: The couple's values: The Lovers or The Devil
paragraphs: The couple's values (its spiritual purpose) answer the question of what the union exists for. In 12-16-22 couples one of two cards stands here: The Lovers in 58.5%, The Devil in 41.5%.

**The Lovers** turn the main task into a choice. Wen compares The Fool's fork in the road with the choice of The Lovers: "in The Lovers card, the choice often has ethical undertones. With The Fool, the choice is not over ethics or morality; it is a choice between two forks in the path." For such a couple, a step into the unknown is not just a road but a decision to choose each other again. Deucalion does it aloud: first blood joined them, then marriage, now danger — and each time the bond is confirmed anew.

**The Devil** points to the chain hidden in the words "we only have each other". With nobody else around, it is easy to start holding on to a partner the way one holds on to a broken mast. Lisovskaya's final thought on The Devil is that nobody belongs to anybody. In Ovid, The Devil and The Tower stand side by side from the very beginning: Lycaon becomes a wolf, and his house falls to the lightning. Waite sets these cards against each other in the same way: The Devil is "the fall into the material and animal state", The Tower "destruction on the intellectual side". For a couple with The Devil in its values, the main thing is not to turn a saving closeness into captivity and not to hold on to what is dead, as Pyrrha holds on to her mother's bones.

sections.h2: How the 12-16-22 tail is formed: an example and three combinations
paragraphs: Each point of the couple's chart is the sum of the same points in two personal charts, reduced to 22. An example with the dates 07.01.1976 and 14.09.1975:

head: Point
Couple
rows: 15 · The Devil (recalculated from the couple's sums, not added)

paragraphs: The partners' personal tails are 21-7-13 and 18-9-9. Neither contains The Hanged Man, The Tower or The Fool: all three cards are born only in the sum.
The 12-16-22 tail occurs in roughly one couple in 215 (0.464%) and ranks 57th of the 97 couple tails. It comes from three combinations of personal tails:

ul: **18-9-9 + 21-7-13** — 56% of these couples (as in the example);

paragraphs: In all three, one partner brings The Moon into the shared entry and the other brings The World. By our count over all dates from 1900 to 2026, the personal tails 21-7-13, 21-10-16 and 21-10-7 together occur in about 3.3% of people, while 18-9-9, 18-6-6 and 18-6-15 occur in about 16.7%: the rare one in this couple is the partner with The World. In 42% of couples The Tower is in one partner's personal tail (21-10-16, as their main task), and the other partner has The Hanged Man in the centre of their personal chart. In the remaining couples both The Tower and The Hanged Man appear only in the sum. Neither The Fool nor The Star is found in any of the six personal tails: The Fool in this tail is born only in the couple, and so is The Star in the centre.

sections.h2: What the 12-16-22 tail asks of a couple
paragraphs: When Lisovskaya analyses a couple's tail, she marks which combination of energies each conclusion comes from. The same is done here.

ul: **Do not mistake a pause for a decision** (12 + 22). There are always clouds in the sky; waiting until "everything is completely calm" can take years.
**Say what each one wants, not only what each one gives up** (12). The language of sacrifice is beautiful, but it has no wishes in it.
**Look in one direction when the familiar falls** (16). First grieve together, then ask together how to go on.
**Let go of the literal reading of old rules** (12 + 16). A parent's "that's how it's done" may have been right for a different world.
**Take the step with no safety net, but together** (22). Each throws their own stones; no one does it for the other.
**Give freedom without checks** (16 + 22). Testing his guest cost Lycaon his house.
**After the collapse, name the bond anew** (16 + 22). The old "we're just together" may no longer describe what there is.
**Allow the new to be rough** (12 + 16 + 22). Ovid's stones become people gradually.

paragraphs.h3: The weak and the strong version

paragraphs: In the weak version, the couple stays in the boat. Its common language is waiting and mutual sacrifice, decisions are postponed, and when the familiar falls, each lives through it alone. The Fool's freedom turns into flight from serious steps, or into the life of two neighbours under one roof.

In the strong version, the couple steps onto the shore. The two grieve together for what has fallen, read the old rules in a new way, name their bond anew and take a step that neither is fully sure of. Their new world looks at first like rough-hewn marble — and comes alive.

paragraphs.h3: Questions a couple can ask itself

ul: What is our "boat" right now — where are we waiting things out, though the water has already gone?
Which rule do we still read literally, though the world in which it was right has ended?
What do we call each other — and does that name fit what is between us?
Which stone is each of us ready to throw behind our back with our own hands?

intro: The three roles in brief:

ul: **12, The Hanged Man — entry to the task.** The couple's common language is pause and care: "let's wait it out", "I'll do it for you". This wish is how the couple enters its task, and the same wish turns into resistance: waiting feels safer than deciding.

**16, The Tower — middle of the task.** The road runs through a collapse. What falls is whatever stood on someone else's foundation: the old way of life, the rule "that's how it's done", the partner as first imagined.

**22, The Fool — main task.** To start again as two — with no safety net, no "must", each with their own hands. The difficulty lies in the serious step: not to run from it and not to freeze in front of it.

intro: This tail's story was written down two thousand years ago. In the first book of Ovid's Metamorphoses, two people are left on earth after the flood: Deucalion and Pyrrha. Their story moves in the same order as the cards, and it even contains a Star that neither of the two has alone.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 12-16-22 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail in which the entry to the task is The Hanged Man, the middle is The Tower and the main task is The Fool. The couple's common language is pause and care, the road runs through the collapse of an old way of life and old rules, and the main task is to start again as two, with no safety net and without running from serious steps. Every such couple has The Star in the centre.

faq.q: Does The Tower in a couple's tail mean a break-up?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events. The Tower in the middle describes a way of walking the path: through the collapse of whatever stood on someone else's foundation — a way of life, rules, invented images. Lisovskaya's key to The Tower in a couple is that trials passed together make the union stronger. In the myth of Deucalion and Pyrrha, the two stay together after the collapse.

faq.q: Why does no personal chart have the 12-16-22 tail?
faq.a: In a personal chart, the entry to the tail equals the main task plus the centre. With a main task of 22, an entry of 12 needs a centre of 17, and no birth date gives The Star in the centre of a personal chart. The middle of a personal tail is also calculated from its ends and would give 7, while a couple's middle is the sum of the partners' middles and equals 16.

faq.q: How is the couple's tail 12-16-22 calculated?
faq.a: The same points of the two personal charts are added, and each sum is reduced to 22. For the dates 07.01.1976 and 14.09.1975: the entry is 21 + 18 = 39 → 12, the middle 7 + 9 = 16, the main task 13 + 9 = 22. The couple's centre is 8 + 9 = 17, The Star.

faq.q: Is there a couple's tail with the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No: among the 97 couple tails, the numbers 12, 16 and 22 appear only in the order 12-16-22. The closest is the tail 12-7-22 — the same ends, with The Chariot in the middle: there the path from pause to freedom runs along a road rather than through a collapse.

report: In the first book of Ovid's Metamorphoses, two people are left on earth after the flood. Deucalion looks down from Parnassus at the empty world and says to his wife: "O sister, O wife, O thou, the only woman surviving… we two are the whole people of the earth." The whole 12-16-22 tail is already written into this scene: a pause in a boat above an upturned world, the ruins of an old order, and a step that neither of the two is sure of.

The tail has an oddity. No single person can have it: such a couple always has The Star in the centre, and The Star never stands in the centre of a personal chart. **The hope that holds these two belongs to neither of them alone** — it appears only when there are two.

report.h3: A declaration of love in the language of sacrifice

report: The entry to the task is The Hanged Man, and it is the couple's common language. It is heard best in Deucalion's speech: "For I, believe me, my wife, if the sea had only carried thee off, should have followed thee, and the sea should have carried me off as well." In Waite's list of meanings for The Hanged Man, "trials, sacrifice" stand side by side. Together, even if it means death.

In a living couple, this entry shows in small things. One partner does not go where they have long wanted to go, so as not to leave the other alone. The two are happy together, away from people. Big decisions wait "for better times", and even marriage needs a push from outside. Ovid's push is the strongest one possible: the rest of the world has gone under water.

The minus of this entry is heard in the same speech. The flood is over, yet Deucalion is still afraid: "even yet do the clouds terrify my mind." **The danger has passed; the waiting has stayed.** There is also someone else's voice inside the couple: Pyrrha refuses to follow the goddess's advice because she "dreads to offend the shades of her mother". Parents' power, "that's how it's done", what people will say — and a model couple that finds it hardest of all to say aloud what each of the two wants.

report.h3: The letter that has to fall

report: The middle of the task is The Tower. The first Tower in this story is the house of King Lycaon: under his roof a guest was tested with a trap, and Jupiter, "with avenging flames, overthrew the house". The house of Deucalion and Pyrrha does not fall. The world around them does: the goddess's temple still stands, but its "altars were standing without fires". This is how the middle of the tail is lived — among the ruins of a way of life that existed before the couple and without it: parents' rules, other people's expectations, plans once made for both, and the partner as first imagined.

The two look at the same empty land, and Ovid gives it a single line: "He thus spoke, and they wept." Deucalion says: "the marriage tie has united to me, and… now dangers themselves unite to me." The collapse in the middle of the tail is not the end of the union but a new knot.

The subtlest Tower is the oracle, which tells the two to throw the bones of their great mother behind their backs. Taken literally, this means desecrating a grave, and Pyrrha freezes. Deucalion finds a second reading: the great mother is the earth, her bones are stones. To move on, the literal reading of an old rule has to collapse. In the myth the roles are divided this way; in a living couple they change places: today one holds on to the letter, tomorrow the other.

report.h3: "But what harm will it do to try?"

report: The main task is The Fool, and here is Ovid's most Fool-like line: "still her hope is involved in doubt; so much do they both distrust the advice of heaven; but what harm will it do to try?" No knowledge, no promise — only the decision to try. The two cover their heads, loosen their belts and throw stones behind their backs without looking round.

This book has two experiments. Lycaon enjoys "this mode of testing the truth" — he tests his guest, and his house falls. Deucalion and Pyrrha try for themselves, with their own hands, and the world comes back. Waite calls The Fool "the spirit in search of experience". **The couple's main task is to choose the second kind of experiment:** freedom without checks.

The Fool's minus is that beginning is easy. After a collapse, such a couple can pack everything into one bag and start on bare ground, while the serious step gets put off. In words everything is settled, yet a shared address, a shared account or a shared "we" never arrives, and the two come to resemble neighbours. Deucalion addresses Pyrrha by three names at once — sister, wife, the only woman left in the world — and adds a new bond: danger. After The Tower the old names may stop fitting, and part of the task is to say aloud who the two are to each other now.

Ovid's stones do not become people at once: at first they look "as if from the marble commenced to be wrought, not sufficiently distinct, and very like to rough statues". "There is no delay," Ovid says of the people, while it is the stones that change slowly. **The Hanged Man's pause does not vanish; it passes from the people into the work.**

report.h3: Hope inside the jar

report: In a personal chart, the entry to the tail equals the main task plus the centre. This couple keeps the rule: The Fool and The Star together make The Hanged Man. Read as a hint, the couple's pause is made not of fear but of its freedom and its hope. The weak version is a waiting in which freedom and hope never turn into a step.

According to Apollodorus, Pyrrha's mother is Pandora. In Hesiod, when the troubles scatter from the jar, "only Hope remained there in an unbreakable home within under the rim of the great jar". Inside, in an unbreakable home — while houses fall all over the earth.

The first thing the two do after the flood is sprinkle their heads and clothes with the very water that destroyed the world. Ovid's flood is "the boundless range of the sea"; Waite describes The Star as a power that gives "in the measure that they can receive her influx". Water without measure drowns; water in measure brings life. In the strong version of the tail, the couple steps out of the boat onto the shore: it grieves together for what has fallen, reads the old rules in a new way and takes a step that neither of the two is fully sure of.

seo.title: Karmic tail 12 16 4 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 16 4 compatibility: The Hanged Man, The Tower and The Emperor — a pause instead of plain words, a day of truth and a house law written by two.

items.title: The couple's karmic tail 12-16-4: The Hanged Man, The Tower and The Emperor
items.short: The Hebrew Bible contains a book in which the name of God never appears, and its heroine bears a name that is read both as "she who hides" and as "star". It is the Book of Esther, and its plot shows through the karmic tail 12-16-4 in compatibility in the same order as the cards: the couple enters its task through a pause and things left unsaid, passes through a day when everything hidden comes out at once, and its main task is the law of its own house.

sections.h2: A book that opens with a decree about marriage
paragraphs: The Persian king Ahasuerus (so in the Hebrew text and the King James Bible; the Russian Synodal translation calls him Artaxerxes) gives a feast lasting a hundred and eighty days, and then another lasting seven. On the seventh day, "when the heart of the king was merry with wine", he sends his chamberlains to bring Queen Vashti, "to shew the people and the princes her beauty". "But the queen Vashti refused to come at the king's commandment."

What happens next is the reason to reread this chapter. A wife's refusal is debated as an affair of state. The adviser Memucan fears not for the king but for what people will say: "this deed of the queen shall come abroad unto all women, so that they shall despise their husbands in their eyes". The ruling is entered "among the laws of the Persians and the Medes, that it be not altered", and letters go out to every province "that every man should bear rule in his own house".

All three cards of the tail stand in that first chapter. The refusal to come and the fear of other people's talk are The Hanged Man. A marriage that falls apart in one evening is The Tower. A law for every house, written by one man, is The Emperor in his heavy version.

The end of the book answers its beginning. The last verse of chapter nine reads: "And the decree of Esther confirmed these matters of Purim; and it was written in the book." A book whose first chapter declares the husband master of the house ends with a decree of the queen. Between those two verses lies the road of the couple 12-16-4: from the pause, through The Tower, to a law written by two.

sections.h2: Entry to the task, 12 — The Hanged Man: "I have not been called to come in unto the king these thirty days"
paragraphs: Esther is an orphan, raised by her cousin Mordecai. She is taken into the palace by royal decree along with other young women, and before she meets the king she spends twelve months in purification: "six months with oil of myrrh, and six months with sweet odours". The Hanged Man is the twelfth arcanum, and in this book the number twelve marks every wait. Twelve months before meeting the king. The lot for destruction is cast "in the twelfth year of king Ahasuerus" and falls "to the twelfth month". And in the twelfth month everything "was turned to the contrary".

"The king loved Esther above all the women" and set the royal crown on her head. But about the main thing Esther keeps silent: "Esther had not shewed her people nor her kindred: for Mordecai had charged her that she should not shew it." She is already queen, yet she still obeys her guardian's word "like as when she was brought up with him". The voice of the parental home sounds louder in the marriage than the husband's voice, and the couple begins its life with a secret that one of them keeps at someone else's request.

The Talmud (tractate Megillah 13a) records a dispute about her names. Rabbi Yehuda holds that her real name was Hadassah, and that she was called Esther "because she concealed the truth about herself" (in the William Davidson translation on Sefaria): the Hebrew root s-t-r means "to hide".

The central scene of the entry is the law of the inner court. When Mordecai asks Esther to plead for her people, she answers: "whosoever, whether man or woman, shall come unto the king into the inner court, who is not called, there is one law of his to put him to death, except such to whom the king shall hold out the golden sceptre, that he may live: but I have not been called to come in unto the king these thirty days." Husband and wife live in one palace, and protocol stands between them. This is life in suspension, as with The Hanged Man: neither a break nor closeness, only waiting to be called.

For the couple 12-16-4 this is the common language. The two know perfectly well when it is better not to approach the other: before dinner, during the silence after work, while someone is "not in the mood". Each waits for the other to speak first. Important things are put off so as not to spoil the evening, and before anything difficult is said, the first thought is what the family will think. In the good version this is tact, rare attentiveness and a fine sense of the other: such a pair can feel each other at a distance and hardly ever wound with a careless word. In the heavy version it is those same thirty days in the inner court, when one does everything for the other, asks nothing for themselves and waits to be called.

Who is the "king" here and who waits in the court has nothing to do with gender. In one and the same couple the roles change from topic to topic: in a conversation about money one of them does the calling, in a conversation about parents the other.

The Hanged Man has a strong side too, and Esther shows it. When the king asks, "What wilt thou, queen Esther? and what is thy request? it shall be even given thee to the half of the kingdom", she asks for nothing and invites the king to a banquet instead. At the banquet he repeats the question, and again she defers: "let the king and Haman come to the banquet that I shall prepare for them, and I will do to morrow as the king hath said." It is a pause, but it has a date — tomorrow. **A pause with a date is the wisdom of choosing the moment. A pause without a date is thirty days of waiting to be called.**

sections.h2: Middle of the task, 16 — The Tower: a tree fifty cubits high
paragraphs: The Tower begins when the pause ends. Esther fasts for three days and goes to the king uncalled, "which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish". The push, as often happens with The Hanged Man, comes from outside. Mordecai sends word to her: "and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"

But in this book the tower itself is built quite literally, and another couple builds it. Haman, the great lord to whom everyone at the king's gate bows except Mordecai, leaves Esther's first banquet happy: the queen invited no one to the banquet with the king except him. At home he tells his wife Zeresh and his friends about his riches, his sons and his honours, and he ends like this: "Yet all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate." His wife and friends reply: "Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high."

The Russian Synodal translation says it outright: a tree, derevo. The Hebrew has ets, the same word as for any tree; the King James Bible renders it gallows. A tree for hanging, raised more than twenty metres high. **The Hanged Man's tree has grown to the height of a tower.** This is how 12 becomes 16: a grievance that hung in the air turns into a construction over one evening's conversation between husband and wife.

That night the king cannot sleep. He commands "the book of records" to be read to him and comes upon an old story: Mordecai once exposed a plot against the king. "What honour and dignity hath been done to Mordecai for this?" — "There is nothing done for him." The debt had hung in the book for years. The Russian Synodal translation reads "the Lord took sleep away from the king" (our translation) at this point: its translators followed the Greek version. In the Hebrew the king simply cannot sleep, and the name of God goes unmentioned here too.

In the morning Haman comes to ask for the hanging and himself devises the honour for "the man whom the king delighteth to honour", never doubting: "To whom would the king delight to do honour more than to myself?" The honour goes to Mordecai, and Haman leads his horse through the city square. At home Zeresh tells her husband what everyone can already see: "If Mordecai be of the seed of the Jews, before whom thou hast begun to fall, thou shalt not prevail against him, but shalt surely fall before him."

At the second banquet Esther finally speaks about the main thing: "For we are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish." The king asks: "Who is he, and where is he, that durst presume in his heart to do so?" — "The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman." In one evening the king learns that his wife belongs to the people he signed away to destruction, and that his chief minister is the enemy. Two images collapse at once: of the wife he turns out not to have known, and of the adviser he trusted. The king rises "in his wrath" and goes out into the palace garden. Even The Emperor needs a pause between the blow and the verdict.

Haman dies on that very tree, and the same day the king gives his house to Esther: the fallen house passes to the one who waited. The book's great reversal is put like this: "in the day that the enemies of the Jews hoped to have power over them, (though it was turned to the contrary...)". The Hebrew here is ve-nahafokh hu — "and it was overturned". The Hanged Man hangs upside down; The Tower turns over whatever was hanging.

For the couple 12-16-4, The Tower in the middle is not a prediction of disaster and not a promise of a break-up. It is the day when one of the two walks into the inner court uncalled and says what both had kept silent about. After such a day it is not the union that falls but the picture: an invented image of the partner, the comfortable version of "everything is fine with us", an order that rested on silence. This Tower has a harsh property worth knowing in advance: what is said on such a day is not forgotten. The words stay in memory like a decree in the book, and that leads straight to the main task.

sections.h2: Main task, 4 — The Emperor: a letter that cannot be revoked
paragraphs: Haman is dead, but his decree lives on. The letters of destruction went out in the king's name, sealed with the king's ring, and not even the king can revoke them. He tells Esther and Mordecai: "Write ye also for the Jews, as it liketh you, in the king's name, and seal it with the king's ring: for the writing which is written in the king's name, and sealed with the king's ring, may no man reverse." The most powerful man in his world cannot take back his own word. He can only allow a second letter, after which the first loses its force in practice.

The whole main task of the couple 12-16-4 is in this scene. For them The Emperor is not a throne but the laws of the house: "that's not how we do things", "I've said what I said", "we agreed once and for all". While such laws serve, they are a support: in Waite's list for The Emperor the first word is "stability". In the good version the four gives the couple what The Hanged Man lacks: clear agreements, savings for a rainy day, the certainty that the other will back them up. Trouble starts when a law once written by one of the two begins to get in the way of its own authors. The law of the inner court protected the king from strangers, and it ended up keeping his own wife from him for thirty days.

What has been said cannot be revoked, least of all after The Tower: the words of the day of truth stay in the book. But a second letter can be written — a new rule agreed aloud on top of the old one and sealed with a shared ring. Not "forget what I said back then" but "from now on, this is how we do it".

The heavy version of The Emperor in this book is not only despotism. King Ahasuerus barely rules at all. He hands his ring to whoever is nearby: first to Haman, to seal a decree against a whole people, then to Mordecai. After the decree of destruction, "the king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city Shushan was perplexed". The household learns the king's mood from a single line: "Then was the king's wrath pacified." In a couple this sounds familiar: "you decide", "do as you like", "I don't care" — and then a face on which no one can tell joy from anger. Deciding for both, and handing over the ring without asking what it will seal, are two sides of one trouble.

The book shows the strong version as well. Three times the king promises to grant Esther's request "even to the half of the kingdom". Not once does she take half the kingdom. She touches the top of the outstretched sceptre, stands before the king and asks not only about the letters but also speaks about herself: "how can I endure to see the destruction of my kindred?" And then she writes: "Then Esther the queen, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew, wrote with all authority." The Russian Synodal translation has "with all insistence" (so vseyu nastoychivostyu, our translation). **A book whose first chapter declares that "every man should bear rule in his own house" ends with "the decree of Esther".** The Emperor's task in a couple is not to split the kingdom in half but to learn to sign the laws together.

And one last turn: irrevocability has not gone anywhere; it has changed its content. In chapter one, the banishment of the queen is written so that "it be not altered". In chapter nine, the days of Purim are fixed so that they "should not fail from among the Jews"; in the Russian text it is the same word as in chapter one. The steadiness that once banished now keeps joy. This is what a mature four looks like in a couple: the rules are still firm, but they are written by two and about what both hold dear.

sections.h2: Clues in Waite and Wen: the veil, the sceptre and truth unveiled
paragraphs: Of The Hanged Man, Waite says plainly that the main thing is not disclosed: "It is a card of profound significance, but all the significance is veiled." For a couple that enters its task through things left unsaid, nothing could be more exact. Nor for a heroine whose name is read as "she who hides".

Waite calls The Tower "a card in particular of unforeseen catastrophe". Unforeseen above all for the one who built: only the day before, Haman had left the banquet "joyful and with a glad heart". And in Wen's section on the reversed Tower there is a reading that might have been written about Ahasuerus: the jolt comes because the Seeker "relied on false impressions made by others". The king signed the decree after believing these words: "There is a certain people … neither keep they the king's laws."

Waite's Emperor holds a sceptre in the form of an ankh: "He has a form of the Crux ansata for his sceptre." Wen explains the signs of his power this way: "The scepter or crux ansata is his sovereignty; the orb is his dominion." In the Book of Esther, the king's power shows precisely in the sceptre: held out, it cancels the death sentence for entering uncalled. The queen "touched the top of the sceptre" — she touched his sovereignty, not his possessions. For a couple this is an exact image of the main task: to hold out the sceptre is to make an exception to one's own law.

Of The Star, which stands at the centre for half of these couples, Waite writes that "for the majority of prepared minds" its naked figure "will appear as the type of Truth unveiled", although he himself also sees in her the Great Mother of the Kabbalah. The entry of the tail is a veil. The centre of half such couples is truth unveiled.

sections.h2: The couple's centre: The Star that no one has alone
paragraphs: At the centre of the couple's matrix — the Atmosphere point, which shows what goes on between two people when no one is watching — the tail 12-16-4 has one of two cards: The Star (17) for 50.1% of couples or Justice (8) for 49.9%.

No birth date ever puts The Star at the centre of a personal matrix: a person's centre can only be 3–14, 16, 18, 20 or 22. Only the sum of two people produces it. A run of the site's engine through every date shows where it comes from: The Star stands at the centre for exactly those 12-16-4 couples in which one partner has the personal tail 3-7-22 with Justice (8) at the centre, and the other has the tail 9-9-18 with The Hermit (9) at the centre. 8 + 9 = 17.

Wen writes that The Star "appears chronologically in the Major Arcana after a great deal of pain: The Hanged Man, Death, The Devil, and The Tower", and that "after the downfall of The Tower, The Star is an indication of a turn upward". Two of the four cards she names stand in this tail, and The Tower comes right before The Star in the deck: 16 and 17. Lisovskaya describes the atmosphere of The Star as a union in which people say straight out what they like and what they don't, and where, for once, the beautiful picture turns out to be true. For a couple that enters its task through silence, that is exactly what opens up after The Tower.

And the name? Most often the name Esther is derived from the Old Persian word for "star" (stāra; setāre in Persian to this day). In the same passage of tractate Megillah where Rabbi Yehuda reads the name as "she who hides", the Talmud gives the view of Rabbi Nehemya: "the nations of the world called her after Istahar, Venus". Both poles of the tail meet in one name: the veil of the entry and the star of the centre. **For half of the 12-16-4 couples, the atmosphere of the union bears the heroine's name.**

Justice, for the other half, comes from this book too. Wen stresses that this is "human-created justice, not divine justice". In the Book of Esther, where God is never named, judgement is done by people: the king, the queen, the scribes with the ring. The atmosphere of a couple with Justice at the centre rests on agreements, fairly shared duties and a sense that the rules are the same for both. Justice does not promise that everyone will get what they deserve; it speaks of how much it matters to these two that the law of the house is not written for one of them.

The couple's values — what the union exists for — are The Lovers for 87.2% of such couples and The Devil for 12.8%. The Lovers are a choice: "the king loved Esther above all the women". In Waite's list of divinatory meanings, The Hanged Man has the word "trials", and The Lovers have "trials overcome". That is what such couples are together for: a choice that went through the pause and did not break. In our reading, where the values sound through The Devil, the union is held by a strong attraction and a shared grip, and the task is to keep that grip from turning into a chain.

sections.h2: Four recipes for the tail 12-16-4
paragraphs: The tail 12-16-4 occurs in roughly one couple in 430 (0.233%), ranking 70th of the 97 couple tails. Every point of a couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, and this triple is built from only four combinations of personal tails. Which one a particular couple has can be seen from both partners' personal tails.
All four share one clue: neither partner has The Hanged Man or The Emperor in their personal tail. The pause and the law are born only between the two.

ul: **3-7-22 + 9-9-18 — half of couples (50%).** One partner's Empress and the other's Hermit give The Hanged Man: a generosity that gives everything away and a solitude that asks for nothing hang together in a pause. The Chariot and The Hermit give The Tower: one rushes ahead, the other withdraws. The Fool and The Moon give The Emperor: freedom and fog together demand a law. These couples always have The Star at the centre.

**6-8-20 + 6-8-20 — a quarter of couples (26%).** Both have the same personal tail. Two choices, The Lovers and The Lovers, give a pause: each waits for the other to choose. Two Justices give The Tower: two judges in one house. Two Judgements give The Emperor. By the engine's count, in every such couple each partner has The Emperor at the centre of their personal chart: the couple's main task is the very card that sits at the centre of each of them. Two kings in one palace learning to write one law. The couple's centre is Justice.

**18-6-15 + 21-10-16 — 16% of couples.** The Moon and The World give The Hanged Man, The Lovers and The Wheel of Fortune give The Tower, The Devil and The Tower give The Emperor. Only in this recipe does one of the two have The Tower personally: it stands on the karmic task of the partner with the tail 21-10-16. The couple's centre is Justice.

**3-13-10 + 9-3-21 — 7% of couples.** The Empress and The Hermit again give The Hanged Man, Death and The Empress give The Tower, The Wheel of Fortune and The World give The Emperor. The couple's centre is Justice.

paragraphs: Together, the first and last recipes account for 57% of couples: in more than half of them, the entry 12 is made of one partner's Empress and the other's Hermit.

The same order 12-16-4 also occurs as a personal tail, for 3,117 dates since 1900, and the site has a separate article about it. That is a different calculation with different roles for the points, and its conclusions do not carry over to a couple. No other couple tail is made of these three numbers: 12-16-4 is the only order.

sections.h2: A worked example: two people born on 07.08.1976
paragraphs: Take two people born on the same day, 7 August 1976 (07.08.1976). Their personal matrices are identical:

ul: karmic task — 7 + 8 + 5 = 20;
entry of the tail — 20 + 4 = 24 → 6, middle — 20 + 6 = 26 → 8.

paragraphs: Each has the personal tail 6-8-20, with The Emperor at the centre. Now add up the matching points of the two matrices:

The couple's centre is 4 + 4 = 8, Justice; the couple's values are 6, The Lovers. Here, as in any couple, the middle comes from adding the two middles, 8 + 8, not from the ends. That it also equals 12 + 4 is a property of the triple itself.

sections.h2: Two couples in one book: the weak and the strong version of the tail
paragraphs: In the Book of Esther the tail 12-16-4 is lived twice, by two couples.

Haman and Zeresh are its heavy version. Their common language is a grievance that hangs in the air: "all this availeth me nothing". Their joint evening project is a tree fifty cubits high. Their law is a decree written in someone else's name and sealed with someone else's ring. And they fall from what they built themselves. In real life the weak version of the tail starts far smaller and without any villainy: with a grievance that two people at the evening table do not talk through but keep building on.

Esther and the king are the strong version. Their pause has a date: "to morrow". The truth is spoken when it can be heard, and it is spoken about oneself. The Tower falls on the lie, not on the marriage. And they write the second letter together: the king gives the ring, the queen writes "with all authority".
Both couples have the same cards. **The difference lies in two things: what the pause is for and whose hand holds the pen.**

sections.h2: What helps a couple with the tail 12-16-4

ul: **Name the couple's own "inner court".** Every such couple has topics one partner does not enter uncalled: money, parents, the past, work. Until they are named, protocol rules them, not agreement.
**Have a sceptre.** A simple sign that lets either come in without an invitation — "is now a good time?" — and an agreement that this question gets an answer, not a brush-off.
**Give the pause a date.** Esther's "to morrow" is wisdom. "Some other time" is thirty days in the court.
**Do not build a tower out of a grievance.** Talk about whatever "gives no peace" while it is still a sentence, not a construction fifty cubits high.
**Go out into the garden, but come back.** On the day of truth, do not pass verdicts at the peak: the king first went out into the garden. But he came back.
**Write a second letter.** Instead of demanding "forget what I said", agree aloud on a new rule on top of the old one.
**Sign the law of the house together.** A decision that concerns both is made by both, and whoever made it explains why. Do not hand over the ring without asking what it will seal.

paragraphs: If the "law of the house" rests on fear, threats or force, it is no longer a task from the cards: it calls for help from a psychologist, and in danger — a call to a local emergency number.

ul: **Entry to the task — 12, The Hanged Man.** The couple's common language is the pause. These two know how not to come in uninvited, how to wait for the right hour and how to keep quiet about the main thing for the sake of peace. This shared wish is where the couple starts, and it is also what turns into resistance.

**Middle of the task — 16, The Tower.** The road from the pause to the task runs through a day of truth: what was kept back for a long time comes out, and the picture the house stood on collapses. Not the union — the picture.

**Main task — 4, The Emperor.** The law of the house. The lesson is not which of the two is in charge but how to write the rules together and rewrite the ones that have started to get in their own authors' way.

intro: The roles of the points follow Yuliana Lisovskaya's book on compatibility. The main point of a couple's tail is the third one, and the first two unfold it; Lisovskaya herself treats the middle as an "addition" to the main task, and the site reads it as the road from the entry to the task.

The first clue lies in the numbers themselves. The middle of a couple's tail is not worked out from its ends: it is the sum of the middles of two personal tails. But this triple has a coincidence built in: 12 + 4 = 16. A pause added to a law gives The Tower. Whatever waits a long time for its hour under strict rules comes out one day, and the Book of Esther shows exactly how that happens.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 12-16-4 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's task written in three cards: the entry through The Hanged Man, the middle through The Tower, and The Emperor as the main task. The two begin with a pause and things left unsaid, pass through a day when what was hidden comes out, and learn to write the rules of their house together rather than by one person's decree.

faq.q: Does The Tower in the middle of a couple's tail mean a break-up?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events or dates. The Tower here is the moment when the pause ends and the truth comes out. What collapses is the picture that rested on silence — an invented image of the partner or the comfortable version of "everything is fine with us" — not the union itself.

faq.q: How does the couple's tail 12-16-4 differ from the personal tail 12-16-4?
faq.a: A personal tail is calculated from a single date, and its points have their own roles. A couple's tail is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, and its points mean the entry to the task, the middle of the task and the couple's main task. The numbers are the same, but the calculation and the meaning are different, so personal conclusions are not carried over to the couple.

faq.q: Which personal tails make up the couple's tail 12-16-4?
faq.a: Only four combinations: 3-7-22 and 9-9-18 (half of couples), 6-8-20 for both (26%), 18-6-15 and 21-10-16 (16%), 3-13-10 and 9-3-21 (7%). To find out which applies, it is enough to look at both partners' personal tails.

faq.q: In a 12-16-4 couple, who is the "king" and who waits for an invitation?
faq.a: The cards do not assign roles by gender or character. Usually the roles change from topic to topic: on one question one partner does the calling, on another the other. It is more useful to notice in which topics the law of the inner court applies to the couple than to look for which of the two is The Emperor.

report: The Book of Esther opens with a decree about marriage: letters go out to every province of Persia "that every man should bear rule in his own house". It closes with the words "the decree of Esther confirmed these matters of Purim". Between those two verses lies the whole tail 12-16-4. The Hanged Man, The Tower and The Emperor come in the book in the same order as in the tail: a pause and things left unsaid, a day when everything hidden comes out at once, and a law of the house that, by the end, two people write.

report.h3: Thirty days in the inner court

report: Esther becomes queen and keeps silent about the main thing: "Esther had not shewed her people nor her kindred: for Mordecai had charged her that she should not shew it." The Talmud reads her name as "she who hides", while the Persian word it is most often derived from means "star". A veil and a star in one name.

The central scene of the entry is the law of the inner court. Whoever comes to the king "who is not called, there is one law of his to put him to death", unless the king holds out the golden sceptre. And the queen admits: **"I have not been called to come in unto the king these thirty days."** Husband and wife live in one palace, and protocol stands between them. That is The Hanged Man: neither a break nor closeness, only waiting to be called.

For a couple with this tail, this is the common language. The two know perfectly well when it is better not to approach the other: before dinner, during the silence after work, while someone is "not in the mood". Each waits for the other to speak first, and important things are put off so as not to spoil the evening. In the good version this is tact and a rare sense of the other: such a pair can feel each other at a distance. In the heavy version it is thirty days in the court, when one does everything for the other and asks nothing for themselves. Who is the "king" here and who waits has nothing to do with gender: the roles change from topic to topic.

Esther shows The Hanged Man's strong side too. The king promises her "even to the half of the kingdom", and she invites him to a banquet, then to a second one: "I will do to morrow as the king hath said." **A pause with a date is the wisdom of choosing the moment. A pause without a date is thirty days of waiting to be called.**

report.h3: A tree grown to the height of a tower

report: In this book the tower is built quite literally, and another couple builds it. The great lord Haman comes home from the banquet, lists his honours to his wife Zeresh and ends: "Yet all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate." His wife and friends reply: "Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high." The Russian Synodal translation says it outright — a tree — and it rises more than twenty metres. **The Hanged Man's tree has grown to the height of a tower.** A grievance that hung in the air turns into a construction over one evening's conversation between husband and wife.

Then everything falls apart in a single evening. Esther goes to the king uncalled — "and if I perish, I perish" — and at the second banquet speaks about the main thing. The king learns that his wife belongs to the people he signed away to destruction, and that his chief minister is the enemy. Two images collapse at once, and the king goes out into the garden: even The Emperor needs a pause between the blow and the verdict. The book's reversal is put as "it was turned to the contrary"; in Hebrew, "and it was overturned". The Hanged Man hangs upside down; The Tower turns over whatever was hanging.

For the couple, this Tower is not a prediction of disaster and not a promise of a break-up. It is the day when one of the two walks into the inner court uncalled and says what both had kept silent about. It is not the union that falls but the picture: an invented image of the partner, the comfortable version of "everything is fine with us". But what is said on such a day is not forgotten.

report.h3: A letter that cannot be revoked

report: Haman is dead, but his decree lives on. Not even the king can take back his own word: "the writing which is written in the king's name, and sealed with the king's ring, may no man reverse." He can only allow a second letter — in the same name and with the same ring.

This is the couple's main task: for them The Emperor is not a throne but the laws of the house. "That's not how we do things", "I've said what I said", "we agreed once and for all". While such laws serve, they are a support. Trouble starts when a law once written by one of the two gets in the way of its own authors: the law of the inner court protected the king from strangers and kept his own wife from him for thirty days. The heavy version of the four is not only despotism. The king hands his ring to whoever is nearby without asking what it will seal, and the household learns his mood from a single line: "Then was the king's wrath pacified." In a couple it sounds like "whatever", "I don't care" — and a face on which no one can tell joy from anger.

The strong version: Esther does not take half the kingdom but writes "with all authority" together with Mordecai. **A book whose first chapter declares that "every man should bear rule in his own house" ends with "the decree of Esther".**

report.h3: What the pause is for, and whose hand holds the pen

report: The book lives this tail twice. Haman and Zeresh build a grievance up into a gallows and fall from what they built. Esther and the king give the pause a date, speak the truth when it can be heard and write the second letter together. Both couples have the same cards. **The difference lies in two things: what the pause is for and whose hand holds the pen.**
What changes the script for such a couple:

ul: name the couple's "inner court" — the topics one partner does not enter uncalled;
have a sceptre: "is now a good time?" — and an agreement that this question gets an answer;
give the pause a date: "to morrow", not "some other time";
talk about whatever "gives no peace" while it is still a sentence, not a construction;
on the day of truth, go out into the garden, but come back;
instead of demanding "forget what I said", write a new rule aloud on top of the old one.

report: If the law of the house rests on fear, threats or force, it is no longer a task from the cards: it calls for help from a psychologist, and in danger — a local emergency number or crisis line.
