unit.meaning: Your task is to give pauses a date, speak the truth in time and write your house laws together, not by one decree.

seo.title: Karmic tail 12 19 16 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 19 16 compatibility: The Hanged Man at the entry, The Sun in the middle, The Tower as the main task — the couple's hidden plot and its test.

items.title: The 12-19-16 karmic tail in compatibility: a happy house with a question under its roof
items.short: For a couple with the 12-19-16 karmic tail, the happy years come not at the end of the road but in the middle, and that is the riddle of these three numbers. The Hanged Man at the entry: the two begin with a pause — a concession, a sacrifice, or a question they agree to leave unsettled for now. The Sun in the middle: a bright, open, enviably successful life together. The Tower as the main task: one day the thing the couple believed in together gives way — shared rules, a picture of the world, the familiar image of each other. The task is not to keep lightning off the house. It is to stay two together after it strikes, once sameness is over.

sections.h2: "This is the Question": The Hanged Man at the entry to the task
paragraphs: Point M in a couple's tail is the "Entry to the task". It is what the two want together: their shared wishes, their agreements, their common language. On the site the same point also appears in the "Relationship and common language" sphere, under the caption "Common language". Through this wish the couple enters its task, and the same wish later turns into resistance. For the 12-19-16 tail the common language is The Hanged Man: the ability to hang a question in the air and go on living.

Darwin's note is almost Hamlet in its heading and pure bookkeeping in its content. Under "Marry": "Children—(if it Please God)—Constant companion, (& friend in old age) who will feel interested in one,—object to be beloved & played with.—better than a dog anyhow." Under "Not Marry": freedom to go where one liked, "conversation of clever men at clubs", "loss of time", "cannot read in the Evenings". The total is reached like a theorem: "Marry—Mary—Marry Q.E.D." On the back a second round begins — when, soon or late? "The Governor", as Darwin called his father, "says soon". The note ends with words that hold more truth than joke: "Never mind my boy—Cheer up… There is many a happy slave."
This is The Hanged Man at the entry: not suffering, but a suspension taken on willingly. A person gives up part of their freedom and knows the price — Darwin even wrote it down in a column.

Before the engagement his father gave him advice that Darwin later recalled in his autobiography: **to conceal carefully his doubts** about religion from his wife. His father, he wrote, had known "extreme misery thus caused with married persons". The son did not take the advice and told his fiancée everything. Ten days after the engagement she replied: "My reason tells me that honest & conscientious doubts cannot be a sin, but I feel it would be a painful void between us. I thank you from my heart for your openness with me." And she asked a favour: to read Christ's farewell discourse to his disciples, which begins at the end of the thirteenth chapter of John. The request ended: "…I don't wish you to give me your opinion about it."
Read it, but do not answer. A question is set down between two people — and left hanging on purpose.

Describing The Hanged Man, Waite explains almost nothing: "all the significance is veiled". The one thing he offers "very simply on my own part" is that the card "expresses the relation, in one of its aspects, between the Divine and the Universe". The Darwins' entry to the task was literally that relation: she with the Gospel of John, he with notebooks in which life on earth was explained without miracles. Between them, a question both agreed not to close.

Soon after the wedding, already living under one roof with her husband, Emma again does not speak but writes: "I do not wish for any answer to all this—it is a satisfaction to me to write it & when I talk to you about it I cannot say exactly what I wish to say." And further: "Don't think that it is not my affair & that it does not much signify to me. Every thing that concerns you concerns me & I should be most unhappy if I thought we did not belong to each other forever." This is the sheet Darwin kissed.

For any couple with the 12-19-16 tail, this is the shape of the entry. The two want to be together so much that they are ready to leave the main thing unsettled. She moves to his city and "for now" does not look for work in her field. He agrees to a church wedding he does not believe in. Both agree to come back to the question of children "in a couple of years", to the question of money "once we're on our feet". This is neither a lie nor a weakness. It is a pause without which the union would never have begun. Lisovskaya writes of the twelfth energy in a couple that such two take a long time to enter a relationship and need a push from outside to marry. Darwin's push was his father with his "soon".

The downside of The Hanged Man at the entry is when the pause turns into silence and the concession into a secret ledger. "I gave it up for you" is not said aloud; it lives in the tone of voice. From outside the couple looks ideal, inside one of them is struggling and keeps quiet, because "that's how it has to be". Emma found a simple remedy: she named the question but did not demand an answer. The question hung, but it hung in plain sight, not in the cellar.

sections.h2: The Sun in the middle of the tail: "a great overgrown child with a new toy"
paragraphs: Point N is the "Middle of the task". Lisovskaya's book gives it no meaning of its own; the site reads it as the road along which the couple moves from the wish of the entry to the main task. For the 12-19-16 tail this road is flooded with sunlight.

Nine days before the wedding Darwin writes to his fiancée from London about the house he is getting ready for the two of them: "I take so much pleasure in the house, I declare I am just like a great overgrown child with a new toy; but then not like a real child I long to have a copartner & possessor." In the same letter he explains why his idea of happiness rests on "quietness & a good deal of solitude": for all five years of the voyage he lived on what passed in his mind while he admired views by himself, crossed deserts and forests, or paced the deck at night. "I think you will humanize me, & soon teach me there is greater happiness, than building theories, & accumulating facts in silence & solitude."

In September 1842 the Darwins move to Down House in Kent and stay there for forty years. Ten children are born into the family. "When you were very young it was my delight to play with you all, and I think with a sigh that such days can never return," he will write to his children in his recollections. And in the same place: "I have indeed been most happy in my family." For many years husband and wife play two games of backgammon every evening. In January 1876 Darwin boasts in a letter to the American botanist Asa Gray: "Now the tally with my wife in backgammon stands thus: she, poor creature, has won only 2490 games, whilst I have won, hurrah, hurrah, 2795 games." Their daughter Henrietta added an important correction to the story: "He won most games, but she won most gammons."

This is the sun of the 12-19-16 tail exactly. In Lisovskaya, The Sun in a couple is just such a house: each partner is busy with their own work and good at it, and the family still comes first. Benebell Wen writes that in love The Sun "indicates a radiant marriage, perhaps one to a spouse with a successful career", and in work it means "high achievement in the arts and sciences". She also has a line that fits this story like a key in a lock: "Key 19 is considered the number of light, the existence of God proven by the very idea of God." The husband's science and the wife's faith meet in one card. That is why the middle of this tail is so bright: in the sunlight both are right.

Darwin summed up these years in words that sound almost like a translation of Waite's divinatory list, where The Sun has "fortunate marriage": "I marvel at my good fortune that she, so infinitely my superior in every single moral quality, consented to be my wife."

sections.h2: An envelope in the drawer: what a sunny noon hides
paragraphs: At noon shadows are shortest. That is physics, but for the 12-19-16 tail it also works as a clue: in the sunny years the hanging question cannot be seen. Guests, children, success for both — why touch what works?

In July 1844, two years after the move, Darwin finishes a sketch of his theory of species and writes his wife a letter in case of his sudden death. It is, in his words, "my most solemn & last request": to spend £400 on publishing the sketch, find an editor and help him sort through the drafts. Nobody knows when Emma first read this letter, but it is addressed to her. The theory that will argue with her faith is placed in her hands. For fifteen more years the sunlit house lives with this envelope: The Tower is already written and lies in a drawer, while over Down House it is noon.

The Sun in the middle of the tail has its own downside, and it is almost always quiet. The couple grows used to being "the sunny ones", and a conversation about something hard starts to feel like spoiling the picture. Among The Sun's tasks for a couple Lisovskaya names the inability to talk about problems and the holding back of feelings. At home it looks ordinary. He has a project, she has a project, in the evenings they laugh at the same series, friends envy them, and in three years nobody once returns to the question they agreed to settle "in a couple of years". Each is sure the other is content, because the other smiles.

Even backgammon at Down House had two scores: in games he was ahead, in gammons she was, and only one of them made it into the letter to a friend. A sunny couple easily lives with two ledgers for the same game and does not notice until the score is needed.

sections.h2: The Tower as the couple's main task: "all my originality… will be smashed"
paragraphs: Point D is the couple's "Main task", its chief trials. It is read above all through the downside: what the couple does not manage and what the two of them have to learn. For the 12-19-16 tail the main task is The Tower. This is not a forecast of disaster and not a date for a catastrophe. It shows where the couple sits its main exam: not in the sunny years, but at the moment the foundation the house stood on stops holding.

At the end of April 1858 Darwin writes to his wife from Moor Park, where he was resting: he fell asleep on the grass and woke to a chorus of birds, squirrels running up the trees and woodpeckers laughing, "& I did not care one penny how any of the beasts or birds had been formed". Seven weeks later, on 18 June, the post brings him a manuscript from a young naturalist, Alfred Russel Wallace, in the Malay Archipelago. It sets out, in essence, his own theory, the one he had worked on for twenty years. That same day Darwin writes to the geologist Lyell: "So all my originality, whatever it may amount to, will be smashed."

A year and a half later, in November 1859, "On the Origin of Species" comes out. Emma helped her husband read the proofs — their daughter remembered it. His old teacher, the geologist and clergyman Adam Sedgwick, answered the book with a letter: "I have read your book with more pain than pleasure." Emma would not show that letter to their daughter.

For the world this was a Tower in the most literal sense: a crack in a house of doctrine that people had lived in for centuries. But a couple's tail speaks of a different house — the one where two people live. And in that house lightning struck both before the book and after it.

In April 1851, at Malvern, the Darwins' ten-year-old daughter Annie died. Her father was with her; her mother stayed at home in Down, expecting a baby. Emma believed in a life after death; it was one of her most cherished beliefs. He no longer had that belief. The two were looking in different directions in the most literal sense: from different towns and from different shores of faith. He writes to her the same day: "We must be more & more to each other my dear wife." She answers the next day: "You must remember that you are my prime treasure (& always have been) my only hope of consolation is to have you safe home to weep together."

Twenty years later, when their daughter was reading the proofs of "The Descent of Man", Emma wrote to her about one of the chapters: "I think it will be very interesting, but that I shall dislike it very much as again putting God further off." On Sundays she took the children to the village church; he had long stopped going.

Among The Tower's tasks for a couple Lisovskaya names the collapse of an invented image of the partner, flight into an extreme — into the spiritual or into the material — and the habit of looking in different directions when bad things happen. The Darwins had all of it at once. Even before the wedding he wrote in a working notebook that love of the deity was an effect of the brain's organisation, and pulled himself up short: "oh you Materialist!" Emma, in a letter soon after the wedding, hoped "you do not consider your opinion as formed": in her eyes his unbelief was not yet final. Each had an extreme to run to, and each saw the other a little differently from how the other really was.

In a couple today the 12-19-16 Tower looks different but is built the same way. One of the two comes to faith or leaves it. Starts calculating destiny matrices while the other laughs — or, the other way round, drops what they have lived by for ten years. Changes profession, city, views on children and money. It turns out that each understood "but we agreed" in their own way. The image cracks: "he's not like that", "she would never". The most dangerous thing at that moment is not the crack itself but two reflexes: to find the one to blame, and to scatter to opposite extremes, one to the sky, the other into the ground.

If there are threats in the house, if there is violence, or if you simply feel afraid for yourself, this is no longer a task of the tail and not a matter for cards: call 112 or your local emergency number and seek help from a psychologist or a crisis service.

sections.h2: The Hierophant at the centre and the two figures on Waite's Tower
paragraphs: In every couple with the 12-19-16 tail, without exception, the centre of the chart holds the fifth arcanum, The Hierophant. The centre of a couple is its atmosphere, what lies between the two when nobody is watching. The Hierophant is tradition, rules, "the proper way", marriage as an institution. Lisovskaya writes that such a couple is often a traditional family, sometimes a religious or an academic one. The Darwins were both at once. Darwin himself had meant as a young man to become a country clergyman and later wrote: "Considering how fiercely I have been attacked by the orthodox, it seems ludicrous that I once intended to be a clergyman."

Waite's divinatory list for The Hierophant begins: "Marriage, alliance, captivity, servitude." In his note of 1838 Darwin managed with almost the same words: "marry" and "many a happy slave". And in the symbolic part Waite calls The Hierophant "the channel of grace belonging to the world of institution as distinct from that of Nature". The centre of this couple stands on the side of institution, while one of the Darwins gave his life to Nature.

In her chapter on The Hanged Man, Benebell Wen compares it with exactly the cards this couple has. "Key 5: The Hierophant is about an orthodox, conventional, institutionalized approach." "Key 9: The Hermit is also about an unorthodox, unconventional approach, but one led in solitude." The Hanged Man is "an approach by the Seeker that offends" the masses. In the 12-19-16 tail all three are in place: The Hierophant at the centre, The Hanged Man at the entry, and The Hermit hidden in the sums, about which more below.

In Lisovskaya, the downside of The Hierophant in a couple is the urge to remake the partner and lecture them; the task is to hold the balance of opposites without moralising. Emma seemed to know this trap and wrote to her husband: "I do not wish for any answer." And in the village church she found her own way to stay both within tradition and within her own faith: when the congregation stood to recite the Creed with its Trinitarian formula, she silently turned the children round to face the rest of the congregation. In a house ruled by rules, each of them had a small deviation of their own. John Brodie Innes, for many years the vicar at Down and Darwin's friend, never accepted his theory — and, by his own account, told a gathering of clergymen that if Darwin met one morning with a fact that contradicted one of his cherished theories, "he would not let the sun set before he made it known". The Hierophant praises The Sun: in this union institution and truth knew how to talk to each other.

Now The Tower itself. On Waite's card two people fall from a tower struck by lightning. Waite argues with those who see in the card a punishment of pride: "The Tower has been spoken of as the chastisement of pride and the intellect overwhelmed in the attempt to penetrate the Mystery of God" — which is how his age might have read the story of "On the Origin of Species". But, he writes, "in neither case do these explanations account for the two persons who are the living sufferers." In a couple's tail those two are the partners. **Here The Tower is never one person's fault and never falls on one person alone**: if the shared house cracks, both fall out of it.

Wen adds a detail that is easy to miss: "The falling crown symbolizes toppling materialism." The Tower brings down not only the house of doctrine but the materialist's crown as well. For this couple that matters: the main task is not for one view to win, but for neither extreme to survive.

sections.h2: What really fell: Emma's note of 1882
paragraphs: Darwin died in April 1882. Six years earlier he had written recollections for his children, spoke there of his "good fortune" in his wife and left a memo in the margin: "(Mem: her beautiful letter to me, safely preserved, shortly after our marriage.)" In 1879, replying to the author of a book on scepticism, he put his position like this: "In my most extreme fluctuations I have never been an Atheist in the sense of denying the existence of a God", and "an Agnostic would be the most correct description of my state of mind". Emma did not stay the same either. Their daughter remembered that as the years went on her beliefs must have greatly changed, "but she kept a sorrowful wish to believe more".

In October 1882, six months after her husband's death, Emma reads his recollections and comes to the place where he explains why he cannot wish Christianity to be true: by the plain language of the text, unbelievers — his father, his brother, almost all his best friends — will be everlastingly punished, "And this is a damnable doctrine." Emma writes in the margin: "I should dislike the passage in brackets to be published. It seems to me raw. Nothing can be said too severe upon the doctrine of everlasting punishment for disbelief—but very few now wd. call that 'Christianity,' (tho' the words are there.)"

So this is what fell. In 1839 Emma was afraid they would not belong to each other for ever, and behind her fear stood exactly this doctrine: if everlasting punishment awaits the unbeliever, a marriage to him ends at the grave. In 1882 she herself writes that nothing can be said too severe about that doctrine. **The Tower brought down not the marriage but a wall inside it.** Neither converted the other. He never called himself an atheist; she did not keep the clear faith of her youth. Both moved, and the "painful void" of 1839 grew smaller.

The passage was left out of the published recollections at the family's wish; Darwin's granddaughter Nora Barlow restored it in 1958. And the letter with the note "kissed and cryed" was found among Emma's papers after her death in 1896. She outlived her husband by fourteen years and kept the sheet on which he had written what she should know once he was gone.

sections.h2: Clues in the numbers: how the 12-19-16 tail adds up in compatibility
paragraphs: The 12-19-16 tail is rare: it turns up in roughly one couple in 1,722, that is 0.058% of couples and 90th place among the 97 couple tails. Running through the dates shows something much stranger as well: in every such couple without exception, one partner was born with the personal tail 18-9-9 and the other with the personal tail 21-10-7. There are no other combinations.
Each point of a couple's tail is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, reduced to 22:

ul: entry: 18 + 21 = 39 → 3 + 9 = 12 — one partner's Moon and the other's World give The Hanged Man;
middle: 9 + 10 = 19 — one partner's Hermit and the other's Wheel of Fortune give The Sun;
main task: 9 + 7 = 16 — one partner's Hermit and the other's Chariot give The Tower.

paragraphs: One of the two carries The Moon and two Hermits: night, quiet, a lantern of their own. The other carries The World, The Wheel and The Chariot: open space, change, moving forward. **One partner's Hermit stands in two of the couple's numbers at once**: from that partner's quiet come both the couple's light and its lightning. The Sun is born when one partner's lantern meets the other's wheel; The Tower, when the same quiet meets a chariot that cannot stand still. In his letter to his fiancée Darwin built his happiness on "quietness & a good deal of solitude" and in the same breath asked her to "humanize" him — that is how a Hermit sounds when it invites someone else's motion into its quiet.

The middle of a couple's tail is not recalculated from the ends. If you add the entry and the main task, 12 + 16 = 28 → 10, you would get The Wheel of Fortune — that is how the middle of a personal tail is calculated. In a couple the middle is made from the partners' middles, and the result is The Sun. The Wheel has not gone anywhere: it is hidden inside The Sun, 9 + 10. In a personal chart such a middle is impossible. The order 12-19-16 is impossible as a personal tail too: there the entry equals the main task plus the centre, and no centre can be added to 16 to give 12.

The couple's centre is fixed as well. A person with the 18-9-9 tail always has a personal centre of 9; a person with the 21-10-7 tail always has 14: The Hermit and Temperance. 9 + 14 = 23 → 5, The Hierophant — in 100% of such couples.

The couple's values — the point also called the spiritual purpose — split in two: in 61.4% of couples it is 15, The Devil; in 38.6% it is 6, The Lovers. Lisovskaya's closing thought on the fifteenth energy in a couple is that nobody belongs to anybody. Emma in 1839 feared they would not belong to each other for ever; Darwin in 1838 consoled himself with "many a happy slave". The Devil among the values asks how to belong to each other without owning each other. The Lovers among the values is a choice the couple makes again, already knowing the price.
There are no other couple tails made of these three numbers: neither 16-19-12 nor any other order occurs in compatibility.
An example on two dates: 14.09.1975 and 18.12.1975. The first person has the personal tail 18-9-9 and centre 9, the second has the tail 21-10-7 and centre 14. Their couple's tail:
The centre of this couple is 9 + 14 = 23 → 5, The Hierophant; the couple's values are 15, The Devil.

sections.h2: How a couple can pass the 12-19-16 tail
paragraphs: The strong version of this tail is not about avoiding The Tower. It is about meeting it with what the couple built up at the entry and in the middle. Here is what works — and all of it is in the Darwins' story.

**Name the hanging question without demanding an answer.** A pause at the entry is normal; a pause without a name is dangerous. It is enough to say: "We haven't decided where we'll live in five years. Let it hang for now, but we both know it's hanging." Emma did exactly this: she named it, asked him to read, and did not wait for an argument.

**Check the sun for shadows.** Once a season, ask each other not "how are things" but "what are we not talking about because everything is fine". The sunny middle is the best time for such a talk: there is strength, and no resentment yet.
**Don't turn a concession into a ledger.** If one partner gave something up at the entry — a city, a job, freedom — the price should be said out loud, not left to live in the tone of voice.

**When the foundation cracks, don't look for one culprit.** Two fall from The Tower. The question is not "who wrecked it" but "what exactly gave way": a rule, an image, a promise each understood in their own way.

**Don't run to extremes.** If one partner goes into the spiritual, the other doesn't have to take refuge in the material, and vice versa. The Darwins disagreed for good — and yet by the end of their lives they stood closer to each other than in 1839.

**Write when you can't say it.** Emma wrote to her husband while living in the same house, because aloud she "cannot say exactly what I wish to say". A note on the table, a message on your phone, a sheet slipped into a book — it doesn't matter. What matters is that the words stay and can be read again. Sometimes forty years later.

In her first letter Emma asked her fiancé to read Christ's farewell discourse and did not explain what exactly she wanted to tell him. But that discourse has a line that sounds like an answer to this tail's Tower: "In my Father's house are many mansions." A couple with the 12-19-16 tail is building exactly such a house: not a house of one truth, where the other must either convert or leave, but a house where different truths have rooms of their own under a shared roof.

sections.h2: Where the quotations come from
paragraphs: The letters of Charles and Emma Darwin are quoted from the Darwin Correspondence Project (University of Cambridge), Darwin's recollections and Emma's note of 1882 from Nora Barlow's complete edition (1958), their daughter's words from Henrietta Litchfield's "Emma Darwin: A Century of Family Letters" (1915). Waite is quoted from "The Pictorial Key to the Tarot", Wen from "Holistic Tarot" (2015).

intro: In the summer of 1838 a twenty-nine-year-old naturalist, two years back from a voyage round the world, divided a sheet of paper into two columns, "Marry" and "Not Marry", and circled the heading: "This is the Question". Six months later he married his first cousin. Soon after the wedding his young wife wrote him a letter about what might part them for ever, and at the end of it he added: "When I am dead, know that many times, I have kissed and cryed over this." The letter was found among her papers after her death, fifty-seven years after it was written. The naturalist was Charles Darwin; his wife was Emma.

Nobody has calculated their tail, and it does not matter. But the Darwins' marriage followed exactly the path written into these three cards: a question left hanging at the entry, forty years of a sunlit house, and a book that cracked the house the two of them shared — the faith she grew up in and he once meant to serve. Their story shows clearly how the 12-19-16 tail works and where such a couple sits its real exam. The roles are not tied to gender: either partner can turn out to be the "Emma".

faq.q: What does the 12-19-16 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of a couple whose entry to the task is The Hanged Man, whose middle is The Sun and whose main task is The Tower. The couple begins with a pause and concessions, lives through bright, open years, and its main exam is to survive the collapse of a shared foundation — rules, a picture of the world or the image of each other — and to stay together without demanding sameness.

faq.q: Does The Tower as the main task mean the couple will split up?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events or dates. The Tower in the main task shows where the couple's chief trial lies: at the moment when what the two believed in together stops holding. The strong version of the tail is a union that, after the crack, rests no longer on sameness but on truth.

faq.q: Why does the 12-19-16 tail never appear in a personal chart?
faq.a: In a personal chart the entry to the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and no centre can be added to 16 to give 12. Besides, the middle of a personal tail is the sum of its ends, and for 12 and 16 it would be 10, not 19. In a couple each point is the sum of the matching points of two people, so such a tail exists only for two.

faq.q: Which personal tails make up the 12-19-16 couple tail?
faq.a: Always the same ones: one partner has the personal tail 18-9-9, the other 21-10-7, in 100% of such couples. The couple's centre is then always 5, The Hierophant: the personal centres 9 and 14 give 23, and 2 + 3 = 5.

faq.q: How common is the 12-19-16 tail among couples?
faq.a: It is rare: roughly one couple in 1,722, that is 0.058% of couples and 90th place among the 97 couple tails. There are no couple tails made of the same numbers in a different order.

faq.q: What does Darwin have to do with it if nobody calculated his tail?
faq.a: His marriage is not a worked example but a story that shows clearly how these three cards work: a question left hanging at the entry, the sunny years, and the collapse of a shared faith that the two lived through together. The worked example in this article uses only two dates, 14.09.1975 and 18.12.1975.

report: "When I am dead, know that many times, I have kissed and cryed over this." Charles Darwin added this note at the end of a letter his wife wrote to him soon after their wedding — a letter about what might part them for ever. It was found among Emma's papers after her death, fifty-seven years later. The Darwins' marriage followed exactly the path written into the three cards 12-19-16: a question left hanging at the entry, forty years of a sunlit house, and the collapse of what the two had once believed in together. The roles are not tied to gender: either partner can turn out to be the "Emma".
The strangest thing about this tail is that **the happy years come not at the end of the road but in the middle**. The exam comes after them.

report.h3: A question left hanging on purpose

report: The Hanged Man at the entry is the couple's common language: the ability to hang a question in the air and go on living. In the summer of 1838 Darwin divided a sheet of paper into "Marry" and "Not Marry", circled the heading "This is the Question", added everything up in columns — "loss of time", "better than a dog anyhow" — and ended with the words: "There is many a happy slave." This is not suffering but a suspension taken on willingly: a person gives up part of their freedom and knows the price.

His father advised him to conceal carefully his doubts about religion from his wife. The son told his fiancée everything. She replied that honest doubts cannot be a sin, but that this would be "a painful void between us", asked him to read Christ's farewell discourse to his disciples — and added that she did not wish him to give her his opinion about it. Read it, but do not answer. Waite says of The Hanged Man that the card expresses "the relation… between the Divine and the Universe". This couple's entry was literally that: she with the Gospel of John, he with a naturalist's notebooks.

For a couple with this tail the entry often looks ordinary. Someone moves "for now", someone agrees to a church wedding they do not believe in, the talk about children is put off "for a couple of years". It is not a lie but a pause, without which the union would never have begun. The downside comes when the pause turns into silence and the concession into a secret ledger. Emma found a remedy: name the question, but do not demand an answer. **The question hung, but it hung in plain sight, not in the cellar.**

report.h3: In sunlight both are right, but at noon nobody sees the shadows

report: The Sun in the middle stands for the years others admire from outside. Ten children were born at Down House. Every evening the couple played two games of backgammon, and Darwin boasted to a friend that she, "poor creature", had won only 2490 games, whilst he had won, "hurrah, hurrah", 2795. Their daughter added: he won most games, but she won most gammons. For Benebell Wen, "Key 19 is considered the number of light, the existence of God proven by the very idea of God", and in work The Sun means "high achievement in the arts and sciences". The husband's science and the wife's faith meet in one card, which is why the middle of this tail is so bright.

But at noon shadows are shortest. In 1844 Darwin finishes a sketch of his theory and writes his wife a letter: "my most solemn & last request" — to publish the sketch if he dies suddenly. The theory that will argue with her faith is placed in her hands, and for fifteen more years the sunlit house lives with that envelope. The Sun's downside is quiet: the couple grows used to being "the sunny ones", and a hard conversation starts to feel like spoiling the picture. Each has a project, friends envy them, and in three years nobody returns to the question put off "for a couple of years".

report.h3: The Tower brings down not the marriage but a wall inside it

report: The main task is The Tower. It is not a forecast of disaster but a pointer to where the exam takes place: the moment the foundation the house stood on stops holding. In the summer of 1858 a manuscript from Alfred Russel Wallace made Darwin write: "all my originality… will be smashed." A year and a half later "On the Origin of Species" came out, and Emma helped him read the proofs. But lightning had struck their house before. In 1851 their ten-year-old daughter died. He was with her, she was in another town; the two were looking in different directions, from different shores of faith. He wrote: "We must be more & more to each other." She replied that her only hope of consolation was to have him safe home, "to weep together".

Today this tail's Tower looks different. One partner comes to faith or leaves it, changes profession, city, views on children, and it turns out that each understood "but we agreed" in their own way. Waite argued with those who saw in The Tower a punishment of pride: that explanation does not account for **"the two persons who are the living sufferers"** on the card. In a couple, they are both partners. The Tower is never one person's fault and never falls on one person alone. The danger is not the crack but two reflexes: finding the one to blame, and scattering to opposite extremes, one to the sky, the other into the ground. If there are threats or violence at home, this is no longer a task of the tail: the thing to do is call 112 or a local emergency number or crisis line and seek help from a psychologist.

In 1839 Emma feared they would not belong to each other for ever, and behind her fear stood the doctrine of everlasting punishment for unbelievers. In 1882, six months after her husband's death, she wrote in the margin of his recollections that "nothing can be said too severe upon" that doctrine. Neither converted the other: he never called himself an atheist, she did not keep the clear faith of her youth. Both moved, and **the "painful void" grew smaller**.

report.h3: A house of many mansions

report: The strong version of this tail rests on simple things. Naming the hanging question without demanding an answer. Asking each other not "how are things" but "what are we not talking about because everything is fine". Writing when it cannot be said: Emma wrote to her husband while living in the same house. The discourse she asked him to read has the line: "In my Father's house are many mansions." A couple with the 12-19-16 tail is building exactly such a house — not a house of one truth, but a house where different truths have rooms of their own under a shared roof.

seo.title: Karmic tail 12 19 7 compatibility: waiting, light and the reins
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 19 7 compatibility: The Hanged Man, The Sun and The Chariot in a couple's matrix, what the three cards mean for two people and what to learn.

items.title: Karmic tail 12-19-7 in compatibility: the second half of Sleeping Beauty
items.short: In Charles Perrault's tale, Sleeping Beauty has no name. Aurora is the name of her daughter, and the daughter arrives only after the wedding, in the second half of the story, the half that later went missing. The couple karmic tail 12-19-7 tells the couple's story whole, second half included: first the waiting, then the light, and the main task begins exactly where storybooks write "and they lived happily ever after".

sections.h2: Why Sleeping Beauty is called Aurora
paragraphs: The version everyone knows was told by the Brothers Grimm in 1812. The prince passes through the briars, kisses the sleeper, she opens her eyes, the cooks and the flies in the palace wake up, there is a wedding, "and they lived happily together all their lives long". Tchaikovsky's ballet (1890) and Disney's film (1959) carry the story to the same wedding, and in both the princess is called Aurora.

Perrault's version, in his collection of 1697, often called the Tales of Mother Goose, is different. There is no kiss: the prince only kneels, and the princess wakes because, in Andrew Lang's English, "the enchantment was at an end". The wedding takes place that same evening, and it is the middle of the tale, not its end. Then the prince lives with his wife in secret for two years and tells his parents he is out hunting. They have two children: a daughter, l'Aurore, and a son, le Jour, Dawn and Day (Lang calls them Morning and Day). When the old king dies, the young one announces the marriage, brings his wife to the capital in state and soon leaves for a whole summer of war. He leaves the kingdom and his family in the care of his mother, and his mother is of the race of ogres.

It seems the daughter's name passed to the mother: everything after the wedding dropped out of the retellings, and all that survived of the second half was a name. In the Neapolitan Pentamerone of Giambattista Basile (1634–1636), where Perrault apparently found the plot, the sleeper's children are named even more plainly: Sun and Moon.

Tail 12-19-7 is the tale uncut. The Hanged Man is a hundred years of sleep and two years of secrecy, The Sun is two children named Dawn and Day, The Chariot is a campaign from which the king barely gets back in time. The part everyone knows is only the entry to the task. The task itself begins after the wedding.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: "You have kept me waiting a long time"
paragraphs: The first point of a couple's tail is what the two want together, their agreements and common language. It is something to lean on, but it stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish can turn into resistance. In this couple the shared wish is expressed by The Hanged Man, and The Hanged Man is life suspended in time.

Perrault's good fairy puts to sleep not just the princess but the whole castle: the maids of honour, the cooks, the beefeaters, the horses in the stables, the little dog on the bed. Even the spits full of partridges fall asleep, "and the fire as well" (et le feu aussi, in Perrault's French). The fairy makes sure the princess will not wake alone in a time not her own: the couple's world falls asleep and wakes together with her. Within a quarter of an hour a wood of trees and brambles grows round the castle, so that the princess "might have nothing to fear from any curious people". Before the prince the wood parts of itself and closes again behind him: none of his people can follow. This castle lets in only one.

A couple with The Hanged Man at the entry to the task recognises this castle: a world of their own where others do not go. The two have their own words and songs, their own jokes and habits, which look old-fashioned from outside. Helping his bride up, the prince notices she is "dressed like his great-grandmother" and tactfully says nothing; at supper the violins play "old tunes, but very excellent, though it was now above a hundred years since they had played". This is the beautiful side of the couple: the two know how to keep what the rest of the world has long since dropped.

In the original, the princess's first words are: "Est-ce vous, mon prince? Vous vous êtes bien fait attendre", that is, "Is it you, my prince? You have kept me waiting a long time." Turgenev, translating into Russian, made it otherwise: "Is it you, prince? And I have long been waiting for you!" (our translation from his Russian; Lang's English even turns it round, "You have waited a long while"). In Perrault it is a gentle reproach, in Turgenev a confession. The waiting is the same, but it is spoken in two different languages. A couple with this tail keeps coming back to this conversation: who waited for whom, for how long, and whether it was worth it. On good days it comes out as "I waited for you", on hard days as "you kept me waiting".

Perrault adds one more fine detail. The prince is more flustered than his bride, and the author explains why: she had had time to think what to say, for "it is very probable (though history mentions nothing of it) that the good Fairy, during so long a sleep, had given her very agreeable dreams". They "talked four hours together, and yet they said not half what they had to say". One of the two comes to the meeting with a ready-made script grown over years of waiting, the other comes with no script at all. A long wait leaves time to expect too much: Lisovskaya lists inflated expectations among the tasks of The Hanged Man in so many words.

In the second act the waiting turns from sweet to sticky. The morning after the wedding the prince returns to his father and says he lost his way while hunting and spent the night in "the cottage of a charcoal-burner, who gave him cheese and brown bread". For two years he goes "hunting" almost every day and never dares confess, because he is afraid of his mother. The decision is postponed until something outside makes it: the prince announces the marriage only when his father dies. Lisovskaya notes the same of a couple with this energy: such two come together slowly, and to get as far as marriage they often need a push from outside.

Today it looks like this. For years the two say "later": we'll move in later, tell the family later, decide later where to live. They are happy together, so "later" does no harm, until something external decides for them: a move, someone else's condition, an offer that cannot be refused. Perrault's prince assures his bride that he loves her "better than he did himself", and that too is the language of The Hanged Man: each is ready to set their own life aside for the other. At its best this is generosity; at its worst neither does anything for themselves and both wait for life to move them.

The main thing is visible already at the entry: in this union much is decided by the right time, not by effort. The princess wakes not from a kiss but because the hundred years are up, and even in Grimm the prince arrives on the very day they run out. That is the couple's gift, because the two can wait for their hour. It is also its risk, because one can wait for a deadline nobody has set.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: children named Dawn and Day
paragraphs: The middle of the tail is our reading of how the couple travels from its wish to its task, what it lives through on the way. For this couple the middle is The Sun, that is, a road through light.

In the tale the middle looks exactly like that. The secret marriage brings two children named after light: Dawn and Day, the son called Day "because he was a great deal handsomer and more beautiful than his sister". The secret comes out into the sun: the king announces his marriage, fetches his wife from the castle in the wood, and she enters the capital in full view, "riding between her two children". The couple that lived behind the briars becomes a couple the whole city watches. Lisovskaya's Sun paints exactly such a couple: bright, warm, noticed, talked about.

**The clue in the numbers.** The Sun is in neither partner's personal tail, in any couple of this kind. Tail 12-19-7 can be assembled from only three combinations of personal tails, and the nineteen in the middle is always the exact sum of the two personal middles: 9 + 10, 7 + 12 or 14 + 5. Neither of the two brings this Sun along. It is born between them, like Dawn and Day, who belong neither to the father nor to the mother alone.

There is a second clue. In almost half of these couples (48%) the two numbers that add up to The Sun are The Chariot and The Hanged Man, the very cards that stand at the two ends of the couple's tail. One partner has The Chariot in the middle of their personal tail, the other has The Hanged Man. Waiting and the road live in two different people, and the light appears only when the two are added together.

Sunlight has a property the tale mentions under its breath. By day everything is visible except what is whispered. "It was even whispered about the Court that she had Ogreish inclinations, and that, whenever she saw little children passing by, she had all the difficulty in the world to avoid falling upon them." The prince knew it, which is why he feared his mother. The Sun brought the marriage into the light, but the danger stayed a rumour: nobody said it out loud, and at the end "no one dared to tell" the king what was going on in his own courtyard. Among the minuses of The Sun in a couple's tasks, Lisovskaya lists not knowing how to talk about problems. For this couple the time of light is the best time to say out loud what the family usually whispers, before the campaign begins.

The second property of light is more treacherous. The brightest season looks like the ending. This is where the popular retellings cut the story: the grand entry, the children, the wedding feast, "happily ever after". In the middle of the tail it is easy for the couple to decide that everything has worked out, while the main task is still ahead.

sections.h2: Main task: war with the Emperor Cantalabutte
paragraphs: The main point of a couple's tail is read mostly through its minus: what does not work for the two and what they need to learn. For this couple the main task is The Chariot: movement, campaign, command, victory, the reins.

"Soon after the King went to make war with the Emperor Contalabutte, his neighbor." Perrault does not explain what the war is for. The neighbour has a comic name, the Emperor Cantalabutte (Lang spells it Contalabutte), and Turgenev turned him into "Tsar Kantalup", that is, a cantaloupe melon. The war lasts all summer, and in the tale it has no aim: it is a campaign that seems to happen by itself, because a Chariot is supposed to ride. Among the minuses of this energy Lisovskaya lists aimlessness, a contest over who leads, and the hard balance between work and family.

Before leaving, the king makes the tale's central mistake, and there is no malice in it. "He left the government of the kingdom to the Queen his mother, and earnestly recommended to her care his wife and children." The reins go to the one whose inclinations were only whispered about at court: she simply happened to be at hand. As soon as he is gone, the regent sends her daughter-in-law and the children to "a country house among the woods", back into the woods, to the beginning of the tale. Then she tells her clerk of the kitchen: "I have a mind to eat little Morning for my dinner to-morrow", with a sauce Robert.

What follows shows what becomes of a house without reins. The young queen is sure her children are dead, and when the clerk comes with a dagger she stretches out her own neck: "Do it; do it… Execute your orders." In the last scene the queen and her children, the clerk, his wife and their maid are brought into the courtyard, and the ogress has given orders that they come "with their hands tied behind them". Whoever was left at home without the reins goes back to the language of the entry: waits, sacrifices themselves, waits for the verdict and the rescuer.

The rescuer comes: "the King (who was not so soon expected) entered the court on horseback (for he came post)". This is The Chariot at its best: its speed and resolve at last working for the home. Only he arrives at the very edge of the tub of snakes.

In life the regent is rarely an ogress mother-in-law. Lisovskaya does list the power of parents over the couple among the minuses of The Hanged Man, but far more often the reins go elsewhere. It may be work that runs the house on its own timetable, tiredness or habit, the phone, relatives, or simply whoever is nearest. A couple with this tail recognises the scene: one sets off on their own summer campaign, a project, a business trip, a career leap or a building job, and tosses over a shoulder "keep an eye on things". The other stays and does not feel entitled to decide: holds the fort and waits for the return. After a while each pulls the blanket their own way, and the house lives a life of its own.

In the tale the roles are handed out the old way: he rides, she waits. In a couple with this tail the roles do not depend on sex. Either of the two may ride and either may wait, and most often they take turns.

The task is not never to leave. The Chariot has to move, and in Lisovskaya's plus of this energy each partner has a life and growth outside the family: walking side by side, each on their own road. The task is something else:

ul: to agree before the campaign, not after, who holds which reins and what gets decided without the one who is away;
not to make a hostage of the one who stays: whoever is at home governs, rather than waiting with tied hands;
to name the status of the relationship and the roles without evasion, since two years of secret marriage were exactly that evasion;
to come back regularly, and not only at the last minute, by post horses, to the very edge of the tub.

sections.h2: The circle of the tail: a tale that begins and ends with waiting
paragraphs: Put the first and last pictures of the tale side by side and the tail's mechanism shows. The first picture is a castle where people cannot move and wait for a rider. The last is a courtyard where people have their hands tied and are again waiting for a rider. Between them lie the light, the children, the grand entry. If the Chariot's task is not solved, the circle closes: waiting, light, campaign, and waiting again, only now not sweet but anxious.

The circle has a price. Years lived in "later". The one who waits grows used to being rescued. The one who rides grows used to coming back a hero at the last moment and does not notice that a regent ran the house all summer. And above all, the couple comes to believe that waiting is its moral.

Perrault's own moral also looks only at the entry. The verses after the tale speak only of the first half, as if there had been no ogress at all: "To wait a while for a husband, rich, well-made, gallant and gentle, is natural enough; but to wait a hundred years, and asleep the whole time, you will not find a woman now who would sleep so calmly." The tale, he goes on, seems to tell us too that the bonds of marriage, when delayed, are often no less happy, "and that one loses nothing by waiting". And at once he does not believe it himself: the fair sex longs for marriage with such ardour that he has "neither the strength nor the heart to preach this moral" to it (our translation). In French the line, on ne perd rien pour attendre, today also sounds like a threat, something like "just you wait". Once again this couple's waiting has two faces.
The moral of tail 12-19-7 is not "wait". The couple knows how to wait from the very entry. Its moral is to drive.

sections.h2: What Waite saw: a spinner, two children and a rider
paragraphs: In the first part of his book Waite describes how The Sun was drawn before him. On older cards there is "a wall suggesting an enclosure—as it might be, a walled garden—wherein are two children", running hand in hand. "Éliphas Lévi says that these are sometimes replaced by a spinner unwinding destinies, and otherwise by a much better symbol—a naked child mounted on a white horse and displaying a scarlet standard." Perrault's tale holds all three versions of the card. The spinner is the old woman at the top of the tower, "alone, spinning with her spindle", who "had never heard of the King's proclamation against spindles": the sleep begins with her. The two children are Dawn and Day. The rider is the king who rides into the courtyard and ends the tale, and a child with a weapon is there too: three-year-old Day, whom the clerk finds "with a little foil in his hand, with which he was fencing with a great monkey". One sentence of Waite's about the old Suns runs through the whole tale, from the tower to the courtyard.

In the same part Waite describes The Hanged Man as a figure "suspended head-downwards", and "the arms are bound behind him". The last scene of the tale divides these two features between its characters. The hands bound behind fall to the queen, the children, the clerk, his wife and the maid. Head down goes the ogress: seeing that all is discovered, she "threw herself head foremost into the tub". In Waite's divinatory list the reversed Hanged Man begins with the word "Selfishness". In the tale the ogress's appetite answers to it: someone else must be the sacrifice.

About The Chariot, Waite reports something curious. Court de Gébelin, the man who in the eighteenth century first declared the Tarot an Egyptian book, said "that it was Osiris Triumphing, the conquering sun in spring-time having vanquished the obstacles of winter". Waite disagrees, but for an eighteenth-century reader the last two cards of this tail were one light: The Sun, and the sun in a triumphal chariot. This is the danger of the middle: light easily turns into triumph, and triumph into a campaign. In Perrault there is a single sentence between the grand entry into the capital and the war.

In her account of The Chariot, Wen writes that "the castle walls and moat behind him represent the domain that he protects". The charioteer protects what lies behind his back, and faces the other way. The first chariot in the tale appears long before the king: the good fairy arrives to put the castle to sleep "in a fiery chariot drawn by dragons". A chariot brings sleep at the beginning; a rider ends the waiting at the end.

Wen has one more detail, the elements of the cards. For her, "the element of Water governs" both The Hanged Man and The Chariot, and in both "yin energy is dominant". The Sun is Fire, with yang dominant. Tail 12-19-7 comes out as water, fire and water again, and the only fire burns in the middle. In Perrault's castle, remember, even the fire in the hearth falls asleep for a hundred years.

sections.h2: How the couple's tail 12-19-7 is worked out
paragraphs: Each point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22: if the sum is greater than 22, its digits are added together. The couple's tail is three points: the entry to the task, the middle and the main task.
An example is a couple with the dates of birth 06.03.1978 and 14.09.1975. The first partner's personal tail is 21-10-16, the second's is 18-9-9. Add them point by point:

Here the sum of the two end numbers also gives 19, because 12 + 7 = 19, but a couple's middle is not worked out that way: it is always the sum of the middles of the two personal tails. In the centre of this couple's matrix stands Temperance (5 + 9 = 14), and in the couple's values, The Lovers.
Tail 12-19-7 occurs in roughly one couple in 192 (0.522%) and ranks 53rd of the 97 couple tails. There are only three ways to assemble it:

There are no other couple tails made of the numbers 12, 19 and 7; this order is the only one. The same order also occurs as a personal karmic tail, for 4,296 birth dates since 1900, but that is a different calculation and the points play different roles. The personal tail 12-19-7 has its own article; this one is only about the couple.

sections.h2: Centre and values: an angel named Time
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's matrix is the atmosphere, what happens between the two when nobody is watching. In couples with tail 12-19-7 the centre is almost always Temperance: in 99.2% of them. The remaining 0.8% have The Hierophant.

Wen quotes P. D. Ouspensky, who called Temperance the Time card: "The name of the angel is Time.… One of the cups the angel holds is the past, the other is the future. The rainbow stream between the cups is the present. You see that it flows both ways." In Perrault time is literally poured from cup to cup. The young queen "was turned of twenty, not reckoning the hundred years she had been asleep", she wears her great-grandmother's dress, and a century-old music plays at supper. Inside such a couple past and future also flow both ways: old dreams pour into the present day, and plans pour back into memory. Lisovskaya's Temperance at its best means quarrels settled by talk and concession, and a balance of rest and movement. This, it seems, is the two people's skill at blending waiting and the road.

In Waite's divinatory list Temperance carries "Economy, moderation, frugality, management, accommodation". All summer the house is saved not by the king or the queen but by the clerk of the kitchen, Perrault's maître d'hôtel, the master of the table. In place of Dawn he serves a lamb, in place of Day a kid, in place of the queen a young hind. Perrault's verb is accommoder une biche, "to dress a hind", from the same root as Waite's accommodation. Temperance at the centre of the couple works like this clerk: quietly substitutes, softens, buys time. That saves the day while the king is away. But if it goes on too long, one partner ends up hiding the trouble in the kitchen instead of bringing it out into the courtyard.

The rare couples with The Hierophant at the centre have a key of their own, and Waite has it too. Among the reversed meanings of Temperance he lists "sometimes even the priest who will marry the Querent". In Perrault the lord almoner, who slept a hundred years along with everyone else, marries the couple right after supper, "without losing any time". For such couples the atmosphere rests on rule, on ritual, on "the way things are done".

The couple's values are what the union exists for. In 61.8% of couples with this tail this is The Lovers, that is, choice. Perrault's prince makes up his mind "sans balancer", "without weighing the matter", the moment the old countryman tells him of the sleeper. For these couples the value lies in choosing each other again, above all at the moment the campaign calls. In 38.2% the values hold The Devil. Lisovskaya's main thought about this energy in a couple is that nobody belongs to anybody. In the tale the ogress treats the house as her table, and the king leaves her his wife and children along with the kingdom, as if they were property. For these couples the value lies in holding the reins, not owning them.

sections.h2: The strong version: four hands on the reins
paragraphs: Tail 12-19-7 makes a couple neither happy nor unhappy. It shows the place where the plot usually breaks, and what mends it.

ul: **Waiting needs a term and a reason.** The fairy had a term, a hundred years. A pause with no term turns into a sleep after which everything in the castle is a century out of date. "We wait until spring, because…" is a decision; "some time later" is that very hedge of briars round the castle.
**In the light, name what is whispered.** The Sun is direct light. The time when the couple is happy and seen is the best time to say aloud what each of them fears, rather than leave it to rumour.
**Agree before the campaign.** Who decides what while one is away, whom the one left behind can lean on, what must not be handed to a "regent", be it work, relatives or habit.
**The one at home governs too.** This couple's Chariot is driven with four hands: one holds the reins of the road, the other the reins of the home, and next time they swap.

**Come back sooner than expected.** Perrault's king arrives earlier than he was expected, and only for that reason does everything end well. In the strong version of the tail this is not a miracle by post horses but a habit.

paragraphs: In the strong version the couple keeps the gift of its entry: the knack of waiting, the slow coming together, the old music only the two of them hear. It does not, however, mistake waiting for fate. It brings its light out into the day and says aloud what used to be whispered. And it drives together: one on the road, the other at home, then the other way round. Then the tale ends not with a tub of snakes but with the words of Perrault's moral, which at last come true: delayed bonds are no less happy.

intro: The three cards of the couple's tail stand in the same order as the three acts of the tale:

ul: **12 · The Hanged Man — entry to the task.** What joins the two is a shared language of waiting: "not yet", "let's wait", a life both are willing to keep on hold for each other's sake. It is how the couple begins, and it is also what holds the couple back.

**19 · The Sun — middle of the task.** The way runs through light: what was hidden comes out into the day, and the couple gains something everyone can see, a shared home, children or a shared venture, a joy that no longer needs hiding.

**7 · The Chariot — main task.** Learning to drive together: not handing the reins of the shared home to someone else when one or both are called away on campaign, and coming back before the last minute.

intro: The tail does not predict what will happen to the couple. It shows a plot in which two people recognise themselves, and the place where that plot tests them in earnest. For this tail, that place is not the meeting but the time after it.

faq.q: How is karmic tail 12-19-7 in compatibility worked out?
faq.a: Two dates of birth are needed. A personal matrix is built for each partner, then the points of the tail are added in pairs and reduced to 22: entry with entry, middle with middle, main task with main task. For example, 06.03.1978 and 14.09.1975 give the personal tails 21-10-16 and 18-9-9, and together 39 → 12, 19 and 25 → 7. The compatibility calculator on the site does this by itself.

faq.q: How does the couple tail 12-19-7 differ from the personal tail 12-19-7?
faq.a: The personal tail 12-19-7 is worked out from one date and describes one person, and its points have their own roles. The couple's tail is built from two personal matrices and describes the task of the union: the entry to it, the middle and the main task. The numbers are the same, but **the calculation and the meaning differ**, so readings of the personal tail do not carry over to the couple.

faq.q: Is tail 12-19-7 a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not predict break-ups, wars or misfortunes, and it does not grade the couple. It shows what the two meet on (waiting), what they pass through (the light of an open shared life) and what they learn (to drive together). The minus of the main task is something to work on, not a verdict.

faq.q: Are there couple tails with the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. From the numbers 12, 19 and 7 a couple can only get the order 12-19-7: The Hanged Man at the entry, The Sun in the middle, The Chariot in the main task. No other arrangement occurs in a couple's matrix.

faq.q: What stands in the centre and in the values of a couple with tail 12-19-7?
faq.a: In the centre of the couple's matrix, 99.2% of such couples have Temperance and 0.8% have The Hierophant. In the couple's values, 61.8% have The Lovers and 38.2% have The Devil. Temperance in the centre is an atmosphere in which the two blend waiting and movement, past and future. The Lovers in the values mean choosing each other again, and The Devil teaches that nobody belongs to anybody.

report: In Charles Perrault's tale, Sleeping Beauty has no name. Aurora is the name of her daughter, and the daughter is born only after the wedding, in the second half of the story, the half that later dropped out of the retellings. Tail 12-19-7 is that tale whole and uncut. The Hanged Man is a hundred years of sleep and two years of secret marriage. The Sun is two children named Dawn and Day. The Chariot is a campaign from which the king barely gets back in time. **The part everyone knows is only the entry to the task; the task itself begins after the wedding.**

report.h3: A castle that lets in only one

report: Perrault's fairy puts the whole castle to sleep: the maids of honour, the cooks, the horses in the stables, the little dog on the bed. Even the spits full of partridges fall asleep, "and the fire as well". A wood of brambles grows up in a quarter of an hour, parts before the prince and closes again behind him, so that none of his people can follow. A couple with The Hanged Man at the entry recognises this castle: the two have a world of their own, their own words and habits, which look old-fashioned from outside. The prince notices that his bride is "dressed like his great-grandmother" and tactfully says nothing, and at supper the violins play music that has not been heard for a hundred years.

The common language of such a pair is waiting. In Perrault the princess's first words are a gentle reproach: she has been kept waiting a long time. Turgenev turned them into a confession that she has long been waiting. The waiting is one, but it speaks two languages, and the couple keeps coming back to the same conversation: who waited for whom, and whether it was worth it. She had had time to think everything over while the fairy gave her agreeable dreams; he arrived flustered and without ready words. A long wait leaves time to expect too much.

Then the waiting turns sticky. For two years the prince goes "hunting", tells his father a story about a night in a charcoal-burner's cottage, and never dares confess to his mother. He brings himself to announce the marriage only when the old king dies. The decision waits for a push from outside, and that is the brake built into this entry: years lived in "later", and a deadline nobody has set.

report.h3: A light in which whispers go unheard

report: The middle of the tail is a road through light. The secret marriage comes out into the day: the king announces it, and his wife enters the capital in full view, riding between her two children. This couple's Sun is in neither partner's personal tail: **it is born only between the two of them**, like Dawn and Day.

But by day everything is visible except what is whispered. "It was even whispered about the Court that she had Ogreish inclinations." The Sun brought the marriage into the light, but the danger stayed a rumour, and at the end "no one dared to tell" the king what was going on in his own courtyard. The season of light is the best time to say aloud what the family usually whispers. There is a second trap too: the brightest season looks like the ending, and that is exactly where the popular retellings stop.

report.h3: A kingdom left to a regent

report: The main task is The Chariot. The king goes off for a whole summer of war with the Emperor Cantalabutte, and the tale never says what the war is for. He leaves the kingdom and his family to his mother, whose inclinations were only whispered about at court. There is no malice in it: the reins simply go to whoever is at hand. The regent sends her daughter-in-law and the children back into the woods, and the young queen, sure that her children are dead, stretches out her own neck: "Do it; do it." In the last scene the queen and her children are brought into the courtyard "with their hands tied behind them". **Without the Chariot's task solved, the couple returns to its entry:** waiting again, sacrificing again, waiting for a rescuer. The rescuer comes, "not so soon expected", on horseback, "for he came post", but he arrives at the very edge of the tub of snakes.

In life the regent is usually not a mother-in-law. It is work that runs the house on its own timetable, tiredness, habit, relatives. One partner sets off on a summer campaign of their own, a project, a business trip or a career leap, and tosses over a shoulder "keep an eye on things". The other stays and does not feel entitled to decide. In the tale he rides and she waits, but in a couple with this tail the roles do not depend on sex: either of the two may ride and either may wait, and more often they take turns.

report.h3: The moral is not to wait

report: Perrault's own moral speaks only of the first half: delayed bonds of marriage are often no less happy, and one loses nothing by waiting. Of the ogress, not a word. **The moral of tail 12-19-7 is not to wait but to drive together.** This couple knows how to wait from the very entry. The Chariot has to move, and each partner may have a road of their own, but the reins of the home are handed to no one. Simple things change the script:

ul: giving the waiting a term and a reason: "we wait until spring, because…" instead of "some time later";
in the light, saying aloud what each one fears;
agreeing before the campaign who holds which reins and what gets decided without the one who is away;
the one at home governs too, rather than waiting with tied hands;
coming back sooner than expected, and making it a habit, not a last-minute miracle.

report: In the strong version the couple keeps its gift: the slow coming together and the old music only the two of them hear. It does not, however, mistake waiting for fate. It brings its light out into the day and **drives with four hands on the reins**: one on the road, the other at home, then the other way round. Then the tale ends not with a tub of snakes but with Perrault's words, which at last come true.
