seo.title: Karmic tail 12 4 19 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 4 19 compatibility: The Hanged Man, The Emperor and The Sun. Why a couple that is good at waiting and building finds open joy the hardest.

items.title: Karmic tail 12-4-19 in compatibility: the happiness a couple hides from the sun
items.short: Waite gives The Sun three divinatory meanings, and the middle one is "fortunate marriage". In a couple with the karmic tail 12-4-19, this card stands on the main task, the point that shows what the two of them find hard. How did a fortunate marriage become a task? The answer is written in the three cards. The couple enters the task through The Hanged Man: a shared pause and a mutual "not yet". It passes the middle through The Emperor: decisions, rules and a given word. And what it has to learn is The Sun: to be glad out loud, in broad daylight. Such a couple has its happiness. It keeps it hidden.

sections.h2: The bower where honeysuckle shut out the sun
paragraphs: Shakespeare wrote Much Ado About Nothing around 1598. He took the story of the slandered bride from Bandello and Ariosto, but the play's second couple, Beatrice and Benedick, he seems to have invented himself: no direct source for them has been found. And it is this second couple that became the heart of the play. Two and a half centuries later Berlioz named his opera after them: Béatrice et Bénédict.

This couple is so close to the 12-4-19 tail that a single speech of the play holds all three of its cards. Hero, Beatrice's cousin, sends her maid to lure Beatrice into the garden so that she will overhear talk about herself:

"And bid her steal into the pleached bower, / Where honeysuckles, ripen'd by the sun, / Forbid the sun to enter, like favourites, / Made proud by princes, that advance their pride / Against that power that bred it."

Hiding to hear what others say about you is The Hanged Man: life in suspension and a view of yourself from someone else's side. Favourites made proud by princes speak the language of The Emperor, of power and order. The sun that is forbidden to enter is the card of the main task. But the mechanism matters more than any of the three cards. The honeysuckle is no enemy of the sun: the sun is what ripened it. What grew in the light keeps the light out, the way a favourite turns against the power that raised him.

That is the secret of the 12-4-19 tail. This couple's pause, its irony, its order all grew out of love — out of how bright and interesting the two of them are together. And they are what bars love's way when it wants to come out into the open. Beatrice and Benedick walk this path in five acts, and they walk it in exactly the order of the cards.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: a merry war instead of a confession
paragraphs: The first thing the audience learns about these two is that they share a language. "There is a kind of merry war betwixt Signior Benedick and her: they never meet but there's a skirmish of wit between them," Beatrice's uncle Leonato warns his guests. Both swear they will never marry. Both mock lovers. Both talk so alike that they seem to be each other's reflection.

This is what The Hanged Man looks like at the entry to the task. This point of a couple's tail is what the two want together: their agreement, their common language. In a 12-4-19 couple the shared wish sounds odd: not to hurry. Not to give in first. Not to name what is between them. Lisovskaya reminds us that the point sits on the line of tasks, so the same wish can turn into resistance. Shakespeare's pair shows exactly that: the language of mockery both protects them and keeps them from each other.

The Hanged Man hangs upside down, and his world is inverted. Hero describes Beatrice in almost those terms: of any man "she would spell him backward" — a fair-faced one should have been her sister, a silent one is "a block moved with none" — "so turns she every man the wrong side out". An inverted gaze is a gift and a trap at once. It notices what others walk past. "I can see a church by daylight," Beatrice boasts of her eyesight. There is one thing such a gaze cannot see: itself.

The two are a mirror here. In the story invented for Benedick's benefit, Beatrice supposedly says of him: "I measure him by my own spirit." The fiction turned out to be the truest line in the play. The same mirror appears in the numbers: in 88.5% of couples with this tail, both partners have The Lovers, 6 and 6, on the personal point "Entry of relationships and the tail". In the "Compatibility of characters" section the site shows this as matching wishes. The two want the same thing, and two identical wishes added together make The Hanged Man — a pause.

What brings such a couple out of suspension? In Shakespeare, a plot by friends. Prince Don Pedro takes it upon himself to match the two mockers and promises: "we are the only love-gods." Benedick hides in the arbour and hears his friends pity Beatrice, who is supposedly pining for him. Beatrice hides in the honeysuckle and hears the same about him. Each learns about themselves from outside, through other people's eyes — the very reversed perspective of The Hanged Man. Describing the twelfth energy in a couple, Lisovskaya notes that such couples take a long time to enter a relationship, and that something from outside often pushes them towards marriage.

In life this is recognisable at once. Two people spend years in the status of "no idea what we are". At other people's weddings they compete in jokes about weddings. After a quarrel each waits for the other to text first — and nobody does. Friends have long been saying "but you're a couple", and both laugh. And in the end something from outside tips the decision: a move, a parent's question, someone else's wedding, a stray remark from a mutual friend.

Beatrice speaks the formula of this entry at the least fitting moment, in a church: "I confess nothing, nor I deny nothing." Neither yes nor no — a suspended answer. It holds all the strength of The Hanged Man: the pause gives two people time to study each other without haste or illusion. And all its danger: a pause can last for years.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: "Enough" — the day the jokes ran out
paragraphs: The suspension ends not in a confession but in a disaster. Midway through the play, the wedding of Hero and Claudio collapses at the altar: on a false accusation, the groom shames the bride in front of everyone. Her father curses her, the friar proposes announcing that she is dead. Beatrice and Benedick are left alone in the empty church — and for the first time they speak in earnest.

"I do love nothing in the world so well as you: is not that strange?" Benedick asks. A minute later he is ready for anything: "Come, bid me do any thing for thee." — "Kill Claudio." — "Ha! not for the wide world." Claudio is his friend and comrade in arms. Beatrice wants a deed, not words: "manhood is melted into courtesies, valour into compliment, and men are only turned into tongue."

This is where The Emperor rises in the play. Before deciding, Benedick asks a single question: "Think you in your soul the Count Claudio hath wronged Hero?" — "Yea, as sure as I have a thought or a soul." — "Enough, I am engaged; I will challenge him." Waite's divinatory list for The Emperor includes "aid, reason, conviction; also authority and will". In Tatiana Shchepkina-Kupernik's Russian translation Beatrice's answer even uses that very word, ubezhdenie — conviction. And at his next meeting with Claudio, Benedick says something his speech has never held before: "You are a villain; I jest not."

The middle of the task is how a couple travels from the wish to the main task — what it does and what it goes through. Lisovskaya gives this point no meaning of its own; this is our reading. In a 12-4-19 couple the road runs through The Emperor: from words to decisions. The jokes end and an alliance begins. For the first time the two stand together against the world — and discover that this is what they do best.

Curiously, Beatrice has already turned down a ready-made Emperor once. In the second act the prince half-jokingly offers himself as her husband: "No, my lord, unless I might have another for working-days: your grace is too costly to wear every day." She has no use for a crown. A 12-4-19 couple doesn't borrow its order either — not from parents, not from other people's models. It builds its own Emperor, and builds it precisely for working days: the household, money, schedules, who is responsible for what.

From outside, the middle of such a couple looks solid. A joint account and a joint plan. Rules agreed once and for all: no quarrels in front of guests, big things decided together, no calling each other at work. In a crisis these two are magnificent: touch one, and the other is already at their side. Love here speaks in deeds — a fixed tap, a pickup at the airport at three in the morning, a debt paid off on time.

Reliability has a reverse side. Benedick proves his love by going off to fight his friend. A couple in the middle of the task risks proving its love the same way — by execution: doing instead of saying. Rules invented in a hard hour stay on after the hour has passed and start to get in the way. Decisions are made for both, and feelings go unspoken: "it goes without saying". Among the tasks of a couple with The Emperor, Lisovskaya names both rules that later get in the way and learning to talk about feelings. The second of these tasks will come back — in the main one.

In the Messina of Shakespeare's day a challenge to a duel is "a man's office", as Beatrice herself says. In a 12-4-19 couple the roles are not split by gender: either partner can take on The Emperor, or the two can take turns. And in the play the duel never happens. The truth is uncovered not by the clever people but by the night watch, led by the pompous constable Dogberry. The captured villain Borachio confesses to the prince: "what your wisdoms could not discover, these shallow fools have brought to light." The order the two relied on cannot reach the truth by itself. Light arrives from the side nobody was watching.

sections.h2: Main task: "by this light"
paragraphs: The main task is the point a couple's tail is read for. Lisovskaya reads it mostly through the minus: what the two find hard and what they need to learn. In a 12-4-19 couple The Sun stands here, and that is the strangest thing about this tail. Waite's divinatory list for The Sun reads: "Material happiness, fortunate marriage, contentment." The card of a fortunate marriage turned out to be a task. What this couple needs to learn is not steadfastness or loyalty — the entry and the middle teach those. What it needs to learn is happiness.

The last scene of the play shows how hard that is. The truth is out, Hero is alive, everyone is gathered, the wedding is set. That morning the prince notices that Benedick's face has not a ray in it: "Why, what's the matter, / That you have such a February face, / So full of frost, of storm and cloudiness?" Benedick asks the friar to marry him, and when the ladies unmask he asks Beatrice in front of everyone: "Do not you love me?" — "Why, no; no more than reason." She asks him — and hears the same. The phrase is exact: "no more than reason". Love is capped by reason once again, a word from The Emperor's list. Having come all the way through the middle, the two hide once more behind their familiar common language.

Their hands save them. Claudio produces "a halting sonnet of his own pure brain, fashion'd to Beatrice", and Hero a poem by Beatrice to Benedick, "stolen from her pocket". Each had secretly written to the other and never handed it over. "A miracle! here's our own hands against our hearts," says Benedick. **This couple's sun rose long ago. They were simply keeping it in a pocket.**

Even now the "yes" does not come out straight. "Come, I will have thee; but, by this light, I take thee for pity." — "I would not deny you; but, by this good day, I yield upon great persuasion; and partly to save your life." Both swear by the daylight — and at once hide under a joke the very thing they swear to. Benedick ends it the only way open to him: "Peace! I will stop your mouth" — and kisses her.

This is what the main task looks like in the minus. Not coldness and not disaster, but an inability to say something good without armour. Such a couple "doesn't do anniversaries, that's not us". One partner learns of the other's success from mutual acquaintances and answers with a quip. "I'm happy with him" or "I'm happy with her" is heard by friends, by parents, by anyone — except the partner. At their own celebration the two keep glancing at the clock. One protects the other so carefully that neither worry nor joy can get through. Among the tasks of a couple with The Sun, Lisovskaya names an inability to talk about problems, holding feelings back, and taking credit for the partner's victories.

When Lisovskaya analyses a couple's tail, she notes in brackets which energies each conclusion comes from. Walk 12-4-19 her way and two forks appear. Inflated expectations are a task she lists for both The Hanged Man and The Sun (12 + 19). Shakespeare gave them a voice in Benedick's soliloquy: "Rich she shall be, that's certain; wise, or I'll none; virtuous, or I'll never cheapen her; fair, or I'll never look on her; mild, or come not near me; noble, or not I for an angel; of good discourse, an excellent musician, and her hair shall be of what colour it please God." Demanding "everything at once" keeps the pause going longer than any fear. Talking about feelings is a task she sets for both The Emperor and The Sun (4 + 19). That is why the heart of this tail is not a deed but a sentence.

The play's finale also shows The Sun's strong side. "Since I do purpose to marry, I will think nothing to any purpose that the world can say against it," Benedick declares — the very man who feared mockery more than anything. "A college of wit-crackers cannot flout me out of my humour." And then he does what The Sun in action is: "let's have a dance ere we are married, that we may lighten our own hearts and our wives' heels." The master of the house objects like an Emperor: "We'll have dancing afterward." — "First, of my word; therefore play, music." Joy here doesn't wait for order to be put in place. Benedick even postpones the punishment of the captured villain: "Think not on him till to-morrow." And among the last lines is the sad prince, to whom Benedick calls: "Prince, thou art sad; get thee a wife, get thee a wife." The Emperor stands aside; the couple dances.

sections.h2: What Waite drew: a nimbus, three faces and two children by a wall
paragraphs: The pictures of Waite's deck add a few more clues to the story. The Hanged Man hangs upside down, and around his head, as Waite himself writes, there is a nimbus: "There is a nimbus about the head of the seeming martyr." The light is there already at the entry to the task. Only it is right at the head, and turned upside down along with it. Our reading: the sun of the main task doesn't come to the couple from outside. It is the same light that was there from the start, only set upright.

Benebell Wen notices faces on the three cards of the tail. The Hanged Man's face is "calm and serene". The landscape behind The Emperor speaks of a "stern, severe nature". And the sun itself on The Sun card, she writes, has a face "somehow both stern and serene". The face of the main task is assembled from the faces of the entry and the middle. The couple doesn't have to give up The Emperor's sternness or The Hanged Man's calm. It has to carry both out into the light.

The most unexpected clue is in Waite himself, in his description of the older decks. There, beneath the sun, stands a wall "suggesting an enclosure—as it might be, a walled garden", and in it two children "gambolling, or running hand in hand". The Sun of the old cards is a couple. Waite replaced the two with a single child on a white horse. For a couple's tail the old version is closer: two figures by a garden wall holding hands — like Beatrice and Benedick stepping out of the bower straight into the dance.

And the centre. Every couple with the 12-4-19 tail has Strength, 11, in the centre, in "The atmosphere inside the couple" — in Waite's deck it is numbered VIII. The woman on this card "is closing the jaws of a lion", and Waite connects Strength itself with "the Divine Mystery of Union". Coming out of the bower, Beatrice promises: "Taming my wild heart to thy loving hand." The last thing Benedick does with her in the play is "Peace! I will stop your mouth" and a kiss. **This couple's strength is a gentleness that tames not each other but their own mockery.**

sections.h2: Clues in the numbers: a light neither of the two carries
paragraphs: A personal chart never has 12-4-19, and the reason is beautiful. For a person with The Sun on the karmic task, the calculation always puts Strength in the centre and The Empress at the entry of the tail: their tail can only be 3-22-19. A 12-4-19 couple has the same Sun on the main task and the same Strength in the centre — in 100% of such couples. But its entry is The Hanged Man and its middle The Emperor, because every point of a couple is the sum of two people's points, not a recalculation. Recalculated by the personal formula, 19 + 11 = 30 → 3, the couple's entry would be The Empress. Our reading: one person reaches the same Sun through abundance and a leap into the unknown, while two reach it through a pause and order.

A couple's main task is the sum of the two personal karmic tasks. In 88.5% of such couples these are Strength and Justice, 11 + 8; in 11.5%, The Wheel of Fortune and The Hermit, 10 + 9. Neither partner has The Sun on their personal karmic task. Running every date since 1900 through the site's engine shows more: in 52% of these couples The Sun appears on none of the fifteen main points of the two personal charts — the points the site uses to compare characters. In 41.3% one partner has it, in 6.7% both do. **Neither of the two brings the light of the main task. It appears only between them.**

Strength and Justice are the very two cards Waite swapped: in his deck Strength is eighth and Justice eleventh. Under either numbering they add up to The Sun. Our reading: one partner's rightness and the other's gentle strength, added together, become light — as long as neither tries to win. Which partner carries which is decided by the birth dates, not by gender or character.

The middle is assembled the same way: in these couples The Emperor's four always comes from 31. In 88.5% that is Temperance and The Star, 14 + 17; in 11.5%, Death and The Moon, 13 + 18. One partner's measure and the other's hope, added together, make order — also our reading.

"The couple's values", the spiritual purpose, is The Lovers in 90.5% of couples with this tail and The Devil in 9.5%. The Lovers is a choice made openly, and that is exactly how the play ends: two people choosing each other in front of everyone. For The Devil, the card of bonds, Shakespeare has a line too. "To bind me, or undo me; one of them," Benedick tells the friar before the wedding.

sections.h2: How the 12-4-19 tail is calculated: an example for 05.11.1975 and 02.01.1976
paragraphs: Every point of a couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices; if the sum is greater than 22, its digits are added together. Take two dates: 05.11.1975 and 02.01.1976. The first partner's personal tail is 6-17-11, the second's is 6-14-8.

The couple's middle is not recalculated from its ends. Here the sum of the ends would give the same four, 12 + 19 = 31 → 4, but the middle is counted differently — from the personal middles, 17 + 14. "The couple's values" are not added up from the personal ones either: they are recalculated from the couple's sums and in this example give 6, The Lovers.

After the tail, Lisovskaya advises checking whether the same energies appear at other points. In this example they do. "What to create together" is 12, 11 + 1: The Hanged Man stands there too. "What can spoil it" is 12 again, 6 + 6. And "What fills the union" is 19, 16 + 3: the sun this couple finds hard to let in is the very thing that fills it. This belongs to the example, not to every such couple. The Sun stands on "What fills the union" in 2.9% of couples with the 12-4-19 tail, The Hanged Man on "What to create together" in 10%, and on "What can spoil it" in 8.9%.

sections.h2: If a couple recognises itself
paragraphs: A couple's tail is neither a verdict nor a forecast. It shows where the two habitually close the door on the sun. Shakespeare left a few hints for this case.

ul: **Hand over the sonnet in person.** Beatrice's and Benedick's poems to each other were produced by friends, one of them stolen from a pocket. A 12-4-19 couple does well not to wait for its confession to be found: say it first, write it, put it in the other's hand.

**One sentence without armour.** Joking is this couple's native language, and there is no need to give it up. But at least one thing a day is worth saying straight, without irony: "I'm happy with you", "I'm proud of you".

**Dance before the wedding.** Don't postpone joy until everything is settled: the renovation finished, the debt paid off, the holidays lined up. The master of the house wanted dancing after the ceremony; the play chose before.

**Check the rules like the honeysuckle.** Every so often, inspect the order invented in a hard hour: has it shut out the very thing that grew it? A rule that stops joy can be cancelled by both partners together.
**Don't wait for conspirators.** A push from outside works, but a couple that has been waiting years for one can more easily push itself: say out loud what the two of them are to each other.
**Celebrate a partner's win as a shared one.** A partner's success is a reason to dance, not to quip. And not a reason to quietly take the credit.
**Tell a pause from a hiding place.** A pause is for seeing each other properly. A hiding place is for not being seen. The Hanged Man gives the first and takes away the second.

sections.h2: Two fictions that made a truth
paragraphs: Commenting on the play, the Russian Shakespeare scholar A. Smirnov named its main device precisely: "Minus times minus gives plus in algebra; two fictions multiplied together give truth in reality" (our translation). Beatrice and Benedick were lied to — each was told that the other was in love — and a lie multiplied by a lie turned out to be the truth. A couple's tail is read through the minus too. But in 12-4-19 the two partners' minuses, added together, give light: this couple's Sun is assembled from what each of them, separately, had as something else entirely. It is already there. All that is left is to stop keeping it in a pocket.

ul: **12, The Hanged Man — entry to the task.** The shared wish the couple starts from: no hurry, no surrendering first, looking at love upside down. In the reading, The Hanged Man appears twice for such a couple — also as the "Common language", because it is the same point.
**4, The Emperor — middle of the task.** How the two travel the road: from a quip to a decision, from words to a deed. The order that protects the union — and the same order that can dry it out.
**19, The Sun — main task.** Learning something simple: speaking about feelings without irony, celebrating, and not keeping in a pocket what was written long ago.

intro: The triple 12-4-19 exists only in a couple's matrix; a personal chart never has it. Lisovskaya calls a couple's tail its karmic program, so the "12 4 19 program" in the destiny matrix is this same tail. It occurs in roughly one couple in 8,416, or 0.012%: 96th of the 97 possible couple tails. Only 18-21-3 is rarer.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 12-4-19 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail in which the entry to the task is The Hanged Man, the middle is The Emperor and the main task is The Sun. The two enter the relationship through a pause and a mutual "not yet", travel the road through decisions and rules, and what they have to learn is open joy: speaking about feelings directly and not hiding the happiness that is already there.

faq.q: Can 12-4-19 appear in a personal destiny matrix?
faq.a: No. A person with The Sun on the karmic task always has Strength in the centre and The Empress at the entry of the tail, so their tail can only be 3-22-19. The triple 12-4-19 appears only in a couple's matrix, where every point is the sum of two people's points.

faq.q: What is the 12 4 19 program in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: The same thing as the couple's karmic tail 12-4-19. Lisovskaya calls a couple's tail its karmic program: tasks that show mostly in the minus, though they can appear in the plus as well. This triple has no separate "program" of its own.

faq.q: Is the 12-4-19 tail a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A tail shows tasks, not fate, and predicts nothing. The difficulty of 12-4-19 is an unusual one: what the couple lacks is not feelings but the ability to show them. The strength of these two is reliability and solidarity in hard times; the task is to allow themselves joy in broad daylight.

faq.q: Why is the middle of the tail 4 if the partners have 17 and 14 there?
faq.a: Because a couple's points are added together: 17 + 14 = 31, and 31 folds into 3 + 1 = 4. The couple's middle is taken from the two people's personal middles, not recalculated from the ends of the couple's tail.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers?
faq.a: No. The first number of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, so 4 and 19 cannot stand at the entry, and a search of all dates finds 12-19-4 in no couple at all. These three numbers form only 12-4-19.

items.title: The 12-7-13 karmic tail in couple compatibility: Koschei on twelve chains
items.short: The Hanged Man, The Chariot, Death. In the deck, cards twelve and thirteen lie side by side, yet in this couple's tail The Chariot has driven in between them. No personal destiny matrix contains this triple: it takes two people to make it. The 12-7-13 karmic tail in compatibility is not about a love that will end. It is about something old that never ended because nobody finished it. It was hung up instead.

sections.h2: The tale with twelve chains
paragraphs: "Marya Morevna" is number 159 in Alexander Afanasyev's "Narodnye russkie skazki" (Russian Folk Tales); the quotations below follow W. R. S. Ralston's English translation of 1873, which spells the villain Koshchei. The tale opens with a death. Prince Ivan's parents, as they lie dying, tell their son about his three sisters: "Give your sisters in marriage to the very first suitors who come to woo them. Don't go keeping them by you!" Ivan obeys. A falcon, an eagle and a raven fly in to woo the sisters, and each time the prince answers in the same spirit: "I will not interfere with her liberty of choice." He knows how to let go.

Left alone, he rides out to look for his sisters and finds a plain covered with a slain army. One woman has slain it all: Marya Morevna. Her first words to Ivan are a question: "whither does God send you? and is it of your free will or against your will?" — "Not against their will do brave youths ride!" — "Well, if your business be not pressing, tarry awhile in my tent." Two nights in the tent, and a wedding.

Then the princess goes off to war. She leaves her husband all the housekeeping and a single prohibition: "Go about everywhere, keep watch over everything, only do not venture to look into that closet there." The next sentence in the tale is five words long: "He couldn't help doing so." In the closet "there hung Koshchei the Deathless, fettered by twelve chains". Koschei begs: "Have pity upon me and give me to drink! Ten years long have I been here in torment." Ivan hands him a bucket, a second, a third. After the third Koschei "regained his former strength, gave his chains a shake, and broke all twelve at once" — and carries Marya Morevna off in a whirlwind.

The middle of the tale is a chase. Three times Ivan finds his wife and three times he takes her away. "Remember not the past; much better fly with me while Koshchei the Deathless is out of sight. Perhaps he won't catch us." When Koschei's horse learns of the escape, it answers its master without any hurry: "It is possible to sow wheat, to wait till it grows up, to reap it and thresh it, to grind it to flour, to make five pies of it, to eat those pies, and then to start in pursuit — and even then to be in time." The second time Ivan no longer hopes to get away: "Suppose he does catch us. At all events we shall have spent an hour or two together." The third time: "Let him hew away! I cannot live without you." Koschei chops him into little pieces, puts them in a barrel, smears it with pitch, binds it with iron hoops and flings it into the blue sea.

The brothers-in-law learn of the disaster from the silver Ivan left them as keepsakes: it has turned black. The Eagle drags the barrel ashore, the Falcon flies for the Water of Life, the Raven for the Water of Death. "The Raven sprinkled them with the Water of Death — the pieces joined together, the body became whole. The Falcon sprinkled it with the Water of Life — Prince Ivan shuddered, stood up, and said: 'Ah! what a time I've been sleeping!'"

And now, for the first time, Ivan asks something other than how to escape. He asks his wife to "find out from Koshchei the Deathless whence he got so good a steed". The answer lies beyond the fiery river, with Baba Yaga: Koschei herded her mares for three days and was given a foal for it. Ivan goes to the same place. The mares scatter, he weeps and falls asleep on a stone, and the herd is driven home for him by a bird, a lioness and a bee whose young and whose honey he spared on the way. From the stable he takes "a sorry colt rolling in the muck" and fattens it in the green meadows until "it turned into a wondrous steed".

The last time, Koschei's horse answers differently: "God knows! Prince Ivan has a horse now which is better than I." Koschei says, "Well, I can't stand it," and gives chase. Ivan's horse strikes him with its hoof, and the prince burns Koschei on a pyre and scatters his ashes to the wind. The ending: "Then Marya Morevna mounted Koshchei's horse and Prince Ivan got on his own."

The numbers do not say which partner in a real couple is Ivan and which is Marya Morevna. The tale itself swaps the usual roles: she rides off to war, he keeps the house. In a couple with this tail both roles usually fall to both people in turn: each of them has a closet, and each has at least once given water to someone else's Koschei.

sections.h2: 12 · Entry to the task: the pact of the locked closet
paragraphs: The entry to the task, point M, is what the couple wants together: its shared language and its agreements. With this wish the two enter the task, and the same wish later pushes back. This couple's entry is The Hanged Man: the wish to stop time.

That is exactly how the tale begins. Not "let us marry", but "if your business be not pressing, tarry awhile". A union with the 12-7-13 tail often forms as a breathing space: two people meet at a breaking point, after their own war or someone else's, and the first thing they give each other is a pause. Nobody hurries here, nobody asks too much, everybody is gentle. For two tired people that is a great deal.

Such a pause has a mechanism: a place nobody looks into. For one couple it is a previous marriage about which "everything has been said". For another it is a parent's voice that still decides for both of them when to buy a flat. For a third it is an abandoned career, a debt, a grudge, a promise made to someone before they met. She does not ask why he rings his mother back every evening at nine. He does not ask why the box with her old life has travelled unopened through three house moves. Peace at home rests on Marya Morevna's rule: go everywhere, only do not look in here.

The catch is that what hangs does not die. Koschei hangs for ten years without food or drink, and he is alive. He is Deathless not because he is stronger than death but because he was hung up rather than killed. Everything the couple has put off "for later" is kept whole in the closet, with all its former strength. Twelve turns up in the tale once more: around Baba Yaga's house stand twelve poles, eleven of them with heads, "the twelfth alone remained unoccupied". Both times it is the number of what hangs and waits for its hour.

The resistance of this point sounds like pity. "Have pity upon me and give me to drink" is a request nobody refuses the first time. One bucket is mercy. The second is habit. After the third the old thing "regained his former strength", and the chains break all at once, all twelve. In a couple's life the third bucket looks innocent: bailing out an ex one more time, one last loan to a brother, one more long talk with the person who used to decide for both of them. Among the difficulties of The Hanged Man in a couple, Lisovskaya names pressure on pity and the inability to say no. The tale shows the same thing without any moral: the old does not need freedom, it needs water.

One more detail. The closet opens not by decision but by impatience: "He couldn't help doing so." The pause ends on its own, while the mistress is far away, and only one of them looks inside. What matters for this couple is not whether the door will open (it will) but whether they open it together or one of them opens it alone, in secret.

sections.h2: 7 · Middle of the task: three escapes on a borrowed horse
paragraphs: The middle of the task, point N, shows how the couple travels from the shared wish to the main task: what it does and what it goes through. Here it is The Chariot — motion, drive, a joint leap forward.

As soon as the closet is open, the couple runs. The tale gives the exact formula of escape: "Remember not the past; much better fly with me… Perhaps he won't catch us." The Russian original ends with "avos ne dogonit": avos is the untranslatable Russian "maybe it will work out somehow". Not a conversation about Koschei, but the road. In a real couple this is a move to another city "with a clean slate", a quick wedding, a new business, a long trip after which "everything will settle down". The trip really does help for about two weeks. Then the old argument catches up with the two of them in the new kitchen, word for word.

The Chariot in a couple is not foolishness. Lisovskaya writes about strong passion at the start of such unions and about how the partners rise to defend each other. The tenderest line of the tale is spoken in flight: "At all events we shall have spent an hour or two together." The two really do get those hours. But an escape on an ordinary horse is a date, not a solution. The old has the better horse, and it is in no hurry: it has time to sow wheat, reap it, thresh it, bake it and eat it, "and even then to be in time".

The three escapes end in a barrel in the sea. This is The Chariot's minus: motion that no longer checks itself against the goal, and strength drawn from the people closest instead of gathered on one's own. Koschei, after all, got his strength back from water out of Ivan's hands.

The turning point of the middle is a single question. Once revived, Ivan stops asking how to escape and asks to learn "whence he got so good a steed". It is Marya Morevna who finds out: she "chose a favorable moment" and questioned the one she knows best of all. For a couple this is the shift from running to investigating: what gives the old script its strength, where it gets that strength, who keeps feeding it. The tale's answer is unexpectedly ordinary. Koschei earned his horse: he herded the mares for three days and did not lose one. The old had no magic, only years of service.

Benebell Wen writes that The Chariot can mean a journey "not for the sake of travel, but for the sake of acquisition". The trip to Baba Yaga is exactly that: Ivan goes not to hide but to earn a horse of his own. The prize looks pitiful: "a sorry colt rolling in the muck". It becomes a wondrous steed only after it has been fattened in the meadows. A couple's own strength begins just as unimpressively: the first honest agreement, the first budget without help from the parents, the first trip that nobody needs to escape from. It has to be raised.

sections.h2: 13 · Main task: letting the Deathless die
paragraphs: The main task, point D, is what the couple has to learn and what does not come easily; it is read above all through the difficulty. Here it is Death. And the enemy in the tale is named as its exact opposite: Koschei the Deathless.

The task of the 12-7-13 tail is not to lose something. It is to let something end that cannot end by itself, because it is hanging. In the deck 12 and 13 are neighbours, and the difference between them is the difference between "postpone" and "complete". As long as the old thing hangs, it is deathless.

Death has two faces in this tale, and that is its most important detail. W. R. S. Ralston, who translated the tale into English in 1873, noticed that a magic water which brings the dead back to life appears in the folklore of all lands, but in the Slavonic stories there are "the two waters, each performing one part only" of the work. The Water of Death does not kill: under it "the pieces joined together, the body became whole". The Water of Life wakes. First the water that belongs to death gathers what was cut apart into a whole, and only then does life return.

For the couple this is the main task read in its plus: an ending that gathers. After three escapes the two are left with pieces — things unsaid, grudges, two different versions of one story. The Water of Death is the last conversation after which no further one is needed. Signed papers. An unpacked box. A flat that has finally been sold. Parents who have heard a calm "we have decided for ourselves". This is not drama but assembly. Afterwards a couple will often say Ivan's line: "Ah! what a time I've been sleeping!"

The tale itself opens with death: with the dying parents' instruction, "Don't go keeping them by you!" Among the tasks of Death in a couple, Lisovskaya names helping each other to separate from parents, moves and partings, and the ability to see one's own mistakes and not only the other person's. In the tale all this fits into a single exchange. Marya Morevna: "why did you disobey me…?" Ivan: "Remember not the past." Each looks at the other's part: she at his curiosity, he right past her closet. Yet the closet was shared: it took both her locked door and his pity.

The minus of this point is a Death that one partner imposes on the other. One demands that the other "finally change". In the present partner one looks for the features of a former one. There are so many changes that the other has nothing left to stand on. The plus is a Death that the two go through together. Lisovskaya describes such couples as living proof that life goes on after something hard, and as a union in which each accepts the partner's past and moves on.

The tale shows this plus in its last line. Koschei is burnt, his ashes scattered; nobody can hang him up again. And then "Marya Morevna mounted Koshchei's horse and Prince Ivan got on his own". The past is not erased: its strength has become her horse. Beside her rides the second rider, on a horse he raised himself. Two horses side by side are The Chariot in its plus: riding together, each on a road of their own.

sections.h2: Waite: the rider who is in no hurry
paragraphs: In Arthur Edward Waite's "The Pictorial Key to the Tarot" these three cards are linked more closely than their numbers suggest.

Waite ends his account of The Hanged Man with Death: whoever understands this symbol "will know that after the sacred Mystery of Death there is a glorious Mystery of Resurrection". And he begins his account of Death with The Hanged Man: the suggestion of death he made at the previous card is to be understood mystically, "but this is not the case in the present instance". The two cards that the tail places at opposite ends talk to each other across a page in Waite. The Hanged Man himself, for Waite, "suggests life in suspension, but life and not death". A ready portrait of Koschei in the closet.

Waite's rider of Death "moves slowly" and "carries no visible weapon", yet "king and child and maiden fall before him". A slow, unarmed rider whom nobody outruns: this is Koschei's horse, which has time for both the wheat and the bread. The Chariot is faster, but Death does not win by speed.

The most unexpected link belongs to The Chariot. Waite recalls that Court de Gébelin saw in it "Osiris Triumphing, the conquering sun in spring-time having vanquished the obstacles of winter", and objects: "Osiris rising from the dead is not represented by such obvious symbolism." Plutarch tells the myth of Osiris ("On Isis and Osiris", chapters 13 and 18, in Babbitt's translation). Typhon shuts his brother in a chest, which the conspirators "fastened by nails from the outside and also by using molten lead", and sends it down the river to the sea. Later he "divided it into fourteen parts", and Isis searches for them, "sailing through the swamps in a boat of papyrus". Ivan has his pitch-smeared barrel, the iron hoops, the blue sea and the pieces gathered by his brothers-in-law. Waite was arguing with a reading of the picture, not with the myth. But the argument itself says a lot: The Chariot was once read as the triumph of someone who had been shut in, thrown into the water, cut apart and put together again. In the 12-7-13 tail The Chariot's true triumph is exactly that: it comes after the Water of Death, not instead of it.

One more of Waite's remarks about Death is useful to a couple. Besides natural death he describes another: entrance "while still in this life" into a state that is "a change in the form of consciousness". This is the death the tail is about: what changes is the form of the union, not the people in it.

sections.h2: Wen: three cards of one water
paragraphs: In "Holistic Tarot" Benebell Wen assigns each card to an element. About The Hanged Man, The Chariot and Death she says the same thing: "The element of Water governs this card." In all three, according to Wen, yin energy is dominant. The 12-7-13 tail is made of water alone.

The tale flows with water too. Ralston explains the name Morevna as "daughter of More, (the Sea or any great water)". Koschei asks for a drink. The barrel with Ivan is flung into the blue sea. Baba Yaga's mares hide in the sea and stand "up to their necks in water". Ivan is raised by the Water of Death and the Water of Life. Fire appears in the tale twice: the fiery river that needs a bridge, and the pyre on which Koschei burns. In this story water preserves and restores strength, including to what ought to end. The old ends only in fire. This is our own reading, but it captures the mechanics of the tail exactly: for a couple made entirely of water, the question is not whether to pour water but which water, and for whom.

Wen also has words about water for each card separately. The Chariot upright is water that "flows quickly forward, with great force"; reversed, it is dammed up. Death asks the Seeker to "be fluid like water" and to "let go of the present and move on". To The Hanged Man Wen gives the pun "hang in there" and a question it shares with The Fool: "will the Seeker fall or fly?" Ivan with his three buckets falls. On his own horse he flies: "it flies just like a bird," he tells his wife.

One more of Wen's readings of Death fits the tale literally: it is the card of revolutions, "the waning of power of one authority and the growing, ascending power of a new". For ten years Koschei ruled the house from the closet. The tail asks the couple to change who rules: not the old order, but the two of them.

sections.h2: Clues in the numbers: a tail that only two can make
paragraphs: **No single person can have it.** In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre of the chart. With a main task of 13, an entry of 12 is impossible with any centre. So 12-7-13 exists only as the sum of two people.
**It is rare.** The tail occurs in about one couple in 3,647 (0.027%) and ranks 93rd of the 97 couple tails.

**It is always built from the same two personal tails.** In every such couple one partner has the personal tail 9-12-3 and the other has 3-13-10. This leads to the main discovery. The twelve at the couple's entry is the middle of the first partner's personal tail. The thirteen in the main task is the middle of the second partner's. The seven in the middle is the sum of the two personal middles: 12 + 13 = 25 → 7. The couple's tail is built entirely from two personal middles. Each partner brings into the union what stands halfway along their own road: one brings what hangs, the other brings what demands an ending. The Chariot appears in neither personal tail: only the couple brings it into the tail.

**The personal tails hook together on The Empress.** The tail 9-12-3 ends with a three, the tail 3-13-10 begins with one, and together they form a single chain, 9-12-3-13-10. In that chain The Empress — home and abundance — stands between The Hanged Man and Death. In the couple's tail her place is taken by The Chariot. Our reading: between the pause and the ending the couple gets not a home but a road, and the home comes after the road. That is how the tale goes. Ralston's version stops at "they went off to their own realm"; Afanasyev's Russian adds the formula "zhit'-pozhivat', dobra nazhivat' da medok popivat'" — they lived on, gathering goods and sipping honey (our translation). The honey, incidentally, comes from the very bee whose hive Ivan left alone.

**The atmosphere inside the couple is always Justice.** This follows from the same two tails. With the tail 3-13-10 the personal centre is always 20, Judgement; with 9-12-3 it is always 6, The Lovers. 6 + 20 = 26 → 8. The tale in which this tail lives is a world of exact accounts. Even Koschei keeps count: "this time I will forgive you, in return for your kindness in giving me water to drink. And a second time I will forgive you; but the third time beware!" The bird, the lioness and the bee return exactly what they received. Justice at the centre of the couple, in its plus, is a fair division of tasks: she rides off to war, he keeps the house, and nobody finds it strange. In its minus it is a ledger of grievances, "I gave you three buckets", promises not kept, like the broken "do not look". Among the tasks of Justice in a couple Lisovskaya lists forgiveness. The tale is a reminder that forgiveness with a counter is not yet forgiveness.

**The couple's values are always The Lovers.** The two came here for a choice. In the tale the key question is asked twice: at the beginning and at the threshold of death. Marya Morevna: "is it of your free will or against your will?" Baba Yaga by her poles: "Is it of your own accord, or on compulsion?" Both times Ivan answers in terms of will, not compulsion: "Not against their will do brave youths ride!" and "I have come to earn from you a heroic steed." He gave his sisters away in the same spirit: "I will not interfere with her liberty of choice." The value of this couple is a union without compulsion, including compulsion by one's own past.

sections.h2: How to calculate the 12-7-13 tail: example 19.03.1979 and 04.01.1976
paragraphs: A couple's matrix is calculated point by point: each point of the couple is the sum of the same points in the two personal matrices, reduced to 22.

First partner, 19.03.1979. Day 19, month 3, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 9 = 26 → 8. Main task 19 + 3 + 8 = 30 → 3, centre 19 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 33 → 6. Entry of the tail 3 + 6 = 9, middle 3 + 9 = 12. Personal tail 9-12-3.
Second partner, 04.01.1976. Day 4, month 1, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5. Main task 4 + 1 + 5 = 10, centre 4 + 1 + 5 + 10 = 20. Entry 10 + 20 = 30 → 3, middle 10 + 3 = 13. Personal tail 3-13-10.

paragraphs.h3: The couple's tail

paragraphs: The couple's centre is 6 + 20 = 26 → 8, Justice. The couple's values for these dates are 6, The Lovers, as in every couple with this tail.

The middle of a couple's tail is not recalculated from its two ends; it is added up from the two personal middles. For 12-7-13 both methods give the same seven: 12 + 13 is both the sum of the ends and the sum of the two personal middles. In shape the tail is built like a personal one, yet no person has it. No other couple tail is made of the numbers 12, 7 and 13.

sections.h2: How a couple goes through the 12-7-13 tail
paragraphs: The tail does not predict events and passes no sentence. It shows where the couple gets stuck and what changes the plot.

ul: **Open the closet together, in daylight.** Do not wait until one of them "couldn't help doing so" while the other is away. Say out loud what is hanging: "this is something we have not settled".
**Give one bucket, not three.** Pity for the past is normal. Pity without a limit gives it back its strength. Help once and say where the help ends.
**Stop running on an ordinary horse.** A move, a wedding, a new project are good in themselves, but they do not replace the conversation about Koschei.
**Ask the old about its strength.** Where did the script get such a horse: who feeds it, what makes it convenient, what holds it up.

**Raise a horse of your own.** One's own strength starts as a sorry colt: small agreements that are kept. Help comes from those the couple did not wrong along the way — people who were treated fairly.
**Give the ending its Water of Death.** Do not tear things off; gather them: the last conversation, the papers, the unpacked boxes. An ending that needs no going back.
**Do not hang it up again.** Burning it and scattering the ashes to the wind means, in real life, not keeping the old "just in case".
**Ride on two horses.** Each has their own road and their own strength, and they ride side by side.

paragraphs: If the old shows itself in a couple as threats or violence, this is no longer a matter for self-reflection: it calls for professional help, and in danger, a local emergency number.

ul: **12, The Hanged Man — entry to the task.** The couple's shared language is pause and pity: "not now", "let it hang for a while", "let's not go there". There is a great deal of tenderness in it. And behind it there is always a door that both of them walk around.

**7, The Chariot — middle of the task.** The two live the task in motion: moves, sudden leaps, new plans, "let's go, maybe it won't catch us". The couple has speed. It does not yet have a horse of its own.
**13, Death — main task.** Not a break-up but the end of an old form: to finish what stayed alive only because nobody touched it.

intro: A Russian fairy tale wrote this plot down almost to the number. In the forbidden closet of Marya Morevna, the fair princess, "there hung Koshchei the Deathless, fettered by twelve chains". The tale knows nothing of tarot or of the destiny matrix, and the twelve chains are a coincidence. But its three acts run in the same order as the cards of the tail: the hanging one, the chase, the death of the Deathless.

faq.q: Does the 12-7-13 tail mean the couple will break up?
faq.a: No. Death in the couple's main task is the end of an old form, not of the union. In the tale it is Koschei who dies, while Ivan and Marya Morevna ride away together, each on their own horse. The numbers do not predict events.

faq.q: Why does the 12-7-13 tail never appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre of the chart. With a main task of 13, an entry of 12 is impossible with any centre, so this triple occurs only in a couple.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. The numbers 12, 7 and 13 form only the 12-7-13 tail, and it occurs in about one couple in 3,647.

faq.q: A couple has the 12-7-13 tail, but the partners' personal tails are different. Is that possible?
faq.a: No. In every couple with this tail the partners' personal tails are 9-12-3 and 3-13-10. If the calculation shows others, the birth dates are worth checking again.

report: Koschei the Deathless is deathless not because he is stronger than death. He was simply hung up instead of killed. The Water of Death is the last conversation after which no further one is needed; signed papers; an unpacked box; parents who have heard a calm "we have decided for ourselves". The minus of the same point is a Death that one partner imposes: one demands that the other "finally change", or looks in the present partner for the features of a former one.

In the tale both mistakes fit into a single exchange. Marya Morevna reproaches him for disobeying her. Ivan answers: "Remember not the past." Each looks at the other's part. Yet the closet was shared: it took both her locked door and his pity.

report.h3: Two horses side by side

report: Arthur Edward Waite's rider of Death "moves slowly" and "carries no visible weapon". Nobody outruns him. In the tale Koschei dies from the hoof of Ivan's horse, burns on a pyre, and his ashes are scattered to the wind: nobody can hang him up again. **The old ends only when it is brought to an end, not when it is hidden.**

The last line of the tale is the strong version of this tail: "Then Marya Morevna mounted Koshchei's horse and Prince Ivan got on his own." The past is not erased: its strength has become her horse. Beside her rides the second rider, on a horse he raised himself. Two horses side by side are The Chariot in its plus: riding together, each on a road of their own.
If the old shows itself in a couple as threats or violence, this is no longer a matter for self-reflection: it calls for professional help, and in danger, a local emergency number or crisis line.

unit.title: Koschei in the locked closet

captions.M: Pity each other and keep the closet shut
captions.N: Run from the old: maybe it won't catch up
captions.D: Bring the old to an end, not hang it up again

unit.meaning: Your task is not to lock the old in a closet or run from it, but to bring it to an end and ride on side by side.

seo.title: Karmic tail 12 7 22 compatibility: Hanged Man, Chariot, Fool
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 7 22 compatibility: why a couple lives in “not now” for years, who holds the reins, and how The Fool asks them to use the door, not the window.

items.title: Karmic tail 12-7-22 in compatibility: the long “not now” and the leap from the window
items.short: The couple's tail 12-7-22 sets a strange riddle: how do two people who can wait for years suddenly decide in a second — and jump the wrong way? The answer is written in three cards, and they have to be read in order. The entry to the task is The Hanged Man: the couple's common language sounds like “not now”, and both are happy to hand their step to a third person. The middle of the task is The Chariot: movement arrives, often someone else's, and everything depends on who holds the reins. The main task is The Fool: learning a freedom that walks out through the door instead of jumping out of the window.

sections.h2: Gogol's Marriage: a tail played out in two acts
paragraphs: In 1842 Gogol published a comedy subtitled “an utterly incredible event in two acts”. He had started it in 1833 as Zhenikhi (The Suitors) and finished it abroad in 1841, so the play itself hung in suspense for eight years. The plot fits in one line: a bridegroom escapes from his own wedding through a window. But read Zhenitba (Marriage) with the cards 12-7-22 in hand and three acts show through, in the order of the tail. Quotations from the play follow E. L. Voynich's translation of 1895; where her version is abridged, the translation is ours and marked as such.

The play opens on a man lying down. Podkolyosin, a court counsellor, smokes his pipe on the sofa. The matchmaker has been calling “for the last three months”, the tailcoat is being made, the boot polish has been bought, and he sighs: “here one goes on, living and living; and one ends by getting quite disgusted with everything. There, I've let the time slip by once more.” He cannot go and see the bride: the weather is dull, “if I go out, I may get caught in the rain.” When the matchmaker describes him to the bride she does not even give his name, but her portrait is exact: “such a slow stick-in-the-mud, there's no getting him out of the house.”

Then his friend Kochkaryov bursts in and goes straight for the same matchmaker: “What the devil did you marry me for?” A minute later he is marrying off somebody else: “Now, my lad, this business mustn't be put off — put on your hat and come along.” In a single day Kochkaryov sees off the rivals, persuades the bride that the other suitors are brawlers, orders the supper, sends for the carriage and dispatches the guests straight to church.

The finale is a leap. The groom is alone in the room, the carriage is at the porch, there are people at the door. He climbs onto the window sill, says “Lord, give Thy blessing!” and drops into the street, and from offstage comes: “Oh! oh! It's a good height though! Hi, drozhki!” The last line goes to the matchmaker: “If he'd run out by the door it would have been another thing, but when the bridegroom pops out of window all I can say is — I wish you joy!”

The play is usually retold as a joke about an indecisive man. But 12-7-22 is the tail of a couple, not of a person, and Gogol, looked at closely, wrote a play about a couple too. The bride speaks the same language.

sections.h2: Entry to the task, 12 — The Hanged Man: the common language of “not now”
paragraphs: For Lisovskaya the entry to the task is what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, a “common language”. The point sits on the line of tasks, so the same wish can also work as resistance. In the tail 12-7-22 this place belongs to The Hanged Man, the card of life held in suspension. What such a couple wants together is not to get it wrong: to wait for the right moment, to be sure, not to fall. Their common language is postponement.

In Marriage both of them speak it. Podkolyosin, already in his tailcoat, tells his friend: “I think you'd better go alone.” Agafya Tikhonovna, with the suitors in the room, whispers to her aunt: “Auntie! stop here instead of me!” He sums up his bachelor life: “I have lived and lived, served, gone to the Department, dined, slept.” She weeps on her wedding day: “I lived and lived — and now I have to get married!” (our translation). For three months he keeps asking his servant whether the tailcoat is coming along and whether the polish shines. She cannot choose a suitor, draws lots — and pulls every slip out of her reticule at once: “Oh! oh! they've all come out!”

And the decisive minute is one they share. Already in her wedding dress, the bride comes into the room and thinks: “Oh! I wish he weren't in the room just this minute; I wish he'd gone out!” The wish comes true to the letter: he is no longer there. **One of them ran, but both of them wanted it** — that is the common language of this tail.

Lisovskaya describes couples with The Hanged Man as if she had read Gogol: they take a long time to enter a relationship, and to marry they need a push from outside — she puts it more bluntly, a kick. In the plus these are delicate, tactful people: they always listen, they sense each other at a distance, and often one does nothing for themselves and everything for the other. Gogol's couple has its plus as well. After their only conversation alone, about the weather, flowers and an outing, both are pleased. “What a superior person! … The best of all is that he doesn't talk small talk,” she says. “I passed the time most agreeably,” he says. At their own slow pace, these two suit each other.

The minus of The Hanged Man in a couple is a life lived for other people's eyes: what others will think and say matters more than what happens inside. For Podkolyosin this is exactly what blocks the door. Before he jumps, he reasons: “there are heaps of people at the door, and everywhere, and they'd ask me why.” In Waite's list of divinatory meanings the reversed Hanged Man includes “the crowd”. The crowd stands in the doorway, and only one exit is left.

Today the language sounds different, but it is instantly recognisable. Two people have lived together for seven years and have discussed the wedding five times: “after the renovation”, “once things settle down with Mum”, “let's do it in summer”. Nobody is against it — each is sure they are waiting for the other. In the end the question is asked not by either of them but by a sister at a family dinner: “So when is it happening?”

sections.h2: Middle of the task, 7 — The Chariot: someone else's carriage and your own cab
paragraphs: The middle of a couple's tail has no meaning of its own in the book: Lisovskaya calls it an addition to the main task. We read it as the road — what the couple does and goes through on the way from the wish at the entry to the task at the end. Here the road is The Chariot: movement, will, the journey. In Russian the word for chariot, kolesnitsa, is built on koleso, “wheel”, and the hero who is supposed to climb into it is called Podkolyosin — a name in which you hear pod kolesom, “under the wheel”. Beside him stands Kochkaryov, whose name echoes kochka, a bump in the road. The literary scholar V. Prozorov pointed out the meaning that arises when these two surnames are read together.

This couple's Chariot often comes from outside. Benebell Wen writes that the charioteer's will can be received: strong external forces “have put the momentum in the Seeker”, which is why the card, for all its outward activity, is “intrinsically yin” — receptive by nature. For The Hanged Man, who needs a push, this is good news: momentum can come from a friend, from family, from circumstances. The only question is whether borrowed momentum becomes a direction of one's own.

Kochkaryov is The Chariot in its purest form. Waite calls the charioteer “above all things triumph in the mind” and adds that “the planes of his conquest are manifest or external and not within himself”. Kochkaryov conquers everything external: the bride's consent, the aunt, the rivals, the supper, the carriage, the guests. Inside the groom he moves nothing at all. Left alone, he cannot tell where he is driving: “And what am I to him — nurse, maiden aunt, mother-in-law, sponsor? … Sometimes there's no making out what a man does a thing for!” Gogol's stage direction for this monologue says that he walks up and down “in strong motion” (in Voynich, “in great agitation”). A Chariot without a goal of its own drives in circles.

Lisovskaya describes two minuses of The Chariot in a couple: a passive one — aimlessness, routine, draining each other's motivation — and an active one: haste, conclusions and events rushed, one partner bending to fit the other. In Marriage they take turns within a single day: three months on the sofa, then “it will be time to go to church and be married in an hour.” Podkolyosin, by the way, asks for something reasonable: “I must have at least a month breathing-time.” In reply Kochkaryov falls on his knees, curses him, wishes that “a tipsy cabman would drive his shafts down your throat”, and later catches him up and shoves him back into the room with both hands. **Here the mechanism of the tail is visible like a blueprint: a “not now” that nobody hears goes out of the window.**

There are two vehicles in the play. Kochkaryov has ordered the carriage for the wedding, and it waits at the porch. Joining the hands of bride and groom, he delivers a little sermon: “Marriage is a kind of thing… It's not like hailing a cab and driving off somewhere; it's a duty of quite another kind” (our translation). A few minutes later the groom does exactly what marriage was compared with: he calls a cab himself — “Hi, drozhki! … All right! Make haste!” — and Dunyashka, the girl of the house, reports it in the same words: “he took a drozhki and drove away.” It is the only time in the whole play that Podkolyosin gives orders to a driver. He does become his own charioteer — but he drives the other way. As for what kind of “duty” marriage is, Kochkaryov promised to explain “afterwards” and never got the chance.

A strong Chariot looks different: the two are quick to get moving, they decide together and fast, each has a road of their own, but they travel in the same direction. Lisovskaya advises such couples not to hurry each other and to settle, clearly and without hints, the status of the relationship and each one's role. A good scene: one of them is offered a job in another city, and the question “shall we go together?” comes up over dinner before the contract is signed, not after. A worrying scene: a move they planned together happens when one of them has already paid the deposit, and the other first hears of it as a done deal.

sections.h2: Main task, 22 — The Fool: a freedom that leaves by the door
paragraphs: Lisovskaya reads a couple's main task mostly through the minus. Her key to The Fool is freedom: in the plus it is the trust that gives freedom, in the minus it is freedom without boundaries and without responsibility. Her description of The Fool in a couple reads like a summary of Gogol's plot: the relationship starts easily and cheerfully, problems arrive as soon as it comes to serious steps, people run away from difficulties and then blame the partner for it. The main thing stays unclear — what these two are to each other.
In Marriage this formula is spoken by the sailor Zhevakin, turned down for the seventeenth time: “At first everything goes all right; and then, when the critical moment comes, they always refuse me.”

In Waite's list of divinatory meanings the reversed Fool includes “absence”. Gogol gives it an exact formula. The bride searches the house for the groom: “— We can't find Ivan Kuzmich. — Can't find him? Has he gone out? — No, he hasn't gone out either.” **“Not here and not gone out” — this is what the minus of The Fool looks like in a couple**: the person is close by, and yet not there; nothing has been said, nothing decided. Lisovskaya describes the same minus from the outside: a couple in name, living like neighbours and doing everything apart.

Kochkaryov, peering under the chairs, adds that the groom “couldn't vanish without going out of the room”. In Russian the verb for “to vanish”, propast', is also the noun propast', a precipice — the very edge on which The Fool stands. Podkolyosin did both: he vanished, and he jumped.

The Fool appears in the play before the window, in the only conversation between bride and groom. Podkolyosin tells her that on the road he takes to the Department every day he passed a plasterer: working men “will stand right on the top”, and this one was “afraid of nothing”. “What a daring race the Russians are!” he marvels. A line earlier he counts on his fingers the days until the outing to Ekaterinhof and arrives at: “in twenty-two days.” Gogol knew nothing of the destiny matrix, so this is a coincidence. But a conversation that began with “Do you like going for rides, madam?” (our translation) has arrived at twenty-two and at a man who stands on a height without fear. The groom admires him from below, from the pavement.

The tail's main task is not “marry at any cost”. The matchmaker's last line matters more than it seems: had the groom run out by the door, “it would have been another thing”. The Fool's freedom includes the right to say “no” and the right to say “not now” — but aloud, face to face, through the door. The window is the same freedom with the words taken away: someone leaves without a word of explanation, and the other is left with the question “not here and not gone out?” Lisovskaya gives couples with The Fool two pieces of advice that seem to pull in opposite directions: give the partner freedom without checks — and think about responsibility before serious steps. **The door is freedom that answers for itself in words.**

Wen describes The Fool as a fork in the road: the next step can send the Seeker “flying into the air over that cliff with impressive accomplishment” — or down, “from naïveté”. She ties The Hanged Man to the same question: will the Seeker fall or fly? The tail 12-7-22 begins and ends with this question: first it is put to the couple, then it becomes their task.

A scene from life: the wedding date is set, the venue is paid for, and a week before, one of the two suddenly has a work emergency — a business trip, a crunch, “let's move it”. The other agrees and feels a relief they do not admit even to themselves. They opened the window together.

sections.h2: Waite: two figures above the void
paragraphs: Lay Waite's cards side by side and you see that the tail begins and ends with a halt. The Hanged Man hangs head downwards by one ankle, his arms bound behind him, and his face, in Waite's words, expresses “deep entrancement, not suffering”. The Fool stands still too: a young man “pauses at the brink of a precipice among the great heights of the world”, and Waite specifies that the urge to walk is still visible in him, “though he is stationary at the given moment”. Both are above the void. The difference is what holds each one there: The Hanged Man is held by a rope, The Fool holds himself.

The Hanged Man's bound arms are in the play as well. The groom never asks for the bride's hand; Kochkaryov does it for him — “he asks your hand”. Afterwards Podkolyosin takes her hand and exclaims “What a lovely little hand!” — but the proposal has already been spoken in someone else's voice.

To whoever understands The Hanged Man, Waite promises “intimations concerning a great awakening that is possible”. Podkolyosin's awakening comes five minutes before the window: “Now, at last, only now, I know what life is; a new world has opened before me.” For a couple with this tail the awakening can be real. The passage from awakening to step is no longer The Hanged Man but The Chariot, and that is exactly where the story breaks.

Of The Fool at the edge Waite writes: “The edge which opens on the depth has no terror; it is as if angels were waiting to uphold him, if it came about that he leaped from the height.” Podkolyosin also asks for support from above — “Lord, give Thy blessing!” — and jumps. The gesture is the same; the direction is not. Waite's Fool looks at the expanse of sky rather than the prospect below, and steps forward; Podkolyosin jumps away from the door. **The Fool steps because he trusts. Podkolyosin jumps because he is afraid.** The couple's main task is to turn the second leap into the first.

sections.h2: The numbers: who brings these cards into the couple
paragraphs: Every point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, reduced to 22. Running through every date shows that the tail 12-7-22 is built from only four combinations of personal tails: 18-3-12 + 21-4-10 (65% of such couples), 6-17-11 + 6-17-11 (18%), 3-22-19 + 9-12-3 (17%) and the very rare 6-14-8 + 6-20-14, a fraction of a per cent. These combinations show who brings what.

Neither partner ever has The Chariot in their personal tail — not in a single such couple. Nobody owns the vehicle: it is assembled only from the sum. In two couples out of three it is made of one partner's Empress and the other's Emperor (3 + 4) — the home and the order. When Kochkaryov talks his friend round, he paints exactly these two cards: “Here there'll be a sofa, there a lap-dog, then a birdcage, and fancy-work lying about”, children, “a whole half-dozen” — and the order that the bachelor admits he lacks. In one couple in six the middle is plainer still: 22 + 12 = 34 → 7, so The Chariot is made of one partner's Fool and the other's Hanged Man. **The couple's vehicle is literally assembled from the other two cards of its tail.**

The Hanged Man, by contrast, is nearly always already familiar to one of the two. In 82% of such couples he is in one partner's personal tail: in 65% as that partner's personal main task, in 17% as the middle. The postponement that becomes a shared language often belonged to one person first.

The couple's Fool is always an exact sum of the two personal main tasks, with no reduction: 12 + 10, 11 + 11, 19 + 3, 8 + 14. In the most common case it is one partner's Hanged Man plus the other's Wheel of Fortune: a suspended man and a turning wheel add up to a leap. You can hear this arithmetic in Podkolyosin's name, too. The Fool appears in a personal tail in only 17% of such couples, and then in one partner only.

In 18% of couples none of the three cards appears in either personal tail. Almost all of them are couples with identical personal tails, 6-17-11: two entries of The Lovers give The Hanged Man (6 + 6), two Stars in the middle give The Chariot (17 + 17 = 34 → 7), two Strengths in the main task give The Fool (11 + 11). Two similar people, and a tail that neither of them has.

This tail has no permutations: the same numbers in another order never occur in a couple's chart. There is, however, a tail with the same ends and a different middle — 12-16-22, where The Tower stands between “not now” and freedom. There, freedom is reached through a collapse. In 12-7-22 it is reached by road.

sections.h2: Atmosphere and values: a Star that no person has
paragraphs: In 81.9% of couples with this tail the centre of the chart — the atmosphere inside the couple — is The Star, 17. No person ever has The Star at the centre of a personal chart: this card in the centre exists only for two. And with it the couple's tail obeys the laws of a personal tail: the entry equals the main task plus the centre (22 + 17 = 39 → 12), the middle equals the entry plus the task (12 + 22 = 34 → 7). In arithmetic terms such a couple is a single person with The Star at the centre — someone who is never born. That person appears only when these two are together.

For Lisovskaya, The Star in the atmosphere is a union that inspires both; often only next to each other do people understand who they want to be. This is Gogol's “a new world has opened before me”. The Star's minus is the same story from the other end: people enjoy being in love but take no responsibility, and may part as soon as marriage or a child comes up. In his dreams Podkolyosin gets to taste “such bliss as one only hears about in fairy-tales” — and jumps. The Star gives the couple a dream; The Fool demands a step.

In the remaining 18.1% the centre is Justice, 8. Such couples, according to Lisovskaya, take a long time to look at each other and a long time to settle in. In the plus they want to make the relationship official and fair; in the minus they do not want to make it official and they break promises. It is the same question of pace, only settled by weighing rather than by dreaming.

The couple's values — the point that says what the union exists for — are held by The Lovers in 71.5% of such couples and by The Devil in 28.5%. These are two sides of Gogol's fear. The Lovers is the card of choice, and choice is exactly what torments Agafya Tikhonovna: “Really, it is a very difficult thing to have to choose.” The Devil is the card of bonds, and bonds are exactly what frighten Podkolyosin: “For all one's life, for ever — you can't get over the fact that you're tying yourself.” Lisovskaya's conclusion about The Devil is that nobody belongs to anybody. For seven couples in ten, the value of the union is to choose each other consciously, and more than once; for three in ten, it is to build a bond that holds without shackling.

sections.h2: Worked example: 05.12.1975 and 14.10.1975
paragraphs: How the tail adds up in practice can be seen on two dates that the site's engine gives for it.

The partner born on 05.12.1975 has the personal tail 18-3-12 — The Moon, The Empress, The Hanged Man — and a centre of 6. The partner born on 14.10.1975 has 21-4-10: The World, The Emperor, The Wheel of Fortune, and a centre of 11. The couple's entry: 18 + 21 = 39, and 3 + 9 = 12. The middle: 3 + 4 = 7. The main task: 12 + 10 = 22, with no reduction. The couple's centre is 6 + 11 = 17, The Star; the values are 15, The Devil.

In this couple The Fool also stands on the point “What to create together” (the birth months: 12 + 10 = 22), and The Hanged Man on “Where it sparks” (7 + 5 = 12). This happens in 3% and 4% of couples with this tail. Lisovskaya reads “What to create together” only in the plus: for these two, freedom is not only a task but also something to build together. And The Hanged Man in the place of quarrels hints at where they come from: from a wait that has dragged on and never been named.

sections.h2: How to get out of the tail: the door instead of the window
paragraphs: A couple's tail is neither a verdict nor a forecast: it is a script that can be recognised and rewritten. Gogol's play shows the worst version of it, and the same play shows where it breaks.

ul: **Name your windows.** Each of the two has a habitual exit for the moment a step becomes serious: work, a trip, the parents, “I need to think”, silence. If the windows are named on a calm day, it is harder to slip out through them unnoticed on a difficult one.

**Say “not now” through the door.** With a reason and a date: “I'm not ready — let's come back to this in March.” Podkolyosin asked for a month, and the request was reasonable. The mistake was that nobody heard it and he did not stand up for it.

**Choose your own pace.** A push from outside — from friends, family, circumstances — does The Hanged Man good. But the route is chosen by the couple, by the two of them, and they get into one carriage, not two different ones.
**Freedom plus a word.** Don't check up on each other and don't hold each other back — and don't vanish in silence. Freedom that answers for itself in words is the strong version of The Fool.

paragraphs: The strong version of this couple looks like this. The Hanged Man gives it depth: these two know how to listen, they don't rush feelings, and they see each other from unexpected angles. The Chariot gives shared movement: moves, common roads, and a road of one's own for each. The Fool gives trust and lightness: such couples start again easily and are not afraid of the unknown. The conversation that Podkolyosin never had takes place in their kitchen: “I'm not ready yet. Let's say March — and in March I'll give an honest answer, yes or no.” And in March that conversation really happens.

intro: The tail 12-7-22 turns up in about one couple in 91, which puts it 33rd among the 97 couple tails. People also search for it as a “12-7-22 programme in the destiny matrix”, but no single person has such a programme. In a personal chart the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and with The Fool as the main task an entry of 12 would need a centre of 17 — and no person ever has The Star at the centre. These three numbers only come together for two people. Lisovskaya calls the couple's tail its karmic programme and reads it above all through the minus: through what the couple cannot manage and has to learn.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 12-7-22 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of a couple's chart: The Hanged Man at the entry to the task, The Chariot in the middle, The Fool as the main task. The story runs from a shared “not now”, through movement that often arrives from outside, to a task of freedom: learning to take a serious step openly, “through the door”, rather than vanishing.
