faq.q: Is there a 12-7-22 programme in a personal destiny matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal chart the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and with The Fool as the main task an entry of 12 would need a centre of 17, while no person has The Star at the centre. The triple 12-7-22 only arises as a couple's tail; Lisovskaya calls a couple's tail its karmic programme.

faq.q: Does this tail mean the couple will never reach the wedding?
faq.a: No. The tail describes a task, not an outcome, and predicts nothing. It shows where the couple is thin-skinned: in long postponement, in someone else's pace and in the temptation to vanish instead of talking. Couples with this tail live both married and unmarried; their task is the same — to take their steps openly.

faq.q: Who plays Podkolyosin in the couple?
faq.a: Either of the two, and more often both in turn: the roles do not depend on gender. In the play both the groom and the bride want to put off the step, and in life the part of Kochkaryov may be played by a partner, by family or by circumstances.

faq.q: How do you work out a couple's tail from the dates of birth?
faq.a: Every point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, reduced to 22. The entry to the task is the sum of the two personal tail entries, the middle is the sum of the personal middles, the main task is the sum of the personal karmic tasks. The couple's middle is not recalculated from its ends: it is added up from the two personal middles.

report: The most decisive act in Gogol's Marriage is performed by its most indecisive man. For three months the matchmaker has been calling on Podkolyosin, a court counsellor, and still he cannot go and see the bride: the weather is dull, “if I go out, I may get caught in the rain.” Yet he jumps out of a window and away from his own wedding in a single minute. The couple's karmic tail 12-7-22 tells the same story in the same order: The Hanged Man, The Chariot, The Fool. Two people can wait for years, then decide in a second — and jump the wrong way.

report.h3: One of them ran, but both of them wanted it

report: The entry to the task is the couple's common language, what the two want together. Here stands The Hanged Man, the card of life held in suspension, and the common language sounds like “not now”. The play is usually read as a joke about a timid groom, but the bride speaks the same language. Podkolyosin, already in his tailcoat, tells his friend he had “better go alone”. Agafya Tikhonovna, with the suitors in the room, whispers to her aunt: “Auntie! stop here instead of me!” He: “I have lived and lived, served, gone to the Department.” She: “I lived and lived — and now I have to get married!” And at the decisive minute the bride, in her wedding dress, thinks: “Oh! I wish he weren't in the room just this minute; I wish he'd gone out!” The wish comes true to the letter. **One of them ran, but both of them wanted it.**

In Lisovskaya's reading such couples take a long time to enter a relationship, and to marry they need a push from outside. In the plus these are tactful people who know how to listen and sense each other at a distance. After their only conversation alone, Gogol's bride and groom are pleased with each other: at their own slow pace, they suit. The minus of The Hanged Man is a life lived for other people's eyes. Before he jumps, Podkolyosin reasons: “there are heaps of people at the door, and everywhere, and they'd ask me why.” In Waite's list of divinatory meanings the reversed Hanged Man includes “the crowd”. The crowd stands in the doorway, and only one exit is left.

report.h3: Someone else's carriage and a cab of one's own

report: The middle of the task is The Chariot: movement that arrives, often from outside. In the play it is brought by his friend Kochkaryov: “Now, my lad, this business mustn't be put off… come along.” In one day he sees off the rivals, orders the supper, sends for the carriage and dispatches the guests to church. Waite writes that the charioteer's conquests are “manifest or external and not within himself”. Kochkaryov conquers everything except the groom himself.

Neither partner has The Chariot in their personal tail: the two own no vehicle of their own, it is assembled only from their sum. That is why it is so easy to climb into someone else's. Podkolyosin asks for something reasonable — “I must have at least a month breathing-time” — and is told the wedding is in an hour. **A “not now” that nobody hears goes out of the window.** Joining the hands of bride and groom, Kochkaryov lectures them: “It's not like hailing a cab and driving off somewhere; it's a duty of quite another kind.” A few minutes later the groom does exactly what marriage was compared with: he calls a cab himself — “All right! Make haste!” He does become his own charioteer — but he drives the other way.

report.h3: Not here and not gone out

report: The main task is The Fool, and Lisovskaya's key to the card is freedom. In the minus, couples with The Fool start easily, and problems arrive as soon as it comes to serious steps; the main thing stays unclear — what these two are to each other. In Waite's list of divinatory meanings the reversed Fool includes “absence”, and Gogol gives it an exact formula. The bride searches the house for the groom: “— We can't find Ivan Kuzmich. — Can't find him? Has he gone out? — No, he hasn't gone out either.” The person is close by, and yet not there; nothing has been said, nothing decided. Kochkaryov, peering under the chairs, says the groom “couldn't vanish without going out of the room”. In Russian the verb for “to vanish”, propast', is also the noun propast', a precipice — the very edge on which The Fool stands.

Waite's Fool feels no terror at the edge of the precipice: “it is as if angels were waiting to uphold him”. Podkolyosin also asks for support from above — “Lord, give Thy blessing!” — and jumps. The gesture is the same; the direction is not. **The Fool steps because he trusts; Podkolyosin jumps because he is afraid.** The couple's main task is to turn the second leap into the first.

report.h3: Had he run out by the door, it would have been another thing

report: Gogol gives the play's last line to the matchmaker: “If he'd run out by the door it would have been another thing, but when the bridegroom pops out of window…” That line holds the way out. The tail's task is not “marry at any cost”. The Fool's freedom includes the right to say “no” and the right to say “not now” — but aloud, face to face, through the door. Lisovskaya advises such couples to give the partner freedom without checks — and to think about responsibility before serious steps. **The door is freedom that answers for itself in words.**

In practice this means naming the windows on a calm day: work, a trip, the parents, “I need to think”, silence. Saying “not now” with a reason and a date. Accepting a push from outside, but choosing the route together and getting into one carriage. The strong version of a couple with this tail is the depth of The Hanged Man, the shared road of The Chariot and the trust of The Fool. The conversation that Podkolyosin never had takes place in such a couple's kitchen: “I'm not ready yet. Let's say March — and in March I'll give an honest answer, yes or no.” And in March that conversation really happens.

unit.title: The door, not the window

captions.M: Waiting for the right moment and putting off the step
captions.N: Choosing your own pace, not someone else's carriage
captions.D: Not vanishing in silence, but saying yes or no at the door

unit.meaning: Your task is to take serious steps openly: say “no” or “not now” out loud instead of slipping away, as if through a window.

seo.title: Karmic tail 12 7 4 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 7 4 compatibility: The Hanged Man, The Chariot and The Emperor in a couple, how the tail adds up and its story in The Captain's Daughter.

items.title: Karmic tail 12-7-4 in compatibility: whose blessing the couple is waiting for
items.short: An odd combination: the couple enters through a card of waiting and sacrifice, and its main task is a card of power. The karmic tail 12-7-4 in compatibility explains it like this. First the two wait for someone older to give their union permission (The Hanged Man). Then an outside force picks them up and carries them along (The Chariot). Only after that does the couple take on the real work: setting up its own order at home, one that belongs to both (The Emperor).

sections.h2: A novel that begins with a tail
paragraphs: The Captain's Daughter opens with a scene that is easy to skim past. A map of the world had been ordered from Moscow for little Petrusha. It "hung on the wall without any use at all", and the boy decided to turn it into a kite. His father walked in "at the very moment when I was fixing a bast tail to the Cape of Good Hope". (Quotations from the novel are our own translation.)

A tail tied to the Cape of Good Hope. It is a coincidence, but a happy one: in 91% of couples with the tail 12-7-4 the centre is The Star, and Waite gives that card a second reading — "hope and bright prospects". The same opening scene already holds everything the tail is made of: a sheet of paper hanging idle, an attempt to fly, and a father who decides everything for everyone in one day. He pulled his son by the ear and threw out the French tutor that same day: "And that was the end of my education." When the son was going on seventeen, the father read the Court Calendar and sent him to serve not in St Petersburg but in the Orenburg steppe.

From there the novel is the story of one couple and one question. Blessings in it are asked for and refused, seen in a dream, given under fire, repeated by the wrong mouth. The order of the cards follows the order of the novel: a love waiting for the father's yes (The Hanged Man), a revolt and journeys by kibitka, a covered sledge (The Chariot), a trial and the Empress (The Emperor).

sections.h2: A clue in the numbers: a tail no single person can have
paragraphs: A couple's tail is added up point by point: one partner's entry with the other's entry, middle with middle, main task with main task; any sum above 22 is reduced by adding its digits. Example: the dates 07.08.1976 and 05.11.1975.

For the first date the day is 7, the month 8, the year 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5. The karmic task is 7 + 8 + 5 = 20, the centre of the chart 7 + 8 + 5 + 20 = 40 → 4, the entry of the tail 20 + 4 = 24 → 6, the middle 20 + 6 = 26 → 8. The personal tail is 6-8-20.

For the second date the day is 5, the month 11, the year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. The karmic task is 5 + 11 + 22 = 38 → 11, the centre 5 + 11 + 22 + 11 = 49 → 13, the entry 11 + 13 = 24 → 6, the middle 11 + 6 = 17. The personal tail is 6-17-11.

The first clue is in the middle. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is not added up but derived from the two ends: entry plus task. 12 and 4 would give 16, The Tower, so no birth date has 12-7-4 as a personal tail. In a couple, both partners bring the middle: it is the sum of their two personal middles. Where a single person would have The Tower between waiting and power, the two of them have The Chariot.

And they bring it in equal shares. In every couple with this tail the two personal middles add up to exactly 25. There are four such sums: Justice and The Star (8 + 17), The Fool and The Empress (22 + 3), Judgement and The Hierophant (20 + 5), The Chariot and The Moon (7 + 18). Each partner carries half of the road.

The second clue is in what is missing. The tail 12-7-4 comes from four pairings of personal tails: 6-17-11 + 6-8-20 (56% of such couples), 3-22-19 + 9-3-21 (31%), 6-20-14 + 6-5-17 (10%), 3-7-22 + 9-18-9 (3%). Neither The Hanged Man nor The Emperor appears in any of these personal tails, and The Chariot appears only in the last, rarest one. In 97% of such couples all three cards are born only in the sum: neither partner brings them ready-made.

The third clue is where The Emperor does live. A person whose personal tail is 6-8-20 always has 4 in the centre of the chart, their comfort zone. So in 56% of couples with the tail 12-7-4 the card of the main task already sits in the centre of one of the two, as it does for the date 07.08.1976. For one of them order is home ground; for the other it is a task. That makes neither of them the boss or the one to blame: the task is shared, they simply start talking about it in different languages.

The rest comes from the site's engine. The couple's centre, its atmosphere, is The Star in 91% of cases and Justice in 9%. No birth date has The Star in the centre of a personal matrix: only a couple can have this card there. The couple's values are The Lovers in 86.6% of cases and The Devil in 13.4%. The tail occurs in roughly one couple in 257 (0.388%), which puts it 64th of the 97 couple tails.

sections.h2: Entry: "Without their blessing there will be no happiness for you"
paragraphs: The Belogorsk fortress turns out to be a hamlet behind a log fence. "But where is the fortress?" Grinyov asks the coachman. "Why, right here." Here, where nothing happens, love begins. Wounded in a duel, Grinyov proposes to Masha, and her first question is not about feelings: "won't your family stand in the way?"

The obstacle arrives by letter. The father gives "neither my blessing nor my consent" and promises "to teach you a proper lesson, like a little boy". Grinyov is ready to do without his father: they will throw themselves at the feet of Masha's parents, marry, and win his father round later. Masha refuses: "I will not marry you without your parents' blessing. Without their blessing there will be no happiness for you. Let us submit to the will of God. If you find the one meant for you, if you come to love another — God be with you, Pyotr Andreich."

The whole entry of the tail is in this scene. The two share one wish: that their union should be right, permitted. That is their common language: both are ready to wait, both are ready to step back for the other's sake. And the same wish turns into resistance. Masha almost stops speaking to him; Grinyov "sank into a gloomy brooding, fed by solitude and idleness". The love has not ended — it is hanging. Later, when Pugachev hands Masha over to him, she will say again that she will be his wife only with his parents' consent. And Grinyov "did not contradict her": by now it is his language too.

In Waite's divinatory list for The Hanged Man the words stand side by side: "Wisdom, circumspection, discernment, trials, sacrifice". Of Masha, Pushkin writes that she "was gifted in the highest degree with modesty and caution". Sacrifice rings out at every step of the novel: "at least you be happy", says Masha; under the gallows, Savelich, the old servant, begs to be hanged instead of his master.

Lisovskaya says of the twelfth energy in a couple what Pushkin showed through the plot: such couples take a long time to commit, and for marriage they need a push from outside. Grinyov describes it himself: he was pulled out of his brooding by "unexpected events" that gave his soul "a strong and salutary shock". That shock was the Pugachev rebellion. Benebell Wen gives The Hanged Man one more reading — "the unsettling calm before a storm". In the novel the storm is literal: a blizzard and a revolt.

Today this entry looks ordinary. The two have been together for three years, and the wedding keeps being put off: let Mum get used to it, let the renovation finish, let Dad stop calling it a whim. Grinyov fears the same thing — that his father will look on his love "as a young man's whim". Both are sure that waiting is noble. Each has given something up for the other: one turned down a move, the other a new job, and neither said it out loud. In the heavy version of the same card, one partner holds the relationship together with all their strength, hears only reproaches in return and cannot leave, while the parents decide about children and moving. The entry to the task is the first question the couple asks itself: whose yes are we waiting for, and what will change when it comes?

sections.h2: Middle: a guide who knows the road
paragraphs: The Chariot turns up in the novel before the love does, in the second chapter. Grinyov is travelling to his post, and a blizzard sweeps over the steppe. The coachman stops: there is no road. A stranger steps out of the snowstorm, and his first advice is to wait: "Better to stop here and wait it out; maybe the storm will die down and the sky will clear, and then we'll find the road by the stars." A minute later he climbs onto the coachman's seat himself: he has caught a smell of smoke, there are houses nearby — "turn right and drive on".

The whole move from the entry of the tail to its middle is in this one remark of the guide. First wait it out, then suddenly drive, and the one holding the reins is not the one travelling. And the stars he promises to steer by stand in the centre of 91% of these couples.

In thanks, Grinyov gives the vagabond his hareskin coat, and Savelich grumbles that "he'll drink it away at the first tavern, the dog". Later this vagabond takes the Belogorsk fortress under the name of Emperor Peter III, and Grinyov, with a noose already round his neck, is let go from under the gallows. Grinyov sums it up himself: "a child's sheepskin coat, given to a vagabond, was saving me from the noose". A gift given early on the road, with no thought of return, came back as rescue.

Then the guide carries him out once more. Orphaned Masha is held under lock and key by Shvabrin, who is forcing her to marry him. The general in Orenburg will not give soldiers and advises him "to have patience". Grinyov rides out to the rebels on his own, is caught, and decides that "providence" has brought him to Pugachev a second time. In the morning the two of them get into the kibitka; "the bell rang out, and the kibitka flew". Grinyov describes his position more precisely than any reading could: "I am an officer and a nobleman; only yesterday I was fighting against you, and today I am riding in the same kibitka with you, and the happiness of my whole life depends on you."

Waite's divinatory list for The Chariot opens with "Succour, providence" and goes on: "also war, triumph, presumption, vengeance, trouble". Reversed, the first word is "Riot", followed by "quarrel, dispute, litigation, defeat". The novel runs through this list almost entirely: the rescue of an orphan, providence, war, the duel with Shvabrin, the commission of inquiry, the rout of the pretender. And the novel's most famous sentence is about the very first word of the reversed list: "God grant that we never see a Russian revolt, senseless and merciless!" The Russian word is bunt, a riot.

For the couple, something else matters more: here The Chariot is a relay. First Grinyov, finding himself before the self-proclaimed "sovereign", pleads with him for Masha. Then Masha travels to the real sovereign to plead for Grinyov. Each in turn carries the other out, and both times the road ends at the door of power, at the card of the main task. The numbers say the same: each partner brings half of the middle of the tail.

Among the tasks of The Chariot in a couple, Lisovskaya names the balance between career and relationship and the decision to move together. In Grinyov this is a single sentence: "Duty demanded that I go where my service could still be useful to my country... But love strongly advised me to stay with Marya Ivanovna." Later he chooses duty: he sends Masha to his parents and stays with his unit. The couple's move is settled, but one of them settled it: at night, after a talk with a friend, and in the morning Grinyov "told her of my intentions". She agreed.

The Chariot has a trap as well. In the same kibitka Pugachev tells a Kalmyk folk tale: the raven lives three hundred years because it eats carrion, the eagle only thirty-three because it drinks living blood, and the eagle decides: "rather than feed on carrion for three hundred years, better to drink living blood once, and then whatever God gives!" A couple with this tail recognises the temptation halfway along the road. In a rush job, a move, in rescuing each other, the two live more brightly than on an ordinary Tuesday, and the even life after the storm seems flat. Grinyov answers the pretender: "to live by murder and robbery is, to my mind, to peck at carrion." For a couple his answer means this: if the two feel alive only in trouble, that is not the eagle's flight, it is the same carrion.

Today the guide can be anything: a redundancy, an offer in another city, a flooded flat, a boss who will "sort it all out", a friend who knows where to rent. In a week the couple does what it has been putting off for years. One flies to a strange city to deal with the other's papers; a year later the other spends nights finding the first a lawyer and money.

sections.h2: The proxy father: when The Chariot takes The Emperor's seat
paragraphs: The most mysterious page of the novel is the dream Grinyov has in the kibitka during the blizzard. He dreams that he has come home and his father is dying. His mother leads him to the bed: "Andrei Petrovich, Petrusha has come... give him your blessing." "Instead of my father I see a peasant with a black beard lying in the bed, looking at me merrily." His mother urges him: "this is your posazhony otets; kiss his hand and let him bless you." Grinyov refuses, the peasant seizes an axe, the room fills with dead bodies, and the terrible peasant calls to him tenderly: "Don't be afraid, come under my blessing."

A posazhony otets, a proxy father, is the man who stands in for the real father at a wedding. The dream comes true in three steps. When Grinyov is taken down from the gallows and set before the pretender, the crowd shouts: "Kiss his hand, kiss his hand!" — he does not. In the Belogorsk fortress Pugachev, having freed Masha, offers it himself: "If you like, I'll be the proxy father." And when he lets them go, he blesses them with words the reader has already heard. Under fire, Captain Mironov blessed his daughter: "If a good man is found, God grant you love and concord." Pugachev, who hanged the captain, says the same: "Take your beauty; take her wherever you like, and God grant you love and concord!" The right words reached the couple from the wrong mouth.

Grinyov himself calls the dream prophetic, and that is one more line from Waite's list: the entry for The Hanged Man ends with "intuition, divination, prophecy". The entry of the tail sees what will happen in the middle.

Waite also explains the mechanism. His Chariot "is really the King in his triumph, typifying, however, the victory which creates kingship as its natural consequence and not the vested royalty of the fourth card", The Emperor. Pugachev is The Chariot in pure form: power seized at full gallop. He knows himself how fragile it is: "My street is narrow; I have little freedom. My lads are too clever by half." The Chariot can carry a couple out of the blizzard, but it has no right to bless. The real emperor drew the same line, only on a title page. For his History of Pugachev, Pushkin travelled in 1833 to Berdskaya Sloboda, the rebels' capital, and questioned the old people there, and Nicholas I changed the title in his own hand to The History of the Pugachev Rebellion. The pretender was left a rebellion, not a history.

Hence the main lesson of the passage from The Chariot to The Emperor. The couple accepts the guide's help — the coat, the horse, the pass — but does not offer him a hand to kiss. Freed, Masha repeats what she said before: she will be a wife only with the consent of Grinyov's parents. This is not meekness. A proxy father cannot replace the real one, and she knows it.

Today the dream is easy to recognise. Someone carried the couple out of a crisis: a boss who gave work and a flat, a relative who paid off a debt, a friend they lived with for six months. Gratitude is natural. The danger comes when the rescuer starts to bless: to decide where the couple should live, when to marry and how to raise children. And the couple, out of The Hanged Man's old habit, waits for his yes.

sections.h2: The main task: two houses where one person decides
paragraphs: In a couple's tail The Emperor is the main task, and it is read mostly through what does not work. Pushkin shows it through two finished marriages, and between them the young couple has to build a third.

The first house is the Grinyovs'. The father, a retired major, receives the Court Calendar every year, a list of dignitaries and their ranks, and reads it with "a remarkable stirring of bile": "Lieutenant-general!.. He was a sergeant in my company!.." The mother knows this weakness and hides the book "as far away as possible", sometimes for months. Above this house stands someone else's hierarchy, and it holds together by one partner's quiet cunning and the other's temper: the father "liked neither to change his intentions nor to put off carrying them out". One reading of the calendar, and the son goes not to the Guards but to the steppe.

The second house is the Mironovs'. Here the wife rules: Vasilisa Yegorovna "looked on the affairs of the service as her own household business and ran the fortress exactly as she ran her little home". The commandant drills his soldiers "in a nightcap and a cotton dressing gown". He tries to hide a secret order from his wife and is caught out: "scheming is not for you". She has one answer to every objection: "are not husband and wife one spirit and one flesh?" The house is warm and funny, and in it, too, one person decides. When Pugachev approaches the fortress, the wife refuses to leave: "Together to live, together to die."

Pushkin sets the two marriages side by side: in one the husband rules, in the other the wife. Neither will do for the young couple, and the point is not who rules. The card is not about gender. It is about the fact that in both houses one person decides, and the other schemes, hides or submits.

Lisovskaya describes the minus of The Emperor in a couple with similar pictures: one decides for everyone, the rules are rigid, and feelings are hidden so deep that you cannot tell joy from anger. Her tasks for the couple sound like an answer to both houses: do not make rules that get in the way later, and learn to talk about feelings.

Among Waite's reversed meanings of The Emperor is the word "immaturity". The novel begins with it: "I lived as a nedorosl, chasing pigeons" — nedorosl, an idle overgrown minor. The main task of the tail is to grow from a nedorosl whose father picks his regiment into the master of his own house, without turning into the father with the calendar.

Today it looks like this. In one home "this is how it's done in our family" collides with "it was different in mine". A rule invented in a crisis — "one of us handles the money", "we don't mention bad news so as not to upset anyone" — lives on for years after the crisis is over. One partner hides from the other whatever irritates them, the way the mother hid the calendar. An argument about where to go on holiday becomes an argument about who is in charge here.

sections.h2: The trial: two silences and one plea
paragraphs: The most exact scene of the tail is the trial. Grinyov is arrested for his friendship with the pretender. He travels to Kazan resolved to tell the plain truth, and at the interrogation he falls silent: "It occurred to me that if I named her, the commission would summon her to answer." He "faltered and got confused", and the judges, who a moment ago had listened to him with goodwill, turn against him again. To protect Masha, he decided for her: her name will not be spoken. The price is a sentence of permanent exile to Siberia.

Masha, meanwhile, is living with his parents, and she too is silent: she "was deeply troubled, but kept silent". She guesses why he did not clear himself, blames herself and "hid her tears from everyone". Then one evening she announces that she is going to St Petersburg, and explains her plan only to Grinyov's mother, alone with her, and only "in part".

This is a pattern of the tail that is easy to mistake for love. The Hanged Man at the entry is sacrifice, The Emperor in the main task is decision. Together they make a decision for the other, taken in silence and with the best intentions. Grinyov decided for Masha that she had better not testify. Masha decided for Grinyov that she had to go. Each protects the other, and each rules alone.

That same evening Pushkin shows how power at home is changing. The father sits with the Court Calendar, "but his thoughts were far away, and the reading did not have its usual effect on him". For the first time the book of other men's ranks does not work. And the father who not long ago refused his blessing answers Masha: "Go, my dear! We do not wish to stand in the way of your happiness."

Next comes the garden at Tsarskoye Selo. On a bench Masha meets a lady "in a white morning dress, a nightcap and a dushegreika", a padded house jacket. The scene is generally thought to be drawn from Borovikovsky's portrait Catherine II Walking in Tsarskoye Selo Park (1794), where the Empress is dressed for home. And inside the novel the detail has an echo: in the seventh chapter, a robber looting Vasilisa Yegorovna's house dressed himself in her dushegreika. On the bench sits not a crowned sovereign but a woman in house clothes who is able to listen.

The conversation is short. "You are an orphan; no doubt you have come to complain of injustice and wrong?" "No, madam. I have come to ask for mercy, not for justice." When the lady coldly calls Grinyov "an immoral and harmful scoundrel", Masha, whom her mother called a coward, answers: "Oh, that's not true!.. It's not true, by God, it's not true!" And she tells everything: "if he did not clear himself before the court, it was only because he did not want to drag me into it." Grinyov's silence would have destroyed him. Masha's speech saved him.

The Empress answers in the language Waite places under The Emperor reversed: "Benevolence, compassion, credit". She is kind to the orphan, acquits the fiancé and says: "I am in debt to Captain Mironov's daughter." Power in this scene does not judge — it acknowledges a debt and shows mercy.

For the couple this gives a simple rule for the main task: in a dispute about power, ask for mercy, not for justice. Do not prove who is right under the law of the house; say what you are asking for. In 9% of couples with this tail the centre is Justice, and among its tasks Lisovskaya names the ability to admit one's own fault instead of accusing. For these couples Masha's sentence is doubly needed.

sections.h2: Under glass and in a frame
paragraphs: In the novel three papers hang on walls. The first is that map of the world in the Grinyovs' house, hanging "without any use at all" until the boy makes a kite of it. The second is in the Mironovs' house: "an officer's commission, under glass and in a frame". After the fortress falls, Grinyov sees it again, "like a sad epitaph to times gone by". The third is in the last paragraph. In the village where the descendants of Grinyov and Masha live, "they show a letter in Catherine II's own hand, under glass and in a frame. It is written to Pyotr Andreyevich's father and contains the acquittal of his son and praise for the mind and heart of Captain Mironov's daughter."

Put the three papers side by side and the whole path of The Emperor in this tail appears. First the wall holds a foreign world one wants to fly away from. Then a father's rank, earned but not the young couple's own. At the end, a paper about the couple itself. The letter is addressed to the father, the man who read the Court Calendar: instead of a list of other men's ranks he received a testimony to his daughter-in-law's mind and heart. The power that used to stand over the house now hangs on their wall. It no longer rules — it is shown to guests.

There is also a scene that is not in the printed novel. Pushkin wrote a chapter in which Grinyov, in the middle of the revolt, makes his way to his home village and finds his father, his mother and Masha tied up in the grain barn, locked in by the rebellious steward. Grinyov looks for a way out, and his father stops him: "Don't bother. I'm not the kind of master whose barns can be got into and out of through thieves' holes." The master built a barn so secure that he cannot get out of it himself. There could be no better picture of a rule that gets in the way later. The way out is found by the same father: when the barn is set on fire, he unlocks the door himself — "Now is the time!" — and leads everyone out through the flames. In the same chapter the parents finally bless the couple, and Grinyov advises the reader "while there is still time, to fall in love and receive your parents' blessing". Pushkin left this chapter out of the final text; it survives in the draft.

sections.h2: The Star in the centre: "It's more frightening at home alone"
paragraphs: The atmosphere of this couple, its centre, is The Star in 91% of cases. Lisovskaya writes of The Star in a couple's centre that the partners often understand who they want to be only together, and open up, sometimes directly with each other's help. Masha is the best example. Her mother says of her in front of a guest: "Masha is a coward. To this day she can't bear the sound of a gunshot." On the rampart, as the rebels approach the fortress, her father asks her: "Well, Masha, are you frightened?" "No, Papa. It's more frightening at home alone." Later this coward travels to Tsarskoye Selo and argues with the Empress, not yet knowing who is in front of her. Grinyov travels the same road from the other side: from a nedorosl chasing pigeons to a man who withstands the gallows and the trial.

For the same Star, Lisovskaya also describes a shadow: the couple enjoys being in love but avoids responsibility and can fall apart as soon as marriage comes up; a partner is chosen under pressure from parents; home life is built on the parents' script. All of these are the novel's questions. The Star holds the couple while the entry and the middle run their course, but it does not settle the question of marriage or of someone else's script. That is The Emperor's work.

sections.h2: How a couple lives 12-7-4 in its plus
paragraphs: In its plus this tail resembles The Captain's Daughter at its best moments. The two know how to wait without losing each other. In the storm they do not abandon each other and take turns coming to the rescue. In the end they build a home of their own — grateful to their elders, but without their calendar. What helps:

ul: **Name whose yes the couple is waiting for.** Not "some day" but specifically: Mum's, Dad's, the boss's — or money for the wedding. And ask each other what will change when it comes, and what happens if it does not.

**Tell the guide apart from the father.** Whoever carried the couple out of the blizzard deserves a coat and gratitude, but not the right to decide how the couple lives from now on. Accept the help; do not offer a hand to kiss.

**Do not decide for the other in silence, even out of love.** Grinyov's silence at the trial nearly cost him Siberia; Masha's speech saved him. When the urge is to protect, first ask the other whether they want that kind of protection.
**Ask for mercy, not for justice.** In an argument about who is in charge, stop collecting evidence and say plainly what you are asking for.
**Write the house rules together and revisit them.** Especially the ones born in a crisis. A rule that cannot be got round "through thieves' holes" will one day lock in the person who made it.
**Do not live from storm to storm.** After rescuing each other, an ordinary Tuesday is not a flat life; it is what the journey was for.

**Change the elders by living, not by revolt.** Grinyov's father did not change his mind because of an argument: Masha lived in his house, and "it was impossible to know her and not love her". The narrator himself addresses the young reader: the best and most lasting changes are those that "come from the improvement of manners, without any violent upheavals".

paragraphs: The minus of The Emperor also means control, pressure and fear. If there are threats or violence in the couple, this is not a "task of the tail" to be endured: it calls for help — the local emergency number, a crisis line, a psychologist.

ul: **12 · The Hanged Man, entry to the task.** The couple's common language is waiting and giving way: "not now", "not without their consent", "for your sake I'll step back". This shared wish is how the couple enters the task, and the same wish becomes its first resistance.
**7 · The Chariot, middle of the task.** The road goes in jolts and most often starts with a push from outside. The two cover it in turns: each, at some point, carries the other out.
**4 · The Emperor, main task.** A law of their own at home: deciding together, not deciding for the other in silence, and not making rules that later lock both of them in.

intro: The whole path is written down in one Russian novel. Pushkin's Kapitanskaya dochka (The Captain's Daughter) is the story of who will bless Pyotr Grinyov and Masha Mironova. The father refuses. In a dream, a peasant with an axe offers to give the blessing. A pretender to the throne volunteers to stand in for the father at the wedding. The last word belongs to the Empress. What follows is an investigation: what is written in the numbers of the tail itself, in Waite, in Lisovskaya and in Pushkin. It is a tool for knowing each partner and the couple, not a forecast: the cards do not say what will happen, they show what the couple goes through and what it learns.

faq.q: Is the karmic tail 12-7-4 a bad sign for compatibility?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not rate compatibility and does not predict how a union will end: the method gives no percentages and no verdicts. It shows a task — the road from waiting for someone else's consent to an order of one's own at home. The difficulty of this tail lies in the minus of The Emperor: decisions made for both, rigid rules, a struggle over who is in charge.

faq.q: Why is there no personal karmic tail 12-7-4?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is derived from its ends: entry plus task. 12 and 4 would give 16, The Tower. In a couple the middle is the sum of two people's personal middles, and in every couple with this tail they add up to 25, that is, 7 — The Chariot.

faq.q: What does it mean if one partner has 4 in the centre of the chart?
faq.a: This happens in 56% of couples with this tail: a person with the personal tail 6-8-20 always has 4, The Emperor, in the centre. Order and rules are familiar ground for that partner and a new task for the other. That makes neither of them the boss or the one to blame: the task belongs to the couple.

faq.q: Where should a couple with the tail 12-7-4 start?
faq.a: With one conversation: whose approval are we still waiting for, and which rules in our home did we not make ourselves. Then agree which decisions are only ever taken together, and do not take them for the other, even to protect them.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. Among couple tails the cards 12, 7 and 4 occur only in the order 12-7-4: The Hanged Man at the entry, The Chariot in the middle, The Emperor as the main task.

report: Masha Mironova refuses to marry the man she loves for one reason: "Without their blessing there will be no happiness for you." The groom's father has withheld his blessing, and the union is left hanging. In Pushkin's The Captain's Daughter the story of the tail 12-7-4 is written down almost word for word. First the two wait for someone older to give their union permission (The Hanged Man). Then an outside force picks them up and carries them along (The Chariot). And the main task turns out to be power — an order of their own at home, shared by both (The Emperor).

report.h3: A common language that turns into resistance

report: The Hanged Man at the entry is what a couple with this tail wants together: for the union to be right, permitted. Both are ready to wait, both are ready to step back for the other's sake. Masha lets him go: if he finds the one meant for him, if he comes to love another, "God be with you". When she repeats her condition, Grinyov "did not contradict her". This is their common language, and it is also the first resistance. Masha almost stops speaking to him; Grinyov sinks into "a gloomy brooding, fed by solitude and idleness". The love has not ended — it is hanging.

Lisovskaya notes that such couples need a push from outside before they marry. Grinyov is pulled out of his stupor by "unexpected events" that gave his soul "a strong and salutary shock". Today it looks ordinary. The wedding is put off until Mum gets used to it and Dad stops calling it a whim. Each has quietly given something up for the other — a move, a new job — and neither has said so out loud.

report.h3: A guide who drives but cannot bless

report: The Chariot in the middle appears in a blizzard. A stranger advises them to "wait it out... and then we'll find the road by the stars", and a minute later climbs onto the coachman's seat himself. First wait, then suddenly drive, and the one holding the reins is not the one travelling. The guide turns out to be Pugachev. He lets Grinyov go from under the gallows for a hareskin coat given to him long before, and drives him in his own kibitka to free Masha. Grinyov puts it more precisely than any reading could: "only yesterday I was fighting against you, and today I am riding in the same kibitka with you, and the happiness of my whole life depends on you."

In this tail The Chariot is a relay. First Grinyov pleads with the self-proclaimed "sovereign" for Masha, then Masha travels to the real sovereign to plead for Grinyov. **Each in turn carries the other out**, and both times the road ends at the door of power.

But The Chariot has no right to bless. Grinyov dreams that a black-bearded peasant is lying in his dying father's bed, and his mother urges him: "this is your posazhony otets; kiss his hand" — the proxy father who stands in for the real one at a wedding. The dream comes true. Pugachev offers to be the proxy father himself and lets the couple go with the words "God grant you love and concord" — the same words with which Captain Mironov blessed his daughter under fire. The right words came from the wrong mouth. Grinyov does not kiss the pretender's hand, and Masha, already free, repeats that she will be a wife only with his parents' consent. Whoever carried the couple out of a crisis — a boss, a relative, a friend — deserves gratitude, **but not the right to decide how the couple lives from now on**.

report.h3: Deciding for the other in silence is power too

report: The main task is The Emperor, and it is read through what does not work. Pushkin shows two finished marriages. At the Grinyovs', the father reads the Court Calendar with "a remarkable stirring of bile" and decides for everyone, while the mother quietly hides the book away. At the Mironovs', the wife "ran the fortress exactly as she ran her little home". In one house the husband rules, in the other the wife, and gender is not the point: in both, one person decides, and the other schemes, hides or submits.

The most exact scene of the tail is the trial. Grinyov stays silent at the interrogation so as not to drag Masha into it, and is sentenced to permanent exile in Siberia. Masha, living with his parents, is silent too, and then decides on her own to go to St Petersburg. The Hanged Man at the entry is sacrifice, The Emperor in the main task is decision. Together they make **a decision for the other, taken in silence and with the best intentions**. Each protects the other, and each rules alone.

What saves them is not silence but speech. In the garden at Tsarskoye Selo, Masha tells an unknown lady in a nightcap: "I have come to ask for mercy, not for justice." When the lady calls the fiancé a scoundrel, the girl her mother thought a coward answers: "Oh, that's not true!" Power listens, shows mercy and admits: "I am in debt to Captain Mironov's daughter."

report.h3: What hangs on the couple's wall

report: In the Mironovs' house hung "an officer's commission, under glass and in a frame" — a father's rank, earned, but not the young couple's own. In the novel's last paragraph, the couple's descendants keep "under glass and in a frame" a letter from the Empress that contains "praise for the mind and heart of Captain Mironov's daughter". The power that used to stand over the house now hangs on their wall and no longer rules.

There is also the opposite picture, from a chapter Pushkin left out of the novel. The family is locked in its own barn, and the father tells his son: "I'm not the kind of master whose barns can be got into and out of through thieves' holes." A rule that cannot be got round locks in the person who made it.
Simple things change the script:

ul: say out loud whose yes the couple is waiting for and what will change when it comes;
thank the guide, but not offer him a hand to kiss;
not decide for the other in silence, even out of love, but ask first;
in an argument about who is in charge, **ask for mercy, not for justice**;
write the house rules together and revisit them, especially those born in a crisis;
change the elders by living, not by revolt: Masha lived in the Grinyovs' house, and "it was impossible to know her and not love her".

report: If there are threats or violence in the couple, this is not a task of the tail to be endured: it calls for help — a local emergency number or crisis line, a psychologist.

unit.title: Your own law after the blizzard

captions.M: Wait for the elders' consent and step back for each other
captions.N: Carry each other out of the storm in turns
captions.D: Decide together, never for each other in silence

unit.meaning: Your task is your own order at home: decide together, wait for no one's blessing, never decide for each other in silence.

seo.title: Karmic tail 15 11 14 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 15 11 14 compatibility: the Devil at the entry, Strength in the middle, Temperance as the main task — and the myth of Heracles sold to Queen Omphale.

items.title: Karmic tail 15-11-14 in compatibility: from “you're mine” to “us”
items.short: You will not find 15-11-14 in any personal matrix: for the Devil to lead into Temperance, the centre of the chart would have to hold the Magician, and in a single person's chart it never does. Only two people can make this tail, and in compatibility it tells the story of the bond itself — how it travels from “you're mine” to “us”. The Devil at the entry is the wish to belong to each other, so strong that it borders on the wish to own. Strength in the middle is a trial of strength: who has tamed whom. Temperance as the main task is an exchange in which the same person does not always give way and each stays themselves.

sections.h2: Why only a couple can have this tail
paragraphs: In a personal matrix the entry to the tail is worked out from the main task and the centre of the chart: M = D + centre. For the Devil (15) to stand at the entry when Temperance (14) is the task, the centre would have to equal one — the Magician. But the Magician never stands at the centre of a personal chart: the centre can only hold the numbers from 3 to 14, plus 16, 18, 20 and 22. So in one person the road from the Devil to Temperance never begins — there is no conjurer to turn one into the other.

In a couple the centre does not enter the tail: each point is the sum of the same points in two personal charts. The entry comes from two entries, the middle from two middles, the main task from two main tasks. That is how a triple appears which neither of the two has alone.

The second clue is the couple's centre. In 80.7% of couples with this tail it holds the Sun (19), in the remaining 19.3% the Wheel of Fortune (10). No date of birth puts the Sun at the centre of a personal matrix: this energy appears in the middle of the chart only when there are two people. The tail itself occurs in about one couple in 233 (0.429%) and ranks 63rd by frequency among the 97 couple tails.

So both this couple's path and its atmosphere are made of what neither partner has alone. That is why the story of this tail is not about the character of either partner but about the bond: what shapes it takes and how it changes.

sections.h2: The myth this couple lives in: Heracles and Omphale
paragraphs: The strongest man of Greek myth was once sold. In Apollodorus' Library (II.6.2–3), Heracles, “going mad again”, threw his guest Iphitus from the walls of Tiryns and fell gravely ill. The oracle at Delphi gave its answer: “for him to be sold, and to serve for three years, and to pay compensation for the murder”. “Hermes sold Hercules, and he was bought by Omphale”, queen of Lydia. Pherecydes, as reported by an ancient commentator on the Odyssey, gives the price: three talents. In Sophocles' Women of Trachis the term is shorter: “a whole year”, “a bought slave to the barbarian Omphale”.

From there the myth breaks into scenes that Roman poets retold with obvious relish. Omphale puts on the skin of the Nemean lion and takes up the club. Heracles, in her dress, sits among her maids spinning wool. And the story has two endings. In Diodorus of Sicily (IV.31) the queen learned who he was, marvelled at his valour, set him free, married him and bore him a son. In Sophocles, Heracles came back from Lydia sworn to enslave the man he blamed for his shame — and the chain moved on.

The three acts of the myth fall onto the three cards of the tail. The purchase is the Devil: a bond that begins with the word “mine”. The lion skin on someone else's shoulders is Strength: the dispute over who holds the power. The exchange of clothes and two couches side by side are Temperance: a measure in which each stays themselves. This is our reading, not a meaning taken from the books: neither Waite nor Lisovskaya writes about Heracles. But the matches are too close to pass by. Latin verse and Saint-Saëns' French are given in our own literal translation; Apollodorus, Diodorus and Sophocles are quoted in the translations by Frazer, Oldfather and Jebb.

sections.h2: Entry to the task, 15: the language of “you're mine”
paragraphs: The entry to a couple's tail is what the two want together, their agreements and their “common language”. In the compatibility reading the same point also appears in the sphere “Relationship and common language”, labelled “Common language”. For this couple, the common language is the Devil's.

The Romans turned it into a whole genre. Love elegy calls the beloved domina — the word a slave used for his mistress — and the lover her slave. Tibullus opens elegy II.4: “Here I see slavery and a mistress waiting for me: farewell now, freedom of my fathers. A bitter slavery is given me, chains hold me, and Love never loosens the bonds of the wretched.” Propertius (III.11) asks a friend: “Why do you wonder if a woman turns my life around and drags under her laws a man handed over to her for debt?” — and a few lines later he remembers Omphale. Propertius' word addictus is legal: it meant a debtor whom the court had handed over to his creditor.

Two thousand years later the same language sounds in every couple, and hardly anyone notices it: “my other half”, “you belong to me”, “I'm all yours”. At the start of a union with this tail such words feel like the highest degree of closeness. The pull is strong, the passion real. Lisovskaya describes the Devil in a couple at its best as well: two people accept each other's dark sides, forgive mistakes and talk openly about what they want.

But the entry stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. One partner is late at work, the other sends a third message in a row, and it no longer says “miss you” but “where are you”. A gift that makes it awkward to say no. Shared passwords “because we have nothing to hide”. The urge to hold on through intimacy, money, a shared child or status — Lisovskaya lists this among the Devil's tasks in a couple, next to keeping silent about one's own wishes. Her closing thought on the fifteenth energy is short: nobody belongs to anybody.

Diodorus has a detail that explains how this happens. Heracles, he writes, “willingly submitted to be sold”, and Omphale bought a slave without knowing who he was: who he was and whose son, she learned later. Only a stranger can be owned. Ownership begins where a role, an image, a function stands in place of a person, and “mine” often answers the question “whose are you?” that gets asked instead of “who are you?”.

Wen adds an important caveat to the Devil: the card “does not necessarily mean the Seeker is entirely to blame”. The Seeker “is not entirely innocent”, but “the greater culpability rests elsewhere”. The myth says the same. In Sophocles the herald asks that no offence be taken at his tale of the sale, since “the deed is found to be Zeus' work”. In this tail the Devil is not the vice of one partner but the shape of the bond the couple starts with. The numbers show this even more clearly, but more on them below.

sections.h2: Middle of the task, 11: who wears the lion skin
paragraphs: The Nemean lion was Heracles' first labour. Its skin, which no weapon could pierce, became his armour and his mark. And it is this skin that Omphale puts on in Lydia. In Ovid's Fasti (II.325) the queen “herself takes the heavy club and the lion's spoil”. In the Heroides, Heracles' wife Deianira writes him a letter full of bitter irony: “You are deceived and do not know it: these are not the lion's spoils but yours. You conquered the beast; she conquered you” (IX.113–114). And further: Omphale “armed her hand with the club, tamer of beasts, and saw in the mirror her consort's arms” (IX.117–118).

The middle of a couple's tail is how the two live the path from the entry to the main task. For this couple the path runs through Strength, that is, through the question “who wins?”. Lisovskaya describes Strength in a couple both ways. At its worst: a fight for leadership, each with their own truth, mockery and humiliation, one partner openly dominating. At its best: the two charge and strengthen each other, sense what the other needs, and one accepts the other's lead where the other is stronger.

The myth shows both. Almost nineteen centuries after Ovid, Camille Saint-Saëns wrote the symphonic poem Le Rouet d'Omphale (Omphale's Spinning Wheel, 1871–1872) and explained its subject himself: “la séduction féminine, la lutte triomphante de la faiblesse contre la force” — feminine seduction, the triumphant struggle of weakness against strength. The spinning wheel, he said, was only a pretext for the rhythm, and an attentive listener would hear “Hercules groaning in bonds he cannot break, and Omphale mocking the hero's vain efforts”. The bonds come from the Devil at the entry, the mockery from Strength at its worst: a victory celebrated over the defeated.

There is another side too. Propertius (III.11.17–20) writes that Omphale rose to such glory that the man who had set up his pillars in a world he had pacified “drew out soft wool with so hard a hand”. Deianira adds that Heracles' “too-mighty hands” more than once crushed the spindles as he twisted the thread with hard fingers (IX.79–80). Strength used to strangling lions cannot hold a spindle: it breaks what is fine. This is the turn towards the main task — strength needs measure.

The history of the card repeats the myth. On one of the oldest surviving tarot cards, from the Milanese Visconti-Sforza deck (about 1450–1480, now in the Morgan Library in New York), Strength is a man who “raises club in both hands above lion”; he is usually taken to be Heracles. Later the lion stays on the card, but beside it stands a woman, and she does not strike it. Over a few centuries the symbol of Strength walked Omphale's path itself: the lion passed from a hero with a club to a woman with bare hands.

Wen explains the difference. The Chariot is “strength to master the world”, Strength is “strength to master the self”. Under this card, she writes, “the Seeker cannot use brute force to exercise will over others; the Seeker must use gentle, subtle influence.” For a couple this means the middle is passed not when someone has won but when the skin can move from shoulders to shoulders and come back. Today one leads the renovation, tomorrow the other handles the bank, and nobody wears the skin as a trophy.

sections.h2: Main task, 14: two couches side by side
paragraphs: A couple's main task is the point that says what the two have to learn, and it is read mostly through what does not work. For Temperance, Lisovskaya says it plainly: one partner always gives way and the other does not even think of it. One saves, the other spends. There is no common language, and at times it is unclear why the relationship exists at all. The task is to reach agreement, not to load one's own fears and wishes onto the partner and not to try to control them.

The most exact scene for this task is in Ovid's Fasti (II.303–358). Ovid explains why the god Faunus dislikes clothes and tells “an old tale full of fun”. Omphale and Heracles are walking to the vineyards of Tmolus. Above the queen is a golden parasol against the warm sun, “and yet it was Hercules' hands that held it”. In a cave, while the servants prepare supper and wine, she dresses Alcides in her own things: fine tunics dyed with Gaetulian purple, her slender girdle. The girdle is too small. To free his huge hands he loosens the ties of the tunic, bracelets not made for such wrists snap, and his big feet tear the “little bonds” of her sandals. She herself takes the heavy club, the lion skin and the arrows.

Here the Latin keeps a clue. Ovid's word for ties and straps is vincula, the same word as Tibullus' “bonds”: “Love never loosens the bonds” (numquam vincla remittit). In the cave Heracles “loosens the ties of the tunics” himself (tunicarum vincla relaxat). One word. In the elegy nobody loosens the bonds; in the scene of exchange the one who wears them loosens them, and the little straps tear at the first step. A chain stops being a chain when the two take turns wearing it.

Then comes the detail that makes the whole scene worth reading. After supper they lie down to sleep “on couches set side by side, apart” (et positis iuxta secubuere toris): in the morning they are to hold a rite for Bacchus, “the discoverer of the vine”, and must come to it pure. Side by side and not merged. Close, and each on their own couch. This is Temperance in a couple: not one cup for two but two cups, with movement between them.

At midnight Faunus creeps into the cave. In the same book Ovid calls him two-horned and horn-hoofed (II.268, II.361); that look, the horns and goat legs, would later pass to the devil. “What does shameless love not dare?” Faunus gropes his way to the first couch, touches the coarse bristles of the lion skin and pulls his hand back in fear — as a traveller pulls back his foot on seeing a snake. On the next couch his fingers find soft cloth, and he is “deceived by a lying sign”. He climbs onto the couch — and Heracles throws him to the floor. The queen calls her servants and asks for light, everything lies open in the glow, and everyone laughs: the servants, Heracles himself, the Lydian queen. Ever since, Ovid concludes, the god who was fooled by a dress has disliked clothes that deceive the eyes, and calls his worshippers to his rites naked.

Our reading: the horned god goes by signs. Bristles mean danger, softness means prey. Swapping roles leaves him nothing to hold on to. And a second point: Heracles in a woman's tunic is still Heracles and throws the intruder off in one move. The exchange does not take strength away; it teaches when to use it.

Wen has a thought about Temperance, said about work but just as true of a couple: “it isn't that new skills need to be learned, but rather that the Seeker need only reconcile his or her existing skills with the task at hand.” A couple with this tail does not need to become different people. It needs to learn to pour. Today one carries the household, tomorrow the other. Money is not “in one pair of hands, by the rules” but in a shared decision. “I'll give way this time” does not turn into “I always give way”. A simple test is to recall who gave way over the last month. If the answer is always the same person, Temperance is at its worst even when there are no quarrels.

The Heroides have one more detail: Heracles “weighs back equal portions” of wool “to his beautiful mistress” (IX.78). A pensum was a spinner's day's work, wool weighed out on scales; in German, Pensum still means a workload. This couple's main task is the same day's work, only now both hold the scales.

sections.h2: What Waite drew: a ring before the altar, a lion and two cups
paragraphs: On Waite's cards the three points of the tail look like one bond in three states.

**The Devil.** “The Horned Goat of Mendes” stands on an altar, a distant relative of Ovid's Faunus. “There is a ring in front of the altar, from which two chains are carried to the necks of two figures, male and female.” Waite likens them to Adam and Eve after the Fall and writes: “Hereof is the chain and fatality of the material life.” “The figures are tailed, to signify the animal nature, but there is human intelligence in the faces.” An altar, a ring, a man and a woman: take away the horned figure and it is the layout of a wedding. Our reading: a union that begins with a ring becomes a chain when someone else holds the ring — habit, fear, “that's how it's done”.

**Strength.** A woman “is closing the jaws of a lion”; “her beneficent fortitude has already subdued the lion, which is being led by a chain of flowers”. “There is one aspect in which the lion signifies the passions,” Waite writes, “and she who is called Strength is the higher nature in its liberation.”

**Temperance.** A winged figure is “pouring the essences of life from chalice to chalice. It has one foot upon the earth and one upon waters.” When the rule of this card holds in our consciousness, according to Waite, “it tempers, combines and harmonises the psychic and material natures.”

Waite also gives a bridge to the couple's centre. Of the Sun he writes that the renewed mind “leads forth the animal nature in a state of perfect conformity”. The same animal nature that sits on a chain in the Devil walks alongside of its own accord in the Sun. The chain holds, the flowers lead, the water flows, the light reveals: the four cards of this couple are four shapes of one bond.

sections.h2: Two endings: the chain is passed on or taken off
paragraphs: The myth has two endings, and both are in the books.

**Sophocles.** The herald tells Heracles' wife that the year of slavery stung the hero so deeply that he swore “to enslave with wife and child the man who had brought that suffering upon him”. He kept the oath: the city of Eurytus was destroyed and its captive women were sent to Heracles' house. Then the tragedy of the Women of Trachis begins. Deianira, afraid of losing her husband, sends him a robe soaked in a centaur's blood: she had been told it would bring back his love. The robe clings to his body and burns like fire; Heracles dies of that torment. Clothing is again at the centre of the story, but now it is not an exchange but an attempt to hold on, and it destroys. The one who was bought starts buying: a chain that is not taken off gets passed on.

**Diodorus.** Omphale sees her slave's courage, learns who he is and who his parents were, “marvelled at his valour, set him free, and marrying him bore him Lamus”. The order is what matters: first know, then free, then choose. The marriage Diodorus puts at the end is possible only between free people.

For a couple with the 15-11-14 tail this is not a forecast of how things will end but two directions that every union with these numbers has. The couple can keep swapping slave and master: today one holds on, tomorrow the other gets even. Or it can cancel the purchase itself — stop asking “whose are you?” and start asking “who are you?”.

sections.h2: Clues in the numbers: a queen and a lion-tamer
paragraphs: A couple's tail is made of two personal tails, and 15-11-14 has only three such combinations: 6-17-11 + 9-12-3 (88% of couples), 12-16-4 + 3-13-10 (10%) and 6-14-8 + 9-15-6 (2%). Every number in them is a clue.

**Nobody brings the Devil.** In 98% of couples with this tail neither of the two personal tails contains a fifteen: the Devil appears only in the sum. Only in the rare combination 6-14-8 + 9-15-6 does it stand in the middle of one partner's personal tail. This couple's chain belongs to neither partner alone — the two forge it together, which is why looking for someone to blame in it is pointless.

**The entry: a hermit and lovers.** In 90% of couples the entry is the sum of 9 and 6: one partner's personal tail begins with the Hermit, the other's with the Lovers. Our reading: one comes into closeness from solitude, the other from the wish to merge. When these two wishes — to keep a distance and to be together — add up, a chain appears: one holds on for fear of losing, the other keeps a distance for fear of dissolving, and the harder the first pulls, the harder the second resists. In the remaining 10% the entry is the Hanged Man (12) and the Empress (3).

**A middle made of the ends.** In 88% of couples the middle is the Hanged Man and the Star (12 + 17), in 10% the Tower and Death (16 + 13). And in 2% it is Temperance and the Devil (14 + 15): in these couples the middle of the tail is literally built from its two ends, and Strength is born where the Devil meets Temperance.

**The main task: a queen and a lion-tamer.** In 88% of couples Temperance is 3 + 11: one partner's personal tail ends with the Empress, the other's with Strength. The myth puts a queen beside the man who killed the lion; the numbers put the same two cards side by side. We do not present this as a law: the meaning of a personal tail does not carry over to a couple's tail; the point is only what the number is made of. In 10% of couples the task is the sum of the Emperor and the Wheel of Fortune (4 + 10), in 2% of Justice and the Lovers (8 + 6).

sections.h2: The Sun at the centre: what daylight shows
paragraphs: A couple's centre is the atmosphere inside the union, what happens between the two when nobody is watching. In 80.7% of couples with this tail it holds the Sun, in 19.3% the Wheel of Fortune.

In Waite's list of divinatory meanings the Sun has three entries: “Material happiness, fortunate marriage, contentment.” At its best, Lisovskaya names for the Sun at a couple's centre respect, harmony, each partner's success in their own field, and the sense of one partner being under the other's protection. The Fasti has a picture for this: Heracles holding a golden parasol against the sun over Omphale. At its worst the same centre brings tyranny and total control, limits on the partner's self-realisation, comparisons. The Sun lights up what is already in the couple, and if the entry says “you're mine”, the light only makes it more visible.

One more observation from Ovid: the trick with the clothes works only in the dark. As soon as the lights were brought, “everything lay open”, and everyone laughed, Heracles included. This tail's Devil lives at night, in what is left unsaid. The Sun at the centre is laughter in daylight, when the swap of roles is visible to both and becomes a game rather than a trap.

The Wheel of Fortune at the centre (19.3%) is an atmosphere in which roles go round: the skin is on one partner today and on the other tomorrow. At its best Lisovskaya describes such an atmosphere as the feeling of a fated meeting and the ability to accept the partner in any state; at its worst, the two do not hear each other and blame fate.

sections.h2: The couple's values: the Empress, the World, the Hanged Man
paragraphs: The sphere “The couple's values” answers what the union exists for. In couples with the 15-11-14 tail it most often holds the Empress (52.9%), then the World (25.7%) and the Hanged Man (21.3%).

The Empress is a home, a full table, what grows and bears fruit; in Waite her list begins “Fruitfulness, action, initiative”. In the myth she is a queen in her own kingdom, and the value here is not power over the other but a shared household that feeds both. The World is a wholeness in which each has a place. The Hanged Man is the value of a pause and of a different angle: to stop and look at the familiar upside down. For a couple learning to swap roles this makes particular sense. The last two readings are ours.

sections.h2: Worked example: 19.03.1979 and 05.11.1975
paragraphs: The personal matrix for 19.03.1979 gives the tail 9-12-3 and the centre 6; the matrix for 05.11.1975 gives the tail 6-17-11 and the centre 13. The couple's points add up pair by pair:

In this tail the middle happens to equal the sum of its ends (15 + 14 = 29 → 11), but it is not worked out that way; it comes from the two personal middles, and here the match is a coincidence, not a rule. “The couple's values” here is the Empress (3).

For this couple the numbers of the tail also recur in other spheres. Temperance also stands in the sphere “Why you met”, at the point “What to create together” (3 + 11 = 14): what the couple has to learn and what it is here to create are one and the same. Strength also stands in the sphere “What fills the union” (22 + 16 = 38 → 11): the trial of strength does not only test these two, it also charges them. Not every couple with this tail has this — it belongs to these particular dates.
There are no other couple tails made of 15, 11 and 14: in the method this triple occurs only in this order.

sections.h2: How to live this tail at its best

ul: **Ask “who are you?”, not “whose are you?”.** Take an interest in what the partner wants, not only in where they have been. Diodorus puts this first: first know, then free.
**Agree who wears the skin where.** Money, renovation, relatives, holidays — each area has its own lead, and every few months this is reviewed out loud.

**Swap roles for real.** Whoever usually drives rides as a passenger for a week; whoever plans everything hands the planning over. Not as a punishment, but as in Omphale's cave: with supper and laughter.
**Laugh together, not at each other.** Laughter in daylight is this couple's Sun; mockery of the defeated is Strength at its worst.
**Leave each other a couch of your own.** Close people need the right to be side by side and apart: their own time, their own affairs, their own silence.
**Count who gives way.** If over a month it was always the same person, that is not peace but Temperance at its worst.
**Do not hold on.** Not with a gift, money, intimacy or a child. In Sophocles, the robe sent to bind ends up burning.

paragraphs: If “you're mine” turns into surveillance, threats or fear, it is no longer the story of the tail and not a task for patience. Then it is time for help from a psychologist, and in danger — a call to the local emergency number.

ul: **Entry to the task — 15, the Devil.** What the couple wants together and the language it speaks: “mine”, “all mine”, “I can't live without you”. The pull is real, and the same pull turns into resistance when the wish to be together becomes the wish to hold on.

**Middle of the task — 11, Strength.** How the couple moves on: through a trial of strength. Who decides, who gives way, who holds the power. At its best, strength passes from hand to hand and comes back; at its worst, it has to be proved.
**Main task — 14, Temperance.** Learning measure and exchange: the same person should not always give way, each should know the weight of the other's load, and neither should dissolve into the other.

intro: An ancient myth tells this path almost word for word. Heracles was sold as a slave to Omphale, queen of Lydia; she put on his lion skin, he sat down to her wool, and in one version it all ended in freedom and a wedding, in another in a new chain. What follows is an investigation: what the cards themselves say, what Waite, Wen and Lisovskaya write, and what the numbers show when every date is checked.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 15-11-14 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's task to travel from “you're mine” to “us”. The entry is the Devil: a strong pull and a wish to belong to each other that easily becomes a wish to own. The middle is Strength: a trial of strength and the question of who holds the power. The main task is Temperance: learning exchange and measure so that the same person does not always give way.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail describes a task, not a verdict, and it is read mostly through what there is to learn. The Devil at the entry gives this couple a rare power of attraction, Strength in the middle gives energy, and in 80.7% of such couples the Sun stands at the centre, which for Waite means, among other things, “fortunate marriage”. The difficulty is one: not to confuse closeness with ownership.

faq.q: Can 15-11-14 be a personal karmic tail?
faq.a: No. In a personal chart the entry to the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and with Temperance as the task, the Devil at the entry would need a centre of 1, the Magician. The Magician never appears at the centre of a personal matrix, so only two people can make this triple.

faq.q: Who is Heracles and who is Omphale in the couple?
faq.a: Both, in turn. The partners' sex does not assign the roles: either can wear the skin, and the whole meaning of the middle of the tail is that it moves from shoulders to shoulders. Getting stuck in one role — “I always decide” or “I always give way” — is exactly what this couple is learning to leave behind.

faq.q: How is the couple tail 15-11-14 calculated?
faq.a: Work out each partner's personal destiny matrix and add the matching points of their tails: entry to entry, middle to middle, main task to main task, reducing any sum above 22 by adding its digits. For example, 19.03.1979 and 05.11.1975 give 9 + 6 = 15, 12 + 17 = 29 → 11 and 3 + 11 = 14.

report: The strongest man of Greek myth was once sold. Heracles, ill after a killing done in a fit of madness, was sent into slavery by the oracle, and Omphale, queen of Lydia, bought him. She put on his lion skin; he sat down to her wool. The three acts of this myth repeat the 15-11-14 tail almost word for word: the purchase is the Devil, the lion skin on someone else's shoulders is Strength, the exchange of clothes is Temperance. No single person has this triple — only two people can make it — and it speaks not about the character of either partner but about the bond itself: how it travels from “you're mine” to “us”.

report.h3: Only a stranger can be owned

report: The entry to the tail is what the couple wants together, and its common language. Here it is the Devil's language: “my other half”, “you belong to me”, “I'm all yours”. The Romans made a whole genre of it: in love elegy the beloved is domina, a slave's mistress, and the lover is her slave. Tibullus complains: “chains hold me, and Love never loosens the bonds of the wretched.”

At the start of the union such words feel like the highest degree of closeness, and the pull in a couple with this tail is real. But the same wish turns into resistance. One partner is late at work, the other sends a third message in a row, and it no longer says “miss you” but “where are you”. A gift that makes it awkward to say no. The urge to hold on through intimacy, money, a shared child.

Diodorus has a detail that explains the mechanism. Heracles “willingly submitted to be sold”, and Omphale bought a slave without knowing who he was. **Ownership begins where a role stands in place of a person**, and “mine” often answers the question “whose are you?” that gets asked instead of “who are you?”. Yet the Devil here is not the vice of one partner. This couple's chain is forged by both, and looking for someone to blame in it is pointless.

report.h3: “You conquered the beast; she conquered you”

report: Strength stands in the middle of the tail, and the couple's path runs through the question “who wins?”. Omphale takes the club and the skin of the Nemean lion — armour no weapon could pierce. In Ovid, Heracles' wife Deianira writes to him: “You are deceived and do not know it: these are not the lion's spoils but yours. You conquered the beast; she conquered you.”

At its worst, Strength is a fight for leadership, each with their own truth, mockery of the defeated. Saint-Saëns, who wrote Omphale's Spinning Wheel, explained that the listener would hear “Hercules groaning in bonds he cannot break, and Omphale mocking the hero's vain efforts”. At its best, the two charge each other, and one accepts the other's lead where the other is stronger.

The myth also points to the next step. Heracles' “too-mighty hands” crushed the spindles: strength used to strangling lions cannot hold what is fine. The middle is passed not when someone has won but when **the skin can move from shoulders to shoulders and come back**.

report.h3: Two couches set side by side

report: The main task is Temperance, and it is read through what does not work: one partner always gives way and the other does not even think of it; one saves, the other spends. The most exact scene for this task is in Ovid's Fasti. In a cave Omphale dresses Heracles in her tunics and girdle. The girdle is too small; to free his hands he loosens the ties, the bracelets snap, his feet tear the sandal straps.

The Latin keeps a clue. Ovid's word for the ties is vincula, the same word as Tibullus' “bonds”. In the elegy Love never loosens the bonds; in the cave Heracles loosens them himself. **A chain stops being a chain when the two take turns wearing it.**

Then they lie down to sleep “on couches set side by side, apart”: a rite awaits in the morning, and they must come to it pure. Side by side and not merged — not one cup for two but two cups, with movement between them. At midnight goat-legged Faunus creeps into the cave. He gropes the lion skin and pulls his hand back in fear, finds soft cloth, climbs onto the couch — and Heracles throws him to the floor. Lights are brought, and everyone laughs. The horned god goes by signs, and swapping roles leaves him nothing to hold on to. And Heracles in a woman's tunic is still Heracles: the exchange does not take strength away, it teaches when to use it.

report.h3: The chain is passed on or taken off

report: The myth has two endings. In Sophocles, Heracles comes back sworn to enslave the man he blames, and tragedy follows: his wife, afraid of losing him, sends him a robe meant to bring back his love, and the robe burns him like fire. The one who was bought starts buying. In Diodorus, Omphale learns who stands before her, marvels at him, sets him free — and only then marries him. **First know, then free, then choose.**
This is not a forecast but two directions open to a couple with this tail. What helps to choose the second:

ul: asking what the partner wants, not only where they have been;
agreeing who leads in which area, and reviewing it out loud from time to time;
swapping roles for real, not as a punishment, with supper and laughter;
laughing together, not at each other;
