leaving each other the right to be side by side and apart;
noticing who gave way over the last month: if it was always the same person, that is not peace but Temperance at its worst;
not holding on with a gift, money or intimacy.

report: If “you're mine” turns into surveillance, threats or fear, it is no longer the story of the tail and not a task for patience. Then it is time for help from a psychologist, and in danger — a call to a local emergency number or crisis line.

seo.title: Karmic tail 15 11 5 compatibility: The Devil, Strength, The Hierophant
seo.description: Karmic tail 15 11 5 compatibility: The Devil, Strength and The Hierophant in a couple's matrix, read through Beauty and the Beast, with a worked example.

items.title: Karmic tail 15-11-5 in compatibility: the secret of Beauty and the Beast
items.short: In the first printed Beauty and the Beast (1740) the Beast asks the same question every evening: will Beauty let him sleep with her. Sixteen years later the governess Leprince de Beaumont retold the tale for her pupils and rewrote the question: "Beauty, will you be my wife?" The couple's karmic tail 15-11-5 is the road between those two questions: from a desire that holds two people like a chain, through the long taming of fear, to the word, the marriage and the families before whom the union has to be named.

sections.h2: One tale in three versions
paragraphs: Most people know Beauty and the Beast from the cartoon, and the cartoon grew out of Beaumont's retelling. But the first to write it was Gabrielle-Suzanne de Villeneuve: in 1740 she placed a long, almost novel-length story in her collection La Jeune Américaine et les contes marins (The Young American and Sea Tales). In Villeneuve, after supper the Beast bluntly asks Beauty whether she will let him sleep with her. The first time she cries out: "Ah, heaven! I am lost." After that the question comes every evening, and the author simply calls it "the usual question".

Jeanne-Marie Leprince de Beaumont, a Frenchwoman working as a governess in England, abridged the tale in 1756 for her Magasin des enfants, known in English as The Young Misses Magazine. It is a textbook written as conversations between a wise governess and her pupils: geography, history, Scripture, and fairy tales in between. Here the Beast's question is different: "Beauty, will you be my wife?" — "No, Beast!" For three months it is asked every evening at nine o'clock. In 1761 the book was translated into Russian as Detskoe uchilishche, "The Children's School, or Moral Conversations between a Wise Teacher and Her Noble Pupils of Various Ages".

The third version is Russian. As a child, Sergei Aksakov heard the tale "not once but dozens of times" from the housekeeper Pelageya. As a schoolboy, lying in the school infirmary, he borrowed Detskoe uchilishche, reached "Beauty and the Beast" and, in his words, recognised his own Alenky tsvetochek (The Scarlet Flower) "from the first lines". He wrote it down in old age and published it in 1858 as an appendix to The Childhood Years of Bagrov the Grandson. In Aksakov there is no question at all: until the last page the monster says nothing of marriage and speaks to the merchant's daughter in letters of fire on a marble wall.

The three versions take the tail apart. In Villeneuve the entry sounds loudest — bodily desire. In Aksakov the middle takes up most of the room — getting used to each other. In Beaumont everything comes down to the main task — the question of marriage and a lesson in what a husband should be.

sections.h2: A curse written in the order of the cards
paragraphs: The strangest clue lies in the second half of Villeneuve's novel, which almost nobody reads. There the prince tells how he became the Beast. He was raised by a fairy protector. When he grew up she demanded his hand, and he refused: "I do not want to lose my freedom so soon." The fairy struck him on the head, and his hands became paws. This is the curse she laid on him (our translation):

"I order you to appear as stupid as you are hideous, and to wait in this state until a young and beautiful girl comes to find you of her own free will, though she is convinced you will devour her. It is also necessary that, once she no longer fears for her life, she grows fond enough of you to propose marriage to you herself."

The sentence holds three conditions, and they come in the order of the tail 15-11-5. To come of one's own will to the place where ruin waits is The Devil, a voluntary captivity. To stop being afraid is Strength: both Waite and Wen see in it a mastery not over an outer beast, but over passions and fear. To propose marriage herself is The Hierophant, a union sealed by a word.

At parting the fairy added a fourth rule: "you must forget who you are. If you let yourself be flattered by empty honours or grand titles, you are lost." This is The Hierophant too, only in its minus: ranks, status, other people's approval.

So the Beast's story begins with a marriage demanded by an older woman with power over him, and ends with a marriage proposed of free will. Both bonds belong to the fifth card. Between them stand a palace where everything is given at once and long evenings in which people learn to be less afraid.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: a palace where every wish comes true
paragraphs: For Lisovskaya the entry M is what the couple strives for together: shared wishes, agreements, a "common language". The point sits on the line of tasks, so the same wish can also become resistance. With The Devil at the entry, a couple enters its task through a strong bond: "I want everything, and now", "you are mine", "I will never let you go".

The Beast's palace works exactly like this. In Aksakov the merchant merely thinks, "All very fine, but there is nothing to eat" (Aksakov is quoted here in our translation) — and a laid table rises before him. He wants to sleep — and a bed of pure gold appears. To the daughter the monster writes on the wall: "whatever you wish, whatever comes into your mind, I will gladly do." Wen puts it plainly: The Devil is "preference for instant gratification over delayed gratification". The palace grants a wish before anyone has managed to say it aloud.

For couples with this tail the beginning is often like that palace. Messages until three in the morning, presents nobody asked for, each other's keys within a month. It feels as if the other person guesses what one wants, so words can be saved. The danger is right there: a wish that is never spoken stays unknown, and later turns into resentment. Among the tasks of the fifteenth energy Lisovskaya names silence about one's own wishes and attempts to hold a partner through closeness, money or status. The palace feeds, dresses, entertains — and holds.

In Aksakov the entry to the task is framed as a bargain. The merchant picked the flower without asking, so he owes a debt. The monster demands "your honest merchant's word and a pledge in your own hand": to send one of his daughters in his place. And at once he sets a condition that breaks the whole contract: "I want no bondmaid: let your daughter come here out of love for you, of her own will and wish." A captivity one can only enter of one's own will is exactly The Devil at the entry to a couple's tail. The bond begins as a chain, but people put this chain on themselves.

The first letters of fire on the wall speak the language of this card turned inside out: "I am not your master but your obedient slave. You are my mistress." Master and slave is The Devil's vocabulary, only here the stronger one calls himself the slave. In a couple this vocabulary can be tender and can be heavy: "I'm all yours", "you'd be nowhere without me", "I gave up everything for you". While it is tender, it looks like love. Once it turns into a tally, it becomes a chain.

In its plus, The Devil at the entry holds the couple's deepest wish: to be accepted together with one's beast. Each brings into the union something they themselves find unsightly: a quick temper, a past nobody mentions, a fear of poverty, a habit of vanishing for a day. In the plus of the fifteenth energy Lisovskaya writes of couples who accept each other's dark sides and forgive mistakes. The condition is the same in all three tales: to love "in the shape of a monster".

And one detail from outside the tale. Pelageya, from whom Aksakov heard The Scarlet Flower, ran away from her former masters to Astrakhan with her father when she was very young and lived there for more than twenty years. On learning that she had "passed" to Aksakov's grandfather, she came back from her flight of her own accord. The grandfather, Aksakov writes, received her kindly "out of respect for so voluntary a return". The tale of a voluntary captivity was told by a woman who had chosen to come back herself. The question at the entry to this tail is not "is there passion" but what in this bond is free will and what is a chain.

The numbers add their own clue: neither partner brings The Devil into the couple. The couple's entry is the sum of the entries of the partners' personal tails, and there one partner has The Hanged Man and the other The Empress (63% of such couples), or one has The Lovers and the other The Hermit (37%). Neither personal tail contains a fifteen, as with other couples who have The Devil at the entry. The palace appears only when the two meet.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: letters of fire, a voice, twilight
paragraphs: Lisovskaya gives the middle N no meaning of its own; it is an "addition" to the main task. We read it as the road: what the couple does to get from the entry to the main task. In this tail the road is Strength.

In Aksakov the taming goes step by step, and no step can be skipped. At first there are only letters of fire. Then a voice — "loud, rough and hoarse", and even then the monster speaks "in an undertone". The merchant's daughter "shuddered at first", but "mastered her fear and did not let it show that she was frightened". Then she asks him to show himself. He agrees only to twilight, when the sun has set behind the forest, and passes at a distance, across the path. She screams and falls senseless. Coming round, she hears someone weeping beside her: "You have destroyed me, my beloved beauty." And then "she mastered her great fear".

Wen opens her reading of Strength in almost the same words: "The Strength card is about domination over the Seeker's fears." And further: "the Seeker cannot use brute force to exercise will over others; the Seeker must use gentle, subtle influence." So it is in the tale: the monster never once raises a paw against her. It is not he who is tamed. What is tamed is fear: hers of his face, his of her leaving.

Both need Strength, and in the Beast it is even more visible. In Beaumont he asks his question every evening for three months and every evening hears "no". In Villeneuve Beauty notes that the Beast "does not persist in his requests and shows no resentment at my refusals". When the prince later complains to the fairy that Beauty will never accept such a proposal, the fairy answers only: "Patience, perseverance, or all is lost." This is Strength in the old sense: fortitude. To ask and hear "no" without revenge is the central skill of the middle of this tail.

Waite's list of meanings for Strength includes the word "magnanimity". In the tale it takes the shape of a ring under the pillow. Agreeing to show himself, the monster says: "I do not want your bondage and endless torment: in your bedchamber, under your pillow, you will find my golden ring." He himself leaves her the key to the way out. The Devil's chain holds; Strength leaves the chance to leave, and that is why the person stays.

In a couple's life the middle of the task looks ordinary. One day a roar breaks through: one partner snaps after a hard day, the other wants to "fall senseless" — slam the door, go back to their mother, go silent for a week. Strength means staying and saying: "I'm frightened when you shout." And for the other, learning to speak in an undertone. Among the tasks of the eleventh energy Lisovskaya names what takes months in the tale: saying from the very start what one likes and what one doesn't, and showing feelings openly. In the minus she has the struggle for leadership and inflated demands on a partner's looks and status. The last sounds almost like a retelling of the tale: "put on something decent, you don't come to my family dressed like that."

There is also the opposite minus: mistaking for taming a patience that silently stores up fear. Beauty and the Beast is not a manual for endurance. In all three versions the Beast does not touch her and hands over the ring himself. If someone in a couple fears for their safety, if there are threats or violence, this is not a story about taming: help is needed — a local emergency number or crisis line, a psychologist.

The numbers say two things about the middle. Strength in the middle of a couple's tail is always assembled from two other cards — from the middles of the personal tails. In 63% of such couples these are The Tower and The Fool: a collapse and a step into the unknown. That is how the tale begins: in Beaumont the merchant loses his fortune at a stroke, and the daughter goes of her own accord to a place nobody expects to return from. The second thing is more surprising. In the same 63% Strength already stands in the centre of one partner's personal chart, while the other has Justice in the centre — the very two cards that Waite swapped. Together they give The Sun in the centre of the couple.

sections.h2: Main task: the word, the sisters and the clocks set back an hour
paragraphs: For Lisovskaya the main task D is read mostly through its minus: what the couple fails at and what it has to learn. With The Hierophant this means family, custom, rule and the word once given. In all three versions the danger at the end comes not from the beast but from the relatives, and the relatives have one weapon — time and the word.

In Aksakov the daughter is allowed home for three days and three nights. Her father blesses her, and it is agreed that she will leave an hour before the deadline. "It vexed" the elder sisters: they "set every clock in the house back a full hour". When the true hour comes, her heart "began to ache and wring", while the sisters ask her "about this and that" and hold her back. She puts on the ring by the slow clocks and, appearing in the palace, cries out that she has returned "a whole hour and a minute before the appointed time". The monster lies on the hillock, his paws around the scarlet flower, "lifeless".

In Beaumont Beauty promises to return in eight days. The sisters plot to keep her longer: "Her stupid Beast will fly into a rage when he finds she has broken her word, and will very likely devour her." They tear their hair, feigning grief, and she promises to remain another eight days. In Villeneuve the spell is already broken and the beast is gone — and then the prince's mother enters the hall. On learning who the bride is, the queen steps back two paces: "What! You are only a merchant's daughter!" — and calls such a marriage "an alliance so shameful for us". The beast has vanished; the relatives remain.

For a couple with this tail, the sisters with the clocks rarely look like villains. A mother rings on Saturday morning: "You are coming, aren't you? At least till the evening." The evening becomes a night, the night becomes a week "all together as a family". The parents have a key to the flat they helped pay for, and they come when it suits them. A sister discusses what the partner is wearing; one of the parents explains how the renovation ought to be done. No clock is ever set back more than an hour, but hour by hour the couple is late for itself. For Lisovskaya the tasks of the fifth energy in a couple are almost all about the same thing: parents, relatives, the partner's family. In the tale all of it fits into one scene with the clocks.

The way out is not to break with the family. Aksakov's daughter leaves each time with her father's blessing, and at the end "the honest merchant gave his blessing". The task is subtler: the two of them set the deadline, and the word they have given each other weighs more than other people's clocks. Lisovskaya advises a couple with the fifth energy to get on with the relatives without letting them inside the couple's borders, and to create holidays and places of their own.

The second half of the task is to name the union. Begging the monster to show himself, Aksakov's heroine tries every name of kinship: "If you are an old man, be a grandfather to me; if middle-aged, be an uncle to me; if you are young, be my sworn brother; and as long as I live, be my heart's friend." Any name will do except one. Only the last one breaks the spell: "Rise, wake up, my heart's friend, I love you as my desired bridegroom!" The condition of the curse, as the prince explains afterwards, is that a girl should love him in the shape of a monster "and wish to be my lawful wife". In Beaumont the same thing is said as a vow: "Here and now I offer you my hand, and swear that I will marry none but you."

In the two words "desired bridegroom" both ends of the tail meet. "Desired" comes from the entry, from The Devil. "Bridegroom" comes from the main task, from The Hierophant. Waite calls The Hierophant "the channel of grace belonging to the world of institution as distinct from that of Nature". Aksakov's monster is a "beast of the forest, wonder of the sea", nature itself, forest and sea. The main task is to bring him into the world of institution: to say aloud, in front of people, who he is. For a modern couple this is our reading, and it need not mean a wedding. The Hierophant asks for a name and a form: who we are to each other, what we promise, which rules in this home are ours. Couples with this tail can live for years as "heart's friends" — together but without a name, while the relatives call the partner "that one of yours".

The form itself has a minus too. Villeneuve's queen measures the union by rank, and the fairy has to reveal that Beauty is in fact a king's daughter. Aksakov's curse cancels this in advance: the maiden may be "of whatever birth and rank she might be". The law is needed; rank is not. And Beaumont shows another temptation of the fifth card — the lesson. "It is neither good looks nor brains in a husband that make a woman happy; it is beauty of character, virtue, kindness," Beauty reasons. Wen writes that "The Hierophant is about the pedagogy of wisdom". A couple with this tail would do well to watch that the union does not become a school where one teaches the other how to be.

And the last thing. The disenchanted prince in Aksakov says: "You loved me in the shape of a hideous monster… now love me in human shape." The good fairy in Beaumont, handing Beauty a crown, adds: "I hope that the pomp of royalty will not destroy your virtues." The Hierophant's task does not end with the vow; it begins with it: to love an ordinary person in an everyday home, without the palace and the letters of fire.

Here too the numbers have left a trace. The couple's main task is the sum of the partners' personal karmic tasks, and in 63% of such couples these are The Emperor and The Sun. Our reading: in the main task the order of the father's house meets a new life — the merchant and his youngest, best-loved daughter.

sections.h2: How the circle closes
paragraphs: In its minus the tail runs in a circle, and each turn shows its own card.

ol: Desire binds quickly. A palace where everything comes true without words, and silence about what one really wants (15).
The beast shows itself: a temper, jealousy, the past. One partner tries to tame by force — control and conditions — the other falls senseless: goes silent, leaves (11 in its minus).
To decide who is right, the couple calls in rules from outside: "normal people don't do this", "let's ask Mum" (5 in its minus).

The relatives take a side and set the clocks back. The two make up where they began — in the palace: with closeness, with a present, without words. Nothing has been named, and the circle starts again.

paragraphs: The price of such a circle is years spent between honeymoon and quarrel, without a name or rules of their own. Every dispute is decided by other people's clocks, and the wishes are never said aloud.

sections.h2: The Sun in the centre: why the Beast comes at twilight
paragraphs: In 71.4% of couples with the tail 15-11-5 The Sun stands in the centre of the matrix. In a personal matrix The Sun never falls in the centre, for any date of birth: this card appears in the centre only for a couple. The centre is "The atmosphere inside the couple", what lies between two people when nobody is watching.

In the tale the Beast lives at twilight. In Aksakov he shows himself only "when the red sun sets behind the forest". In Beaumont he comes at nine in the evening. In Villeneuve the real prince visits Beauty only in her dreams. And at the very moment Beaumont's vow is spoken, the castle suddenly becomes "ablaze with lights". The tale moves from twilight to light, and the couple's centre stands where the tale ends. Our reading: inside such a couple the beast finds it hard to hide in the half-dark for long. A sunlit atmosphere makes everything visible, and the beast has to be met in daylight, not at dusk.

In the remaining 28.6% the centre holds The Wheel of Fortune: fate that turns. Beaumont's tale also begins with a turn of the wheel — the merchant loses his fortune at a stroke, and later carries a chest of gold away from the palace.

"The couple's values" in such couples are most often The Empress (55.6%), less often The Hanged Man (25.4%) and The World (19%). The Empress is a garden where things grow if they are tended. The scarlet flower grows in a garden on a hillock, and it is there that the merchant's daughter finds the monster for the last time. The Hanged Man recalls the very first turn of the plot: the daughter goes to the beast "in his stead", taking on another's fate of her own free will.

sections.h2: What Waite saw: a beast above people, a woman with a beast, people without a beast
paragraphs: On Waite's card of The Devil a horned figure stands on an altar, and chains run from a ring on the altar to the necks of a man and a woman. The chained figures have tails, "to signify the animal nature, but there is human intelligence in the faces". Of the one exalted above them Waite writes that he "is not to be their master for ever. Even now, he is also a bondsman" — like the monster who writes on the wall that he is a slave. And tails beneath human faces are the Beast of the tale: an animal body and a human mind that he is forbidden to show. In Beaumont the wicked fairy "forbade me to betray any sign of intelligence"; in Villeneuve she ordered him "to appear as stupid as you are hideous". That is why the Beast's question in Villeneuve is so crude. Later the prince admits that he spoke in words the fairy had "chosen on purpose to be low and childish".

On the card of Strength (VIII for Waite, 11 in the matrix) a woman is closing a lion's jaws, and the lion follows her on a chain of flowers. For Waite, "her beneficent fortitude has already subdued the lion": the picture shows not a fight but what comes after it. He explains: "There is one aspect in which the lion signifies the passions, and she who is called Strength is the higher nature in its liberation." The beast is still in the picture, but it is no longer above people; it is beside a human being.

On the card of The Hierophant there is no beast. The high priest sits between pillars, crossed keys at his feet, two ministers kneeling before him. The three cards of the tail show where the beast goes: first it is above people, then beside a woman, then it is gone. In the tale it vanishes at the very moment the vow is spoken.

sections.h2: Worked example: the couple's tail for 09.05.1976 and 14.04.1975
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the matching points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22. First the personal tails are calculated.
The year is reduced by adding its digits: 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5, and 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Now the couple's tail:

This is the most common version of the tail: the personal tails 12-16-4 and 3-22-19 produce it in 63% of cases. One partner has Strength in the centre and the other Justice, so the couple's centre is 11 + 8 = 19, The Sun. "The couple's values" here are The Hanged Man, 12.

This couple has a rare detail. The Hierophant stands not only in the main task but also in the spheres "How others see the couple" (9 + 14 = 23 → 5) and "What fills the union" (14 + 18 = 32 → 5). Three or more fives occur in only 3% of couples with this tail. Lisovskaya advises adding up repeated energies: 5 + 5 + 5 = 15. The sum gives The Devil again — the card of the entry. Anyone who likes such coincidences will see the whole tale in them: marriage, custom and family, added together, lead back to the desire where it all began.

sections.h2: Why 15-11-5 is never a personal tail
paragraphs: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail equals the sum of the entry and the main task. From 15 and 5 that would give 20, the tail 15-20-5 with Judgement in the middle. In a couple the middle is not recalculated: it is added up from the middles of the partners' personal tails, and the result is 11. So 15-11-5 exists only for a couple, and the Strength in its middle is something no single person carries in their own tail.

No other couple's tails are made of the same three numbers: the calculation never produces the permutations 5-11-15 or 11-15-5. If Lisovskaya's book or another calculator shows 5-11-15, it is the same tail written in reverse order, from the main task to the entry.

sections.h2: The strong version: a ring on one's own finger
paragraphs: In the strong version of the tail all three cards remain, but they change sign. The Devil becomes attachment in the good sense: the two know each other's dark sides and do not turn them into weapons. Strength becomes the ability to hold without a chain. The Hierophant becomes a union with its own rules, where the relatives are loved but only the owners of the house set its clocks.
What helps a couple through this tail:

ul: say wishes aloud instead of waiting for the palace to guess;
ask, and hear "no" without punishment — the Beast heard it for three months;
leave each other a "ring under the pillow": the right to go to one's family and come back;
set the deadlines with relatives together and keep the word once given, even if someone's clocks run slow;
do not turn the union into a school: no lecturing, no remaking each other;
name the union in one's own words: who we are to each other and what we promise.

paragraphs: In the tale it is she who speaks the last word, but in a couple with this tail the roles are not divided by sex. Each of the two, on some evening, is the Beast who asks and the Beauty who decides whether to say "yes".

Aksakov's ring works on one condition only: "whoever puts it on the little finger of the right hand will find himself wherever he wishes." It is not put on someone else; it is put on oneself. That is the difference between a chain and a vow. A chain is put on another person. A ring a person puts on themselves, and it leads to the place they have chosen to return to.

ul: **15 — The Devil, "Entry to the task".** Where the couple starts and what it wants together: to be everything to each other, to have it all at once, to belong. This is its common language and its first resistance.

**11 — Strength, "Middle of the task".** What the couple goes through: taming. Not chaining the "beast" and not running from it, but learning to stay close to fear, anger and jealousy — one's own and the other's.

**5 — The Hierophant, "Main task".** What the couple has to learn: to turn a bond into a union with its own word and its own rules, with parents, relatives, customs and other people's clocks all around.

intro: The secret of this tail is hidden in the tale itself. The spell is broken not by a kiss and not by beauty, but by one word spoken of one's own free will. The Devil's chain and The Hierophant's vow bind two people equally tightly. The difference between them is settled in the middle, on the card of Strength: is a person being held, or do they stay of their own accord.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 15-11-5 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of a couple's matrix, the main line of its tasks. **At the entry stands The Devil**: the couple begins with a strong desire and attachment, which can become both a common language and a chain. **In the middle stands Strength**: the road leads through taming fear, anger and jealousy without brute force. **The main task is The Hierophant**: to build a union with its own word and rules and to keep its borders in the face of relatives and other people's customs.

faq.q: Is the 15-11-5 tail bad compatibility?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail shows tasks, not a verdict, and the method gives no compatibility percentages. The Devil at the entry does not mean addiction or violence: it is a theme of desire and freedom that the couple works through together. In their strong version the same three cards describe a deep attachment, the ability to hold without a chain, and a union with rules of its own.

faq.q: Is the tail 5-11-15 the same tail?
faq.a: Yes, it is the same tail written in reverse order. On the site a couple's tail is read from the entry to the main task — M, N, D — while Lisovskaya writes it in her book from the main task: D, D2, D1. No other couple's tails are made of the numbers 15, 11 and 5.

faq.q: Does the 15-11-5 tail occur in a personal matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is the sum of the entry and the main task, and 15 and 5 would give the tail 15-20-5. In a couple the middle is added up from the middles of the two personal tails, so Strength in the middle is possible only for a couple.

faq.q: How common is the couple's tail 15-11-5?
faq.a: About one couple in 208 has it, which is 0.481% of all couples and 55th place among the 97 couple's tails. Most often it is formed by the personal tails 12-16-4 and 3-22-19 (63% of such couples), less often by 6-8-20 and 9-3-21 (28%), 6-20-14 and 9-9-18 (9%), and 6-20-14 and 9-18-9 (1%).

report: In the first printed Beauty and the Beast (1740) the Beast asks Beauty every evening whether she will let him sleep with her. Sixteen years later the governess Leprince de Beaumont retold the tale for her pupils and rewrote the question: "Beauty, will you be my wife?" The couple's karmic tail 15-11-5 is the road between those two questions: from a desire that holds two people like a chain, through the long taming of fear, to the word, the marriage and the families.

In the second half of the first version, by Gabrielle-Suzanne de Villeneuve, the prince tells how he became the Beast. The fairy who raised him demanded his hand, and he refused: "I do not want to lose my freedom so soon." The curse ran like this: wait until a young beauty comes to him of her own free will, though convinced he will devour her, and then, "once she no longer fears for her life", grows fond enough of him to propose marriage herself. **The three conditions come in the order of the cards of the tail.** To come of one's own will to the place where ruin waits is The Devil. To stop being afraid is Strength. To propose marriage is The Hierophant.

report.h3: A captivity entered of one's own free will

report: In Aksakov's The Scarlet Flower, the Russian version of the same tale, the palace grants a wish before anyone has managed to say it aloud: "whatever you wish, whatever comes into your mind, I will gladly do." Wen calls The Devil a "preference for instant gratification over delayed gratification". For a couple with this tail the beginning is often like that palace: messages until three in the morning, presents nobody asked for, a sense that the other guesses everything without words. The danger is right there: a wish that is never spoken stays unknown, and later turns into resentment. The palace feeds, dresses, entertains — and holds.

In Aksakov the entry to the task is framed as a bargain: the merchant picked the flower without asking and must send a daughter in his place. And at once the monster sets a condition that breaks the whole contract: "I want no bondmaid: let your daughter come here out of love for you, of her own will and wish." **The bond begins as a chain, but people put this chain on themselves.** The first letters of fire on the wall speak The Devil's language turned inside out: "I am not your master but your obedient slave." In a couple this vocabulary can be tender — "I'm all yours" — and it can be heavy — "I gave up everything for you". Once it turns into a tally, it becomes a chain.

In its plus, The Devil at the entry holds the couple's deepest wish: for a person to be accepted together with their beast — a quick temper, a past nobody mentions, a fear of poverty. The condition is the same in every version of the tale: to love "in the shape of a monster".

report.h3: It is fear that gets tamed, not the beast

report: In Aksakov the taming goes step by step: first letters of fire, then a voice, "loud, rough and hoarse", then a meeting at twilight, when the sun has set behind the forest. The merchant's daughter screams and falls senseless, and on coming round she hears someone weeping beside her. And then "she mastered her great fear". Wen writes about Strength in almost the same words: "The Strength card is about domination over the Seeker's fears." The monster never once raises a paw against her. It is not he who is tamed but fear: hers of his face, his of her leaving.

In Beaumont the Beast asks his question every evening for three months and every evening hears "no". When the prince in Villeneuve complains to the fairy that Beauty will never accept such a proposal, the fairy answers only: "Patience, perseverance, or all is lost." **To ask and hear "no" without revenge is the central skill of the middle of this tail.** And the "magnanimity" that Waite lists among the meanings of Strength takes the shape of a ring under the pillow in the tale: the monster himself leaves her the key to the way out. A chain holds; Strength leaves the chance to leave, and that is why the person stays.

Beauty and the Beast is not a manual for endurance: in every version the Beast does not touch her and hands over the ring himself. If someone in a couple fears for their safety, if there are threats or violence, help is needed — a local emergency number or crisis line, a psychologist.

report.h3: The sisters set back the clocks

report: The main task is read mostly through its minus, and at the end of the tale the danger comes not from the beast but from the relatives. In Aksakov the elder sisters "set every clock in the house back a full hour", and the heroine returns to the palace sure that she is in time — and the monster lies "lifeless". In Beaumont the sisters hold Beauty back so that she breaks her word. In Villeneuve the spell is already broken, and the prince's mother steps back two paces: the bride is "only a merchant's daughter". The beast has vanished; the relatives remain.

For a couple with this tail, the sisters with the clocks rarely look like villains: "at least till the evening", the evening becomes a night, the night becomes a week "all together as a family". No clock is ever set back more than an hour, but hour by hour the couple is late for itself. The way out is not a break with the family — Aksakov's daughter leaves each time with her father's blessing. **The two of them set the deadline, and the word they have given each other weighs more than other people's clocks.**

report.h3: The spell is broken by a word

report: Aksakov's heroine tries every name of kinship for the monster: "be a grandfather to me", "be an uncle to me", "be my sworn brother", "be my heart's friend". Only the last word breaks the spell: "I love you as my desired bridegroom!" In those two words both ends of the tail meet: "desired" comes from The Devil, "bridegroom" from The Hierophant. The main task is to name the union: who we are to each other, what we promise, which rules in this home are ours. And to remember the words of the disenchanted prince: "now love me in human shape" — without the palace and the letters of fire.

Aksakov's ring works on one condition: "whoever puts it on the little finger of the right hand will find himself wherever he wishes." **A chain is put on another person. A ring a person puts on themselves**, and it leads to the place they have chosen to return to.

unit.title: A ring, not a chain

captions.M: Want everything at once, without words
captions.N: Tame fear and hear "no" without revenge
captions.D: Name your union and keep your word against others' clocks

unit.meaning: Your task is to go from a desire that chains to a union with your own word: name who you are and set deadlines together.

seo.title: Karmic tail 15 14 8 compatibility: the Pygmalion story
seo.description: Karmic tail 15 14 8 compatibility: The Devil, Temperance and Justice, with The Tower at the centre of every such couple. A story of two people who sculpt each other.

items.title: Karmic tail 15-14-8 in compatibility: a couple who sculpt each other
items.short: The three numbers 15-14-8 in compatibility are The Devil, Temperance and Justice, and every couple with this tail has The Tower at the centre of its matrix. This is the Pygmalion story told for two: the couple is drawn together by the wish to make each other their own, the road runs through a slow mutual recasting, and the main task is to see in the partner not one's own handiwork but a separate person with a design of their own. The Tower at the centre is the moment when the invented image collapses and a living person turns out to be underneath.

sections.h2: First clue: a middle that one person never has
paragraphs: Each point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The couple's middle is not recalculated from the two ends: it is added up from the partners' middles. A personal matrix follows a different rule: the middle of the tail is the sum of the entry and the main task. By that formula 15 and 8 would give 23 → 5, The Hierophant, and that personal tail, 15-5-8, exists. One person never has the tail 15-14-8.

Running through every date since 1900 shows where the fourteen comes from. The tail 15-14-8 arises from a single combination of personal tails: one partner has 6-5-17, the other 9-9-18. That holds for one hundred per cent of such couples. The cards add up in pairs, and in our reading each sum is a small story:

ul: **The Lovers of one and The Hermit of the other give The Devil.** The wish for union plus the habit of solitude: the love of a recluse who makes himself a beloved.

**The Hierophant of one and The Hermit of the other give Temperance.** The teacher is there — The Hierophant stands in one partner's personal tail. But in the couple he is blended with The Hermit, and instead of a lectern there are two cups.
**The Star of one and The Moon of the other give 35, that is, Justice.** The ideal and the imagination are laid on the two pans of the scales.
**The Chariot of one and The Hermit of the other give The Tower at the centre.** Triumph plus withdrawal — and a fall.

paragraphs: One more clue is The Hermit. In one partner's numbers he stands three times: at the entry and the middle of the personal tail and at the centre of the personal chart. So in the couple's sums he appears three times — at the entry, in the middle and at the centre. A person with their own lamp, used to their own company, meets a person with The Lovers at the entry, The Hierophant in the middle and The Chariot at the centre. This is not a portrait and not a casting of roles: the numbers speak of the themes each brings into the couple, not of who is right.
Both personal tails are rare: 6-5-17 falls to about one date in 57, 9-9-18 to one in 50. Hence the rarity of the couple's tail: about one couple in 1,419 has it (0.07%), and it ranks 86th of 97.

sections.h2: Ovid: a statue no woman could be born like
paragraphs: The best-known story of a man who made himself a beloved is in the tenth book of Ovid's Metamorphoses (X, 243–297). Orpheus sings it, and it comes straight after two short tales of Cyprus: the Cerastae, who had horns growing on their foreheads, and the Propoetides, the first women to sell their bodies, who were turned to stone. Horns and stone, right at the threshold.

Pygmalion had seen the Propoetides and, in Henry Riley's 1851 prose translation, "he lived a single life without a wife, and for a long time was without a partner of his bed". A hermit. From snow-white ivory he carved a woman and gave her a form "qua femina nasci nulla potest" — in Riley's words, "a beauty with which no woman can be born". And he fell in love with his own work.

Ovid then describes the love of a maker for his piece with details that anyone will recognise who has ever loved their dream of a person more than the person. Pygmalion touches the statue and will not admit to himself that it is ivory. "He gives it kisses, and fancies that they are returned." He is afraid his fingers will leave a bruise on her. He brings presents: shells, smooth pebbles, little birds, flowers, amber — the "tears of the Heliades" — rings, necklaces, earrings. He dresses her, lays her on purple coverlets and "calls her the companion of his bed".

At the feast of Venus he does not dare to ask for the statue itself: he prays for a wife and "did not dare to say 'this ivory maid,' but 'like to this statue of ivory.'" Venus understands. At home the ivory grows warm under his hand: "The pressed ivory becomes soft, and losing its hardness, yields to the fingers, and gives way, just as Hymettian wax grows soft in the sun, and being worked with the fingers is turned into many shapes, and becomes pliable by the very handling." The girl who has come alive blushes and, "raising her timorous eyes towards the light of day, she sees at once her lover and the heavens." For the first time she has a gaze of her own — and there Ovid leaves her. What she thinks of her maker the poet never says. She has no name either: the statue would be called Galatea only in the eighteenth century.

The three moves of this story are the three cards of the tail. To make a person to one's own measure and love one's own handiwork is The Devil. To soften the ivory not by force but by warmth and repetition, until the material becomes "pliable by the very handling", is Temperance. The girl who looks for herself for the first time is the beginning of Justice: the second one now has an opinion of the first.

In Riley's English prose translation of 1851 this fable is followed by an "Explanation": the story is most probably an allegory of a man of virtuous principles who "took a great deal of care in training the mind and conduct of a young female", kept her from the prevailing vices and then made her his wife. Some sixty years later Bernard Shaw put that allegory on the stage — and asked what Ovid leaves unsaid.

sections.h2: Shaw: a deal for a shilling
paragraphs: Shaw's Pygmalion was first performed in 1913 in Vienna, in German, and in the spring of 1914 in London, with Herbert Beerbohm Tree as Higgins and Mrs Patrick Campbell as Eliza.

It all begins with a deal, and in it each wants something from the other. The flower girl Eliza Doolittle comes to Henry Higgins, professor of phonetics, in Wimpole Street to buy lessons: she wants to be "a lady in a flower shop" and offers a shilling an hour. Higgins works out that this is two-fifths of her day's income and declares it "the biggest offer I ever had". Colonel Pickering bets the expenses of the whole experiment. Higgins catches fire: "I shall make a duchess of this draggletailed guttersnipe." Eliza's father leaves with five pounds, and later Higgins says of her: "She doesn't belong to him. I paid him five pounds for her."

Higgins's mother, having listened to her son and Pickering, calls them "a pretty pair of babies, playing with your live doll". Higgins and Pickering talk over each other about what they do: teaching Eliza, dressing Eliza and, in Higgins's own words, "inventing new Elizas". Two men are inventing new Elizas while the real one sits beside them.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — The Devil: a common language that belongs to one
paragraphs: For Lisovskaya, point M is what the couple strives for together: shared wishes, agreements, a "common language". The point lies on the line of tasks, so the same wish also becomes resistance. In the tail 15-14-8 it holds The Devil, the card of a strong bond and of unfreedom. Lisovskaya's closing thought on the fifteenth energy in a couple: nobody belongs to anybody.

In Pygmalion the common language is literal. Higgins gives Eliza his language — vowels, intonation, words — and in the last act she says: **"I am a child in your country. I have forgotten my own language, and can speak nothing but yours."** This is what The Devil means at the point of the common language: the language two people speak turns out to be the language of one.

In a living couple it looks peaceful, even tender. One brings into the union their pet words, tastes, music, their way of arguing, and a year later the other catches themselves using someone else's phrases. "We don't wear that sort of thing." "This is how we go on holiday." "That's not like you." Presents become corrections: a course, a new wardrobe, a gym pass, a book "you really ought to read". In Ovid the presents go to the statue: they are given not to a person but to an image. In the plus this is passion and growth, two people who can honestly say "we made each other". In the minus each holds the other by what they have put into them.

Shaw sees that both hold the chain. Higgins remakes Eliza, and over the months she becomes indispensable: she knows where his things are, remembers his appointments, brings his slippers. In the last act he tells her what Lisovskaya would list in the minus of the fifteenth energy: "You call me a brute because you couldn't buy a claim on me by fetching my slippers and finding my spectacles." One currency is creation, the other is service. **Both buy a claim on a person.**

On the night after the ball Eliza asks a question that could stand as the epigraph to this tail: "Do my clothes belong to me or to Colonel Pickering?… All I want to know is whether anything belongs to me." She hands back the hired jewels and takes off the ring Higgins bought her in Brighton. He dashes the ring into the fireplace. When he has gone, slamming the door, Eliza goes down on her knees by the hearth to look for the ring. A bond that is renounced aloud is held on to by hand.

Another minus of The Devil in Lisovskaya is silence about one's own wishes. For five acts Eliza talks about slippers, dresses and the bet, and only at the end says what she wants: "I want a little kindness." For a 15-14-8 couple this is the first work at the entry: to say the wish out loud rather than wait for the other to sculpt it. Wen links The Devil with "preference for instant gratification over delayed gratification", and Higgins promises a duchess "in six months—in three if she has a good ear and a quick tongue". At the entry the couple wants results now. The middle of the tail will teach it another kind of time.

sections.h2: Waite's cards: two people chained to each other
paragraphs: On Waite's Devil a male and a female figure are chained to a ring in front of the altar. Wen opens her description of the same card with the words "The Lovers from Key 6 are chained by a horned beast". In the couple's tail it comes out exactly so: The Lovers of one plus The Hermit of the other give The Devil.

Waite himself opens his description of the design with an unusual word: it is "an accommodation, mean or harmony, between several motives". The same word, accommodation, ends his divinatory list for Temperance: "Economy, moderation, frugality, management, accommodation." Waite's Devil is a middle too, only a counterfeit one. Higgins describes such a middle better than any commentator: **"One wants to go north and the other south; and the result is that both have to go east, though they both hate the east wind."**

The second detail: he who is exalted above the chained figures "is not to be their master for ever. Even now, he is also a bondsman". In Pygmalion the master depends no less: "I have grown accustomed to your voice and appearance. I like them, rather." When Eliza hands back the jewels, Higgins thrusts them into his pockets, "unconsciously decorating himself with the protruding ends of the chains" — so runs Shaw's stage direction.

The third detail is almost a hint for the couple's tail. In the part of his book on older packs, Waite notes that in Papus's version the small demons of The Devil are replaced by "naked human beings, male and female, who are yoked only to each other", and adds: "The author may be felicitated on this improved symbolism." Nobody stands above such a pair. The chain is the two of them.

Of The Tower Waite writes that "there is a sense in which the catastrophe is a reflection from the previous card" — The Devil: one card is concerned with "the fall into the material and animal state", the other signifies "destruction on the intellectual side". In the tail 15-14-8 The Devil stands at the entry and The Tower at the centre, and Waite draws the link between them himself. As for Temperance, in his words "it tempers, combines and harmonises the psychic and material natures" — the very work for which this couple walks the middle.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — Temperance: two cups instead of a lectern
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya the middle of a couple's tail has no meaning of its own: it is an addition to the main task. Our reading: the middle shows how the couple travels from the wish at the entry to the main task. In the tail 15-14-8 the road runs through Temperance, the card of measure and blending.

Here the arithmetic of the first clue is at work. One person on this road would pass through The Hierophant: teacher, rule, pupil. Shaw's play is built as a course of lessons, but by the end the lessons run both ways. Eliza tells Pickering that her real education began not with phonetics but on the day he called her "Miss Doolittle". Higgins admits: "I have learnt something from your idiotic notions: I confess that humbly and gratefully." And Eliza throws at him: "If you can preach, I can teach." **In a 15-14-8 couple the teacher is not abolished but diluted:** each pours their own into the common cup.

The best scene of Temperance in progress is the third act, the at-home at Higgins's mother's. Eliza has strict orders to keep to two subjects, the weather and how everybody is. She delivers the weather like a meteorological bulletin, her vowels are flawless, and the content comes straight from Lisson Grove: her aunt, she insists, was done in for the sake of a new straw hat — "them as pinched it done her in". Two waters are poured into one cup but have not yet blended. On her way out Eliza drops "Not bloody likely" — at the London premiere in 1914 that line brought the house down.

In her example about work, Wen describes Temperance as fusing what a person already has with what is expected of them: "it isn't that new skills need to be learned, but rather that the Seeker need only reconcile his or her existing skills with the task at hand". For the couple this turns the whole story round. Its middle is not to remake a person but to fuse what both already have. Higgins describes his own work as "filling up the deepest gulf that separates class from class and soul from soul". Temperance is a bridge over that gulf, not the moving of one bank onto the other.

In Ovid the ivory comes alive not under the chisel but under a warm hand, and the wax, as he puts it, becomes pliable by the very handling. Time is an ally in this middle: the blend is not made in three months.

In life the middle of this couple is a long blending. Whose holidays, whose cooking, whose weekend rhythm, whose friends at the table. In the plus, after a few years the two speak a third language that neither had before. In the minus, as Lisovskaya puts it, one always gives way while the other does not even notice. From outside it looks like compromise; inside, both are walking into the east wind. Another minus of Temperance is perfectionism and dependence on other people's opinion: in Shaw the exam is set by guests at a society party, and Eliza passes it so brilliantly that everyone forgets about her.

Lisovskaya advises a couple with the fourteenth energy not to jump to conclusions about the partner, not to shift their own fears and wishes onto them, and to know how to wait for the right moment. For the tail 15-14-8 this is a rule against Pygmalion: not to sculpt the other after one's own fear and one's own wish.

sections.h2: The couple's centre — The Tower: the night after the ball
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's matrix is the atmosphere between the two, what is inside and not on show. Every couple with the tail 15-14-8 has The Tower there: The Chariot of one and The Hermit of the other. In Lisovskaya The Tower in the plus means trials the couple goes through hand in hand, after which the union is stronger; in the minus, the collapse of an invented image of the partner.

The fourth act of Pygmalion is The Tower almost word for word. Midnight, the laboratory in Wimpole Street, Eliza in diamonds after the garden party, the dinner and the opera. The bet is won. Pickering congratulates Higgins on his triumph — that is The Chariot. Higgins answers with relief: "Thank God it's over!" The whole thing has been a bore, and now he can go to bed at last "without dreading tomorrow" — that is The Hermit going back into himself. Nobody notices Eliza. When Higgins, outside the door, asks what the devil he has done with his slippers, she hurls them at him: "There are your slippers. And there. Take your slippers; and may you never have a day's luck with them!"

Both images collapse. Higgins sees not his handiwork but a person with claws, and refuses to believe it: "It's only imagination." Eliza sees that to him she is "not so much as them slippers", and asks what nobody thought of at the entry: **"What's to become of me?"** The Chariot's triumph plus The Hermit's solitude — and The Tower stands at the centre.

This Tower has its material too. Pygmalion worked in ivory, and the "ivory tower" is an old image of seclusion. In the Song of Songs the beloved's neck is "as a tower of ivory", and in 1837 Sainte-Beuve called the poet Alfred de Vigny's retreat his tour d'ivoire. A hermit carving his ideal alone lives exactly there. The Tower at the centre of this couple is a closed world for two, where an image is easy to create and hard to keep in daylight.

Shaw understood the force of this card. In his sequel he writes that nothing could alter the relations of Eliza and Higgins but "some emergency or calamity great enough to break down all likes and dislikes, and throw them both back on their common humanity" — and adds at once: "and may they be spared any such trial!" The Tower at the centre does not promise calamity. It says something else: in this couple the truth comes through a shaking, and after it the two can see each other as people.

In the last act Higgins finds the word himself. Five minutes ago, he tells Eliza, "you were like a millstone round my neck. Now you're a tower of strength". The millstone round the neck is The Devil. The tower of strength is The Tower lived through together: after the fall, an equal stands before him.

sections.h2: Main task — Justice: on what terms
paragraphs: The main point of the tail is D, and Lisovskaya reads it mostly through the minus: what the couple fails at and what it has to learn. In the tail 15-14-8 it is Justice, arcanum 8 (XI in Waite's numbering).

In Pygmalion the question of this card is asked by Higgins's mother back in the third act, when nobody wants to hear it: **"But on what terms? Is she a servant? If not, what is she?"** At the entry the couple had a wish. It had no terms. The main task is to agree on them after the fact.

Eliza's answer in the last act is the best definition of Justice for this couple: "the difference between a lady and a flower girl is not how she behaves, but how she's treated." Higgins replies with his own definition: the great secret is "having the same manner for all human souls" and behaving as if in Heaven, "where there are no third-class carriages". "He treats a flower girl as if she was a duchess," Eliza says of Pickering. "And I treat a duchess as if she was a flower girl," Higgins replies. Formally he is just: he is rude to everyone alike. Eliza answers with a line that leaves nothing to argue about: **"I notice that you don't notice me."**

This is the minus of the eighth energy in Lisovskaya: measuring everything by oneself and not noticing what hurts the partner. The justice of this couple is not one rule for everyone but attention to one person. The same scales for all do not yet mean that the person beside you has been weighed on them.

Towards the end Shaw shows the other pan as well. "And you may throw me out tomorrow if I don't do everything you want me to?" Eliza asks. "Yes; and you may walk out tomorrow if I don't do everything YOU want me to." For the first time the two have equal terms: both have the right to leave — which means staying can also be a free choice.

Roman jurists defined justice as the constant will to render to each what is due to them: suum cuique. Eliza's question from the night after the ball — what belongs to me — is the same question. And she answers it herself: "You can't take away the knowledge you gave me." What was given becomes one's own.

The main task is added up from two personal ones: The Star of one partner and The Moon of the other. In Waite the figure of The Star "expresses eternal youth and beauty", and The Moon "represents life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit". Pygmalion's statue is exactly that: eternal beauty seen by the imagination. The sum gives the scales. Our reading: the couple's task is to lay the ideal on one pan and what the imagination has filled in on the other, and see what a living person weighs.

In daily life the justice of this couple is tested by questions that are awkward to ask. Who decided the other needed that degree — they themselves, or the one who "knows better"? Whose plan was it: the move, the renovation, the wedding for a hundred guests? Who apologised after the last quarrel, and who thinks there is nothing to apologise for, because "I only wanted what was best"? Lisovskaya sees in the minus of the eighth energy an over-responsibility that turns into control, and advises the couple to set limits on advice and help and to let go of idealising the partner. For a couple who sculpt each other this is a rule of the workshop: **help ends where someone else's design begins**.

The conversation about Freddy, who writes to Eliza "twice and three times a day", is a short summary of the whole tail. "Can he MAKE anything of you? That's the point," says Higgins. "Perhaps I could make something of him," Eliza answers. "But I never thought of us making anything of one another; and you never think of anything else. I only want to be natural." The Devil asks who will make whom. Justice asks whether one may simply be.

sections.h2: Pygmalion or Michelangelo: what psychologists measured
paragraphs: This story has a scientific sequel. In 1999 the American psychologists Stephen Drigotas, Caryl Rusbult and their co-authors described the "Michelangelo phenomenon": close partners sculpt each other. How one sees the other and treats them gradually becomes part of the other's character.

The name comes from the sculptor. Michelangelo held that the figure is already enclosed in the block: his sonnet 151 says that the best artist has no idea that a single marble does not contain "col suo superchio" — within its excess (our translation). The chisel only removes what is superfluous. In Rusbult's words, Michelangelo "described sculpting as a process whereby the artist releases an ideal figure from the block of stone in which it slumbers", and a good partner works the same way: sees in the other that person's own ideal — who they themselves dream of becoming — and helps that figure emerge.

In one study, married partners were filmed discussing a goal that mattered to one of them, and four months later the researchers asked whether it had been reached. Those whose partners helped and supported them in the conversation, rather than criticising, were more likely to have achieved their goals.

Rusbult has a name for the opposite case too — the "Pygmalion phenomenon": a partner who perceives and treats the other "in ways that are consistent with the partner's ideal self (irrespective of the target's ideal self)". In a 2009 review the authors write that it is "negatively associated with diverse indices of personal and couple well-being", and conclude: **"it is unwise to foist one's ideal self representations onto others."** Ironically, the notion of the "ideal self" on which this whole line of work rests was taken from a psychologist named Higgins — E. Tory Higgins, author of self-discrepancy theory (1987).

The tail 15-14-8 fits into these two names. The entry is Pygmalion: sculpting in one's own image. The main task is Michelangelo: seeing the figure already present in the other. The middle is the work of the chisel, and it takes time: the same review says the sculptor "must not only understand the ideal form slumbering in the block, but must also understand the block per se – what possibilities are inherent in the block, and what flaws must be circumvented".

sections.h2: Three endings of one play
paragraphs: The argument about how this story ends has gone on for more than a hundred years — and it resembles the choice the tail 15-14-8 puts before a couple.

Ovid's ending is happy and brief: the goddess attends the wedding, nine moons later Paphos is born, and the island will take that name. In Shaw, Eliza leaves for her father's wedding, while Higgins, left alone, is sure she will buy him a ham, a Stilton cheese and gloves all the same. In 1914 Beerbohm Tree, the first Higgins, added a romantic gesture at the end without the author's knowledge. The exchange with Shaw became an anecdote: "My ending makes money; you ought to be grateful." — "Your ending is damnable; you ought to be shot."

In 1916 Shaw added a sequel to the play, "What Happened Afterwards". Eliza marries Freddy; they open a flower shop with Pickering's money and attend bookkeeping classes and even the London School of Economics: "business, like phonetics, has to be learned". Eliza spars with Higgins for the rest of her life. The sequel's last sentence: **"Galatea never does quite like Pygmalion: his relation to her is too godlike to be altogether agreeable."**

The cinema disagreed with Shaw. In the 1938 film, for whose screenplay Shaw and his co-writers won an Oscar, Eliza comes back, and Higgins, his back turned, asks about his slippers. The musical My Fair Lady (1956) took that ending, and its last line is: "Eliza, where the devil are my slippers?" The devil is in the last line. If the work of Justice is skipped, the story returns to its entry: to the slippers, to service, to The Devil.

The tail does not choose the couple's ending. Staying together or parting is not its question; its question is on what terms. The same couple may go back to the slippers, or stay as equals — and then each finds their own slippers.

sections.h2: The couple's values: what grows out of the workshop
paragraphs: The couple's values are its spiritual purpose, the answer to what the union exists for. Couples with the tail 15-14-8 most often have The Empress there (54.1%), then The World (32.2%) and The Hanged Man (13.7%).

For Lisovskaya The Empress means fruitfulness, abundance and growth, and in money her advice is to grow through shared goals in such a way that each partner has their own fulfilment. Ovid ends his story with a birth; Shaw, with a flower shop that did not pay for a long time and then began to prosper, and the former flower girl became its owner. The value of such a couple is what grows when the workshop turns into a garden: a shared venture in which each has their own bed.

The World means freedom and the wide world. "If I can't have kindness, I'll have independence," says Eliza. For a couple with The World among its values, each partner's independence is not a threat to the union but its aim.

The Hanged Man is a view turned upside down: the pupil suddenly announces that she will teach. For a couple with The Hanged Man the value lies in changing places from time to time and looking at the union from the other's side.

sections.h2: Worked example: 10.01.1977 and 11.02.1976
paragraphs: The example was calculated by the site engine. First, the partners' personal tails.

ul: **10.01.1977.** Day 10, month 1, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 7 = 24 → 6. Karmic task 10 + 1 + 6 = 17, centre 10 + 1 + 6 + 17 = 34 → 7. Entry of the tail 17 + 7 = 24 → 6, middle 6 + 17 = 23 → 5. Personal tail 6-5-17.

paragraphs: The couple's points are the sums of the same points:

If the middle were counted by the personal formula, it would be 15 + 8 = 23 → 5. But a couple's points are added point by point: the middle from the middles, which gives 14. The couple's values in this example are 3, The Empress.

sections.h2: What helps a couple with the 15-14-8 tail

ul: **Saying wishes out loud.** Not waiting for the other to guess and sculpt them: it took Eliza five acts to say one sentence, "I want a little kindness".
**Asking about the other's ideal instead of offering one's own.** "Who do you want to become?" before "that would suit you". This is the difference between Pygmalion and Michelangelo.
**Checking presents and advice.** Who is the present for — the person or the image? A course, a book, a new haircut are good when the one receiving them wants them.
**Blending slowly.** A couple's common language takes years to form. If the same one always gives way, it is not Temperance but the east wind.
**Talking after a triumph.** A wedding, a move, a thesis defended, the end of a renovation — that is the night after the ball. It is the moment to ask what happens now to each of the two.
**Agreeing on terms.** Who is responsible for what, and what belongs to whom. The right to leave and the right to stay belong to both.
**Owning one's share.** Justice begins with the words "I sculpted too", not with "I only wanted what was best".

paragraphs: If there are threats, violence or fear for one's safety in the relationship, that is not a task of the tail to be "worked through" but a reason to call the local emergency number or a crisis line and to seek help from people close to you and from professionals.

intro: The three roles in brief:

ul: **Entry to the task — 15, The Devil.** What the couple wants together: a bond in which each "makes" the other. The common language of two easily becomes the language of one.
**Middle of the task — 14, Temperance.** The road is walked not by command but by measure: the two blend like water from two cups, and both change — slowly, like wax under warm fingers.

**Main task — 8, Justice.** To give each their own: their own goals, their own voice, their own right to leave and to stay. In the minus, measuring the partner by oneself and not noticing what hurts them.

intro: The riddle of this tail is written in its arithmetic. A middle of 14 is impossible in a personal matrix: a person walking alone from The Devil to Justice would pass through The Hierophant, the card of the teacher. A couple passes through Temperance. There is a teacher in such a couple, but in the sum he dissolves. What follows is the evidence: the site engine's numbers, Ovid, Bernard Shaw, Waite, Wen, Yuliana Lisovskaya and the psychologists who measured how partners sculpt each other.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 15-14-8 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail with The Devil as the entry to the task, Temperance in the middle and Justice as the main task, and The Tower always at the centre of the matrix. The couple is drawn together by a strong wish to make each other their own, the road runs through mutual measure, and what it has to learn is justice: seeing the partner as a separate person with their own goals and rights.

faq.q: Why does the tail 15-14-8 never occur in a personal matrix?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail equals the sum of the entry and the main task: 15 + 8 = 23 → 5, which would give the tail 15-5-8. In a couple's matrix the middle is added up from the partners' middles, here 5 + 9, which gives 14.

faq.q: Does The Devil at the entry mean the couple is dependent?
faq.a: No. The card does not establish dependencies or anyone's actions. At the entry point The Devil describes the couple's shared wish: a strong bond in which two people change each other. In the plus it is passion and growth; in the minus, an attempt to hold the other by what has been put into them.

faq.q: Does The Tower at the couple's centre mean a break-up?
faq.a: No, the card does not predict events. The Tower at the centre is a quality of the atmosphere: an invented image of the partner does not last long here, and the truth comes through a shaking. For Lisovskaya, trials gone through together make such a union stronger.

faq.q: How common is the 15-14-8 tail in a couple?
faq.a: About one couple in 1,419 has it (0.07%), which ranks it 86th of the 97 couple tails. It arises from a single combination of personal tails: one partner has 6-5-17, the other 9-9-18.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. The method has no other couple tails made of 15, 14 and 8: the order 15-14-8 is the only one.

report: Ovid tells of a sculptor who lived alone, carved a woman out of ivory with "a beauty with which no woman can be born", and fell in love with his own work. Pygmalion kisses the statue, "fancies that they are returned" and brings it shells, rings and necklaces. The presents go not to a person but to an image. The karmic tail 15-14-8 is this story told for two. At the entry stands The Devil: the couple is drawn together by the wish to make each other their own. In the middle stands Temperance: the road runs through a slow mutual recasting. The main task is Justice: to see in the partner not one's own handiwork but a separate person with a design of their own. And at the couple's centre stands The Tower — the moment when the invented image collapses.

report.h3: A common language spoken by one

report: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together: its agreements and its "common language". The Devil stands here, the card of a strong bond and of unfreedom, and the common language of two easily becomes the language of one. In Bernard Shaw's Pygmalion this is said literally: Professor Higgins gives the flower girl Eliza his vowels, his intonation and his words, and in the last act she admits that she has forgotten her own language and can speak nothing but his.

In a living couple it looks peaceful, even tender. One brings their pet words, tastes, music and way of arguing, and a year later the other catches themselves using someone else's phrases: "we don't wear that sort of thing", "we don't do it that way". Presents become corrections — a course, a new wardrobe, a book that simply "must be read". In the plus this is passion and growth, two people who can honestly say "we made each other". In the minus each holds the other by what they have put into them.

Shaw sees that both hold the chain. Higgins remakes Eliza, and she becomes indispensable: she remembers his appointments and brings his slippers. One currency is creation, the other is service. **Both buy a claim on a person.** On the night after the ball Eliza asks who her clothes belong to and then says the main thing: "All I want to know is whether anything belongs to me." Waite writes approvingly of a version of The Devil with a man and a woman "yoked only to each other": nobody stands above such a pair, and the chain is the two of them.

report.h3: The teacher is not abolished but diluted

report: The middle of the tail shows how the couple travels its road. Here stands Temperance, the card of measure and blending: there is a teacher in such a couple, but that voice is blended with the voice of the other, and instead of a lectern there are two cups. Shaw's play is built as a course of lessons, and by the end the lessons run both ways. Higgins admits that he has learnt something from Eliza — "humbly and gratefully". Eliza announces that she will teach herself.

In Ovid the ivory comes alive not under the chisel but under a warm hand: it softens like wax in the sun and becomes "pliable by the very handling". The blend is not made in three months. In the plus, after a few years the two speak a third language that neither had before. In the minus the same one always gives way while the other does not even notice. Higgins described such a middle himself: **"One wants to go north and the other south; and the result is that both have to go east, though they both hate the east wind."**

report.h3: The night after the ball

report: The fourth act of Pygmalion is The Tower almost word for word. The bet is won, Eliza is still in her diamonds, and Higgins says with relief: "Thank God it's over!" Nobody notices her. When he asks what the devil has become of his slippers, she hurls them at him. Both images collapse: he sees not his handiwork but a person with claws, she sees that to him she is "not so much as them slippers". And a question is heard that nobody thought of at the entry: "What's to become of me?"

The Tower at the centre does not promise calamity. It says something else: an invented image does not last long here, the truth comes through a shaking, and after it the two can see each other as people. In the last act Higgins tells Eliza that five minutes ago she hung round his neck like a millstone, and now she is "a tower of strength".

report.h3: Scales that weigh a living person

report: The question of Justice is asked by Higgins's mother, and nobody wants to hear it: "But on what terms? Is she a servant? If not, what is she?" At the entry the couple had a wish and no terms. Eliza's answer is the best definition of this card for such a couple: **"the difference between a lady and a flower girl is not how she behaves, but how she's treated"**. Higgins replies that he has "the same manner for all human souls", and formally he is just: he is rude to everyone alike. Eliza retorts that what she notices is that he does not notice her. This is the minus of Justice: measuring everything by oneself and not seeing what hurts the partner.

Psychologists who study couples have two names for this. The "Michelangelo phenomenon" is when a partner sees in the other that person's own ideal and helps the figure emerge, as a sculptor frees it from the block. The "Pygmalion phenomenon" is when a partner sculpts the other after their own ideal; it is linked to lower well-being for both the person and the couple. The authors' conclusion: "it is unwise to foist one's ideal self representations onto others." For a couple with the tail 15-14-8 this is a rule of the workshop: **help ends where someone else's design begins**.

Shaw ended the sequel to his play with the sentence: "Galatea never does quite like Pygmalion: his relation to her is too godlike to be altogether agreeable." The musical My Fair Lady brought Eliza back to Higgins, and its last line is "Eliza, where the devil are my slippers?" If the work of Justice is skipped, the story returns to its entry: to the slippers, to service, to The Devil. The tail does not choose the couple's ending; its question is on what terms two people stay side by side.

What changes the script: saying wishes out loud instead of waiting for the other to guess; asking about the other's own ideal before saying what would suit them; after every shared triumph, talking about what happens next to each of the two; agreeing on who is responsible for what and what belongs to whom; owning one's share — **"I sculpted too"** instead of "I only wanted what was best". If there are threats, violence or fear for one's safety in the relationship, that is not a task of the tail but a reason to call a local emergency number or crisis line and to seek help.
