seo.title: Karmic tail 15 5 8 compatibility: meaning for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 15 5 8 compatibility: the Devil at the entry, the Hierophant in the middle, Justice as the main task, told through Jacob, Rachel and Laban.

items.title: Karmic tail 15-5-8 in compatibility: seven years for Rachel and the heap of witness
items.short: In late Victorian England, lovers about to part gave each other rings and brooches bearing a single word: Mizpah. Beside it they engraved a verse from Genesis: "The LORD watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another." Fashion turned these words into a vow of faithfulness across distance. Who first spoke them, and to whom, was never engraved on the brooches.

sections.h2: How a couple gets the tail 15-5-8
paragraphs: A couple's matrix is not calculated from one date. Each of its points is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22: if the sum is greater than 22, its digits are added together. The couple's tail is three such sums: the entry to the task M, the middle N and the main task D.
Example: a couple born on 09.05.1976 and 05.07.1975. The first partner's personal tail is 3-22-19, the second partner's is 12-19-7. The points are added in pairs:

The middle of a couple's tail is not recalculated from the two outer numbers: the five here is the sum of the middles of the two personal tails, 22 and 19. For the tail 15-5-8 it happens to match the sum of the ends anyway: 15 + 8 = 23 → 5. That is why the same order also occurs as one person's personal tail, for 4,275 dates since 1900. It is a different calculation with different roles for the points; the personal tail has its own article, and its conclusions do not carry over to the couple.

No other order of these numbers occurs for a couple. The first number of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, and of 15, 5 and 8 only 15 is. The tail itself occurs in roughly one couple in 96 (1.043%), 35th place among the 97 possible couple tails. For the couple in the example, the centre is 11 + 5 = 16, The Tower, and the couple's values are 21, The World. The investigation will come back to both numbers.

sections.h2: First clue: neither partner brings the Devil
paragraphs: Everyone has an entry to their personal tail, and in couples with the tail 15-5-8 only two combinations meet at these entries. In 78% of couples one partner has The Hanged Man (12) there and the other The Empress (3). In the rest it is The Lovers (6) and The Hermit (9). Neither partner has 15 there, and neither can: the sum has to come to exactly 15. **The Devil of this tail does not live in either partner alone. It appears only between them.**

In Jacob's story this is visible from the first scene, if it is read through the cards (the reading is ours). Jacob on his own is a man of service and waiting: The Hanged Man, whose list in Waite includes "trials, sacrifice". Rachel on her own is the shepherdess of her father's flocks, of whom the text says she "was beautiful and well favoured" (Genesis 29:17). Abundance and beauty belong to The Empress. Apart, there is nothing dark in either of them. But the moment they meet, a bargain appears: "I will serve thee seven years for Rachel" (Genesis 29:18). That is how Genesis casts the roles; in a living couple either partner may turn out to be The Hanged Man or The Empress, and gender decides nothing here.

Waite's divinatory list for The Devil includes "vehemence" and "extraordinary efforts". A stone lay over the well that the shepherds rolled away only all together: "We cannot, until all the flocks be gathered together" (Genesis 29:8). Jacob saw Rachel and rolled it away alone. Then he kissed her, "lifted up his voice, and wept". And the seven years of service "seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her" (Genesis 29:20). That is how this entry works: desire compresses time and moves stones.

In the sixteenth century the Portuguese poet Camões wrote a sonnet about this, one of the best known in his language. It has a line that names the hook more precisely than any commentary: Jacob served "not the father, he served her, and her alone he sought as his reward" (our translation). Reward: this is where the Devil hides inside love. The term runs out, and Jacob says to Laban: "Give me my wife, for my days are fulfilled" (Genesis 29:21). That is how people speak of wages at the end of a contract.

For Lisovskaya, the couple's entry to the task is what the two want together: their shared wishes and their "common language". The point stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish can turn into resistance. For a 15-5-8 couple, the common language at the entry is the language of price. "I moved cities for us." "I waited three years for a decision." "I left my job so we could be together." The desire is real, and so is the price. But a price paid in silence turns into an IOU, and one day it is presented for payment. Lisovskaya sums up the fifteenth energy in a couple in one thought: nobody belongs to anybody.

sections.h2: Second clue: "it must not be so done in our country"
paragraphs: Jacob gets his wedding by all the rules: "Laban gathered together all the men of the place, and made a feast" (Genesis 29:22). The midrash Genesis Rabbah (70:19) tells what it looked like from the inside. Laban took a pledge from the neighbours that no one would give the secret away, and with those pledges he bought wine, oil and meat for the feast. The guests knew about the switch and that evening sang before the groom "ha laya, ha laya". In Aramaic this sounds both like praise ("it is fitting, it is fitting") and like "she is Leah, she is Leah", but the groom heard only praise. The bride was brought in once the lamps had been covered. All night Jacob called her Rachel, and she answered.

"In the morning, behold, it was Leah" (Genesis 29:25). To the question "wherefore then hast thou beguiled me?" Laban has an answer ready, and it is the answer of the Hierophant in shadow: "It must not be so done in our country, to give the younger before the firstborn" (Genesis 29:26). The agreement of two people is cancelled by the custom of the place. Arguing is useless: the rule is older than the agreement, and the one who keeps the rule is the one who judges it. Wen describes the upright Hierophant as a person who "relies on another, a figure of authority or an institution, to define for the Seeker what is right and wrong". Laban is exactly such an institution in one person.

Then come seven more years of service for the woman he had served the first seven for, and after that six years for the flocks. "Your father hath deceived me, and changed my wages ten times" (Genesis 31:7). This is the middle of the tail lived in its minus: life in someone else's house, where the rules change on the way and the last word always belongs to the elders. Among the tasks of the fifth energy in a couple, Lisovskaya names living with the parents or on their support, relatives interfering even in the choice of partner, and conflict with the partner's family. Genesis has all of it at once: the son-in-law lives with his father-in-law, works for his father-in-law, and his wife is chosen by his father-in-law.

In the end Jacob has two wives, and the pain of unloved Leah in Genesis is real. But what matters for the couple's tail is not a third person; it is what replaced the one who was chosen. In a modern couple, what gets brought in on the morning after the wedding is not another person but an order of things: who comes first, what is proper, the parents' plans for the young couple. The flat where the young couple will "stay with us for now". The holiday table where everything was decided long before this couple existed. Financial help whose terms are a little different every year: the very wages changed ten times.

The numbers show why the middle feels different to each of the two. In 40% of couples with this tail, one partner has The Hierophant in the centre of their personal chart, the comfort zone. For that partner, established order is home; for the other, it is a foreign order they have come to serve. This is neither guilt nor merit, just a difference in temperature: one is at home, the other is a guest. And in 16% of couples the partners carry in the middles of their personal tails exactly the two ends of the couple's tail: one has Justice there, the other The Devil. Their sum gives The Hierophant. 15 + 8 = 23 → 5: this couple's established order is made of desire plus justice.

sections.h2: Third clue: gods under the camel's saddle
paragraphs: Jacob leaves in secret while Laban is away shearing his sheep. Two sentences side by side in Genesis read like a clue about a couple: "Rachel had stolen the images that were her father's", and Jacob, in the Hebrew, "stole the heart of Laban the Aramean", because he did not tell him he was fleeing (Genesis 31:19–20; the King James Version smooths the second into "stole away unawares"). In the Hebrew text the verb is the same, ganav, to steal. Both of them steal, each in his or her own way, and neither knows about the other's theft.

The images are the teraphim, the household gods of the father's house. Wen writes of The Devil: "The theme of The Devil is the worship of false idols." The text does not say why Rachel took them. In 1940 the Assyriologist Cyrus Gordon linked the theft to the tablets from Nuzi, where household gods went together with the right of inheritance; the hypothesis was later disputed, for example by Moshe Greenberg in 1962. But the daughters' grievance is in the text even without the tablets: "Is there yet any portion or inheritance for us in our father's house? Are we not counted of him strangers? for he hath sold us, and hath quite devoured also our money" (Genesis 31:14–15). Perhaps Rachel took her share herself, in secret, since no one intended to give it to her. That too is a court, only without witnesses.

Laban catches up with the fugitives and asks a question there is no escaping: "wherefore hast thou stolen my gods?" Jacob, sure of his own people, answers with a sentence: "With whomsoever thou findest thy gods, let him not live" (Genesis 31:32). And the text adds at once: "For Jacob knew not that Rachel had stolen them." Rachel hides the idols under the camel's saddle and sits on them: "Let it not displease my lord that I cannot rise up before thee" (Genesis 31:35). The search finds nothing.

The commentators remembered this sentence. Rashi, following the midrash, wrote: "In consequence of this curse Rachel died on the journey." A verdict passed in the heat of the moment and blind strikes the person closest. Waite's reversed Justice includes "excessive severity", and this is what it means: justice that hurries ahead before the tent has been searched.

For a 15-5-8 couple this may be the main secret of the middle of the tail. Each partner carries little gods out of the parental home: how money should be spent, who apologises first, whose holiday matters most, what is shameful and what is sacred. They are not put on the table; they travel under the saddle, and someone sits on them when anyone looks into the tent. The other partner does not know about them and so judges too confidently: "nothing like that exists here, and it never could."

sections.h2: Fourth clue: a court with no judge
paragraphs: On Mount Gilead there is no third party to sort things out. There are only the two of them and the relatives on both sides. "Set it here before my brethren and thy brethren, that they may judge betwixt us both" (Genesis 31:37). And Jacob delivers a speech that could be called a family audit: "This twenty years have I been with thee… That which was torn of beasts I brought not unto thee; I bare the loss of it… in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep departed from mine eyes. Thus have I been twenty years in thy house" (Genesis 31:38–41).

The audit is honest, and that is the strength of Justice: Waite's list for the card begins "Equity, rightness, probity". But it is also twenty years of silent bookkeeping presented in a single evening. Among the tasks of the eighth energy in a couple, Lisovskaya names debts and arrears, over-responsibility that slides into control and pressure, and the ability to admit one's own fault instead of blaming everyone else. Jacob counts his losses precisely, down to the last sheep torn by beasts. His own share in the story he does not count.

The midrash says what Genesis leaves unsaid. On the morning after the wedding Jacob throws at Leah: "Deceiver, daughter of a deceiver! Did I not call thee Rachel all night, and thou didst answer me?" Leah replies: "Is there a master without apprentices? Did not thy father call thee 'Esau', and thou didst answer him?" (our translation). Shortly before he fled to Laban, Jacob himself had passed for his brother before his blind father and taken a blessing that was not his. Wen explains Justice with Newton's third law: "to every action there is always an equal and opposite reaction". A deception in the dark came back to Jacob as a deception in the dark.

Laban answers the audit, and in his words the Devil of the entry speaks in the Hierophant's voice: "These daughters are my daughters, and these children are my children, and these cattle are my cattle, and all that thou seest is mine" (Genesis 31:43). But right here the story turns. Laban does not demand a trial; he proposes something else: "let us make a covenant, I and thou" (Genesis 31:44). For Wen, Justice is a balance set by people rather than by heaven, and on Mount Gilead it is set by two.

A couple recognises this easily. For years the two keep silent accounts, each their own: how much money, how many concessions, how many weekends with the other's family. Then comes the evening when the account is read out in full, like an indictment, and it turns out that the other partner has a ledger too. The main task of the tail is not to win that trial. It is to keep the account from piling up for twenty years.

sections.h2: The morning when "it was Leah": The Tower in the couple's centre
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's matrix is the atmosphere between the two, what is inside and not on show. In couples with the tail 15-5-8 it is almost always the same: in 82.9% it is The Tower (16), in the remaining 17.1% The Chariot (7).

The Tower here is built in two ways, and both speak about the tail. In 40% of couples it is The Hierophant in one partner's centre and Strength in the other's: 5 + 11 = 16. And in 38% of couples both partners have Justice in the centre of their personal charts: 8 + 8 = 16. **Two pairs of scales in one house make a Tower.** Each partner carries an exact measure of what is right, and each measure is right in its own way until it collides with the other.

Waite's divinatory list for The Tower contains the word "deception", and above all it is a card of the unforeseen. For the tail 15-5-8, The Tower is that very morning when "behold, it was Leah": the truth comes out all at once and the imagined picture collapses. Lisovskaya sees both sides of such an atmosphere. In the minus: barbs, irritation and threats to leave. In the plus: support in which trials are faced hand in hand, and calm in the face of unexpected trouble. This atmosphere does not promise disasters. It promises that whatever is secret in this couple will not stay secret for long.

The Chariot in the centre gives the same story a different character: a couple that solves things by moving. Lisovskaya describes the atmosphere of The Chariot as constant motion, in which decisions are made together and both rush to defend those close to them. In Genesis it is the night when Jacob sets his children and wives on camels and crosses the river, because he is afraid his father-in-law will take his daughters back.

sections.h2: Waite's cards: two in chains, two on their knees, two on the scales
paragraphs: In the deck of Waite and Pamela Colman Smith, the tail's cards show a pair of people who change position from card to card and on the third card disappear. On The Devil a man and a woman are bound to a ring in front of the altar: "There is a ring in front of the altar, from which two chains are carried to the necks of two figures, male and female." They have tails, but, as Waite writes, "there is human intelligence in the faces, and he who is exalted above them is not to be their master for ever." Waite himself links this card to The Hierophant: the Devil's raised hand is, in his words, "the reverse of that benediction which is given by the Hierophant in the fifth card".

On The Hierophant the two are below again: "two priestly ministers in albs kneel before him", with the crossed keys at his feet. There are no chains, but a third figure still stands above the two, and he decides. Waite's divinatory list for this card opens with "Marriage, alliance", and the middle of the tail 15-5-8 rests on those words.

On Justice the two are gone altogether. A single figure sits between pillars, holding a sword and scales. Nobody stands above people any more, because there are no people left on the card, only two pans. In our reading this is the path of the tail: two people, first held in chains by a third and then blessed by a third, become the two pans of the scales. The figure in the middle is no longer a master or a priest but the agreement they have made themselves.

Waite separates this justice from a higher one: the moral law "deals unto every man according to his works", while gifts and election are not handed out by merit. Camões has a line about exactly that gap. When Jacob was given Leah instead of Rachel, he began to serve another seven years "as though he had not earned her" (our translation). Love is not a salary; it can be neither earned nor underpaid. The account of Justice covers contributions, obligations and debts, the things that can be placed on a pan. The person is never placed on the pan.

sections.h2: The heap with two names: the strong version of the tail
paragraphs: The covenant on Mount Gilead is sealed by three things, and each is a hint for a 15-5-8 couple. First a stone set up as a pillar, and a heap piled by the hands of relatives from both sides. Then a shared meal: "they did eat there upon the heap" (Genesis 31:46). And then the heap is named, and it has two names. "And Laban called it Jegar-sahadutha: but Jacob called it Galeed" (Genesis 31:47). Laban speaks Aramaic, Jacob Hebrew, and both names mean the same thing: "heap of witness".

This answers the riddle of the entry. For Lisovskaya, the point at which a couple enters the task is their "common language". At the start of the tail, the common language of the two was the language of price: years, sacrifices, IOUs. At the end, nobody needs to speak the same dialect. What is needed is for two words to mean the same thing. One partner's family may call this agreement "letting the young ones live by their own lights", the other's "not interfering", and the two themselves "our rules". The words are different; the heap is one.

The border in this covenant is drawn not by flight but by words: neither I to thee nor thou to me, "for harm". Laban writes in his own condition: not to mistreat his daughters. The parents' care stops being control and becomes a clause in the agreement. And the last verse of the chapter sounds like the resolution of the whole middle of the tail: "And early in the morning Laban rose up, and kissed his sons and his daughters, and blessed them: and Laban departed, and returned unto his place" (Genesis 31:55). The Hierophant's blessing finally stands in its proper place: after the agreement, not instead of it. And the parent goes back home.
What changes the script for a couple with this tail:

ul: **Name the price aloud while it is still small.** A move, a wait, a job given up: these are contributions to be agreed on, not IOUs to be kept. A beloved person is not "earned", and love is not bought with gifts.

**Take the gods out from under the saddle.** Each partner names the rules of the parental home they carry with them, and the two decide together which to bring into their own home and which to leave where they came from.
**Start the couple's own holidays and rules.** Get along with the family without letting it inside the couple's borders, and agree in advance where advice and help end.

**Check the account regularly, not once every twenty years.** Calmly, without a speech for the prosecution: who put in what, what is hard, what needs dividing again. And in that conversation count one's own share too, not only the other's.

**No verdict before the tent has been searched, and no searches.** Asking aloud is better than looking under the saddle. And it is not by chance that Lisovskaya lists forgiveness among the tasks of the eighth energy.

paragraphs: If there are threats, violence or fear for one's safety in a couple, this is not a matter for reading cards. What is needed then is help: a local emergency number, a crisis line, a psychologist.

The Victorian lovers engraving Mizpah on their brooches were not wrong after all. The treaty of two distrustful men became a word given before parting, because an honest border is itself a form of faithfulness. A 15-5-8 couple walks this whole path: from a bargain made for love to an agreement the two can sign together.

sections.h2: The couple's values: the road to a land of one's own
paragraphs: The couple's values are the spiritual purpose, one more answer to the question of why the two met. Couples with the tail 15-5-8 have three possible values. In 54.2% it is The World (21). Waite's divinatory list for The World includes "recompense, voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place". That is almost word for word the end of Jacob's story with Laban: "Return unto the land of thy fathers, and to thy kindred" (Genesis 31:3). The value of such a couple is a land of its own, where nobody changes the wages any more.

In 32% of couples the values card is The Hanged Man (12): Waite's list for it begins with "wisdom, circumspection, discernment", that is, the ability to wait without losing one's head, which Jacob learned over fourteen years. In 13.8% it is The Empress (3), for Waite "fruitfulness": the multiplied flocks Jacob led out of Laban's house. This is our reading, not a statement from the books, but all three converge on one thing: this couple's path leads out of someone else's house into its own.

intro: A father-in-law said them to his son-in-law. Laban said them to Jacob on Mount Gilead, after a seven-day pursuit and a search of the tents. Two men who had lived side by side for twenty years and did not trust each other piled up a heap of stones and swore "that I will not pass over this heap to thee, and that thou shalt not pass over this heap… unto me, for harm" (Genesis 31:52). The tenderest words of parted lovers were born as a border treaty. The whole story of Jacob and Rachel, from the well to that heap, is the couple's karmic tail 15-5-8.

**The tail in brief.** The union begins with a desire that both are willing to pay for, passes through someone else's house and someone else's rules, and arrives at the main task: an honest reckoning and an agreement that carries both signatures. The three cards in order:

ul: **15, The Devil — Entry to the task.** A strong "I want to be with you, whatever it costs". The strength of this entry and its hook are the same thing: the beloved easily becomes a reward that has been earned, and the years of waiting become a debt that someone has to repay.

**5, The Hierophant — Middle of the task.** The path runs through established order: the wedding, the parents, "this is how we do things", the rules of the parental homes that each partner brings along. Here the agreement of the two is constantly rewritten by a third party, whether custom or family.

**8, Justice — Main task.** To settle the account honestly: to say aloud who put in what and who owes what, to own one's share and not only the other's, and to draw the border with the parental homes by agreement rather than by flight.

intro: This is not a prediction and not a verdict. The couple's tail shows where the two of them are most likely to stumble and what they can learn together. What follows is the evidence: what is written in the cards themselves, in the books of Waite, Wen and Lisovskaya, and in the numbers shared by every couple with this tail.

faq.q: Is the karmic tail 15-5-8 in compatibility a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not predict events and does not pass a verdict on the union. It shows a task: a desire the two pay for, a middle where established order and family press on the couple, and a main lesson in honest reckoning and agreement. Lisovskaya reads a couple's main task mostly through its difficulties, so the description sounds stern, but the same task, solved together, becomes a support for the union.

faq.q: How is the couple's tail 15-5-8 different from the personal tail 15-5-8?
faq.a: They are different calculations. A personal tail is calculated from a single date of birth, and its points mean something else. A couple's tail is added up from the points of two personal matrices, and its roles belong to the couple: the entry to the task, the middle of the task, the couple's main task. A personal tail 15-5-8 in one partner never produces a couple tail 15-5-8: the entry of the couple's tail has to add up to exactly 15, and for that each partner needs a number below fifteen at their own entry.

faq.q: Can a couple have the tail 5-8-15 or 8-15-5?
faq.a: No. The first number of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, and of the three numbers 15, 5 and 8 only 15 is. So these cards stand in a couple's tail in only one order: The Devil at the entry, The Hierophant in the middle, Justice as the main task.

faq.q: Does the Hierophant in the middle mean the couple has to get officially married?
faq.a: No. The Hierophant describes a path through established order (marriage, families, traditions, shared rules), not an obligation to go through a ceremony. The question in the middle of this tail is not "are we registered" but "whose rules live in our home, and who chose them". A couple can live by its own rules with a marriage certificate or without one.

faq.q: Why do couples with this tail almost always have The Tower in the centre?
faq.a: That is how the numbers add up: in 38% of couples both partners have Justice in the centre of their personal charts (8 + 8 = 16), in 40% one has The Hierophant and the other Strength (5 + 11 = 16). In all, The Tower stands in the centre for 82.9% of such couples and The Chariot for 17.1%. The Tower in a couple's atmosphere does not promise misfortune: it says that what is hidden here comes out quickly and that the couple goes through such moments together.

faq.q: How can a couple find out whether its tail is 15-5-8?
faq.a: Calculate both personal matrices and add the matching points of the tail: entry to entry, middle to middle, main task to main task, reducing sums above 22. The easier way is to enter both dates of birth into the compatibility calculator: it shows the couple's tail, the centre and the couple's values at once.

report: In nineteenth-century England, lovers about to part gave each other brooches bearing the word Mizpah and a verse from Genesis: "The LORD watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another." The first to speak these words was not a lover but a father-in-law addressing his son-in-law. Laban said them to Jacob on Mount Gilead, after a pursuit and a search of the tents, when two men who had distrusted each other for twenty years piled up a heap of stones and swore not to cross it "for harm". The tenderest words of parted lovers were born as a border treaty. The tail 15-5-8 is the whole road that leads to such a heap.

The union begins with The Devil: a desire that both are willing to pay for. The middle is The Hierophant: someone else's house, established order, family and "this is how we do things". The main task is Justice: **to settle the account honestly and make an agreement that carries both signatures.**

report.h3: Neither partner brings the Devil

report: In a couple with this tail, neither partner has The Devil at the entry of their personal tail. It appears only between them. In Jacob's story, read through the cards, this is visible from the first scene. Jacob on his own is a man of service and waiting. Rachel on her own is a beauty, the shepherdess of her father's flocks. Nothing dark. But the moment they meet, a bargain appears: "I will serve thee seven years for Rachel." The seven years "seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her."

In the sixteenth century Camões wrote a sonnet about this that names the hook more precisely than any commentary: Jacob served "not the father, he served her, and her alone he sought as his reward". Reward: this is where the Devil hides inside love. The term runs out, and Jacob says: "Give me my wife, for my days are fulfilled." That is how people speak of wages.

A couple with this tail recognises itself not in passion but in the bookkeeping of passion. "I moved cities for us." "I waited three years for a decision." The desire is real, and so is the price. But **a price paid in silence turns into an IOU**, and one day it is presented for payment. Lisovskaya sums up the fifteenth energy in a couple in one thought: nobody belongs to anybody.

report.h3: The rule is older than the agreement

report: Jacob gets his wedding by all the rules, with a feast for all the men of the place. The midrash adds a detail: the guests knew about the switch and sang "ha laya" to the groom, which sounds both like praise and like "she is Leah". In the morning, behold, it was Leah. To the question "wherefore then hast thou beguiled me?" Laban has the Hierophant's answer in shadow ready: "It must not be so done in our country, to give the younger before the firstborn." The agreement of two people is cancelled by the custom of the place. Then come seven more years of service, and a father-in-law who "changed my wages ten times".

In a modern couple, what gets brought in on the morning after the wedding is not another person but an order of things: "stay with us for now", a holiday table where everything was decided long before this couple existed, financial help whose terms are a little different every year. The agreement of the two is constantly rewritten by a third party.

report.h3: Gods under the saddle and a blind verdict

report: When Jacob leaves in secret, Genesis puts two sentences side by side: Rachel stole her father's idols, and Jacob "stole the heart of Laban" by not telling him he was going. In the Hebrew text the verb is the same. Both of them steal, and neither knows about the other's theft. Laban catches up and asks about his gods. Jacob, sure of his own people, passes sentence: "With whomsoever thou findest thy gods, let him not live." And the text adds: "For Jacob knew not that Rachel had stolen them." She is sitting on the idols, hidden under the camel's saddle.

This is the main secret of the middle of the tail. Each partner carries little gods out of the parental home: how money should be spent, who apologises first, whose holiday matters most. They are not put on the table; they travel under the saddle. And the other partner, not knowing about them, **judges too confidently and strikes the person closest.**

report.h3: Twenty years of silent bookkeeping

report: On Mount Gilead there is no judge, only the two of them and the relatives on both sides. Jacob delivers a family audit: "This twenty years have I been with thee… That which was torn of beasts I brought not unto thee; I bare the loss of it… Thus have I been twenty years in thy house." The audit is honest, but it is also twenty years of accounts presented in a single evening. His own share Jacob does not count. The midrash keeps the reply Jacob heard from Leah on the morning after the wedding, when he accused her of deceit: "Is there a master without apprentices? Did not thy father call thee 'Esau', and thou didst answer him?" A deception in the dark came back to him as a deception in the dark.
The main task of the tail is not to win that trial. It is to keep the account from piling up for twenty years.

report.h3: A heap with two names

report: Laban answers: "all that thou seest is mine", and at once proposes not a trial but a covenant. The heap receives two names: Laban names it in Aramaic, Jacob in Hebrew, and both mean "heap of witness". Two families do not need to speak one language; they need their words to mean the same thing. In the morning Laban blesses his daughters and grandchildren, and the text says that he "returned unto his place". **The blessing comes after the agreement, not instead of it.**

What changes the script: naming the price aloud while it is still small; taking the gods out from under the saddle and deciding together which rules of the parental homes to bring into a home of one's own; starting the couple's own holidays and agreeing in advance where the family's advice and help end; checking the account regularly, counting one's own share too; passing no verdict before the tent has been searched.

If there are threats, violence or fear for one's safety in a couple, this is not a matter for reading cards: what is needed is help, from a local emergency number or crisis line, or from a psychologist.

The lovers with their Mizpah brooches were not wrong. The treaty of two distrustful men became a word of faithfulness, because an honest border is itself a form of it. A 15-5-8 couple walks this whole road: from a bargain made for love to an agreement the two can sign together.

seo.title: Karmic tail 15 8 11 compatibility: the riddle of the lion and honey
seo.description: Karmic tail 15 8 11 compatibility: The Devil at the entry, Justice in the middle, Strength as the main task, and why its plot is written in the Book of Judges.

items.title: Karmic tail 15-8-11 in compatibility: The Devil, Justice and Strength
items.short: At his own wedding Samson put a riddle to the guests: "Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness." The answer was bees and honey in the carcass of a lion he had torn apart with his bare hands. The karmic tail 15-8-11 in a couple's compatibility asks the two of them the same riddle: how to make sweetness come out of their strength, rather than a defeated partner.

sections.h2: Tail to tail: how a couple's 15-8-11 is formed
paragraphs: The same story holds the most literal picture of a couple's tail there is. Wronged by his father-in-law, Samson "caught three hundred foxes, and took firebrands, and turned tail to tail, and put a firebrand in the midst between two tails" (Judges 15:4). A couple's tail is made the same way: neither partner brings it, it is tied together from two personal tails. Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, reduced to 22.

An example: a couple born on 05.12.1976 and 05.07.1975. The first partner's personal tail is 3-7-22, the second's is 12-19-7. Entries are added to entries, middles to middles, main tasks to main tasks:

The couple's middle is counted from the two personal middles, not from the couple's outer numbers. Here the two happen to agree (15 + 11 = 26 → 8), but that is a result, not a method. This couple's centre is 13, Death (8 + 5), and the couple's values are 12, The Hanged Man.

Now the first clue. The couple's tail 15-8-11 arises from five combinations of personal tails, and in all five the entries are 3 and 12 or 6 and 9. Neither partner has a fifteen at the entry of their own tail: the couple's Devil is born only between them, like a firebrand tied between two tails. Nobody brings the wish to hold the other whole into the union — it appears when the two meet.
The rest also comes from checking every date:

ul: the tail occurs in about one couple in 120 (0.834%), ranking 43rd of the 97 couple tails;
in 65% of such couples the partners' personal tails are 12-19-7 and 3-7-22, as in the example;
in 21% they are 6-17-11 and 9-9-18: one partner already has Strength as the main task of their own tail, and the couple's task sounds familiar to them;
in 11% they are 6-5-17 and 9-3-21; two more combinations give about one per cent each.

paragraphs: No other couple tail is made of these numbers. The first number of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, so 8 and 11 cannot stand at the entry, and the order 15-11-8 never comes up across all dates. 15-8-11 is the only one.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — The Devil: "wherewith thou mightest be bound"
paragraphs: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, its "common language". In this tail the common language is the language of the tether. Delilah speaks it in her very first line: "Tell me, I pray thee, wherein thy great strength lieth, and wherewith thou mightest be bound to afflict thee" (16:6).

What follows is usually retold as betrayal, though at first the text reads more like a game. Samson answers: seven green withs. She binds him and cries "The Philistines be upon thee, Samson" — and he breaks the withs "as a thread of tow is broken when it toucheth the fire". Then new ropes. Then seven locks woven into the web. Three times she binds him, three times he breaks free — and he does not leave. The text does not say why, but the game repeats, and both play it: one binds, the other shows he can break the bonds. As long as it is a game, the ropes snap like thread.

This is what The Devil at the entry looks like in ordinary life. The two are pulled towards each other with a force that would do for ten. Jealousy is taken for proof of love, "where were you?" for care. Each wants to know everything about the other and keeps testing whether the knot still holds. In Lisovskaya this is both the energy's plus — passion, readiness to accept the partner's dark sides, open talk about desires — and its minus: only closeness holds the couple together, one presses while the other keeps quiet about what they want, and people are held by the body, by money, by a child, by status. The entry stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish can turn into resistance: the harder they hold, the harder they pull away.

There is a detail that is easy to miss. Samson is a Nazarite from birth, and the Nazarite law forbids him anything from the vine (Numbers 6:3–4). Yet he loves a woman "in the valley of Sorek" — and in Hebrew soreq means "choice vine" (the same word names the choicest vine in Isaiah 5:2 and the noble vine in Jeremiah 2:21). He meets the lion by the vineyards of Timnath, and his foxes with their firebrands burn the corn along with the vineyards. He is always drawn to where he is not allowed to go. That is the entry of The Devil: a desire that grows stronger the less it is permitted.

Why bind at all? The Bible does not explain; Milton did. In his drama Samson Agonistes (1671) Dalila is no longer a lover but Samson's wife, and her visit to her blinded husband in prison reads like a marital quarrel. She says what the Book of Judges never does: she "feared lest one day thou wouldst leave me / As her at Timna". She knew that liberty "Would draw thee forth to perilous enterprises, / While I at home sate full of cares and fears". Here he would be with her day and night — "Mine and Love's prisoner, not the Philistines', / Whole to myself". Beneath the wish to bind lies the fear of being left. Among the tasks of the fifteenth energy Lisovskaya lists exactly this: fear, and attempts to hold on.

Samson's reply is half a line, and the way out of this entry rests on it: "Love seeks to have love." And one more line: "This gaol I count the house of liberty / To thine whose doors my feet shall never enter." If the wish to hold goes unseen, home becomes a cage, and a prison cell feels freer.

An important caveat. In the story one partner betrays and the other is betrayed. In a couple's tail that never happens: there is one tail for two. Samson binds too — the foxes tail to tail, the wedding guests with a wager of thirty garments — and he hides things too: he told not even his father and mother about the lion and the honey. The tail does not say which partner is Samson and which is Delilah, and gender has nothing to do with it. Each asks "what can I bind you with?", and each hides a lock of their own.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — Justice: "thou hast mocked me these three times"
paragraphs: The middle of the task is how the couple lives the road from the wish to the main task. Here the road runs across the scales. Delilah keeps count out loud: "Behold, thou hast mocked me, and told me lies", "Hitherto thou hast mocked me", and finally: "How canst thou say, I love thee, when thine heart is not with me? thou hast mocked me these three times" (16:10–15). Love has become a ledger: you say "I love thee" — show me your heart. Samson answers the count in his own way: three times he invents new bonds.

Two chapters earlier the same scene has already played out, in almost the same words. His wife from Timnath weeps: "Thou dost but hate me, and lovest me not: thou hast put forth a riddle unto the children of my people, and hast not told it me." Samson answers by his own measure: "Behold, I have not told it my father nor my mother, and shall I tell it thee?" (14:16). Two ledgers: in hers, closeness is proved by a secret; in his, my parents come before you. The women differ, the quarrel is the same. This is how the middle of the tail works: the same account keeps coming back until it is settled differently.

And there is one more detail that makes the skin crawl. While Delilah binds Samson, "there were men lying in wait, abiding with her in the chamber" (16:9, 16:12). In every test there is someone else, out of sight. A couple has such a third party too — a mother who "always said so", a friend, an ex whose opinion matters. The ledger is kept not for the two of them but for whoever is sitting behind the curtain. Among Lisovskaya's recommendations for Justice is to set limits on advice and help from others.

Samson in this story is not just a strongman — he is a judge. "And he judged Israel in the days of the Philistines twenty years" (15:20), and again in the very last line (16:31). Yet the story does not show a single case he judged. His justice is a mirror: "As they did unto me, so have I done unto them" (15:11); "Now shall I be more blameless than the Philistines, though I do them a displeasure" (15:3). Benebell Wen describes reversed Justice almost as this plot: "actions that may be unjust rather than just", "prompted by the Seeker's feeling that what happened was not fair".

In a couple this looks peaceful, but recognisable. "I told you everything — and you?" "Last time it was me who gave in." "We always visit your parents, never mine." Honesty turns into an instrument of control, responsibility into pressure. Among the minuses of Justice Lisovskaya names over-responsibility that slides into control, the habit of measuring everyone by oneself, and the inability to admit one's own fault. Among the pluses: a fair share of duties, promises kept, "a cool head and a warm heart". And among the tasks of the eight she names forgiveness.

In Milton the argument over forgiveness is the heart of the whole scene. Dalila asks for her offence to be weighed "By itself, with aggravations not surcharged, / Or else with just allowance counterpoised". Then she makes an offer that is hard to call unfair: "Let weakness then with weakness come to parle, / So near related, or the same of kind; / Thine forgive mine". She reminds him that he himself gave the secret away under pressure, and asks him not to exact "More strength from me than in thyself was found". Samson answers with perfect justice: take for your deed exactly the pardon I give my own folly — "Impartial, self-severe, inexorable". One measure for both, and therefore no mercy at all.

That is the trap in the middle of the tail. Justice in the minus is not necessarily deceit or counting in one's own favour. More often it is an honest ledger without forgiveness: "I don't forgive myself either, so don't expect it." The scales are the middle of the road; one cannot settle down and live on them.

sections.h2: Main task — Strength: a lion that need not be torn
paragraphs: The couple's main task is read mostly through its minus — what does not work out and what has to be learned. From the first scene Samson's strength is a strength that tears. A young lion "roared against him", and Samson "rent him as he would have rent a kid, and he had nothing in his hand" (14:6). Then the gates of Gaza, posts, bar and all, on his shoulders. Then the jawbone of an ass. Not once does his strength become gentle, and it never comes by his choice: "the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him" — so begin the lion, Ashkelon and Lehi (14:6, 14:19, 15:14). Strength overtakes him like a storm.

Delilah's question "wherein thy great strength lieth" is the very question of the main task. In the Hebrew one and the same verb stands behind it three times, and the King James Bible keeps it each time: the lords want "to bind him to afflict him" (16:5), Delilah asks what will bind him "to afflict thee" (16:6), and after the shaving "she began to afflict him" (16:19). The Russian Synodal Bible renders the last of these as "and he began to weaken" — and takes the verb out of her hands. In the original, strength in this story is a thing that can be taken away: find the secret, shave it off, bind it.

This is what the minus of the eleventh energy looks like in a couple, according to Lisovskaya: a struggle for leadership, suppression and fear, each with their own truth, mockery of the other's weakness. Strength is either hidden like a weapon or someone tries to worm it out and disarm it. And the strongest man has a fear he repeats from answer to answer: "then shall I be weak, and be as another man". What he fears is not pain but becoming ordinary. For a couple with Strength as the main task this fear is familiar: to show the other your weakness, because it can be used.

Benebell Wen opens the Strength card with the words "Triumph of love over hate" — and goes on: "the Seeker cannot use brute force to exercise will over others; the Seeker must use gentle, subtle influence." Both of Samson's women speak to him about hate: "Thou dost but hate me, and lovest me not." Milton's Dalila turns this around: "And what if love, which thou interpret'st hate, / The jealousy of love… / Caused what I did?" The task of Strength in this tail is to tell love from hate where they speak in the same words. Reversed Strength Wen describes as reliance on brute force and as being "too stubborn and obstinate".

The most important sentence in Judges for this tail is 16:20. Shaven, Samson wakes and says: "I will go out as at other times before, and shake myself." The old way — breaking the bonds — no longer works. "And he wist not that the LORD was departed from him." His strength left not with his hair but with the broken vow: the secret was not a mechanism but a promise. For a couple this is the main key: the strength of a union lies not in what each hides from the other, but in what both keep.

And finally the scene in which the whole task of the tail can be seen. Milton's Dalila asks: "Let me approach at least, and touch thy hand." Samson: "Not for thy life, lest fierce remembrance wake / My sudden rage to tear thee joint by joint. / At distance I forgive thee, go with that." He tore a lion apart in his youth, and now the lion sits inside him, and he can forgive only at a distance, because up close the lion would break loose. Just before this Dalila tells him: "If thou in strength all mortals dost exceed, / In uncompassionate anger do not so."

The main task of 15-8-11 is the reverse of "at distance I forgive thee". To let a hand come near one's lion and not tear it. To stay close while the anger has not yet passed. Lisovskaya puts it in everyday words: work with aggression, learn mutual respect, say from the very start what you like and what you don't, express feelings openly. Milton himself, incidentally, knew this choice not only from books: his first wife, Mary Powell, left him for her mother soon after their wedding in 1642, came back in 1645 — and he took her in. His Samson forgives at a distance; the poet himself forgave up close.

sections.h2: What Waite's cards show: fire on the tail and a hand at the jaws
paragraphs: The pictures here are those of the classic Waite–Smith deck; the cards on this site are drawn differently. But Waite's three cards read like illustrations to the Book of Judges.

**The Devil.** Two tailed figures are chained to a ring by the altar, and above them stands a horned figure with a torch pointing down to the earth. Benebell Wen notices what most people pass over: the torch "appears to be lighting the primordial man's tail on fire", while "the female figure's tail bears fruit" (in the picture, a bunch of grapes). Fire on a tail and the vine — exactly Samson's foxes: a firebrand between two tails, let loose into the standing corn, burned the vineyards and the olives too. There are two chains on the card, and in Gaza Samson was "bound with fetters of brass" (16:21; the Hebrew uses the dual, "a pair of bronzes"). In Waite's divinatory list the reversed Devil includes "weakness" and "blindness", and Samson in the prison house is both weak and blind.

**Justice.** A figure with a sword and scales sits between two pillars. The last scene of Samson the judge is between pillars too: "they set him between the pillars" (16:25), and he takes hold of "the two middle pillars upon which the house stood". His last prayer is about settling a score: "that I may be at once avenged of the Philistines for my two eyes". A judge who spent his life settling scores settles the last one at the end and brings the house down with himself inside. A couple knows this in a peaceful form: a quarrel in which the aim is not to agree but to bring the score to zero loosens the pillars of the shared home.

**Strength.** A woman holds her hands at a lion's jaws, and the lion does not resist. This is exactly the scene missing from Samson's story: his lion is either torn apart or sits inside him and roars "at distance". In Waite's divinatory list Strength has "Power, energy, action, courage, magnanimity", and reversed Strength has, among other things, "abuse of power, weakness, discord, sometimes even disgrace". Samson came to know disgrace at the end: he was fetched from prison so that he might "make us sport" at the feast. The word "weakness" stands in Waite's lists for both the reversed Devil and reversed Strength: the most famous strongman of the Bible spends the whole story afraid of becoming weak, and weak is what he becomes. (In Waite's deck Strength and Justice swap numbers; on this site 8 is Justice and 11 is Strength.)

sections.h2: The couple's centre and values: honey in the carcass of a lion
paragraphs: The couple's centre is the atmosphere inside the union, what lies between two people and is not for show. In three couples out of four with this tail (76.4%) the centre is 13, Death. This is not about anyone dying. Waite writes of the thirteenth card as "change, transformation and passage from lower to higher". In Lisovskaya the atmosphere of Death in the plus is accepting the partner's past and moving on, taking changes in each other easily; in the minus, emotional swings and attempts to remake the other.

With Samson's riddle this fits literally. "Out of the eater came forth meat": the one who ate became food, and the honey was found where the lion was already dead. For sweetness to appear in a couple, something in it has to end — an old form of strength, the duel, the game of who binds whom. The guests' answer to Samson — "What is sweeter than honey? and what is stronger than a lion?" — has long been read by scholars as a second riddle. The German biblical scholar Hermann Stahn suggested in 1908 that it was a wedding riddle whose answer was "love"; among the other answers proposed is "death". Both answers meet in a single verse: "for love is strong as death" (Song of Songs 8:6).

In 21.4% of couples the centre is 22, The Fool: an atmosphere of lightness, freedom and play. Samson plays too — he wagers garments on a riddle, he lets himself be bound. The Fool makes the game of the tether lighter and more dangerous: in the minus it becomes a relationship as a game, with no boundaries and no responsibility. In 2.2% the centre is 4, The Emperor — order and authority, when "who is in charge" is settled by rules.

The couple's values are what the union exists for. In 41.7% they are 12, The Hanged Man. In prison, at the darkest point of the story, there is a quiet verse: "Howbeit the hair of his head began to grow again after he was shaven" (16:22). Waite calls The Hanged Man "life in suspension, but life and not death". The value of such a couple is a pause in which what was cut off grows back, and the ability to look at one's own strength from the other side. In 31.9% of couples the values are 21, The World: wholeness, a shared outlook, accepting the partner even in the minus. In 26.4% they are 3, The Empress: fruitfulness, home, plenty — the honey itself. In the example above the centre is Death, the values are The Hanged Man, and Strength also stands on the point "What fills": what the couple is learning is also what restores it.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail: out of the strong came forth sweetness
paragraphs: Since 1885 the tins of Britain's Lyle's Golden Syrup have shown a lion with bees above it and the words "Out of the strong came forth sweetness". In 2006 Guinness World Records named it the world's oldest branding and packaging. Samson's riddle has stood on kitchen shelves for almost a century and a half as a sign of sweetness. But the lion on the tin is dead. The tail 15-8-11 asks about another version: can honey be had from a living lion?

The strong version of the tail looks like this. Passion stays passion but does not become a cage: "love seeks to have love", not a prisoner. Secrets are told by choice, not on the seventh day of tears. The ledger is kept, but there is one for both, with a column marked "forgiven". Strength and weakness are shown to each other before anyone has to ask "wherein thy great strength lieth". And forgiveness does not come from a distance.
What helps a couple through this tail:

ul: not prying: a secret extracted under pressure brings no closeness, it becomes evidence;
noticing when "I love thee" starts being tested with "thine heart is not with me";
asking who else is "abiding in the chamber" during a quarrel — whose opinion, whose voice, whose ledger;
not settling scores at the peak of anger, and not mistaking justice for punishment;
speaking of one's own "lock" — the vulnerable place — oneself, rather than waiting for it to be found;
moving closer when the urge is to forgive from a distance.

paragraphs: If there are threats, physical violence or fear for one's safety in a couple, that is not "the task of the tail" and not a reason to put up with it. It is a reason to call for help: a local emergency number, a crisis line, a psychologist.

Samson's guests answered his riddle with a question: "What is sweeter than honey? and what is stronger than a lion?" A couple with the tail 15-8-11 answers it not in words but in the way they live: when the strength of two stops being a duel, out of the strong comes forth sweetness.

ul: **15 · The Devil — entry to the task.** What draws the couple together is the wish to hold each other whole: passion, jealous closeness, the very question Delilah puts to Samson — "wherewith thou mightest be bound".
**8 · Justice — middle of the task.** The road runs through a ledger: who opened up, gave and forgave how much. "How canst thou say, I love thee, when thine heart is not with me?"
**11 · Strength — main task.** To learn a strength that needs neither to bind nor to hide: to come close to the other's "lion" and not tear it apart.

intro: This is not a verdict and not a forecast. The tail describes a road the couple walks together, and the Book of Judges records that road almost word for word — from a riddle at a wedding to a prison in Gaza.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 15-8-11 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of the couple's chart: **The Devil** at the entry to the task, **Justice** in the middle, **Strength** as the main task. The couple is drawn together by a strong wish to hold each other, the road runs through a ledger of openness and grievances, and the main task is strength without a struggle for power: a closeness in which nothing needs to be bound and nothing vulnerable needs to be hidden.

faq.q: Is the couple's tail 15-8-11 a bad sign for a relationship?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not grade the union and predicts nothing: it shows what the two have to learn. The Devil at the entry is both passion and the risk of jealous possession; Justice is both fair agreements and the counting of grievances; Strength is both respect and a struggle for leadership. Which side shows depends on what the couple does.

faq.q: How is the couple's tail 15-8-11 different from the personal tail 15-8-11?
faq.a: The personal tail 15-8-11 is calculated from a single date of birth and read through the roles of a personal chart. In a couple each point is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, and the roles are different: the entry to the task, the middle, and the couple's main task. Even with the same numbers it is a different calculation, and conclusions about a person do not carry over to a couple.

faq.q: How can a couple find out whether they have the tail 15-8-11?
faq.a: Enter both dates of birth in the compatibility calculator: the tail appears in the sphere "The couple's karmic tail". Most often it is formed from the personal tails 12-19-7 and 3-7-22, but other combinations occur too, for example 6-17-11 and 9-9-18.

faq.q: Can a couple's tail have the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. From the numbers 15, 8 and 11 a couple can only get the order 15-8-11: the first number of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, and the order 15-11-8 never comes up across all dates.

faq.q: What should a couple with the tail 15-8-11 do?
faq.a: Speak about their wishes and fears directly instead of testing each other; keep one honest ledger for both and forgive up close, not from a distance; never settle who is in charge by force. If there are threats or violence in the relationship, help is needed: a local emergency number, a crisis line, a psychologist.

report: Samson put a riddle to the guests at his own wedding: "Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness." Only he knew the answer: bees had settled in the carcass of a lion he had torn apart with his bare hands, and there was honey. A couple with the tail 15-8-11 faces the same riddle, only it is put to two people: how to make sweetness come out of their strength, rather than a defeated partner. The Book of Judges records the road to the answer almost word for word, in three lines of dialogue.

report.h3: The first line: "wherewith thou mightest be bound"

report: Delilah asks: "Tell me, I pray thee, wherein thy great strength lieth, and wherewith thou mightest be bound to afflict thee." This is The Devil at the entry to the task — what the couple wants together. Its common language is the language of the tether. At first it all looks like a game: seven green withs, new ropes, locks woven into the web. She binds him, he breaks the bonds and does not leave. As long as it is a game, the ropes snap like thread.

In a couple's life this looks familiar. The two are pulled towards each other with a force that would do for ten. Jealousy passes for proof of love, questioning for care. Each wants to know everything about the other and keeps testing whether the knot still holds. The harder they hold, the harder they pull away.

Why bind at all was explained by Milton. In his drama Samson Agonistes Dalila confesses that she feared he would one day leave her, and wanted him with her day and night — **"Mine and Love's prisoner, not the Philistines', / Whole to myself"**. Beneath the wish to bind lies the fear of being left. Samson's answer is a few words, and the way out rests on them: "Love seeks to have love." If the wish to hold goes unseen, home becomes a cage, and a prison cell feels freer.

In the story one partner betrays and the other is betrayed. In a couple's tail that never happens: there is one tail for two. The tail does not say which partner is Samson and which is Delilah, and gender has nothing to do with it. Each asks what the other could be bound with, and each hides a lock of their own.

report.h3: The second line: "thou hast mocked me these three times"

report: The middle of the task is Justice, and the road runs across the scales. Delilah keeps count out loud: "How canst thou say, I love thee, when thine heart is not with me? thou hast mocked me these three times." Love has become a ledger: say "I love thee" — show the heart. Two chapters earlier his wife from Timnath wept in almost the same words, and Samson answered by his own measure: "Behold, I have not told it my father nor my mother, and shall I tell it thee?" The women differ, the quarrel is the same. The account keeps coming back until it is settled differently.

The text holds a detail that makes the skin crawl: while Delilah binds Samson, **"there were men lying in wait, abiding with her in the chamber"**. In every test there is someone else, out of sight. In a couple it is a mother who "always said so", a friend, an ex — and the ledger is kept not for the two of them but for whoever is sitting behind the curtain.

Samson, meanwhile, judged Israel for twenty years, yet the story does not show a single case he judged. His justice is a mirror: "As they did unto me, so have I done unto them." In Milton, Dalila offers an honest peace: "Let weakness then with weakness come to parle, / So near related, or the same of kind; / Thine forgive mine". Samson answers with flawless justice: she gets exactly as much pardon as he gives himself — "Impartial, self-severe, inexorable". One measure for both, and therefore no mercy at all. That is the trap in the middle: not deceit, but an honest ledger without forgiveness.

report.h3: The third line: "I will go out as at other times before"

report: The main task is Strength, and it is read through what does not work out. From the first scene Samson's strength tears: he "rent him as he would have rent a kid", carries the gates of Gaza on his shoulders, strikes with the jawbone of an ass. Not once does it become gentle. In this story strength is a thing that can be taken away: find the secret, shave it off, bind it. This is what the minus of Strength looks like in a couple: a struggle for leadership, each with their own truth, the fear of showing weakness because it can be used. The strongest man fears one thing: "then shall I be weak, and be as another man".

Shaven, Samson wakes and says: "I will go out as at other times before, and shake myself." The old way no longer works. "And he wist not that the LORD was departed from him." His strength left not with his hair but with the broken vow: the secret was not a mechanism but a promise. **The strength of a union lies not in what each hides from the other, but in what both keep.**

report.h3: Forgiveness that does not keep its distance

report: Milton has a scene in which the whole task of the tail can be seen. Dalila asks: "Let me approach at least, and touch thy hand." Samson: "Not for thy life, lest fierce remembrance wake / My sudden rage to tear thee joint by joint. / At distance I forgive thee, go with that." He tore a lion apart in his youth, and now the lion sits inside him, and he can forgive only at a distance.

**The main task of 15-8-11 is the reverse of "at distance I forgive thee".** To let a hand come near one's lion and not tear it. To stay close while the anger has not yet passed. Since 1885 the tins of Britain's Lyle's Golden Syrup have shown a lion with bees and the words "Out of the strong came forth sweetness", but the lion there is dead. The tail asks about something else: can honey be had from a living lion?

The strong version of the tail looks like this. Passion stays passion but does not become a cage. Secrets are told by choice, not on the seventh day of tears. The ledger is kept, but there is one for both, with a column marked "forgiven". The simple things help:

ul: not prying: a secret extracted under pressure brings no closeness, it becomes evidence;
noticing who else is "abiding in the chamber" during a quarrel — whose opinion, whose voice, whose ledger;
not settling scores at the peak of anger, and not mistaking justice for punishment;
speaking of one's own "lock" — the vulnerable place — oneself, rather than waiting for it to be found.

report: If there are threats, physical violence or fear for one's safety in a couple, that is not "the task of the tail" and not a reason to put up with it. It is a reason to call for help: a local emergency number, a crisis line, a psychologist.
