seo.title: Karmic tail 15 8 20 compatibility: the Devil, Justice, Judgement
seo.description: Karmic tail 15 8 20 compatibility: the Devil at the entry, Justice in the middle, Judgement as the main task, read through Tolstoy's Resurrection.

items.title: Karmic tail 15-8-20 in compatibility: The Devil, Justice and Judgement
items.short: A hundred roubles in an envelope: in Tolstoy's Resurrection this sum opens an account between two people that neither money nor marriage can close. The couple's karmic tail 15-8-20 tells the same story. The couple enters the task through the Devil: an attraction that easily starts to name a price. It passes through the middle by way of Justice: an attempt to settle up and make amends. And its main task is Judgement: to stop keeping accounts and wake up to a life in which nobody pays with themselves.

sections.h2: A hundred roubles: where the story came from
paragraphs: In June 1887 the lawyer Anatoly Koni was a guest at Yasnaya Polyana and told Tolstoy a case from his years as a prosecutor in St Petersburg. A young man from high society had come to him asking to pass a letter to a prisoner, Rozalia Oni. Her story went like this. An orphan, the daughter of a tenant farmer, she grew up in the house of a rich St Petersburg lady; at sixteen she was seduced by a relative of her mistress, and when she became pregnant, the mistress turned her out. Rozalia gave the baby to a foundling home and slowly sank to the very bottom. One day, in a den near the Haymarket, she stole a hundred roubles from a drunken guest. She was tried before a jury, and among the jurors, by chance, sat the very man who had seduced her. He recognised her and decided to marry her.
Koni tried to talk him out of it and advised him to get to know his bride first. Lent put off the wedding, and at the end of Lent Rozalia died of typhus. That was where the real story ended.

Tolstoy asked Koni for the plot and for years called the project "the Koni story" in his diary. He wrote it on and off for ten years, finished it on 16 December 1899, and gave the fee to the resettlement of the Doukhobors in Canada. He called the novel Resurrection (Voskreseniye). Quotations below follow Louise Maude's translation of 1900; where the translation is ours, it is marked.

One detail changed sides on its way from life into the book. In Rozalia's case the hundred roubles are stolen money, the money she is tried for. In the novel the same sum ends up in another hand: it is the hundred-rouble note the seducer pushes on the girl as he leaves. The money she was tried for became the money with which he tried to close his account.

The novel's three acts follow the order of the tail. The Easter night and the envelope are the Devil. The jury room and the attempt to pay are Justice. Siberia, the refusal and the Gospel in the last chapter are Judgement. The novel is not a portrait of any particular couple, nor a script waiting for one: Tolstoy pushed everything to the limit. But the mechanism he took apart on an extreme case can be recognised, in a softer form, in ordinary married life.

sections.h2: The entry: the Devil, or love that names a price
paragraphs: Point M is the entry to the task: what the couple wants together, what it agrees on, which common language it speaks. It lies on the line of tasks, so the same desire that brought two people together can in time become resistance.

The Easter matins is the brightest scene in Resurrection. To Nekhlyudov it seems that everything in the church exists for Katyusha, "because she was the centre of all". Tolstoy calls that night the zenith of love, a moment when it is "unconscious, unreasoning, and with nothing sensual about it". A few hours later the hero is ruled by "the animal man, seeking only his own happiness", as Tolstoy calls him. And Nekhlyudov does what, as it seems to him, everyone does.

The most exact word about the Devil comes the next day. As he leaves, Nekhlyudov decides he must give her money, "not for her sake, not because she might need it, but because that is what is always done, and he would be thought dishonest if, having made use of her, he did not pay for it" (our translation; Maude softens the line). He pushes the envelope at her and runs to his room "as if he had burnt himself" (our translation). **Closeness converted into payment, and called honesty into the bargain**: that is this tail's entry in its extreme form.

Waite describes the Devil as the chain of material life and adds that the one exalted above the chained figures is not free either: he is "blind to the liberty of service". For Benebell Wen the Devil is above all a "preference for instant gratification over delayed gratification". Tolstoy hears the same voice: "Take care I don't let the opportunity for your own happiness, your own enjoyment, slip by!" Wen and Tolstoy alike see here not a monster but ordinary human selfishness.

In an ordinary couple, 15 at the entry is not a drama of seduction. It is a common language in which closeness is easily translated into what was given and what was received. After a quarrel an expensive present turns up instead of a talk. In an argument someone says "I gave you everything". A decision rests on "that's how everyone lives". One partner wants the other to be theirs alone, and jealousy passes itself off as love. Among the tasks of a couple with this energy, Lisovskaya names attempts to hold on to the partner through closeness, money, status or a child, silence about one's own desires, and a union that drags both down. Her main thought about the fifteenth energy is short: **nobody belongs to anybody**.

The entry has its strength too. Fifteen gives a couple the courage to want and to speak openly about desire, to accept each other's dark sides and to forgive mistakes. The danger is not desire but the moment when "I want you" turns into "you owe me".

sections.h2: The middle: Justice, or the attempt to pay
paragraphs: Point N is the middle of the task. Lisovskaya gives it no meaning of its own; it completes the main task. We read it as the couple's path from the desire of M to the task of D: what the two do and what they go through.

Ten years later Nekhlyudov sits on a jury and recognises the defendant. In the jury room he thinks: "Yes, all that horrible business had not yet happened on that Easter eve!" The Easter night and the room where a verdict is reached stand in a single sentence: the tail's entry meets its middle.

Then Tolstoy shows how human judgement works. The jury finds Maslova guilty "without intent to rob" and forgets to add "without intent to take life". Tolstoy lists the reasons. This time the presiding judge forgot to suggest the wording. The colonel told the story of his brother-in-law's wife at great length. Nekhlyudov was too excited. One juror had left the room. And "chiefly because, being tired, and wishing to get away as soon as possible, all were ready to agree with the decision which would bring matters to an end soonest". An innocent woman is sent to four years of penal servitude. Nekhlyudov's first feeling is relief: "Siberia and penal servitude at once cut off every possibility of any kind of relations with her."

In a couple, a verdict like that is reached at half past one in the morning, when both are too tired to argue. The decision is taken not because it is right but because after it one can go to bed. Justice in its minus, for Lisovskaya, means both failing to notice that the partner is hurt and the habit of measuring everything by oneself.

Then comes the attempt to pay. In prison Nekhlyudov says he wants "to atone for my sin, not by mere words, but in deed. I have made up my mind to marry you." Katyusha answers: "You did not feel so then, but threw me 100 roubles. That's your price." And then: **"You've got pleasure out of me in this life, and want to save yourself through me in the life to come."** The whole tail is in one sentence: the Devil ("pleasure"), Judgement ("save yourself") and, between them, an account in which she twice becomes the means of payment.

Tolstoy himself stumbled at this step. On 5 January 1897 he wrote in his diary: "I began rereading Resurrection and, when I reached his decision to marry, threw it aside in disgust. It is all untrue, invented, weak" (our translation). To save the book he resolved "to describe his and her feelings and life by turns". A Justice that weighs only one pan stops being justice.

But the middle is not useless. Leaving the prison, Nekhlyudov understands: "If he had not tried to expiate his guilt he would never have found out how great his crime was. Nor was this all; she, too, would never have felt the whole horror of what had been done to her." **The attempt to pay shows the real size of the debt**, and shows that it cannot be closed with money or with marriage. The scales in the middle of the tail are there to see what happened, not to settle the account.

Wen has an exact pair of formulas for this card. Justice upright: "What is fair will feel fair." Reversed: "What is fair will not feel fair." Nekhlyudov's proposal is fair by the ledger, yet to Katyusha it sounds like a new price. Tolstoy names another trap of this card: until then Nekhlyudov "had played with a sensation of self-admiration, had admired his own remorse". The pleasure of being in the right is also a payment to oneself.

In a couple's life the middle 8 shows in small things. A tally runs in someone's head: who gave in how many times, who pulled whom out. An apology becomes a project: one partner is ready to do everything but never asks whether it is wanted. Help is later presented as a bill. After a quarrel someone says "we're quits". Among the tasks of the eight, Lisovskaya names owning one's guilt instead of blaming everyone; over-responsibility that turns into control and pressure; debts; forgiveness. In its plus the same card gives honest agreements, clear rules and "a cool head and a warm heart".

sections.h2: The main task: Judgement, or "Where is the use of our reckoning?"
paragraphs: Point D is the couple's main task, its chief trials. It is read mostly through the minus: what does not work for the two and what they have to learn.

Lisovskaya's key to the twentieth energy is kin and family: relatives, traditions, inheritance, the influence of parents. In its minus this is a union "for the sake of something", love hindered by age, status or tradition, a partner who decides nothing without the parents, and an inability to admit one's own mistake.

In Resurrection the family court speaks before any other. When he learns that Katyusha left to give birth and "had gone quite to the bad", Nekhlyudov hears from his aunts that "she had inherited her mother's depraved nature". Tolstoy adds: "he was pleased to hear this opinion of his aunts'. It seemed to acquit him." **The family's verdict suits whoever needs to be acquitted.** Next to it stands the difference in station that Katyusha throws in his face: "I am a convict and you a prince." And a marriage "for the sake of something": for the sake of his salvation.

The turn comes in Siberia. Waite's divinatory list for Judgement begins with the words "Change of position, renewal, outcome". Katyusha's sentence is commuted, and Nekhlyudov comes to tell her she may settle wherever she likes. She answers that she will follow the political prisoner Simonson. "No, Dmitri Ivanovitch, you must forgive me if I am not doing what you wish... You must live, too." She tries to thank him, he refuses her thanks, and she answers: **"Where is the use of our reckoning? God will make up our accounts."** At parting she says, as Tolstoy notes, not "Good-bye" but "Forgive me". In Russian both words, proshchaite and prostite, are imperatives of one verb, "to forgive", in its two aspects.

Before Siberia, Nekhlyudov wrote in his diary that Katyusha "does not wish to accept my sacrifice; she wishes to make a sacrifice herself. She has conquered, and so have I." And further: "she seems to be coming back to life".

The last chapter closes the books for good. At night in a hotel Nekhlyudov opens the Gospel an Englishman had given him and lands on Matthew 18. There is the parable of the hundred sheep, and then Peter's question: "How oft shall my brother offend me and I forgive him? Until seven times?" — and the answer: "until seventy times seven". The novel opens with these same verses; they are its epigraph. Then comes the parable of "a certain king which made a reckoning with his servants". The king forgives a servant a debt of ten thousand talents, and the servant goes out and takes by the throat a fellow-servant who owes him "a hundred pence". "And is this all?" Nekhlyudov exclaims aloud, and the inner voice answers: "Yes, it is all."

**The novel that began with a hundred roubles ends with a hundred pence**, a hundred denarii in the Russian text. Between them lies the whole course of the tail: from a price, through the account, to a judgement that stops counting. It becomes clear to Nekhlyudov that "we should forgive always an infinite number of times because there are no men who have not sinned themselves".

Waite writes that Judgement is a transformation in answer to a summons which "is heard and answered from within". Wen adds: "Events currently happening in the Seeker's life will be the catalyst to a personal awakening." For Nekhlyudov the catalyst was the "strange coincidence" in court which, in Tolstoy's words, "demanded from him the acknowledgment" of what he had done.

For the couple, the main task 20 is to own its part without putting the other on trial. To keep its own judgement apart from the family's verdict. Not to turn the union into a means of salvation. To let the other live their own life, as Katyusha let Nekhlyudov: "You must live, too." To forgive not from above, writing off a debt, but by ceasing to keep it. In its plus the twentieth energy gives a couple what Tolstoy's heroes so lacked: a union in which a difference in age, status or faith does not get in the way, mistakes are forgiven, and a partner is supported even when in the wrong.

sections.h2: A clue in the numbers: the Devil and Judgement on the scales
paragraphs: The strangest detail of this tail shows up in the arithmetic. 15 + 20 = 35, and 3 + 5 = 8. **Justice in the middle is the sum of the Devil and Judgement.** The couple's middle is not recalculated from its ends: it is added up from the middles of the two people's personal tails. And still the same sum comes out.
The couple's tail 15-8-20 is built from two combinations of personal tails:

ul: **6-20-14 and 9-15-6 — 79% of such couples.** Judgement stands in the middle of one person's personal tail, the Devil in the middle of the other's. 20 + 15 = 35, an eight. Both ends of the couple's tail are already in the personal charts, and their meeting gives the scales.
**6-17-11 and 9-18-9 — 21% of such couples.** The middles hold the Star and the Moon, hope and fog. 17 + 18 = 35, an eight again.

paragraphs: In both cases the entry 15 is made of one partner's Lovers (6) and the other's Hermit (9). The Lovers are not in the couple's tail, but in 79% of couples they appear in both personal tails: at the entry for one, at the end for the other. Like the Easter night Nekhlyudov remembers all his life: the love was there, but it enters the couple's shared story already as the Devil.

This is not a casting of roles. Whoever has 15 in their personal tail is not "the couple's Devil", and whoever has 20 is not its judge: a personal tail has its own points and its own meaning. In the novel both pans belong to both. Nekhlyudov carries both the "animal man" and the resurrection. Katyusha first defends herself with the same price, "my price is a ten-rouble note", and then decides her own fate and, in Nekhlyudov's words, is "coming back to life". The scales stand between two people, not in the hands of one of them.

sections.h2: The atmosphere: Death or the Emperor at the centre
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's matrix is the atmosphere: what happens between the two when nobody is watching. For the tail 15-8-20 the centre depends on which personal tails have met. In 79% of couples (6-20-14 and 9-15-6) it is 13, Death; in 21% (6-17-11 and 9-18-9) it is 4, the Emperor.

**Death between the Devil and Judgement.** In the real story Koni told, there is no resurrection: Rozalia died at the end of Lent, before the wedding. Life stopped at death, and Tolstoy called the book Resurrection. Waite writes that Death also has an entrance "while still in this life", as a change in the form of consciousness. Before leaving for Siberia, Nekhlyudov says the same in his own words in his diary: "Tomorrow a new life will begin. A final good-bye to the old!" In such a couple's atmosphere something is always ending. Lisovskaya sees in the plus of the thirteenth energy a couple that accepts the partner's past and moves on, takes changes in each other easily and helps the other out of destructive relationships. In the minus one forces the other to change and notices only the other's mistakes. The question of the atmosphere is whether endings become renewal or merely losses.

**The Emperor at the centre.** Where the centre is 4, the atmosphere is held by rules, order and someone's power to decide. In the novel this is the whole machinery of the state: the Senate, the petition to the Emperor, the paper with the pardon. In Waite's divinatory list the Emperor reversed reads "Benevolence, compassion, credit": mercy lives inside the same card as power. Lisovskaya describes, in the plus, passion, trust and strictness without fanaticism behind an outward reserve; in the minus, rigid rules, control and decisions made for everyone.

sections.h2: The couple's values: the World, the Empress, the Hanged Man
paragraphs: "The couple's values" in the compatibility matrix is the spiritual purpose, what the union exists for. For the tail 15-8-20 it is the World for 57.7% of couples, the Empress for 31% and the Hanged Man for 11.3%. Our reading: all three appear in the last part of Resurrection as three different answers to the question "what for".

ul: **The Empress — a home and the continuation of life.** In the general's house Nekhlyudov is shown the sleeping children and feels envious. An hour later, seeing Katyusha come in, he thinks: "I wish to live, I want a family, children, I want a human life."

**The Hanged Man — a sacrifice, but one's own.** Nekhlyudov realises that Katyusha may "not in the least require the sacrifice I imagined I was bringing her". In his diary he writes that she "does not wish to accept my sacrifice; she wishes to make a sacrifice herself". Wen links Justice reversed directly to the Hanged Man reversed, to "martyrdom": resentment at injustice easily turns into sacrifice for show.

**The World — a life in which nobody needs to be owned.** The last chapter goes beyond a single couple: Nekhlyudov thinks of a new order of life for everyone. Lisovskaya names in the World's plus full acceptance of the partner even in the minus and no pressure; in its minus, remaking the partner to suit oneself.

paragraphs: For a tail that begins with a price, the values sound like an answer: a home, not a deal; a sacrifice by one's own choice, not as payment; a world big enough for nobody to belong to anybody.

sections.h2: How the tail 15-8-20 is formed, and why it is not a personal programme
paragraphs: Each point of the couple's matrix is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices, reduced to 22: if the sum is above 22, its digits are added. The middle of the couple's tail is not recalculated from its ends; it, too, is added up from the personal middles.

Example: the couple born 08.01.1976 and 14.05.1976. For the first person the day is 8, the month 1, the year 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5. Karmic task 8 + 1 + 5 = 14, centre 8 + 1 + 5 + 14 = 28 → 10, entry to the tail 14 + 10 = 24 → 6, middle 14 + 6 = 20. Personal tail: 6-20-14. For the second, the day is 14, the month 5, the year 5. Task 14 + 5 + 5 = 24 → 6, centre 14 + 5 + 5 + 6 = 30 → 3, entry 6 + 3 = 9, middle 6 + 9 = 15. Personal tail: 9-15-6.
Their couple's centre is 10 + 3 = 13, Death, and the couple's values are 21, the World. This is the most common combination of those described above.

In a personal matrix this triple never occurs. There the tail's entry M equals the sum of the main task D and the centre. With D = 20, any such sum lies between 23 and 42 and reduces to 12 at most, so fifteen at the entry is impossible with any centre. If 15, 8 and 20 stand on a chart, it is a couple's chart.

The tail 15-8-20 is rare: it occurs in about one couple in 1,123 (0.089%) and ranks 83rd of the 97 couple tails. No other couple tail is made of these three numbers: the Devil, Justice and Judgement meet on a couple's tail only in this order.

Resurrection has a judge, Matvei Nikitich, who likes to tell fortunes by numbers. Walking into the courtroom, he makes a guess about his new regimen: if the number of steps to his chair divides by three, the regimen will work. There are twenty-six steps, so he squeezes in a little extra one to make twenty-seven. At the decisive moment he adds up the figures of a number on a paper: if the sum divides by three, he will back the presiding judge. It does not divide, yet "his kindness made him agree all the same". The first number of a couple's tail also always divides by three, here it is 15, but that is a property of addition, not an omen. The tail's numbers do not tell the outcome. As in the novel, people decide.

sections.h2: Living the tail 15-8-20 at its strongest
paragraphs: The strong version of this tail is a couple whose desire is honest, whose agreements are clear, and whose past has been lived through rather than presented as a bill. Lisovskaya advises a couple with the fifteenth energy not to buy love with presents, and to admit their secret desires and talk about them. The novel itself suggests the rest.

ul: **Noticing the moment when a present, a favour or "after all I did for you" starts replacing a conversation.** That is the Devil's entry: desire being converted into a price.
**Not making important decisions "just to get it over with".** That is how Tolstoy's jury sent an innocent woman to penal servitude.
**Putting things right by asking what the other needs, not by assigning them one's own atonement.** Nekhlyudov proposes marriage and is told that he wants to save himself through her.
**Keeping one's own judgement apart from the family's.** The aunts' verdict suited, above all, the one who wanted to be acquitted.

**Starting with oneself.** Nekhlyudov writes in his diary: "If only we could manage to see the beam in our own eye in time, how kind we should be." It is the novel's second epigraph, retold in his own words.
**Forgiving means ceasing to keep the account,** not pretending that nothing happened.

paragraphs: Tolstoy did not promise his hero a happy ending. The last sentence of the novel reads: "How this new period of his life will end time alone will prove." The tail 15-8-20 promises nothing either and passes no sentence. It shows where an account begins between two people and where they can stop keeping it.

ul: **15 · The Devil — entry to the task.** What the couple wants together and which language it speaks: strong attraction, a wish to possess, and a habit of measuring closeness by what has been given and received.
**8 · Justice — middle of the task.** How the couple walks the path: weighing who owes whom, trying to put things right by deeds and to settle matters by the rules.

**20 · Judgement — main task.** What the couple has to learn: to own its part without looking for someone to blame, to keep its own judgement apart from the family's, and to forgive so that each can live their own life.

intro: People also look up "15 8 20" as a programme in the destiny matrix. In a personal chart, by our method, this tail does not occur: it belongs to couples. Yuliana Lisovskaya, whose book the compatibility calculation follows, calls the three numbers on a couple's tail its karmic programme. This is neither a forecast nor a verdict: the numbers show which story comes most easily to the couple and where it turns.

faq.q: What does 15-8-20 mean in a couple's destiny matrix?
faq.a: It is the couple's karmic tail: the Devil at the entry to the task, Justice in the middle, Judgement as the main task. The story of the tail runs from closeness that starts being measured by price, through an attempt to settle up, to the ability to own one's part and forgive.

faq.q: Does 15-8-20 occur in a personal destiny matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal chart the tail's entry equals the sum of the main task and the centre, and with a main task of 20 the entry cannot be fifteen. The triple 15-8-20 occurs only in a couple's matrix.

faq.q: Why is 15 8 20 called a programme?
faq.a: Lisovskaya calls the three numbers on a couple's tail its karmic programme. It is the same M–N–D triple, not a separate calculation: the programme describes the couple's tasks, not a fate assigned to it.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail is read mostly through its difficulties because it is about tasks, not about a verdict. In the plus the same cards give the courage to talk about desire, honest agreements and the ability to forgive.

faq.q: Which partner is the Devil and which is the judge?
faq.a: Neither. The numbers of a couple's tail belong to the couple as a whole. Even if one partner has 15 in their personal tail and the other has 20, these are not the roles of culprit and judge but two pans of the same scales.

report: In the case the lawyer Anatoly Koni told Tolstoy in 1887, a girl was tried for a hundred roubles stolen from a drunken guest. Among the jurors, by chance, sat the man who had once seduced her, and he decided to marry her. In Resurrection the same sum ends up in another hand: the hundred roubles are pushed on the girl at parting by the seducer himself. The money she was tried for became the money with which he tries to close his account.

The couple's tail 15-8-20 follows the same road. The Devil at the entry is an attraction that easily starts to name a price. Justice in the middle is an attempt to settle up and make amends. Judgement as the main task is the ability to stop keeping accounts.

report.h3: A payment that calls itself honesty

report: The Easter night in the novel is the zenith of love, a moment when, in Tolstoy's words, it is "unconscious, unreasoning, and with nothing sensual about it". A few hours later the hero is ruled by "the animal man, seeking only his own happiness". And the next day Nekhlyudov decides to give her money "because that is what is always done, and he would be thought dishonest if, having made use of her, he did not pay for it" (our translation). **Closeness converted into payment, and called honesty into the bargain**: that is this tail's entry in its extreme form.

In an ordinary couple it looks softer. After a quarrel an expensive present turns up instead of a talk. In an argument someone says "I gave you everything". A decision rests on "that's how everyone lives". Jealousy passes itself off as love, and the partner has to be "mine alone". Lisovskaya's main thought about the fifteenth energy is short: nobody belongs to anybody. The entry has its strength too, the courage to want and to speak openly about desire. The only danger is the moment when "I want you" turns into "you owe me".

report.h3: A verdict reached out of fatigue

report: Ten years later Nekhlyudov sits on a jury and recognises the defendant. The jurors forget to add "without intent to take life" to their answer, and an innocent woman is sent to four years of penal servitude. Tolstoy names the main reason plainly: "being tired, and wishing to get away as soon as possible, all were ready to agree with the decision which would bring matters to an end soonest". The hero's first feeling is relief: "Siberia and penal servitude at once cut off every possibility of any kind of relations with her."

In a couple, a verdict like that is reached at half past one in the morning, when both are too tired to argue. The decision is taken not because it is right but because after it one can go to bed. The middle of the tail shows in small things too: a tally runs in someone's head of who gave in how many times and who pulled whom out, help is later presented as a bill, and after a quarrel someone says "we're quits".

report.h3: "Save yourself through me"

report: Then comes the attempt to pay. Nekhlyudov wants "to atone for my sin, not by mere words, but in deed" and proposes marriage to Katyusha. She answers: "You did not feel so then, but threw me 100 roubles. That's your price." And then: **"You've got pleasure out of me in this life, and want to save yourself through me in the life to come."** The whole tail is in one sentence: the Devil, Judgement and, between them, an account in which she twice becomes the means of payment.

Tolstoy himself stumbled at this step. In 1897 he wrote in his diary that on reaching the hero's decision to marry he "threw it aside in disgust. It is all untrue, invented, weak" (our translation). He resolved to save the book by choosing "to describe his and her feelings and life by turns". A Justice that weighs only one pan stops being justice.

But the middle is not useless. Nekhlyudov understands that had he not tried to expiate his guilt, "he would never have found out how great his crime was". **The attempt to pay shows the real size of the debt**, and shows that it cannot be closed with money or with marriage. The scales are there to see what happened, not to settle the account.

report.h3: "Where is the use of our reckoning?"

report: The main task is Judgement, and it is read mostly through its difficulties: a union "for the sake of something", the family's court, an inability to admit one's own mistake. In the novel the family court speaks before any other: the aunts decided that Katyusha "had inherited her mother's depraved nature", and "he was pleased to hear this opinion of his aunts'. It seemed to acquit him." **The family's verdict suits whoever needs to be acquitted.**

The turn comes in Siberia. Katyusha chooses another fate and lets Nekhlyudov go: "You must live, too." When the talk turns to gratitude, she answers: "Where is the use of our reckoning? God will make up our accounts." At parting she says, as Tolstoy notes, not "Good-bye" but "Forgive me".

In the last chapter Nekhlyudov opens the Gospel at Matthew 18, the chapter the novel's epigraph comes from. There he finds the parable of "a certain king which made a reckoning with his servants": the king forgives a servant a debt of ten thousand talents, and the servant takes by the throat a fellow-servant who owes him "a hundred pence". "And is this all?" Nekhlyudov exclaims, and the inner voice answers: "Yes, it is all." **The novel that began with a hundred roubles ends with a hundred pence.** Between them lies the whole course of the tail: from a price, through the account, to a judgement that stops counting.
For a couple with this tail, a few simple things follow:

ul: noticing the moment when a present, a favour or "after all I did for you" starts replacing a conversation;
not making important decisions "just to get it over with";
putting things right by asking what the other needs, not by assigning them one's own atonement;
keeping one's own judgement apart from the family's;
forgiving as ceasing to keep the account, not as pretending that nothing happened.

report: Tolstoy did not promise his hero a happy ending: "How this new period of his life will end time alone will prove." The tail 15-8-20 promises nothing either. It shows where an account begins between two people and where they can stop keeping it.

seo.title: Karmic tail 18 12 12 compatibility: the Moon and two Hanged Men
seo.description: Karmic tail 18 12 12 compatibility: the Moon at the entry, the Hanged Man twice. Read through Oblomov: Casta Diva, raised bridges and a way out of waiting.

items.title: Karmic tail 18-12-12 in compatibility: a couple waiting for the bridges
items.short: The Moon, followed twice by the Hanged Man. The 18-12-12 tail exists only in a couple: two people enter the union through a shared dream that is never said aloud, and then hang between "already" and "not yet". The main task of such a couple is not to love more, but to stop living in the future tense: to choose the person who is here now, not the one they might someday become, and to answer rather than wait.

sections.h2: A song about a secret confided to the moon
paragraphs: Oblomov has not yet met Olga. In the second part of the novel he comes home late one evening, grumbling, puts on his dressing gown, lies down on the sofa and tells Stolz what an ideal day would be like: dinner, guests, the fields. Towards evening "fog hangs over the rye like an upturned sea", lights come on in the house — and here Oblomov starts to sing: "Casta diva... Casta diva! I can't recall Casta diva without being moved... What sorrow there is in those sounds!.. And nobody around knows anything... She is alone... **A secret weighs on her; she confides it to the moon...**"
Stolz replies: "You love that aria? I'm very glad: Olga Ilyinskaya sings it beautifully. I'll introduce you." So this couple's love begins with a song, before the first meeting.

Who is "she", the woman weighed down by a secret? She is Norma from Bellini's opera (1831), a druid priestess. She has secretly broken her vows and borne two children to the Roman proconsul Pollione, and her people know nothing of it. In the scene with the aria the Gauls wait for her signal to rise against Rome. Norma declares that the time has not yet come, cuts the mistletoe and prays to the moon for peace. To herself she admits that she cannot destroy Pollione and wants everything to be as it was. The first lines of the aria:
Casta Diva, che inargenti / queste sacre antiche piante, / a noi volgi il bel sembiante / senza nube e senza vel.
"Chaste goddess, you who silver these sacred ancient trees, turn your fair face to us — without cloud and without veil" (our translation).

The whole tail is already in one aria. A secret union confided to the moon — that is the Moon. A decision put off because "the time has not come" — the Hanged Man. A broken vow and an attachment that can be neither admitted nor broken — the Devil at the centre. And in the same conversation, on the same pages, Stolz invents the word the novel will end on: "Some kind of... Oblomovism" (oblomovshchina). Going off to bed, he says from the doorway: "Now or never — remember!" The name of the chain and the only way out of it are spoken before the heroine has even appeared. And Oblomov sings his aria to the moon lying on the sofa in his dressing gown. The dressing gown is described on the very first page of the novel, and it will turn out to be the third character in this story.

sections.h2: Entry to the task, 18: a love that speaks in hints
paragraphs: The evening when Olga first sings for Oblomov Goncharov sets under the moon, though it takes place in her aunt's drawing room: "They lit a lamp, which shone through the ivy on the trellis like the moon. The dusk hid the outlines of Olga's face and figure and threw something like a crape veil over her; her face was in shadow: all one could hear was a soft but strong voice." At the end of the evening Olga sings Casta diva. Oblomov falls in love with a voice whose face he can barely see.

After that the couple develops a language of its own. Olga picks a sprig of lilac and hands it to him without a word, drops lilies of the valley on the path, Oblomov catches her glances. Goncharov later calls this period "the moment of symbolic hints, meaningful smiles, sprigs of lilac". Oblomov tells Olga that her look seems to say: "I need no words, I can read your looks", and at once admits: "But when you are not there, such a tormenting game of doubts begins." After one meeting he comes home "beaming, as if with 'a crescent moon on his brow', as his nanny used to say", sits down on the sofa and writes in the dust on the table with his finger: "Olga".

The entry point of a couple's tail is what the two want together: shared wishes, agreements, a common language. With this wish the couple enters its task. With 18 the common language is lunar: images, music, hints, signs that only the two understand. It is a real gift. Such couples understand each other from half a word and can build a world no one else can enter. But the entry stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. What is understood without words never gets said. Such a couple may have a whole dictionary of private jokes and songs, while the question "what are we to each other" or "are we living together" is never asked once. The plan exists as a mood.

The funniest thing is that Oblomov had described the wife of his dreams in advance, and the description has the line: "No moon, no sadness needed." He wanted a love without the moon and fell for a voice singing to the moon.

The entry holds an arithmetic clue as well. The couple's M point is the sum of the two partners' M points, and for the 18-12-12 tail it is always made as 9 + 9: each partner's personal tail begins with the Hermit. Two habits of living inside oneself, added together, give the Moon. The couple builds a shared inner world, like a second room for two with its own language. Only that room is also easy to lock oneself into.

sections.h2: A light that gives no warmth
paragraphs: Both lovers in the novel describe their love, and both with the same image — reflected light. Of Olga the author writes: "She weighed her power over him in an instant, and she liked this role of a guiding star, a ray of light that she would pour over a stagnant lake and that would be reflected in it." Oblomov, in a letter, describes her love as "an unconscious need to love which, for want of real nourishment, for want of fire, burns with a false light that gives no warmth".

Each sees a mirror in the other. Olga sees in Oblomov a lake in which her light will be reflected. Oblomov sees in her love a light that does not warm. Moonlight is not its own but reflected — one of Waite's best-known thoughts about the Moon — and in the novel it is the lovers themselves who say it. Benebell Wen adds one more trait to the Moon that fits this couple well: "There is a strong theme of **conservation in the card, rather than exploration or expansion**", "a sense of needing to feel protected, and thus forming the tough outer shell", and at the same time "a profound vulnerability that the Seeker is trying to conceal from others". Oblomov's shell is the dressing gown and the sofa. Olga's shell is pride and her role.

The most precise passage in the novel is the letter Oblomov writes after a sleepless night to break things off while it is not too late. He warns Olga: "You are mistaken; the man before you is not the one you were waiting for, the one you dreamed of. Wait — he will come, and then you will wake up." And the key sentence: **"your present 'I love you' is not real love but future love"**.

This is the trap of the lunar entry: love for a future image. A few months later Olga says the same thing in her own words: "I loved the future Oblomov!" Later still Stolz reads the letter aloud and sums it up: "You had parted even before you separated, and you were faithful not to love but to its ghost, which you had invented yourselves — that is the whole secret." The letter turned out to be a prophecy. The last word in Waite's divinatory list for the Hanged Man is precisely "prophecy".

That same day in the park, in a conversation about the letter, the Hanged Man appears too. Oblomov asks: "Am I not giving you up because I foresee your happiness ahead, because I am sacrificing myself to it?" Olga answers that he hid in the bushes to see whether she would cry: "this is not love, this is..." — "Selfishness!" Oblomov finishes himself. In the same list Waite gives the Hanged Man "sacrifice", and in the reversed position "selfishness". Here that pair of words is acted out in person.

sections.h2: Middle of the task, 12: "Katya, have they put the bridges back?"
paragraphs: Summer is ending, and love, in Goncharov's words, "began to turn into some kind of duty; mutual rights appeared". The couple is secretly engaged. Olga's aunt has been told nothing, and Oblomov is waiting for a letter from his estate, for money and for a flat. Meanwhile the servants give the secret away. Zakhar asks his master when the wedding is and explains how he found out: "Katya told Semyon, Semyon told Nikita, Nikita told Vasilisa, Vasilisa told Anisya, and Anisya told me..." Oblomov is horrified: "Olga kept silent, I didn't dare even think aloud, and in the servants' hall they've settled everything!" — and he shouts at Zakhar that it is all "nonsense, absurdity, lies, calumny". Waite's list for the Moon has exactly that word, calumny. A lunar couple is secretive even when all is well, and that is why rumours grow around it.

Then autumn comes. Oblomov lives on the Vyborg Side, Olga on the other bank of the Neva. "The bridges had already been taken up, and the Neva was about to freeze." He could cross over and stay closer to Olga, and Oblomov even puts his feet on the floor, "but, after thinking a little, with a careworn face and a sigh, slowly lay down again in his place". He hides from the servant Olga has sent and replies by note that he is unwell. The book she sent him he put down open at page 105, face down, and there it has lain for several days. Every morning the first thing he asks is whether the bridges are back.
And here Goncharov makes the move that makes the novel worth rereading:
"Katya, have they put the bridges back?" Olga asked her maid, waking up that same morning. And the question was repeated every day. Oblomov had no idea of it.

This is the middle of the tail. Two people wait for the same bridge, each on their own bank. There is not one idler here: both are hanging, and each waits for the other to cross the river. The N point shows how the couple lives the way from the wish to the task. For 18-12-12 that way runs through a pause: "And he was still at the same point of being unable to move forward."

There is a numerical clue too. If 18-12-12 were a personal tail, the middle would be counted from the ends: 18 + 12 = 30, 3 + 0 = 3, the Empress. In a couple the middle is added up from the two partners' middles, and here it is always 9 + 3 = 12. Where personal logic would put the Empress — home, wedding, children — the couple has the Hanged Man. A personal matrix never has such a middle at all. The Empress is exactly what Oblomov saw in his dreams: a bride "at the altar, with a long veil, then at the head of the marriage bed... and at last a mother among a group of children". The picture of home stays a picture, and the life between the dream and the home hangs.

In a couple today it looks quite ordinary. The wedding date floats: "after the renovation". Meeting the parents is put off "until the holidays", moving in "until the lease runs out". Each secretly checks whether the other has already crossed. According to Lisovskaya, couples with the twelfth energy get going slowly, and they often need a push from outside to marry. In the novel the push came from the servants' gossip, only it did not push — it froze.

sections.h2: Main task, 12: "I am waiting not for assurances of love but for a short answer"
paragraphs: The main point of a couple's tail is read mostly through difficulties: what the two cannot manage and what they have to learn. Goncharov gives a whole scene to this at the end of the third part. Some remember it as a break-up, but it is built as an exam on the main task.

Olga begins with a confession: "I thought I would bring you back to life, that you could still live for me — but you died long ago." And she adds: "A stone would have come to life from what I did." Oblomov answers with what their whole middle rested on: "But perhaps..." — and hesitantly adds: "in a year..." Olga gives him one more chance: "If you say yes boldly and after thinking it over, I take back my decision: here is my hand, and let us go wherever you like — abroad, to the country, even to the Vyborg Side!" He begins: "If only you knew how I love..." And then Olga says the key line of the tail: **"I am waiting not for assurances of love but for a short answer."**
When everything has already been decided, Oblomov finds the right words: "Take me as I am, love what is good in me." Olga shakes her head, and a little later says: "I loved the future Oblomov!"

It is easy to read this scene as a verdict on one of the two, but a couple's tail describes the task of both. Olga holds the union up with all her strength, puts a summer, her pride and her reputation into it, and gets postponements in return. Oblomov is tormented by guilt and hides deeper. According to Lisovskaya, this is what the Hanged Man looks like in the main task: one partner carries the relationship and gets reproaches, there are no shared goals, expectations of the partner are too high. Only here both are hanging. Olga is suspended on the project of bringing him back to life, Oblomov on the hope that someday he will be ready. Both love a future person: she loves the future Oblomov, he loves his future self.

Waite has a sentence about the Hanged Man that most retellings pass by: "He who can understand that the story of his higher nature is imbedded in this symbolism will receive intimations concerning a great awakening that is possible". The awakening is promised to the one who has understood his own story, not to the one who tries to wake someone else. Olga was wrong not in her feeling but in her craft: no one can be woken from the outside, not even by a voice singing Casta diva.

The couple's main task is made up of the partners' main tasks: one has the Moon, 18, in this place of the personal tail, the other has the World, 21. Together 39, 3 + 9 = 12. Fog plus a hunger for the whole world gives suspension. In one sentence of Olga's both halves of this sum can be heard: "this is not enough for me, I need something more, and what — I don't know!"

In a couple today the task sounds like this. One books, explains, suggests, waits, gets tired and starts to reproach. The other answers "let's see", feels guilty and withdraws even further. A year later both are surprised that "nothing happened", though the main thing did: the decision was never made.

sections.h2: The atmosphere inside the couple, 15: a chain neither of the two owns
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's chart is the atmosphere of the union, what is between the two when nobody is watching. Every couple with the 18-12-12 tail has 15, the Devil, at the centre. There are no exceptions: the centre is added up from the partners' centres, and with this tail they are always 9 and 6, the Hermit and the Lovers. One more clue: no birth date ever gives 15 at the centre of a personal matrix. Neither of the two brings this chain. It appears only when a hermit and a lover sit down side by side.

Goncharov describes this atmosphere without any cards. In such a "comedy or tragedy", he writes, the two almost always have the same roles: **"of the tormentor, male or female, and the victim"**. Of Olga it is said that she "triumphed in her primacy in this duel in all sorts of ways". Olga tells Oblomov: "What I have once called mine I will not give back, unless it is taken from me." And Oblomov, in his letter, fears something else: "And what will happen when I become attached... How will I tear myself away then?" One holds on by power, the other by dependence, and both are chained.

But this couple has a third character as well. Back in summer, in the park, Olga asks: "if not even another woman, but your dressing gown becomes dearer to you?" On the night after the break-up Oblomov comes home, and Goncharov ends the chapter with a single object: Zakhar undressed him, pulled off his boots "and threw over him — the dressing gown!" The Devil at the centre of this couple is not a wicked partner. It is whatever each holds dearer than the other: comfort, pride, the role of rescuer, "the way it was". Wen writes that "The Devil is not a literal beast or demon; The Devil personifies human selfishness", and speaks of a **"preference for instant gratification over delayed gratification"**. The dressing gown is the instant gratification. The delayed one is the road to Olga across the river.

Olga's last question in that scene sounds like an incantation: "Who cursed you, Ilya? What have you done?.. What has ruined you? There is no name for this evil..." — "There is," he answers barely audibly, and to her questioning look whispers: "Oblomovism!" The evil gets a name, and it is the name not of a person but of a way of living. Wen specifically notes that "The Devil card does not necessarily mean the Seeker is entirely to blame". The guilt in this couple does not split into "him" and "her": the chain is shared.

In Waite's divinatory list the Devil has a clause that fits the fact "every couple, without exception": "that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil". And the description of the card says that the one exalted above the chained figures "is not to be their master for ever". In Lisovskaya the conclusion about the fifteenth energy in a couple is that **no one belongs to anyone**. For this couple it is not a moral but a technique: the chain weakens when it is named aloud.

sections.h2: The couple's values: the peace that comes after the road
paragraphs: The couple's values are what the union exists for. Couples with the 18-12-12 tail have two cards here: the Hermit in 76.3% and the Moon in 23.7%.

The Hermit among the values means quiet, depth, unhurriedness, honesty. In the novel Stolz names them when he explains to Olga what she still loves in Oblomov: "an honest, faithful heart! That is his natural gold", and, remembering himself, adds "dove-like tenderness". In itself this is no vice. Oblomov dreamed of a wife "as peace itself", and there is nothing shameful in that dream.

The difference lies in when the peace comes. Wen's Hermit is a man who "has been on a long journey" and at the end of it "has found peace". Oblomov wanted peace instead of the journey: when Stolz suggests leaving in two weeks, he answers "perhaps in three months or so". For a couple with this tail quiet is a real value, only it should be the quiet of a hermit who has arrived, not the quiet of a sofa nobody ever got up from.

In one such couple in four the values hold the Moon. Then the union exists for the dream itself: shared poetry, a secret world of their own, music for two. That is a value too, but it is easy to spend it on hiding.

sections.h2: The way out: into the moonlight, face to face
paragraphs: In the fourth part Olga is married to Stolz. She is tormented by a strange sadness, which she hides. One evening they are walking along an avenue of poplars, and Goncharov writes: "He led her out of the avenue and turned her face to the moonlight. 'Look at me!'" For the first time Olga names aloud what troubles her. A few turns of the avenue later she, "in her turn, led him out into the moonlight and looked questioningly into his eyes". Stolz explains to her: "This is the sadness of a soul questioning life about its secret", and suggests: "we will bow our heads and humbly live through the difficult moment".

This is the very request of Casta diva, finally granted: to turn one's face to the other "without cloud and without veil". The moon is the same as at the start of the novel. The difference is that the two stand in its light face to face and say aloud what used to be a hint. The Hanged Man is here too, but chosen: to bow their heads together for a difficult moment is a pause the two take together, not a hook on which each hangs alone.

The novel gives Olga a different husband, but a couple's tail does not advise changing partners. It speaks about what these two should do. Translated into the language of the tail, the novel's hints come out like this.

ul: **Turn hints into sentences.** A sprig of lilac is lovely, but the sentence "I want us to live together" is stronger. The Moon at its best is a couple that can talk about feelings and does not invent things on the other's behalf.
**Give a short answer.** A date, a decision or an honest "no" instead of "in a year". A pause is good when it has an end and both have chosen it.
**Love the one who is there.** "Take me as I am" — the partner is not a draft of a future person. A project of bringing someone else back to life is a beautiful form of the same chain.

**Find the third at the centre and name it.** Whatever each holds dearer than the other: the dressing gown, the role of rescuer, pride, "the way it was". A chain that has been named holds less tightly.
**Each crosses their own bridge.** No one can wake the other; one can wake up oneself and hold out a hand from the other bank.

paragraphs: And a last clue, from the author's life. The novel about a suspended life was itself suspended for a long time. Goncharov conceived it in 1847, published "Oblomov's Dream" separately, then broke off for years and sailed on the frigate Pallada. In the summer of 1857, in Marienbad, he finished three parts in a few weeks. A pause after which a whole thing ripens is the Hanged Man too. That is the side of the card for whose sake a couple with this tail is worth learning to wait differently.

sections.h2: How the 18-12-12 tail comes about: an example with two dates
paragraphs: Each point of a couple's chart is the sum of the same points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22. Take the dates 11.02.1976 and 02.01.1980.

paragraphs: The couple's values in this example are 9, the Hermit.
What else a run through all birth dates shows:

ul: the 18-12-12 tail occurs in roughly one couple in 929 (0.108%), 81st place out of 97 couples' tails;
it is made by only one combination of personal tails: 9-9-18 in one partner and 9-3-21 in the other;
so the couple's centre is always 15, and the values are 9 or 18;
there are no other couples' tails from these numbers: the couple calculation never gives 12-18-12 or 12-12-18, and there is no personal tail 18-12-12.

intro: The three numbers of a couple's tail are read in order, and each has its own role.

ul: **18, The Moon — entry to the task.** What the couple wants together and the language in which they agree. Here it is a language of half-tones: songs, hints, private words, a secret for two. The wish is there, but it lives in the imagination, not in words.

**12, The Hanged Man — middle of the task.** How the couple moves from the wish to the task: through a pause. Moving in, the wedding, meeting the family — all "a little later", and each quietly waits for the other to move first.

**12, The Hanged Man — main task.** What the couple has to learn: to take the union off the hook of waiting. Not to wait until the partner becomes the person they imagined, but to choose them as they are today — or honestly say "no".

intro: The strangest thing about this triple is the repeat. The pause the couple walks through is its main task as well: the middle and the end of the tail are the same card. And at the centre of the chart every such couple has the Devil, the card of attachment, which no personal destiny matrix ever has at its centre. Neither of the two brings it: it is born only between them.

Russian literature knows this plot almost by heart, though it is usually read as the story of one idle man. In fact it is the story of a couple. Ivan Goncharov, Oblomov, 1859: Ilya Ilyich Oblomov and Olga Ilyinskaya. (Quotations from the novel here are our own translations from the Russian.)

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 18-12-12 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: These are the couple's tasks, not a personal programme of one partner. The Moon at the entry: the couple comes together through a shared dream and a language of hints. The Hanged Man in the middle: the way to the goal runs through pauses and postponements. The Hanged Man as the main task: learning to step out of waiting, to choose the partner as they are today and to answer briefly.

faq.q: Why does the Hanged Man appear twice in this tail?
faq.a: A repeat does not double the card; each point has its own role. In the middle the Hanged Man describes how the couple lives: through a pause. In the main task it describes what to learn: to manage that pause so that it is chosen and has an end, rather than turning into a hook.

faq.q: Does the 18-12-12 tail occur in a personal destiny matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is derived from the ends, and with ends 18 and 12 it would be 3. In a couple the middle is added up from the two partners' middles, so 18-12-12 occurs only in a couple.

faq.q: Does the 18-12-12 tail mean the couple is doomed to wait or to part?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events or dates; it shows where the couple easily gets stuck and what to learn. Goncharov's novel is one version of this plot; the scene of Olga and Stolz in the moonlight shows the same Moon and the same Hanged Man at their best.

faq.q: How can you tell a couple has the 18-12-12 tail without a calculator?
faq.a: Look at the partners' personal karmic tails: one must have 9-9-18, the other 9-3-21. This couple's tail cannot be made any other way. The most reliable way is to calculate the couple's chart in the compatibility calculator.

report: Russia's most famous novel about idleness is really about a couple waiting for the bridges to go back. The 18-12-12 tail — the Moon, followed twice by the Hanged Man — is played out in Goncharov's Oblomov almost note for note, and it begins with a song.

Oblomov has not yet met Olga. Late one evening, in his dressing gown on the sofa, he tells Stolz about the ideal life and starts singing Casta diva: "A secret weighs on her; she confides it to the moon..." It is Norma's aria from Bellini's opera. The priestess is secretly bound to a Roman, her people wait for her signal to rise up, and she declares the time has not yet come and prays to the moon for peace. A secret union confided to the moon, a decision put off until later, a bond that can be neither admitted nor broken — the whole tail is already in one aria. Stolz replies that Olga Ilyinskaya sings this aria beautifully.

report.h3: A language in which the main thing is never said

report: Olga sings for Oblomov in a drawing room where the lamp shines "like the moon" and the singer's face is in shadow: "all one could hear was a soft but strong voice." Then the couple develops its own language: a sprig of lilac, lilies of the valley on the path, glances. Goncharov calls this period "the moment of symbolic hints, meaningful smiles, sprigs of lilac".

A couple's entry to the task is what the two want together, their common language. With the Moon that language is lunar: images, music, signs only the two understand. It is a real gift, but the entry stands on the line of tasks, and **what is understood without words never gets said**. There is a whole dictionary of private jokes and songs, but "what are we to each other" is never asked. Oblomov had even dreamed in advance of a wife without mists: "No moon, no sadness needed." And he fell for a voice singing to the moon.

He described the trap of the lunar entry himself, in a letter to Olga: the love she feels now "is not real love but future love". Months later Olga says the same in her own words: "I loved the future Oblomov!" **Both love a future person**: she loves the future Oblomov, he loves his future self.

report.h3: Two people on two banks waiting for one bridge

report: The couple is secretly engaged. Nobody has told the aunt, and the servants are first to talk of the wedding. In autumn Oblomov lives on the Vyborg Side and Olga on the other bank of the Neva; "the bridges had already been taken up". Each morning he first asks whether the bridges are back. And here Goncharov makes his best move:
"'Katya, have they put the bridges back?' Olga asked her maid, waking up that same morning. And the question was repeated every day. Oblomov had no idea of it."

The middle of the tail shows how the couple moves from the wish to the task. For 18-12-12 that way runs through a pause. There is not one idler here: **both are hanging, and each waits for the other to cross the river**. In a couple today it looks quite ordinary: the wedding date set "after the renovation", meeting the parents put off "until the holidays", and each secretly checking whether the other has already crossed.

report.h3: The main task: a short answer instead of "in a year"

report: The break-up scene in the novel is built as an exam on the main task. Olga confesses that she meant to bring him back to life, that he could still live for her — but, in her words, he "died long ago". Oblomov answers with what their whole middle rested on: "But perhaps..." — and hesitantly adds: "in a year..." Olga says the key line of the tail: **"I am waiting not for assurances of love but for a short answer."** Oblomov finds the right words only when all is decided: "Take me as I am, love what is good in me."

It is easy to read this scene as a verdict on one of the two, but a couple's tail describes the task of both. One carries the union and gets postponements in return; the other is tormented by guilt and hides deeper. Olga is suspended on the project of bringing him back to life, Oblomov on the hope of someday being ready. Waite says of the Hanged Man that "a great awakening that is possible" is promised to the one who has understood his own story — not to the one who tries to wake someone else.

report.h3: A chain that appears only between two people

report: At the centre of the chart, couples with this tail have the Devil, the card of attachment, which no personal destiny matrix ever has at its centre. Neither of the two brings it: it is born only between them. Goncharov describes this atmosphere without any cards: the two have the roles "of the tormentor, male or female, and the victim". Olga says: "What I have once called mine I will not give back, unless it is taken from me." Oblomov fears getting too attached to tear himself away.

This couple has a third character as well — the dressing gown. In summer Olga asks whether his dressing gown will become dearer to him than she is. On the night after the break-up Zakhar undressed him, pulled off his boots "and threw over him — the dressing gown!" The Devil at the centre is not a wicked partner but whatever each holds dearer than the other: comfort, pride, the role of rescuer, "the way it was". To Olga's "There is no name for this evil..." Oblomov whispers: "Oblomovism!" The evil gets a name, and it is the name not of a person but of a way of living. **The chain weakens when it is named aloud**: no one belongs to anyone.

report.h3: The way out: face to face in the moonlight

report: In the last part Olga, now married to Stolz, hides a strange sadness. One evening on a walk "he led her out of the avenue and turned her face to the moonlight. 'Look at me!'" A few turns later she, "in her turn, led him out into the moonlight and looked questioningly into his eyes". This is the request of Casta diva, finally granted: to turn one's face "without cloud and without veil". The moon is the same as at the start. The difference is that the two stand in its light face to face and say aloud what used to be a hint. The Hanged Man is still here, only chosen: "we will bow our heads and humbly live through the difficult moment".
A couple's tail does not advise changing partners. It suggests something else to these two:

ul: turn hints into sentences;
give a short answer: a date, a decision or an honest "no" instead of "in a year";
love the one who is there, not a draft of a future person;
find what each holds dearer than the other, and name it;
each crosses their own bridge: no one can wake the other; one can wake up oneself and hold out a hand from the other bank.

report: A pause is good when it has an end and both have chosen it.
