seo.title: Karmic tail 18 12 21 compatibility: Moon, Hanged Man, World
seo.description: Karmic tail 18 12 21 compatibility: what the Moon, the Hanged Man and the World mean for two people, and how Ibsen's Peer Gynt tells this tail scene by scene.

items.title: Karmic tail 18-12-21 in compatibility: night, a threshold and a whole world
items.short: The couple's tail 18-12-21 begins at night and ends with a whole world, and the Hanged Man stands between them. The story was written long ago: Ibsen's Peer Gynt, the tale of Peer and Solveig. The Moon (18) is the entry to the task: the couple comes together over a fairy tale, a secret and a lot of guessing. The Hanged Man (12) is the middle: two people get stuck on a threshold, one "going roundabout", the other promising to wait. The World (21) is the main task: to make two lives into one whole and finally walk into their own house, instead of searching for "the whole world" at the far end of the earth.

sections.h2: What 18-12-21 means in a couple's destiny matrix
paragraphs: A couple's tail is three points on the line of tasks in the compatibility matrix; in the reading it is the sphere called "The couple's karmic tail". Yuliana Lisovskaya, whose book the compatibility calculation follows, calls such a triple a karmic programme, which is why people search for "18 12 21 programme". The tail is read in the order M–N–D. The entry to the task (M) is what the couple wants together, its shared language; the point stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish easily turns into resistance. The middle of the task (N) is how the couple travels from that wish to the task. The main task (D) is the central test, and it is read mainly through its minus: what the two cannot manage yet and what they have to learn.
In the tail 18-12-21 the roles fall like this:

ul: **Entry to the task — 18, The Moon.** The couple wants a shared secret: to understand each other without words, to live in its own fairy tale, to see more in each other than anyone else does. The resistance is the same Moon: guessing instead of asking, and an image instead of a person.

**Middle of the task — 12, The Hanged Man.** The road runs through a pause. Decisions are put off, one carries something heavy alone, the other waits. The pause can become a change of view, or it can stretch over years.

**Main task — 21, The World.** To build a whole: a shared world in which both stay themselves and what was started gets finished. In the minus the World is a closed circle: a private universe behind a locked door, or an endless search for "real life" somewhere else.

paragraphs: The atmosphere inside these couples is always the same: the centre of the couple's matrix holds 15, The Devil, the card of attraction and attachment. No birth date ever gives a personal matrix with 15 at the centre, so this atmosphere is born only in the couple. The couple's values are The Hermit (in 69.3% of these couples) or The Moon (in 30.7%).

Why Peer Gynt? Ibsen wrote this dramatic poem in 1867 on Ischia and in Sorrento, and the book came out on 14 November. In 1876 it was staged in Christiania with Grieg's music, and "Morning Mood", "In the Hall of the Mountain King" and "Solveig's Song" are known even to people who have never opened the play. The plot goes like this. Peer, a village liar, meets quiet Solveig at a wedding, lands among the trolls and builds a hut in the forest. Solveig comes to live with him, and he leaves, supposedly for a while, and spends decades looking for himself all over the world. The cards of the tail appear in the play in their own order: night and trolls, a half-open door, the whole world and the way home.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — The Moon: "Peer, you're lying!"
paragraphs: The play opens with an accusation. The first line belongs to his mother, Åse: "Peer, you're lying!" Peer has just told her how he rode a reindeer along a mountain ridge and plunged with it into the abyss. As they fell, something whitish below rushed up to meet them: "Mother, 'twas our own reflection in the glass-smooth mountain tarn, shooting up towards the surface." The buck from above met the buck from below, and both went under. Åse gasps, thanks God for saving her son — and suddenly stops: she heard this story as a girl, and it happened to Gudbrand Glesnë. "Yes, a lie, turned topsy-turvy, can be prinked and tinselled out," she says.

The first image of the play is a man falling towards his own reflection. Waite calls the light of the Moon a reflection and puts "deception" on its list of meanings. Peer shines in exactly this way: someone else's tale told as his own, with himself as the hero.

A few scenes later Solveig enters the wedding yard, and Peer sees her the way couples with this tail first see each other: "How fair! Did ever you see the like! Looked down at her shoes and her snow-white apron—! … And carried a psalm-book wrapped up in a kerchief—!" When she hears his name, Solveig pulls her hand away: the gossip about Peer has reached her before Peer himself. Lisovskaya writes that couples with the Moon stay secretive even in the plus and so "become overgrown with rumours and false images" (our translation); for Peer and Solveig this began before they had even met. She refuses to dance, and Peer threatens her: "I can turn myself into a troll! I'll come to your bedside at midnight to-night." He says it outright: "I'm a were-wolf at night" — varulv in the original. And at once, "as if in dread", he changes his tone: "Dance with me, lass!" Her answer: "You were ugly then."

One short exchange holds the whole Moon. Desire and fear arrive together. Each meets not a person but an image: he sees a saint; she first hears the gossip, then sees a monster. Neither image is entirely a lie, and neither is the truth.

For a couple's tail, the Moon at the entry means this. The two are drawn together by a secret: the feeling that they knew each other without words, their own pet names and private jokes, talks until dawn, a shared legend about themselves — "as if we had always known each other". Lisovskaya writes that in the plus of the Moon partners understand each other by intuition and keep discovering something new in each other every year. This is the couple's shared language.

But the entry to the task sits on the line of tasks, and the same Moon turns into resistance. A fairy tale does not like questions. To "What's wrong?" one answers "Nothing", and by nightfall the other has built three versions of what happened and checked none of them. The past gets told in a flattering light, like Peer's reindeer ride. People grow jealous of things they invented. The image made at the start protects the couple as long as nobody touches it, so nobody touches it for years. Wen writes of the Moon that "the tame side and the wild side are at odds" — and that is how Peer and Solveig met: in one speech he is first a werewolf, then a suitor begging for a dance.

This Moon has arithmetic. The partner whose personal tail is 12-19-7 brings The Hanged Man to the entry; the partner with 6-20-14 brings The Lovers: 12 + 6 = 18. Our reading: one partner's suspension and the other's choice add up to a night in which the fairy tale is easy to see and the road is not.

sections.h2: The atmosphere — The Devil: the hall where the bridegroom gets a tail
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's matrix is its atmosphere, what goes on between the two away from view. Every couple with the tail 18-12-21 has 15, The Devil, here, and it follows from arithmetic. The partner with the personal tail 12-19-7 always has a personal centre of 5, The Hierophant; the partner with 6-20-14 always has 10, The Wheel of Fortune. 5 + 10 = 15. A card that never sits at the centre of a personal matrix appears only when two people are added together.

In Ibsen this atmosphere is the hall of the Dovre-King, the king of the trolls — the very hall of Grieg's "In the Hall of the Mountain King". Peer is courting the king's daughter, and the conditions are homely. First the home-brewed drink: "The cow gives cakes and the bullock mead; ask not if its taste be sour or sweet; the main matter is, and you mustn't forget it, it's all of it home-brewed." Then the clothes. Then the tail: "None comes courting my child with no tail at his rear." Peer grumbles and gives in: "It's true, as the saying goes: Man's but a mote. And it's wisest to follow the fashion a bit. Tie away!"

The most important thing the king says separately, like a motto for a coat of arms: "Out yonder, under the shining vault, among men the saying goes: 'Man, be thyself!' At home here with us, 'mid the tribe of the trolls, the saying goes: 'Troll, to thyself be—enough!'" Then he adds that "Enough" is "that most potent and sundering word". In the original the two mottoes differ by exactly one word: "Mand, vær dig selv!" and "Trold, vær dig selv — nok!". A man is told to be himself; a troll is told to be enough for himself.

The last condition is the eye. "In your left eye, first, I'll scratch you a bit, till you see awry; but all that you see will seem fine and brave." Here Peer digs in his heels. The tail, he says, is no problem — "no doubt I can loose what the Chamberlain tied" — breeches can be buttoned on again, an oath can be eaten. But "to live as a hill-troll for all one's days — to feel that one never can beat a retreat… that is a thing I can never agree to."

For the atmosphere of a couple this is an exact picture of the Devil. In the plus: a strong pull, their own customs, their own mead, their own language that outsiders watch in puzzlement. Lisovskaya writes that such partners accept each other's dark sides and speak openly about their desires. In the minus: the same "enough" — "the two of us are enough", friends slowly become superfluous, closeness turns into the only glue, the wish is to own rather than to be beside. For the sake of peace it is easy to accept small tails: the other's habits, the other's holidays, the other's catchphrases. The danger is something else — the scratched eye, when, to keep things calm, both agree to see what is crooked as beautiful. Wen writes that "The Devil is not a literal beast or demon; The Devil personifies human selfishness and indulging in that selfishness." Lisovskaya's chapter on the Devil ends with the line "no one belongs to anyone".

In the fifth act the old Dovre-King appears again and announces that Peer has lived his whole life by that motto: "You've lived as a troll, but have still kept it secret." As proof he pulls out a troll newspaper, which declares that "horns and a tail are of little importance, so long as one has but a strip of the hide". A couple's karmic tail is not about a tail either. It is about the word "enough".

sections.h2: The Boyg: an enemy that does not fight
paragraphs: From the troll hall Peer stumbles into pitch darkness. Something slimy and shapeless blocks his way. "Who are you?" — "Myself. Can you say the same?" The creature calls itself the Boyg. In the Norwegian it is Bøygen, a monster from the folk tale of Peer Gynt that Asbjørnsen published in 1848. Ibsen's English translators, William and Charles Archer, derive the name from a root meaning "to bend"; a German translator called it "der Krumme", and in the Russian translation by Anna and Peter Hansen it is Krivaya, "the Crooked One". It has one piece of advice: "Go roundabout, Peer!" Peer shouts "No, through!" and lashes out, but his blows land on nothing: "Forward or back, and it's just as far; out or in, and it's just as strait! He is there! And there! And he's round the bend! No sooner I'm out than I'm back in the ring." The Boyg does not strike back: "The great Boyg conquers, but does not fight."

Critics argued over what it is. Georg Brandes saw in the Boyg the spirit of compromise. The Swedish critic Vasenius saw Peer's inability to take a decisive step — to go through an obstacle instead of skirting round it. For the couple 18-12-21 the second reading fits better. This is a moonlit enemy: shapeless, nocturnal, immune to a quarrel. Such couples rarely break over a big scandal. They spend years going round the same subject — money, parents, an old story, the question of children, a move. Each detour makes sense on its own: "not now", "let's not spoil the evening". Together the detours close into a ring, and inside it the two walk in circles.

In the play the Boyg is not beaten by fists. Church bells and psalm-singing are heard far away, and it "shrinks up to nothing", gasping: "He was too strong. There were women behind him." Before he falls, Peer manages to call to the girl with the psalm-book: "Your clasp-book! Hurl it straight into his eyes!" The fog is lifted not by force but by a voice close by. In a couple that voice belongs to whoever is the first to say out loud what both have been going round.

Remember the ring. Archer's Peer is "back in the ring"; the original is more exact still: as soon as he gets out, he is standing "midt i ringen" — in the very middle of the ring. That ring will come back at the end of the tail.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — The Hanged Man: the half-open door
paragraphs: Act three. Peer is an outlaw living in the forest; he builds a hut and fixes a bar to the door — against "troll-folk, and men, and women", against "cantankerous hobgoblin-thoughts". Solveig comes over the snow on skis. She has left her father, her mother and her little sister, and to those who asked "Whither go you?" she answered, "I go home." "The path I have trodden leads back nevermore." Peer forgets about the bar, yet his words still carry moonlight: "Solveig! Let me look at you! Not too near! Only look at you!" He is ready to carry her in his arms — and to hold her "far out from me", so as not to soil her.

Peer goes to fetch wood, and out of the thicket comes the Woman in Green, the Dovre-King's daughter, with an ugly brat — his son from that night in the mountains. "Even as your hut was builded, mine built itself too," she says, and promises to come every day, sit by them and "ask for my share". Left alone, Peer remembers: "The Boyg said, 'Go roundabout!'—so one must here." Going in to Solveig now would mean to "speak, yet be silent; confess, yet conceal". In the Russian translation this almost turns into a pun: the Boyg is Krivaya, "the Crooked One", and Peer wonders whether to krivit dushoy — literally "to make the soul crooked", the Russian idiom for lying.
Then come five lines on which the whole middle of the tail rests:

— You must wait. It is dark, and I've got something heavy to fetch. — Wait; I will help you; the burden we'll share. — No, stay where you are! I must bear it alone. — …Be my way long or short—you must wait. — Yes, I'll wait!

The stage direction: "Solveig remains standing in the open half-door." On that half-open door the play hangs for decades. In the original Peer's refusal says even more: "Jeg får bære det hele" — "I must carry all of it", literally "the whole". That word, hele, will return in the last scene.

This is the middle of the tail 18-12-21: not betrayal and not a quarrel, but a refused offer to share the burden. Here the Hanged Man has two faces. One carries the weight alone and calls it care: "Don't worry about it, I'll sort it out myself." The other waits and calls it loyalty. Both sacrifices look noble, and together they make a door that is neither open nor shut. Lisovskaya writes that with the Hanged Man a couple takes a long time to commit and often needs a push from outside to marry; in its sacrificial version one partner does everything for the other and nothing for themselves, and the picture outside looks better than the life within. In ordinary life this means years of "after the renovation", "when the project is over", "when things settle down"; an old debt one partner keeps quiet about "so as not to cause worry"; a move that gets discussed every holiday.

But the Hanged Man is not only standing still. It is also the ability to see from the other side, and Lisovskaya notes a rare plus in these couples: the partners sense each other at a distance. Solveig's song is sung thousands of miles from Peer: "Maybe both the winter and spring will pass by, and the next summer too, and the whole of the year; — but thou wilt come one day, that know I full well; and I will await thee, as I promised of old." In her last song she still remembers that very burden: "Is thy burden heavy, take time, take time." In the original Solveig repeats the words of that evening exactly. Peer left saying "jeg har noget tungt at hente" — "I've got something heavy to fetch". She sings: "Har du tungt at hente, så und dig frist" — "if what you went to fetch is heavy, take your time". Wen writes that the Hanged Man raises the question "will the Seeker fall or fly?" and sends the message to "hang in there". The middle of the tail is not a verdict but a pause whose outcome is not written down.

The number of the middle confirms that there is no way round it. The couple's middle is counted from the personal middles: 20 + 19 = 39 → 12. One partner's Sun and the other's Judgement, two cards of light and awakening, fold together into suspension. And if the outer numbers of the tail are added, 18 + 21, the result is the same 39. Whichever way it is counted, the two arrive at the same door.

sections.h2: Main task — The World in the minus: emperor of the earth and the onion
paragraphs: The main task is read through its minus, and Ibsen gives the minus of the World a whole act. In act four Peer is rich, entertains guests on the Moroccan coast and declares his life's goal: "To be Emperor." — "Where?" — "O'er all the world." In the same breath he recalls a Gospel line and retells it his own way: "if you gained the whole wide world, but lost yourself, your gain were but a garland on a cloven skull." And asked what his Self is, he answers: "The world behind my forehead's arch."

Here it is worth going back to the troll hall. The king said that men are taught to be themselves "out yonder, under the shining vault". Peer puts his world behind the arch of his own forehead. In the original both lines use the same word, hvælv, "vault": the world of men lies under the sky, Peer's world under his brow. That is the World in the minus: a whole universe that fits inside one head.

The original holds one more echo, and Archer kept it. The king calls "enough" the "sundering", splitting word — kløvende. And in Peer's version of the Gospel line, the victory of a man who gained the world and lost himself is a garland round a "cloven" temple, kløvet tinding. The troll's "enough" splits, and a world bought without a self crowns a split head.

Then comes the madhouse in Cairo. The director explains that here everyone is "oneself, and nothing whatever besides": "No one has tears for the other's woes; no one has mind for the other's ideas." Peer is crowned with a wreath of straw: "Long life, long life to Self-hood's Kaiser!" And in act five, back in the forest, he peels a wild onion and names every layer: the shipwrecked man, the gold-digger, the Prophet. One layer looks like a crown, and Peer throws it away. There is no kernel: "nothing but swathings — each smaller and smaller."

Lisovskaya describes the World in the minus with scenes that are easy to recognise in these pictures. One partner draws the shared world to their own plan and takes offence if the other has a different map: re-educates, imposes views. Friends and relatives drop away one by one: "we don't need anyone". The relationship goes round the circle of "together — apart", like Peer, who left supposedly for a while and came back decades later. Life becomes a Groundhog Day of roles — parents, hosts, colleagues — and when the roles come off, the middle is empty, like the onion. Waite's divinatory list for the World includes "voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place", and reversed, "inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence". In the play these lists are divided between two people, and neither of them reaches the World alone.

sections.h2: A button on the vest of the world: how the World comes together
paragraphs: In act five an old Peer is visited by the Button-moulder with his casting-ladle: Peer's soul is to be melted down with the rest of the spoilt goods. He is no villain — even the Devil, whom Peer meets a little later, will turn him down — and that is the whole point. "Now, you were designed for a shining button on the vest of the world; but your loop gave way." A button without a loop is only good for melting: there is nothing to sew it to.

Here is the main task of the tail 18-12-21 put in the simplest words. Not an emperor of the world, and not a troll who is "enough" for himself, but a button with a loop: a small place sewn into a larger cloth. Wen writes that the World stands for "oneness with his or her greater calling" and for "the Seeker's importance in the greater cosmic landscape". A couple with this tail builds its world not by walling itself off from everyone, and not when one of the two goes looking for "real life" on the other side of the earth. It builds it when the two acquire a shared loop: a home, a cause, a circle of people they are sewn to together.

The main task is plain addition with no reduction. The partners' personal main tasks, The Chariot (7) and Temperance (14), add up to 21. Our reading: the World is made of movement and measure, and neither the one who only travels nor the one who only waits and keeps can assemble it alone.

Peer understands this before he dares to act. He passes a familiar hut and hears Solveig singing: "One that's remembered,—and one that's forgot. One that has squandered,—and one that has saved.— Oh, earnest!—and never can the game be played o'er! Oh, dread!—here was my Kaiserdom!" In the original it is "O, angst! — Her var mit kejserdom!" Everything he had sought "o'er all the world" stood in the forest, behind a half-open door.

The finale answers the Boyg word for word. Peer walks up to the hut and repeats its words: "Forward and back, and it's just as far. Out and in, and it's just as strait." He stops: "Round about, said the Boyg!" And for the first time in his life: "Ah no; this time at least right through, though the path may be never so strait!" On the threshold stands Solveig, dressed for church, "with a psalm-book wrapped in a kerchief". This is exactly how Peer first saw her at the wedding in act one: the circle of the play closes on the same detail. Solveig gropes for him. Peer sets her a riddle: "Where was I, as myself, as the whole man, the true man? Where was I, with God's sigil upon my brow?" The answer: "In my faith, in my hope, and in my love." In the original Peer asks where he was "den hele, den sande" — the whole one, the true one. That is the word of the World: whole. And it is the same hele he once meant to carry off alone. He turned out to be whole in the place where he had been offered a share of the burden.

But Ibsen does not end on a full stop. Peer hides his face in Solveig's lap — "My mother; my wife; oh, thou innocent woman!" — she sings a lullaby, the sun rises, and from behind the house comes the Button-moulder's voice: "At the last cross-road we will meet again, Peer; and then we'll see whether——; I say no more." There is no verdict, only a reprieve. For a couple this is the most honest moment of the tail. A cradle is a circle too, but in it one holds and the other hides. The main task of the World is a circle in which both are whole: the one who went away comes back by the straight road, and the one who waited stops being a door and becomes a person with a life of their own again.

Peer and Solveig's last meeting falls on Whitsun morning. The church-goers walking through the forest sing of the morning "when the tongues of God's kingdom struck the earth like to flaming steel". After a life lived by the rule "speak, yet be silent", the play ends on the feast of speech. Solveig's name contains the Norwegian sol, "sun", and the last stage direction has her singing "in the full daylight": a tail that began at night ends in broad day.

sections.h2: Clues in Waite: the wolf, the tails and the garland
paragraphs: The pictures of the classic Rider–Waite–Smith deck add three clues to this story. The cards on the site have their own artwork, so what follows is about Waite's cards and his text only.

**The Moon.** On Waite's card a dog and a wolf bay at the moon, and a road runs off between two towers. Waite writes: "The path between the towers is the issue into the unknown. The dog and wolf are the fears of the natural mind in the presence of that place of exit, when there is only reflected light to guide it." At their first meeting Peer called himself a werewolf. The first step of a couple with this tail is taken by reflected light, and the fear in it speaks with an animal's voice.

**The Devil.** The figures chained to the altar on Waite's card have tails. "The figures are tailed, to signify the animal nature," Waite writes, "but there is human intelligence in the faces, and he who is exalted above them is not to be their master for ever." This is Peer in the Dovre-King's hall: the tail tied on, the human eye kept. Waite also recalls Papus's version of the card, where the little demons are replaced by "naked human beings, male and female, who are yoked only to each other", and says "the author may be felicitated on this improved symbolism". For a couple with the Devil at the centre the formula is exact: no one stands above them; their chain is one for two.

**The World.** In Waite this is a female figure dancing inside an oval wreath, "an elliptic garland, as if it were a chain of flowers intended to symbolize all sensible things". Now add up the rings Peer has passed through. The Boyg's ring in the dark, where he stands in the very middle and sees nothing. The onion — rings with nothing at the centre. The straw wreath of "Self-hood's Kaiser". The World card is the same ring, but with a living figure in the middle, and she is dancing. The shape is the same, the content the opposite: the entry of the tail already carries its main task, only in negative.

Ibsen himself supplies the word. The Devil whom Peer meets in act five talks about photography: a picture can be straightforward or negative, and in a negative "the lights and the shades are reversed, and they're apt to seem ugly to commonplace eyes; but for all that the likeness is latent in them, and all you require is to bring it out." The Boyg's ring is the negative of the World's garland. The Hanged Man, who sees everything from the reverse side, is the time it takes the picture to develop. Wen notes "the tau cross in the legs" of the Hanged Man "reemerging in Key 21: The World, suggesting that it is the hanged man who shall attain the fulfillment of the World card, not the mob."

sections.h2: The couple's values: a light in a forest hut
paragraphs: "The couple's values" is the spiritual purpose, the road the two are meant to walk together. For couples with the tail 18-12-21 only two cards appear here: The Hermit in 69.3% and The Moon in 30.7%.

The Hermit in Ibsen is two huts. Before the finale Peer looks back on his life and says to the sun: "Thou beautiful sun, thou hast squandered away thy glory of light in an empty hut. There was no one within it to hearten and warm;— the owner, they tell me, was never at home." A few minutes later he asks the Button-moulder what is shining in the forest, and hears: "Only light from a hut." An empty hut whose owner was never home, and a hut with a light in it. The Hermit among a couple's values is the second: a quiet fire of one's own, a time and place of solitude for each, love shown in deeds rather than speeches. The minus is the same as on Peer's first night in the forest: a bar on the door, each on their own, troubles piling up in silence. When Solveig came, Peer said: "Away, away then with nails and planks! No need now for bars against hobgoblin-thoughts." The value of such a couple is the light in the window, not the bar on the door.

The Moon among the values is the night heath of act five. Thread-balls roll under Peer's feet: "We are thoughts; thou shouldst have thought us." A sighing in the air says "We are songs; thou shouldst have sung us!", and dewdrops fall from the branches: "We are tears unshed for ever. Ice-spears, sharp-wounding, we could have melted." For couples whose values hold the Moon, imagination is not only the entry but also the road: shared dreams, night thoughts, music, everything that lives after dark. This Moon asks one thing: to finish the thoughts, sing the songs, shed the tears — to bring what belongs to the night out into the light.

sections.h2: How the tail 18-12-21 is calculated: an example
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points in the two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The example is the couple 08.01.1976 and 05.07.1975, calculated by the site's engine.
For 08.01.1976: day 8, month 1, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5. Karmic task 8 + 1 + 5 = 14, centre 8 + 1 + 5 + 14 = 28 → 10. Personal tail: 6-20-14.
For 05.07.1975: day 5, month 7, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Karmic task 5 + 7 + 22 = 34 → 7, centre 5 + 7 + 22 + 7 = 41 → 5. Personal tail: 12-19-7.
The couple's centre is 10 + 5 = 15, The Devil. The couple's values in this example are 9, The Hermit.
A few more facts, checked by running through every date:

ul: The tail 18-12-21 occurs in roughly one couple in 516 (0.194%) and ranks 73rd by frequency among the 97 couple tails.
It is always made the same way: one partner has the personal tail 12-19-7, the other 6-20-14. There are no other combinations.
These couples always have 15 at the centre. A personal matrix never has 15 at the centre: this atmosphere exists only in a couple.

18-12-21 never occurs as a personal karmic tail. In a personal matrix the entry M is the main task D plus the centre. With D = 21, the sum with any centre lies between 24 and 43, and such numbers reduce to 12 at most, so an entry of 18 is impossible.
There are no other couple tails made of 18, 12 and 21: these three cards form a tail only in this order.

sections.h2: What helps a couple with the tail 18-12-21
paragraphs: The cards do not predict how two people's story will end. They show where this couple usually turns off "roundabout". A few habits that follow directly from the plot:

ul: **Name the Boyg.** Find the subject both partners keep going round and say it out loud in a single sentence. Fists cannot beat the Boyg, but a voice makes it dissolve.

**Share the burden.** When one says "I'll handle it myself", ask what exactly is heavy. "Wait; I will help you; the burden we'll share" is the line after which, in Ibsen, everything could have gone differently.

**Wait with a loop.** "You must wait" without an agreement leaves the door half-open. Waiting holds when both know what they are waiting for, what each will do in the meantime and when they will come back to the conversation.
**Check the reflection.** Instead of three night-time versions, ask one daytime question. Moonlight is reflected light: it shows whatever the onlooker brought along.
**Don't scratch the eye.** Accepting small tails for the sake of peace is fine. Seeing what is crooked as beautiful for the sake of calm is not.
**Open the hut.** Friends, family, guests, a shared cause for others. A couple's world should not fit behind one forehead, or even two.

**Travel together.** Lisovskaya advises couples with the World to travel together and to go through difficulties together rather than run from them. Peer crossed half the globe alone; a couple's World is a road both of them walk.

paragraphs: If the waiting or the "burden" comes with fear for one's own safety, reading the tail will not help: that calls for a psychologist, and in danger, the local emergency number.

faq.q: What does 18-12-21 mean in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: It is the karmic tail of a couple's matrix: The Moon at the entry to the task, The Hanged Man in the middle, The World as the main task. The couple comes together over a shared secret, goes through a long pause and learns to build a common whole instead of searching for it separately.

faq.q: Why is the tail 18-12-21 called a programme?
faq.a: Yuliana Lisovskaya, whose book the compatibility calculation follows, calls the triple on a couple's tail a karmic programme. The 18-12-21 programme and the couple's karmic tail 18-12-21 are one and the same thing.

faq.q: Can 18-12-21 appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: Not as a personal karmic tail: in a personal matrix, when the main task is 21, the entry cannot be 18. This triple appears only in the compatibility matrix of two people.

faq.q: Is the tail 18-12-21 a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. The tail shows a couple's task, not its fate: where the two usually get stuck and what they have to learn together. It occurs in roughly one couple in 516, and it contains no forecast.

faq.q: How can a couple quickly tell they have the tail 18-12-21?
faq.a: Look at the partners' personal karmic tails: if one has 12-19-7 and the other 6-20-14, the couple's tail is 18-12-21. There is no other way to get it; the most reliable check is to calculate the couple's matrix from both birth dates.

report: Peer Gynt searched the whole world for his kingdom, and it was waiting for him in a forest hut, behind a half-open door. Ibsen wrote the story in 1867, and the three cards of the tail 18-12-21 appear in it in their own order: The Moon is night and a fairy tale, The Hanged Man is the threshold where two people get stuck, The World is the whole that has to be built by both.

report.h3: A fairy tale that dislikes questions

report: The play opens with his mother's words: "Peer, you're lying!" Peer has just told her how he plunged into the abyss on a reindeer, and how their own reflection rose to meet them from the depths of a mountain tarn. His mother remembers hearing this story as a girl, and it happened to someone else. The first image of the play is a man falling towards his own reflection. Waite calls the light of the Moon a reflection and puts "deception" on its list.

Love begins the same way. At a wedding Peer sees Solveig: "How fair! Did ever you see the like!" She hears his name and pulls her hand away: the gossip about him arrived before he did. He threatens to turn into a troll and come at midnight, and a moment later, "as if in dread", he begs: "Dance with me, lass!" Each meets not a person but an image.

For the couple this is the entry to the task. The two are drawn together by a secret: understanding without words, private pet names, a shared legend about themselves. This is their common language. But the same Moon turns into resistance: **a fairy tale does not like questions.** To "What's wrong?" one answers "Nothing", and by nightfall the other has built three versions and checked none of them. The image made at the start protects the couple as long as nobody touches it — and nobody touches it for years.

report.h3: An enemy that does not fight

report: Then Peer finds himself in pitch darkness, where something slimy and shapeless blocks the way: the Boyg. It has one piece of advice: "Go roundabout, Peer!" Peer punches at nothing: "Forward or back, and it's just as far … No sooner I'm out than I'm back in the ring." And the Boyg replies: "The great Boyg conquers, but does not fight."

Couples with this tail rarely break over a loud scandal. They spend years going round the same subject: money, parents, an old story, a move. Each detour makes sense on its own — "not now", "let's not spoil the evening" — but together the detours close into a ring, and the two walk it in circles. In the play the Boyg is scattered not by fists but by voices from afar. The fog lifts when someone is the first to say out loud what both have been going round.

report.h3: The half-open door

report: Solveig comes to Peer's forest hut, leaving her family behind. He goes to fetch wood and runs into his own past. Then come five lines on which the whole middle of the tail rests:

— You must wait. It is dark, and I've got something heavy to fetch. — Wait; I will help you; the burden we'll share. — No, stay where you are! I must bear it alone. — …Be my way long or short—you must wait. — Yes, I'll wait!

The stage direction: "Solveig remains standing in the open half-door." There the play hangs for decades. In the original Peer says "Jeg får bære det hele" — "I must carry all of it", literally "the whole".

This is the Hanged Man of the couple 18-12-21: not betrayal and not a quarrel, but **a refused offer to share the burden.** One carries the weight alone and calls it care: "Don't worry about it, I'll sort it out myself." The other waits and calls it loyalty. Both sacrifices are noble, and together they make a door that is neither open nor shut: years of "after the renovation", "when things settle down".

But the Hanged Man is also a pause whose outcome is not written down. Such partners sense each other at a distance. Decades later Solveig sings to a Peer who is far away, and repeats his words from that evening: if the thing he went to fetch is heavy, let him take his time.

report.h3: Here was my kingdom

report: Peer goes off to look for the world. Grown rich, he declares his goal: "To be Emperor." Where? "O'er all the world." He describes his Self like this: "The world behind my forehead's arch." In a madhouse he is crowned with a wreath of straw: "Long life, long life to Self-hood's Kaiser!" In old age he peels an onion, layer after layer, and finds no kernel. This is the World in the minus: a universe that fits inside one head. In a couple's life it is a shared world drawn to one partner's plan, friends dropping away one by one, "we don't need anyone", the circle of "together — apart".

Near the end the Button-moulder comes to Peer and explains why he is to be melted down: "Now, you were designed for a shining button on the vest of the world; but your loop gave way." **The main task of the tail is not a kingdom over the world but a button with a loop:** a small place sewn into a larger cloth — a home, a cause, a circle of people the two are sewn to together.

Passing a familiar hut, Peer hears the song and understands: "Oh, dread!—here was my Kaiserdom!" The Boyg once told him to go roundabout. In the last scene he says: "Ah no; this time at least right through." On the threshold stands Solveig, and Peer sets her a riddle: where was he himself, "the whole man, the true man"? The answer: "In my faith, in my hope, and in my love." In the original he asks where he was "den hele" — whole. The very word with which he once refused to share the burden. **He turned out to be whole in the place where he had been offered a share of it.**

Ibsen does not end on a full stop. Peer hides his face in Solveig's lap, she sings a lullaby, and from behind the house comes: "At the last cross-road we will meet again, Peer; and then we'll see whether——" A cradle is a circle too, but in it one holds and the other hides. A couple's World is a circle in which both are whole: the one who went away comes back by the straight road, and the one who waited becomes a person with a life of their own again, not a door.

What changes the script: naming the subject both keep going round; meeting "I'll handle it myself" with a question about what exactly is heavy; waiting by agreement rather than "be my way long or short"; asking one daytime question instead of building three night-time versions; keeping the door of the hut open to friends and family. If the waiting or the "burden" comes with fear for one's own safety, what is needed is not a reading of the tail but a psychologist, and in danger, a local emergency number or crisis line.

seo.title: Karmic tail 18 12 3 compatibility: the tower, the braid and the garden
seo.description: Karmic tail 18 12 3 compatibility — The Moon, The Hanged Man and The Empress: why a couple builds a secret world, lives by a thread and learns to come home.

items.title: Karmic tail 18-12-3 in compatibility: a tower that two people build together
items.short: No single person has the karmic tail 18-12-3: in a personal destiny matrix it cannot occur. It appears only when two people work out their compatibility, and with it The Devil takes the centre of the couple's chart — a card that neither partner has on their own. The three cards of this tail retell the story of Rapunzel. The Moon at the entry is the couple's shared wish for a secret world of their own. The Hanged Man in the middle is a union that hangs by a thread for years. The Empress is the main task: to come down from the tower and grow a garden of their own in daylight.

sections.h2: A tail that no single person has
paragraphs: The first clue lies in the numbers themselves. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail is worked out from two other points: entry M equals the main task D plus the centre. For the entry to be 18 when the task is 3, the centre would have to be 15. But no birth date ever gives a centre of 15: The Devil cannot stand in the centre of a personal matrix. So no individual has the tail 18-12-3.

A couple's points are counted differently: each point of the couple is the sum of the same points in the two personal matrices, reduced to 22. And a run through every date shows something strange: the tail 18-12-3 forms in one way only. One partner always has the personal tail 3-7-22, the other 15-5-8. There are no other combinations. Add them point by point and this is what comes out:

ul: entry: one partner's Empress (3) plus the other's Devil (15) — **The Moon (18)**;
middle: The Chariot (7) plus The Hierophant (5) — **The Hanged Man (12)**;
main task: The Fool (22) plus Justice (8), 30 → **The Empress (3)**.

paragraphs: The personal tails also fix the personal centres: the tail 3-7-22 always comes with centre 8, Justice, and the tail 15-5-8 always with 7, The Chariot. Their sum is 15. That is why The Devil sits in the centre for 100% of couples with this tail.
Three observations follow from this arithmetic, and they hold for every such couple.

ol: **One partner's centre stands in the other's tail.** Justice, the centre of the partner with 3-7-22, is the main task of the personal tail 15-5-8. The Chariot, the centre of the partner with 15-5-8, is the middle of the tail 3-7-22. Where one feels at ease, the other has a lesson to learn.

**The entries of both tails do not vanish — they move.** The Empress, which opens the personal tail 3-7-22, becomes the couple's main task. The Devil, which opens 15-5-8, becomes the atmosphere inside the couple.
**Nobody brings The Devil into the centre.** It appears only between the two: Justice from one plus The Chariot from the other. The atmosphere of this couple is something they create together.

paragraphs: There is a fourth detail. If the middle were counted by the personal formula, from the two ends, it would be 18 + 3 = 21 — The World, completion and fullness. But the couple's middle is built from the partners' middles, and instead of The World it comes out as The Hanged Man. At the point where the road could have ended, it stalls.

The tail occurs in about one couple in 185 (0.539%) and ranks 52nd of the 97 couple tails. The rarity has a simple cause. The tail 15-5-8 is one of the most common personal tails — every eleventh birth date has it. But 3-7-22 belongs to only one date in 34.

sections.h2: A tale about a tower, rewritten for two hundred years
paragraphs: There is a story that begins with exactly this sum — The Empress and The Devil — and then runs through The Moon and The Hanged Man back to The Empress. It is "Rapunzel".

The tale has a long pedigree. In 1634 the Neapolitan Giambattista Basile published "Petrosinella": the heroine's name means "parsley". In 1698 the Frenchwoman Charlotte-Rose de Caumont de La Force brought out "Persinette" — again from the word for parsley, persil. In 1790 Friedrich Schulz retold it in German and swapped the parsley for rapunzel, a bellflower with a sweetish root that is eaten in salads. The Brothers Grimm took the tale from Schulz: in their collection it is number 12, and between the first edition of 1812 and the last of 1857 they rewrote it more than once. To the end the Grimms believed it was a folk tale — told "undoubtedly from oral tradition", as their notes put it in Margaret Hunt's 1884 English translation. Their notes say not a word about a French aristocrat's literary tale lying underneath.

The life of La Force herself is another clue. In 1687 she married a man six years younger than she was. The Church recognised the marriage, but her husband's father opposed it, and after two years in court the Parlement of Paris dissolved it. In 1697 the king sent her to the abbey of Gercy, and a year later her "Tales of Tales" came out, with "Persinette" among them. The girl who is loved in a tower without a door was invented by a woman whose husband's family would not let her have a home of her own.

The first page of the tale is that very sum of two personal tails. In the Grimms (quoted here and below in the same translation by Hunt) a small window at the back of a house looks into someone else's garden, "full of the most beautiful flowers and herbs", behind a high wall. A pregnant wife longs for the rampion in one of its beds. Her husband climbs over the wall twice, and both times at dusk — "in the twilight of evening", then "in the gloom of evening". The enchantress catches him and names her condition: he must give her the child. "It shall be well treated, and I will care for it like a mother." The garden and its plenty are The Empress. A bargain that speaks in the voice of care is The Devil. From the two of them comes a girl in a tower whom people visit only in the evening. For couples with 18-12-3, The Empress plus The Devil give The Moon at the entry. For the Grimms, that is how the tale begins.

And one more coincidence, too exact to pass over: "When she was twelve years old, the enchantress shut her into a tower, which lay in a forest, and had neither stairs nor door." In La Force the girl is already "a marvel" before she reaches her twelfth year — and that is when the fairy builds her a tower. The Hanged Man, the middle of this tail, is the twelfth arcanum. The tale knew nothing of the matrix, yet the number stands exactly where the suspended life begins.

sections.h2: The Moon: a shared language overheard from the gaoler
paragraphs: The prince does not look for Rapunzel — he hears her. Riding through the forest, he hears singing, looks for a door and finds none. Every day he comes back and listens from behind a tree until he learns the words that open the tower: "Rapunzel, Rapunzel, Let down thy hair." "If that is the ladder by which one mounts, I will for once try my fortune," he says, and the next day, "when it began to grow dark", he speaks the password himself. This couple's shared language is a set of words overheard from the gaoler.

La Force is even more precise. The prince "admirably counterfeited the Fairy's voice" (our translation from the French), and Persinette, "deceived by the sound of that voice", lets down her hair. Later the fairy pays him back in kind: she sings in Persinette's voice, and the prince climbs straight into the trap. Both enter the tower in someone else's voice. Even the light in Persinette's tower is not sunlight: the fairy built it of silver, the metal of the Moon in old alchemy, and its rooms are lit by the fire of carbuncles, "as bright as if the light of the sun had entered them".

This is what The Moon at the entry looks like. Point M is what the couple wants together — its agreements and its "shared language". With The Moon that language belongs to the night: pet names, jokes nobody else would get, understanding that needs no explaining, the feeling that together they know something about the world that others do not. Lisovskaya sees the bright side of this energy as high sensitivity, intuitive understanding and respect for each other's private space; here a partner is first of all a friend. But the tale's rule — "the old woman comes by day, you come in the evening" — has a price. The couple ends up with two lives: a daytime one for relatives, colleagues and acquaintances, and an evening one that is theirs. They take a long time to introduce each other to their families, each goes home to their own people for the holidays, and friends learn about the big events after the fact.

The Moon stands on the line of tasks, so its wish is also a form of resistance. In the tale the same password turns against the couple: the enchantress ties the cut braids to the window hook, and the familiar words bring down a trap. In everyday life it looks ordinary: something only the two of them knew becomes an argument in a quarrel — "you told me so yourself". Lisovskaya describes the shadow side of The Moon in a couple in just these terms: a partner's secrets become weapons, and jealousy grows out of stories that were made up. In Basile the secret is given away by the ogress's crony, "who was for ever prying into things that did not concern her" (John Edward Taylor's 1848 translation). Lisovskaya has this too: a Moon couple is secretive even at its best, and so it gathers rumours.

Benebell Wen writes that The Moon speaks of "the hidden condition of the Seeker's situation that will reveal itself in time", and that "the repressed latent will always surface, and any strong intention to repress will cause a violent surfacing". In the tale the secret surfaces in a way that is both funny and frightening. In the first edition of 1812 Rapunzel innocently complains: "My little clothes are getting so tight" (our translation from the German). In the last, of 1857, she lets it slip: "Tell me, Dame Gothel, how it happens that you are so much heavier for me to draw up than the young King's son—he is with me in a moment." The scissors follow the slip at once — "snip, snap".

sections.h2: The Hanged Man: everything hangs by a hair
paragraphs: This couple's middle draws itself: in the tower everything hangs. The braids are wound round the window hook and fall twenty ells to the ground. The enchantress climbs them, and so does the prince. English would say a union like this hangs by a thread; Russian says it hangs na voloske — by a single hair. Here the hair is real.

In the edition of 1850 the Grimms added a scene that had not been there before. Rapunzel says to the prince: "I will willingly go away with thee, but I do not know how to get down. Bring with thee a skein of silk every time that thou comest, and I will weave a ladder with it, and when that is ready I will descend, and thou wilt take me on thy horse." Until then, they agreed, he would come every evening, "for the old woman came by day".

Readers have long asked why the prince did not simply bring a ladder. The tail answers the question: a ladder can be seen, but a skein of silk hides in a sleeve. The secret with which the couple entered the union also sets the speed of the way out of the tower — one thread per visit. The Hanged Man here is not a punishment but a way of life the couple chose for itself: everything is being prepared, nothing is being decided.

The arithmetic of the middle tells the same story. The couple's Hanged Man is built from the partners' middles — The Chariot (7) and The Hierophant (5). The tale has both. Below, a horse is waiting: The Chariot, readiness to break away and ride off. Above, a routine is in force — "the old woman by day, you in the evening": The Hierophant, an order the couple did not set up themselves. The wish to leave plus the habit of "this is how things are done here" add up to suspension.

Suspension can be happy, and that is its trap. In the 1812 edition the lovers in the tower "lived merrily and joyfully for a good while" (our translation). Lisovskaya's bright side of The Hanged Man in a couple is tact, attention, willingness to give way, the ability to sense each other at a distance. Yet she also makes an observation that reads like a summary of the tale: such couples are slow to enter a relationship, and they need a push from outside to marry. In the tale the push comes from a pair of scissors. In no edition of the Grimms is the ladder ever finished: the couple leaves the tower not by its own ladder but by a fall.

In real life the middle sounds familiar: "we'll move in together once we have a flat", "we'll tell our parents after the holidays", "we'll marry when everything is settled". Usually one partner holds the whole structure up — carries the silk, works out how to keep things hidden, how to fit everything in. In return they hear that everything is too slow, and by now they cannot leave. This too belongs to the shadow side of the twelfth energy in a couple: one partner holds the relationship together with all their strength, there are no shared goals, and nobody knows how to say no.

Wen compares The Hanged Man's sense of suspension to the question The Fool poses: "will the Seeker fall or fly?" The prince answers it literally — he leaps from the tower. "He escaped with his life, but the thorns into which he fell, pierced his eyes." For some years he wanders through the forest, eats "nothing but roots and berries", and finds Rapunzel not with his eyes but by her voice: "He heard a voice, and it seemed so familiar to him." It was by her voice, too, that he found her the first time.

sections.h2: The Empress: from someone else's garden to a kingdom of their own
paragraphs: The tale has two Empresses, and this is the tail's central secret. The first stands on the first page: someone else's garden behind a high wall, entered at dusk like a thief and paid for with a bargain. The second stands on the last: "He led her to his kingdom where he was joyfully received, and they lived for a long time afterwards, happy and contented." The main task of an 18-12-3 couple is to get from the first to the second: from plenty taken in secret and on credit to something of their own that needs no hiding.

In Basile the ogress, finding her parsley gone, swears to teach the thief a lesson and quotes a Neapolitan saying: "every one should eat off his own platter, and not meddle with other folks' cups". The ogress is the villain of the tale, but the saying is right, and it is almost word for word The Empress's task for this couple.

The most interesting thing is that the kingdom did not appear in the tale at once. The first edition of 1812 ends in the wilderness: Rapunzel's tears fall on the prince's eyes and he can see again — full stop. The line about the kingdom was added in the 1837 edition, the words "where he was joyfully received" by 1850, together with the silk ladder. The home in this tale took twenty-five years to build. It is the same for the couple: The Empress does not arrive on her own after a hard middle — she has to be written in.

Among the tasks of a couple with a three on this point, Lisovskaya names breaking free of the influence of a mother and relatives, swings of feast and famine, childishness and practicality. The tale has a scene for each of them.

The first is about family. The Grimms' enchantress promises to care for the child "like a mother", and it is exactly this motherly care that becomes the tower. In La Force the fairy softens at the end, arrives for the family in a gleaming chariot and drives them to the palace. But she seats herself "in the middle of these fortunate lovers". The picture is familiar: parents help with housing, money, grandchildren — and sit between the two. The Empress's task is not to refuse help but to change seats: nobody should sit between the partners.

The second is about money. Persinette's tower is bursting with riches: wardrobes as magnificent as those of the queens of Asia, jewels in every drawer, the most delicate dishes at every meal. In exile she has a hut of leaves by the sea and a basket of biscuits. On the very first evening after the reunion, a biscuit in the prince's hand turns to stone and the water turns to crystal. Plenty given by someone else's hand is taken away by the same hand: feast or famine in its purest form. What is truly the couple's own begins where the home and the income depend on the two of them, not on whoever is driving the chariot.

The third is about growing up. Rapunzel gives the secret away with a childish slip, the escape plan is meant to take years, the prince leaps from the tower in despair. Wen stresses that "the element of Earth governs this card". Everything that happens up high in the tale, in the air, on a braid, is a task of bringing it down to earth. In the tale the scissors do it: the cut braids "lay on the ground", the prince fell into thorns. The couple can come down by itself — by its own ladder.

The arithmetic of the main task says the same. The Fool (22), the task of one partner, plus Justice (8), the task of the other. The lightness of a leap and the sobriety of the scales, taken apart, give either a leap without looking or endless weighing. Together they give The Empress — a decision after which something begins to grow.

sections.h2: The Devil in the centre: "I thought I had separated thee from all the world"
paragraphs: When she learns the truth, the enchantress cries to Rapunzel: "I thought I had separated thee from all the world, and yet thou hast deceived me!" It is the most precise formula of The Devil in the whole tale: a love that wants to cut someone off from the world. The couple's centre is the atmosphere inside the union, what lies between the two and is not on show. Lisovskaya ends her chapter on the fifteenth energy in a couple with a single thought: nobody belongs to anybody.

For an 18-12-3 couple it matters who builds the tower. The enchantress in the tale is a third party, but there is no third party in the numbers: The Devil in the centre is made from the partners' own centres, and neither of them has it alone. So the temptation of this couple is not someone else's ill will but their shared wish to become a tower for each other. "We don't need anyone", "we have our own world", "let nobody know" — that is how it sounds from inside, and at first it sounds like happiness.

At its best a centre of 15 means passion and a rare ability to accept each other's dark sides and forgive mistakes. At its worst it is that very "separated from all the world": jealousy of friends, of work, of the past, and attempts to hold on to a partner through intimacy, money, a shared roof. If the wish to possess turns into surveillance, prohibitions and threats, it is no longer a question of the tail but of safety: in that situation the thing to do is call a local emergency number or crisis line and seek help from a psychologist.

In a note of 1812 the Grimms warned that the shutting of a maiden in a tower occurs in many old songs — of Hildburg, of Brynhild — "and is therefore not exactly to be taken for a prison" (our translation). In the old songs a tower is not only a dungeon but also a shelter. A centre of 15 is not a verdict for this couple either: it is a shelter that becomes a prison once nobody keeps a door in it.

sections.h2: What Waite saw in these cards
paragraphs: The cards do not illustrate the tale. But Arthur Edward Waite, whose descriptions the classic deck was drawn from, left details that read like a commentary on it.

On Waite's Moon a road runs off to the horizon between two towers. He calls it "the issue into the unknown", and the dog and the wolf "the fears of the natural mind in the presence of that place of exit". Basile has a scene the Grimms lack. Petrosinella and the prince make a rope ladder themselves and climb down from the tower, and the ogress gives chase. Then the heroine throws three gallnuts onto the road, and up spring a Corsican bulldog, a lion and a wolf. At the very exit from the tower the same beasts appear that howl on the road between Waite's towers — only here they do not frighten the runaways but stop the pursuit. The fears at the exit work for those who have decided to leave.

Waite refused to call The Hanged Man a card of martyrdom: "the tree of sacrifice is living wood", "the face expresses deep entrancement, not suffering", and the figure as a whole "suggests life in suspension, but life and not death". The prince who "escaped with his life" and the happy evenings in the tower both fit this formula.

On Waite's Devil, chains run from a ring in front of the altar to the necks of two figures, male and female. Waite calls this "the chain and fatality of the material life" and at once adds that he who is exalted above them "is not to be their master for ever. Even now, he is also a bondsman". In the tale this is literal: every day the enchantress herself climbs the same braid. The keeper of the tower is tied to it no less than the one she keeps. In the same passage Waite calls The Devil "the Dweller on the Threshold without the Mystical Garden when those are driven forth therefrom who have eaten the forbidden fruit". "Rapunzel" begins with a forbidden garden bed.

And the sceptre of The Empress, Waite writes, "is surmounted by the globe of this world". The enchantress wanted to separate Rapunzel "from all the world"; The Empress holds that world in her hand. The couple's main task is to return to the world, not to hide from it.

sections.h2: The couple's values: a light in the tower window
paragraphs: The couple's spiritual purpose — on the site this is the sphere "The couple's values", the road the two are meant to walk together — comes in two kinds with this tail. For 73% of couples it is The Hermit (9), for 27% The Moon (18).

The Hermit among the values explains why the tower is so attractive in the first place. Rapunzel sings "in her solitude". La Force's Persinette "was never bored in her solitude: she read, she painted, she played instruments". Such a couple truly values quiet, depth and time of one's own: Lisovskaya, describing the nine at its best, writes that each partner has a time and a place to be alone, and that love is shown in deeds, not words. The task is not to give up solitude but to let it shine rather than lock the door. Waite says of The Hermit's light: "His beacon intimates that 'where I am, you also may be.'" In the tale that is how the song from the window sounds: it carries through the forest, and by the voice the prince finds Rapunzel — first at the tower, then in the wilderness.

If the couple's values are The Moon, night becomes not only the entry but also the shared road: the inner world, imagination, a pull towards the hidden. Then it matters all the more that this world has a door through which one can go out to people and come back.

sections.h2: How the circle closes
paragraphs: The couple enters the union through a shared secret world — The Moon. To protect it, the important things are put off — The Hanged Man: silk is brought one skein at a time, and the ladder is never finished. No garden of their own appears, The Empress is left undone, and the couple lives on what belongs to others: help from relatives, temporary housing, an endless "later". Having nothing of their own tightens the attachment — The Devil in the centre: apart from each other they have nothing, and letting go is frightening. And the more frightening it is, the more tightly the tower is shut.

In La Force the fairy builds the tower out of fear: "since the Fairy knew her fate, she resolved to steal her away from her destinies". And once found out, she admits: "destinies cannot be avoided, and my foresight has been quite in vain". A tower built out of fear of life does not stop life — it only decides who will be in charge of it: the two of them or some outside force.

sections.h2: The way out: a tower needs a door
paragraphs: In the Grimms an outside force makes the exit for the couple: a slip of the tongue, scissors, a leap, years apart. In Basile, the oldest version, it is all different. The lovers make a rope ladder themselves, climb down themselves, fight off the pursuit themselves and reach the kingdom, where the prince takes Petrosinella to wife "with his father's free consent". The tail promises neither scenario. It shows where the couple can get ahead of the scissors:

ul: finish the ladder: name one concrete step — moving in together, meeting the families, a shared budget — and take it themselves, without waiting for circumstances to decide;
bring the shared language into the light: say to the "daytime" people — family and friends — what the two have agreed between themselves;
let nobody sit in the middle: accept help from elders in a way that leaves decisions with the couple;
test care for a leash: if "I take care of you" means "you can't go anywhere without me", it is no longer The Empress but The Devil;
never bring up in a quarrel what was entrusted between the two;
keep their night-time world, but not live in it alone: a home can have a window at the top as long as it also has a door at the bottom.

paragraphs: A strong 18-12-3 couple is the same two people who recognise each other's voice in the dark but no longer hide. Their Moon is a fine understanding without words and the ability to discover something new in the partner every year. Their Hanged Man is patience and the capacity to look at a situation from the other side. Their Empress is a home in which what they started together keeps growing. La Force ended "Persinette" with a moral in verse, and its last lines would do for this couple's motto: fortune is defied and fate overcome "as long as two spouses are of one accord" (tant que deux époux sont d'accord).

sections.h2: How 18-12-3 is calculated: an example
paragraphs: Take two dates: 05.12.1976 (5 December 1976) and 14.08.1975 (14 August 1975). First each person's personal matrix is worked out.

For the first date the day gives 5, the month 12, the year 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5. Main task: 5 + 12 + 5 = 22. Centre: 5 + 12 + 5 + 22 = 44 → 8. Entry of the tail: 22 + 8 = 30 → 3, middle: 22 + 3 = 25 → 7. Personal tail — 3-7-22.

For the second date the day is 14, the month 8, the year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Main task: 14 + 8 + 22 = 44 → 8. Centre: 44 + 8 = 52 → 7. Entry: 8 + 7 = 15, middle: 8 + 15 = 23 → 5. Personal tail — 15-5-8.
Now the matching points are added together:
The couple's values in this example are The Hermit, 9.

This tail can be recognised without the whole matrix, from a single sum for each partner: the arcana of the day, month and year of birth. A day above 22 is reduced by adding its digits; the year arcanum is the sum of the year's digits, reduced to 22. For one partner the sum is exactly 22, for the other 26, 35, 44 or 53 — that is, above 22 and reducing to 8. In the example these are 5 + 12 + 5 = 22 and 14 + 8 + 22 = 44.

sections.h2: 18-12-3 and 18-3-12: the same cards in a different order
paragraphs: The same numbers form one more couple tail, 18-3-12. It is rarer (0.147% of couples), its centre is always The Lovers rather than The Devil, The Empress stands in the middle and The Hanged Man becomes the main task; its middle equals the reduced sum of the ends, and it also occurs as a personal tail.

ul: **Entry to the task — 18, The Moon.** What the couple wants together: a world hidden from other eyes, understanding without words, a private language that only the two of them speak. On the line of tasks the same wish also works as resistance: the secret makes it hard to step outside.

**Middle of the task — 12, The Hanged Man.** How the couple travels the road: in suspension. The relationship exists, but everything that matters — a home, a decision, a talk with the family — is put off until "the ladder is ready".

**Main task — 3, The Empress.** What the couple has to learn: to build its own life on solid ground — a home, a household, a shared plan — and not hand it over to anyone else: relatives, circumstances, chance.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 18-12-3 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's task, not a verdict. The entry is The Moon: a shared secret world and a language only the two of them understand. The middle is The Hanged Man: a union that lives in suspension for a long time and keeps putting off what matters. The main task is The Empress: their own home, their own household and their own decisions in daylight, with no one else's hand over the union.

faq.q: Why does this tail never appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre. With a task of 3 and an entry of 18, the centre would have to be 15, and no person ever has a centre of 15. A couple's points are sums of personal points, so 18-12-3 is possible for a couple — always as the sum of the personal tails 3-7-22 and 15-5-8.

faq.q: Is The Devil in the couple's centre a bad sign?
faq.a: No. It is an atmosphere of strong attachment. At its best it means passion and the ability to accept each other whole; at its worst, a wish to possess and jealousy. A centre of 15 appears only in a couple: two people create it, and the two of them decide whether their shared world will be a shelter or a tower without a door.

faq.q: How can a couple tell it has the tail 18-12-3 without working out the whole matrix?
faq.a: Add up the arcana of the day, month and year of birth for each partner. If one gets exactly 22 and the other 26, 35, 44 or 53, the couple has the tail 18-12-3. There is no other route to it: the partners' personal tails are always 3-7-22 and 15-5-8.

faq.q: Does this tail predict a separation or a hard fate for the couple?
faq.a: No. A karmic tail does not predict events, dates or outcomes. The tale shows the worst scenario, in which scissors and years apart make the way out of the tower. The cards show something else: where the couple can get ahead of that scenario and come down on its own.

faq.q: Which partner is Rapunzel and which is the prince?
faq.a: Neither. The roles of the tale are not divided by gender or between the partners. Both build the tower: The Devil in the centre is made from the centres of both, and the secret world belongs to both of them. Coming down from it is a task for both as well.

report: Readers of "Rapunzel" have long asked why the prince did not simply bring a ladder. For a couple with the tail 18-12-3 this child's question has a grown-up answer. The three cards of the tail — The Moon, The Hanged Man and The Empress — come in the same order as the tale: evening visits to a tower without a door, a life that hangs by a hair and, at last, a kingdom of their own.

report.h3: The tale begins with the same sum

report: No single person has this tail: 18-12-3 is born only between two. One partner's personal tail begins with The Empress, the other's with The Devil, and together they give The Moon at the entry. The first page of the Grimms' tale adds up the same way. A window looks into someone else's garden, "full of the most beautiful flowers and herbs", behind a high wall. A husband climbs in twice for the rampion "in the twilight of evening", and the enchantress names her condition: he must give her the child. "I will care for it like a mother." The garden is The Empress. A bargain that speaks in the voice of care is The Devil. Out of the two grows a girl in a tower whom people visit only in the evening.

report.h3: A shared language overheard from the gaoler

report: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together, its "shared language". With The Moon that language belongs to the night. The prince does not look for Rapunzel; he hears her singing, stands behind a tree and learns the words that open the tower: "Rapunzel, Rapunzel, Let down thy hair." In La Force's French version the prince "admirably counterfeited the Fairy's voice", and later the fairy sings in Persinette's voice and lures him into a trap. Both enter the tower in someone else's voice.

The couple lives the same way: pet names and private jokes, understanding without explanation, a feeling that together they know something about the world that others do not. And the tale's rule — the old woman by day, the beloved in the evening: a daytime life for relatives and acquaintances, an evening life that is theirs. But the same password can turn against the couple. The enchantress ties the cut braids to the window hook, and the familiar words bring down a trap. In everyday life it looks ordinary: something only the two of them knew becomes an argument in a quarrel.

report.h3: Why the ladder was never finished

report: The middle of the task is The Hanged Man, and in the tower everything really does hang: the enchantress climbs the braid, and so does the prince. The union hangs **by a single hair**. In the edition of 1850 the Grimms added Rapunzel's request: "Bring with thee a skein of silk every time that thou comest, and I will weave a ladder with it." A ladder can be seen; a skein of silk hides in a sleeve. The secret with which the couple entered the union also sets the speed of the way out: **one thread per visit**. Everything is being prepared, nothing is being decided: "we'll move in together once we have a flat", "we'll tell our parents after the holidays".

Suspension can be happy: in the first edition the lovers "lived merrily and joyfully for a good while". That is the trap. Lisovskaya observes that such couples need a push from outside to marry. In the tale the push comes from a pair of scissors. The ladder is never finished in any edition, and the tower is left not by the ladder but by a fall.

report.h3: Two gardens and someone sitting in the middle

report: The main task is The Empress, and the tale has two of them. The first is someone else's garden, entered like a thief and paid for with a bargain. The second is "his kingdom where he was joyfully received". The couple's task is **to get from someone else's garden to their own**, one that needs no hiding. The Grimms added the kingdom only in 1837, and the first edition ends in the wilderness. The home in this tale had to be built on later — and the couple, too, has to write it in for itself.

In La Force the fairy softens at the end and drives the family to the palace in her chariot, but she seats herself "in the middle of these fortunate lovers". The picture is familiar: elders help with housing and money — and sit between the two. Plenty given by someone else's hand is taken away by the same hand. The Empress's task is not to refuse help but to make sure nobody sits between the partners.

report.h3: Two people build the tower

report: When she learns the truth, the enchantress cries: "I thought I had separated thee from all the world." This is the formula of The Devil, who stands in the centre of the couple, in its atmosphere. But the enchantress in the tale is a third party, and there is no third party in the numbers: The Devil appears only between the two. The temptation of this couple is **to become a tower for each other**: "we don't need anyone", "let nobody know". At its best this is passion and the ability to accept each other's dark sides; at its worst, jealousy and the wish to possess. Waite wrote of his Devil: "Even now, he is also a bondsman." In the tale the enchantress herself climbs the same braid every day. If the wish to possess turns into surveillance, prohibitions and threats, it becomes a matter of safety: the thing to do is call a local emergency number or crisis line and seek help from a psychologist.

In the oldest version of the tale, Basile's, the lovers made a rope ladder themselves and climbed down. The way out for a couple with this tail is the same: name one step — moving in together, meeting the families, a shared budget — and take it themselves; tell the "daytime" people what the two have agreed between themselves; never bring up in a quarrel what was entrusted; keep their night-time world, but **leave the tower a door**. La Force ended "Persinette" with a line that would do for this couple's motto: fate is overcome "as long as two spouses are of one accord".
