seo.title: Karmic tail 18 15 6 compatibility: The Moon, The Devil, The Lovers
seo.description: Karmic tail 18 15 6 compatibility: The Moon at the entry, The Devil in the middle, The Lovers as the main task, and why no single person's chart has it.

items.title: Karmic tail 18-15-6 in compatibility: hold me fast and fear me not
items.short: The Moon, The Devil, The Lovers: read card by card, the couple's road seems to have a dark middle. Yet the 18-15-6 tail tells a story of rescue, not of a fall. The couple enters the task through a shared secret and a language only the two of them understand (The Moon). The road runs through a strong attachment, in which each sees the other at their worst and does not let go (The Devil). And the main task is to choose each other with open eyes, then unclench the hands once the other has become themselves again (The Lovers).

sections.h2: The riddle of the middle: a six that was never reduced
paragraphs: Each point of a couple's tail is the sum of the same points in two personal charts. The entry is added from two entries, the middle from two middles, the main task from two main tasks. The couple's middle is not recalculated from its own ends, and that is the whole point. In the example the partners' middles are 3 and 12. Their sum, 15, is below 22, there is nothing to reduce, and The Devil stays in the middle. Counted by the personal formula, from The Moon to The Lovers, it would have come to 24 → 6. **Twenty-four and fifteen are different numbers with the same digit sum**: 2 + 4 = 6 and 1 + 5 = 6.

Hence a simple rule. In couples with The Moon at the entry and The Lovers as the main task, the middle comes in only two kinds. Either it is 6, which gives the 18-6-6 tail, found in about 1.5% of couples. Or it is 15, which gives 18-15-6: about one couple in 210 (0.476%), 56th of the 97 couple tails. The second variant never occurs in a personal chart: there the middle must be the sum of the ends, and The Devil cannot stand between The Moon and The Lovers.

The second clue is who brings what into the couple. The 18-15-6 tail is formed by only two combinations of personal tails: 15-8-11 + 3-7-22 (52% of such couples) and 9-12-3 + 9-3-21 (48%). None of the four personal tails contains The Moon or The Lovers: both cards are born only in the sum. The Devil belongs to just one partner in the first combination, at the entry of the 15-8-11 tail. In the second combination nobody has it. **This tail belongs to neither of the two alone**, and the attachment in its middle cannot be charged to one person's account.

The third clue is subtler. The tails 9-12-3 and 9-3-21, each added to a copy of itself, give 18-6-6: 12 + 12 = 24 → 6, and 3 + 3 = 6. The Devil appears only when the partners' middles differ: one partner's Hanged Man and the other's Empress (12 + 3), or Justice and The Chariot (8 + 7). Fifteen is born not of sameness but of the meeting of two different ways of walking the road.

And the last. In the 9-12-3 + 9-3-21 combination both partners have The Lovers in the centre of their personal charts. The card that is the couple's main task is, for each of the two, their own comfort zone. And 6 + 6 = 12, so The Hanged Man ends up in the centre of the couple. We will come back to it.

Our reading of all the clues: the couple goes from The Moon to The Lovers not directly but through The Devil, that is, through the same love before it has been reduced to a choice. To see what this looks like in life, one needs a story in which love passes through captivity and comes out of it. Such a story exists, and it is nearly five hundred years old.

sections.h2: The ballad of Tam Lin: this couple's story
paragraphs: In The Complaynt of Scotland (1549), a company of shepherds passes an evening telling tales, and among them is "The Tayl of the ȝong Tamlene". A little later the same shepherds dance a dance called "Thom of Lyn". The text of the ballad itself was written down only in the eighteenth century. The best-known version was sent by Robert Burns to James Johnson's collection, The Scots Musical Museum. Francis James Child made it number 39 in The English and Scottish Popular Ballads and wrote: "This fine ballad stands by itself, and is not, as might have been expected, found in possession of any people but the Scottish."

The setting is real. Carterhaugh, Walter Scott wrote in his introduction to the ballad in Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border, "is a plain, at the conflux of the Ettrick and Yarrow, in Selkirkshire, about a mile above Selkirk". The peasants pointed out rings on the plain, traces of the fairy revels, and the spots where "the stands of milk, and of water, in which Tamlane was dipped" had been placed. There, they said, "the grass will never grow".

The plot falls into three acts, and they run in the same order as the cards of the tail. Quotations here and below follow Child's version 39A in the original Scots; the plain-English glosses in brackets are ours.

head: Card
Point of the tail
Act of the ballad
rows: the forbidden wood of Carterhaugh, a rose by the well, the question "were you ever christened?" and secret signs for Halloween night
captivity with the Queen of Fairies and the tithe to hell; at Miles Cross Janet holds Tam Lin while he turns into a snake, a bear, a lion, iron and fire
a naked knight comes out of the well water, she covers him with her green mantle, and the Queen threatens him with eyes of wood

sections.h2: The Moon at the entry: Carterhaugh, where nobody asks leave
paragraphs: The ballad opens with a ban: "O I forbid you, maidens a', / That wear gowd on your hair, / To come or gae by Carterhaugh, / For young Tam Lin is there." Whoever passes leaves a pledge: "Either their rings, or green mantles, / Or else their maidenhead." Janet kilts her green kirtle above her knee and goes. By the well stands a horse without a rider. She pulls a double rose, and the knight starts up before her: why pull the rose, why come "withoutten my command"? Janet's answer is the first thing worth knowing about this couple: "Carterhaugh, it is my ain, / My daddie gave it me; / I'll come and gang by Carterhaugh, / And ask nae leave at thee."

The entry to the task is what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, a common language. For 18-15-6 it is the wish for a wood of their own, where outsiders are not let in and nobody has to ask leave of anyone. The Moon in its plus, according to Yuliana Lisovskaya, whose book the site uses to calculate compatibility, is understanding without words, mystery, the feeling of being desired, games for two; the partner is first of all a friend, and even after years something new keeps turning up in them. The scenes are recognisable: messages that begin at night; pet names nobody else hears; a trip they do not mention even to their closest people.

This door has a shadow. At home Janet tells her father that her love is "an elfin grey". She does not yet know who he is, and she fills him out into a creature from another world. Couples with The Moon enter the task this way too: at first each loves a slightly invented person. Lisovskaya describes the minus of The Moon in a couple's tasks in exactly these terms: an image made at the start that later collapses; jealousy and resentment over stories the two made up themselves; tenderness hidden as if it were weakness. One is an hour late, and the other already has a story ready that contains everything except the actual person. One goes quiet, and the other decides it must be about them.

Janet does what needs doing at the entry: she goes back to the wood and asks straight out. "O tell me, tell me, Tam Lin," she says, "For's sake that died on tree, / If eer ye was in holy chapel, / Or christendom did see?" And he tells her everything at once. He is an earthly knight, Roxbrugh's grandson. One cold day, coming home from the hunt, he fell from his horse, and the Queen of Fairies caught him "in yon green hill to dwell". He had not lied. He had been enchanted.

Benebell Wen draws the same distinction. The High Priestess, she writes, "suggests secrets that a person is withholding", while The Moon represents "the hidden condition of the Seeker's situation". **For a couple with The Moon at the entry, the secret is most often not a lie but a condition**: what each has brought along and not yet spoken of, whether an earlier attachment, fear or tiredness. Guesswork turns this into an elf. A straight question turns it into a person.

The entry stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish can turn into resistance. Janet and Tam Lin's common language is signs. "But how shall I thee ken, Tam Lin, / Or how my true-love know, / Amang sae mony unco knights / The like I never saw?" And he answers: "My right hand will be glovd, lady, / My left hand will be bare, / Cockt up shall my bonnet be, / And kaimd down shall my hair, / And thae's the takens I gie thee." A couple with this tail needs its own signs: a word that at a noisy party means "I feel awful, let's go"; a look by which one finds the other in a crowd. Resistance begins where the signs replace the conversation: the two understand each other without words, and for years never say the main thing aloud.

In his introduction Child retells a story from Scott's notes that runs opposite to the ballad. A farmer in Lothian had lost his wife to the fairies. She appeared to him and told him how to win her back. At Halloween he waited in a plot of furze, but "at the ringing of the fairy bridles, and the wild, unearthly sound which accompanied the cavalcade, his heart failed him, and he suffered the ghostly train to pass by". The last thing he heard was his wife's voice, "lamenting that he had lost her forever". At midnight Janet hears the same ringing ("She heard the bridles ring") and is "as glad at that / As any earthly thing". One sound. For one it is terror, for the other it is the sound long awaited. **The Moon at the entry tests not love but fear**: in the dark a couple is let down not by a monster but by its own "what if".

sections.h2: The Devil in the middle: hold me fast and fear me not
paragraphs: Lisovskaya gives the middle of a couple's tail no meaning of its own: it is an "addition" to the main task. Our reading for the site is how the couple travels from the wish at the entry to the main task. For 18-15-6 this road runs through The Devil, and the ballad shows what that looks like.

Fairyland, Tam Lin admits, is pleasant. "And pleasant is the fairy land, / But, an eerie tale to tell, / Ay at the end of seven years / We pay a tiend to hell; / I am sae fair and fu o flesh, / I'm feard it be mysel." From the inside, The Devil's attachment rarely looks like a chain. It looks like a pleasant country that somehow cannot be left.

Then comes the great night. Dark, midnight, Miles Cross. The fairies ride past: let the black go by, let the brown go by, pull the rider down from the milk-white steed. And in her arms he turns into "an esk and adder" [a newt and a snake], "a bear sae grim, / And then a lion bold", "a red het gaud of airn" [a red-hot bar of iron], "the burning gleed" [a live coal]. Each time the same words: **"hold me fast, and fear me not"**.

In a couple's life these transformations are recognised at once. In a quarrel one becomes a snake: cold, quiet, stinging. The other becomes a bear: loud, heavy, impossible to shift. The red-hot iron is words that burn the hands of the one holding on. The burning coal is a person who burns themselves out with work, resentment, worry. The middle of the 18-15-6 tail is the years in which two people see each other in all these shapes and stay. Lisovskaya describes The Devil in its plus in just this way: the partners accept each other's dark sides and forgive mistakes, and between them there is passion, powerful support and a readiness to change for love.

But there are two ways to hold, and the ballad shows both. The Queen of Fairies holds Tam Lin for years. Janet holds him for one night. The motif of holding on through transformations, Child writes, connects the Scottish ballad "with Greek popular tradition older than Homer". On the centaur Chiron's advice, Peleus seized the sea goddess Thetis and did not let go, "though she turned, now into fire, now into water, and now into a beast", as Apollodorus tells it in Frazer's translation. Child calls it plainly "the forced marriage of Thetis with Peleus". Later Thetis left her son and went back to the Nereids. In a Cretan tale that Child sets beside it, a young man held a nereid by the hair until cock-crow while she became a dog, a snake, a camel, fire. He got a wife who did not utter a word for a whole year and then vanished.

The grip is the same. The difference is who asked for it. Tam Lin asks for it himself: "Then win me, win me, an ye will, / For weel I wat ye may" [win me if you will, for well I know you can]. **To hold someone who asks to be held is rescue. To hold someone who is struggling free is captivity**, even if the one holding calls it love.

The minus of The Devil in a couple's tasks, as Lisovskaya lists it, is the Queen herself: the wish to possess, control, attempts to keep the partner through closeness, money, status, children; fear and hopelessness; silence about one's own desires. In a couple's life the Queen of Fairies is not a rival but whatever holds one of the two: a former life, habit, fear. The danger of the middle is not that the couple will meet its Devil. The danger is that the one who did the rescuing will start holding on like the Queen: checking, reminding the other how much has been done, repeating "you'd be lost without me". Lisovskaya's chapter on the fifteenth energy ends with a simple thought: nobody belongs to anybody.

Wen adds a caveat that matters for a couple. The Devil card "does not necessarily mean the Seeker is entirely to blame": the person is never quite innocent, but "the greater culpability rests elsewhere". Tam Lin did not choose the hill; he fell from his horse. The numbers say the same: The Devil of the middle is born in the sum of two tails, not in the tail of one. There is no point in hunting for which of the two "tied up" the other. Such a couple's attachment is shared, and untying it is also a job for two.

Among Waite's divinatory meanings for The Devil there is a line that fits the night at Miles Cross: "extraordinary efforts, force, fatality; that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil". For this couple the dark middle is not a verdict but the place where strong hands are needed.

sections.h2: The Lovers as the main task: a naked knight under a green mantle
paragraphs: The couple's main task is read mostly through the minus: what does not work and what has to be learned. In the ballad it takes two stanzas. Tam Lin's last shape is a burning coal, and he must be thrown into well water. "And then I'll be your ain true-love, / I'll turn a naked knight; / Then cover me wi your green mantle, / And cover me out o sight." Child notes that immersion in water is the step required to pass from an enchanted shape back into a human one, and that version A "is the only version which has preserved an essentially correct process". The ballad began at a well ("Tam Lin was at the well"), and it ends at one.

At the end Janet holds a green mantle. At the very start of the ballad, green mantles are the pledge Carterhaugh takes from every girl who passes, along with rings. **What the enchanted wood took as payment becomes the cover for the one set free.** The mantle does not hold. It hides him from other eyes, but not from hers.

The Lovers as the main task means loving a real person. Not the elf invented by The Moon at the entry, nor the monster shown by The Devil in the middle, but the one who remains when everything magical has been washed off by water: wet, naked, without enchantment. Among this energy's tasks Lisovskaya names idealisation and perfectionism, the insecurity from which jealousy and control grow, dependence on relatives, learning to love oneself within the couple, and leaving a hard past behind together. In scenes it looks like this. One wants the other to be "like at the beginning" again, and the beginning was by moonlight. The other is jealous not of a person but of their own insecurity. Both look round at relatives and friends before deciding that they themselves are happy.

The choice in the ballad is free. "Win me, an ye will": Tam Lin does not demand, he asks. Janet chooses for herself, at home before her father and his knights, at night before the whole fairy train. From the castle wall an old grey knight sighs: "Alas, fair Janet, for thee / But we'll be blamed a'." Janet tells him to hold his tongue, and to her father she says she would not give her true love "for nae lord that ye hae". The Lovers ask the same of a couple with this tail: to choose each other without permission from "the old knight on the wall", meaning relatives, friends, general opinion. Lisovskaya gives the same advice: look less to the people around and do not remake the partner to fit one's own standards.

The last word belongs to the Queen. First she concedes: "Them that has gotten young Tam Lin / Has gotten a stately groom." Then she says the essential thing about her kind of love: "But had I kend, Tam Lin," she says, "What now this night I see, / I wad hae taen out thy twa grey een, / And put in twa een o tree." In other versions she would also have taken out his heart of flesh and put in a heart of stone. Child explains the threat this way: mortals who have been among the fairies can see them afterwards when they are invisible to others, and the Queen would have taken that sight away. **Possession wants a partner with wooden eyes**, one who sees nothing but the one who holds. The Lovers want him with his own grey eyes.

Hence the formula of the main task. Reducing 15 to 6 does not mean giving up the strength of hand that The Devil taught. It means turning the grip into an open palm: holding while the other becomes themselves, and letting go once they have.
What helps a couple with this tail:

ul: **Ask instead of filling in the blanks.** The question "were you ever christened?" instead of a story composed alone: in such a couple a secret is more often a condition than a lie.
**Agree on signs, and do not mistake them for silence.** A private language is needed, but the main things are still said aloud.
**Hold, but do not hold back.** "Fear me not" in the ballad is addressed to the one who holds: it is about their fear, not about power over the one being held.
**Put desires into words.** The Devil is strong where desires go unspoken; Lisovskaya advises admitting secret desires and talking about them.
**Unclench the hands.** When the hard time is over, the grip that rescued should become an embrace: a mantle, not a chain.
**Choose each other in front of people.** Without permission from the old knight on the wall.

sections.h2: What Waite saw: a ring, chains and living wood
paragraphs: The site's cards have drawings of their own. But in the descriptions of the deck that Pamela Colman Smith drew to Arthur Edward Waite's design there are details that read like stage directions to the ballad.

The Moon. Out of the water comes a crayfish, "the nameless and hideous tendency which is lower than the savage beast". "It strives to attain manifestation, symbolized by crawling from the abyss of water to the land, but as a rule it sinks back whence it came." What surfaces in a couple at the entry usually sinks again, unless someone asks a straight question. Waite calls the card itself "life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit". In the ballad this is the "elfin grey" whom Janet has not yet asked who he is.

The Devil. "There is a ring in front of the altar, from which two chains are carried to the necks of two figures, male and female." Rings were the first pledge Carterhaugh took. And Waite's caveat follows at once: he who is exalted above them "is not to be their master for ever. Even now, he is also a bondsman." In the ballad this is literal: the whole of fairyland pays the tithe to hell ("We pay a tiend to hell", says Tam Lin). Child notes that one version (39H) "makes the queen fear for herself". The one who holds is on a chain too.

The Lovers. Waite describes a man and a woman "unveiled before each other" and love "before it is contaminated by gross material desire". In the ballad the naked knight is hidden by the mantle from other eyes, but not from the woman who covered him.

The Hanged Man, the card of the couple's centre. "The tree of sacrifice is living wood, with leaves thereon"; "the face expresses deep entrancement, not suffering"; the figure suggests "life in suspension, but life and not death". The ballad has three trees. Janet swears by Him "that died on tree". The Hanged Man hangs from living wood. And the Queen would have given Tam Lin "twa een o tree": eyes of dead wood.

The Hermit, the most frequent card among such couples' values. Waite notes that his card differs from the conventional models in one thing only: "the lamp is not enveloped partially in the mantle of its bearer". In this tail the mantle is needed not to hide the light but to cover the one who has become human again.

sections.h2: The Hanged Man in the centre: a pleasant country in suspension
paragraphs: In every couple with the 18-15-6 tail, The Hanged Man (12) stands in the centre. The couple's centre is the atmosphere inside the union: what lies between the two and is not for show. Lisovskaya describes the twelfth energy here as tact, empathy, attentiveness and a readiness to yield; one partner often does nothing for themselves and everything for the other; the two feel each other at a distance. Such couples take a long time to enter a relationship, and to marry they need a push from outside.

Tam Lin lives exactly like this: he fell from his horse and hangs between worlds, in a country where life is pleasant. The push is a deadline: "But the night is Halloween, lady, / The morn is Hallowday", and so "win me" is said now rather than some day. The minus of this centre, in Lisovskaya, is a sacrifice nobody asked for: one gives up their own interests for the other; decisions are made "because that's how it should be" and because of what people will say. Next to The Devil in the middle this shows especially clearly. A pleasant suspended state is that very fairyland where the tithe is paid.

Wen's advice to the person who draws The Hanged Man is to "hang in there": to endure, to stay suspended a little longer. The ballad's verb is a neighbouring one: "hold me fast". One means to endure, the other to act. **The couple's centre teaches the first, the tail teaches the second**, and a couple with this tail needs both skills.

One clue from the numbers adds a detail. In almost half of such couples, in the 9-12-3 + 9-3-21 combination, both partners have The Lovers in the centre of their personal charts, and together they make twelve. Our reading: two people for each of whom love is a familiar home together create an atmosphere of waiting, where each expects the other to make the first move.

sections.h2: The couple's values: each walks to Miles Cross alone
paragraphs: The couple's values are its spiritual purpose, what the union exists for. In 64.6% of couples with this tail The Hermit (9) stands here, in 35.4% The Moon (18) again. In the example couple it is The Hermit.

"Gloomy, gloomy was the night, / And eerie was the way, / As fair Jenny in her green mantle / To Miles Cross she did gae." The rescue takes two, but each walks to Miles Cross alone. The Hermit among a couple's values, according to Lisovskaya, means each partner's own time and place for solitude, love shown in deeds, deep conversations, respect for boundaries. Wen writes that the Hermit's lantern can be read as "someone who sees the world through his or her own light". For a couple with The Devil in the middle this is the antidote. Each must keep a lantern of their own, or there will be no one left to do the holding: the two will become one chain.

When The Moon returns among the values, the shared wood turns out to be not only the entry but the meaning of the union. Lisovskaya says to look separately at energies that repeat in a couple's chart, and here the repetition is plain. Such couples need a Carterhaugh of their own (a shared world, dreams, a secret for two) as a value, not as a place to hide from everyone else.

First partner, 02.01.1980: day 2, month 1, year 1 + 9 + 8 + 0 = 18. Karmic task 2 + 1 + 18 = 21, centre 2 + 1 + 18 + 21 = 42 → 6, entry to the tail 21 + 6 = 27 → 9, middle 21 + 9 = 30 → 3. Personal tail: 9-3-21.
Second partner, 19.03.1979: day 19, month 3, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 9 = 26 → 8. Karmic task 19 + 3 + 8 = 30 → 3, centre 19 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 33 → 6, entry 3 + 6 = 9, middle 3 + 9 = 12. Personal tail: 9-12-3.

This couple's values: The Hermit (9). If the couple's middle were recalculated from its ends, as in a personal chart, it would come to 18 + 6 = 24 → 6 and the tail would be 18-6-6. That is not how it is done: the couple's middle is the sum of the partners' middles, and here it is The Devil.

intro: This tail has an oddity that only the numbers reveal. In one person's chart the middle of the tail is the sum of its ends: 18 + 6 = 24 → 6, so between The Moon and The Lovers there would stand The Lovers again. In a couple the middle is added up from the middles of two personal tails, and the result is 15, The Devil. And 1 + 5 = 6. **Here The Devil is the same six, only unreduced**, and the whole plot of the tail is how fifteen becomes six: how attachment becomes choice.
This is how the numbers add up for the couple born on 2 January 1980 and 19 March 1979, whose personal tails are 9-3-21 and 9-12-3:

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 18-15-6 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: A couple's tail is read from the entry to the main task. The Moon at the entry is the shared wish for a secret world and a language only the two understand. The Devil in the middle is a road through strong attachment, where each sees the worst in the other. The Lovers as the main task means choosing each other freely and with open eyes. It is a tail about love that passes through captivity and comes out of it, not about a fall.

faq.q: Is The Devil in the middle a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. The card does not predict events or pass verdicts. The Devil in the middle is the way the couple travels the road: passion, attachment, dark sides that have to be accepted. Among Waite's meanings for the card is "that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil". The difficulty lies elsewhere: a grip that rescues can turn into control.

faq.q: Why can a single person's chart never have the 18-15-6 tail?
faq.a: In a personal chart the middle of the tail is the sum of the entry and the task: 18 + 6 = 24 → 6, which would give the tail 18-6-6. In a couple the middle is added up from the two partners' middles (3 + 12 or 8 + 7), and the result is 15. That is why 18-15-6 occurs only in compatibility, in about one couple in 210.

faq.q: How is 18-15-6 different from 18-6-15?
faq.a: In 18-6-15 the same cards stand in a different order: The Lovers are the middle of the road and The Devil is the main task, so the couple deals with attachment at the end rather than along the way. That tail occurs in 0.697% of couples, and their centre is different: The World in 81.8% or The Empress in 18.2%. In 18-15-6 the centre is always The Hanged Man.

faq.q: How is a couple's tail calculated?
faq.a: Calculate both personal charts and add the same points of the tails: entries with entries, middles with middles, tasks with tasks, reducing any sum above 22. The couple's middle is not recalculated from its own ends. The compatibility calculator on the site does this automatically.

report: A girl holds her lover while in her arms he turns into a snake, a bear, a lion, red-hot iron, a burning coal. He asked for it himself: "hold me fast, and fear me not". This is the Scottish ballad of Tam Lin, a tale shepherds were already telling in 1549, and its three acts run in exactly the order of the 18-15-6 cards: The Moon, The Devil, The Lovers.

Read card by card, the couple's road seems to have a dark middle. But what stands in the middle is not a fall. If this were one person's tail, the middle would be the sum of the ends and would give The Lovers again. In a couple it is added up from the middles of the two partners, and the result is 15. And 1 + 5 = 6. **Here The Devil is the same six, only unreduced**: the same love, before it has become a choice. The whole tail is about how fifteen becomes six.

report.h3: An elf who has to be asked who he is

report: The ballad opens with the forbidden wood of Carterhaugh. Whoever passes leaves a pledge: "Either their rings, or green mantles, / Or else their maidenhead." Janet goes without asking leave: "Carterhaugh, it is my ain." This is how a couple with this tail enters the task: with a wood of their own, where nobody has to ask leave of anyone, with private pet names and messages that begin at night.

The shadow of the entry is an invented person. At home Janet calls her love "an elfin grey": she does not yet know who he is, and she fills him out into a creature from another world. Couples with The Moon at the entry know this well. One is an hour late, and the other already has a story ready that contains everything except the actual person. Janet does what is needed: she goes back and asks straight out whether he was ever christened. And she hears the truth: he is an earthly knight who fell from his horse and was caught by the Queen of Fairies. He had not lied; he had been enchanted. Benebell Wen draws the same distinction: The Moon is not a secret a person withholds but "the hidden condition of the Seeker's situation". **In such a couple the secret is most often not a lie but a condition**: an earlier attachment, fear or tiredness that has not yet been spoken of.

The two share a language of secret signs: a gloved right hand, a bare left one, a bonnet cocked up. Signs are needed, but resistance begins where they replace the conversation. And there is one more test at the entry. Walter Scott recorded the story of a farmer who set out to win his wife back from the fairies, heard the ringing of the fairy bridles, and lost his nerve: he let the whole procession pass. At midnight Janet hears the same ringing and is "as glad at that / As any earthly thing". The Moon at the entry tests not love but fear.

report.h3: One grip, two outcomes: rescue or captivity

report: Fairyland, Tam Lin admits, is pleasant, except that every seven years it pays a tithe to hell. From the inside, The Devil's attachment rarely looks like a chain; it looks more like a pleasant country that somehow cannot be left. The night at Miles Cross is the middle of the tail in a single scene. In a quarrel one partner becomes a snake: cold, quiet, stinging. The other becomes a bear that cannot be shifted. The red-hot iron is words that burn the hands of the one holding on. The middle of 18-15-6 is the years in which two people see each other in all these shapes and stay.

But there are two kinds of grip. The ballad collector Francis James Child found the same motif in Greek myth: Peleus held Thetis while she turned into fire, water and a beast. Child calls it a forced marriage, and Thetis later left. In a Cretan tale a young man held a nereid in the same way and got a wife who did not utter a word for a year and then vanished. Tam Lin asks for it himself: "Then win me, win me, an ye will." **To hold someone who asks to be held is rescue. To hold someone who is struggling free is captivity.**

The danger of the middle is that the one who did the rescuing will start holding on like the Queen: checking, reminding the other how much has been done, insisting that the other would be lost without them. Hunting for the guilty party is pointless here. Wen notes that The Devil card does not mean a person is entirely to blame, and Tam Lin did not choose the hill: he fell from his horse. The Devil in the middle is born in the sum of two tails, not in the tail of one, and untying this attachment is also a job for two.

report.h3: A mantle instead of a chain

report: Tam Lin's last shape is a burning coal. He is thrown into well water, and out comes a naked knight: "Then cover me wi your green mantle, / And cover me out o sight." Green mantles appeared at the very start of the ballad, as the pledge the enchanted wood took. **What the wood took as payment becomes the cover for the one set free.** The mantle does not hold; it covers.

The Lovers as the main task means loving a real person: not the elf from the entry, nor the monster from the middle, but the one who remains when the magic has been washed off by water. The difficulty here is idealisation (the wish for things to be "like at the beginning" again, when the beginning was by moonlight), jealousy born of one's own insecurity, and looking round at relatives. Janet chooses for herself. When an old knight on the castle wall sighs "Alas, fair Janet, for thee / But we'll be blamed a'", she tells him to hold his tongue.

The last word belongs to the Queen of Fairies: had she known in advance, she would have taken out Tam Lin's grey eyes and put in eyes of wood. **Possession wants a partner with wooden eyes**, one who sees nothing but the one who holds. The Lovers want him with his own.

report.h3: How fifteen becomes six

report: Reducing 15 to 6 does not mean giving up the strength of hand that The Devil taught. It means turning the grip into an open palm. Asking instead of filling in the blanks. Keeping private signs and still saying the main things aloud. Putting desires into words. Holding on while the other becomes themselves, and unclenching the hands once they have. In the strong version of the 18-15-6 tail, the couple knows each other in every shape and still chooses each other, in front of people and with open eyes.

seo.title: Karmic tail 18 18 18 compatibility: three Moons of a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 18 18 18 compatibility: three Moons and The Hermit at the centre — what the tail means for a couple and why its story is a truth seen in a mirror.

items.title: The 18-18-18 tail in compatibility: three Moons and a truth seen in a mirror
items.short: The Moon, The Moon and The Moon again: the 18-18-18 tail holds no other card, and it turns up in roughly one couple in 1,684. In compatibility this karmic tail means that two people come together over a mystery, live their union in half-light, where each sees the other by reflected light, and are handed a single main task — to stop knowing each other by reflection.

sections.h2: The novel where the key evidence was seen in a mirror
paragraphs: In 1868 Wilkie Collins published The Moonstone, a novel T. S. Eliot would later call "the first, the longest, and the best of modern English detective novels". At its centre is a yellow diamond. Legend says it was set in the forehead of an Indian god of the Moon, its lustre "growing and lessening … with the waxing and waning of the moon"; hence the stone's name. A will leaves the diamond to Rachel Verinder as a present for her eighteenth birthday, 21 June 1848. The Moon is the eighteenth arcanum too. Collins knew nothing of the destiny matrix, and a coincidence stays a coincidence, but it is an easy one to remember.

That same night the stone vanishes. Suspicion falls on a housemaid with a dark past, on Indian jugglers prowling round the house, and finally on Rachel herself: the celebrated Sergeant Cuff seriously concludes that she has stolen her own diamond. Yet Rachel knows from the first minute who the thief is. She saw him. It is Franklin Blake, her cousin and the man she loves.

She did not see him directly. He stood with his back to her at the Indian cabinet, and Rachel watched in a mirror: "There are three glasses in my sitting-room. As you stood there, I saw all that you did, reflected in one of them." Three mirrors in the room, three Moons in the tail. The key evidence in this love story is a reflection, and a true one: the hand really did take the stone from the drawer. Everything else was wrong. Franklin remembered nothing: he had been secretly dosed with laudanum, and that night he walked as if in a dream.

Collins said himself what the book stands on. In the preface of 1868: "The conduct pursued, under a sudden emergency, by a young girl, supplies the foundation on which I have built this book." That conduct is silence. Rachel saw, and said not a word — not to her mother, not to the police, not to him. The plot of the novel stands on that silence, and so does the plot of a couple with three Moons. Quotations from the novel here and below are Collins's own words.

sections.h2: The first Moon, entry to the task: a door painted by two
paragraphs: Entry to the task is the first card of the couple's tail. For Lisovskaya it is what two people want together, their agreements and their "common language". The point sits on the line of tasks, so the same wish can also turn into resistance. With The Moon at the entry, the couple's common language is mystery.

In the novel that language is visible before the theft. For weeks Rachel and Franklin decorate the door of her little sitting-room with griffins, birds, flowers and cupids, copied from designs by a famous Italian painter. They mix the paint with a "vehicle" Franklin invented himself; it stinks so badly that the very dogs sneeze when they come into the room. The old house-steward Betteredge grumbles but admits that the two never seemed to tire of it, sitting over the door "with their heads together, as busy as bees". They finish on the birthday itself, by three in the afternoon. The pattern is beautiful and so tangled that, Betteredge says, "you felt them unpleasantly in your head for hours after".

And what draws them to each other is what cannot be seen to the end. Of the diamond Betteredge writes that a stone you could hold between finger and thumb "seemed unfathomable as the heavens themselves". Of Rachel he says almost the same: "The difficulty was to fathom Miss Rachel." Franklin, as Betteredge describes him, has "his French side, and his German side, and his Italian side", with the original English foundation only now and then showing through; Rachel teases him about which side is uppermost. Each loves in the other a depth with no bottom.

Now the catch. The vehicle takes twelve hours to dry, and Franklin painted the last morsel of the pattern himself, at about three in the afternoon. At night the paint is still wet, and whoever passed brushed against it. The smear on the door became the first clue. The couple's shared picture keeps a trace of every night. This is the double nature of the entry: the world of images two people create together is their language and, at the same time, the place where their future misunderstanding is written down.

The numbers add their own clue. In this couple the Moon at the entry is always folded from two different cards: one partner has The Devil (15) at this point, the other The Empress (3). Our reading: enchantment plus shared creation. Betteredge confesses that the diamond "laid such a hold on" him that he cried out "O" along with the young ladies; The Empress is the generosity that grows living, beautiful things. Together they make a door covered in cupids.

In life this is recognisable at once. The couple has pet words no third person would understand, an invented world of their own — a city, a game, a series, an unusual shared passion. They like it that even friends understand them only in part. In Lisovskaya, The Moon fills a union with fantasy and play for two, and at the entry that is the glue. Resistance starts with a sentence that sounds like a compliment: "we understand each other without words". From it the next one follows easily: so words need not check anything.

sections.h2: The second Moon, the middle: a year of silence for the other's sake
paragraphs: The middle of the task is how the couple travels from their shared wish to the main task. With The Moon in the middle, that road runs through dusk.

Rachel later describes the birthday night. At about one o'clock she cannot sleep, lights her candle and means to fetch a book from the sitting-room. There is light under the door, footsteps. She thinks it is her mother, who spent the evening begging to take charge of the diamond, and blows out her own candle so as to seem asleep. From the dark she sees Franklin "in your nightgown — with your bedroom candle in your hand". In the mirror she watches him open the drawers, take out the stone and stand still for a long time: "I saw your face sideways in the glass. You looked like a man thinking, and dissatisfied with his own thoughts." Then his light went away, and she was left alone in the dark.

Then comes a year. Rachel raises no alarm. She refuses to have her wardrobe examined, cries out to the police officer that she never sent for him and that nobody will ever find the diamond, cuts off all contact with Franklin and tells no one why. Before morning she writes him a letter that names nothing openly: only a hint that she knows of his debts, and a private offer to lend him money. The letter never reaches him. Franklin sees only that the woman he loves has turned to ice and will not see him. He leaves England.

So two versions of one story appear. In hers he is a thief who also pretends to zeal and hunts for himself. In his she has come to hate him for no reason at all. Among The Moon's tasks for a couple Lisovskaya names jealousy and grievances that most often grow out of invented stories. The novel shows how such stories are born: from a real fact seen only in part.

The hardest thing about the middle is that the silence here is not a lie. Betteredge remembers Rachel as a child: when a friend she loved was at fault, she took the blame, never confessed and never lied. She looked you straight in the face and said plainly, "I won't tell you!" Her mother kept saying: "Rachel's best friend and Rachel's worst enemy are, one and the other — Rachel herself." The grown-up Rachel is silent out of love: "I spare him, when my heart is breaking; I screen him when my own character is at stake." And from outside, a silent person looks guilty — the detective suspected her of all people.

In Paul's hymn to love, charity "beareth all things" (1 Cor 13:7). The Greek verb is στέγει, from στέγη, "roof": to cover, to keep under a roof, to keep silent. Thayer's lexicon notes that some interpreters read the verse exactly so — love covers and hides the faults of others; Thayer himself prefers "beareth", but the Greek word holds both senses. Rachel loved in just that way, by covering. Yet one line earlier the same hymn says that love "rejoiceth in the truth". To cover without knowing the truth — that is the second Moon.

The numbers leave a clue here as well. The middle of this couple's tail is folded from The Hierophant (5) of one partner and Death (13) of the other. Our reading: a rule plus a rupture. "One doesn't talk about such things", "I won't humiliate him with a question" — and instead of a conversation, a door closes. The year of fog is made of a code of honour and a break.

In life it looks ordinary. One partner notices a fragment — an odd pause in a conversation, a phrase half overheard, a closed door — and does not ask, so as not to humiliate either of them. The other feels the chill and does not ask either, so as not to seem clingy. Each protects the other with silence and runs a private investigation. Nobody lies, and both are wrong.

All this time the key evidence lay at the bottom. Franklin's nightgown with the smear of paint was found by a housemaid secretly in love with him, who hid it in a tin case in the Shivering Sand by the sea. Of that quicksand Betteredge writes that at the turn of the tide "something goes on in the unknown deeps below", and the whole surface begins to tremble. A truth hidden out of love lies down there and shudders with every tide. That is how the second Moon feels: nothing has been said aloud, yet everything keeps shaking.

sections.h2: The third Moon, the main task: "I saw you with my own eyes"
paragraphs: The main task is the anchor point of the tail. Lisovskaya reads it mostly through its minus: what the couple cannot manage and what it has to learn.

A year later Franklin finds the case in the sand, unrolls the nightgown and looks for the owner's mark. The mark bears his own name: "on the unanswerable evidence of the paint-stain, I had discovered Myself as the Thief." He manages to see Rachel. The conversation opens with reproaches on both sides, and Rachel breaks: "You villain, I saw you take the Diamond with my own eyes!"

Franklin answers with words that hold the whole tail: "I can't explain the contradiction in what I am going to tell you. I can only speak the truth as you have spoken it." There are two truths, and they are opposites. Then he finds the exact words: "You are the victim, and I am the victim, of some monstrous delusion which has worn the mask of truth." And the most important: "You have tried by yourself. You have not tried with me to help you."

Even then the conversation breaks down. Having heard her account of the night, Franklin reproaches her — if only she had spoken then… — and a year of silence comes out in a single cry. Wen, writing of The Moon reversed, has an exact phrase: "any strong intention to repress will cause a violent surfacing". What is held down does not vanish; it waits for an occasion.

Among The Moon's tasks Lisovskaya also names the habit of hiding feelings and taking tenderness for weakness, and an image created at the start that later collapses. The novel shows why The Moon is more dangerous than an ordinary lie. The image "Franklin the thief" was built not on gossip but on her own eyes, and that is why it lasts a whole year. A mistake taken from someone else's words is easy to check. A mistake seen with your own eyes you do not want to check: "but I saw it".

The numbers hint at how this mistake is built. The couple's main task is folded from Justice (8) of one partner and The Wheel of Fortune (10) of the other. Our reading: a verdict plus circumstances makes fog. Rachel passed an honest verdict on what she saw. She did not know the circumstances: at dinner Mr Candy, the family's medical man, had argued with Franklin about medicine and decided to teach the scoffer a lesson, and the laudanum was slipped to him in secret. In his preface Collins says he set out "to trace the influence of character on circumstances", and the couple's main task lies exactly at that seam. Character is not to blame, circumstances are not to blame; the mistake is a verdict passed alone.
For a couple with 18-18-18 the main task sounds simple: before saying "I know", say "I saw" — and ask. Not because eyes lie. Because they are looking into a mirror.

sections.h2: Ezra Jennings's black ink and red
paragraphs: The way out of the fog is found by a man nobody thinks of at first. Ezra Jennings is Mr Candy's assistant, an outsider with startling white and black hair. For years he has lived under "the cloud of a horrible accusation" that he cannot even bring himself to name; he can only assert his innocence. When the slander first struck him down, he parted with the woman he loved rather than make her share his disgrace. A man who has spent his life inside someone else's false image knows better than anyone the price of silence kept out of love.

When Mr Candy lay in a fever, Jennings took down his delirium in shorthand. Then he copied the fragments in black ink and filled the gaps between them in red, so that what was said and his interpretation stood side by side and could be checked against each other. "I have penetrated through the obstacle of the disconnected expression, to the thought which was underlying it connectedly all the time." Out of black fragments and red links a story grew. At dinner Franklin had quipped in front of everyone that "taking medicine and groping in the dark mean one and the same thing", and Mr Candy decided to give him "five-and-twenty minims of laudanum … without his knowing it" and confront him with the truth in the morning.

For a couple with three Moons this is the best working tool. The Moon writes in red ink and forgets that it is red. "He came home late" is black. "He is hiding something" is red. As long as both colours are visible to both people, any story can be checked. When red is passed off as black, a year of silence begins.

Jennings's second step is bolder. He proposes not to interrogate but to repeat the night. On 25 June 1849, almost a year after the birthday, the house is set back the way it was that night, an imitation stone goes into the cabinet drawer, and Franklin is given laudanum again. Rachel stands in her room behind a door left ajar, her light put out. Franklin gets up with a candle, mutters "How do I know? The Indians may be hidden in the house", goes to the sitting-room, opens the drawers and takes out the stone — exactly as a year before. The celebrated Cuff looked for someone to blame and was wrong about the main thing. The outsider Jennings rebuilt the circumstances and showed how it had all happened.
Wen has a short comparison of two cards: "Key 5: The Hierophant is about orthodox wisdom; Key 9 is the unorthodox solitary path to wisdom." Cuff and Jennings are those two cards in person.

sections.h2: The Hermit at the centre: a silence made of three Moons
paragraphs: At the centre of the chart every couple with the 18-18-18 tail has The Hermit (9), and he stands in the couple's values too, without exception. This is one of the strongest clues in the tail.

Lisovskaya suggests adding up repeated energies: 18 + 18 + 18 = 54, which folds to 9. The sum of the three Moons is The Hermit. By her rule, a sum that does not appear on the chart sounds in the couple only as a faint trail. Here it is no trail: it stands at the very centre.

There is a second piece of arithmetic. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is built from its ends, and between two Moons The Hermit would stand: 18 + 18 = 36 → 9. For a couple the middle is taken from the partners' middles, 5 + 13, so a third Moon appears. The silence missing from the middle of the tail has moved to the centre of the chart. In our search through all dates, the partners' personal centres in such couples are also always the same: The Chariot (7) for one, Judgement (20) for the other. Two loud cards, drive and calling, add up to silence.

For Lisovskaya the couple's centre is the atmosphere between the two, what lies inside and is not on show. With The Hermit it is a couple where each has a time and a corner of their own, where love is proved by deeds rather than words, and no step is hurried. In the minus the same Hermit paints another picture: each on their own, with difficulties piling up in silence. The scene is familiar: an evening, two people in different rooms, each "sorting it out alone" so as not to burden the other. This is exactly where the fog of the second Moon thickens.

In The Moonstone The Hermit even slips into the comedy. In every trouble old Betteredge opens Robinson Crusoe at random and reads the answer as prophecy; he has worn out six copies, and his mistress gave him a seventh. The oracle of that house is a book about a man who lived twenty-eight years on a desert island.

Waite, meanwhile, insists that The Hermit is not isolation. Reading the card through "occult isolation" he calls one of the "frivolous renderings"; for him it is "a card of attainment", a figure "holding up his beacon on an eminence". That is how Jennings leaves the novel. Before he dies he asks that not even the plainest stone mark his grave: "Let me sleep, nameless. Let me rest, unknown." The light that led the couple out of the fog was held by a man who asked for nothing in return. The values of a couple with The Hermit are his path: patient attention instead of a verdict.

sections.h2: Face to face
paragraphs: After the experiment Franklin falls asleep on the sofa in that same sitting-room. Rachel asks to sit with him, watches him all night and does not set a single stitch of her needlework. By eight in the morning, Jennings writes, she is kneeling by the sofa: "She has so placed herself that when his eyes first open, they must open on her face."
In this scene the plot of the tail closes. A year earlier she saw him in a mirror, sideways, by the light of someone else's candle. Now it is face to face.

Near its end, the same hymn to love that "beareth all things" says: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known" (1 Cor 13:12). Paul's Greek says literally "through a mirror, in a riddle". The Russian Synodal Bible renders "in a riddle" as gadatel'no, a word from fortune-telling. The couple's three Moons fit into a single line here: the mirror, the riddle, knowledge in part. And so does the way out: not only to know the other, but to let oneself be known — "even as also I am known".

Collins built the whole novel on this principle. The plan comes from Franklin himself: each witness in turn is to write the story of the Moonstone "as far as our own personal experience extends, and no farther". No narrator knows everything. The truth appears only when the partial accounts are laid side by side. That is the form of conversation that suits a couple with three Moons: each speaks of what they saw themselves, and the story is put together by two.

Rachel and Franklin were married on 9 October 1849. In the epilogue the diamond shines again in the forehead of the Moon god, and the last narrator writes: "So the years pass, and repeat each other; so the same events revolve in the cycles of time." For a couple with the 18-18-18 tail this is not a sentence but a description of the mechanism: the same night will keep repeating until the two of them look at it together.

sections.h2: What changes the script

ul: **Two colours of ink.** Say "I saw" and "I thought" separately. Black is the fact, red is the guess, and both colours are visible to the partner.
**Don't guard with silence.** Rachel's silence was love, and it cost a year. The one who protects is not the one who kept quiet but the one who asked, in time and gently.
**Investigate together.** "You have tried by yourself. You have not tried with me" — in this couple a suspicion is taken apart at a shared table, not inside one head.

**Reconstruct, don't interrogate.** Go back to the moment where the versions parted and walk through it again: who was where, what each saw, what each thought. Interrogation looks for someone to blame; reconstruction looks for the picture.
**Keep the solitude, but don't hide in it.** The Hermit at the centre needs time alone; difficulties are not hidden there but set aside for a conversation.
**Leave the mystery room to play.** Fantasy, pet words and a shared invented world are the couple's strength. Mystery as a game — yes; mystery as a rule of conduct — no.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail
paragraphs: Wen puts The Moon briefly: "Key 18 represents poetry and mystery." A couple with three Moons has more of that poetry than most. Lisovskaya, describing The Moon in its plus, draws a union where the partner is first of all a friend, where each understands the other from half a word, and where every year a person reveals a new side to the other. That is the strong version of 18-18-18: two people who never stop surprising each other, because they do not turn mystery into a weapon.

A strong couple with this tail keeps its door with the griffins — its shared world — and can still read the smear on it out loud. It is not afraid of silence, because The Hermit at the centre teaches them to be quiet together, not apart. And it knows the price of a reflection: a mirror honestly shows the hand, but not the thought behind it.

On the wedding day Betteredge opened Robinson Crusoe at page three hundred and eighteen and, of course, took it for a prophecy. The couple's tail prophesies nothing. It shows where to look: not into the mirror, but into the face.

sections.h2: How the 18-18-18 couple tail is calculated
paragraphs: Each point of a couple is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, folded down to 22. The middle of the tail is not recalculated from the couple's ends: it is the sum of the partners' middles.
An example with the dates 14.08.1975 and 04.01.1976. The first date has the personal tail 15-5-8 and centre 7, the second the tail 3-13-10 and centre 20.
What every couple with this tail has in common:

ul: **Rarity.** Roughly one couple in 1,684 (0.059%), 88th place out of 97 couple tails.

**One combination.** The tail comes only from the personal tails 15-5-8 in one partner and 3-13-10 in the other. The rarity comes from the second: in our search, since 1900 the 3-13-10 tail has fallen on only 149 birthdays, against 4,275 for 15-5-8.
**Nobody's Moon.** Neither partner has The Moon in their personal tail; the three Moons appear only in the sum.
**The Hermit.** The couple's centre is The Hermit in 100% of such couples, and the couple's values are The Hermit in 100% too.
**The middle.** It does not equal the folded sum of the ends: 18 + 18 would give 9, while the couple has 18.

paragraphs: As a personal tail the order 18-18-18 does not occur: in a personal matrix the entry equals the main task plus the centre, and with a main task of 18 an entry of 18 is impossible whatever the centre. The tail has no permutations, since all three numbers are the same; 18-9-18 is a different couple tail. In our example the whole couple chart is written with two numbers, 9 and 18, but that is rare: in our search, 0.85% of couples with this tail. Usually other arcana stand on the remaining points.

ul: **M · Entry to the task — The Moon.** The couple's common language is mystery. What draws them together is what cannot be seen to the bottom, and very quickly they build a world of their own: words, games and images no one else understands.

**N · Middle of the task — The Moon.** The road runs through dusk. Each notices something, guesses at something and stays silent to protect the other — and two different versions of one story live under one roof.
**D · Main task — The Moon.** To separate what was seen from what was filled in, and to check the versions together instead of passing sentence alone.

intro: At the centre of the chart every such couple has The Hermit, and The Hermit again in the couple's values: a silence in which the fog either gathers or clears. What follows is an investigation. The evidence lies in the numbers themselves, in the books of Waite, Benebell Wen and Yuliana Lisovskaya, and in a novel where the key evidence of a love affair was seen in a mirror.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 18-18-18 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is three Moons in a couple's tail. At the entry the couple is bound by a mystery and a shared world of images; in the middle each stays silent to protect the other and keeps a private version of events; and the main task is to learn to separate what was seen from what was filled in, and to check the versions together. At the centre such couples always have The Hermit: a silence in which the fog either gathers or clears.

faq.q: How does the couple tail 18-18-18 come about?
faq.a: Each point of a couple's tail is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, folded down to 22. The 18-18-18 tail occurs only when one partner has the personal tail 15-5-8 and the other 3-13-10: 15 + 3, 5 + 13 and 8 + 10 give three Moons. An example is the couple 14.08.1975 and 04.01.1976.

faq.q: Why is the middle of the tail 18 and not 9?
faq.a: The middle of a couple's tail is not recalculated from its ends but added up from the partners' middles: 5 + 13 = 18. By the personal formula 18 + 18 would fold to 9, giving a different tail, 18-9-18. The Hermit does not disappear, though: in every couple with this tail he stands at the centre of the chart.

faq.q: Does the 18-18-18 tail occur in a personal matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and with a main task of 18 an entry of 18 is impossible whatever the centre. Three Moons in a row is a tail that only a couple can have.

faq.q: Is the 18-18-18 tail a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not predict events or pass sentence on the union. It shows what the two have to learn: to say "I saw" before "I know", not to guard each other with silence, and to work through misunderstandings together. In its strong version this is a couple with a rich shared imagination who understand each other from half a word.

report: Three mirrors hung in Rachel Verinder's sitting-room, and in one of them she watched the man she loved steal her diamond. This scene from Wilkie Collins's The Moonstone describes the couple tail 18-18-18 almost word for word: three Moons in a row are three mirrors in which two people see each other. The reflection was true: Franklin Blake's hand really did take the stone from the drawer. Everything else was wrong. Franklin had been secretly dosed with laudanum; that night he walked as if in a dream and remembered nothing. **A couple with this tail knows each other by reflection: the fact is seen precisely, the meaning is not.**

report.h3: The door that remembered the night

report: The first Moon is the entry to the task, the couple's common language. Here that language is mystery. Before the theft Rachel and Franklin spend weeks decorating the door of her sitting-room with griffins, birds and cupids, sitting over it "with their heads together, as busy as bees". Of the diamond the old house-steward Betteredge writes that it "seemed unfathomable as the heavens themselves"; of Rachel, that "the difficulty was to fathom Miss Rachel". What draws the two together is a depth with no bottom.

A couple with this tail also builds a world of its own early on: pet words, games, an invented city that only the two of them understand. It is the glue of the union. But in Collins the paint on the door was still wet that night, and the smear on it became the first clue. The shared picture keeps a trace of every night. And resistance starts with a sentence that sounds like a compliment: "we understand each other without words". From it the next one follows easily: so words need not check anything.

report.h3: A silence that was love

report: The second Moon is the middle of the road, and the road runs through dusk. Rachel saw everything and said nothing — not to her mother, not to the police, not to him. She cuts off all contact with Franklin and writes him a letter that names nothing openly, and the letter never reaches him. Franklin sees only a sudden chill and leaves England. So two versions of one story appear: in hers he is a thief, in his she has come to hate him for no reason. Nobody lies, and both are wrong.

The trap is that this silence is not a lie. As a child Rachel took the blame for a friend she loved and met every question with a flat "I won't tell…" As a grown woman she says: "I spare him, when my heart is breaking; I screen him when my own character is at stake." In Paul's hymn to love, charity "beareth all things"; the Greek στέγει comes from the word for "roof": to keep under a roof, to keep silent. Yet one line earlier it says that love "rejoiceth in the truth". **To cover without knowing the truth — that is the second Moon.**

In life it is ordinary. One partner notices a fragment of a phrase or an odd pause and does not ask, so as to humiliate no one. The other feels the chill and does not ask either. Each protects the other with silence and runs a private investigation. Meanwhile the evidence lies at the bottom, like Franklin's nightgown in the Shivering Sand, which shudders with every tide: nothing has been said aloud, yet everything keeps shaking.

report.h3: "With my own eyes"

report: The third Moon is the main task. A year later Franklin finds that nightgown, sees his own name on the mark and manages to see Rachel. She breaks: she saw him take the diamond "with my own eyes". He answers that he can only speak the truth as she has spoken it. There are two truths, and they are opposites. He calls them both victims "of some monstrous delusion which has worn the mask of truth" and says the most important thing: she tried to work it out by herself, not together with him.

This is why The Moon is more dangerous than an ordinary lie. A mistake taken from someone else's words is easy to check. A mistake seen with one's own eyes nobody wants to check: "but I saw it". For a couple with 18-18-18 the main task sounds simple: **before saying "I know", say "I saw" — and ask.**

report.h3: Black ink and red

report: The way out is found by Ezra Jennings, a lonely outsider who has lived for years under a false accusation. He took down the delirium of the feverish Mr Candy in fragments and copied it out: what was said in black ink, his own guesses between the words in red, so that the two could be checked against each other. That is how it came out that Mr Candy had decided to teach the scoffer a lesson and gave Franklin laudanum without his knowing it. The Moon writes in red ink and forgets that it is red. "He came home late" is black. "He is hiding something" is red. As long as both colours are visible to both people, any story can be checked.

Then Jennings proposes not to interrogate but to repeat the night. A year later the house is set back the way it was, Rachel stands in the dark behind a door left ajar, and Franklin, candle in hand, again takes a stone from the drawer, this time an imitation. The celebrated detective looked for someone to blame and was wrong; the outsider rebuilt the circumstances and showed how it had all happened. And in the morning Rachel kneels by the sofa so that when Franklin opens his eyes, the first thing he sees is her face. A year ago, a mirror; now, face to face.

At the centre of such a couple's chart stands The Hermit: a silence in which the fog either gathers or clears. It gives each of the two a time and a corner of their own; trouble begins when difficulties are hidden in that corner. Paul fits the whole road into one line: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face." In Greek it is literally "through a mirror, in a riddle". **The strong version of the tail is a couple with a rich shared imagination that does not turn mystery into a weapon:** it keeps its door with the griffins and can read the smear on it out loud.

On the wedding day Betteredge opened Robinson Crusoe at page three hundred and eighteen and took it for a prophecy. The couple's tail prophesies nothing. It shows where to look: not into the mirror, but into the face.
