seo.description: Karmic tail 18 3 3 compatibility: the Moon at the entry, the Empress twice, the Devil in the centre of every such couple, read through The Merchant of Venice.

items.title: Couple karmic tail 18-3-3 in compatibility: how a moonlit game becomes a home
items.short: The couple tail 18-3-3 is built strangely. Its main task is written twice: The Empress stands both in the middle and at the end. And in the centre of the chart every such couple has The Devil, a card that never appears in anyone's personal chart. The answer to the riddle is that this union enters its task through The Moon: through play, hints and night-time enchantment. Its whole work is to make sure that love born in a glance does not die "in the cradle where it lies", but grows into a home that feeds both.

sections.h2: Venice and Belmont: the two personal tails that add up to 18-3-3
paragraphs: The plot in brief. Bassanio, a Venetian, wants to court Portia, a rich heiress from Belmont, but he has no money. His friend Antonio, a merchant, borrows for him from the moneylender Shylock and pledges a pound of his own flesh. By her father's will Portia goes to whoever picks the right one of three caskets: gold, silver and lead. Bassanio picks right, Antonio's ships are lost, and Portia, disguised as a young lawyer, saves him in court. As her fee she begs from her husband her own wedding ring. Alongside runs a second story: Shylock's daughter Jessica escapes from her father's house at night with Lorenzo.

The stage direction says: "Partly at Venice, and partly at Belmont, the seat of Portia". The two places are built as opposites. Venice is the bond, the court and the knife. Belmont is the estate, the casket lottery, the disguises and Portia's "sunny locks", which in Bassanio's words "Hang on her temples like a golden fleece".

The 18-3-3 tail is made of the same two halves. The site's engine has run through every date: in **100% of couples** with this tail one partner has the personal tail 15-8-11 — The Devil, Justice, Strength — and the other has 3-22-19 — The Empress, The Fool, The Sun. Bond, law and force on one side; garden, play and sun on the other. Calling them the Venetian and the Belmont tail is our reading, not a rule of the method. But the cards ask to be set on this stage.
Each point of a couple's tail is the sum of the matching points of two personal tails, reduced to 22:

ul: **Entry:** The Devil + The Empress = 15 + 3 = 18, The Moon. Bond plus garden gives night. And the main meetings of the two places in the play happen at night: Jessica escapes from Venice in the middle of a masque, and at the end all the couples gather at Belmont by moonlight.

**Middle:** Justice + The Fool = 8 + 22 = 30 → 3, The Empress. Court plus masquerade: a young woman disguised as a lawyer turns law into mercy, and the merchant she has saved tells her, "Sweet lady, you have given me life and living".

**Main task:** Strength + The Sun = 11 + 19 = 30 → 3, The Empress. In Waite, Strength leads a lion on a chain of flowers, and the first words of The Sun in his divinatory list are "Material happiness, fortunate marriage". Strength that does not tear, plus happiness that does not hide, gives a home.

paragraphs: Of the six cards in the two personal tails only one survives in the couple's tail, The Empress, and it stands there twice. The Devil disappears from the tail but turns up in the centre, by a different arithmetic described below. If the middle were worked out by the personal formula, it would be 18 + 3 = 21, The World. In the couple, The Empress stands in The World's place: the circle does not close on the whole world, it comes back to the garden.

sections.h2: The Moon at the entry: love that is "engender'd in the eyes"
paragraphs: Bassanio speaks of Portia in the very first scene, and the order of his words is honest to the point of embarrassment. First: "In Belmont is a lady richly left". Then that she is fair. And only then the main thing: "Sometimes from her eyes / I did receive fair speechless messages". An 18-3-3 couple begins with exactly such a wordless greeting.

The Moon stands on the point "Entry to the task": what the two want together, their common language. On the chart the same point M closes the relationship line and is labelled there "Common language". This couple's language is lunar: a look instead of a word, a hint instead of a request, a joke that is half true.
Shakespeare hid the whole tail in the song that is sung while Bassanio chooses a casket:

"Tell me where is fancy bred, / Or in the heart or in the head? / How begot, how nourished? / Reply, reply. / It is engender'd in the eyes, / With gazing fed, and fancy dies / In the cradle where it lies."

"Fancy" is a shortened form of "fantasy", that is, imagination. The song asks about The Moon: love as imagination, living on gazes. And it answers in The Empress's words: begot, nourished, a cradle. The song has nine lines, and the whole task of the tail is in them. **Lunar feeling is born at once, but it can also die in its own cradle.** Whether it grows is a question not for fate but for whether it is fed with anything besides gazing.

The song has a false bottom that readers and directors have argued about for generations. Portia is bound by her father's will and dares not give a hint: "I could teach you / How to choose right, but then I am forsworn". Yet the first rhymes of the song, bred and head, chime with lead, and Bassanio chooses the lead casket. Whether it was a hint cannot be proved from the text. But this is exactly the common language of a lunar couple: said so that only one person will hear it, while the oath stays formally unbroken. In the standard Russian translation the hint disappears, the way such a phrase disappears when it is retold to a third person.

What does Bassanio find in the right casket? Not Portia but her portrait. He admires it and admits himself that "so far this shadow / Doth limp behind the substance". This is what the 18-3-3 entry looks like: the two first receive each other's image, slightly retouched by their own imagination, and only later the person. In Waite, The Moon shines with reflected light. Wen says the card "represents poetry and mystery" and writes of "the hidden condition of the Seeker's situation that will reveal itself in time".

In life it shows in small things. The two tell the story of how they met like a legend, a little differently each time. Much between them is understood without words, and a direct question feels rude. One tests the other without asking: "if you love me, you'll guess". Portia says it almost word for word: "If you do love me, you will find me out."

Here, too, lies the resistance: the entry point sits on the line of tasks, and the wish the couple starts from gets in the way of going further. The lunar wish needs things to be magical, and magic is hard to turn into a home. Before the caskets Bassanio delivers a speech against ornament, "The world is still deceiv'd with ornament", and in it one hears this couple's chief fear: what if what we got is not real? In Lisovskaya, the minus of The Moon includes a false image created at the start that later collapses. Bassanio himself came to Belmont that way: on borrowed money, playing a rich suitor. Later, in a confession prompted by a letter, he says: "I should then have told you / That I was worse than nothing".

It is curious where Shakespeare found Belmont. In a novella from Giovanni Fiorentino's collection Il Pecorone (around 1378) the Lady of Belmonte is a greedy widow. She gives her suitors a sleeping draught, and whoever falls asleep loses his whole fortune. Shakespeare replaced the sleeping potion with the riddle of the caskets and kept the ring and the disguise. For the tail this is a fork inside The Moon itself: in its minus it is sleep that robs, in its plus a riddle that tests. The entry is the same for every such couple; whether it leads to the potion or to the riddle is up to the two of them.

sections.h2: The middle of the task: a house given together with a ring
paragraphs: Once the casket is open, Portia makes the most generous speech in the play. She would be "trebled twenty times myself, / A thousand times more fair, ten thousand times / More rich": The Empress has her own arithmetic, she only multiplies. And then she gives everything away:

"But now I was the lord / Of this fair mansion, master of my servants, / Queen o'er myself; and even now, but now, / This house, these servants, and this same myself / Are yours,—my lord's. I give them with this ring, / Which when you part from, lose, or give away, / Let it presage the ruin of your love, / And be my vantage to exclaim on you."

"Queen o'er myself" is The Empress herself, laying down her crown. But a condition is sewn into the last lines of the gift: the ring is a pledge, and losing it is a "vantage to exclaim" written out in advance. **This is what the middle of the 18-3-3 tail looks like.** The couple moves through the house and through generosity: one lets the other into their home, a joint budget forms quickly, the gifts are large. But next to The Devil in the centre, generosity easily becomes a contract nobody read aloud. "It's all yours", and in the small print, "just don't lose it".

The other side shows in the same scene. On learning that his friend has pledged his own body for Bassanio's debts, Portia orders: "Pay him six thousand, and deface the bond. / Double six thousand, and then treble that", and promises "gold / To pay the petty debt twenty times over". Her speech ends with a line that the standard Russian translation softens: "Since you are dear bought, I will love you dear." Love and purchase sit in a single sentence.

Then the house passes from hand to hand. Leaving, Portia tells Lorenzo: "I commit into your hands / The husbandry and manage of my house". The runaways Lorenzo and Jessica live in someone else's mansion as its masters. In Waite, The Empress is refugium peccatorum, "refuge of sinners", and Belmont really does become a refuge for everyone who has fled Venice. Many 18-3-3 couples recognise themselves here too: years in a parent's flat, in a rented place, in one partner's home — comfortable, generous, and still not theirs.

The sharpest point of the middle is the trial. By the sum of the middles this Empress is born of one partner's Justice and the other's Fool, and in Act IV it is literally visible. Into the Venetian court walks a lawyer called Balthazar, of whom the learned Bellario writes: "I never knew so young a body with so old a head." It is Portia in men's clothes, law plus masquerade. And she speaks not of law but of mercy:
"The quality of mercy is not strain'd, / It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven / Upon the place beneath. It is twice blest, / It blesseth him that gives and him that takes."

Describing The Moon, Waite notes a detail that is easy to miss: on his card "the moon is increasing on what is called the side of mercy". The lunar entry of this tail is turned towards mercy. The middle of the task is learning to give so that the blessing is double, for the one who gives and for the one who takes. A gift that leaves the other in debt for life blesses only one.

sections.h2: The main task: whose garden is it?
paragraphs: The second Empress, on the point "Main task", is read mostly through its minus: what the couple fails at and what it must learn. In the play the answer is visible in the list of characters. There are three women: "PORTIA, a rich heiress", "NERISSA, her waiting-woman", "JESSICA, daughter to Shylock". **Not one mother.** Only one mother is mentioned — Leah, Shylock's wife, who never appears, and all that remains of her is a turquoise ring. Jessica trades it in Genoa for a monkey. "I would not have given it for a wilderness of monkeys," Shylock cries.

A play with two Empresses in which The Empress's place is empty. All its abundance is inherited or borrowed. Portia is rich through a dead father and bound by the same dead father: "so is the will of a living daughter curb'd by the will of a dead father". Jessica runs from her father's house with a casket of ducats and calls that house hell: "Our house is hell". Bassanio lives on Antonio's credit, Antonio on Shylock's. Nobody has a garden of their own.

Hence the minus of the main task. In Lisovskaya it runs like this: getting out from under the family's influence, surviving feast and famine, growing out of childishness, arriving at shared values. In the play the swing shows in figures. Jessica spends in Genoa "one night, fourscore ducats". Every one of Antonio's ventures fails, and at the end "three of your argosies / Are richly come to harbour suddenly". Nerissa said it already in Act I: "they are as sick that surfeit with too much as they that starve with nothing." Portia herself begs her happiness for measure: "In measure rain thy joy; scant this excess!"

Wen describes The Empress briefly: "She produces. She makes things happen." And of the reversed card she writes: "There is a sense of emptiness and no production after much work and effort." The main task of 18-3-3 runs between these two sentences. **A garden that was handed down is not yet the couple's garden.** It has to be grown: with money whose source is clear, with decisions made by the two and not by a will, and with work of one's own for each. Lisovskaya advises such couples that each partner find fulfilment separately. Portia, incidentally, shows herself best while away — in a court where nobody recognises her.

Why The Empress stands twice, Shakespeare shows as well: in the play the same ring is given twice. The first time in Act III, together with the house and a condition. The second time in Act V, after a test. What changed between the two gifts is visible in the night scene below.

Even the manna at the end has a bitter taste. Nerissa hands Lorenzo and Jessica a deed of gift for everything Shylock will leave at his death. Lorenzo answers: "Fair ladies, you drop manna in the way / Of starved people." But that deed was wrung from Shylock in court together with his conversion, by sentence and not by free will. Shakespeare does not hide where the manna comes from, and the play is cruel to Shylock: today it is hard to read without saying so. For the couple the conclusion is simple: abundance with someone else's bond behind it has not yet become one's own.

sections.h2: The Devil in the centre: spouses are a team in harness
paragraphs: The centre of a couple is "The atmosphere inside the couple": what lies between the two and is not on show. Every 18-3-3 couple has The Devil there. And it is a card a person never has in the centre: no birth date gives a personal centre of 15. The Devil appears only when two people are added together. The arithmetic is simple: the partner with tail 15-8-11 always has centre 4, The Emperor, and the partner with tail 3-22-19 always has 11, Strength. One partner's order plus the other's tamed passion: 4 + 11 = 15.

Waite suggests how to read this. In The Devil's divinatory list, beside the grim words, stands a reservation: "that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil". A card that stands in the centre of every such couple is exactly that case. And in his historical section Waite praises Papus, who removed the demons from the card and left "naked human beings, male and female, who are yoked only to each other": "The author may be felicitated on this improved symbolism." **The couple's Devil is that picture without a master: two people bound to each other.**

Language remembers this better than fortune-telling books. English "conjugal" goes back to Latin coniux, "spouse", from the same root as iugum, "yoke"; Greek σύζυγος, "spouse", is literally "yoked together". Russian is even blunter: according to Vasmer's etymological dictionary, Old Russian suprug ("spouse") meant both "married couple" and "a team in harness", from the same root as zapryagat', "to harness". Spouses are those harnessed together. Portia says the same thing about companions "Whose souls do bear an equal yoke of love". The yoke is not only shared but equal; the standard Russian translation drops the word "equal".

The whole Merchant can be read as a play about bonds. Leaving the house, Shylock throws his daughter a proverb: "Fast bind, fast find." Bassanio introduces Antonio to his wife as the man "To whom I am so infinitely bound". Portia answers with a pun: "You should in all sense be much bound to him, / For, as I hear, he was much bound for you." Of Gratiano's ring she says it is "A thing stuck on with oaths upon your finger, / And so riveted with faith unto your flesh" — flesh again, in a play about a pound of it. And that ring bears the posy "Love me, and leave me not", which Gratiano himself compares to "cutlers' poetry / Upon a knife". Love, an oath and a knife in a single engraving. Wen names the theme of The Devil "the worship of false idols" and notes that the card often turns up for "those plagued by consumer debt". The whole Venice of the play lives on credit, and the golden casket holds a scroll that begins "All that glisters is not gold".

In life this centre is recognised by the strength of the bond both feel from the first months. In its plus, as Lisovskaya has it, there is passion, powerful support, the ability to accept each other's dark sides and to forgive. In its minus, the wish to possess, jealousy, drama, attempts to hold on with a gift, money or status. And a question that sounds louder in these couples than in others: who belongs to whom. Jessica asks Lorenzo from the window: "who knows / But you, Lorenzo, whether I am yours?" Portia gets tangled in halves: "And so though yours, not yours." Lisovskaya ends her chapter on The Devil with a phrase that would make a motto for this centre: nobody belongs to anybody.

The border between a chain and a yoke is visible in Waite on a neighbouring card. Strength stands in one partner's tail and in the other partner's centre. She leads the lion on a chain of flowers, and Waite speaks of it in Gospel language, "the sweet yoke and the light burden" (compare Matthew 11:30, "my yoke is easy, and my burden is light"; the Latin Vulgate has iugum suave, "sweet yoke"). The Devil's chain is iron, Strength's is made of flowers. An 18-3-3 couple always has bonds; the question is what they are woven from. If the bond has turned into fear, surveillance or threats, that is no longer a question for the cards: it calls for a psychologist, and in danger, a local emergency number or crisis line.

sections.h2: Night at Belmont: what the couple does with its secret
paragraphs: Act V takes place at night in the avenue outside Portia's house, and almost all of it is about The Moon. Lorenzo begins: "The moon shines bright. In such a night as this…", and the two take turns recalling lovers who had the same moon: Troilus, Thisbe, Dido, Medea. A strange choice for a love duet. Troilus will be betrayed by Cressida, Thisbe will die, Dido will be abandoned. Medea is the princess of Colchis who helped Jason win the golden fleece and was later abandoned by him; in Act I Bassanio himself called Belmont "Colchos' strond" and himself one of its "many Jasons". Then the lovers come to themselves: Lorenzo swore he loved Jessica "with many vows of faith, / And ne'er a true one"; and "In such a night / Did pretty Jessica, like a little shrew, / Slander her love, and he forgave it her."

**This is the common language of a lunar couple in its pure form.** The two tease each other with stories that end badly and, under the joke, test what is real: were the vows false? In Lisovskaya, the minus of The Moon includes jealousy and hurt built on invented stories, when it is unclear whether the two are friends or enemies. The plus of the same Moon is that the partner is first of all a friend, understanding without words, and the feeling that every year one discovers something new in the other.

A few minutes later Portia stages the same play in earnest. She comes home before her husband, asks about the ring and, hearing that it went to the young lawyer, threatens: "Now by mine honour which is yet mine own, / I'll have that doctor for mine bedfellow." Jealousy over an invented story, since the lawyer in question was Portia herself. And when everything comes out, Bassanio says the line that holds the whole plus of this card: "Were you the doctor, and I knew you not?" In such a couple each partner always contains a person the other has not yet seen. The Moon in its plus is joy at that discovery; in its minus, suspicion.

Before her husband arrives Portia stops the music: "Peace! How the moon sleeps with Endymion, / And would not be awak'd!" In the myth Selene put Endymion into an endless sleep so that he would belong to her alone. This is the temptation of the entry: to stay in the night, where everything is magical and nobody leaves, and not go into the house. The whole of Act V takes place outside. Portia says it plainly: "I have not yet / Enter'd my house."

Shakespeare's way out is simple. The ring comes back to Bassanio through Antonio — the man who once pledged his body for his friend and now says: "I dare be bound again, / My soul upon the forfeit, that your lord / Will never more break faith advisedly." **The very same ring is given a second time:** the first time with a condition and a right to accuse, the second after a test and through a guarantor. The bond that nearly cost a life becomes a surety for a marriage. The Devil does not vanish; the contract changes. And Portia calls everyone into the house: "It is almost morning, … Let us go in, / And charge us there upon inter'gatories, / And we will answer all things faithfully."

One secret Portia still keeps: "You shall not know by what strange accident / I chanced on this letter", the letter about the rescued ships. Shakespeare never explains where it came from. A lunar couple does not need to give up secrets altogether; it needs its secrets not to become weapons. To answer every question faithfully and leave one miracle unexplained: that is what The Moon looks like once it has reached the house.

sections.h2: Candle and moon: the values of an 18-3-3 couple
paragraphs: The couple's values, its spiritual purpose, come in two kinds for 18-3-3: in 59.8% of couples it is 9, The Hermit, in 40.2% it is 18, The Moon. Shakespeare placed both cards side by side, in two consecutive lines. Approaching the house, Portia sees a light in the window: "How far that little candle throws his beams! / So shines a good deed in a naughty world." Nerissa replies: "When the moon shone we did not see the candle."

For couples whose value is The Hermit, the main thing is the candle in the hall: a small light of their own that someone coming home late can see, and deeds instead of words. In Wen, The Hermit is "someone who sees the world through his or her own light". The play also contains a parody of this card. A servant reports that his mistress is accompanied by "None but a holy hermit and her maid", and Portia herself announced she was leaving "To live in prayer and contemplation" at a monastery. There is no hermit: it is cover for the trip to the court. In Waite, The Hermit reversed means precisely "Concealment, disguise". The value is one, but it can show itself as a candle or as a mask.

Couples whose value is The Moon stand under that card twice: at the entry and in the values. Their shared path is the world of imagination itself: night-long conversations, shared creative work, a game that lasts for years. Nerissa is right that the candle cannot be seen by moonlight. Such a couple needs to keep the great light from outshining the small one — the simple deeds that can be seen in the window.

sections.h2: Worked example: 09.05.1976 and 14.10.1976
paragraphs: An example on two dates, calculated by the site's engine. The first partner (09.05.1976) has the personal tail 3-22-19 and centre 11, the second (14.10.1976) the tail 15-8-11 and centre 4. Each point of the couple's tail is the sum of the matching points of the two personal tails:

The couple's centre: 11 + 4 = 15, The Devil. The couple's values for these dates: 9, The Hermit. The middle of a couple's tail is not recalculated from the two outer numbers: the personal formula would give 18 + 3 = 21, The World, but in a couple the middle is the sum of the partners' middles, 22 and 8. No personal chart has such a middle, just as no personal chart has the 18-3-3 tail itself: for an entry of 18 with a main task of 3, a person would need a centre of 15.

A quick check needs no chart: it is enough to add up each partner's arcana of the day, month and year of birth (a day above 22 and the year are reduced by adding digits). The partner with tail 3-22-19 gets exactly 19, the partner with 15-8-11 exactly 29. In the example: 9 + 5 + 5 = 19 and 14 + 10 + 5 = 29, where 5 comes from 1976 → 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5.

The tail 3-22-19 occurs in 2.2% of birth dates, 15-8-11 in 4.2%. An 18-3-3 couple arises only when these two tails meet, which makes it rare: about one couple in 529 (0.189%), 74th of the 97 couple tails. There are no couple tails made of the same numbers in a different order: neither 3-18-3 nor 3-3-18 ever comes up for a couple.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail: a house two people walk into
paragraphs: The cards do not say what will happen to a couple; they show where its forks lie. 18-3-3 has three: potion or riddle at the entry, gift or contract in the middle, a garden of its own or someone else's manna at the end. The roles of Portia and Bassanio are not assigned by gender here: either partner can be the one who gives the house or the one who arrives at it empty-handed. What changes the script:

ul: **At least once, say it straight where a hint is tempting.** Not everyone hears the hint in the song, and Bassanio might not have.
**Keep the gift apart from the condition.** If a gift carries "and if you lose it…", that is worth saying aloud before the condition becomes a "vantage to exclaim".

**Check whose garden it is.** What in the couple's house belongs to the couple, and what to a will, to parents, to a loan. One's own begins small: with a decision two people made without anyone else's signature.
**Grow apart and together.** Each has work of their own; the two have a shared goal both put into.
**Play knowing that it is a play.** A lunar performance is good as long as it ends with "we will answer all things faithfully".
**Leave one secret the right to stay secret,** as long as it is not a weapon.

paragraphs: In its strong version 18-3-3 is a couple with a language of its own and a house of its own. It still talks in hints and laughs at stories that end badly, but a candle burns in its house that can be seen from the road. Its bond is like the ring given a second time: the same metal, but a surety instead of a pledge. The Merchant of Venice ends two hours before dawn, on the threshold: the couples are still in the avenue, and only at the end does Portia call everyone into the house. The 18-3-3 tail is about taking that step.

ul: **18 · The Moon — entry to the task.** Together the couple wants mystery: a language of hints that only the two of them understand, a game in which each is slightly in disguise. The same wish slows them down: testing each other is easier than asking straight out.

**3 · The Empress — middle of the task.** The path runs through the house and through generosity. The two give, invest, let each other into their household, and a condition is easy to sew into a gift.
**3 · The Empress — main task.** To make abundance their own: a garden that belongs to both of them, not to someone else's will, someone else's money or a feast-or-famine swing.
**15 · The Devil in the centre.** The atmosphere inside the couple is a bond. The whole question is whether it becomes a chain or "an equal yoke of love".

intro: All of this has been staged before. In Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice (around 1596) two pairs of lovers walk through the 18-3-3 tail almost literally. They begin with a riddle and an elopement by moonlight, receive a house as a gift together with a ring, and spend the last night of the play in the avenue outside that house: they are called inside only at the very end. What follows is an investigation: what is written in the three cards, in the books of Waite and Wen, in the engine's numbers and in the text of the play. Shakespeare is quoted from the original text.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 18-3-3 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple tail in which **The Moon** stands at the entry to the task and **The Empress** both in the middle and in the main task. The couple enters the relationship through mystery, play and enchantment, and its main task is to turn this into a shared home and an abundance that belong to both of them, not to relatives, debts or someone else's conditions.

faq.q: Is 18-3-3 a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not predict events or pass sentence: it shows what the two have to learn. With 18-3-3 the difficulty is that the lunar game may never become a home, and generosity may turn into a contract. The strength of the same tail is a common language only the two of them understand and the ability to grow a home together.

faq.q: Why does every 18-3-3 couple have The Devil in the centre?
faq.a: Because this tail is built only from the personal tails 15-8-11 and 3-22-19, whose centres are always 4 and 11. The sum is 4 + 11 = 15. A personal chart never has 15 in the centre, so The Devil in this couple's atmosphere is born only of the two together: it is the bond, passion and the question of who belongs to whom.

faq.q: Does the 18-3-3 tail occur in a personal chart?
faq.a: No. In a personal chart the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and with a main task of 3 an entry of 18 would require a centre of 15, which no person has. The 18-3-3 tail exists only for couples, and no permutation of the same numbers occurs among couple tails either.

faq.q: How to tell from two birth dates that a couple has tail 18-3-3?
faq.a: Add up each partner's arcana of the day, month and year of birth. If one gets exactly 19 and the other exactly 29, the couple has tail 18-3-3. For example, 09.05.1976 and 14.10.1976: 9 + 5 + 5 = 19 and 14 + 10 + 5 = 29.

report.h3: Love that is born in the eyes

Shakespeare hid the whole tail in the song sung while Bassanio chooses a casket: fancy "is engender'd in the eyes, / With gazing fed, and fancy dies / In the cradle where it lies". "Fancy" is a shortened form of "fantasy", imagination. The song asks about The Moon and answers in The Empress's words: begetting, nourishment, a cradle. **Lunar feeling is born at once, but it can also die in its own cradle.**

People have long argued over whether Portia gave her suitor a hint: the song's first rhymes, bred and head, chime with lead, and the lead casket is the right one. That is the common language of a lunar couple — said so that only one person will hear it. Yet the right casket holds not Portia but her portrait, and Bassanio admits that "this shadow / Doth limp behind the substance". First the two receive each other's image, retouched by imagination, and only later the person. Hence the resistance at the entry: testing is easier than asking, and the worst fear is that what came to them is not real.

report.h3: A house given together with a ring

report: The middle of the task is The Empress again, and in the play it takes the form of the most generous speech. Portia was "Queen o'er myself" and gives her suitor everything — the house, the servants, herself — together with a ring. But a condition is sewn into the last lines of the gift: losing the ring would hand her a "vantage to exclaim". This is how an 18-3-3 couple travels its path: through the house and through generosity, where a contract nobody has read aloud is easy to hide.

Shakespeare put the way out of this trap into the speech at the trial, where Portia, disguised as a lawyer, speaks of mercy: "It is twice blest, / It blesseth him that gives and him that takes." A gift that leaves the other in debt for life blesses only one. And Waite notes that on his card "the moon is increasing on what is called the side of mercy": the lunar entry of this tail is turned towards mercy.

report.h3: Whose garden is it?

report: The main task is read through its minus, and in the play the minus shows in the list of characters: a rich heiress, a waiting-woman, a daughter. **Not one mother.** All the abundance is inherited or borrowed. Portia is bound by a will: "so is the will of a living daughter curb'd by the will of a dead father". Jessica runs from her father's house and calls it this: "Our house is hell". Bassanio lives on credit; the ships first sink to the last one, then come home richly laden. Lisovskaya calls this feast or famine and the influence of the family. The task is to grow a garden that belongs to the two of them, not to a will, to parents or to a loan, with work of one's own for each.

report.h3: Spouses are a team in harness

report: The Devil in the centre is the atmosphere inside the couple, and no person has such a centre: it is born only of two. Waite writes of it as "that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil". And he praises a design that removed the demon from the card and left a man and a woman "yoked only to each other". The Russian word suprug, "spouse", once also meant "a team in harness", according to Vasmer: spouses are those harnessed together. Portia speaks of companions "Whose souls do bear an equal yoke of love".

This couple always has bonds; the question is what they are woven from. In the plus there is passion, support, the ability to accept the dark in each other and to forgive. In the minus, the wish to possess, jealousy, an attempt to hold on with a gift or with money. Lisovskaya ends her chapter on The Devil with a phrase that works as a motto: nobody belongs to anybody. On the neighbouring card in Waite, Strength leads the lion on a chain of flowers — "the sweet yoke". If the bond has turned into fear, surveillance or threats, that is no longer a question for the cards: it calls for a psychologist, and in danger, a local emergency number or crisis line.

report.h3: A ring given twice

report: In Act V Portia stages the lunar play in earnest: she acts out jealousy over an invented story about the young lawyer, who was in fact herself. And Bassanio is left with the discovery that holds the whole plus of The Moon: the lawyer was his own wife, and he never recognised her. In such a couple each partner always contains a person the other has not yet seen.

Then **the very same ring is given a second time**, just as The Empress stands twice in the tail. The first time with a condition, the second after a test and through a guarantor: Antonio, who once pledged his body for his friend, now pledges his soul. The bond becomes a surety for the marriage. The Devil does not vanish; the contract changes. And Portia calls everyone: "Let us go in", promising to answer every question faithfully. One secret she still keeps — where the letter about the ships came from. The Moon that has reached the house does not give up its secrets; it simply stops turning them into weapons.

captions.M: To want mystery and a language only the two of you share
captions.N: To give the house and generosity without hidden terms
captions.D: To grow your own garden, not live on other people's wealth

unit.meaning: Your task is to bring the moonlit game home: give without hidden terms and grow what is shared instead of living on credit.

seo.title: Karmic tail 18 6 15 compatibility: The Moon, The Lovers, The Devil
seo.description: Karmic tail 18 6 15 compatibility: a couple meets through an image of each other, learns to choose the living person and to stop holding on to “mine”.

items.title: Karmic tail 18-6-15 in compatibility: a couple and its phantom
items.short: For ten years Greeks and Trojans fought over Helen, and yet, if Stesichorus, Herodotus and Euripides are to be believed, she was never in Troy. In Euripides, Paris carried off a phantom woven out of air. The karmic tail 18-6-15 in compatibility tells the same story about a couple. Two people come together through an image of each other (The Moon), they have to recognise and choose the living person (The Lovers), and the main task is to stop serving the image and holding on to the thought “you are mine” (The Devil).

sections.h2: A war over a cloud
paragraphs: The first to tell this story was the poet Stesichorus, who lived at the turn of the seventh and sixth centuries BC. At first, like everyone else, he sang of Helen the runaway, the woman who started the war. According to the legend Plato retells in the Phaedrus, the poet was struck blind for it. Plato names his fault precisely — κακηγορία, evil-speaking. Stesichorus understood the cause and composed a palinode, a song of recantation: “That saying is not true; thou didst not go within the well-oared ships, nor didst thou come to the walls of Troy” (trans. H. N. Fowler). As soon as he finished it, he could see again.

In the second book of his Histories (chapters 112–120) Herodotus wrote down what the Egyptian priests told him. A storm drove Paris's ship to Egypt, King Proteus kept Helen with him, and she spent the whole war there. The Trojans honestly told the Greeks that Helen was not in their city, but the Greeks would not believe them, “although they spoke the truth” (trans. A. D. Godley). Herodotus adds that Homer, in his opinion, knew this version but rejected it because it suited epic poetry less well.

In 412 BC Euripides turned this into a tragedy, Helen. Hera, offended by the judgement of Paris, gave him not Helen but “a phantom endowed with life, that she made in my image out of the breath of heaven”, as E. P. Coleridge translates it. In the prologue Helen says: “Paris thought that I was his, although I never was — an idle fancy!” The Greek line is shorter and harder: καὶ δοκεῖ μ᾽ ἔχειν — κενὴν δόκησιν, οὐκ ἔχων, “and he thinks he has me — an empty seeming, not having me” (our translation). And the prize of the war was a name: “yet not I, but my name alone”.

Waite's divinatory list for The Moon reads: “Hidden enemies, danger, calumny, darkness, terror, deception, occult forces, error.” It is almost a table of contents for the myth. The hidden enemy is Hera. The calumny is Stesichorus's evil-speaking and the phantom's own last words about Helen, who “hath borne an evil name without reason”. The deception is the substitution. The error is a ten-year war over a cloud. For Waite, The Moon is “life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit”, a light that only reflects. Euripides' phantom is exactly that kind of light: a reflection that walks, speaks and is embraced.

sections.h2: One word at both ends of the tail
paragraphs: In Euripides, Helen's phantom is called εἴδωλον. The word comes from the verb “to see”, and it means an image, a reflection in water or a mirror, a shade, a ghost. A century and a half to two centuries later the translators of the Bible into Greek took the same word. In the book of Exodus (20:4) the commandment reads: οὐ ποιήσεις σεαυτῷ εἴδωλον οὐδὲ παντὸς ὁμοίωμα ὅσα ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ ἄνω. In Brenton's English Septuagint: “Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol, nor likeness of anything, whatever things are in the heaven above.”

Put Euripides' prologue next to it. Hera “made like me” (ὁμοιώσασα) a “phantom” (εἴδωλον) composed “of heaven” (οὐρανοῦ). The same three ideas as the commandment, from the same Greek roots: idol, likeness, heaven. The translators of the Torah were of course not quoting a tragedian. All the more striking, then, that the language itself linked them: in Greek “phantom” and “idol” are one word, and the English word idol comes from it.

For Benebell Wen, “the theme of The Devil is the worship of false idols.” Waite says of The Moon: “The intellectual light is a reflection.” The tail 18-6-15 begins with the eidolon as reflection and ends with the eidolon as idol. Between them stand The Lovers — the only one of the three cards where, in Waite, two people stand “unveiled before each other”. That is the hidden plot of the tail: the image with which the couple began will either become a living person or become an idol to be served. This link through the Greek word is our own reading; neither Waite nor Wen draws it.

A similar link, without any cards, was drawn by Plato. In book nine of the Republic (586b–c) he speaks of pleasures mixed with pain: they are “phantoms of true pleasure”, they “beget mad loves of themselves in senseless souls”, and they are “fought for, as Stesichorus says the wraith of Helen was fought for at Troy through ignorance of the truth” (trans. Paul Shorey). Just before this he describes people who, like cattle, kick and butt one another “with horns and hooves of iron” in their insatiable greed for such pleasures. For Plato, Helen's phantom is no longer a myth but a name for passion for a likeness. It is very close to the passage from The Moon to The Devil written into this tail.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: a common language of guesses
paragraphs: The entry to the task shows what the couple wants together, what common language it speaks and what it agrees on. The Moon in this place wants mystery. Not a dull “how was your day”, but a world only the two of them understand: half-hints, games, night-time talks, the feeling that the other sees what nobody else sees. In its plus, Lisovskaya describes The Moon in a couple as intuition, respect for personal space and the habit of discovering something new in the partner every year.

Wen makes an observation about The Moon that takes the blame off this entry: “the first light of the divine, the first clarity to be offered,” may come “from the moon, the reflection, rather than from the sun itself.” Two people really do see each other first by reflected light — in the light of their own hopes. That is not a mistake; it is a way in. In Richard Strauss and Hugo von Hofmannsthal's Die ägyptische Helena (The Egyptian Helen, first performed on 6 June 1928 in Dresden), Menelaus raises a dagger over his wife, but the lights in the hall go down, only moonlight falls inside, a beam lands on Helen's face, and the hand with the dagger drops. The stage direction says he stands as if spellbound by her beauty. At the entry The Moon saves: the image stops the blow.
But the entry stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. The common language of guesses quietly becomes a language of assumptions:

ul: He is silent at dinner, she already knows why, and she spends the evening arguing not with him but with her version of him.
One of them keeps the image of “who you were that first summer” and measures the present person against it, and the present person never quite measures up.
The couple has a lovely legend for friends — “we understood each other at first sight” — and everything that does not fit it gets hidden: tiredness, boredom, disagreement.
One of them plays the role they were loved for, and a year later the role irritates them both.

paragraphs: Among the couple's tasks in the minus of The Moon, Lisovskaya names exactly this: a false image created at the start that later collapses, jealousy and resentment born of invented stories, adapting to the partner in a way that ends in irritation. Euripides shows the mechanism in a single exchange. Menelaus, seeing his living wife, calls on the night goddess of the crossroads: “O Hecate, giver of light, send thy visions favourably!” Helen replies: “In me thou beholdest no spectre of the night, attendant on the queen of phantoms.” Someone who has lived a long time with an image sees a ghost in a living person. Helen's answer is the best advice for this entry: check things by daylight.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: “the greatness of my troubles convinces me”
paragraphs: The middle of the task is how the couple travels from the wish to the main task. In Waite, The Lovers is “the card of human love”; in Wen, it is “partnership with one other person” and a choice with a moral price. In this tail the choice is very concrete: whom to believe — the image or the person.

Euripides' recognition scene reads like the minutes of such a choice. Menelaus pushes his wife away: “Nor yet am I in my single person the husband of two wives.” The other one, he explains, is “the inmate of yonder cave, whom I from Troy convey”. Then he looks closer and admits: “Thy form resembles her, but the real truth robs me of this belief.” Helen: “Who then shall teach thee, unless it be thine own eyes?” And finally the key line: “The greatness of my troubles at Troy convinces me; thou dost not.” The Greek is just as blunt: “the greatness of my toils there persuades me, not you” (our literal translation).

This is why people hold on to an image: it has been paid for. Ten years of war and seven years of wandering would turn into nonsense if the woman in the cave were a phantom. Menelaus believes not his eyes but the price. In a couple this sounds familiar: “I have put so much into this”, “I have put up with so much for this person” — and what has been invested gets in the way of seeing who is actually standing there.

In Euripides the resolution is simple. A messenger runs in: the cave is empty, the phantom has risen into the sky. As it left, it told the truth: they all died “in the false belief that Helen was in the hands of Paris”. Only after that comes the embrace. The image did not have to be smashed: it left by itself, having “stayed my appointed time”. For a couple like this, the middle of the task is a series of small recognitions. The strong one turns out to be lost, the light one vulnerable, the mysterious one simply tired. Each time it is possible to resent the person for not matching the image, and each time it is possible to choose them again.

Among the tasks of The Lovers, Lisovskaya names idealisation and perfectionism in the relationship, the insecurity from which jealousy and control grow, and self-love inside the couple, which one partner sometimes teaches the other. In its plus the same card brings sincerity, no secrets and shared decisions even in small things. For this tail the plus of The Lovers is the ability to say: I see you not as I imagined you, and I choose you as you are.

sections.h2: Main task: “he thinks he has me”
paragraphs: The couple's main task is read mostly through its minus. For The Devil in a couple, Lisovskaya lists control and pursuit, jealousy and the wish to own, attempts to hold the partner through intimacy, a child, money or status, obsession with a person, silence about one's own desires, and a union that drags both down. Her closing thought on the fifteenth energy is that nobody belongs to anybody.

Euripides builds the play on the verb ἔχειν — “to have, to hold”. Paris “thought that I was his, although I never was”. The phantom tells the Greeks they died believing Paris had Helen, whom he never had. Menelaus explains why he cannot believe his wife: “Herein is my dilemma; I have another wife” — and again the Greek word is ἔχω. The whole play is about people sure they hold what they do not have. Here is the Devil of this couple in one image: a cave on the shore where sailors guard a likeness of a wife, and a husband who calls it “mine”.
In everyday life the cave looks ordinary:

ul: “Mine” turns into rights: to know passwords, to approve friends, to decide what the partner wears — all in the name of the image: “that's not like you”.
Sacrifices turn into a bill. Menelaus's “greatness of my troubles” becomes “I gave things up for you”, “I wasted my best years on you”. The bill holds both of them tighter than any chain.
The couple is held together by a shared mortgage and a shared legend, and both are afraid to admit that the legend stopped being about them long ago.
Each guards the image of “the good partner” and so keeps quiet about what they really want. Desire goes underground and comes back out as resentment.

paragraphs: There are always two in the cave: the one who is guarded and the one who guards. Neither is free. In the myth the husband holds the image, but in a real couple the roles are not handed out by gender: either partner can hold on to the image and to “mine”, and more often both do, by turns.

The Devil has a plus too, and for this tail it matters most. Lisovskaya describes it as attachment in the good sense: the partners accept each other's dark sides, forgive mistakes, talk openly about desires, and there is a lot of passion and readiness to change for love. A couple with 18-6-15 reaches this plus not when it gets rid of the mystery, but when it stops guarding it.

If control in a couple has already turned into threats, surveillance or violence, this is not a “karmic task” to be sat out to the end. In danger, call a local emergency number; for support, turn to a psychologist or a crisis line.

sections.h2: Two cups: Hofmannsthal turns Euripides inside out
paragraphs: Two thousand three hundred years after Euripides, Hofmannsthal wrote his own Helen for Strauss and turned the myth inside out. In The Egyptian Helen the phantom is no longer the truth but a merciful lie. The sorceress Aithra gives Menelaus lotus, the drink of forgetting, and tells him that when Paris reached for his wife, the gods secretly looked after the husband and laid in the abductor's arms “an airy image, a fragrant ghost, the kind they fool mortal men with” (ein Luftgebild, ein duftig Gespenst — our translation). And the real Helen, she claims, slept all those years in a castle on the slopes of the Atlas. “Drink with me!” says Aithra, and the stage direction specifies that she herself only pretends to drink.

The drug of forgetting is old in this couple's story. Already in book four of the Odyssey, Helen, back home in Sparta, casts into the wine a drug she received from the Egyptian woman Polydamna, “a drug to quiet all pain and strife, and bring forgetfulness of every ill” (trans. A. T. Murray). Hofmannsthal said what Homer left unsaid: at what price.

The lotus worked, and Helen saw what it had done to her. Her husband now takes her “for a strange woman you brought him in the night, and thinks that with me he has betrayed the Helen he believes dead” (Er kennt mich für ein fremdes Weib… — our translation). The image of the “pure” wife has made the living wife a stranger and the husband an adulterer: unfaithful to her, with her. The loop of The Moon and The Devil could not be drawn more sharply.

Aithra's casket holds two flasks. The second is remembrance, “the drink of hell” from which, she says, even the blessed gods flee. Helen seizes exactly that one: “This is the drink I need! Remembrance!” Aithra warns her: let it touch your lips and you will become a living dead woman. Helen answers that it was the first potion that made her dead while alive, that very night.

The couple's final exchange could stand as an epigraph to this tail. Helen asks: “Do you belong so wholly to her?” Menelaus answers: “Hast du mich jemals besessen? Laß mich der Toten und lebe!” — “Did you ever possess me? Leave me to the dead woman, and live!” (our translation). The German besessen here means “possessed” in the sense of owned, but the same word also means “possessed” as in obsessed. Menelaus thinks the cup holds poison and will not let his wife drink. Helen raises the cup to her lips: “You drink it to the other one — I drink with you!” Almost the same words Aithra said for show, Helen says in earnest, and she drinks first.

Menelaus drinks remembrance and sees his wife anew: “I see you as no mortal man has ever yet seen his wife!” And then: “Faithless one, ever the one, ever new!” (Ungetreue, ewig eine, ewig neue — our translation). He stops splitting her into the woman who was at Troy and the woman he loves: the libretto says the two are now united into one. This is the way out of The Devil into its plus: to accept the partner's dark side instead of guarding a likeness of them. And at the same time it is a return to The Lovers, where two people stand unveiled before each other.

Hofmannsthal does not preach forgiving everything. He shows that peace bought with forgetting rests on a substitution. For a couple with tail 18-6-15 this is the main temptation: to agree not to remember, to edit each other's past into a beautiful image and live with the image. The way out is to remember together.

sections.h2: The empty tomb: how a couple leaves the cave
paragraphs: In Euripides one word recurs at three key moments — κενός, “empty”. The empty seeming of possession in the prologue. The empty bed that Menelaus is ready to carry off instead of his wife — in Coleridge's version: “What! wilt leave me, and take that phantom bride away?” And the empty tomb through which the couple escapes.

The plan is Helen's: “Dost thou consent to be dead in word, though not really so?” Menelaus agrees — “I am ready to be dead in word, though not in deed” — but grumbles that “there is something stale about this story” (our translation). Helen asks the king of Egypt for a ship so that she can bury her drowned husband at sea, in an empty tomb. On that ship the two of them sail away together.

To leave the cave, what gets buried is not a person but a role: the Menelaus who fought ten years over a cloud. They do it together, by a shared plan, and here The Lovers work as an alliance. For a couple with this tail the story yields several practices:

ul: **Palinode.** Stesichorus regained his sight when he took back his evil-speaking. Now and then a couple can take back an old story about the partner, out loud: “For years I said you always ruin everything. It isn't true.” In the Phaedrus, Socrates uncovers his head before speaking his own palinode about love: he gave his first speech with his head covered for shame.
**The daylight check.** Telling “I know” from “I imagine”. Asking rather than guessing, especially late in the evening, when The Moon writes the scripts.
**Price is not proof.** Noticing the moment when “I have put so much in” replaces “I see”.
**Drink with, not to.** Remembering the hard chapters together, without turning the partner into either a stranger or a saint.
**Desires out loud.** The Devil grows where desires are kept silent. In its plus it is precisely about talking about them openly.
**“Mine” is not a right.** Friends, time alone and private messages stay with each person. Closeness that runs on permissions is a cave, not a home.

sections.h2: What the numbers show
paragraphs: The tail 18-6-15 occurs in roughly one couple in 143 (0.697%) and ranks 49th of the 97 couple tails — right in the middle of the list, neither rare nor ordinary.

It is formed by only four combinations of the partners' personal tails. In 86% of such couples they are 12-16-4 and 6-17-11, in 9% 15-20-5 and 3-13-10, in 3% 12-19-7 and 6-14-8, in 2% 9-15-6 and 9-18-9. Hence the main clue: in 89% of such couples neither partner has either The Moon or The Devil in their personal tail. Someone brings their own Moon in only 2% of couples, their own Devil in 11%. The image and the tether of this tail are almost always born between two people rather than brought in by one of them. As in Euripides: Hera made the phantom “out of the breath of heaven”, and it belonged to neither spouse.

There is an arithmetical detail too. In each of the four combinations the middles of the personal tails add up to exactly 33: 16 + 17, 20 + 13, 19 + 14, 15 + 18. The couple's middle six always comes from one and the same sum.

The centre of the chart in such couples is “The atmosphere inside the couple”, what happens between two people when nobody is watching. In 81.8% it holds 21, The World, in 18.2% 3, The Empress. The World never appears in the centre of a personal chart for any date of birth: this card in the centre exists only for a couple. In Lisovskaya, The World in a couple's atmosphere means, in its plus, full acceptance of the partner even in their minus, and in its minus, re-educating the partner to suit oneself and illusions about the relationship. It is the same fork as in the tail: accept the living person or remake them to fit the image.

“The couple's values” hold 9, The Hermit, in 75.5% of cases and 18, The Moon, in 24.5%. Of the Hermit's lantern Waite writes: “It is a star which shines in the lantern.” A light of one's own instead of a reflected one is not a bad value for a couple that began with a reflection. And in every fourth such couple The Moon stands both at the entry and among the values: mystery is itself a value for them, and the task is not to kill it but to stop worshipping it.

sections.h2: Example calculation: 14.04.1975 and 05.11.1975
paragraphs: Each point of the couple is the sum of the same points in the two personal charts, reduced to 22. The middle of the couple's tail is not recalculated from the two outer numbers: it too is the sum of the partners' middles.

First partner, 14.04.1975: day 14, month 4, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Main task 14 + 4 + 22 = 40 → 4, centre 14 + 4 + 22 + 4 = 44 → 8, entry to the task 4 + 8 = 12, middle 4 + 12 = 16. Personal tail: 12-16-4.
Second partner, 05.11.1975: day 5, month 11, year 22. Main task 5 + 11 + 22 = 38 → 11, centre 5 + 11 + 22 + 11 = 49 → 13, entry 11 + 13 = 24 → 6, middle 11 + 6 = 17. Personal tail: 6-17-11.

This is the most common combination, accounting for 86% of such couples. This couple's centre is 8 + 13 = 21, The World, and “The couple's values” are 9, The Hermit. And on the point “What to create together” (the month, 4 + 11) stands another Devil, 15. Lisovskaya reads this point only in its plus and writes that fifteen there very often means a way out of dependence. In this couple The Devil is both the task and what they are to create together: a union where attachment does not turn into a tether.

The same numbers form the couple tail 18-15-6. It occurs in 0.476% of couples, and its centre is always 12, The Hanged Man. The order changes the meaning: there The Devil stands in the middle and The Lovers are the main task. A couple with 18-15-6 goes through the tether in order to learn to choose. A couple with 18-6-15 goes through the choice in order to learn not to hold on.
There is also a personal karmic tail 18-6-15 — one person's, from a date of birth. It is a different calculation with different roles for the points, and the site has a separate article about it.

sections.h2: Sources

ul: Euripides, Helen (412 BC): translation by E. P. Coleridge (1891); Greek text from the Perseus edition; where marked, our translation.
Plato, Phaedrus, 243a–b: the story of Stesichorus and his palinode (trans. H. N. Fowler); Republic, IX, 586b–c: “phantoms of true pleasure” (trans. Paul Shorey).
Herodotus, Histories, book II, 112–120: the Egyptian priests' account of Helen at the court of Proteus (trans. A. D. Godley).
Homer, Odyssey, IV, 220–221: Helen's drug against “all pain and strife” (trans. A. T. Murray).
The Septuagint, Exodus 20:4, in the Greek and in Brenton's English translation.
H. von Hofmannsthal and R. Strauss, Die ägyptische Helena (The Egyptian Helen, 1928): libretto; translations of quotations are ours.
A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, reissued 1922): The Moon, The Lovers, The Hermit.
Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015): The Moon, The Lovers, The Devil.
Yuliana Lisovskaya, Matritsa sudby: sovmestimost (The Destiny Matrix: Compatibility, 2024): the meaning of the couple's points and energies 6, 9, 15, 18 and 21 in a couple.

**Entry to the task — 18, The Moon.** What the couple wants together: mystery, depth, being understood without words. This wish is how the couple enters the task, and it is also what resists: a shared language of guesses easily turns into a language of assumptions.

**Middle of the task — 6, The Lovers.** What the couple goes through: recognition and choice. Sooner or later they have to decide whom to believe — the image they have paid so much for, or the person standing next to them.
**Main task — 15, The Devil.** The couple's main trial, read through its minus: attachment to an image, the wish to own, control. What has to be learned is that nobody belongs to anybody.

intro: A couple's tail does not predict what will happen to two people. It shows where their union most often stumbles and where it keeps its reserves of strength. What follows is the evidence: in a Greek tragedy, in one Greek word, in an opera of 1928 and in the numbers themselves.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 18-6-15 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of a couple's chart: entry to the task 18 (The Moon), middle 6 (The Lovers), main task 15 (The Devil). The couple comes together through an image of each other, goes through recognising and choosing the living person, and its main trial is attachment to the image and the wish to own the partner.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail shows tasks, not a verdict. The Devil as the main task is read through its minus — control, jealousy, living for an image — but in its plus it is passion, acceptance of each other's dark sides and open talk about desires. This method gives no compatibility percentages.

faq.q: Who in the couple holds the image, and who carries it?
faq.a: The cards do not hand out roles by gender or character and do not assign blame. In the myth it is Menelaus who holds the image, but in a real couple it can be either partner, and more often both, by turns.

faq.q: How is the couple's tail 18-6-15 different from a personal tail 18-6-15?
faq.a: A personal tail is calculated from one date of birth, and its points have their own roles. A couple's tail is formed from two personal charts: each point is the sum of the partners' points. Texts about one do not carry over to the other.

faq.q: How do you calculate the couple's tail 18-6-15?
faq.a: Calculate the two personal charts and add up the matching points of the tail: the entries, the middles and the main tasks, reducing sums above 22. For example, 14.04.1975 (tail 12-16-4) and 05.11.1975 (tail 6-17-11) give 18-6-15. The middle is not recalculated from the couple's outer numbers.

report: For ten years men fought at Troy over a woman who was not there. So it goes in Euripides: Hera gave Paris not Helen but a living phantom made out of the breath of heaven. Helen herself sums it up in one line: “he thinks he has me — an empty seeming, not having me”. The tail 18-6-15 tells the same story about a couple. The entry to the task is The Moon: two people come together through an image of each other. The middle is The Lovers: recognising and choosing the living person. The main task is The Devil: to stop serving the image and holding on to “mine”.

In Greek, Helen's phantom is called εἴδωλον — an image, a reflection, a ghost. A century and a half to two centuries later the translators of the Bible took the same word for the commandment “Thou shalt not make to thyself an idol”. The English word idol comes from it. For Waite, the light of The Moon is “a reflection”; for Benebell Wen, “the theme of The Devil is the worship of false idols.” The tail begins with the eidolon as reflection and ends with the eidolon as idol. Hence its hidden plot: **the image with which the couple began will either become a living person or become an idol to be served.** This link through the Greek word is the article author's reading, not a teaching of Waite or Wen.

report.h3: “No spectre of the night”

report: The Moon at the entry to the task wants mystery: a world only the two of them understand, half-hints, night-time talks, the feeling that the other sees what is invisible to everyone else. Wen observes that the first clarity may come from the moon, the reflection, rather than from the sun itself. Two people really do see each other first in the light of their own hopes. That is not a mistake; it is a way in.

But the entry stands on the line of tasks, and the common language of guesses quietly becomes a language of assumptions. He is silent at dinner, she already knows why, and she spends the evening arguing not with him but with her version of him. One of them keeps the image of the partner “from that first summer”, and the present person never quite measures up to it. Euripides shows the mechanism in a single exchange. Menelaus, seeing his living wife, calls on the goddess of the night: “O Hecate, giver of light, send thy visions favourably!” Helen replies: “In me thou beholdest no spectre of the night.” Someone who has lived a long time with an image sees a ghost in a living person. **Helen's answer is the best advice for this entry: check things by daylight.**

report.h3: An image held up by its price

report: The middle of the task is The Lovers, a choice: whom to believe, the image or the person. Menelaus looks at his wife and admits: “Thy form resembles her, but the real truth robs me of this belief.” Then he says the key line: “The greatness of my troubles at Troy convinces me; thou dost not.” Ten years of war and seven years of wandering would turn into nonsense if the woman in the cave were a phantom. Menelaus believes not his eyes but the price.

In a couple this sounds familiar: “I have put so much into this”, “I have put up with so much”, and what has been invested gets in the way of seeing who is standing there. For a couple with this tail, the middle is a series of small recognitions: the strong one turns out to be lost, the light one vulnerable, the mysterious one simply tired. Each time it is possible to resent the person for not matching the image, and each time it is possible to choose them again. The plus of The Lovers here is the ability to say: this is not the person I imagined, and this is the person I choose.

report.h3: A cave where a likeness is guarded

report: The main task is read through its minus, and Euripides builds the play on the verb “to have”. Paris thinks he has Helen. The Greeks die believing Paris has her. Menelaus cannot believe his wife because he has “another wife”: sailors guard her in a cave on the shore. Here is the Devil of this couple in one image — a likeness of a wife that someone calls “mine”.

In everyday life the cave looks ordinary. “Mine” turns into rights: to know passwords, to approve friends, to decide what the partner wears — in the name of the image: “that's not like you”. Sacrifices turn into a bill: “I wasted my best years on you”. Each guards the image of “the good partner” and keeps quiet about what they really want. There are always two in the cave: the one who is guarded and the one who guards — and neither is free. The roles are not handed out by gender: either partner can hold on to the image, and more often both do, by turns. If control has already turned into threats, surveillance or violence, this is not a task to be sat out: in danger, call a local emergency number; for support, turn to a psychologist or a crisis line.

The Devil has a plus too: accepting each other's dark sides, forgiving mistakes, talking openly about desires. **A couple with 18-6-15 reaches it not when it gets rid of the mystery, but when it stops guarding it.**

report.h3: Drink with, not to

report: In 1928 Hofmannsthal and Strauss turned the myth inside out in the opera The Egyptian Helen. There the phantom is a merciful lie: a sorceress gives Menelaus the lotus of forgetting and assures him that only “an airy image” was at Troy, while the real Helen slept all those years. The lotus worked, and the husband began to take his wife for a strange woman with whom he was betraying the “pure” Helen. The image made the living wife a stranger. So Helen herself chooses the second flask — the drink of remembrance. Menelaus asks: “Did you ever possess me?” She raises the cup to her lips: “You drink it to the other one — I drink with you!” Having drunk remembrance, he sees her anew: “Faithless one, ever the one, ever new!” **Peace bought with forgetting rests on a substitution; the way out is to remember together.**

In Euripides the couple escapes through an empty tomb: Menelaus agrees to be “dead in word, though not in deed”, and the two of them sail away on a ship begged for a funeral. What gets buried is not a person but a role — the man who fought ten years over a cloud. Several practices follow from this. Now and then, take back an old story about the partner out loud, like the poet Stesichorus, who by legend regained his sight when he recanted his slander of Helen. Tell “I know” from “I imagine”, and ask rather than guess. Notice when “I have put so much in” replaces “I see”. And remember that “mine” is not a right: friends, time alone and private messages stay with each person.
