seo.title: Karmic tail 18 6 6 compatibility: The Moon, then The Lovers twice
seo.description: Karmic tail 18 6 6 compatibility in a couple's destiny matrix: The Moon at the entry, The Lovers twice, and what A Midsummer Night's Dream reveals about it.

items.title: The 18-6-6 karmic tail in compatibility: a midsummer night's dream for two
items.short: The 18-6-6 karmic tail in destiny matrix compatibility is The Moon at the entry followed by The Lovers twice in a row. The oddity shows at once: the couple's shared task opens with a night card, and its middle and its goal are the same card. The answer is this: it is the tail of two people who enter love through mystery, imagination and a world of their own, and who have to learn to repeat their choice of each other by daylight — knowing the living person rather than the image the night painted.

sections.h2: A Midsummer Night's Dream: the play that stages the 18-6-6 tail
paragraphs: The play was written around 1595. Theseus, Duke of Athens, is waiting to marry Hippolyta, and the moon sets the date: the wedding is to be at the new moon. "But, O, methinks, how slow / This old moon wanes!" Theseus complains. By the same day young Hermia must give her answer: her father, Egeus, is giving her to Demetrius, but she loves Lysander. The law of Athens leaves her three roads: obedience, death or the convent. The lovers decide to run — at night, through the forest. Demetrius follows them, and Helena, who loves Demetrius, follows him.

The forest has masters of its own, Oberon, king of the fairies, and Titania, his queen, and they are quarrelling. Oberon sends Puck for a flower whose juice, laid on a sleeper's eyelids, makes him fall in love with the first creature he sees on waking. Puck muddles the Athenians, and in one night everything turns over: both young men now swear love to Helena, Hermia cannot understand what has happened, and Titania embraces the weaver Bottom, who wears an ass's head. At dawn hunting horns wake the four. The spells are lifted — all but one. Theseus overrules the father, and three weddings are held in the temple. At the feast the craftsmen perform "Pyramus and Thisbe", and one of the parts is played by the Moon itself.

Open the text and it is plainly a play about The Moon and The Lovers, quite literally. We counted the words in the spoken lines of all 37 plays in the MIT edition of Shakespeare: moon, moonshine and moonlight occur 45 times in the Dream, against 12 in The Tempest, which comes next. And no other play talks about eyes so densely: 65 times in sixteen thousand words. The moon and eyes — the light by which people look, and those who look.

Even the title carries the Moon. "’Tis Midsummer-moon with you" was what English speakers said to someone who had gone mad; Brewer's Dictionary of Phrase and Fable records the saying in its 1894 edition. In Shakespeare's own Twelfth Night, Olivia calls the antics of her love-struck steward "midsummer madness". And Theseus speaks the key to the play in the fifth act:
The lunatic, the lover and the poet / Are of imagination all compact.

Lunatic comes from the Latin luna — "moon-struck". The first two words of the famous speech are the first two cards of the tail: the moon-struck and the lover. Fyodor Tyutchev published his Russian version of this passage in 1833: "Lyubovniki, bezumtsy i poety / Iz odnogo voobrazhenya sliti" — lovers, madmen and poets, fused out of one imagination.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: The Moon, or what the couple wants together
paragraphs: The entry to the task is the point that holds the couple's shared desire and their common language. The play describes that language in its very first scene — through the mouth of someone who does not understand it. Egeus complains to the Duke about Lysander: "Thou, thou, Lysander, thou hast given her rhymes, / And interchanged love-tokens with my child: / Thou hast by moonlight at her window sung, / With feigning voice verses of feigning love". To the father this is deceit and witchcraft: "This man hath bewitch'd the bosom of my child". To the two of them it is a language nobody else speaks: verses, bracelets of hair, trinkets that mean something only to the two of them.

A couple with The Moon at the entry wants the same thing. A world of its own that outsiders cannot enter. Words only the two of them understand: nicknames, jokes, glances across the table. Night conversations after which the morning feels foreign. The feeling that the other understands without explanation and that every year reveals something new in them. Lisovskaya describes The Moon in a couple, on its bright side, in almost the same way: the two understand each other by intuition and guard each other's private space, and what holds them together is play and mystery.

The Moon even stands in the very name of the beginning. A honeymoon is, word for word, a moon of honey; in Russian, mesyats means both a month and the crescent in the sky. The first explanation of the word was left by Richard Huloet in his dictionary of 1552: the proverb so calls the newly married, who do not quarrel at first and love each other beyond measure, though it is already plain that this excess will ebb — "the likelihood of their exceadinge love appearing to aswage, ye which time the vulgar people call the hony mone". The moon got into the name because it changes. At the end of the play, watching Moonshine in the craftsmen's show, Hippolyta will say: "I am aweary of this moon: would he would change!" — and Theseus will reply that "he is in the wane; but yet, in courtesy, in all reason, we must stay the time". **The Moon at the entry is a phase, not a permanent state.** The couple's task begins where it wanes.

paragraphs.h3: When the same entry turns into resistance

paragraphs: The entry to the task stands on the line of tasks, so the same desire turns into resistance. The wish to protect the magic becomes a reluctance to speak plainly: important things are put off "so as not to spoil it". A question is replaced by a guess. Theseus described the mechanism more precisely than many psychologists: imagination, if it expects joy, sees joy's messenger, and "in the night, imagining some fear, / How easy is a bush supposed a bear!"

In a couple's life the bush looks like this. One is late to reply — by midnight the other already knows why, and that knowledge is worse than any truth. One is silent at dinner from tiredness — the other hears a verdict in the silence. The partner has not said a word yet, and the other already has a whole story with a beginning and an end. Among The Moon's tasks for a couple Lisovskaya names exactly this: jealousy and grievances born of invented stories, an image created at the start that later collapses, secrets that one day become weapons.

Shakespeare showed the price of such a bush — and showed it as comedy. In the fifth act the craftsmen perform "Pyramus and Thisbe", a story from Ovid's Metamorphoses. The lovers have agreed to meet at night by a tomb; Thisbe is frightened by a lion and drops her mantle, which the lion mauls with its bloody jaws; Pyramus finds the mantle, decides she is dead and stabs himself, and Thisbe dies over him. The whole tragedy is a single misread clue by moonlight. Pyramus even thanks the Moon "for thy sunny beams": he takes moonlight for daylight. The four, just back from the forest, laugh at the show — and fail to notice that they are watching the night they themselves barely survived.

paragraphs.h3: A forest that belongs to no one

paragraphs: The Moon in this tail has an oddity that only the numbers reveal. Each point of a couple is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices, and the entry of a personal tail is always a multiple of three. So the 18 at the couple's entry can be formed in only three ways: 3 + 15 (The Empress and The Devil), 6 + 12 (The Lovers and The Hanged Man) or 9 + 9 (two Hermits). **Neither of the two brings a Moon of their own to the entry.** The forest belongs neither to Hermia nor to Lysander: it appears only when they leave the city together. In one such couple in four (26%) The Moon is formed by two Hermits — two people carrying lanterns. That is exactly how Shakespeare brought the Moon on stage: in the craftsmen's show it is played by a man with a lantern.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: the flower that confuses the choice
paragraphs: The passage of the play that fits the middle of the tail best is Oberon's account of where the magic flower came from. Cupid took aim at a maiden in the west, "But I might see young Cupid's fiery shaft / Quench'd in the chaste beams of the watery moon" — and the arrow fell on a little flower, "Before milk-white, now purple with love's wound". Love's arrow passed through moonlight and became a juice that changes what the eyes see. This is the tail's step from 18 to 6: The Lovers, having passed through The Moon.

The flower has a name: love-in-idleness, which the standard Russian translation by Tatiana Shchepkina-Kupernik renders as "Lyubov v prazdnosti". It is the wild pansy, and pansy comes from the French pensée, "thought"; in Hamlet Ophelia will say: "there is pansies, that's for thoughts". In Russian the flower is called anyutiny glazki — "Annie's little eyes". A thought dropped onto the eyes: falling in love has never been described more exactly. Helena says the same without any flower:
Love looks not with the eyes, but with the mind; / And therefore is wing'd Cupid painted blind.

Love looks with the mind, not the eyes, and that is why Cupid is painted blind. The Russian translation has Helena say "heart", but Shakespeare wrote precisely "mind": love sees what it has imagined. And further: love is called a child "Because in choice he is so oft beguiled".

The middle of the task is how the couple lives the road from shared desire to the main task. For 18-6-6 the road runs through choice, and the choice is not made once. Where to live and whose friends to spend Saturday with. Whose side to take when a mother calls. Whether to stay in or go out. Every such decision is a small "you or not you". Among the things that fill a couple with The Lovers, Lisovskaya names precisely shared decisions even in small matters — that is, the act of choosing together.

But here the choice is made by moonlight, and sometimes it gets tangled. Yesterday the partner seemed the best person on earth; today, a stranger. The one who adored suddenly cools and is sure reason brought them there; Lysander, under the juice, says just that: "The will of man is by his reason sway'd". After the night Hermia puts this state better than anyone: "Methinks I see these things with parted eye, / When every thing seems double." And Helena answers: "And I have found Demetrius like a jewel, / Mine own, and not mine own."

**"Mine own, and not mine own" is the formula of the tail's middle.** The partner is chosen but not owned; found but not possessed. The downside of The Lovers in Lisovskaya — jealousy, checking, suspicion — grows exactly from the attempt to make "mine" what also remains "not mine". A caveat: the swaps in the forest are the flower's work, that is, the work of perception. The Lovers in the tail do not mean a third person in the couple.

sections.h2: Main task: the same choice by daylight
paragraphs: The morning in the play begins with Theseus's question: "But speak, Egeus; is not this the day / That Hermia should give answer of her choice?" The night is over, and the tail's main task is stated plainly: to choose. A couple's main task is read mostly through its downside — what does not work for the couple and what it has to learn. For The Lovers on this point Lisovskaya sees several such tasks, and in the play each one has a scene of its own.

**To choose with your own eyes, not someone else's.** "I would my father look'd but with my eyes," says Hermia. "Rather your eyes must with his judgment look," the Duke replies. Lysander lists what stands in love's way, and Hermia reacts most bitterly to "the choice of friends": "O hell! to choose love by another's eyes." For a couple with this tail, other people's eyes come in many forms: a mother's "he's not the one", a friend who keeps count of the other's faults, a picture of someone else's happiness to measure one's own against. Lisovskaya calls this dependence on relatives; in the play it has a name — Egeus.

**To believe that you were the one chosen.** Abandoned in the forest, Helena says of herself: "No, no, I am as ugly as a bear". And when a minute later Lysander, under the juice, swears his love to her, she is not glad but offended: she decides she is being mocked. The task that Lisovskaya puts as love for oneself within the couple looks exactly like this: a person who is loved hears mockery in a compliment and keeps checking whether the choice has been cancelled. Sometimes one partner teaches this to the other.

**Not to turn insecurity into control.** That same night Hermia, deciding that Helena has stolen Lysander from her, flies at her friend. Helena cries "you puppet, you!", Hermia answers "thou painted maypole" and threatens that "my nails can reach unto thine eyes" — the quarrel is about height, that is, about who is worse than whom. The jealousy of The Lovers on its downside grows from insecurity, not from love, and in a couple it looks familiar: a read message thread, an interrogation about "who were you with", words that cannot be taken back.

**To love a person, not an image.** The lover, Theseus says, "Sees Helen's beauty in a brow of Egypt". Titania tells an ass, "Thou art as wise as thou art beautiful" — and the ass himself, Bottom the weaver, turns out soberer than the queen: "reason and love keep little company together now-a-days". Lisovskaya places idealisation among the tasks of The Lovers next to perfectionism: demanding a picture from the relationship and conformity to it from the partner.

paragraphs.h3: Two sixes: the night choice and the day choice

paragraphs: The middle and the main task of this tail are one card. The road and the goal coincide: to choose in order to choose. Lysander chooses Hermia twice — in Athens, under her window by moonlight, and in the morning after the forest, when the spell is lifted. It is the same person, but the second choice is made by daylight, after a night in which everything seemed double. **The hidden plot of 18-6-6 is not finding "the one" but choosing the one you have already chosen — now knowing them.**

With Demetrius Shakespeare is bolder: his spell is never lifted, right to the end of the play. He tells the Duke himself: "I wot not by what power,— / But by some power it is,—my love to Hermia, / Melted as the snow" — and at once: "Now I do wish it, love it, long for it, / And will for evermore be true to it." The play does not ask love to prove where it came from. It asks something else: that a choice made at night be confirmed by day, aloud and in front of others. For a couple this is an honest thought: a beginning does not have to be reasonable for what follows to be real.

sections.h2: How the night becomes constancy
paragraphs: The play has a line that readers usually skip, though it holds the way out of the tail. On waking, Demetrius calls the others to the temple: "And by the way let us recount our dreams." The four walk and compare what each of them saw. Later Theseus refuses to believe their story: "More strange than true". Hippolyta objects — and in the original her answer is stronger than in the familiar Russian translation:
But all the story of the night told over, / And all their minds transfigured so together, / More witnesseth than fancy's images / And grows to something of great constancy.

In plain prose: the whole story of the night, told over again, and all their minds changed together, testify to more than fantasy and grow into something very constant. In Shchepkina-Kupernik's translation Hippolyta speaks more softly — "it seems to me there is truth in this" — and the word constancy disappears. Yet here it is the key word. Waite gives The Moon reversed the meaning "inconstancy"; Juliet begs Romeo not to swear by "the inconstant moon". **Hippolyta names the opposite: a night told by two becomes constancy.**

Wen closes The Moon reversed with a similar formula — "everything that rises must converge". The night visions of the four converge into one story, and the story proves sturdier than any single vision. For a couple with the 18-6-6 tail this is a working method, not a metaphor: The Moon at the entry stops frightening once the night has been talked through aloud and the versions compared. In practice it looks like this:

ul: to tell each other the story of how it began — each their own version — and find where the versions differ;
to turn a guess into a question: not "that hurt" but "did that hurt?";
to call a bush a bush, aloud: "right now I'm afraid that…" — and let the other answer;
to leave room in the couple for mystery and play, but not for silence about what matters;
to choose aloud, in small things, remembering that choosing each other is repeated, not done once and for all;
not to measure the couple against other people's eyes — parents', friends', those on a screen.

sections.h2: The centre of the couple: a sleep in the forest or a whole world
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's matrix is "The atmosphere inside the couple" — what happens between the two when nobody is watching. Couples with the 18-6-6 tail have only two cards in the centre: The Hanged Man in 69.9% and The World in 30.1%.

**The Hanged Man** is the four lovers' sleep in the forest: between night and morning they lie on the grass, and everything is settled without them. Lisovskaya describes couples with The Hanged Man in the centre this way: they take a long time to enter a relationship, and marriage needs a push from outside. In the play the push comes from Theseus: "Egeus, I will overbear your will". And on the downside of the same card she names the power of parents over the couple — that is, Egeus, who came to the Duke demanding the law. Both sides of the centre are in one scene. There is arithmetic too: Lisovskaya allows repeated energies to be added up, and the tail's two sixes give 6 + 6 = 12 — the very Hanged Man that stands in the centre of seven couples out of ten.

**The World** is a card that never appears in the centre of a personal matrix, for any birth date: in the centre it arises only in a couple. Among couples with the 18-6-6 tail it comes from every couple of one combination of personal tails — 15-20-5 + 3-22-19 — and only that one. The atmosphere of such a couple is a whole world with its own weather. In Shakespeare this shows in the play's second couple, Oberon and Titania: their quarrel confuses the seasons, frost falls on roses, "the mazed world, / By their increase, now knows not which is which" — and Titania admits: "We are their parents and original." They make peace with a dance and a blessing of someone else's house. On the bright side of The World in the centre Lisovskaya sees full acceptance of the partner, much talk and compromise; on the downside, many secrets and illusions about the relationship. With The Moon at the entry this follows directly: a world for two is good as long as people live in it, not illusions alone.

sections.h2: The couple's values: Diana's cell and the Hermit's lantern
paragraphs: In the first scene the Duke lists what awaits Hermia if she does not submit to her father's choice: death or a vow at Diana's altar — "To live a barren sister all your life, / Chanting faint hymns to the cold fruitless moon." For the Romans Diana was a goddess of the moon. Solitude under a cold moon — that is the punishment for a choice of one's own.

In the matrix of a couple with the 18-6-6 tail these same two cards stand in "The couple's values" — the point read for what the union exists for and which road it should walk together: The Hermit in 64% of such couples, The Moon in 36%. What Athens threatens as a sentence turns out, for the couple, to be a value — only not instead of the union but within it. Each has their own time and place for solitude, and love is shown in deeds more than words — this is how Lisovskaya describes The Hermit in a couple. And to a couple with The Moon she advises accepting the partner's need to withdraw into themselves at times: it is a way to recover, not a lack of love.

Waite insists that The Hermit is not a card of "occult isolation": his beacon intimates that "where I am, you also may be". A lantern, not a wall. Shakespeare's Moonshine holds a lantern too: "This lanthorn doth the horned moon present". **The value of a couple with this tail is not to merge into one but to light the way for each other.**

sections.h2: Clues in Waite: inconstancy, a dog and marriage
paragraphs: The cards in the reading on this site are drawn in their own style. This section is about the Waite–Smith deck and Waite's book The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910).

Waite defines The Moon in a sentence Theseus could have spoken: "The card represents life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit". His divinatory list gives The Moon deception and error, and reversed: "Instability, inconstancy, silence". On the Waite–Smith card a dog and a wolf howl at the moon. In Shakespeare Moonshine comes on with a dog of his own — "this dog, my dog" — and in Puck's last song "the wolf behowls the moon".

Waite describes The Lovers on the Waite–Smith card as two figures "unveiled before each other". That is where the tail leads: from an image in the half-dark to two people who see each other uncovered.

One more clue lies in the numbers. Waite also gives The Lovers an older name: "The Lovers or Marriage". And his lists hold two more cards with the word marriage: the meanings of The Hierophant begin with "Marriage, alliance", and The Sun has "fortunate marriage". **In 52% of couples with the 18-6-6 tail one of the two sixes is formed from exactly these two cards:** The Sun in one partner and The Hierophant in the other give 19 + 5 = 24 → 6. In the combination 15-20-5 + 3-22-19 (30% of such couples) this is how the main task is formed; in 12-19-7 + 6-5-17 (22%), the middle. A wedding in the temple in the morning sun — the very ending of the play.

sections.h2: Worked example: 09.05.1976 and 17.01.1976
paragraphs: A couple's tail is worked out from two personal matrices. A person born on 09.05.1976 has the personal tail 3-22-19; a person born on 17.01.1976 has 15-20-5. This is the most common combination for 18-6-6: 30% of such couples. The points are added, and a sum above 22 is reduced by adding its digits.

The couple's middle is taken from the middles of the two personal tails, 22 and 20, not from the couple's two outer numbers. In this tail it happens to match the sum of the outer numbers (18 + 6 = 24 → 6), but it is still worked out separately.

The Moon at the entry here is one partner's Empress and the other's Devil. The main task is one partner's Sun (19) and the other's Hierophant (5): that very pair of Waite's "marriage" cards. The centre is 11 + 10 = 21, The World, which never occurs in a personal matrix. "The couple's values" is 9, The Hermit. "Image of the couple" is 8, Justice. And "What to create together" is 6, so The Lovers appear three times in this couple. Repeats, according to Lisovskaya, can be added: 6 + 6 + 6 = 18 — The Moon, the very card of the entry. The circle closes on itself.

sections.h2: How to recognise the 18-6-6 couple tail and what not to confuse it with
paragraphs: The compatibility calculator on this site works out a couple's tail from two birth dates for free. By hand it takes three steps: find both personal tails (entry, middle, main task), add entry to entry, middle to middle and task to task, and reduce any sum above 22.

The 18-6-6 tail occurs in roughly one couple in 67 (1.499%) and ranks 24th of the 97 couple tails. It is formed from six combinations of personal tails: most often 15-20-5 + 3-22-19 (30%), then 12-16-4 + 6-8-20 and 12-19-7 + 6-5-17 (22% each), 9-12-3 + 9-12-3 (12%), 9-15-6 + 9-9-18 (9%) and 9-3-21 + 9-3-21 (5%). In one such couple in six the partners' personal tails are identical — the two enter the forest by the same path. And neither partner has the personal tail 18-6-6 in any of the six combinations.

There are no other couple tails made of the same numbers: 18, 6 and 6 cannot be rearranged. There is, however, a personal 18-6-6 tail — for 3,001 birth dates since 1900. That is a different calculation with different roles for the points: a personal tail speaks about one person, a couple's tail about a task that appears only for two. Texts for one do not carry over to the other.

sections.h2: Sources

ul: William Shakespeare, A Midsummer Night's Dream (around 1595): English text from The Complete Works of William Shakespeare on the MIT site; Russian translation by T. L. Shchepkina-Kupernik; the passage "The lunatic, the lover and the poet…" in the Russian translation by F. I. Tyutchev (1833).
Shakespeare, Hamlet (Ophelia on pansies), Twelfth Night (midsummer madness), Romeo and Juliet (the inconstant moon).
Ovid, Metamorphoses, book IV: Pyramus and Thisbe.
E. Cobham Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1894), entry Midsummer-Moon Madness.
Richard Huloet, Abcedarium Anglico-Latinum (1552), entry hony mone — as quoted by the Oxford English Dictionary.
A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910): The Moon, The Lovers, The Hermit, The Hierophant, The Sun.
Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015): The Moon.
Yuliana Lisovskaya, Matritsa sudby: sovmestimost (Destiny Matrix: Compatibility, 2024): the meaning of a couple's points, energies 6, 9, 12, 18, 21.
Frequencies, centres, values and combinations of personal tails — a run of the site's engine over every birth date since 1900.

**M · Entry to the task — 18, The Moon.** What the couple wants together: a world of its own that outsiders cannot enter, understanding without words, a shared secret. The same entry easily turns into resistance: things left unsaid, guesses instead of questions, fears grown in the half-dark.
**N · Middle of the task — 6, The Lovers.** How the couple travels the road: through a choice that has to be made again and again — in small things, in doubt, sometimes blindly.

**D · Main task — 6, The Lovers.** What the couple has to learn: to love a person, not an image; to choose with their own eyes, not someone else's; not to mistake love for jealousy, control and idealisation.

intro: This tail has a play in which it is acted out almost point by point: Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream. Two lovers run away into the forest at night: that is the entry. In the forest a magic flower confuses who chooses whom: that is the middle. In the morning everyone has to choose again, this time in front of others and in sunlight: that is the main task. What follows is an investigation — of what is written in the cards themselves, in the numbers of the couple's matrix and in the text of the play.

faq.q: Is the 18-6-6 tail a bad sign for a couple's compatibility?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not rate the union and does not predict how it will end. It shows a task: for 18-6-6 it is the road from love by moonlight — mystery, guesses, imagination — to choosing each other by daylight. The tail's difficulties are what the couple has to learn, not a verdict.

faq.q: Do The Lovers in a couple's tail mean infidelity or a rival?
faq.a: No. The Lovers do not prove that there is a third person in the couple. In A Midsummer Night's Dream the swaps are the flower's work, that is, the work of perception: each sees not a person but what they imagined. The tail's task lies exactly here — to see the partner, not an image.

faq.q: Does The Moon at the entry mean a partner is hiding something?
faq.a: No. The Moon at the entry to the task speaks of the couple's wish for a world of its own and of the language of hints the two speak. Its flip side is things left unsaid and guesses, but that is a habit shared by both, not one person's secret. Besides, neither partner brings The Moon to the entry: it is formed only from the two personal matrices.

faq.q: What can a couple with the 18-6-6 tail do?
faq.a: Talk the night through aloud: tell each other how each sees the beginning of the relationship and what is happening between them; turn guesses into questions; make small choices aloud and not measure themselves against other people's eyes. If jealousy turns into control, threats or fear, that is no longer the tail's task but a reason to see a psychologist, and in danger, to call a local emergency number or crisis line.

faq.q: How does the 18-6-6 couple tail differ from the personal 18-6-6 tail?
faq.a: A personal tail is worked out from one birth date and speaks about one person. A couple's tail is made up of two personal tails and speaks about a task that exists only for the two together. The numbers coincide; the roles of the points and the meaning differ.

report: Two lovers run from Athens into the forest at night, because in the city nobody will let them choose each other. That is how Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream begins — and the 18-6-6 tail is built the same way: The Moon at the entry, then The Lovers twice in a row. In the forest a magic flower confuses who chooses whom. In the morning everyone has to choose again, this time in front of others and in sunlight. In the fifth act Theseus says: "The lunatic, the lover and the poet / Are of imagination all compact." Lunatic comes from the Latin luna — "moon-struck". The first two words of the famous speech are the first two cards of the tail: the moon-struck and the lover.

report.h3: A common language that looks like witchcraft from outside

report: The entry to the task is the point that holds the couple's shared desire and their common language. The play describes that language in its very first scene — through the mouth of someone who does not understand it. Hermia's father complains to the Duke about Lysander: "Thou hast by moonlight at her window sung, / With feigning voice verses of feigning love". To the father this is deceit and witchcraft: "This man hath bewitch'd the bosom of my child". To the two of them it is a language nobody else speaks.

A couple with The Moon at the entry wants the same thing: a world of its own that outsiders cannot enter, nicknames and jokes only the two of them understand, night conversations after which the morning feels foreign. The Moon even stands in the very name of the beginning: a honeymoon is, word for word, a moon of honey. In 1552 Richard Huloet explained that the newly married are so called because at first they love each other beyond measure, though it is already plain that this excess will ebb. **The Moon at the entry is a phase, not a permanent state.** The couple's task begins where it wanes.

The entry stands on the line of tasks, and the same desire turns into resistance. Protecting the magic comes to mean not speaking plainly: important things are put off "so as not to spoil it", and a question is replaced by a guess. Theseus says: "in the night, imagining some fear, / How easy is a bush supposed a bear!" One is late to reply — by midnight the other already knows why, and that knowledge is worse than any truth. One is silent at dinner from tiredness — the other hears a verdict in the silence.

Shakespeare showed the price of such a bush as comedy. The craftsmen perform "Pyramus and Thisbe": Pyramus finds a bloodied mantle, decides Thisbe is dead and stabs himself. The whole tragedy is a single misread clue by moonlight. The four, just back from the forest, laugh at the show — and fail to notice that they are watching the night they themselves barely survived.

report.h3: A thought dropped onto the eyes

report: In Shakespeare the middle of the task is a flower. Cupid took aim at a maiden in the west, "But I might see young Cupid's fiery shaft / Quench'd in the chaste beams of the watery moon" — and the arrow fell on a little flower. Love's arrow passed through moonlight and became a juice that changes what the eyes see. This is the tail's step from 18 to 6: The Lovers, having passed through The Moon. The flower is the wild pansy, and pansy comes from the French pensée, "thought"; in Russian it is anyutiny glazki, "Annie's little eyes". A thought dropped onto the eyes: falling in love has never been described more exactly.

The road of a couple with this tail runs through choice, and the choice is not made once: where to live, whose friends to spend Saturday with, whose side to take when a mother calls. By moonlight it sometimes gets tangled: yesterday the partner seemed the best person on earth; today, a stranger. After the night Hermia says: "Methinks I see these things with parted eye, / When every thing seems double." And Helena answers: "And I have found Demetrius like a jewel, / Mine own, and not mine own."

**"Mine own, and not mine own" is the formula of the tail's middle.** The partner is chosen but not owned. Jealousy, checking and suspicion grow exactly from the attempt to make "mine" what also remains "not mine". The swaps in the forest are the flower's work, that is, the work of perception: The Lovers in the tail do not mean a third person in the couple.

report.h3: Choosing the one already chosen

report: The morning begins with the Duke asking whether this is the day Hermia must give her answer. The main task is to choose, and the play shows what gets in the way. Other people's eyes: "O hell! to choose love by another's eyes." — a father in the play, a mother's "he's not the one" in life. Disbelief at being the one chosen: Helena says of herself "No, no, I am as ugly as a bear", and takes a declaration of love for mockery. Insecurity turned into control: Hermia, jealous, threatens her friend with her nails. An image instead of a person: the lover, Theseus says, "Sees Helen's beauty in a brow of Egypt".

The middle and the main task of this tail are one card. Lysander chooses Hermia twice: in Athens, under her window by moonlight, and in the morning after the forest, when the spell is lifted. It is the same person, but the second choice is made by daylight, after a night in which everything seemed double. **The hidden plot of 18-6-6 is not finding "the one" but choosing the one already chosen — now knowing them.** With Demetrius Shakespeare is bolder: his spell is never lifted, right to the end of the play. The play does not ask love to prove where it came from. It asks that a choice made at night be confirmed by day, aloud and in front of others.

report.h3: A night told by two becomes constancy

report: The way out of the tail hides in a line that readers usually skip. On waking, Demetrius calls the others to the temple: "And by the way let us recount our dreams." Theseus refuses to believe their story, and Hippolyta objects: "But all the story of the night told over, / And all their minds transfigured so together, / More witnesseth than fancy's images / And grows to something of great constancy." A night told over again, and together, grows into something very constant. Waite gives The Moon reversed the meaning "inconstancy". **Hippolyta names the opposite.**
In practice this means:

ul: to tell each other the story of how it began — each their own version — and find where the versions differ;
to turn a guess into a question: not "that hurt" but "did that hurt?";
to call a bush a bush, aloud, and let the other answer;
to leave room in the couple for mystery and play, but not for silence about what matters;
to choose aloud, in small things, remembering that choosing each other is repeated, not done once and for all.

report: The strong version of this tail is a couple whose night has not been taken away but told: the mystery and the play remain, and the choice of each other has been made by daylight.

seo.title: Karmic tail 18 9 18 compatibility: two Moons and the Hermit
seo.description: Karmic tail 18 9 18 compatibility: the Moon at the entry, the Hermit in the middle, the Moon again as the main task — read through Cyrano de Bergerac.

items.title: The 18-9-18 karmic tail in compatibility: a couple who recognise each other in the dark
items.short: The Moon, the Hermit and the Moon again: the 18-9-18 tail begins at night and ends at night, with a long silence between the two nights. Nobody has this tail in a personal chart; it appears only in the sum of two charts. It belongs to a couple who understand each other best in half-light — in letters and messages, in hints, in talk after midnight — and who keep quiet about the main thing in daylight longer than anyone else.

sections.h2: A tail that belongs to no one
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. A couple's tail is read in the order M–N–D: entry to the task, middle of the task, main task. The 18-9-18 tail has an oddity, and the investigation starts there: it never occurs as a personal tail. In a personal matrix the entry M equals the main task D plus the centre of the chart, and with D = 18 no centre can give an entry of 18. So neither partner brings this tail into the relationship. It arises only between the two of them.

It occurs in roughly one couple in 104 (0.963%), 38th of the 97 couple tails. And it is almost always assembled from two particular personal tails: 12-19-7 in one partner and 6-17-11 in the other (85% of such couples), or 12-16-4 and 6-20-14 (15%). A third route, two identical 9-18-9 tails, is arithmetically possible but so rare that it rounds to zero.
Break the couple's points down into their sums and the first clues appear:

ul: **Entry:** the Moon is made of one partner's Hanged Man and the other's Lovers, 12 + 6. The entry almost never has any other components.
**Middle:** the Hermit is born of the Sun and the Star (19 + 17 = 36 → 9) or of the Tower and Judgement (16 + 20 = 36 → 9). Two lights of the sky, the Sun and the Star, add up to a single lantern.
**Main task:** the Moon is made of the Chariot and Strength (7 + 11) or of the Emperor and Temperance (4 + 14). Two cards of will and self-command together give the card of fog.

paragraphs: Rostand wrote lines that sound like a description of this arithmetic. Cyrano offers the handsome Christian an alliance: one will supply the words, the other the face. "Will you complete me, and let me complete you?" he asks, in the 1898 translation by Gladys Thomas and Mary F. Guillemard quoted here throughout; and then, more briefly: "Let me be wit for you, be you my beauty!" Roxane will fall in love with a man who does not exist on his own. He exists only as the sum of two.

The 18-9-18 tail works the same way, but this is not a story about a love triangle: in a real couple there is no third person. "Christian" here is the pleasant version of oneself that is fit for daylight, the one each partner pushes forward while the real voice speaks from the shadow.

sections.h2: Act III: the whole tail in one night
paragraphs: Act III is called "Roxane's Kiss". It lasts one night on a small square in old Paris, and its three main scenes come in exactly the order of the tail's cards.

**The Moon.** Christian cannot talk to Roxane, so Cyrano stands under her balcony, in the dark: first he prompts, then he speaks himself. He refuses to climb into the light and explains why — it is "the rare occasion, when our hearts can speak / Our selves unseen, unseeing!" And at once he gives the formula of the whole couple: "I but a shadow--you a radiance fair!"

**The Hermit.** In the middle of the declaration a Capuchin friar appears on the square. Rostand's stage direction: he enters "with a lantern. He goes from house to house, looking at every door." Cyrano greets him with a joke: "What do you, playing at Diogenes?" Diogenes, as Diogenes Laërtius tells it, walked about in broad daylight with a lit lamp, saying he was looking for a man. The friar is looking for Roxane's house and carries a letter for her; Cyrano sends him the wrong way, and he comes back when the kiss has already happened. Once the wedding is settled, the friar turns his lantern on Cyrano — "'Tis you?" — and only after Christian answers "'Tis I!" does he move the light to the handsome face. The lantern finds first the man Roxane has really fallen in love with that night: this is our reading, but the words and stage directions are Rostand's. The wedding itself takes place inside the house, with no audience, and it will be announced after the fact.

**The Moon again.** To keep de Guiche from going in and stopping the wedding, Cyrano pulls his hat down over his eyes, changes his voice and drops from the balcony on a branch, as if he had crashed from the sky: "Like a bomb / I fell from the moon!" While the wedding goes on inside, he lists the ways of rising to the Moon and names the tide as the seventh: "I' th' witching hour when the moon woos the wave". Then he speaks in his own voice: "The quarter's gone--I'll hinder you no more: / The marriage-vows are made." Footmen bring out candelabra, Cyrano takes off his hat — and in the light he is known by his voice and by his nose.

The same scene holds a detail that will return at the end. Roxane first reads de Guiche's letter to herself by lantern light, and aloud she reads something else entirely: that the Cardinal orders her to marry Christian at once. "Am I not apt at reading letters?" she whispers to the bridegroom. **The union begins with a letter read falsely.** Fifteen years later there will be another letter and another reading.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — the Moon: talking without seeing each other
paragraphs: The entry to the task shows what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, that very "common language". In the compatibility reading this point carries a second label too — "Common language". For 18-9-18 the common language is lunar. The two are happiest where neither has to show themselves completely: in long correspondence, in voice messages after midnight, in jokes only they understand, in things left unsaid that stir more than a plain word.

Cyrano explains why night makes it easier: "In the tender, sheltering dusk / I dare to be myself for once,--at last!" This is the paradox of the lunar entry. Darkness hides the face and frees the voice. A person in such a couple often says the truest things where they cannot be seen: they write what they would never say at the table, and at the table they joke about what they wrote in earnest at night.

Roxane hears the difference at once — "'Tis true, your voice rings with a tone that's new" — and asks nothing. She likes the mystery, and the mystery suits her. This is the other side of point M: it stands on the line of tasks, and what the two want can become their resistance. A wish for mystery easily turns into an unspoken agreement not to ask awkward questions.

This is how an image, rather than a portrait, forms at the start of the union. Each partner fills the other in by reflected light — from letters, from a couple of phrases, from their own hopes. Already in Act I Cyrano tells a friend how it goes. On a spring evening, in a garden, he watches a knight with a lady on his arm and dreams for a moment "To saunter thus 'neath the moonshine" — and then: "--The shadow of my profile on the wall!" The same moon gives him both the dream and the shadow of his nose. That is how the lunar entry works: the half-light that makes a meeting magical also draws the fear of looking ridiculous.

Later Christian speaks for everyone who has to live beside such an image: "Too long I've borne about within myself / A rival to myself". For a couple with this tail the rival is usually not a person. More often it is that first version of oneself — from the letters, from the start of the romance — that one has to compete with for years.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — the Hermit: fifteen years of Saturdays
paragraphs: Act V is called "Cyrano's Gazette". Fifteen years have passed: 1655, autumn, the park of the Sisters of the Holy Cross in Paris. The stage direction puts "an enormous plane tree in the middle of the stage, standing alone". Roxane lives here as a widow, in a black veil, and wears Christian's last letter on her breast. Cyrano comes every Saturday at the same hour. Roxane says of him: "I hear,--for now I never turn to look-- / Too sure to hear his cane tap down the steps".

The middle of the task is how the couple lives the path from the shared wish to the main task. The Hermit in the middle is loyalty and silence at once. The plus here is real: not a single Saturday missed, the chair in the shade, the embroidery he teases with the same joke every time, love shown in deeds rather than words. The minus is just as real: each of them sits under this tree with a wound and keeps it hidden.

Cyrano recites to Roxane her "gazette", the news of the week. The King overate on fruit preserve and was bled; hundreds of candles burned at the Queen's ball; Madame d'Athis's little dog had to take a dose. News of everyone — and not a word about himself. To the nuns he boasts, "Sister, I eat meat on Friday!", while the Mother Superior knows that the last time he came he had not eaten for two days. No one can help him: "He permits not."

On the last Saturday he arrives wounded, his hat pulled down over his eyes, and explains his faint by an old wound from Arras. Roxane answers, "Each of us has his wound; ay, I have mine,-- / Never healed up", and puts her hand on her breast, where the letter hangs. Both speak of wounds. He passes off a fresh wound as an old one. She shows her old one and does not know that the author of the letter under which she aches is sitting in the next chair.

In a modern couple this Hermit looks ordinary. There is a ritual — Sunday dinner, an evening walk, a call at the same time every day — and it holds the union together for years. Inside the ritual they discuss colleagues, relatives, TV series, prices. About "I'm scared", "I'm tired", "I miss you" they keep quiet: sometimes out of care, so as not to worry the other, sometimes out of pride, so as not to look weak. Each withdraws into a shell exactly when things are hard, though the Hermit's task in a couple is the opposite: not to hide at a hard moment, but to share and to help.

This act holds an exchange that reads like a caption to the card. De Guiche, having heard dangerous rumours, asks Le Bret to warn his friend: "Let him stay in--be prudent!" Le Bret raises his arms to heaven: "Prudent! He!..." Cyrano, who all his life has thrown himself alone against a hundred swords, is the least prudent man in the play. And the most cautious in love: for fifteen years he guards a single sentence. Even news about himself he will deliver the Hermit's way: after the fact, in the third person, as the last line of his "gazette".

sections.h2: Main task — the Moon: "How can you read? It is too dark to see!"
paragraphs: A couple's main task is read mainly through its minus: what the two cannot manage and what they have to learn. For 18-9-18 this is the Moon again, the same card as at the entry. But in the finale of the play it works the other way round.

Cyrano asks to read the very letter of Christian's that he once wrote himself. The stage directions follow one another: "Twilight begins to fall." "The shades of evening fall imperceptibly." "The darkness deepens." He reads aloud, and Roxane is no longer listening to the words but to the voice: "It is not the first time I hear that voice!" She quietly steps behind the chair, looks at the letter and puts her hand on his shoulder: "How can you read? It is too dark to see!"

In the original the two night scenes share the same words. Under the balcony Cyrano excuses his faltering: "C'est qu'il fait nuit" — "it is because it is night". In the convent garden Roxane says: "Il fait nuit" — "it is night". **The same night that hid him at the start gave him away at the end.** This is the meaning of one card at both ends of the tail. The couple does not need to escape the Moon. It needs the darkness to stop being a shelter for the image and to become the place where people are recognised by their voice.

Rostand shows the minus of the main task without mercy. The image built at the start collapses, and Roxane loses one man twice: "I loved but once, yet twice I lose my love!" Cyrano denies everything to the last, and the denial gives him away by itself: "No, my sweet love, I never loved you!" The lie is spoken, but "my sweet love" already tells the truth.

There is also a piece of evidence he had forbidden himself. In Act I Cyrano will not let himself weep: "Think, how vilely suited / Adown this nose a tear its passage tracing!" Tenderness seems ridiculous to him, and he hides it. But on the farewell letter he composed for Christian, his tear remained — "A tear!", Christian noticed at the time. In the finale it is this tear that settles the matter: "The tears were your tears?" — "The bloodstains were his." **What he hid as weakness turned out to be the only proof of his love.**

Benebell Wen, discussing the reversed Moon, writes: "The repressed latent will always surface, and any strong intention to repress will cause a violent surfacing." The harder something is held down, the more sharply it breaks out. Rostand lets fifteen years of silence break out in a few minutes of dusk. And Roxane asks the question that an 18-9-18 couple can ask itself before it gets dark: "Why, why keep silence".

The bitterest line in the scene is hers: "I should have guessed, each time he said my name!" She heard the other voice already under the balcony. The knowledge was with her for all fifteen years; what was missing was the question.

sections.h2: Two Moons: each lights the other with reflected light
paragraphs: Rostand's hero had a model: Savinien de Cyrano de Bergerac (1619–1655), poet and freethinker. Twenty months after his death his friend Henry Le Bret published his fantastic novel about a journey to the Moon, the Comical History of the States and Empires of the Moon (1657); today it is often known as The Other World. The novel opens with an argument on a night road: a full moon, friends guessing what it might be, and the narrator saying: "I believe that the Moon is a world like this one, to which ours serves as a moon" (our translation).

For a couple with two Moons in its tail there is no better formula. Each sees the other as a moon: by reflected light, in whatever phase their own hopes and fears allow them to make out. And each forgets that to the other they are a moon too — shining not with their own light but with what the other puts into them.

Rostand knew the book. His Cyrano calls the Moon "that saffron-colored ball", and the real Cyrano, on the first page of his novel, a "boule de safran", a saffron ball. And the first of the seven ways of reaching the Moon with which Cyrano bamboozles de Guiche — rising with dew that the sun draws upwards — is the very way the novel's hero flies off. In the finale of the play the Moon and Roxane stand side by side. Cyrano tells Roxane: "I owe it to you that I had at least one woman friend" (our translation; Thomas and Guillemard have "But I have had your friendship"). Le Bret points to the moonlight between the branches: "Your other friend is here, come to see you" (our translation). In Thomas and Guillemard's version the line is "Your other lady-love is come." Two friends, and both are Moons. One of them he saw all his life from below, from afar, by reflected light. And to her he was a voice from the dark.

The real story around the play is lunar too. Roxane's model was Cyrano's cousin on his mother's side, Madeleine Robineau, Baroness de Neuvillette. Her husband, Baron Christophe de Neuvillette, died at the siege of Arras in 1640. Widowed, she gave up worldly life and turned to devotion. Mother Marguerite of Act V is real as well: Marguerite de Senaux, in religion Marguerite de Jésus, was prioress of the Daughters of the Cross, the convent that Cyrano's sister Catherine entered in 1641. And the anecdote collection Menagiana preserved a detail about the real Cyrano that might have come straight from the Moon card: because of his disfigured nose he could not bear to be looked at.

sections.h2: Waite and Wen: a Capuchin with a lantern and a generous deception
paragraphs: Arthur Edward Waite, in The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, lists the old names of the Hermit. In common parlance, he writes, "he is also the Capuchin, and in more philosophical language the Sage." By placing a Capuchin friar with a lantern between the two moon scenes, Rostand repeats the card's old name literally. Wen, too, links the Hermit with friars of a mendicant order — the Hermits of Saint Francis of Paola, "later known as the Minim Friars".

Waite's divinatory meanings for the Hermit begin with "Prudence, circumspection". For the reversed card he gives "Concealment, disguise, policy, fear, unreasoned caution". It is almost an exact portrait of Cyrano in love — a man whom Le Bret cannot even imagine being prudent.

In Waite's divinatory list the Moon has "deception", and the reversed card "lesser degrees of deception and error". In the original, Roxane calls the whole story "la généreuse imposture", a generous imposture ("the generous counterfeit" in Thomas and Guillemard). The lunar deception in this couple is not about gain or malice. It is the deception of shame: a person hides not to take something that belongs to someone else, but because they do not believe their real self will be accepted. The card does not prove that anyone in the couple is lying: it shows where the two can easily mistake each other.

sections.h2: A worked example: 05.07.1975 and 05.11.1975
paragraphs: Two dates from the same year and even the same day of the month, four months apart. The partners' personal tails:
Now add up the matching points:

The couple's middle is the sum of the two personal middles; it is not recalculated from the couple's outer numbers. The couple's centre, the atmosphere inside the union, is the Moon here too: so it is in 91.1% of couples with this tail, while the other 8.9% have the Hermit in the centre. The couple's values in the example are 9, the Hermit: so it is in 71.5% of such couples, and 28.5% have the Moon. One more Moon stands in the point "What to create together", which is made from the birth months (7 + 11 = 18). The tail's two cards spread across the whole matrix: night and lantern are not an episode here but the climate.

sections.h2: How to rewrite the ending
paragraphs: The play ends in darkness, but the numbers predict neither its ending nor any other. The tail shows a plot, not a fate, and it can be lived differently. Rostand himself left hints for an 18-9-18 couple — at the places where the plot could have turned.

ul: **Believe the permission already given.** In Act IV Roxane tells Cyrano she would love Christian ugly — "Yes, ugly!" — and to "Disfigured" she answers "Ay!". Cyrano believes it for a moment — "My God! it's true, perchance, love waits me there!" — and does not get to finish. In an 18-9-18 couple the permission to be oneself has often already been given. The task is to take it seriously.

**Ask instead of filling in.** Roxane hears "a tone that's new" and asks no question. The Moon in the main task asks for guesses to be checked with words — "what did you mean?" — rather than with one's own version of the answer, and for one's fears not to be loaded onto the partner.

**Say in daylight what is easy to write at night.** Letters and night conversations are this couple's native language, and there is no need to give them up. But one sentence said aloud, face to face, weighs more than a dozen letters.

**Add a line about oneself to the "gazette".** The Hermit's ritual is the couple's strength, and it does not have to be invented. It has room for one piece of news that is not about the world but about oneself: "I'm tired", "I'm scared", "I'm happy with you".

**Tell solitude from disappearance.** The Hermit needs time of his own, and withdrawing into oneself is a way to restore strength, not a lack of love. But it is said aloud: "I need some time alone" is not at all the same as a silence fifteen years long.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail
paragraphs: In the plus, both cards give the two a rare gift. The Moon gives intuition: Roxane recognised the voice in the dark, by its tone, after fifteen years. The Moon also gives imagination and play, a shared secret world in which the partner keeps surprising the other years later. The Hermit gives a loyalty that needs no witnesses, the ability to be together without unnecessary words, a friendship that lasts for decades.

A strong 18-9-18 couple keeps its night language and adds a daytime one. It can still talk for hours in the dark — but it no longer hides there. Its "il fait nuit" means only one thing: time to light the lamp and finish the conversation.

sections.h2: How 18-9-18 differs from 9-18-18 and 18-18-9
paragraphs: The same numbers make two more couple tails. In 9-18-18 (1.228% of couples, the Moon in the centre for 66.8%) the couple enters through the Hermit — wanting quiet and a corner of its own — and then lives and learns through the Moon. In 18-18-9 (0.221% of couples, the Hermit in the centre for 82%) the couple enters and lives through the Moon, and the Hermit becomes the main task: learning a solitude that does not drive the two apart. In 18-9-18 the Moon stands at both ends, and the Hermit's silence becomes a bridge between two nights.

ul: **Entry to the task — The Moon.** What the two want together: mystery, understanding without words, a private language of half-tones. Along with that wish an image enters the union: each shows the other a slightly polished version of themselves.
**Middle of the task — The Hermit.** How the couple lives its path: loyalty, rituals, respect for each other's solitude — and the habit of carrying the hardest things alone.
**Main task — The Moon.** What the couple has to learn: to tell the living person from the image formed at the start, and to speak about feelings in daylight instead of waiting for dark.

intro: This story has already been written. In Edmond Rostand's Cyrano de Bergerac (first performed on 28 December 1897) the whole romance rests on a voice from the dark, and the 18-9-18 tail is played out in it twice: within a single night in Act III, and across the fifteen years between the balcony and the convent garden. What follows is an investigation: the clues in the numbers, in the text of the play and in the books about the cards.

faq.q: What does the 18-9-18 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail in which the entry to the task and the main task are the Moon and the middle is the Hermit. The two are drawn together by a language of mystery and half-tones, they walk their path in loyalty and silence, and what they have to learn is to tell the living person from the image and to speak about feelings directly, in daylight.

faq.q: Can 18-9-18 be the karmic tail of a personal destiny matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre of the chart, and with a main task of 18 no centre gives an entry of 18. Anyone who sees the triple 18-9-18 is looking at a couple's matrix: this tail exists only in compatibility.

faq.q: How is the 18-9-18 couple tail calculated?
faq.a: Add up the matching points of the two personal tails and reduce the sums to 22: entry with entry, middle with middle, main task with main task. For example, 12-19-7 and 6-17-11 give 12 + 6 = 18, 19 + 17 = 36 → 9 and 7 + 11 = 18.

faq.q: Is 18-9-18 a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. The tail shows a couple's tasks, not a verdict, and the method gives no compatibility percentages. The Moon and the Hermit have real strengths — intuition, imagination, loyalty, deep friendship. There is one difficulty, and it can be seen in advance: the habit of hiding the main thing and loving an image instead of a person.

faq.q: How common is the 18-9-18 couple tail?
faq.a: Roughly one couple in 104 (0.963%), 38th of the 97 couple tails. In 85% of cases it is made of the personal tails 12-19-7 and 6-17-11, in 15% of 12-16-4 and 6-20-14.

report: Roxane, in Cyrano de Bergerac, fell in love with a man who did not exist on his own. Cyrano gave him the words; the handsome Christian gave him the face. Cyrano proposes the deal himself: he will be the wit, Christian the beauty. The 18-9-18 tail works the same way: nobody has it in a personal chart, and it appears only in the sum of two charts. It belongs to a couple who understand each other best in half-light — in letters and messages, in hints, in talk after midnight — and who keep quiet about the main thing in daylight longer than anyone else. In a real couple there is no third person: "Christian" here is the version of oneself fit for daylight, the one each partner pushes forward while the real voice speaks from the shadow.

report.h3: The whole tail in one night

report: Act III of the play lasts a single night, and its three scenes come in exactly the order of the cards. First the Moon. Cyrano stands in the dark under Roxane's balcony and refuses to climb into the light; it is "the rare occasion, when our hearts can speak / Our selves unseen, unseeing!" Night makes it easier for him: "I dare to be myself for once,--at last!" Darkness hides the face and frees the voice.

Then the Hermit. A Capuchin friar crosses the square with a lantern in his hand, and Cyrano jokingly calls him Diogenes. Among the Hermit's old names Waite gives this one too: "he is also the Capuchin". The friar is looking for Roxane's house, and once the wedding is settled his lantern falls first on Cyrano — and only then on the bridegroom's handsome face. The wedding itself takes place inside the house, with no audience.

And the Moon again. So that nobody can stop the ceremony, Cyrano pulls his hat over his eyes, changes his voice and drops from the balcony: "Like a bomb / I fell from the moon!" The union begins with a lunar fib — and with a letter that Roxane read aloud falsely.

For this couple the entry to the task is a common language of half-tones. The two are happiest where neither has to show themselves completely: in long correspondence, in voice messages after midnight, in jokes only they understand. Roxane notices that Christian's voice has suddenly changed, and asks nothing. A wish for mystery easily becomes an unspoken agreement not to ask awkward questions.

report.h3: Fifteen years of Saturdays

report: Act V is a convent garden fifteen years later. Roxane lives there as a widow and wears Christian's last letter on her breast. Cyrano comes every Saturday at the same hour and recites her "gazette": the King overate on fruit preserve, hundreds of candles burned at the ball. News of everyone — and not a word about himself. He boasts to the nuns that he ate meat on Friday, when in fact he has not eaten for two days. On the last Saturday he arrives wounded and passes off a fresh wound as an old one. Roxane answers that each of us has a wound "Never healed up", and puts her hand on the letter, not knowing that its author is sitting in the next chair.

This is the Hermit in the middle: **loyalty and silence at once.** Not a single Saturday missed, love shown in deeds — and each carries the hardest things alone. In a modern couple it is the Sunday dinner or the call at the same time every day, where everything is discussed except "I'm scared" and "I feel lonely". When Le Bret is asked to warn his friend to be prudent, he raises his arms to heaven: "Prudent! He!..." A man who throws himself alone against a hundred swords guards a single sentence for fifteen years. Waite's divinatory meanings for the Hermit begin with "Prudence", and for the reversed card they end with "unreasoned caution".

report.h3: One night hides, another gives away

report: The main task is the Moon again, but in the finale it works the other way round. Cyrano asks to read Christian's letter — the one he once wrote himself. The stage directions follow in turn: "Twilight begins to fall." "The shades of evening fall imperceptibly." "The darkness deepens." Roxane listens no longer to the words but to the voice; she looks over his shoulder and asks how he can read: "It is too dark to see!"

In the original the two night scenes share the same words. Under the balcony Cyrano excused his faltering: "c'est qu'il fait nuit", "it is because it is night". In the garden Roxane says: "il fait nuit". **The same night that hid him at the start gave him away at the end.** An 18-9-18 couple does not need to escape the Moon. It needs the darkness to stop being a shelter for the image and to become the place where people are recognised by their voice.

Rostand shows the price of silence to the very end. Cyrano denies everything, calling her "my sweet love" in the very sentence in which he swears he never loved her — the endearment tells the truth before the denial is finished. He had forbidden himself tears back in Act I: tenderness seemed ridiculous to him. But his tear remained on the farewell letter, and it is this tear that becomes the evidence. **What he hid as weakness turns out to be the only proof of love.** "I should have guessed, each time he said my name!" says Roxane. She had heard the other voice already under the balcony; what was missing was the question.

The hero had a model, the real Cyrano, and he wrote a novel about a journey to the Moon. It opens with the claim that the Moon is a world like this one, "to which ours serves as a moon". Each partner in such a couple sees the other by the reflected light of their own hopes and fears — and forgets that to the other they are a moon too.

report.h3: How to rewrite the ending

report: The numbers do not predict the ending of the play: the tail shows a plot, not a fate. Rostand himself left hints at the places where the plot could have turned.

ul: **Believe the permission already given.** Roxane said she would love Christian ugly, even disfigured: "Ay!" Cyrano believed it for a moment and did not get to finish.
**Ask instead of filling in.** Check a guess with words, not with one's own version of the answer, and do not load one's fears onto the partner.
**Say in daylight what is easy to write at night.** One sentence said aloud, face to face, weighs more than a dozen letters.
**Add a line about oneself to the "gazette".** The couple's ritual has room for one piece of news about oneself: "I'm tired", "I'm glad we're together".
**Tell solitude from disappearance.** Withdrawing into oneself is a way to restore strength, not a lack of love, as long as it is said aloud.

report: In the plus this tail is a rare gift: an intuition that recognises a voice in the dark after fifteen years, a shared secret world and a loyalty that needs no witnesses. A strong 18-9-18 couple keeps its night language and adds a daytime one. Its "il fait nuit" means only one thing: time to light the lamp and finish the conversation.
