seo.title: Karmic tail 18 9 9 compatibility: The Moon and two Hermits
seo.description: Karmic tail 18 9 9 compatibility in the destiny matrix: a shared secret at the entry, a path walked apart and the task of not letting solitude become silence.

items.title: Karmic tail 18-9-9 in compatibility: a secret for two and the task of not falling silent
items.short: The karmic tail 18-9-9 in destiny matrix compatibility is The Moon at the entry to the task and The Hermit twice: in the middle and in the main task. The couple comes together over a secret only the two of them understand, walks the path apart, each with a lantern of their own, and its main task is to keep solitude from turning into silence.

sections.h2: Letters planned on day one
paragraphs: In early twelfth-century Paris the most famous teacher was Peter Abelard. The most learned young woman in the kingdom was Heloise, niece of the canon Fulbert. Abelard set out to win her, and later, in his Historia calamitatum, he explained why he chose her. One of the reasons: "so, even if we were parted, we might yet be together in thought with the aid of written messages. Perchance, too, we might be able to write more boldly than we could speak".

The whole tail is already in that sentence. "To write more boldly than we could speak" is the language of The Moon: things said in half-light, not face to face. "Even if we were parted" is The Hermit, who has not arrived yet but is already on his mind. Abelard provided for separation before the first meeting. Some fifteen years later it came true to the letter: the two lived in two monasteries and wrote to each other. Only the first letter that arrived was not about love. It was about silence.

This article does not claim that an 18-9-9 couple is headed for a monastery. The cards do not predict events: no partings, no catastrophes, no dates. What matches is the mechanism — a secret at the entry, withdrawal in the middle, silence as the main task. It is worth taking apart step by step: the evidence is in the letters, in Waite's and Wen's books and in the numbers themselves.

sections.h2: Entry to the task, 18 — The Moon: "secret retreats"
paragraphs: The first point of a couple's tail is what the two want together: shared wishes, agreements, a common language. On the site the same point also appears in the sphere "Relationship and common language" under the label "Common language". For an 18-9-9 couple the common language is The Moon. The point lies on the line of tasks, so the same wish can also become resistance.

For Abelard and Heloise the common language was lessons. Fulbert took the famous teacher into his house and entrusted his niece to him, to be taught "no matter whether by day or by night". Abelard says he was astounded by such simplicity: it was as if the uncle "had entrusted a tender lamb to the care of a ravenous wolf". Then: "Under the pretext of study we spent our hours in the happiness of love, and learning held out to us the secret opportunities that our passion craved. Our speech was more of love than of the book which lay open before us".

Abelard's Latin is sharper: secretos regressus, "secret retreats". Two words — a secret and a retreat — and the tail fits into one phrase: The Moon's secrecy and The Hermit's withdrawal. From the very start the two withdrew not from each other but together, from everyone else.

The Moon has a strange property: a secret for two quickly becomes a rumour for all. Abelard wrote songs about his love, and, as he says, "some have become widely known and have been sung in many lands". Only one man failed to guess: the thing "could deceive only a few, no one, methinks, save him whose shame it chiefly bespoke, the girl's uncle, Fulbert". Everyone found out except the one they were hiding from.

Then the entry turns into resistance. When the secret came out, Abelard offered to marry, on one condition: "provided only the thing could be kept secret". They were married early in the morning after a night of prayer in a church, before the uncle and a few friends. When Fulbert's household began to talk about the marriage, Heloise, Abelard writes, "swore that they were speaking the most absolute lies". Every cover demanded the next one: the lessons hid the love, the secret marriage hid the love from gossip, and the nun's habit in which Abelard himself dressed Heloise at Argenteuil hid the wife from her family's anger. The end came at night: Fulbert's people bribed a servant and mutilated Abelard in his sleep.

Among the tasks of a couple with The Moon, Lisovskaya names an image created at the start which later collapses. Abelard and Heloise created that image not for each other but together, for the world. The same often holds for an 18-9-9 couple: The Moon at the entry is less a deception of the partner than a shared conspiracy against outsiders.

In today's life it looks familiar. An affair kept from colleagues for six months. A relationship the parents learned about last. Messages in which both are bolder than at dinner: confessions in writing, jokes in person. Private nicknames, private words, the feeling of being read without words. That is the strength of The Moon: intuition, play, a world for two. The weakness grows from the same root: the agreement "we don't talk about the important things" first hides the couple from the world and then starts working inside it. Jealousy over an invented story, hurt over words the partner never said — that is The Moon too, only turned inward.

sections.h2: Middle of the task, 9 — The Hermit: "by separate ways"
paragraphs: Lisovskaya gives the middle of a couple's tail no meaning of its own: it is an "addition" to the main task. In our reading the middle shows how the couple walks from the shared wish to the main task. For 18-9-9 that road runs through The Hermit, through each partner withdrawing into their own.

For Abelard the middle begins on the day of the wedding. Straight after the secret ceremony, he writes, "We departed forthwith stealthily and by separate ways, nor thereafter did we see each other save rarely and in private". From the shared secret to the main task the road runs through two separate doors.

The Hermit in the middle is not necessarily coldness. After their first parting, when Fulbert learned everything, Abelard writes: "Each grieved most, not for himself, but for the other", and "The very sundering of our bodies served but to link our souls closer together". Distance can bring people closer. In Lisovskaya's description the positive Hermit looks quite ordinary: each has a corner of the home and an hour of quiet, and love shows in deeds rather than words.

Then came two monasteries, Saint-Denis and Argenteuil. Abelard withdrew to wasteland near Troyes and there "built with reeds and stalks" an oratory. Students followed him, built huts above the river Arduzon, "so that they seemed hermits rather than scholars". Abelard named the oratory the Paraclete — Greek for "the Consoler". At Argenteuil Heloise became the head of her community. Each grew into a lantern of their own.

The danger of the middle is time. A pause that was chosen becomes the default. Two people at two desks, in two pairs of headphones. One on shifts, the other studying. A long-distance relationship where "we don't call every day, and we're fine". It really is fine while the quiet remains a choice. The tail tests something else: whether the two will notice when it stops being one.

sections.h2: Main task, 9 — The Hermit: a consolation sent to a friend
paragraphs: The main point of a couple's tail is its task and trial; Lisovskaya reads it mostly through its weak side. For 18-9-9 it is The Hermit again, but in another role: the middle shows the path, the task shows what has to be learned on it.

In 1129 the nuns were driven out of Argenteuil, and Abelard made over his Paraclete to Heloise, "together with everything pertaining thereto". A few years later he wrote the Historia calamitatum as a letter of consolation to an unnamed friend. The letter reached Heloise. Her reply is the central scene of this tail.

"You wrote your friend a long letter of consolation, about his misfortunes indeed, but about your own. Recalling them so carefully in order to console him, you have greatly added to our desolation." And then: "Tell me one thing, if you can: why, after our entry into religion, which you alone decided on, have I fallen into such neglect and oblivion with you that I am neither refreshed by your talk when you are here nor consoled by your letters when you are away?" (Heloise's letters are quoted in our translation from the Latin.)

The man who named his retreat the Consoler and wrote a consolation to a friend did not console the one closest to him. He knew the weight of that word himself. Having left the Paraclete to become an abbot in Brittany, he wrote: "Justly has this sorrow come upon me because I deserted the Paraclete, which is to say the Consoler, and thrust myself into sure desolation". In Heloise's Latin the words rhyme: his consolatio for a friend became her desolatio — comfort for one turned into desolation for the other.

In Lisovskaya, the weak side of The Hermit in a couple is the same picture: trouble piles up in silence, and when things get hard each retreats into their own shell instead of reaching out a hand. Heloise adds a precise image: "You tend a vineyard of another man's vines, which you did not plant… Consider what you owe to your own, you who spend such care on another's."

In a modern couple the letter to a friend looks like this. She learns how hard his autumn was from his conversation with a friend. He learns about her doubts from her own post. There is light, but it burns for others: colleagues, students, clients, followers. At home it is quiet and polite.

sections.h2: "Do not think me strong": how the trap closes
paragraphs: Abelard replied. His first sentence is the most recognisable line of this tail: "If since our conversion from the world to God I have not yet written you any word of comfort or exhortation, this must be put down not to my negligence but to your wisdom, in which I have always had the greatest confidence. I was sure it needed nothing of the kind" (our translation).

In today's words it is shorter: "You're strong, you'll manage." Heloise had answered that before she heard it: "the more secure I have made you, the more neglect I have to bear." And in her second letter, directly: "Do not think me strong, or I may fall before you can hold me up as I slip." And again: "Always fear for me, I beg you, rather than trust in me, so that your care may always help me."

This is the mechanism of the main task. In a couple whose task is The Hermit, respect for the other's independence quietly becomes a reason not to ask. Trust turns into inattention, and inattention looks like trust. Lisovskaya puts the task her own way: to sense when to support and when to leave the other in peace. Abelard chose "leave in peace" where "support" was needed, and sincerely believed it was respect.

There is a second half to the trap. Abelard gave Heloise his retreat with everything in it: The Hermit's love is shown in deeds. She asked for something else: "In vain do I hope for you to be generous in deeds if I find you a miser with words." A renovated flat, a car, paid-for courses — and not one "how are you?". In an 18-9-9 couple one partner often gives in deeds while the other waits for words.

And one more detail without which the story is not honest. Heloise was hiding too. The flawless abbess whom bishops praised writes: "Men call me chaste because they have not found out the hypocrite", and to Abelard: "For a long time my pretence deceived you, as it deceived many, so that you took hypocrisy for piety." The silence was double: he kept his troubles from her, she kept her real self behind the image of a model abbess. In an 18-9-9 couple either partner can be the silent one, and more often both take turns.

Heloise's comparison shows how the tail changed from entry to task: "When long ago you sought me for base pleasures, you visited me with letter after letter, and with song after song you put your Heloise on every tongue." The Moon spoke easily — in hints, songs and letters. The Hermit fell silent. The main task is to bring the words back without giving up the solitude.

sections.h2: The Moon and The Hermit in Waite and Wen
paragraphs: In Waite's divinatory list the reversed Moon includes the word silence: "Instability, inconstancy, silence, lesser degrees of deception and error". A calculated number is never reversed, and this is no verdict on the couple. But the vocabulary is telling: The Moon already knows silence, and The Hermit will make it a task.

Benebell Wen separates The Moon from The High Priestess with a pair of sentences: "Key 2 is about disguise. Key 18 is about revelation of the inner self". The Priestess is disguise, The Moon is the inner self coming out. For a couple that matters: The Moon at the entry is not a card of deceit but a card of what has not been said yet and is asking to come out.

Of the crayfish crawling out of the water on Waite's Moon card, Wen writes: "there is a sense of needing to feel protected, and thus forming the tough outer shell. Simultaneously, there is a profound vulnerability that the Seeker is trying to conceal from others". A tough shell and a vulnerability hidden under it. In Lisovskaya, the task of a couple with The Hermit is not to hide "in one's shell" when things get hard. The Moon's shell and The Hermit's shell are one and the same defence. The mask of the flawless abbess was such a shell, and "do not think me strong" was the vulnerability finally coming ashore.
On the same Waite card a dog and a wolf bay at the moon. Describing the beginning, Abelard called himself the wolf.

Wen describes The Hermit this way: "The Hermit is a guardian of higher thoughts and contemplation". The word "guardian" will come back. And in Waite's divinatory list The Hermit has, besides prudence, dissimulation — the very pretence Heloise confessed to.

sections.h2: A room with two cards: the evidence in the numbers
paragraphs: The 18-9-9 tail occurs in 1.754% of couples, about one in 57; it ranks 18th of the 97 couple tails. The site's engine shows more: this tail locks the couple inside two cards.

The Moon and The Hermit are the only cards from 1 to 22 divisible by nine. Reducing a number to 22 by adding its digits does not change its remainder after division by nine. And the inner points of the matrix are all derived from the main task: by that remainder the centre equals two main tasks, the entry three, the middle four and the values six. If the main task is divisible by nine, so is everything else. That is why, in a couple with The Hermit as the main task, the entry, the middle, the centre and "The couple's values" can only be The Moon or The Hermit. The arithmetic lets no other card in.

Every ninth couple is built this way: in 11.1% the main task is The Hermit or The Moon. There are eight tails made only of these two cards, and all eight occur. 18-9-9 is the third most frequent of them, after 9-9-18 and 9-9-9.

What this means for the atmosphere. The couple's centre, that is "The atmosphere inside the couple", is The Moon in 57.1% of 18-9-9 couples and The Hermit in 42.9%. "The couple's values" are The Hermit in 64.3% and The Moon in 35.7%. Together: in 36.4% of couples The Moon is in the centre and The Hermit in the values, in 27.9% The Hermit is in both, in 20.7% The Moon is in both, and in 15% The Hermit is in the centre and The Moon in the values. With The Moon in the centre the partner is a friend first and understanding comes without words, while on the weak side it is unclear whether the two are friends or rivals, and secrets become weapons. With The Hermit in the centre each has a corner and a time of their own, while on the weak side each lives on their own.
When Lisovskaya reads a couple's tail, she adds its energies in pairs and all three together. The Moon and The Hermit give 18 + 9 = 27, which is 9 again. Two Hermits give 18, The Moon.
Now add up all three numbers.
18 + 9 + 9 = 36, and 3 + 6 = 9. No combination leads out of the two cards: the tail keeps returning to itself, like two people walking from cell to cell.

Where these cards come from in the two partners. The 18-9-9 tail is formed by five combinations of the partners' personal tails. Most often these are 15-20-5 and 3-7-22 (34% of such couples), 12-19-7 and 6-8-20 (26%), 15-5-8 and 3-22-19 (24%). In 83% of couples neither partner has The Moon or The Hermit in their personal tail: this room appears only between them. In 16%, couples with the personal tails 9-12-3 and 9-15-6, both personal tails begin with a nine, and two Hermits together give The Moon at the couple's entry.

sections.h2: An example: how a couple gets 18-9-9
paragraphs: Take two dates: 07.08.1976 and 05.07.1975. The first partner's personal tail is 6-8-20, the second's is 12-19-7. Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22 if the sum is larger.

The couple's middle is calculated from the partners' middles, not from the two outer numbers of the couple. Here the result would be the same, but the rule is different, and in other couples the difference shows.

In this couple The Hermit reaches far beyond the tail. The centre is 4 + 5 = 9. "The couple's values" are also 9: they are recalculated from the couple's own sums, not added from the partners' values (3 and 15 would give The Moon). Further:

sections.h2: The strong version: guardians of solitude
paragraphs: For Abelard and Heloise the correspondence did not end in reproach. In his first reply Abelard wrote: "write to me about whatever you wish, so that I may answer you" (our translation). Heloise began to ask, and never stopped. She asked him to tell how communities of women began and to write a rule for a women's house; Abelard wrote both. For the Paraclete he composed hymns. Later Heloise sent him forty-two questions on difficult passages of Scripture, and he answered every one. The two remained hermits, each in their own monastery. But their solitude became a conversation.

Heloise became a lantern herself. Abelard writes of her as head of the Paraclete: "The less often she allowed herself to be seen, shutting herself up in her cell to devote herself to sacred meditations and prayers, the more eagerly did those who dwelt without demand her presence and the spiritual guidance of her words." His retreat became her home, and, in his own words, "the place proved itself a true Paraclete to them". When Abelard died in 1142, his body was secretly carried to the Paraclete. Later Heloise was buried beside him. In 1817 their remains, as is generally believed, were moved to Père Lachaise cemetery, and by tradition people bring letters there.

Rilke wrote down the formula of the strong version eight centuries later. In a letter to Emanuel von Bodman of 17 August 1901 he called a good marriage "that in which each appoints the other guardian of his solitude, and shows him this confidence, the greatest in his power to bestow". And he added that the measure for choosing a person must be "whether one is willing to stand guard over the solitude of a person and whether one is inclined to set this same person at the gate of one's own solitude, of which he learns only through that which steps, festively clothed, out of the great darkness".

Here is the 18-9-9 tail in one picture. The great darkness is The Moon of the entry. The solitude is The Hermit. The main task is to stand at the gate rather than move to another city, and to bring to the gate what was born in the dark. Abelard was at first a guardian who had left his post. With her letters Heloise brought him back to it.
What helps a couple with this tail:

ul: **Name the withdrawal.** "I need some time alone; it's not about us" — a silence with a name is not frightening.
**Don't take strength for having no needs.** Ask "how are you?" of exactly the one who always copes.
**Add a word to the deed.** A repair, a gift, a paid bill — and one sentence about why.
**Tell the partner about the trouble first, and a friend second.** Not the other way round.
**Keep a shared Paraclete.** A place or ritual where two silences meet: an evening walk, a weekly letter, a morning hour without phones.
**Keep the secret for two, and keep no secrets from each other about what matters.** The Moon of the entry is an alliance against the world, not a wall inside the couple.
**Don't put out the other's hermitage.** Among the tasks of a couple with The Hermit, Lisovskaya lists not extinguishing a partner's interest in their own pursuits.

paragraphs: If the silence in a couple rests on fear, bans or threats, it is no longer about the tail: it is a reason to call a local emergency number or crisis line, or to see a psychologist.

sections.h2: 18-9-9, 9-9-18 and 9-18-9: the same cards in a different order
paragraphs: The same numbers make two more couple tails. In 9-9-18 the couple enters the task through The Hermit, with a wish for quiet and space of its own, and the main task becomes The Moon: fears, invented stories, trust in what is left unsaid. It occurs in 3.26% of couples, and their centre is The Moon in 74% of cases.

In 9-18-9 the entry and the task are The Hermit, while the middle passes through The Moon: the path runs through fog, secrets and misunderstandings. That is 1.136% of couples, with The Moon in the centre in 81.3%. Only in 18-9-9 does the secret come at the start and the solitude in the lesson.
The personal karmic tail 18-9-9 is a different calculation with different roles for the points; the site has a separate article on it, and its conclusions do not carry over to the couple.

sections.h2: Where the quotations come from

ul: Peter Abelard, Historia calamitatum, translated by Henry Adams Bellows (1922). Heloise's letters and Abelard's reply are quoted in our translation; Latin words checked against the text of the Historia and of Heloise's first letter.
A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, 1922 reissue — divinatory meanings of The Moon and The Hermit.
Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot, 2015 — the chapters on The Moon and The Hermit.
Yuliana Lisovskaya, Matritsa sudby: sovmestimost (The Destiny Matrix: Compatibility), 2024 — the meaning of a couple's points and of energies 9 and 18 in a couple.
R. M. Rilke, letter to Emanuel von Bodman of 17 August 1901, from Letters of Rainer Maria Rilke, 1892–1910, translated by Jane Bannard Greene and M. D. Herter Norton (1945).

intro: The riddle of this tail is that a union in which two people understand each other without words is given words as its task. The three roles in brief:

ul: **18 · The Moon — entry to the task.** Where the couple starts and what it agrees on: a common language of hints and half-sentences, a world for two hidden from everyone else. The same wish for secrecy also becomes resistance: it is easier to keep quiet about what matters most.

**9 · The Hermit — middle of the task.** How the couple walks the path: each withdrawing into their own work, study, quiet or separate room. Distance can bring them closer here, but pauses easily turn into habit.
**9 · The Hermit — main task.** What the two have to learn: not to leave the other alone with their trouble, not to mistake a partner's strength for having no needs, and to put care into words.

intro: About one couple in 57 has this tail. Eight hundred years ago two people lived out its plot, Peter Abelard and Heloise, and she left the most precise words about it.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 18-9-9 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of a couple's matrix: The Moon at the entry to the task, The Hermit in the middle and in the main task. The couple comes together over a shared secret and an understanding without words, walks the path with each withdrawing into their own, and the main task is to keep solitude from becoming silence: share troubles, ask the strong one too, add words to deeds.

faq.q: Is the 18-9-9 tail a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail shows a task, not a rating of the union; the method gives no compatibility percentages. This tail's strength is right there in the cards: the two can be close without getting in each other's way, and they understand more than they say. The difficulty comes from the same source: silence is easy to mistake for calm.

faq.q: Does 18-9-9 mean the couple is destined to live apart?
faq.a: No. The cards predict neither partings nor moves. The Hermit in the middle and in the task speaks of how the couple walks its path and what it learns: to protect each partner's solitude while not leaving the other alone. The story of Abelard and Heloise is an example of the mechanism, not a forecast.

faq.q: Why is the centre of an 18-9-9 couple only The Moon or The Hermit?
faq.a: Because of the arithmetic of reduction. Adding digits does not change the remainder after division by nine, and by that remainder the couple's centre, entry, middle and values depend on the main task. If the task is The Hermit, they are all divisible by nine, and only two cards are: 9 and 18. In 57.1% of 18-9-9 couples the centre is The Moon, in 42.9% The Hermit.

faq.q: If one partner has the personal tail 18-9-9, is it the same thing?
faq.a: No. A personal tail is calculated from one date, and its points have different roles. A couple's tail is the sum of the points of two matrices. In 83% of couples with the 18-9-9 tail neither partner has The Moon or The Hermit in their personal tail: these cards appear only when the two are together.

faq.q: How is a couple's tail calculated?
faq.a: A personal matrix is calculated for each partner, then the matching points are added and the sum is reduced to 22. The entry to the task is the sum of the partners' entries, the middle the sum of their middles, the main task the sum of their main tasks. For example, 07.08.1976 and 05.07.1975 give 6 + 12 = 18, 8 + 19 = 27 → 9 and 20 + 7 = 27 → 9.

report: Peter Abelard chose Heloise partly because, even if they were parted, they could write to each other: "we might be able to write more boldly than we could speak". He thought about separation before the first meeting. Some fifteen years later the two lived in two monasteries and wrote letters. The first of them was not about love but about silence.

This twelfth-century story holds the couple's karmic tail 18-9-9: The Moon at the entry to the task, The Hermit in the middle and in the main task. The cards promise no monasteries and no partings. What matches is the mechanism: **a secret at the entry, withdrawal in the middle, silence as the main task.**

report.h3: A secret two people retreat into

report: The entry to the task is what the two want together: their agreements and their common language. For Abelard and Heloise the common language was lessons: her uncle took the famous teacher into his house and entrusted his niece to him. "Under the pretext of study we spent our hours in the happiness of love." Abelard's Latin calls what learning offered them secretos regressus, "secret retreats". The Moon's secrecy and The Hermit's withdrawal — the whole tail in one phrase.

A secret for two quickly became a rumour for all: Abelard's songs about his love were sung in many lands, and only the uncle failed to guess. When everything came out, Abelard agreed to marry on one condition: "provided only the thing could be kept secret". Every cover demanded the next: the lessons hid the love, the secret marriage hid the love from gossip, the nun's habit hid the wife from her family's anger.

For a couple with this tail, The Moon at the entry is less a deception of the partner than **a shared conspiracy against outsiders**. An affair kept from colleagues for six months. Messages in which both are bolder than at dinner. Private words and the feeling of being read without words. The weakness grows from the same root: the agreement "we don't talk about the important things" first hides the couple from the world and then starts working inside it.

report.h3: Straight after the wedding, by separate ways

report: The middle of the tail shows how the couple walks its path. For 18-9-9 it runs through each partner withdrawing into their own. Straight after the secret ceremony, Abelard writes, "We departed forthwith stealthily and by separate ways, nor thereafter did we see each other save rarely and in private".

The Hermit here is not necessarily coldness. After their first parting Abelard notes: "The very sundering of our bodies served but to link our souls closer together". Then came two monasteries. Abelard built an oratory in the wasteland "with reeds and stalks" and named it the Paraclete — Greek for "the Consoler". Each grew into a lantern of their own.

The danger of the middle is time. Two people at two desks, in two pairs of headphones; "we don't call every day, and we're fine". It really is fine while the quiet remains a choice and does not become the default pause.

report.h3: A consolation sent to a friend

report: Years later Abelard made over his Paraclete to Heloise, and then wrote the Historia calamitatum, a letter of consolation to an unnamed friend. The letter reached Heloise. Her reply is the central scene of the tail: "You wrote your friend a long letter of consolation… Recalling them so carefully in order to console him, you have greatly added to our desolation." And then: "Tell me one thing, if you can: why… have I fallen into such neglect and oblivion with you that I am neither refreshed by your talk when you are here nor consoled by your letters when you are away?"

**The man who named his retreat the Consoler did not console the one closest to him.** In Heloise's Latin the words rhyme: his consolatio for a friend became her desolatio. Today it looks like this: she learns how hard his autumn was from his conversation with a friend. There is light, but it burns for others — colleagues, students, clients. At home it is quiet and polite.

report.h3: "Do not think me strong"

report: Abelard replied, and his excuse is the most recognisable line of this tail: his silence came not from negligence but from her wisdom, "in which I have always had the greatest confidence. I was sure it needed nothing of the kind". In short: **"You're strong, you'll manage."**

Heloise had answered that in her first letter: "the more secure I have made you, the more neglect I have to bear." And in her second, directly: "Do not think me strong." This is the mechanism of the main task: in an 18-9-9 couple, respect for the other's independence quietly becomes a reason not to ask. Trust turns into inattention, and inattention looks like trust.

The second half of the trap is deeds instead of words. Abelard gave Heloise his retreat with everything in it; she asked for something else: "In vain do I hope for you to be generous in deeds if I find you a miser with words." And in fairness: Heloise was hiding too, behind the image of a flawless abbess — "men call me chaste because they have not found out the hypocrite", she writes of those who praised her. Either partner can be the silent one, and more often both take turns.

report.h3: A guardian at the gate

report: The correspondence did not end in reproach. Abelard asked: "write to me about whatever you wish, so that I may answer you". Heloise began to ask, and never stopped. Abelard wrote a rule for her community and hymns for the Paraclete, and answered her forty-two questions on difficult passages of Scripture one by one. The two remained hermits, each in their own monastery, but **their solitude became a conversation.**

Eight centuries later Rilke called a good marriage "that in which each appoints the other guardian of his solitude" — and the guardian learns of that solitude only "through that which steps, festively clothed, out of the great darkness". The great darkness is The Moon of the entry, the solitude is The Hermit, and the main task is to stand at the gate rather than move to another city.
What helps a couple with this tail:

ul: name the withdrawal: "I need some time alone; it's not about us";
ask "how are you?" of exactly the one who always copes;
add a word to the deed — one sentence about why;
tell the partner about the trouble first, and a friend second;
keep a shared Paraclete — a walk, a letter, an hour without phones, where two silences meet.

seo.title: Karmic tail 21 10 16 compatibility: World, Wheel and Tower
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 10 16 compatibility: The World at the entry, The Wheel of Fortune in the middle, The Tower as the main task, read through Antony and Cleopatra.

items.title: Karmic tail 21-10-16 in compatibility: when a whole world is not enough for two
items.short: The couple's karmic tail 21-10-16 begins with The World, the fullest card in the deck, and runs into The Tower. Why does a union that enters its task with the words "we have everything" learn its lesson through a collapse? The answer is written into three roles. The World at the entry to the task is the shared wish to be a whole world to each other, without measure or limits. The Wheel of Fortune in the middle is a path in circles: rise, quarrel, reconciliation and rise again. The Tower as the main task is the day the invented image of the partner falls apart; what the couple has to learn is to meet that day together, not each inside a fortress of their own.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: "new heaven, new earth"
paragraphs: The play opens with two people measuring their love. Their very first exchange (Shakespeare is quoted in the original throughout, Plutarch in Bernadotte Perrin's translation):
— If it be love indeed, tell me how much. — There's beggary in the love that can be reckon'd. — I'll set a bourn how far to be beloved. — Then must thou needs find out new heaven, new earth.

The last line is almost word for word the Book of Revelation: "And I saw a new heaven and a new earth" (21:1), where the old world passes away and a new one opens. The chapter number matches the card's number by chance; the meaning does not. The World at the entry to the task is exactly that promise of a new heaven and a new earth: two people begin by declaring their love bigger than everything else.

In Lisovskaya's reading, point M is what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, a "common language". For a 21-10-16 couple that language is the language of the whole. Antony speaks it in the same scene: "Let Rome in Tiber melt, and the wide arch / Of the ranged empire fall! Here is my space. / Kingdoms are clay." And, embracing Cleopatra, he binds "the world to weet / We stand up peerless". Two people become the measure for the whole world.

Plutarch shows how this language sounds in everyday life. At night Antony, dressed as a servant, roamed Alexandria, stopping at the doors and windows of ordinary people to mock them, and Cleopatra went with him, "wearing the garb of a serving maiden". Once he was fishing, the fish would not bite, and he ordered divers to fasten fish already caught to his hook in secret. Cleopatra saw through the trick, invited her friends to watch the next day, and had one of her own people fasten a salted Pontic herring to his hook. Amid the laughter she said: "Imperator, hand over thy fishing-rod to the fishermen of Pharos and Canopus; thy sport is the hunting of cities, realms, and continents" (Plutarch, Life of Antony, 29). That is The World at the entry: the partners set each other's scale. A joke, an adventure, a dare, and every one of them the size of a world map.

In its plus, such a couple can be seen from far away. The two live unlike everyone else: they move, travel, build a philosophy of life of their own, and many people see them as an ideal couple. But M stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. In the very first scene a messenger brings news from Rome, and Antony answers: "Grates me: the sum." Everything beyond the two of them is noise. Later, handing out kingdoms to his children, Antony gave his son Armenia, Media and Parthia, Parthia, as Plutarch notes, "when he should have subdued it" (54). It was never subdued. The World at the entry easily becomes a world on credit: the couple has already arranged the furniture in a house not yet bought and shared out a future that does not yet exist.

Hence the first clue. A love that has declared itself a whole world cannot make room for a crack. In an ordinary couple a failure is a failure. In a couple with The World at the entry any crack looks like the end of the world, because no spare world was ever planned.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: Cleopatra's twenty deaths
paragraphs: How do you keep a whole world alive if it cannot stand still? You spin it. Cleopatra sends a servant to Antony with precise orders: "See where he is, who's with him, what he does: / I did not send you: if you find him sad, / Say I am dancing; if in mirth, report / That I am sudden sick."

Her attendant Charmian advises the opposite: "In each thing give him way, cross him nothing." Cleopatra answers: "Thou teachest like a fool; the way to lose him." And Antony's Roman friend Enobarbus remarks drily that Cleopatra, at the least noise of bad news, "dies instantly; I have seen her die twenty times upon far poorer moment".

This is The Wheel of Fortune in the middle of the task: for such a couple the path from the wish at M to the task at D runs in circles. And in Shakespeare the wheel works. Enobarbus explains why Antony will never leave Cleopatra: "Age cannot wither her, nor custom stale / Her infinite variety." Other women cloy the appetites they feed, "but she makes hungry / Where most she satisfies". Antony goes to Rome, marries Caesar's sister there ("And though I make this marriage for my peace, / I' the east my pleasure lies") and comes back. Rome, Egypt, Rome again, Egypt again.

Lisovskaya calls the ten a symbol of cycles: rises and crises in a couple follow one another, and the change itself has to be accepted, not fought. In its minus it is a swing of "calm, then conflict", and the feeling that being together is hard and yet something holds. This couple's wheel shows in small things. After a quarrel, a week of model tenderness. Then a chill with no explanation. Then a trip that mends everything. Friends know the cycle by heart and no longer ask what has happened this time.

Plutarch left the most vivid scene of such a wheel, and it is set in a kitchen. A young man studying in Alexandria at the time was shown round by the royal cooks and saw "eight wild boars a-roasting". He assumed a crowd of guests was expected. The cook laughed: there were only about twelve guests, but Antony might ask for supper at once, or put it off and get caught up in conversation, so "not one, but many suppers are arranged; for the precise time is hard to hit" (28). The home of a couple with The Wheel in the middle keeps eight boars at different stages of readiness: in case of tenderness, in case of a quarrel, in case of a sudden departure.

The numbers say the same. The middle of the couple's tail is the sum of the two personal middles, and for couples with this tail it always comes to 37. That is more than 22: the sum overflows and is reduced, 3 + 7 = 10. This couple's Wheel is always born of excess. The play's first line is about excess too: the Roman Philo complains that his general's dotage "o'erflows the measure".

Charmian names the danger of the Wheel in the same scene: "In time we hate that which we often fear." Among the tasks of the ten, Lisovskaya also lists moving away from manipulation, grudges and hysterics. A wheel turned by hand teaches the partner to fear the next turn. And a scene rehearsed twenty times will one day be played at the moment when the game is already over.

sections.h2: Main task: The Tower that struck more than once
paragraphs: The main point of the tail is D, and it is read mostly through the minus: what the couple fails at and what it has to learn. Lisovskaya's first task of The Tower is the collapse of the invented image of the partner, when the person turns out to be someone else entirely. Next to it she sets a second, very recognisable one: when something bad happens, the two look and walk in different directions. The play tests the couple on both tasks twice.

The first time is at Actium. In the thick of the sea battle Cleopatra's sixty ships turn and flee, and Antony, in the words of one of his officers, "like a doting mallard", leaves the fight and flies after her. Plutarch describes what happened on board afterwards. Antony did not look at her: he sat down at the prow holding his head in both hands, and "he spent three days by himself at the prow, either because he was angry with Cleopatra, or ashamed to see her" (67). Only at Taenarum "the women in Cleopatra's company at first brought them into a parley, and then persuaded them to eat and sleep together".

Shakespeare compresses those three days into one scene. Antony: "O, whither hast thou led me, Egypt?" Cleopatra: "Forgive my fearful sails! I little thought / You would have follow'd." Antony: "My heart was to thy rudder tied by the strings." The reproach is spoken, the fault admitted, and then comes a decision, the main task lived in its plus:
Fall not a tear, I say; one of them rates All that is won and lost: give me a kiss; Even this repays me.

"All that is won and lost" is the Wheel's ledger, its gains and losses. A partner's tear is not part of that ledger: it is worth more than the whole account. Antony ends the scene by defying fortune: "Fortune knows / We scorn her most when most she offers blows." The collapse has been lived through together.

The second time is at Alexandria. Before Antony's eyes his fleet raises its oars, salutes Caesar's ships and goes over to the enemy. Antony cries: "All is lost; / This foul Egyptian hath betrayed me." Cleopatra, "fearing his anger and his madness", as Plutarch puts it, shuts herself in her tomb near the temple of Isis, a monument "built surpassingly lofty and beautiful" (74), and has the drop-doors let fall. Then she chooses the Wheel's old move, one more death:
Mardian, go tell him I have slain myself; Say, that the last I spoke was "Antony," And word it, prithee, piteously: hence, Mardian, And bring me how he takes my death.

"Bring me how he takes my death" is a test, a game played with feelings at the moment when the game is already over. Antony believes it. A little later another messenger arrives with the truth and says: "I dread, too late."

What makes the second scene different from the first? After Actium the two, even if on the third day and with someone else's help, talk to each other face to face. At Alexandria they do not speak once until it is too late: between them go messengers, a false report and a test. Each is in a tower of their own. Hers is the tomb with its bolts. He had built his even earlier: after Actium he settled on a mole at Pharos, named the dwelling the Timoneum after the Athenian misanthrope, and, Plutarch says, "hated and distrusted all mankind" (69, 71). That is this couple's Tower in its minus: not the lightning as such, but two fortresses where two people wait out the lightning alone.

Shakespeare's ending is literal. The dying Antony is hoisted on ropes to the window of the monument, and Cleopatra, with her two women, pulls him up with her own hands: "How heavy weighs my lord!" They are together again, at the top of the tower, where nothing can be changed any more. This is tragedy, and Shakespeare plays the minus out to the end. The matrix does not predict endings. It shows a mechanism, and the play contains the way out of it too: the scene after Actium.

One note for real life. Cleopatra's pretended death is a stage device. If someone in a real couple threatens to harm themselves, even "as a test", this is no longer a conversation about cards but a reason to call a local emergency number or a crisis line.

sections.h2: "A tower'd citadel" in the clouds: what really collapses
paragraphs: Before he believes the false report, Antony speaks the strangest speech in the play, a speech about clouds: "Sometimes we see a cloud that's dragonish; / A vapour sometime like a bear or lion, / A tower'd citadel, a pendent rock… / That which is now a horse, even with a thought / The rack dislimns, and makes it indistinct, / As water is in water."

Among the clouds stands "a tower'd citadel", a fortress with towers. Shakespeare's tower is literally made of cloud, and what falls apart is what was only an image. Then Antony speaks about himself: "here I am Antony: / Yet cannot hold this visible shape." This is the play's central discovery about the tail 21-10-16. Lisovskaya writes that the task of The Tower is the collapse of the invented image of the partner. Shakespeare adds that one's own image collapses along with the partner's, because it was built around the other person. Cleopatra was the one "whose bosom was my crownet, my chief end".

What words does Antony find for the betrayal? The language of cards: "she, Eros, has / Pack'd cards with Caesar, and false-play'd my glory / Unto an enemy's triumph." In plain terms, she has stacked the deck with Caesar and played away his glory into an enemy's triumph. In Shakespeare's day triumph was also the name of a card game with trumps, and the English word trump is traced back to triumph. In fifteenth-century Italy the cards that later became the Major Arcana of the tarot were called trionfi, "triumphs". Antony describes his Tower as a hand of cards in which his partner gave the trump to the enemy.

A few minutes later he refutes himself with the same word. Dying, he says: "Not Caesar's valour hath o'erthrown Antony, / But Antony's hath triumph'd on itself." The trump that beat him was in his own hand. And was there a betrayal at all? The play never proves it. Cleopatra's messenger says Antony suspected her of dealing with Caesar, "which never shall be found". The image fell before the facts were known.

In the last act Cleopatra does the opposite. Antony is gone, and she rebuilds his image to the size of the universe: "I dream'd there was an Emperor Antony… / His legs bestrid the ocean: his rear'd arm / Crested the world." Then she asks the Roman Dolabella whether such a man could ever have existed. "Gentle madam, no," he answers. The task of a 21-10-16 couple is to do this in the reverse order: to let go of the invented image while the living person is still beside them.

sections.h2: The Hierophant in the centre: a third voice in the couple
paragraphs: Every couple with the tail 21-10-16 has 5, The Hierophant, in the centre. One hundred per cent, no exceptions. For Lisovskaya the couple's centre is the shared atmosphere between the partners, what lies inside and is not on show. The couple enters its task speaking a language "without measure", yet inside it lives the card of measure: rules, traditions, marriage as an institution, the voice of "how things should be".

In the play that voice is Rome. It is there from the first scene: messengers, letters, an Antony suddenly lost in thought. "He was disposed to mirth; but on the sudden / A Roman thought hath struck him," Cleopatra observes. Rome also arrives as a marriage of alliance: Antony marries Octavia to seal his peace with Caesar, and Enobarbus predicts that "the band that seems to tie their friendship together will be the very strangler of their amity", and that "that which is the strength of their amity shall prove the immediate author of their variance". About Octavia he says three words that read like a portrait of the fifth card: "holy, cold, and still". In Waite's divinatory list for The Hierophant stand exactly "Marriage, alliance, captivity, servitude".

But The Hierophant lives inside the passion itself as well. Enobarbus says of Cleopatra that "vilest things / Become themselves in her: that the holy priests / Bless her when she is riggish". The holy priests bless her even in her wantonness. And in Plutarch the couple founds an institution of its own: "they had an association called The Inimitable Livers, and every day they feasted one another" (28). Two people who have abolished other people's rules at once create their own, with a name and rites. The Alexandrians, Plutarch writes, said that Antony "used the tragic mask with the Romans, but the comic mask with them".

In the lovers' first exchange the centre and the entry are already arguing. "Tell me how much", "I'll set a bourn how far to be beloved": this is The Hierophant's question, a request for measure and form. "Then must thou needs find out new heaven, new earth" is The World's answer. In a living couple this argument is not divided by gender and often changes sides: today one partner asks "let's settle at least something", tomorrow the other.

The Hierophant in the centre is not a third person between the partners but a third voice. In its plus this is a couple where the partners are also friends: they always have something to talk about, and if someone in the house has the last word, it is because both decided so. Lisovskaya advises such couples to create holidays and places of their own. In its minus the same voice turns into a teacher: "it's all wrong", "I know better". The scene is familiar: two people who meant to live unlike everyone else quarrel over whose parents to spend New Year with and who, by the rules, should call first after a fight.

Plutarch also shows the darkest turn such a rite can take. After Actium Antony and Cleopatra "dissolved their famous society of Inimitable Livers, and founded another, not at all inferior to that in daintiness and extravagant outlay, which they called the society of Partners in Death" (71). The same feasts, the same guests; only the name changed. This is how the Wheel turns a couple's own ritual: the form stays, the meaning changes sign. "Us against everyone" quietly becomes "we are doomed". The easiest place to notice it is in the words a couple uses to name itself.

sections.h2: A world made of a chain and a choice: where the three numbers come from
paragraphs: Each point of the couple's matrix is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices. Running through all dates shows that the tail 21-10-16 forms in only two ways. In 96% of such couples one partner has the personal tail 15-20-5 and the other 6-17-11. Then The World at the entry is 15 + 6, The Devil and The Lovers. The Wheel in the middle is 20 + 17 = 37, Judgement and The Star. The Tower as the main task is 5 + 11, The Hierophant and Strength. In the remaining 4% the partners' tails are 12-19-7 and 9-18-9: The World is 12 + 9, The Hanged Man and The Hermit; The Wheel is 19 + 18, The Sun and The Moon; The Tower is 7 + 9, The Chariot and The Hermit. Personal tails have meanings of their own, and those meanings are not carried over here. Here they are only the material from which the couple's cards are built.

Now the second clue. In "The couple's values", the sphere that reads the shared path and what the two are together for, such couples have only two cards: The Devil in 53.6% and The Lovers in 46.4%. Exactly the two from which The World at the entry is assembled in 96% of couples. This couple's whole world is glued together from attachment and choice, and the couple's values show which of the two halves leads.

In Antony both halves sound in a single scene. After hearing the messengers from Rome he says: "These strong Egyptian fetters I must break, / Or lose myself in dotage." That is The Devil's chain, fetters that hold against one's will. But he will not break them; again and again he will choose Egypt, and that is already the choice of The Lovers. Waite's list for The Lovers, incidentally, includes "trials overcome". Lisovskaya names the main lesson of the fifteenth energy as this: nobody belongs to anybody. For a 21-10-16 couple it is the question after every turn of the Wheel: do the two stay together because the fetters will not let go, or because they have chosen each other again?

The rare variant has a detail of its own. There The Wheel is built from The Sun and The Moon, day and night taking turns. In the last act Cleopatra describes Antony's face as the sky: "His face was as the heavens; and therein stuck / A sun and moon, which kept their course, and lighted / The little O, the earth." A sun and a moon keeping their course above a little circle: that is the Wheel.

sections.h2: Waite and Wen: deception is written into The Tower
paragraphs: Waite gives The Tower this divinatory list: "Misery, distress, indigence, adversity, calamity, disgrace, deception, ruin," and adds: "It is a card in particular of unforeseen catastrophe." The last three words come in the same order as the events of the play. Disgrace is Actium, after which Antony says: "I have offended reputation." Deception is the false report of death. Ruin is the ending. The play walks through this list in order three hundred years before Waite's book.

Benebell Wen says two things about the reversed Tower that meet in a single scene. The blow comes because the Seeker "relied on false impressions made by others", and the card may also mean that the Seeker "has been falsely accused of something". At Alexandria both happen at once: Antony falsely accuses Cleopatra of betrayal, and she creates in him the false impression of her death. In its minus, the collapse of a 21-10-16 couple is rarely pure lightning from the sky. More often it involves an untruth told out of fear and an accusation made before the facts.

Waite has a thought about The World that explains this couple's entry. He writes that the card "is perhaps more especially a story of the past, referring to that day when all was declared to be good, when the morning stars sang together". A couple with The World at the entry will recognise this: their common language often sounds like a memory of the beginning, of that trip, of that summer. Among the things that fill a couple with this energy, Lisovskaya names returning to places with good memories. But a story of the past has a reverse side, a demand: "be again who you were then". The dying Antony asks Cleopatra to please her thoughts by "feeding them with those my former fortunes / Wherein I lived, the greatest prince o' the world".
For the reversed Wheel Waite writes not "bad luck", as popular retellings have it, but "Increase, abundance, superfluity": the very eight boars in the Alexandrian kitchen.

On Waite's card the figure of The World dances inside an oval wreath, which he himself calls a garland, "an elliptic garland". When Antony dies, Cleopatra says: "The crown o' the earth doth melt. My lord! / O, wither'd is the garland of the war." The same garland has withered. The World with which the couple entered its task withers at the end of its Tower. The play is a tragedy precisely because Antony and Cleopatra did not play the scene after Actium a second time.

sections.h2: How to get through The Tower together
paragraphs: The main task of the tail does not promise a catastrophe. It says where the couple learns. The play also gives the opposite recipe, the one that worked after Actium.

ul: **Speak face to face, not through messengers.** Antony and Cleopatra's second Tower is played out entirely through go-betweens. The first was survived when the two finally spoke for themselves, even if on the third day.

**Do not turn the Wheel by hand.** "If you find him sad, say I am dancing" works while it is a game. Disappearing "so they miss me", threats to leave and tests of "how will they take it" turn into a false report on the day of a real collapse.

**Separate the event from the verdict on the person.** "The fleet went over to Caesar" is a fact. "She betrayed me" is a conclusion reached in a minute. In the first hours after a blow it is better not to decide who the partner "really" turned out to be.
**Do not keep a ledger of gains and losses.** "Fall not a tear, I say; one of them rates / All that is won and lost": this line takes the couple off the Wheel.

**Call in a third person who brings together rather than judges.** After Actium the couple was reconciled by the women of Cleopatra's household. In life this is a friend both partners trust, or a couples counsellor.

**Remember that what is said in a collapse stays.** In her reading of a couple with The Tower in the centre, Lisovskaya notes that words spoken in a quarrel stay in the memory forever. "Triple-turn'd whore!" is never taken back in any scene.

paragraphs: And the last point, the most unexpected one. The answer to the riddle of this tail lies in the play's very first scene. Cleopatra asked love for a boundary; Antony refused it any measure. A world without measure cannot survive a crack, and every failure becomes the end of the world. **This couple's world needs a measure**, the very one The Hierophant holds in the centre. Then another turn of the Wheel stays a turn, and The Tower becomes the rebuilding of a house rather than the death of a universe.

sections.h2: How to calculate the couple's karmic tail 21-10-16
paragraphs: A couple's tail is not calculated from a single date. Each point of the couple's matrix is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22: if the sum is greater than 22, its digits are added together. The middle of the couple's tail is also added up from the partners' middles, not recalculated from the couple's two outer numbers.
An example: the dates 17.01.1976 and 05.11.1975. The first partner's personal tail is 15-20-5, the second's is 6-17-11. Adding point by point:
In the centre of this couple's chart stands 5, The Hierophant, as in every couple with this tail. In "The couple's values" stands 6, The Lovers.

The tail 21-10-16 occurs in roughly one couple in 107 (0.931%) and ranks 39th of the 97 couple tails. No other couple tails are made of these three numbers: neither 16-10-21 nor any other order forms in a couple. The same order 21-10-16 also occurs as a personal tail, but that is a different calculation with different roles for the points.

intro: Shakespeare put such a couple on stage around 1606. Antony and Cleopatra is a play about two people for whom the whole Roman world is too small, about a love kept alive by constant change, and about a collapse after which each of them locks themselves in a tower. Shakespeare took the story from Plutarch, at times almost word for word. Both of them share a detail that makes this story worth reading for a couple with this tail: Antony and Cleopatra go through a collapse more than once. They come out of the first one together and out of the last one apart. The difference between those scenes is the main task of the tail 21-10-16.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 21-10-16 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of the couple's matrix: The World at the entry to the task, The Wheel of Fortune in the middle, The Tower as the main task. The couple enters its shared task wanting to be a whole world to each other, lives through circles of rises, quarrels and reconciliations, and learns the main thing: to live through the collapse of the invented image of the partner together, not each in a fortress of their own.

faq.q: Is The Tower as the main task a verdict on the couple?
faq.a: No. The main task is read through difficulties, but it does not predict events or dates. The Tower shows where the couple learns: how it meets a blow and what it does with the image of the partner when that image no longer matches the living person. In Shakespeare's play the couple gets through its Tower together at least once, after Actium.

faq.q: How is the couple's tail 21-10-16 different from the personal tail 21-10-16?
faq.a: A personal tail is calculated from one date of birth, and its points mean something else. A couple's tail is the sum of the points of two personal matrices: here 21 is the couple's shared wish, 10 its path, 16 the main task of the union. With this couple tail, the partners' own personal tails are most often 15-20-5 and 6-17-11, not 21-10-16.

faq.q: Can a couple have the tail 16-10-21 or another order of these numbers?
faq.a: No, running through all dates confirms it: only 21-10-16 forms in a couple. The reason is arithmetic. The first number of a couple's tail is always divisible by three, and of these numbers only 21 is. The order 21-16-10 does not work either: the middle of the tail depends on its ends, and between 21 and 10 there can be no 16.

faq.q: Why do such couples always have The Hierophant in the centre?
faq.a: That is how the partners' personal centres add up: with this tail their sum always reduces to 5. The atmosphere inside the couple is The Hierophant: rules and rites of its own and the voice of "how things should be". In its plus this means trust, loyalty and friendship inside the union; in its minus, lecturing and attempts to remake the partner.

faq.q: What should a couple with the tail 21-10-16 do?
faq.a: Talk directly rather than through go-betweens and tests; do not rock the relationship on purpose to keep interest alive; after a blow, separate the fact from the verdict on the partner; do not keep score of gains and losses; call in someone who reconciles rather than judges. And give the shared world a measure: then a crack stays a crack rather than the end of the world.

report: The lovers' first exchange in Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra is an argument about measure. "If it be love indeed, tell me how much," says Cleopatra. "There's beggary in the love that can be reckon'd," Antony answers. "I'll set a bourn how far to be beloved." — "Then must thou needs find out new heaven, new earth." The last line is almost word for word the Book of Revelation. The whole karmic tail 21-10-16 is already written into this exchange: the couple enters its task with The World, travels it on The Wheel of Fortune and learns its lesson from The Tower.

report.h3: A world with no room for a crack

report: The World at the entry is the couple's shared wish, its "common language". For this couple that language is the language of the whole. Antony speaks it from the first scene: "Let Rome in Tiber melt… Kingdoms are clay." Plutarch tells how Cleopatra once made fun of his fishing and said: "thy sport is the hunting of cities, realms, and continents." The two set each other the scale of a world map: they live unlike everyone else, move, travel, and many see them as an ideal couple.

The same wish has a reverse side. Handing out kingdoms to his children, Antony gave his son Parthia, "when he should have subdued it". It was never subdued. The World at the entry easily becomes a world on credit. Above all, **a love that has declared itself a whole world cannot make room for a crack**. In an ordinary couple a failure is a failure. Here any crack looks like the end of the world, because no spare world was ever planned.

report.h3: Cleopatra's twenty deaths

report: How to keep a whole world alive if it cannot stand still? Spin it. Cleopatra sends a servant to Antony with orders: if he is sad, "Say I am dancing; if in mirth, report / That I am sudden sick." Her attendant advises the opposite: "In each thing give him way, cross him nothing." — "Thou teachest like a fool; the way to lose him." And Antony's friend Enobarbus remarks: "I have seen her die twenty times upon far poorer moment."

This is The Wheel of Fortune in the middle of the task, and in Shakespeare it works: "Age cannot wither her, nor custom stale / Her infinite variety." In a living couple the wheel shows in small things: a week of model tenderness after a quarrel, then a chill with no explanation, then a trip that mends everything. Plutarch even left us the kitchen of such a couple: eight wild boars roasting for twelve guests, because "the precise time is hard to hit".

The danger is named in the same scene: "In time we hate that which we often fear." **A wheel turned by hand teaches the partner to fear the next turn.** And a scene rehearsed twenty times will one day be played at the moment when the game is already over.

report.h3: Two Towers in one play

report: The main task is The Tower: the collapse of the invented image of the partner, and the habit of looking in different directions when things go wrong. The play tests the couple on this twice.

At Actium Cleopatra's ships flee the battle, and Antony rushes after them. Plutarch writes that "he spent three days by himself at the prow, either because he was angry with Cleopatra, or ashamed to see her", until the women of her household brought the two into a parley. In Shakespeare the reproach is spoken, the fault admitted, and then comes a decision: "Fall not a tear, I say; one of them rates / All that is won and lost." The collapse is lived through together.

At Alexandria the fleet goes over to Caesar, and Antony cries: "This foul Egyptian hath betrayed me." Cleopatra locks herself in her tomb and sends a messenger to say she has killed herself: "And word it, prithee, piteously: hence, Mardian, / And bring me how he takes my death." The Wheel's old move, a test, is played at the hour of collapse. Antony believes it. The messenger with the truth arrives saying: "I dread, too late."

The difference between the two scenes is the key to the tail. After Actium the two talk face to face; at Alexandria, only through messengers. **Each is in a tower of their own**: she in the tomb with its bolts, he, even earlier, in a dwelling on a mole at Pharos, named after the misanthrope Timon. The play is a tragedy and plays the minus out to the end; the tail predicts no endings, it shows a mechanism. If someone in a real couple threatens to harm themselves, even "as a test", that is a reason to call a local emergency number or a crisis line.

report.h3: The trump in his own hand

report: Before he believes the false report, Antony watches the clouds: now a dragon, now a lion, now "a tower'd citadel", and suddenly everything loses its outline, "as water is in water". "Here I am Antony: / Yet cannot hold this visible shape." With the partner's image one's own collapses too, because it was built around the other person: Cleopatra was the one "whose bosom was my crownet, my chief end".

Antony describes the betrayal in the language of cards: she has "pack'd cards with Caesar, and false-play'd my glory / Unto an enemy's triumph". Triumph was a game with trumps, and the word trump comes from it; in fifteenth-century Italy "triumphs" were the cards that later became the Major Arcana. Dying, Antony says: "Not Caesar's valour hath o'erthrown Antony, / But Antony's hath triumph'd on itself." **The trump that beat him was in his own hand.** The play never proves the betrayal: the image fell before the facts were known.

report.h3: The measure that was missing

report: Such couples always have The Hierophant in the centre: rules, rites, the voice of "how things should be". It is not a third person but a third voice. In the play it sounds as Rome and as the couple's own rites: they called their circle the Inimitable Livers, and after Actium they dissolved it and founded a new one, the Partners in Death. The same feasts, a different name: this is how the Wheel changes the sign of a ritual, and "us against everyone" quietly becomes "we are doomed".
The play itself suggests the way out:

ul: speak face to face, not through messengers and tests;
do not turn the Wheel by hand: disappearing "so they miss me" and threats to leave turn into a false report during a real collapse;
separate the event from the verdict on the person: "the fleet went over to Caesar" is a fact, "she betrayed me" is a conclusion reached in a minute;
call in a third person who brings together rather than judges, a friend or a couples counsellor.

report: The answer to the riddle of the tail lies in the first scene. Cleopatra asked love for a boundary; Antony refused it any measure. **This couple's world needs a measure**, the one The Hierophant holds in the centre. Then a turn of the Wheel stays a turn, and The Tower becomes the rebuilding of a house rather than the death of a universe.

unit.title: A whole world and one crack

captions.M: To be a whole world to each other, without measure
captions.N: To live in circles: tenderness, chill, reconciliation
captions.D: To meet the collapse together, not each in a tower
