seo.title: Karmic tail 21 16 22 compatibility: The World, The Tower, The Fool
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 16 22 compatibility: a couple who enter through The World, pass The Tower and must learn The Fool, read through Tevye and Golde's story.

items.title: Karmic tail 21-16-22 in compatibility: the fiddler on the roof
items.short: In a couple with the karmic tail 21-16-22, the entry to the task is The World, the last card of the deck; the middle is The Tower; and the main task is The Fool, the card with which the tarot journey only begins. The answer to the riddle is unexpected: this couple starts with a ready-made world for two, goes through its collapse, and learns what the ready-made world never could — to keep their balance without walls, travelling light, choosing each other again.

sections.h2: The fiddler on the roof: the whole tail in one monologue
paragraphs: The most accurate portrait of this tail was written long before compatibility calculators. For twenty years, from 1894 to 1914, Sholem Aleichem published the monologues of Tevye the Dairyman — a village poor man who carts cheese and butter to the summer folk of Boiberik and the townsfolk of Yehupetz, argues with God in quotations from Scripture and marries off his daughters. In 1964 these stories became the Broadway musical Fiddler on the Roof (book by Joseph Stein, music by Jerry Bock, lyrics by Sheldon Harnick); in 1971 Norman Jewison made it into a film. In Russia the same story is also known through Grigory Gorin's play Pominalnaya molitva ("A Memorial Prayer"), staged by Mark Zakharov at the Lenkom theatre in 1989 with Yevgeny Leonov as Tevye.

The title was suggested by Marc Chagall's paintings, where a fiddler plays above the roofs of a shtetl. And the musical opens with Tevye's monologue — read it next to the three cards, and the whole of the tail 21-16-22 is in it, together with the couple's centre:

"A fiddler on the roof. Sounds crazy, no? But in our little village of Anatevka, you might say every one of us is a fiddler on the roof, trying to scratch out a pleasant, simple tune without breaking his neck. <…> You may ask, why do we stay up there if it's so dangerous? We stay because Anatevka is our home. And how do we keep our balance? That I can tell you in a word: Tradition!" (Here and below, lines from the musical and the film are quoted in the original English.)

Tradition is The World, the entry to the task: a whole way of life in which, as Tevye puts it, "everyone knows who he is and what God expects him to do". The roof is The Tower, the middle: a house that holds until it is shaken. The fiddler is The Fool, the main task: to play at the very edge and not fall. And the balance is Justice, which stands in the centre for every couple with this tail. The whole musical is about what happens when tradition stops keeping the balance and the roof becomes the only place left to stand.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — The World: twenty-five years without one question
paragraphs: Tevye and Golde married the way it was done: they were matched. "The first time I met you was on our wedding day," he reminds her twenty-five years later. Their parents told them back then that they would learn to love each other. Nobody spoke of love again: there was the house, five daughters, the cow, the Sabbath candles — there was a world in which everything stood in its place.

The World at the entry to a couple's tail is exactly this wish to have a whole. For Lisovskaya, the entry point is what the two want together: their agreements, their "common language". For a 21-16-22 couple the common language is a way of life. Such two assemble the picture of their life quickly and completely: how they celebrate holidays, where they go in summer, who handles the money, what the house will be like, who the children will become. From outside this often looks like the ideal couple — settled, understandable, "doing it properly". Inside it is real peace: there is no need to negotiate every day, because everything has already been agreed.

But the entry point sits on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. A whole world has nowhere to grow. New friends, new ideas, a new job have to pass through customs: "that's not how we do things". The partner is gradually adjusted to fit the shared picture, and the picture cannot be argued with — it belongs to both. For The World reversed, Waite gives four words that read like an inventory of such a flat: "Inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence." Wen calls The World "the supreme balance between good and evil" — and Tevye also speaks of balance, only in his case tradition is what holds it.

What this world is made of can be heard in Tevye's best-known song, "If I Were a Rich Man". He dreams of a big house with rooms by the dozen, where one staircase only goes up, another, even longer, only comes down, and a third leads nowhere, just for show. In the couple's tail The World is built from the partners' personal tails as The Moon plus The Empress, a dream plus a house (more on this in the section on the calculation). This couple's world is exactly such a house: built from a dream, full, beautiful — and with a staircase that leads nowhere.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — The Tower: a world that falls stone by stone
paragraphs: In Anatevka the roof cracks not from lightning but from the daughters. The eldest, Tzeitel, refuses the rich butcher she has been matched with and gives her word to a poor tailor — herself, with no matchmaker. The second, Hodel, follows the revolutionary Perchik to Siberia. The third, Chava, marries a Russian boy, Fyedka, and here Tevye, who has weighed every decision all his life, says: "If I try and bend that far, I'll break." Then a pogrom bursts into Tzeitel's wedding, and at the end the constable brings an order: in Sholem Aleichem the Jews are given three days to sell everything and leave the village.

In Waite's historical description of The Tower there is a phrase that fits this story literally: "It is assuredly a card of confusion." The Tower's blow is not necessarily loud. More often it is the day when the finished picture stops matching life: one of the two is still following the old map, the other is already following the terrain.

For a 21-16-22 couple the middle of the path is made of such days. A move that cancelled everything. A job that stopped being a support. A child who chose something other than what was planned for them. A partner who turned out not to be the person the other had imagined — but someone alive and inconvenient. This is not a forecast of events: the middle of the tail describes how the couple go from their wish to their task — through the collapse of the picture, not along a smooth road.

In the plus, The Tower pulls the couple together. When the roof cracks, it turns out the two know how to hold: one offers a shoulder while the other cannot stand, decisions are made quickly and without unnecessary words, and in place of the imagined partner the real one finally appears. In the minus, the same blow drives them apart: each saves their own part of the world and looks their own way, and in the heat of the moment someone says "then go".

The musical has a scene that shows how The Tower enters such a couple from the inside. To break off the match with the butcher, Tevye wakes Golde in the middle of the night and tells her an invented nightmare: her grandmother has come from the other world to bless the tailor, and the butcher's late wife threatens terrible revenge. Golde interprets the dream and herself demands that their daughter marry the tailor. In Waite's divinatory list for The Tower, the word deception stands between disgrace and ruin, but this deception is a special one. In this house the shared picture cannot be argued with, so it is changed in secret: the old agreement is broken not head-on but through the language in which the wife speaks to the world. This is the hidden mechanism of a couple with The World at the entry: when the picture cannot be challenged, changes arrive in disguise.

The Tower in this story has a second half too. At the end, Golde sweeps the floor of the house they are leaving forever: "I don't want to leave a dirty house!" The walls go, but the care for them stays.

sections.h2: Main task — The Fool: "You're a fool!" — "I know"
paragraphs: In the middle of the collapse, when Hodel is already engaged to Perchik without asking her parents, Tevye comes to his wife and says: "It's a new world, Golde. A new world. Love." And he asks the question he has not asked in twenty-five years: "Do you love me?"

At first Golde does not understand the question, then decides her husband has indigestion and sends him to lie down. Then she snaps: "You're a fool!" — and Tevye answers: "I know." And asks again. So she lists the twenty-five years: she washed his clothes, cooked his meals, cleaned his house, gave him children, milked the cow, fought with him, starved with him — if that's not love, what is? The song ends on the thought that it doesn't change a thing, but after twenty-five years it's nice to know.

Here is the main task of the tail 21-16-22, told in a single scene. **The Fool as the main task is not carelessness to be defeated but a beginner's question that the couple must learn to ask after everything.** "You're a fool!" — "I know": only someone willing to play the fool asks about what "goes without saying". Lisovskaya reads a couple's main task mostly through the minus, and among The Fool's minuses she lists an undefined status of the relationship. Tevye and Golde's status is more firmly defined than anyone's: matched, married, five daughters. Only the main thing is undefined — whether they chose each other. Formally everything is clear, yet it has never once been said aloud.

This minus has other faces as well. A lightness that turns into flight at the first serious step. Rules that one partner strictly holds the other to and breaks themselves. A quarrel after which it is easier to drive off than to stay. Tevye knows this too: in Sholem Aleichem, Chava steps out to meet him on a forest road and grabs the horse by the bridle, and he whips up the horse and drives away — and all the way home it seems to him that she is running after the cart.

The Fool's plus is the other side of the same coin: the ability to start from zero, humour when it is frightening, trust without checking. Tevye goes broke, loses his home, argues with God and keeps joking; that humour is his safety margin. The Fool is the card of the road travelled light, and that is its lesson for a couple who came in through a whole world: **the most important thing in a union cannot be inherited along with the way of life — it is chosen, again and aloud.**

sections.h2: "Get thee out": a road that cannot be walked alone
paragraphs: The last chapter of Tevye the Dairyman is called "Lekh-Lekho", usually rendered in English as "Get Thee Out". These are the first words with which God addresses Abraham. Tevye retells them his own way: "Get out, Tevye, 'from your country and from your birthplace'… 'to the land that I will show you' — wherever your eyes may lead!" And to his daughter, who asks where they are to go now, he answers: "When God appeared to our father Abraham and told him, 'Get thee out of thy country,' did Abraham ask where to?" (Sholem Aleichem is quoted in our translation.)

This is The Fool: the one who leaves without knowing where. But in the book Tevye hears "Get thee out" alone. Golde has died earlier, in the chapter "Tevye Leaves for the Land of Israel", and her last words are about caring for him: "I'm dying, Tevye — who will cook your supper?" And Tevye, not yet believing it, answers with a saying: "Golde, you've been faithful to me all these years — will you leave me a fool in my old age?" In the Russian translation the Fool's word sounds even here — v durakakh, "left a fool" — beside his dying wife, just as in the musical it will sound in the song about love.

The musical changed this fate: two people leave Anatevka. Tevye and Golde set off for America with their youngest daughters. In the film Golde calls after Chava, whom her father has forbidden them even to mention: "We will be staying with Uncle Avram!" — and so leaves her daughter an address. Tevye grumbles: "The whole world has to know our business!" The uncle the couple are going to bears the same name as the first man who heard "Get thee out".

The numbers of the tail say the same. **In a personal matrix the tail 21-16-22 is impossible:** for a single person the entry to the tail equals the karmic task plus the centre of the chart, and with The Fool as the karmic task, The World at the entry cannot come out with any centre. From The World to The Fool there is no way alone — only together. Sholem Aleichem sent Tevye down the road alone; the musical sent a couple, and that is the only version this tail allows.
At the end, as the family sets off, the fiddler begins to play, Tevye beckons with a nod, and the fiddler follows them out of the village. There is no roof any more, but the music leaves with them.

sections.h2: Justice in the centre: "on the other hand"
paragraphs: Every couple with the tail 21-16-22 has 8, Justice, in the centre. This is no accident: such couples are always formed from the personal tails 18-3-12 and 3-13-10, and the centres that go with these tails are always 6 and 20; 6 + 20 = 26, 2 + 6 = 8. The centre in a couple's matrix is the atmosphere between the two — what is inside and not for show.

Tevye is Justice in the flesh, and Sholem Aleichem shows it in the very first story. Tevye stands on the veranda of the rich and turns to God: "You are great, merciful and just! What kind of order is it, that to one You give everything and to another — nothing?" And straight away, without drawing breath: "But on the other hand, I think, you are a great fool, Tevye!" The scales and The Fool in a single sentence: the weighing ends with the one who weighs calling himself a fool.

The musical turned "on the other hand" into a refrain. Motel the tailor asks for Tzeitel's hand: on the other hand, he has absolutely nothing; on the other hand, things could never get worse for him, only better. Hodel gets engaged without a matchmaker: "On the other hand, our old ways were once new, weren't they?" And when Chava marries an outsider: "On the other hand… No! There is no other hand!"

This is the atmosphere of this couple. In the plus it is honest: everything is discussed, duties are shared equally, and Lisovskaya also sees in Justice at the centre respect for the traditions of both families and a wish to make the relationship official and proper. Weighing keeps the house in balance, the way tradition keeps the fiddler. In the minus, the scales lose their second pan. Everything is measured by one's own yardstick, responsibility turns into control, and a moment comes when one of the two says "there is no other hand". Waite's divinatory list for Justice reversed includes "bigotry, bias, excessive severity" — that is what scales with one pan look like.

The musical shows where this couple's second pan is. Tevye has forbidden any talk of Chava — Golde shouts her an address as they part. Tevye has turned away from his daughter — and at once prompts Tzeitel to add: "God be with you." **A couple's justice rests not on one person doing the weighing but on two: when one of them has no other hand, the partner holds it.**

sections.h2: The couple's values — The Lovers: Adam and Eve had a matchmaker too
paragraphs: "The couple's values" is the spiritual purpose, the path the two are to walk together. For every couple with this tail it holds 6, The Lovers. A couple who enter the task through a ready-made way of life end up valuing not the way of life but the choice.

Tevye put this into words as well. Blessing Hodel and Perchik, who got engaged without a matchmaker, he argues with himself: "On the other hand, did Adam and Eve have a matchmaker? Yes, they did. And it seems these two have the same matchmaker." The joke is precise: nobody matched the first couple in the world except the one who created them both — and a union by love turns out to be not a breach of order but its beginning.

For a 21-16-22 couple this means something simple. A union that began as a given holds because it is chosen. Tevye and Golde's marriage was arranged by their parents; their value is a question asked twenty-five years later and the answer "I suppose I do". The tail shows the road; The Lovers show what the road is walked for.

sections.h2: What Waite and Wen saw: confusion, a bundle and the edge of a cliff
paragraphs: In the books on tarot this tail has several clues that match Tevye's story with surprising precision.

Waite calls The Tower "a card of confusion", and of The Fool he writes that this card "reverses, under high warrants, all the confusions that have preceded it". Waite meant the muddle of the commentators, but the word is the same, and in a couple's tail it works literally: The Fool stands right after The Tower and answers its confusion. In Anatevka the confusion ended not with a new rule but with a simple question: "Do you love me?"

Wen describes The Fool with a bundle over one shoulder holding "all his earthly possessions". In Sholem Aleichem, before leaving, Tevye walks into the emptied house: "On the floor — bundles, bundles, bundles! A cat sits on the stove ledge like an orphan." And Chava, on hearing of the expulsion, decides to share it with her family and brings her own bundle, "tied up in a red kerchief": "Our exile is her exile."

Waite's Fool stands at the edge of a precipice and looks not down but at the sky, and the edge does not frighten him — "it is as if angels were waiting to uphold him, if it came about that he leaped from the height". This is the same fiddler on the roof: a man who plays at the edge and does not fall, because he is not looking into the abyss.

Wen explains The Fool reversed with a psalm: "The fool says in his heart, 'There is no God.'" Tevye is a Fool of another kind. He is ruined, driven out, reproaches God ("Why have You fastened on Tevye?"), yet never once says there is no God. For a couple the difference is the same: there is a lightness that does not care, and a lightness that argues but does not walk away.

Waite describes The Lovers as Adam and Eve in paradise and writes that his card replaced "the old card of marriage", which showed "father and mother, with their child placed between them". Tevye's joke about the matchmaker argues with exactly this: the old card of marriage is a family that was arranged; the new one is two people who chose.
And finally — a coincidence now, not a clue: the first Tevye on Broadway in 1964 was Zero Mostel. Zero — and zero, for Waite, is the number of The Fool.

sections.h2: Example calculation: 05.12.1975 and 04.01.1976
paragraphs: A couple's tail is not derived from its two outer numbers: each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. A person born on 05.12.1975 has the personal karmic tail 18-3-12 (The Moon, The Empress, The Hanged Man) and centre 6. A person born on 04.01.1976 has the tail 3-13-10 (The Empress, Death, The Wheel of Fortune) and centre 20. Add point to point:

head: Point
Arcanum
How it is derived
rows: 12 + 10: The Hanged Man and The Wheel of Fortune

paragraphs: The couple's values for these dates are 6, The Lovers. And this is not one possibility among many but the only one: a couple's tail 21-16-22 is formed only from the personal tails 18-3-12 and 3-13-10, so such couples always have 8 in the centre and 6 in the values. It occurs in about one couple in 3,742 (0.027%) — 94th place out of 97 couple tails.

The middle here is not the reduced sum of the outer numbers: 21 + 22 = 43, 4 + 3 = 7. By the logic of a single person, The Chariot would stand between The World and The Fool — a vehicle that carries one to the goal. In a couple this place holds The Tower, built from the partners' middles, 3 + 13 = 16. In a personal matrix such a middle is impossible. This couple are not carried from their world onto the road — they tumble out onto it.

What follows is our reading of the arithmetic. The Empress stands in the personal tails of both partners, in the middle for one and at the entry for the other, and in the couple's tail she goes into two cards at once: with The Moon she gives The World, with Death she gives The Tower. The house is this couple's common material: their world is built from it, and it is also what collapses in the middle of the path. The Fool, in turn, is made of The Hanged Man and The Wheel of Fortune — of the ability to hang in uncertainty and a turn of fate. Tevye describes this mechanism himself: "if God wants the wheel to turn the other way, everything flies to the devil", and then — "now up, now down!" The main task is born where the two stop holding on to the wheel and agree to hang for a while as it turns.

sections.h2: How a couple live the tail 21-16-22: the circle and the way out
paragraphs: The circle in the minus looks like this. The two quickly build a shared world and settle down: everything is agreed. The world closes up — anything new has to pass through customs, the main thing goes unsaid because it "goes without saying". Then life shifts one wall, and it turns out that the shared picture cannot be argued with and changing it openly is frightening. Changes arrive in disguise, quarrels arrive suddenly, in trouble each saves their own part of the house. When it comes to a serious step, someone turns the cart around. And the question everything was for remains unasked.

The way out is the same path in the plus. The world stays, but becomes portable: whatever can be carried in a bundle — habits, jokes, rituals, a common language. The Tower stops being a verdict: the couple discover that they can hold together. The Fool turns from flight into a road: the two choose each other aloud and travel on light, and the fiddler follows.
What helps along the way:

ul: **Ask Tevye's question.** From time to time ask directly: "Do you love me?", "Would you choose this again?" — and answer not with a list of chores but with words.
**Tell custom from balance.** A custom is a tool, not a roof. Once a year, review the couple's rules: which still hold, and which are held up by inertia alone.
**Keep the second pan.** In an argument, first restate the partner's point so well that they agree with the restatement, and only then object.
**Build a portable world.** Cherish what does not depend on walls: shared jokes, songs, rituals, private words. They can be taken anywhere.
**In trouble, together first.** When a wall falls, don't argue about whose wall it was; sort that out later.
**Practise zero on a small scale.** A new place, a new project, a week without a plan — together, so that the big start from zero is not the first one.
**Don't turn the cart around.** When the urge comes to run from a hard conversation, say so aloud and stay.

**Entry to the task — 21, The World.** The couple want a whole world for two: a shared way of life, a shared picture of life where everything has its place. Everything starts from this wish — and the couple run up against the same wish when life asks for change.

**Middle of the task — 16, The Tower.** The path runs through moments when the finished picture stops matching life: the order collapses, the imagined image of the partner collapses. Here The Tower does not promise misfortune; it describes how the couple walk their path.

**Main task — 22, The Fool.** To learn to live without a ready-made world: to start from zero, to trust without checking, to joke when it is frightening, and to choose each other not by custom but of their own free will.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 21-16-22 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail in which the entry to the task is The World (21), the middle is The Tower (16), and the main task is The Fool (22). The couple start with the wish for a whole shared world, go through the collapse of the finished picture and learn the main thing: to live without the ready-made, to choose each other again, to trust and to start from zero.

faq.q: Does The Tower in the middle mean the couple will split up?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events. The Tower in the middle describes how the couple walk their path: through moments when the finished picture stops matching life. In the plus such moments pull the couple together, in the minus they drive them into separate corners, and which way it goes is decided by the two of them, not by the card.

faq.q: Why is the middle 16 if 21 + 22 = 43 → 7?
faq.a: The middle of a couple's tail is not derived from the outer numbers. It is made from the middles of the partners' personal tails: 3 + 13 = 16. Reducing the outer numbers would give 7, The Chariot, but in a couple this place holds The Tower, and no personal matrix has such a middle.

faq.q: Can the tail 21-16-22 appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the entry to the tail equals the karmic task plus the centre of the chart, and with The Fool as the karmic task an entry of 21 cannot come out with any centre. This tail exists only for couples.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. From the numbers 21, 16 and 22 a couple's tail comes out in only one order — 21-16-22 — so there is nothing to confuse it with.

faq.q: How common is this tail?
faq.a: About one couple in 3,742 (0.027%), 94th place out of 97 couple tails. All such couples are formed from the personal tails 18-3-12 and 3-13-10, so they always have Justice in the centre and The Lovers in their values.

report: After twenty-five years of marriage, Tevye the Dairyman asks his wife: "Do you love me?" Golde decides her husband has indigestion and sends him to lie down. Then she snaps: "You're a fool!" — and Tevye answers: "I know." They were matched long ago, and in all those years they never once spoke of love.

This scene from Fiddler on the Roof is the shortest retelling of the tail 21-16-22. The musical, staged in 1964 from Sholem Aleichem's stories, opens with Tevye's monologue: everyone in their village is a fiddler on the roof, "trying to scratch out a pleasant, simple tune without breaking his neck". "And how do we keep our balance? That I can tell you in a word: Tradition!" Tradition is The World, the entry to the task. The roof is The Tower, the middle of the path. The fiddler is The Fool, the main task: to play at the very edge and not fall.

report.h3: A finished world with nowhere to grow

report: The World at the entry is the couple's wish to have a whole. Such two assemble a shared picture of life quickly and completely: how they celebrate holidays, who handles the money, what the house will be like, who the children will become. From outside it is the ideal couple; inside it is real peace: everything has already been agreed, there is no need to negotiate again. This couple's common language is a way of life.

But the same wish turns into resistance. A whole world has nowhere to grow. New ideas and new people have to pass through customs: "that's not how we do things". The partner is gradually adjusted to fit the shared picture, and the picture cannot be argued with — it belongs to both. For The World reversed, Waite gives four words that read like an inventory of such a flat: "Inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence."

report.h3: Changes arrive in disguise

report: The middle of the tail is The Tower. In Anatevka the roof cracks not from lightning but from the daughters: one gives her word to a poor tailor herself, with no matchmaker; another follows a revolutionary to Siberia; a third marries an outsider, and Tevye says: "If I try and bend that far, I'll break." For a 21-16-22 couple the middle of the path is made of such days, when the finished picture stops matching life: one of the two is still following the old map, the other is already following the terrain. This is not a forecast of events but a description of how the couple walk their path.

The Tower in this couple has a hidden mechanism. To break off the match with the butcher, Tevye wakes Golde in the middle of the night and tells her an invented nightmare — and his wife herself demands that their daughter marry the tailor. **When the shared picture cannot be argued with, changes arrive in disguise.** In the plus, The Tower pulls the couple together: one offers a shoulder while the other cannot stand, and in place of the imagined partner the real one appears. In the minus, each saves their own part of the world, and in the heat of the moment someone says "then go".

report.h3: Only a fool asks what goes without saying

report: The main task is The Fool, and the scene with the question about love shows it whole. **The Fool as the main task is not carelessness to be defeated but a beginner's question that the couple must learn to ask after everything.** Only someone willing to play the fool asks about what "goes without saying". Among The Fool's minuses Lisovskaya lists an undefined status of the relationship, and in this couple it looks like a paradox: formally everything is clear — matched, married, five daughters — yet the main thing, whether they chose each other, has never once been said aloud.

This minus has other faces too: a lightness that turns into flight at the first serious step, rules that one partner strictly holds the other to and breaks themselves. In Sholem Aleichem, Chava steps out to meet her father on a forest road, and he whips up the horse and drives away. The Fool's plus is the other side of the same coin: the ability to start from zero, humour when it is frightening, trust without checking. **The most important thing in a union cannot be inherited along with the way of life — it is chosen, again and aloud.**

report.h3: From The World to The Fool there is no way alone

report: The book's last chapter is called "Get Thee Out" — the words with which God sent Abraham on his way. Tevye explains to his daughter: "Did Abraham ask where to?" But in the book he hears "Get thee out" alone: Golde has died earlier. The musical changed this fate, and two people leave Anatevka. Before they go, Golde sweeps the floor of the house they are leaving forever: "I don't want to leave a dirty house!" The walls go, but the care for them stays. And this tail is not given to a single person: **from The World to The Fool there is a way only for two.**

The way out is the same path in the plus. The world stays, but becomes portable: whatever can be carried in a bundle — habits, jokes, rituals, a common language. The Tower stops being a verdict: the couple discover that they can hold together. The Fool turns from flight into a road. What it takes:

seo.title: Karmic tail 21 16 4 compatibility: The World, The Tower, The Emperor
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 16 4 compatibility: what The World, The Tower and The Emperor mean for a couple, how it is worked out, and why its happy ending comes first.

items.title: Karmic tail 21-16-4 in compatibility: the couple whose ending comes first
items.short: The couple's karmic tail 21-16-4 begins with The World — the card of completion, the "final message" of the Major Arcana — and ends with The Emperor, one of the first cards in the row. It runs backwards: first "happily ever after", then the foundation that such happiness rests on. The couple enters the task feeling that they already have everything, lives through the collapse of that feeling, and learns the main thing: how to build a shared order in which both of them have a voice.

sections.h2: How the 21-16-4 tail is calculated: an example with two dates
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices; if the sum is above 22, its digits are added together. Take the dates 05.12.1976 and 14.09.1975. The first partner's personal tail is 3-7-22, the second's is 18-9-9. Add top to top, middle to middle, bottom to bottom:

Here is the first oddity. Add the two ends of the tail, 21 + 4 = 25 → 7, and you would get The Chariot. But a couple's middle is not derived from the ends: it is the sum of the partners' middles, 7 + 9. With these two ends, the personal formula could never produce a sixteen in the middle.

The whole 21-16-4 tail is impossible for one person, too. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, so to have The World on top with a four at the bottom, the centre would have to be The Star, 17. No birth date puts The Star in the centre of a personal matrix. A couple's matrix can hold it: our partners' centres are 8 and 9, which make 17. Both this tail and this Star exist only for two.

About one couple in 137 has 21-16-4 — 48th place among the 97 couple tails. It is put together in two ways: from the personal tails 18-9-9 and 3-7-22, as in our example (71.5% of such couples), or from 15-8-11 and 6-8-20 (28.5%). No couple tail uses the same numbers in another order: a search through every date produced neither 21-4-16 nor any order with 16 or 4 in front.

sections.h2: A romance that begins with the wedding
paragraphs: Around 1170 Chrétien de Troyes wrote "Erec and Enide", one of the earliest Arthurian romances. In the prologue he boasts that he has drawn from "a tale of adventure" une mout bele conjointure — "a most beautiful joining". The word means a skilfully assembled plot, but literally it is a "joining together", parts fitted into a whole. A couple's matrix is built the same way: two matrices added into a third.

The romance is built in an unusual way. The knight Erec, son of King Lac, meets a poor girl in an old dress, wins the prize for the fairest lady for her in single combat and brings her to Arthur's court. The wedding comes at about line two thousand out of nearly seven thousand: where a fairy tale puts a full stop, Chrétien is only starting. The reader does not even learn the bride's name until the altar, because "a wife is not wed unless she is called by her rightful name". Her name is Enide. Everything else is about what happens after "happily ever after".

The 21-16-4 tail is built the same way: the final card stands at the entrance. The three acts of the romance fall on the three cards in order. This is our reading, not Chrétien's design, but there are too many matches to walk past. The quotations below are our own translations from the Old French.

sections.h2: The World: "I lacked for nothing"
paragraphs: After the wedding Erec takes Enide to his father's town of Carnant, which has everything: forests and meadows, vineyards, orchards and rivers. He loves his wife so much that he gives up tournaments and arms, and often gets up when it is already past noon. He still hands out horses and armour to his knights generously, but he himself goes nowhere. The world shrinks to one room, and in that room nothing is lacking.

From outside, this world looks different. The court whispers that Erec has turned recreant — a knight who has given up, a coward — and Enide gets the blame: she has supposedly ensnared him. Enide hears all of it and says nothing, because her husband would take offence if she spoke. One morning, while he sleeps, her tears break through, and with them a short sentence: "Con mar i fus!" — "Ill-fated you are!" Erec is only dozing, and he hears.

Getting ready for the road, Enide names the loss herself: "I was too much at ease: there was nothing I lacked." It is worth remembering that "nothing I lacked", in Old French ne me faloit nule chose. It comes back in the last scene of the romance.

This is what The World looks like at the entry to the tail. What a 21-16-4 couple wants together is a full, finished world for two. In its bright form this means freedom, a shared outlook, the open road. In its shadow it means closedness and secrets. It can go like this: the two are happy together, meetings with friends are cancelled one after another, relatives tell one of the partners "you two have vanished" — and that partner does not pass it on, so as not to spoil things. The world is full, except that everything said about it from outside piles up inside one of the two. That is why the entry to the task so easily becomes resistance: the more perfect the world for two, the more frightening it is to change anything in it.

Among the wedding guests, by the way, is the lord of the Isle of Glass, where "no thunder is heard, no lightning falls and there is no storm". The World this tail begins with is exactly that kind of country. There is no Tower in it yet.

sections.h2: The Tower: she rides ahead and keeps silent
paragraphs: Erec does not argue. "You were right," he says, "and those who blame me are right." And at once he tells her to get up, put on her finest dress and saddle her best horse. He arms himself, refuses an escort — only his wife will go with him — and leads her off, in Chrétien's words, "not knowing where, at a venture". On the road he gives an order that alone is worth rereading the romance for:
"Take care not to be so bold that, whatever you may see, you tell me of it. Do not speak to me unless I address you first. Ride ahead, and fast."

"She went ahead and fell silent. Neither said a word to the other." Enide whispers to herself: "To such great joy had God raised me up — and in a short hour He has cast me down." This is The Tower in a single line: the height you fall from and the short hour of the fall.

Chrétien never says why Erec does this. In the Welsh retelling of the same story, "Geraint son of Erbin", the husband suspects his wife of loving another man and makes her wear her worst dress. In Chrétien there is no jealousy and no rival, and the dress is the finest. What collapses is not fidelity but two invented images. Erec, "the best knight in the world", learns how others see him. Enide, who "lacked for nothing", learns that her happiness is called his disgrace. And suddenly each sees the other as a stranger: on the road Erec will throw at her that he "knew very well all along that you hardly value me at all".

Lisovskaya describes The Tower among a couple's tasks in almost the same picture: the invented image of the partner collapses, hard events come one after another, and in trouble the two look in different directions. In Chrétien it is not a metaphor. Enide rides in front, Erec behind, and she is forbidden even to turn round.

Then come blow after blow: three robbers, then five, a count who wants to take Erec's wife from him, two giants. Again and again Enide sees the danger first and has to choose between the ban and her husband. "He will kill me. Let him kill me! I will not keep silent — I will tell him." Erec wins and scolds her every time: next time I will not forgive you. The voice that saves him is punished for having spoken.

In a modern couple, the middle of 21-16-4 can look entirely ordinary. After a hard conversation the two live "in business mode": they sort things out, pay the bills, drive the children around — and barely talk. One of them, like Enide, is the first to notice what is coming and decides each time whether to break the silence. The other, like Erec, copes alone and is annoyed at being warned. Difficulties come in a row, and the two go through them not hand in hand, but one after the other.

Here the numbers of the tail drop a clue. In 71.5% of couples with this tail, The Tower is made of 7 and 9 — The Chariot and The Hermit, the road and solitude. That is exactly what Chrétien wrote: a ride without words. In the other 28.5% the middle is 8 + 8, two Justices. And the line with which Erec gets out of bed is about two rights: in "you were right, and those who blame me are right" the Old French uses droit both times — "right, being in the right". The road begins with a double verdict.

sections.h2: The voice that wakes
paragraphs: The turning point comes at Limors. Badly wounded, Erec collapses senseless and is taken for dead. Count Oringle carries the body and Enide to his castle and that same evening marries her against her will. She refuses to eat; the count strikes her and speaks a formula in which the shadow of The Emperor shows without disguise: "The lady is mine and I am hers, and I will do with her as I please." Enide answers that she fears neither his blows nor his threats.

At that moment Erec comes to — "when he heard his wife's voice". The voice that was forbidden to speak brings him back to life. The guests flee shouting "Run, run, the dead man!", and Erec puts Enide in front of him on a single horse. "The horse carries them both." A moment ago they rode apart, she in front and he behind. Now they share one saddle.

That same night he tells her: "Sweet sister, I have tested you to the full. Now I love you more than ever before, and I know that you love me with a perfect love. From now on I am wholly at your command, as I used to be." It is easy to decide here that the way out is simply to change who gives the orders. The romance does not end like that: the garden and the two crowns are still ahead.

Here, too, the numbers know more than it seems. In 28.5% of couples with this tail, The Emperor is made of 11 and 20 — Strength and Judgement. Strength is Enide facing the count; Judgement is the card of waking and of the call: Erec rises at the call of a voice. In 71.5% of couples The Emperor is the sum of 22 and 9, The Fool and The Hermit: the road taken "at a venture" and the decision to ride without an escort. Partners with the tails 18-9-9 and 3-7-22 have no Emperor either in the personal tail or in the centre: it is born only in the sum. In the pairing of 15-8-11 and 6-8-20 it is the other way round: both partners carry The Emperor in the centre of their personal matrix, and in the couple's centre 4 + 4 gives Justice — two rulers and a pair of scales between them.

sections.h2: The Emperor: two crowns and a robe on which the world is measured
paragraphs: The last scene of the romance is Christmas at Nantes. Erec's father dies, and Arthur crowns the new couple. Two crowns of fine gold are brought out: two maidens hold one, two knights the other. The bishop anoints Erec, and Arthur puts in his hand a sceptre of solid emerald on which every fish, beast, man and bird in the world is carved. Then Enide receives her crown. The woman who was forbidden to speak is crowned beside her husband.

Erec wears a robe embroidered by four fairies. The first portrayed Geometry — how she measures "how far the heavens and the earth extend, so that nothing is lacking", and so "measures the whole world". The second portrayed Arithmetic, who counts the days and hours, the drops of the sea, the grains of sand and the stars: "numbers never deceived her". The third embroidered Music, the fourth Astronomy.

Here is the promised return. "So that nothing is lacking" on the robe — de rien nule n'i faut — uses the same verb as Enide's morning lament: ne me faloit nule chose. In bed, the fullness of the world was given as a gift and measured by nothing. On the king's robe it is measured: height, width, depth, number. The World from the entry of the tail comes back at the end, but now as measure. **In the 21-16-4 tail The Emperor does not cancel happiness: he draws its plan.**

The romance shows The Emperor in shadow twice, and both forms are easy to recognise. First the empty throne: a king's son who does not rule, does not ride out and decides nothing, while gossip rules in his place. Then the decree: "do not speak unless I address you". Enide breaks it again and again, each time for her husband's sake. It is a rule that later gets in its own author's way: he has to forgive his wife for saving him. And Erec has no face that shows what he feels — all along the road Enide wonders whether this is anger or a test.

The couple's main task is to turn "we have everything" into "we have it all worked out". Who decides about money and who about holidays. How much time belongs to each partner's friends. What to do if one of them hears something unpleasant about the couple. Which rules are shared, and which have long been in the way and survive only out of habit. This is The Emperor's order in a couple: not a throne for one and not a decree, but a structure the two have agreed on out loud.

sections.h2: The garden behind a wall of air
paragraphs: Before the coronation Chrétien places an episode that feels like a dream. The castle of Brandigan is so strong that it "fears neither king nor emperor". By the castle lies a garden with no wall and no fence around it, only air, yet the enchanted air holds as if the garden were closed in iron. Flowers and ripe fruit grow there all year round. The fruit may be eaten inside, but whoever tries to carry even one piece out will not find the way out until he puts it back in its place.

A couple lives in the garden. The knight Mabonagrain once promised his beloved to grant her a request — "I pledged my word to her, and did not know to what". She demanded that he never leave the garden until someone defeated him in combat. He stayed, and did not let her see how hard it was for him: he was afraid she would take back her heart. They had left her home in secret, "so that no one knew of it but the two of us". When Enide and the lady recognise each other as cousins, Enide tells her own story differently: she was given in marriage so that "my father knew, and my mother rejoiced".

Erec defeats Mabonagrain and blows the horn that no one before him could sound. The captive is free, and the celebration is called "the Joy of the Court": the joy of two becomes the joy of all. This is the mirror of the 21-16-4 tail — a World the couple never left. A perfect garden, a secret union, a vow made blind, displeasure hidden out of love — and strangers pay for this closed harmony: in the garden stand stakes with the helmets of the defeated. The tail shows what happens if a couple stays at the entrance for ever.

One more clue is "The couple's values", the spiritual purpose. In 69% of couples with this tail it holds The Lovers, the card of choice; in 31%, The Devil, the card of a bond that holds. In our example it is The Devil. For couples with The Devil, Mabonagrain's garden is a warning about a bond held by a vow rather than by desire. For couples with The Lovers, it is a reminder that a choice is not made only once. Erec and Enide leave their Tower precisely by choosing: she chooses to speak, he chooses to listen.

sections.h2: What Waite says: a song at the laying of a stone
paragraphs: Having called The World "this final message of the Major Trumps", Waite adds that it is "perhaps more especially a story of the past, referring to that day when all was declared to be good, when the morning stars sang together and all the Sons of God shouted for joy". The words come from the Book of Job (38:7), and the verses before them are worth reading: "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?.. Who hath laid the measures thereof?.. Whereupon are the foundations thereof fastened? or who laid the corner stone thereof". The joy with which Waite explains The World is the joy at the laying of a stone.

Waite's Emperor "is executive and realization", and the author notes that "he is occasionally represented as seated on a cubic stone". So the first and last cards of the tail are already linked in Waite's own text: the song of The World rings out over The Emperor's stone. A 21-16-4 couple hears the song before laying the stone. The likeness to Erec's robe, embroidered with measure, number, music and stars, is our observation, not Chrétien's intent: the four arts were the standard set of medieval learning. But next to Job it rings true.

In his list of divinatory meanings Waite calls The Tower "a card in particular of unforeseen catastrophe". And in the centre of 71.5% of such couples stands The Star — the card that follows The Tower in the deck. Waite's figure on it pours "on the waters of the soul some part and measure of her priceless possession". The atmosphere inside this couple is what comes after the lightning: not armour, but water. In Chrétien, once the danger is past, Enide takes Erec's armour off, washes and binds his wounds, and lets no one else touch him. In the other 28.5% of couples the centre holds Justice — the scales on which the two weigh their rights.

sections.h2: How a couple steps out of the 21-16-4 script
paragraphs: The romance gives no recipe, but it shows exactly where things break and where they mend. Here is what follows from it for two people.

ul: **Say by day what is heard at night.** Enide kept the gossip to herself until it broke out one morning in bed, through tears, over her sleeping husband. Other people's words about the couple — from relatives, friends, colleagues — are better brought into the conversation while they are still news, not a verdict.

**Do not answer pain with a decree.** "Don't speak to me" is the natural reaction of someone who has been hurt. But rules like that later have to be broken for the sake of the very person who made them. If the urge is to forbid, it is more honest to say that it hurts.
**Ride side by side after the blow.** Troubles are not split into "yours" and "mine". In a hard period, decide together and out loud, even if one of the two has more strength right now.

**Measure your world.** Translate "we have everything" into agreements: money, home, time for oneself and for friends, who is responsible for what. And revise them when life changes: a rule that is never revised turns into a garden behind a wall of air.

**Two crowns, not one.** Order does not mean that one gives orders and the other obeys, nor that the two swap roles. Each has an area where they decide, and there are shared questions where both decide.
**Let people into the garden.** Friends, family and shared projects with other people keep a world for two from becoming an enchanted garden.

paragraphs: If in a real couple one partner forbids the other to speak, threatens them or raises a hand, this is not "a lesson of The Emperor" but danger. What is needed here is help from people: a local emergency number, a crisis line, a psychologist.

sections.h2: The strong version of the couple's 21-16-4 tail
paragraphs: The strong version of this couple is two people who have been through their Tower and know each other's voice. Their order was not invented by one of them: it was measured by both, like Erec's robe. Their world is not closed — others are glad of it too, as of "the Joy of the Court". Lisovskaya writes that many see a couple with The World in its bright form as ideal. For 21-16-4 this is not a shop window at the start but the result: an ideal that was built, not given.

After "the Joy of the Court" Chrétien slips in a line that is easy to miss: "Nor was Enide mute as she took leave of the barons: she greeted them all by name." The girl with no name until her wedding, the wife who was forbidden to speak, now calls every person by name. That is the whole road of the 21-16-4 tail: **from a world that needs no words to an order in which everyone has a voice.**

ul: **Entry to the task — 21, The World.** What the couple wants together: a whole world for two, full and finished, with nothing left to add. It is also the resistance: a world like that easily closes itself off from everyone else.

**Middle of the task — 16, The Tower.** The road runs through the collapse of invented images — of oneself and of the partner. What was left unsaid breaks out, and for a while the two travel in silence, one behind the other rather than side by side.
**Main task — 4, The Emperor.** To build how the union works: agreements instead of orders, rules that both of them made, and a voice for each.

intro: This plot has a twin in literature, and it is more than eight centuries old. What follows is an investigation: what is written in the three cards, in the numbers of the couple's matrix, and in an old romance that begins where fairy tales end.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 21-16-4 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of a couple who begin with a sense of a finished, complete world for two (The World, 21), live through the collapse of invented images of themselves and of each other (The Tower, 16) and learn the main thing — to build a shared order with agreements and a voice for both (The Emperor, 4). The main point is The Emperor: that is where the couple has the most work to do.

faq.q: Can 21-16-4 appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and for The World over a four at the bottom the centre would have to be The Star, 17. No birth date gives a person that centre, so 21-16-4 occurs only in a couple's matrix.

faq.q: Why is the middle 16 and not 7?
faq.a: A couple's middle is not recalculated from the ends; it is the sum of the middles of the two personal tails: 7 + 9 or 8 + 8. Adding the ends, 21 + 4, would give 7, but the couple takes its middle straight from the partners, and the result is The Tower.

faq.q: Does the 21-16-4 tail predict a crisis or a break-up?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events or dates. The Tower in the middle describes how the couple travels towards its task: through a change in how they see themselves and each other, not through an appointed catastrophe. How that road goes depends on whether the two talk to each other.

faq.q: What is in the centre for couples with the 21-16-4 tail?
faq.a: In 71.5% of these couples the centre is The Star, 17 — a card that never appears in the centre of a personal matrix. In the other 28.5% the centre is Justice, 8: this happens when the tail is built from the personal tails 15-8-11 and 6-8-20.

faq.q: Are there couple tails with the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. A search through every date produces neither 21-4-16 nor any order with 16 or 4 in front. A tail of The World, The Tower and The Emperor appears in a couple only in the order 21-16-4.

report: In the 21-16-4 tail the happy ending comes first. It opens with The World — the card of completion, the "final message" of the Major Arcana — and closes with The Emperor, one of the first cards in the row. First "happily ever after", then the foundation such happiness rests on. A couple with this tail is given fullness before structure, and its main task is to lay the foundation after the fact.

Around 1170 Chrétien de Troyes wrote a romance built in exactly this way. In "Erec and Enide" the wedding comes at about line two thousand out of nearly seven thousand: where a fairy tale puts a full stop, Chrétien is only starting. Even the bride's name is first spoken at the altar, because "a wife is not wed unless she is called by her rightful name". The three acts of the romance fall on the three cards in order — a reading, not the author's design, but the matches are too exact to ignore.

report.h3: A world with nothing left to add

report: After the wedding Erec loves his wife so much that he gives up tournaments and often gets up when it is already past noon. The world shrinks to one room, and in that room nothing is lacking. Outside, the court whispers that Erec has turned coward and blames Enide. She hears all of it and says nothing — her husband would take offence. One morning, over her sleeping husband, her tears break out in a sentence: "Ill-fated you are!" Erec is only dozing, and he hears.

Later Enide names the loss herself: "I was too much at ease: there was nothing I lacked." This is the entry to the tail: what the couple wants together is a full, finished world for two. It is also the resistance. Meetings with friends are cancelled one after another, someone close tells one of the partners that the two have "vanished completely" — and that partner does not pass it on, so as not to spoil things. **The world is full, except that everything said about it from outside piles up inside one of the two.**

report.h3: She rides ahead and keeps silent

report: Erec does not argue — "you were right" — and orders her to get ready for the road. He leads his wife off "not knowing where, at a venture" and gives an order: "Do not speak to me unless I address you first. Ride ahead, and fast." "She went ahead and fell silent. Neither said a word to the other." Enide whispers: "To such great joy had God raised me up — and in a short hour He has cast me down." This is The Tower in a single line.

There is no jealousy and no rival in Chrétien. What collapses is not fidelity but two invented images: "the best knight in the world" learns how others see him, and the wife who "lacked for nothing" learns that her happiness is called his disgrace. In trouble the two literally look in different directions: she in front, he behind, and she is forbidden to turn round. Dangers come one after another, and again and again Enide must choose between the ban and her husband: "He will kill me. Let him kill me! I will not keep silent — I will tell him." Erec wins and scolds her. **The voice that saves him is punished for having spoken.**

In real life this middle can be entirely ordinary: after a hard conversation the two live "in business mode", sort things out, pay the bills and barely talk. One of them is the first to notice what is coming and decides each time whether to break the silence. The other copes alone and is annoyed at being warned.

report: The turning point comes when the badly wounded Erec is taken for dead, and a count marries Enide by force and speaks a formula in which the shadow of The Emperor shows without disguise: "The lady is mine and I am hers, and I will do with her as I please." Enide fears neither his blows nor his threats. And Erec comes to — "when he heard his wife's voice". He puts her in front of him on a single horse: "The horse carries them both." A moment ago they rode apart; now they share one saddle.

The romance ends with a coronation. Two crowns are brought out: one for Erec, the other for Enide, who not long ago was forbidden to speak. Erec's robe is embroidered with Geometry, who measures "how far the heavens and the earth extend, so that nothing is lacking". It is the same turn of phrase as in Enide's morning lament. In bed, fullness was given as a gift and measured by nothing; on the king's robe it is measured. **In the 21-16-4 tail The Emperor does not cancel happiness: he draws its plan.**

report.h3: Two crowns, not one

report: The romance shows The Emperor in shadow twice. First the empty throne: a king's son who decides nothing, while gossip rules in his place. Then the decree "do not speak", which Enide breaks for her husband's sake — a rule that gets in its own author's way. The couple's main task is to turn "we have everything" into "we have it all worked out": who decides about money and who about holidays, how much time belongs to each partner's friends, which rules are shared and which survive only out of habit.

What follows for the two of them: say by day what is heard at night, while other people's words about the couple are still news, not a verdict. Divide the areas where each one decides, rather than simply changing who gives the orders. And if in a real couple one partner forbids the other to speak, threatens them or raises a hand, this is not a lesson of the cards but danger: what is needed is help from people — a local emergency number or crisis line, a psychologist.

There is a line in the romance that is easy to miss: "Nor was Enide mute as she took leave of the barons: she greeted them all by name." The girl with no name until her wedding, the wife who was forbidden to speak, calls every person by name. That is the road of the tail: **from a world that needs no words to an order in which everyone has a voice.**
