seo.title: Karmic tail 21 19 16 compatibility: The World, The Sun, The Tower
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 19 16 compatibility: what The World, The Sun and The Tower mean for a couple who live in plain sight, and how to survive a fallen image.

items.title: Karmic tail 21-19-16 in compatibility: the bridal chorus and the forbidden question
items.short: In much of the world brides walk down the aisle to the bridal chorus from Wagner's Lohengrin, and few people remember where that chorus leads in the opera itself: to a bedroom where the marriage collapses that same night over a single question. Karmic tail 21-19-16 in compatibility tells this story in three cards. The couple enters the union wanting a whole world for two, lives it brightly and in plain sight, and the main task begins when the beautiful image of the partner cracks.

sections.h2: An opera that calls the three cards by name
paragraphs: Wagner wrote Lohengrin entirely himself, words and music; it was first staged in Weimar on 28 August 1850, with Franz Liszt conducting. The plot fits in a few lines. Elsa of Brabant is accused of doing away with her younger brother. She cannot defend herself and tells only a dream: a knight came to her. The king's trumpeters turn to the four quarters of the world and call for a champion. Down the Scheldt comes a knight in silver armour, in a boat drawn by a swan on a golden chain. He defeats the accuser and takes Elsa as his wife on one condition: she must never ask who he is or where he comes from.

The wedding is the next day. The chorus escorts the newlyweds to the bridal chamber and sings (here and below, quotations from the libretto are in our translation): "Fragrant room, adorned for love, now take them in, far from the splendour." The knight sits with Elsa by the window: "We are alone, alone for the first time since we met. Now we have escaped the world." A few minutes later Elsa asks the forbidden question. In the morning, before all the people, the knight names himself — Lohengrin, son of Parzival, knight of the Grail — and sails away.

In the German text the first two cards of the tail have words of their own. Splendour, Glanz, is what the opera calls the radiance of the knight and of the feast. The world, Welt, is everything before whose eyes the story happens. **Both stay outside the bedroom door, and inside, where there is neither world nor splendour, The Tower strikes.** Now, card by card.

sections.h2: The World: "Never shall you ask me"
paragraphs: The World stands at the entry to the task, the point of the couple's shared wishes. In the paid reading the same point appears again, in the sphere "Relationship and common language". This couple's common language is the whole at once. In the opera both of them speak it. At their first meeting Elsa sinks at the knight's feet: "To you I give all that I am." He answers with a condition: "Never shall you ask me, nor trouble yourself to know, whence I sailed here, nor what my name and lineage." And on the wedding night he explains why questions are needless: "We who had never seen each other had divined each other… I had no need to find out your lineage: my eye saw you, and my heart understood you."

In real life this is recognisable at once. The two feel they have always known each other, and the slow stage of getting acquainted is skipped: within a month a shared home, within a year another city or another country, a philosophy for two, private words, their own map of the world. In plus The World gives the couple something rare. One comes home angry and worn out, and the other does not demand that they first become pleasant, but puts the kettle on. They argue at length and out loud, and come out of the argument with an agreement rather than a victory. From outside, such a couple looks like a model.

The resistance grows from the same root. Accept the whole, and there seems to be nothing left to ask about. One says nothing about their former life, their family, their money before the two met, and the other accepts this as the price of the whole. The secrets multiply, the picture of the partner looks less and less like the partner, and the couple stops hearing each other even while talking a great deal.

Benebell Wen describes the hard side of The World (the card drawn reversed) through two states that look like opposites. In the first, the person is "consciously and knowingly in denial" and is "remaining willfully ignorant". The second is "the Great Skeptic", who will "question all, and doubt all". Elsa goes through both in one opera: first an oath to know nothing, then a doubt that within a single day drives her to the question. Ignorance by agreement and suspicion grow from one and the same World, accepted without questions.

In two thirds of these couples The World is made of one partner's The Moon and the other's The Empress, that is, of a dream and of land. Elsa brings the knight exactly this: the dream in which she saw him, and the crown of her father's land — "in my father's lands let him wear the crown". A whole world, given away on the strength of a dream.

sections.h2: The Sun: a life before witnesses
paragraphs: Everything Elsa and the knight live through before the bedroom happens in front of everyone. The trial is held at noon, and the king orders the call: "The sun already stands high at noon — it is time to summon the champion." The crowd looks at the arriving knight and cannot bear to look: "How his armour shines! The eye fails before such splendour!" After the duel both are lifted on shields and carried off amid cheering. In the morning the herald announces the wedding and, in the same breath, a campaign: "Today he celebrates his wedding feast with you, but tomorrow you shall come armed for battle." The bridal procession walks to the cathedral through a living corridor, and Wagner's stage direction specifies that everyone can see Elsa. Only in the bridal chamber are they alone for the first time.

The Sun in the middle of the task shows how the couple travels from the wish to the task. This couple travels it in the light. In readings about love and relationships, Wen calls The Sun "a radiant marriage" and says plainly: "It could suggest a power couple." A home where friends gather. A shared venture they are proud of. Children whose achievements get shared. Together they know how to be a couple in public: they tell one story in two voices, and catch each other's jokes on the fly. In plus each is good at their own work, and one's success does not overshadow the other's: at one partner's award ceremony the other claps loudest, and a month later they swap places.

The difficulty shows in the same scene for anyone who stays to the end of the evening. The guests have gone, the dishes are in the sink, and it turns out there is nothing to talk about, the two of them alone, except plans. Problems go unmentioned so as not to darken the picture. There is so much work that there is no minute for "how are you really": today the wedding, tomorrow the campaign. Expectations rise — of the partner, of oneself, of the union. At an anniversary party one of them tells how "we" built the business, while the other silently counts how many times "I" was said.

In two thirds of these couples The Sun is made of one partner's The Lovers and the other's Death, that is, of a choice and of what was left behind for its sake. Lohengrin speaks of it on the wedding night almost like an accountant: "Your love must richly repay me for what I left behind for you." A light that has a price easily turns into a bill.

sections.h2: The Tower: the question asked in the bedroom
paragraphs: The scene in the bridal chamber is the most exact description of this couple's main task to be found anywhere. In it the question ripens step by step, and a couple can recognise every step.

First Elsa asks for very little — the sound of his name, and only for the two of them: "How sweetly my name slips from your lips! Will you not grant me the sound of yours?.. Alone, when everyone is asleep. The world shall never hear it!" The knight refuses.

Then he reassures her in the language of The Sun: "For I do not come from night and sorrow — I come from splendour and bliss!" It is exactly this that breaks her: "You came to me from bliss, and you long to go back!.. Shall I count the days you still will stay with me?" The radiant image of the partner becomes a source of fear: whoever came from the light will go back to the light.

Then Elsa imagines the swan already swimming to fetch him, and the whole question comes out: "Tell me your name! Whence did you come? What is your lineage?" Lohengrin: "Alas, now all our happiness is gone!" The candles burn down towards dawn.

In the morning comes the denouement, and the opera's main lesson is hidden in it. The truth refused in private, the knight speaks in front of everyone: "Before the whole world, before king and realm, I reveal my secret." First he even accuses his wife for all to hear. **The name that could have been whispered for Elsa alone rings out in the public square, and the marriage ends with it.**

Among the tasks of a couple with The Tower, Yuliana Lisovskaya names three that are acted out in this scene. The collapse of an invented image of the partner — Elsa loved the knight of her dream long before they met. The loss of self-control — the question is asked at the wrong moment and in the wrong way. And the habit of looking in different directions when trouble comes: she looks into the past, at his secret; he looks at the river, where the swan will come for him.

In life the trigger can be anything: a detail from a former life surfaces, someone's status suddenly changes, the one who was always strong is suddenly tired. After a long time in the light, the two meet for the first time without an audience and see an ordinary person where a radiant one used to stand. The hardest thing at that moment is not to sail away on one's own swan: into resentment, into work, into "nobody understands me here".

sections.h2: The Sun and The Tower: one light at different distances
paragraphs: In 1851 Wagner wrote "A Communication to My Friends", in which he explained where Lohengrin came from. He found the outline of the story already among the Greeks: "Who does not know the story of 'Zeus and Semele'?" (in William Ashton Ellis's translation, as are the other quotations from this essay). The god loves a mortal woman and comes to her in human shape. She, "urged by Love's own ardour, demands that her spouse shall show himself to physical sense in the full substance of his being". Zeus knows it will destroy her and still grants the wish — and, Wagner writes, "the fatal splendour of his godlike presence strikes Semele dead".

In the German original that splendour is again Glanz. The very word that in the opera shines on the knight's armour and stays outside the bedroom door kills in Wagner's own account. **The Sun and The Tower in this tail are one and the same light at different distances.** From afar, in public, it warms and dazzles. When it is demanded whole and all at once, at close range, it strikes like lightning.

Running through every date since 1900 turns up one more clue. Neither partner in such a couple has The World or The Sun — not in their personal karmic tail, not in the centre of their personal matrix. The World and The Sun are born only in the sum of the two dates. This couple's radiance is shared: it exists between two people, not in each of them separately. In the opera the knight really did come from the light. In a living couple the light works differently, and in the moment of The Tower each sees the other without the shared radiance — simply because neither has it alone. This is not the unmasking of a fraud. It is meeting a person who until now has only been seen in the light of the couple.

Hence the task. Its point is not that the question must never be asked. The couple needs to learn a third, ordinary light: to see each other neither from afar, as at a celebration, nor in a flash, as on the night of the question, but by day, piece by piece, without demanding that everything be shown at once.

sections.h2: Why Wagner took Elsa's side
paragraphs: The usual moral of this story is "she should have trusted and not asked". Wagner himself thought otherwise. In the same "Communication" he writes that he found Elsa "so justified in the final outburst of her jealousy" that this very outburst taught him "the purely-human element of love". He describes her question as the moment she "wakes first from out the thrill of worship into the full reality of Love". And he admits that Elsa "made me a Revolutionary at one blow".

One more detail from the same text. "Infected", as he puts it, "with the doubting spirit of Criticism", Wagner sketched a different ending: Lohengrin, once revealed, would "put aside his higher nature" in favour of "a sojourn upon earth with Elsa". He then rejected it as "utterly unsatisfactory" and "unnatural", and put the knight back in the boat.

Wagner's source, Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival (early thirteenth century), tells the same story in fewer than a hundred lines, and more calmly. There the Duchess of Brabant does not even have a name. Before all the people the knight sets his condition: "Never ask who I am — then I can stay with you" (our translation from Middle High German, as below). He becomes a good judge, "together they had fine children", and only then does the question come. He leaves, in Wolfram's word, "unwillingly", and leaves behind a sword, a horn and a little ring. Wolfram judges more harshly than Wagner: the knight had warned her, after all, when he came to her out of the sea.

Eight centuries lie between the two verdicts, and a couple with this tail needs both. From Wagner, the right to ask: Elsa's question is not a sin of curiosity but a step from worship to a living person. From Wolfram, the years and the children between the oath and the question — that is, a Sun lived long enough for there to be something to protect. In plus, Lisovskaya's Tower sounds like this: trials gone through together make the union stronger, and in sudden trouble the two calmly hold on to each other. **The ending Wagner sketched and rejected — the knight said his name and stayed — is exactly this couple's main task.**

sections.h2: The Hierophant in the centre: the rule about what may be shown
paragraphs: A couple with tail 21-19-16 always has the same centre — The Hierophant, the fifth arcanum, in 100% of such couples. In two thirds of them it is made of the personal centres 12 and 20 (The Hanged Man and Judgement), in the rest of 7 and 16 (The Chariot and The Tower).

Waite describes The Hierophant's gesture: with his raised right hand he gives a sign "distinguishing between the manifest and concealed part of doctrine". The opera knows this rule. Telling the story of the Grail, Lohengrin explains why he kept silent: "So sublime is the Grail's blessing that, once revealed, it must flee the layman's eye." The knight is not secretive by nature — he serves a rule under which one thing may be shown and another may not. Waite also warns about the danger of this card: "it may so happen that the pontiff forgets the significance of this his symbolic state and acts as if he contained within his proper measures all that his sign signifies". Then the rule starts living in place of the people.

The couple's centre is its atmosphere, what happens between the two when nobody is watching. For this couple The Hierophant lives there. In plus this is a couple with its own holidays and its own order: a Sunday breakfast that is never cancelled, a word that is kept, and decisions that one partner makes for both with the other's full consent. And the partners remain friends. In minus the same Hierophant gives lectures: one knows how things should be done and patiently remakes the other, and the couple's door is closed to everyone, sometimes even to the partners themselves. For tail 21-19-16 what matters most is which rule sits in the centre. "We don't quarrel in front of guests" protects both. "In our house we don't talk about your parents" hides something, and rules like that store up the question to come.

sections.h2: The couple's values: the swan's golden chain
paragraphs: In the sphere "The couple's values" such couples have The Devil (78.6%) or The Lovers (21.4%).

The swan that brings the knight draws the boat on a golden chain. In the finale Ortrud, the sorceress and Elsa's chief enemy, gloats: by the little chain she herself wound around the swan, she knew who it was — Elsa's lost brother, the heir of Brabant. Lohengrin takes the chain off the swan, and a boy rises from the river. The radiance came to Brabant drawn by an enchanted chain.

Waite himself links The Devil with The Hierophant. The Devil's raised hand is "the reverse of that benediction which is given by the Hierophant in the fifth card", and the two chained figures at his feet "are analogous with those of the fifth card". The chain, for Waite, is "the chain and fatality of the material life". In the couple's centre there is a blessing; in its values, the same blessing turned inside out. In plus, The Devil in the values is a passion nobody is ashamed of: the two know each other's dark sides and say their wishes out loud, even the awkward ones. In minus it is the wish to own: to check, to hold on, to tie the other down with money or status — and silence about what one really wants. The closing thought of Lisovskaya's section on The Devil deserves to hang over this couple's door: nobody belongs to anybody. Lohengrin takes the chain off only after The Tower. The couple would do well to take it off sooner.
Where the values hold The Lovers, the value becomes the choice itself: the union rests not on an oath given once by a river, but on a decision the two keep making again.

sections.h2: The Sun instead of the Wheel: how tail 21-19-16 is worked out
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22. Example: the dates 04.07.1975 and 04.01.1976. The first partner's personal tail is 18-6-6, the second's is 3-13-10.
The couple's centre: 12 + 20 = 32 → 3 + 2 = 5, The Hierophant. "The couple's values" in this example are 15, The Devil.

The couple's middle is not recalculated from the ends. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is the sum of its ends: 21 + 16 = 37 → 10, The Wheel of Fortune. That is why 21-19-16 never occurs as a personal tail. For a couple the middle is added up from the two personal middles: 6 + 13 = 19.

Here is one more clue. A personal middle is the sum of its own ends, so a couple's middle always reduces to the same digit as the sum of its ends: 37 → 10 → 1. Of the numbers up to 22, only 10 and 19 reduce to one, and one itself never appears in a couple. So a couple that enters the task through The World and works on The Tower can only have The Wheel or The Sun in the middle. The Wheel comes up in one couple in 107 — that is tail 21-10-16. The Sun comes up in one in 1,572 (0.064%, 87th place of 97 couple tails). Among couples with these ends, roughly one in sixteen gets The Sun.

The Sun appears only when the partners' middles add up to exactly 19 without reduction: 6 + 13 (personal tails 18-6-6 and 3-13-10, 66% of such couples) or 5 + 14 (15-5-8 and 6-14-8, 34%). Tails 3-13-10 and 6-14-8 are among the rarest personal tails: since 1900 they have fallen on 149 and 55 birth dates, almost all between January and April. Hence the rarity.

What this means. Almost every couple with the same entry and the same main task has The Wheel in the middle: life turns now up, now down, and reminds them by itself that luck changes. This couple has The Sun at its height where The Wheel would stand. Luck seems to have stopped at noon, "the sun already stands high", and The Wheel's lesson — everything changes — arrives all at once, through The Tower.
This tail has no permutations: the numbers 21, 19 and 16 in any other order do not form a couple tail.

sections.h2: How to live tail 21-19-16 in plus

ul: **Ask by daylight.** Do not save up "who are you really" until the night after a celebration, but ask a little at a time on ordinary days, when the answer breaks nothing. In the opera the question is asked at night, by guttering candles, and the answer is given in full daylight — when it is already too late.

**Answer in private.** If the partner asks for a truth meant for the two of them only, that is the best form a question can take. Refusing it, as Lohengrin does, usually ends with the truth told in front of everyone.
**Review the rules in the centre.** Every so often, go through the couple's own "we don't do that here" together and separate the rules that protect from the rules that hide.
**Keep the collapse out of the public square.** No judging each other in front of friends, family or followers. The Tower is a matter for two.

**Check the image against the person.** Each names honestly what in the partner they invented themselves and what they saw with their own eyes. The invented part is not the partner's lie but one's own dream, and the dreamer answers for it.
**Share The Sun.** Tell the couple's success as a shared one, and do not take the other's part for oneself.
**Stay after the name.** When the truth has been spoken, do not step into the boat. Wagner turned down the ending where the knight stays, but nothing stops a couple from writing it.

**The World (21), entry to the task.** The shared wish is to accept each other at once and entirely, without questions, as if the partner had arrived ready-made from a distant land. The same wish turns into resistance when "don't ask" becomes a rule.

**The Sun (19), middle of the task.** The couple travels its road in the light: celebrations, successes, a home open to friends, and everyone around saying "the perfect couple". In plain sight it is easy to love an image, because everyone can see it, the partners included.

**The Tower (16), main task.** To live through the moment when the two are alone for the first time, with no audience and no radiance, and ask each other "who are you?" — and then not to part, but to build again, this time on the truth.

intro: The tail does not predict a break-up or a disaster. It describes a plot that each couple lives with its own force and in its own time. The roles in this plot are not split by sex: either partner may stay silent or ask, and they often swap places.

faq.q: Is karmic tail 21-19-16 in compatibility a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail describes tasks, not a verdict. The World at the entry gives this couple a rare ability to accept each other whole, The Sun in the middle gives warmth, success and respect. The Tower shows where all this wealth needs a foundation: in truth told in time.

faq.q: Does The Tower in a couple's tail mean the couple will split up?
faq.a: No. The Tower as the main task describes the collapse of an invented image of the partner and of the couple, not an event with a date. In plus, Lisovskaya links it to trials gone through together, after which the union is stronger. One can part with the image and stay with the person.

faq.q: How does tail 21-19-16 differ from tail 21-10-16?
faq.a: They share the entry, The World, and the main task, The Tower, but the middles differ. In 21-10-16 the middle is The Wheel: the couple's life turns, and changes come gradually. In 21-19-16 the middle is The Sun: the couple lives in a long noon, and change comes all at once, as a blow. The second tail is almost fifteen times rarer.

faq.q: Can one person have karmic tail 21-19-16?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail equals the sum of its ends, and 21 + 16 give 10, The Wheel. The triple 21-19-16 exists only for a couple, because its middle is added up from the middles of the two partners.

faq.q: Who in the couple is Elsa, and who is Lohengrin?
faq.a: Either of the two, and more often by turns. In one situation a partner arrives "from splendour" and asks not to be questioned; in another the same partner saves up a question and asks it at the wrong moment. Sex decides nothing here.

report: In much of the world brides walk down the aisle to the bridal chorus from Wagner's Lohengrin. In the opera itself that chorus escorts the newlyweds to a bedroom where the marriage collapses that same night over a single question. Couple tail 21-19-16 tells this story in three cards: The World, The Sun and The Tower.

Elsa of Brabant stands accused, and down the river a knight in silver armour sails to her aid, in a boat drawn by a swan on a golden chain. He defends her and takes her as his wife on one condition: "Never shall you ask me, nor trouble yourself to know, whence I sailed here, nor what my name and lineage." In return Elsa gives him "all that I am". This is The World at the entry to the task, the couple's shared wish: to accept each other at once and entirely, without questions, as if the partner had arrived ready-made from a distant land. The roles are not split by sex: either partner may stay silent or ask, and they often swap places.

report.h3: The world and the splendour stay outside the door

report: Everything the two live through before the wedding night happens in front of everyone. The trial is held at noon. The crowd looks at the arriving knight and cannot bear to look: "The eye fails before such splendour!" Both are lifted on shields, and on the wedding day itself the herald is already announcing a campaign for tomorrow.

This is The Sun in the middle of the task: the couple travels its road in the light. Benebell Wen writes that in readings about love this card "could suggest a power couple", two people who are strong and visible together. A home where friends gather. A shared venture they are proud of. One story told in two voices. And the evening when the guests have gone and there is nothing to talk about, the two of them alone, except plans: problems go unmentioned so as not to darken the picture.

The chorus escorts the newlyweds to a chamber "far from the splendour", and the knight says to Elsa: "We are alone, alone for the first time since we met. Now we have escaped the world." **The world and the splendour stay outside the bedroom door, and inside, where there is neither, The Tower strikes.**

report.h3: The truth refused in private

report: In the bridal chamber the question ripens step by step. First Elsa asks only for the sound of his name, and only for the two of them: "Alone, when everyone is asleep. The world shall never hear it!" The knight refuses. Then he reassures her in the language of The Sun: "I come from splendour and bliss!" It is exactly this that breaks her: whoever came from the light will go back to the light. "Shall I count the days you still will stay with me?" At last the whole question comes out: "Tell me your name! Whence did you come? What is your lineage?"

In the morning the knight names himself before all the people: "Before the whole world, before king and realm, I reveal my secret." And he sails away. **The name that could have been whispered for Elsa alone rings out in the public square, and the marriage ends with it.**

Among the tasks of a couple with The Tower, Yuliana Lisovskaya names the collapse of an invented image of the partner, the loss of self-control and the habit of looking in different directions when trouble comes. All three are in that bedroom. Elsa loved the knight of her dream long before they met. The question is asked at the wrong moment and in the wrong way. And in trouble she looks at his secret, he looks at the river the swan will come down. In life the trigger can be anything: a detail from a former life, a sudden change of status, the tiredness of the one who was always strong. After a long time in the light, the two meet for the first time without an audience and see an ordinary person where a radiant one used to stand.

report.h3: One light at different distances

report: Wagner himself found the outline of this story in the Greek myth of Zeus and Semele. A mortal woman demands that the god show himself to her in full, and she is killed by "the fatal splendour of his godlike presence". In the German original that splendour is the same word as the shine on the knight's armour: Glanz. **The Sun and The Tower in this tail are one and the same light at different distances.** From afar, in public, it warms. When it is demanded whole and all at once, at close range, it strikes like lightning.

There is a clue in the numbers too. Neither partner in such a couple has The World or The Sun — not in their personal karmic tail, not in the centre of their personal matrix. The radiance exists only between the two, not in each of them separately. So in the moment of The Tower each sees the other without the shared light. This is not the unmasking of a fraud, but meeting a person who until now has only been seen in the light of the couple.

At the centre of such couples there is always The Hierophant — the rule about what may be shown and what may not. "We don't quarrel in front of guests" protects both. "In our house we don't talk about your parents" hides something, and rules like that store up the question to come.

report.h3: The ending Wagner turned down

report: The usual moral of the opera is "she should have trusted and not asked". Wagner thought otherwise: he found Elsa "so justified in the final outburst of her jealousy" that this very outburst taught him "the purely-human element of love". He even sketched an ending in which Lohengrin, once revealed, stays on earth with Elsa, and then rejected it. **For a couple with this tail, the main task is exactly that ending: the truth has been spoken, and nobody steps into the boat.** In plus, Lisovskaya's Tower means trials gone through together, after which the union is stronger.
What helps a couple with this tail:

ul: asking by daylight, a little at a time on ordinary days, instead of saving up "who are you really" until the night after a celebration;
answering in private: a request for a truth meant for the two alone is the best form a question can take, and refusing it usually ends with the truth told in front of everyone;
separating the rules that protect from the rules that hide;
keeping the collapse out of the public square: The Tower is a matter for two;
checking the image against the person: what in the partner was invented and what was seen with one's own eyes.

seo.title: Karmic tail 21 19 7 compatibility: the World, the Sun, the Chariot
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 19 7 compatibility: the World at the entry, the Sun in the middle, the Chariot as the main task, and an Indian myth of the Sun's wife.

items.title: The 21-19-7 karmic tail in compatibility: the Sun's wife and a team of two
items.short: Book Ten of the Rigveda describes a wedding to which "all the world" comes, and a bride who vanishes from it. The groom is Vivasvat, the Shining One. Later texts call him the Sun outright and tell the rest of the story: the bride could not bear his light, left a shadow in her place and fled as a mare, and her husband found her only when he became a horse himself. The World, the Sun, the Chariot: the cards of the couple's karmic tail 21-19-7 stand in the same order. The couple enters its shared task wanting a whole world for two and lives that task brightly, in full view, and in that light one partner can start to shine while the other quietly slips into the shadow. The main task is the Chariot: learning to run in one harness so that nobody has to disappear.

sections.h2: How the 21-19-7 tail is built and why only a couple can have it
paragraphs: A couple's tail belongs to neither partner. Each of its points is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. Here is an example with the dates 02.01.1980 and 14.04.1975.

The first partner has day 2, month 1 and year 1 + 9 + 8 + 0 = 18. Their karmic task is 2 + 1 + 18 = 21, their centre 42 → 6, their personal tail 9-3-21. The second partner has day 14, month 4 and year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. The karmic task is 40 → 4, the centre 44 → 8, the personal tail 12-16-4. Now the points of the two tails are added in pairs:
This couple's centre is 6 + 8 = 14, Temperance, and the couple's values are 6, The Lovers. Both cards will be needed later.

A personal matrix cannot hold this triple. There the middle of the tail is the reduced sum of the entry and the main task: 21 + 7 = 28 → 10, The Wheel of Fortune. A couple's middle is not recalculated from its two ends; it is added up from the middles of two people, and instead of the Wheel it comes out as the Sun, a number that only two people can produce. The method does not reduce numbers up to 22, yet the Wheel can still be read in the digits of the Sun: 1 + 9 = 10. It is worth remembering: in the myth it will turn up as the lathe on which the Sun is cut down.

The 21-19-7 tail falls to roughly one couple in 269 (0.371%), which puts it 66th among the 97 couple tails. In 98% of these couples it is made of the personal tails 12-16-4 and 9-3-21, as in the example; in 2% it is made of 18-6-15 and 3-13-10. In the main variant the couple's World is built from The Hanged Man and The Hermit, two cards in which a person is alone: one has stopped in a pause, the other has walked away from people. The Sun is built from The Tower and The Empress, a sudden blow and abundance. The Chariot comes from The Emperor and The World, power and a whole world. These are not the partners' roles, because a personal tail is read differently. This is what the numbers are made of, and it says a great deal: this couple's wish for a whole world grows out of two solitudes.
This tail has no permutations. The entry of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, so 7 and 19 cannot stand there, and no pair of birth dates produces the order 21-7-19.

sections.h2: A myth older than the cards: the Shining One and the Swift One
paragraphs: The oldest version takes up two stanzas of the Rigveda (X, 17, 1–2). In Ralph Griffith's translation (1896):

"Tvaṣṭar prepares the bridal of his Daughter: all the world hears the tidings and assembles. But Yama's Mother, Spouse of great Vivasvān, vanished as she was carried to her dwelling. From mortal men they hid the Immortal Lady, made one like her and gave her to Vivasvān. Saraṇyu brought to him the Aśvin brothers, and then deserted both twinned pairs of children."

The hymn says nothing more: not why she vanished, not where she went. The whole story is told by the Puranas, written down many centuries later: the Markandeya Purana (cantos 77–78) and the Vishnu Purana (book III, chapter 2). The daughter of the heavenly craftsman marries the Sun and cannot bear his radiance. She makes a body of her own out of shadow, leaves it in her husband's house in her place and goes to her father. Her father sends her back to her husband, and she goes north instead, to the Northern Kurus, and lives there as a mare. The Sun lives with the shadow for a long time and never notices the substitution, until the deceit comes out through the children. Then the Sun himself asks his father-in-law to reduce his radiance, takes the form of a horse and finds his wife. From that meeting the Ashvins are born, the twin horsemen of the sky.

The names in this story speak for themselves. Vivasvat means "the Shining One". Saranyu means "the Swift One", from a root meaning "to run, to flow". In the Puranas the bride is called Sañjñā, and among the meanings of the word the Monier-Williams dictionary gives "agreement, mutual understanding, harmony". The double is called Chhāyā, "Shadow". In the Puranas the bride's father is Vishvakarman, "the Maker of All". The cards of the tail sit in these names almost word for word. The World is the wedding to which all the world comes, and the father who made everything. The Sun is the groom. The Chariot is the bride whose name is Swift. And the bride's second name, Agreement, is exactly what the couple has at the entry to its task: a common language.

The story reaches beyond India. A nineteenth-century Sanskrit dictionary notes that some scholars connected the name Saranyu with the Greek Erinys. And Pausanias recorded an Arcadian myth in which Demeter turned into a mare to escape Poseidon, he caught her in the form of a stallion, and for her anger at this the goddess was called Erinys there (Description of Greece, VIII, 25).

sections.h2: The World at the entry: a wedding the whole world comes to
paragraphs: For Yuliana Lisovskaya, the entry to the task is the point of shared wishes and agreements, the couple's "common language". It sits on the line of tasks, so the same wish can also become resistance. This couple has the World at the entry, and its wish is the size of the world.

Couples like this begin with something big. They have not yet decided where to live, but they already know which countries they will travel to, what the house will be like, whom they will invite to the table and how they will look at life. They agree quickly, and they are at ease together on the road, in a move, in a strange city. From outside they often look like the perfect couple. Waite calls the World "the perfection and end of the Cosmos", and at the entry this is exactly what the couple wants: a whole in which nothing is missing.

The Rigveda adds one detail to this picture, and it is unsettling. The whole world gathered for the wedding, and the bride vanished on the way, in the wedding procession itself, "as she was carried to her dwelling". Nobody noticed, because she was replaced by "one like her". The Sanskrit word, savarṇā, literally means "of the same colour". This is where the World's minus in a couple begins: the picture stays whole, but the person is no longer in it.

In everyday life this looks ordinary. The couple still has shared plans, shared friends, shared photographs. But one partner has long been the only one talking about "our world", while the other nods. Decisions get made, but there is no agreement: nobody has checked it since it put itself together in the first months. Lisovskaya puts it briefly: such partners do not hear each other. The World at the entry asks not for scale but for a check: do both of them live in this world, or is one of them only playing at being there?

The same wish has a reverse side. A world built to one person's design turns into a workshop where the other is remade to fit the plan: the right friends, the right interests, the right faith. Whatever does not fit the design is quietly cut away, and the whole world for two becomes very small.
In Waite's list of divinatory meanings, the World includes "voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place". In the myth, the flight on that list happens literally.

sections.h2: The Sun in the middle: a light that makes eyes close
paragraphs: The middle of the task is how the couple travels from the shared wish to the main task: what it does and what it goes through. This is how the site reads it; for Lisovskaya it is an "addition" to the main task. Here stands the Sun, and this couple's road is bright.

The Sun in a couple means warmth, success, a house that always has guests, children, shared victories and the feeling that someone reliable is close by. Waite's divinatory list for the Sun has three entries: "Material happiness, fortunate marriage, contentment." Benebell Wen is even more direct: "a radiant marriage, perhaps one to a spouse with a successful career", "a power couple". The middle of the tail holds the card of a happy marriage, and the myth tells what such a marriage costs.

"Sañjñā used to shut her eyes when the Sun gazed on her": so the story begins in the Markandeya Purana, in F. E. Pargiter's translation (1904). The Sun answers in anger: because you always close your eyes when you see me, you will give birth to Yama, "the imprisoner of mankind". The Sun is no villain. He shines as he can and wants to be looked at: for Wen, the Sun is a card "about dominance and captivating the attention and respect of others". But the one beside him cannot look into direct light. "It was with pain that Sañjñā, the noble lady, endured the Sun's splendour," the text says, and then come her questions: "What am I to do? Where am I to go? Where shall I go that I may find ease? And how shall the Sun, my husband, control his wrath?"

The scene is a familiar one. One partner is the sun: work, projects, friends, energy, and the house revolves around them. The other basks in it at first, then grows tired of being lit up all the time and starts to squint: falls silent, agrees, withdraws. The first sees only the closed eyelids and feels hurt: "You won't even look at me." Of everything Lisovskaya writes about the Sun among a couple's tasks, one thing matters most here: not knowing how to talk about problems. Sañjñā does not say a single word to her husband. She goes straight to making a shadow.

The instructions she leaves the shadow are frightening in their precision: "Remain thou here in the Sun's house even as I; and behave thou becomingly to the children even as to the Sun. And though questioned say nothing of this my going away; say always this, 'I am she indeed, Sañjñā by name.'" And the shadow agrees to keep the secret "as far as suffering my hair to be seized and as far as undergoing curses".

In a living couple the shadow is the partner who goes on doing everything properly — dinners, school runs, a smile for the guests, "everything's fine" — while they themselves have long been elsewhere. The shadow is obedient, friendly and recognisable at first sight; she is "of the same colour". In the myth the Sun lives with her for a long time, three children are born, and all the while the Sun takes Chhāyā for his wife Sañjñā, as the Vishnu Purana says. The substitution is given away by a small thing nobody planned: the shadow is fonder of her own children than of the others. Yama, offended, raises his foot at her, she curses him, and the boy runs to his father: "this great marvel was never seen by any one, that a mother casting love away imprecates a curse on her son."

In the myth the Sun is the husband and the wife is the one who leaves a shadow. In a living couple this is not divided by sex and not fixed forever: either partner can shine, either can slip into the shadow, sometimes by turns. The tail belongs to the couple, not to the one who shines.

What the numbers are made of explains where this Sun gets its force. In the main variant it is built from The Tower and The Empress, a sudden blow and abundance. The same light that makes a home and children grow can also blind.

sections.h2: The Chariot as the main task: two horses instead of a sun and a shadow
paragraphs: A couple's main task is read mostly through its minus, through what does not work and what has to be learned. With the Chariot in a couple the minus is easy to recognise: anger that immediately looks for someone to punish, and running alone instead of a shared road. The myth has both, and it shows where they lead.

Anger settles nothing. The Sun curses his wife for closing her eyes, the shadow curses the son, and the Sun is ready to curse the shadow too. Reversed, Waite's Chariot means "Riot, quarrel, dispute, litigation, defeat", and that is what a house looks like when everyone answers with force. Not one curse brings Sañjñā back.

Something else does. The Sun learns where she is: among the Northern Kurus, in the shape of a mare, practising austerities. And he understands why she went there. The Markandeya Purana records the purpose of her austerities in a single line: "May my husband become mild in body, beautiful in form." She ran not away from him but so that it would be possible to live beside him. And the Sun does what she never once asked for aloud: "Pare down my splendour now," he tells his father-in-law.

Then the Sun takes the form of a horse and goes north. Sañjñā, not recognising him and afraid of a stranger, "went towards him face to face, intent on guarding her rear". They meet nose to nose, the way horses meet, and from that meeting the Ashvins are born. Only then does the Sun show his true form, "and she gazing upon his true form felt a keen joy". Both return home in their own shapes.

This is the whole of this couple's Chariot. The one who shines turns down the light himself, by his own will and in measure. The one who ran stops running and turns to face the other, but still guards her back: a face-to-face conversation does not require surrendering one's boundaries. They meet not as a sun and a shadow but as two horses, as equals. And each keeps their own run. Sañjñā's austerities among the Northern Kurus are not a betrayal of the marriage but her own path. This is exactly the plus of the Chariot in a couple: each has their own work and their own growth outside the home, clear roles and decisions made together.

The Chariot itself was once read as the sun. Waite reports that Court de Gébelin saw in it "Osiris Triumphing, the conquering sun in spring-time having vanquished the obstacles of winter", and he does not agree. In the 21-19-7 tail the Chariot comes after the Sun, and its meaning is the opposite: it is the place where the Sun stops conquering. He crosses the sky every day. A home cannot be conquered that way.

Lisovskaya writes that a couple with the Chariot looks, from outside, more like friends and a team than like lovers. The Indian wedding rite ends with the same word. Bride and groom take seven steps together, and after the seventh come the words "Friend! be with seven steps (united to me)" (Paraskara Grihya Sutra, I, 8, 1, in Hermann Oldenberg's translation). Seven is the number of the Chariot. This is a coincidence, not proof, but its sense is exact: this couple's main task is to become companions who walk in step.

sections.h2: The Ashvins: a wagon made of mind and wheels made of hearing
paragraphs: The children of that meeting are the Ashvins, "the Horsemen", twin riders. In the Rigveda they have a three-wheeled chariot, and in it they come to the most famous wedding of the Vedic hymns, the wedding of Surya, the Sun's daughter (X, 85). Verses of this hymn are still recited at Indian weddings, and the bride's wagon is described in it like this (our literal translation):
"Her mind was the wagon, heaven was its cover… Thy two ears were the wheels… breath was fitted in as the axle. Surya mounted the wagon made of mind as she set out for her husband."

This is an answer to the myth about her family. In Saranyu's story nobody hears anybody: she keeps silent, he does not notice, the shadow repeats her learned line, "I am she indeed". In the hymn the wheels of the wedding wagon are made of hearing. This couple's Chariot runs on the same thing: the ability to listen.

Another stanza of the same hymn reads like a riddle: "The Brahmans, by their seasons, know, O Sūrya, those two wheels of thine: One kept concealed, those only who are skilled in highest truths have learned." Read as a parable about a couple, the two visible wheels are the two people. The third, hidden one is what lies between them, and it is what keeps the chariot moving. This is how a 21-19-7 couple learns to travel: not on one partner's light and the other's shadow, but on three wheels, one of which is never shown to anyone.

The hymn ends with a blessing that suits this couple better than any advice: "Be ye not parted; dwell ye here; reach the full time of human life." And in its last stanza: "So may the Universal Gods, so may the Waters join our hearts."

sections.h2: What Waite's cards show: two children under the sun and a sun on the angel's brow
paragraphs: Waite's Sun is a naked child on a white horse. But Waite himself writes that in older cards two children stood under the sun by a water, "gambolling, or running hand in hand", and that Éliphas Lévi said these are sometimes replaced by "a naked child mounted on a white horse". The Sun of the old deck is a card of two. In the same Rigveda wedding hymn the Sun and the Moon are called two playing children going round the sacrifice: "One of the Pair beholdeth all existing things; the other ordereth seasons and is born again" (X, 85, 18).
Reversed, the Sun in Waite's divinatory list means "The same in a lesser sense". The Sun of the myth, once cut down, looks just like that: it shines less but is still the Sun.

Temperance, the card of the centre in 97.8% of these couples, Waite opens with the words "A winged angel, with the sign of the sun upon his forehead". And he adds at once that "it is, moreover, untrue to say that the figure symbolizes the genius of the sun, though it is the analogy of solar light". Here the sun does not blind; it is a sign on the brow of the one who is "pouring the essences of life from chalice to chalice".

Waite's Chariot is drawn by two sphinxes, but "in the eighteenth century", he writes, "white horses were yoked to the car". And Benebell Wen notices on Waite's chariot an Indian emblem, the lingam and yoni, a union of two principles, and writes that it continues "certain themes that ran through Key 6: The Lovers". The Lovers are the values of most couples with this tail.

sections.h2: The couple's centre: Temperance, or the Sun on the lathe
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's matrix is the shared atmosphere between the partners, what is inside and not for show. In 97.8% of couples with the 21-19-7 tail it is Temperance, in 2.2% The Hierophant.

Temperance is the myth's answer to the question of what to do with a Sun that is too bright. In the Vishnu Purana, Vishvakarman puts the Sun on his lathe and grinds off part of his radiance: "and in this manner reduced it an eighth, for more than that was inseparable" (H. H. Wilson's translation, 1840). In the Markandeya Purana the craftsman pares away fifteen parts out of sixteen, and the Sun keeps one. The Puranas disagree about the measure. They agree on the main thing: the light is reduced, not put out. The Sun cannot stop being himself entirely. In the Matsya Purana, as Wilson notes, the craftsman trimmed the sun "every where except in the feet, the extent of which he could not discern".

The light that was cut away was not lost. From it Vishvakarman forged the discus of Vishnu, the trident of Shiva and the weapons of other gods, all "from the superfluous rays of the sun". This is our reading, but for a couple it is exact: one partner's surplus of brightness does not have to blind, nor does it have to vanish. It can be given over to protecting both.

Lisovskaya describes the atmosphere of Temperance as arguments settled by talking and an understanding of what the other needs. For Wen, Temperance comes to "cool what was too hot, heat up what was too cold", and in a relationship it calls for "a greater need for cooperation and tempering of extreme emotions, such as anger, resentment, hostility". Lisovskaya describes the minus of Temperance in a couple in a single phrase, and it sounds like a retelling of the myth: one partner always gives way, and the other does not even notice. That is the house of the Sun and the Shadow.

In rare couples the centre holds The Hierophant: tradition, order, doing things "properly". In the myth it has a voice too, Sañjñā's father: "Dwelling a long time among kinsmen brings no good repute to women; kinsmen hold a woman's proper residence is in her husband's house." Advice by the rules solved nothing: the daughter went not home but north.

sections.h2: The couple's values: The Lovers or The Devil
paragraphs: A couple's values are its shared path and what the two are together for. In 60.3% of couples with this tail the values are The Lovers, in 39.7% The Devil.

For Wen, The Lovers is first of all a choice, not romance: "in every traditional interpretation of The Lovers, the card is about a moral choice". The myth has two choices, and both are turning points: the Sun chooses to reduce his light, Sañjñā chooses to turn and face him. The myth begins with closed eyes and ends with a gaze: "she gazing upon his true form felt a keen joy". For this couple the value of The Lovers is to look at each other openly, without squinting and without pretending.

The Devil in the values speaks of something else: a role that holds like a chain. The shadow agreed to play someone else's life until her hair was seized. Lisovskaya's closing thought on The Devil in a couple is that "nobody belongs to anybody", and in its plus this card accepts the dark sides and forgives mistakes. That is exactly what the myth does with the shadow: she is not driven out. Her children receive their places: one son becomes the planet Shani, another will be one of the future Manus, and her daughter becomes the river Tapati. A shadow that has a place of her own no longer needs to pass herself off as someone else.

sections.h2: How to live the 21-19-7 tail: what changes the story
paragraphs: The myth does not promise the couple a happy ending. It shows the places where the story turns.

ul: **Speak about the light out loud.** Sañjñā never once tells her husband that it is hard for her; she goes straight to making a shadow. Saying "it blinds me" is harder than withdrawing, but only that gives the other a chance to turn the light down.

**Notice the shadow.** If one partner has long been answering "everything's fine" and doing everything properly while not really being there, this is not peace in the couple but a copy of it "of the same colour".
**Turn down the light by choice and in measure.** The Sun asks to be pared down himself, and an eighth is ground away: "more than that was inseparable". There is no need to put oneself out entirely.
**Do not bring anyone back with anger.** Not one curse in the myth mended anything. A visit to the craftsman and the shape of a horse did.
**Meet face to face while guarding one's back.** A hard conversation does not require surrendering one's boundaries.
**Leave each partner their own run.** Each needs time and work where the other's light does not reach. Sañjñā's Northern Kurus are not a betrayal of the union but her own path.
**Travel in the wagon made of mind.** Its wheels are ears.

paragraphs: If there are threats in the couple, if one partner fears for their safety or there is violence, this is no longer a matter of the tail. It calls for professional help, and in danger, a call to a local emergency number.

ul: **21 · The World — entry to the task.** What the couple wants together: a whole world of its own — a home, the road, a shared view of life in which everything fits. This is the couple's common language and its first resistance: in a whole world it is easy to miss that one of the two no longer lives there.

**19 · The Sun — middle of the task.** How the couple moves towards its goal: warmly, brightly, with success, guests and children, to the envy of others. The risk is one partner's light, which makes the other start closing their eyes.

**7 · The Chariot — main task.** What the couple has to learn: to travel together instead of taking turns to shine and to run. The card's minus is anger and running alone; its plus is two people who run side by side, each at their own pace, and steer together.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 21-19-7 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a task for the couple, not for one person. The couple enters it wanting a whole world for two (The World), travels the road brightly, warmly and in full view (The Sun), and has to learn the Chariot: to travel together as equals, so that one partner's brightness does not drive the other into the shadow and running away does not replace talking.

faq.q: Can the 21-19-7 tail appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail equals the reduced sum of the entry and the main task, so with an entry of 21 and a task of 7 it would be 10, The Wheel of Fortune. The Sun in the middle comes only from adding the middles of two people.

faq.q: Which partner is the Sun, and which one slips into the shadow?
faq.a: The tail does not say: it is one tail for two. Either partner can shine, either can slip into the shadow, and the roles change over time. Sex has nothing to do with it, even though in the myth the Sun is the husband.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a relationship?
faq.a: The tail does not predict a couple's fate and does not pass judgement on it. It shows the task the two of them work on together. In the myth the story ends with a return home, after the Sun has reduced his light and his wife has turned to face him.

faq.q: Are there other couple tails made of the same numbers?
faq.a: No. The entry of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, so 7 and 19 cannot come first, and the order 21-7-19 does not occur for any pair of dates. 21-19-7 is the only tail made of these three cards.

faq.q: Where does the story of the Sun's wife come from?
faq.a: From the Rigveda (X, 17, 1–2), where it fits into two stanzas, and from the Puranas, where it is told in full: the Markandeya Purana (cantos 77–78) and the Vishnu Purana (III, 2). The wedding hymn of Surya is Rigveda X, 85. The Rigveda is quoted in Ralph Griffith's translation except for the wagon stanzas, which are our own literal translation; the Markandeya Purana in F. E. Pargiter's, the Vishnu Purana in H. H. Wilson's.

report: The Rigveda describes a wedding to which "all the world" comes, and a bride who vanishes from it. Her husband is Vivasvat, the Shining One; later texts call him the Sun outright. The bride could not bear his light, left a shadow in her place and fled as a mare, and her husband found her only when he became a horse himself. The World, the Sun, the Chariot: the three cards of the couple's tail 21-19-7 stand in the same order.

report.h3: The whole world at the wedding, and a substitution nobody noticed

report: At the entry to this couple's task stands the World. It is the couple's common language and shared wish, and the wish is the size of the world: a home, the road, other countries, a shared view of life in which everything fits. From outside, such couples often look perfect.

The Rigveda adds a detail that is unsettling. The bride vanished in the wedding procession itself, "as she was carried to her dwelling", and nobody noticed, because she was replaced by "one like her". The Sanskrit word literally means "of the same colour". **The picture stays whole, but the person is no longer in it**: this is how the World's minus begins. The shared plans and shared friends are still there, but one partner has long been the only one talking about "our world", while the other nods.

The names in this myth speak for themselves. The groom is "the Shining One". The bride is Saranyu, "the Swift One", and in later texts Sañjñā, a word whose meanings include "agreement, mutual understanding". The double is called Chhāyā, "Shadow". What stands at the couple's entry is agreement, and agreement is the first thing to leave.

report.h3: A light that makes the eyes close

report: The middle of the task is the Sun: a road the couple travels brightly and warmly, with success, guests and children. Waite's list for the Sun includes "fortunate marriage"; Benebell Wen writes of "a radiant marriage" and "a power couple". And the myth tells what such a marriage costs.

"Sañjñā used to shut her eyes when the Sun gazed on her," the Markandeya Purana begins. The Sun is angry. He is no villain: he shines as he can and wants to be looked at. But living beside direct light is hard. "What am I to do? Where am I to go? Where shall I go that I may find ease?" Sañjñā asks herself. She says not a word to her husband. She makes a body of her own out of shadow and leaves it instructions: "behave thou becomingly to the children even as to the Sun… say always this, 'I am she indeed, Sañjñā by name.'"

The scene is familiar. One partner is the sun: work, projects, energy, and the house revolves around them. The other grows tired of being lit up all the time, falls silent, agrees and goes on doing everything properly: dinners, school runs, a smile for the guests, "everything's fine". **The shadow is obedient and recognisable at first sight, but no living person lives in it.** In the myth the Sun lives with the shadow for a long time and notices nothing, until a small thing gives the substitution away: the shadow is fonder of her own children than of the others.
In the myth the Sun is the husband. In a living couple either partner can shine, and either can slip into the shadow, sometimes by turns. The tail belongs to the couple, not to the one who shines.

report.h3: The Sun who asked to be pared down

report: The main task is the Chariot, and it is read through what does not work. Anger settles nothing here: the Sun curses his wife for closing her eyes, the shadow curses the son, and not one curse brings Sañjñā back.

Something else does. The Sun learns where she is: in the north, in the shape of a mare, practising austerities. And he understands why she went there. The purpose is recorded in a single line: "May my husband become mild in body, beautiful in form." **She ran not away from him but so that it would be possible to live beside him.** And the Sun himself tells his father-in-law, the heavenly craftsman: "Pare down my splendour now." In the Vishnu Purana an eighth is ground away, "for more than that was inseparable". The light is reduced, not put out.

Then the Sun takes the form of a horse. Sañjñā, afraid of a stranger, "went towards him face to face, intent on guarding her rear". They meet as two horses, as equals, and only after that does the Sun show his true form, "and she gazing upon his true form felt a keen joy". The myth begins with closed eyes and ends with a gaze.

This is the whole Chariot of a 21-19-7 couple. **The one who shines turns the light down himself, by his own will and in measure.** The one who ran turns to face the other but still guards her back: a hard conversation does not require surrendering one's boundaries. And each keeps their own run: time and work where the other's light does not reach.

report.h3: A wagon whose wheels are ears

report: The children of that meeting are the Ashvins, twin horsemen with a three-wheeled chariot. They come to the wedding of Surya, the Sun's daughter, and in that Rigveda hymn the bride's wagon is described like this: "Her mind was the wagon… Thy two ears were the wheels… breath was fitted in as the axle." In Sañjñā's story nobody heard anybody: she kept silent, he did not notice, the shadow repeated her learned line. In the hymn the wheels are made of hearing.

The same hymn says that the Brahmans know two of the wheels, while the third is concealed and known only to those skilled in the highest truths. Read as a parable about a couple, the two wheels are the two people, and the third is what lies between them. That is what keeps the chariot moving.

For a couple with this tail the myth yields a few rules: speak about the light out loud instead of closing one's eyes; notice when "everything's fine" has become a shadow; turn down one's own brightness without putting oneself out entirely; bring no one back with anger; leave each partner their own run. If there are threats in the couple, if one partner fears for their safety or there is violence, this is no longer a matter of the tail: it calls for professional help, and in danger, a local emergency number or crisis line.

captions.N: Shine brightly without driving the other into shadow
