seo.title: Karmic tail 21 7 13 compatibility: The World, The Chariot, Death
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 7 13 compatibility: a dream of a whole world, a chariot on the road and Death as the task: end the old life, not change the address.

items.title: The couple's karmic tail 21-7-13: a world sought in a change of place
items.short: The three cards of the couple's tail 21-7-13 read like an itinerary: The World is travel and moving abroad, The Chariot is the vehicle, Death is the end of the line. It looks like a one-way ticket, but the tail reads the other way round. The couple enters the task with a shared picture of a whole, proper life waiting for them somewhere else, and they head for it on anything that moves. Yet the main task, Death, asks them to end the old shape of the union where they stand: not to change the address, but to change the life.

sections.h2: A novella about a couple who keep leaving
paragraphs: Chekhov finished The Duel in the summer of 1891 on the Bogimovo estate. Ivan Andreitch Laevsky, a civil servant of about twenty-eight, and Nadyezhda Fyodorovna, another man's wife, left Petersburg two years earlier for a small seaside town in the Caucasus. The novella opens with Laevsky standing shoulder-deep in the sea, asking his friend Samoylenko, an army medic, what to do once you have stopped loving. It closes with the two of them staying on the same shore: married, poor and, it seems, alive for the first time.

Why this novella? Its plot runs in the same order as the three cards. First the dream of a whole world for which they left. Then endless plans to leave and the duel itself — The Chariot. At the end, the night before the shot and the morning when the old life is over and nobody has died. Even the number fits: the novella has exactly twenty-one chapters. That is a coincidence, not proof, but it makes the tail easier to remember.

sections.h2: The World at the entry: one dream, two pictures
paragraphs: What does a 21-7-13 couple want together? Yuliana Lisovskaya, whose book the compatibility calculation follows, describes the entry point as the couple's wishes and agreements, its "common language". The World here is the wish for a whole life: not to fix one thing, but to start everything at once and properly, preferably somewhere else. For Laevsky the dream sounds almost like a plan: "We pictured our future like this: to begin with, in the Caucasus, while we were getting to know the people and the place, I would put on the Government uniform and enter the service; then at our leisure we would pick out a plot of ground, would toil in the sweat of our brow, would have a vineyard and a field, and so on."

Four chapters later Chekhov shows the same dream through Nadyezhda Fyodorovna's eyes, and it is a different picture. She had imagined she "would find here on the first day a cosy nook by the sea, a snug little garden with shade, with birds, with little brooks, where she could grow flowers and vegetables, rear ducks and hens, entertain her neighbours". He saw a vineyard, a field and toil in the sweat of his brow. She saw a little garden, ducks and neighbours. They travelled to one world and never once compared the pictures.

When the world failed to happen, the couple came to an agreement — in silence. Chekhov writes that "they seemed to be in a tacit compact never to allude to a life of hard work". This is how the entry point becomes resistance: the couple's common language turns into a common silence. She is sure he is angry with her over the life of labour that never came, and her reasoning goes one step further: "He was silent about it, she thought, because he was angry with her for being silent about it." Each carries the guilt for a dream they never talked through.

For a couple today it need not be a move to the sea. It can be "once we buy the house", "once we leave, everything will settle", "once the renovation is done, we will really live". The World at the entry is never modest: it promises everything at once. And while it stays a picture, it can be neither tested nor corrected.

The dream of a whole world has a reverse side, which Lisovskaya describes as routine and "Groundhog Day". In the novella it can be heard in one line at dinner: "The same thing every day." The zoologist Von Koren lays out Laevsky's day by the hour: "in the morning, slippers, a bathe, and coffee; then till dinner-time, slippers, a constitutional, and conversation…" The whole world has shrunk to a timetable, and once more the whole world seems to be wherever the couple is not: "he conceived that wonderful world as real and possible, not on this sea-front… but there in the North". Two years ago salvation was the Caucasus; now it is Petersburg.

The novella also has the plain words. Laevsky says of Nadyezhda Fyodorovna that she "has followed you to the ends of the earth". The couple already stands at the edge of the world and still looks for it further on.

sections.h2: The letter in the pocket: an ending that has already come
paragraphs: In the very first chapter Laevsky has a secret: two days earlier a letter arrived saying that Nadyezhda Fyodorovna's husband has died. He hides it: "To show her that letter would be equivalent to 'Come to church to be married.' And we should first have to make our relations clear."

This is the tail's main task, arriving before anything else. Death in the couple's main task is not about people dying but about a form coming to an end. The life the couple had been living as if provisionally, for the time being, ended on the day the letter came. The old obstacle is gone, and now they will have to choose: make the union official or part honestly. Both of them stall.

He carries the letter in his pocket, the letter "which he had been intending every day to read to her", as Chekhov puts it. She, once she knows, answers Marya Konstantinovna, who is already eager to play matchmaker: "What should we be married for? I see no necessity for it. We'll go on living as we have lived." He wants to end the union and she wants to keep it as it was, yet both resist the same thing — a change of form. The World at the entry wants everything to stay "as we have lived", only better. Death replies that "as we have lived" is already over.

For a couple today such a letter can be any news that changes the shape of the union: a divorce finalised, a job offer in another city, an inheritance, the sale of a parent's flat, a talk about children. The trap of the 21-7-13 tail is that news like this is easy to carry in a pocket. It is put off not out of malice but in order to "make our relations clear first". Yet it is exactly this news that makes them clear.

sections.h2: The Chariot in the middle: an escape for each
paragraphs: The middle of the task is how the couple lives the road from the dream to the ending. In this tail the middle is The Chariot, and in The Duel it never stops moving. In the second chapter alone Laevsky says the same words seven times: "Run away!" His imagination lays out the route to the last station: "he would go aboard the steamer and then would have some lunch, would drink some cold beer… then would get into the train at Sevastopol and set off. Hurrah for freedom! …then Kursk, Moscow…"

Chekhov names exactly how the road replaces thought: "He would get into the train and set off, and thereby the problem of his life would be solved, and he did not let his thoughts go farther." The Chariot at its worst is not speed. It is the belief that motion will settle by itself what has to be settled in words.

The subtlest thing in the novella is that there is more than one escape. Nadyezhda Fyodorovna, tangled in debts and in a secret of her own, also decides to leave: "I am going away. Ivan Andreitch may stay, but I am going." She thinks of going away from him secretly, living in some remote place and sending him money "anonymously". He means to leave alone and send for her later. Two people under one roof are plotting two separate routes and not telling each other about them.

Even to the picnic the couple rides separately: he in a char-à-banc with Samoylenko, she in a coach with the ladies. On the way back, after his rude remark, they climb into different carriages, each with strangers. The couple has a chariot, but each rides in it alone.

The central question of the middle is spoken aloud in the novella. Samoylenko, who is scraping together money for Laevsky's journey, asks: "why shouldn't you take Nadyezhda Fyodorovna with you?" — "You queer fellow. How is that possible? One of us must stay, or our creditors will raise an outcry." Among the couple's tasks for The Chariot Lisovskaya lists exactly this one: to make up their minds to move together. Not to move as such, but to move together. The Chariot in this tail asks not "where to" but "the two of us?"

Laevsky borrows the money for the journey, and Lisovskaya puts loans and dodging responsibility on the negative side of The Chariot. It is recognisable without the Caucasus: an escape hatch for each, talk of moving in which "we" means "me now, you later", one partner bending to the other's plans instead of a shared decision.

sections.h2: The duel: a war that drives the wrong way
paragraphs: The Chariot is a card of motion and victory, and Waite's list of its meanings includes war. But in The Duel the couple does not fight each other. The tension goes outwards. Laevsky snaps not at Nadyezhda Fyodorovna but at Samoylenko and at Von Koren, who has long despised him: "I will fight you!" — and the zoologist accepts the challenge. Waite's reversed Chariot reads "Riot, quarrel, dispute, litigation, defeat". All of it fits into one scene in a drawing-room, and that evening Von Koren is already asking what the penalty for a duel would be.

Von Koren explains the mechanics of The Chariot better than any commentator: "we shall not stop, we shall go there and fight. So there is some force stronger than our reasoning." Laevsky, for his part, sees the duel as one more means of transport: "this duel was so far good in that it made it impossible for Laevsky to remain in the town afterwards." Even a shot is a way out of town for him.

For a 21-7-13 couple this is a familiar substitution: instead of talking to each other, a battle with the outside world. With relatives, with neighbours, with work, with the town that is "to blame for everything". A war outside gives a sense of motion, but it solves the wrong problem.
They fight where the picnic was held: by Kerbalay's duhan, where the Black River meets the Yellow. The road on which the couple so often meant to leave brings them back to the same spot.

sections.h2: The night before the shot: the death that did not happen
paragraphs: The tail's main task is Death, and Lisovskaya reads this point mainly through its negative side: what the couple fails at and what it has to learn. In The Duel the lesson takes one night. On the eve of the duel Laevsky learns Nadyezhda Fyodorovna's secret, the one she had kept quiet about. At night a storm breaks. He sits down at the table: "On the eve of death one ought to write to one's nearest relation."

The first word of the letter is "Mother!" His mother had never forgiven him this liaison, and all his plans of escape rested on her money and on lying to her. He wants to beg his mother to give Nadyezhda Fyodorovna shelter and warmth — and crosses the word out. Then he writes it again several more times. Among the couple's tasks for Death, Lisovskaya puts first helping each other to separate from their parents. Here it happens literally: a man crosses out the hope that his parent's home will decide things for him.

Towards morning Laevsky arrives at the thought for which the novella seems to have been written: "the man who seeks salvation in change of place like a migrating bird would find nothing anywhere, for all the world is alike to him." It is a verdict not on the Caucasus and not on Petersburg, but on the itinerary. The World at the entry promised salvation somewhere else. Death in the main task answers that the place decides nothing.

Before getting into the carriage he goes into the bedroom. Nadyezhda Fyodorovna starts up in bed and says she expected him to "turn me out of the house into the rain and storm, but you delay . . . delay . . .". He takes her in his arms and realises that she is "the one creature near and dear to him, whom no one could replace". Then comes a short sentence on which the whole tail rests: "When he went out of the house and got into the carriage he wanted to return home alive." For the first time the chariot is not driving away but holding a return ticket.

Chekhov builds the morning of the duel on the words "for the first time in his life". Von Koren sees green rays at sunrise for the first time in his life. Laevsky "saw the sunrise now for the first time in his life". The young officers acting as seconds are at a duel for the first time, and nobody present knows how a duel is done. Death in this tail is an experience the couple has not had before: further down it turns out that 13 appears in neither partner's personal tail.

Von Koren aims at the forehead. The deacon, who has crept along to watch, shouts from the maize: "He'll kill him!" — and the bullet only grazes the neck. Nobody has died. But on the drive home it seems to Laevsky "as though they were all coming back from a graveyard in which a wearisome, insufferable man who was a burden to others had just been buried". "Everything is over," he thinks of his past. This is Death at its best: what dies is not a person but a way of living that could not go on.

And at home comes a scene Lisovskaya would call the positive side of the thirteenth energy: the couple accepts each other's past and moves on. Nadyezhda Fyodorovna hurries to tell him everything and fears he will curse her, "but he listened to her, stroked her face and hair, looked into her eyes and said: 'I have nobody but you. . . .'"

sections.h2: What Waite and Wen see: "change of place"
paragraphs: Arthur Waite's list of meanings for The World sounds like a steamship timetable: "Assured success, recompense, voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place." It ends on change of place. In 1916 Constance Garnett translated The Duel into English, and Laevsky's night thought came out in her version in those very words: "the man who seeks salvation in change of place like a migrating bird would find nothing anywhere, for all the world is alike to him". The words that close Waite's list for The World are exactly what Laevsky gives up on the night before the duel. And where Chekhov wrote zemlya vezde odinakova, "the earth is the same everywhere", Garnett wrote "all the world".

Waite's reversed World ends with the words "stagnation, permanence" — the very Groundhog Day people run from. The World at the entry holds both extremes at once: to tear oneself away and to freeze on the spot. Either one lets a couple avoid changing the shape of its life.

Benebell Wen describes the reversed World almost as a scene from the first chapter: "there was a major change presented in the Seeker's life that could have been great for the Seeker's future, but the Seeker is afraid of change and is hesitating to take the necessary actions"; the Seeker may be "consciously and knowingly in denial". The letter in Laevsky's pocket and Nadyezhda Fyodorovna's "we'll go on living as we have lived" are both versions at once.

Of Death, Wen writes that the card is "a call to let go of the present and move on". To move on is not to move away. The World tempts the couple to change the place; Death asks it to change the stage. The difference is one word, and the whole tail stands on it.

One more detail comes from Wen's description of The Chariot as drawn in the Rider-Waite-Smith deck: in front of the chariot are "two sphinxes, one dark and one light". In The Duel both the picnic and the shot happen where the Black River falls into the Yellow and "the water black as ink stains the yellow and struggles with it". Time after time the couple's carriage arrives at the place where two different forces contend in one channel.

sections.h2: Justice at the centre: a couple forever being weighed
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's chart is the atmosphere, what lies between the partners and is not on show. Every couple with the tail 21-7-13 has the same card there: 8, Justice. No exceptions. And The Duel is a novella about a couple who are weighed all the time.

Everyone judges them. Von Koren considers Laevsky harmful and reminds his listeners that "People are judged by their actions". Marya Konstantinovna tells Nadyezhda Fyodorovna, "At the bottom of my heart I blamed you", and demands a wedding. On his way to the duel the deacon asks a question fit to be the motto of the eighth arcanum: "By what standard must one measure men's qualities, to judge rightly of them?" And the two judge themselves most harshly of all: he asks whether it is his fault that her husband died; she feels "hopelessly guilty towards him".

The other side of Justice is the ledger. In the novella money is counted all the time. Laevsky owes about two thousand roubles; he already owes Samoylenko about four hundred and asks for three hundred more to leave. Nadyezhda Fyodorovna owes three hundred roubles at Atchmianov's shop, and in delirium she repeats: "At first a hundred . . . then another hundred . . . and then the third hundred. . . ." Even the medic at the duel names his fee: "Each side is to pay me fifteen roubles, and in the case of the death of one party, the survivor is to pay thirty."

For Lisovskaya, Justice in a couple's atmosphere means a wish to make the relationship official and an honest division of duties; on the negative side come reluctance to marry, broken promises, debts and the habit of blaming instead of admitting one's own fault. It reads almost like the table of contents of The Duel. And almost like instructions for its ending: in the last chapter Laevsky is married, and "He sits from morning till night, he's always at work. He works to pay off his debts."

Here is the tail's most beautiful arithmetic. Justice at the centre plus Death in the main task give The World at the entry: 8 + 13 = 21. The world the couple dreams of is made of two terms: an honest ledger and the end of the old life. That is exactly the world Laevsky and Nadyezhda Fyodorovna receive at the end — not a vineyard and not a garden with ducks, but a wedding, work to pay the debts and "the little house with three windows" in the same small town. It is smaller than the dream. But it is real.
Justice at the centre does not mean that one of the two is right. The harshest judge in the novella, Von Koren, says as he leaves: "No one knows the real truth."

sections.h2: The numbers: what every such couple shares
paragraphs: The tail 21-7-13 occurs in about one couple in 148 (0.677%) and ranks 50th of the 97 couple tails. Each point of the couple's chart is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts; a sum above 22 is reduced by adding its digits. This tail arises from only three combinations of the partners' personal tails.

**The Chariot in the middle is born only in the couple.** Neither partner has it in the middle of a personal tail: there you find The Sun and The Devil, The Tower and The Moon, or Judgement and Temperance. The couple's middle is exactly 34 every time, and 34 reduces to 7. And 34 = 21 + 13: the middle of a personal tail is the sum of its two ends, so the couple's middle adds up the entry and the main task. This is not a metaphor but the way the numbers are built: the road of this couple is made of the dream and the ending. Laevsky would put it more briefly — on the train "the problem of his life would be solved".

**The World at the entry is made of two retreats.** In 96% of such couples the entry is built from one partner's Hanged Man and the other's Hermit: 12 + 9. Our reading: a pause, life on hold, and a withdrawal into one's own territory are two ways of stepping back from the world, and together they produce the dream of a whole world. Laevsky and Nadyezhda Fyodorovna live "on this empty, desolate coast, always expecting something better" — the pause and the solitude at once. In the remaining 4% the entry is The Devil plus The Lovers, 15 + 6.

**Death is new to both of them.** The main task is always an exact sum — 7 + 6, 4 + 9 or 5 + 8 — and 13 appears in neither partner's personal tail. In 92% of couples the couple's Death is made of one partner's personal Chariot (that tail ends in 7) and the other's personal Lovers: of a road and a choice. In the novella the end of the old life comes exactly so: from the drive to the duel and the choice made at the bedside that morning.

**The centre is always 8.** And 13 + 8 = 21, 21 + 13 = 34 → 7: in this tail the couple's arithmetic matches the personal one. That is why the same order 21-7-13 also occurs as a personal tail, for 678 dates since 1900. But that is a different calculation with different roles for the points; this page is only about the couple's tail. Here too the couple's middle is not recalculated from the ends: it remains the sum of two personal middles, and the result simply coincides.
There are no permutations of this tail: no other couple tails are made of the numbers 21, 7 and 13.

sections.h2: A worked example: 14.05.1976 and 05.07.1975
paragraphs: Two dates that give the couple's tail 21-7-13. First each person's own chart is calculated, then the matching points are added.

This couple's values card is 6, The Lovers. And The World appears in its chart in one more place: in the sphere "What can spoil it", at the point "Where it sparks". The dream at the entry is here also a source of quarrels. That is a feature of this one couple, not of every couple with the tail 21-7-13.

sections.h2: The couple's values: The Lovers or The Devil
paragraphs: The couple's values are its spiritual purpose, what the union exists for. Couples with the tail 21-7-13 have one of two cards here: The Lovers in 75.8% and The Devil in 24.2%. Both are about the bond between two people, but the knot is different. The Lovers are held together by choice. The Devil by attachment: habit, debt, the fear of being left alone. Lisovskaya ends her chapter on the fifteenth energy with the thought that no one belongs to anyone.

The Duel has both knots. At first Laevsky speaks of Nadyezhda Fyodorovna as of an object: he is for her "an indispensable, integral part of her boudoir", and it would be as hard for her to do without him "as to do without her powder or her curl-papers". Von Koren describes his life as a "narrow programme" within which his existence is confined "like an egg within its shell". That is the language of The Devil. At dawn before the duel the language of The Lovers is heard: "the one creature near and dear to him, whom no one could replace". The same person, the same house, a different knot.

Wen distinguishes The Lovers from Justice like this: "The Lovers is about making an ethical decision that involves the Seeker", while Justice "is about making an ethical decision that involves an external condition, others who matter to the Seeker, or a situation outside of the Seeker." For this tail it is an exact map of the ground. At the couple's centre stands judgement and reckoning from outside, the eight. In its values stands a decision only the two of them can make, the six. However much the neighbours, duellists and creditors judge, the decision is still theirs.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail: a boat that takes two steps forward
paragraphs: In the last chapter Von Koren leaves. Laevsky and Nadyezhda Fyodorovna stay exactly where they had spent two years planning to escape from. Laevsky sees the zoologist off at the quay and watches the boat being flung about on the waves: "she makes two steps forward and one step back; but the boatmen are stubborn, they work the oars unceasingly, and are not afraid of the high waves." And he thinks: "So it is in life. . . ."

This is The Chariot at its best. Not a carriage to Petersburg and not a steamer out of here, but a boat rowed by several people at once, against the waves, towards lights that cannot yet be seen. The tail 21-7-13 does not require the couple to stay put. It asks that the motion be shared and that it not take the place of ending what has already ended.

paragraphs.h3: What changes the pattern

ul: **Compare the pictures of the dream.** Say aloud what "our new life" looks like for each of you: a vineyard and a field, or a little garden with ducks and neighbours. The World at the entry is sturdier when there is one picture for two, not two silent ones.
**Do not carry the letter in a pocket.** News that changes the shape of the union is told the same day. It cannot be "made clear first": it is the clarification itself.

**One route for two.** Plans to leave, to move to a new city or take a new job are discussed as shared plans. "I'll go now, you'll come later" is a sign that the chariot is once again carrying one person at a time.

**Tell a change of place from a change of life.** Before a big step, ask each other what exactly has to end. If the answer is "everything here", it is worth checking whether that "everything" would leave together with the suitcases.

**Keep the ledger together.** Debts, promises and grievances out loud and on a list, not in one's head and not in delirium. Justice at the centre works for the couple when the two of them keep the accounts, not the neighbours.
**Bury the past, not each other.** The end of the old shape of a union is not a verdict on the union. Sometimes, as in The Duel, only after such an ending does a couple have its first real day.

paragraphs: Chekhov promises his characters no happiness. Von Koren, saying goodbye, thinks: "What pitiful figures they are, though! The life they are living does not come easy to them." But this life is theirs, and for the first time it is not somewhere else. That is the secret of the tail 21-7-13: the whole world the couple travels towards turns out to be not a place on the map but the next chapter. And it can only begin where the previous one ended.

ul: **21 · The World — entry to the task.** Where the couple starts: a dream of a whole world for two, a life in which everything finally falls into place. The same dream turns into resistance when life refuses to match the picture.
**7 · The Chariot — middle of the task.** How the couple travels: by motion, plans, departures and a struggle for the reins. Here the road easily takes the place of a conversation.

**13 · Death — main task.** What there is to learn: to let what is worn out come to an end — the provisional way of living, the unspoken agreements, the hope that a parent's home will sort things out — and to start the next chapter together.

intro: About one couple in 148 has this tail. It is best explained not by a textbook but by Chekhov's novella The Duel: the story of two people who ran away to the ends of the earth for a new life and spent two years planning to run away again.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 21-7-13 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's tasks read in the order "entry to the task — middle — main task". The couple enters with a dream of a whole world (21, The World), lives the road through motion, plans and struggle (7, The Chariot), and learns the main lesson: to let a worn-out shape of life and union come to an end (13, Death).

faq.q: Is Death in a couple's main task a sign of a break-up?
faq.a: No. The card speaks of the end of a form, not of people and not of the union: old agreements, a provisional way of living, the hope that a parent's home will help. The number does not predict events. In The Duel the only shot that could have killed missed, and what ended was the couple's former life.

faq.q: Does a couple with the tail 21-7-13 have to move?
faq.a: No. In this tail a move can be both a task and a trap. Among the couple's tasks for The Chariot Lisovskaya lists making up their minds to move together, and the key word is "together". The trap is expecting a new place to settle by itself what has to be ended.

faq.q: How does the couple's tail 21-7-13 differ from the personal tail 21-7-13?
faq.a: A personal tail is calculated from one date and describes one person's tasks; its points have different roles. A couple's tail is the sum of the points of two personal charts, and the partners themselves have other tails: in 92% of such couples they are 12-19-7 and 9-15-6.

faq.q: How common is the tail 21-7-13 among couples?
faq.a: About one couple in 148: that is 0.677% of couples and 50th place among the 97 couple tails. Every such couple has Justice at the centre, and in the values either The Lovers (75.8%) or The Devil (24.2%).

report: The three cards of the tail 21-7-13 read like an itinerary: The World is travel and moving abroad, The Chariot is the vehicle, Death is the end of the line. It looks like a one-way ticket. But the tail reads the other way round, and nothing explains it better than Chekhov's novella The Duel — the story of two people who ran away to the ends of the earth for a new life and spent two years planning to run away again.

report.h3: One dream, painted twice

report: Laevsky and Nadyezhda Fyodorovna left Petersburg for the Caucasus in search of a whole, proper life. That is The World at the entry: the wish to start everything at once, preferably somewhere else. His picture: "we would pick out a plot of ground, would toil in the sweat of our brow, would have a vineyard and a field, and so on". Her picture, four chapters later: "a snug little garden with shade, with birds, with little brooks… rear ducks and hens, entertain her neighbours". They travelled to one world and never once compared the pictures.

When the world failed to happen, the couple came to an agreement in silence: "they seemed to be in a tacit compact never to allude to a life of hard work". This is how the entry to the task turns into resistance: **the couple's common language becomes a common silence**. And once more the whole world seems to be wherever the couple is not. Two years ago salvation was the Caucasus; now it is Petersburg.

report.h3: An ending carried in a pocket

report: In the first chapter a letter arrives: Nadyezhda Fyodorovna's husband has died. Laevsky hides it: "To show her that letter would be equivalent to 'Come to church to be married.'" Once she knows, she says: "We'll go on living as we have lived." He wants to end the union and she wants to keep it as it was, yet both resist the same thing — a change of form. Death in the couple's main task is not about people dying but about a form coming to an end: the provisional life ended on the day of the letter. For a couple today such a letter can be any news that changes the way they live, and it is far too easy to carry in a pocket.

report.h3: Two escapes under one roof

report: The middle of the task is The Chariot, and in the novella it never stops moving. In the second chapter Laevsky says "Run away!" seven times. Chekhov names exactly how the road stands in for thought: "He would get into the train and set off, and thereby the problem of his life would be solved, and he did not let his thoughts go farther."

The subtlest thing is that there is more than one escape. Nadyezhda Fyodorovna also decides to leave, secretly: "Ivan Andreitch may stay, but I am going." Two people under one roof plot two routes and keep quiet about them. Asked why they do not leave together, Laevsky replies: "One of us must stay." **The Chariot in this tail asks not "where to" but "the two of us?"**

The tension goes outwards: Laevsky snaps not at her but at acquaintances, and a quarrel turns into a duel. Even a shot is a way out for him: the duel "made it impossible for Laevsky to remain in the town afterwards". A war outside gives a sense of motion, but it solves the wrong problem.

report.h3: The death that did not happen

report: On the night before the duel Laevsky writes "Mother!" and crosses it out: the hope that his parent's home will decide things for him comes to an end. Towards morning he reaches the central thought of the novella: "the man who seeks salvation in change of place like a migrating bird would find nothing anywhere, for all the world is alike to him." Waite's list of meanings for The World ends with the very same words, "change of place". And in Constance Garnett's English translation Laevsky's night thought comes out exactly so: "seeks salvation in change of place". The World at the entry promised salvation somewhere else. Death answers that the place decides nothing.

Before the shot he takes Nadyezhda Fyodorovna in his arms and realises that she is "the one creature near and dear to him, whom no one could replace", and as he gets into the carriage he wants to "return home alive". The bullet only grazes his neck. Nobody has died, yet on the drive home it seems to Laevsky as though they are all "coming back from a graveyard in which a wearisome, insufferable man who was a burden to others had just been buried". **What dies is not a person but a way of living.** At home she hurries to tell him everything, and he listens and says: "I have nobody but you. . . ."

report.h3: A world made of a ledger and an ending

report: Every couple with this tail has Justice at the centre, and the novella is full of scales. The neighbours and the zoologist judge the couple, the two judge themselves most harshly of all, and money is counted to the rouble: debts, loans for the journey, three hundred owed at a shop. Justice at the centre plus Death in the main task give The World at the entry: 8 + 13 = 21. **The world the couple dreams of is made of an honest ledger and the end of the old life.** That is the world the two receive at the end: not a vineyard and not a garden with ducks, but a wedding, work to pay off the debts and "the little house with three windows" in the same small town. It is smaller than the dream, but it is real.

The last picture in the novella is a boat in a storm: "she makes two steps forward and one step back; but the boatmen are stubborn". This is The Chariot at its best, when the motion is shared and does not take the place of ending what has already ended. Simple things change the pattern: comparing the two pictures of the dream out loud; telling news that changes the shape of the union the same day; making plans to leave as shared plans, without "I'll go now, you'll come later"; asking before a big step what exactly has to end; keeping the ledger together, not in one's head.
The secret of the tail 21-7-13 is that **the whole world turns out to be not a place on the map but the next chapter**. And it can only begin where the previous one ended.

unit.meaning: Your task is to let the old shape of your union end, not to seek salvation in a change of place.

seo.title: Karmic tail 21 7 22 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 7 22 compatibility: The World, The Chariot and The Fool in a couple's tail, read through Waite, Wen and Jules Verne's race round the world.

items.title: The 21-7-22 karmic tail in compatibility: the whole world, the road and a day off the timetable
items.short: The 21-7-22 karmic tail in compatibility turns the order of the Major Arcana upside down: the couple's task opens with The World, the last card of the deck, and closes with The Fool, the card of beginnings. It belongs to two people who find a shared world before they take a shared step. They agree quickly on the big picture and travel the road in motion and to a plan, and what they have to learn is what others start with: to take the serious step freely, out of trust, and to leave room for the unforeseen.

sections.h2: How to read the 21-7-22 tail in a couple's chart
paragraphs: On the site these three numbers sit in the sphere “The couple's karmic tail” under the captions “Entry to the task” (M), “Middle of the task” (N) and “Main task” (D). Each number is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, reduced to 22. The main point is D: it shows what the couple has to learn and is read above all through what does not work.

M is the shared wish with which the two enter the task. The same point appears in the sphere “Relationship and common language” under the caption “Common language”, and the wish in it easily turns into resistance: what the couple wants together starts to hold it in place. N is how the couple lives the road from the wish to the task. This is our site's reading: Lisovskaya gives this point no meaning of its own and calls it an addition to the main task.

In the deck the Major Arcana run from The Fool to The World. For Waite The Fool is zero, the card without a number, and The World is fullness and completion. In the destiny matrix The Fool carries the number 22, right after The World. The 21-7-22 tail walks this road backwards: the couple starts from the result, from a whole world, and its main work lies in the first step.
The tail does not say whether the couple will marry or part, and it sets no dates. It describes the shape of the task: where the two of them find things easy and where they skid.

sections.h2: A novel about a couple, read as a novel about travel
paragraphs: Verne's novel came out in 1872; quotations below follow George Makepeace Towle's English translation of 1873 unless marked otherwise. People remember it as a race with steamers and an elephant. But read next to this tail, another book shows through: two people travel together for eighty days without knowing what they are to each other, and everything is decided by a day that was not on the timetable.

Phileas Fogg lives at No. 7, Saville Row as if the world had already been gone round. He breakfasts and dines at the club at the same hours, at the same table. He has dismissed his last servant for bringing “shaving-water at eighty-four degrees Fahrenheit instead of eighty-six”. His only pastimes are the papers and whist, a game that for him is “a contest, a struggle with a difficulty, yet a motionless, unwearying struggle”. And yet nobody at the club knows the map of the globe better: “He must have travelled everywhere, at least in the spirit.” One more line from the first chapter will be needed at the end: Fogg was not known to have “either relatives or near friends”.

The wager is born at the card table. “The world is big enough,” says a partner. “It was once,” Fogg replies in a low tone. A newspaper has already worked out the route: eighty days. What about storms, wrecks, torn-up rails? “All included.” And delays? “The unforeseen does not exist.” Fogg stakes twenty thousand pounds that he will walk into the club on Saturday, 21 December, at a quarter before nine in the evening — in 1,920 hours. The papers would call the scheme madness.

In India he is joined by Aouda, a young widow he saves from being burned on her husband's funeral pyre. Beside him all the way is Passepartout, his new servant: a former itinerant singer, circus rider and rope dancer who took service with “the most exact and settled gentleman in the United Kingdom” in order “to taste the sweets of domestic life” — and set off round the world that same evening.

The three cards of the tail stand in the novel in order. The World is the wager on the whole globe, gone round in the head beforehand. The Chariot is eighty days of steamers, trains, sledges and connections. The Fool is the evening when all is lost, and the question Aouda asks.

sections.h2: The World at the entry: “All included”
paragraphs: In Waite's divinatory list The World upright means “Assured success, recompense, voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place”, and reversed “Inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence”. In the novel's first chapters the two lists stand side by side. Fogg in London is The World reversed: the same hours, the same table, water at exactly eighty-six degrees. The wager is The World upright: a route, a voyage, a promised reward. This is how the “Entry to the task” works: the wish for a whole world and the resistance to it live in one point.
Even “emigration” from the list is in the book. In Hong Kong it turns out that the relative Aouda was travelling to has gone to live in Europe, and her road becomes a shared road with Fogg.

Wen calls The World “the card of synthesis” and recalls the Gaia hypothesis: the world as a living, evolving organism. Fogg's world is a table from a newspaper: London to Suez, seven days; Suez to Bombay, thirteen; total, eighty. The difference between a living world and a timetable of the world is the first thing worth seeing for a couple with this tail.

In life the entry looks like this. Two people meet, and within a month they share a map. They think alike about money and freedom, they want to live by the sea or in another country, they have agreed that each stays themselves and the chores are split in half. They talk until three in the morning about how it will all be. Friends call them the perfect couple, and that is no exaggeration: the two really do speak one language, and that language is the language of the big picture.

The resistance grows out of the same picture. A world drawn together is no longer redrawn. When one of them changes — a new job, a new circle, a new wish — the other hears it as a betrayal of the shared plan and starts correcting: “but we agreed”. The same holiday route every year, the same arguments to the same script, and the most dangerous sentence of all: “we already know everything about ourselves”. Fogg would put it more briefly: “All included.”

sections.h2: The Chariot in the middle: “not travelling, but only describing a circumference”
paragraphs: The middle of the task shows how the couple travels the road, and with this tail it travels on The Chariot. The novel has a sentence that describes this card better than any handbook. On a train in India General Cromarty would gladly tell his fellow passenger about the country, but Fogg asks nothing: **“Phileas Fogg, who was not travelling, but only describing a circumference,** took no pains to inquire into these subjects; he was a solid body, traversing an orbit around the terrestrial globe, according to the laws of rational mechanics.” The general studies him and wonders “whether a human heart really beat beneath this cold exterior”.

Mechanics reaches this card from two sides. Wen, explaining The Chariot, writes that “Key 7 might be likened to Newton's second law of motion: force is mass times acceleration”, and The Chariot is the force that is enough to accelerate the mass of the problem. Waite calls the charioteer “above all things triumph in the mind”. Almost a century and a half before Wen, Verne described his hero in the words of the same physics: a body, an orbit, the laws of mechanics.

But Waite's divinatory list for The Chariot does not open with victory; it opens with “Succour, providence”. And when Fogg's machine leaves the schedule of its own accord, it is to help: in India he saves Aouda, on the American prairie he goes to rescue Passepartout, taken by a war party. In the jungle the guide tells them of the widow who is to be burned at dawn. “Suppose we save this woman.” — “I have yet twelve hours to spare; I can devote them to that.” The general is astonished: “Why, you are a man of heart!” “Sometimes,” replied Phileas Fogg, quietly; “when I have the time.” Those words hold the whole danger of the tail's middle: the heart is there, but it switches on by the timetable.

From then on Aouda travels with him, and her position is never named. “What ought I to do, Mr. Fogg?” — “It is very simple… Go on to Europe… You do not intrude, nor do you in the least embarrass my project. Passepartout!… Go to the ‘Carnatic,’ and engage three cabins.” On board he visits her at fixed hours, listens, makes sure she wants for nothing, but “with the precision of an automaton, the movements of which had been arranged for this purpose. Aouda did not quite know what to make of him.”

Near the end The Chariot shows what speed costs. In the middle of the Atlantic the steamer Henrietta runs short of coal. Fogg buys the ship and has her wood burned in the furnaces: “the poop, cabins, bunks, and the spare deck were sacrificed.” The next day the masts go. The ship burns its own cabins so as not to lose speed.

A couple with this tail recognises itself in the best chapters of the race. They are a team: they move house, renovate, start a business together, pull each other out of trouble and stand up for each other in front of strangers. Each goes their own way, but side by side, and it is exciting to travel together.

And it recognises itself in the worst. Conversation shrinks to logistics: who is meeting whom, where the connection is, whether the bill is paid. Talking about “us” can happen when there is time — after the move, after the project, after the holiday. There is a quiet struggle for the reins: who drives. Tiredness comes out as irritation over nothing. One expects the other to put a goal aside for the sake of the shared route. And the cabins go into the furnace — sleep, weekends, a home where one can simply be. Among the tasks of The Chariot in a couple Lisovskaya names this one too: learning to restore strength with care instead of taking it from those close by.

sections.h2: The Fool as the main task: what are we to each other?
paragraphs: In Waite The Fool has two faces, and Waite himself keeps them apart. In the symbolic account The Fool is “the spirit in search of experience”, “a prince of the other world on his travels through this one”. In the divinatory list he is “Folly, mania, extravagance, intoxication, delirium, frenzy, bewrayment”, and reversed “Negligence, absence, distribution, carelessness, apathy, nullity, vanity”.

In the novel The Fool appears in both forms. In Verne's French the papers call Fogg a maniaque and a fou, a maniac and a madman (our translation; Towle has “lunatic”) — words from the same roots as “mania” and “folly” at the head of Waite's list. The journey swallows nearly nineteen thousand pounds: an elephant for two thousand, a steamer bought for firewood. And at the pyre in India Fogg has to be held back by force, because he, “in an instant of mad generosity, was about to rush upon the pyre”. The folly of the wager and the generous folly are two different Fools, and the couple's task is to tell one from the other.

The main task of the tail is read through what does not work, and with The Fool that is above all uncertainty. What is Aouda during those eighty days? A rescued woman, a fellow traveller, a guest, a ward? Three cabins. Fogg looks after her flawlessly and says not one word about what is between them. Wen writes of The Fool reversed: “If in a relationship, it is a spontaneous one.” And of The World reversed, that such a person “thrives in ambiguity”, is at home in it like a fish in water. On the downside the two cards of the tail meet on one thing: it suits both partners not to name anything.

A couple with this tail can live for years in such a “for now”. Together, but without a name: not husband and wife, not “just seeing each other”, but “we have our own kind of relationship”. Everything begins easily and beautifully, and as soon as it comes to a serious step — moving in, getting married, taking out a joint loan, moving abroad together — one of them suddenly has an urgent trip, a new project, a “let's do it later”. The freedom both were proud of turns into two flatmates with a shared calendar. There is a flip side as well: the one who dislikes rules starts to be jealous and to check up, and at the first difficulty walks out with a reproach — “you were the one who said we didn't need a piece of paper”.

The upside of The Fool in a couple is trust, and freedom grows out of it. The two do not check up on each other, each is self-sufficient and enters the union consciously, they can laugh and start from zero. The task is not to crush The Fool inside and become a Fogg with a daily routine. The task is to make the leap.

In the novel Aouda makes it, at the worst moment possible. Fogg is sure he came back to London five minutes too late: the wager is lost, the fortune gone. In the evening he comes to apologise for bringing her to England, where he can no longer provide for her. “But what will become of you, Mr. Fogg?” — “As for me, madam, I have need of nothing.” “Your friends—” — “I have no friends, madam.” “Your relatives—” — “I have no longer any relatives.” And then she rises: **“Mr. Fogg, do you wish at once a kinswoman and friend? Will you have me for your wife?”**

Her question answers the first chapter, where Fogg was not known to have “either relatives or near friends”. For eighty days the status had no name — and now it is named in one sentence. Fogg shuts his eyes, opens them and says: “I love you!… I am entirely yours!” The Fool has stepped off the edge, and the edge here is real: ruin.

sections.h2: The day that was not on the timetable
paragraphs: Passepartout runs to the Reverend Samuel Wilson to arrange the wedding for tomorrow, Monday, and soon comes back without his hat, knocking passers-by over. “Marriage—impossible… Impossible—for to-morrow.” — “Why so?” — “Because to-morrow—is Sunday!” — “Monday,” replied Mr. Fogg. — “No—to-day is Saturday… You have made a mistake of one day!”

Fogg has lived the whole day as 22 December, and it was the 21st. There are ten minutes left before the wager closes. A cab, a hundred pounds promised to the driver, two dogs run over, five carriages overturned — and he walks into the club saloon as the clock shows a quarter before nine.

Verne gives the solution with figures. Travelling east, towards the sun, Fogg shortened his day by four minutes for every degree of longitude; three hundred and sixty degrees at four minutes each make exactly one day. He saw the sun pass the meridian eighty times, his partners in London seventy-nine.

The secret was written in the book long before the ending. Back in India General Cromarty explained to Passepartout that, going eastward, “the days were shorter by four minutes for each degree gone over”. Passepartout “obstinately refused to alter his watch”; already in Suez he had told the detective: “So much the worse for the sun, monsieur. The sun will be wrong, then!” And in the very first chapter, hiring him, Fogg notes that the new servant's watch is exactly four minutes slow: “No matter; it's enough to mention the error.” The novel opens with four minutes and closes with the same four minutes multiplied by 360.

Now the main thing. Fogg names the cause of his victory himself. In the evening he tells Aouda: **“If you had not suggested our marriage, my servant would not have gone to the Reverend Samuel Wilson's, I should not have been apprised of my error, and—”** The error in the calendar was uncovered not by calculation and not by speed, but by the decision to marry. The serious step gave back the whole world.

That is the hidden plot of the 21-7-22 tail. The couple's main task, The Fool, is not the price of the road and not an obstacle on it, but the key to the entry. While the two race by the timetable, they feel they are late and have lost everything. Clarity about what they are to each other gives them back a day that was not on the calendar: time that, it turns out, they had in hand.

The morning after the wedding Passepartout bursts in with a discovery: the world could have been gone round in seventy-eight days. “No doubt,” returned Mr. Fogg, “by not crossing India. But if I had not crossed India, I should not have saved Aouda; she would not have been my wife, and—” The shortest route is The Chariot's route. The detour on which the meeting happened is the couple's route.

This ending has a forerunner. In 1841 Edgar Allan Poe published a story he later called “Three Sundays in a Week”. An old uncle promises Kate to the hero “when three Sundays come together in a week” — that is, never. The condition is met by two sea captains who have sailed round the globe in opposite directions: for one Sunday was yesterday, for the other it will be tomorrow. The bride is the first to see the answer, and a captain sums it up: “there can be no philosophical reason assigned why the idea of one of us should have preference over that of the other.” Whether Verne knew the story has not been established. But in both, an extra day settles a question of marriage, each side keeps its own time, and both are right.

Three coincidences are worth recording precisely as coincidences, with no conclusions drawn. The novel's decisive mix-up is between 21 and 22 December, and the couple's tail ends with the same numbers: The World and The Fool. The Paris daily Le Temps ran the novel from 6 November to 22 December 1872, so the last instalment appeared the day after Fogg's deadline. And Wen, timing The Chariot by the sign of Cancer, gives the dates “June 21–July 22”. The numbers of the tail do not steer the plots of books, but coincidences like these are easy to remember.

sections.h2: What the numbers of the 21-7-22 tail show
paragraphs: The 21-7-22 tail occurs in about one couple in 84 (1.19%) and ranks 30th among the 97 couple tails. It cannot be a personal tail: in a personal chart the entry M is the main task D plus the centre, and with D = 22 an entry of 21 is impossible with any centre. This tail exists only between two people.
It is built from four combinations of the partners' personal tails:

This table holds three clues. The first: none of the tail's three cards appears in either partner's personal tail — no World, no Chariot, no Fool. The tail is born only in the sum; on their own, neither partner has it.

The second: in all four combinations the middle is 25, reduced to 7. Two personal paths added together do not fit into the deck and fold into The Chariot. This couple's Chariot belongs to no one: it is the speed of two, not the habit of one.

The third: the entry is always an exact sum of the two personal entries, 15 + 6 or 12 + 9. Were the couple a single person with the main task 22 and The Star at the centre, the personal formula would give the entry 22 + 17 = 39 → 12, The Hanged Man. The couple has 21 at the entry — the same digits in reverse. The Hanged Man is the card of suspended waiting; this couple enters its task not through waiting but straight through a whole world, because the entry is put together by two.

And one more piece of arithmetic. In three combinations out of four (77% of couples) one partner enters their personal tail through The Devil (15) and the other through The Lovers (6), and the shared World at the entry is their sum. The same two cards become the couple's values: The Lovers in 71.1%, The Devil in 28.9%. The points and the calculation are different here, so this is arithmetic only; our reading is that this couple's world is made of choice and attachment.

sections.h2: The Star at the centre and the couple's values
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's chart is the atmosphere between the two, what is not on show. In 96.7% of couples with this tail it holds The Star, in 3.3% Justice. The Star never stands at the centre of a personal chart for any date: this card appears only in a couple.

Waite quotes the mottoes of The Star and calls them true: “Waters of Life freely” and “Gifts of the Spirit”. Wen writes of hope, inspiration and “divine charity”, a generosity that gives more than it receives. In the novel The Star is hidden in the coldest man. “Whenever he knew that money was needed for a noble, useful, or benevolent purpose, he supplied it quietly and sometimes anonymously”; his winnings at whist went to his charities. The thousand pounds left after the wager he divides between Passepartout and Fix, the detective who arrested him. Outside, mechanics; inside, a quiet spring.

In a couple, The Star at the centre is a union that inspires both: next to each other the two understand who they want to be. On the downside, in Lisovskaya, the same Star enjoys being in love and backs away from responsibility when the question of marriage or a child comes up. The atmosphere and the main task rhyme here: on the downside The Star and The Fool stumble over the same serious step, and on the upside both cards give a hope that needs no receipt.

In 3.3% of couples with this tail Justice holds the centre, and the atmosphere is different: honest accounts and clear duties. This is the Fogg who deducts from Passepartout's share “the cost of the gas which had burned in his room for nineteen hundred and twenty hours, for the sake of regularity”, while they were travelling. The values of such couples are always The Lovers.

The couple's values answer what the union is for. The Lovers (71.1%) make it a union for choosing: choosing each other again and again, as Aouda chooses Fogg with her question “will you have me?”. The Devil (28.9%) makes it a union for sorting out its bonds: which hold by choice, and which by habit, by fear, or like a wager that can no longer be lost. With this tail The Devil appears among the values only when The Star is at the centre.

sections.h2: Worked example: 08.01.1976 and 14.08.1975
paragraphs: The dates 08.01.1976 and 14.08.1975 give the couple's tail 21-7-22. The first partner's personal tail is 6-20-14, the second's 15-5-8; this is the rarest of the four combinations, 16% of such couples.

The middle is calculated from the two personal middles, not from the couple's outer numbers: 20 + 5 = 25, and 25 reduces to 2 + 5 = 7. The couple's centre is 10 + 7 = 17, The Star. The couple's values are 15, The Devil. And this couple has The Fool at one more point, “How you are seen”: 8 + 14 = 22. That happens in 4.3% of couples with this tail: The Fool, which is a task for the two of them, looks to others like lightness, brightness and a touch of frivolity.
The compatibility calculator on the site works out every point itself: just enter two dates of birth.

sections.h2: How the loop of this tail turns
paragraphs: The loop is recognised by repetition. First the shared world: the two sit down again and draw a plan — a new country, a new home, a new life. Then The Chariot: tickets, deadlines, arrangements, a race in which there is no time to ask “how are you”. Then a serious step comes up, and it is not on the schedule. One disappears into work, the other takes offence. Someone says “let's not spoil everything with formalities”, someone gets jealous because it is unclear what they have a right to. And the couple returns to the start — to a new plan that once again promises the whole world.

The price of the loop is years in three cabins. Side by side, with flawless care for each other, and nobody knows what is between them. Weariness from a speed nobody chose. And the feeling of always running late, although in fact there is a day in hand.

sections.h2: What changes the script

ul: **Name the status in words.** Not “it will sort itself out”, but Aouda's question: what are we to each other. It is a conversation, not an item on the plan.
**Do not wait for the edge.** In the novel the proposal comes on the day of ruin. A couple need not be brought to the brink to say the main thing — Passepartout is right: “Never too late.”
**Mention the error instead of resetting the other's watch.** Each has their own time, and almost always both are right, like Poe's captains. It is enough to notice the difference and agree on it.
**Keep a day off the timetable.** A shared calendar needs a day with nothing booked — not a planned rest, but an empty square.
**Do not burn the cabins.** Sleep, weekends, home and the talk about “us” are not firewood for speed.
**Value the detour.** The shortest route belongs to The Chariot; meetings happen on detours.
**Give freedom without checking up.** And live by the same rules one expects of the other.

sections.h2: The strong version of the 21-7-22 tail
paragraphs: On the upside this is one of the freest stories two people can have. The world for them is a living horizon, not a table: they travel a lot, move easily, can live in different countries and never lose their common language. The Chariot is their shared vehicle, not their master: they decide quickly, protect each other, and each has their own road. The Fool becomes trust: no checking up is needed, starting from zero holds no fear, and the two can laugh at what others call a disaster.

The novel's last chapter is called “In which it is shown that Phileas Fogg gained nothing by his tour around the world, unless it were happiness”. And its last lines are a question: “What had he really gained by all this trouble? What had he brought back from this long and weary journey? Nothing, say you? Perhaps so; nothing but a charming woman, who, strange as it may appear, made him the happiest of men!”
For Waite The Fool is zero. The strong version of the 21-7-22 tail is a couple that has gone round a whole world and brought home “nothing”: the main thing, which fits into no timetable.

ul: **21 · The World — “Entry to the task”.** The shared wish that brings the two of them into the task: a whole world — shared views, open space, the road. The same point is the couple's “Common language”. The resistance hides here too: a world drawn together once is no longer redrawn.

**7 · The Chariot — “Middle of the task”.** How the couple travels the road: in motion, projects and moves, with a clear route and victories over obstacles. The risk is that the union turns into a timetable, and the heart gets whatever time is left “when there is time”.

**22 · The Fool — “Main task”.** What the couple has to learn: to name what they are to each other and take the serious step not as an escape and not on schedule, but freely. On the downside: an easy start, years of uncertainty and a swerve away whenever things come to the point.

intro: This tail is lived almost word for word in a novel everyone read as a child and hardly anyone read as the story of a couple. In Jules Verne's Around the World in Eighty Days, Phileas Fogg stakes his fortune on the whole world, crosses it by the timetable and wins only because his bride proposes to him on a day that was not on his calendar. The novel's decisive mix-up is between 21 and 22 December.

faq.q: What does the 21-7-22 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of a couple with The World (21) at the entry to the task, The Chariot (7) in the middle and The Fool (22) as the main task. The two quickly find a shared picture of life and travel the road in motion and to a plan. What they have to learn is the serious step, clarity about what they are to each other, and a freedom that rests on trust rather than on escape.

faq.q: Is it a hard tail? Does it mean the couple will not marry?
faq.a: No. The tail predicts no weddings, break-ups or dates. It shows where the couple finds things easy — in a shared world and in motion — and where it skids: in an unnamed status and before serious steps. The strong version of this tail is a free couple that knows how both to travel and to stay.

faq.q: Why does the 21-7-22 tail never occur in a personal chart?
faq.a: In a personal chart the tail's entry M equals the main task D plus the centre, and with D = 22 an entry of 21 is impossible with any centre. In a couple each point is the sum of two personal ones, so the entry 21 is made of 15 + 6 or 12 + 9, and the tail becomes possible.

faq.q: How is 21-7-22 different from 12-7-22 and 3-7-22?
faq.a: They share the middle and the main task — The Chariot and The Fool — but the entry differs. In 12-7-22 the couple enters the task through The Hanged Man, through pause and waiting; in 3-7-22 through The Empress, home and plenty; in 21-7-22 straight through a whole world. The numbers 21, 7 and 22 form no other couple tail in a different order: this order is the only one.

faq.q: How can a couple find out whether they have the 21-7-22 tail?
faq.a: Enter both dates of birth in the compatibility calculator: it adds up the matching points of the two charts and shows the three numbers in the sphere “The couple's karmic tail”. For example, the dates 08.01.1976 and 14.08.1975 give exactly 21-7-22, with The Star at the centre and The Devil among the values.

faq.q: What changes if the couple's centre holds Justice instead of The Star?
faq.a: That happens in 3.3% of couples with this tail, and their values are then always The Lovers. The atmosphere rests on honest accounts and clear duties. The Fool's task is the same, but next to it the question “what are we to each other” easily shrinks to “who has put how much into the shared road”.

report: Phileas Fogg, in Jules Verne's novel, won his wager on the whole world only because his bride proposed to him on a day that was not on his calendar. The 21-7-22 tail tells the same story. The couple's task opens with The World — the last card of the Major Arcana, the end of the road — passes through The Chariot and closes with The Fool, the card of beginnings. A couple with this tail starts from a whole world, and what it has to learn is the first step.

report.h3: A world where everything is “All included”

report: The entry to the task is the shared wish of the two, and here it is a whole world: shared views, open space, the road, a life by the sea or in another country. The two agree quickly on the big picture and speak one language — the language of the grand plan. Fogg staked twenty thousand pounds that he would go round the globe in eighty days, and to every objection he answered: “All included” and “The unforeseen does not exist.”

That is where the resistance lies. A world drawn together is no longer redrawn. When one of them changes — a new job, a new circle, a new wish — the other hears it as a betrayal of the shared plan: “but we agreed”. The most dangerous sentence for such a couple is “we already know everything about ourselves”.

report.h3: A heart that switches on by the timetable

report: The middle of the task is The Chariot. The couple travels the road in motion, projects and moves, like a team that stands up for each other in front of strangers. Verne has a sentence that beats any handbook: **“Phileas Fogg, who was not travelling, but only describing a circumference”**. A solid body on an orbit, “according to the laws of rational mechanics”. In India he spends twelve hours of his margin to save a widow who is to be burned at dawn. The general is amazed that this man has a heart at all. “Sometimes,” replied Phileas Fogg, quietly; “when I have the time.”

On the downside such a couple's conversation shrinks to logistics: who is meeting whom, where the connection is, whether the bill is paid. Talking about “us” can wait — until after the move, the project, the holiday. There is a quiet struggle for the reins, and tiredness comes out as irritation over nothing. In Verne the steamer Henrietta runs short of coal in the middle of the Atlantic, and Fogg has her wood burned in the furnaces: “the poop, cabins, bunks, and the spare deck were sacrificed.” The ship burns its own cabins so as not to lose speed. A couple burns sleep, weekends and the home where one can simply be in the same way.

report.h3: Eighty days in three cabins

report: The main task is The Fool, and it is read through what does not work. Above all, that means uncertainty. Aouda, once rescued, travels with Fogg for eighty days, and her position is never named: “engage three cabins.” He looks after her flawlessly, but “with the precision of an automaton”, and she “did not quite know what to make of him”.

A couple with this tail can live for years in such a “for now”: together, but without a name. Everything begins easily and beautifully, and as soon as it comes to a serious step — moving in, getting married, moving abroad together — one of them suddenly has an urgent trip or a new project, a “let's do it later”. The freedom both were proud of becomes two flatmates with a shared calendar. The one who dislikes rules starts to be jealous and to check up, and at the first difficulty walks out with a reproach.

In the novel it is Aouda who leaps, at the worst moment. Fogg is sure he arrived five minutes late and is ruined. “I have need of nothing.” “I have no friends, madam.” “I have no longer any relatives.” Then she rises: **“Mr. Fogg, do you wish at once a kinswoman and friend? Will you have me for your wife?”** For eighty days the status had no name — and now it is named in one sentence.

report.h3: The day a serious step gave back

report: Passepartout runs to the Reverend to arrange the wedding for Monday and comes back without his hat: “Because to-morrow—is Sunday!… No—to-day is Saturday.” Travelling east, towards the sun, Fogg gained a day without knowing it. He lived the whole day as 22 December, and it was the 21st, with ten minutes left before the wager closed.

Fogg names the cause of his victory himself: **“If you had not suggested our marriage, my servant would not have gone to the Reverend Samuel Wilson's, I should not have been apprised of my error, and—”** The error was uncovered not by calculation and not by speed, but by the decision to marry. That is the hidden plot of the 21-7-22 tail: **the main task is not the price of the road but the key to it.** While the two race by the timetable, they feel they are late and have lost everything. Clarity about what they are to each other gives back time that, it turns out, was in hand all along.

What changes the loop. Name the status in words and do not wait for the edge: a couple need not be brought to the brink to say the main thing. Do not reset the other's watch; notice the difference instead. In the first chapter Fogg says of his servant's slow watch: “No matter; it's enough to mention the error.” Keep a day in the shared calendar with nothing booked. Do not burn the cabins. And value the detour: the morning after the wedding Passepartout worked out that the world could have been gone round in seventy-eight days, “by not crossing India”. But without India there would have been no Aouda.

report.h3: Nothing, unless it were happiness

report: On the upside this is one of the freest stories two people can have. The world for them is a living horizon, not a table. The Chariot is their shared vehicle, not their master: they decide quickly and protect each other, and each has their own road. The Fool becomes trust: no checking up is needed, and starting from zero holds no fear. Verne's last chapter is called “In which it is shown that Phileas Fogg gained nothing by his tour around the world, unless it were happiness”.
