seo.title: Karmic tail 21 7 4 compatibility: The World, The Chariot, The Emperor
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 7 4 compatibility: a couple who want the whole world, live on the road and must learn to rule a kingdom of two by counsel, not by decree.

items.title: 21-7-4 in compatibility: the whole world, a ship and a kingdom for two
items.short: 21-7-4 in a compatibility reading is the couple's karmic tail: The World at the entry, The Chariot in the middle, The Emperor as the main task. Such a couple starts with a dream the size of the whole world, lives it out on roads, in moves and separations, and learns to build a kingdom for two — a home, money and decisions ruled by counsel rather than decree. This triple never occurs in a personal destiny matrix: it can only come from two dates.

sections.h2: How the 21-7-4 tail is formed and why a personal matrix never has it
paragraphs: Each point of the couple's matrix is the sum of the matching points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The couple's tail works the same way: entry is added to entry, middle to middle, main task to main task. The middle is not recalculated separately — it is a sum just like the other two points.
An example: the dates 05.12.1975 and 09.05.1976. The first partner has the personal tail 18-3-12 and centre 6, the second has the tail 3-22-19 and centre 11.
The couple's centre in this example is 6 + 11 = 17, The Star; the couple's values are 6, The Lovers.

There is no other way to 21-7-4. Going through every date gives one single pair of personal tails: **18-3-12 and 3-22-19, in a hundred per cent of such couples**. This shows what the three cards are made of. The couple's World is The Moon plus The Empress (18 + 3). The Chariot is The Empress plus The Fool (3 + 22). The Emperor is The Hanged Man plus The Sun (12 + 19). Personal tails are read by their own rules, and their meaning cannot be carried over to the couple; but the arithmetic says one thing: The Empress sits in both partners' tails, and The Emperor in neither. The ruler of this union is born only in the sum. And the tale this page turns to next opens with "If I were the tsaritsa" said three times, and the tsar in it steps out from behind a fence.

Why no single person has this tail: in a personal matrix the entry of the tail M equals the main task D plus the centre. For the entry to be 21 when D = 4, the centre would have to be 17 — and 17 never stands at the centre of a personal matrix, for any date. In the couple the same equation holds exactly: **4 + 17 = 21**, The Emperor plus The Star give The World. That is why The Star stands at the centre of every such couple, without exception.

The tail is rare: about one couple in 537 (0.186%), 75th of the 97 couple tails. There are no couple tails made of the same numbers in another order. The first number of a couple's tail is always divisible by three, so 4-7-21 and 7-21-4 are impossible for a couple, and the calculation never gives 21-4-7 for any dates. If 21, 7 and 4 stand in a row in a destiny matrix, it is compatibility, and they should be read as a task for two.

sections.h2: "If I were the tsaritsa": entry to the task — The World
paragraphs: "The Tale of Tsar Saltan" begins with three wishes spoken aloud late one evening. The first sister would "prepare a feast for the whole christened world", the second "alone would weave linen for the whole world", the third would "bear a bogatyr" — a hero — for the tsar. (Quotations from Pushkin here are our own close translation.) All this time the tsar stood "behind the fence", and "the last one's speech pleased him most of all". He married her that same evening.

These lines hold a detail that appears only next to the source. In 1824 Pushkin wrote down a folk version of the tale, most likely from his nanny, and there the eldest sister boasted that she would "feed the state with a single grain". Pushkin replaced the state with "the whole world", and the word for world, mir, occurs in the tale exactly twice — in these two wishes. After that the world is called svet, and the merchants measure it: "We have sailed round the whole world" is heard eight times. The state did not vanish from the tale. It moved to the end, to the island of Buyan. The tale runs the same way as the tail: from the whole world to a kingdom of one's own.

The entry to the task is the couple's common language and shared wishes. For a 21-7-4 couple this language is wide. Early dates are about countries rather than flats: a year in another country, a house by the sea, a business of their own, friends from all over the world around one table. Lisovskaya describes The World in a couple through freedom, travel, a shared outlook, moves and even a marriage across nationalities. The two recognise each other by their scale.

But the entry point stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. The three sisters have three different "whole worlds": one wants a feast for everyone, another work for the whole world, the third a family. In a couple it is the same. One means guests and celebration by "the whole world", another a venture that will make a name, a third children and a line. Each is sure the dream is shared, until they have to decide what to spend a Saturday, money and ten years of life on. In the minus of The World, Lisovskaya has no agreements, each pulling the blanket their own way, re-educating the partner into one's own outlook, and mocking the partner's plans.

The card has a second side too. Six days after his wedding, on 24 February 1831, Pushkin wrote to Pletnyov: "I am married — and happy; my one wish is that nothing in my life should change — I shall wait for nothing better." He finished the tale that same summer at Tsarskoye Selo: a scrap of the manuscript is dated 29 August 1831. In Waite's divinatory list for The World, "voyage" and "change of place" stand side by side, and reversed comes "permanence". A 21-7-4 couple wants both at once: the whole world — and for everything to stay forever as it was on the first evening.

sections.h2: A ship, a barrel and a bumblebee: middle of the task — The Chariot
paragraphs: The Chariot enters the tale right after the wedding night: "In those days there was a war." The tsar mounts "his good steed" and rides away. From then on everything in the tale rides and sails. The barrel with the tsaritsa and her son rocks on the ocean, ships pass Buyan to the refrain "The wind roams over the sea and drives the little ship along", and the prince flies after a ship three times — as a mosquito, a fly and a bumblebee. Rimsky-Korsakov's famous "Flight of the Bumblebee" comes from the opera based on this tale (1900): it is the music to which Gvidon, as a bumblebee, flies after the ship.

The middle of the task is how the couple travels from the shared wish to the main task. For a 21-7-4 couple that road is motion. Such couples often get on best on the move: they pack a flat overnight, find a home and work in a strange city within a week, become a team on a trip. Lisovskaya writes that a Chariot couple looks from outside more like friends and a team than like lovers: each develops outside the home, decisions come fast, and they defend their own at once. That is how the Swan is saved in the tale. The young prince breaks off an oak bough, strings it with the silk cord from his cross, shoots — and the kite falls into the sea.

Wen notes something important about The Chariot: it is "travel not for the sake of travel, but for the sake of acquisition". The merchants in the tale trade in sables, horses and damask steel. Gvidon first asks "to get a wondrous wonder", then: "I would like to bring a marvellous marvel into my domain." A 21-7-4 couple is always acquiring something too: a new city, a new post, the next project. The Chariot can also sting. Lisovskaya names aggression first among The Chariot's tasks, and every flight of Gvidon's ends in a sting: one aunt in the right eye, the other in the left eye, the old woman on the nose.

But the tale's real disaster happens not at war but on the road between two people. When the tsar hears of the "unknown little beast", he first wants in his anger to hang the messenger, then softens and acts wisely: he orders them "to wait for the tsar's return for a lawful decision". On the way the messenger is made drunk, the letter is swapped, and the boyars read aloud a decree that is no longer his. In the language of a couple: one is away, the other at home, and everything important travels through go-betweens. A voice message heard in a taxi. News "Mum passed on". A row in a chat where each answers not the words but the tone they read into them. A decision taken while the other was not there, and announced aloud by somebody else.

In the minus, Lisovskaya's Chariot means hasty conclusions, conflicts out of nothing, rivalry over who leads, and a habit of drawing strength from those close rather than restoring it oneself. Among the couple's tasks she also names this one: to dare a joint move. In the tale the move is forced — in a tarred barrel. They get out of it not because someone unlocks it. The son braces his head against the bottom and says, "How could we cut a window out to the yard?" — and "knocked out the bottom and walked out".

sections.h2: The city on Buyan: main task — The Emperor
paragraphs: The morning after the Swan is saved, a city stands on the empty island: crenellated walls, golden domes, a harbour "with a strong customs post". The court meets the young prince "in golden carriages", and at once "crowns him with a prince's cap". The Chariot and The Emperor in two neighbouring lines: the carriages roll up — and the crown goes on.

Then Pushkin describes in detail how the kingdom works. For the squirrel that cracks golden nuts the prince builds a crystal house, sets a guard on her "and made a clerk keep strict account of the nuts. Profit to the prince, honour to the squirrel." Coins are cast from the shells, emeralds are poured into the storerooms, "everyone on that island is rich, there are no huts, only palaces everywhere". The thirty-three bogatyrs are "all equal, as if hand-picked" and patrol the city. The Pushkin scholar Sergei Bondi believed that the image of an ideal sea-kingdom was brought into the folk tale by Pushkin himself. The result is almost word for word Waite's divinatory list for The Emperor: "Stability, power, protection, realization".

The couple's main task is read mostly through the minus: what does not work and what to learn. For The Emperor, Lisovskaya names a struggle for leadership, decisions made for everyone, rigid rules that later get in their own makers' way, and a coldness that makes it impossible to tell joy from anger. The tale has a portrait of this minus. Three times in a row, word for word: "Tsar Saltan sits in his hall, on the throne and in his crown, with a sad thought on his face." Around him sit the weaver, the cook and the matchmaker Babarikha, who "look him in the eyes". The tsar does not say what saddens him. The tsar does not go himself. Three times he promises, "I will visit the wondrous island", — and stays. He learns about the world from other people's stories, and each time his wish to visit the wondrous island is put out by the story of a bigger wonder — "you won't surprise us with that", as the weaver says. In the folk note of 1824 the tsar is called "Sultan Sultanovich, the Turkish sovereign", and the Arabic word sultan means "power". Power sits on the throne — and sees through other people's eyes.

In a couple this looks ordinary. The rule "I keep the budget" was set when one earned and the other studied, and kept long after it all turned the other way round. "Holidays at my parents'" was decided in the first year and never revisited. One sits silent and sad on a throne, the other rules by reports and by the look on a face. And both are sure the house is in order.

The tale's own words divide it into two kingdoms. In the first half, "order", "letter" and "decree" rule — five times in twenty-four lines, and all of it by messenger. At the end the same matters are settled by "counsel": the Swan says "I will serve you with counsel", and the mother blesses the young pair "to live in counsel and love". The word for order survives on the island too, but now it serves the wonder: a chancery clerk — in Russian a d'yak prikaznyi, literally a "clerk of orders" — counts the nuts. The Emperor does not have to disappear. He has to stop writing decrees through go-betweens.

Gvidon gets the squirrel and the bogatyrs the same way: he longs, asks and receives. The third "marvel" begins with the same formula: "Grief and longing eat at me: people marry; I look around — only I go unwed." And here the Swan stops him for the first time: "But a wife is no mitten: you can't shake her off your white hand, nor tuck her into your belt… Think it all through well, so as not to repent later." A squirrel can be put under guard, a coin can be sent around the world. A person cannot be acquired, tucked into a belt or kept under guard. For the couple's Emperor this is the main lesson: **a partner is not a mitten, not a treasury and not a subject**. In the tale, sex hands out the roles. In a 21-7-4 couple either of the two can turn out to be the tsar, the messenger or the Swan, and usually both take turns.

The Emperor grows up in the tale in a single line. Hearing for the fourth time about the wonders of Buyan, Saltan stops listening to the aunts: "What am I — a tsar or a child? — he says, not joking. — I'm going today!" In Waite's reversed list for The Emperor the last word is "immaturity". The child-tsar learns about the world from stories at court. The grown tsar boards a ship and sees for himself. And at the end the truth is revealed without words: Gvidon leads his father into the city "saying nothing", and "the tsar looks — and recognises".

sections.h2: A star on her brow: a centre that belongs to neither partner
paragraphs: The star on the brow appears in the tale five times, and Babarikha is the first to mention it: "By day she outshines God's light, by night she lights the earth, the moon gleams beneath her braid, and on her brow a star burns." In the folk note these marks belonged to another hero. There the tsaritsa gives birth to a wonderful boy: "a star on his brow, a moon at the nape". The star on the brow was the child's — the one born of two. Pushkin gave it to the bride.

The same happens to the centre of a 21-7-4 couple. The centre is the couple's atmosphere, what is between two people when nobody is watching. Here it is The Star for everyone without exception, and it is a card no person ever has at the centre. These two have no "my" Star and "your" Star. It appears only between them. Lisovskaya writes about The Star at the centre of a couple with striking precision: such people often understand only in the couple who they want to be, and open up, sometimes with the partner's direct help.

That is exactly what happens in the tale. Four times the Swan finds the prince on the shore and asks the same thing: "Why are you quiet as a rainy day? What makes you sad?" Four times he confesses his longing, and she helps: three times she splashes him with water so that he can fly after the ship, she gives him the squirrel, sends her brothers the bogatyrs, and the fourth time she reveals who she is. Waite writes that the figure on The Star "pours Water of Life", and that the card's mottoes are "Waters of Life freely" and "Gifts of the Spirit". Wen sees in The Star the generosity of "giving more than the Seeker receives", and an inner compass: "Guidance is not coming from others, but rather it is coming from within."

Stars first appear in the tale above the barrel: "Stars sparkle in the blue sky, waves lash in the blue sea." Waite's divinatory list for The Star opens with "Loss, theft, privation, abandonment" and only then says "another reading says — hope and bright prospects". The night scene holds both readings: mother and child are cast into the sea, but the stars are above them, and the wave carries the barrel ashore.

There is one more coincidence that is hard to miss, though it proves nothing. The Swan's portrait is made of three lights: the moon, a star, and a radiance that outshines the day. In the Major Arcana these three cards come in a row: 17 — The Star, 18 — The Moon, 19 — The Sun. In a 21-7-4 couple The Moon stands in one partner's personal tail, The Sun in the other's, and The Star at the centre of their shared matrix. Pushkin, of course, knew nothing of the matrix.

Lisovskaya's minus of The Star is love for an image instead of a person, comparison with others, fitting the partner to a picture. Gvidon falls in love with a rumour: he hears about the princess from Babarikha while sitting as a bumblebee at his father's court, and doubts it himself: "But come — is it true?" The answer comes not from rumour but from the one who has been beside him the whole tale: "Why go far? Know that your fate is near: that princess is me." This is the turn of the whole tail. The World at the entry and The Chariot in the middle pull the couple far away, to the wonder beyond the sea. The Star at the centre says the main wonder is already here, and that neither of the two creates it alone.

sections.h2: Two weddings in one tale: the tail in the minus and in the plus
paragraphs: "Saltan" has two couples, and both marry by the same formula: "The tsar did not take long: he married that same evening" — "The prince did not take long, he married the princess." The son repeats his father's words but lives the tail differently. Two weddings — two ways to live 21-7-4.

paragraphs: A window frames the tale. It begins at a window: "Three maidens by the window were spinning late one evening" and dreamed of the whole world. Near the end there is a window again: "By the window Gvidon sits, silently gazing at the sea." The sea that "lashed" at the start now "does not roar, does not lash, only barely, barely trembles". And this time the prince does not fly to the world — the world comes to him: "Across the plains of the Ocean sails the fleet of Tsar Saltan." A couple that has built its kingdom stops chasing the world. The world sails in to visit.

The last thing Pushkin changed in the folk tale concerns The Emperor. In the 1824 note the ending is short: "and the stepmother dies". In Pushkin the three envious women hide in corners, are found, confess everything — and "the tsar, for such joy, let all three go home". A tsar who has seen the truth with his own eyes no longer needs an execution. Order rests not on fear but on joy.

sections.h2: What a 21-7-4 couple has to learn
paragraphs: Lisovskaya analyses a couple's tail this way: each conclusion carries, in brackets, the cards it follows from. Below are the tasks of a 21-7-4 couple taken apart the same way: from pairs of cards to the whole tail.

ul: **The World + The Emperor: rules agreed on, not rules inherited.** The freedom of The World and the order of The Emperor do not have to be at war. The task is to set shared rules together and revise them when life changes. A good test: can each of the two remember when and why a rule appeared, and do they agree with it today?

**The Chariot + The Emperor: decide important things with both present.** Saltan is wisest when he orders them "to wait for the tsar's return for a lawful decision". Nothing big about money, housing, children or family is decided by message, through go-betweens or in the other's absence. Waiting for the return is easier than fishing a barrel out of the sea later.

**The World + The Chariot: the road together, not apart.** A 21-7-4 couple comes alive in motion, but each may have their own road, and then home is only a change of trains. The task is to choose at least part of the way together: a city, a trip, a shared project. Gvidon flies after the ship alone while he is sad. Once married, he stays at home, and the motion comes to him by itself.

**The Emperor: say feelings out loud.** "With a sad thought on his face" is the portrait of someone who rules but does not say what is wrong. Among The Emperor's tasks Lisovskaya names exactly this: learning to talk about feelings. Four times the Swan opens a conversation with "What makes you sad?" — and it works better than any decree.

**The Chariot: restore strength rather than take it from those close.** After a business trip, a rush job or a move, The Chariot's tank is empty, and the easiest refuelling is at the partner's expense — irritation, demands, complaints. The task is to know in advance what restores each of the two, and not to mistake rest for winning an argument.

**The World + The Chariot + The Emperor: don't import the wonder from overseas.** As long as the couple measures its life by other people's tales of "such a wonder in the world", its own island will always seem too small. The task is to notice that the main thing in this union — The Star at the centre — is already there, and to build the kingdom around it, not around rumours.

paragraphs: If the "decree" in a couple rests on fear, threats or force, it is no longer a subject for reading the tail. Then a specialist is needed — a psychologist, and in danger, the local emergency number.

sections.h2: The couple's values: The Lovers or The Devil
paragraphs: "The couple's values" in the compatibility matrix answer what the union exists for. A 21-7-4 couple has only two options here.

83.8% of such couples have The Lovers. Waite calls it "the card of human love", and his divinatory list includes "trials overcome". For a 21-7-4 couple this fits the tale well: the union rests on a choice made with open eyes, after "think it all through well", and on the blessing "to live in counsel and love". The Lovers explain what the kingdom is built for: for the two, not for the throne.

16.2% of couples have The Devil in their values. For Lisovskaya it is a union of passion, a vivid bond and strong attachment, and even in the plus she warns that one partner may wake up wanting to possess the other. For such couples the Swan's words sound twice as loud: a wife is no mitten, and nor is a husband. The stronger the attachment, the more important it is not to confuse it with a right to keep someone tucked in a belt.

sections.h2: What Waite writes about The World, The Chariot and The Emperor
paragraphs: In the Major Arcana these three cards stand in the reverse order: The Emperor is fourth, The Chariot seventh, The World the last. The couple's tail runs against this current: from completion to foundation, from the whole world to a home of one's own. Waite describes The Chariot as "the victory which creates kingship as its natural consequence and not the vested royalty of the fourth card", that is, of The Emperor. In the 21-7-4 tail these two powers stand side by side: power won on the road, and power that has to be held at home.

On Waite's card The Emperor holds a sceptre and "a globe in his left hand". Wen explains: "The scepter or crux ansata is his sovereignty; the orb is his dominion." In Russian this orb is called derzhava, and the same word means a state, a power. Both senses come from the verb derzhat', "to hold". The World at the entry of the tail is the whole wide world, and in the main task it becomes an orb in the hand: something held. The couple's task is to hold their kingdom without crushing it in a fist.

On The World Waite sees a dancing figure in an oval garland and calls it an image "of joy attained in the body", "still guarded by the Divine Watchers". And on The Star, besides the woman with two ewers, there is "a shrub or tree, whereon a bird alights". Wen writes that "the bird perched on the tree conveys new opportunities that will restore hope". In Pushkin, hope also comes as a bird: "Look — over the flowing waters swims the white swan."

intro: The triple has an oddity that shows only in the numbers. The centre of the chart of every couple with the 21-7-4 tail is The Star, and no single person ever has The Star at the centre, whatever the date of birth. The brightest thing in this union belongs to neither of the two. Pushkin described such a couple long before any matrix: a prince is ready to walk after a bride with a star on her brow "even beyond thrice-nine lands", and the Swan answers him: "Why go far?"

ul: **M · Entry to the task — 21, The World.** The couple's common language is big plans: countries, moves, a life "for the whole world". The couple enters the union with this dream and stumbles over it too, because each has their own "whole world".

**N · Middle of the task — 7, The Chariot.** How the couple moves towards the task: in motion. Roads, projects, business trips, the chase after the next wonder — and decisions made on the move and at a distance.

**D · Main task — 4, The Emperor.** What the couple has to learn: to build their own kingdom — home, order, money, rules — without turning the partner into a subject. The key question of this tail is not "who is right" but "who decides, and how".

faq.q: Can 21-7-4 appear in a personal destiny matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and 21 with a main task of 4 needs a centre of 17, which no person has. If 21, 7 and 4 stand in a row in a calculation, it is the karmic tail of a couple's matrix, that is, the compatibility of two people.

faq.q: What does "21-7-4 programme" mean in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: It is the same couple's karmic tail. Yuliana Lisovskaya, whose book the compatibility calculation follows, calls the triple on a couple's tail a "karmic programme". There is no separate entity behind the word "programme": these are the couple's tasks, read from the main point, The Emperor, through The Chariot and The World.

faq.q: Are there couple tails with the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. The first number of a couple's tail is always divisible by three, so 4-7-21 and 7-21-4 are impossible, and the calculation never gives 21-4-7 for any dates. The 21-7-4 tail is one of a kind, and in every such couple it comes from the personal tails 18-3-12 and 3-22-19.

faq.q: Is the 21-7-4 tail bad compatibility?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail shows tasks, not a verdict or a forecast, and the method gives no compatibility percentages at all. By the method the main task of the tail is read mostly through the minus, because it is about what to learn. A 21-7-4 couple has The Star at the centre — an atmosphere of inspiration and mutual help that neither of the two has alone.

faq.q: Who is The Emperor in a 21-7-4 couple?
faq.a: Nobody by default, and not by sex. The Emperor here is the couple's task, not one partner's role. In different years and in different matters, first one and then the other turns out to be the "tsar". The task is to divide power into areas and decide important things together, by counsel rather than decree.

report: The brightest thing in a 21-7-4 couple belongs to neither of the two. At the centre of the chart of every such couple stands The Star, and no single person ever has this card at the centre of a personal matrix. It appears only between two people. Around it stand the three cards of the tail: The World at the entry, The Chariot in the middle, The Emperor as the main task. And behind them a story shows through, one that Pushkin finished in the summer of 1831, in the first year of his own marriage. A prince is ready to walk after a bride with a star on her brow "even beyond thrice-nine lands", and the Swan answers him: "Why go far?"

report.h3: Pushkin changed one word, and the tale followed the tail

report: In the folk note of 1824 the eldest of three sisters boasted that she would "feed the state with a single grain". Pushkin replaced the state with the world: "If I were the tsaritsa… I would prepare a feast for the whole christened world." The word for world, mir, occurs in the tale exactly twice, in the first two wishes. After that the world is called svet, and the merchants measure it: "We have sailed round the whole world." The state did not vanish. It moved to the end, to the island of Buyan. **The tale runs the same way as the tail: from the whole world to a kingdom of one's own.**

The World at the entry is the couple's common language. Early dates here are about countries rather than flats: a year in another country, a house by the sea, a business of their own, friends from all over the world around one table. But the entry stands on the line of tasks, and the dream turns into resistance. The three sisters have three different "whole worlds": a feast for everyone, work for the whole world, a family. In a couple it is the same. Each is sure the dream is shared, until they have to decide what to spend a Saturday, money and ten years of life on.

report.h3: The disaster happens not at war but on the road

report: The Chariot rides into the tale right after the wedding night: "In those days there was a war." From then on everything rides and sails: the tsar on his steed, the barrel on the ocean, ships to the refrain "the wind roams over the sea", the prince flying after a ship three times as a mosquito, a fly and a bumblebee. From outside, a Chariot couple looks more like a team: it packs a flat overnight and finds a home and work in a strange city within a week.

But the tale's real disaster happens between two people, halfway. When the tsar hears of the "unknown little beast", he acts wisely: he orders them "to wait for the tsar's return for a lawful decision". On the way the messenger is made drunk, the letter is swapped, and the boyars read aloud a decree that is not his. In the language of a couple it looks like this: one is away, the other at home, and everything important travels through go-betweens. A voice message heard in a taxi. News "Mum passed on". A decision taken without the other, announced aloud by somebody else. **Big things about money, housing, children and family are decided with both present**: waiting for the return is easier than fishing a barrel out of the sea later.

report.h3: A tsar with a sad thought on his face

report: Three times in a row, word for word: "Tsar Saltan sits in his hall, on the throne and in his crown, with a sad thought on his face." Around him sit the envious women who "look him in the eyes". The tsar does not say what saddens him and does not go himself. He learns about the world from other people's stories. In the folk note he is called "Sultan Sultanovich", and the Arabic sultan means "power". Power sits on the throne — and sees through other people's eyes.

This is the minus of The Emperor in the couple's main task. The rule "I keep the budget" was set when one earned and the other studied, and kept long after it all turned the other way round. One sits silent and sad on a throne, the other rules by reports. The tale's own words divide it into two kingdoms. In the first half, "order", "letter" and "decree" rule, and all of it by messenger. At the end the same matters are settled by counsel: the young pair are blessed **"to live in counsel and love"**.

A squirrel with golden nuts can be put under guard, with "strict account" kept of her. When the prince asks for a third marvel, a wife, the Swan stops him for the first time: "But a wife is no mitten: you can't shake her off your white hand, nor tuck her into your belt." **A partner is not a mitten, not a treasury and not a subject.** In the tale, sex hands out the roles. In a 21-7-4 couple either of the two can be the tsar, the messenger or the Swan, and usually both take turns.

The Emperor grows up in a single line: "What am I — a tsar or a child? I'm going today!" In Waite's reversed list for The Emperor the last word is "immaturity". The child-tsar learns about the world from stories at court. The grown one boards a ship and sees for himself: "the tsar looks — and recognises".

report.h3: The Star is not imported from overseas

report: In the folk tale the star on the brow belonged to a child — the one born of two. Pushkin gave it to the bride. Four times the Swan asks the prince the same thing: "Why are you quiet as a rainy day? What makes you sad?" — and each time she helps. The Star at the centre of a couple works just like this: beside the partner, a person understands who they want to be. It has a minus too: love for a picture instead of a person. Gvidon falls in love with a rumour and doubts it himself: "But come — is it true?" And the answer comes from the one who has been beside him the whole tale: "Know that your fate is near: that princess is me."

A window frames the tale. At the start "three maidens by the window" dream of the whole world. Near the end "by the window Gvidon sits, silently gazing at the sea", and the sea "does not roar, does not lash". Once married, the prince no longer flies — and the world sails in to visit him with Tsar Saltan's fleet. The last thing Pushkin changed in the folk tale: there "the stepmother dies", while in his version "the tsar, for such joy, let all three go home". **Order rests not on fear but on joy.**
If the "decree" in a couple rests on fear, threats or force, it is no longer a subject for reading the tail: a psychologist is needed, and in danger, a local emergency number or crisis line.

unit.title: Counsel instead of decree

captions.M: To want the whole world for two and live by big plans
captions.N: To live on the road and not leave big things to go-betweens
captions.D: To rule together without making the partner a subject

unit.meaning: Your task is to decide big things together and face to face, by counsel, not by decree through go-betweens.

seo.title: Karmic tail 3 10 16 compatibility: a garden, a wheel and lightning
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 10 16 compatibility: The Empress, the Wheel of Fortune and The Tower. Why a turning wheel stands where the Sun should be, and how to work it out.

items.title: The couple's tail 3-10-16: The Empress, the Wheel of Fortune and The Tower in compatibility
items.short: The karmic tail 3-10-16 in compatibility begins with a garden and ends with lightning. Between them the arithmetic of the matrix leaves room for only two cards, The Sun or the Wheel of Fortune, and in almost three couples out of four with these two ends it is the Wheel. This is the tail of a couple who want to grow abundance together, live that wish through turns in which one rises while the other sinks, and learn the main thing: how to survive the collapse of what they invented — the image of the partner and of their shared future — and remain one tree.

sections.h2: The chestnut by its old roots: the novel where tail 3-10-16 lives
paragraphs: Many readers know the story. Jane, an orphan, works as a governess at Thornfield Hall. Its master, Mr Rochester, is twenty years older and stands so high on the English ladder of rank that between them, in Jane's words, lies "the wider ocean—wealth, caste, custom".

Chapter 23. Midsummer Eve, sunset. Jane goes out into the orchard: "No nook in the grounds more sheltered and more Eden-like." She sees "trees laden with ripening fruit"; Rochester takes "a ripe cherry from the wall". Down the laurel walk he leads her to a giant horse-chestnut: "here is the chestnut tree: here is the bench at its old roots." On that bench he proposes, and Jane feels herself "called to the paradise of union".

Then the chestnut "writhed and groaned", wind roars down the walk, a spark leaps out of a cloud — "a crack, a crash, and a close rattling peal". In the morning little Adèle runs in with the news: "the great horse-chestnut at the bottom of the orchard had been struck by lightning in the night, and half of it split away."

One night holds the whole tail in miniature. The garden where two people agree on their future is The Empress. Weather that overturns within the hour is the Wheel. Lightning in the very tree at whose roots the "yes" was spoken is The Tower. The novel then unfolds the same three acts over a year: the wedding will be stopped at the altar, Jane will leave with nothing, fortune will raise her and bring him down, Thornfield will burn. And Brontë does not forget the tree until her last chapters.

On the eve of the wedding Jane goes back to it: "The cloven halves were not broken from each other, for the firm base and strong roots kept them unsundered below; though community of vitality was destroyed… as yet, however, they might be said to form one tree—a ruin, but an entire ruin." And she speaks to the wreckage as if it were alive: "You did right to hold fast to each other."

A year later the blinded Rochester will say of himself: "I am no better than the old lightning-struck chestnut-tree in Thornfield orchard." Jane will answer with the sentence that closes the tail: "You are no ruin, sir—no lightning-struck tree… Plants will grow about your roots." A garden at the entry, lightning in the main task — and a garden again, this time around a split trunk. The cards show how a couple gets there.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: The Empress and two dialects of one garden
paragraphs: M is the Entry to the task. For Lisovskaya it holds the couple's shared wishes and agreements, their "common language"; in the reading the same point also appears in the sphere Relationship and common language. The point lies on the line of tasks, so the wish with which a couple enters the task easily becomes resistance.

Here the wish is The Empress: to grow. A home, a family, a shared venture, a move closer to the land, an "our" budget, the feeling of a full cup. Jane and Rochester share the wish but speak it in different dialects.

Jane's dialect is home as a person. Coming back to Thornfield, she blurts out: "wherever you are is my home—my only home." Rochester's dialect is home as a gift. The morning after the proposal he has already written to his banker for the family jewels and hopes "to pour them into your lap": "the diamond chain round your neck, and the circlet on your forehead", bracelets, rings, satin and lace. Jane replies: "And then you won't know me, sir… an ape in a harlequin's jacket." At the silk warehouse he picks an amethyst silk and a pink satin; she fights him down to black satin and pearl-grey silk, and Rochester vows "he would yet see me glittering like a parterre".

Jane states her terms in words that could hang over any joint budget: "I will not be your English Céline Varens." Céline was Rochester's former mistress, a French opera-dancer he had showered with diamonds. "I shall continue to act as Adèle's governess; by that I shall earn my board and lodging, and thirty pounds a year besides… and you shall give me nothing but— … Your regard; and if I give you mine in return, that debt will be quit."

Beneath The Empress hides a second role. Rochester asks Jane for more than her hand. Three chapters before the proposal he asks her, as if about some abstract man, whether "the wandering and sinful, but now rest-seeking and repentant, man" may bind a gentle stranger to himself for ever, "thereby securing his own peace of mind and regeneration of life". On the night of the proposal he repeats: "It will atone—it will atone." Waite calls The Empress "not Regina coeli, but she is still refugium peccatorum" — the refuge of sinners. That is exactly the post Rochester offers Jane. She declines it in advance: **"a wanderer's repose or a sinner's reformation should never depend on a fellow-creature."**

Among the reasons The Empress brings a couple together Lisovskaya lists this one too: to thaw after past unhappy relationships. On the bright side the union really does warm. On the dark side one partner enters it as a shelter, and the other is handed the duty of being the garden where the first will be saved. In daily life it looks ordinary: "after everything I've been through, you're all I live for", "why work, I'll give you everything", gifts that leave the other feeling in debt, and a quiet separate account the other opens so as not to be kept.

Jane opens exactly such an account. Driving home from the shops, she remembers her uncle in Madeira, who once meant to make her his heir: "if I had ever so small an independency; I never can bear being dressed like a doll by Mr. Rochester, or sitting like a second Danae with the golden shower falling daily round me." That same day she writes to tell her uncle about the marriage. The letter reaches him while Mason is staying with him — the brother of Rochester's first wife, of whom Jane knows nothing. A few weeks later Mason and a solicitor stop the wedding. **The Empress's wish not to enter the union empty-handed is what sets the Wheel turning, and the Wheel brings the lightning.** Wen pins the same shadow to The Empress: her fruition "might also be a foreshadowing of unintended or unanticipated consequences".

Even Danaë is the right choice. Horace's ode (III.16) opens with "Inclusam Danaen turris aenea" — "Danaë, shut in a tower of bronze" (our translation, as with the Latin below). Horace goes on to say that gold loves to pass through guards and to break through rock "more powerfully than the lightning's stroke", that a seer's house fell "for gain", and he sums up: "Multa petentibus desunt multa" — those who seek much lack much. One ode holds gold, a tower and lightning. At the entry to the task Jane fears that the garden she is being given will turn out to be a bronze tower with a golden shower inside.

sections.h2: Why the Sun is not between the garden and the lightning
paragraphs: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is the sum of the entry and the main task. By that formula The Sun would stand between The Empress and The Tower: 3 + 16 = 19. In a couple the middle is not derived from the two ends; it is added up from the personal middles of two people. But addition has a memory. Reducing a number does not change its remainder after division by nine, so by that remainder the couple's middle always matches the sum of entry and task. With an entry of 3 and a task of 16, only two cards are allowed in the middle: 19 or 10 (28 reduces to 10).

So couples with The Empress at the entry and The Tower as the task have only this choice: The Sun or the Wheel. Tail 3-19-16 occurs in 1.26% of couples, 3-10-16 in 3.35%. **In almost three cases out of four what stands between the garden and the lightning is not steady light but a turn.**

The Sun does not vanish from the people themselves. In half of the couples with this tail (49%) one partner carries it in the middle of their own tail: their personal tail is 12-19-7. In the couple this Sun is added to the other partner's nine, The Hermit, and becomes the Wheel: 19 + 9 = 28 → 10. The light of one does not shine evenly on both — it starts to rotate. This is our reading; the arithmetic is checked by going through all birth dates.

Brontë got there first here too. Rochester, speaking of himself as if of a stranger, says: "your sun at noon darkens in an eclipse, which you feel will not leave it till the time of setting." A month before the wedding Jane writes of Rochester: "He stood between me and every thought of religion, as an eclipse intervenes between man and the broad sun… of whom I had made an idol." Each of the two has an eclipse. And on the evening before the wedding Jane catches herself thinking that "my fortune had passed its meridian, and must now decline". The meridian is the highest point, where the sun stands at noon. The Sun reaches its height, and then the wheel begins.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: the Wheel on which two change places
paragraphs: N is the Middle of the task. Lisovskaya gives this point no meaning of its own: it adds to the main task. In our reading the middle shows how a couple lives the road from the wish to the task. In 3-10-16 that road is the Wheel: highs and lows take turns, and what matters most in this energy, for Lisovskaya, is to accept the change itself rather than fight it.

Above all, the Wheel does one thing to this couple: it makes the two change places. At Thornfield Rochester is the master. He has the estate, the money and the right to decide where the governess goes: on the night of the proposal he first tells her she will have to go to Ireland. Jane, as he puts it himself, is in a "responsible and dependent position". A year later it is all reversed. Jane has inherited a fortune, and when Rochester asks who will look after her now, she answers: **"I am independent, sir, as well as rich: I am my own mistress."** Rochester is blind, his left arm maimed; he lives in a house buried in a wood and calls himself "a blind lameter".

Brontë even names the turn with a card word. Hearing about the twenty thousand pounds, Jane thinks: "Here was a new card turned up! It is a fine thing, reader, to be lifted in a moment from indigence to wealth." Indigence is a word from Waite's list for The Tower, while "abundance" is on his list for the reversed Wheel. The Wheel in the middle of the tail carries the couple from The Tower's word to The Empress's and back.

And at once it is clear which dialect of the garden Jane speaks now. She finds cousins: "This was wealth indeed!—wealth to the heart!… not like the ponderous gift of gold." She divides the inheritance four ways: "Twenty thousand pounds shared equally would be five thousand each, justice—enough and to spare."

The Wheel has a dark side as well, and in the novel Rochester plays it out. He turns the wheel himself to test feelings. He lets a rumour spread that "my fortune was not a third of what was supposed" and watches the society beauty everyone took for his bride grow cold. Disguised as a gypsy fortune-teller, he tells Jane her fortune and probes whether she is waiting for him: "Chance has meted you a measure of happiness… It depends on yourself to stretch out your hand, and take it up." Among the Wheel's tasks Lisovskaya lists leaving manipulation and grudges behind, no longer blaming fate and each other, accepting the partner with their flaws, looking for solutions instead of complaints. A test by turning the wheel is the same attempt to steer the wheel instead of living on it.

In the life of a 3-10-16 couple the turns look ordinary. One loses a job while the other is promoted the same year. The one who always carried the load suddenly needs support. A good year gives way to a hard one, quiet to a quarrel, and the argument is no longer about the matter but about places: "you've changed", "you used to be stronger", "now you're keeping me". The test of the middle is not to fix each other in the roles of the first act: master and governess, provider and the one provided for. A place on the wheel is a place, not a character. Rochester knows it from experience: "Fortune has knocked me about since: she has even kneaded me with her knuckles, and now I flatter myself I am hard and tough as an India-rubber ball."

One more detail from the numbers. In a quarter of couples with this tail the partners' personal tails are identical: both have 15-5-8. Their Wheel is made of two identical Hierophants (5 + 5 = 10). The turn is not born from the two being different — the union itself creates it.

sections.h2: Main task: The Tower strikes what was invented
paragraphs: D is the Main task. It is read mostly through its shadow side: what the couple cannot manage and what it has to learn. In Lisovskaya's card for The Tower the first of the couple's tasks is **the collapse of an invented image of the partner**, and her key to the energy is that trials lived through together make the union stronger.

In Jane Eyre both of them are invented. Rochester invents Jane: he calls her a fairy, an elf, "you almost unearthly thing", wants to dress her in satin and "make the world acknowledge you a beauty". Jane invents Rochester, and calls it an idol herself. On the eve of the wedding she shuts the wardrobe on her wedding dress with "I will leave you by yourself, white dream", and cannot bring herself to fix the address cards marked "Mrs. Rochester" to her trunks: "Mrs. Rochester! She did not exist: she would not be born till to-morrow." In the morning it turns out that a Mrs Rochester has existed for years. Rochester is married; his mad wife Bertha is kept locked up on the third storey of Thornfield. The lightning struck the image of the future wife — literally.

What Jane writes after the wedding that never happened is an exact formula for The Tower in a couple: **"Mr. Rochester was not to me what he had been; for he was not what I had thought him."** Right after it comes The Empress's whole garden, turned over by the Wheel in a single night: "A Christmas frost had come at midsummer; a white December storm had whirled over June; ice glazed the ripe apples, drifts crushed the blowing roses; on hayfield and cornfield lay a frozen shroud."

Later the tower falls in the literal sense too. Bertha sets the house on fire and throws herself from the battlements. Rochester will not leave until everyone else is out, and on the staircase the house comes down on him. When Jane returns, she sees what she once saw in a dream: of the front only a tall, fragile wall is left, "no roof, no battlements, no chimneys—all had crashed in".

In real life this Tower does not have to be a catastrophe. More often the blow lands on the picture. A partner does something "not like them". An old secret or a debt comes out. The plan for a house, a move, a shared venture — the plan around which "we" was built — collapses. The Tower's shadow side for Lisovskaya is that at such moments the two look in different directions: one rescues the plan, the other rescues themselves. They lose their temper, throw out words in shock that are hard to take back, threaten to leave in order to hold on. The task is not to keep the lightning from striking. The task is to tell the person apart from the picture each has painted of them, and to let the picture fall rather than the person.

sections.h2: What Waite drew: a field, a wheel's rim and a sun on the forehead
paragraphs: The cards on this site have their own artwork. But the Waite–Smith deck, and Wen's commentary on it, hold four details that read as clues to this tail.
**The Empress.** In front of her, Waite writes, "a field of corn is ripening". In Brontë, after the wedding that never happened, a frozen shroud lies on the cornfield.

**The Wheel.** Waite drew the card after Lévi's reconstruction, with "a Hermanubis rising with the wheel" and "a Typhon on the descending side"; Waite "presented Typhon in his serpent form". Two figures on one rim, and one goes up exactly when the other goes down. That is Jane and Rochester in the second year of their story.

**The Tower.** Waite argues against reading the card as the chastisement of pride: such readings, he says, do not "account for the two persons who are the living sufferers". Two people fall. And Wen, describing the card, writes: "Yellowing leaves from the Tree of Life float down from the heavens." The Tower has a tree as well.

**Temperance, the centre of these couples.** Waite's angel has "the sign of the sun upon his forehead". Waite adds that it is "untrue to say that the figure symbolizes the genius of the sun, though it is the analogy of solar light". The Sun that is missing from the middle of the tail is painted on the forehead of the couple's centre.

sections.h2: An entire ruin: what holds the two halves
paragraphs: The main secret of this tail is written in its numbers. The centre of the matrix in 3-10-16 couples is Temperance, 14, practically always: The Hierophant stands in the centre for four couples in ten thousand. And 16 + 14 = 30, which reduces to 3. **The main task added to the couple's atmosphere gives exactly the entry.** In a personal matrix every tail is built this way: the entry equals the main task plus the centre. A 3-10-16 couple obeys the same rule. Lightning plus what the two patiently blend between them gives back the garden.

For Lisovskaya the couple's centre is their shared atmosphere, what happens between two people when nobody is watching. Wen writes of Temperance as forces that "restore what was lost, cool what was too hot, heat up what was too cold". Lisovskaya's shadow side of this centre is just as precise: one always gives way, and the other never even thinks of it. Temperance breaks when only one of them is doing the blending.

Brontë shows it in a small thing. Walking away from the split chestnut, Jane gathers up "the apples with which the grass round the tree roots was thickly strewn" and divides "the ripe from the unripe". The garden goes on at the roots of the struck tree. The last word on Waite's list for The Tower is "ruin", and that is exactly what Brontë calls the chestnut: a ruin, but an entire one.

At the end of the novel a gesture from the beginning comes back. Their first meeting is a fall: on an icy road, "Man and horse were down". Rochester has sprained his ankle and says: "necessity compels me to make you useful." He "laid a heavy hand on my shoulder, and leaning on me with some stress, limped to his horse". In the wood at Ferndean, blind now, he "stretched his hand out to be led", and Jane lets it pass round her shoulder: "I served both for his prop and guide." The first fall and the last support are one movement, only now it is not made out of necessity.

Jane's answer about the chestnut, in full: "You are no ruin, sir—no lightning-struck tree: you are green and vigorous. Plants will grow about your roots, whether you ask them or not, because they take delight in your bountiful shadow; and as they grow they will lean towards you, and wind round you, because your strength offers them so safe a prop." And the sum of ten years of marriage: "To be together is for us to be at once as free as in solitude, as gay as in company. We talk, I believe, all day long: to talk to each other is but a more animated and an audible thinking." The common language with which the couple entered the task has become the air they breathe. "Perfect concord", Jane writes, and that is a word for Temperance.

In the penultimate chapter Rochester thanks God that, "in the midst of judgment, he has remembered mercy". Wen's description of the reversed Tower has a similar line: "There will be mercy and some will be saved."

sections.h2: The couple's values: The Lovers or The Devil
paragraphs: The Couple's values sphere is the spiritual purpose, what the union exists for. In couples with tail 3-10-16 it holds The Lovers (69.5%) or The Devil (30.5%). Matching them with the novel is our reading.

On the night of the proposal Jane breaks out of Rochester's arms: "I am no bird; and no net ensnares me; I am a free human being with an independent will." Rochester replies: "And your will shall decide your destiny." Will and destiny — The Lovers and the Wheel in one line. For such a couple the value of The Lovers is a choice made again after every turn, not once under the chestnut. The last chapter opens with "Reader, I married him", and the subject of that sentence is she.

The Devil is a chain. In the same weeks Rochester jokes that once he has her, he will "—figuratively speaking—attach you to a chain like this", touching his watch-guard. Jane refuses two chains: life with Rochester without marriage after the broken wedding, and marriage without love to St John Rivers ("I scorn your idea of love"). Lisovskaya's closing thought on The Devil is that no one belongs to anyone. Brontë says the same from inside a marriage: "I am my husband's life as fully as he is mine." When both belong to each other, it is no longer a chain.

sections.h2: How tail 3-10-16 is worked out: 05.07.1975 and 14.09.1975
paragraphs: Each point of the couple's matrix is the sum of the same points in the two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The couple's tail is assembled from two personal tails: entry with entry, middle with middle, task with task. A person born on 05.07.1975 has the personal tail 12-19-7; a person born on 14.09.1975 has 18-9-9.

By the personal formula, this couple's entry plus task would give 3 + 16 = 19, The Sun. But the couple's middle is 19 + 9, the middles of two people, and the first partner's Sun literally becomes the Wheel here. Elsewhere in this couple's matrix the centre is 5 + 9 = 14, Temperance; The Devil stands in Values; The Sun (19) stands on Image of the couple, which is how others see them, and that happens in 4.3% of couples with this tail. What to create together holds The Tower again (16), as in 6.8% of such couples: a couple whose main task is The Tower is also called to build together.
What a run through every birth date since 1900 showed:

ul: **Frequency.** Tail 3-10-16 occurs in one couple in 30 (3.353%), sixth place among the 97 couple tails.

**Where the cards come from.** Four combinations of personal tails: 12-19-7 + 18-9-9 (49% of such couples), 15-5-8 + 15-5-8 (25%), 15-20-5 + 15-8-11 (25%) and the vanishingly rare 21-10-7 + 9-18-9 (0.04%).

**No one's and shared.** In 99.96% of such couples none of the three tail cards appears in either partner's personal tail. The Empress at the entry always comes from 30 (12 + 18, 15 + 15 or 21 + 9): no one brings an Empress of their own to the entry. The Tower is always an exact sum with no reduction: 7 + 9, 8 + 8 or 5 + 11. The whole tail is born between two people.
**Centre.** Temperance in 99.96% of couples; The Hierophant only in the rarest, fourth combination.
**Values.** The Lovers in 69.5%, The Devil in 30.5%.

paragraphs: In couples with two identical 15-5-8 tails each card of the couple is a doubled card of each partner: two Devils make The Empress (15 + 15 = 30 → 3), two Hierophants make the Wheel, two Justices make The Tower (8 + 8 = 16). If two people are equally sure they know what is fair, together they risk building the very tower that will be struck. This is our reading.

sections.h2: What helps a couple with tail 3-10-16

ul: **Divide the garden into two plots.** Each has their own work, their own income, their own "thirty pounds a year". Abundance that one gives and the other only receives turns, at this entry, into a golden shower inside a bronze tower.

**Do not appoint the partner as a refuge.** One person's peace should not depend wholly on the other. Friends, one's own work, support outside the couple; with the Wheel, Lisovskaya advises not to close in on each other.
**Call a place on the wheel a place.** "Things are hard for you right now" instead of "you've become weak". The roles of the early years — who earns, who decides, who takes care — are not for life.
**Do not test by turning the wheel.** A rumour of ruin, a question like "if I lost everything, would you stay?" — that is an attempt to spin the wheel by hand. An answer comes, and trust shrinks.
**When the blow comes, look in one direction first.** The first hours are not for verdicts or decisions. First "what has happened to us", then, if it is still needed, "whose fault was it".
**Tell the person apart from the picture.** Ask what in the ruins was one's own invention. Jane's line "he was not what I had thought him" is the start of the work, not its end.
**Build from the root.** After the blow, list what is still alive: conversations, shared jokes, the habit of leaning on the other's shoulder. The new garden grows from there.

paragraphs: If the blow is threats, violence, or fear for oneself or for the children, it is not "The Tower's lesson". That calls for help: a local emergency number or a crisis line.

ul: **3 · The Empress — entry to the task.** The couple's common language is the language of growth: a home, a family, a shared venture, plenty. The couple enters the task with this wish, and the same wish turns into resistance when one wants to give the other a garden and the other wants to grow one of their own.

**10 · The Wheel of Fortune — middle of the task.** The path does not run in even sunlight but in turns: whoever was on top ends up below, and the other way round. The test of the middle is not to mistake a place on the wheel for a character.
**16 · The Tower — main task.** The lightning does not strike the couple; it strikes what each of them invented. The task is to let the picture fall and keep the root.

intro: This tail has a novel in which all three cards stand in a single scene. In Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre (1847) the proposal is made in a garden, on a bench by the old roots of a chestnut tree, and that night lightning strikes the chestnut.

faq.q: What does the program 3-10-16 mean in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: In the destiny matrix a program is a stable combination of three arcana; Lisovskaya also calls the tail of a couple's matrix a karmic program. The numbers 3-10-16 are a couple's tail. The entry to the task is The Empress: a shared wish to grow a home, a venture, plenty. The middle is the Wheel of Fortune: a road through turns in which the partners change places. The main task is The Tower: the collapse of the invented image of the partner and of the shared future, and the ability to stay together after it.

faq.q: How is tail 3-10-16 different from 3-19-16?
faq.a: Both have the same ends, The Empress and The Tower, but a different middle, and with these ends the middle can only be The Sun or the Wheel. In 3-19-16 the road runs through The Sun, steady growth in the light; that tail occurs in 1.26% of couples. In 3-10-16 the road runs through a turn in which one rises and the other sinks; it occurs in 3.35% of couples, almost three times as often.

faq.q: Can tail 3-10-16 appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail equals the sum of the entry and the task, so with 3 and 16 it would be 19. What is more, in a person's matrix The Tower as the main task appears only in the tail 21-10-16, where the Wheel also stands before it and The World stands at the entry. Tail 3-10-16 appears only when two matrices are added together.

faq.q: Is tail 3-10-16 a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not predict events and passes no verdict on the union. It shows where the main test lies: wherever the two of them hold an invented image. Lisovskaya's key to The Tower in a couple is that trials lived through together make the union stronger. And in the numbers of this tail, The Tower together with the couple's atmosphere gives back The Empress.

report: In Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre the proposal is made in a garden, on a bench by the old roots of a giant chestnut. That same night lightning strikes the chestnut, and by morning half of it has split away. One night holds the whole of tail 3-10-16: the garden where two people agree on their future is The Empress; weather that overturns within the hour is the Wheel of Fortune; the blow to the very tree at whose roots the "yes" was spoken is The Tower. And Brontë gives her main answer a year later, when she comes back to the tree.

report.h3: A garden to be given, and a garden to be grown

report: The entry to the task is The Empress. It is the couple's common language, the wish to grow something together: a home, a family, a shared venture, a full cup. The two lovers share the wish but speak it in different dialects. For Jane home is a person: her home is wherever he is, and she has no other. For Rochester home is a gift. The morning after the proposal he sends for the family jewels and drags her to the silk warehouse. Jane sets terms that would suit any joint budget: "I shall continue to act as Adèle's governess; by that I shall earn my board and lodging, and thirty pounds a year besides."

Beneath The Empress hides a second role. Rochester looks to Jane for the "regeneration of life", and on the night of the proposal he repeats: "It will atone—it will atone." Waite calls The Empress refugium peccatorum, the refuge of sinners. Jane declines the post in advance: **"a wanderer's repose or a sinner's reformation should never depend on a fellow-creature."** On the dark side of this entry one partner comes into the union as into a shelter, and the other is obliged to be the garden where the first will be saved.

And the entry itself sets everything else in motion. So as not to sit "like a second Danae" under a golden shower, Jane writes to her uncle in Madeira: she wants to enter the marriage with something of her own. The letter reaches the brother of Rochester's first wife, of whom Jane knows nothing, and a few weeks later the wedding is stopped at the altar. **The Empress's wish is what sets the Wheel turning, and the Wheel brings the lightning.**

report.h3: Between the garden and the lightning: a wheel, not a sun

report: By the arithmetic of a single person, The Sun would stand between The Empress and The Tower — steady light. In the couple the Wheel stands there, and it makes the two change places. At Thornfield Rochester is the master, and Jane is in a "dependent position". A year later she inherits a fortune and says: "I am independent, sir, as well as rich: I am my own mistress." He has gone blind and calls himself "a blind lameter". Brontë even names the turn with a card word: "Here was a new card turned up!"

The sun in the novel is covered twice. Rochester speaks of a sun that "at noon darkens in an eclipse". Jane writes that he stood between her and God "as an eclipse intervenes between man and the broad sun", and that she had made an idol of him. On the eve of the wedding she feels that her fortune "had passed its meridian, and must now decline".

In everyday life such turns are ordinary. One loses a job, the other is promoted. The one who always carried the load suddenly needs support. The argument is no longer about the matter but about places: who has changed, who is keeping whom. The test of the middle is not to fix each other in the roles of the early years. A place on the wheel is a place, not a character. Rochester plays out the Wheel's dark side himself: he lets a rumour spread that his fortune is "not a third of what was supposed", to test someone's feelings. A test by turning the wheel is an attempt to spin the wheel by hand.

report.h3: The lightning strikes what was invented

report: The main task is The Tower, and it is read through its shadow side: the collapse of an invented image of the partner. Here both are invented. Rochester calls Jane a fairy and an elf and wants to dress her in satin. Jane has made herself an idol. On the eve of the wedding she cannot bring herself to fix the address cards for the new bride to her trunks: "Mrs. Rochester! She did not exist: she would not be born till to-morrow." In the morning it turns out that a Mrs Rochester has existed for years. After the wedding that never happened, Jane writes down the formula of this Tower: **"he was not what I had thought him."** And the whole garden freezes overnight: "A Christmas frost had come at midsummer… ice glazed the ripe apples."

In real life this Tower does not have to be a catastrophe. The blow lands on the picture: a partner does something "not like them", an old secret comes out, the plan around which "we" was built collapses. At such moments the two look in different directions and throw out words that are hard to take back. The task is to tell the person apart from the picture and to let the picture fall rather than the person.

report.h3: A ruin, but an entire one

report: On the eve of the wedding Jane walks up to the split chestnut. The cloven halves have not broken from each other: the firm base and strong roots hold them together below, and for now it is still one tree — **"a ruin, but an entire ruin"**. Jane tells the wreckage, as if it were alive, that the halves did right to hold fast to each other. Then she gathers up the apples strewn round the roots.

The numbers of the tail say the same. The centre of such couples holds Temperance, the shared atmosphere, what the two patiently blend between them. The Tower together with Temperance gives exactly The Empress: lightning plus that blending gives back the garden.

Their first meeting is a fall: Rochester and his horse go down on an icy road, and he gets back to the saddle leaning on Jane's shoulder. At the end, blind now, he stretches out his hand to be led, and Jane lets it pass round her shoulder: "I served both for his prop and guide." When he compares himself to the old chestnut, Jane answers that he is no ruin and that plants will grow about his roots. She sums up the marriage like this: "to talk to each other is but a more animated and an audible thinking." The common language with which the entry began has become the air the couple breathes.

What helps: each partner keeps their own work and their own income; the partner is not a refuge; a place on the wheel is called a place; in the first hours after a blow, no verdicts, and both look in one direction; rebuilding starts from what is still alive. If the blow is threats, violence or fear for oneself, it is not "The Tower's lesson": it calls for help, a local emergency number or a crisis line.
