seo.title: Karmic tail 3 10 7 compatibility: a house on wheels
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 10 7 compatibility: The Empress, The Wheel of Fortune and The Chariot. Why this couple's home keeps moving, and who holds the reins.

items.title: The 3-10-7 karmic tail in compatibility: a house, a wheel and a wagon
items.short: In a compatibility matrix the three numbers of the 3-10-7 tail add up on their own: 3 + 7 = 10. The Empress is the house, The Chariot is the wagon, and together they make The Wheel of Fortune. This is the tail of a couple whose home is always on the road: the shared wish is a nest of their own and a full larder, the path runs through rounds of good and bad luck, and the main task is to decide together where to go and who holds the reins.

sections.h2: The first clue: the middle is the sum of the ends
paragraphs: The middle of a couple's tail is not calculated from the two outer numbers. Each point of the couple is counted on its own: add the matching points of the two personal matrices and reduce the sum to 22 or less. The couple's middle is the sum of the two personal middles, not the entry plus the main task. So the coincidence in 3-10-7 is a property of these particular numbers, not a rule of the calculation: The Empress plus The Chariot equal The Wheel exactly, with no reduction needed.

The site's engine shows where it comes from. In 92.5% of couples with this tail, the partners' personal tails are 21-7-13 and 9-3-21. The first has The Chariot in the middle of their personal tail, the second has The Empress. In the couple's matrix these two cards move out to the edges: The Empress becomes the entry, The Chariot the main task. And the couple's middle is made of the two of them: 7 + 3 = 10. One partner's wagon and the other's house, added together, make a wheel.

In the remaining 7.5% of couples the partners' tails are 21-10-16 and 9-18-9. There the couple's Wheel is the middle of one partner's own personal tail, with the other partner's Moon added to it: 10 + 18 = 28, and 2 + 8 = 10. The entry, though, is built the same way for every couple with this tail: one partner's World and the other's Hermit, 21 + 9 = 30, which reduces to 3. The wide world and a lonely light in a cabin together make The Empress — a house in the middle of open country.

The tail is rare: it turns up in roughly one couple in 1,171 (0.085%), 84th of the 97 couple tails. As a personal tail, 3-10-7 does not exist at all. In a personal matrix the entry M is the main task D plus the centre of the chart, and with a 7 as the main task no centre can produce a 3 at the entry. So no one brings this triple with them: it only appears in a couple.
History has a well-known name for a house set on wheels: the settlers' covered wagon. And one such family lived the 3-10-7 tail in such detail that their daughter wrote it all down, scene by scene.

sections.h2: Little House: the family that carried its home in a wagon
paragraphs: Laura Ingalls Wilder wrote a series of books about her family: eight came out between 1932 and 1943, and a ninth was published after her death, in 1971. In them Ma and Pa — Caroline and Charles Ingalls — travel from the Big Woods of Wisconsin to Kansas, back to Wisconsin, to Plum Creek in Minnesota and on to Silver Lake in Dakota. Bows go up on the wagon, the canvas is stretched over them, beds are made underneath. Almost every time they arrive, Pa builds a house, and almost every time the house is left behind.
Wilder is quoted here in her own words, from the original American editions.

In the books it is Pa who wants the road and Ma who guards the home. In a couple with the 3-10-7 tail the roles are not split by gender, and Wilder herself shows it. When Laura, still a girl, begs to go on West, Pa tells her: "You and I want to fly like the birds." The wandering foot passed to the daughter, and in the next generation she is the one who takes the reins.

sections.h2: Entry — The Empress: the shepherdess comes out only at home
paragraphs: In the Big Woods Pa carves a Christmas bracket for Ma: a carved back, a little vine around the edge, a star at the top. Ma stands her china woman on it — a shepherdess with a china bonnet and little gilt china shoes. From that moment the family has a sign of home, and it is made by two pairs of hands: the shelf is his, the figure is hers.

The shepherdess travels half a continent with them and never breaks. In Kansas Pa lays a floor of oak puncheons, Ma sets the figure on the mantel-shelf and says: "There. Now we're living like civilized folks again." At Silver Lake the family lives in a makeshift shanty at the railroad camp, and Pa asks: "But where's the china shepherdess, Caroline?" Ma answers: "I haven't unpacked the shepherdess, Charles. We aren't living here, we're only staying till you get our homestead." It comes out only on their own claim, when Pa says, "We're settled at last on our homestead claim," and drives the nail for the bracket himself.

This is **the couple's common language** — point M, the entry to the task. Both need a home where the shepherdess stands on the shelf rather than lying in a box. The Empress in this tail is not the card of one "home-loving" partner. It is a wish the couple shares completely.

But the entry stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. Look at Ma and Pa arguing when Pa is offered work in Dakota. Pa: "We can get a hundred and sixty acres out west, just by living on it, and the land's as good as this is, or better." Ma: "But we're settled here. We've got the farm." Both are speaking the language of The Empress — land, plenty, a place of their own. The only difference is where that place lies: for one it is already here, for the other a little further on, where there is more. The argument of a couple with this tail is rarely house against road. More often it is two houses against each other: the one they have and the one they might have.

Benebell Wen has a word that gives away this Empress's secret. She writes that The Empress "can harness the laws of nature in her favor". Harness is a driver's word. The mistress of the garden is a driver too: she harnesses rain, sun and season. So in a couple with this tail the question "who is driving?" comes up already at the entry — it is just still about the vegetable beds, not the road.

In a couple today this looks familiar. Two people rent a flat, and one of them never unpacks the boxes: "We're only here for now." Two people renovate and argue not about tiles but about whether to put money into walls they will leave anyway. Two people talk about a house of their own for years and cannot agree which town it is in.

sections.h2: Middle — The Wheel of Fortune: a bet with Uncle Sam
paragraphs: The middle of the tail is how the couple lives the way from the wish to the task. Waite calls The Wheel "the perpetual motion of a fluidic universe" and "the flux of human life". For Ma and Pa that flux can be read in a single field.

On Plum Creek Pa sows wheat and, when it is barely up, brings home a wagon piled high with lumber. "Here's your new house, Caroline!" — "But the wheat's hardly up yet!" — "That's all right. They let me have the lumber, and we'll pay for it when we sell the wheat." A house of sawed lumber, with glass windows, built on the strength of a harvest. When the heads are already heavy, Pa lists what will come after the harvest: out of debt, a buggy for him, a silk dress for Ma. All three cards are already in that dream: plenty, the luck of the harvest, and a carriage. Then at Saturday dinner Pa says he has never seen such a crop: they are rich now and can have anything they want. Laura looks through the open door, and the sunshine dims. It is a cloud of grasshoppers. The Wheel turns at the very moment the couple reaches its top.

What follows is the reason to read this chapter. Pa says: "Don't worry, Caroline. We did all we could, and we'll pull through somehow." Ma slips a pillow under his head while he sleeps on the floor. No one blames anyone for the lumber. Soon Pa sets out on foot to the east, where the grasshoppers did not reach, to hire out for other men's harvest, and walks two hundred miles. A man who all his life has pulled west goes east, because the home needs it. The night before, he plays "Oh, Susanna" on his fiddle: "I'm going to California."

Yuliana Lisovskaya, whose book the site follows for couples, describes The Wheel in a couple through two poles. In the minus, the couple blames fate and each other, lives on a swing between silence and quarrel, and finds it hard to be together while something still holds them. In the plus, a partner is accepted in any state, and change becomes a reason to move. The Wheel does not ask permission. The couple decides only one thing: whether each turn of it becomes a charge against the other.

The Wheel had already turned earlier, when they left Kansas. That day the family eats for dinner the seed potatoes they had been saving for planting, and Pa says: "There's no great loss without some small gain." The store for next year's crop becomes a meal for the road. This is how The Wheel treats The Empress: what was saved for later has to be eaten now.

And at Silver Lake Pa states the law of The Wheel outright. To get a claim, the law says you must live on it for five years, and Pa tells his daughters: "I've bet Uncle Sam fourteen dollars against a hundred and sixty acres of land, that we can make out to live on the claim for five years." Ma answers: "I don't like to think of it as gambling." Pa: "Everything's more or less a gamble, Caroline." One couple, two views of The Wheel: for him life is a bet, for her an order with no room for chance. Waite, as it happens, is on Ma's side: behind the symbol of The Wheel he sees "the denial of chance". But both are right, and it helps a couple with this tail to know which of the two sees the bet and which sees the order.

The most exact image of the middle is in The Long Winter. Blizzard after blizzard cuts the little town off from the trains, and the family grinds wheat in a hand coffee mill to bake bread. "The coffee mill's handle ground round and round, it must not stop." A small wheel inside the kitchen holds the house together while the big wheel of winter turns outside. Pa says: "It can't beat us! It's got to quit sometime and we don't." A couple with this tail today has its own coffee mill too: the work nobody notices and without which no crisis can be got through.

sections.h2: Main task — The Chariot: who holds the reins
paragraphs: The main task of the tail is read above all through what the couple fails at. With Ma and Pa it is visible from the first pages of Little House on the Prairie. Pa says: "Seeing you don't object, I've decided to go see the West." Ma only answers: "Oh, Charles, must we go now?" One decided, the other kept quiet. The reins are in one pair of hands, and silence counts as consent.

A year later word comes that soldiers will move the settlers out of Indian Territory: the family, as Pa himself admits, has settled three miles over the line, on Osage land. Ma asks: "What is the matter, Charles? Where are we going?" Pa answers: "Durned if I know! But we're going." This is a Chariot without a direction. Wen writes of the reversed Chariot that the Seeker **must reconsider direction** and make sure the movement is going the right way. The wagon has power, but no aim.

Lisovskaya sets out The Chariot among a couple's tasks very concretely: to dare a move together, not to compete for the lead, to balance work and the relationship, not to demand that a partner give up their own goals for someone else's. She also writes that couples with The Chariot often move house in search of a home of their own. It could have been written about the Ingalls family.

Yet Ma and Pa did have an agreement, and in the end it stopped the wagon. Pa tells Laura: "Your Ma was a school-teacher when we met, and when she came West with me I promised that our girls would have a chance to get book learning. That's why we stopped here, so close to a town that has a school." Ma agreed to the road on a condition. A few years later Laura begs to go further, and Pa answers: "You and I want to fly like the birds. But long ago I promised your Ma that you girls should go to school. You can't go to school and go West."

The last lines of that scene are the main task of the tail. Pa says: "Just so you're content, Caroline, I'm satisfied." Wilder adds: "That was true, but he did want to go West." The agreement is kept, and the wish remains. Years later Pa again gazes west from the doorway, and Ma says she was so tired of being dragged from pillar to post. He answers: "Well, I guess we are, Caroline. Don't fret. It's just that my wandering foot gets to itching, I guess."

The Chariot of this tail is not solved by one of them giving in. If the reins simply pass from one to the other, someone is still riding where they did not want to go. The road Pa gave up lived on in his fiddle: he played songs about California in a house that was not going anywhere any more. In a couple with this tail each needs a fiddle of their own — their own work, their own path — so that the shared home does not become someone's cage.

Wen gives The Chariot two observations that fit this story. First, The Chariot is **"travel not for the sake of travel, but for the sake of acquisition"**. Pa never travelled for the sake of the road; he went after land and game, that is, after The Empress. The driver in this tail carries the house rather than running from it. Second, according to Wen, the chariot bears a badge of "the union of the external sphere of rulership by man and the internal sphere of rulership by woman". In a couple with the 3-10-7 tail these spheres are not tied to gender, but the core remains: one wagon has both the world outside and the order inside in harness.

There is a small coincidence too. When Pa's sister brings him the offer of work in Dakota, Ma says: "It does seem providential, fifty dollars a month." Waite's list of meanings for The Chariot begins with the words "Succour, providence".

sections.h2: The next generation: the reins in two pairs of hands
paragraphs: Laura grew up with her father's wandering foot. At fifteen she teaches school twelve miles from home, and every Friday Almanzo Wilder comes for her in a sleigh. Once he sets out when it is forty below zero. Laura hesitates for a long time, then tells him straight: "I am going with you only because I want to get home. When I am home to stay, I will not go with you any more." The relationship begins with an honest talk about the sleigh: who is carrying whom, and why.

Later Almanzo has a young horse, Barnum, who rears as he starts. Laura asks: "Let me drive him; I would like to see if I could." Almanzo seems doubtful but gives her the lines: "Keep a tight rein on him." She drives the length of the little town, her arms tire, and she hands the lines back, warning him that she will want to drive again. Almanzo answers: "You may drive all you want to. It gives my arms a rest, too." The next time Laura says: "I do believe Barnum knows I'm driving." Almanzo takes the lines and notes: "He leans on the bit, with me." The same horse pulls differently in different hands. It is the best description of this tail's Chariot one could find: the reins pass from hand to hand, and the wagon grows lighter for it.

Before the wedding Laura asks about the reins directly: "Do you want me to promise to obey you?" Almanzo answers: "Of course not. I know it is in the wedding ceremony, but it is only something that women say. I never knew one that did it, nor any decent man that wanted her to." Laura explains why it matters to her: "I can not make a promise that I will not keep, and, Almanzo, even if I tried, I do not think I could obey anybody against my better judgment." — "I'd never expect you to." The minister marries them without the word "obey". The couple agreed on the reins before they set off.

In the posthumous book The First Four Years Laura admits she did not want to marry a farmer: a farm is too hard a place for a woman. Almanzo proposes a deal: try farming for three years, and if it does not work, turn to something else. The term is later extended. Hail flattens the wheat just before harvest, later hot dry winds ruin the crop again, the debts grow. The Wheel turns just as it did for her parents.

But near the end of the book a single long sentence shows that this couple's Chariot has found a different direction: "The incurable optimism of the farmer who throws his seed on the ground every spring, betting it and his time against the elements, seemed inextricably to blend with the creed of her pioneer forefathers that 'it is better farther on' — only instead of farther on in space, it was farther on in time, over the horizon of the years ahead instead of the far horizon of the west."

The whole tail is in that sentence, in order. Seed in the ground — The Empress. A bet against the elements — The Wheel. "Better farther on" — The Chariot. And the main discovery: The Chariot changed its axis. The father looked for something better beyond the next hill, the daughter in the next year. A wagon does not have to travel across a map to move forward.

And yet The Chariot did travel. In 1894 the Wilders loaded a covered wagon and left Dakota for Missouri, for Rocky Ridge Farm. That is where Laura wrote her books, and today it is a museum that keeps Pa's fiddle. The road the father gave up ended in the house where it was written down.

sections.h2: What Waite and Wen saw: unlike beasts in one harness
paragraphs: This section is about the cards of the Waite–Smith deck as Waite and Wen describe them; the cards on the site are drawn in their own way.

In Waite's account The Chariot is drawn by two sphinxes: the driver "has thus replied to the sphinx", and that is why they are in harness. In the historical part of his book he recalls that "in the eighteenth century white horses were yoked to the car", and that other animals have drawn the triumphal chariot too — "for example, a lion and a leopard". Two pull The Chariot, and they need not be alike: sphinxes, horses, a lion with a leopard. One driver holds them. For a couple with this tail they are two wishes in one harness: the house and the road, "here" and "farther on".

Wen points out a detail that links the two ends of the tail. The Empress is "crowned with a laurel wreath and stars", and the wreath, Wen says, "denotes victory". The charioteer, too, "wears the laurel wreaths of victory", and the curtains of his chariot are printed with stars. The house and the road wear the same insignia: there is victory both in holding your ground and in getting there.

The centre of the matrix for most couples with this tail is Temperance, and Waite writes of its angel: **"It has one foot upon the earth and one upon waters."** That is the stance of a couple living between the firm ground of the house and the moving water of the road.

And one coincidence that is hard to miss. In Waite's reversed meanings for Temperance stand "competing interests" and even "the priest who will marry the Querent". Laura and Almanzo had competing interests — the farm or the town — and a minister who would not use the word "obey" himself. It is only a coincidence, but very much in the spirit of the tail.

sections.h2: Atmosphere and values: what holds the house and the wagon together
paragraphs: In 92.5% of couples with this tail the centre of the matrix — the atmosphere inside the couple — is Temperance, 14. It is made of the personal centres: the partner with the 21-7-13 tail always has a centre of 8, the partner with 9-3-21 always has 6. Waite lists Temperance as "Economy, moderation, frugality, management, accommodation", and describes its main work like this: under its rule "we know in our rational part something of whence we came and whither we are going". This couple's atmosphere gives it a compass — whence and whither. Leave the compass unused, and The Chariot drives at random.

Lisovskaya sums up the minus of Temperance in one line: one partner always gives way, and the other does not notice. That is "seeing you don't object". In the plus, Temperance in a couple settles arguments by talk and compromise, keeps a balance between motion and rest, and gives a sense that things are going to plan. For the 3-10-7 tail this is a direct answer to the main task: talk about direction out loud while the wagon is still standing.

In 7.5% of couples the centre is The Hierophant, 5. Then rules and traditions set the atmosphere, and the couple's agreement resembles Pa's promise: "the girls will go to school". Among Lisovskaya's tasks for the 5 are interference from relatives and attempts to remake each other. For a tail with a wagon in it, this means that it may be a whole family, not just two people, arguing over the direction.

The couple's values — the spiritual purpose — are The Lovers in 63.7% of couples with this tail and The Devil in 36.3%. The Lovers is a choice: Ma once chose to go West, and the strength of their union rests on the choice having been hers. Waite's list for The Lovers includes "trials overcome". The Devil is what binds: lumber on credit against a harvest, a claim the law says you must live on for five years. Lisovskaya closes her chapter on The Devil with the thought that nobody belongs to anybody. For a couple with a wagon this matters: commitments can be taken on together, but neither of the two becomes the other's baggage.

sections.h2: How a couple recognises itself in the 3-10-7 tail
paragraphs: This tail is recognised by scenes, not descriptions.

ul: **Boxes in the hallway.** One partner settled in long ago, the other lives "for now". A shepherdess in a box is not a whim: for one of the two, home has not been found yet.
**"Seeing you don't object."** One partner decides about a move, a job or a big purchase, and the other stays quiet. A year later it turns out the silence was not consent but fatigue.
**Lumber against the harvest.** The couple builds, buys, moves on credit against future income. When the harvest fails, the real question is not money but who will blame whom.
**A fiddle by the door.** One gave way and stayed, but their road did not vanish. It sounds in talk of "if only we had", in other people's photos, in longing for another town.

paragraphs: What changes the script can be seen in the books too:

ul: ask "where to?" before "we're going", not after;
agree on a date to review the decision, as Laura and Almanzo did with their three years;
unpack the shepherdess where you live now, even if it is for a while;
take turns with the reins, and notice that the horse goes differently under the other hand;
leave each a fiddle of their own — work in which one can travel further without moving the shared home;
argue with each other about decisions, but not about the wheel: grasshoppers are no grounds for a reckoning.

paragraphs: The strong version of this tail is a couple that carries its home and does not lose it on the way. It has a shared "place of our own", it lives through the turns of the wheel without keeping score, and it knows where it is going and who is driving right now. Its "farther on" does not have to lie beyond the horizon. Sometimes it is the next year on the same land.

sections.h2: A worked example: 07.01.1976 and 02.01.1980
paragraphs: A couple's tail is counted from three points. Each is the sum of the matching points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22 or less if the sum is larger.

The person born on 07.01.1976 has the personal tail 21-7-13: entry 21, middle 7, main task 13, centre of the chart 8. The person born on 02.01.1980 has the personal tail 9-3-21: entry 9, middle 3, main task 21, centre of the chart 6.

The couple's centre: 8 + 6 = 14, Temperance. The couple's values for these dates are 6, The Lovers. This is the most common variant: personal tails 21-7-13 and 9-3-21, The Chariot in the middle for one partner and The Empress in the middle for the other.

ul: **M = 3, The Empress — entry to the task.** The couple's common language is "a place of our own": a house, land, plenty that keeps growing. Both want the same thing, but each may picture that place somewhere else.

**N = 10, The Wheel of Fortune — middle of the task.** The path goes in circles: harvest and crop failure, debt against future income, moves. The couple gets through it when they stop blaming the wheel and each other.
**D = 7, The Chariot — main task.** Choosing a direction together. Not "seeing you don't object, I've decided", but an agreement on where the house is going, and reins that pass from hand to hand.

intro: The tail does not predict moves or ruin. It shows what this couple's main conversation will be about. No one has written that conversation down in more detail than Laura Ingalls Wilder in her Little House books, the ones the TV series was later based on. Her parents carried their home in a wagon for more than ten years, and Laura and her husband faced the same task again — and solved it differently.

faq.q: What does 3-10-7 mean in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: In a compatibility matrix, 3-10-7 is a couple's karmic tail: The Empress at the entry, The Wheel of Fortune in the middle, The Chariot as the main task. The couple wants a shared home and plenty, goes through turns of luck, and learns to choose a direction together and share the reins.

faq.q: Can 3-10-7 appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: As a karmic tail in a personal matrix, 3-10-7 never occurs: with a 7 as the main task, no centre can give a 3 at the entry. But the same numbers in the same order do appear on other lines of a personal chart. Most often it is the talent line — for people born in March with a centre of 4 or 22. Less often it is the relationship line. There the numbers have other roles, and they cannot be read as a couple's tail.

faq.q: Is 3-10-7 a programme?
faq.a: Lisovskaya calls a couple's tail the couple's karmic programme. So a search for "programme 3 10 7" in compatibility is about the same thing: the task a couple goes through together. It is the programme of a union, not of one person.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. From the numbers 3, 10 and 7 a couple can only get the 3-10-7 tail: the order "entry — middle — main task" is the only one here.

faq.q: Which partner is The Empress and which is The Chariot?
faq.a: All three cards belong to the couple as a whole, not to one partner, and gender has nothing to do with it. But in 92.5% of such couples one partner has The Chariot in the middle of their personal tail and the other has The Empress. So often one is closer to the road and the other to the house, and it is in the couple that these wishes add up to a shared wheel.

faq.q: Is the 3-10-7 tail a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict ruin, moves or break-ups. It shows the couple's main conversation — about home, about turns of luck and about direction. A couple that has this conversation out loud and hands each other the reins gets its strength from this tail: the ability to carry its home and not lose it on the way.

report: In this family the china shepherdess was unpacked only once they were sure they had come home. For more than ten years Ma and Pa Ingalls carried their home in a covered wagon, and their daughter, Laura Ingalls Wilder, wrote the journey down in her Little House books. Read alongside those books, the 3-10-7 tail unfolds almost scene by scene.

report.h3: A house set on wheels

report: The three cards of the tail add up on their own: The Empress is the house, The Chariot is the wagon, and 3 + 7 = 10, The Wheel of Fortune. This is not a rule of the calculation but a property of these particular numbers. A house set on wheels is exactly what a settlers' covered wagon is.

A couple with this tail shares one wish: a nest of their own and a full larder. The way to the main task runs through rounds of good and bad luck. And the task itself is to decide together where the house is going and who holds the reins.

report.h3: A shepherdess in a box

report: In the Big Woods Pa carves a Christmas bracket, and Ma stands her china shepherdess on it. The sign of home is made by two pairs of hands: the shelf is his, the figure is hers. In a makeshift shanty at Silver Lake Pa asks where the shepherdess is, and Ma answers: "I haven't unpacked the shepherdess, Charles. We aren't living here, we're only staying…" It comes out only on their own claim.

This is **the couple's common language**: both need a home where the shepherdess stands on the shelf. But the same wish turns into resistance. Pa is drawn West: a hundred and sixty acres there "just by living on it", and land as good or better. Ma answers: "But we're settled here. We've got the farm." Both speak the language of The Empress, of land and plenty. The argument of a couple with this tail is rarely house against road. **More often it is two houses against each other**: the one they have and the one they might have.

report.h3: The Wheel turns at the top

report: Pa builds a house of lumber taken on credit against the wheat harvest. At Saturday dinner he says he has never seen such a crop: they are rich now. Laura looks through the open door, and the sunshine dims. It is a cloud of grasshoppers. The Wheel turns at the very moment the couple reaches its top.

Then comes what matters most. Pa says: "Don't worry, Caroline. We did all we could, and we'll pull through somehow." Ma slips a pillow under his head while he sleeps on the floor. No one blames anyone for the lumber. Then a man who all his life has pulled west sets out on foot to the east, to other men's harvest, two hundred miles away, because the home needs it. The Wheel does not ask permission. The couple decides only one thing: whether each turn of it becomes a charge against the other.

The same couple holds two views of The Wheel. Pa calls the homestead claim a bet with Uncle Sam. Ma answers: "I don't like to think of it as gambling." Pa: "Everything's more or less a gamble, Caroline." Both are right, and it helps to know which of the two sees the bet and which sees the order.

report.h3: Reins in one pair of hands

report: The main task is read through what goes wrong. At the start of the road Pa says: "Seeing you don't object, I've decided to go see the West." One decided, the other kept quiet. A year later, leaving Kansas, Ma asks: "Where are we going?" Pa answers: "Durned if I know! But we're going." The wagon has power, but no direction.

Ma and Pa did have an agreement: she went West on condition that the girls would go to school. In the end that agreement stopped the wagon. Pa says: "Just so you're content, Caroline, I'm satisfied." Wilder adds: "That was true, but he did want to go West." The agreement was kept, the wish remained, and it lived on in his fiddle. **The Chariot of this tail is not solved by one of them giving in**: each needs a fiddle of their own — their own work and their own path — so that the shared home does not become someone's cage.

The daughter solves the same task differently. Laura asks Almanzo Wilder to let her drive his young horse Barnum. The next time she says: "I do believe Barnum knows I'm driving." Almanzo notes: "He leans on the bit, with me." The same horse pulls differently in different hands. Before the wedding Laura asks whether he wants her to promise to obey him, and hears: "Of course not." The couple agreed on the reins before they set off.

report.h3: "Farther on" need not lie beyond the horizon

report: Near the end of The First Four Years there is a sentence that holds the whole tail in order. The farmer throws his seed on the ground every spring, "betting it and his time against the elements", and the pioneer creed that "it is better farther on" now means **"instead of farther on in space, it was farther on in time"**. Seed is The Empress, the bet is The Wheel, "farther on" is The Chariot. The father looked for something better beyond the next hill, the daughter in the next year.

What changes the script: ask "where to?" before "we're going"; agree on a date to review the decision, as Laura and Almanzo did with their three years on the farm; unpack the shepherdess where they live now; take turns with the reins; argue about decisions, but not about the wheel.

The strong version of this tail is **a couple that carries its home and does not lose it on the way**. It has a shared "place of our own", it lives through the turns of the wheel without keeping score, and it knows where it is going and who is driving right now. Sometimes its "farther on" is the next year on the same land.

seo.title: Karmic tail 3 13 10 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 13 10 compatibility: the Empress, Death and the Wheel of Fortune in a couple's tail, and why the romance ends midway while the union goes on.

items.title: Karmic tail 3-13-10 in compatibility: the romance that ends in the middle
items.short: When a couple's tail reads 3-13-10, Death stands in the middle of their shared task, and the first question is always the same: does it mean a break-up? No. This tail tells of a different ending: halfway through a life together the romance ends, and the union stays. The Empress at the entry is what the couple wants together: a home, a garden, a shared harvest, and for all of it to last for ever. Death in the middle is the time when the first form of love is spent and held together only by habit. The Wheel of Fortune in the main task is learning that every season of life has its own love, and not trying to bring back the first summer.

sections.h2: A novella with the wedding exactly in the middle
paragraphs: In 1859 Tolstoy published Family Happiness (Semeynoye schastiye) in The Russian Messenger. The story is told by its heroine, seventeen-year-old Masha. She spends the winter after her mother's death in the old house at Pokrovskoye, and in spring her guardian arrives: Sergey Mikhaylych, a friend of her late father, a man of thirty-six. Tolstoy took the material from his own life: «Then the main, the most serious one… that was Arsenyeva, Valeria… I was almost her fiancé (Family Happiness)», he wrote many years later to Pavel Biryukov. Quotations from the novella follow Louise and Aylmer Maude's translation; where it is loose or silent, the translation is ours.

The novella has nine chapters. Many novels of the time end with a wedding, but Tolstoy puts it in the fifth chapter, exactly in the middle. The second half of the book is about what happens to love once the romance has been written to its end. And the wedding day itself, read closely, begins with a memorial service: «Before dinner we walked to our church, to attend a memorial service for my father».

The shape of the novella matches the tail. First the garden, the lilac, the nightingales and the harvest: The Empress. In the middle the wedding, then a frozen winter and three years in which their relations «seemed to have taken a fixed shape». That is Death. At the end, the same veranda, the same bench, the same sonata, and a conversation about how «each time of life has its own kind of love». That is the Wheel. The last sentence of the novella: «That day ended the romance of our marriage; the old feeling became a precious irrecoverable remembrance; but a new feeling of love for my children and the father of my children laid the foundation of a new life and a quite different happiness».

sections.h2: The Empress at the entry: a garden, a harvest and the words «for ever»
paragraphs: A couple's entry to the task is what the two of them want together: shared wishes, agreements, a common language. The point stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish can turn into resistance. Lisovskaya's key to The Empress is fertility, abundance and growth. Tolstoy shows them as scenes rather than words.

Late May, the veranda, the samovar, cream and cracknels, a nightingale in the lilac. Sergey Mikhaylych says: «I wish I could spend all my life here, sitting in this veranda». Katya answers: «Well, do then!» And he: «That's all very well, but life won't sit still». **The tail's main task is spoken aloud on the very first summer evening**, before any confession: the entry wants to sit like this all its life, and the Wheel already knows that life won't sit still.

The first, unintended confession comes during the harvest. From the garden Masha watches the loaded carts of sheaves creak along the road while the field turns to stubble before her eyes: «as if summer had turned into autumn before my eyes». She thinks of happiness as a harvest that needs somewhere to go: «am I to blame for being happy? And how can I share my happiness?» That same evening, in the fenced cherry garden, she hears Sergey Mikhaylych, sure that nobody can see him, softly say: «Darling Masha!»

The couple's shared dream is set down in his words before the wedding: «A quiet secluded life in the country… then work… then rest, nature, books, music, love for one's neighbor -- such is my idea of happiness». Masha answers: «I have always wished for and loved only this quiet family life». That is The Empress at the entry: a house where there is plenty of everything and everything grows.

The resistance hides in a single word. On summer nights Masha felt «a wish never to leave that room -- a wish that dawn might never come», and she thought «that it might always be like this, that such a feeling is given for nothing». Walking in the moonlit garden she felt «that the whole scene must remain fixed for ever in its beauty». On the morning of her wedding: «Can this new life really be for ever?» Some years later, at a German spa: «Let us go to the country, and for ever». Her husband answers: «as for "for ever", that is a dream». **The minus of this entry is the wish for a garden without seasons.**

The couple's common language grows from the same entry: the two of them talk about themselves as if about other people. On the first evening he opens the music at the adagio of Beethoven's «sonata quasi una fantasia», the Moonlight: a sonata «in the manner of a fantasy». He declares himself through «the story about A and B»: an «old and worn-out» Mr A fell in love with young Miss B and decided to go away. The story, he says, has «two different endings». Masha invents a third — «the third ending is that he did not love her, but hurt her» — and on that word confesses her own love. This is The Empress in the plus: a tale told in the third person helps to tell the truth. The minus shows later: «conversation flowed more easily in the presence of a third person».

The numbers hold their own clue. The Empress at the entry is formed the same way in every such couple: one partner has 21, The World, at the same point of the personal matrix, and the other has 9, The Hermit. The whole world and the lantern of solitude add up to a garden. In the novella both terms are heard in one conversation: «Oh, I should like to go round the world with you» — and straight after: «What about my mother? What about my business?» The Russian word svet means both "the world" and "society". A year later the couple quarrels precisely over svet, society: balls, receptions, a prince. And in the last chapter the husband says: «No, it was not society, my dear». This is our reading, not a rule of Lisovskaya's.

sections.h2: Death in the middle: the romance ends, not the union
paragraphs: The middle of the task is our reading: how the couple travels from the wish of the entry to the main task. In this tail the road runs through Death. Waite describes it as a change of form: «The veil or mask of life is perpetuated in change, transformation and passage from lower to higher». What ends is not life but the mask it has worn until now.

The first small death happens in the church itself. Masha expected a miracle, but «nothing extraordinary, nothing worthy of the Sacrament I had just received, had taken place in myself». The kiss felt strange: «Is this all?» Right afterwards, in the carriage, her fear turns into «a new love still more tender and stronger than the old». This is how the middle works in the plus: the old form ends, and another one grows in its place at once.

Then the minus begins. The mother-in-law's house, where «the whole household went like a clock»: floors scrubbed and carpets beaten every Saturday, a service on the first of every month, name days celebrated for the whole district. The husband says «le mieux est l'ennemi du bien», the best is the enemy of the good, and admits: «I'm frightened. Life must go on, something may change; and nothing can be better than the present». Masha feels «that life was repeating itself», and that her love «had stopped and grew no more». And then the key sentence: «custom was daily petrifying our lives into one fixed shape… The morning always found us cheerful; we were polite at dinner, and affectionate in the evening».

This is worth pausing on. In the moonlit garden Masha felt that everything «must remain fixed for ever in its beauty». A few months later the same image returns as custom that hardens their life into «one fixed shape»; in the Russian original Tolstoy uses one verb for both, zakovat', to put in chains. **The wish of the entry came true literally, and became Death in the middle.** In this tail love does not freeze because of something bad. It freezes because two people wanted too much to hold on to something good.

The same middle shows in the roles. The romance began as a lesson: the guardian promises, «I shall put you through an examination in spring», and all her thoughts at that time were, in her words, «not mine but his thoughts and feelings». His gaze «draws out of me the very thought he wants». In Petersburg it pleased her «to find myself in these surroundings not merely his equal but his superior», and now it is she who pulls him to the balls. After the quarrel over a reception she notes: «We had changed parts». Wen writes that Death can suggest «the waning of power of one authority and the growing, ascending power of a new». What dies in the couple is the form "the elder leads, the younger learns", and for a long time nothing shows what will take its place. Among the difficulties of the thirteenth energy Lisovskaya names this one too: one partner forces the other to change. In the novella they both do it, by turns.

The bitterest line of the middle belongs to the husband: «So you make a sacrifice! Well, so do I. What could be better? We compete in generosity -- what an example of family happiness!» After it, for three years, their relations «seemed to have taken a fixed shape which could not become either better or worse». Wen calls this state, in Death reversed, a plateau: the transition is due, but nothing moves.

sections.h2: Who is to blame when Death stands in the middle
paragraphs: The whole second half of the novella is a search for the guilty one. «How am I guilty before you?» — «I am to blame». «You loved too little». — «I was to blame». Tolstoy gives the answer to the husband in the last chapter: «time is to blame for that, and we ourselves», and a little later, more honestly still: «Who is to blame, I do not know».

The numbers answer the same way. Thirteen is not in the personal tail of either partner in any couple with the 3-13-10 tail. Nobody brings Death into the middle; the two of them put it together. In about 77% of such couples it is 4 + 9: one partner's Emperor and the other's Hermit. In the remaining 23% it is 3 + 10: one partner has The Empress in the middle of the personal tail, the other has The Wheel of Fortune. **The two other cards of the tail reach the couple from two sides, and their meeting makes Death**: a house that wants «for ever» meets a wheel that turns. There is no culprit in such a sum.

The novella also offers a temptation to skip the middle. At the spa an Italian marquis who resembles the husband «by his smile and the expression of his brow» explains to a friend: «To make life a romance is the one thing worth doing. And with me romance never breaks off in the middle». It is the promise of a romance without Death. Masha nearly gives in, and that same evening takes the train to her husband. Such a romance is not on offer to a 3-13-10 couple: they always have a middle, and the only question is what the two of them carry out of it.

One more detail — a coincidence, not a clue, but hard to miss. On the day he gives himself away, Sergey Mikhaylych says of himself: «I feel like a boy of thirteen -- I want to play at horses and climb trees». After the wedding, when Masha asks him to say the prayers with her, he laughs: «It's as if I were ten years old again». Tolstoy put two numbers of the 3-13-10 tail into his mouth at moments of happiness.

sections.h2: The Wheel of Fortune: each time of life has its own love
paragraphs: A couple's main task is read mostly through the minus: what does not work and what they will have to learn. Lisovskaya's key to the Wheel is cyclicity: highs and lows replace each other, and the fight is not with the change itself but with the habit of blaming fate and each other for it. In the novella the minus of the Wheel is the last conversation on the veranda, in the spring rain.

Masha accuses: «Why did you give me a freedom for which I was unfit? Why did you stop teaching me? If you had wished it… none of all this would have happened!» Then she pleads: «Let everything be as it was before… It can be, can't it?» These are two attempts to stop the wheel: find who pushed it, and turn it back. At first he answers too smoothly: «No; I might as well wish to have wings. It is impossible». Then honestly: «I weep for that past love which can never return… Love remains, but not the old love».

The plus of the Wheel is in his own words: «Each time of life has its own kind of love». And: «Don't let us try to repeat life… Don't let us make pretences to ourselves». He explains what happened in the middle: «In that summer when I first knew you, I used to lie awake all night, thinking about you, and I made that love myself… So again, in Petersburg and abroad, in the course of horrible sleepless nights, I strove to shatter and destroy that love, which had come to torture me. I did not destroy it, but I destroyed that part of it which gave me pain. Then I grew calm; and I feel love still, but it is a different kind of love». In this speech Death and the Wheel work together: the old form is broken, while love itself has turned and stayed.

The Wheel shows in the scenery as well. The story returns to the house at Pokrovskoye: «the garden visible through the window… the very same bench over there above the dell, the same song of the nightingale by the pond, the same lilacs in full bloom, the same moon shining above the house; and yet, in everything such a terrible inconceivable change!» Masha plays the sonata quasi una fantasia again and looks round at the corner where he used to listen: «his chair, long unmoved, was still in its place». In her girlhood room there are two beds, and one of them is her own, where her elder son now sleeps. Her husband points to the younger one: «Now we must stand aside and make room -- for him».

The turn comes quietly: «Suddenly I realized clearly and calmly that the past feeling, like the past time itself, was gone beyond recall, and that it would be not only impossible but painful and uncomfortable to bring it back». Then the baby smiles, and Masha looks into her husband's eyes «with an ease and happiness which I had not felt for a long time». **The task of the Wheel is not to bring back the first summer but to recognise love in a new season.**

The numbers add a detail of their own. The Wheel of Fortune is in the personal tail of one of the partners in every couple with the 3-13-10 tail: in 77% it is that partner's own main task (the tail 21-4-10), in 23% the middle of the personal tail. That does not make this partner the teacher. The couple's Wheel is a sum: 10 + 18 in most couples, 16 + 21 or 7 + 21 in the rest. A task that one of them knows from a personal chart becomes shared in the couple and looks different.

sections.h2: Waite and Wen: the field, the scythe and the wheel
paragraphs: Of The Empress Waite writes: «A field of corn is ripening in front of her, and beyond there is a fall of water», and calls her «universal fecundity». It is the very field Masha watches on the day he gives himself away.

Of Death he recalls the old design of the card: «The scene is the field of life», living heads stick out of the grass, and a skeleton «with a great scythe is in the act of mowing it». The meaning, Waite adds, is transparent — death — «but the alternatives allocated to the symbol are change and transformation». On his own card «king and child and maiden» fall before the rider. Our reading for this couple: in the middle the three roles of the romance come to an end — the husband who, as Masha saw it, «had to be a demigod on a pedestal», the «dear child who has to be calmed down», and the «violet», as he called her when she was a girl.

Of the Wheel: «the perpetual motion of a fluidic universe and for the flux of human life». Reversed, Waite lists «Increase, abundance, superfluity». That is The Empress's vocabulary. The end of the tail speaks in the words of its beginning, and the tail closes into a ring.

Tolstoy leads the couple through all three pictures. The first confession comes at harvest. On the wedding day, walking back from the memorial service, they cross «the beaten and trampled stubble»; to one side a peasant is «ploughing a black strip which grew wider and wider», and ahead «a field of winter corn… showed black with occasional patches of green». Mown, ploughed and already sown — in one field, on one day.

Wen writes that the Wheel suggests «samsara… the endless cycle of birth and death». All three cards of the tail are in that phrase: birth (for Wen The Empress is «the card of fruition»), death and the circle. The village church in the novella is built the same way: the same voice had read «at Sonya's christening, at memorial services for my father, and at my mother's funeral»; the priest wears «a cope made of the pall that had covered my father's coffin»; and he is the one who marries Masha: «I christened you and by God's mercy have lived to marry you». The book opens in mourning for a mother and closes with a baby's smile.

sections.h2: Atmosphere and values: family around, choice within
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's matrix is the atmosphere, what lies between the two and is not on show. In 81.5% of couples with this tail the centre holds Judgement. Lisovskaya's key to the twentieth energy in a couple is kin and family: relatives, traditions, the influence of parents. The novella opens with this centre. Masha's mother once said that she «would like such a husband for me», her father joked «you should marry my Masha», and at the memorial service before the wedding Masha feels her father's blessing upon her. The young couple live in the house of his mother, where everything was set up before them. The minus of the same centre is a sharp cooling, when neither can say what they feel. In Tolstoy: «Never had he looked at me so coldly, never had he spoken to me so coldly». With a centre of 20 the couple's tail follows the same arithmetic as a personal matrix: the main task plus the centre give the entry, 10 + 20 = 30 → 3.

In 18.5% of couples the centre holds Strength. In the minus of the atmosphere Lisovskaya describes it as a struggle for leadership in which each partner has their own truth. In Tolstoy this is Masha's line, said coldly: «You are always in the right».

The couple's values are The Lovers in 71.1% of cases and The Devil in 28.9%. The Lovers here are love as a choice that is made again: Sergey Mikhaylych says «I made that love myself», and later he remade it himself. The Devil is the shadow of that choice: passion and the wish to possess. Lisovskaya's closing thought on the fifteenth energy in a couple: no one belongs to anyone. In the novella Masha reproaches her husband: «Why did you not exercise your authority?», and he explains that he «had no right to put pressure on» her. This is our reading: the value of such a union is a freedom that never had to be taken away.

sections.h2: How a couple lives this tail in its strong version
paragraphs: The strong version of the tail does not promise that Death will pass the couple by. It changes the way the two of them meet it.

ul: **Call the end of the romance the end of a form, not of the union.** A wedding, a move, the birth of a child or a new job can end the old way of being together. That is not yet the end of the couple.

**Don't keep the garden «for ever».** A home needs habits. But when feelings run to a timetable — «cheerful» in the morning, «polite» at dinner, «affectionate» in the evening — the form has outlived its content.
**Don't look for a culprit in the turn.** The sum 4 + 9 or 3 + 10 belongs to no one. "What do we need now?" is a more useful question than "Who started it?"
**Tell the stories through to the third ending.** A couple can talk about itself through «Mr A and Miss B» as long as this helps to tell the truth rather than to avoid it.
**Grieve for the past, but don't repeat it.** «I weep for that past love» and «Don't let us try to repeat life» stand side by side in the novella and do not get in each other's way.

**Open the house.** Lisovskaya advises couples with the Wheel not to shut themselves up in each other. The last scene of the novella is full of people: Katya and Sonya wet from the rain, the nurse with Vanya, laughter on the veranda.

sections.h2: Example calculation: 11.02.1976 and 14.10.1975
paragraphs: Each point of a couple is the sum of the same points in the two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The couple's middle is not derived from the two outer numbers: it is added up from the personal middles.

The partner born on 11.02.1976 has the personal tail 9-9-18, the partner born on 14.10.1975 has 21-4-10. This is the most common combination for the couple tail 3-13-10: 77% of such couples are formed this way. In the rest, one partner has the tail 21-10-16 (19%) or 21-10-7 (4%), and the other has 9-3-21.

The example shows the whole story of the numbers. The Wheel is the second partner's personal main task. The couple's centre is 9 + 11 = 20, Judgement; the couple's values are 6, The Lovers. Point H of the couple's matrix also holds 10, and the reading marks The Wheel of Fortune as a card that appears both in the tail and at an additional point: in the couple method this reinforces the theme of the section. This happens in about 16% of couples with this tail. The Empress from point M appears twice in the reading: in the tail and in the sphere «Relationship and common language», where she is labelled «Common language».

intro: About one couple in 227 has this tail. Literature has an exact double for it: a novella by Tolstoy whose last page says «That day ended the romance of our marriage» and calls it the beginning of happiness.

faq.q: Does Death in a couple's 3-13-10 tail mean a break-up?
faq.a: No. Numbers do not predict events. Death in the middle of a couple's tail speaks of a change of form: the first way of loving each other ends, and with it roles, habits and expectations. The union goes on, as long as the couple does not mistake the end of the romance for the end of the relationship.

faq.q: How is the couple tail 3-13-10 different from the personal tail 3-13-10?
faq.a: It is a different calculation with different roles for the points. The personal tail 3-13-10 occurs for 149 dates since 1900 and describes the task of one person; the site has a separate article about it. A couple's tail is added up from two personal matrices and describes the shared task of two people: the entry is what the couple wants together, the middle is how it travels, the main task is what it has to learn.

faq.q: Why is the middle 13 if 3 + 10 also make 13?
faq.a: A coincidence of arithmetic. The couple's middle is the sum of the partners' personal middles: 4 + 9 in 77% of such couples and 3 + 10 in 23%. It is not recalculated from the outer numbers of the couple's tail, even though here the result happens to be the same.

faq.q: Are there couple tails with the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. The entry of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, so 10 and 13 never come first, and the order 3-10-13 does not occur for any couple. Of these three numbers only the tail 3-13-10 is possible for a couple.

faq.q: How rare is the couple tail 3-13-10?
faq.a: It occurs in about one couple in 227, which is 0.44% of all couples, and ranks 60th of the 97 possible couple tails.

report: Tolstoy wrote a novella about a couple in which the wedding stands exactly in the middle of the book, and the last sentence sounds like a verdict but turns out to be a promise: «That day ended the romance of our marriage». The 3-13-10 tail is built the same way. The Empress at the entry, Death in the middle and the Wheel of Fortune in the main task tell not of a break-up, but of how the romance ends halfway through a shared life while the union goes on.

report.h3: A garden that does not want seasons

report: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together. For The Empress this is a house where there is plenty of everything and everything grows. In Family Happiness this entry is written down almost word for word. Sergey Mikhaylych's dream is «A quiet secluded life in the country», then work, rest, nature, books, music, love for one's neighbour. Masha answers that this is all she has ever wanted. The first, unintended confession comes during the harvest, when before her eyes summer turns «into autumn».

Yet on the very first summer evening on the veranda he says: «I wish I could spend all my life here, sitting in this veranda». A moment later he adds: «life won't sit still». The tail's main task is spoken aloud before the love has even begun.

The resistance of the entry hides in two words: «for ever». In the moonlit garden Masha feels «that the whole scene must remain fixed for ever in its beauty». **The minus of this entry is the wish for a garden without seasons.**

Such a couple also has a common language of its own: the two talk about themselves as if about other people. Sergey Mikhaylych declares himself through the story of Mr A and Miss B, which has «two different endings», and Masha invents a third and makes her own confession through it. A tale told in the third person helps to tell the truth, until it starts helping to avoid it. Later Masha will note: «conversation flowed more easily in the presence of a third person».

report.h3: A wish that came true literally

report: A few months after the wedding the same image returns. Now it is custom that is «daily petrifying our lives into one fixed shape… The morning always found us cheerful; we were polite at dinner, and affectionate in the evening». **The wish of the entry came true literally, and became Death in the middle.** In this tail love freezes not because of something bad, but because two people wanted too much to hold on to something good.

Waite describes Death as a change of form: what ends is not life but the mask it has worn until now. What ends in the couple is the form in which the romance lived: one leads, the other learns. At first Masha's thoughts were «not mine but his thoughts and feelings»; later «We had changed parts». The bitterest line of the middle belongs to the husband: «We compete in generosity -- what an example of family happiness!»

There is also a temptation to skip the middle. A marquis at the spa promises a romance that «never breaks off in the middle». Such a romance is not on offer to a 3-13-10 couple: they always have a middle, and the only question is what the two of them carry out of it.

report.h3: No culprit, even in the numbers

report: The second half of the novella is a search for the guilty one: she asks how she is guilty before him, she tells him he loved too little, he answers «I was to blame». The answer comes in the last chapter: «time is to blame for that, and we ourselves», and then, more honestly still: «Who is to blame, I do not know».

The numbers answer the same way. The thirteenth card is not in the personal tail of either partner: nobody brings Death into the middle, only the couple puts it together. Sometimes it is made, quite literally, of the other two cards of the tail: one partner has The Empress in the middle of the personal tail, the other has the Wheel. A house that wants «for ever» meets a wheel that turns.

report.h3: Each time of life has its own love

report: The main task is read through the minus. The minus of the Wheel is two attempts to stop the turn: find who pushed it, and bring everything back. «Let everything be as it was before… It can be, can't it?» Masha pleads.

The plus of the Wheel is spoken in reply: «Each time of life has its own kind of love» and «Don't let us try to repeat life». Sergey Mikhaylych admits that he destroyed not love but only «that part of it which gave me pain», and «I feel love still, but it is a different kind of love». And straight away, honestly: «I weep for that past love». Grieving for the past is allowed; repeating it is not.

The Wheel shows in the scenery too: the same garden, the same bench above the dell, the same nightingale and the same moon above the house, «and yet, in everything such a terrible inconceivable change!» Masha's girlhood bed now holds her son. Reversed, the Wheel in Waite's list means increase, abundance, superfluity: The Empress's vocabulary, so the end of the tail speaks in the words of its beginning.

**The task of the Wheel is not to bring back the first summer but to recognise love in a new season.** The strong version of this tail does not skip Death in the middle. It calls the end of the romance the end of a form, not of the union, looks for no culprit in the turn, and opens the house to people, children and shared work. Tolstoy's novella ends exactly this way: the romance is over, and «a new life and a quite different happiness» has only just been founded.

unit.title: Each season has its own love

captions.M: To want a home where everything grows — for ever
captions.N: To live through the end of the romance, not the union
captions.D: To recognise love in a new season, not repeat the past

unit.meaning: Your task is to live through the end of your first romance, blame no one, and recognise your love in a new season.

seo.title: Karmic tail 3 13 19 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 13 19 compatibility: why Death stands between The Empress and The Sun, how the tail is built, and what the tale of Savitri knows about it.

items.title: The couple's karmic tail 3-13-19: The Empress, Death and The Sun
items.short: The karmic tail 3-13-19 turns up in roughly one couple in 129: The Empress at the entry, Death in the middle, The Sun as the main task. It looks like a story with a bad middle, but the answer lies elsewhere. Death here is the end of an old form of life, and the two go through it together. The real difficulty hides in The Sun: one partner knows and keeps quiet, protects and smiles, while the other lives on knowing nothing. The couple's task is to bring what one of them knows into a light both can see by.

sections.h2: A tale that lays out the three cards in order
paragraphs: The story of Savitri and Satyavan sits in the Forest Book of the Mahabharata (chapters 277–283 in the critical edition). The sage Markandeya tells it to King Yudhishthira as consolation, and it opens with a childless king, Aswapati. For eighteen years he keeps strict vows and makes offerings while reciting the Savitri — the famous prayer to the solar god Savitr. The goddess of that verse rises from his fire and promises him a daughter "of great energy". The girl is named Savitri.

She grows up so bright that no one asks for her hand: the text says that, "overpowered by her energy, none could wed" her. Her father sends her to choose a husband herself. Savitri travels from one forest hermitage to the next and chooses Satyavan, son of a blind king whom an enemy has driven from his throne. The sage Narada praises the young man without pause and then names the one defect that outweighs all his virtues: "Within a year from this day, Satyavan, endued with a short life will cast off his body!" Savitri does not change her choice. Then come the wedding, a year in the hermitage, the appointed day, Yama the god of death with his noose, a conversation on the move, five boons and a journey home by night.
The three acts follow the order of the cards:

ul: **The Empress:** eighteen years of praying for offspring, then a wedding and a home in the forest, where the new daughter-in-law tends and shelters everyone;
**Death:** a year counted day by day, and a god who comes for the husband in person;
**The Sun:** the road back through the night, the truth told by the fire, and the sunrise that brings good news to the hermitage.

paragraphs: The Sun in this story does not have to be read between the lines — it is named outright. Savitri bears the name of the solar verse. Narada says that "in energy Satyavan is like unto the sun"; the Sanskrit names Vivasvat, the Sun himself. Yama appears "effulgent as the Sun", and Savitri addresses him as the son of Vivasvat. In this myth Death is the son of the Sun. The middle of the tail and its main task are father and son.
Quotations from the Mahabharata here and below follow K. M. Ganguli's English translation (1883–1896), checked against the Sanskrit.

sections.h2: The evidence in the numbers: why the middle is Death and not The Fool
paragraphs: The first oddity is plain to see. In a personal chart the middle of the tail comes from its two ends: entry plus main task. If 3-13-19 belonged to one person, the card between The Empress and The Sun would be 3 + 19 = 22 — The Fool, a light step into the unknown. No person has such a tail. In a couple, each point is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, and the middle is built from the partners' middles. In place of the light step stands Death — a step after which the old life does not come back.

The second clue is the make-up. Running every possible date gives a single recipe: one partner has the personal tail 15-5-8, the other 15-8-11, and this holds for **100%** of such couples. The sums go point by point:

ul: entry: 15 + 15 = 30 → 3, The Empress made of two Devils;
middle: 5 + 8 = 13, Death made of one partner's Hierophant and the other's Justice;
main task: 8 + 11 = 19, The Sun made of Justice and Strength.

paragraphs: Personal tails are read by their own rules, and their meanings do not carry over into the couple's tail. But the pattern of the sums is evidence, and the tale answers each line. In Waite's list, The Devil is also "that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil". Savitri's story begins with exactly that: a prediction. The Hierophant and Justice are teaching and law; we will come back to them when Savitri starts talking to Death. And The Sun is made of Justice and Strength — of honest reckoning and gentle firmness. These, not heroics, are what bring her husband back.
The third clue is the centre. In every such couple, without exception, the atmosphere inside the couple is 11, Strength: the two personal centres are always 7 and 4. It gets a chapter of its own.
In frequency the tail sits mid-table: about one couple in 129 (0.778%), 46th of the 97 couple tails.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: a house where nobody asks for anything (3 · The Empress)
paragraphs: The Empress at the entry is what the couple wants together. Here it is a home where things grow: children or a shared business, a garden or a kitchen where someone is always eating. The common language of such couples is care given with the hands: to feed, to fix, to fetch, to drive someone somewhere. The couple enters the task through this wish, and the same wish becomes resistance.

The tale shows exactly how. After the wedding Savitri's father leaves, and that very day she puts off all her ornaments and clothes herself in bark, as people live in a hermitage. She dresses and tends her mother-in-law; she gratifies her father-in-law, in Ganguli's words, "by worshipping him as a god and controlling her speech"; she pleases her husband "by her honeyed speeches, her skill in every kind of work" and "the indications of her love in private". A model household. And a year later the father-in-law says something easy to miss: "Since Savitri hath been bestowed by her father as my daughter-in-law, I do not remember that she hath ever spoken any words couching a request." Her first request in a year comes on the day her husband is to die: to let her go into the forest with him.

In Waite, The Empress is "fruitfulness, action, initiative", followed at once by "the unknown, clandestine". In this house the secret has lived there from the first day. Waite is sharper still in his account of the symbolism: The Empress is "the outer sense of the Word", but "she does not herself carry its interpretation". The Empress speaks through deeds. Couples with this entry understand each other for years through a laid table, and put the words off.

The other hero has an Empress of his own — his parents'. Satyavan lives in his father and mother's hermitage. The moment he wakes from death and sees that night has fallen, he thinks not of what has happened to him but of his parents: "Even before it is twilight my mother confineth me within the asylum"; more than once the old couple wept to him at night that he was "the crutch of these blind ones" and that on him "doth perpetuity of our race depend", and without them he will not live. The couple lives in someone else's house, by its clock.

Among the tasks of this energy, Lisovskaya names getting out from under the influence of the mother and the wider family and leaving infantility behind; among her advice to the couple is to speak about wishes directly. In life it shows in small things. Sunday lunches at the parents' that cannot be missed. A shared country house where the couple has no say. A family business that feeds everyone except its owners. And a partner who never asks for anything, next to a partner who never notices: the couple's wish is shared, but the requests belong to no one.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: a year lived as a farewell (13 · Death)
paragraphs: The middle of the couple's tail is how the couple walks the path from the wish to the task. This is our reading: the book gives the point no meaning of its own, and Lisovskaya treats it as an addition to the main task. With Death the path runs through endings: something keeps ending so that something else can grow.

Savitri walks this path alone. "The words spoken by Narada were present night and day" in her mind. She counts the days, and three days before the appointed one she takes a vow to fast for three nights. Her father-in-law begs her to spare herself, and she begins "to look (lean) like a wooden doll". On the appointed morning she goes into the forest with her husband, "in seeming smiles although her heart was racked with grief". The woods ring with peacocks, and Satyavan leads her on, pointing: "Behold these rivers of sacred currents and these excellent trees decked with flowers!" She has not left the hermitage for almost a year. And she looks at her husband and, the text says, "considered her husband as already dead".

This is the minus of Death in the middle: the ending is lived in advance, and inside one head. One partner has already said goodbye to the old life — to a city, a job, the parents' house, the role of newlyweds — while the other is still pointing out the flowers. Waite writes of Death: "The veil or mask of life is perpetuated in change." Savitri's smile on the way to the forest is that mask.

Lisovskaya lists tasks under the thirteenth energy that read like a list of endings: to separate from the parents, to buy a home of one's own, to move, to accept a partner unlike the previous one, to go through separations and crises as a test, to see one's own mistakes and not only the other's. In the minus there are emotional swings, when there is so much change that the other has nothing to lean on, and attempts to remake the partner. In the plus there is a couple who accept each other's past and move on, take changes in the partner easily and are living proof that life goes on after hard times.

Wen writes that Death "assuages the tendency in human nature to resist change" and calls it "a call to let go of the present and move on". Resistance here comes in two kinds: clinging to the old form with all one's strength, or burying it silently without saying a word to the other.

sections.h2: Death talked round: seven steps and the King of Dharma
paragraphs: Then the tale does something no one expects from a story about death. Satyavan is chopping wood when his head starts to split; he lays it in his wife's lap. Yama appears — in yellow robes, noose in hand, "effulgent as the Sun". "By main force" he pulls out of the body a person "of the measure of the thumb" and sets off to the south. Savitri follows.

Yama tells her to turn back and perform the funeral rites. She answers: "Whither my husband is being carried, or whither he goeth of his own accord, I will follow him thither. This is the eternal custom." And she adds: "It hath been declared by wise men endued with true knowledge that by walking only seven paces with another, one contracteth a friendship with one's companion." The seven steps are the **saptapadi**, the heart of the Hindu wedding: in the old ritual manuals, at the seventh step the groom says to the bride, "Be friend with seven steps". Under India's Hindu Marriage Act of 1955, a marriage that includes this rite "becomes complete and binding when the seventh step is taken". Savitri walks the wedding steps with Death and calls it friendship. She does not fight and does not beg — she walks alongside and talks.

Every speech of hers pleases Yama, and for each he grants a boon — anything but her husband's life. One of the speeches runs: "Thou art the powerful son of Vivaswat. It is for this that thou art called Vaivaswata by the wise. And, O lord, since thou dealest out equal law unto all created things, thou hast been designated the lord of justice!" Dharmaraja, the King of Dharma, is Yama's standing title.

Now back to the sum. This couple's Death is made of one partner's Hierophant and the other's Justice. Waite's divinatory list for The Hierophant begins "marriage, alliance"; the list for Justice begins "equity, rightness, probity". Teaching and law. In the tale, Death is the King of Dharma, and Savitri's weapon is the formula "the wise have declared". She defeats Death with its own law, set out in the language of teachers.

For the couple this is an important hint. Endings in such a union do not strike like lightning: they have rules, and they can be talked to — what ends, what stays, on what terms, by when. The mistake is to treat the middle as a disaster to be fought or got through in secret. The strong move is to walk next to the ending and speak to it aloud, together.

sections.h2: The key was at the entry: a boon Death could not keep
paragraphs: There are five boons, and their order matters. First Savitri asks for her father-in-law's sight, that he may "become strong 'like either fire or the Sun!'" Then for his kingdom back. Then for a hundred sons for her own father. The fourth boon is a hundred sons for herself: "Both of me and Satyavan's loins, begotten by both of us, let there be a century of sons." Yama agrees — and walks into a trap. Savitri says: "Thou thyself hast bestowed on me the boon, namely, of a century of sons; yet thou takest away my husband!… May Satyavan be restored to life, for by that thy words will be made true." The King of Dharma cannot break the law. "With cheerful heart" he unties his noose.

Nobody tricks Death here. It is bound by its own word, and that word was given to The Empress's wish — to fruitfulness, to lineage, to a shared future. **The entry of the tail turns out to be the key to its middle.** The wish the couple started from is neither ornament nor naivety: it is the argument that carries the two of them through the end.

A couple with the tail 3-13-19 recognises this move in its own life. When something ends — a move, a change of job, leaving the parents' house, the end of the first and easiest season — what holds them is not the attempt to keep everything as it was. What holds them is the shared wish said aloud: this is what we are growing, and it needs both of us. A wish with room for both is stronger than any ending. A wish one partner carries in silence holds no one.

sections.h2: Main task: "Wherefore didst thou not awake me?" (19 · The Sun)
paragraphs: The couple's main task is read mainly through its minus — through what does not work. And the tale shows that minus with merciless precision.

Satyavan opens his eyes and looks at his wife "like one come home after a sojourn in a strange land". His first words: "Alas, I have slept long! Wherefore didst thou not awake me? And where is that same sable person that was dragging me away?" Savitri replies: "The night deepens. I shall, O prince, relate everything unto thee on the morrow." At the hermitage the ascetics ask why the pair came back so late. Satyavan explains: his head ached and he fell into a deep sleep — "This is all that I remember… There is no other reason for this." Satyavan means "the one who has truth"; the Brahmanas named him so because "his father speaketh the truth and his mother also is truthful in her speech". And here the man named for truth tells his own story without one false word and without knowing its main point. He is the only one who does not know he was saved.

This is the minus of The Sun in a couple. One partner knows, decides and rescues; the other lives in an ignorance created for them out of love. Among the couple's tasks under the nineteenth energy, Lisovskaya names the inability to talk about problems, holding back feelings, over-protection, inflated expectations and claiming the partner's victories. In life it looks ordinary. One partner learns about a debt, a redundancy, the parents' decision to sell the house — and "sorts it out alone". The other finds out later, from the bank, from friends, from a mother-in-law. The story of the rescue belongs to one person, and it has a single narrator. The rescuer gets a year of loneliness; the rescued gets the role of a child protected from the truth.

Tradition has remembered the tale in just this way. In the Indian month of Jyeshtha, married women keep the Vat Savitri fast: they walk around a banyan tree, winding a thread about it, and pray for their husbands' long life. In the folk version of the tale, it all happened under a banyan. What survives of the whole story is the vow of one partner for the other. The Mahabharata itself ends differently.

Savitri has a formula of her own, spoken back in front of Narada, when her father urged her to choose someone else: "Having first settled a thing mentally, it is expressed in words, and then it is carried out into practice." With the prophecy she walked this path with a gap. She settled it in her mind and carried it out in deeds — the vow, the walk into the forest, the conversation with Death — but put off the words to her husband for a year and one more night.
