seo.title: Karmic tail 3 16 22 compatibility: The Empress, The Tower, The Fool
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 16 22 compatibility: why it forms only when both partners have the tail 15-8-11, and what such a couple can never gamble away.

items.title: Karmic tail 3-16-22 in compatibility: what a couple cannot gamble away
items.short: The couple's karmic tail 3-16-22 looks like a verdict: The Empress builds a house, The Tower knocks it down, The Fool walks off with nothing. In compatibility these three cards tell a different story: how a couple stripped of everything external recognise each other by what cannot be taken.

sections.h2: A tale told to someone who has lost everything
paragraphs: In the third book of the Mahabharata, King Yudhishthira sits in the forest dressed in deerskins. He has lost his wealth and his kingdom at dice, his wife has been dragged before the assembly in disgrace, and long years of exile lie ahead. He puts to the sage Brihadashva the question anyone asks when their house has fallen: "Is there a king on this earth who is more unfortunate than myself?"

The sage answers with a story. There was a king called Nala — handsome, a master of horses, truthful and generous. There was a princess called Damayanti, more beautiful than any god or mortal had seen. They fell in love without meeting, through what others told them, and golden messenger birds brought them together. She chose him over the gods; for twelve years they lived happily and had a son and a daughter. Then Nala lost everything to his brother at dice, down to his last garment, went into the forest with his wife, left her asleep, was turned into an ugly man by a serpent, served as a stableman to a foreign king — and in the fourth year his wife recognised him by the taste of the food he had cooked.

In India this is one of the best-loved tales. In Europe generations began learning Sanskrit with it: Franz Bopp published "Nala" with a Latin translation in 1819, and textbooks placed it first. In Russian the tale was retold by Vasily Zhukovsky in 1844, from Friedrich Rückert's German version, and in 1904 the Bolshoi Theatre staged Anton Arensky's opera "Nal and Damayanti" to a libretto by Modest Tchaikovsky.

For the tail 3-16-22 something else matters more. The tale's three acts run exactly in the order of the three cards: the choice and the flourishing kingdom — The Empress; the game of dice — The Tower; the forest, nakedness and the road — The Fool. And it is told not as a prophecy but as a remedy, to a man for whom everything has already happened.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: The Empress who chose a mortal
paragraphs: A svayamvara is a ceremony at which the bride herself chooses a husband from the assembled suitors. Kings came to Damayanti's svayamvara, and so did four gods. The gods wanted her for themselves, and when they learned that she loved Nala, they took on his form. Damayanti entered the hall and saw "five persons all alike in appearance".

The marks of the gods that her elders had told her about showed on none of them. So she prayed: "For the sake of truth, O, let the gods reveal him to me." The gods assumed their own attributes. They do not sweat, they do not blink, their garlands do not fade, no dust settles on them, and they stand without touching the ground. Ganguli's translation puts it this way: she beheld "the celestials unmoistened with perspiration, with winkless eyes, and unfading garlands, unstained with dust, and staying without touching the ground", while Nala "stood revealed to his shadow, his fading garlands, himself stained with dust and sweat, resting on the ground with winking eyes". She chose the one with a shadow, sweat and a wilting garland. Nala answered with a vow: "Since thou, O blessed one, hast chosen a mortal in the presence of the celestials, know me for a husband even obedient to thy command."

That choice contains the whole Empress at the entry to the couple's tail. What these two want together is not an ideal but a living, earthly life where everything grows and everything wilts: a home that smells of cooking, a garden that needs watering, children, guests, a shared venture. The couple fill their life remarkably fast. Within six months a rented flat becomes a home, plants climb up the windowsills, people gather at weekends, and both enjoy having plenty around them.

For Lisovskaya, the entry point of the couple's tail stands for shared wishes, agreements and a "common language". In the reading on the site the same 3 also stands at the end of the line "Relationship and common language": this couple's language is the language of home. They easily agree on a renovation, a trip or a celebration, and find it hard to talk about the possibility of losing the home.

The wish is strong because it is doubled. Each partner brings The Devil — 15 — into the couple, the card of a strong personal "I want", of attachment and passion. Two fifteens make thirty, and thirty folds into three: two wishes to possess add up to a wish to grow. But the entry point stands on the line of tasks, and Lisovskaya warns that such a wish can turn into resistance. The Empress in the minus is a home to be preserved at any cost, money that comes in "feast or famine", a jealous count of which of the two has grown and which has fallen behind.

At the wedding of Nala and Damayanti the gods gave gifts, and they are worth remembering: they will be needed at the end. Fire comes whenever Nala wishes, water wherever he desires, his garlands keep their celestial fragrance, and his food gains a subtle taste. The kings rode away and Nala took his wife home. Zhukovsky describes their happiness like this: he lived "drop by drop drinking life from a single cup together with her" (our translation).

sections.h2: Middle of the task: The Tower that waited twelve years
paragraphs: One more suitor arrived late for the svayamvara: Kali, the spirit of strife and of the losing throw at dice. Learning that Damayanti had chosen a mortal in the presence of the gods, he swore revenge and settled in Nala's kingdom. He waited for a crack to open in the righteous king, "always watching for a hole". In the Mahabharata he had to wait twelve years (in Zhukovsky, six). One day Nala said his evening prayers "without having previously washed his feet", and Kali entered him through that tiny lapse.

From here on it is The Tower card at work. Nala's brother Pushkara challenged him to play, and Nala could not refuse for long: "Thus challenged in the presence of Damayanti, the lofty-minded king could not long decline it." He lost gold, chariots and robes, and the more he lost, the hotter he burned. The citizens came to the gate, Damayanti passed on their pleas, and he did not say a word. The people went home saying, "He liveth not." The game went on for many months.

Waite calls The Tower "a card in particular of unforeseen catastrophe" and reads it as "the ruin of the House of Life, when evil has prevailed therein". In Wen the key word is suddenness: "What seemed stable and solid to the Seeker is not so; it is in fact destructible." But the tale holds a detail that changes everything. When the sage first describes Nala, among his virtues — truthful, a master of horses, commander of a mighty army — stands one more: "fond of dice". The crack was in the very first line, among the virtues. The catastrophe looks unforeseen only to those who skipped the first line.

In a couple's life the Tower in the middle rarely looks like a bolt from the blue. More often one of the two disappears headlong into something — work, a project, a principle, a grievance, a game of any kind — while the other knocks at a closed door and hears no answer. The house falls not in a day but over "many months", and the whole time both hope the next throw will put things right. Among The Tower's tasks Lisovskaya gives an exact description of this picture: in bad times the partners look in different directions. There is another one too: the collapse of an imagined image of the partner. Nala, whom Damayanti chose because he stood on the ground, suddenly turns out to be possessed, deaf and a stranger.

Why The Tower stands in the middle of the tail can be seen from the numbers. Each partner brings Justice — 8 — into the couple: their own scales and their own sense of what is right. Eight plus eight is sixteen: two versions of "this is the right way" meet in one house. Nala does not sit down to play out of greed: the challenge was thrown in front of his wife, and a king's honour forbids refusing. In a couple this looks familiar: each acts by their own code of honour, and at some point the two codes strike each other like lightning striking the top of a tower.

Inside The Tower the tale also shows the card's plus. Damayanti does not wait for it all to end. She calls the charioteer, puts the children into a chariot drawn by her husband's favourite horses and sends them to her father. Lisovskaya writes of The Tower in a couple: the ability to take serious decisions quickly and calm in unexpected trouble. And one more detail: Damayanti refuses to name a culprit. "I do not think," she says, "that in this the high-souled Naishadha is to blame."

The last throw matters as well. When everything is lost, Pushkara laughingly offers to stake Damayanti. Nala silently takes off his ornaments and leaves the city in a single garment. That is where The Tower stopped: he did not stake a person.

sections.h2: Main task: The Fool whose last garment the birds took
paragraphs: Nala and Damayanti spent three nights outside the city walls: Pushkara proclaimed that anyone who helped them would be put to death. Then they went into the forest and lived on roots. One day the hungry Nala saw some birds with golden plumage and thought they would be his meal and his wealth. He threw his last garment over them, and the birds rose into the sky with it. From above they spoke, in Ganguli's translation:
"O thou of small sense, we are even those dice. We had come hither wishing to take away thy cloth, for it pleased us not that thou shouldst depart even with thy cloth on."

That is how The Fool is born: a naked man at the edge of the forest, called a fool by his own dice — and in Zhukovsky the dice even sing him off with "farewell, reckless one; a happy journey!" (our translation). At the beginning of the tale golden birds brought love: Nala caught one and let it go, and it flew off to tell Damayanti about him. At the end golden birds carried off his last possession: these he tried to hold on to. For Waite The Fool is zero, the card without a number. Nala reached zero literally.

The Fool as the main task is not about irresponsibility as such. It is about what two people do when they have nothing. Wen writes of The Fool as a fork: "One fork will lead to attainment (flying, transcending the cliff) and the other will lead to likely demise (falling off the cliff)." Nala points out the fork at once. He starts explaining the roads to Damayanti: this one leads south, this one to the mountains, and this one to her father's country. She understands before he does where he is heading: why are you showing me the way? And she replies that "in every sorrow there is no physic equal unto the wife". Nala agrees and promises not to part from her.

Next comes the image that makes the whole tale worth reading. The two of them have one cloth between them: Damayanti covers her husband with half of her own garment, and they walk on "both attired in one cloth". This is the couple's Fool in the plus: two people who own nothing but one piece of cloth and each other — and that is enough to keep walking.

And here is The Fool in the minus. At night in an empty shelter Nala cannot sleep and reasons: she will be better off without me, she will go back to her family, and with me only grief awaits her. He finds a blade lying unsheathed near the shelter, cuts their shared cloth in half and leaves. Then he comes back, weeps over her as she sleeps, leaves again. Ganguli's translation compares him to a swing, "dragged away by Kali but drawn back by love"; Zhukovsky has him pulled "now by the mighty foe, now by love" (our translation). In the end he goes.

Here another clue from the numbers shows up. The centre of the matrix in every couple with this tail is 8, Justice, without exception. The atmosphere inside such a couple is a pair of scales: fair, equal, each paying their own way. That is a strength as long as the subject is the budget and the chores. But in the tale the blade appears at the most terrible moment and works like the sword of Justice: the cloth is divided exactly in half so that the two can part. The most dangerous thing this tail knows how to do is to split everything equally and leave "for the other's good". Among The Fool's tasks Lisovskaya names running away from problems and a couple who seem to be together but do everything separately and live like neighbours. Nala decided for both of them what was best for Damayanti and did not ask her.

sections.h2: Two Strengths that make freedom
paragraphs: The separation in the tale is Kali's doing, and there is no need to repeat it. But in the forest each of the two shows a Strength of their own. The personal tails of both partners end with card 11, Strength: the ability to endure, to face the beast and not back away. Eleven twice is twenty-two, The Fool.

Damayanti walks alone through a forest full of tigers. A tiger comes out to meet her and she decides: "Even him will I accost fearlessly" — and asks the king of beasts whether he has seen Nala. Meanwhile Nala hears a voice from a burning forest, "O righteous Nala, come hither", walks into the flames saying "Fear not", and carries out the serpent Karkotaka. The serpent bites him and changes his form. In Zhukovsky the serpent explains: "You are transformed, you have parted with yourself, and from now on, as nobody, you cannot be recognised even by your own wife" (our translation).

Our reading: two Strengths in one couple make not a double wall but a road. When both know how to endure and hold on, there is nothing left to hold — what remains is to walk. Lisovskaya describes The Fool in the plus as a couple where each is self-sufficient, where trust brings a great deal of freedom, and where starting from zero comes easily. The tale shows where this lightness comes from: each of the two learned separately that they would hold out. She learned to search and to act; he learned to serve and to be nobody.

Nala becomes Bahuka (Vahuka in Ganguli's translation): "of unsightly appearance and possessed of short arms", as the text says, a stableman and cook at the court of King Rituparna. That court never had a better stableman. Every evening he recites a verse about the woman who is hungry and worn out somewhere in the forest. When a companion asks whom he is weeping for, Nala tells his own story in the third person: "A certain person devoid of sense had a wife." The Fool calls himself by his own name.

sections.h2: Recognition: what The Tower could not take
paragraphs: Meanwhile Damayanti had returned to her father and sent Brahmins out to every kingdom. At every court they repeated her words: "O beloved gambler, where hast thou gone cutting off half of my garment, and deserting the dear and devoted wife asleep in the forest?" Only one man answered — the short-armed stableman. He spoke up for the runaway: a wife "should not be angry with one that was deprived by birds of his garment while striving to procure sustenance". Only Nala knew about the birds.

To bring him back, Damayanti announced that tomorrow she would choose a husband again. Only someone who drove horses like Nala could arrive within a single day. Bahuka carried King Rituparna to her city, and Damayanti sent her maid to watch what this man did. The maid came back amazed. Low doorways rise up before him by themselves. Empty vessels fill with water as soon as he looks at them. A handful of grass bursts into flame in his hand. He touches fire and is not burnt. Flowers pressed in his palms do not crumple but grow fresher, and in Zhukovsky a withered rose comes back to life in his hand.

This is the answer to the tail's riddle. Zhukovsky names it outright: "these were clear signs of Nala, these were the gifts he had received from the gods on his very wedding day, and she… saw with her heart the longed-for Nala where her eyes still saw Vahuka" (our translation). Damayanti arranged the last test herself: she asked for a piece of meat cooked by Bahuka, tasted it and recognised the flavour. A subtle taste in food was also a wedding gift. In Zhukovsky the serpent had already reminded Nala in the forest of "the elemental gifts received from the gods on your wedding day; they are not lost to you" (our translation).

The dice took the kingdom, the clothes and even his face. They did not take the wedding gifts: what was received at the entry to the tail survived The Tower and became the way to recognise each other at zero. Waite says something strange about Justice, the card at the centre of this couple. He separates the law that deals unto every man according to his works from spiritual justice, which is like the possession of gifts: "we have them or have not". The law of stakes takes away whatever has been staked. A gift is never put on the table.

For the couple 3-16-22 this is the main discovery. Their Empress is not a flat or furniture. It is the ability of the two of them to make life around them alive: to feed, to warm, to fill, to bring the withered back. The Tower can take the walls, the job, the familiar way of life and the familiar image of each other. It does not take the ability to make things grow, and by it the two recognise each other when everything external is already lost.

The tale tells the rest quickly. Damayanti calls the wind, the sun and the moon to witness, and the wind answers from the sky: she is pure. In Ganguli's translation the wind sums it up in words as symmetrical as the scales at the centre: "thou hast obtained Bhima's daughter, and she hath also obtained thee." Nala puts on the garment the serpent gave him and regains his former form. They spend the night telling each other what each of them lived through in the forest. Zhukovsky writes that "the living tale of what they had suffered apart" became shared, and "the sad true stories turned into a merry tale" (our translation). The Fool's main task is solved not by a return to the old palace but by the forest becoming a shared story.

sections.h2: The Chariot missing from the tail
paragraphs: If 3-16-22 were a personal tail, the middle would come out differently: in the personal matrix the middle is the folded sum of the two ends, and 3 + 22 = 25 → 7, The Chariot. In the couple's tail that place belongs to The Tower. The Chariot does appear in the tale after all — but after The Tower, not instead of it.

Nala drives someone else's chariot. The lean horses he picked fall to their knees at the first jolt; he raises them with the reins, and they race so fast the chariot seems to fly. On the way King Rituparna's upper garment blows off and the king asks to turn back. Nala answers: "The sheet is dropped down far away. We have travelled one yojana thence. Therefore, it is incapable of being recovered." The third lost garment in the tale — and this time nobody goes back for it.

Then the king boasts that at a glance he has counted the leaves and fruits on a vibhitaka tree. Nala fells the tree, counts, finds the king right and proposes an exchange: his art of horses for the king's art of dice. At the very moment Nala grasps the secret of the game, Kali leaves him and hides in that same vibhitaka. In Zhukovsky the tree withers on the spot.

The detail is no accident. Vibhitaka nuts were India's ancient dice. The gambler's hymn of the Rigveda (X.34), one of the oldest texts about gambling, opens by praising these nuts, "sprung from tall trees on windy heights", and towards the end passes on the advice of the god Savitr: "Play not with dice, cultivate your corn-land… There are your cattle, there your wife, O gambler" (Griffith's translation, revised after Macdonell). The quarrel between The Empress and The Tower was written down some three thousand years ago: the cornfield against the dice.

Our reading is this: speed, command of direction and the ability to steer come to this couple not before the collapse but after it — and as service, not as ownership. Nala drives a chariot that is not his, and that is exactly how he wins back what is his.

sections.h2: The three cards according to Waite: a cornfield, lightning and the edge of a cliff
paragraphs: The cards in the reading are drawn for the site and have their own pictures. Waite describes his cards in words, and the tale of Nala can be recognised in those descriptions.

Waite writes of his Empress: "A field of corn is ripening in front of her, and beyond there is a fall of water." It is the very cornfield Savitr advises ploughing instead of gambling, and the water that by a god's gift fills Nala's vessels. Above all, for Waite, The Empress is "universal fecundity". The entry to the couple's tail is exactly that: two people enter a shared life through the wish to make it grow.

Waite's Tower is struck by lightning, and of the two falling figures he writes: "The one is the literal word made void and the other its false interpretation." The tale has two such empty words: "a king does not refuse a challenge" and "she will be better off without me". Both sound noble, and both bring the house down.

Waite places his own Fool at the brink of a precipice: "The edge which opens on the depth has no terror." But in his historical survey he also recounts an older design: the Fool does not know he is on the brink of a precipice, "but a dog or other animal—some call it a tiger—is attacking him from behind, and he is hurried to his destruction unawares." The tale has both Fools. Nala, driven by Kali, does not see the edge. Damayanti walks up to the tiger herself and speaks to it without fear.

sections.h2: Why only doubles form 3-16-22
paragraphs: Now for the numbers — checked by running every date through the site's engine.

The tail 3-16-22 occurs in roughly one couple in 563 (0.178%) and ranks 76th of the 97 couple tails. It forms in one way only: both partners have the same personal tail, 15-8-11 — The Devil, Justice, Strength. A person has that tail roughly once in 24 cases. Couples in which both partners have it produce 3-16-22.
Each point of the couple's tail is the sum of the matching points of the two personal matrices, folded down to 22. Here all three numbers are doublings:

The example: 14.10.1976 and 14.10.1976, two people born on the same day. Each has the personal tail 15-8-11 and centre 4, The Emperor. In the couple's matrix the tail is 3-16-22, the centre is 8 and the couple's values are 6.

Centre 8, Justice, appears in 100% of such couples, and the reason is in the numbers too. Everyone with the tail 15-8-11 has 4, The Emperor, at the centre of their personal matrix, without exception. Four plus four is eight. Our reading: two people, each used to being master of their own life, create between them an atmosphere of scales — respect, fair division and an endless weighing of who has given how much.

The middle, 16, is itself what makes the tail impossible in a personal matrix. There the middle is calculated from the ends: 3 + 22 → 7. Here it is added up from the partners' middles, 8 + 8. That is why The Chariot, which would be "due" under the personal formula, gives way to The Tower in the couple's tail.

There is also a clue visible right in the couple's reading. The "Compatibility of characters" sphere checks whether one partner's point of wishes sounds in the other's chart. In these couples that point is the same for both: 15, The Devil. So every reading of a couple with the tail 3-16-22 shows a match in wishes: the same "I want" in both. Added together, it produces The Empress at the entry.

And the tale, as if it knew, is built entirely of pairs. Five identical Nalas at the svayamvara. Golden birds at the beginning and at the end. Two children — a son, Indrasena, and a daughter, Indrasenā: one name for two, told apart in Sanskrit by a single long vowel. Two bride's choices — a real one and a pretended one. Two kings who trade their arts: horses for dice. And the formula with which the messenger bird brings the lovers together: "The union of the best with the best is happy."

There are no couple tails made of the same three numbers in another order: 3-16-22 is the only one. The partners' personal tail 15-8-11 is read by its own rules, and its conclusions do not carry over to the couple's tail: the couple has different points and different roles.

sections.h2: The couple's values: a choice made again
paragraphs: The couple's values are its spiritual purpose, "what your union exists for". In 93.2% of couples with the tail 3-16-22 this is 6, The Lovers. Waite's divinatory list for this card contains words that read like a summary of the tale: "Attraction, love, beauty, trials overcome." The old Lovers card, he writes, "is said to have been entitled Simulacrum fidei, the symbol of conjugal faith".

The Lovers is a card of choice, and in the tale the choice is made twice. The first time Damayanti chooses a mortal over the gods. The second time she announces a new svayamvara — not to choose someone else but to call the same man back. When they meet, Nala bitterly asks whether any devoted wife could seek a second husband. She answers with the words of her first choice: "passing over the celestials themselves, I choose thee as my lord." This couple's value is a choice that is not made once and for all but confirmed after every loss.

In 6.8% of couples the values are 15, The Devil — the very card with which both partners' personal tails begin. For these couples the bond itself, passion and attachment, is the highest value. The task is to keep the bond from becoming a chain: in the gambler's hymn the dice "give gifts like boys [do], and then snatch them back from the winner" (Griffith's translation, revised after Macdonell).

sections.h2: How karmic tail 3-16-22 lives in a couple: the circle and the way out
paragraphs: In the minus the circle usually runs like this. First the two build abundance and enjoy it. A small crack remains in the foundation — something "we don't discuss": one partner's passion, the other's code of honour, an old grievance, a habit of escaping into work. One day something big enters through that crack, and one of the two stops hearing. The other knocks, then saves what can be saved. Once the house has fallen, the couple at zero faces The Fool's two temptations: to scatter "so as not to be a burden", or to stay under one roof but live apart, like neighbours.

In the plus the circle looks different. A couple that has already lost everything once without losing each other starts from zero more easily than almost anyone: they know their wealth is not in the walls. Such a pair can turn misfortune into a shared story and later tell it with laughter. They are recognisable by the way life starts growing around them again.
What helps this couple:

ul: name the crack aloud while it is small: whatever has gone unspoken in the house for years is exactly where The Tower will come in;
agree in advance on what is never staked — in an argument, with money, in the heat of a game: each couple has its own list, but a person is never on it;
in trouble, do not decide for the other what would be better for them: Nala left "for her good" and never asked her;
do not split everything in half at a moment of fear: the scales at the centre are good for the budget and the chores, not for running away;
look after the gifts, not just the property: what each can do with their hands and heart outlives any loss;
after a hard period, tell each other your "forest" — what each of you went through alone — so that it becomes a shared story rather than a secret.

paragraphs: If the "game" in a couple is a real addiction, debt or a threat to safety, it is no longer a question of cards: specialist help is needed, and in danger, the emergency services.

intro: **Entry to the task — 3, The Empress.** The couple's shared wish is a life that grows: a home, plenty, beauty, children or a joint venture. The couple enters the task through this wish, and the same wish later resists change.

**Middle of the task — 16, The Tower.** The road from the wish to the task runs through the collapse of whatever rested on habit and on an imagined picture. More often it is not a blow from outside but a crack nobody noticed for years.

**Main task — 22, The Fool.** To learn freedom and trust without a safety net: to start from zero together, not to run from each other, and not to split everything in half when things get frightening.

This tail holds a riddle that others do not. It is formed only by two people with the same personal tail, 15-8-11, so every card of the couple turns out to be one person's card doubled. And its plot is told best of all in an ancient Indian tale about King Nala and Princess Damayanti.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 3-16-22 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail: the entry to the task is The Empress (the shared wish to grow a home and a life), the middle is The Tower (the collapse of what rested on habit and image), and the main task is The Fool (freedom and trust without a safety net, the ability to start from zero together and not run from each other).

faq.q: Does The Tower in the middle of the couple's tail mean a break-up?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events. The Tower in the middle describes what the couple goes through on the way to its task: a review of what was built on habit. How and when this is lived through, and whether it is turbulent at all, the cards do not say.

faq.q: Why does this tail never appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is the folded sum of the ends: 3 + 22 → 7. Here the middle is 16, added up from the two partners' middles (8 + 8), so the order 3-16-22 is possible only in a couple's matrix.

faq.q: If both partners have the tail 15-8-11, does the couple have the same tasks?
faq.a: No. The personal tail 15-8-11 is read by the rules of the personal matrix, and the couple's tail by its own. The match between the personal tails only explains where the couple's numbers come from: each of its cards is one partner's card doubled.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. The numbers 3, 16 and 22 form only one order in a couple: 3-16-22. No other arrangement of these numbers exists among couple tails.

faq.q: How is the couple's tail calculated?
faq.a: Calculate both partners' personal matrices and add up the matching points of the tail, folding any sum above 22 by adding its digits. For example, two people born on 14.10.1976 have personal tails 15-8-11, which give the couple's tail 3-16-22. The compatibility calculator does it more conveniently.

report: A wife recognised her husband by the taste of the meat he had cooked. His face was a stranger's, his name was a stranger's, he worked as a stableman for a foreign king, yet his gift was the same. The scene comes from the tale of Nala and Damayanti in the Mahabharata, and it holds the answer to the couple's tail 3-16-22. The tale's three acts run exactly in the order of the three cards: the flourishing kingdom — The Empress; the game of dice — The Tower; the forest and nakedness — The Fool.

report.h3: Five identical bridegrooms

report: At the ceremony where the bride chooses her own husband, four gods came to Damayanti, and all of them took on Nala's form. She saw "five persons all alike in appearance", prayed, and when the gods assumed their own attributes, she told the real one apart by earthly marks. The gods do not sweat, their garlands do not fade, they stand without touching the ground. Nala, in Ganguli's translation, "stood revealed to his shadow, his fading garlands, himself stained with dust and sweat, resting on the ground".

That choice holds the whole Empress at the entry to the task. What a couple with this tail wants together is not an ideal but a living, earthly life where everything grows and everything wilts: a home that smells of cooking, guests, children, a shared venture. Such a pair fill their life remarkably fast. Their common language is the language of home: a renovation or a celebration is easy to agree on, the possibility of losing the home is hard to talk about. The wish is doubled: each partner brings a strong personal "I want", The Devil, into the couple, and together they add up to a wish to make things grow. But the same wish later resists change.
At the wedding the gods gave Nala gifts: fire comes at his will, water wherever he desires, and his food gains a subtle taste. These gifts will be needed later.

report.h3: A crack awaited for twelve years

report: Kali, the spirit of strife and of the losing throw, arrived late for the bride's choice and swore revenge. For twelve years he waited for a crack to open in the righteous king, and he entered Nala through a single lapse. Nala's brother challenged him to play, and months later the kingdom was lost. The citizens stood at the gate, his wife passed on their pleas, the king did not answer.

Waite calls The Tower "a card in particular of unforeseen catastrophe". Yet in the very first description of Nala, among his virtues, stand the words "fond of dice". **The crack was in the first line.** In a couple's life the Tower in the middle rarely looks like a bolt from the blue. More often one partner disappears headlong into work, a principle, a grievance or a game of any kind, while the other knocks at a closed door. Each brings their own scales into the couple — two Justices — and The Tower rises where two versions of "this is the right way" strike each other: Nala sits down to play because a king's honour forbids refusing a challenge.

Inside The Tower the tale also shows its plus. Damayanti sends the children to her father while her husband is still playing, and refuses to name a culprit. And when the brother offers to stake her herself, Nala silently leaves the city in a single garment. **He did not stake a person.**

report.h3: Dice that wish a happy journey

report: In the forest the hungry Nala throws his last garment over birds with golden plumage, and they fly off with it. From above they speak: "O thou of small sense, we are even those dice." Zhukovsky's Russian version adds a parting line: "farewell, reckless one; a happy journey!" That is how The Fool is born: a man at zero whose own dice wish him a good road. The couple's main task is what two people do when they have nothing.

The tale gives both answers. In the plus, the two walk on "both attired in one cloth": one cloth for two, and that is enough. In the minus, at night Nala decides his wife will be better off without him, cuts their shared cloth in half and leaves. The centre of every such couple is Justice, an atmosphere of scales: fair, equal, each paying their own way. **The most dangerous thing this tail knows how to do is to split everything equally and leave "for the other's good".** Nala decided for both of them and did not ask.

report.h3: What can never be staked

report: Nala turns into a homely stableman; Damayanti sends messengers out with the question "O beloved gambler, where hast thou gone?" To bring him back she announces a new choice of husband, and her maid reports on the strange stableman: vessels fill with water at his glance, grass bursts into flame in his hand, a withered rose comes back to life. Zhukovsky names the answer outright: "these were the gifts he had received from the gods on his very wedding day, and she… saw with her heart the longed-for Nala where her eyes still saw Vahuka." The last test is a piece of meat cooked by the stableman.

**The dice took the kingdom, the clothes and even his face, but not the wedding gifts.** Waite has a strange thought about Justice, the card at this couple's centre: the law deals with each according to his works, while gifts "we have them or have not". The law of stakes takes whatever has been staked. A gift is never put on the table. This couple's Empress is not a flat or furniture but the ability of the two of them to make life around them alive: to feed, to warm, to bring the withered back. The Tower can take the walls and the familiar image of each other. It does not take the ability to make things grow, and by it the two recognise each other when everything external is already lost.

The night after their meeting, Nala and Damayanti tell each other what each lived through in the forest, and in Zhukovsky "the sad true stories turned into a merry tale". The Fool's task is solved not by a return to the palace but by the forest becoming a shared story.

What helps a couple with this tail: naming the crack aloud while it is small; agreeing in advance on what is never staked; in trouble, not deciding for the other what would be better for them; not splitting everything in half at a moment of fear; looking after the gifts, not just the property; after a hard period, telling each other the story of the "forest".

unit.title: What is never staked

captions.M: To want a living home where everything grows
captions.N: To live through the collapse of what rested on habit
captions.D: To start from zero together, not split in half out of fear

unit.meaning: Your task is to go through loss together: don't decide for each other, don't split everything, guard what you can grow.

seo.title: Karmic tail 3 16 4 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 16 4 compatibility: why a couple's Empress and Emperor have the Tower between them, not the Chariot, and what the tale of Aladdin knows.

items.title: The couple's karmic tail 3-16-4: from the Empress to the Emperor through the Tower
items.short: The couple's tail 3-16-4 opens with the Empress and closes with the Emperor — the queen and king of the major arcana, whom an old tradition, Waite notes, takes for husband and wife. Between them stands the Tower, struck by lightning. The riddle is that by the ordinary arithmetic of the matrix the Chariot should have stood there. The answer is written in the numbers themselves: the couple enters the task wanting a home with plenty of everything, passes through the collapse of what rested on one partner's knowledge and the other's ignorance, and learns the main thing — to hold power and order together, not in one person's pocket.

sections.h2: How the 3-16-4 tail is formed: a worked example
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices, reduced to 22: if the sum is above 22, its digits are added. The middle of the couple's tail is also built from the partners' middles, not worked out from the two outer numbers.

The example uses two dates, 07.01.1976 (7 January 1976) and 11.02.1976 (11 February 1976). The first person has the personal tail 21-7-13 (The World, The Chariot, Death) and centre 8. The second has 9-9-18 (The Hermit, The Hermit, The Moon) and centre 9.

This meeting is the only road to the tail. In 100% of couples with the tail 3-16-4, one partner has the personal tail 21-7-13 and the other 9-9-18. Neither personal tail is common: 21-7-13 belongs to roughly one person in 68, 9-9-18 to one in 50. Hence the couple's rarity: one couple in 1,712 (0.058%), 89th place among the 97 couple tails.

As a personal tail, 3-16-4 does not occur for any date. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and with a main task of 4 an entry of 3 is impossible whatever the centre. This is a tail that exists only for two.
The couple in the example has 6, The Lovers, in its values. More on them, and on the Star in the centre, below.

sections.h2: The first clue: the Chariot could have stood where the Tower is
paragraphs: Add the outer numbers of the tail the way a personal matrix does: 3 + 4 = 7, the seventh arcanum, The Chariot. Between the Empress and the Emperor the arithmetic of the matrix leaves exactly two options. In every personal tail the middle is the reduced sum of the entry and the task, and reduction never changes the remainder after division by nine. So the couple's middle leaves the same remainder as 3 + 4: it can only be 7 or 16. The tail 3-7-4, with the Chariot, occurs in one couple in 217. The tail 3-16-4, with the Tower, in one in 1,712 — eight times rarer.

And the Chariot is here. It stands in the middle of one partner's personal tail, 21-7-13. The other partner simply brings a Hermit to the same point, and 7 + 9 make 16. **This couple's Tower is built from a chariot that drives off and a lantern that stays at home.**

Waite's divinatory lists hint at what the two halves are made of. His Chariot is "Succour, providence; also war, triumph, presumption", and its conquests, Waite writes, are "manifest or external and not within himself". The Hermit reversed is "Concealment, disguise, policy, fear, unreasoned caution." One rides out after victories. The other guards something and keeps quiet. Taken apart, these are just two different temperaments, and neither is dangerous on its own. Added together at one point of the couple's matrix, they make lightning.

This is no verdict on anyone's character: that is how the numbers add up, and in real life both partners get to play both parts. How exactly a chariot and a lantern bring a house down is shown best not by the tarot but by a fairy tale.

sections.h2: The tale this couple lives in
paragraphs: "Aladdin" has no Arabic original. On 5 May 1709 the orientalist Antoine Galland wrote in his Paris diary: "In the morning, the Maronite Hanna of Aleppo finished telling me the tale of the Lamp." Hanna Diyab, a young traveller who had come to France with the antiquities collector Paul Lucas, told Galland more than a dozen stories. "The Story of Aladdin, or the Wonderful Lamp" came out in the ninth and tenth volumes of Galland's "Thousand and One Nights" in the early 1710s. The Arabic manuscripts of the tale found later turned out to be back-translations from the French, as the Nights scholar Muhsin Mahdi showed. That is why every quotation below follows Galland, in our own translation from the French.

In the children's version this is a story about a boy and a genie. In Galland it is a story about a marriage, and it runs in the order of the tail's three cards. First, a palace that grows overnight opposite the sultan's palace: the Empress. Then a lamp given away as a joke while the master is out hunting, and the palace vanishing overnight with the wife inside: the Tower. At the end, two people on one throne: the Emperor. Between the second and third acts there is one more scene, without which the tale would be about magic rather than about a couple — a conversation in Africa about whose fault it was.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — The Empress: a palace with one unfinished window
paragraphs: The entry point is what the couple wants together, its shared wishes and agreements. In the relationship section of the reading the same point is labelled "Common language". For a 3-16-4 couple the common language is abundance. A home they want furnished at once. Gifts that speak instead of words. Plans in which everything is big: a flat, children, travel, a business of their own. The urge to build is shared from the first day, and it easily turns into action.

Galland gives this wish an exact shape. Aladdin puts off the wedding: first there must be a palace "worthy to receive the princess". The genie builds it overnight — porphyry, jasper, agate, and at the top a domed hall with twenty-four windows set with diamonds, rubies and emeralds; a garden, kitchens, storerooms, stables and, as a separate line of the order, "not forgetting a hunting train". The Chariot is built into the house from day one.

One window Aladdin orders to be left unfinished. The sultan, his future father-in-law, is puzzled: was it forgotten? was there no time? Aladdin replies that it was done on purpose, so that His Majesty might have the glory of completing the hall. The sultan's jewellers spend a month and the treasury's stones and do not finish even half. Galland says it plainly: Aladdin "concealed the real reason" — the sultan simply did not have enough jewels. The window was a polite trap, a place left to the in-laws so that they could see for themselves that this house was beyond them.

The same entry also shows the downside of the Empress that Lisovskaya writes about: the task of getting out from under the family's influence. The palace stands "opposite the sultan's palace, at a proper distance", and the genie lays a velvet carpet from the father-in-law's door to the princess's rooms. Every morning, as was his habit, the sultan steps up to an open window to admire the young couple's palace. The couple lives in full view of the family, on the family's carpet, with the family's window in its own hall. That kind of task does not begin with a quarrel; it begins with a carpet.

Waite seems to describe both faces of this entry in a single line. His Empress is "Fruitfulness, action, initiative" and, straight after, "the unknown, clandestine; also difficulty, doubt, ignorance". A palace and ignorance in one card. A few years later, ignorance will become the key detail of the tale.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — The Tower: "Who will exchange old lamps for new?"
paragraphs: The middle of a couple's tail is how the couple lives the road from the shared wish to the main task. Lisovskaya gives this point no meaning of its own — it only adds to the main task; we read it as the road. For 3-16-4 the road runs through the Tower.

Galland stages the scene with a watchmaker's precision. Aladdin goes hunting for eight days — he goes hunting every week. The lamp without which he would have neither palace nor wife he puts on the cornice of the hall of twenty-four windows himself, "for fear of losing it". The rest of the time he carries it on him. In his absences neither the maids nor the eunuchs nor the princess herself had ever paid it any attention.

A few days later a madman with a basket of shiny new copper lamps appears under the windows, crying: "Who will exchange old lamps for new?" The children jeer, a maid comes back into the hall choking with laughter, and the princess, watching her, laughs too. Another maid remembers the old lamp on the cornice: the master will hardly mind finding a new one in its place. The princess, Galland writes, did not know how precious the lamp was, and she "went along with the joke". At night the magician rubs the lamp, and the palace, with the princess in it, is carried off to Africa.

Here Galland does something rare for a fairy tale: he stops and speaks to the reader. "It will be said that Aladdin's precaution was a good one, but that he should at least have locked the lamp away. That is true; but such mistakes have been made in every age, they are made still, and they will never stop being made." No better caption could be written for this couple's Tower.

In the morning the sultan, as usual, goes to the window to admire the palace and sees an empty space, "just as it was before anything was built there". He rubs his eyes and reasons: had the palace collapsed, there would be heaps of stone; had the earth swallowed it, there would be some trace. There is neither. Waite's Tower is "Misery… deception, ruin", "in particular of unforeseen catastrophe". **This couple's Tower is often exactly that: from outside nothing is broken, and yet the old home is gone.**

The mechanism is now in full view. Neither of the two caused the collapse. One held the house's support in hand and, leaving, put it where it could not be seen — out of caution, not cunning. The other did not know it was a support and, in a good-faith joke, swapped the old for the new. The chariot drove off, the lantern stayed unexplained, and together they made the Tower. Among the Tower's tasks Lisovskaya also lists partners who, in trouble, look in different directions. The tale shows this literally: the sultan demands Aladdin's head, while in Africa the magician tells the princess her husband has been executed. Each is left with half of the truth.

sections.h2: After the lightning: taking the blame on yourself
paragraphs: Lisovskaya's key to the Tower in a couple is that an ordeal survived together makes the union stronger. Galland shows where "together" begins. Aladdin finds the princess in Africa, and the first thing he asks is where the old lamp from the cornice went. What follows is a dialogue that children's versions cut down to a single line.
The princess: "I did suspect that our shared misfortune came from that lamp, and what torments me most is that I am the cause of it myself!"
Aladdin: "Do not take the blame; it is all mine — I should have kept it more carefully. Let us think only of how to repair this loss."

These two lines turn the Tower towards the Emperor. Each takes the blame, and so there is no longer any need to look for a culprit. The one who held the lamp admits that it was his to guard. And straight away there is a plan with roles: Aladdin promises to be back by noon and explain what the princess must do for it to succeed.

The plan rests on a second exchange. The princess puts on her finest dress, receives the magician kindly and at supper offers to swap cups: "with us in China", she says, lovers hand each other their cups and drink to one another. Her cup holds Aladdin's powder, and the fairy-tale villain gets what he deserves. **The first exchange she made without knowing what it meant, and the palace vanished. The second she made understanding it better than anyone at the table, and the palace came back.** Later she will tell her father about the measures they took "jointly". The difference between the Tower and its repair fits into that one word.

sections.h2: The roc's egg: when a shared wish becomes resistance
paragraphs: The entry point stands on the line of tasks, and so it has a second face: the wish that leads the couple can become its resistance. Galland shows this in an episode that cartoons usually leave out.

The magician had a younger brother. He kills the holy woman Fatima, a recluse who left her cell only on Mondays and Fridays, puts on her dress and veil, and the princess, who has long wanted to meet the saint, herself gives her rooms in the palace. Aladdin is out hunting again, for the sixth day. The false Fatima looks round the hall and says humbly: "As far as a recluse who knows nothing of what the world calls beautiful can judge, one thing is missing here." A roc's egg hanging from the dome.

Aladdin comes home to find his wife a little cool. "I believed, as you did, that our palace was the most magnificent and perfect in the world," she says, and now the palace lacks an egg. Aladdin answers with a sentence that holds the Empress's whole common language: "It is enough that you find a roc's egg missing here for me to find the same flaw." He rubs the lamp, and the genie lets out a cry that shakes the hall: "Is it not enough that my companions and I have done everything for you — and now you demand that I bring you my master and hang him in the middle of this dome?" The wish, the genie explains, came not from them but from an enemy in disguise.

This is a precise drawing of how a 3-16-4 couple's entry turns into resistance. Danger arrives not as an enemy but as modest advice from under someone else's veil: "everyone has one already", "the home only lacks…", "you have to, for the children". A couple whose common language is abundance picks the wish up at once: if you want it, then so do I. The genie hears sacrilege in the request: to hang under the dome his own master, the power he himself serves. In the same way the last thing "for perfect completeness" can demand that a couple hang under the dome the very source of everything else: strength, money, the freedom of one of the two. Waite describes the Hermit reversed with the words "Concealment, disguise", and in the tale trouble comes a second time from a false hermit — again while the master is out hunting.

sections.h2: Main task — The Emperor: "They reigned together"
paragraphs: The main point of the tail is the couple's main task, and it is read mostly through its downside: what does not work and what has to be learned. Here it is the Emperor: power, structure, rules, responsibility. Waite's Emperor is "Stability, power, protection, realization… also authority and will". Waite himself stresses that this card and the Empress "do not precisely represent the condition of married life, though this state is implied", and in his historical survey he calls the Emperor "by imputation the spouse of the former". The tail 3-16-4 is the road from a queen to her husband, and it leads through the Tower.

Here is Galland's ending. A few years later the sultan dies at a great age. He has no sons, and the princess, "as lawful heir", succeeds him and shares the supreme power with Aladdin. "They reigned together for many years."

In Andrew Lang's "Blue Fairy Book" (1889), one of the best-known English retellings, the ending is shorter: "He succeeded the Sultan when he died, and reigned for many years." The heiress and the word "together" are gone. **The reteller did to the end of the tale what the Emperor at his worst does to a couple: one crown, one head.**

Wen offers a guess about the models for these two cards, and calls it speculation herself: the Empress as Joan I of Navarre, the Emperor as her husband Philip IV of France. The guess has the same shape as Galland's ending. Joan became Queen of Navarre in her own right before she was two; Philip ruled Navarre together with her. The kingdom comes through one, and two rule it.

What does this Emperor demand of a 3-16-4 couple? The downside of the Emperor that Lisovskaya describes shows up in such a couple as scenes. One partner runs the budget and announces decisions already made. A rule invented in a hard year gets in both partners' way five years later, yet dropping it feels like admitting weakness. "Are you upset?" is met with "I'm fine", and the argument about who is in charge replaces the conversation about what hurt. The tale adds one subtle point to the list. After Africa, Aladdin always carries the lamp on him, wherever he goes: the lesson has been learned as control, not as shared knowledge. And the next trouble comes through another door — through his wife's wish and a stranger's veil. One hand on the lamp does not save the house if the other partner does not know what holds it up.

The last clue comes from Scheherazade herself. Having finished the tale, she explains to her sultan husband what it teaches: a good and just monarch risks even losing his throne when "through unreasonable haste he condemns an innocent man without being willing to hear his defence". She means the father-in-law, who nearly beheaded Aladdin on the first morning after the palace disappeared. For a 3-16-4 couple this is the Emperor at his best: listen first, decide afterwards.

sections.h2: The Star in the centre: what Waite saw in the Hermit's lantern
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's matrix is the shared atmosphere, what lies between the two and is not on show. In every 3-16-4 couple the Star stands there, 17. No person ever has 17 in the centre: this card appears in the centre only for a couple. It is built from the partners' personal centres — Justice (8) for the owner of the tail 21-7-13 and the Hermit (9) for the owner of 9-9-18.

In the deck the Star comes straight after the Tower: the sixteenth card is the lightning, the seventeenth is the light that follows it. This couple's atmosphere is the card that arrives after the collapse.

And in his description of the Hermit, Waite left a sentence that links the middle of the tail to the couple's centre: "It is a star which shines in the lantern." The Hermit is the very card whose nine turned the Chariot into the Tower. His lantern is both the lamp on the cornice and the star in the centre. **The same knowledge, hidden with one partner, brings the palace down; shared between two, it becomes the light the couple lives in.**

Waite's divinatory list for the Star is split in two: "Loss, theft, privation, abandonment; another reading says—hope and bright prospects". The tale of Aladdin fits into that line: the theft of the lamp, the lost palace, the princess abandoned in Africa — and the hope with which Aladdin wakes under her window to birdsong.

Lisovskaya describes the Star in a couple's atmosphere in a way that echoes the whole task of the tail. At its best the union inspires both, and this is the rare case when the pretty picture really is the truth. At its worst come things left unsaid and an infatuation that takes no responsibility. The Star feels at home in a beautiful palace. The Emperor demands that the palace have a foundation both of them know about.

sections.h2: The couple's values: The Lovers or The Devil
paragraphs: The couple's values are one more answer to the question of what the two are together for. In 3-16-4 couples one of two cards stands there.

**The Lovers, 6 — in 75.5% of such couples.** Waite gives them the list "Attraction, love, beauty, trials overcome" and recalls an old title of the card, Simulacrum fidei, "the symbol of conjugal faith". This is the value of choice: the union holds because the two choose each other again, including after the Tower. In Africa the princess chooses Aladdin while the magician tells her every day that her husband is dead.

**The Devil, 15 — in 24.5%.** In Waite this card is "the chain and fatality of the material life". In the tale it has an exact double: the genie, who calls himself the slave "of all who have the lamp in hand". He serves Aladdin, he serves the magician — whoever holds the lamp. The strength of such a couple is that what they share holds them firmly: the home, the business, what they have built. The risk is that the couple starts serving its palace, while the palace serves whoever holds the lamp. Here the Emperor's task is sharpest of all: power in the home must not go to whoever grabs the lamp first.

sections.h2: How to recognise yourselves in this tale
paragraphs: The tale is not a prediction. The Tower in the tail does not promise that the home will vanish, nor the Emperor that someone will become a tyrant. It is the outline of a task, and it is usually recognised by small things.

ul: **The lamp on the cornice.** One of the two knows what holds the home up: where the documents and passwords are, how the payments and debts work, what was agreed with the landlord or the family, where the money in the shared business really comes from. They are not hiding it — it is just "safer this way" and "why burden you with it".
**The hunt.** The same person is often away: a project, business trips, a season, a big goal. The Chariot rides out after victories, and that is temperament, not a vice.

**The exchange in jest.** The other, not knowing that the "old" thing holds the home up, swaps it for something new in good faith: throws out papers that look useless, accepts a relative's generous offer, closes a "spare" account. It is all done lightly, sometimes with a laugh.
**The velvet carpet.** The family lives close by and admires the home from its own window; inside the home there is a place left to them "for the glory", and advice comes in through that place.
**The roc's egg.** The home always lacks one more thing, and one partner's wish instantly becomes both partners' wish.
**The empty space.** When the collapse comes, it looks less like a row than like a disappearance: nothing is smashed, and yet the old life is gone.

paragraphs: The roles are not fixed and have nothing to do with gender. Whoever holds the lamp today may swap someone else's lamp for a new one tomorrow. Recognising oneself in both roles is already half the task.

sections.h2: What changes the script: an inventory of lamps
paragraphs: The strong version of the tail 3-16-4 is Galland's ending: the same palace, ruled by two. In Lisovskaya the Emperor at his best is a couple whose rules suit both, where each has an area of responsibility and strictness never turns into fanaticism. For a 3-16-4 couple it is made of a few habits.

ul: **An inventory of lamps.** Every so often, list together what holds the home up: money, documents, access, obligations, agreements with the family. The point is not inspection but making sure no lamp stands on a cornice that only one partner knows about.
**Leaving? Leave a map.** Before the "hunt", say where things are and what must not be changed without a call. One sentence would have been enough for Aladdin.
**Rules for two — with a review date.** The Emperor at his worst makes rules that later get in the way. A rule the couple wrote itself, it can also rewrite.
**After a collapse, the formula from Africa.** Do not look for a culprit; take your share of the blame and go straight to the plan: "let us think only of how to repair".
**The roc's egg test.** Before adding the last thing "for perfect completeness", ask whose wish it is and who suggested it.
**Listen first, decide afterwards.** Scheherazade's rule for a monarch works in any kitchen where decisions are made for two.

paragraphs: If threats, pressure or fear for each other appear in the home, this is no longer a tale about a lamp or a task of the tail. Then a psychologist is needed, and in danger a local emergency number or crisis line.

ul: **Entry to the task — 3, The Empress.** What the couple wants together: a home, prosperity, growth, everything big and everything at once. This is their common language, and it turns into resistance when the wishes outgrow the foundations.
**Middle of the task — 16, The Tower.** How the couple travels the road: through a sudden collapse. What falls is whatever rested on a secret that one kept out of caution and the other never knew.
**Main task — 4, The Emperor.** What the couple has to learn: shared order, rules and power agreed by both; responsibility without despotism and without hunting for someone to blame.

intro: This couple's plot was written down long ago, and everyone knows it. Aladdin's palace rose in a single night and vanished in a single night, while its master was out hunting and his wife, laughing, handed a street trader an old lamp from the cornice, not knowing that the whole palace rested on it. What follows is an investigation: clues in the numbers, in Waite and Wen, and in the first, French text of the tale, whose ending is not the one in the children's version.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 3-16-4 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the task of a couple who enter the relationship with a shared wish for a home and abundance (The Empress, 3), pass through a sudden collapse of what rested on one partner's knowledge and the other's ignorance (The Tower, 16), and learn to build shared order and share power (The Emperor, 4). The tail exists only for couples, roughly one in 1,712.

faq.q: Why is the Tower in the middle and not the Chariot, if 3 + 4 = 7?
faq.a: The middle of a couple's tail is not worked out from the outer numbers: it is built from the middles of the partners' personal tails. For every 3-16-4 couple this is 7 + 9 = 16 — one partner's Chariot and the other's Hermit. By the rules of reduction, only 7 or 16 can stand between 3 and 4; the variant with the Chariot, 3-7-4, occurs eight times more often.

faq.q: Does the tail 3-16-4 occur in a personal matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail is the sum of the main task and the centre, and with a main task of 4 an entry of 3 is impossible whatever the centre. 3-16-4 is a tail of the couple's matrix only, and in every such couple it is built from the personal tails 21-7-13 and 9-9-18.

faq.q: Does the Tower mean the couple is heading for a break-up?
faq.a: No. The matrix does not predict events or dates. The Tower in the middle of the tail describes how the couple lives its task: through rethinking what holds the home up. In the tale of Aladdin the palace comes back, and two people rule it.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. Out of 3, 16 and 4 a couple's matrix forms only the order 3-16-4. The closest in meaning is 3-7-4: the same entry and the same main task, but with the Chariot in the middle.

faq.q: Who in the couple is Aladdin, and who is the princess?
faq.a: Either partner, and the roles change. The numbers speak about the couple, not about gender: the Chariot and the Hermit come from the partners' personal tails, but in real life both get to keep the lamp on the cornice and both get to swap it for a new one.

report: Aladdin's palace rose in a single night and vanished in a single night — while its master was out hunting and his wife, laughing, handed a street trader an old lamp from the cornice, not knowing that the whole palace rested on it. In the children's version this is a tale about a boy and a genie. In Antoine Galland's first, French text it is the story of a marriage, and it runs exactly in the order of the three cards of the tail 3-16-4: The Empress, The Tower, The Emperor. The queen and king of the major arcana, whom an old tradition takes for husband and wife, with lightning between them.

The entry to the task is the Empress, and the common language of a 3-16-4 couple is abundance. A home they want furnished at once, gifts instead of words, plans in which everything is big. Galland gives this wish a shape: a palace built overnight opposite the sultan's palace, with a velvet carpet from the father-in-law's door and one window that Aladdin deliberately left unfinished "for the glory" of the sultan, concealing the real reason. Waite's Empress is "Fruitfulness, action, initiative" and, in the same line, "the unknown, clandestine; also difficulty, doubt, ignorance". A palace and ignorance in one card.

report.h3: The chariot drove off, the lantern stayed

report: The riddle of the tail is in the middle. Add the outer numbers the ordinary way, 3 + 4 = 7, and the Chariot would stand between the Empress and the Emperor. And the Chariot is here: it stands in the middle of one partner's personal tail. The other partner brings a Hermit to the same point, and 7 + 9 make 16. **This couple's Tower is built from a chariot that drives off and a lantern that stays at home.**

Waite's Chariot is "Succour, providence; also war, triumph, presumption", and its conquests are "manifest or external". The Hermit reversed is "Concealment, disguise, policy, fear, unreasoned caution." One rides out after victories, the other guards something and keeps quiet. Taken apart, these are just two temperaments, and in real life both partners get to play both parts. Added together at one point, they make lightning.

report.h3: The lamp on the cornice

report: Aladdin goes hunting for eight days. The lamp on which everything rests he puts on the cornice himself, "for fear of losing it"; the rest of the time he carries it on him, and no one in the house knows what that lamp is. A madman appears under the windows: "Who will exchange old lamps for new?" The maids roar with laughter, and the princess, in Galland's words, "went along with the joke". At night the palace, with her inside it, is carried off to Africa.

Here Galland stops and speaks to the reader: "It will be said that Aladdin's precaution was a good one, but that he should at least have locked the lamp away. That is true; but such mistakes have been made in every age, they are made still, and they will never stop being made." In the morning the sultan sees an empty space where the palace stood, "just as it was before anything was built there": no heap of stone, no trace. **This couple's Tower is often exactly that: from outside nothing is broken, and yet the old home is gone.**

Neither of the two caused the collapse. One held the house's support and, leaving, put it where it could not be seen — out of caution, not cunning. The other did not know it was a support and, in a good-faith joke, swapped the old for the new. In real life the lamp can be anything: documents and passwords, how the debts and payments work, an agreement with the family, an understanding of where the money in a shared business comes from. It is kept not out of malice but because it is "safer this way" and there seems no need to burden the other with it.

report.h3: "It is all mine"

report: Aladdin finds the princess in Africa, and a dialogue follows that children's versions cut down to a single line. She: "I did suspect that our shared misfortune came from that lamp, and what torments me most is that I am the cause of it myself!" He: "Do not take the blame; it is all mine — I should have kept it more carefully. Let us think only of how to repair this loss."

Each takes the blame, and so there is no longer any need to look for a culprit. A plan with roles appears at once. At supper the princess offers the magician an exchange of cups, and the fairy-tale villain gets what he deserves. **The first exchange she made without knowing what it meant, and the palace vanished. The second she made understanding it better than anyone at the table, and the palace came back.** Later she will tell her father about the measures they took "jointly".

report.h3: They reigned together

report: The main task is the Emperor: power, rules, responsibility. At his worst he is recognised by scenes: one partner runs the budget and announces decisions already made; a rule from a hard year gets in both partners' way five years later; the argument about who is in charge replaces the conversation about what hurt. After Africa, Aladdin always carries the lamp on him — the lesson has been learned as control, and the next trouble comes through another door.

Through that door comes the Empress's second face. While Aladdin is out hunting again, an enemy disguised in the dress of a holy recluse settles in the palace and lets drop that the hall lacks "one thing" — a roc's egg hanging from the dome. Now the princess wants the egg, and Aladdin at once finds the same flaw: whatever she lacks, he lacks too. The shared wish instantly becomes resistance, and the genie, with a cry, refuses to hang his own master under the dome. The last thing "for perfect completeness" can demand the very source of the couple's strength as its price.

Galland's ending: the sultan dies, the princess, "as lawful heir", takes the throne and shares the supreme power with Aladdin. "They reigned together for many years." In Andrew Lang's well-known English retelling what remains is "He succeeded the Sultan when he died, and reigned for many years." **The reteller did to the end of the tale what the Emperor at his worst does to a couple: one crown, one head.**

The strong version of the tail is Galland's ending. Every so often, list together what holds the home up, so that no lamp stands on a cornice only one partner knows about. When leaving, leave a map: where things are and what must not be changed without a call. Write the rules together and review them. After a collapse, the formula from Africa: one's own share of the blame, then straight to the plan. Before the last thing "for perfect completeness", ask whose wish it is. And the rule Scheherazade draws for a monarch: listen first, decide afterwards.
If threats, pressure or fear for each other appear in the home, this is no longer a task of the tail: a psychologist is needed then, and in danger a local emergency number or crisis line.
