seo.title: Karmic tail 3 22 10 compatibility: waiting for something to turn up
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 22 10 compatibility: The Empress, The Fool and The Wheel of Fortune in a couple, read through Lisovskaya, Waite and Dickens's Micawbers.

items.title: The 3-22-10 karmic tail in compatibility: a home, a leap and a wheel
items.short: The Empress, The Fool and The Wheel of Fortune turn up together in compatibility for roughly one couple in 111. It is the tail of a union that wants a home and plenty (3), travels towards it light, from despair to cheerfulness in half an hour (22), and has one thing to learn: not to wait for the wheel to turn by itself (10). The riddle sits in the middle: neither partner has The Fool in their personal tail; it is born only in the couple. And the most exact portrait of such a union was written by Dickens: Mr and Mrs Micawber, whose motto is "in case anything turned up".

sections.h2: The riddle: a Fool that neither partner has
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's tail is the sum of the same points in two personal charts. So for any of its cards one can find out what it is made of. The 3-22-10 tail can be assembled in only two ways, and both say the same thing.

In 97% of such couples one partner has the personal tail 12-16-4 and the other 18-6-6. The entry is built from 12 and 18 (30 → 3), the middle from 16 and 6, the main task from 4 and 6. Neither The Empress, nor The Fool, nor The Wheel appears in these people's personal tails. Another 3% of couples have the personal tails 21-10-7 and 9-12-3: here the partners already carry The Wheel and The Empress, but still not The Fool — it is made from 10 and 12.

So the lightness with which this couple jumps from trouble to celebration is not "his" trait or "hers". It is weather that the two create only together. When one blames the other for being careless, the tail disagrees: neither partner has The Fool in their personal tail.

The second oddity is arithmetic. In a personal chart the middle of the tail equals the sum of its ends, and between 3 and 10 there would stand 13, Death. In a couple the middle is added up from the middles of two people, so the result is 22. As a personal tail the triple 3-22-10 does not exist: no single person has this story, only a union does.
Dickens noticed this long before any matrix. Having described Mr Micawber weeping at supper and then planning an extension at bedtime, he added one sentence: "And Mrs. Micawber was just the same."

sections.h2: The Micawbers: a family waiting for something to turn up
paragraphs: In David Copperfield (1849–1850) young David lodges with the Micawbers in London. The centre of the street door is covered with "a great brass-plate, on which was engraved 'Mrs. Micawber's Boarding Establishment for Young Ladies'". Only, Dickens writes, "I never found that any young lady had ever been to school there; or that any young lady ever came, or proposed to come". Creditors came instead.

Mr Micawber could "come home to supper with a flood of tears, and a declaration that nothing was now left but a jail", and then "go to bed making a calculation of the expense of putting bow-windows to the house, 'in case anything turned up', which was his favourite expression". Mrs Micawber could be "thrown into fainting fits by the king's taxes at three o'clock, and to eat lamb chops, breaded, and drink warm ale (paid for with two tea-spoons that had gone to the pawnbroker's) at four". She almost always had one of the twins in her arms.

Then come the debtors' prison and release under the Insolvent Debtors Act, Plymouth, where the relations received them coolly, coal on the River Medway, Canterbury, corn on commission, service under Uriah Heep, the exposure of Heep and, at last, Australia. And through all of it runs one sentence of Mrs Micawber's, repeated at every turn: "I never will desert Mr. Micawber."

The Micawbers are not invented. Dickens drew them from his own parents. His father, John Dickens, was imprisoned for debt in London's Marshalsea in 1824, and there he told his twelve-year-old son the very rule Micawber would later repeat: twenty pounds a year in income and nineteen pounds nineteen shillings and sixpence spent is happiness, a shilling the other way is wretchedness. His mother, Elizabeth Dickens, decided to save the family with a school, and a brass plate reading "Mrs. Dickens's Establishment" appeared on the door of a house in Gower Street. "Yet nobody ever came to school," Dickens recalled in the autobiographical fragment published by his friend and biographer John Forster. "Under similar disguises my own father and mother are in my books," Dickens admitted himself. And later he said of his father: "The longer I live, the better man I think him."

This matters for reading the tail. The Micawbers are funny, but they are written with love, and there is no culprit in their story. Nor are there roles by gender: in a 3-22-10 couple either partner can turn out to be "Mr Micawber", and more often both take turns. The novel is not a forecast but a mirror: it shows how the circle works and how they got out of it.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: The Empress and the language of home
paragraphs: Lisovskaya calls this point what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, a "common language". And she warns that the point stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish can also become resistance. On the site this couple sees The Empress twice: at the entry to the tail and in the sphere "Relationship and common language".

The Micawbers' common language is the language of home. There is nothing to eat, and Mrs Micawber talks about the larder: "I was accustomed to speak of the larder when I lived with papa and mama, and I use the word almost unconsciously. What I mean to express is, that there is nothing to eat in the house." Mr Micawber has his eye on a terrace fronting Hyde Park and wonders where to throw out a bow-window or carry up the roof another storey. Twins, boarding school, bow-window, terrace — all of it is The Empress, the wish for a full cup. On this subject the two never argue.

Wen has a short formula for The Empress: "She produces. She makes things happen." The Micawbers' brass plate is The Empress turned inside out: the sign of a home instead of a home, the board of a school nobody will ever attend. Wen describes The Empress reversed almost as this scene: "Efforts of creation and innovation won't yield results. There is a sense of emptiness and no production after much work and effort."

But the main clue lies in Waite's divinatory list. For The Empress it begins brightly: "Fruitfulness, action, initiative, length of days". And it ends in shadow: "the unknown, clandestine; also difficulty, doubt, ignorance". Now Mrs Micawber, on the evening the court released her husband: "Mr. Micawber may have concealed his difficulties from me in the first instance… I do not deny that he has kept me in the dark as to his resources and his liabilities both." **Concealed, difficulties, in the dark: the shadow half of one card in one speech.** In the novel "difficulties" is the family word for debts: "When I lived at home with papa and mama, I really should have hardly understood what the word meant, in the sense in which I now employ it."

This is how the entry becomes resistance. A 3-22-10 couple talks easily about the home, and that is exactly why the home is such a convenient place to hide the bills. An evening on the sofa: the two choose kitchen tiles for a flat whose first instalment has not yet been paid, and it is a happy evening. Nobody raises the overdue payment: it would spoil the language in which they feel so good. In Lisovskaya, The Empress's tasks for a couple include surviving "feast or famine", learning to be practical and getting out from under the relatives' influence. With the Micawbers all three appear in a single chapter: feast and famine on the same day, a boarding school without a single pupil instead of a business, and "my family" deciding where they should go.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: The Fool, or elasticity
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya this point has no meaning of its own: it is an addition to the main task. The site reads it as the path — what the couple does and goes through between the wish and the task. This is our reading, and in 3-22-10 the path runs through The Fool.

Dickens found the exact word for it: elasticity. After a creditor's visit Mr Micawber "would be transported with grief and mortification", "but within half-an-hour afterwards, he would polish up his shoes with extraordinary pains, and go out, humming a tune". On the day of his arrest he told David that "the God of day had now gone down upon him" — "But I heard, afterwards, that he was seen to play a lively game at skittles, before noon." The Fool measures distance in his own way: Micawber set off for Canterbury as if for the farthest limits of the earth, and for Australia as if for a little trip across the Channel. "The distance is quite imaginary."

Waite calls The Fool "the spirit in search of experience", and in the divinatory list puts first "Folly, mania, extravagance". Mrs Micawber, without disowning her husband, admits exactly this: "I do not deny that he is improvident." Lisovskaya describes The Fool in a couple with the same two sides. With him it is easy to start from nothing, find a way out, laugh, set off on the road. It is hard when it comes to serious steps that need boundaries and responsibility. A 3-22-10 couple recognises itself in both halves. Three moves in five years, and every time "this one is for good". The last money spent on a celebration because "we deserve it". Laughter on the hardest evening, which has saved the union more than once.

The Fool also has a leap. Micawber uses the word himself: "You find me, fallen back, FOR a spring; and I have every reason to believe that a vigorous leap will shortly be the result." Wen places The Fool at the edge of a cliff: the next step "could either send the Seeker flying into the air over that cliff with impressive accomplishment or falling down hard from naïveté"; before him is a choice "between two forks in the path". The Micawbers leapt twice, and the novel shows both forks. The first leap was an advertisement in all the papers, "Now employ me, on remunerative terms", paid for with a new bill; Uriah Heep answered it. The second was Australia. What separates one leap from the other is something a 3-22-10 couple spends its whole life finding out, and the answer lies in the main task.

sections.h2: Main task: the Wheel they wait for
paragraphs: Lisovskaya reads the main task mostly through its downside: what does not work for the couple and what it has to learn. The Wheel of Fortune in a couple means cycles: rises and falls follow each other, and the struggle is not with the change itself but with how the couple meets it. On the downside: a seesaw of "silence and conflict", life in debt, the habit of blaming fate, the feeling that being together is hard and yet something holds them.

Micawber's motto is a ready formula for this downside. In English it reads "in case anything turned up", and "turn up" is also what a card does when it is turned over from the pack: to "turn up trumps". In the same chapter Dickens himself slips into the language of cards: Micawber goes in for "anything that might be on the cards". The Russian translators, A. V. Krivtsova and Yevgeny Lann, rendered it "esli schastye ulybnyotsya", "if happiness smiles". And happiness, felicity, is the last word in Waite's list for the Wheel: "Destiny, fortune, success, elevation, luck, felicity." **In both languages the couple's motto is a Wheel that is supposed to turn by itself.**
Yet Waite explains the Wheel the other way round: behind the symbol, he writes, "there lies the denial of chance". The Micawbers live as if there were nothing but chance.

Wen compares the wheel to the unit circle of trigonometry: sine and cosine reveal "the philosophy of oscillations between zeniths and nadirs". With the Micawbers the oscillation can be read off the clock: fainting at three, lamb chops at four. It even has an exact amplitude — the famous rule: "Annual income twenty pounds, annual expenditure nineteen nineteen and six, result happiness. Annual income twenty pounds, annual expenditure twenty pounds ought and six, result misery." Between happiness and misery lies one shilling. On the downside a 3-22-10 couple lives exactly on this line and keeps stepping over it by sixpence.

The most exact scene of the downside is the day of release from prison. David expects a celebration, but the Micawbers are inconsolable: "Mr. and Mrs. Micawber were so used to their old difficulties, I think, that they felt quite shipwrecked when they came to consider that they were released from them." **This is the Wheel's trap: the seesaw becomes home.** A quiet month feels suspicious, a quarrel and reconciliation feel like proof of love, and money enters the conversation only when the bank calls. And the one to blame is always someone else: the Custom House, where "they would rather NOT have a man of Mr. Micawber's abilities", the relations in Plymouth, society. The Micawbers never blame each other — that is their strength. But they blame fate all the time.

sections.h2: The turn: "assist to turn them up"
paragraphs: The formula for the way out comes from Mrs Micawber, in the chapter called "Mr. Micawber's Gauntlet": "I am convinced, myself, and this I have pointed out to Mr. Micawber several times of late, that things cannot be expected to turn up of themselves. We must, in a measure, assist to turn them up." **This is the main task of the 3-22-10 tail in one sentence: from "in case anything turned up" to "assist to turn them up".**

But the first attempt fails, and the novel shows honestly why. Mrs Micawber's way of assisting is to throw down the gauntlet to society, advertise in all the papers and, since advertising is expensive, raise the money "on a bill". It is still waiting, only louder, and still debt. The gauntlet was taken up by Uriah Heep. Micawber sends David a solemn letter: "something has turned up". Later he reads aloud a different letter: his salary from Heep was "the pittance of twenty-two shillings and six per week", the advances from Heep "were secured by I.O.U.'s", "And that I thus became immeshed in the web he had spun for my reception?" What turned up by itself turned out to be a hook.

Micawber gets out of the web not by chance but by an act: he gathers evidence against Heep and exposes him in front of everyone. The secret that held him stops being a secret. After that David's aunt suggests Australia. Mrs Micawber asks whether there will be room for her husband's talents, and hears that there is "no better opening anywhere, for a man who conducts himself well, and is industrious". She repeats the words like a formula: "Precisely." And before sailing she says the main thing: "I wish Mr. Micawber… to be the Caesar of his own fortunes."

How it all ended Dickens reports through an Australian newspaper. Micawber worked in the Bush so hard that, in Mr Peggotty's words, his bald head was "a perspiring in the sun… till I a'most thowt it would have melted away"; in the original Peggotty's highest praise is that he "turned to with a will" (the Russian translation drops the phrase). He paid off every debt he had left in England, "even to Traddles's bill". Now he is Port Middlebay District Magistrate, and in his speech at a public dinner he warns the young against the shoals of "pecuniary liabilities which they were unable to liquidate".

The Wheel turned after the couple stopped waiting for it. The strong version of the 3-22-10 tail loses neither The Empress nor The Fool: in Australia the Micawbers still love dinners, songs and fine words, and the family is as big and noisy as ever — at the dinner in the father's honour the son sings. Only one thing changes: who turns the wheel.

sections.h2: Centre and values: the family court and the choice that gets reread
paragraphs: Every couple with this tail has 20, Judgement, at the centre. The centre of a couple is the atmosphere inside the union, what is not on show. In Lisovskaya the key to Judgement in a couple is lineage and family: relatives, traditions, the influence of parents.

In the Micawbers' home this court sits all the time. "My family" is what Mrs Micawber calls her relations, and she "always said those two words with an air, though I never could discover who came under the denomination". The family decides that Mr Micawber must go to Plymouth, the family recommends coal, the family does not answer letters. "Papa and mama" keep coming up in her speech. Even the wedding was hurried by papa's maxim "never do tomorrow what you can do today", and Micawber sighs that the marriage "was so far prematurely entered into, in consequence, that I never recovered the expense". The downside of Judgement in a couple is living under the relatives' eye and checking every decision against their verdict. The upside sounds on the last evening before sailing, when Mrs Micawber speaks of her children's children: "However vigorous the sapling, I cannot forget the parent-tree." The family stops being a judge and becomes a root.
The couple's values are another answer to the question of what this union is for. In 73% of such couples this point holds The Lovers, in 27% The Devil.

The Lovers are a choice. Before leaving for Canterbury Mrs Micawber tells how, the night before, she read the marriage service over by candlelight, with the words "I, Emma, take thee, Wilkins", and drew her conclusion: "that I never could desert Mr. Micawber". A choice made once she makes again — from the text, like an exam. When The Lovers stand in the values, the union rests on this repeated "yes".

The Devil is what binds. Young David kept hearing about a certain "Deed" in the Micawber house and was "conscious of having confounded it with those demoniacal parchments which are held to have, once upon a time, obtained to a great extent in Germany". Then came the I.O.U.s and Heep's "web". If The Devil stands in the values, the couple has to tell two kinds of ties apart: those that hold them together and those that hold them on a leash.

paragraphs.h3: Coincidences that are not clues

paragraphs: These couples have the twentieth arcanum at the centre, and Micawber's rule starts with twenty pounds. Heep paid him twenty-two shillings and sixpence a week — for the leap that turned into a fall — and the couple's Fool carries the number 22. Mrs Micawber once declares that her husband has "the judicial mind", and the novel ends with him becoming a magistrate — under a centre called Judgement. Dickens knew nothing of the destiny matrix, and no conclusions are drawn from these numbers here. But they are hard not to notice.

sections.h2: What helps a couple with the 3-22-10 tail
paragraphs: Not a recipe, but what can be seen in the cards themselves and in the novel:

ul: **Name your own "twenty pounds".** The month's sum and the line beyond which debt begins are shared knowledge, not one person's secret.
**Do not keep each other "in the dark".** Talk about money on a schedule, once a month, not when the bank calls. The Empress is strong when her house stands on the truth.

**Check the fork before the leap.** An advertisement on borrowed money and a ticket to Australia with a plan of work are both leaps. There is one question: is this a step towards the work or one more way of waiting?
**Assist things to turn up.** One concrete step a week instead of "if only": call, send, count.
**Do not mistake the seesaw for closeness.** A calm month is not a shipwreck. If the two are bored without a crisis, that is the Wheel's habit, not a measure of love.
**Keep the lightness.** Laughter and the knack of starting from nothing are this couple's strength. They need no correcting, only a direction.
**Keep the promise "I never will desert" — but not as a vow of silence.** Loyalty and honesty about the bills do not get in each other's way.

paragraphs: If the debts no longer fit into the family budget, that is work for a lawyer or a financial adviser, not for waiting. Micawber, too, was let out of prison not by chance but by the Insolvent Debtors Act.

sections.h2: Worked example: 14.04.1975 and 04.07.1975
paragraphs: A couple's tail is not recalculated from its two end numbers: each of its points is added up from the same points of two personal charts and reduced to 22. A person born on 14.04.1975 has the personal tail 12-16-4, a person born on 04.07.1975 has 18-6-6.

If the middle were calculated by the personal formula, it would be 3 + 10 = 13, Death. In a couple it is added up from the middles of two people: 16 + 6 = 22. This couple's centre is 20 (8 + 12), Judgement, and its values are The Lovers.

sections.h2: How 3-22-10 differs from its neighbours
paragraphs: This tail has no permutations: among couples' tails the numbers 3, 22 and 10 occur only in this order. But it has two neighbours with the same ends. By our count over all dates from 1900 to 2025, the tail 3-4-10 occurs in about 1% of couples and 3-13-10 in 0.44%. All three share one wish, a home and plenty, and one task, keeping their footing on the Wheel. The road differs: through The Emperor's order, through Death's ending of the old, or through The Fool's leap.

The Fool in the middle of a couple's tail is rare in general: it stands there in about 4 couples out of 100, and only five tails have it. In 3-22-10 it is especially striking, because neither partner has it in their personal tail.

sections.h2: Sources

ul: Charles Dickens, David Copperfield (1849–1850): chapters 11–12, 17, 27–28, 52, 57 and 63; the Russian translation by A. V. Krivtsova and Yevgeny Lann for the Russian wording of the motto.
John Forster, The Life of Charles Dickens (1872–1874), volume I: Dickens's autobiographical fragment on the Marshalsea and the school in Gower Street.
A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910): The Empress, The Fool, The Wheel of Fortune.
Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015): The Empress, The Fool, The Wheel of Fortune.
Yuliana Lisovskaya, Matritsa sudby: sovmestimost (Destiny Matrix: Compatibility, 2024): the meaning of a couple's points, energies 3, 10, 20 and 22.
Frequencies and combinations: a run over all dates with the site's engine.

**3 · The Empress — entry to the task.** What the couple wants together: a home, a full larder, a family, growth. It is also their common language: the two agree most easily when they talk about the home.

**22 · The Fool — middle of the task.** How the couple moves towards the goal: lightly, in leaps, with moves and fresh starts from nothing. The lightness rescues them in a crisis and fails them when a long stride is needed.

**10 · The Wheel of Fortune — main task.** Ups and downs follow each other in this couple. The task is to stop waiting for the turn and learn to turn the wheel themselves, without letting go of each other's hands.

faq.q: What does the 3-22-10 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: These are the couple's tasks in three cards. The Empress at the entry is the shared wish for a home, plenty and a family. The Fool in the middle is a light path of leaps and fresh starts. The Wheel of Fortune as the main task is learning to go through ups and downs together without waiting for things to sort themselves out.

faq.q: Why is The Fool in the middle if 3 + 10 = 13?
faq.a: That is how a personal tail is calculated. In a couple's chart each point is the sum of the same points of two people, and the middle is added up from their middles: for example, 16 + 6 = 22. That is why a single person never has the 3-22-10 tail.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail shows a task, not a verdict. On its downside it resembles the Micawbers' life on the seesaw, on its upside their Australia: the same lightness and the same full house, but they turn the wheel themselves.

faq.q: Does the 3-22-10 tail mean debts?
faq.a: No. The cards do not establish anyone's financial situation. The Wheel speaks of change and of how the couple meets it, and money is simply where this shows most often.

faq.q: Who plays Mr Micawber in the couple?
faq.a: Either partner, or both by turns. The cards do not assign roles by gender, and in this tail neither partner has The Fool on their own — it belongs to both.

report: On the Micawbers' street door hung a great brass plate: "Mrs. Micawber's Boarding Establishment for Young Ladies". Not a single young lady ever came; only creditors did. Dickens drew this family for David Copperfield from his own parents, and the result is the most exact portrait of a couple with the 3-22-10 tail. The Empress at the entry is the shared wish for a home and a full cup. The Fool in the middle is a path travelled light, from despair to cheerfulness in half an hour. The Wheel of Fortune as the main task is change, which the couple has grown used to waiting for and must learn to turn itself.

report.h3: A home where the bills hide in the conversation

report: This couple's common language is the language of home. There is nothing to eat, and Mrs Micawber talks about the larder: "I was accustomed to speak of the larder when I lived with papa and mama, and I use the word almost unconsciously." Mr Micawber comes home to supper "with a flood of tears, and a declaration that nothing was now left but a jail", and at bedtime calculates "the expense of putting bow-windows to the house, 'in case anything turned up'". About the home the two never argue.

But in Waite's divinatory list The Empress has a shadow half: "the unknown, clandestine; also difficulty, doubt, ignorance". Mrs Micawber speaks it almost whole in a single speech: "Mr. Micawber may have concealed his difficulties from me in the first instance… I do not deny that he has kept me in the dark as to his resources and his liabilities both." **Concealed, difficulties, in the dark: the shadow half of one card in one speech.** This is how the wish becomes resistance. Choosing kitchen tiles for a flat whose first instalment has not been paid is easy and joyful. Nobody raises the overdue payment: it would spoil the language in which the two feel so good.

report: For The Fool, Dickens found the exact word: elasticity. After a creditor's visit Mr Micawber "would be transported with grief and mortification", "but within half-an-hour afterwards, he would polish up his shoes with extraordinary pains, and go out, humming a tune". And Dickens added at once: "And Mrs. Micawber was just the same." The couple's tail says the same thing: neither partner has The Fool in their personal tail; it is born only when the two are together. Blaming each other for carelessness makes no sense — this is weather the two create themselves.

The Fool rescues: with him it is easy to start from nothing and laugh on the hardest evening. And he fails when a long stride is needed. The Fool also has a leap, and Micawber names it himself: he has only "fallen back, FOR a spring". The novel shows two leaps. The first is an advertisement in all the papers, paid for with a new bill. Uriah Heep answered it, and Micawber "became immeshed in the web he had spun for my reception". The second leap is Australia.

report.h3: When the seesaw becomes home

report: In English Micawber's motto reads "in case anything turned up", and "turn up" is also what a card does when it is turned over from the pack. The Russian translation has "if happiness smiles", and felicity is the last word in Waite's list for the Wheel. **In both languages the couple's motto is a Wheel that is supposed to turn by itself.** Waite himself writes that behind the symbol of the Wheel "there lies the denial of chance".

The price shows in Micawber's famous rule: "Annual income twenty pounds, annual expenditure nineteen nineteen and six, result happiness. The most exact scene is the day Micawber is let out of the debtors' prison. Instead of celebrating, the two are inconsolable: they "were so used to their old difficulties, I think, that they felt quite shipwrecked when they came to consider that they were released from them". **This is the Wheel's trap: the seesaw becomes home.** A quiet month feels suspicious, and money enters the conversation only when the bank calls. The Micawbers never blame each other — that is their strength. But they blame fate all the time.

report.h3: "We must assist to turn them up"

report: The way out is put into words by Mrs Micawber: "things cannot be expected to turn up of themselves. We must, in a measure, assist to turn them up." **This is the main task of the 3-22-10 tail in one sentence: from "in case anything turned up" to "assist to turn them up".** The first attempt, an advertisement on borrowed money, turned out to be the same waiting, only louder. The turn began with an act: Micawber gathered evidence against Heep and exposed him in front of everyone. Before sailing, his wife said the main thing: "I wish Mr. Micawber… to be the Caesar of his own fortunes." In Australia Micawber works in the Bush, pays off every debt he left in England and becomes Port Middlebay District Magistrate. The dinners, songs and fine words stay with him. Only one thing changes: who turns the wheel.
What the cards and the novel show:

ul: name the couple's own "twenty pounds" — the month's sum and the line beyond which debt begins — and let both know it;
keep no one "in the dark": talk about money on a schedule, not when the bank calls;
check the fork before a leap: is it a step towards the work or one more way of waiting;

report: The vow "I never will desert Mr. Micawber" remains the main strength of such a couple — as long as it is a promise of loyalty and not a vow of silence about the bills.

seo.title: Karmic tail 3 22 19 compatibility: from the garden into the sun
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 22 19 compatibility: The Empress at the entry, The Fool in the middle, The Sun as the main task, read through the Song of Songs, with an example.

items.title: Karmic tail 3-22-19 in compatibility: out of the enclosed garden into the sun
items.short: The Song of Songs has a verse that holds this whole tail. A young woman asks not to be stared at: "Look not upon me, because I am black, because the sun hath looked upon me: my mother's children were angry with me; they made me the keeper of the vineyards; but mine own vineyard have I not kept." In the next line she asks her beloved where he rests "at noon", "for why should I be as one that turneth aside", a stray among the flocks. The vineyard is The Empress, the sun is The Sun, the stray is The Fool. Karmic tail 3-22-19 in compatibility describes a couple whose task is to bring their love out of a closed garden into daylight and still keep a vineyard of one's own for each of them.

sections.h2: A book in which a couple speaks in two voices
paragraphs: The Song of Songs is eight short chapters, and almost all of it is a conversation between two people. The title itself is built like "Holy of Holies": a superlative, the finest of songs. She calls, he answers, and they describe each other in the same words: he tells her "thou hast doves' eyes", she says of him, "His eyes are as the eyes of doves by the rivers of waters". Out of such echoes a couple's common language grows. On the compatibility chart the common language sits on the same point as the entry to the task.

There is no running plot in the book, only scenes. But read in order, they follow the order of this tail. The opening has vineyards, "a garden inclosed" and a mother's house. The middle has a roe leaping on the mountains, night searches through the city and a door opened too late. The ending has the sun, a seal upon the heart and the line "My vineyard, which is mine, is before me", which answers the complaint of the first chapter.

The speakers are a woman and a man, but the roles of the tail are not divided by sex. In a living couple either of the two can be the one who calls "Rise up… and come away" and the one who did not open the door in time.

sections.h2: Earth, air, fire
paragraphs: The first clue lies in the elements. Benebell Wen gives each card an element: for her The Empress is governed by Earth, The Fool by Air, The Sun by Fire. The Song of Songs follows the same order. First comes earth bearing fruit behind a fence: "A garden inclosed is my sister, my spouse; a spring shut up, a fountain sealed." Then air, and no stranger opens the garden: the bride calls the wind herself. "Awake, O north wind; and come, thou south; blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out." At the end comes fire: "the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame. Many waters cannot quench love".

For a couple this is a route through three states. At first love can be touched: home, food, things, a shared household. Then it cannot be held: it is on the road, in change, in the wind. At the end it shines and warms, and if there is too much fire, it burns. Wen makes the centre of this couple a fire card too: Strength, she writes, is governed by Fire. The atmosphere and the main task burn with one flame.

The second clue lies in Waite's divinatory lists. Under The Empress he has "the unknown, clandestine". Under The Fool, "bewrayment", an old word usually glossed as the revealing of a secret. The Sun he calls direct light, "the antithesis of the reflected light". Secret, disclosure, daylight: the same road the couple of the Song of Songs walks.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: honey and milk under the tongue
paragraphs: "Thy lips, O my spouse, drop as the honeycomb: honey and milk are under thy tongue". What lies under this couple's tongue is food, garden and harvest. The love talk of the book is rural through and through: vineyards, pomegranates, fig trees, lilies, spikenard and saffron. Love here is measured in fruit, not in vows.

The entry to the task is what the couple wants together and where their shared road begins. With The Empress it is a wish for fullness. The two quickly start speaking the language of care: who cooked what, what to buy for the house, what the kitchen will look like, where to go out of town at the weekend. Lisovskaya sums up the Three in three words, fertility, abundance and growth, and holds that the couple met for the sake of the area where these will grow. For some it is a family and a shared table, for others a business that lifts both of them within a couple of years, for others a house out of town instead of a rented flat. The Song of Songs has a scene that reads like the programme of such a union: "Come, my beloved, let us go forth into the field; let us lodge in the villages. Let us get up early to the vineyards; let us see if the vine flourish… which I have laid up for thee, O my beloved." To go out into the field, see what has blossomed and show what has been saved: this is what Empress love looks like.

Wen writes that The Empress has "an incredible gift for harnessing interpersonal relationships to yield success and harmony". Couples like this know how to make a home that guests are drawn to, and a shared venture that grows faster than either partner's would alone.

But the entry to the task stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish can turn into resistance. The garden in the book is beautiful and locked. The heroine brings her beloved not to a place of her own but "into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her that conceived me", and in the eighth chapter she dreams again of bringing him into her mother's house. Her work was decided by her brothers: "they made me the keeper of the vineyards". The first of The Empress's tasks for a couple, in Lisovskaya's list, is getting out from under the influence of the mother and the wider family. In real life this is a couple whose every holiday is spent at the parents', and whose renovation is first cleared with the elders. Or a couple where one feeds and settles the other so diligently that the other has no reason to get up from the cushions, and a few years later one has grown and the other has not.

One more line is about small things: "Take us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vines: for our vines have tender grapes." A vineyard in blossom is spoiled not by bears but by fox cubs. It is the same with this couple: the union is rarely broken by a great misfortune; it is worn down by small things nobody mentioned. "Fine, I'll do it myself", a forgotten promise, a present instead of a conversation. Wen describes the reversed Empress as "a sense of emptiness and no production after much work and effort". That is how a home feels where much work was done and no harvest is in sight.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: a roe behind the wall
paragraphs: "The voice of my beloved! behold, he cometh leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills. My beloved is like a roe or a young hart: behold, he standeth behind our wall, he looketh forth at the windows, shewing himself through the lattice." The Fool of the Song of Songs stands right behind the garden fence. And he calls: "Rise up, my love, my fair one, and come away. For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone".

In Lisovskaya's book the middle of the task has no meaning of its own; it is an "addition" to the main task. On the site we read it like this: how the couple lives the road from the wish of the entry to the main task. For this couple the road goes through The Fool, which means in leaps. The two may move to another city half a year after meeting, drop a secure job for a shared venture, start from zero after a failure and find a way out where others would sit down to grieve. On the bright side Lisovskaya sees in The Fool a trust that grows into freedom: the two live like best friends and do not cling to things. Such a couple is bored standing still, and it is movement that takes it out of the locked garden.

For Wen, The Fool is a card of a fork in the road: the next step "could either send the Seeker flying into the air over that cliff with impressive accomplishment or falling down hard from naïveté". Every leap this couple makes is such a fork. How it ends is more often decided not by the leap itself but by whether the two jump together.

The price of the leaps is in the most recognisable scene of the book. At night he knocks: "Open to me… for my head is filled with dew". She has already gone to bed: "I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?" She gets up and opens, "but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone". One came with an impulse when the other had settled into comfort; when the second was ready, the first was gone. Lisovskaya describes this shadow of The Fool precisely: starting is easy, and trouble comes as soon as it is time for serious steps. In daily life it is the endless "let's do it later", and the question "what are we to each other" hangs in the air for years. One has found a flat in another city, the other says "not now". One is ready for a wedding while the other is in a phase of freedom, and a year later it is the other way round.

After the unopened door the heroine goes looking for her beloved through the city at night, asks the watchmen, and then begs everyone she meets: "if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love." The secret of the garden goes out into the street. This is the "bewrayment" from The Fool's list: the disclosure without which there is no reaching The Sun. The middle of the tail drags what was hidden into the light, awkwardly, at night, in front of strangers, but it does drag it out.

The numbers show something odd about this couple's Fool. It is always the sum of the two personal tail middles, exactly 22 with no reduction, and neither partner has The Fool in their own tail, not in a single couple of this kind. The roe lives in neither of the two houses; it leaps between them. And in 64% of such couples the personal middles are The Sun (19) for one partner and The Empress (3) for the other. The road from the garden into the sun is literally built from one partner's garden and the other's sun.

sections.h2: Main task: the sun that looks
paragraphs: Back to the verse where it all began: "Look not upon me, because I am black, because the sun hath looked upon me". The Hebrew verb in this verse means "to catch sight of, look on", and the King James Bible keeps that sense: the sun has looked at her. In the Song of Songs the sun is a gaze. That is why this couple's main task is about how the two look at each other and how they are seen.

Lisovskaya reads a couple's main task mostly through its shadow: what the two cannot manage and what they have to learn. For The Sun this shadow is scorching light, and its first form is named in the same verse. The heroine kept other people's vineyards and neglected her own. In a couple this is the one whose talent spends years working for the shared home, for the other's career, for the family business, while their own stands idle. Lisovskaya calls this a failure to realise oneself and taking credit for the partner's victories. It is easy to spot by the pronouns: "we got the PhD", "I'm the one who pulled him through", "our success", in which nobody remembers any more whose it was.

The second form is light that presses down. In the sixth chapter they say of the heroine: "Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?" Clear and terrible in one line. Admiration easily becomes a demand: "you can do better", "look how others manage", "I was counting on you". Lisovskaya puts this into the shadow of The Sun: expectations higher than the person, comparisons, and control over whom the partner sees and where they grow. Wen writes that The Sun "could suggest a power couple" and that it is "a card about dominance and captivating the attention and respect of others". For two people with Strength in the centre and The Sun as their task this is a trap: two strong people under one sky start arguing over whose light comes first.

The third form is love that may not go out into the street. "O that thou wert as my brother… when I should find thee without, I would kiss thee; yea, I should not be despised." All the tenderness stays at home, at night, behind the wall, and in public there is restraint. Lisovskaya also counts an inability to talk about problems and holding feelings back among the tasks of The Sun. The couple lives beautifully in its own garden, but every difficult conversation is put off until night, and at night until tomorrow.

There is also the opposite extreme: light for show. The chorus in the book cries: "Return, return, O Shulamite; return, return, that we may look upon thee", and the answer comes: "What will ye see in the Shulamite?" A sunny couple easily starts living for an audience: beautiful photographs, the right image, a compulsory brightness that tires sooner than love does.

On the bright side of The Sun, for Lisovskaya, each partner succeeds in their own work, and the growth of one pushes the growth of the other. The book has one line for this: "his banner over me was love". What flies over this couple should be love, not status, not a ranking and not a score of who pulled whom through.

If control in a couple turns into fear or threat, it is no longer a matter for reading cards. Real help is needed: a psychologist, close friends and family, and in danger, a local emergency number or crisis line.

The numbers hold this task as precisely as they hold the entry. The couple's Sun is always the exact sum of the two personal karmic tasks, with no reduction. In 64% of such couples it is The Chariot (7) of one partner and The Hanged Man (12) of the other: one rushes ahead, the other knows how to wait, and together they make 19.

sections.h2: Centre of the couple: "love is strong as death"
paragraphs: The centre of a couple is its atmosphere, what happens between the two when nobody is watching. Tail 3-22-19 has only one centre: 11, Strength, in 100% of such couples. And the Song of Songs has the most famous line in the book for it: "Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death". In the Latin Vulgate: fortis est ut mors dilectio. Waite calls this card "Strength, or Fortitude", and in his divinatory list simply "Fortitude", from the same Latin fortis. The atmosphere of this couple is a love that holds fast.

The same line gives the shadow at once: "jealousy is cruel as the grave". The shadow of Strength in a couple shows up as an argument in which both are right and neither gives way: for Lisovskaya this is a struggle for leadership in which each has their own truth. On the bright side she describes Strength as a couple in which each senses keenly what the other needs, and tension goes not into a quarrel but into passion.

Three times the book repeats the same refrain: "I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please." The Hebrew says simply "love" (ahavah), not "my love": do not wake love until it wants to wake. This is the formula of Strength at its best. Wen writes that the card "is a reminder that the Seeker cannot use brute force to exercise will over others; the Seeker must use gentle, subtle influence". For a couple with The Fool in the middle this matters especially. A leap the other was dragged into by force turns into that same night of the unopened door.

Strength has its lion in the book as well. The bridegroom calls the bride: "Come with me from Lebanon, my spouse… look from the top of Amana, from the top of Shenir and Hermon, from the lions' dens, from the mountains of the leopards." Love comes down into the garden from the lions' dens.

And the last clue is in the first part of Waite's book. The highest degree of this virtue he calls "the state of Royal Fortitude, which is the state of a Tower of Ivory and a House of Gold". These are two titles of the Virgin Mary from the Litany of Loreto, and the tower of ivory came into the litany from the Song of Songs: "Thy neck is as a tower of ivory", in the Vulgate turris eburnea. Waite describes the highest form of this couple's centre card with an image from this couple's own book.

The image has a sequel. In 1837 Sainte-Beuve turned it into a phrase that is still in use: the poet Vigny, he wrote, "Comme en sa tour d'ivoire, avant midi, rentrait", "withdrew, as into his ivory tower, before noon" (our translation). So the Strength of this couple acquires a shadow: a fortress the two retreat into before noon, that is, before their Sun. A strong couple closed off from the world may never come out into the light.

sections.h2: Three cards in Waite: the banner, the morning and the open jaws
paragraphs: The Waite deck, drawn by Pamela Colman Smith, adds three details to the story.

On Waite's Sun card a naked child on a white horse displays "a red standard". The Song of Songs names the banner outright: "He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love." Describing the same card, Wen notes that its sun "has a face, somehow both stern and serene". It is the same doubleness as in "clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners".

Waite sets The Fool at the edge of a precipice and names the hour: it all happens "amidst the morning glory, in the keen air". The Fool is morning, The Sun is full day. The couple of the book keeps hours too. "Until the day break, and the shadows flee away", the roe leaps on the mountains. And the heroine's first question to her beloved is where he rests "at noon". The middle of this tail is dawn; the main task is noon.

On Waite's Strength card the woman is closing the lion's mouth. But in the first part of his book Waite adds a note: in the earlier form printed by Court de Gebelin "she is obviously opening it". The closing version, he says, "is better symbolically". A couple whose main task is to speak in daylight does well to remember that Strength once had two gestures: it can hold back the roar, and it can let the voice out.

sections.h2: The couple's values: from "he is mine" to "I am his"
paragraphs: "The couple's values" are the spiritual purpose, the road the two are to walk together. This tail has only two options there: The Lovers (6) in 63.4% of couples and The Devil (15) in 36.6%. Both cards are about belonging, and the Song of Songs has a ladder that shows the difference.

It is worth writing three lines one under another. Chapter two: "My beloved is mine, and I am his". Chapter six: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine". Chapter seven: "I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me." At first "he is mine" comes first. Then "I am his". At the end the word "mine" disappears altogether, leaving "I am his, and he desires me".

Our reading: this is the road from The Devil to The Lovers. The Devil among the values is the temptation to hold love as property. Lisovskaya writes about attempts to keep a partner by closeness, money or status, and sums up the card in the phrase "nobody belongs to anybody". The book answers in chapter eight: "if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned." All the riches of The Empress are not enough to buy what is given only by choice. The Lovers are that choice, repeated in daylight.

The word "desire" in chapter seven (teshuqah) occurs only three times in the Bible. The first time is in Genesis, where it stands next to power: "and thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee." The biblical scholar Phyllis Trible, in God and the Rhetoric of Sexuality (1978, the chapter "Love's Lyric Redeemed"), reads the line of the Song as an answer to those words: the desire remains, the rule is gone. For a couple with The Devil among its values this is the very work: keep the attraction and remove the power.

sections.h2: The strong version: a vineyard of one's own for each
paragraphs: The last chapter of the Song of Songs gathers the way out of this tail into four movements.

First the brothers again decide for their sister: "If she be a wall, we will build upon her a palace of silver: and if she be a door, we will inclose her with boards of cedar." And for the first time she answers for herself: "I am a wall… then was I in his eyes as one that found favour." Where the King James has "favour", the Hebrew word is shalom, peace. The Empress no longer lives by the family's plan: the two decide for themselves where they have a wall and where a door.

Then the vineyard. Solomon lets out his vineyard to keepers for a thousand pieces of silver. The heroine replies: "My vineyard, which is mine, is before me". The complaint of the first chapter, "mine own vineyard have I not kept", is closed. This is The Sun at its best: each has their own work, their own harvest and their own joy, and instead of competing they warm the shared home.

Then the voice. "Thou that dwellest in the gardens, the companions hearken to thy voice: cause me to hear it." In the second chapter the heroine was hiding "in the clefts of the rock", and her beloved asked, "let me hear thy voice". By the end everyone hears her voice, and he asks to hear it too. Love has come out into the light, and its main listener has stayed close.

And the last line of the book: "Make haste, my beloved, and be thou like to a roe or to a young hart upon the mountains of spices." In chapter two the word was "turn, my beloved, and be thou like a roe", that is, come back. In chapter eight it is a different verb, which the King James softens to "make haste" and which in Hebrew means "flee". The book ends not with a lock but with freedom, and that freedom comes after the seal upon the heart. The Fool in the strong version of the tail is trust: the two let each other go because they are not afraid of losing each other.
In the everyday life of a couple with tail 3-22-19 it looks like this:

ul: **A vineyard of one's own for each.** One's own work, money and friends next to the shared garden. Lisovskaya plainly advises such couples to find self-realisation separately and to learn to make decisions alone.
**Catch the little foxes while the vine is in blossom.** Mention a small irritation the same day, while it is still small.
**Leap by agreement.** Before a big step, ask whether the other is "dressed", and name a date instead of "later". Think about responsibility before the leap, not after it.
**Call victories by their names.** Say out loud whose success it is, give thanks, and do not turn it into "ours" without asking.
**Love in the street too.** Tenderness, plans and difficult conversations belong not only to the night and not only to the home. But not to the chorus that cries "return, return" either.
**Do not wake love by force.** Do not drag the other into a decision they have not grown into yet.
**Freedom with a seal.** Let the other go without checking up, on a trip, to friends, into their own work, and bear temporary separations calmly.

sections.h2: How tail 3-22-19 comes about: a worked example
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices, reduced to 22. A couple's tail is not recalculated from its outer numbers: the couple's middle is added up from the partners' middles. Example: the couple born 05.12.1975 and 05.07.1975. The first partner has the personal tail 18-3-12 and centre 6, the second has 12-19-7 and centre 5.

This couple's middle is put together exactly as described above: The Empress from one partner's personal tail and The Sun from the other's give The Fool. The Sun appears twice more in this couple's matrix. On the point What to create together (12 + 7 = 19), where it occurs in only 4.1% of couples with this tail. And on the Way into money (10 + 9 = 19), in 4.9%. So for this couple the main task and the reason they met coincide. Strength repeats too: in the centre and on the point What fills (17 + 12 = 29 → 11), which happens in 6.8% of these couples. By Lisovskaya's rule, repeated energies can be added: 11 + 11 = 22, which gives The Fool, already standing in the middle of the tail. The couple's values are 6, The Lovers.
The other numbers describe all couples with this tail at once. They come from running every date since 1900 through the site's engine:

ul: tail 3-22-19 occurs in roughly one couple in 83 (1.204%), 29th place among the 97 couple tails;
the couple's entry to the task is always the sum 30: 12 + 18 (78%) or 21 + 9 (22%), and neither partner has The Empress on their own personal entry;
the middle is always exactly 22 and the main task always exactly 19, with no reduction;

neither partner ever has The Fool in their personal tail; The Empress is in one partner's tail in 74.7% of couples, The Sun in 64%; in 25.3% of couples none of the three cards appears in the personal tails, and the tail is formed entirely between two people;
the centre is Strength in 100%; from the personal centres it adds up as 5 + 6 (74.7%), 3 + 8 (22.3%) or 18 + 11 (3%);
the values are The Lovers (63.4%) or The Devil (36.6%).

paragraphs: There is no couple tail made of the same numbers in a different order: neither 3-19-22 nor 22-3-19 nor any other permutation occurs for couples. The triple 3-22-19 does, however, occur as a personal karmic tail, for 1,038 dates since 1900. That is a different calculation with different roles for the points, and the site has a separate article about it.

ul: **Entry to the task — 3, The Empress.** The two want a fruitful life: a home and a garden of their own, a full table, care that can be tasted. The same wish keeps them in comfort and in the parental home, where nobody ever leaves.

**Middle of the task — 22, The Fool.** The road goes in leaps: moves, fresh starts from zero, a sudden "let's go", freedom and play. The price is missed timing: one calls the other outside when the other is not ready yet.

**Main task — 19, The Sun.** Learning to live in view and in truth: saying hard things out loud, being glad of the other's success without taking it over, growing something of one's own for each. The shadow of The Sun is a scorching gaze: control, inflated expectations, comparisons and somebody's abandoned vineyard.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 3-22-19 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the task of a couple that starts from a wish for a full, fruitful life (The Empress), moves towards its goal through leaps and changes (The Fool) and learns the main thing, which is to live in daylight: to talk about hard things, to be glad of the other's success and to keep work of one's own for each (The Sun).

faq.q: How does a couple get tail 3 22 19?
faq.a: Each point of a couple's tail is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices, reduced to 22. In such couples the entry to the task always gives 30 → 3, the middle exactly 22 and the main task exactly 19. Most often (64%) the tail is made from the personal tails 12-19-7 and 18-3-12.

faq.q: How is couple tail 3-22-19 different from personal tail 3-22-19?
faq.a: A personal tail is calculated from one date and describes one person's task, with its own roles for the points. A couple's tail is added up from two matrices and speaks of what the two have to learn together. The same numbers do not make these readings interchangeable.

faq.q: Are there couple tails with the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. From the numbers 3, 22 and 19 a couple can only get the order 3-22-19: permutations such as 3-19-22 or 19-22-3 do not occur in the compatibility matrix.

faq.q: Does tail 3-22-19 predict what will happen to a couple?
faq.a: No. The tail is a symbolic map of a task, not a forecast of events and not a verdict on the union. It shows where the couple's difficulties repeat and which version of the story is stronger, and the choice belongs to the two of them.

report: A young woman in the Song of Songs asks not to be stared at: "Look not upon me, because I am black, because the sun hath looked upon me: my mother's children were angry with me; they made me the keeper of the vineyards; but mine own vineyard have I not kept." In the next line she asks her beloved where he rests "at noon", and does not want to be "as one that turneth aside", a stray. The vineyard, the sun and the stray are The Empress, The Sun and The Fool: the whole of tail 3-22-19 in two verses. A couple with this tail starts in a closed garden, moves in leaps and learns the main thing: **to bring love out into daylight so that each partner keeps a vineyard of their own.**

report.h3: Love measured in fruit

report: The love talk of this book is rural through and through: "honey and milk are under thy tongue", pomegranates, vineyards, lilies. A couple with The Empress at the entry speaks the same way. Its common language is care: who cooked what, what to buy for the house, where to go out of town, what the home will be like, which guests it will draw. Wen sees The Empress's gift in "harnessing interpersonal relationships to yield success and harmony".

But the garden in the book is locked: "A garden inclosed is my sister, my spouse; a spring shut up, a fountain sealed." The heroine brings her beloved "into my mother's house", and her brothers decided what her work would be. This is what resistance at the entry looks like: every holiday at the parents', a renovation cleared with the elders first, one partner settling the other so diligently that the other has no reason to get up from the cushions. And a vineyard in blossom is spoiled not by bears but by "the little foxes": small things nobody mentioned, "fine, I'll do it myself", a present instead of a conversation.

report.h3: A door opened too late

report: The Fool stands right behind the garden fence: "behold, he cometh leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills… he standeth behind our wall, he looketh forth at the windows". And he calls: "Rise up, my love, my fair one, and come away." The middle of the tail is a road of leaps. Such a couple may move half a year after meeting, drop a secure job for a shared venture, start from zero after a failure. It is movement that takes them out of the garden.

The price of the leaps is in the most recognisable scene of the book. He knocks at night, and she has already gone to bed: "I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on?" She gets up and opens, "but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone". One arrives with an impulse when the other has settled into comfort; when the second is ready, the first is gone. Starting is easy; trouble comes with the serious steps. In daily life it is the endless "let's do it later", and the question "what are we to each other" hanging in the air for years.
Neither partner brings this couple's Fool: it is absent from both personal tails and appears only between the two. **The roe lives in neither of the two houses; it leaps between them.**

report.h3: The sun that looks

report: The Hebrew verb in that first verse means "to look on": the sun has looked at the heroine. In this book the sun is a gaze, and the couple's main task is about how the two look at each other and how they are seen.

Scorching light comes in three kinds. The first is named in the same verse: one partner keeps other people's vineyards and neglects their own. That talent spends years working for the shared home or the other's career, and later the success sounds like "we got the PhD" or "I'm the one who pulled him through". The second is light that presses down. The heroine is called "clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners", and admiration easily turns into a demand, the familiar "could do better". Wen writes that The Sun "could suggest a power couple", and for two people with Strength in the centre this is a trap: **two strong people under one sky argue over whose light comes first.** The third is love that may not go out into the street: "when I should find thee without, I would kiss thee; yea, I should not be despised." Tenderness stays at home, behind the wall, and a difficult conversation is put off until night, and at night until tomorrow.

If control in a couple turns into fear or threat, it is no longer a matter for reading cards: real help is needed, a psychologist, close friends and family, and in danger a local emergency number or crisis line.

report.h3: A tower before noon

report: The centre of every such couple is Strength, and the book gives it its most famous line: "love is strong as death", in the Vulgate fortis est ut mors dilectio. Waite calls the card Fortitude, from the same fortis. The same line holds its shadow: "jealousy is cruel as the grave". And the refrain repeated three times gives its bright side: the Hebrew says "love", not "my love", so it reads as "do not wake love until it wants to wake". A leap the other was dragged into by force ends in a night with an unopened door.

Waite describes the highest Fortitude as "a Tower of Ivory", an image that came from the same Song of Songs. And in 1837 Sainte-Beuve wrote of a poet who "withdrew, as into his ivory tower, before noon". That is the shadow of the centre: a strong couple can retreat into its fortress before noon, that is, before its Sun.

report.h3: My vineyard, which is mine, is before me

report: The last chapter of the book gathers the way out. The brothers once more decide for their sister, and for the first time she answers for herself: "I am a wall". Solomon lets out his vineyard to keepers for a thousand pieces of silver, and the heroine says: "My vineyard, which is mine, is before me". The complaint of the first chapter is closed: **each has their own work and their own harvest, and both warm the shared home.** Her beloved asks to hear the voice that everyone already hears. And the last line of the book is not a lock but freedom: "Make haste, my beloved, and be thou like to a roe". That freedom comes after the seal upon the heart.

The book also shows the ladder of the couple's values: "My beloved is mine", then "I am my beloved's", then "I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me". The word "mine" disappears. In our reading this is the road from The Devil to The Lovers: a love that "all the substance of his house" cannot buy is held by choice, not by ownership.

In practice this means a vineyard of one's own for each next to the shared garden, little foxes caught the same day, leaps by agreement with a date instead of "later", victories called by their names, tenderness and difficult conversations not only at night, and freedom without checking up.
