seo.title: Karmic tail 3 7 22 compatibility: meaning for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 7 22 compatibility: The Empress, The Chariot and The Fool — what the three cards say about a couple and why Justice always stands at the centre.

items.title: The 3-7-22 karmic tail in compatibility: a home, a road and the edge of the roof
items.short: For a couple with the 3-7-22 tail, the three cards make a route: The Empress is the home, The Chariot is the road, The Fool is the edge beyond which the whole world opens. The riddle is that such couples often walk the whole route and end up exactly where they started. The answer is written in the cards themselves: the main task of this union is a freedom the two choose for themselves — not an escape, and not a retreat out of fear.

sections.h2: The fairy tale in which the couple recognises itself
paragraphs: In 1845 Hans Christian Andersen published "The Shepherdess and the Chimney-Sweep" (in Danish, "Hyrdinden og Skorsteensfeieren"). On a table under the mirror stand two china figures: a shepherdess with golden shoes, a red rose and a crook, and a chimney-sweep with his ladder. Close by stands an old porcelain mandarin three times their size, who can nod his head and says he is the shepherdess's grandfather. In the middle of an old carved chest a little man is carved, with a goat's hind legs, little horns and a long beard; the children call him General-Headquarters-Hindquarters-Gives-Orders-Front-and-Rear-Sergeant-Billygoat-Legs. He asks for the shepherdess's hand, the grandfather nods, and the wedding is set for that night.

The lovers run. They climb down from the table, hide in a drawer, climb out, make their way through the stove and up the chimney, sit down on its rim — and see the starry sky and all the roofs of the town. The shepherdess weeps: "The wide world is too big." The two climb back down. The grandfather, running after them, has fallen off the table and broken into three pieces. He is glued together, a rivet is put through his neck, and he can no longer nod. Billygoat-Legs never gets his answer, and the porcelain couple stays side by side.

The three scenes of the tale are the three cards of the tail, in the same order. The table under the mirror is The Empress. The way through the stove and the chimney is The Chariot. The rim of the chimney above the wide world is The Fool. The nodding grandfather, on whom the decision depends, is Justice at the centre of the couple. And Billygoat-Legs' proposal against the two's own choice is the fork in the values: The Devil or The Lovers.

The tale also has a mirror scene. The runaways hide in a drawer of the window-seat. Inside lie three or four decks of cards, not quite complete, and a little puppet theatre where a play is on. The queens of every suit sit in the front row fanning themselves with tulips, and behind them the knaves line up, "showing that they had heads both at the top and at the bottom, as face cards do have" (here and below the tale is quoted in Jean Hersholt's translation). The play is about two people who are not allowed to marry, and it makes the shepherdess cry "because it was so like her own story". A person who has calculated compatibility and is looking at the three cards of the tail is sitting in the same drawer. And every card, like a knave, has two heads: what holds the couple together in the plus stops it in the minus.

One caveat. In the tale the cards are handed out to the characters like parts in a puppet show: the shepherdess wants to go home, the sweep knows the way. In a living couple all three cards belong to both, and gender decides nothing here. Today one pulls towards the roof and the other asks to go back to the shelf; a year later it is the other way round.

sections.h2: The Empress at the entry: "having been placed there, they had become engaged"
paragraphs: Andersen explains how this union begins in a single sentence: "They had both been put on the table where they stood and, having been placed there, they had become engaged because they suited each other exactly. Both were young, both were made of the same porcelain, and neither could stand a shock." Not a meeting and not a choice, but a place. They were put on the same table, and that was enough.

The Empress at the entry to the task is the wish with which the couple enters a shared life. For Lisovskaya, the key to the Three in a couple is fertility, abundance and growth: such two meet in order to grow something together, and sometimes in order to thaw after earlier relationships that went wrong. In life it looks very simple. Within a month a rented flat turns into a home: plants on the windowsill, a shared blanket, a Sunday pie, talk about where the nursery or the business will go. The two find a common language fastest when they talk about the nest. The happiest arguments of the first years are about curtains.

Waite calls The Empress the Earthly Paradise and a refuge: "She is not Regina coeli, but she is still refugium peccatorum", the refuge of sinners. The table under the mirror is such a refuge: it is warm there, with golden shoes and a rose. In Waite's divinatory list this card has "fruitfulness, action, initiative" side by side with "difficulty, doubt", and reversed there is one more word — "vacillation". That is the shepherdess's whole line. The initiative is hers: "Please let's run away into the big, wide world." So is the doubt: "It looks very black in there." And the vacillation will come on the rim of the chimney.

The most exact clue is one sentence that the shepherdess says twice. On the table: "I'll never be happy until we are out in the big, wide world." On the roof: "I'll never be happy until I stand there again, just as before." The same words, the opposite direction. This is how the entry point of a couple's tail works. It stands on the line of tasks, so a shared wish can turn into resistance. The dream of a nest of their own first pushes the couple onto the road: away from other people's rules, to build something of their own. Then the same dream pulls them back: "we're fine where we are".

The Empress has her own scenes in the minus. Comfort one is afraid to lose, so that any suggestion of change sounds like a threat. Prosperity measured by who has brought more into the home. Relatives who feel entitled to decide because they once helped. Among the tasks of the Three, Lisovskaya names getting out from under the influence of relatives and leaving childishness behind. In the tale the grandfather "claimed that this gave him authority over her", although "he couldn't prove it".

sections.h2: The Chariot in the middle: "I'll do just what you want me to"
paragraphs: The middle of the tail shows how the couple travels from the wish to the task. The 3-7-22 couple travels by chariot: in motion, in a rush, with a clear direction and with someone holding the reins.

In the tale the reins belong to the sweep. "My way lies up through the chimney," he says. "Once we get there, I'll know what to do." Then comes a road that Waite would call a trial: his charioteer is conquest "in certain trials of initiation" too. Through the stove, through the stovepipe "where it was pitch-black night", up a terribly steep way. The sweep "lifted her up, held her safe, and found the best places for her little porcelain feet". Above them a star shines down "as if it wished to show them the way". The first two words in Waite's divinatory list for The Chariot are "succour, providence". The tale has both: the hand that lifts and the star that guides.

Lisovskaya writes about the Seven in a couple almost literally about these two: such couples often move house in search of "a home of their own", and among their tasks is deciding on a move together. Andersen's tale is the story of a move that never happened. In the middle of this tail a couple often lives like a crew: a mortgage and a renovation, a move to another city, two jobs, a business of their own, a marathon towards the first big income. The Chariot is good at one thing — taking an obstacle. The two did get through the chimney.

This card has a dark side too, and the tale shows it. The sweep says "yes" twice. The first time at the start: "I'll do just what you want me to," he tells her. "Let's run away right now." The second time on the roof, when the shepherdess begs to go home: "he had to do as she said, though he thought it was the wrong thing to do." The one who has a way of his own hands over the reins twice. Lisovskaya names this among the minuses and tasks of the Seven: one partner adjusts to the other, a partner is expected to give up their own goals for someone else's. The chariot is driven by the one who knows the chimney, and the direction is set by the one who cries. Who really decides in this couple, nobody knows — the two least of all.

The second dark side is running instead of talking. In the whole tale nobody ever speaks to the grandfather. The two hide in a drawer, think of climbing into the pot-pourri vase of rose petals and lavender to "throw salt in his eyes", climb the chimney — but never walk up to the table to say "no". Wen notes that the Chariot person "likes to appear in control, but has a tendency to run from his or her problems". Couples with the 3-7-22 tail know this: it is easier to start a renovation, change city or job, than to say out loud, just once, what does not suit them.

sections.h2: The Fool, the main task: the rim of the chimney and a world too big
paragraphs: The couple's main task is The Fool. This point is read mostly through the minus: what does not work for the couple and what it has to learn.

The tale brings its heroes exactly to this card. "Overhead was the starry sky, and spread before them were all the housetops in the town." Waite describes The Fool at the same point: a young man "pauses at the brink of a precipice among the great heights of the world; he surveys the blue distance before him—its expanse of sky rather than the prospect below." And: "The edge which opens on the depth has no terror." In Andersen two sit on the same edge, but they look in different ways. The sweep is at home on the roof: this is his way. The shepherdess sees all the roofs of the town spread before her, and she is frightened: "The poor shepherdess had never thought it would be like that."

One more clue. Waite writes that The Fool is "a prince of the other world on his travels through this one". Andersen writes of the sweep at the very start that "he was only an ornamental chimney-sweep. If the china-makers had wanted to, they could just as easily have turned him out as a prince". A prince of roofs and chimneys, dressed up in soot, is this couple's Fool — the part of it that feels cramped at home.

The tale shows the price of freedom in one detail: the shepherdess "sobbed so many tears that the gilt washed off her sash". The Empress's gold does not stay on up on the roof. Then comes the sentence where all the cards of the tail meet: "I followed you faithfully out into the world, and if you love me the least bit you'll take me right home." In it are the home, the road, the tally of concessions and the love used to pay for the way back.

The Fool in the minus, for Lisovskaya, is an easy start and trouble as soon as serious steps come up. Down below, the sweep asks the shepherdess whether she has thought "about how big it is, and that we can never come back here". "I have," she says. On the rim of the chimney it turns out she had not. A modern couple has its own chimney rim: signing for a flat, getting married, deciding to have a child, leaving on a contract abroad, quitting a job for a business of their own. They reached the edge easily, and at the edge one of them says the world is too big.

The Fool's minus has other faces too. A relationship with no defined status: "we live together, we'll see". Two people under one roof, each on their own, like neighbours. Running from difficulty with reproaches to the partner: "I climbed into that chimney for you." A freedom with no room for commitments — or strict rules for the other while one's own are not kept.

It matters that the tale does not make the return itself the mistake. Wen describes The Fool as a fork in the path: "One fork will lead to attainment (flying, transcending the cliff) and the other will lead to likely demise (falling off the cliff)." For the reversed card she even says that "it would behoove the Seeker to turn back and take the other fork". The mistake of the shepherdess and the sweep is not that they came back but how. She came back out of fear and on the condition "if you love me"; he, "though he thought it was the wrong thing to do". Neither of them chose the return. Waite's Fool will come back too, but "by another path after many days". The porcelain couple came back by the same path, the same night.

sections.h2: Justice at the centre: scales that bring everything back to zero
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's matrix is the atmosphere inside the union, what happens between the two when nobody is watching. For couples with the 3-7-22 tail it holds 8, Justice. Not for most of them — for all.

In the plus this is a good atmosphere: honesty, a clear agreement, duties shared equally, "a cool head and a warm heart", as Lisovskaya writes of the Eight in a couple. Such couples take a long time to look each other over and a long time to settle in, but afterwards they can be relied on.

The tale shows how these scales work inside the tail. The shepherdess's sentence on the roof is built like a calculation, and in Andersen's Danish it is even more symmetrical: "now I have followed you out into the wide world, now you may follow me home again, if you care for me at all" (my translation). A concession for a concession, a step for a step. The scales balance exactly, and the couple ends up at zero. Back on the table, the sweep sums up: "Back where we started from. We could have saved ourselves a lot of trouble." The Danish is sharper still: "See how far we got!" An honest exchange of concessions does not move this union a single step. It returns it to where it was.

Then comes guilt. Seeing the grandfather on the floor, the shepherdess wrings her hands: "poor old grandfather is all broken up, and it's entirely our fault." Among the tasks of Justice in a couple, Lisovskaya names admitting one's own fault instead of blaming everyone, and learning to forgive. This task has a reverse side: guilt holds people in place as well as glue does.

And finally the grandfather himself, whose nod decides the couple's fate. In English such a figure is a nodding mandarin; Russian calls it kitaisky bolvanchik, the "little Chinese dummy", and uses the name for anyone who nods along: the porcelain head rocks and agrees with whatever is said. He "couldn't prove" he was her grandfather, yet he nodded to Billygoat-Legs, and that was enough. Waite's reversed Justice includes the words "bias, excessive severity". In a 3-7-22 couple anything can stand in the grandfather's place: relatives, "the way things are done", a shared ledger kept in the head, one's own inner judge. Justice at the centre easily turns into a nodding mandarin that nods on behalf of both.

This centre also has its own story in numbers. In 98% of such couples the partners' personal centres are 3 and 5: one has The Empress at the centre of their personal chart, the other The Hierophant, keeper of rules and of blessing. In the remaining 2% they are 8 and 18. One partner's comfort and the other's sense of rules together give the couple an atmosphere of scales.

sections.h2: The couple's values: The Lovers or Billygoat-Legs
paragraphs: The couple's values (the spiritual purpose) are what the union exists for. For the 3-7-22 tail there are only two options here: The Lovers for 65.2% of couples and The Devil for 34.8%. The tale gives both of them a face.

The Lovers is the card of choice. In the story of the shepherdess and the sweep it is the main question nobody asks: are they together because they chose each other, or because, "having been placed there", they simply got engaged? Waite writes that the old Lovers card "is said to have been entitled Simulacrum fidei, the symbol of conjugal faith". The china figures on the table are exactly such a symbol, literally. Among Waite's reversed meanings is "marriage frustrated" — the play in the drawer, where two lovers are not allowed to marry. For a couple with The Lovers in its values, the path is to turn the image into a choice: not just to stand side by side, but one day to tell each other that they stand here because they want to.

The Devil in the values is the theme of who belongs to whom. Billygoat-Legs, with his little horns and goat's legs, wears the usual face of the devil in European fairy tales. He is rich: "He has the whole chest full of silver, and who knows what else he's got hidden away in his secret drawers?" — and in there he already has "eleven china wives". His last question is an owner's question: "Am I to have her, or am I not?" But Waite has a phrase that explains Billygoat-Legs too: he who is exalted above the chained figures "is not to be their master for ever. Even now, he is also a bondsman". Billygoat-Legs is carved into the chest. In the whole tale he only jumps and shouts "They're running away! They're running away!", but he never leaves his place: at the end he "was standing where he always stood, looking thoughtful". The threat the two fled through the chimney could never have caught them. Only the nodding mandarin gave chase — and broke.

Lisovskaya's final thought on the fifteenth energy in a couple is that nobody belongs to anybody. For a couple with The Devil in its values the lesson lies here: the dark chest full of silver — comfort, money, the fear of loss — frightens more than it can hold. And it holds only those who believe in it themselves.

sections.h2: How the 3-7-22 tail is calculated for a couple: an example and the clues in the numbers
paragraphs: Each point of the couple's matrix is the sum of the same points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22. An example: the partners were born on 05.05.1976 and 05.07.1975. The first has the personal karmic tail 18-6-15, the second 12-19-7. Add them point by point:

The couple's middle is not derived from the two outer numbers: it is the sum of the two personal middles. The 3-7-22 tail occurs in roughly one couple in 292 (0.342%) and ranks 67th of the 97 couple tails. No couple tail is made of the same three numbers in another order.
Going through all dates since 1900 shows that this tail is assembled from only three combinations of the partners' personal tails:

head: Partners' tails
Share of such couples
What The Fool is made of

paragraphs: This table holds three clues. First: in such couples the entry is always exactly 30, the middle exactly 25 and the main task exactly 22, with no reduction — a couple's Fool comes only from an exact sum. Second: neither partner has The Fool in their personal tail, and in 38% of such couples it is absent from every main point of both personal charts. The freedom the couple is learning does not come from either of the two: it is born only between them. Third, a coincidence that is hard to pass by. In 69% of couples The Fool is made of one partner's Chariot and the other's Devil, 7 + 15. That is exactly the tale: flight (The Chariot) from Billygoat-Legs (The Devil) brings the two to the edge of the wide world. It is a coincidence of numbers, not a law, but the picture is exact.

The example couple has two more marks. The Fool stands not only in its main task but also at the point "What fills" — this happens in 5.4% of couples with this tail. And at the point "Where it sparks", which shows what causes serious quarrels, stands 21, The World — as in 4% of such couples. So freedom both gives this couple strength and is exactly where it may spark: around the big world — plans, moves, going out into it.

A personal 3-7-22 tail exists too: 1,353 dates since 1900 have it. But that is a different calculation, with different roles for the points. If 3-7-22 appears in compatibility, it has to be read by the couple's roles.

sections.h2: How the circle closes
paragraphs: Put the cards of the tail together with the centre and the values, and Andersen's tale becomes a circle that a 3-7-22 couple can go round more than once.

ol: **The nest.** The couple is joined by the wish for something of their own: a home, plenty, a shared business. The two stand side by side because that is how things turned out, and they are happy.
**Someone else's decision.** A nod hangs over the nest: relatives, circumstances, "the way things are done". Nobody dares to name it aloud.

**The dash.** The couple throws itself into motion: a move, a renovation, a new project. One knows the way and leads, the other holds on. The one who leads puts their own goals aside: "I'll do just what you want me to."
**The edge.** The couple reaches the freedom it set out for — and one of them is frightened: "the wide world is too big".
**The tally.** The way back is paid for with a concession and with love: I followed you, now you take me home, if you love me.
**Zero.** The couple returns by the same path to the same place, with guilt on top. "Back where we started from."

**The rivet.** The question of the couple's status is closed not by the couple but by a circumstance: money, a contract, someone's silence. The couple thanks the rivet, and everything stays as it was.

paragraphs: The last step looks like a happy ending, and in the tale it is one: the two keep on loving each other "until the day they broke". Only their freedom came not from their will but from grandfather's rivet. The tale begins with the two being placed side by side and ends with them staying side by side. In the whole story the two themselves decided nothing.

sections.h2: How to break the circle: freedom with a way back
paragraphs: For this couple The Fool does not demand leaving home at all costs, nor staying at all costs. Its task is for the two to decide it themselves — on the rim of the chimney, aloud and together.

ul: **Talk to "the grandfather" before running.** Name who or what nods on the couple's behalf: relatives, money, habit, an inner judge. Saying "no" at the table is easier than climbing the chimney later.

**Do not demand the whole world at once.** The sweep's question about "how big it is, and that we can never come back here" puts the couple before the whole world in one go. The world really is too big to enter in one night. One can go out to the edge more often and for short spells: a trip, a trial month, a small shared risk. That is how a big step is prepared rather than put off.
**Do not pay with love.** "If you love me" is a poor currency for decisions. A concession for which a return concession is later demanded is no longer care but a debt book.

**Each has a way of their own.** The sweep knows the chimney, the shepherdess her table. Lisovskaya advises a couple with The Chariot to walk side by side but each on their own path, and a couple with The Fool to give the partner freedom without checks and to take temporary separations calmly. One can go off to their own roofs and come back; the other can keep the home.
**Settle the status before the rivet does.** Who we are to each other and where we are going — let the couple answer that, not a circumstance that one day will stop nodding.
**Notice "I'll do just what you want me to".** When one partner agrees to everything for a long time, the bill will be presented sooner or later.

paragraphs: The strong version of 3-7-22 looks like this. The couple has a home, but it is a base, not a shelf: they leave it and come back to it. The couple starts from zero easily and finds a way out where others see a cliff — this is how Lisovskaya describes The Fool in the plus. The two are like best friends: each is self-sufficient and stays in the union by their own choice. The Empress gives them what they met for — growth and abundance. The Chariot gives them the knack of taking obstacles together. And The Fool gives them the freedom to come home by another path, no longer the people who left.

ul: **Entry to the task — 3, The Empress.** The couple is joined by the wish for a home of their own, for plenty, for something grown together. Later the same wish holds them in place.
**Middle of the task — 7, The Chariot.** The couple travels its path in motion: moves, dashes, projects, where one leads and the other holds on.
**Main task — 22, The Fool.** Learning freedom as two: taking serious steps into the unknown and not running from them, forwards or backwards.

intro: At the centre of the matrix every such couple has Justice; in the values, The Lovers or The Devil. All these cards are already laid out in one fairy tale by Andersen, from the little table under the mirror to the rim of a chimney.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 3 7 22 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's task, written in three cards: The Empress at the entry (a shared wish for home and plenty), The Chariot in the middle (a path in motion, where one leads), The Fool in the main task (freedom as two). Most often this is a couple that builds a nest, moves a lot and learns to take serious steps into the unknown by itself — not by someone else's decision and not out of fear.

faq.q: Is it a difficult tail for a couple?
faq.a: A couple's tail is not a verdict and not a forecast; it shows what the two have to learn together. For 3-7-22 the difficulty is that comfort and freedom pull in different directions, and decisions are made through an exchange of concessions. The strength is the ability to start from zero, to move together and to trust each other.

faq.q: How is the couple's 3-7-22 tail different from the personal 3-7-22 tail?
faq.a: A personal 3-7-22 tail belongs to 1,353 dates since 1900 and is calculated from a single date of birth. A couple's tail is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, and its points mean something else: the entry to the task, the middle of the task and the couple's main task. Personal readings do not carry over to the couple.

faq.q: Why do all couples with this tail have Justice at the centre?
faq.a: That is how the numbers add up. The tail is assembled from only three combinations of personal tails, and in each of them the partners' personal centres add up to 8: in 98% of couples these are 3 and 5, in 2% they are 8 and 18. So the atmosphere of such couples is a pair of scales: an honest agreement, duties shared equally and the habit of counting who gave way to whom.

faq.q: How can a couple find out whether it has the 3-7-22 tail?
faq.a: Calculate the compatibility matrix from the two dates of birth and look at the couple's karmic tail. For example, partners born on 05.05.1976 and 05.07.1975 have the personal tails 18-6-15 and 12-19-7, and their point-by-point sum gives 3-7-22.

report: "Here we are," says the chimney-sweep in Andersen's tale. "Back where we started from. We could have saved ourselves a lot of trouble." He is back with his bride on the very table under the mirror they had run away from. "The Shepherdess and the Chimney-Sweep" is laid out exactly along the cards of the 3-7-22 tail: the table is The Empress, the way through the stove and up the chimney is The Chariot, the rim of the chimney above the wide world is The Fool. Justice, which stands at the centre of every such couple, is there too: the old porcelain mandarin who says he is the shepherdess's grandfather and with a nod gives her to Billygoat-Legs, the little man carved into the chest. In the tale the parts are handed out to the characters; in a living couple they are not fixed, and the pull towards the roof comes now from one, now from the other.

report.h3: Placed side by side, and so engaged

report: Andersen explains the engagement in one sentence: "having been placed there, they had become engaged because they suited each other exactly". Not a meeting and not a choice, but a place. The Empress at the entry is the shared wish: a home of their own, plenty, something grown together. The two find a common language fastest when they talk about the nest.

But this point stands on the line of tasks, and here a wish easily turns into resistance. The shepherdess says the same sentence twice. On the table: "I'll never be happy until we are out in the big, wide world." On the roof: "I'll never be happy until I stand there again, just as before." **The dream of a nest of their own first pushes the couple onto the road, then pulls it back.**

report.h3: The one who knows the way hands over the reins twice

report: The middle of the tail is The Chariot: the couple moves towards its task in motion, in a rush, and someone holds the reins. "My way lies up through the chimney… Once we get there, I'll know what to do," says the sweep, and he lifts his bride and finds the best places for her little porcelain feet. In Waite's list for The Chariot the first words are "succour, providence", and above the runaways a star really does shine down "as if it wished to show them the way". In life such a crew is easy to recognise: a mortgage and a renovation, a move to another city, two jobs, a business of their own.

Only the sweep says "yes" twice: "I'll do just what you want me to" at the start, and on the roof "he had to do as she said, though he thought it was the wrong thing to do". The chariot is driven by the one who knows the chimney, and the direction is set by the one who cries. And in the whole tale nobody ever speaks to the grandfather: climbing a chimney is easier than saying "no" at the table.

report.h3: The edge where the world is too big

report: The couple's main task is The Fool, and it is read through what does not work. "Overhead was the starry sky, and spread before them were all the housetops in the town." Waite's Fool stands at the brink of a precipice, and for him "the edge which opens on the depth has no terror". The sweep is at home on the roof: no wonder the china-makers "could just as easily have turned him out as a prince", while Waite's Fool is "a prince of the other world on his travels through this one". The shepherdess is frightened: "The wide world is too big." Her tears wash the gilt off her sash, and The Empress's gold does not stay on up on the roof.

Then comes the sentence where the whole tail meets: "I followed you faithfully out into the world, and if you love me the least bit you'll take me right home." **A concession for a concession — that is how the scales of Justice work, and they balance at zero.** The couple returns by the same path to the same place, with guilt on top: "it's entirely our fault".

A modern couple has its own chimney rim: getting married, signing for a flat, moving away, leaving a job for a business of their own. They reached the edge easily, and at the edge one of them says the world is too big. Hence a relationship with no defined status, life under one roof but apart, and reproaches like "I climbed into that chimney for you".

report.h3: A rivet instead of a decision

report: The tale ends happily. The grandfather, chasing the runaways, fell and broke; he was glued together and a rivet was put through his neck, and he was as good as new, "except that never again could he nod his head". Billygoat-Legs gets no answer, and the couple stays together. But their fate was settled not by their will but by the rivet. **The tale begins with two figures placed side by side and ends with them staying side by side.** In the whole story they themselves decided nothing.

In English such a figure is a nodding mandarin; Russian calls it kitaisky bolvanchik, the "little Chinese dummy": a head that nods to everything. In a living couple anything can stand in the grandfather's place — relatives, "the way things are done", money, one's own inner judge. Coming home is not a mistake in itself: Waite's Fool will come back too, but "by another path after many days". The porcelain couple came back by the same path, the same night, and neither of the two chose the return.

The strong version of the tail is deciding on the rim of the chimney themselves, aloud and together. Naming who nods on the couple's behalf, and saying "no" before running. Going out to the edge more often and for short spells: the world is too big to enter in one night. Not paying for decisions with the words "if you love me". Letting each other go off to their own roofs and calmly waiting for the return. Settling the status of the relationship themselves, before another rivet does it for the couple. **Then the home becomes a base rather than a shelf, and The Fool becomes the freedom to come home by another path.**

seo.title: Karmic tail 3 7 4 compatibility: who rules in the couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 7 4 compatibility: the Empress, the Chariot and the Emperor. A couple that wants a shared garden, travels apart and has to learn to share power.

items.title: Karmic tail 3-7-4 in compatibility: the Empress, the Chariot and the Emperor
items.short: The couple's tail 3-7-4 looks like a ready-made equation: the Empress plus the Emperor equals the Chariot. In this compatibility karmic tail the couple enters the task through a wish for a shared garden and plenty, lives it out on the road, where each partner drives a chariot of their own, and arrives at the main lesson: agreeing on power — who rules what in the couple, and how to keep a promise without letting it become a chain.

sections.h2: How the 3-7-4 tail is formed: two royal cards in the middles
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The entry to the task is the sum of the two personal entries, the middle is the sum of the two personal middles, and the main task is the sum of the two karmic tasks. This is how it looks for the dates 02.01.1980 and 14.10.1975.

The partners' personal tails are 9-3-21 and 21-4-10. This is not a quirk of the example: a check of every date shows that the couple's tail 3-7-4 is built only from these two personal tails, in 100% of such couples. There is no other way to reach it.

Now look at the middles. The person with the tail 9-3-21 has the Empress in the middle; the person with 21-4-10 has the Emperor. The couple's tail begins with that same Empress, ends with that same Emperor, and in its middle stands the Chariot, made of both: 3 + 4 = 7. **The two royal cards the partners carry inside their own tails stand at the two ends of the couple's road, and in the middle of it they ride in one chariot.**

This does not mean that one of the two is "the Emperor" and the other "the Empress". Sex has no effect on the numbers, and the middle of a personal tail is not a role in the couple. The coincidence says something else: both kinds of power, the soft and the firm, are present in this couple from the first day, and the main task is not to choose one of them but to bring them together into a shared order.

The centre works the same way. With the tail 21-4-10 the personal centre is always 11, Strength; with 9-3-21 it is always 6, the Lovers. Their sum is 17, the Star, and it stands in the centre of 100% of couples with this tail. Neither partner has the Star in the centre, and neither can: no date of birth ever gives 17 in the centre of a personal matrix. This card appears only when the two are counted together.

Nor does 3-7-4 exist as a personal tail. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and with a task of 4 an entry of 3 is impossible whatever the centre. No other couple's tail is made of the numbers 3, 7 and 4: this triple occurs only in this order. The tail appears in about one couple in 217 (0.461%), which puts it 58th of the 97 couple's tails.

sections.h2: The Franklin's Tale: a marriage that began with an agreement about power
paragraphs: In Chaucer's Canterbury Tales (late fourteenth century) pilgrims take turns telling stories, and several stories in a row argue about one thing: who should have the upper hand in marriage. The Wife of Bath demands power for the wife; meek Griselda in the Clerk's Tale endures any will of her husband's. In 1912 the American scholar George Lyman Kittredge read these tales as a single debate on marriage, and they have been called the "Marriage Group" ever since. The Franklin's Tale is usually read as the answer to the whole debate.

The teller himself seems to be made of two of our cards. In the General Prologue we learn that in the Franklin's house "it snewed ... of mete and drinke" — it snowed food and drink — and that his table stood laid in the hall all day long, while at the court sessions "ther was he lord and sire"; he had been a sheriff and sat as knight of the shire. A host of plenty and a man of power in one person. Even his title speaks of freedom: a franklin is a free landholder, from Old French franc, "free". Keep that word in mind: the tale will end on it.

The Franklin claims to be retelling an old Breton lay. In fact the nearest source is Boccaccio: a question of love in Book IV of the Filocolo (the 1330s) and the fifth story of the tenth day of the Decameron. The root of the plot is older still, and Indian: in the Vetala tales about a girl who made a rash promise, the same final question is asked — which of the three was the most generous. Here and below Chaucer is quoted in the original Middle English from Skeat's edition, with plain glosses where needed; Boccaccio is quoted in our own translation from the Italian.

The story goes like this. In Brittany the knight Arveragus long courts the noble lady Dorigen, and she agrees to marry him. Then Chaucer does something Boccaccio does not: before telling us about the marriage, he spells out its contract. Of his own free will Arveragus swears never to take mastery over his wife against her will, never to show jealousy, and to obey her in everything, as a lover obeys his lady — **"save that the name of soveraynetee"**, the name of sovereignty, which he will keep for himself "for shame of his degree". Dorigen answers that since he offers her "so large a reyne", such a loose rein, she will be his humble, true wife. And the Franklin adds a word of his own:

"Frendes everich other moot obeye, if they wol longe holden companye. Love wol nat ben constreyned by maistrye; whan maistrie comth, the god of love anon beteth hise winges, and farewel! he is gon! Love is a thing as any spirit free; wommen of kinde desiren libertee, and nat to ben constreyned as a thral; and so don men, if I soth seyen shal" (lines 762–770).

The contract ends in "an humble wys accord": she has taken him as both servant and lord — "servant in love, and lord in mariage". It is hard to imagine a better agreement. The 3-7-4 tail begins with exactly such an agreement, and the whole tale tests whether it will survive the road.

The tail fits the tale almost act by act. The Empress is the first year of marriage and the garden in May. The Chariot is the husband's departure in search of glory and everything that happens while he is away. The Emperor is his return and the decision he takes for both of them. And in the middle of the plot, where the couple has the Star in its centre, sits an astrologer from Orléans, counting the stars.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — the Empress: a garden asked for in January
paragraphs: Point M in a couple's tail is what the two want together: shared wishes, agreements, a common language. Here the Empress is the wish to live in plenty: a home of their own, a generous table, a garden, children or a joint venture, prosperity that can be seen. Chaucer describes the first years of such a couple in a single line: who could tell, unless he had been married, "the joye, the ese, and the prosperitee that is bitwixe an housbonde and his wyf"? The last of those words is the Empress's own: plenty that keeps growing. For a year and more Arveragus and Dorigen live "in blisse and in solas". This is the Empress at the entry: the two are happy together, and everything around them grows.

But the entry of the tail stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish can turn into resistance. With the Empress the resistance looks soft: agree "out of love" without spelling anything out; give the reins a little more slack; hurt nobody with a refusal. That is exactly how trouble begins in Chaucer. In a garden on "the sixte morwe of May", a garden like no other "but-if it were the verray paradys", the young neighbour Aurelius confesses his love to Dorigen. She answers firmly: never. Then, seeing how he suffers, she adds — "in pley", Chaucer stresses — that she will love him if he clears every rock from the coast of Brittany, stone by stone. **"For wel I woot that it shal never bityde."**

In Boccaccio the same scene comes even closer to the Empress. The lady of the Filocolo wants to be rid of a persistent suitor and asks for an impossible gift: "in the month of January, in this land, a fine large garden, full of grass and flowers and trees and fruit, as if it were May". And she tells herself: "This is impossible — that is how I will get him off my back." In the Decameron Madonna Dianora asks for the same thing — a garden in January as lovely as in May. Chaucer swapped the garden for the rocks, but the motif stayed: the wish that it should always be May turns into a promise that someone will one day come to collect.

In a couple with the 3-7-4 tail this mechanism is easy to recognise. One partner cannot say "no" without softening it — "well, unless…" — and the softening sounds like a promise. The other agrees to a move, a loan, a joint business "some day", because right now it seems impossible. While it is May in the house, such words cost nothing. The task of the entry is to speak about wishes directly and not to hand out promises that rest only on the certainty that they will never have to be kept.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — the Chariot: two years in England and the black rocks
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya's book point N has no meaning of its own: it is an addition to the main task. We read it as the road — what the couple does and goes through on the way from the wish to the task. In the 3-7-4 tail that road is the Chariot: movement, a road of one's own for each, a race of one's own and victories of one's own.

In Chaucer the Chariot begins a year after the wedding. Arveragus leaves for England "to seke in armes worship and honour; for al his lust he sette in swich labour" — all his delight was in such labour — and stays there two years. He writes letters home, doubts nothing, and on his return "no-thing list him to been imaginatyf": he has no wish to imagine whether anyone spoke of love to his wife while he was away. Dorigen, meanwhile, weeps, lies awake, walks with her friends along the high shore counting ships — and every time she looks down she sees the "grisly rokkes blake" on which his ship might break.

Her prayer on the shore is already about the main task of the tail: "Eterne god, that thurgh thy purveyaunce ledest the world by certein governaunce" — eternal God, who guides the world by sure governance — why did you make these rocks, which do nobody any good? The one who stayed at home argues about who rules the world and how, while the one who left seeks glory in arms. **The Chariot in the middle of the tail divides the couple like this: one gets the road and the glory, the other the shore and the fear.** Each sees their own: the one who travels does not see the rocks, and the one who waits sees nothing else.

In a modern couple this is rotation work, a long project, study in another city, a start-up that eats every evening, or simply working "until the last". Or both are in chariots — and then the argument is about whose road matters more, who will adjust and who will give way first. Among the tasks of a couple with the Chariot, Lisovskaya names the balance between career and relationship and the rivalry for leadership. The bright side of the Chariot is visible in Chaucer too: Arveragus is not jealous, he keeps his vow never to "kythe hir jalousye", and the letters keep coming home. The Chariot does not have to separate — it has to come back.

In Boccaccio the middle of the plot is a chariot in the literal sense. The suitor has searched the whole West for a sorcerer and finds him in Thessaly: a poor old man called Tebano, gathering herbs. At night Tebano stretches out his arms to the stars, calls on the night, the stars, Hecate and Ceres for help — and "the stars did not shine in vain: swifter than the flight of any bird a chariot drawn by two dragons came before him; he mounted it, took the reins in his hands and rose into the air". For three days he flies over mountains and rivers, cutting herbs, and the dragons, breathing in their scent, shed their old skins and grow young again. The Chariot gives strength back to the one who drives it towards a goal rather than away from something.

One more detail. Chaucer's marriage contract is phrased from the start in the language of harness: Dorigen thanks her husband for letting the reins run so loose. The question of who holds the reins stands at this couple's entry, is settled on the road, and becomes the main task at the end.

sections.h2: Main task — the Emperor: "Is ther oght elles, Dorigen, but this?"
paragraphs: Point D is the couple's main task: what does not work for it and what it has to learn; it is read above all through the shadow side. The Emperor in this point means power, order, rules, responsibility. On the shadow side: decisions made for everyone, rigidity, rules that later get in the way of the very people who made them, and a face on which nobody can tell joy from anger. On the bright side: support and protection, an agreement on boundaries that lets both feel safe.

In Chaucer the task arrives in a single evening. For two years Aurelius lies "in langour and in torment"; then his brother takes him to a learned astrologer in Orléans. For a thousand pounds of gold the man undertakes to remove the rocks, arrives in Brittany in "the colde frosty seson of Decembre", and makes it so that "for a wyke or tweye, it semed that alle the rokkes were aweye". Aurelius comes to Dorigen: "wel I woot the rokkes been aweye!" For two days she weeps alone — her husband is away from home — and on the third night Arveragus returns and asks why she is crying. She tells him everything.

The husband's first words are the Emperor at his best. He answers "with glad chere, in freendly wyse": **"Is ther oght elles, Dorigen, but this?"** — is there anything else, Dorigen, but this? And then: "lat slepen that is stille" — let sleeping dogs lie; it may yet turn out well. No shouting, no accusation, no jealous scene. His next words are the Emperor's shadow, in the same minute: "Ye shul your trouthe holden, by my fay! … Trouthe is the hyeste thing that man may kepe." With that word he burst into tears and said: "I yow forbede, up peyne of deeth" — on pain of death — ever to tell anyone of this; he would bear his grief as best he could and show no sign of sorrow, so that people should think no harm of her. A squire and a maid take her towards the garden; nobody knows why.

The man who at the wedding gave up power over his wife against her will gives an order for the first time in a crisis. The "name of sovereignty", kept for other people's eyes, turns into sovereignty overnight. And everything in his decision is noble: he puts his wife's word above his own pain, guards her good name, hides his tears. But the decision is taken for two, the rule is placed above the person, and the grief is hidden for the sake of onlookers. Chaucer himself expects the listeners' indignation: "Paraventure an heep of yow, y-wis, wol holden him a lewed man in this, that he wol putte his wyf in jupartye; herkneth the tale, er ye up-on hir crye" — perhaps many of you will think him a fool for putting his wife in jeopardy; hear the tale before you cry out against her.

This is what the main task of 3-7-4 looks like in everyday life. The couple agreed that each decides for themselves — until the first crisis, when one suddenly decides for both, "for our sake". Someone once said in passing, "your parents are your business", "we each keep our own money", "if it comes to that, we split without drama" — and a rule spoken in May starts being carried out to the letter in December. In public they keep up appearances; at home they do not talk about what matters. Among Lisovskaya's tasks for a couple with the Emperor there are two that read like a summary of Chaucer: **do not create rules that later get in the way, and learn to talk about feelings.**

In Boccaccio the husband's act is judged by a court of love. Queen Fiammetta finds a legal answer: at the wedding both partners swear to be content with each other, and "no later oath can override the first one lawfully made". So the wife's promise to her suitor was worthless from the start. The verdict translates easily into a couple's language. Sooner or later any two people make promises on the side — to work, to parents, to friends, to the bank, to themselves. The main task of the tail is to know which agreement comes first, and not to let a later one cancel an earlier one.

Her companion Menedon objects with a phrase that suits a couple with the Emperor as their main task very well: "whoever gives what he cannot refuse gives little". A concession made by the rule is not yet a gift.

sections.h2: The Chariot in Waite and Wen: two powers in one carriage
paragraphs: Put the three cards of the tail side by side in the books, and the coincidences become almost awkward. Waite describes the Empress and the Emperor as a pair: the Emperor is "by imputation the spouse of the former", and he adds at once that the two cards "do not precisely represent the condition of married life, though this state is implied". In the 3-7-4 tail the couple travels from one of them to the other.

The Chariot between them is, for Waite, "really the King in his triumph", "typifying, however, the victory which creates kingship as its natural consequence and not the vested royalty of the fourth card". In this tail the seventh card leads straight to the fourth: the couple wins first and then learns to rule. Waite's chariot is drawn by two sphinxes, Boccaccio's by two dragons: two forces in one harness.

The most precise clue is in Benebell Wen. The chariot, she writes, bears a badge with the lingam and the yoni — Shiva and Shakti — and its traditional meaning is **"the union of the external sphere of rulership by man and the internal sphere of rulership by woman"**. Two powers in one carriage: exactly what the tail builds from the Emperor and the Empress. The split by sex is an old tradition here, not a rule for the couple: Chaucer's knight himself hands power to his wife and keeps only the name. The question of the 3-7-4 tail is not which sphere belongs to whom by birth, but who rules what by agreement.

In Wen both of them hold a sign of power. The Empress "holds up her baton of sovereignty"; for the Emperor, "the scepter or crux ansata is his sovereignty; the orb is his dominion". The soft power of plenty and the firm power of order are both power, not power and submission. Sovereignty, soveraynetee, is the very word Arveragus kept for himself "in name".
One last detail will matter when we come to the stars: in Waite the arms of the Emperor's throne "are fronted by rams' heads", and Wen links the card to the sign of Aries.

sections.h2: The Star in the centre: what the astrologer from Orléans measured by the stars
paragraphs: The couple's centre is its shared atmosphere, what lies between the two and is not on show. In every couple with the 3-7-4 tail it holds the Star — a card no single person ever has in the centre. In Lisovskaya's reading, the Star in a couple's centre at its best is a union that inspires both partners: they say plainly what they like and what they do not, they know how to forgive, and the beautiful picture, for once, turns out to be true. On the shadow side: things left unsaid, a showy wrapping, ultimatums.

In the middle of the Franklin's Tale stands a man with the stars. The astrologer from Orléans brings out his "tables Toletanes", works out the mansions of the moon and, as Chaucer puts it, "knew ful wel how fer Alnath was shove fro the heed of thilke fixe Aries above that in the ninthe speere considered is" — how far the star Alnath had been pushed from the head of the fixed Aries of the ninth sphere. This is a calculation of precession: the stars slowly drift away from the point they were once fixed to. Just before this the Franklin assures us, "I ne can no termes of astrologye" — I know no terms of astrology — and then pours them out. Chaucer knew them perfectly well: in 1391 he wrote a treatise on the astrolabe for his little son Lewis.

**Our own observation, not a teaching of the sources: the astrologer measures the distance between a star and the Ram — between the card in this couple's centre and the sign of its main task.** That is exactly what a couple with the 3-7-4 tail has to do from time to time: check how far their shared star — hope, inspiration, faith in each other — has drifted from the fixed point of their first agreement. Not to drag it back into place by force, but to know where it stands now.

The Star's shadow is in this story too. The rocks did not vanish — they only "semed" to be gone for a week or two. An atmosphere of hope is good at producing appearances: "it will work out somehow", "that will never happen", "everything is fine with us". And right beside it is the Star at its best: Dorigen tells her husband everything, hiding nothing. The trouble will end precisely because the truth was spoken aloud — and nearly begins again when the husband forbids her to speak it to anyone else.

Waite gives the Star two mottoes: "Waters of Life freely" and "Gifts of the Spirit". Wen calls it "a card of divine charity": it is about "giving more than the Seeker receives". In Boccaccio, Menedon speaks of generosity in words that sound like a description of this card: "it is a great thing to bear a long thirst, reach the fountain and not drink, so as to let another drink". And the Franklin said before his story had even begun: "Love is a thing as any spirit free." In the centre of this couple stands a card of the gift — and, as the ending will show, it is the gift, not the rule, that solves the main task.

sections.h2: The couple's values: free choice or bonds
paragraphs: The couple's spiritual purpose is its values, what the union exists for. Couples with the 3-7-4 tail have one of two cards there: the Lovers (6) in 59% and the Devil (15) in 41%. Both answer the question of the main task, only from different sides.

The Lovers are the value of choice. What matters to such a couple is that the two choose each other again and again, and every rule is tested by one thing: does it take that choice away? For them the Franklin's line is almost a charter: love will not be constrained by mastery, and when mastery comes, the god of love flies off. Such a couple needs the Emperor of its main task as a frame in which choice can live, not as a lock on the door.

The Devil is the value of bonds, of what ties people together. Such couples are held by promises, shared debts and obligations, an attachment that is hard to break. In Chaucer the bonds are literally visible: Dorigen complains to Fortune, who has "unwar wrapped" her "in thy cheyne", Aurelius owes the astrologer a thousand pounds of gold, and the resolution sounds like a legal formula: "I yow relesse, madame, in-to your hond quit every surement and every bond." Lisovskaya ends her chapter on the Devil with the thought that nobody belongs to anybody. For such a couple the main task is to keep the bonds a union and not let them become a chain.

sections.h2: Who was the most generous: how the 3-7-4 tail opens up at its best
paragraphs: Chaucer's ending is a chain of releases. Aurelius meets Dorigen in the street; she is going "un-to the gardin, as myn housbond bad, my trouthe for to holde, allas! allas!". Seeing her grief and her husband's nobility, he lets her go: "and right as frely as he sente hir me, as frely sente I hir to him ageyn". The astrologer, hearing of this, forgives Aurelius the debt: shall a clerk not do a noble deed as well as a knight and a squire? The Franklin ends with a question to his listeners: **"Which was the moste free, as thinketh yow?"** The man whose title means "free" asks who was the freest of them all.

People have answered the question in different ways. Boccaccio's Fiammetta names the husband: he gave away the dearest thing, his honour. Menedon disagrees: the sorcerer was the most generous, because the old man returned of his own will to poverty. The king in the Indian Vetala tale thinks the thief was the noble one. The cards of the 3-7-4 tail answer differently: **in this couple power is settled not by whoever holds the rule most tightly, but by whoever lets go first.** Waite's Emperor reversed means "benevolence, compassion, credit", and the tale ends with exactly that: Aurelius's compassion and the respite on his debt, which the astrologer turns into forgiveness.
What helps a couple with this tail live it at its best:

ul: **Agree on power aloud and by area.** Who decides about money, the home, moving, children or the joint venture — and make sure the "name of sovereignty" shown to relatives and friends does not differ from how things really work at home.
**Make no promises "in jest"** or "because it will never happen": the impossible does sometimes happen, and someone comes to collect.
**Talk about the rocks before the journey.** Before a departure, a new job or a big project, discuss what frightens the one who stays, not only what the one who goes stands to win.
**In a hard moment, start with a question, not a decision:** "is there anything else but this?" — and decide together, even if one of you is sure they know the nobler way.
**Do not hide grief for the sake of other people's opinion.** An Emperor who keeps up a face for the public is left alone with his throne.
**Check the star against the Ram.** From time to time revisit the first agreement: not "but we agreed", but "where are we now compared with what we agreed".

paragraphs: Chaucer's last lines about the couple are the strong version of this tail: "Arveragus and Dorigene his wyf in sovereyn blisse leden forth hir lyf. Never eft ne was ther angre hem bitwene; he cherisseth hir as though she were a quene; and she was to him trewe for evermore." The road from the Empress to the Emperor closes on the Empress, but now she is crowned not by the softness of a May agreement but by an order tested in winter. The garden that Boccaccio's sorcerer raised by magic in January, such a couple can grow itself: **plenty that rests not on an endless May but on an agreement that has come through December.**

ul: **3 — The Empress, entry to the task.** The shared wish: a home, a generous table, a joint venture, a life where there is enough of everything. The same wish for softness turns into resistance when the time comes to agree on something seriously.
**7 — The Chariot, middle of the task.** How the couple moves towards its goal: in motion, often apart, with departures, races and an argument about who holds the reins.
**4 — The Emperor, main task.** What the couple has to learn: power shared by two — rules that suit both, and decisions that are not taken on the other's behalf, even out of nobility.

intro: The equation 3 + 4 = 7 only looks simple. The middle of a couple's tail is not worked out from its two ends: it is the sum of the middles of two personal tails, and those middles hold exactly the same two cards — the Emperor in one person's tail and the Empress in the other's. And the plot of this tail was written, almost scene by scene, more than six hundred years ago: in Geoffrey Chaucer's Franklin's Tale a marriage begins with an agreement about power and ends with the question of who was the most generous of all.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 3-7-4 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail: the Empress at the entry to the task, the Chariot in the middle and the Emperor as the main task. The couple wants shared plenty and a home, travels towards it through movement, departures and races, and has to learn power shared by two — agreements that suit both, and decisions that are not taken on the other's behalf.

faq.q: Is the 3-7-4 tail a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail describes a task, not a verdict and not a forecast. It shows where such a couple stumbles — soft promises, separate roads and decisions made for two — and what it can learn. The main task is read through its shadow side because it is a lesson, not a judgement of the union.

faq.q: Why do couples with the 3-7-4 tail always have the Star in the centre?
faq.a: The 3-7-4 tail is built only from the personal tails 21-4-10 and 9-3-21. With the first the personal centre is always 11, Strength; with the second always 6, the Lovers; and 11 + 6 = 17. No date of birth gives the Star in the centre of a personal matrix, so a couple receives this card only as two.

faq.q: Can 3-7-4 be a personal karmic tail?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and with a task of 4 an entry of 3 is impossible whatever the centre. So 3-7-4 is only a couple's tail, and texts about personal tails do not apply to it: the calculation and the points are different.

faq.q: Who is "the Emperor" in a couple with the 3-7-4 tail?
faq.a: Nobody by appointment. One partner has the Emperor in the middle of their personal tail and the other has the Empress, but that is about numbers, not about who leads. Sex does not affect the calculation. The main task is shared: both have to learn a kind of power that keeps order without taking away the other's voice.

report: At his wedding a knight swears never to take mastery over his wife against her will — "save that the name of soveraynetee", the name of sovereignty, which he keeps "for shame of his degree". Geoffrey Chaucer's Franklin's Tale opens with this proviso, and the 3-7-4 tail follows the tale almost scene by scene. The Empress at the entry is the wish for a shared garden and plenty. The Chariot in the middle is a road on which each partner drives a carriage of their own. The Emperor as the main task is power shared by two: who rules what, and how to keep a promise without letting it become a chain. The Empress and the Emperor — two royal cards that Waite describes as husband and wife — stand at the two ends of the road, and in its middle they ride in one chariot.

report.h3: A promise made in jest

report: Chaucer describes the first year of the marriage in the Empress's own words: "the joye, the ese, and the prosperitee that is bitwixe an housbonde and his wyf". A couple with this tail is happy together, and everything around it grows: the home, the table, the joint venture. But the entry of the tail stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish for softness turns into resistance. Agree "out of love" without spelling anything out. Give the reins a little more slack. Hurt nobody with a refusal.

That is how trouble begins in Chaucer. In a May garden like no other "but-if it were the verray paradys", a neighbour confesses his love to Dorigen. She refuses him firmly — and then, seeing how he suffers, promises "in pley" to love him if he clears every rock from the coast of Brittany. **"For wel I woot that it shal never bityde."** In Boccaccio, Chaucer's source, the lady's request comes even closer to the Empress: a garden in January, full of flowers and fruit, "as if it were May". The wish that it should always be May turns into a promise that someone will one day come to collect.

In everyday life this is "well, unless…" instead of a plain "no", or agreeing to a move or a joint business "some day", because right now it seems impossible. While it is May in the house, such words cost nothing.

report.h3: One gets the road, the other the rocks

report: A year later the husband leaves for England "to seke in armes worship and honour" and stays there two years. He writes letters and doubts nothing. His wife counts ships from the high shore and sees below the "grisly rokkes blake" on which his ship might break. Her prayer there is already about the main task: why did God, who guides the world "by certein governaunce", make these rocks at all?

**The Chariot in the middle of the tail divides the couple like this: one gets the road and the glory, the other the shore and the fear.** The one who travels does not see the rocks; the one who waits sees nothing else. In a modern couple this is a long project, rotation work, study in another city — or two chariots at once and an argument about whose road matters more. The Chariot does not have to separate — it has to come back. It is no accident that Chaucer's marriage contract is phrased in the language of harness: the wife thanks her husband for letting the reins run so loose.

report.h3: "Is ther oght elles, Dorigen, but this?"

report: The astrologer from Orléans makes it so that for a week or two the rocks "semed" to be gone. Dorigen tells her husband everything. His first words are the Emperor at his best: **"Is ther oght elles, Dorigen, but this?"** — is there anything else, Dorigen, but this? No shouting, no jealousy. His next words are the Emperor's shadow, in the same minute: "Trouthe is the hyeste thing that man may kepe." He burst into tears, forbade her "up peyne of deeth" ever to tell anyone, and promised to show no sign of sorrow, so that people should think no harm of her.

The man who gave up power over his wife gives an order for the first time in a crisis. Everything in his decision is noble, but the decision is taken for two, the rule is placed above the person, and the grief is hidden for the sake of onlookers. In everyday life this is "each of us decides for ourselves" — until the first crisis, when one decides for both, "for our sake"; a rule dropped in passing in May that is carried out to the letter in December. The couple's main task is to create no rules that later get in the way, and to learn to talk about feelings. In Boccaccio a court of love adds that no later oath can override the first one lawfully made. The couple needs to know which of its agreements comes first.

Benebell Wen sees on the Chariot a badge that traditionally stands for the union of two spheres of rulership, the external and the internal. Two powers in one carriage — exactly what this tail is made of. The question is not which sphere belongs to whom, but who rules what by agreement.

report.h3: A star checked against the Ram

report: A couple with this tail always has the Star in the centre — a card no single person ever has there: only two people together can produce it. At the centre of the tale stands a man with the stars as well. The astrologer works out "how fer Alnath was shove fro the heed of thilke fixe Aries", how far the star Alnath had drifted from the head of the fixed Ram, and in Wen the Ram is the Emperor's sign. This is our own observation, not a teaching of the sources, but it is exactly the work the couple has to do: from time to time, check how far their shared hope has drifted from the point of their first agreement.

The ending is a chain of releases. The neighbour lets Dorigen go once he sees her grief: "and right as frely as he sente hir me, as frely sente I hir to him ageyn". The astrologer forgives him the debt. The Franklin, whose title means "free", asks his listeners "which was the moste free". **In this couple power is settled not by whoever holds the rule most tightly, but by whoever lets go first.**
What helps a couple live this tail at its best:

ul: agreeing on power aloud and by area — money, the home, moving, children or the joint venture;
making no promises "in jest" or "because it will never happen";
talking about the rocks before the journey, not after it;
in a hard moment, starting with a question rather than a decision, and deciding together;
not hiding grief for the sake of other people's opinion.

report: Chaucer's last lines about the couple: "Never eft ne was ther angre hem bitwene; he cherisseth hir as though she were a quene." The road from the Empress to the Emperor comes back to the Empress. Boccaccio's January garden was raised by magic, but such a couple can grow one itself: **plenty that rests not on an endless May but on an agreement that has come through December.**

unit.title: A pact that outlasted December

captions.M: To want a shared garden, a home and plenty
captions.N: To each drive your own road and come back
captions.D: To share power and keep your word without chains
