seo.title: Karmic tail 6 11 14 compatibility: the couple's tail explained
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 11 14 compatibility: The Lovers, Strength and Temperance. Why a couple has Strength where Judgement should stand, and who tames whom.

items.title: The 6-11-14 karmic tail in compatibility: a taming with no winner
items.short: The couple's karmic tail 6-11-14 — The Lovers, Strength and Temperance — holds an oddity that only the numbers reveal. For a single person, the road from The Lovers to Temperance always runs through Judgement: 6 + 14 = 20. For a couple, that place is taken by Strength, 11. Where one person alone would face a verdict from outside, two people are left alone with each other, and they start taming each other.

sections.h2: The first clue: Strength where Judgement should stand
paragraphs: A couple's tail is counted differently from a personal one. Each of its three points is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. So the middle of a couple's tail is not derived from its two ends, as it is for one person; it is assembled from the middles of two personal tails. By the personal formula this place would hold Judgement: a personal 6-20-14 tail does exist. A personal 6-11-14 tail does not exist at all — only two people can add it up.
Running through every date since 1900 shows how couples assemble their Strength:

ul: **20 + 9 → 11** — in 45% of couples: one partner has Judgement in the middle of the personal tail, the other has The Hermit;
**5 + 6 = 11** — in 30%: one partner's Hierophant and the other's Lovers;
**19 + 19 → 11** — in 22%: both have The Sun in the middle, and their personal tails are identical, 12-19-7;
the remaining 3% — the combinations 19 + 10 and 20 + 18.

paragraphs: In almost half of these couples (46%), Judgement has not gone anywhere: one of the two carries it in their personal matrix. But added to the other partner's card, it stops being Judgement and becomes Strength. One person's verdict turns into the strength of two — or into a struggle between two, depending on how they use it.

The second clue is stricter still. In these couples, neither partner has Strength or Temperance in their personal tail — not in any of the five combinations. The Lovers appear in one partner's personal tail in 30% of couples, and in 70% of couples none of the three cards appears in either personal tail. Nobody brings the middle or the main task of this tail with them: these cards appear only between the two.

The ends of the tail, meanwhile, behave just as they would for one person: the entry equals the main task plus the centre. With The Sun at the centre, 14 + 19 = 33 → 6; with The Wheel of Fortune, 14 + 10 = 24 → 6. Only the middle breaks the rule — the very point where a single person would have Judgement.

And one coincidence is too exact to pass over. In The Taming of the Shrew a servant describes a "taming-school" whose master is Petruchio, teaching "tricks eleven and twenty long". The phrase alludes to the card game thirty-one: 11 + 20 = 31, meaning "exactly right". Eleven and twenty are the very two cards that compete for the middle of this tail. Shakespeare knew nothing of the destiny matrix, of course, but his master of taming counts in exactly these numbers.

sections.h2: Two plays about one husband
paragraphs: Shakespeare wrote The Taming of the Shrew in the early 1590s. Some twenty years later John Fletcher — Shakespeare's co-author on his late plays and his successor as chief playwright of the King's Men — wrote a sequel: The Woman's Prize, or The Tamer Tamed. Katherina is dead by now, Petruchio marries Maria, and on the very first night Maria shuts herself up in the house with her allies and sets her husband terms.

In November 1633 the two plays were performed one after the other before Charles I and Queen Henrietta Maria at St James's Palace: Shakespeare's on Tuesday the 26th, Fletcher's on Thursday the 28th. The Master of the Revels, Sir Henry Herbert, noted that the first was "liked" and the second "very well liked". In a single week the king and queen saw both ends of one story.

Shakespeare's play has a frame that is often forgotten. A drunken tinker, Christopher Sly, is picked up outside an alehouse, carried to a lord's bed and assured that he is a lord. The play is performed for him, and as a remedy: "Seeing too much sadness hath congeal'd your blood, / And melancholy is the nurse of frenzy, / Therefore they thought it good you hear a play". Fletcher's prologue repeats the prescription: if you fall sick of melancholy, "see't agen. / 'Tis no dear Physick". Both plays about a couple present themselves as a way to restore measure.

In the anonymous 1594 play The Taming of a Shrew, a close relative of Shakespeare's, the frame closes. Sly wakes outside the alehouse and announces, "I know now how to tame a shrew" — and sets off home to try it on his wife. The recipe for taming turns out to be a drunken tinker's dream. This is worth keeping in mind: everything that follows between Petruchio and Katherina is a dream that another person can be remade, and the play itself warns that it is a dream.

The cards of the tail fall onto the two plays in order. The wooing and the first sparring match are The Lovers. Shakespeare's taming and Fletcher's counter-taming are Strength. Fletcher's epilogue is Temperance.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: The Lovers, whose common language is sparring
paragraphs: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together, its agreements and its common language. On the couple's chart it is the same point as "Common language" on the relationship line. Katherina and Petruchio find their common language with the first line they exchange, and it is the language of sparring. A minute after meeting, they are already finishing each other's puns:
— Who knows not where a wasp does / wear his sting? In his tail. / — In his tongue.

The sting of these two really is in the tongue. Her sister's suitors are afraid of Katherina, her father is worn out by her, her music teacher left with a lute broken over his head. Petruchio is the first to answer her at her own speed. That is The Lovers at the entry: attraction to a person with whom there is no need to pretend. Waite calls this card simply "in all simplicity the card of human love".

But the entry stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. Shakespeare shows where Katherina's shrewishness comes from before the wooing even begins: her sister is loved, and she is not. "She is your treasure, she must have a husband; / I must dance bare-foot on her wedding day," she throws at her father. When Petruchio comes to woo, her father tells him the main thing is to win her love, "for that is all in all". Petruchio replies: "Why, that is nothing." At the entry the two want the same thing — a love in which you are the one chosen — and at once argue over whether it is needed at all.

For Wen, The Lovers is above all a card of choice, and this wooing is exactly where the choice is missing. The father and the suitor settle the dowry without the bride. "Will you, nill you, I will marry you," says Petruchio — willing or not. Consent is skipped in the very first scene. Katherina will say her "yes" not at the altar but much later — on the road and in the middle of a street.

In the life of a couple with this tail, the entry is easy to recognise. The two find a tone only they understand: teasing, arguing for the sake of it, flirting through challenge. Others think they are quarrelling; they think they are talking. The trouble starts when tenderness can no longer be heard in this language and only the score of jabs is left. Lisovskaya describes the minus of The Lovers in a couple as a swing of "peace, then war", words that wound more than intended, and jealousy that grows out of self-doubt. Such a couple can be loud in public too. At the wedding Petruchio swears so loudly that the priest drops his book, and when he stoops to pick it up, the groom cuffs him; the whole church hears the kiss.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: Strength, or the taming-school
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya's book the middle of a couple's tail has no meaning of its own: it is an addition to the main task. We read it as the road — what the couple does and goes through on its way from the wish to the task. For these two, the road runs through Strength.

Shakespeare names it outright: "For I am he am born to tame you Kate, / And bring you from a wild Kate to a Kate / Conformable as other household Kates." The pun in the original rests on the name: Kate sounds like cat, and Petruchio promises to turn a "wild Kate" into a "household" one.

He describes his method as a falconer would: "My falcon now is sharp and passing empty… Another way I have to man my haggard… That is, to watch her, as we watch these kites". The meat is "burnt", the bed is badly made, and all of it is done "in reverend care of her". A servant sums it up in one line: "He kills her in her own humour." Another does the arithmetic more precisely: "By this reckoning he is more shrew than she." Petruchio wins by becoming more of a shrew than the shrew.

This is the first trap of Strength in a couple: the two compete over who can hold out longer. Petruchio explained the arithmetic himself before the wedding: "And where two raging fires meet together / They do consume the thing that feeds their fury". Two fires are an exact picture of the middle 11 in every fifth couple with this tail, where it is made of one partner's Sun and the other's.

Wen writes about Strength what Petruchio missed: a person "cannot use brute force to exercise will over others" and must use "gentle, subtle influence". For her, Strength is mastery of the self, while The Chariot is mastery of the world around. Lisovskaya describes the minus of Strength in a couple as a competition: each wants to be in charge, each has their own truth, and the other's view is not accepted. In the plus is what the play reaches only in its fifth act: one partner accepts the other's lead, flexibility appears, and tension turns into passion.

In daily life the middle 11 shows itself in small things that decide whose word is last: who picks the road, who decides whether the food is "all right", who falls silent first and stays silent longer. Pressure rarely looks like an order. More often it looks like care that leaves the other no choice. Shakespeare's Petruchio is the extreme case: hunger and sleeplessness. In a real couple this is not the task of the tail but a boundary. If one partner holds the other through fear, by withholding food, sleep, money or contact, or through threats, outside help is needed: a psychologist, a crisis line, and in danger — a local emergency number.

paragraphs.h3: The tamer who had been tamed before

paragraphs: Fletcher saw in Shakespeare's play what Shakespeare had left offstage: Strength works both ways. In the very first scene of the sequel, friends recall the late Katherina: she "turn'd his temper, / And forc'd him blow as high as she"; the bare remembrance of her "will make him start in's sleep". Petruchio himself calls that taming "my twelve strong labours to reclaim her, / Which would have made Don Hercules horn mad, / And hid him in his Hide". Hercules' hide, as everyone knows, was a lion's. The tamer came out of his first marriage tamed and never noticed.

Maria answers Petruchio in his own language. In Shakespeare he trained a "haggard", a wild hawk caught full-grown. Maria declares: "I am no more the gentle, tame Maria… I have a new soul in me / Made of a North wind, nothing but tempest" — and praises the free haggard, "that woman, that hath wing, and knows it". Her means are the same as his: refusal, siege, a bet on who will hold out longer. Across two plays one and the same man was both the tamer and the tamed. The role in the middle of this tail is tied neither to sex nor to character: it passes from hand to hand.

paragraphs.h3: A Judgement staged in a coffin

paragraphs: Then Fletcher stages a Judgement — the very card that is missing from the middle of the couple's tail. Petruchio pretends to be dead and is carried in in a coffin. Over the coffin Maria pronounces her verdict: she weeps not for him but for his life — "His poor unmanly, wretched, foolish life". The dead man cannot bear it, rises, and a few lines later says, "I am born again."

The scene is funny, but the mechanism is serious. When two people lack honest Strength, they stage a Judgement for themselves: a loud scene with a verdict and a resurrection, after which everything seems to start with a clean slate. In a comedy it works. In a couple such a scene brings relief but not measure: the score has not been reset; only the winner has changed.

sections.h2: The couple's atmosphere: an argument about the sun
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's chart is the atmosphere — what happens between the two when nobody is watching. In 77% of couples with the 6-11-14 tail the centre is The Sun; in 23% it is The Wheel of Fortune. No date ever puts The Sun at the centre of a personal chart: only two people can light it. Most often it comes from centres 9 and 10 (The Hermit and The Wheel, 45% of couples) or 7 and 12 (The Chariot and The Hanged Man, 30%).

The most famous scene of The Taming of the Shrew is the argument about the sun. Petruchio and Katherina are riding to her father's, it is broad day, and Petruchio says: "Good Lord, how bright and goodly shines the moon!" She objects: it is the sun. He orders the horses turned back. And then Katherina answers in a way that can be heard in two ways:

Then, God be bless'd, it is the blessed sun: / But sun it is not, when you say it is not; / And the moon changes even as your mind. / What you will have it named, even that it is; / And so it shall be so for Katharina.

This is The Sun at the centre of the couple in both of its forms at once. In the minus, one partner decides what counts as the sun, and the atmosphere rests on the other agreeing; Lisovskaya names total control and attempts to restrict the partner among the minuses of The Sun. The plus begins a minute later. An old man comes towards them, Petruchio greets him as a fair young maid, and Katherina takes up the game with such zest that the old man calls her "my merry mistress". Then she "apologises": her eyes, she says, "have been so bedazzled with the sun / That everything I look on seemeth green". For the first time the two laugh not at each other but together. Waite's list of meanings for The Sun includes "fortunate marriage". In the play this sun rises at the very moment the argument becomes a shared game.

Right after this scene comes the kiss in the street. "First kiss me, Kate, and we will." — "What, in the midst of the street?" — "What, art thou ashamed of me?" — "No, sir, God forbid; but ashamed to kiss." He threatens to turn for home, and she kisses him: "Nay, I will give thee a kiss: now pray thee, love, stay." Here, for the first time, she calls him "love". The entry of the tail, The Lovers, is fulfilled in public, without the father and without the dowry.

paragraphs.h3: When the Wheel of Fortune is at the centre

paragraphs: In 23% of couples the centre is The Wheel. Then the couple's atmosphere is a game of chance and a wager. In the last scene of the Shrew the husbands bet on whose wife is the most obedient, and the widow teases Petruchio with a proverb: "He that is giddy thinks the world turns round." Lisovskaya sees in a couple's Wheel an alternation of rises and crises and advises not to fight the alternation itself. Such a couple will easily recognise itself in Cole Porter's musical Kiss Me, Kate (1948): divorced actors play Petruchio and Katherina and, in the course of the show, live through their own story a second time.

sections.h2: Main task: Temperance, or two drops of equal weight
paragraphs: The main point of the tail is Temperance. It is read mostly through its minus: what the couple cannot manage and what it has to learn. For all their differences, both plays end in the same minus, the one Lisovskaya describes for a couple with Temperance: one partner keeps giving way, and the other never even thinks of it.

In Shakespeare this is Katherina's famous speech. Three husbands bet a hundred crowns on whose wife will come at the first call. Only Katherina comes, and she lectures the headstrong wives on duty: "But now I see our lances are but straws, / Our strength as weak, our weakness past compare, / That seeming to be most which we indeed least are." Two cards of the tail meet in one speech. Strength is declared an illusion, and measure — lower your pride, she tells the wives — is demanded of one side only.

Whether this is meant seriously or ironically has been argued for four hundred years. The last line of the play leaves the question open: "'Tis a wonder, by your leave, she will be tamed so." She will be tamed — that is, she lets herself be. The taming Petruchio dreamed of as his victory rests on her consent.

In Fletcher the score is reversed. Over the coffin Maria has got her way, and at once she says: "From this hour make me what you please: I have tam'd ye, / And now am vow'd your servant… Dare you kiss me? / Thus I begin my new love." Again one side gives everything away — only now it is the other one. And again the play ends with a kiss and a new love: the tail returns to its entry, to The Lovers.

In daily life the minus of Temperance looks ordinary. The same partner always apologises. Peace in the house rests on the other keeping quiet. A quarrel is not taken to a real conversation but put out by surrender, and resentment piles up until one day the score flips, as it does in Fletcher. Among the tasks of Temperance in a couple Lisovskaya names lost balance, suppressed feelings, haste and the wish to control the partner — and all of them can be seen in these two marriages.
Fletcher put the answer to the main task into Maria's mouth earlier, when Petruchio demands "due obedience" from her:
Take two small drops of water, equal weigh'd, / Tell me which is the heaviest, and which ought / First to descend in duty?

The question is not who is right but who gives way. Two drops of equal weight are two people, neither of them heavier. And Petruchio takes his first step towards measure in reply: "I urge not service from you, nor obedience / In way of duty, but of love, and Credit".
The play's epilogue reads like a formula for the main task, one a couple could write about itself:

The Tamer's tam'd, but so, as nor the men / Can find one just cause to complain of, when / They fitly do consider in their lives, / They should not reign as Tyrants o'er their wives. / Nor can the Women from this president / Insult, or triumph; it being aptly meant, / To teach both Sexes due equality; / And as they stand bound, to love mutually.

Its last two lines hold the whole formula: due equality, and mutual love between two people who are bound together. Neither victory nor surrender — equality between two people tied to each other. For Wen, Temperance is "the fusion of two contrasting elements and bringing them into harmony". And when the question is love in a relationship, the card, in her words, calls for "cooperation and tempering of extreme emotions, such as anger, resentment, hostility".

paragraphs.h3: The remedy Petruchio passed off as a trick

paragraphs: Shakespeare himself gave this couple a recipe for Temperance — through Petruchio's mouth, and as part of a trick. Throwing away the "burnt" meat, he says it is better for them to fast, "Since, of ourselves, ourselves are choleric". In the theory of temperament of the time, choler was the hot, angry humour, and two choleric people must not be given more fire. The trick becomes the truth once it is turned on oneself: when both are hot, anger is not fed — neither with food nor with words.

And at the wooing, Petruchio described Katherina with the very word of the main task: "She is not hot, but temperate as the morn". At the time it was a lie told to her father. The word spoken at the entry of the tail turned out to be the address the tail leads to.
If the links of this tail are put together the way Lisovskaya teaches one to connect the energies of a couple's tail, they come out like this:

ul: **The Lovers and Strength:** the common language of sparring easily becomes a struggle — flirting through challenge quietly turns into a score of jabs, and love starts being proved by winning.
**Strength and Temperance:** the main trap is who will out-stubborn whom; the way out is not to stop arguing but to stop adding fuel when both are hot.
**The Lovers and Temperance:** a love in which you were chosen rests on equality — giving way in turns, not by rank.
**All three cards:** a taming with no winner — every victory for one is recorded as a defeat for the couple.

sections.h2: The Lovers, Strength and Temperance in Waite: a chain of flowers and an angel without sex
paragraphs: The cards on this site have their own artwork. In the Rider–Waite–Smith deck, the three cards of this tail each add one detail to the story.

ul: **The Lovers.** A man and a woman beneath a winged figure, "unveiled before each other". The play begins the same way: from the first minute the two tell each other exactly what they think.

**Strength.** A woman closes a lion's jaws, and Waite stresses that the struggle is already over: "her beneficent fortitude has already subdued the lion, which is being led by a chain of flowers". The lion is not starved or kept awake — it is led on a chain of flowers. This is a direct answer to Shakespeare's falcon: a taming after which the beast stays a lion and walks alongside of its own accord. Petruchio wanted to turn a wildcat into a house cat; on Waite's Strength card the lion does not become a kitten.

**Temperance.** A winged figure pours "the essences of life from chalice to chalice", one foot on the earth and the other on the water. And one sentence of Waite's reads as if written for two plays about the war of the sexes: "I speak of him in the masculine sense, but the figure is neither male nor female." The angel of the main task is neither a man nor a woman.

paragraphs: Now it is clear why Maria's question about two drops is a question of Temperance: her card is water passing between two vessels. Wen quotes P. D. Ouspensky on this angel: "One of the cups the angel holds is the past, the other is the future. The rainbow stream between the cups is the present. You see that it flows both ways." The answer to Maria's question is that no drop is bound to run down first: the water goes back and forth. Even Katherina, in her final speech, compares an angry wife to a troubled fountain, "Muddy, ill-seeming, thick, bereft of beauty" — only she demands clear water from one side alone.

The plot of the two plays rests on the question of who tames whom — husband the wife or wife the husband. The main task of the tail removes the question: the figure of Temperance has no sex, so in this couple the role of tamer belongs to no one in particular. Measure is held by whoever can hold it at the moment.

sections.h2: The couple's values: a house, the world and an upside-down view
paragraphs: The couple's values are the point that shows what the union exists for. Couples with the 6-11-14 tail have one of three cards there: The Empress (47.9%), The World (29.1%) or The Hanged Man (23%). How they echo the plays is our own reading.

ul: **The Empress — a house in which something shared grows.** In Fletcher the house becomes a weapon: Maria demands that it be rebuilt and that a garden "of some twenty Acres" be laid out "of the Italian fashion", and every word from her husband about "due obedience", she says, "Shall cost you many a pound more". The value of The Empress is a house that two build together, not a fortress that one of them besieges.

**The World — acceptance without re-education.** In the minus of this card Lisovskaya sees remaking the partner to suit oneself — exactly Petruchio's programme. In the plus she sees full acceptance of the partner even at their worst, and no pressure at all. For these couples The World is a value that is the direct opposite of taming.

**The Hanged Man — the world upside down.** Katherina agrees to see the moon by day and a maiden in an old man, and in her agreement play can be heard for the first time, not defeat. Lisovskaya writes that couples with The Hanged Man often need a push from outside before they marry. Katherina's marriage really was pushed by other hands: her sister's suitors promised to pay Petruchio's wooing expenses, provided the elder sister was married off first. The value of The Hanged Man is the ability to look at the world through another person's eyes without losing one's own.

sections.h2: Example: the 6-11-14 tail for the couple 05.07.1975 and 05.07.1975
paragraphs: The site's engine gives the 6-11-14 tail to a couple whose two dates of birth are the same — 05.07.1975. This is the extreme case of the most "mirrored" combination: both partners have the personal tail 12-19-7 and the personal centre 5. The couple is the sum of two identical matrices:

Two Hanged Men make The Lovers, two Suns make Strength, two Chariots make Temperance. Each of the two, alone, is learning to drive their own chariot: 7 stands in the personal karmic task of both. Together the task is different — not to race each in their own chariot, but to blend. The middle is two Suns, the very "two raging fires" Petruchio spoke of before the wedding. Couples with identical personal tails 12-19-7 make up 22% of all couples with the 6-11-14 tail, and all of them have The Wheel of Fortune at the couple's centre: 5 + 5 = 10.

In this couple Temperance also stands at the point "What to create together": measure here is not only the task but also what the two met for. The Lovers recur at "What fills", "Path to prosperity" and "Where it leaks"; The Wheel stands both at the centre and at "Image of the couple"; at "Values" is The Empress. And the Judgement missing from the middle of the tail turns up at the point "Parents together".

sections.h2: How to live the 6-11-14 tail at its strongest
paragraphs: The tail predicts nothing. It shows where the same circle keeps repeating between two people, and what opens it.

ul: **Notice who names the sun.** If one partner always decides what counts as true, the atmosphere rests on the other's consent rather than on a game played by two.
**Tell sparring from war.** The common language of jabs is alive as long as tenderness can be heard in it. When only the score is left, it is time to change the conversation, not to win it.
**No taming by deprivation.** Not with food, sleep, money or silence. The Strength of this tail is the kind that leads, not the kind that keeps someone hungry.
**The rule of two drops.** Give way in turns, not by rank. If the same partner always yields first, it is no longer measure.
**When both are hot, add no fuel.** Putting a conversation off until morning is better than winning it at night.
**Write your own epilogue.** Agree that nobody has the right to reign and nobody may triumph over the one who lost.

paragraphs: The strong version of the 6-11-14 tail is a couple that has been through both plays and got stuck in neither. They still talk to each other in their own sharp language and still argue about where the sun is, but the argument has become a game against the world, not against each other. Whoever finds it easier at the moment gives way. They have no winner — not because their strength is equal, but because in this tail one partner's victory is always a defeat for both.

intro: That is the hidden plot of this tail. Two people are drawn together by a wish for love without masks; their road runs through a contest over who will tame whom; and their main task is to blend two hot tempers so that neither a tamer nor a tamed one is left in the couple.

ul: **6 · The Lovers — entry to the task.** What the two want together: a love where each can be themselves and where each was chosen. From the first meeting they share a common language — the language of sparring. It also becomes their first resistance.
**11 · Strength — middle of the task.** What the couple goes through: a trial of strength, a fight for the last word, and the discovery that you can only tame someone who has agreed to it.

**14 · Temperance — main task.** What to learn: measure. Not letting the same person give way every time, not adding fuel when both are hot, and seeing that here one partner's victory is always a defeat for both.

intro: Four hundred years ago this plot was played out in two plays about one and the same husband. In Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew, Petruchio tames Katherina. In the sequel written by John Fletcher, the same Petruchio marries again — and this time he is the one being tamed. Together the two plays walk the 6-11-14 tail from start to finish, and Fletcher put the answer to its main task into his epilogue.

faq.q: How is the 6-11-14 couple tail different from a personal karmic tail?
faq.a: There is no personal 6-11-14 tail: for one person the middle of the tail is the reduced sum of the entry and the main task, and with an entry of 6 and a task of 14 it is always 20, Judgement. In a couple each point is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, so Strength ends up in the middle. The roles of the points differ too: entry to the task, middle of the task and the couple's main task, not one person's karma.

faq.q: Are there couple tails with the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. Among the 97 couple tails these three numbers occur only in the order 6-11-14. The order matters: the entry to the task always comes first and the main task last.

faq.q: Does the 6-11-14 tail mean that one partner will dominate the other?
faq.a: No. The tail describes a theme the two go through, not an outcome. Strength in the middle speaks of a trial of strength, and the main task, Temperance, of leaving it with no winner. The roles of tamer and tamed are tied neither to sex nor to character, and in a real couple they often swap.

faq.q: How common is the 6-11-14 karmic tail in compatibility?
faq.a: Roughly one couple in 25 has it — 3.95% of couples; it is the fourth most common of the 97 couple tails. It is made up of five combinations of personal tails, most often 15-20-5 and 18-9-9 (45% of such couples), 15-5-8 and 18-6-6 (30%), and two identical 12-19-7 tails (22%).

faq.q: Why does the couple have The Sun at the centre if one person never does?
faq.a: The couple's centre is the sum of two personal centres. For one person 19 never falls at the centre, whatever the date, but for two it adds up from 9 and 10, from 7 and 12 or, more rarely, from 5 and 14. So The Sun at the centre of these couples is an atmosphere that neither of the two brought along: they can only create it together.

report: The middle of the 6-11-14 tail holds a card that could never stand there for a single person. One person alone always travels from The Lovers to Temperance through Judgement: 6 + 14 = 20. In a couple the middle is added up by two, and in the place of Judgement stands Strength. No verdict comes from outside — the two are left alone with each other, and they start taming each other.

Four hundred years ago this plot was played out in two plays about one and the same husband. In Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew, Petruchio tames Katherina. In John Fletcher's sequel, The Tamer Tamed, the same Petruchio marries again — and this time he is the one being tamed. Together the plays walk the tail in order: the wooing is The Lovers, taming in both directions is Strength, the epilogue is Temperance.

report.h3: A sting hidden in the tail

report: A couple with this tail is drawn together by a wish for a love in which each can be themselves, and its common language appears with the very first line — the language of sparring. A minute after meeting, Katherina and Petruchio are finishing each other's puns: "— Who knows not where a wasp does wear his sting? In his tail. — In his tongue." Petruchio is the first to answer her at her own speed. With him there is no need to pretend.

But the same wish turns into resistance at once. Katherina's shrewishness grows from the fact that her sister is loved and she is not. Her father tells the suitor that her love is the main thing, "all in all"; Petruchio replies, "Why, that is nothing" — and marries her willing or not. Others think such a pair is quarrelling; the two think they are talking. The trouble starts when tenderness can no longer be heard in the language of jabs and only the score is left.

report.h3: The taming-school works both ways

report: Petruchio promises to turn a "wild Kate" into a "household" one — Kate sounds like cat — and tames her as a falconer tames a hawk: with hunger and sleeplessness, all of it "in reverend care of her". The servants sum it up: "He kills her in her own humour" — "he is more shrew than she". He had warned of it himself: "where two raging fires meet together / They do consume the thing that feeds their fury". **The first trap of Strength in a couple is competing over who can hold out longer.** Pressure here rarely looks like an order; more often it looks like care that leaves the other no choice. If one partner holds the other through fear, by withholding food, sleep or money, or through threats, this is no longer the task of the tail but a boundary: outside help is needed — a psychologist, a crisis line, and in danger, a local emergency number.

Fletcher saw what Shakespeare had left offstage. The late Katherina, friends recall, "turn'd his temper" and forced Petruchio to storm as high as she did; he calls that taming twelve labours that would have driven even Hercules mad. His second wife, Maria, declares, "I am no more the gentle, tame Maria" — and turns his own means against him: refusal, siege, a bet on endurance. One and the same man was both the tamer and the tamed. **The role in the middle of this tail is tied neither to sex nor to character** — it passes from hand to hand.

When honest Strength runs short, the two stage a Judgement. In Fletcher, Petruchio pretends to be dead, Maria pronounces a verdict over the coffin on his "foolish life", and he rises and says, "I am born again." In a comedy it works. In a couple such a scene brings relief but not measure: only the winner has changed.

report.h3: Who names the sun

report: The most famous scene of The Taming of the Shrew is an argument on the road. It is broad day, Petruchio insists it is the moon, and he orders the horses turned back. Katherina answers that whatever he chooses to name it, "even that it is; / And so it shall be so for Katharina." It can be heard as surrender: one decides what counts as the sun, the other agrees. Or it can be heard as the start of a game. A minute later Petruchio greets an old man as a fair young maid, and Katherina joins in so warmly that the old man calls her his merry mistress. For the first time the two laugh not at each other but together. Right after this Petruchio asks for a kiss in the middle of the street, and she kisses him, calling him "love" for the first time. The entry of the tail is fulfilled not at the altar but here.

report.h3: Two drops of equal weight

report: The main task is Temperance, and both plays end in its minus: one gives way, the other never thinks of it. In her final speech Katherina tells the wives to lower their pride, so measure is demanded of one side only; the last line of the play has its doubts: it is a wonder, it says, that she lets herself be tamed so. Maria, having won, at once vows to be her husband's servant. The score has flipped, but it has not disappeared.

Fletcher had put the answer into Maria's mouth earlier: "Take two small drops of water, equal weigh'd, / Tell me which is the heaviest, and which ought / First to descend in duty?" The question of Temperance is not who is right but who gives way. The epilogue answers: the play is meant "To teach both Sexes due equality; / And as they stand bound, to love mutually." In Waite, the figure of Temperance pours water from chalice to chalice and, in his words, is "neither male nor female"; and the lion of his Strength is led on a chain of flowers, with nobody starving it.

There is also a Shakespearean recipe passed off as a trick. Throwing away the "burnt" meat, Petruchio explains that such food is not for them, "Since, of ourselves, ourselves are choleric". **When both are hot, anger is not fed — neither with food nor with words.** And at the wooing he lied to her father that Katherina was "not hot, but temperate as the morn". The word spoken at the entry turned out to be the address the tail leads to.

The strong version of the 6-11-14 tail is a couple that has been through both plays and got stuck in neither. The two still talk in their own sharp language and still argue about where the sun is, but the argument has become a game against the world, not against each other. Whoever finds it easier at the moment gives way. **They have no winner: in this tail one partner's victory is always a defeat for both.**

seo.title: Karmic tail 6 11 5 compatibility: The Lovers, Strength, The Hierophant
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 11 5 compatibility: how a couple's wish to choose each other passes a trial of strength and becomes the couple's own law.

items.title: The 6-11-5 tail in compatibility: how a couple's love becomes its law
items.short: The karmic tail 6-11-5 in compatibility — The Lovers, Strength and The Hierophant — never occurs in a single person: in a personal destiny matrix it would need The Sun in the centre of the chart, and no one is born with The Sun there. Couples get it about one time in 32. It is the tail of a union that begins with the wish to choose each other, passes through a trial of strength and arrives at its main task: to write the couple's own law instead of living by someone else's rulebook.

sections.h2: What 6-11-5 means in a couple's destiny matrix
paragraphs: A couple has its own karmic tail: each of its points is the sum of the same points of the two personal matrices, reduced to a number from 1 to 22. Yuliana Lisovskaya, whose book the site uses to work out compatibility, calls this line the couple's tasks and says plainly that its trials may be called karmic or simply part of life. The line is read mostly through its minus — through what the couple fails at and has to learn.

The word "programme", which people type next to "6 11 5", comes from the same school: Lisovskaya calls a couple's tail a "karmic programme". She writes it from the main task, so in her book it appears as 5-11-6. Nor is it a random choice among many: when the author of the book on compatibility shows how to join the three energies of a tail into one conclusion, this is the triple she picks. Her analysis is a list of tasks, each marked with the combination of cards it comes from. Here it serves as a reference for what the points mean; the plot of this couple is its own.
The three points of the tail work like this:

ul: **entry to the task** — the couple's shared wishes and agreements, its "common language". The point sits on the relationship line, so what the couple wants together can also become what it resists with;

**middle of the task** — in Lisovskaya's book it has no meaning of its own and only complements the main point. We read it as the road: what the couple does and goes through on the way from the wish to the task. This is the site's reading, not a statement of the book;
**main task** — the couple's main trials and what it has to learn.

paragraphs: **The first clue is in the names.** In the historical part of his book Arthur Edward Waite gives the sixth card a double name: "The Lovers or Marriage". And his divinatory list for The Hierophant opens with the same word — "Marriage". The 6-11-5 tail begins with marriage as a feeling and ends with marriage as an institution.

**The second clue is in the arithmetic.** 6 + 5 = 11. The middle of this tail is exactly the sum of its two ends: Strength here is made of The Lovers and The Hierophant, of love and law. What that means in practice is best seen in the tale.

sections.h2: The tale this couple lives in
paragraphs: "The Tale of Peter and Fevronia of Murom" was written by the monk Ermolai-Erasmus in the late 1540s at the request of Metropolitan Macarius. Peter and Fevronia are venerated as patrons of marriage, and since 2008 their feast day, 8 July, has been marked in Russia as the Day of Family, Love and Fidelity. Quotations from the tale below are our own translations from the Old Russian.
The plot rests on three acts, and each is one card of the tail:

ol: a prince and the daughter of a tree-climber make a deal: she will get him back on his feet if he takes her as his wife — **The Lovers**, choice and condition;
a serpent killed with a sword, and scabs taken away with sourdough — **Strength**, two kinds of strength in one story;
boyars, the law, and a stone coffin with a thin partition — **The Hierophant**, the question of whose rulebook governs this marriage.

paragraphs: The tale is not offered here as a model to copy, nor as a prediction. It is a mirror: in it one can see clearly how the three cards behave when they stand in a row.

sections.h2: The entry: The Lovers, or love with a condition
paragraphs: The prince's servant finds Fevronia in Laskovo, a village in the Ryazan lands. She is sitting at her loom, and a hare is leaping in front of her. The first thing he hears from her is a riddle: "It is unseemly for a house to be without ears and a temple without eyes." The servant does not understand. Fevronia explains: the ears of a house are a dog, which would have barked at a stranger; the eyes are a child, who would have seen the guest first. Her father and mother have gone "to weep on loan" — to a funeral, to weep for others so that one day others will weep for them. Her brother is a tree-climber who gathers wild honey; he looks down "through his legs into the land of the dead", so as not to fall.

So this union begins with a language not everyone understands. For a couple's tail that is no small thing. **The entry to the couple's task is its common language** — words and jokes that only two people get, agreements nobody else knows about. For a 6-11-5 couple this is where the road to the main task begins: pet names, private words, decisions like "with us it will be different from our parents".

Then comes the condition. The servant asks her to get the prince back on his feet. Fevronia answers that it can be done, but "if I am not to be his wife…" — then there is no reason for her to nurse him. Love here starts not with a sigh but with a contract spoken out loud. This is The Lovers as Benebell Wen reads the card: "in every traditional interpretation of The Lovers, the card is about a moral choice", and in matters of love it marks "the beginnings of romance and, simultaneously, the beginnings of temptation."

Temptation arrives at once. Hearing the condition, Peter thinks: "How can I, a prince, take a tree-climber's daughter as my wife!" He agrees for appearances' sake, and afterwards he sends gifts. The tale answers in three words: "She did not accept."

The whole minus of the entry is in this scene. The wish to be chosen argues with status, and a present arrives instead of a promise. Among the minuses of the six, Lisovskaya lists gifts given "with a calculation", and in her analysis of this tail — the chase after status. In a real couple it looks mundane: a new phone instead of the conversation that was asked for; weekend tickets instead of "I was wrong"; silence in front of the family instead of "yes, I choose you" — and flowers later. The gift is nice, but the condition was something else.
The roles of Peter and Fevronia are not handed out by sex. In a 6-11-5 couple either partner may be the one who sets the condition, and either may be the one who tries to pay with gifts.

sections.h2: The middle: Strength, or the sword and the sourdough
paragraphs: To understand the middle, one has to go back to the start of the tale. The prince's trouble began with a serpent. The serpent visited the wife of Peter's brother, Prince Paul of Murom, and to other people it looked like the prince himself, "as if the prince were sitting with his wife". A serpent wearing the face of the lawful husband — the same shadow that coils round the tree on The Lovers card: a desire that passes itself off as one's own.

Peter kills the serpent with the sword of Agrikov. It is a victory by force, and it wounds the victor: the serpent "sprinkled the blessed prince Peter with its blood", and from that blood the prince's body broke out in scabs and sores. The sword worked. The price was his skin.

Here Waite offers an unexpected hint. His description of Strength ends: "It has walked upon the asp and the basilisk and has trodden down the lion and the dragon." This is a verse of Psalm 91 — Psalm 90 in the Greek and Slavonic numbering — which in the Church Slavonic psalter reads "Thou shalt tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and trample the lion and the serpent". In Russia this psalm, known by its opening words Zhivyi v pomoshchi, "He that dwelleth in the help", is among the best known of all. So Strength has two faces: the one who tramples the serpent, and the one who leads the lion without a fight. **In the tale the two faces belong to two different people**: Peter has the sword, Fevronia has the sourdough.

Her remedy is deliberately ordinary. Fevronia "took a small vessel, scooped up some of her leaven and blew on it" — her bread sourdough and her breath. A quieter force is hard to imagine. And one condition: "and let him leave one scab unanointed." One scab must be left untouched.

Peter anointed himself, rose well again, broke his word — and "from that scab many scabs began to spread over his body". Everything came back from the one untouched spot. The prince returned in shame, and Fevronia repeated her condition: "If he is to be my husband, he will be made whole." This time he married her.

paragraphs.h3: One scab kept in reserve

paragraphs: Fevronia is right: the scab is a pledge for the word. But in a couple this scene has a shadow. Sometimes each partner keeps "one scab in reserve" — an old hurt that was never spoken and never let go, kept just in case. It lies quiet while things are good and spreads in the first quarrel: "And remember the time you…" In her analysis of this tail Lisovskaya describes the same mechanism in other words: an unspoken "I don't like this" settles inside and grows like a weed — into insecurity, passive aggression, jealousy and manipulation.

paragraphs.h3: The flax and the log

paragraphs: The tale also has a third force — neither the sword nor submission. Before the wedding Peter decides to test her wisdom. He sends a bundle of flax with the order: "If she is wise, let her make me from this flax a shirt, trousers and a towel" — while he is in the bathhouse. Fevronia has a small piece cut from a log and sends it back: "let him first make me from this little stick a loom and all its fittings, on which his linen can be woven."

She neither argues nor obeys. She holds the demand up like a mirror: the impossible comes back as the impossible. Wen separates two neighbouring cards this way: The Chariot "is typically associated with the strength to master the world", while Strength "is associated with strength to master the self." And among the meanings of Strength reversed she names "being too stubborn and obstinate" — strength applied in the wrong place.

paragraphs.h3: A strength that belongs to neither partner

paragraphs: The strangest clue of this tail lies in the full run of dates. Strength never stands in the middle of a personal karmic tail: a check of every birth date since 1900 does not find it there once. So in a 6-11-5 couple the eleven in the middle is never brought by one partner — each time it is assembled from two other cards. One partner's Emperor and the other's Chariot (4 + 7). Judgement and The Hermit (20 + 9 = 29 → 11). Justice and The Empress (8 + 3). And in one such couple in six it is literally one partner's Hierophant and the other's Lovers, 5 + 6.
That is why this tail has no "born tamer". The couple's strength is shared; it arises between the two. Whoever starts taming the other is taking what belongs to both.

In daily life the middle of the tail shows up in arguments about big decisions — moving, a job, money. One partner presses with arguments as if with a sword. The other answers with sarcasm, and now there are two swords. Lisovskaya names this directly for the eleven: a struggle for leadership, each with a truth of their own. And the plus of the same card, in her book, is a fine sense of what the other needs, and a way of turning tension into passion rather than war. The strong move here resembles Fevronia's log: not "no" and not "fine", but "to do that, this is needed — let's start with the loom".

If strength in a couple has turned into fear, threats or physical violence, that is not "the task of the tail" and not a reason to endure. It is a reason to get help — from a local emergency number or a crisis line.

sections.h2: The main task: The Hierophant, or whose rulebook governs this marriage
paragraphs: After the wedding the longest trial begins. Peter becomes prince of Murom, and the boyars dislike the princess "because of her birth". The boyars' wives complain: she has a peasant habit — after a meal she gathers the crumbs from the table into her palm. Peter takes her hand, opens her fingers — and sees "fragrant incense and frankincense".

For the fifth card this is a precise scene. The Hierophant is the card of established order: how things are done, what is proper, who is an equal. The boyars' wives measure another man's wife by their own rulebook. And in her palm lies what is burned in church: the "low" habit turns out to be a rite as well — just not the one the court is used to.

Then the boyars speak plainly: "Let her take as much wealth as she likes and go wherever she wants!" Peter does not decide for her: "Say it to Fevronia, and whatever she says, we shall hear." Her answer: "I ask for nothing else but my husband, Prince Peter." The prince cites the words of the Gospel — that whoever puts away his wife and marries another commits adultery — and, in the tale's words, "did not love temporal rule above the commandments of God". The boyars give them boats on the Oka, and they sail away from their own city.

Here the two faces of The Hierophant collide. One is the norm of the court: who is fit to be princess. The other is the law of the union: the word that was given. **Peter uses the law to protect the couple from the norm.** That is the main task of the 6-11-5 tail: not to choose between love and order, but to make order serve the union instead of breaking it apart.

paragraphs.h3: Where it shows in a couple's life

paragraphs: Among the tasks of the five Lisovskaya names relatives meddling, even in the choice of a partner; conflict with the other's family; attempts to remake each other; lectures about how "everything is wrong". For a 6-11-5 couple the scenes are familiar:

ul: a holiday that "we have always spent at our place", with nobody asking where the two of them would like to spend it;
"that's not how it's done in our family" — the sentence by which someone else's rulebook walks into the shared home;
one partner becomes the other's high priest, teaching how to eat, dress, spend and talk, because "that's what normal people do";
the couple takes a ready-made template of marriage — their parents', a book's, other people's photos — and suffers because their union does not fit it.

paragraphs.h3: Water from both sides of the boat

paragraphs: On the same river there is a short scene. A man sailing in the same boat as Fevronia lets his eyes rest on her. She tells him to scoop up water from one side of the boat and drink it, then from the other side and drink again. "Is this water the same, or is one sweeter?" The same, he says. Then she finishes the lesson: what he was gazing at is no different either — so why leave what is his and think about what belongs to another?

For a 6-11-5 couple this scene holds the trap of comparison, and not only with other people. Someone else's marriage on the far side of the boat looks sweeter: everything there is by the book, their relatives never call, they never quarrel. Measuring one's own marriage by another's canon is the same as drinking from the other side.

paragraphs.h3: Stakes that became trees

paragraphs: In the evening the exiles make camp on the bank. The cook cuts thin saplings to hang the cauldrons on. Fevronia blesses them: "Let these be great trees by morning, with branches and leaves." In the morning, where the stakes stood, there are tall trees in full leaf.

This is the best image of where a couple's own rulebook comes from. Not from an inheritance and not from a book, but from the camping rules of two people in exile, made up in a hurry: where the pot goes, who does the dishes, what we do when we are scared. The temporary comes alive if nobody pulls it out.

Soon the same boyars come sailing after them: the city has torn itself apart in a fight for power — please come back. Peter and Fevronia return and rule, says the tale, "like a father and mother who love their children". This is the plus of the five in Lisovskaya's book: an authority everyone accepts willingly, not because that is the custom.

sections.h2: A thin partition: the ending that did not make the canon
paragraphs: In old age both take monastic vows: Peter under the name David, Fevronia as Euphrosyne. She is embroidering an altar cover with the faces of saints for the cathedral. Peter sends word that he is dying and waits for her, so that they may depart together. She answers: "Wait, my lord, until I finish the cover for the holy church." He sends a second time, then a third. Then she "thrust her needle into the cover and wound the thread round it" — and went.

Even the shared ending waited until she had finished her own work. In her analysis of this tail Lisovskaya writes separately that each partner needs a circle of like-minded people of their own and achievements they can see apart from the other. And among the pluses of the five she lists respect for personal space and support in which each grows in their own field.

Now the heart of it. The couple asked to be laid together and had an unusual tomb made for themselves: "in one stone two coffins, with only one partition between them". **One stone, one shared fate — and a thin wall, so each has a place of their own.** No closer formula for the main task of this tail exists: a union that does not swallow the two.

People decided otherwise: "it is not fitting to lay saints who have taken the monastic habit in one coffin". Peter was placed in a separate coffin in the city, Fevronia outside the city, in a convent. In the morning the separate coffins were empty, and both were found in the shared stone, in the city cathedral. They were moved apart once more — and again by morning they lay together. The rule of the institution lost to the rule of the couple.

The last clue lies not in the tale but in what happened to it. Macarius commissioned the text, and the council of 1547 numbered Peter and Fevronia among the saints, yet the Metropolitan left the tale out of the Great Menaion Reader, the main collection of saints' lives of the time; scholars explain this by its "exceptionally legendary" character. The institution accepted the saints and turned down their story: riddles, a hare, sourdough and empty coffins did not fit the canon. The couple held up as an example for almost five hundred years was never recognised as a model in form.

The Hierophant likes to turn a couple into a model — for others, for a holiday, for a photograph. The tale shows that this couple's real law was something else: a language of riddles, a condition spoken aloud, one stone for two and a thin partition inside.

sections.h2: What Waite saw: two unveiled, a lion on a chain of flowers, the keys
paragraphs: The cards on the site have their own artwork; this section is about the Waite–Smith deck of Arthur Edward Waite and Pamela Colman Smith.

**The Lovers.** In Waite the man and the woman stand "unveiled before each other". There is nothing to hide; in Lisovskaya's book the plus of the six includes having no secrets. Behind the woman stands the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil, and "the serpent is twining round it". The tale of Murom begins with that serpent.

**Strength.** A woman is closing the jaws of a lion, and Waite adds what matters most: "her beneficent fortitude has already subdued the lion, which is being led by a chain of flowers." The struggle happened before the picture. The card shows what comes afterwards: the lion is held by a chain of flowers, which means that what holds him is not the strength of the chain.

**The Hierophant.** At the pontiff's feet lie the crossed keys, and two ministers kneel before him. Waite agrees with the writer who signed himself Grand Orient that this card is "the power of the keys". Keys bind and loose: who holds the keys to this marriage — the two of them, the relatives, or "society"? The divinatory list of the fifth card splits in two. Upright: "Marriage, alliance, captivity, servitude". Reversed: "Society, good understanding, concord, over-kindness, weakness". The main task of the tail runs between captivity and concord. And there is a second boundary: concord that melts into "over-kindness" is no rulebook either.

sections.h2: The Sun in the centre: the person who cannot exist
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's matrix is the atmosphere between the partners, what is not on show. In couples with the 6-11-5 tail the centre holds one of two cards: The Sun (19) in 56.8% of them, The Wheel of Fortune (10) in 43.2%.

Here lies the answer to why this tail never occurs in a person. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre. For the entry to be 6 when the main task is 5, the centre would have to be 1 or 19: 5 + 19 = 24, 2 + 4 = 6. No person has a centre of 1 or 19: a personal centre can only be 3–14, 16, 18, 20 or 22. **But a couple's centre can be 19 — and with it the 6-11-5 tail adds up exactly by the personal formula.** In more than half of these couples the union is built like a single person with The Sun in the centre — a person who cannot exist.

In his list for The Sun Waite writes: "Material happiness, fortunate marriage, contentment." And in older decks, he recalls, beneath the luminary there was a wall, "as it might be, a walled garden", with two children inside "gambolling, or running hand in hand". The card that no human being has in the centre once showed two.

In Lisovskaya's book The Sun in a couple's centre means respect, a cosy home, a sense of being safe next to the other; its minus is control and comparison. The Wheel of Fortune in the centre is the feeling of a fated meeting and a similar outlook on life; its minus is a seesaw of "silence, then conflict". Two atmospheres for one tail: a walled garden, and a wheel that lifts and lowers.

In the couple's values — the spiritual purpose — such unions have one of three cards: The Empress (3) in 48.3%, The World (21) in 33.8%, The Hanged Man (12) in 17.9%. The Empress, for Lisovskaya, is growth and abundance in whatever sphere the couple met for. The World is a shared philosophy of life, and among its pluses there is a detail that seems to continue the main task of the tail: the couple makes the budget rules together. The Hanged Man, in Waite, is "wisdom, circumspection, discernment, trials, sacrifice": for the sake of what is shared, one sometimes has to look at one's own things upside down.

sections.h2: How to work out the 6-11-5 tail: an example couple
paragraphs: Take two dates: 08.01.1976 and 14.09.1975. First each personal matrix is worked out.

For 08.01.1976: day 8, month 1, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5. Main task 8 + 1 + 5 = 14, centre 8 + 1 + 5 + 14 = 28 → 10. Entry of the tail 14 + 10 = 24 → 6, middle 14 + 6 = 20. The personal tail is 6-20-14.
For 14.09.1975: day 14, month 9, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Main task 14 + 9 + 22 = 45 → 9, centre 14 + 9 + 22 + 9 = 54 → 9. Entry 9 + 9 = 18, middle 9 + 18 = 27 → 9. The personal tail is 18-9-9.
Now the couple's tail: each point is the sum of the same points.
The couple's centre is 10 + 9 = 19, The Sun. The couple's values are 21, The World.

The couple's middle is worked out from the partners' middles, not from the ends of the couple's tail. For 6-11-5 both ways happen to give the same result — 6 + 5 = 11 — but the rule is still one: the same points are added together.

The 6-11-5 tail occurs in about one couple in 32 — 3.1% — ninth among the 97 couple tails. It is assembled from 13 combinations of personal tails. The most common are 21-4-10 with 3-7-22 (16% of such couples), 15-20-5 with 9-9-18 (13%) and 15-8-11 with 18-3-12 (11%).

One more detail from the full run of dates: in two out of three couples with this tail, neither partner has The Lovers at their own entry or The Hierophant at their own main task. This triple is rarely brought by one person — two people make it.
No other couple tail is made of these three numbers. If the notation 5-11-6 turns up, it is the same tail read from the main task, as Lisovskaya writes it.

sections.h2: What changes the script
paragraphs: The tail passes no sentence and promises no events. It shows where this couple's knot lies. Here is what the tale and the cards suggest as a way out:

ul: **The condition — aloud and at the start.** Like Fevronia: not "if you loved me, you would guess", but "this is what I need". An agreement spoken plainly holds better than one that has to be guessed.
**No gifts in place of a word.** A present is fine in itself, but not instead of what was asked for.
**No scab kept in reserve.** Talk about a hurt while it is fresh, rather than storing it as a lever for the next quarrel.
**Meet pressure with a log.** Not with a sword and not with surrender, but with a counter-question: "to do that, this is needed".
**The keys to the union stay with the two.** In this home relatives are guests, not high priests.
**A rulebook of the couple's own.** A few rules both partners chose themselves — and the right to revise them. Stakes turn into trees if nobody pulls them out.
**A thin partition.** Each has a needle of their own: their own work, their own circle, their own time.
**Drinking from one's own side.** Someone else's marriage is not sweeter; it is just on the other side of the boat.

sections.h2: The strong version of the 6-11-5 tail
paragraphs: In its strong version this tail is the same tale, only told by two people for themselves. The couple starts with its own language and an honest condition, goes through the trial of strength without taking up the sword or keeping a scab in reserve, and writes a law nobody could have handed it: a shared stone with a thin wall inside. Such a union may not look like a model one — just as the tale of Peter and Fevronia does not look like a proper saint's life. But its rulebook is its own.

ul: **Entry to the task — 6, The Lovers.** Where the couple starts: choosing each other and coming to terms — a private language, conditions of its own, its own "we". The same wish later turns into resistance.
**Middle of the task — 11, Strength.** What the couple goes through: who holds whom, who nurses whom back, who tries to tame whom. This is where strength and power part ways.

**Main task — 5, The Hierophant.** What the couple has to learn: to turn love into a rulebook both of them accepted freely — not their parents', not "what normal people do", and not one written by one partner for the other.

intro: The best-known story of marriage in Old Russian literature is built exactly like this tail: in three acts, in the same order. What follows is an investigation — into what is written in the three cards, in the couple's numbers, and in a tale that has been read as a model of marriage for almost five hundred years and yet was never admitted into the great church collection of saints' lives.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 6-11-5 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's task, running from The Lovers through Strength to The Hierophant. The couple enters it through the wish to choose each other and come to terms, passes through a trial of strength — who holds and tames whom — and learns the main thing: to create the union's own rulebook instead of living by the rules of relatives, society or one of the partners.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail is read through its minus because it shows what the union has to learn, but it is never a verdict. The 6-11-5 tail does not say whether the relationship will last and does not predict events: it describes a knot this couple needs to untie — joining love and order so that order serves both partners.

faq.q: Can 6-11-5 appear in a personal destiny matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and an entry of 6 with a main task of 5 needs a centre of 1 or 19. No person has such a centre. A couple can, and in 56.8% of couples with this tail the centre is exactly The Sun.

faq.q: How is 6-11-5 different from 5-11-6?
faq.a: It isn't: it is one tail written from opposite ends. On the site a couple's tail is read from the entry to the main task: 6-11-5. Yuliana Lisovskaya, in her book on compatibility, writes it from the main task — 5-11-6. No other couple tail is made of these three numbers.

faq.q: Does The Hierophant on the main task mean the couple must get married?
faq.a: No. The Hierophant speaks of the law, tradition and order of a union, but it does not demand a marriage certificate, a church wedding or any particular form of relationship. The task is for the couple's rules to be accepted freely by both, rather than inherited from relatives or imposed by one partner on the other.

faq.q: What does "programme 6-11-5" mean in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: It is the same thing as the karmic tail 6-11-5. Lisovskaya calls a couple's tail a "karmic programme", and this is the very triple she chose in her book to show how the three energies of a tail are joined into one conclusion about the couple's tasks.

report: The best-known Old Russian tale of marriage begins not with love but with a condition. A girl from Laskovo, a village in the Ryazan lands, agrees to get Prince Peter of Murom, covered in scabs, back on his feet — but only if he takes her as his wife. The couple tail 6-11-5 is built the same way as "The Tale of Peter and Fevronia": in three acts and in the same order. The Lovers at the entry, Strength in the middle, The Hierophant on the main task.

The first clue is in the names. Arthur Edward Waite gives the sixth card a double name: "The Lovers or Marriage". And his divinatory list for The Hierophant opens with the same word — "Marriage". The tail begins with marriage as a feeling and ends with marriage as an institution. The second clue is in the arithmetic: 6 + 5 = 11. **The Strength in the middle of this tail is made of love and law.**

report.h3: Love spoken as a condition

report: Fevronia talks in riddles: "It is unseemly for a house to be without ears and a temple without eyes." The ears are a dog, the eyes a child. The prince's servant does not understand, and that is the point: the union begins with a language not everyone understands. The entry to the couple's task is its common language — pet names, private words, decisions like "with us it will be different from our parents".

Then comes the condition, spoken aloud. And temptation follows at once. Peter thinks: "How can I, a prince, take a tree-climber's daughter as my wife!" He agrees for appearances' sake and sends gifts. The tale answers in three words: "She did not accept."

The whole minus of the entry is in this scene: the wish to be chosen argues with status, and a present arrives instead of a promise. In a real couple it looks mundane — a new phone instead of the conversation that was asked for; weekend tickets instead of "I was wrong". The gift is nice, but the condition was something else. The roles are not handed out by sex: in a couple with this tail either partner may set the condition, and either may try to pay with gifts.

report.h3: The sword, the sourdough and one scab kept in reserve

report: Peter killed the serpent with the sword of Agrikov, and the serpent's blood covered him in scabs. A victory by force wounded the victor. Waite's description of Strength ends with a verse of Psalm 91: "It has walked upon the asp and the basilisk and has trodden down the lion and the dragon." The card has two faces — the one who tramples the serpent and the one who leads the lion without a fight. **In the tale the two faces belong to two different people: Peter has the sword, Fevronia has the sourdough.** She scooped up some of her bread leaven, blew on it and set one condition: "let him leave one scab unanointed."

Peter rose well again, broke his word — and everything came back from the one untouched spot. Fevronia is right: the scab is a pledge for the word. But the scene has a shadow. Sometimes each partner keeps **one scab in reserve** — an old hurt that was never spoken and never let go. It lies quiet while things are good and spreads in the first quarrel: "And remember that time…"

There is a third force too, neither the sword nor submission. Peter sends Fevronia a bundle of flax: if she is so wise, let her make him a shirt, trousers and a towel from it while he is in the bathhouse. She sends back a small piece of a log: let him first make a loom out of it. She neither argues nor obeys — the impossible comes back as the impossible.

The strangest clue of this tail: no person ever has Strength in the middle of a personal tail. In this couple the eleven is born each time from two other cards. So there is no born tamer here. Whoever starts taming the other is taking what belongs to both. If strength in a couple has turned into fear, threats or physical violence, that is not "the task of the tail" and not a reason to endure, but a reason to get help — from a local emergency number or crisis line.

report.h3: Whose rulebook governs this marriage

report: The boyars' wives dislike a princess of humble birth: after a meal she gathers the crumbs into her palm. Peter opens her fingers — and sees fragrant incense. The "low" habit turns out to be a rite as well, just not the one the court is used to. The boyars offer her as much wealth as she likes if she will leave. Peter does not decide for her: "Say it to Fevronia, and whatever she says, we shall hear." She asks only for her husband. He cites the Gospel's words on keeping faith with one's wife — and sails away with her down the Oka, out of his own city.

Here the two faces of The Hierophant collide: the norm of the court and the law of the union. **Peter uses the law to protect the couple from the norm.** That is the main task of the tail: not to choose between love and order, but to make order serve both. In daily life it is the holiday "we have always spent at our place"; the sentence "that's not how it's done in our family"; a partner who has become the other's high priest, teaching how to eat, spend and talk.

On the river bank Fevronia blesses the thin saplings the cook has hung the cauldrons on, and by morning they stand as tall trees. A couple's own rulebook grows the same way: from the camping rules of two people, not from an inheritance. The temporary comes alive if nobody pulls it out.

report.h3: One stone and a thin wall

report: The couple asked to be laid "in one stone two coffins, with only one partition between them". **One stone for two and a thin wall, so each has a place of their own** — no closer formula for this tail exists. People decided that monks must not lie in one coffin and moved the bodies apart: one into the city, the other outside it. By morning both lay in the shared stone. The rule of the institution lost to the rule of the couple. And Metropolitan Macarius himself, who commissioned the tale, left it out of the main collection of saints' lives — scholars explain this by its "exceptionally legendary" character.
The strong version of the tail resembles this fate: the union may not look like a model one, but its rulebook is its own. What helps to get there:

ul: saying the condition aloud and at the start, rather than waiting for it to be guessed;
not replacing a word with gifts;
talking about a hurt while it is fresh, rather than keeping a scab in reserve;
meeting pressure with a log — a counter-question: "to do that, this is needed";
keeping the keys to the union with the two: relatives in this home are guests, not high priests;
leaving each partner their own work and their own circle — a thin wall inside the shared stone.

unit.title: One stone and a thin wall

captions.M: Choose each other and say the condition aloud
captions.N: Pass the trial of strength without taming each other
captions.D: Write your own rulebook, not live by someone else's

unit.meaning: Your task is to turn love into a rulebook of your own, where order serves you both, not your relatives or one of you.

seo.title: Karmic tail 6 14 17 compatibility: The Lovers, Temperance, The Star
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 14 17 compatibility: how a couple moves from admiration, through time, to a star of its own — the three cards, the maths and The Little Prince.

items.title: Karmic tail 6-14-17 in compatibility: a rose, time and stars that laugh
items.short: The karmic tail 6-14-17 in compatibility is the story of a couple that begins with admiration and has to learn a light that needs no audience. The Lovers stand at the entry, Temperance in the middle, The Star in the main task. Between the first "how beautiful you are" and a star of their own, this couple has not a rule but time. No personal destiny matrix holds such a tail: only two people together can make it.

sections.h2: The riddle of the middle: why 14 and not 5
paragraphs: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is not chosen: it is the sum of the two ends. If 6-?-17 were someone's personal tail, The Hierophant would stand in the middle: 6 + 17 = 23, and 23 reduces to 5. A teacher, a rule, "how love ought to be done". This couple has Temperance in that place, and it is not a calculation error. Each point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, so the couple's middle is built from the partners' middles, not from its own ends.

A run of the site's engine through every date shows what this tail is made of. It occurs in roughly one couple in 45 (2.246%) and ranks 14th among the 97 couple tails. Only three combinations of personal tails produce it:
There are three clues in this table.

**First: the plot belongs to the union, not to either person.** Neither partner carries Temperance or The Star in a personal tail, in any combination. The Lovers appear in only a quarter of couples, in the tail 18-6-6. In three couples out of four, neither of the two has any of the three cards: the entry, the middle and the task come to this couple only together.

**Second: The Hierophant has not gone anywhere.** In 73% of these couples it stands in the middle of one partner's personal tail (15-5-8). Added to the other partner's Hermit, it stops being a rule and becomes a measure: 5 + 9 = 14. Our reading: the "this is how it's done" that one of them brings meets the other's quiet, and the rule turns into time.

**Third: The Lovers made of The Devil and The Moon.** In 97% of these couples The Lovers at the entry are the sum of one partner's Devil and the other's Moon. Wen separates The Lovers from The Devil this way: "Key 6 is about one choice. Key 15 is about being led astray." Our reading: this couple's admiration is made from the start of attachment and night-time imagination, and the choice inside it has yet to be made.

sections.h2: The Little Prince as the story of one couple
paragraphs: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry wrote the tale in 1942 in New York and in Asharoken on Long Island, and it came out in 1943 in English and French at once. It is usually read as a parable about friendship and childhood. But inside it is a love story between two very young creatures, the prince and the rose, and it is told in three acts, exactly in the order of the tail 6-14-17.

The first act is the prince's planet: the rose opens at sunrise, they admire each other, misunderstand each other and part. The second is the Earth: a garden of five thousand identical roses, the Fox and his lesson about time. The third is the stars: from the businessman who counts them and locks them in a drawer to stars that know how to laugh.

The roles here are not split by sex. The prince and the rose are not "him" and "her" but two ways of loving, and in every couple with this tail both partners are sometimes one and sometimes the other. The rose — when the wish is to be admired and tenderness hides behind a whim. The prince — when words are taken literally and leaving is easier than guessing what lies behind them.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — The Lovers: "Oh! How beautiful you are!"
paragraphs: The rose prepared her entrance for a long time. Still hidden in "her green chamber", she chose her colours and adjusted her petals one by one: "It was only in the full radiance of her beauty that she wished to appear." She opened "exactly at sunrise" and promptly yawned: "Ah! I am scarcely awake. I beg that you will excuse me. My petals are still all disarranged..." The prince "could not restrain his admiration": "Oh! How beautiful you are!" — "Am I not? And I was born at the same moment as the sun..."

In Lisovskaya's reading, the Entry to the task point is what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, a common language. The point stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish also turns into resistance. For a 6-14-17 couple the wish at the entry is this: to admire and to be admired. Wen writes of The Lovers in questions of love: "the beginnings of romance and, simultaneously, the beginnings of temptation", and at the start "a strong feeling of paradise, at least in the beginning". Such unions are said to be made in heaven. The rose really did come from the sky: she grew "from a seed blown from no one knew where".

The resistance hides in that same language. The rose prepared for days, yet pretends she has only just woken. Then come the tigers that do not live on the planet, the draughts, the screen, and the cough "in order to put the little prince in the wrong". The prince hears every word. "He had taken seriously words which were without importance, and it made him very unhappy." In a couple's life this is recognisable at once. One complains in order to be noticed, and the other answers the complaint instead of the request. One says "go, then, if you've decided" and waits to be stopped, and the other picks up a coat.

The prince only draws the conclusion later, on Earth: **"I ought to have judged by deeds and not by words."** And straight after: "She cast her fragrance and her radiance over me. I ought never to have run away from her... I ought to have guessed all the affection that lay behind her poor little stratagems."

There is no culprit in this scene, and that matters for the whole tail. Saying goodbye, the rose tells him: "Of course I love you. It is my fault that you have not known it all the while.
