That is of no importance. But you, you have been just as foolish as I." And at once, so that he will not see her tears: "You have decided to go away. Now go!" This was the choice of The Lovers, made in the language of pride. Not "I don't love you" but "I won't show you that it hurts". The task at the entry is not to stop admiring. This couple's admiration is real. The task is to hear the tenderness behind the performance and to stop staging performances.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — Temperance: the time wasted for the rose
paragraphs: On Earth the prince finds a garden where five thousand roses bloom, exactly like his. "I thought that I was rich, with a flower that was unique in all the world; and all I had was a common rose." He lies down in the grass and cries. This is how this couple's chief enemy enters the story — comparison. But the answer to it comes not from The Star but from the middle of the road: the Fox.

The Fox explains that taming means "to establish ties" and teaches how it is done: "You must be very patient. First you will sit down at a little distance from me, like that, in the grass... you will say nothing. Words are the source of misunderstandings. But you will sit a little closer to me, every day..." This is a direct answer to the entry to the task. The common language of The Lovers is words, and it failed. Temperance offers not new words but a distance that shrinks by one blade of grass a day.

Then the Fox talks about the hour: **"If, for example, you come at four o'clock in the afternoon, then at three o'clock I shall begin to be happy."** And about rites: they "are what make one day different from other days, one hour from other hours". The hunters have their Thursday, when they dance with the village girls, and that day is wonderful. Wen recalls that twentieth-century writers called Temperance the Time card. The Fox describes time exactly so: the coming hour pours into the present one, and happiness begins an hour before the meeting.

And now the key clue of the whole article. In parting, the Fox tells the prince his secret. In the French original it runs: "C'est le temps que tu as perdu pour ta rose qui fait ta rose si importante." Katherine Woods, in the first English translation of 1943: "It is the time you have wasted for your rose that makes your rose so important." Andrei Sharov's Russian version: "because you gave her all your time" (our translation). And Nora Gal's canonical Russian translation, the one through which almost every Russian reader knows the tale (our translation):
**"Your rose is so dear to you because you gave her your whole soul."**

Time has turned into soul. Nora Gal does this twice. In the original, the switchman's children lose time over a rag doll: Woods has "They waste their time over a rag doll", Sharov "they don't begrudge the time they spend fussing over a rag doll". In Nora Gal they "give their whole soul to a rag doll". It is a beautiful translation, but for a 6-14-17 couple the difference is real. A soul can be given in a single rush, at dawn, at the sight of a beauty: that is The Lovers. Time cannot be given that way, only an hour at a time, and that is Temperance. The word itself matters too: in Saint-Exupéry, time is not "invested" but "lost", wasted. The Fox praises not an investment but a spending without calculation.

Right after the Fox the book sets his opposite — a merchant selling pills that quench thirst. "Because they save a tremendous amount of time... With these pills, you save fifty-three minutes in every week." The prince thinks: **"If I had fifty-three minutes to spend as I liked, I should walk at my leisure toward a spring of fresh water."** Among Waite's divinatory meanings for Temperance the first is economy. This couple's middle teaches the opposite: to save time for each other, not at each other's expense.

At its worst, Temperance in Lisovskaya is one partner always giving way while the other never even notices. It is haste, and a feeling that nobody knows what the relationship is for. In the tale, haste is shown by the switchman: express trains thunder past in both directions, and "not even the locomotive engineer knows" what the passengers are looking for. "No one is ever satisfied where he is," he says in Woods; Nora Gal gives him the Russian proverb "Tam khorosho, gde nas net" — "it is good wherever we are not". Waite writes that under the rule of Temperance we know "something of whence we came and whither we are going". A couple in the shadow of the middle rides an express without knowing where to. A couple at its best knows its own four o'clock.

And one more detail that is easy to miss: who tamed whom? The prince tells the Fox: "There is a flower... I think that she has tamed me..." The ties of this middle run both ways. When the prince goes back to the five thousand roses, he lists what sets his rose apart from them. Nothing but the time they lived through: "because it is she that I have watered... because it is she that I have listened to, when she grumbled, or boasted, or even sometimes when she said nothing. Because she is my rose." What defeats comparison with others is not being different, but this list.

sections.h2: Main task — The Star: stars in a drawer and stars that laugh
paragraphs: The Main task point is read mostly through its shadow side: what the couple fails at and what it has to learn. At its worst, The Star in Lisovskaya is a beautiful wrapping with nothing inside and a union put on display. It is comparison with others and pride in status, when one partner belittles the other. It is treating the partner as a fan. It is fear of fulfilling one's own dream and a habit of getting in the way of the partner's. And it is being in love without responsibility. The prince's journey across the planets reads as a gallery of these shadows.

On the second planet lives a conceited man. "Ah! Ah! I am about to receive a visit from an admirer!" he cries when he sees the prince from afar: "For, to conceited men, all other men are admirers." He asks for applause, raises his hat and explains that to admire means to regard him as "the handsomest, the best-dressed, the richest, and the most intelligent man on this planet". — "But you are the only man on your planet!" A couple in the shadow of The Star recognises itself here easily. One partner expects applause from the other on demand and takes offence when it is too faint. Or both expect it from an audience and live for the photograph.

The businessman counts the stars: "Five-hundred-and-one million, six-hundred-twenty-two thousand, seven-hundred-thirty-one. I am concerned with matters of consequence: I am accurate." He owns them: he writes the number on a little paper and locks it in a drawer. The prince answers him with a line that could serve as the formula of the main task: "I myself own a flower, which I water every day... It is of some use to my volcanoes, and it is of some use to my flower, that I own them. But you are of no use to the stars..." Another person's light can be counted as property and kept in a drawer. Or it can be watered.

The lamplighter is the only one the prince does not find ridiculous: "When he lights his street lamp, it is as if he brought one more star to life, or one flower." His trouble is his orders — in Nora Gal, his "agreement": once he put the lamp out in the morning and lit it in the evening, but now "from year to year the planet has turned more rapidly and the orders have not been changed!" This speaks directly to the Entry to the task point, where the couple's shared agreements live. The agreement of the first days works while the planet turns slowly. When life speeds up and the agreement stays the same, the light goes on and off every minute and there is not a second left for rest.

The prince answers the whole gallery on his last night: **"Where I live everything is so small that I cannot show you where my star is to be found. It is better, like that. My star will just be one of the stars, for you."** This couple's star is not the one that gets displayed. "All men have the stars, but they are not the same things for different people. For some, who are travellers, the stars are guides. For others they are no more than little lights in the sky. For others, who are scholars, they are problems. For my businessman they were wealth. But all these stars are silent." For the one who loved, though, the stars will laugh. His friends will be astonished to see him laughing at the sky and will think he is crazy. A light that only two people understand looks strange from outside, and that is what makes it real.

Even a number changes its meaning here. The businessman locked half a billion stars in a drawer — as a number on a little paper. At the end the prince gives the pilot the same number, only alive: "You will have five hundred million little bells, and I shall have five hundred million springs of fresh water..." For him the stars are now "wells with a rusty pulley. All the stars will pour out fresh water for me to drink..."

The Fox has one last lesson too: **"You become responsible, forever, for what you have tamed. You are responsible for your rose..."** In Lisovskaya, The Star at its worst is a couple that enjoys being in love until the question of responsibility comes up. The Fox answers before the question is asked: admiration lived through time becomes responsibility.

The whole tail fits into one sentence about the water from the well that the pilot and the prince reached at daybreak. **"This water was indeed a different thing from ordinary nourishment. Its sweetness was born of the walk under the stars, the song of the pulley, the effort of my arms."** The long walk is Temperance. Under the stars is The Star. And it was sought for one thing only: "what they are looking for could be found in one single rose, or in a little water."

sections.h2: What Waite's cards show: noon, two cups and the stars
paragraphs: These are the drawings of the Waite–Smith deck; the cards on this site are drawn differently. But in Waite the three cards of the tail add up to a single day, from the noon sun to the stars.

On The Lovers "the sun shines in the zenith", and beneath it is a winged figure with arms extended. Waite calls it "in all simplicity the card of human love", love before it is contaminated by "gross material desire". The rose, remember, "was born at the same moment as the sun".

On Temperance the angel has "the sign of the sun upon his forehead". He pours liquid from chalice to chalice, and "a direct path goes up to certain heights on the verge of the horizon", above which shines a great light. Waite adds: "I speak of him in the masculine sense, but the figure is neither male nor female." For the middle of a couple's tail this is a precise hint: the work of time is not divided into "his" and "hers". Wen quotes P. D. Ouspensky's The Symbolism of the Tarot: "The name of the angel is Time... One of the cups the angel holds is the past, the other is the future. The rainbow stream between the cups is the present. You see that it flows both ways." The Fox at four o'clock, happy from three, is that same stream.

On The Star the sun is gone: a great star of eight rays and seven lesser ones shine, and a woman pours water from two great ewers onto the land and into the pool. Wen compares her with Temperance: there, a balancing; here, "a pouring out in one direction". The middle of the tail is an exchange; the main task is a light that pours out without expecting a return. Waite adds that on other planes the card "has been certified as immortality and interior light". The tale describes that interior light exactly: the pilot carries the sleeping prince and sees in him "the image of a rose that shines through his whole being like the flame of a lamp, even when he is asleep".

And a small thing that proves nothing but raises a smile. Waite notes that in some later cards the bird on The Star's tree was replaced by "a butterfly on a rose". And the rose, saying goodbye to the prince, tells him: "Well, I must endure the presence of two or three caterpillars if I wish to become acquainted with the butterflies."

sections.h2: The rose who had a voice of her own
paragraphs: The rose had a real model, and her story adds the tail's last clue. Consuelo Suncín was born in 1901 in El Salvador; she wrote, painted and sculpted. She and Antoine de Saint-Exupéry met at the end of 1930 in Buenos Aires and married in the spring of 1931. The marriage was stormy: he left and came back many times. Consuelo had asthma, and the rose in the tale coughs. Biographers see her as the model for the capricious, vain and fragile flower. In 1942, while the tale was being written, they lived at Bevin House on Long Island.

On 31 July 1944 Saint-Exupéry did not return from a reconnaissance flight. Consuelo wrote a memoir of the marriage, and the manuscript lay in a trunk for a long time. Mémoires de la rose (in English, The Tale of the Rose) came out only in 2000 and was translated into many languages. Earlier still, in 1945, her book Oppède appeared in New York with her own drawings.

This is not a model for a couple and not a forecast. It is a detail that clarifies the main task. The rose in the tale speaks in hints, tigers and coughs. The living woman behind that rose told the story herself, in her own voice. The Star in the tail 6-14-17 is not a role played in someone else's light, but each partner's own light.

sections.h2: How this tail's circle closes and where it opens
paragraphs: Put the three acts together and a circle appears, one that a couple with this tail can walk for years without noticing it is a circle:

ol: **A performance of admiration.** One shows themselves in the best light and waits for delight; the other admires. Both are in paradise, like the rose and the prince at sunrise.
**Words instead of deeds.** Requests come out as complaints, tenderness hides behind barbs. The other hears the words literally, feels guilty and leaves — the room, for work, into silence.
**Time on the run.** Meeting "when we can", life on an express train, fifty-three minutes saved at each other's expense. One keeps adjusting, the other does not see it.

**Five thousand roses.** The couple starts comparing itself with other couples, and the partner with other people. Someone lies down in the grass and cries: "that doesn't make me a very great prince". Someone chooses the shop window and looks for admiration from an audience.
**Hunger for admiration again.** The less time and truth there is, the stronger the wish for someone to applaud. The circle returns to the first step.

paragraphs: It opens at every step with a move of its own, and every one of these moves is in the tale:

ul: **Judge by deeds.** Hear a request in a complaint, and "it hurts" in "now go".
**Keep a four o'clock of their own.** A time that repeats and is never moved: a Thursday, an evening, a ritual that belongs to the two of them.
**Waste time together.** Do not economise on those fifty-three minutes: the middle of the road grows out of them.
**Revise the lamplighter's orders.** Check the agreements of the first days against how the planet turns now.
**Do not count the other's stars.** Support the other's dream instead of owning it and locking it in a drawer.
**Answer for what has been tamed.** When admiration quietens down, the thing the whole road was for begins.

paragraphs: If threats, pressure or fear for personal safety have entered the relationship, that is no longer a matter for the tail. Then it is worth seeing a psychologist, and in danger, calling a local emergency number.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail 6-14-17
paragraphs: At its best, The Star in Lisovskaya is a union that inspires both. The partners say plainly what they like and what they don't, and often it is only as a couple that they understand who they want to be. It is the rare case where the pretty picture is true. A 6-14-17 couple has beauty from the very entry, and the main task is not to give it up. The task is for the picture to stop being a performance.

The tale has this version too. At six, the pilot gave up drawing because grown-ups did not understand his boa constrictors. Beside the prince he draws again — a sheep, a box, a muzzle — and in the end illustrates the book himself. The prince asks nothing of his drawings; he only laughs that the baobabs "look a little like cabbages" and reassures him: "children understand." The Star at its best is when, beside another person, someone dares to take up what they once abandoned.

sections.h2: Worked example: 14.08.1975 and 14.09.1975
paragraphs: The two dates that give the couple tail 6-14-17 were calculated by the site's engine. The first partner's personal tail is 15-5-8, the second's 18-9-9 — the most common combination, 73% of such couples.

The couple's values for these dates are 12, The Hanged Man. The Star stands here twice, and that is not a doubling but two different roles. In the main task it is read through its shadow side, as a lesson: the shop window, comparisons, another's light in a drawer. On the What to create together point, which is read only at its best, it is what the couple is meant to create: a light of its own that inspires both.

The check of the middle on these dates is plain to see. By the personal formula, 6 + 17 would give 5. In the couple the middle is the sum of the partners' middles: 5 + 9 = 14. The first partner's Hierophant is literally visible in the sum, and together with the second partner's Hermit it turns into Temperance.

sections.h2: The Tower at the centre and the couple's values
paragraphs: In 97.5% of couples with this tail the centre holds 16, The Tower; in the remaining 2.5%, 7, The Chariot. In Lisovskaya the couple's centre is the atmosphere inside the union, what is not on show. The Tower at its best means trials passed hand in hand, calm in sudden trouble, often an unusual story of how they met. At its worst, barbs and threats of a break-up used as leverage. Wen observes that The Star comes straight after The Tower in the deck: "After the downfall of The Tower, The Star is an indication of a turn upward." The tale begins the same way — with a forced landing in the desert: "Something was broken in my engine." The stars appear in it only after the crash. Saint-Exupéry had such a crash himself: in 1935 he came down in the Libyan Desert and, with his mechanic, wandered for four days without water until a Bedouin gave them a drink. He told the story in Terre des hommes, whose English title is Wind, Sand and Stars.

There is an arithmetic detail as well. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail equals the sum of the main task and the centre. For this couple the formula holds with both possible centres: 17 + 16 = 33 → 6 and 17 + 7 = 24 → 6. The admiration at the entry is literally made of a star and a crash.

The couple's values (spiritual purpose) in such couples are 21, The World (49.3%), 3, The Empress (27.1%), and 12, The Hanged Man (23.7%). What follows is our reading through the tale. The World is the journey across the planets that leads back home to the rose. The Empress is the garden and the care of a living thing, that same watering every morning. The Hanged Man is the ability to look at the same sky differently: "all men have the stars, but they are not the same things for different people".

ul: **Entry to the task — 6, The Lovers.** The couple enters its task through delight and beauty: it wants to love and be loved the way it did on the first day. Its common language is the language of admiration, hints and little performances, and that same language is the first thing to get in the way of understanding.

**Middle of the task — 14, Temperance.** The road runs through measure and time: drawing closer little by little, keeping an hour that belongs to the two of them, never saving time at each other's expense.

**Main task — 17, The Star.** Learning a light that does not need to be put on show: each becoming themselves beside the other and not dimming the other's dream. At its worst: a shop window, comparisons, and a partner cast as a fan.

intro: This plot was written down long ago, and almost everyone read it as a child. In Saint-Exupéry's The Little Prince, the story of the prince and the rose runs exactly in the order of the tail: a beauty at sunrise, the Fox and his lesson about time, stars that know how to laugh. The key to the middle is hidden in a single line of the Fox's — and the classic Russian translation gives it in a different form from the one the author wrote.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 6-14-17 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the task of a couple that enters a relationship through admiration and beauty (6, The Lovers), lives it through time, measure and patience (14, Temperance) and learns a light that needs no audience (17, The Star). The main task is read through its shadow side: a shop window, comparison with others, a partner cast as a fan, fear of fulfilling one's own dream and of getting in the way of the other's.

faq.q: Why is the middle of the tail 14 if 6 + 17 gives 5?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle is built from the ends of the tail, while in a couple's matrix each point is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices. The couple's middle 14 comes from the partners' middles: 5 + 9, 8 + 6 or 10 + 4. That is why the tail 6-14-17 never occurs in one person's personal chart.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers?
faq.a: No. The entry of a couple's tail can only be 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 or 21, so 14 and 17 cannot stand there, and the order 6-17-14 does not arise from any two dates. 6-14-17 is the only couple tail made of these three numbers.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail? Does it mean the couple will break up?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events or pass verdicts: it describes a task, not an outcome. This couple's task is to learn to judge by deeds, to give the relationship time and not to confuse an audience's admiration with a light of its own.

faq.q: How common is the karmic tail 6-14-17?
faq.a: It occurs in roughly one couple in 45, which is 2.246% of all couples and 14th place among the 97 couple tails. It is made of three combinations of personal tails: 15-5-8 and 18-9-9 (73%), 15-8-11 and 18-6-6 (24%), 21-10-7 and 21-4-10 (2%).

report: One of the best-known lines in The Little Prince reaches Russian readers in a different form from the one Saint-Exupéry wrote. In the French original the Fox speaks of time lost, and Katherine Woods' English keeps it: "It is the time you have wasted for your rose that makes your rose so important." Nora Gal's canonical Russian translation reads (our translation): **"Your rose is so dear to you because you gave her your whole soul."** For a couple with the tail 6-14-17, that difference is the whole plot.

The tail reads as the three acts of that tale. At the entry to the task stand The Lovers: the couple comes in through admiration and beauty. In the middle, Temperance: the road runs through measure and time. In the main task, The Star: a light that needs no audience. In one person's personal chart The Hierophant would stand between The Lovers and The Star — a rule, "how love ought to be done". This couple has time in that place, and only two people together can make it.

report.h3: Admiration that begins as a performance

report: The rose prepared her entrance for days, choosing her colours and adjusting her petals: "It was only in the full radiance of her beauty that she wished to appear." She opened "exactly at sunrise" and promptly yawned: "Ah! I am scarcely awake..." The prince "could not restrain his admiration": "Oh! How beautiful you are!" — "Am I not? And I was born at the same moment as the sun..."

That is the couple's common language at the entry: to admire and to be admired. The delight is real, but it speaks in hints and little performances. The rose complains of draughts and coughs "in order to put the little prince in the wrong". The prince hears every word literally and leaves. In a couple's life this is recognisable at once. One partner complains in order to be noticed, and the other answers the complaint instead of the request. One says "fine, go" and waits to be stopped, and the other picks up a coat.

There is no culprit in this scene. Saying goodbye, the rose says: "It is my fault that you have not known it all the while... But you, you have been just as foolish as I." The prince only draws the conclusion later: **"I ought to have judged by deeds and not by words."**

report.h3: A soul is given in one rush, time only an hour at a time

report: On Earth the prince finds a garden where five thousand roses just like his are in bloom, lies down in the grass and cries: his only one has turned out to be "a common rose". This is how the couple's chief enemy enters the story — comparison. The Fox answers it.

The Fox teaches taming, which means "to establish ties". First sit at a little distance and say nothing, because "words are the source of misunderstandings", and every day sit a little closer. Come back at the same hour: if the prince comes at four, "then at three o'clock I shall begin to be happy." Wen recalls that Temperance was called the Time card. The Fox describes time exactly so: the coming hour pours into the present one.

Here the difference between translations becomes a clue. A soul can be given in a single rush, at dawn, at the sight of a beauty — that is The Lovers. Time cannot be given that way, only an hour at a time — that is Temperance. And in Saint-Exupéry it is not invested but lost, wasted. Next to the Fox the book sets a merchant selling pills that save fifty-three minutes a week, and the prince thinks he "should walk at my leisure toward a spring of fresh water". **The middle of this couple's road teaches saving time for each other, not at each other's expense.** What defeats comparison with five thousand roses is not being different but the time lived together: "because it is she that I have watered".

report.h3: The star that cannot be shown

report: The main task is read through its shadow side, and the prince's journey across the planets is a gallery of that shadow. The conceited man cries "Ah! Ah! I am about to receive a visit from an admirer!" and asks for applause, though there is nobody else on his planet. That is the partner cast as a fan, and applause on demand. The businessman counts the stars, writes the number on a little paper and locks it in a drawer. The prince answers him: "it is of some use to my flower, that I own them. But you are of no use to the stars..." Another's light can be kept in a drawer like property, or it can be watered.

The lamplighter lights his lamp, and "it is as if he brought one more star to life, or one flower". But his orders never change, though "from year to year the planet has turned more rapidly". The agreements of the first days work while the planet turns slowly.

The prince gives the answer on his last night: his star is too small to point out, and **"It is better, like that."** For everyone else the stars are silent, but for the one who loved they will laugh, and friends will think he is crazy. A light that only two people understand looks strange from outside, and that is what makes it real. The businessman locked half a billion stars in a drawer; the prince gives the same number away alive, as "five hundred million little bells" and "five hundred million springs of fresh water". The Fox's last lesson is about this too: "You are responsible for your rose..." Admiration lived through time becomes responsibility.

report.h3: Water born of the walk under the stars

report: The whole tail fits into one sentence about the water from the well that the pilot and the prince reached at daybreak: **"Its sweetness was born of the walk under the stars, the song of the pulley, the effort of my arms."** The long walk is Temperance, the stars are The Star, and it was sought for one thing only: "what they are looking for could be found in one single rose, or in a little water."
The circle of this tail opens with the same moves as in the tale:

ul: judge by deeds, and hear "it hurts" in "now go";
keep a four o'clock of the couple's own that is never moved;
waste time together instead of saving it at each other's expense;
check the agreements of the first days against how the planet turns now;
support the other's dream instead of locking it in a drawer.

report: The rose had a living model, Consuelo de Saint-Exupéry. In the tale the rose speaks in hints and coughs, but the living woman told the story of the marriage herself, in her own voice, in a book of her own. The Star in this tail is not a role played in someone else's light, but each partner's own light.

If threats, pressure or fear for personal safety have entered the relationship, that is no longer a matter for the tail: it is worth seeing a psychologist, and in danger, calling a local emergency number or crisis line.

unit.title: Time wasted for the rose

captions.M: To want admiration and to speak in hints
captions.N: To draw closer hour by hour, not save time on each other
captions.D: To shine without an audience, not lock up the other's dream

unit.meaning: Your task is to move from admiration, through time, to a light that needs no audience, and to guard each other's dreams.

seo.title: Karmic tail 6 14 8 compatibility: Pride and Prejudice in a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 14 8 compatibility: The Lovers at the entry, Temperance in the middle, Justice as the main task and The Tower at the centre in 9 couples of 10.

items.title: Karmic tail 6-14-8 in compatibility: from first impressions to a fair verdict
items.short: In nine couples out of ten with the karmic tail 6-14-8, the centre of the matrix holds The Tower, the card of sudden collapse. It is an odd neighbour for a tail that opens with The Lovers and closes with Justice. The answer to the riddle is that 6-14-8 is not a story about love at first sight but about putting first sight on trial. The couple enters the task through attraction and a first opinion of each other, lives it as a slow blending of two characters, and learns the main thing: to judge fairly — each other, themselves and what happened between them. The Tower at the centre is the moment when an opinion built on a first impression falls down. More than two hundred years ago Jane Austen wrote this plot.

sections.h2: The novel that was first called First Impressions
paragraphs: In October 1796 the twenty-year-old Jane Austen sat down to a novel and finished it by the following August. It was called First Impressions. Her father offered the manuscript to the London publisher Thomas Cadell and was turned down. Sixteen years later, in January 1813, the reworked book came out under another title: Pride and Prejudice.

Austen took the new title from someone else's novel. In Fanny Burney's Cecilia (1782), Dr Lyster sums up the heroes' troubles, and two words of his speech are printed in capitals: "The whole of this unfortunate business has been the result of PRIDE and PREJUDICE." Then comes the sentence worth remembering him for: "if to PRIDE and PREJUDICE you owe your miseries, so wonderfully is good and evil balanced, that to PRIDE and PREJUDICE you will also owe their termination."

The two titles of one book are the two ends of the tail 6-14-8. First Impressions is the entry, The Lovers: attraction, choice, an instant judgement. "So wonderfully is good and evil balanced" is the scales of Justice, the main task. Between them lie a long middle and an explosion at the centre. Many remember the plot: at a ball the proud Mr Darcy makes a cutting remark about Elizabeth Bennet, she believes the handsome story told by the charming Wickham, Darcy unexpectedly proposes and is refused with accusations, he answers with a letter — and from then on the two slowly revise their view of each other. Austen named the novel not after love but after what stands in love's way.

sections.h2: The Lovers at the entry: a first impression is already a verdict
paragraphs: Point M in a couple's tail is the "Entry to the task": what the two want together, what they agree on, what language they speak. The couple enters the task through this wish. But the point stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish easily becomes resistance.

The novel opens with a law nobody ever passed: "It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife." The neighbours have not yet seen the new tenant of Netherfield, and he already "is considered as the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters." A few pages later comes the first ball, and the verdict is passed in a single evening. For the first half of the evening Darcy is admired; then "his character was decided. He was the proudest, most disagreeable man in the world." He returns the favour: Elizabeth, in his words, is "tolerable: but not handsome enough to tempt me."

Waite's divinatory list for The Lovers opens with the words "Attraction, love, beauty." At the entry of this couple, attraction arrives together with an assessment: handsome or not, one of us or a stranger, suitable or "not handsome enough." Benebell Wen writes of The Lovers in love readings that "there is a strong feeling of paradise, at least in the beginning," but "not all is as it seems." In the novel the paradise of first sight goes to Wickham: "His countenance, voice, and manner, had established him at once in the possession of every virtue." Neither of Elizabeth's two first impressions will prove right.

In a 6-14-8 couple this looks quite ordinary. The story of how they met, told to guests, is already a small verdict: "he didn't even look my way that night," "I thought she was terribly stuck-up." Nicknames and jokes grow out of those first judgements, and a common language grows out of the jokes. While the language is funny, it binds. When a role gets stuck in it — "you're always like that" — each starts proving that the first opinion was a mistake, or, on the contrary, that it was right. In Yuliana Lisovskaya's account, The Lovers at their worst mean idealisation, perfectionism and the insecurity from which jealousy and control grow. At this entry they are easy to recognise: one keeps checking whether they are still looked at as on the first evening, the other feels constantly assessed.

sections.h2: The Tower at the centre: a house built on a first opinion
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's matrix is the "Atmosphere": what happens between two people when nobody is watching. In 89.6% of couples with the tail 6-14-8 it holds The Tower; in the remaining 10.4%, The Chariot. There is no third option.

The scene at Hunsford, one of the best known in the novel, is The Tower itself. Darcy declares his love in such a way that the declaration sounds like a list of arguments against it: inequality, damage to his name, the bride's relations. Elizabeth answers just as directly, and her central sentence is built like an account of a construction site: his manners, from the first moment of their acquaintance, "were such as to form that groundwork of disapprobation, on which succeeding events have built so immovable a dislike." Darcy sums it up like a bookkeeper: "My faults, according to this calculation, are heavy indeed!" Within one day both buildings will fall: his certainty that he cannot be refused, and her certainty about Wickham.

Now take Benebell Wen's description of The Tower (Holistic Tarot, 2015). Upright, the card is a downfall through pride and ego: "the Seeker's ego will be struck down to humility. This is good news, actually. There will be a lesson in humility." Reversed, it is the jolt felt by someone who "relied on false impressions made by others"; sometimes, someone who "has been falsely accused." And after the jolt, in Wen's words, "the aftermath is truth." Pride, false impressions taken from someone else's words, a false accusation and truth after the blow — this is not the theme of the novel but its main events, and in the same order.

A calculated card has no upright or reversed position: the number 16 at the centre lies neither way. The couple gets the whole Tower, both halves of the description. In the novel they went to two people: the pride to Darcy, the borrowed impressions to Elizabeth. In a living couple the halves are not handed out as roles: pride and trust in other people's stories are found in each partner. And the "lesson in humility" returns word for word at the end of the book, in Darcy's mouth: "You taught me a lesson, hard indeed at first, but most advantageous. By you, I was properly humbled."

Among the tasks of a couple with The Tower, Lisovskaya names the collapse of an invented image of the partner, and in her reading of a couple with The Tower at the centre she warns that what is said in a quarrel stays in the memory. Austen shows it literally: months later Darcy repeats her reproof word for word — "Had you behaved in a more gentlemanlike manner" — and admits how those words have tortured him. The Tower at the centre does not predict disasters. It describes how truth comes to this couple: not drop by drop, but in a blow, when the accumulated opinion can no longer bear its own weight. A quarrel in such a couple is rarely about an unwashed mug. It is about "you've been like this from the very start…" — and at that moment one can see how many storeys have been added on top of the first impression.

One more clue lies in the arithmetic. In a personal matrix, the entry to the tail equals the sum of the task and the centre. A couple's matrix is not calculated that way, yet in 6-14-8 with The Tower the formula holds by itself: Justice plus The Tower, 8 + 16 = 24 → 2 + 4 = 6, gives The Lovers. Scales plus collapse — love again. In the novel the second proposal comes only after the collapse and after an honest reckoning. With The Chariot at the centre the equation does not work: 8 + 7 = 15.

sections.h2: Darcy's letter: a speech for the defence on two charges
paragraphs: The couple's main task, point D, is Justice. Lisovskaya reads this point mostly through its minus: what the couple does not manage and what it has to learn. Austen shows both the minus and the way out of it in a single chapter.

The morning after the refusal Darcy hands Elizabeth a letter: two sheets "written quite through, in a very close hand," and even the envelope full. It is a real speech for the defence. "Two offences of a very different nature, and by no means of equal magnitude, you last night laid to my charge," he begins, answers each in turn, offers a witness and asks not for pity but for a hearing: "I demand it of your justice." Elizabeth reads like a judge trying not to decide in advance: she "weighed every circumstance with what she meant to be impartiality — deliberated on the probability of each statement — but with little success. On both sides it was only assertion." The scales stand level. What tips them is not a new argument but a second reading.

And then the main thing happens: Elizabeth passes her first fair verdict not on Darcy, not on Wickham, but on herself. "How humiliating is this discovery! Yet, how just a humiliation! … But vanity, not love, has been my folly. Pleased with the preference of one, and offended by the neglect of the other, on the very beginning of our acquaintance, I have courted prepossession and ignorance… Till this moment, I never knew myself." The last sentence is the shortest of all, and the heaviest.

Waite's list for Justice reversed ends with the words "bigotry, bias, excessive severity"; bias is prejudice by another name. Wen sums the card up in one formula: upright, "What is fair will feel fair"; reversed, "what is fair will not feel fair." That is an exact description of the minute over the letter: everything Darcy writes is true, and that is precisely why it is unbearable to read.

In a 6-14-8 couple, Justice at its worst rarely looks like a court with a sword. More often it is a quiet habit of measuring the partner by oneself and not noticing what hurts them; of displaying their faults to look better; of collecting evidence instead of asking. One partner ends up as prosecutor, the other as defendant; the roles may swap, but the court never rises. The tasks Lisovskaya sets a couple with Justice repeat Elizabeth's road: to admit one's own fault instead of blaming everyone; to forgive; to let go of idealising the partner. Justice does not prove that anyone deserved their grievance. It asks which scales the grievance was weighed on.

sections.h2: Temperance in the middle: on Waite's card the water flows uphill
paragraphs: The middle of the tail, point N, has no meaning of its own for Lisovskaya — it is an "addition" to the main task. We read it as the road: what the couple does and goes through on the way from the wish at the entry to the task at the end. In 6-14-8 that road is Temperance.

Austen, unusually, names it outright. When Elizabeth, after the letter and after the visit to Pemberley, realises that her feelings have changed, the author steps into the story herself: "If gratitude and esteem are good foundations of affection, Elizabeth's change of sentiment will be neither improbable nor faulty." And she compares it with the other way of falling in love — with what "is so often described as arising on a first interview with its object, and even before two words have been exchanged." Elizabeth has already tried the first way on Wickham and now turns to "the other less interesting mode of attachment." Austen's word is pointedly dry. Two ways of loving in one paragraph — exactly the entry and the middle of the tail: The Lovers at first sight and Temperance, which blends feeling slowly, out of esteem and gratitude.

For Wen, Temperance "is the fusion of two contrasting elements and bringing them into harmony," and for a couple it suggests "a greater need for cooperation and tempering of extreme emotions, such as anger, resentment, hostility." On Waite's card an angel pours water between two cups, and Wen asks an unexpected question: does the water flow "from the higher cup to the lower cup, with gravity, or from the lower cup to the higher cup, against gravity, against the laws of physics"? In Austen the water flows uphill. Darcy is richer, better born and eight years older, yet it is Elizabeth who teaches him. He admits it himself: "As a child I was taught what was right, but I was not taught to correct my temper." Temper and temperance are one word at the root.

There is a clue in the numbers too. Card 14 does not appear in the personal tail of either partner — not in any of the nine combinations that add up to 6-14-8. The couple's middle is something nobody brought along. It is gathered from the two personal middles: in 42% of such couples it is The Hermit and The Hierophant (9 + 5), in 30% The Lovers and Justice (6 + 8), in 16% The Wheel of Fortune and The Emperor (10 + 4), in 12% two Chariots (7 + 7). In almost a third of couples, one partner carries The Lovers in the middle of their personal tail and the other carries Justice, and only together do they make Temperance. Even without that coincidence, the middle of 6-14-8 equals the sum of its ends exactly: 6 + 8 = 14. A couple's middle is never worked out from the outer numbers, but here it adds up — Temperance literally blends The Lovers and Justice.

In a living couple the middle is work that cannot be seen from outside. Two people blend two ways of life: in one family they quarrelled loudly and made up at once, in the other they went silent for a week. One apologises in words, the other in deeds, and neither notices the other's apologies. Lisovskaya advises a couple with Temperance to catch how the partner speaks of love, since everyone does it in their own way. Darcy declares himself in deeds: he secretly finds the runaway Lydia and settles her fate, and when Elizabeth thanks him on her family's behalf he replies: "your family owe me nothing. Much as I respect them, I believe I thought only of you." At its worst, Temperance means one partner always gives way and the other does not notice: the water pours in one direction only. And Lisovskaya's advice not to jump to conclusions about the partner reads like a direct antidote to "first impressions."

sections.h2: Justice as the main task: blame shared in half
paragraphs: When the two finally have it out, Austen stages a strange argument. Darcy asks: "What did you say of me that I did not deserve? … my behaviour to you at the time had merited the severest reproof." Elizabeth will not let him take it all: "We will not quarrel for the greater share of blame annexed to that evening. The conduct of neither, if strictly examined, will be irreproachable." The two argue about who is more to blame, and each pulls the larger share towards himself or herself.

This is a couple's Justice at its best: not a verdict on one of the two, but blame shared in half. The first thing Darcy does after the reconciliation is to go to his friend and confess that his "former interference in his affairs" was "absurd and impertinent"; the friend forgives him. A Justice that began with accusations ends with a confession.

Austen adds to the scales the one thing without which they turn into bookkeeping. Darcy hopes the letter has been destroyed, and Elizabeth promises: "The letter shall certainly be burnt." She sets out her philosophy: "Think only of the past as its remembrance gives you pleasure." Darcy objects: "Painful recollections will intrude, which cannot, which ought not to be repelled." Both are right. Justice in a 6-14-8 couple means keeping the lesson and burning the case file: not bringing a closed case back into every new quarrel.

It has a third face as well — equality. Lady Catherine de Bourgh arrives to forbid the engagement and exclaims: "Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?" Elizabeth answers with a formula worthy of the scales: "He is a gentleman; I am a gentleman's daughter; so far we are equal." Not equality of fortune — equality of standing. Burney promised that pride and prejudice would themselves end the miseries, and Austen keeps her word: Lady Catherine's pride brings Darcy back. Her account of the conversation with Elizabeth, he says, "taught me to hope."

Justice at its best, for Lisovskaya, means a fair division of duties, restraint in words, "a cool head and a warm heart." In a couple with this tail it shows in small things: a hurt is named aloud the same day, not a year later on a general list; the argument is about the deed, not the character; "I was wrong" is heard no less often than "you were wrong."

sections.h2: The couple's values: The World, The Hanged Man and The Empress
paragraphs: "The couple's values" is the spiritual purpose, one more answer to the question of why the two met. In couples with the tail 6-14-8 only three cards appear here: The World in 51.1%, The Hanged Man in 26.8%, The Empress in 22.1%. What follows is our reading, not a statement from the books.

Wen describes The World as "the supreme balance between good and evil, a complete reconciliation of the universe's dichotomy and duality" — almost Dr Lyster's words about good and evil "so wonderfully balanced." For half of these couples the value is a whole in which both pride and prejudice have found their place, and there is no longer any need to settle whose share was bigger. Waite's list for The Hanged Man begins with "Wisdom, circumspection, discernment," and Elizabeth reproached herself precisely over her discernment: "I, who have prided myself on my discernment!" The value of The Hanged Man is clear sight that comes once one's view has been turned upside down. Waite's Empress is above all "Fruitfulness"; Austen's ending is the house at Pemberley, where the closest friends are Elizabeth's uncle and aunt Gardiner — the very relations whose condition in life Darcy once called "so decidedly beneath my own," and who, "by bringing her into Derbyshire, had been the means of uniting them."

sections.h2: Worked example: 11.02.1976 and 14.08.1975
paragraphs: Each point of a couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22: if the sum is greater than 22, its digits are added together. A person born on 11.02.1976 has the personal tail 9-9-18; a person born on 14.08.1975 has 15-5-8.

The middle comes from the two personal middles, 9 and 5, and is not worked out from the entry and the task. The centre of this couple is 9 + 7 = 16, The Tower, as in most such couples. "Image of the couple" is The Chariot (11 + 14 = 25 → 7), "What to create together" is The Wheel of Fortune (2 + 8 = 10), "Values" is The Empress.

Justice appears twice in this couple: in the main task and at the point "What fills" (13 + 22 = 35 → 8). A repeat does not double the card — each point has its own role. In the task, Justice is read through what does not work yet; in "What fills", through what gives the couple back its strength. The same honest conversation that comes hardest is also what restores the union after a hard stretch.

The combination of the personal tails 15-5-8 and 9-9-18 is the most common route to 6-14-8: 23% of such couples are built this way. The second partner already has Justice at the end of the personal tail, but that says nothing about who is the "judge" in the couple: a personal tail and a couple's tail are calculated differently, and their points mean different things.

sections.h2: Which personal tails add up to 6-14-8
paragraphs: The tail 6-14-8 occurs in roughly one couple in 62 (1.621%) and ranks 21st of the 97 couple tails. It comes from nine combinations of personal tails; the most common are 15-5-8 + 9-9-18 (23% of such couples), 18-6-6 + 6-8-20 (20%) and 18-9-9 + 6-5-17 (19%).
In 28% of couples neither partner has The Lovers, Temperance or Justice in their personal tail. A couple's tail is not the sum of two characters but a new plot that appears only when there are two.

No other couple tails are made of these three numbers: the entry to a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, and the order 6-8-14 does not occur in any couple. The order 6-14-8 also exists as a personal karmic tail — for 55 dates since 1900 — but that is a different calculation with different roles for the points, and the site has a separate article about it.

sections.h2: What helps a 6-14-8 couple
paragraphs: The tail passes no sentence on the union. It shows where this couple's knot is and what unties it.

ul: **Check the first opinion.** What is it built on — one's own experience or someone else's story, as with Elizabeth and Wickham?
**Argue about the deed, not the character.** The phrase "you've been like this from the very start…" adds another storey to The Tower.
**Share the blame out loud.** When both are at fault, don't compete over who is more to blame — in accusation or in repentance.
**Reread the letter.** Elizabeth understood Darcy on the second reading; an important conversation deserves a second attempt.
**Take turns giving way.** Notice who in the couple always gives way, and swap roles.
**Burn the case file.** Don't bring a closed case into a new quarrel.

paragraphs: If quarrels turn into threats, stalking or fear for one's safety, this is no longer a task of the tail but a reason to call a local emergency number and seek a psychologist's help.

ul: **M · Entry to the task — The Lovers (6).** What the couple wants together: attraction, choosing each other, a common language. This is also where the first opinion of each other is born, and the same wish can turn into resistance.

**N · Middle of the task — Temperance (14).** How the couple walks the road: blending two characters and looking for the measure at which both can live. Neither partner brings this card into the couple.

**D · Main task — Justice (8).** What there is to learn: to judge without bias and without keeping score of grievances, to own one's share of the blame, to see the other as an equal. It is read mostly through what does not work yet.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 6-14-8 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: These are the couple's tasks in the order M–N–D. The entry is The Lovers: attraction, choice, a common language and a first opinion of each other. The middle is Temperance: a slow blending of two characters. The main task is Justice: a fair verdict on oneself and the partner, blame shared in half, equality. The key point is Justice; the other two unfold it.

faq.q: Is the tail 6-14-8 a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not predict events and does not decide whether two people suit each other. It shows where the couple stumbles and what it learns: to revise first impressions and to judge fairly. This method gives no compatibility percentages.

faq.q: Why do such couples almost always have The Tower at the centre?
faq.a: The numbers of the tail and the centre are linked: in every personal matrix the entry to the tail equals the task plus the centre, and this kinship survives when two matrices are added. So a couple with the tail 6-14-8 can only have 16 or 7 at the centre, and The Tower comes up in 89.6% of couples. It describes the atmosphere: truth arrives in a blow, when an opinion built on a first impression collapses.

faq.q: How does the couple tail 6-14-8 differ from the personal tail 6-14-8?
faq.a: A personal tail is calculated from one date and occurs for 55 dates since 1900; its points mean something else. A couple's tail is the sum of the points of two matrices, reduced to 22, and it is read as the tasks of the union. Readings cannot be carried over from one to the other.

faq.q: Are there couple tails with the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. The entry to a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, so 8 and 14 never stand at the entry, and the order 6-8-14 does not occur in any couple. Of the numbers 6, 14 and 8, only the couple tail 6-14-8 can be formed.

report: Jane Austen gave one book two titles, and both are written into the three cards of the tail 6-14-8. The novel the whole world knows as Pride and Prejudice was called First Impressions in its first version. Austen took the new title from Fanny Burney — from a sentence saying that pride and prejudice bring miseries and also end them, because "so wonderfully is good and evil balanced." First impressions are the entry of the tail, The Lovers. Good and evil in balance are its main task, Justice. Between them lies Temperance, and at the centre of such a couple's matrix there most often stands The Tower. **This is not a story about love at first sight but about putting first sight on trial.**

report.h3: A first impression is already a verdict

report: The novel opens with a law nobody ever passed: "It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife." A few pages later the neighbours pass a verdict on a newcomer in a single evening: "his character was decided." Darcy returns the favour — Elizabeth is "tolerable: but not handsome enough to tempt me." Wickham, on the contrary, needs only first sight: "His countenance, voice, and manner, had established him at once in the possession of every virtue." Neither of Elizabeth's two first impressions will prove right.

At the entry of a 6-14-8 couple, attraction arrives together with an assessment. The story of how they met, told to guests, is already a small verdict: "he didn't even look my way that night." Jokes and nicknames grow out of those first judgements, and a common language grows out of the jokes. While it is funny, it binds. When a role gets stuck in it — "you're always like that" — the same wish that brought the two together becomes resistance: one keeps checking whether they are still looked at as on the first evening, the other feels constantly assessed.

report.h3: The Tower built on a first opinion

report: The refusal at Hunsford is The Tower in its pure form. Elizabeth explains it like an account of a construction site: from the first moment of their acquaintance Darcy's manners "were such as to form that groundwork of disapprobation, on which succeeding events have built so immovable a dislike." Within one day both buildings will fall: his certainty that he cannot be refused, and her certainty about Wickham.

Benebell Wen describes The Tower in two halves. One is a downfall through pride, after which "there will be a lesson in humility." The other is a jolt for someone who "relied on false impressions made by others." Pride and borrowed impressions are exactly the two heroes of the novel. A calculated card has no upright or reversed position: the couple gets both halves at once, and in a living couple they are not handed out as roles. And the lesson returns word for word at the end of the book, in Darcy's mouth: "By you, I was properly humbled."

The Tower at the centre does not predict disasters. It describes how truth comes to this couple: **not drop by drop, but in a blow, when the accumulated opinion can no longer bear its own weight.** A quarrel here is rarely about an unwashed mug — it is about "you've been like this from the very start…". Even the arithmetic holds this plot together: Justice and The Tower add up to The Lovers. Scales plus collapse — love again.

report.h3: The first fair verdict falls on oneself

report: The morning after the refusal Darcy hands over a letter — a speech for the defence on two charges: "I demand it of your justice." Elizabeth weighs every circumstance, and it comes out a draw: "On both sides it was only assertion." The second reading tips the scales, and she passes her first fair verdict not on him but on herself: "How humiliating is this discovery! Yet, how just a humiliation!" And then the shortest line of all: "Till this moment, I never knew myself." Wen sums Justice up in a formula that fits this very minute: reversed, "what is fair will not feel fair."

In a 6-14-8 couple, Justice at its worst rarely looks like a court with a sword. More often it is a habit of measuring the partner by oneself and collecting evidence instead of asking. One partner ends up as prosecutor, the other as defendant; the roles swap, but the court never rises.

report.h3: The other less interesting mode of attachment

report: The middle of the tail is Temperance, and Austen names it outright. Of Elizabeth's change of feeling the author writes: "If gratitude and esteem are good foundations of affection…" — and compares it with what "is so often described as arising on a first interview with its object, and even before two words have been exchanged." Elizabeth has tried the first way on Wickham and now turns to "the other less interesting mode of attachment." Two ways of loving in one paragraph — the entry and the middle of the tail.

Neither partner brings this card into the couple: Temperance is absent from both personal tails. Yet it equals the sum of the two outer cards exactly — The Lovers and Justice make Temperance. **The couple's middle is what appears only when there are two.** In everyday life it is the blending of two ways of life: one apologises in words, the other in deeds, and neither notices the other's apologies. Darcy declares himself in deeds — he secretly settles the fate of the runaway Lydia — and does not turn it into a debt: "your family owe me nothing. Much as I respect them, I believe I thought only of you."

report.h3: Blame in half and a burnt case file

report: When the two finally have it out, they argue about who is more to blame, and each pulls the larger share towards themselves. Elizabeth stops the argument: "We will not quarrel for the greater share of blame annexed to that evening. The conduct of neither, if strictly examined, will be irreproachable." **A couple's Justice is not a verdict on one of the two but blame shared in half.** Another of its faces is equality: "He is a gentleman; I am a gentleman's daughter; so far we are equal."

Elizabeth promises to burn Darcy's letter. That is the strong version of the tail: keep the lesson and burn the case file, never bringing a closed case into a new quarrel. Check what the first opinion is built on — one's own experience or someone else's story. Argue about the deed, not the character. Share the blame out loud. Take turns giving way. If quarrels turn into threats, stalking or fear for one's safety, this is no longer a task of the tail but a reason to call a local emergency number or crisis line and seek a psychologist's help.
