seo.title: Karmic tail 6 17 11 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 17 11 compatibility: what The Lovers, The Star and Strength mean in a couple's destiny matrix, and why its story is Cupid and Psyche.

items.title: Karmic tail 6-17-11 in compatibility: The Lovers, The Star and Strength
items.short: The 6-17-11 tail sounds like a wedding toast: love, a star, strength. In a couple's destiny matrix, though, it is not a wish but a task, and its story is ancient — Apuleius's tale of Cupid and Psyche. The couple enters the task through the wish for love (6, The Lovers), lives it out in a light that shows everything that was hidden (17, The Star), and has one main thing to learn: to handle the force of their own feelings so that the union holds neither a beast nor a tamer (11, Strength).

sections.h2: The tale told to a bride
paragraphs: In the second century Apuleius set into his novel the Metamorphoses, better known as The Golden Ass, a tale that outlived both the novel and the empire. It is told by a drunken old woman in a robbers' cave to a girl who has been kidnapped straight from her wedding. "But I will take your mind off it at once with pretty stories and old wives' tales," she says (here and below, Apuleius is quoted in our own translation from the Latin). A bride whose wedding was stolen is told about a wedding that looks like a funeral.

A king has three daughters, and the youngest, Psyche, is so beautiful that people forget the way to the temples of Venus. The offended goddess sends her son, Cupid, to make the girl fall for the lowest of mortals. And the oracle of Apollo orders her father:

"King, on a crag of a high mountain set the girl / adorned for a funeral wedding; / hope for no son-in-law of mortal stock, / but a cruel, wild, viperish evil. / … / Jupiter himself trembles before it, and the gods are afraid."

The wedding torches blacken with soot, the flute slips into a mournful key, and "tearful Psyche goes not to her wedding but to her own funeral." From the cliff the west wind, Zephyr, carries her off to a palace where invisible servants wait on her and where, at night, a husband comes whom she must never see. Her sisters visit, see the gold and grow envious. They convince Psyche that a huge serpent sleeps with her at night and teach her to hide a razor in the bed and a lamp under a pot. At night Psyche raises the lamp and sees "the gentlest and sweetest of all wild beasts — that very Cupid himself." A drop of hot oil falls on the god's shoulder; he wakes and flies away.

Then come wanderings and four impossible tasks set by Venus. The last of them is a descent to the underworld for a box of beauty, which Psyche opens on the way back, and she falls into a deathlike sleep. Cupid wakes her with a prick of his arrow. Jupiter summons the gods, promises that the marriage "will not be unequal" and hands Psyche a cup of ambrosia — the mortal becomes immortal. The couple have a daughter, "whom we call Pleasure."

The three cards of the 6-17-11 tail are three acts of this tale. The Lovers are the night palace, where one loves without seeing a face. The Star is the lamp in whose light everything shows. Strength is the beast of the oracle, the one everyone feared, who turned out to be love. And at the centre of the chart, for 98.8% of these couples, stands 13, Death — that very wedding in funeral dress. The tale promises the couple neither monsters nor trials set by a goddess. Its use is different: in it one recognises the order in which the three forces stand in the tail, and what happens between them.

sections.h2: Waite's clues: Cupid, the butterfly and the mystery of union
paragraphs: Linking the tale to the tail is our reading, but it rests on more than the plot: the clues are in the writing of Waite, the author of the classic deck. The pictures he discusses come from old decks and from the Waite–Smith deck; the cards on this site do not show these details, but Waite's words concern the meaning of the cards themselves.

The first clue is in The Lovers. Describing an old eighteenth-century card on which father, mother and child stand beneath a flying Cupid, Waite calls the pagan god a misapplied emblem of marriage and explains why: "The Cupid is of love beginning rather than of love in its fulness, guarding the fruit thereof." The formula of the tail's first point is written almost word for word. The couple's entry to the task is Cupid, love that is only beginning. The task is to reach fullness.

The second is in The Star. In his historical notes Waite remarks in passing: "A bird is perched on a tree near her; for this a butterfly on a rose has been substituted in some later cards." In Greek, ψυχή, psyche, means soul, and Aristotle uses the same word for a butterfly. Artists have often given Psyche butterfly wings. In the middle of the tail stands a card on which Psyche once settled.

The third is in Strength. Waite writes that "Fortitude, in one of its most exalted aspects, is connected with the Divine Mystery of Union", and that "there is one aspect in which the lion signifies the passions." The couple's main task stands on the card of union, and its beast is not an enemy outside but passion. That is exactly what Apuleius told: the viperish evil of the oracle, before which Jupiter trembles, is the god of love.

The fourth is in Death, the card of the centre. Waite's divinatory list contains a line that seems copied from Psyche's wedding: "for a maid, failure of marriage projects." And his description of the symbol holds the way the tale ends: "The veil or mask of life is perpetuated in change, transformation and passage from lower to higher."

sections.h2: Entry to the task: The Lovers, or loving without seeing a face
paragraphs: The first point of a couple's tail is what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, a common language. The task begins with this wish. But the point stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish can also turn into resistance.

In the 6-17-11 tail the wish is love itself. Not so much a home, a project or a joint venture as a state: to be in love, to choose and be chosen, to live as if it were still the beginning. Waite calls The Lovers "the card of human love". Wen sees in them "a strong feeling of paradise, at least in the beginning", and warns that "the feeling of paradise may be evanescent if caution is not observed."

Apuleius has a sentence that names this entry better than any other. Studying her sleeping husband's weapons by lamplight, Psyche tests the point of one of his arrows and pricks her finger until it bleeds. "So, without knowing it, Psyche of her own accord fell in love with Love." To fall in love with Love is a wonderful start and an honest wish. It becomes resistance when love of love crowds out interest in the person.

Even before the lamp, Psyche tells her invisible husband: "Whoever you are, I love you desperately, as my own soul, and I would not compare you even with Cupid himself." The irony is that there is no one to compare him with: he is Cupid. But the key words are "whoever you are". It is easy to love without knowing who is beside you: wishes fill in the portrait.

This is exactly where the sisters catch her out. The first time, she describes her husband as a young man "whose cheeks are just shaded with down", a hunter. The second time, as a middle-aged merchant "with a sprinkling of grey". "Either the wretch made it all up, or she has never set eyes on her husband," the sisters conclude. For a couple this is a familiar scene: to a friend the partner is described one way, to the parents another, to oneself a third, and all three portraits are sincere. This is not a lie. It is a person no one has yet seen in the light.

In Lisovskaya, The Lovers among a couple's tasks are recognised by scenes: the relationship is measured against an ideal and always comes up short; insecurity rereads someone else's messages at night; no decision is taken without a family council. In the tale all of this fits into two words: in tears, Psyche calls her palace "a blissful prison". The wish to keep the enchantment quietly grows prohibitions — don't ask, don't look, don't talk about hard things, so as not to scare it away. Cupid sets his wife exactly this condition. For a couple it is more often a silent agreement that nobody ever announced out loud.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: The Star, the lamp and the drop of oil
paragraphs: Lisovskaya does not interpret the middle of a couple's tail separately: it is an "addition" to the main point. On this site it is read as the path — what the couple does and goes through on the way from the wish to the main task. This is the product's reading, not a statement from the book.

For this couple the path is lit by The Star, the card of open truth: Waite connects it with "Truth unveiled". For two people these are the moments when the partner is suddenly seen whole: the first honest talk about money or fears, a weakness seen without the scenery, a dream said out loud for the first time. Of The Star at its best, Lisovskaya writes that such partners often understand who they want to be only as a couple, and tell each other plainly what they like and what they don't. This is the case where the pretty picture of a union turns out to be true.

Psyche's lamp shows exactly this. She went to kill a serpent and saw the one she had loved blindly. In the light, this couple is more likely to discover the best than the worst — that is hope, The Star's second name.

But light here is never free. Psyche's hand trembles, and the lamp — "or because it, too, longed to touch and, as it were, to kiss so fair a body" — spits oil on the god's shoulder. Apuleius cannot help himself and turns to address it: "Oh bold and reckless lamp, worthless servant of love, you burn the very god of all fire!" Truth seen in secret burns. Waite's list of meanings for The Star, by the way, begins not with hope but with "loss" and "abandonment" — what Psyche receives a minute after the light.

The Star among a couple's tasks has a reverse side, and the tale knows it too. Psyche shows her sisters around the palace and loads them with gold — she puts her happiness on display, and displayed happiness breeds envy. In the book's worked example where The Star falls among a couple's tasks, Lisovskaya notes that such a couple's tasks may play out in public. The Star's downside shows in scenes: the couple's photos are better than its evenings; the partner is compared with other people's husbands and wives; one is quietly fitted to an image that is convenient to show; one's own dream is shelved, and the other's dream is obstructed along the way.

The most precise scene is Proserpina's box. Psyche opens it to take a little of the divine beauty and "so please that beautiful lover of mine", but there is "nothing there at all, no beauty whatever, only an infernal sleep, a truly Stygian one." Beauty fetched for the picture turns out to be an empty box.

sections.h2: Main task: Strength and the beast of the oracle
paragraphs: The main point of a couple's tail is its main task, its chief difficulties and trials. Lisovskaya reads this point mostly through its downside: what the couple is not managing and what it has to learn.

The oracle promised Psyche a monster, "a cruel, wild, viperish evil", before which Jupiter himself trembles. It is a portrait of Cupid: winged, armed with fire and arrows, stronger than the gods. The beast feared in this tale is love, or rather its force: passion, jealousy, the power of one person over another. Strength as the main task tells the couple the same thing: the main trial is not an outside enemy but the energy that lives between two people.

Wen writes that "the Strength card is about domination over the Seeker's fears" and reminds that "the Seeker cannot use brute force to exercise will over others; the Seeker must use gentle, subtle influence." In Lisovskaya, Strength at its worst is an argument over who is in charge at home that drags on for years; each has their own truth, and both are loud; a jibe in front of guests, after which the other says nothing until evening. And the task is respect: to share the housework fairly, to balance work and family, and from the very start to say what one likes and what one doesn't.

In Apuleius's tale there is not a single equal agreement. Cupid sets the condition: don't look and don't ask. Psyche answers with a razor hidden in the bed. Venus declares her daughter-in-law a runaway servant, and one of her household shouts at Psyche: "So, most worthless of maids, have you at last learned that you have a mistress?" The sisters advise murder. And in Aksakov's The Scarlet Flower (Alenky tsvetochek), a Russian relative of this tale, power is turned the other way round: the forest monster writes on the wall in letters of fire: "I am not your master but your obedient slave. You are my mistress" (our translation). Master and slave, tamer and beast — two versions of the same inequality.

For a couple it looks mundane. One decides what may be asked. The other silently gathers a "razor" — grievances, arguments, messages to be produced one day. Each is sure they are defending themselves from a beast, and each, in the other's eyes, slowly becomes one. Cupid puts it with bitter precision: he wounded himself with his own arrow and made Psyche his wife "so that, it seems, I should look like a beast to you, and you would cut off with a blade this head of mine, which carries these eyes that love you."

The tale knows another kind of strength too. When Psyche persuades her husband to let her sisters visit, she whispers endearments — "My honey, my husband, sweet soul of your Psyche!" — and "to the force and power of love's whisper the husband yielded against his will." In Apuleius, the god of love is overcome not by a razor but by a whisper.

The most precise advice about Strength comes from a reed by the river, when Venus sends Psyche for golden wool. Do not go near the sheep while the sun scorches them and "they are usually seized by a savage frenzy"; wait until "the frenzy of the sheep has died down" — and gather the wool "caught everywhere among the tangled branches". **Here the gold is not torn from a raging beast — it is picked up once the beast has calmed down.**

If strength in the couple has already become a threat and someone fears for their safety, this is not a matter for reading a tail. What is needed is real help: a local emergency number, a crisis line, a psychologist.

sections.h2: Atmosphere: Death at the centre, or a wedding in funeral dress
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya, the centre of a couple's chart is the atmosphere between the partners — what is inside and not on show. In couples with the 6-17-11 tail it is almost always 13, Death: in 98.8% of them. In the remaining 1.2% it is 22, The Fool. There are no other options.

This is no accident: here the centre is all but set by the tail itself. In a personal chart the entry of the tail is calculated as the sum of the karmic task and the centre. In a couple's chart it is not: each point is added up from the matching points of the two partners. But in the 6-17-11 tail the personal arithmetic works out by itself. The centre of such couples is always one of the two cards that, together with Strength, give The Lovers: 11 + 13 = 24, and 2 + 4 = 6; with the rare Fool, 11 + 22 = 33 → 6. And further: 6 + 11 = 17. If the numbers are read as a record, **Strength passed through Death gives The Lovers, and The Lovers together with Strength give The Star.** The couple's middle is calculated separately, from the middles of the two personal tails, and still matches the sum of the ends. This does not hold for every tail: in 50 of the 97 couple tails the middle and the sum of the ends differ.

Death in a couple's atmosphere is neither a threat nor a forecast. At its best, in Lisovskaya, it is a steady union with shared goals: the partner's past is accepted and left behind, changes in the partner are met calmly, and sometimes one helps the other leave a destructive relationship. At its worst it is a swing: so many changes that the other has nothing to lean on; one hurries the other to change; the features of an ex are glimpsed in the current partner; nitpicking over every trifle. Waite writes of the card's symbol as a passage "from lower to higher", Wen of the end of a stage and of how painful it is to part with the old.

Apuleius's tale is built exactly like this: each part of it dies so that the next can begin. The wedding is the funeral of a girl who was only a king's daughter. The night palace ends in lamplight. The wanderings end in sleep from a box. Psyche's mortal life ends with a cup of ambrosia. No stage is saved by being preserved — only by being allowed to end. For a couple with this tail this is perhaps the main secret of its atmosphere: the union holds not because nothing changes, but because the old is let go in time — first infatuation, old roles, the agreement "don't look".

sections.h2: The loop of the tail: the same mistake twice
paragraphs: When Lisovskaya analyses a couple's tail, she links the energies in pairs and all three together: each conclusion follows from its own combination. For 6-17-11 the links read like this.

ul: **The Lovers and The Star (6 + 17).** The wish for love meets the light. At best, a couple that is not afraid to see each other and becomes itself beside the other. At worst, love of the picture: a union that is shown first and lived afterwards.

**The Lovers and Strength (6 + 11).** The wish to be chosen meets power: who chose whom, who owes whom, who sets the terms. Hence jealousy and control — in Lisovskaya they grow from insecurity, not from strength.

**The Star and Strength (17 + 11).** Truth meets power. The same truth can be held up like a lamp, or like a razor. Constant criticism from The Star's downside and jibes from Strength's downside are one mistake: truth used as a weapon.

**All three (6 + 17 + 11).** Enchantment guarded by a prohibition breeds fear of what cannot be seen. Fear prepares a secret check. The check burns, and one of the two pulls away. Then comes the urge to bring the magic back — a little beauty from the box — and the couple falls into the same sleep again.

paragraphs: The tale says outright that the loop repeats. Waking Psyche, Cupid says: "Look, poor thing, you nearly perished again from the same curiosity." Psyche's two mistakes are really one: **she takes in secret what can only be received openly.** The first time, her husband's face; the second, beauty. The 6-17-11 tail does not condemn the wish to see — seeing is its very middle. It shows what becomes of a glance cast at night, in fear, with a razor in the other hand.

sections.h2: The way out: a marriage "not unequal"
paragraphs: The tale does not end with one side defeating the other. Jupiter gathers the gods and announces: "I will make this marriage not unequal, but lawful and in keeping with civil law." Psyche drinks ambrosia and becomes immortal — that is, her husband's equal. The unequal marriage of a mortal and a god is evened out not because someone won, but because both left their former positions: Cupid, the role of the invisible master of the night; Psyche, the role of the one who may not ask.

The strong version of the 6-17-11 tail is a couple that began as lovers in a dark palace and arrived at a union of two people who know each other in the light. **Strength in such couples is not the ability to endure or the ability to subdue, but the capacity to stay close to strong feelings, one's own and the other's, without turning them into either a weapon or a cage.**

paragraphs.h3: What changes the script

ul: to say from the very start what one likes and what one doesn't, instead of guarding the enchantment with silence: Psyche was forbidden to ask — and she took up a razor;
to test doubts with a question asked with both present, not in secret and at night;
not to settle the big things at the peak: to wait until "the frenzy of the sheep has died down", and only then gather the gold;
to share power: no single partner controls the decisions, the money and the housework;
to hear the "sisters" — relatives, friends, other people's stories in the feed — as voices, not as a plan of action;
less shop window and fewer comparisons: a union does not have to look like a fairy tale to be one;
to let go of the union's former shapes once they have run their course, rather than mending them at any cost.

paragraphs: Eighteen centuries after Apuleius, C. S. Lewis retold this story from the point of view of Psyche's sister in his novel Till We Have Faces (1956). The narrator spends her life accusing the gods, and at the end understands why they are silent: "How can they meet us face to face till we have faces?" For a couple with the 6-17-11 tail this is perhaps the best formula for the main task. Love begins in the dark, with Cupid. Fullness begins when both have faces.

sections.h2: How the 6-17-11 tail comes about: an example with 14.08.1975 and 19.03.1979
paragraphs: Each point of a couple's chart is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, folded down to 22 by adding the digits. The couple's tail is not recalculated from its ends: entry is added to entry, middle to middle, task to task.

First partner, 14.08.1975. Day — 14, month — 8, year — 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Karmic task — 14 + 8 + 22 = 44 → 8. Centre — 14 + 8 + 22 + 8 = 52 → 7. Tail entry — 8 + 7 = 15, middle — 8 + 15 = 23 → 5. Personal tail — 15-5-8.

Second partner, 19.03.1979. Day — 19, month — 3, year — 1 + 9 + 7 + 9 = 26 → 8. Karmic task — 19 + 3 + 8 = 30 → 3. Centre — 19 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 33 → 6. Tail entry — 3 + 6 = 9, middle — 3 + 9 = 12. Personal tail — 9-12-3.
The couple's tail adds up like this:
Centre of the couple's chart — 7 + 6 = 13, Death. The couple's values — 12, The Hanged Man.

Neither of the two has The Lovers, The Star or Strength in their personal tail. The 6-17-11 tail is not one partner's inheritance; it is born only between them. This couple also has an echo of its own: The Lovers also stand on the point "Image of the couple" (14 + 19 = 33 → 6), and Strength on "What to create together" (8 + 3 = 11). This is a feature of these particular dates, not of every couple with this tail.

sections.h2: 6-17-11 in numbers: which couples it comes from
paragraphs: Going through every date since 1900 gives 97 different couple tails. 6-17-11 occurs in roughly one couple in 65 (1.545%) and ranks 23rd by frequency.

It is made up of just six combinations of personal tails. Most often it is 15-5-8 and 9-12-3, as in the example: that is 51% of such couples. Next come 18-9-9 and 6-8-20 (28%) and 15-8-11 and 9-9-18 (11%); the remaining three combinations make up 10% between them. In 61% of such couples, neither of the two personal tails contains any of the three cards. And nobody, ever, has The Star in their personal tail: the couple's middle, 17, is always made up of two other middles — 5 and 12, 9 and 8, 8 and 9, or 10 and 7. **This couple's Star belongs to the couple alone.**

The couple's values — the spiritual purpose, the path the two are to walk together — are one of three cards for such couples: 21, The World, in 39.5%; 12, The Hanged Man, in 34.5%; 3, The Empress, in 26%. This is a separate sphere of the reading, but the end of the tale, if you like, has all three. The feast of the gods, where the Muses sing and Venus herself dances, is The World, the circle completed. Psyche, hanging from the leg of her departing husband, "a hanging companion through the cloudy heights", and, in the underworld, refusing the soft seat and sitting down "humbly at the feet" of Proserpina, is The Hanged Man — the view from below and the refusal of the easy way. The daughter named Pleasure is The Empress. This is our reading, not a rule of the method.

ul: **Entry to the task — 6, The Lovers.** What the couple wants together: to be in love, to choose each other and to be chosen. Everything starts with this wish, and the same wish digs in its heels when the enchantment has to be tested by light.

**Middle of the task — 17, The Star.** How the couple travels its path: through openness and hope, through moments when the partner is seen whole, unveiled — and through the temptation to swap the truth for a pretty picture.

**Main task — 11, Strength.** What the couple has to learn: to deal with passion, anger, fear and power over each other with neither a knife nor a cage. Not to defeat the "beast" in the other, but to stop fearing it — and to make the union equal.

intro: A couple's tail does not predict events or pass sentence on a union. It is a pattern in which a couple recognises itself: where it is strong, where it stalls and what changes the script. What follows is an investigation: what the cards themselves say, what Arthur Edward Waite, Benebell Wen and Yuliana Lisovskaya, the author of the compatibility method, write about them, and what the numbers from the site's engine show.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 6-17-11 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's task, written in three points of the compatibility chart: entry to the task — The Lovers, middle — The Star, main task — Strength. The couple begins with the wish for love and enchantment, travels through openness and moments when everything is seen without embellishment, and has one main thing to learn — to handle passion, anger, fear and power over each other without suppression and without a cage, so that the union becomes equal.

faq.q: Is this the same as the personal karmic tail 6-17-11?
faq.a: No. The same three numbers also occur as a personal tail — for 2,052 birth dates since 1900 — but it is a different calculation, and the points have different roles. A personal tail is calculated from one date; a couple's tail is the sum of the points of two charts and is read as a task for two. Personal readings do not carry over to the couple; the personal tail has its own article on the site.

faq.q: Can a couple's tail have the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. Among the 97 couple tails produced by all dates since 1900, the numbers 6, 17 and 11 occur only in this order. The same set in another sequence does not come up for a couple.

faq.q: Is Death at the centre of the chart a bad sign for such a couple?
faq.a: No. The centre of a couple's chart is the atmosphere between the partners, and 13 there speaks of a union that goes through change and renewal, not of a threat. In couples with the 6-17-11 tail, Death stands at the centre in 98.8% of cases: it follows from the numbers themselves. The difficulty of this atmosphere is the swings and the attempts to remake the partner; its strength is the ability to let go of what has run its course, in time.

faq.q: Is the 6-17-11 tail a sentence or a prediction?
faq.a: Neither. The tail does not predict events, dates or break-ups, and does not say whether a couple suits each other. It shows where the couple stumbles and what it can learn together. As in Apuleius's tale, the main work is not to overcome the other but to see them in the light.

faq.q: Do the partners need The Lovers, The Star or Strength in their personal charts?
faq.a: No. In 61% of such couples neither of the two personal tails contains any of these cards, and neither partner ever has The Star in their personal tail. A couple's tail is born from the sum of two charts, so its theme may be new to both.

report: The most frightening bridegroom in ancient literature was promised by an oracle: "a cruel, wild, viperish evil", and "Jupiter himself trembles before it". The bride was dressed for a funeral, and "tearful Psyche goes not to her wedding but to her own funeral." The bridegroom turned out to be Cupid, the god of love.

Apuleius's tale of Cupid and Psyche lays itself out across the three cards of the 6-17-11 tail with almost nothing left over. The Lovers at the entry are the night palace, where one loves without seeing a face. The Star in the middle is the lamp in whose light everything shows. Strength as the main task is the beast of the oracle, the one everyone feared, who turned out to be love. It is no accident that the centre of the chart of such couples almost always holds Death — that very wedding in funeral dress. The tale predicts nothing for the couple. It shows the order in which these forces stand in the tail, and what happens between them.

report.h3: Love that is only beginning

report: The first thing a couple with this tail wants is love itself: to be in love, to choose and be chosen, to live as if it were still the beginning. Waite, discussing Cupid on an old Lovers card, gave the formula for this entry: "The Cupid is of love beginning rather than of love in its fulness." In Apuleius, Psyche pricks her finger on her sleeping husband's arrow: "So, without knowing it, Psyche of her own accord fell in love with Love."

To fall in love with Love is a wonderful start. The trouble is that it is easy to love without knowing who is beside one: wishes fill in the portrait. "Whoever you are, I love you desperately," Psyche tells her invisible husband. To her sisters she describes him first as a youth with the first down on his cheeks, then as a middle-aged merchant going grey. This is not a lie — it is a person no one has yet seen in the light. The wish to keep the enchantment grows prohibitions: don't ask, don't look, don't talk about hard things, so as not to scare it away. In tears, Psyche calls her palace **"a blissful prison"**.

report.h3: The light that burns

report: This couple's path runs through The Star — through moments when the partner is suddenly seen whole: an honest talk about money or fears, a weakness without the scenery, a dream said out loud for the first time. Psyche went to kill a serpent, and by lamplight she saw "the gentlest and sweetest of all wild beasts — that very Cupid himself." In the light, such a couple is more likely to discover the best than the worst.

But light here is never free. The hand trembles, a drop of hot oil falls on the god's shoulder, and he flies away. **Truth seen in secret burns.** The Star has a reverse side too: Psyche shows her sisters around the palace and loads them with gold, and displayed happiness breeds envy. In life this downside looks like this: the couple's photos are better than its evenings, and the partner is compared with others and quietly fitted to an image that is convenient to show.

report.h3: Not a single equal agreement

report: The couple's main task stands on Strength, and it is a task about power. In the tale there is not a single equal agreement. Cupid sets the condition: don't look and don't ask. Psyche answers with a razor hidden in the bed. In Aksakov's The Scarlet Flower, power is turned the other way round: the forest monster writes in letters of fire, "I am not your master but your obedient slave." Master and slave, tamer and beast — two versions of the same inequality.

In daily life it looks mundane. One decides what may be asked. The other silently gathers a "razor" — grievances, arguments, messages to be produced one day. Each is sure of defending themselves from a beast, and each, in the other's eyes, slowly becomes one. Cupid says bitterly that he made Psyche his wife only to look like a beast to her — so that she would take a blade to "this head of mine, which carries these eyes" full of love for her.

The loop repeats. Psyche opens Proserpina's box to take a little beauty for her husband, and inside there is "nothing there at all, no beauty whatever, only an infernal sleep". Waking her, Cupid says: "Look, poor thing, you nearly perished again from the same curiosity." Both mistakes are one: **to take in secret what can only be received openly.** The first time, her husband's face; the second, beauty.

report.h3: Gold is gathered once the beast has calmed

report: The tale knows another kind of strength. In Apuleius, the god of love is overcome not by a razor but by a whisper: "to the force and power of love's whisper the husband yielded against his will." And the most precise advice about Strength comes from a reed by the river: do not go near the sheep while "they are usually seized by a savage frenzy", wait until "the frenzy of the sheep has died down", and gather the golden wool from the branches. **The gold is not torn from a raging beast — it is picked up once the beast has calmed down.**

Hence the practice: to say from the very start what one likes and what one doesn't, instead of guarding the enchantment with silence; to test doubts with a question asked with both present, not in secret and at night; not to settle the big things at the peak; to share power, so that no single partner controls the decisions, the money and the housework; to let go of the union's former shapes once they have run their course. If strength in the couple has already become a threat and someone fears for their safety, this is not a matter for reading a tail: real help is needed — a local emergency number or crisis line, a psychologist.

The tale does not end with one side defeating the other. Jupiter promises: "I will make this marriage not unequal," and Psyche becomes immortal, her husband's equal. The strong version of the 6-17-11 tail is a couple that began as lovers in a dark palace and arrived at **a union of two people who know each other in the light**. C. S. Lewis, who retold this story eighteen centuries later, found a formula for it: "How can they meet us face to face till we have faces?" Love begins in the dark. Fullness comes when both have faces.

seo.title: Karmic tail 6 17 20 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 17 20 compatibility: The Lovers, The Star and Judgement. Why the middle is The Star, not Justice, and how Shakespeare's Pericles tells it.

items.title: The 6-17-20 karmic tail in compatibility: The Lovers, The Star and Judgement
items.short: The 6-17-20 couple's tail holds an oddity that needs no mysticism to see: Justice ought to stand in the middle, and The Star stands there instead. In a personal chart the middle is the sum of the two ends, 6 + 20 → 8. In a couple's chart it is put together differently and comes out as 17 — a number that hides the same eight in its digits: 1 + 7. This is the tail of a couple that enters its task by choosing each other (6, The Lovers), lives a long stretch of the road on hope and things left unsaid (17, The Star), and whose main task is to tell its own story aloud, among its own people, and to recognise each other anew (20, Judgement).

sections.h2: Why the middle is The Star, not Justice
paragraphs: In a personal destiny matrix the tail follows simple arithmetic: the middle is the sum of the ends. If 6-…-20 were a personal tail, the middle would be 6 + 20 = 26 → 8, Justice. That personal tail, 6-8-20, does exist in the method. A 6-17-20 tail never appears in a personal chart.

In a couple's chart each point is counted separately: the matching points of two personal charts are added together. The couple's middle comes from the partners' middles, not from its own ends. In nine couples out of ten with this tail, one partner's personal middle is 8, Justice, and the other's is 9, The Hermit. 8 + 9 = 17.

Add the digits and 1 + 7 = 8. That is no coincidence. Reducing a number by adding its digits never changes its remainder when divided by nine, so a couple whose ends are 6 and 20 can have only one of two middles: 8 or 17. This calculation allows no third option. Some couples carry the measure openly in the middle, as Justice. This couple carries the same measure hidden in the digits of The Star.

The difference between the two cards is the plot of the tail. Justice weighs: two pans, a tally, who owes whom how much. Waite gives its meanings as "Equity, rightness, probity". The Star does not weigh: its mottoes are "Waters of Life freely" and "Gifts of the Spirit", and among its readings is "hope and bright prospects". The 6-17-20 couple walks the middle of its road not by the tally but by hope: it gives, waits, trusts and does not check. That is its generosity. It is also its blind spot: when nobody weighs, nobody notices that the two have long been living not with each other but with an image of each other.

sections.h2: Pericles: a story told by a man risen from the dead
paragraphs: Around 1608 Shakespeare, together with the playwright George Wilkins, wrote Pericles, Prince of Tyre. The plot comes from a book that Europe, in the words of the Russian classicist Faddei Zelinsky, read for fourteen centuries — the anonymous late-antique History of Apollonius, King of Tyre — and from its retelling in a poem by John Gower, Chaucer's contemporary. Gower comes on stage himself as the narrator, and his first words are about resurrection: "To sing a song that old was sung, / From ashes ancient Gower is come". The play is told by a man who had died two hundred years before its premiere.

The play itself had a similar fate. Audiences adored it, yet Shakespeare's fellow actors left it out of the first collected edition of his plays in 1623. In 1629 Ben Jonson sneered at it as "some mouldy tale, / Like Pericles". It entered the collected works only in 1664, in the third edition, and for another century editors kept dropping it and bringing it back.

The story is simple. Pericles, ruler of Tyre, flees King Antiochus after solving his terrible riddle, is shipwrecked and lands in Pentapolis, where he wins a tournament and the hand of Princess Thaisa. On the voyage home, in a storm, Thaisa gives birth to a daughter and, as everyone believes, dies. Her body is laid in a pitch-sealed chest and thrown into the sea. The chest washes up at Ephesus, Thaisa is brought back to her senses, and she becomes a priestess in the temple of Diana. Their daughter Marina grows up in a stranger's house, and Pericles spends years in mourning. Fourteen years later the father finds his daughter, and in Diana's temple, his wife. The three movements run in the order of the tail: a choice, a long life on hope, a judgement and a resurrection.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: a father's armour and the motto "In this hope I live"
paragraphs: Pericles reaches Pentapolis with nothing: the sea has taken his ship and his men. Fishermen haul a rusty suit of armour out of the water in their net, and it turns out to be his dead father's. Dying, the father had told him: "Keep it, my Pericles; it hath been a shield / 'Twixt me and death". In that armour, rust and all, the son goes to the tournament for the princess's hand. The ancient source has no such scene — there the hero wins a ball game. The father's armour pulled from the sea is the play's own addition.

Before the joust the knights pass before Thaisa and show the devices on their shields. One carries a torch turned upside down and the motto "What feeds me puts me out". Pericles carries "A wither'd branch, that's only green at top" and the motto In hac spe vivo: "In this hope I live". The courtiers laugh at the rust. King Simonides, the bride's father, answers them: "Opinion's but a fool, that makes us scan / The outward habit by the inward man." One device holds the whole tail: the dry branch is the past and the inheritance, the green at the top is hope, and the knight hands his shield to the bride himself.

At the feast neither of them can eat. Pericles says the dishes "resist me, she but thought upon"; Thaisa finds every dish "unsavoury, / Wishing him my meat". To her he looks among the other knights "like diamond to glass". And Pericles looks at Simonides and sees his own father: "Yon king's to me like to my father's picture", who "Had princes sit, like stars, about his throne". The stars and the father — the other two cards of the tail — already sit at the table of love's feast.

When Simonides tells his daughter to ask who the knight is, Thaisa asks and then retells his answer to her father in her own words: the name, Tyre, the shipwreck. Lisovskaya writes that couples with The Lovers complete each other's stories beautifully. Here the couple's common language is born in exactly this way: she tells his story for him.

Then comes the letter. Thaisa writes to her father that she will "wed the stranger knight, / Or never more to view nor day nor light." The other suitors are told that the princess has vowed to wear "Diana's livery" for twelve more moons. Simonides stages a fit of anger, calls Pericles a traitor and ends like this: "Either be ruled by me, or I will make you — / Man and wife". The two answer together: "Yes, if it please your majesty."

Point M in a couple's chart stands for shared wishes and agreements, the couple's "common language". Here it is the wish to choose each other openly and beautifully, in front of their own people, and to be blessed. Wen writes of The Lovers: "there is a strong feeling of paradise, at least in the beginning." But M sits on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. The first thing Pericles says on reading the letter is: "'Tis the king's subtlety to have my life." Not long before, he had fled Antioch, where a beautiful bride turned out to be a riddle with a death sentence attached. Once burned, he sees a trap in the gift. Among the tasks of a couple with The Lovers, Lisovskaya names insecurity, from which jealousy and control grow, and dependence on relatives. In this couple it looks like this: love is so wanted that it is frightening to believe in, and the two people's "yes" is spoken in the father's voice.

One more detail of the entry. The excuse made to the suitors — a year in Diana's service — will later become fourteen years of Thaisa's life. In the play, words said at the entry "for show" become the rule in the middle. A couple with this tail would do well to look at its own first words — about freedom, about "we don't need anyone", about "breaking up is easy" — and check whether they have quietly become law.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: fourteen years on a single hope
paragraphs: The storm catches the ship as Thaisa is giving birth. The nurse brings out the baby and tells Pericles: "Patience, good sir; do not assist the storm." Pericles answers the gods: "Why do you make us love your goodly gifts, / And snatch them straight away?"

Then the sailors come: the sea "will not lie till the ship be cleared of the dead". "That's your superstition," says Pericles. "With us at sea it hath been still observed: and we are strong in custom." And he gives way: "As you think meet." Not because he believes them, but because someone else's custom has proved stronger. Thaisa is laid in a pitch-sealed chest with jewels and a letter: whoever finds her should give her burial, for "She was the daughter of a king".

At Ephesus the chest is opened by Cerimon, a lord who has spent his life studying herbs and stones. The first thing he says is: "They were too rough / That threw her in the sea." And then: "Death may usurp on nature many hours, / And yet the fire of life kindle again / The o'erpress'd spirits." He calls for music, and Thaisa opens her eyes: "Where am I? Where's my lord? What world is this?"

Now the heart of the middle. From the letter Thaisa knows that her husband survived that night: it is his handwriting. And she decides: "since King Pericles, / My wedded lord, I ne'er shall see again, / A vestal livery will I take me to, / And never more have joy." Pericles, leaving his daughter at Tarsus, swears that his hair shall stay "Unscissor'd" until she marries, "Though I show ill in't". Years later, at his daughter's false tomb, he puts on sackcloth, swears never to wash his face, and for three months speaks to no one. Gower, standing by that tomb, tells the audience: "See how belief may suffer by foul show!"

Two people keep faith with each other, and neither checks. He never once doubts her death. She never once writes to Tyre, although a king is not hard to find. Each makes a vow alone, and each vow is a picture of loyalty that the other cannot see.

This is The Star in the middle, both its sides. For Lisovskaya, The Star in a couple is a union that inspires both partners, and the rare case where the beautiful picture is true. Its shadow is the same picture with nothing inside, and things left unsaid. In the play the shadow is not vulgar: nobody shows off. But instead of a conversation the two have a picture: a tomb, a priestess's robes, uncut hair. Waite opens The Star's list of meanings with "Loss, theft, privation, abandonment" — and the middle of the play goes through all four literally: the wife is lost at sea, the daughter is stolen by pirates, the father refuses food and speech, the child is left in a stranger's house.

The middle of a couple's tail is our reading of how the couple travels from the wish of M to the task of D. The 6-17-20 couple travels it on hope. It may be a long stretch: work in another city, a child, a move, caring for parents. Each protects the other and keeps quiet about the hardest things. Both are faithful — and both are lonely. The measure is there inside, the very eight hidden in the digits of seventeen, but nobody takes it out.

In the fifth act Pericles looks at an unknown girl, not yet knowing she is his daughter, and says: "thou look'st / Modest as Justice, and thou seem'st a palace / For the crown'd Truth to dwell in". Justice and Truth in one line — 8 and 17, the measure and The Star. Both old Russian translations lost Justice: Pyotr Kanshin has "as modest as pravda", Pavel Kozlov "modest as holy truth". In Russian the loss barely shows: in Old Russian pravda meant both truth and law — the law code of Yaroslav the Wise is called Russkaya Pravda. A measure hidden inside truth — like an eight hidden inside seventeen.

sections.h2: The couple's atmosphere: a death that turned out to be sleep
paragraphs: The tail is read together with the rest of the couple's chart. In 91% of couples with the 6-17-20 tail the centre of the chart — the sphere "The atmosphere inside the couple" — holds 13, Death. In 6.7% it is The Emperor, in 2.4% The Fool.

Waite calls Death "more especially a card of the death of Kings", and writes that "the alternatives allocated to the symbol are change and transformation". In Pericles kings die one after another: Antiochus with his daughter, Pericles's father whose armour came up from the sea, and finally Simonides. And two living people are buried: Thaisa in the sea, Marina in a tomb at Tarsus. Pericles says of his daughter: "Thou that wast born at sea, buried at Tarsus, / And found at sea again!" And of her too: "thou dost look / Like Patience gazing on kings' graves, and smiling / Extremity out of act." The Star gazes at the graves of kings — the middle of the tail gazes at the centre of the chart.

Wen notes that The Star "appears chronologically in the Major Arcana after a great deal of pain: The Hanged Man, Death, The Devil, and The Tower." This couple is built the same way: the hope of the middle grows right beside Death in the atmosphere. Inside the union one can clearly hear that everything ends. Hence the couple's strength — the ability to let go of what has truly ended — and its main danger: mistaking sleep for death. A quarrel for a break-up, a cooling for an ending, a pause for a grave. Cerimon puts it more precisely than any reading: death may rule for a long while, and still the fire kindles again.

sections.h2: Main task: telling everything in front of everyone
paragraphs: Act five. Pericles's ship lies off Mytilene. He himself lies behind a curtain; for three months he has spoken to no one, nor taken food "But to prorogue his grief". They bring him a girl who sings — Marina. He does not hear. She speaks to him, and he pushes her away. She says she has endured a grief that "Might equal yours, if both were justly weigh'd" — the scales again. She wants to leave, but something "whispers in mine ear, 'Go not till he speak.'"

Step by step: her name is Marina. Why Marina — because she was born at sea. Her mother died the minute she was born. Pericles cannot believe it, asks to be struck "Lest this great sea of joys rushing upon me / O'erbear the shores of my mortality", and at last: "O, come hither, / Thou that beget'st him that did thee beget". And at once: "Give me fresh garments."

The play has an exact architecture. It opens in the palace of Antiochus with a riddle in which one and the same man is "father, son, and husband": a family whose every boundary has been erased by violence. It closes with a line of the same shape: a daughter who gives birth to her father. The roles change places again, but now through a gift, not a crime. The American Shakespeare scholar C. L. Barber took this line as the title of his 1969 essay.

Then Pericles hears music. "The music of the spheres! List, my Marina." — "My lord, I hear none." He alone hears the summons that Waite describes for Judgement, one that "is heard and answered from within". In a dream Diana appears to him and tells him to sail to Ephesus and there, "Before the people all", to "Reveal how thou at sea didst lose thy wife". The ancient source has the same: the goddess orders Apollonius to tell his fate aloud before her altar.

In the temple Pericles tells everything: who he is, how he married, how his wife died at sea in childbirth, how his daughter grew up and nearly died. The high priestess faints: "Voice and favour!" Then: "Like him you spake, / Like him you are: did you not name a tempest, / A birth, and death?" Thaisa recognises her husband by his story. Pericles still argues: "I threw her overboard with these very arms." A moment later: "O, come, be buried / A second time within these arms." The same arms, the same verb: a burial becomes an embrace. Thaisa's proof is a family one — the ring her father gave Pericles. And straight away comes the news: "My father's dead." Pericles answers: "Heavens make a star of him!" The last star of the play is a dead father, and the couple will live out their days in his kingdom.

For Lisovskaya, Judgement is the card of lineage and family: relatives, traditions, inheritance, the influence of parents. Pericles has all of it, and all of it decides the couple's fate. The father's armour was a shield against death. The father's game blessed the marriage. The sailors' custom proved stronger than love. Marina's foster mother, Dionyza, cannot bear that the girl outshines her own daughter — comparison, The Star's shadow, lives here among relatives. The father's ring proves who is who, and in the end the couple inherits the father's kingdom. Lisovskaya reads point D mainly through its minus, and her tasks for a couple with Judgement are these: to admit mistakes; to manage to say what one feels and what one dislikes; to find boundaries — such couples tend to have either none at all or impenetrable ones. In the play Antiochus has no boundaries at all, while Pericles's three months of silence are impenetrable. The way out is a full account in front of witnesses.

For the couple, the main task of Judgement arrives as a summons: a moment comes when silence is no longer possible. The whole story has to be told — to each other and to their families — with the losses, the mistakes and whatever each has already buried alone. Waite's divinatory meanings for Judgement are "Change of position, renewal, outcome", and in the play the renewal can be seen: fresh garments, the vow lifted, and the hair that "this fourteen years no razor touch'd" trimmed for the daughter's wedding. In Wen, Judgement reversed means the Seeker "has misinterpreted the facts or evidence presented and has arrived at the wrong conclusion". The play's main mistake is exactly that: both believed in a death neither of them saw. On the plus side, Lisovskaya's Judgement means forgiving mistakes, and the way everything lived through together binds a couple. Pericles tells the gods in the temple: "your present kindness / Makes my past miseries sports". The past does not vanish. It becomes a story that can be told.

sections.h2: Waite and Wen: a star in the lantern and coffins on the water
paragraphs: A few more pieces of evidence lie in the drawings of Waite's deck — by Pamela Colman Smith — and in how Waite and Wen describe them. These are drawings from their deck, not the cards on our site.

Of The Hermit, Waite writes: "It is a star which shines in the lantern." And he quotes the old explanation that The Hermit "is said to be in search of that Truth which is located far off in the sequence, and of Justice which has preceded him on the way." In the Marseille order our site uses, Justice, 8, stands immediately before The Hermit, 9. Waite himself disagrees: for him this is "a card of attainment" rather than "a card of quest". But the couple's arithmetic repeats the old reading: in nine couples out of ten the middle is built from one partner's Justice and the other's Hermit, and the sum is The Star, whose figure, Waite says, will appear to "the majority of prepared minds" as "the type of Truth unveiled".

Wen compares The Star with Temperance: both show a figure at the water, but in Temperance "there is a balancing", while The Star "depicts a pouring out in one direction". That is the difference between 8 and 17 in the middle: scales with two pans, and a jug that pours without expecting anything back.

Of Judgement, Wen writes of "the body of water that the coffins float upon", and she assigns the card to the element of Water. In Shakespeare, Thaisa's coffin is a pitch-sealed chest on the waves, which the sea itself carries to the shore.

And one word links the entry and the middle. Waite's Lovers are "two human figures, male and female, unveiled before each other", and the figure of The Star is for him "Truth unveiled". First the two are open to each other. Then they have to open up before the truth. And in the finale — before everyone.

sections.h2: How the 6-17-20 tail looks in a couple's life
paragraphs: Lisovskaya advises reading a tail in links between cards and saying, for every conclusion, which combination it follows from. The 6-17-20 tail has four such links.

ul: **The Lovers and The Star (6 + 17).** A love that is pleasant to look at. Such partners often discover who they want to be precisely within the couple, and help each other open up. The shadow is the one beautiful photographs have: the picture of happiness takes the place of life, comparisons with other couples begin, and the waiting for an ideal.

**The Star and Judgement (17 + 20).** Hope against family. They wait a long time: until the relatives accept them, until there is a home of their own, until one partner is ready for the child the other already wants. Each carries the hardest part alone. The plus of this link is the ability to forgive and start again after a long stretch.

**The Lovers and Judgement (6 + 20).** A choice made under the eyes of the family. Parents bless the union or withhold their blessing, and the couple needs to tell its own choice apart from someone else's custom — to say, as Pericles said to the sailors, "That's your superstition", but this time not to give way.
**All three cards (6 + 17 + 20).** A story told aloud. At the start the two tell each other's stories, in the middle they keep silent, at the end they have to tell everything — among their own.

paragraphs: What it looks like in daily life. They have known each other a month and already tell their friends each other's story better than their own. Then comes a long period when each protects the other and keeps quiet. Sometimes, after a hard quarrel, one of them silently puts up a gravestone over the relationship — "that's it, it's over" — while the other, in a temple of their own, vows never to be happy again. The main task arrives not as a catastrophe but as a conversation: to sit down and tell everything in order, the tempest, the birth and the death, without embellishment.

This is not a forecast. The tail says nothing about events or dates, or about who is right and who is to blame. It shows a plot two people may recognise in themselves — and the place where that plot turns.

sections.h2: What helps a couple with the 6-17-20 tail

ul: **Checking before burying.** Before deciding "it's all over", asking: what did I see myself, and what did I simply believe? Thaisa recognised her husband's handwriting and still put on a priestess's robes.
**Saying aloud what was sworn in silence.** A silent vow of loyalty is a picture the other cannot see. Spoken, it becomes an agreement that can be discussed.

**Telling someone else's custom from one's own decision.** Relatives, traditions, "this is how we do things" — all of it deserves respect and is worth passing on, but decisions about the couple are made by the two.

**Not living inside a picture.** Not comparing each other with an ideal or with other couples, not standing in the way of the partner's dream, and not forcing a choice between the partner and their work.
**Marking the end of a hard time.** Pericles had his hair trimmed for his daughter's wedding. A couple, too, benefits from a visible sign: the waiting is over, ordinary life begins.
**Telling their story together.** First to each other — in full, with the losses and the mistakes. Then, if needed, to their families.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail
paragraphs: The strong 6-17-20 couple is the one that can tell its story to the end. In it the storm becomes a chapter, not the finale. Such partners recognise each other by voice and by story, as Thaisa recognised Pericles. Their choice was blessed, then held for a long time on a single hope, and it all ends not in resignation but in recognition.

Shakespeare's ending gathers the whole tail. A father made into a star — Judgement, turning the past into light. Marina, "Modest as Justice" — the measure hidden inside The Star. The arms that threw her into the sea are the same arms that embrace.

The couple's values — its spiritual purpose — are most often The Empress (45.7%), The World (36.7%) or The Hanged Man (17.6%) in such couples. To our reading, the play's ending holds all three: a mother to whom her daughter returns — "Flesh of thy flesh, Thaisa"; two kingdoms and a whole sea, from Tyre to Ephesus; and fourteen years of a life suspended between hope and mourning. This is our reading, not a rule of the method.

sections.h2: How to calculate the 6-17-20 couple's tail: an example
paragraphs: The example is a couple born on 14.09.1975 and 14.10.1976.
First partner: day 14, month 9, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Karmic task: 14 + 9 + 22 = 45 → 9. Centre: 14 + 9 + 22 + 9 = 54 → 9. Tail entry: 9 + 9 = 18, middle: 18 + 9 = 27 → 9. Personal tail: 18-9-9.

Second partner: day 14, month 10, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5. Karmic task: 14 + 10 + 5 = 29 → 11. Centre: 14 + 10 + 5 + 11 = 40 → 4. Tail entry: 4 + 11 = 15, middle: 15 + 11 = 26 → 8. Personal tail: 15-8-11.
The couple's tail is the sum of the matching points:

Check: 6 + 20 = 26 → 8, yet the middle is 17. The couple's middle is not recalculated from its ends; it is added up from the partners' middles. The couple's centre in this example is 9 + 4 = 13, Death, and the couple's values are 3, The Empress.
The 6-17-20 tail occurs in roughly one couple in 121 (0.825%) and ranks 44th of the 97 couple tails. It is formed by four combinations of the partners' personal tails:

ul: 15-8-11 and 18-9-9 — 91% of such couples;

paragraphs: Four different roads lead to the same Star: Justice and The Hermit (8 + 9), The Emperor and Death (4 + 13), The Empress and Temperance (3 + 14), The Wheel of Fortune and The Chariot (10 + 7). The Star is in none of these personal tails: only the couple puts it together.

ul: **6 · The Lovers — entry to the task.** The couple's shared wish: to love openly and beautifully, to choose each other and to hear a "yes" from their families. The same impulse can turn into resistance — when it is frightening to believe the gift is real.

**17 · The Star — middle of the task.** How the couple walks its road: on hope, generously, without weighing. In its shadow, a beautiful picture instead of a conversation, and vows each partner makes in silence.

**20 · Judgement — main task.** Lineage, family, inheritance and the ability to admit a mistake. The main test is to say aloud what has been carried inside for years — and not to bury what is still alive.

intro: What follows is an investigation. There are three kinds of evidence: arithmetic that does not match the personal chart; the books of Waite, Benebell Wen and Yuliana Lisovskaya; and Shakespeare's play Pericles, whose three movements run exactly in the order of this tail — a tournament and a wedding, fourteen years apart, a recognition in a temple.

faq.q: What does the 6-17-20 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: These are the couple's tasks in the order "entry — middle — main task". The entry is The Lovers: the wish to choose each other openly and with the blessing of their families. The middle is The Star: a road travelled on hope and generosity, where it is easy to replace a conversation with a beautiful picture. The main task is Judgement: lineage, family, admitting mistakes and the ability to tell one's story aloud.

faq.q: Why is the middle 17 if 6 + 20 gives 8?
faq.a: In a couple's chart the middle of the tail is not calculated from its ends. It is added up from the middles of two personal tails, most often 8 + 9 = 17. Reducing by digits keeps the remainder when divided by nine, so with ends of 6 and 20 the middle can only be 8 or 17 — and the digits of seventeen add up to the same eight.

faq.q: Does the 6-17-20 tail mean the couple will break up?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events, dates or break-ups, and it does not say who in the couple is right. It describes a task: not to live for years on a single hope and silent vows, but to check, to speak and to recognise each other anew.

faq.q: Does the 6-17-20 tail occur in a personal matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail equals the sum of its ends, and with ends of 6 and 20 the tail would be 6-8-20. The order 6-17-20 is possible only in a couple's chart. There are no other couple tails made of the numbers 6, 17 and 20 either.

faq.q: How can a couple find out whether they have the 6-17-20 tail?
faq.a: By calculating the compatibility matrix from the two birth dates: find each partner's personal tail, then add their matching points and reduce any sum above 22. In the example above, 14.09.1975 and 14.10.1976 give 18 + 15 → 6, 9 + 8 = 17 and 9 + 11 = 20.

report: In Shakespeare's Pericles a husband throws overboard, with his own hands, the coffin of a wife who is still alive — and then keeps faith with her for years. Fourteen years later he says to her: "O, come, be buried / A second time within these arms." Between these two gestures lies the whole 6-17-20 tail: choosing each other, a long life on a single hope, and recognition.

The tail's oddity shows in the numbers themselves. In a personal chart the middle is the sum of the ends, and here it would be 6 + 20 → 8, Justice. In a couple's chart the middle is added up from the middles of two personal tails, and it comes out as 17, The Star. The digits of seventeen hide the same eight: 1 + 7. **This couple has a measure, but it is hidden inside The Star.** Justice weighs: two pans, a tally, who owes whom how much. The Star does not weigh: its mottoes are "Waters of Life freely" and "Gifts of the Spirit". The 6-17-20 couple walks the middle of its road not by the tally but by hope — it gives, waits, trusts and does not check.

report.h3: A love that begins with someone else's story

report: The entry to the task is The Lovers: the shared wish to choose each other openly, beautifully and with the blessing of their own people. Pericles comes to the tournament for Princess Thaisa's hand in his dead father's rusty armour, which fishermen hauled out of the sea in their net. On his shield is "A wither'd branch, that's only green at top" and the motto "In this hope I live". This is how the couple's common language is born: **she tells his story for him.** But the entry sits on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. On reading her love letter, Pericles says: "'Tis the king's subtlety to have my life." Once burned, he sees a trap in the gift. Love is so wanted that it is frightening to believe in, and the two people's "yes" is spoken in the father's voice: the king stages a fit of anger and ends by declaring them man and wife.

report.h3: Two loyalties the other knows nothing about

On another shore the chest is opened, and the first words spoken over it are: "They were too rough / That threw her in the sea." Thaisa opens her eyes, recognises her husband's hand in the letter — and decides: "since King Pericles, / My wedded lord, I ne'er shall see again, / A vestal livery will I take me to, / And never more have joy." Pericles swears not to cut his hair, puts on sackcloth at his daughter's false tomb and for three months speaks to no one. The play's narrator remarks: "See how belief may suffer by foul show!"

In a couple's life it is a long stretch — work in another city, a child, a move, caring for parents — when each protects the other and keeps quiet about the hardest things. Both are faithful — and both are lonely.

Later Pericles will say to an unknown girl, not yet knowing she is his daughter: "thou look'st / Modest as Justice, and thou seem'st a palace / For the crown'd Truth to dwell in". Justice and Truth in one line — the eight and The Star. This couple's main danger is mistaking sleep for death: a quarrel for a break-up, a cooling for an ending, a pause for a grave. The play says it more precisely than any reading: "Death may usurp on nature many hours, / And yet the fire of life kindle again / The o'erpress'd spirits."

report.h3: The main task is to tell everything in front of everyone

report: The main task is Judgement, the card of lineage and family: relatives, traditions, inheritance, the influence of parents. It is read above all through what fails: admitting mistakes, saying what one feels, keeping boundaries — such couples tend to have either none at all or impenetrable ones.

It is his daughter who brings Pericles out of his silence. He recognises her step by step and at last says: "O, come hither, / Thou that beget'st him that did thee beget". Then he alone hears music, and the goddess tells him to reveal, "Before the people all", how he lost his wife at sea. In the temple he tells everything, and the high priestess faints: "Voice and favour!" **Thaisa recognises her husband by his story** — by the tempest, the birth and the death. Pericles still argues: "I threw her overboard with these very arms." A moment later: "O, come, be buried / A second time within these arms." The proof is the ring her father gave Pericles. And straight away comes the news of that father's death. Pericles answers: "Heavens make a star of him!"

For a couple with this tail, Judgement arrives as a summons: a moment comes when silence is no longer possible. The whole story has to be told — to each other and to their families — with the losses, the mistakes and whatever each has already buried alone.

report.h3: Hands that buried learn to embrace

report: Simple things change the script. Checking before burying: what was seen, and what was merely believed. Saying aloud what was sworn in silence: a silent vow is a picture the other cannot see, a spoken one is an agreement that can be discussed. Telling someone else's custom from one's own decision: relatives and traditions deserve respect, but decisions about the couple are made by the two. Marking the end of a hard time — Pericles had the hair that "this fourteen years no razor touch'd" trimmed for his daughter's wedding.

The strong 6-17-20 couple is the one that can tell its story to the end. **In it the storm becomes a chapter, not the finale.** Such partners recognise each other by voice and by story, and the past does not vanish — it becomes a story that can be told. In the temple Pericles tells the gods that their present kindness turns his past miseries into sport.
