items.title: Karmic tail 6-20-14 in compatibility: Romeo and Juliet's second sonnet
items.short: The first words Romeo and Juliet say to each other form a sonnet: fourteen lines for two voices, rhymed without either of them planning it. They start a second sonnet straight away and never finish it. The Nurse comes in: "Madam, your mother craves a word with you." That scene holds the whole of the couple's karmic tail 6-20-14: a love that speaks one language from the first minute, a family that walks into the room in mid-line, and a sense of measure the couple still has to learn.

sections.h2: A sonnet for two voices: The Lovers at the entry to the task
paragraphs: The sonnet is one of the strictest forms in English verse: fourteen lines, three quatrains and a couplet, a fixed rhyme scheme. Shakespeare gives the first quatrain to Romeo ("If I profane with my unworthiest hand / This holy shrine, the gentle fine is this"), the second to Juliet, the third they share between them, and the couplet they break in half: one line hers, one his. Two strangers, speaking for the first time, fall into the metre. Quotations from the play are given in Shakespeare's original throughout.

For point M this is an exact picture. In Lisovskaya's reading, the entry of a couple's tail is what the two strive for together: shared wishes, agreements and a "common language". With The Lovers in this place the common language is not built over years; it turns up on the first evening. Such couples recognise themselves in small things: from the first conversation they seem to have known each other for ages; one starts a sentence and the other finishes it; the private jokes arrive before the mutual friends.

The second thing written at the entry is a shared wish. On the balcony Juliet says it in full: "Deny thy father and refuse thy name", "What's in a name? that which we call a rose / By any other name would smell as sweet". The wish of a 6-20-14 couple at the entry is to be two, apart from surnames, from "that's how we do things in our family", from other people's expectations. But point M sits on the line of tasks, and in Lisovskaya the same wish can turn into resistance. The name the two want to throw away at the entry will come back to them, full size, in the middle of the tail.

The third is an agreement given in a single night. Juliet sees the danger herself: "It is too rash, too unadvised, too sudden; / Too like the lightning, which doth cease to be / Ere one can say 'It lightens.'" A few minutes later she sets the terms herself: "If that thy bent of love be honourable, / Thy purpose marriage, send me word to-morrow". The Lovers at the entry to the task are a love that signs before the contract has been read to the end.

And last: this love has no measure, and it is proud of it. "My bounty is as boundless as the sea, / My love as deep; the more I give to thee, / The more I have". At the wedding Juliet is plainer still: "They are but beggars that can count their worth; / But my true love is grown to such excess / I cannot sum up sum of half my wealth." The card of the entry refuses to count. The card of the main task, Temperance, is the art of counting. The whole tail lies between two words: "excess" and "measure".

Benebell Wen writes something about The Lovers that reads like a stage direction for the first scene. When the question is love, the card indicates "the beginnings of romance and, simultaneously, the beginnings of temptation", and "a strong feeling of paradise, at least in the beginning". Romeo and Juliet's first sonnet is written entirely in the words of a church: pilgrims, saints, a shrine, prayer. A 6-20-14 couple's common language at the entry is often the same: lofty, almost sacred, and without a single word yet about housework, money or relatives.

sections.h2: "Your mother craves a word with you": Judgement in the middle of the road
paragraphs: Lisovskaya's key to the twentieth energy in a couple is family and kin: parents, relatives, traditions, inheritance, the influence of the older generation on the union. She gives point N no meaning of its own; for her it simply adds to the main task. We read the middle as a road: what the couple goes through on its way from the wish at the entry to the task at the end. This is the product's reading, not a statement from the book. For the 6-20-14 tail the road runs through two families.

Shakespeare shows it relentlessly: every time the lovers speak to each other, the house interrupts. The second sonnet is cut off by the Nurse with a message from the mother. On the balcony the Nurse calls from inside three times, and three times Juliet answers "anon", without finishing what matters. Then she says the line that holds the whole downside of the middle: "Bondage is hoarse, and may not speak aloud; / Else would I tear the cave where Echo lies" — tear it with "repetition of my Romeo's name".

Judgement is named after the Last Judgement, and the Last Judgement begins with a trumpet: at its sound the dead rise. A trumpet does not whisper. The middle of the 6-20-14 tail demands the same: the union has to sound out loud, before both families. In Shakespeare it never does. The marriage stays a secret of the friar's cell, of two go-betweens — the Nurse and the friar — and of one night. Friar Laurence even has the right plan in his head: "Where thou shalt live, till we can find a time / To blaze your marriage, reconcile your friends, / Beg pardon of the prince, and call thee back". To announce, to reconcile, to call back — that is Judgement at its best: a summons that was answered. Not one point of the plan comes true.

When the family does come in, it comes in as a court. Juliet's father passes sentence the way it is passed in the downside of the twentieth energy: "Speak not, reply not, do not answer me" — and then: "Nor what is mine shall never do thee good". Lisovskaya's list for the downside of this energy describes the same scene almost word for word. Among the couple's difficulties: neither partner can say what they feel. Among its tasks: a union built on the parents' approval or arranged through relatives, and "unaccepted love", when two people love each other but cannot be together because of position or tradition. Among its money troubles: being disinherited. Count Paris, the match planned for Juliet, is a union arranged by the family. The secret marriage to Romeo is the unaccepted love. Both marriages at once are the whole middle of the tail.

The second image of the Last Judgement is the dead rising from their tombs. Shakespeare draws it literally. Juliet, holding the vial, pictures the family vault, "an ancient receptacle, / Where, for these many hundred years, the bones / Of all my buried ancestors are packed", and fears she will wake and "madly play with my forefather's joints". The play never once names the cause of the feud between the Montagues and the Capulets. The Prologue speaks only of an "ancient grudge", and old Montague asks: "Who set this ancient quarrel new abroach?" The past of two families rises from its graves by itself and without explanation. In an ordinary couple this is instantly recognisable: parents' habits, an old grievance of one family against the other, "we have never done it that way" — all of it comes up in the middle of the road, though neither of the two started it.

paragraphs.h3: What the couple's Judgement is made of

paragraphs: The number in the middle of a couple's tail is the sum of the middles of the two personal tails, not recalculated. In 6-20-14 couples neither partner brings Judgement: checking every date since 1900 found no such couple in which either partner has the 20 in their personal tail. The couple's Judgement is always made of two other cards:

Our reading: Shakespeare has all three main pairs. The power of a father whose care "day, night, hour, tide, time, work, play" was "to have her match'd", and the collapse of his house — The Emperor and The Tower. Friar Laurence's rite and the passion he secretly blesses — The Hierophant and The Devil. The prince's sentence and the forty-two hours Juliet spends between life and death — Justice and The Hanged Man. The family's court is made not of wicked people but of ordinary forces: power, tradition, law. What makes them dangerous is only that they meet a secret.

sections.h2: Poison and medicine in one flower: Temperance as the main task
paragraphs: The main point of a couple's tail is D. Lisovskaya reads it mostly through the downside: what is not working for the couple and what it has to learn. For Temperance her list of the couple's tasks includes haste, suppressed emotions, idealisation, dependence on other people's opinions and the wish to control, and among her recommendations are not to jump to conclusions about the partner, to learn to wait for the right moment to act, and to look for the golden mean instead of extremes. In Romeo and Juliet this card has its own voice, and it walks onto the stage with a basket of herbs.

Friar Laurence's first speech is a lecture on Temperance, though the word itself never appears. "The earth that's nature's mother is her tomb; / What is her burying grave that is her womb". And then, about the flower in his hand: "Within the infant rind of this small flower / Poison hath residence and medicine power: / For this, being smelt, with that part cheers each part; / Being tasted, slays all senses with the heart." One and the same substance is medicine or poison; measure decides. The forces that meet in a 6-20-14 couple work the same way: the love of the entry and the family of the middle are neither bad nor good in themselves. What decides is the proportion in which they are mixed. As soon as Romeo walks into the cell he hears from the friar a word of the same root: anyone up at that hour shows "a distemper'd head". Distemper literally means "wrong mixing", from the same Latin temperare as Temperance.

Three scenes later, at the wedding, Laurence states the tail's main task in full: "These violent delights have violent ends", and then, "Therefore love moderately; long love doth so; / Too swift arrives as tardy as too slow." The ending of the play runs exactly by this line. Romeo reaches the tomb too swiftly: he dies minutes before Juliet opens her eyes, and as she kisses him she says, "Thy lips are warm." Friar Laurence arrives too slowly, and his first words in the churchyard are: "how oft to-night / Have my old feet stumbled at graves!" The very friar who warned Romeo: "Wisely and slow; they stumble that run fast."

Everyone in Verona is in a hurry, not only the lovers — and that is an important clue. In the first act Juliet's father tells Paris: "Let two more summers wither in their pride, / Ere we may think her ripe to be a bride." In the third he already fixes the wedding for Thursday and asks himself: "do you like this haste?" Then, delighted by his daughter's apparent consent, he moves it to Wednesday — a day earlier. Because of that shift Juliet takes the potion a day before the friar planned, and his letter to Mantua has a day less to arrive. The letter will fail anyway: its messenger is held in the city because of the plague. Even Laurence hurries at the wedding: "Come, come with me, and we will make short work". Measure is the main task not of one partner, and not only of the two, but of the whole system of two houses.
Shakespeare lays out Lisovskaya's downside of Temperance scene by scene, as if he had read her list:

ul: **a hasty conclusion about the partner** — Romeo hears one sentence from his servant and in the same scene goes to buy poison; the servant begs, "I do beseech you, sir, have patience", and is too late;
**suppressed feelings** — "Speak not, reply not, do not answer me"; Juliet asks her father to "hear me with patience but to speak a word", and that word is never spoken;
**one partner shutting out the family's problems** — Juliet sends the Nurse away and says: "My dismal scene I needs must act alone";
**extremes instead of the middle** — Lady Capulet cuts her husband short: "You are too hot." Wen writes that Temperance comes to "cool what was too hot, heat up what was too cold".

paragraphs: The image worth remembering this play for, Shakespeare keeps for the very end. Juliet wakes and sees in Romeo's hand "a cup", and says: "O churl! drunk all, and left no friendly drop / To help me after?" The couple's main task in 6-20-14 is written in this line in reverse: **do not drink the cup alone**. A decision that concerns two is not taken alone and in one gulp. Why this is precisely Temperance's image shows on Waite's card — more on that below.

paragraphs.h3: The fourteenth line

paragraphs: Shakespeare opens the second act with a sonnet too, spoken by the Chorus. Its first lines are about a deathbed and an inheritance: "Now old desire doth in his death-bed lie, / And young affection gapes to be his heir". And the fourteenth, the last, runs: "Tempering extremities with extreme sweet". In line fourteen Shakespeare uses the verb of that very card, to temper, and at once shows the counterfeit: one extreme is damped with another. This is the downside of the main task. The Temperance of the 6-20-14 tail is not about sweetening the conflict of two houses with strong feeling; it is about mixing two waters in proportion.

Wen defines the card as "the fusion of two contrasting elements". Writing about work, she adds a thought that fits a couple too: "it isn't that new skills need to be learned, but rather that the Seeker need only reconcile his or her existing skills with the task at hand." A 6-20-14 couple does not need to become different people or give up its families. It needs to blend what each has already brought: two ways of celebrating, two attitudes to money, two styles of quarrelling and making up.

The numbers say the same. In half of 6-20-14 couples (50.9%) Temperance appears in none of the main points of the personal chart — for either partner. Neither of the two brings measure into this union; it appears only when they are together. And the couple's main task is the exact sum, with no folding, of the two personal karmic tasks, most often 4 and 10, 6 and 8, or 3 and 11. The couple's measure is assembled from two different tasks and belongs to neither of them.

sections.h2: Five days instead of nine months: a clue in the history of the plot
paragraphs: Shakespeare had a source: Arthur Brooke's poem The Tragicall Historye of Romeus and Juliet (1562). Its plot is almost the same, with two differences, and both lead to our tail. The poem's editor, J. J. Munro, worked it out in 1908: in Brooke the action stretches over more than nine months, while in Shakespeare it fits into five days — the lovers meet on a Sunday, die on the night of the fifth day, and the play ends on the morning of the sixth. In Brooke, after the secret wedding, the couple has "the summer of their bliss", which lasts "a month or twain"; in Shakespeare, one night. Munro says outright that this compression is the dramatist's own invention. And the second: Brooke's Juliet is sixteen, while Shakespeare's is not yet fourteen.

So the haste in this story was added by Shakespeare. The plot of two feuding families existed before him. He sped it up until time itself became the protagonist of the tragedy. Laurence says "too swift arrives as tardy as too slow", and the play becomes the proof of that line.

Brooke did something else: he judged. In his preface "To the Reader" he explains why the poem was written: to describe "a couple of unfortunate lovers", "neglecting the authority and advice of parents and friends; conferring their principal counsels with drunken gossips and superstitious friars", "abusing the honourable name of lawful marriage to cloak the shame of stolen contracts; finally by all means of unhonest life hasting to most unhappy death". This is Judgement's downside in its purest form: a verdict passed from outside, before the story has been told. Shakespeare lifted that verdict. In his Prologue it is not the children who are to blame but "their parents' strife", and at the end the prince spreads the blame over everyone: "Some shall be pardon'd, and some punished", and earlier, "all are punish'd".

The numbers in the play are coincidences, not clues: Shakespeare knew nothing of the destiny matrix. But they are amusing. In the first act the word "fourteen" is spoken six times, and all six times it is about Juliet's age; when the Nurse asks how long it is until the day she turns fourteen, the mother answers: "A fortnight and odd days." There are three sonnets, forms of exactly fourteen lines, in the play: the Prologue about the two households, the lovers' first exchange, and the Prologue to the second act. And on the night of the balcony Juliet, having agreed to send a messenger to Romeo at nine, sighs: "'tis twenty years till then."

sections.h2: Waite's cards: a trumpet over the tombs and two cups
paragraphs: This section is about the pictures in the classic Waite–Smith deck; the cards on our site differ in their details.

**The Lovers.** Waite calls VI "in all simplicity the card of human love, here exhibited as part of the way, the truth and the life". On the card a man and a woman stand beneath a winged figure, with two trees behind them. For the reversed card Waite gives "Failure, foolish designs". The plan with the sleeping potion, the letter and the flight to Mantua is just such a design, built by a loving heart and a clever friar.

**Judgement.** Waite describes it with a Latin formula: an angel sounds his trumpet "per sepulchra regionum", and the dead arise. It is a line from the medieval hymn Dies irae: "Tuba mirum spargens sonum / Per sepulchra regionum" — "the trumpet, scattering its wondrous sound through the tombs of every land". On the card the trumpet carries a banner with a cross. In the Capulet vault Romeo speaks of banners: "beauty's ensign yet / Is crimson in thy lips and in thy cheeks, / And death's pale flag is not advanced there." The friar had promised Juliet that with the potion "the roses in thy lips and cheeks shall fade / To paly ashes" for a time. Romeo sees the roses have returned and does not grasp what it means: he never received the letter explaining it. The sign of life over the coffin is right before his eyes, and he reads it as a sign of death. Wen calls this the downside of Judgement: misreading the evidence that lay in plain sight. And one more small thing from Waite: he mockingly reports that Court de Gébelin pointed out that "if the grave-stones were removed it could be accepted as a symbol of creation". The middle of the 6-20-14 tail works the same way: the very forces of the family that rise from the tombs become, once the gravestones are gone, the forces from which the couple builds its own life.

**Temperance.** The angel is "pouring the essences of life from chalice to chalice", with "one foot upon the earth and one upon waters". There is drink in both cups at once. In the vault Romeo does the opposite: "drunk all, and left no friendly drop". Waite writes that the card is called Temperance because, when its rule obtains in our consciousness, "it tempers, combines and harmonises the psychic and material natures". And he adds a sentence that ties the main task to the middle: under that rule "we know in our rational part something of whence we came and whither we are going". Whence we came — the two families of the tail's middle. Whither we are going — the couple's shared future. Temperance holds both cups. Even Waite's reversed meaning reads like a stage direction for Shakespeare: "sometimes even the priest who will marry the Querent", and next to it, "disunion, unfortunate combinations, competing interests".

sections.h2: The Sun or the Wheel of Fortune at the couple's centre
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's matrix is the atmosphere of the union, what lies between two people when nobody is watching. 6-20-14 couples have exactly two: The Sun (19) for 53.6% and The Wheel of Fortune (10) for 46.4%.

The Sun never appears at the centre of a personal chart, for any date. It is possible only for a couple, and here it is always made by personal centres 8 and 11 — Justice and Strength, the very two cards Waite swapped. Shakespeare named this atmosphere in one of the most famous lines of the play: "It is the east, and Juliet is the sun. / Arise, fair sun, and kill the envious moon". In Lisovskaya, The Sun at the centre means warmth, respect, family first, closeness. Its downside lists among the tasks an inability to talk about problems and holding feelings back — the same thing as in the downside of Judgement in the middle. A warm atmosphere easily becomes a reason to stay silent: it seems a pity to spoil the sun with a conversation about relatives. The play's last speech is about the same sun: "A glooming peace this morning with it brings; / The sun, for sorrow, will not show his head".

Couples with The Wheel of Fortune at the centre have a different atmosphere. Lisovskaya describes it as the feeling of a fated meeting, and in its downside as a habit of blaming fate and each other. Shakespeare has this too: the "star-cross'd lovers" of the Prologue, Romeo's cry after Tybalt's death, "O, I am fortune's fool!", and his "Then I defy you, stars!" in Mantua. The trap of this atmosphere is calling one's own haste fate.

If the order 6-20-14 stood in one person's personal chart, the centre could only be The Wheel: that personal tail belongs to 484 dates since 1900, and all of them have centre 10. The sunlit atmosphere comes with this tail only for two.

sections.h2: The couple's values: The Empress, The World or The Hanged Man
paragraphs: The couple's values are its spiritual purpose, one more answer to the question of why the two met. 6-20-14 couples have three cards here. The links with the play are our reading.

**The Empress — 49%.** Waite's list for her opens with "Fruitfulness, action, initiative, length of days". Then comes "the unknown, clandestine". And for the reversed card, "public rejoicings". One card holds the whole road Shakespeare's lovers never travelled: from a clandestine wedding to an open celebration and length of days. In Lisovskaya, The Empress means family and marriage, and among the tasks in her downside is getting out from under the influence of one's mother and relatives. The value of these couples is a home of their own that lasts long, not five days.

**The World — 29.8%.** Banished, Romeo tells the friar: "There is no world without Verona walls". The line carries the card's own name. The value of these couples is a world wider than the walls of one city and one family. Shakespeare's ending shows the same card's downside: the Montagues and the Capulets promise to raise statues of the lovers "in pure gold". Waite's reversed World is "Inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence". A love turned into a monument is The World without movement.

**The Hanged Man — 21.2%.** Waite's list for it includes the word "circumspection" — the very virtue Verona lacked. And the forty-two hours Juliet lies between life and death are the plot's image of The Hanged Man: a halt, a view from the other side, life on pause. The value of these couples is the ability to wait and see a situation differently before acting.

sections.h2: Worked example: 14.10.1975 and 14.04.1975
paragraphs: Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, folded down to 22. The couple's middle is not recalculated from the couple's entry and task; it too is the sum of the personal middles.
The first date has personal tail 21-4-10 and centre 11. The second has 12-16-4 and centre 8. This is the most common combination of personal tails among 6-20-14 couples: 54% of them.
The couple's centre is 11 + 8 = 19, The Sun. The couple's values are 21, The World. The image of the couple is 10, The Wheel of Fortune.

For this couple the tail's cards stand outside the tail as well. Temperance appears again at "What to create together" (10 + 4 = 14). The Lovers appear three more times: at "What fills" (6 + 18 = 24 → 6), at "Path to prosperity" (15 + 18 = 33 → 6) and at the point "Where it leaks", which on the relationship line is also "Success and the union" (9 + 15 = 24 → 6). Lisovskaya advises adding up repeated energies. Two Temperances give 14 + 14 = 28 → 10, and that is The Wheel of Fortune — exactly the card standing at the couple's "Image of the couple". Our reading: the measure these two are learning on the inside is seen from the outside as their "fate". There is only one Judgement in this matrix: the middle of the tail.

Other combinations of personal tails give the same couple tail less often: 15-5-8 + 9-15-6 for 29% of couples, 15-8-11 + 9-12-3 for 17%, the remaining two under 1%. In 70.4% of 6-20-14 couples neither partner has any of the three cards in their personal tail. A 6 in a personal tail appears only in the second combination (9-15-6) and in the rare fourth, and nobody has Judgement in a personal tail. This tail is almost never brought in by one of the two: the couple puts it together.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail: how to finish the second sonnet
paragraphs: Romeo and Juliet has a version in which everyone lives. In 1935 Prokofiev wrote a ballet to a scenario by Adrian Piotrovsky and Sergei Radlov with a happy ending: Friar Laurence reaches Romeo in time and explains that Juliet is asleep. Prokofiev put the choice simply: only living people can dance. The ending stirred controversy among Soviet cultural officials, and by the Leningrad premiere of 1940 the tragedy was back. The original score was found in a Moscow archive by the musicologist Simon Morrison, and in 2008 it was danced for the first time, in a production by Mark Morris. The difference between tragedy and happy ending in this story is a few minutes. That is Temperance: not a different love and not different parents, but a different timing.
The strong version of the 6-20-14 tail is a couple that lives the same play slowly. What changes the script:

ul: **Announce the union out loud.** Tell both families what matters in one's own words, not through go-betweens and not after the fact. A Nurse and a friar as the union's only witnesses are the downside of the middle.
**Reread night-time agreements by day.** What was decided on the first evening gets checked in a second, calm conversation.
**Do not judge the partner by a single sentence.** Especially a sentence passed on by a third person.
**Mix the two households in proportion.** Holidays, money, child-rearing, daily routine — agree how much comes from whose house, instead of seizing territory.
**Do not answer "speak not" with silence.** A suppressed feeling in this tail does not vanish; it waits for its vault.
**Do not drink the cup alone.** A decision that concerns two is made by two.

paragraphs: If pressure from relatives turns into threats or violence, it is no longer a task of the tail. Then help is needed: a local emergency number and a psychologist.

The Prologue promises that only the children's death will "bury their parents' strife": only the death of the young could reconcile the two houses. The task of a 6-20-14 couple is to do the same while alive, slowly and with measure. Friar Laurence named it the morning after the first meeting: "this alliance may so happy prove, / To turn your households' rancour to pure love." The strong version of the tail is a couple that finishes the second sonnet, broken off after its first quatrain, and finishes it with the mother already in the room.

ul: **Entry to the task — 6, The Lovers.** The couple enters its task through a shared language found at once, and through a shared wish: to be simply two people, without names and surnames.

**Middle of the task — 20, Judgement.** The road to the main task runs through two families: parents, house rules, old grudges and a past that rises from its graves. The union has to be announced out loud.
**Main task — 14, Temperance.** Learning measure: not deciding everything in one night, mixing two households in proportion, and not drinking the cup alone.

intro: The 6-20-14 tail falls to about one couple in 47, which makes it 15th of the 97 couple tails. It is neither a verdict nor a forecast. Shakespeare's play is this tail lived at a run, in five days, and that is exactly why it shows so clearly where a couple needs measure. What follows is an investigation: what is written in the cards themselves, in the books of Waite, Wen and Lisovskaya, in the history of the plot and in the numbers.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 6-20-14 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of the couple's matrix: entry to the task — 6, The Lovers; middle of the task — 20, Judgement; main task — 14, Temperance. The couple enters its task through a shared language and the wish to be two, passes through the meeting with two families, and learns the main thing: measure — not rushing, not deciding for both alone, and mixing two households in proportion.

faq.q: Is the 6-20-14 tail a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail describes a task, not an outcome. It contains no forecast of events or dates: it shows where the union will find things hard and what the two have to learn. Romeo and Juliet is this tail lived at a run; the same story also exists in Prokofiev's version, where the lovers stay alive.

faq.q: How does the couple's tail 6-20-14 differ from the personal tail 6-20-14?
faq.a: A personal tail is calculated from one date of birth, and its points mean different things. A couple's tail is the sum of two personal charts, and its points stand for the couple's shared wishes, the road through its trials and the union's main task. Even with the same numbers it is a different calculation with different roles. The personal tail 6-20-14 always has The Wheel of Fortune at the centre; a couple with this tail has The Sun there in half of cases.

faq.q: How is the 6-20-14 tail calculated in a couple's matrix?
faq.a: Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, folded down to 22: entry with entry, middle with middle, task with task. For example, 14.10.1975 and 14.04.1975 give 21 + 12 = 33 → 6, 4 + 16 = 20 and 10 + 4 = 14. The couple's middle is not recalculated from the two outer numbers.

faq.q: Is there a couple tail with 6, 20 and 14 in a different order?
faq.a: No. Among the 97 couple tails these three numbers occur only in the order 6-20-14. The entry of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, and of the three cards only the 6 meets that condition, while the order 6-14-20 is produced by no pair of dates.

faq.q: What should a 6-20-14 couple do if relatives oppose the union?
faq.a: The tail suggests neither war nor flight, but the slow road of the middle: announce the union directly, in one's own words, ride out the relatives' first reaction, and make no decisions at the peak of emotion. If the pressure turns into threats or violence, it is no longer a task of the tail: help is needed — a local emergency number and a psychologist.

report: The first words Romeo and Juliet say to each other form a sonnet: fourteen lines for two voices, rhymed without either of them planning it. They start a second sonnet straight away and never finish it. The Nurse comes in: "Madam, your mother craves a word with you." That scene holds the whole of the 6-20-14 tail. The Lovers at the entry: a shared language found at once. Judgement in the middle: a family that walks in mid-line. Temperance as the main task: the measure Shakespeare's lovers never had.

report.h3: A love that refuses to count

report: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together, its agreements and its common language. With The Lovers this language is not built over years: from the first conversation the two seem to have known each other for ages, one starts a sentence and the other finishes it. Juliet speaks the shared wish of the entry in full on the balcony: "Deny thy father and refuse thy name". To be simply two people, without surnames and other people's rules. But the entry sits on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance: the name the two throw away on the first evening will come back to them in the middle of the road.

This love has no measure, and it is proud of it. At the wedding Juliet says: "They are but beggars that can count their worth; / But my true love is grown to such excess / I cannot sum up sum of half my wealth." The card of the entry refuses to count. The card of the main task is the art of counting. **The whole tail lies between the words "excess" and "measure".**

report.h3: A trumpet that never sounded

report: The middle of the tail is the road the couple travels from wish to task. With Judgement that road runs through two families: parents, house rules, old grudges. Shakespeare shows it relentlessly: every time the lovers speak, the house interrupts. The second sonnet is cut off by a message from the mother; on the balcony the Nurse calls three times. And Juliet says the line that holds the whole downside of the middle: "Bondage is hoarse, and may not speak aloud".

Judgement is named after the Last Judgement, and the Last Judgement begins with a trumpet. A trumpet does not whisper. **The middle of the 6-20-14 tail demands that the union sound out loud before both families.** In Shakespeare it never does: the marriage stays a secret of the friar's cell, the Nurse and one night. The friar even had the right plan in his head — "To blaze your marriage, reconcile your friends". Not one point of it comes true. When the family does come in, it comes in as a court: "Speak not, reply not, do not answer me". And the play never names the cause of the feud between the two houses: the past rises from its graves by itself and without explanation, the way parents' habits and "we have never done it that way" rise up in any couple.

report.h3: Poison and medicine in one flower

report: Temperance's voice in the play is Friar Laurence with his basket of herbs. His first speech is about a flower in whose "infant rind" both "poison hath residence and medicine power": measure decides. At the wedding he states the tail's main task in full: "Therefore love moderately; long love doth so; / Too swift arrives as tardy as too slow."

The ending runs exactly by this line. Romeo reaches the tomb too swiftly and dies minutes before Juliet opens her eyes: "Thy lips are warm." The friar arrives too slowly, his "old feet stumbled at graves" — the very friar who had warned: "Wisely and slow; they stumble that run fast." Everyone hurries: Juliet's father first wanted to wait "two more summers", then fixed the wedding for Thursday, then moved it to Wednesday. **Measure is the task not of one partner but of the whole system of two houses.**

Shakespeare added this haste to the story himself. In Arthur Brooke's poem, his source, the action stretches over more than nine months; in Shakespeare, five days. Brooke judged the lovers: in his preface they go "hasting to most unhappy death". Shakespeare lifted the verdict and made time the protagonist.

report.h3: Do not drink the cup alone

report: Near the end Juliet sees in Romeo's hand "a cup": "O churl! drunk all, and left no friendly drop / To help me after?" Waite's Temperance angel is "pouring the essences of life from chalice to chalice", so that there is drink in both cups. Romeo drank it all. **A decision that concerns two is not taken alone and in one gulp.**

Shakespeare even named this card's counterfeit. The Prologue to the second act is a sonnet too, and its fourteenth line runs: "Tempering extremities with extreme sweet". The Temperance of a 6-20-14 couple is not about sweetening the conflict of two houses with strong feeling, but about mixing two waters in proportion: two ways of celebrating, two attitudes to money, two styles of quarrelling and making up.

The story also has a version in which everyone lives. In the first scenario of Prokofiev's ballet (1935), Friar Laurence reaches Romeo in time. The difference between tragedy and happy ending is a few minutes: not a different love and not different parents, but a different timing. What changes the script:

ul: announcing the union to both families in one's own words, not through go-betweens;
rereading night-time agreements by day;
not judging the partner by a single sentence, especially one passed on by a third person;
mixing the two households in proportion instead of seizing territory;
not drinking the cup alone.

report: If pressure from relatives turns into threats or violence, it is no longer a task of the tail: help is needed — a local emergency number or crisis line, and a psychologist. The strong version of the tail is a couple that finishes the second sonnet, and finishes it with the mother already in the room.

seo.title: Karmic tail 6 20 5 compatibility: Lovers, Judgement and Hierophant
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 20 5 compatibility: a choice made by two, the verdict of two families and whose law the couple lives by, read through Manzoni's The Betrothed.

items.title: The 6-20-5 karmic tail in compatibility: who marries the couple?
items.short: The 6-20-5 karmic tail in compatibility is made of The Lovers, Judgement and The Hierophant, and it hides a question couples rarely ask out loud: when does a union become real — when two people have said "yes" to each other, or when other people have accepted that "yes"? The cards answer in order. The couple enters its task through a choice of its own, passes through the judgement of two families and of its own conscience, and learns the main thing: to live by a law written by both of them — not by someone else's law, and not by the law of one of the two.

sections.h2: This wedding shall not happen: a novel about a couple nobody will marry
paragraphs: On the evening of 7 November 1628 a village priest, Don Abbondio, is walking home along a road above Lake Como, and at a fork two armed men of the local lord, Don Rodrigo, are waiting for him. They give him one sentence: "This wedding shall not happen — not tomorrow, not ever." The wedding is set for tomorrow. The groom is Renzo Tramaglino, a silk spinner; the bride is Lucia Mondella. Everything between them is settled, the families agree, the guests are invited.

Then come thirty-eight chapters. Renzo and Lucia try to marry on their own, flee their village and lose each other. Lucia is hidden in a convent and then abducted; Renzo is caught up in a bread riot in Milan and flees across the border of the duchy; then comes the plague of 1630. And in the last chapter the couple is married by the very same Don Abbondio. The novel came out in 1827, the final version in 1840, and Italian schools still teach it: modern literary Italian owes a great deal to this book.

The 6-20-5 tail reads in it as three acts. **Act one — The Lovers:** two people choose each other and try to become husband and wife by their own words. **Act two — Judgement:** separation, family, fear, a night in which the biggest decisions are made and unmade, and a plague after which each of them looks at themselves again. **Act three — The Hierophant:** who will join these two, and under what law — and what rule the couple will draw up for itself at the end.

sections.h2: The entry: "the priest has to be there, but he needn't be willing"
paragraphs: The plan comes not from the bride or the groom but from Lucia's mother, Agnese. She explains the old way: two reliable witnesses, and everything done in front of the priest. "The man says: Signor Curate, this is my wife; the woman says: Signor Curate, this is my husband" — and the marriage is done, "as holy as if the Pope himself had made it". And the key line: "You do need the priest, yes, but he needn't want to; it's enough that he's there."
Lucia is against it. "If a thing isn't right, it shouldn't be done," she says, and also: "I want to be your wife, but by the straight road, in the fear of God, at the altar."

This is the entry to the 6-20-5 couple's task, packed into one conversation. Both want the same thing — to marry. Where they part is the question of what makes a union a union. For Renzo two sentences, said about each other, are enough. Lucia needs the altar. And neither of them is wrong: The Lovers are a choice two people make, The Hierophant is the form that choice is looking for. For Lisovskaya, point M is what the couple strives for, its shared wishes and agreements. But it sits on the line of tasks, so the same wish can turn into resistance. In a 6-20-5 couple the resistance runs both ways: "we decided, and nobody tells us what to do" — and "until we are recognised, it isn't real".

That night they go to Don Abbondio anyway. Renzo manages to say: "Signor Curate, before these witnesses: this is my wife." Lucia gets out only "and this…" — the priest throws the cloth from his table over her head, the sexton rings the alarm bell, the whole village wakes up. The bride's words break off in the middle, and those were the very words that were meant to make them husband and wife.

Today that evening looks different. A couple quietly signs the register and presents the parents with a done deal, announces the wedding date as settled, moves in together without asking anyone. Sometimes this is freedom. Sometimes it is the same surprise wedding: a decision meant to shield the union from other people's judgement becomes the first thing other people judge.

In the couple's reading the same point M also appears in the sphere "Relationship and common language", under the caption "Common language". In every 6-20-5 couple The Lovers stand there too. In the novel the common language literally passes through go-betweens. Renzo and Agnese cannot read or write: a scribe writes Renzo's letters for him, and Agnese has them read to her by a cousin. Manzoni describes it with bitter precision: the scribe "partly understands, partly misunderstands", and afterwards the two sides argue about what the words mean. The downside of the Six at the entry often looks exactly like this: two people talking to each other through third parties — through mothers, friends, retellings, screenshots. Other downsides walk beside it: the picture of "we'll never be like them" that does not survive the first quarrel, and an insecurity that looks for reassurance now in jealousy, now in other people's approval.

sections.h2: A clue: who makes a marriage — the two, or the witness?
paragraphs: Agnese did not make anything up. In 1563 the Council of Trent, in the decree Tametsi, declared valid only a marriage contracted before the parish priest and two or three witnesses. But the law required the priest's presence, not his consent. People used this: they turned up at the priest's door without warning, spoke the words in front of him, and the marriage counted as made. In Italy this was called matrimonio a sorpresa, a marriage by surprise. The loophole was closed only by the decree Ne temere, issued in 1907 and in force from Easter 1908: from then on the priest himself had to ask for the couple's consent and receive it. Agnese's trick lived in church law for almost three and a half centuries.

Beneath this legal history lies a deeper question. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (§ 1623) says that in the Latin Church the spouses themselves perform the sacrament: "the spouses, as ministers of Christ's grace, mutually confer upon each other the sacrament of Matrimony by expressing their consent before the Church." The priest is a witness. In the Eastern rite it is different: the priest, having received the consent, crowns the bride and groom. The Russian word for a church wedding, venchanie, comes from venets, "crown", and keeps exactly this answer. Two churches answer differently the question of who makes a marriage a marriage.

A 6-20-5 couple carries both answers at once. The Lovers say: a union is made by the two. The Hierophant says: a union needs a form and a witness. And Judgement in the middle shows what happens between these two truths: the road from one to the other runs through the family, through fear and through a second look.

sections.h2: Don Abbondio's Latin: a rule spoken so as not to be understood
paragraphs: In the morning Renzo comes to be married, and Don Abbondio, sick with fear, spins excuses, then suddenly switches to Latin: "Error, conditio, votum, cognatio, crimen, Cultus disparitas, vis, ordo, ligamen, honestas, Si sis affinis…" It is a schoolroom rhyme of the canon lawyers, a list of impediments to marriage: error, unfree status, vow, kinship, crime, difference of faith, force, holy orders, an existing marriage, public propriety, affinity. Renzo cuts him short: "Are you making fun of me? What do I want with your Latin?" In Italian he does not say "Latin" but the mocking latinorum, and the word entered the language. The Treccani dictionary defines it as the Latin of someone who does not want to be understood — and, more broadly, as any speech made obscure on purpose.

There is a detail that is easy to miss. Don Abbondio stops at "Si sis affinis". After the Council of Trent the rhyme went on with the words "si clandestinus" — if the marriage is secret — and the next line began "Raptave sit mulier" — or if the woman has been abducted. The priest falls silent one word away from the plot. A few chapters later the couple will attempt a secret marriage, then Lucia will be abducted, and the "votum", the vow he did pronounce, will come back into the story from Lucia's own lips. A list read out to scare them off becomes this couple's road.

This is what the Hierophant of the main task looks like at its worst. Don Abbondio is no villain. Manzoni calls him an earthenware pot forced to travel in the company of iron ones, and later he himself admits to the cardinal: "Courage — a man can't give it to himself." Behind the Latin stands fear. In a couple, Latin sounds like this: "that's how it's done", "normal people do it this way", "in our family we don't do that", "Mum knows best". The rule is spoken not to explain but to end the conversation. One partner lectures: "you're doing it all wrong". The other quietly does it their own way. Someone runs the shared money "out of care", someone tries to remake the partner to their own family's standard. Lisovskaya lists all these stories on the downside of the Five; in life they seldom look like a quarrel over principles — more often like an argument about where to spend the holidays and who decides what to save for.

Benebell Wen describes the upright Hierophant as someone who "relies on another, a figure of authority or an institution, to define ... what is right and wrong"; the reversed Hierophant "defines right and wrong by self-determination". And she adds a line any couple with this tail can use: "We are not the keeper of others." Waite agrees with the formula that the Hierophant is "the power of the keys". Keys are sometimes needed to lock things. Don Abbondio uses them only that way. The novel will show their other use.

sections.h2: The middle: Judgement — the night when verdicts are passed
paragraphs: The middle of the novel coincides with the middle of the tail. After the failed night the couple separates. Lucia and her mother take refuge in a convent in Monza. Renzo goes to Milan, falls into a bread riot, makes a speech in the square, lingers too long at an inn, is arrested, is freed by the crowd and flees across the river Adda to a cousin, where he lives under another name. And Lucia, on Don Rodrigo's orders, is abducted and taken to the castle of a robber lord whom the novel simply calls the Unnamed.

That night two verdicts are passed in the castle. Lucia, alone in a locked room, vows to the Madonna to remain a virgin: "I renounce for ever that poor man of mine." She does not say Renzo's name. And the lord of the castle cannot sleep. Towards morning he hears distant festive bells, sees people in their best clothes hurrying down the valley, and asks himself: "What is all this joy? What have they all got to be glad about?" That same morning he will meet the cardinal and come out a different man. Waite writes of Judgement as a summons "heard and answered from within"; in the novel it sounds as ordinary church bells.

For Lisovskaya, the Twentieth energy is family and lineage. In the novel the family stands in every scene of the couple. Agnese invents the surprise wedding, goes everywhere with her daughter, has her letters read by a cousin. A cousin saves Renzo from destitution. The role of father to both is played by a Capuchin friar, Fra Cristoforo, whom everyone calls "Padre". For a 6-20-5 couple the middle of the road also runs through the families. The first holidays at the parents' and the question of whose traditions come first. A partner who decides nothing without Mum. A union the families approved — or didn't. A difference in age, standing or faith that the families notice before the lovers do. And at its best — what Lisovskaya puts on the strong side of the Twenty: the ability to forgive mistakes, support even when the partner is wrong, and a family that takes in a stranger as one of its own.

Then the plague comes. Renzo catches it and survives. In Milan a crowd takes him for an untore, an "anointer" — someone supposedly smearing the walls with contagion — and he escapes by jumping onto the cart of the gravediggers carrying away the dead. The false verdict of a crowd preoccupied Manzoni so much that he attached to the final edition of the novel the History of the Column of Infamy — about the real Milan trial of summer 1630, when the barber Gian Giacomo Mora and the sanitary commissioner Guglielmo Piazza were executed as anointers on a baseless accusation, and a column of shame was put up on the site of Mora's demolished house. Judgement has two faces: the summons that wakes, and the verdict passed too soon.

In the plague hospital Fra Cristoforo leads Renzo to the dying Don Rodrigo: "It may be punishment, it may be mercy." And Renzo, who more than once dreamed of getting even with Don Rodrigo, says: "I forgive him! I truly forgive him, I forgive him for ever!" In the middle of the book two "for evers" are spoken: Lucia renounces for ever, Renzo forgives for ever. One closes the road, the other opens it.

Here lies a clue in the numbers as well. In a personal destiny matrix the middle of the tail is the sum of its ends, and a person with ends 6 and 5 would get 11, Strength, in the middle. Couples can have that tail too — 6-11-5. But a couple's middle is built not from the ends but from the middles of the two partners, most often 3 + 17, and the result is 20 — a middle that a personal matrix with these ends never has. One person would travel from love to law through Strength, through endurance and will. Two travel through Judgement: through verdicts that are passed and then reviewed.

sections.h2: The main task: one person's vow for two
paragraphs: The plague hospital, chapter thirty-six. Renzo finds Lucia: she has survived the plague. And he hears from her: there is a vow; forget me. Renzo is in despair, and then proposes the thing that changes everything: "Promise Her that the first daughter we have, we'll name Maria." Fra Cristoforo hears them both out and tells Lucia the essential thing: she could not offer to God "the will of another, to whom she was already bound by her word". And "with the authority I have from the Church" he declares her free of the vow.

The whole main task of 6-20-5 is in this scene. A rule for two cannot be set by one. Lucia's vow is sincere, made in terror, at night, alone — and it disposes of Renzo's life without Renzo. In couples such vows sound ordinary: "we will never live near your mother", "there will be no children until I decide", "I'm never going to your family's again". One person makes them, in a moment of fear or hurt, and they bind both. The task of the Five in a couple, as Lisovskaya puts it, is to reach a shared decision about the family and to hold opposites in balance without lecturing. Renzo shows what this looks like: he does not argue with the vow, he turns it into a promise of two — "we have", "we'll name".

And here are the keys. The Gospel formula of the power of the keys: "whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven" (Matthew 16:19). To release someone from a vow is to loose a knot. Fra Cristoforo says the same in Italian: "sciolta" — untied. Don Abbondio used the keys to lock; Fra Cristoforo used them to untie. A couple's Hierophant can be either of the two.

And one more clue from the same canon-law vocabulary. Don Abbondio's list goes back to a rhyme by the canonist Tancred, written early in the thirteenth century, and that rhyme opens with the line "Ecclesiae vetitum, tempus, sponsalia, votum": betrothal and vow stand side by side in it. The title of the novel is the same word: I promessi sposi, "the betrothed". In the plague hospital the betrothal and the vow collide, and the betrothal wins — because two people made it.

The numbers say the same thing. The 6-20-5 tail is made from six combinations of the partners' personal tails, and not one of them contains The Hierophant or Judgement. Both cards are born only in the sum. This couple's main task belongs to neither partner alone — exactly what Fra Cristoforo explained to Lucia.

And the wedding happens "by the mouth of Don Abbondio". The form has not changed: the same priest, the same rite, the same church. What has changed is the couple's attitude to the form. Now it is a witness, not a wall.

sections.h2: "The juice of the whole story": the rule a couple draws up for itself
paragraphs: The last chapter. Renzo loves to tell what he has learned: "I've learned not to get mixed up in riots; I've learned not to make speeches in the square; I've learned not to lift my elbow too often; I've learned not to hold a door knocker when there are hotheads about." Every item is one of his own mistakes from the novel, named out loud. Lucia replies: "I didn't go looking for trouble — trouble came looking for me."

And then, Manzoni writes, "after long debating and searching together" they concluded: troubles often come because we have given them cause; but the most cautious and innocent conduct is not enough to keep them away; and when they come — "by our fault or without fault" — trust in God softens them and makes them useful for a better life. Manzoni calls this conclusion "the juice of the whole story".

Here is The Hierophant at its best. It is a teaching, but one written by two people, from their own experience, without hunting for the guilty one: "by our fault or without fault". Wen writes of Judgement: "An important life lesson will be learned." Of The Hierophant — that it is about "the pedagogy of wisdom". Renzo has both. His "I've learned" is the lesson of Judgement. And his decision that all his children will learn to read and write — "since this roguery exists, they might as well get the good of it too" — is the Hierophant's pedagogy: the Latin that locked the door in chapter two becomes a family tradition of literacy. Their first child is a girl, and she is named Maria. The vow is untied, the promise of two is kept. (This last link is our reading, not Manzoni's words.)

The strong version of the 6-20-5 tail looks like this: the couple has rules of its own, said in plain words; after every storm the two review them together; the families stand nearby as witnesses, not as judges.

sections.h2: How the 6-20-5 tail is formed: the calculation and the clues in the numbers
paragraphs: Each point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The example uses the dates 05.12.1975 and 05.11.1975.

The first partner has day 5, month 12, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Main task D = 5 + 12 + 22 = 39 → 12, centre = 5 + 12 + 22 + 12 = 51 → 6, entry M = 12 + 6 = 18, middle N = 18 + 12 = 30 → 3. Personal tail: 18-3-12. The second has day 5, month 11, year 22: D = 38 → 11, centre 49 → 13, M = 11 + 13 = 24 → 6, N = 6 + 11 = 17. Personal tail: 6-17-11.
Running through every date produced several facts, and each one is a clue.

ul: **The tail is rare, but not exceptional.** It occurs in roughly one couple in 232 (0.432%) and ranks 62nd of the 97 couple tails.

**It is usually built from the same tails.** In 85% of such couples one partner has the personal tail 18-3-12 and the other 6-17-11, as in the example. Another 5% are two 21-10-16 tails, 4% are 3-13-10 and 3-7-22; the remaining three combinations are rarer. None of the six contains 20 or 5: this couple's Judgement and Hierophant appear only in the sum.
**No single person has this tail.** In a personal matrix the entry M = main task D + centre. For the entry to be 6 when D = 5, the centre would have to be 1 or 19, and no person has such a centre.

**The Sun is almost always at the centre.** In 79.3% of such couples the centre of the chart is 19, The Sun; in 20.7% it is 10, The Wheel of Fortune. No date gives a personal matrix centre 19: this atmosphere exists only between two people.

**The couple's values.** In the spiritual purpose there is 3, The Empress, in 54.9%; 21, The World, in 24.7%; 12, The Hanged Man, in 20.4%. In the example it is The Empress. Our reading: the law this couple is heading towards matters not for its own sake but for the home it holds up — as in Manzoni, whose book ends not with a ceremony but with children.

paragraphs: The example also has coincidences of its own that other couples may not share: The Hierophant also stands at the point "What to create together", and The Lovers at the point "What fills". Couple tails made of the same three numbers in a different order do not exist.

sections.h2: What a couple with this tail can do
paragraphs: This is not a prediction and not a verdict: the tail does not say whether there will be a wedding, a church ceremony or a divorce. It shows the question through which the couple grows. The novel suggests a few moves.

ul: **Tell the couple's own rules from Latin.** It helps to say out loud, at least once, whose each rule in the house is: mine, yours, Mum's, ours. A rule that cannot be explained in plain words, only pronounced to end an argument, is Don Abbondio's Latin.

**Make no vows for two.** Every "never" and "not for anything" that affects both is decided by both. If one partner has already promised something in fear or hurt, the way out is Renzo's: turn one person's vow into an agreement of two.
**Family as witnesses, not judges.** Agnese's formula works here too: for the family "it's enough to be there". It can be invited, heard and respected, but the decision stays inside the couple.

**Review the verdicts.** This couple's quarrels often end in a verdict: "you always", "your family never". Judgement in the middle of the tail is a reminder that a verdict can be reviewed and that forgiveness is a decision too.

**After every storm, a "juice of the story" of its own.** One sentence drawn up together: what was learned, without hunting for the guilty one. Over time such sentences add up to the couple's own law — the very thing The Hierophant in the main task asks it to create.

paragraphs: Form is not the enemy. Lucia wanted the altar and was no less right than Renzo. A 6-20-5 couple does not choose between love and form: its task is to make the form its own.

sections.h2: Sources

ul: Alessandro Manzoni, The Betrothed (I promessi sposi), 1840 edition, chapters I, II, VI, VIII, XXI, XXV, XXVII, XXXIII, XXXV, XXXVI, XXXVIII; quotations in our own translation from the Italian. History of the Column of Infamy (Storia della colonna infame), appended to the 1840 edition.
Council of Trent, Session XXIV (1563), decree Tametsi; decree Ne temere (1907, in force from 1908).
Catechism of the Catholic Church, § 1623.
Catholic Encyclopedia, "Canonical Impediments": Tancred's rhyme and its post-Tridentine version.
Vocabolario Treccani, entry "latinorum".
A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911); Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015); Yuliana Lisovskaya, Matritsa sudby: sovmestimost (The Destiny Matrix: Compatibility, 2024).

**6 · The Lovers — "Entry to the task".** The couple is set in motion by a choice two people made: "we decided". This is their common language — and their first resistance: "nobody tells us what to do".

**20 · Judgement — "Middle of the task".** The road runs through the family line: parents, their blessing and their disapproval, old family scores. And through a review after which each partner owns their share of the mistakes.

**5 · The Hierophant — "Main task".** Whose rulebook the union lives by. At its worst: the elders' rules, lectures, one partner deciding for both. At its best: rules and traditions of the couple's own, drawn together from their own experience.

intro: This tail has a book in which it is lived out from beginning to end: Alessandro Manzoni's The Betrothed. The wedding is set on the first page and held on the last, and everything in between is laid out in the order of the three cards.

faq.q: What does the 6-20-5 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail with The Lovers as the entry to the task, Judgement in the middle and The Hierophant as the main task. The couple is joined by its own choice, passes through the judgement of the families and a review of its own decisions, and learns to live by a shared law written by both — not by the elders' rules and not by the will of one partner.

faq.q: Is the 6-20-5 tail bad for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail speaks about tasks, not about the fate of the union. For Lisovskaya the main task is read mostly through its downside: what the couple cannot yet manage. Here that means other people's rules, lectures and one partner deciding for both. The same card at its best gives the couple traditions of its own and the ability to agree without Latin.

faq.q: Does such a couple have to marry in church or register the marriage?
faq.a: No. The Hierophant does not prescribe a rite. It asks whose law the couple lives by. One couple needs an altar, another a signature at the registry office, a third an agreement with no witnesses at all. The task is for both to make this choice, not one partner or somebody's family.

faq.q: Why is the middle of the tail Judgement and not Strength?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle is the sum of the ends: 6 + 5 = 11, Strength. In a couple's matrix the middle is built from the middles of the two partners, most often 3 + 17 = 20. That is why this couple's road runs not through one person's endurance but through a review of two people's decisions.

faq.q: Can one person have the 6-20-5 tail?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the entry M = main task D + centre. For the entry to be 6 when D = 5, the centre would have to be 1 or 19, and no person has such a centre. The 6-20-5 tail exists only for a couple.

faq.q: Are there couple tails with the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. Running through every date gives not a single couple with any rearrangement of 6, 20 and 5. So the 6-20-5 tail has no twin with the same cards in different roles.

report: Renzo and Lucia's wedding was set on the first page of the novel and held on the last, and they were married by the very priest who had refused to marry them. Between those pages lie the thirty-eight chapters of Alessandro Manzoni's The Betrothed, and the 6-20-5 tail lies in them whole, in the order of its cards. The Lovers at the entry: two people chose each other themselves. Judgement in the middle: separation, family, a night of verdicts. The Hierophant in the main task: under whose law these two will become husband and wife — and under whose law they will live.

"This wedding shall not happen — not tomorrow, not ever," two armed men of the local lord tell the village priest Don Abbondio on the evening of 7 November 1628. The wedding is set for tomorrow, and everything between bride and groom is settled. The question of the novel, like the question of this tail, is not whether the two love each other. It is what makes a union a union: the "yes" two people say to each other, or the "yes" that others have accepted.

report.h3: The priest has to be there, but he needn't be willing

report: The way out is invented by Lucia's mother, Agnese. The old method: come to the priest with two witnesses and say in front of him "this is my wife" and "this is my husband". "You do need the priest, yes, but he needn't want to; it's enough that he's there." Lucia is against it: she wants to marry "by the straight road, in the fear of God, at the altar". They want the same thing and part on the main point — who makes a marriage. That night the attempt fails: Renzo gets his sentence out, but the priest throws the cloth from his table over Lucia's head, and her words break off at "and this…".

The argument is older than the novel. In the Latin Church the spouses themselves perform the sacrament of marriage, and the priest is their witness; in the Eastern rite the priest crowns the bride and groom. **A 6-20-5 couple carries both answers.** The Lovers say: a union is made by the two. The Hierophant says: a union needs a form and a witness. Hence two resistances at the entry: "we decided, and nobody tells us what to do" — and "until we are recognised, it isn't real". Today the surprise wedding looks like a quiet signature at the registry office and parents presented with a done deal. A decision meant to shield the union from other people's judgement becomes the first thing other people judge.

report.h3: Latin spoken so as not to be understood

report: As he refuses, Don Abbondio switches to Latin — to the canon lawyers' rhyme listing impediments to marriage: "Error, conditio, votum, cognatio, crimen…" Renzo cuts him short: "What do I want with your Latin?" In Italian he says the mocking latinorum, and the word entered the language as the Latin of someone who does not want to be understood. The priest falls silent at the word "affinis", and after the Council of Trent the rhyme went on with "si clandestinus" — if the marriage is secret — and "Raptave sit mulier" — if the woman has been abducted. A few chapters later there will be both a secret marriage and an abduction, and the "votum", the vow, will come back from Lucia's own lips. A list read out to scare them off becomes this couple's road.

This is **the Hierophant of the main task at its worst**. Behind Don Abbondio's Latin stands fear: "Courage — a man can't give it to himself," he later admits to the cardinal. In a couple, Latin sounds different: "that's how it's done", "in our family we don't do that", "Mum knows best". The rule is spoken not to explain but to end the conversation. One partner lectures, the other quietly does it their own way, someone runs the shared money "out of care".

The middle of the road is Judgement, and in this tail it runs through the family line. In the novel the family stands in every scene of the couple: the mother invents the secret wedding, Renzo hides with a cousin under another name, the role of father to both is played by a friar whom everyone calls "Padre". On the night of the abduction two verdicts are passed in one castle. Lucia makes a vow and renounces her groom "for ever", without saying his name, while the lord of the castle lies awake until dawn and that same morning becomes a different man. Then the plague comes, and in the plague hospital Renzo says of his enemy: "I forgive him for ever!" One "for ever" closes the road, the other opens it.

report.h3: One person's vow for two

report: In the plague hospital Lucia tells Renzo: there is a vow; forget me. The friar, Fra Cristoforo, explains to her what the whole main task of this tail comes down to: she could not offer to God "the will of another, to whom she was already bound by her word" — and he unties the vow. **A rule for two cannot be set by one.** In couples such vows are ordinary: "I'm never going to your family's again", "there will be no children until I decide". One person makes them, in fear or hurt, and they bind both.

Renzo does not argue with the vow. He turns it into a promise of two: "the first daughter we have, we'll name Maria." The numbers say what the friar said: **partners with this tail carry neither Judgement nor The Hierophant in their personal tails**; both cards are born only in the sum. The couple's main task belongs to neither partner alone. And in the end they are married by the same Don Abbondio. The form has not changed; the attitude to it has: now it is a witness, not a wall.

report.h3: The juice of the whole story

report: In the last chapter Renzo lists what he has learned: not to get mixed up in riots, not to make speeches in the square, not to lift his elbow too often. Lucia replies: "I didn't go looking for trouble — trouble came looking for me." And "after long debating and searching together" they draw up a shared rule: troubles often come because we have given them cause, but the most cautious and innocent conduct is not enough to keep them away; and when they come — "by our fault or without fault" — trust in God softens them and makes them useful for a better life. Manzoni calls this conclusion "the juice of the whole story".

This is **The Hierophant at its best**: a teaching written by two people, from their own experience and without hunting for the guilty one. Renzo decides that all his children will learn to read and write — the Latin that locked the door becomes a family tradition of literacy. Their first daughter is named Maria. The strong version of a couple with this tail is one whose rules are said in plain words and reviewed together after every storm, with the family standing nearby as a witness, not a judge.
