seo.title: Karmic tail 6 5 17 compatibility: two lights in one house
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 5 17 compatibility: The Lovers, The Hierophant and The Star — how love passes through other people's rules and learns to let two lights shine.

items.title: The 6-5-17 karmic tail in compatibility: love, rules and two lights under one roof
items.short: The 6-5-17 karmic tail in compatibility reads like a novel with the ending in the wrong place. First The Lovers, then The Hierophant — the card of the teacher, the rite and the rules — and only after them, in the place of the main task, The Star. An ordinary love story ends with the wedding. For a 6-5-17 couple the main thing begins the next morning: how two people, each with a light of their own, can live under one roof without putting each other out.

sections.h2: The main card comes after the wedding
paragraphs: The most famous love story in music is usually told up to a single date. On 12 September 1840, in the church at Schönefeld near Leipzig, Robert Schumann and Clara Wieck were married — after three years of secret engagement, her father's ban and a lawsuit against him. That is usually where the story stops.

What happened the next day is more interesting. On 13 September Clara turned twenty-one, and Robert gave his wife a notebook, making the first entry himself. It was to be a diary of everything that touched their household and married life, he wrote — "a book of the requests which we have to make of each other, when words fail to express our meaning", and a book of reconciliation if they ever misunderstood each other. They would write in turn, a week each, and hand the book over every Sunday. Anyone who wrote less than a page in a week would receive a punishment to be devised later. At the end came three words, as a talisman: industry, frugality and loyalty. Under his name Clara wrote: "Your wife, who is devoted to you with her whole heart, Clara."

The Lovers, The Hierophant, The Star — their story went in exactly that order. A declaration made in a language understood by one person in the hall. A book of rules — first her father's, then their own. And a question that neither the court nor the wedding could settle: how two talents can live in one house. In 1840 the public knew Clara Wieck's name better than her husband's: she had been playing at the Leipzig Gewandhaus since the age of nine, while many people took his originality for immaturity.

The Schumanns are not presented here as "a couple with the 6-5-17 tail": the calculator does not work with dates before 1900, and dates are not the point. Their story is a plot in which this tail can be read from the first card to the last — and from documents: letters, diaries, a court ruling.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: a declaration played in public
paragraphs: The point "Entry to the task" shows what the couple want together, what they have agreed on, which "common language" they speak. Lisovskaya places this point on the line of tasks, which makes it double-edged: the very wish that started the union can later turn into resistance.

For the Schumanns the common language was literally music. For a year and a half Clara's father kept them from seeing or writing to each other. On 13 August 1837 Clara gave a morning concert in Leipzig and put Robert's F-sharp minor sonata on the programme — the one published without his name, "dedicated to Clara by Florestan and Eusebius", his two invented alter egos. Later she explained: "I played because I knew no other means of showing you what was in my heart. I could not do it secretly, so I did it in public." That same day Robert wrote her his first letter in eighteen months: "Are you still firm and true?" — and asked for a simple "yes".

This is the six at the entry in its purest form: choosing each other against everyone, and a language in which something said before a full hall is heard by one person. Three years later, on the eve of the wedding, Robert gave his bride the song cycle Myrthen (Myrtles). Its first song, "Widmung" (Dedication), to a poem by Rückert, is about a love that makes a person dearer to himself: "That you love me makes me worthy in my own eyes… Lovingly you lift me above myself" (our translation). There is no better formula for the entry to this tail: love as the first mirror in which each of them likes what they see.

That mirror has a reverse side. If your love is what gives me my worth, then without it I am worth nothing, and the shared wish "for things between us to be beautiful, chosen, true" turns into a test. Lisovskaya describes the minus of the six as two kinds of couple: the noisy one, with jealousy and daily showdowns, and the closed one, where nobody speaks about what matters. In life these are often the same two people: in company they finish each other's sentences, at home every small thing becomes an exam on "do you still love me?". A common language easily becomes a field that has to be divided. That is exactly what happened to the Schumanns: the music that joined them became, in marriage, the subject of a quiet dispute — over silence, over hours at the piano, over the right to be heard.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: a book someone else writes for you
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya's book the middle of a couple's tail has no meaning of its own: it is an "addition" to the main task. In our reading it is the path — what the couple does and goes through between the wish and the task. For 6-5-17 the path runs through The Hierophant. Benebell Wen says the card "is about the pedagogy of wisdom and divine knowledge" and describes someone who "relies on another, a figure of authority or an institution, to define for the Seeker what is right and wrong".

The Schumanns had one Hierophant between them: Friedrich Wieck, Clara's father and the teacher of both. In 1830 Robert moved into his house as a pupil. Wieck taught his daughter from early childhood and kept her diary for her. The first page of her first diary bears, in her father's hand, the words: "My diary, begun by my Father, May 7 1827, and to be continued by Clara Josephine Wieck." The first volume is almost entirely his — written in her voice. In the autumn of 1828 nine-year-old Clara reports "herself" that her father has noticed again that she is "still lazy, careless, disorderly, obstinate, and disobedient". Her biographer Berthold Litzmann, who worked with all forty-seven volumes of her diaries, remarks that until the summer of 1838 they reflect "not her thoughts and opinions, but her father's".

Wen has a sentence about The Hierophant that describes Wieck completely: one may shield another person from knowledge with the best of intentions, but the result will be negative, because "We are not the keeper of others." In June 1836, on her father's orders, Clara sent Robert back all his letters. Then came the court: the couple asked for permission to marry without her father's consent. At the hearing on 18 December 1839 Wieck was so passionate that "the President of the court had to call him to order", and Clara wrote that the day had torn to pieces "the tender bond between father and child". The ruling came on 1 August 1840. The Hierophant in this story is doubled: one law held the couple back, another set them free.

The most interesting part is what became of the book of rules after the wedding. The couple did not abolish The Hierophant; they replaced him. The marriage diary is the father's diary again, except that now two people are supposed to write it, in turn. Litzmann calls Robert's rules the laws of an "order of matrimony" and notes straight away that "the lawgiver himself was the chief offender". Carried away by composing, Robert wrote less and less, then stopped, and after the Russian tour of 1844 the book stayed with Clara alone. A written dialogue about "questions which they hesitated to discuss by word of mouth in the bustle of the day" became a monologue again.

The teacher stayed in the house too — only now he was the husband. In the second week of their marriage they worked through The Well-Tempered Clavier together. Clara wrote: "Robert scolded me sharply; I had been doubling a passage in octaves, and so had added a fifth voice, incompatible with four-part writing." In the same book, where she praises Mendelssohn's fugues, Robert added an objection in the margin — the names of three other masters. A fifth voice that has no place in someone else's order is a coincidence, but an exact one: the middle of this tail is a five, and it is the five that tests whether the shared order has room for one more voice.

The quietest Hierophant lived in Clara herself. In November 1839 she wrote: "I once thought that I possessed creative talent, but I have given up this idea; a woman must not desire to compose — not one has been able to do it, and why should I expect to? It would be arrogance." Here "the way things are done" speaks in her own voice and calls the dream arrogance — the very word that opens Waite's list for The Star reversed.

In a 6-5-17 couple the middle of the task is easy to recognise without the nineteenth century. Whose family decides how to celebrate, how to spend, how to bring up children. A parent's voice that suddenly comes out of the partner's mouth. One partner teaching the other — how to dress, speak, work — and sure of knowing better. The constant glance at "what will people say". Among the tasks of the five Lisovskaya names interference from relatives, attempts to remake each other, and a shared decision about the family that has to be reached without lecturing. Rules are not the enemy in themselves: in its plus The Hierophant is trust, loyalty, shared views, the traditions a home rests on. The question of the middle is a different one — whose rules they are, and who holds the pen.

sections.h2: Main task: two pianos that may not sound at once
paragraphs: The couple's main task is read mostly through the minus: what does not work for the couple and what they have to learn. For 6-5-17 it is The Star — the card of a light that can be seen.

There were two grand pianos in the Schumanns' house, but they were not both allowed to be heard at the same time: the walls were thin, and Robert was composing. In January 1841 Clara wrote: "My playing is getting all behindhand, as is always the case when Robert is composing. I cannot find one little hour in the day for myself!" Robert saw it. At the end of 1840 he wrote: "For too often she has to buy my songs at the price of silence and invisibility." And he added: "So must it be in an artist's life, and if two people love each other, it is right enough."

Silence and invisibility is an exact definition of The Star in the minus: the light is there, but it has been put out so as not to disturb the other. Among this card's tasks Lisovskaya names the fear of fulfilling one's own dream and the habit of getting in the way of the partner's. In the Schumann house both halves lived under one roof, and without any ill will at all.

Then came the mirror scene. In February 1842, on tour, an invitation arrived from the court of Oldenburg — for Clara alone. She went and came back pleased. Robert wrote that "the thought of my undignified position in such cases, prevented me from feeling any pleasure". A few weeks later they parted: Clara went on to give concerts in Copenhagen, while he returned to their little daughter and his journal. On 14 March Robert left in their shared book the most honest lines of their marriage: "The separation has once more made me very conscious of my peculiar and difficult position. Am I to neglect my own talent, in order to serve you as a companion on your journeys? Have you allowed your talent to lie useless, or ought you to do so, because I am chained to the paper and to the piano? […] But what will the world say? Thus I torture myself with thinking. Yes, it is most necessary that we should find some means by which we can both utilise and develop our talents side by side."

The whole tail is in one paragraph. "A companion on your journeys" — the partner as an entourage. "What will the world say?" — The Hierophant who has moved into one's head. "Our talents side by side" — a formula for the main task that could not be bettered.

Even the biographer speaks in the voice of the tail's middle. Litzmann calls the young Clara Wieck a "girl-priestess" who, "like the star which shines out of a purer atmosphere, and in quiet silent beauty sheds its light abroad" — and at once explains that when such gifts are weighed against each other, the husband's creative power must outweigh the wife's interpretive one, and that Clara, as he puts it, realised "it was at once her highest duty and her highest happiness to lose herself in him". The Star and The Hierophant in a single paragraph: the light is acknowledged, but the order decides whom it is for.

The Star also has a quiet form of the minus — comparison. In 1846 Clara wrote a piano trio, her largest work. At the first rehearsal she was delighted: "There is nothing greater than the joy of composing something oneself, and then listening to it." And in the same entry: "of course it is only a woman's work, which is always lacking in force, and here and there in invention." A year later, when the printed copies came, she set her trio beside Robert's, and "after Robert's (D minor), it sounded effeminate and sentimental". In her recommendations to a couple with this tail Lisovskaya advises moving away from comparing oneself with one's partner and with other couples. Clara was not comparing her husband with someone else; she was comparing herself with her husband — and losing before the game began.

Her trio is Op. 17. Under the same number Robert has the Fantasie in C major; on 18 March 1838 he wrote to his bride that its first movement was "a deep lament for you". This is a coincidence, not evidence, but the picture is exact: under one number, a light directed at a beloved person, and one's own light, which its owner judged weak.

In a modern couple this card is recognised without any notes. One partner's success becomes the union's shop window, and the other turns into the "plus one" on the invitations. One is too shy to say what they want and backs this with sensible reasons; the other, meaning well, talks the partner out of a risky dream. The partner is compared with exes, with other couples, with who they "ought to be". The photos together are lovely — and not a word has been said about what matters. In her analysis of this tail Lisovskaya names what is perhaps the sorest point: much is left unsaid, especially about feelings, and resentment and jealousy grow out of what is unsaid. If mockery and pressure in the couple have become constant and it feels frightening to be near the partner, this is no longer a question for the cards: it calls for a psychologist, and if there is a threat, for a local emergency number or crisis line.

sections.h2: Clues in Waite: open to each other, the Hierophant's sign, the Star's two ewers
paragraphs: The pictures of the Waite–Smith deck lay out the same story in three frames. This is about his cards: the cards on the site are drawn differently in places.

On The Lovers Waite sees a man and a woman "unveiled before each other" and calls it "in all simplicity the card of human love". Before each other, not before the world: this is the couple's entry, their language for two.

The Hierophant gives a sign with his right hand which, according to Waite, is "distinguishing between the manifest and concealed part of doctrine". Two priestly ministers kneel before him. In the older decks, Waite recalls, the card was "called also Spiritual Father". The one who decides for two people what to show and what to hide — for the Schumanns this was a father in the most literal sense.

"For the majority of prepared minds," Waite writes, the figure of The Star "will appear as the type of Truth unveiled". From "unveiled before each other", through "what to show and what to hide", to a truth that is open to everyone — that is how the couple's openness changes along the tail. And one more detail: "She pours Water of Life from two great ewers, irrigating sea and land." One figure, two streams. In the language of a couple The Star demands what Robert wrote about: two channels for two talents, not one into which everything is poured.

Wen adds two sentences to this line. Her Hierophant is someone who relies on an authority to define what is right. Of The Star she writes: "Guidance is not coming from others, but rather it is coming from within." That is the whole path from the middle of the tail to its task: from someone else's voice deciding who gets to shine, to one's own. And one more of her observations: "Unlike Temperance, where there is a balancing between the levels of awareness, The Star card depicts a pouring out in one direction." For a couple this is a warning: if one only shines and the other only receives the light, The Star turns into service.

sections.h2: What the numbers record
paragraphs: The 6-5-17 tail is not rare: one couple in 28 has it (3.539%), fifth place among the 97 couple tails. A great many couples live through the plot "love — rules — star".

**Neither of the two owns the couple's Star.** The seventeen in the couple's main task is always an exact sum of the two personal karmic tasks, with no reduction: 7 + 10, 5 + 12, 6 + 11, 4 + 13, 8 + 9. So the partners in such a couple never have The Star as their personal karmic task, and in a personal tail it appears in only 16% of these couples — in the partner whose tail is 6-17-11, and even then in the middle. The main card of the tail is a shared light, assembled from two different tasks and belonging to neither. The question "which of us is the star" is put wrongly from the very start.

**The couple does not bring this story with them.** The tail is formed by eight combinations of personal tails. In almost half of the couples (45%) it is one and the same combination: 12-19-7 in one partner and 21-4-10 in the other; next come 15-20-5 + 18-3-12 (24%) and 18-6-6 + 6-17-11 (16%). In 50.5% of the couples neither partner has The Lovers, The Hierophant or The Star in their personal tail. The tail arises between the two — just as the Schumanns' question of "talents side by side" could not have arisen for either of them alone.

**The couple's rules are made of its love and its star.** The middle of a couple's tail is counted from the two personal middles, and it always comes out by reduction: the sum is 23, and 2 + 3 = 5 (most often 19 + 4). But this tail has another coincidence: the entry and the main task together also give the middle, 6 + 17 = 23 → 5. And in 16% of the couples The Hierophant is literally assembled from one partner's Lovers and the other's Star — the personal middles of the tails 18-6-6 and 6-17-11. Our reading: the couple's book of rules is written from what the two of them love and from what each of them wants to shine with.

**The couple is built like one person.** The centre of the couple's matrix in these couples is only ever of two kinds: The Tower (16) in 74% and The Chariot (7) in 26%. With both, the formula of a personal matrix holds — "main task plus centre gives the entry": 17 + 16 = 33 → 6 and 17 + 7 = 24 → 6. Arithmetically a 6-5-17 couple looks like one person with this tail, but it is read differently — more on that below.

**An example from the book.** The only couple on which Lisovskaya demonstrates a full consultation in her book is a couple with this tail. She writes it from the end to the beginning, 17-5-6, and calls it the couple's "karmic programme". That couple's centre is also The Tower, and the partners' personal tails are the same 12-19-7 and 21-4-10 as in the example below.

sections.h2: How the 6-5-17 tail comes about: an example with 05.07.1975 and 14.10.1975
paragraphs: Each point of a couple is the sum of the matching points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22: if the sum is greater than 22, its digits are added.

ul: **05.07.1975.** Day 5, month 7, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Karmic task 5 + 7 + 22 = 34 → 7, centre 5 + 7 + 22 + 7 = 41 → 5, entry to the tail 7 + 5 = 12, middle 7 + 12 = 19. Personal tail: 12-19-7.

paragraphs: The couple's tail is assembled from these two tails point by point:

The middle of a couple's tail is counted only from the two personal middles. Here the sum of the couple's outer numbers also gives 5, but that is a property of this particular tail, not a way of calculating.

In this couple The Star stands in two more places: in the point "What to create together" (birth months 7 + 10 = 17), which Lisovskaya reads only in the plus, and in the point "Parents together". One card is both the couple's main trial and what they are meant to create together. Lisovskaya suggests adding up repeats: 17 + 17 + 17 = 51 → 6 — The Lovers, the card of the entry. The couple's centre is 5 + 11 = 16, The Tower; "The couple's values" is 12, The Hanged Man.

sections.h2: The Tower, The Chariot and the couple's values
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's matrix is "The atmosphere inside the couple" — what happens between the two when nobody is watching. In three couples out of four with this tail it holds The Tower. In the plus Lisovskaya describes it as a union that goes through any trial hand in hand, in which the partners see and bring out each other's potential. In the minus — the collapse of an invented image of the partner. For a couple whose task is The Star, this is one theme seen from two sides: the image the other is made to fit will sooner or later fall, and it is well if what falls is the image and not the union. Her analysis of a couple with this tail and The Tower in the centre also contains an everyday warning: in such an atmosphere what is said in the heat of the moment stays in the memory for a long time. And in money matters The Tower in the plus means strict order by rules the two have invented together; the Schumanns' book with its laws is exactly such an attempt.

Every fourth couple has The Chariot in the centre. Then the atmosphere is movement: each has their own development outside the family, and what matters, according to Lisovskaya, is to walk side by side but each on their own road. Its minus is rivalry for leadership and the demand that the partner give up their goals for someone else's. Robert's question — whether he should neglect his own talent to become his wife's companion on her journeys — is The Chariot asking The Star.

"The couple's values" answer what the union exists for. In half of these couples (50.4%) it is The World — a whole in which everyone has a place; in the plus Lisovskaya writes of full acceptance of the partner and of rules created together, in the minus of re-educating the other to suit oneself and mocking their plans. In 28.6% it is The Hanged Man: in the plus, the care of one partner who does everything for the other; in the minus, sacrifice "because that's how it must be" and a lovely picture outside with heaviness inside. In 21% it is The Empress: home, children, creation, and yet each must have their own fulfilment, while the minus is contempt for the one who has "fallen behind" in growth. Our reading: in all three variants the couple's values come up against the same fork as the tail — a union is valuable when both grow in it, not one at the other's expense.

sections.h2: What changes the script
paragraphs: The tail is neither a verdict nor a forecast: it is a theme the couple will live through one way or another. The script is changed not by promises but by a few quite ordinary decisions.

ul: **Writing its own book of rules.** Not living by the statutes of the parental families and "the way things are done", but agreeing on its own: holidays, money, whose time is when. Lisovskaya advises a couple with a five to create their own holidays and places and to get on with relatives without letting them inside the couple's borders.

**Keeping a book of requests.** For the Schumanns it was a notebook for what is hard to say aloud. A 6-5-17 couple needs its own channel for what goes unsaid — a note, an agreed weekly conversation — as long as it is regular and for the two of them, not only after a quarrel.

**Giving the second piano its hours.** If there are two talents in the house, each needs their own hours and their own place, not the leftovers of someone else's schedule. "Our talents side by side" is a timetable, not a slogan.
**Not measuring oneself by the partner.** Comparison is the quiet form of The Star's minus. It was not a critic who called Clara's trio "only a woman's work", but a voice in her own head.
**Not putting out another's light out of care.** Talking a partner out of a dream "for their own good" is exactly the guardianship Wen means: we are not the keeper of others.

**Not living for show.** Lisovskaya advises this couple not to put their relationship on display and not to share everything intimate. A lovely picture for others is The Star's minus; a light that the two of them see is its plus.

sections.h2: The strong version: songs with no composer's name
paragraphs: The best thing the Schumanns did with this tail fits into one songbook. In the winter of 1841 Robert took up the idea of publishing songs together with his wife, chose poems from Rückert's Liebesfrühling (Love's Spring) for her, and wrote nine songs himself in a week. Clara could not get anywhere; she wrote: "I have no talent at all for composing." Then in the first week of June she wrote four songs and gave them to her husband for his birthday. Three went into the joint volume — twelve songs under a double number: Robert's Op. 37 and Clara's Op. 12. Which song was whose, the edition did not say. Robert gave Clara the first printed copy on 13 September 1841 — her birthday and the anniversary of their shared book. Rückert answered them both with a poem.

One of Clara's songs in this volume is "Liebst du um Schönheit", and its text reads like an exam on the tail's main task: "If thou lovest for beauty, O love not me: love the sun with her golden hair. If thou lovest for youth, O love not me: love the spring, which is young every year. If thou lovest for treasure, O love not me: love the mermaid, she has many pearls. If thou lovest for love, O yes, love me" (our translation). The Star in the minus is love for a picture: for beauty, youth, status, for how the couple looks from outside. The Star in the plus is when people love the one who shines, not the light.

Sixty years later Gustav Mahler set the same poem — for his wife Alma, whom shortly before their wedding he had asked to give up composing: there would be one composer in their house. One poem and two marriages. In one, the wife writes the song, and her name stands on the cover next to her husband's. In the other, the song is written for a wife who is not supposed to compose. Between them lies exactly the difference between a Hierophant the couple wrote themselves and a Hierophant handed to them.

The end of the Schumanns' story has nothing to do with the tail: the cards do not predict events. But one scene from the last years of their marriage is worth telling. At the end of 1853, on a triumphant tour of Holland, Clara played at a soirée given by a prince. Afterwards their host asked Robert: "Are you musical, too?" — and, hearing "yes", went on: "And what instrument do you play?" Litzmann writes that in earlier years this would have hurt Robert deeply, but now he only smiled. This is The Star lived to the end: a light that no longer needs to be recognised at court.

After Robert's death in 1856 Clara lived another forty years. She wrote almost nothing more for the public, but to the end of her life she played his music and prepared the complete edition of his works. She had done the same before: in May 1844 in Moscow, at a matinée for thirty or forty listeners, she played his piano quintet, which could not be performed at the big concert because of the size of the hall. A Star that pours water on her own land and on someone else's.

sections.h2: The 6-5-17 tail in a couple and in one person
paragraphs: The same three numbers also occur as a personal tail — on 818 dates since 1900. But that is a different calculation with different roles for the points: a personal tail describes one person's programme, a couple's tail describes a task that arises between two people and that neither of them has alone. Readings of one cannot be carried over to the other, even when the numbers are the same.

These numbers do not occur in any other order in a couple. A couple's entry to the task is always a multiple of three, so 17-5-6 or 5-6-17 will not appear in a couple's matrix. Lisovskaya's 17-5-6 is the same tail, read from the main task back to the entry.

sections.h2: Where the quotes come from

ul: The Schumanns' diaries and letters — from Berthold Litzmann's biography Clara Schumann: ein Künstlerleben nach Tagebüchern und Briefen (1902–1908), in Grace E. Hadow's English translation, Clara Schumann: An Artist's Life (1913).
Robert's letter of 18 March 1838 about the Fantasie — from the preface to the Henle edition.
A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot; Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015).
Yuliana Lisovskaya, Matritsa sudby: sovmestimost (Destiny Matrix: Compatibility, 2024).
Friedrich Rückert's poems "Widmung" and "Liebst du um Schönheit" — our translation.
**Entry to the task — 6, The Lovers.** Where the couple starts and what they want together: to choose each other and to speak a language only the two of them understand.
**Middle of the task — 5, The Hierophant.** How the couple moves on: through rules — first other people's (parents, teachers, "the way things are done"), then rules they write themselves.
**Main task — 17, The Star.** What the couple learns: to let both of them shine — without turning the union into a shop window, the partner into an audience, or one's own dream into a sacrifice.

faq.q: What does the 6-5-17 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's task, running from The Lovers through The Hierophant to The Star. The couple enters it by choosing each other and finding a common language, passes through rules — first other people's, then their own — and the main thing they learn is to let both of them shine: without a shop window, without comparisons, and without one going dark for the sake of the other.

faq.q: Is the 6-5-17 tail bad for a couple?
faq.a: No. It is neither a verdict nor a forecast but a theme of the union, and the tail is common — one couple in 28 has it. The main task is read through the minus because it shows where the couple has to learn; in the plus the same Star is a union in which each, beside the other, understands who they want to be.

faq.q: Which partner is responsible for The Star?
faq.a: Neither alone. The Star in the couple's main task is always an exact sum of the two personal karmic tasks, and neither partner has it as a personal task. There is no point looking for whose light it is: it appears only when the two are together.

faq.q: Why does Lisovskaya write this tail as 17-5-6?
faq.a: Lisovskaya writes a tail from the main task to the entry, while the site writes it from the entry to the main task. Her 17-5-6 and the site's 6-5-17 are one and the same couple tail. These numbers do not occur in any other order in a couple: a couple's entry to the task is always a multiple of three.

report: The 6-5-17 couple tail reads like a novel with the ending in the wrong place: the wedding sits in the middle. First The Lovers, then The Hierophant — the card of the teacher, the rite and the rules — and only after them, in the place of the main task, The Star. An ordinary love story ends at the altar. For this couple the main thing begins the next morning: how two people, each with a light of their own, can live under one roof without putting each other out.

The most famous couple in the history of music lived this plot, and left the documents. On 12 September 1840 Robert Schumann and Clara Wieck were married — after three years of secret engagement, her father's ban and a lawsuit against him. On 13 September Robert gave his wife a notebook, a diary for two: "a book of the requests which we have to make of each other, when words fail to express our meaning". They would write in turn, a week each. The Schumanns are not "a couple with the 6-5-17 tail" — theirs is a plot in which the tail can be read from the first card to the last.

report.h3: A declaration in a language for one

report: The entry to the task is The Lovers: what the couple want together and which common language they speak. For the Schumanns that language was music. When her father forbade them to meet, Clara put Robert's sonata on her concert programme and later explained: "I could not do it secretly, so I did it in public." Something said before a full hall was heard by one person.

Such an entry has a reverse side. The shared wish "for things between us to be beautiful, chosen, true" easily turns into a test, and the common language into a field that has to be divided. The music that joined the Schumanns became, in marriage, the subject of a quiet dispute — over silence, over hours at the piano, over the right to be heard.

report.h3: A book of rules in someone else's hand

report: The middle of the task is The Hierophant, the path through rules. The Schumanns' first Hierophant was Clara's father, the teacher of both. Her childhood diary opens in his hand: "My diary, begun by my Father, May 7 1827, and to be continued by Clara Josephine Wieck." He wrote almost the whole first volume in her voice: nine-year-old Clara reports "herself" that she is "still lazy, careless, disorderly, obstinate, and disobedient".

The marriage diary is the father's diary again, except that now two people are supposed to write it. That is the movement of the tail's middle: from someone else's book of rules to one's own. But the quietest Hierophant lived in Clara herself. In November 1839, before the wedding, she wrote: "a woman must not desire to compose — not one has been able to do it, and why should I expect to? It would be arrogance." Here "the way things are done" speaks in her own voice and calls the dream arrogance. In a modern couple this is a parent's voice coming out of the partner's mouth, one partner's habit of teaching the other, and the constant glance at "what will people say". **The question of the middle is not whether rules are needed, but who holds the pen.**

report.h3: Silence and invisibility

report: The main task is The Star, the card of a light that can be seen, and it is read through the minus. There were two grand pianos in the Schumanns' house, but they were not both allowed to be heard at the same time: Robert was composing. He himself wrote that too often his wife had **"to buy my songs at the price of silence and invisibility"**. The light is there, but it has been put out so as not to disturb the other — and without any ill will at all.

Then came the mirror scene: an invitation arrived from the court of Oldenburg for Clara alone, and Robert wrote of his "undignified position". A few weeks later, when Clara went on to give concerts in Copenhagen, he left the most honest lines of their marriage in the shared book, asking whether he was to neglect his own talent in order to serve as her companion on her journeys, and whether her talent was to lie useless because he was "chained to the paper and to the piano". "But what will the world say?" And the conclusion: **"it is most necessary that we should find some means by which we can both utilise and develop our talents side by side"**. The whole tail is in one paragraph: the partner as an entourage, The Hierophant in one's head, and a formula for the main task.

The Star also has a quiet form of the minus — comparison. Of her own trio Clara said: "of course it is only a woman's work", and beside Robert's trio it "sounded effeminate and sentimental". She was not comparing her husband with someone else; she was comparing herself with her husband — and losing before the game began. In a modern couple this card is recognised without any notes: one partner's success becomes the union's shop window, the other becomes the "plus one" on the invitations, the partner is talked out of a dream "for their own good", and not a word has been said about what matters, especially about feelings.

report.h3: A light that belongs to neither

report: The numbers of this tail hold a clue: the seventeen in the couple's main task is always assembled from the two personal karmic tasks, and neither partner has The Star as a personal task. **The question "which of us is the star" is put wrongly from the very start** — this light appears only when the two are together. In Waite the figure of The Star "pours Water of Life from two great ewers, irrigating sea and land": two channels for two talents, not one into which everything is poured. Wen writes of The Star: "Guidance is not coming from others, but rather it is coming from within."

The script is changed by quite ordinary decisions: writing one's own book of rules instead of the statutes of the parental families; keeping a book of requests for what goes unsaid, rather than waiting for a quarrel; giving the second piano its own hours, not the leftovers of someone else's schedule; not measuring oneself by the partner; not putting out another's dream out of care.

The best thing the Schumanns did with this tail is a joint songbook to poems by Rückert: twelve songs under a double number, and which song was whose, the edition did not say. One of Clara's songs is "Liebst du um Schönheit": "If thou lovest for beauty, O love not me… If thou lovest for love, O yes, love me." The Star in the minus is love for a picture. The Star in the plus is when people love the one who shines, not the light. Years later, on a tour of Holland, a prince who had heard Clara play asked Robert whether he was musical too, and on hearing "yes", which instrument he played. Robert only smiled. This is The Star lived to the end: a light that no longer needs to be recognised at court.

seo.title: Karmic tail 6 5 8 compatibility: love, form and a fair account
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 5 8 compatibility: The Lovers at the entry, The Hierophant in the middle, Justice as the main task — the couple's story told through Beaumarchais.

items.title: The 6-5-8 karmic tail in compatibility: The Lovers, The Hierophant and Justice
items.short: In one person's chart, a tail that runs from The Lovers to Justice always has 14, Temperance, in the middle. A couple has 5 there instead — The Hierophant, the card of rites, rules and other people's "that's how it's done". The 6-5-8 karmic tail in compatibility describes the road of two people who chose each other for love: through the form of their union — marriage, families, roles — to the main task, a fair account between the two of them.

sections.h2: Three plays about one couple
paragraphs: Almost everyone knows one of them — The Marriage of Figaro, or Mozart's opera Le nozze di Figaro (1786). But for Beaumarchais it is the middle part of a trilogy about Count Almaviva and his wife Rosine.

The Barber of Seville, or The Useless Precaution (1775): the young Count carries Rosine off from under her guardian's lock and marries her for love. The Mad Day, or The Marriage of Figaro (1784): the marriage is three years old, the Count has cooled towards his wife, and the wedding of his servants Figaro and Suzanne falls apart all day long — right up to a court case. The Guilty Mother, or The Other Tartuffe (1792): twenty years have passed, each of the spouses carries an old fault, and the family has to decide what to do with it.

The actors proposed playing the three pieces on three evenings in a row, as "the whole novel of the Almaviva family", and Beaumarchais approved. In the preface to the third play he explains the plan: on the first day the audience laughed at the Count's "turbulent youth", on the second at "the faults of his manhood", on the third it will see "the picture of his old age". And he adds a sentence worth remembering. Had the drama shown the faults themselves rather than their consequences twenty years on, it would have been called not The Guilty Mother but The Unfaithful Wife, or **The Guilty Spouses**.

The guilty spouses — plural. Love, marriage, a trial — and at the end a guilt that turns out to be shared. That is the 6-5-8 tail, read in order. Matching the trilogy to the cards is our reading; the plot, the court scene and every line quoted below come from Beaumarchais's text (translations from the French are ours).

How far these plays touched the established order we know from a witness. According to the memoirs of Madame Campan, Louis XVI, after hearing The Marriage of Figaro read aloud, said that the Bastille would have to be destroyed before the play could be allowed on stage. It opened all the same, in 1784.

sections.h2: Why the middle is The Hierophant and not Temperance
paragraphs: In a personal matrix the karmic tail follows one formula: the middle equals the entry plus the main task. For 6 and 8 that is 14, Temperance. So nobody has a personal 6-5-8 tail.

In the couple's matrix every point is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The couple's middle is not worked out from the two ends: it is the sum of the two personal middles. Running every date shows that for 6-5-8 couples this sum always goes past 22: in 65% of cases it is 32, in 35% it is 23. Both reduce to 5. Exactly 14 never comes out.

Add up the digits of 14 and you get 5. The couple gets the same Temperance, only spilled over the brim. The Latin temperantia comes from temperare, "to mix in due measure", and in one person the middle of the tail works just like that: he or she blends two sides within. Two people cannot do it that way: between them they need a vessel on the outside — an agreement, a rite, a shared form that both accept. That is The Hierophant. The reading is ours; the arithmetic is the site's engine.

The two ends of the tail, meanwhile, behave as they would in one person. In a personal matrix the entry equals the main task plus the centre. In 98.3% of 6-5-8 couples the centre is The Tower, and 8 + 16 = 24 → 6: the formula holds. Such a couple looks like one person with The Tower in the centre, different only in the middle.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: "to be loved for oneself"
paragraphs: The Barber of Seville opens with the Count hiding under a false name. He calls himself Lindor, a poor bachelor of arts, and stands under Rosine's window because he is tired of conquests "that self-interest, convenience or vanity keep putting in our way". And he says: "How sweet it is to be loved for oneself!"

This is the formula of the entry into the 6-5-8 tail. In Lisovskaya, point M is what the couple strives for, its shared wishes and its "common language". Here the common language is the language of choice: we found each other ourselves, nobody arranged it, we are not like everyone else. You can hear it in how the couple tells the story of how they met, how they guard their private words and rituals, how they defend their right to decide without advisers.

Wen writes of The Lovers that at the start partners have a strong feeling of paradise, but "the feeling of paradise may be evanescent if caution is not observed". Beaumarchais shows how quickly paradise runs into paperwork. At the end of The Barber the notary arrives with two marriage contracts at once: one for the Count and Rosine, the other for her guardian Bartholo and the same Rosine. "The young ladies must be two sisters with the same name," the notary supposes. The contract that gets signed is the one in which Rosine is chosen. Love decides which paper becomes a marriage — but a paper is signed all the same. The entry leads into form.

Point M stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish can turn into resistance. In the second play the Count, who once asked to be loved "for himself", explains one night in the garden to his disguised wife (he thinks she is Suzanne) what he looks for elsewhere: "less sameness… now and then a refusal". The wish to choose and be chosen again does not sit easily with what has already been decided. Hence jealousy without love. The Countess throws it at her husband: "Did I unite myself with you to be forever given over to neglect and jealousy — which you alone manage to combine?" Lisovskaya lists among the tasks of the 6 the insecurity from which jealousy and control grow. The Count locks the doors of his wife's rooms and takes the key, while on the same day he arranges a meeting with her maid.

Figaro and Suzanne have the same entry, only a merry one. The play opens with Figaro measuring the floor of their future room with a measuring rod — "nineteen feet by twenty-six" — while Suzanne, at the mirror, pins to her hair the little spray of orange blossom "called the bride's hat". The two are building something of their own. And the first shadow falls at once: the room, the bed and even the dowry are gifts from the Count. The room lies exactly midway between the Count's apartments and the Countess's. Suzanne refuses it and explains to her bridegroom where such generosity comes from: "Did you think, my good boy, that this dowry was for the beaux yeux of your merit?"

sections.h2: Middle of the task: "I am no longer that Rosine"
paragraphs: Three years after the escape from under the lock, the Count says to his disguised wife a sentence that holds the whole move from the 6 to the 5: "I love her very much; but three years of union make marriage so respectable!" Love has become respectable — respected, and far away.

In the second act the Countess answers him herself. In the heat of a quarrel the Count calls her by her name: "Rosine!…" — and hears: "I am no longer that Rosine you pursued so hard! I am the poor Countess Almaviva, the sad, forsaken wife you no longer love." The name under which she was chosen is hidden by a title. This is The Hierophant in the middle of the road: the two begin to live in roles — wife, husband, mistress of the house, head of the family — and the role speaks in place of the person.

Waite sets The Hierophant apart from nature. He belongs to "the world of institution as distinct from that of Nature" and expresses doctrine "when it has passed into the utmost rigidity of expression". In The Marriage of Figaro the institution rules every step. Servants cannot marry without their lord. The old droit du seigneur the Count abolished in public at his own wedding, and now he wants to buy it back from Suzanne in secret. He puts it himself like this: abolishing a shameful right is "only the payment of a debt to decency". Even about love the Count talks in the language of debts, and that is the bridge to the last card.

The other side of The Hierophant is families. Lisovskaya lists among the tasks of the 5 interference from relatives, even in the choice of a partner, and conflict with the partner's family. Beaumarchais takes this to farce. Marceline tries to stop Figaro's wedding through the court — and turns out to be his mother. Wen writes of The Lovers reversed: "meddling from an in-law, relative". Here the meddler is his own mother, who does not yet know it.

Suzanne's uncle, the gardener Antonio, refuses to give his niece "to one who is nobody's child" and lays down the order: in family weddings the parents' wedding goes first. The judge Brid'oison, stammering, answers him with the key line of this card: "Can such a th-thing be, you fool? One is al-always somebody's child." Marceline asks her newly found son: "Did nature never tell you so, a thousand times?" — "Never." Nature is silent; the institution speaks. Figaro sums it up: "All the fools of Andalusia, I do believe, have been let loose against my poor marriage!"

Beaumarchais shows the strength of the 5 as well. In the first act Figaro brings the peasants to thank the Count for abolishing the right and asks him to place on Suzanne, before everyone, the white bridal headdress, "symbol of the purity of your intentions", and to "adopt this ceremony for all marriages". A rite performed before witnesses binds the Count by his own word. "I'm caught," the Count says aside, and postpones the ceremony. This is The Hierophant at its best: a public form holds a promise where feeling alone is not enough.

In the middle of the tail the couple passes exactly here — between the rite that holds the word and the role that takes away the name. This is our reading of point N: Lisovskaya gives it no meaning of its own, it is an "addition" to the main task.

sections.h2: Main task: "and" or "or"
paragraphs: The third act of The Marriage of Figaro is a court hearing, and here the tail reaches its main point. Long ago Figaro borrowed two thousand piastres from Marceline and gave her a written promise. It is read out in court: "…which sum I shall repay her on demand, in this castle, and I shall marry her by way of acknowledgement." Figaro objects: the paper says not "and" but "or". Repay the money — or marry.

The argument is conducted in earnest. Bartholo, counsel for the plaintiff, insists on "the copulative conjunction AND", Figaro on "the alternative conjunction OR". The clerk takes the paper and reads it himself: "AND… OR… AND… OR… The word is so badly written… there's a blot." Then they argue over a comma: "No comma." — "There is one." — "No comma, gentlemen." — "There was one." The fate of a marriage hangs on a conjunction, a blot and a comma.

This is more than a comedy of pettifogging. **"And" or "or" is the central question of Justice for a 6-5-8 couple.** Do love and obligation go together — or does one stand in for the other? Can a debt be paid off with a marriage? Figaro asks whether a man who marries must also pay. "Yes: we marry with separate property," Bartholo replies. "And we with separate persons, since marriage is not a receipt."

The chief task of the 8 in Lisovskaya is to own one's guilt instead of blaming everyone; next to it stand broken promises and debts. Beaumarchais's court shows what happens when this task goes unsolved. The verdict is given by the Count himself: he judges the servant whose bride he wants to take, and rules — pay the two thousand piastres or marry the plaintiff "this very day". "I've won!" Figaro manages to rejoice. "I've lost." And the Count says aside: "At least I am avenged — that's a relief." Among the meanings of Justice reversed Waite names "bias"; the Count shows it in pure form — a judge in his own case.

The voice of the card itself in this scene belongs to Marceline and Figaro. Marceline, reproached all act long for the sins of her youth, tells the judges: "A man who judges us severely here has perhaps ruined a dozen unfortunate girls in his time!" Figaro adds: "The guiltiest are the least generous; that's the rule."

Then comes the moment that makes the act worth reading to the end. Figaro declares that he is a gentleman and cannot marry without the consent of his noble parents, shows a mark on his arm — and Marceline recognises her lost son. Bartholo turns out to be the father. "It's clear: he won't m-marry her," the judge concludes. And Marceline hands Figaro that very paper: "Take back your note — it is yours, it is your dowry."

**The IOU that in the morning could have wrecked the wedding becomes a wedding gift by evening.** The words on the paper are the same. Only one thing has changed: what the people are to each other — parties to a lawsuit, or family. This is what Justice at its best looks like for a 6-5-8 couple: the same account, the same debts and promises, but kept by one's own people, not by opponents.

sections.h2: The judge asks for forgiveness
paragraphs: The fifth act ends with a scene that opera-goers know from two words of Mozart. At night in the garden the Count catches, as he believes, his wife at a rendezvous. He drags the "faithless woman" out before witnesses; one by one everybody kneels and begs for mercy, and the Count answers: "No, no… Not if there were a hundred of you!" Then the real Countess steps out of the other pavilion and kneels too: "At least I shall make up the number."

The Count realises he has spent the whole evening courting his own wife in Suzanne's dress, and pleads: "Only a very generous pardon…" The Countess answers with a line that holds both her character and the whole of the 8: "In my place you would say 'No, no'; and I, for the third time today, grant it without condition." Mozart and da Ponte compress this into "Contessa, perdono" — "Countess, forgive me" — and the reply "Più docile io sono, e dico di sì": "I am gentler, and I say yes."

Back in the second act the Countess had set a condition that is the very measure of Justice: "You ask for yourself a pardon you refuse to others… If ever I agreed to forgive, I would insist that the amnesty be general." One measure for oneself and for the other. The Count lives by a double measure. In the night scene he explains to "Suzanne" that wives must know how to keep their husbands. "So they owe everything?" — "And the man nothing." Among the meanings of Justice reversed Wen names "chauvinism", and here it is in one exchange: an account in which one side owes everything and the other nothing. The gender here is a mark of the eighteenth century, not a rule of the card: in a couple either partner can keep a double measure.

Before the closing songs the Countess hands out the gifts the Count gave the false Suzanne that night in payment for "the right I no longer have": the purse to Figaro, the diamond to Suzanne. "Each shall have what belongs to them." This is almost word for word the ancient definition of justice: to give each their due. And Figaro, who caught the slap meant for the page, grumbles: "That's how the great dispense justice!"

sections.h2: Twenty years later: guilt for two
paragraphs: In The Guilty Mother twenty years have passed. The Countess has a grown son, Léon, and his father is not the Count. The Count has a goddaughter and ward, Florestine, who is in fact his daughter. Each keeps an old fault, and a third person knows both — Bégearss, the friend of the house whom the whole family trusts. In the preface Beaumarchais calls him "the Tartuffe of probity": Molière's Tartuffe dressed up in religion, this one in decency.

Bégearss is a dark Hierophant passing himself off as Justice. A man of "the proper way", through whom the family judges itself, and who profits from the scales never balancing. He frightens the young people into believing they are brother and sister — and very nearly marries Florestine himself.

The resolution is the most exact scene of the 6-5-8 tail in the whole trilogy. When Bégearss is unmasked, the Countess holds out her hand to her husband and asks: "Almaviva! Isn't it true that she is my daughter?" The Count answers: "And he is my son; here are our two children." **Two faults go onto the two pans of the scales at the same moment, and instead of a verdict there is one family.** Justice here is not punishment but balance: nobody weighs the other's fault without setting their own beside it.

In his last long speech the Count says to his wife and children: "There comes an age when decent people forgive each other their wrongs, their old weaknesses… Rosine (it is the name your husband gives back to you), let us go and rest from the labours of the day." The name that the title hid in the second play comes back in the third. The entry — Rosine at the window. The middle — the Countess Almaviva. The main task — Rosine again, but after a fair account.

In the same preface Beaumarchais writes that he composed this drama "with the cool head of a man and the burning heart of a woman". Among the strengths of the 8 in a couple Lisovskaya names "a cool head and a warm heart". The formula is nearly the same, with one difference: in Beaumarchais both halves are held by one person, not shared out between two by role.

sections.h2: Clues in the numbers: neither partner has Justice
paragraphs: The 6-5-8 tail occurs in about one couple in 47 (2.144%) and ranks 16th of the 97 possible couple's tails. It is built from eight combinations of the partners' personal tails, and running every date turns up three clues in them.

**Neither partner has Justice in their personal tail.** In none of the eight combinations does the 8 stand on any point of a personal tail. The couple's main task is always made of two other cards: 5 + 3 (40% of couples), 5 + 21 = 26 (25%), 4 + 4 (21%), and more rarely 15 + 11, 12 + 14, 16 + 19. Nobody brings Justice in — it appears only as a shared account. Just as in The Guilty Mother, where the scales balance only when both faults are on them.

**The partners carry the other two cards themselves, but not in the tail.** In two couples out of three (65%) one partner has the personal tail 15-20-5, and The Hierophant is their own karmic task. In these couples the other partner has The Lovers in the centre of the personal matrix; across all 6-5-8 couples that is 69%. The layout resembles the trilogy: one has choice and feeling in the centre of the chart, the other has form and rule as a life task. This is not a sharing-out of blame or of roles by gender, but the themes each brings into the union.

**In one couple in five the partners are mirror images.** In 21% of couples both have the same personal tail, 12-16-4, and both have Justice in the centre of the personal matrix. Two Justices in the centres give the couple The Tower (8 + 8 = 16), and the couple's tail is the personal one doubled: 12 + 12 → 6, 16 + 16 → 5, 4 + 4 = 8.
And finally: in a quarter of couples (25.4%) neither partner has a 6, a 5 or an 8 in their personal tail. This tail is not handed to the couple by one of the two — the two make it together.

sections.h2: The Tower in the centre: a mad day
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's matrix is the atmosphere inside the union, what happens between the two when nobody is watching. In 6-5-8 couples it is almost always The Tower (98.3%), occasionally The Chariot (1.7%).

The other title of The Marriage of Figaro is The Mad Day, and it is a good picture of The Tower in the centre. In a single day in the Count's house a dressing-room door is about to be broken in, the page leaps from the bedroom window straight into the flower beds, the gardener demands that the windows "be barred at last", the Countess threatens to retire to the Ursuline convent. By nightfall everything the Count has built on secret rendezvous and convenient verdicts comes down. Waite sees in The Tower not just ruin but "the rending of a House of Doctrine. I understand that the reference is, however, to a House of Falsehood." For a couple with The Hierophant in the middle this is an exact link: the atmosphere of the union tests everything that rests on form without truth.

Lisovskaya sees strength in a couple's Tower too: trials passed together make the union stronger. For the 6-5-8 tail she gives an important detail: such a couple's money rests on strict rules the two have invented together, and that is The Hierophant without anyone else's voice. On the downside she names threats of a break-up used as pressure. The Ursuline convent of the second act is exactly such a threat: spoken to be heard, not in order to leave.
Mozart ended the opera with words that suit this centre: "This day of torment, of caprice and of folly, only love can turn into contentment and joy."

The Chariot in the centre is an atmosphere of movement and victory. Among its reversed meanings Waite lists "Riot, quarrel, dispute, litigation, defeat": even here the tail pulls the couple towards court. Only with The Chariot the formula of the two ends no longer holds: 8 + 7 = 15, not 6.

sections.h2: The couple's values: The World, The Hanged Man, The Empress
paragraphs: The couple's values are the spiritual purpose of the union, the answer to what it exists for. The 6-5-8 tail has three variants, and each answers the tail in its own way. The links below are our reading.

**The World (46.6%).** Waite writes of the garland on The World: according to P. Christian it should be made of roses, "and this is the kind of chain which Éliphas Lévi says is less easily broken than a chain of iron". For a couple that has passed through The Hierophant — through bonds, vows and the "captivity" of his divinatory list — this is the answer: what holds is not the iron of obligation but a chain of roses. The heroine of the trilogy, by the way, has a flower's name.

**The Hanged Man (42.1%).** Wen compares him directly with The Hierophant: The Hierophant is "an orthodox, conventional, institutionalized approach", The Hanged Man is "seeing the same issues as others, but through a different perspective". She also writes that the card has "a component of grace" and that the Seeker must forgive, and, for the reversed card, that "it is not for the Seeker to administer judgment, vengeance, or penance". For a couple with Justice as the main task this is a correction from above: the account is kept honestly, but for the sake of forgiveness, not of a verdict. The Countess who forgives "for the third time today, without condition" lives by exactly this value.

**The Empress (11.3%).** Among the reversed meanings of The Empress Waite lists "the unravelling of involved matters, public rejoicings". That is how every Beaumarchais comedy ends: the knot untied, a wedding, songs. The value here is a fruitful house where tangles are unravelled, not hidden.

sections.h2: Worked example: two people born on the same day
paragraphs: The clearest example is a couple in which both partners were born on 14 April 1975. The site's engine gives this couple the 6-5-8 tail.

Each of them has the same personal matrix: day 14, month 4, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. The karmic task D = 14 + 4 + 22 = 40 → 4. The centre E = 14 + 4 + 22 + 4 = 44 → 8. The entry of the tail M = D + E = 12, the middle N = D + M = 16. The personal tail is 12-16-4, with Justice in the centre.
The couple's matrix adds up the same points of the two personal matrices:
The couple's centre is 8 + 8 = 16, The Tower. The couple's values are 12, The Hanged Man.

In this couple Justice appears three more times: on "What to create together", in "Home and things" and on "Parents together". Lisovskaya advises adding up repeated energies, and four eights give 32 → 5 — the very Hierophant from the middle of the tail. The Tower repeats in "Where it sparks", and The Lovers on "Way into money"; in the relationship sphere the same point M is labelled "Common language".

The doubling shows the mechanics of the tail in pure form. Each of the two, separately, has Justice in the centre of the personal chart. Added to the same date, it moves from the centre to the couple's main task, and The Tower takes its place in the atmosphere of the union.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail
paragraphs: Beaumarchais's trilogy is not a forecast but a picture: a funny first evening, a heavy third and a reconciliation at the end. The 6-5-8 tail does not say what will happen to a couple. It shows the question the two stumble over and what changes the script.
The strong version of this tail is a couple whose form serves love and whose account is kept in the open:

ul: **The name before the role.** The Lovers at the entry are the right to be chosen for oneself. The roles of husband, wife, parents, master of the house are needed, but they do not cancel the person who was chosen. Rosine stays Rosine under a countess's title too.

**A rite to keep one's word, not to hide behind.** The Hierophant is strong when an agreement is spoken aloud and before witnesses, the two alone or with the family, and weak when form covers what goes unsaid. House rules are better invented together than taken ready-made from parents or from "the way people do it".

**"And" or "or" — before signing.** Many quarrels of such a couple are arguments over a conjunction in a sentence both thought they shared. What was promised: both things — or one instead of the other? It is worth settling while there is no blot on the paper.

**Marriage is not a receipt.** Love does not pay off debts, and debts are not collected in love. Money, favours and concessions are more honestly counted separately, so that they do not turn into "look how much I gave you".

**No judging in one's own case.** The Count is ridiculous not because he is jealous but because he judges the servant whose bride he wants to take. In a quarrel between two it helps to check whether one has become the judge in one's own lawsuit.
**One measure for two.** "You ask for yourself a pardon you refuse to others." If forgiving — then with an amnesty for both. If weighing — then putting one's own fault on the scales too.

paragraphs: Beaumarchais gives Suzanne a line as she refuses to argue: "To prove that I am right would be to grant that I could be wrong." Justice begins exactly with that admission. And in Figaro's monologue there is a line the newspaper Le Figaro later took as its motto: "Without the freedom to criticise, there is no flattering praise." For a 6-5-8 couple it is a bridge between the first card and the last. A compliment from The Lovers is worth something only when it sits next to the right to an honest "you're wrong here". And the honest criticism of Justice is borne by those who keep choosing each other.

sections.h2: Sources

ul: Beaumarchais: The Barber of Seville, or The Useless Precaution (1775); The Mad Day, or The Marriage of Figaro (1784); The Guilty Mother, or The Other Tartuffe (1792), with its preface "Un mot sur la Mère coupable". Quotations are our translation from the French edition of the Œuvres complètes (Laplace, 1876).
Mozart and Lorenzo da Ponte, Le nozze di Figaro (1786), finale of Act IV.
Madame Campan, Memoirs of the Private Life of Marie Antoinette: Louis XVI's words about the play.
A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1922 reissue): The Lovers, The Hierophant, Justice, The Tower, The Chariot, The World, The Empress.
Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015): The Lovers, Justice, The Hanged Man.
Yuliana Lisovskaya, Matritsa sud'by: sovmestimost' (The Destiny Matrix: Compatibility, 2024): the meaning of the couple's points and of energies 5, 6, 8 and 16.
Calculations and statistics: the site's engine, run over every date of birth.

**M · Entry to the task — 6, The Lovers.** The couple's shared wish is to be chosen for who they are, not for gain, propriety or someone else's will. The two enter the task with this wish, and later the same wish pushes back against any routine.

**N · Middle of the task — 5, The Hierophant.** The road runs through form: ritual, status, families, house rules, the roles of husband and wife. Form keeps a promise — and can hide the person behind it.
**D · Main task — 8, Justice.** To learn to measure oneself and the other by one measure: to own one's share of the blame, to keep promises, not to sit as judge in one's own case.

intro: This road — with a contract, a court case, an ink blot on an IOU and forgiveness at the end — was written down more than two hundred years ago by Beaumarchais. He wrote three plays about one married couple, and they follow the order of these cards.

faq.q: What does the 6-5-8 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's road from love by choice (6, The Lovers, entry to the task), through the form of the union — marriage, families, rules, roles (5, The Hierophant, the middle) — to the main task of a fair account between the two (8, Justice). The couple has to learn to measure themselves and each other by one measure, to keep promises and to own their share of the blame.

faq.q: Why is there no 6-5-8 tail in a personal matrix?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail equals the entry plus the main task: 6 + 8 = 14, Temperance. In a couple the middle is the sum of the two personal middles, and for 6-5-8 couples that sum is always above 22 — 23 or 32 — so it reduces to 5.

faq.q: How is the 6-5-8 tail different from the couple's tail 6-14-8?
faq.a: The entry and the main task are the same — The Lovers and Justice. The difference is in the middle: in a 6-14-8 couple the road goes through Temperance, a gradual blending of two characters, and in a 6-5-8 couple through The Hierophant, an outward form: an agreement, a rite, family rules.

faq.q: Are there couple's tails 5-6-8 or 8-5-6?
faq.a: No. The first number of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three: every person's personal entry to the tail is a multiple of three, and so is the sum of two such numbers. Running every date shows that only one couple's tail is built from 6, 5 and 8 — 6-5-8.

faq.q: Does the 6-5-8 tail mean a couple needs an official marriage?
faq.a: No. The Hierophant in the middle speaks of form in general: agreements, rites, house rules and relations with families. The tail does not predict events and does not demand a marriage certificate; it shows what the couple passes through on its road and where it has to learn a fair account.

report: It took Beaumarchais three plays and twenty years of stage time to give his heroine back her name. In The Barber of Seville Count Almaviva falls in love with Rosine and carries her off from under her guardian's lock. In The Marriage of Figaro, in the third year of their marriage, she tells him in the middle of a quarrel: "I am no longer that Rosine… I am the poor Countess Almaviva, the sad, forsaken wife." In The Guilty Mother the Count at last says: "Rosine (it is the name your husband gives back to you)." Between these lines lies the 6-5-8 tail: The Lovers at the entry, The Hierophant in the middle, Justice as the main task.

report.h3: First, to be chosen for oneself

report: The Count began in disguise. He called himself Lindor, a poor bachelor of arts, because he was tired of conquests "that self-interest, convenience or vanity keep putting in our way". And he said: "How sweet it is to be loved for oneself!" This is the entry of a couple with this tail — a shared wish to be chosen as a person, not for a title, for gain or as a convenient option. Hence the couple's common language: we found each other ourselves, we are not like everyone else.

But at the end of the same play the notary arrives with two marriage contracts for one Rosine — one for the Count, the other for the guardian. Love decides which of them gets signed, yet what is signed is still a paper. The entry leads into form. And the same wish to be chosen later pushes back against what has been settled: three years on, the Count looks elsewhere for "less sameness… now and then a refusal".

report.h3: When the role speaks for the person

report: "I love her very much; but three years of union make marriage so respectable!" the Count admits. Love has become respectable — respected, and far away. This is The Hierophant in the middle of the road: the two begin to live in the roles of wife, husband, master of the house, and the role speaks in place of the person. Waite places this card in "the world of institution as distinct from that of Nature". In The Marriage of Figaro the institution rules every step: servants cannot marry without their lord, the bride's uncle will not give her "to one who is nobody's child", and the wedding is nearly stopped in court by a woman who turns out to be the bridegroom's mother.

In one person the middle of such a tail would hold Temperance — the ability to blend two sides within oneself. Two people need a vessel on the outside: an agreement, a rite, a rule that both accept. The Hierophant has a strong side too. Figaro asks the Count to place the bridal headdress on Suzanne before everyone and to "adopt this ceremony for all marriages", and the public form binds the Count by his own word. **Form either keeps the word or takes away the name**, and the middle of the tail runs exactly between the two.

report.h3: Marriage is not a receipt

report: The central scene is the trial in the third act. Long ago Figaro borrowed money from Marceline and wrote that he would repay the sum "and marry her". He claims the paper says "or". The clerk reads it aloud: "AND… OR… AND… OR… The word is so badly written… there's a blot." Then they argue over a comma. **The fate of a marriage hangs on a conjunction, a blot and a comma** — and this is the central question of Justice for a couple with this tail: do love and obligation go together, or does one stand in for the other? Figaro answers with a formula: marriage "is not a receipt".

The verdict is given by the Count, a judge in his own case: he judges the servant whose bride he wants to take, and lets drop aside: "At least I am avenged — that's a relief." Among the meanings of Justice reversed Waite names "bias". Then Marceline recognises Figaro as her lost son and hands him that very paper: "Take back your note — it is yours, it is your dowry." **The IOU that in the morning could have wrecked the wedding becomes a wedding gift by evening.** The words are the same. Only one thing has changed: what the people are to each other — parties to a lawsuit, or family.

report.h3: Two faults on one pair of scales

report: All through the mad day the Count lives by a double measure: wives, he says, must know how to keep their husbands. "So they owe everything?" — "And the man nothing." The Countess sets a different condition: "You ask for yourself a pardon you refuse to others… If ever I agreed to forgive, I would insist that the amnesty be general." At the end, realising he has spent the whole evening courting his own wife in another woman's dress, the Count begs for mercy. She answers that "for the third time today" she grants it "without condition". And as she hands out his night-time gifts, she speaks the ancient formula of justice: "Each shall have what belongs to them."

Twenty years later each of the spouses carries an old fault: the Countess has a son who is not her husband's, the Count a ward who is in fact his daughter. The resolution is the most exact scene of this tail. The Countess asks: "Almaviva! Isn't it true that she is my daughter?" The Count answers: "And he is my son; here are our two children." **Two faults go onto the two pans at the same moment, and instead of a verdict there is one family.** Only after that does Rosine become Rosine again.

The strong version of the tail rests on a few simple things: the name before the role; a rite to keep one's word, not to hide behind; "and" or "or" settled before signing, not after the blot; one measure for two — owning one's share of the blame before weighing the other's. Beaumarchais wrote a line that the newspaper Le Figaro later took as its motto: "Without the freedom to criticise, there is no flattering praise." A compliment from The Lovers is worth something only next to the right to an honest "wrong here". And a fair account is borne by those who keep choosing each other.

unit.title: Marriage is not a receipt

captions.M: To want to be chosen for who you are
captions.N: To pass through roles and rites without losing your names
captions.D: To measure yourselves and each other by one measure

unit.meaning: Your task is a fair account with no double measure: keep your word, own your share of the blame, never judge your own case.

seo.title: Karmic tail 6 8 11 compatibility: The Lovers, Justice and Strength
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 8 11 compatibility in the couple's destiny matrix: why love turns into a race here, and what Strength asks of the two people in it.

items.title: Karmic tail 6-8-11 in compatibility: when love becomes a race
items.short: The three numbers 6-8-11 in a couple's matrix — The Lovers, Justice and Strength — make one of the most common karmic tails in compatibility: roughly one couple in 23 has it. It is also one of the strangest: no single person can have this tail, only two people together can write it. It is the story of a couple who enter their task through falling in love, walk it like a fair contest with rules, and learn the main thing — a strength that has no need to beat the other.

sections.h2: Why 6-8-11 never appears in a personal destiny matrix
paragraphs: In a personal matrix, the middle of the tail is always the sum of the two outer numbers. A person with The Lovers at the entry and Strength in the task gets 6 + 11 = 17 in the middle — The Star: that personal tail exists, it is 6-17-11. One person never has the triple 6-8-11 anywhere — not in the tail, not in the money, relationship or talent lines: they are built the same way, with the middle equal to the sum of the ends. Anyone searching for "6 8 11 in the destiny matrix" will find these numbers in a row only in a couple's matrix.

In a couple, the middle is added up not from the ends but from the two partners' personal middles. So where one person would have The Star burning, the two of them have Justice. Waite remarks in passing that the figure of Justice "is said to be Astræa". Astraea's name means "the starry one". In the first book of Ovid's Metamorphoses she is the last of the gods to leave the earth — "last of all the virgin deity, Astraea vanished from the blood-stained earth" — and the constellation Virgo, next door to Libra, the Scales, is hers. Our reading: where a single person holds the star of hope, a couple holds a star that has taken up the scales. Not "it'll all work out", but "let's keep it fair".

The second clue is who Strength belongs to. The site's engine went through every date: in no couple with the tail 6-8-11 does either partner have Strength in their personal tail. The couple's Strength is always made of two other cards:

ul: The Hierophant and The Lovers (5 + 6) — in 45.1% of these couples;
The Emperor and The Chariot (4 + 7) — in 29.4%;
Justice and The World (8 + 21 = 29 → 11) — in 11.3%;
The Wheel of Fortune and The Sun (10 + 19 = 29 → 11) — in 9.1%; the other combinations are rarer.

paragraphs: And in 39.6% of couples, neither partner has any of the three cards in their personal tail. Neither of them brings this tail. It appears when the two are added together — like the lions in the myth below: neither hero was a lion, they became lions as a pair.

sections.h2: The myth this couple lives in: Atalanta and Hippomenes
paragraphs: Book Ten of Ovid's Metamorphoses is sung by Orpheus, and inside his song Venus, lying with Adonis on the grass under a poplar, tells him a story, "mingling kisses with her words". The tale is meant to explain why the goddess of love hates lions. Quotations below follow Brookes More's 1922 translation; where a literal rendering matters, it is marked.

Atalanta ran faster than men, and "you could not have said whether her swift speed or her beauty was more worthy of your praise". An oracle told her: "You, Atalanta, never will have need of husband… and while yet living you will lose yourself." She went to live in the woods and set her suitors a condition: "I will not be won… till I am conquered first in speed… A wife and couch shall both be given to reward the swift, but death must recompense the one who lags behind. This must be the condition of a race."

Hippomenes came to watch the race and to condemn the madmen who risked their lives for a wife. He saw her — and begged forgiveness of the men he had just been judging. He challenged her himself. For the first time, Atalanta was unsure whether she wanted to win. Hippomenes prayed to Venus, and she brought him three golden apples from her field on Cyprus. As they ran he threw them one after another, Atalanta turned aside for the gold — and lost.

Having won, Hippomenes forgot to thank Venus. The goddess turned against them both.
