seo.title: Karmic tail 9 12 12 compatibility: the climb without looking back
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 12 12 compatibility: The Hermit at the entry and two Hanged Men. Why no person has this tail, what holds the couple, how to end the suspension.

items.title: Karmic tail 9-12-12 in compatibility: two who must not look back
items.short: The triple 9-12-12 cannot be found in any personal destiny matrix. To become a person's tail, it would need The Devil in the centre of the chart, and no person ever has The Devil in the centre. A couple does: 82.4% of couples with this tail. What holds these two together belongs to neither of them — it appears only between them.

sections.h2: A tail that no single person has
paragraphs: In a personal matrix the tail obeys a strict rule: the entry M is the reduced sum of the main task D and the centre of the chart. If the task is 12 and the entry is 9, the centre has to be 15: 12 + 15 = 27, 2 + 7 = 9. But the centre of a personal matrix can only be 3–14, 16, 18, 20 or 22. Fifteen never appears there, for any date of birth. So 9-12-12 is impossible as a personal tail.

In a couple's matrix every point is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The couple's centre is built from two personal centres, and The Devil appears in the sum easily: 10 + 5, 8 + 7. Going through every date shows that 82.4% of couples with the 9-12-12 tail have exactly 15 in the centre. For them the tail is built by the law of a personal tail — only the missing card comes not from one person but from two. The remaining 17.6% have The Lovers (6) in the centre.

The middle is not personal either. In a personal chart the middle of the tail comes from its two ends, and 9 + 12 would give 21, The World. A couple's middle is added up from the partners' middles, and it comes out as 12. That is why the triple 9-12-12 appears nowhere in a personal chart: not in the tail, and not on the money, relationship or talent lines, where the middle number is also always the sum of the outer two. Whoever sees these three numbers is looking at a couple's matrix.
The tail is not rare: about one couple in 42 has it (2.389%), the 13th most common of the 97 couple tails.

The arithmetic can be read as an image. For most of these couples the entry is the sum of the main task and the centre: The Hermit is The Hanged Man plus The Devil. **This couple's silence is made of suspension and attachment** — an attachment so strong that a careless word feels dangerous. This is our reading, not a rule of the method, but the numbers suggest it on their own.

sections.h2: Why Orpheus and Eurydice
paragraphs: The marriage of Orpheus and Eurydice in Ovid's Metamorphoses (Books X and XI) lasts a few lines. Hymen, the god of weddings, comes to the feast, but without songs or good omens. Soon the bride dies of a snakebite. Orpheus goes down to the underworld and sings before its rulers, Persephone and her husband. The song is so beautiful that they let Eurydice go on one condition: Orpheus must not turn round until he has left the valleys of Avernus. The two climb in silence. Near the very edge he looks back, and she vanishes a second time.

This story holds everything the 9-12-12 tail is made of. Two people walk one behind the other in silence, each alone with their own thoughts — The Hermit. The whole road rests on a condition and on waiting — The Hanged Man. The main trial is to hold on without checking — The Hanged Man again. And between them lies the strongest attachment and a fear of loss that rises right at the threshold — The Devil in the centre.

The myth is not a prediction. Ovid and Virgil end it in grief, Gluck's opera of 1762 ends it happily, and Ovid himself gives one more ending in the following book. The tail shows which scene keeps repeating in a couple, but not how it will end. Nor are its roles tied to gender: either of the two may walk in front.

sections.h2: A wedding without words: The Hermit at the entry
paragraphs: Ovid begins this love story with silence. Here is Hymen at the wedding, in Brookes More's translation:

Truly Hymen there / was present during the festivities / of Orpheus and Eurydice, but gave / no happy omen, neither hallowed words / nor joyful glances; and the torch he held / would only sputter, fill the eyes with smoke, / and cause no blaze while waving.

There is light, but it will not blaze, and no solemn words are spoken. For the 9-12-12 tail this is an exact image of the entry: the fire is already burning, quietly and low, and words seem unnecessary.

The entry to the task is what the couple wants together: its shared wishes and common language. With The Hermit on this point, both want the same thing — a world of their own where nothing has to be proved. Love is shown by deeds: meeting the six o'clock train, fixing the tap without a word, buying that particular book. Friends hear about important things once everything is already decided. Each has their own time and their own corner, and that is respected. No step is rushed — not the first confession, not moving in, not the wedding.

Benebell Wen offers two readings of The Hermit's lantern. The first is the familiar one: a light in the darkness for others. The second fits this entry better: someone "who sees the world through his or her own light", who "walks in the direction of his own thoughts only". At the 9-12-12 entry each partner carries their own lantern and sees the other by its light — as the other appears to them.

In Virgil's Georgics, Orpheus after his loss sings of his wife like this: "you, sweet wife, you he sang, alone with himself on the lonely shore, you as the day came, you as it went" (our translation). This is The Hermit's love in its purest form: a conversation with the other that goes on inside oneself.

The entry stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish turns into resistance. "We understand each other anyway" turns into "we don't talk about that". Questions pile up in silence, each lives in a room of their own, and one day it turns out that the two have long been walking side by side without seeing each other. From outside such a couple can look cold, even though inside something is burning — like Hymen's torch, which smokes but does not go out.

sections.h2: The climb in silence: The Hanged Man in the middle
paragraphs: Ovid describes the condition and the road in a few lines; in Brookes More's translation:

Pluto told him he / might now ascend from these Avernian vales / up to the light, with his Eurydice; / but, if he turned his eyes to look at her, / the gift of her delivery would be lost. / They picked their way in silence up a steep / and gloomy path of darkness.

The middle of the task is how the couple walks from the wish to the main task. With The Hanged Man here, the path runs through suspension. On this path Eurydice is no longer dead and not yet alive; in Ovid she walks "with slow steps, yet halting from her wound". Orpheus has found her and has not: she is one step behind, but he may not see her. Waite writes of The Hanged Man: "life in suspension, but life and not death". Eurydice's climb is that kind of life, literally.

In a couple's life the middle 12 looks like this. The big decision waits "for better times": moving in after the renovation, marrying once things settle at work, having the talk when the right moment comes. One leads — knows where and why — and the other follows without knowing the plan. The one in front does not look back and does not explain, believing that this is how it must be, that it is safer. The one behind keeps quiet so as not to get in the way. Sometimes only a push from outside can move the couple — news, a move, someone else's wedding.

This middle has a strong side too. The Hanged Man knows how to wait and how to see a situation from the other side. Such couples sense each other at a distance, give way without keeping score, and do a great deal for each other in silence. One of the card's messages, in Wen's words, is to "hang in there": suspension can be endured. The question is whether it ends.

sections.h2: The backward glance: The Hanged Man in the main task
paragraphs: Here are the lines on which the whole myth rests, in Brookes More's translation:
in fear he might again / lose her, and anxious for another look / at her, he turned his eyes so he could gaze / upon her. Instantly she slipped away.

There are two motives, named outright: fear and longing. Not indifference and not betrayal — Ovid calls Orpheus amans, "the lover", at that very moment (flexit amans oculos, "the lover turned his eyes"). Orpheus looked back to make sure she was there. The main task of the tail is read mostly through its minus, and the minus of The Hanged Man here is not the sacrifice itself but the fact that the sacrifice cannot bear the silence and breaks into checking.

Russian has a word for this — oglyadka, "a backward glance". Zhit' s oglyadkoy, "to live with a backward glance", means to be over-careful and keep checking: is it still there, have we lost it, what will people say. Lyubit' bez oglyadki, "to love without a backward glance", means to give oneself completely. **A couple with the 9-12-12 tail wants the second and lives the first.** In Waite's divinatory lists, both The Hermit and The Hanged Man carry the word circumspection, from the Latin circumspicere, "to look around". In the 9-12-12 tail that circumspection is written three times.

What the backward glance looks like in a couple. Every evening one asks: "Are you sure you're not upset? Are we really all right?" The other says "yes" and feels checked up on. Decisions are made "the proper way", with one eye on the family: what the parents will think, how it looks from outside. The picture outside is flawless; inside are two people trying very hard and very tired. One of them holds everything together with all their strength and hears reproaches in return. They cannot leave, and they cannot explain either.
Three authors told this scene in different ways, and together they show how the main task unfolds.
In Ovid, Eurydice does not reproach him: "what had she to complain of — his great love?"

In the fourth book of Virgil's Georgics she cries out: "Who has ruined both poor me and you, Orpheus? What madness is this?" Virgil himself calls the act "a sudden madness", one "to be forgiven, if the dead knew how to forgive". Then Orpheus clutches at shadows and wants "to say many things" — but there is no one left to say them to (our translations).

In Gluck — the opera Orfeo ed Euridice, Vienna, 1762, libretto by Ranieri de' Calzabigi — the twist is the most exact. Eurydice does not know the condition. Love tells Orpheus: "Gli sguardi trattieni, affrena gli accenti" — "hold back your glances, rein in your words". She walks behind a husband who will not look at her and will not say why. She begs for a single glance, calls him faithless and a tyrant, says that death is dearer to her than life with him. He answers: "Ben potrò morir d'affanno, ma giammai dirò perché" — "I may well die of grief, but I will never say why." She asks: "What secret is Orpheus hiding from me?" — and weeps that he has abandoned her. And Orpheus turns round: not from his own fear, but from her pain (our translations).

This is the mechanism of the 9-12-12 main task. One keeps silent for the sake of the couple and is sure this is a sacrifice. The other sees only the silence and reads it as coldness or betrayal. In Waite's list for The Hermit, "treason" and "dissimulation" stand right next to "prudence": "Prudence, circumspection; also and especially treason, dissimulation". Prudent silence from inside and betrayal from outside are one and the same silence, seen from two sides. The longer the condition lasts, the louder the reproach, and the more certain it is that someone will turn round — not because they have stopped loving, but because they can bear no more.

So the couple's task is not to endure even more: The Hanged Man is not just patience. The task is to **say the condition out loud**. "I can't explain right now — and here is why." "I'm putting this off until spring, not for ever." "I'm afraid you'll fall behind, so I keep looking back." A condition that has been spoken stops being a secret, and so it stops working as a wall.

sections.h2: Seven days on the bank: when suspension becomes a home
paragraphs: After the second loss Orpheus tries to go back for Eurydice, but the ferryman will not let him across. In Brookes More's translation:
Seven days he sat upon Death's river bank, / in squalid misery and without all food — / nourished by grief, anxiety, and tears — / complaining that the Gods of Erebus / were pitiless.

Orpheus cannot go back and cannot leave. He sits by the river, feeds on grief and blames his misfortune on the "pitiless" gods, and then for three years he shuns everyone. The suspension that used to be a road becomes a home.

In couples with this tail it can happen quietly. After a failed attempt — a move that fell through, a talk that ended in a quarrel — the couple stops trying. Circumstances are to blame, or work, or parents, or "fate". Each goes back to their own lantern, and everything returns to the entry: silence, only now with more hurt in it. That is how the tail closes into a circle — The Hermit, The Hanged Man, The Hanged Man, and The Hermit again.

sections.h2: The Dweller on the Threshold: the couple's centre in Waite and Wen
paragraphs: The couple's centre is the shared atmosphere, what lies between the two and is not on show. In 82.4% of couples with the 9-12-12 tail, The Devil sits there.

In The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, Waite says that what this card signifies is "the Dweller on the Threshold without the Mystical Garden when those are driven forth therefrom who have eaten the forbidden fruit". The figure of the Dweller on the Threshold came into occult writing from Bulwer-Lytton's novel Zanoni (1842). Orpheus loses exactly at the threshold: in Ovid there remained "but little more to climb till they would touch earth's surface"; in Virgil it happens "right at the edge of the light". The Devil in these couples' centre is what rises at the threshold: when almost everything has worked out, the fear of losing grows stronger than trust.

Wen opens her description of The Devil on the Waite–Smith card like this: "The Lovers from Key 6 are chained by a horned beast". So the centre of 9-12-12 couples holds either The Lovers (17.6%) or the same Lovers in chains (82.4%). Wen also links The Devil with Mara, the tempter of the Buddha, who personifies "the thirst for existence, the thirst for pleasure, the thirst for power". In Ovid, Orpheus turns round avidus videndi, "greedy to see".

In its plus, The Devil in a couple's atmosphere is strong attraction, passion and a rare acceptance: here no one has to hide their dark side, and mistakes are forgiven. In its minus it is the wish to possess, jealousy, control and silence about one's own desires. Together with The Hermit's silence at the entry this is a risky mix: desires go unspoken, while the two hold on to each other very tightly. Waite leaves hope in the description of the card itself: the one who is exalted over the chained figures "is not to be their master for ever".

Orpheus himself speaks the key to this centre when he pleads with the rulers of the underworld. Brookes More renders it as "I ask of you / possession of her few days as a boon". The Latin is sharper: pro munere poscimus usum — "I ask not for a gift, but for a loan" (our translation). A beloved person cannot be owned; one can only walk beside them. In her advice to couples with energy 15, Yuliana Lisovskaya reaches the same thought: nobody belongs to anybody.

sections.h2: What such a couple is made of
paragraphs: A couple's tail is the sum of the partners' personal tails, and for 9-12-12 there are only three combinations.

ul: **12-19-7 + 15-20-5 — 78% of these couples.** One partner's personal tail begins with The Hanged Man, the other's with The Devil. In the couple these two cards go deeper: The Hanged Man becomes the main task, The Devil the centre. The middle is the sum of The Sun and Judgement, cards of clarity and awakening: 19 + 20 = 39 → 12. Two bright lights add up to suspension.

**18-6-6 + 18-6-6 — 18%.** Both have the same personal tail, and both have The Hanged Man in the centre of their personal chart. In the couple the cards swap places: The Lovers from the two personal tails give the Hanged Men of the couple's tail, and the two Hanged Men from the personal centres give The Lovers in the couple's centre.

**3-7-22 + 6-5-17 — 4%.** The Empress and The Lovers at the entries give The Hermit, The Chariot and The Hierophant give The Hanged Man in the middle, The Fool and The Star give The Hanged Man in the task.

paragraphs: None of these five personal tails contains The Hermit. **Neither partner brings the silence at the entry with them — it is born between them.** The numbers cannot say who is "to blame" for the silence or for the backward glance: both are made by two.

sections.h2: The couple's values: a second Hermit or The Moon
paragraphs: The couple's values are its spiritual purpose, the path the two are to walk together. In 65.7% of couples with the 9-12-12 tail this is The Hermit again; in 34.3% it is The Moon.

The second Hermit changes the meaning of the first. At the entry silence hides; in the values it deepens: conversations after which something changes, respect for the other's quiet, the ability to learn from each other. The lantern each carried for themselves becomes a light in which both can be seen.

The Moon in the values is a path through the dark, where trust has to rest not on the eyes but on feeling. This is exactly what Orpheus's climb teaches: to walk without seeing the other, and to know that they are there.

sections.h2: A worked example: 17.01.1976 and 05.07.1975
paragraphs: The person born on 17.01.1976 has the personal tail 15-20-5 and The Wheel of Fortune (10) in the centre. The person born on 05.07.1975 has the tail 12-19-7 and The Hierophant (5) in the centre. The couple's matrix adds their points pair by pair:

The middle 12 comes from the partners' middles, not from the ends of the couple's tail: 9 + 12 would have given The World. This couple's values are The Hermit (9), and that is not the sum of the personal values either: 3 + 15 would have given The Moon, but the couple's values are recalculated from the couple's own points. In this couple The Hermit also sits on the attitude to material things (5 + 22 = 27 → 9), and in Lisovskaya, The Hermit in money means unhurried spending and something always put aside for a rainy day.

sections.h2: The way out: side by side, then each in front
paragraphs: In Book XI Ovid brings Orpheus back to Eurydice and describes how they walk now. In Brookes More's translation:
Then lovingly they wandered side by side, / or he would follow when she chose to lead, / or at another time he walked in front, / looking back, safely, — at Eurydice.

Ovid sets this scene in the fields of the blessed — a poetic convention, not a promise. But the way of walking he describes can be taken into life. It corrects both mistakes of the first climb: no one is always in front, and a look back is no longer a check.

There is a hint in the numbers too. Lisovskaya adds up repeated energies: the tail's two Hanged Men give 12 + 12 = 24 → 6. Add up the whole tail, 9 + 12 + 12 = 33 → 6 — The Lovers again. Lisovskaya herself notes that such a sum sounds faintly if its card does not appear in the matrix; in 17.6% of 9-12-12 couples The Lovers stand right in the centre. **Beneath the silence and the suspension The Lovers are hidden** — the card of choice. In Gluck the ending is brought by Love. For a 9-12-12 couple it is brought by a choice made out loud.
What this means in practice:

ul: **Name the condition.** If one partner is silently carrying something "for us", say what it is, why, and until when. Gluck's whole disaster lies in the words "I will never say why".
**Give "later" a deadline.** The Hanged Man is a pause, not a home. A postponed decision needs a date, or at least a next step.
**Change places.** Whoever is always in front should sometimes walk behind: with money, with holidays, in talks with the family. Whoever is always behind gets the right to lead.
**Ask instead of checking.** "Are you there?" asked out loud costs less than a secret backward glance, and it sounds like care rather than control.
**Don't pay with sacrifice.** Agree on what each keeps for themselves — time, money, friends — so that "everything for the other" does not turn into a silent ledger.

**Call for help when it is frightening.** If constant fear, control or pressure have settled into the couple, that is a reason to see a family psychologist. If there is danger, call a local emergency number or crisis line.

paragraphs: The strong version of the 9-12-12 tail is a couple that can be silent without fear. Its silence is trust, not a wall: each can withdraw into themselves, knowing the other will not vanish. It knows how to wait and knows what it is waiting for. And it looks at the other the way Orpheus does at the end of the myth: without fear.

sections.h2: Where the quotations come from

ul: Ovid, Metamorphoses, X, 1–77 and XI, 61–66; translation by Brookes More (1922). The Latin words pro munere poscimus usum are X, 37; the other Latin and the English renderings of them are ours.
Virgil, Georgics, IV, 464–506; translations ours.
Gluck, Orfeo ed Euridice (1762), libretto by R. de' Calzabigi, Acts I and III; translations ours.
A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910): The Hermit, The Hanged Man, The Devil.
Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015): The Hermit, The Hanged Man, The Devil.
Yu. Lisovskaya, Matritsa sud'by: sovmestimost' (Destiny Matrix: Compatibility, 2024): the meaning of the couple's points and energies 9, 12, 15.

intro: The karmic tail 9-12-12 in compatibility is the task of a couple that enters the union through silence and lives in suspension. **The Hermit at the entry** is the shared wish: a quiet world for two, where words are not needed and no step is rushed. **The Hanged Man in the middle** is how the couple walks the path: postponing, waiting, with one of them silently carrying the load for both. **The Hanged Man in the main task** is what the couple has to learn: to stop paying for the union with silent sacrifice and an endless "later", to trust without checking, and to say out loud what the silence costs.

The story of these three cards is older than any matrix. Ovid wrote it down: two people climb out of the underworld in complete silence, he in front, she behind, and he must not turn round. What follows is an investigation: what the numbers themselves say, what Waite and Benebell Wen write about the cards, and why the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice fits the 9-12-12 tail so closely.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 9-12-12 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the task of a couple that enters the union through silence and lives in suspension. The Hermit at the entry is the wish for a quiet world of two. The Hanged Man in the middle is a path of waiting and silent sacrifice. The Hanged Man in the main task means learning not to pay for the union with silence, to give "later" a deadline, to trust without checking and to say out loud what the silence costs.

faq.q: Can 9-12-12 appear in a personal destiny matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal tail the entry equals the reduced sum of the task and the centre, so a task of 12 and an entry of 9 would need a centre of 15, which no person has. On the money, relationship and talent lines the middle number is the sum of the outer two, and 9 + 12 gives 21. The triple 9-12-12 exists only in a couple's matrix.

faq.q: Why does the couple tail 9-12-12 have two Hanged Men?
faq.a: The middle and the main task of the couple are built from different points of the partners: the middle from the middles of their personal tails, the task from their karmic tasks. In couples with this tail both sums reduce to 12. These are two different roles: in the middle The Hanged Man shows how the couple walks the path, in the task — what it has to learn.

faq.q: What does The Devil in the centre mean for a couple with the 9-12-12 tail?
faq.a: It sits in the centre of 82.4% of these couples and describes the atmosphere of the union: strong attraction and acceptance, but also fear of loss, the wish to possess, silence about one's own desires. No person has The Devil in the centre — this card appears only in a couple. The remaining 17.6% have The Lovers in the centre.

faq.q: Is the 9-12-12 tail a verdict on the couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not predict a break-up and does not say how the union will end. It shows a recurring difficulty — suspension, silent sacrifice and checking — and the direction of the work. The strong version of this tail is a couple that can be silent without fear and can wait, knowing what it is waiting for.

faq.q: Is there a couple tail 12-9-12 or 12-12-9?
faq.a: No. Among the 97 couple tails these numbers appear only in the order 9-12-12, with The Hermit at the entry and two Hanged Men after it.

report: Ovid explains the most famous backward glance in literature in two words. Orpheus was leading Eurydice out of the underworld, he was forbidden to turn round, and near the very edge he turned — "in fear he might again lose her, and anxious for another look at her". Not out of indifference: Ovid calls him amans, "the lover", at that very moment. The couple tail 9-12-12 tells this story in three cards — The Hermit, The Hanged Man, The Hanged Man — and shows why two people who treasure each other so much are so afraid of one careless word.

report.h3: A silence that neither of them brings

report: The Hermit at the entry is what the couple wants together: a quiet world for two, where nothing has to be proved. Love is shown by deeds: meeting the six o'clock train, fixing the tap without a word, buying that particular book. Friends hear about important things once everything is already decided. No step is rushed — not the confession, not moving in, not the wedding.

Ovid begins Orpheus's marriage with the same silence. Hymen, the god of weddings, brings "neither hallowed words nor joyful glances", and the torch in his hand "would only sputter, fill the eyes with smoke, and cause no blaze while waving". There is fire, there are no words, and words seem unnecessary.

A curious detail: neither partner has The Hermit in their personal tail. **Nobody brings this silence with them — it is born between the two.** The entry stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish turns into resistance: "we understand each other anyway" becomes "we don't talk about that". Questions pile up in silence, and one day it turns out that the two have long been walking side by side without seeing each other.

report.h3: The climb in silence

report: Orpheus accepted the condition, and then "they picked their way in silence up a steep and gloomy path of darkness". On this path Eurydice is no longer dead and not yet alive. This middle has a strength too: such couples know how to wait, sense each other at a distance and do a great deal for each other without words. The only question is whether the suspension ends.

report.h3: Why Orpheus turned round

report: The main task is The Hanged Man again, and it is read through its minus. Russian has an exact word for it: oglyadka, "a backward glance". To live with a backward glance is to keep checking: is it still there, have we lost it, what will people say. To love without a backward glance is to give oneself completely. **A couple with the 9-12-12 tail wants the second and lives the first.** Every evening one asks: "Still not upset? Are we really all right?" The other says "yes" and feels checked up on. Decisions are made "the proper way", with one eye on the family. One of them holds everything together with all their strength and hears reproaches in return.

Gluck showed the mechanism most precisely, in his opera of 1762. There Eurydice does not know the condition. Her husband will not look at her and will not say why; she begs for a single glance and calls him faithless. He answers: "I may well die of grief, but I will never say why." And he turns round — not from his own fear, but from her pain.

One keeps silent for the sake of the couple and is sure this is a sacrifice. The other sees only the silence and reads it as coldness or betrayal. In Waite's divinatory list for The Hermit, "treason" and "dissimulation" stand right next to "prudence": one and the same silence, seen from two sides. So the task is not to endure even more. **The task is to say the condition out loud.** "I can't explain right now — and here is why." "I'm putting this off until spring, not for ever." "I keep looking back because I'm scared of finding no one behind me."

report.h3: Not a gift, but a loan

report: Most of these couples have The Devil in the centre — a card that never appears in the centre of anyone's personal matrix. Waite calls it the Dweller on the Threshold, and Orpheus loses exactly at the threshold, when almost everything has worked out. The Devil in a couple's atmosphere is strong attraction and a rare acceptance, but also fear of loss, the wish to possess, silence about one's own desires. Wen notes that on Waite's Devil card the figures in chains are the same Lovers. And in the tail's numbers they are hidden in plain sight: the two Hanged Men together give 12 + 12 = 24 → 6, the card of choice.

Orpheus himself speaks the key to this centre when he pleads for Eurydice: pro munere poscimus usum — "I ask not for a gift, but for a loan". **A beloved person cannot be owned; one can only walk beside them.**

How people walk once this is understood, Ovid shows in the next book: "Then lovingly they wandered side by side, / or he would follow when she chose to lead, / or at another time he walked in front, / looking back, safely, — at Eurydice." No one is always in front, and a look back is no longer a check. For a couple this means giving every "later" a deadline, changing places with money, holidays and talks with the family, asking out loud instead of checking in secret, and agreeing on what each keeps for themselves. If constant fear, control or pressure have settled into the couple, it is worth seeing a family psychologist, and if there is danger, calling a local emergency number or crisis line.

The strong version of the 9-12-12 tail is a couple that can be silent without fear. Its silence is trust, not a wall: each can withdraw into themselves, knowing the other will not vanish. It knows how to wait and knows what it is waiting for. And it looks at the other the way Orpheus does at the end of the myth: without fear.

seo.title: Karmic tail 9 12 21 compatibility: a secret union and the world
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 12 21 compatibility: the Hermit, the Hanged Man and the World. Why a union without witnesses stalls and how a couple brings it into the world.

items.title: The 9-12-21 karmic tail in compatibility: a union the world does not know about
items.short: The couple's karmic tail 9-12-21 is written as a sum: the Hermit plus the Hanged Man equals the World, 9 + 12 = 21. The couple begins with a union hidden from other people's eyes, lives for a long time in suspension, and its main task is to carry what was born between the two of them out to other people without losing it on the way.

sections.h2: A tail no single person can have
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points in the two personal matrices, reduced to 22. Take the dates 05.12.1975 and 14.09.1975 (calculated by the site's engine). The first partner has the personal tail 18-3-12 and centre 6, the second has the tail 18-9-9 and centre 9. The points are added in pairs:

The first oddity is the middle. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail comes from the ends: entry plus main task. By that rule it would be 9 + 21 = 30 → 3, the Empress. But in a couple the middle is the sum of the partners' middles, and the result is 12. That is why 9-12-21 never appears as a personal tail for any date: it is a tail for two only.

The second oddity matters more. The rule is turned upside down: it is not the middle that equals the sum of the ends, but the end that equals the sum of the entry and the middle. **9 + 12 = 21** — no reduction, nothing left over. The main task does not come at the couple from outside. It is made of what the couple wants (the Hermit) and what it goes through (the Hanged Man). The World in this tail is not a new place to move to; it is quiet for two plus a pause endured, once both parts are finally added together.

The third is the centre. Every couple with this tail has 15, the Devil, at the centre. No one has 15 as a personal centre: a person's centre can be 3–14, 16, 18, 20 or 22. So neither partner brings the Devil into the couple's atmosphere. It arises only in the air between them.

The 9-12-21 tail occurs in about one couple in 53 (1.894%), seventeenth of the 97 couple tails. It is built from four combinations of personal tails: 18-3-12 with 18-9-9 (39% of such couples), 15-8-11 with 21-4-10 (38%), 15-5-8 with 21-7-13 (14%), 18-6-15 with 18-6-6 (9%). In every case the couple's entry comes from 36: either from two Moons, when both partners' personal tails begin with 18, or from the Devil in one partner and the World in the other. And in the most common combination, as in the example, the partners' personal karmic tasks are 12 and 9: one has the Hanged Man, the other the Hermit. The couple's tail sets them side by side and draws the line under them: 9 + 12 = 21.

sections.h2: Shakuntala: a play about a marriage the world never saw
paragraphs: Kalidasa, the classic of Sanskrit drama, is generally thought to have lived in the fourth or fifth century. William Jones translated his Shakuntala into English in 1789, a German version followed two years later, and Goethe answered the play with a quatrain. In E. B. Eastwick's English it ends: "Would'st thou the Earth and Heaven itself in one sole name combine? I name thee, O Sakoontalá! and all at once is said." Earth and heaven under one name — that is the World, the last card of the tail.

The plot is short. King Dushyanta, out hunting, drives into the forest hermitage of the sage Kanva. The master is away, and guests are received by his foster daughter Shakuntala. The two marry without a rite and without witnesses — the old law allowed two people to marry this way if both wished it. The king leaves for his capital and puts a ring with his name on her finger. While Shakuntala sits thinking of him, the irascible sage Durvasas comes to the hut. She does not hear the guest, and he curses her: the one she is thinking of will forget her. Her friends beg for a softening — the king will remember when he sees the token he gave her. On the way to the palace the ring slips into the river. The king does not recognise his wife, and a light from heaven carries her away. Later a fisherman finds the ring in a fish's belly, the king remembers everything and tortures himself with remorse. They meet years later in another hermitage, on a mountain between heaven and earth, where Shakuntala's son is growing up.

The play is laid out across three places. The first four acts pass in the forest hermitage, the fifth and sixth in the palace, the seventh on a heavenly mountain. This is the 9-12-21 tail performed on stage: the Hermit's retreat, the palace where everything hangs, and the summit from which the whole world can be seen.

One more clue. Kalidasa took the story from the Mahabharata and changed its core. In the epic the king forgot nothing. Shakuntala waited six years for the army he had promised to send to bring her to the capital (1.67.20; 1.68.5), gave up waiting and came herself, with her son. And the king, in K. M. Ganguli's translation, "hearing these her words, and remembering everything said, 'I do not remember anything'" (1.68.18). Later he explained: their union had been made out of the world's sight, and had he accepted the son on her word alone, the world would have had doubts (1.69.36; 1.69.40). Kalidasa invented the curse and the ring so that the king's forgetting would be innocent. His translator Arthur W. Ryder says as much: in the epic "the king is decidedly contemptible. Somehow or other, his face must be saved."
So there are two versions of one misfortune, and both sit in the main task of the tail. In one, the world blots out memory. In the other, a man disowns his love for the world's sake.

Quotations from the play here and below follow Arthur W. Ryder's translation (1912), checked against Monier Monier-Williams (1855); lines from the Mahabharata are from K. M. Ganguli's translation or, where marked, our own translation from the Sanskrit of the Critical Edition, Book 1.

sections.h2: 9 · Entry to the task: one enters a hermitage without jewels
paragraphs: The first thing the king does at the hermitage gate is take off his jewels and hand his bow to the charioteer: "One should wear modest garments on entering a hermitage." The second is to hide who he is. When the girls ask, he calls himself a student of Scripture on a tour of inspection for the king. The union is born where a royal title weighs nothing and nobody knows who these two are.

This is the entry of 9-12-21. Point M is what the couple wants together, its agreements and its common language. The Hermit here is the wish for a place outsiders do not enter. Friends of such a couple hear about the engagement, the move or the renovation only afterwards — from a photo in which everything is long since done. Each of the two has an hour of their own to be alone, love shows in deeds, and every next step is taken slowly. In the palace old Gautami puts it to the king better than anyone: "Did she with father speak or mother? Did you engage her friends in speech? Your faith was plighted each to other."

The common language of such a couple is like the memory Shakuntala tries to bring back to the king at court. Once he held out a lotus-leaf cup of water to her fawn. The fawn would not drink from a stranger's hand, but drank from hers. The king smiled: "Every one trusts his own sort. You both belong to the forest." For the two of them that scene holds a whole world. In the palace, before witnesses, the same story sounds like an invention, and the king answers it with an insult.

The Mahabharata gives such a union an almost legal definition. Kanva tells his daughter that she has broken no law: for a kshatriya, a member of the warrior class, the best marriage is the union "of a desiring woman with a desiring man, without sacred words, in secret" (1.67.25–26, our translation). Two cards of this couple stand in one line: the secret — the Hermit at the entry; the desire — the Devil at the centre.

But point M stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. "Let nobody know for now" first protects the union and then locks it in. Wen notes that the Hermit's light can be "the shining of light in the darkness for others" — or the sign of "someone who sees the world through his or her own light". A lamp for two lights two faces and leaves everything else in the dark. **An agreement known to two people lives exactly as long as their memory does.**

At court the Shakuntala of the Mahabharata says a strange thing to the king: "You think, 'I am alone', and you do not know the ancient sage who dwells in your heart" (1.68.27, our translation). The Sanskrit word is muni — the word for the sages of the forest. So the Hermit has two faces. One says: nobody knows about this. The other is the inner witness who knows everything and needs no proof. Both stand at this couple's entry, and the task of the tail begins with choosing between them.

sections.h2: 12 · Middle of the task: a spring forbidden to bloom
paragraphs: The middle of a couple's tail is our reading: how the couple walks from the wish at M to the task at D. Here it is the Hanged Man, life on pause. In the play the pause begins with a farewell. Leaving, the king puts the ring on Shakuntala's finger and says, in Monier-Williams's version: "Repeat each day one letter of the name Engraven on this gem; ere thou hast reckoned The tale of syllables, my minister Shall come to lead thee to thy husband's palace." The agreement becomes a countdown. The minister never comes. In the epic the promised army did not come in six years.

The Hanged Man in this couple is a union that exists and yet seems not to. The two of them know about it, and they will start living by it "later": when work settles down, when there is a good moment to introduce each other to the parents, when "everything is sorted out". One counts the days. The other is swallowed by outside life and does not notice "later" becoming a habit. Lisovskaya writes of the Hanged Man in a couple that such people take a long time to enter a relationship and need a push from outside to marry. And she describes another scene of the same energy: one partner holds the relationship together with all their strength and gets reproaches in return.

The pause in this tail rests on a silence kept with the best intentions. Shakuntala's friends heard the curse but decide not to tell her: "We two must keep this thing to ourselves… Would any one sprinkle a jasmine-vine with scalding water?" Pity turns into misfortune: Shakuntala goes to the palace not knowing she may not be recognised. Couples do the same: they keep quiet about the hard thing so as not to hurt, and the hurt is put off until later along with everything else.

The ring is lost on the way — at a holy pool of the Ganges where Shakuntala worships the water. The token of the union disappears exactly on the border between two worlds, the forest and the capital. And in the palace the king looks at the veiled woman and can neither remember her nor turn away: "like a bee That hovers round a jasmine flower at dawn, While frosty dews of morning still o'erweave it… I cannot taste the sweet, and cannot leave it." That is the Hanged Man in one line: unable to take, unable to let go.

The most exact scene of the tail is the sixth act. The ring has been found, the king remembers everything, and to punish himself he has forbidden the spring festival. The chamberlain reports that spring itself has obeyed the royal order: "The mango branches are in bloom, Yet pollen does not form; The cuckoo's song sticks in his throat, Although the days are warm; The amaranth-bud is formed, and yet Its power of growth is gone." Monier-Williams puts it plainly: the cuckoo "suspends the liquid volume of his song".

Now back to the numbers. By the personal formula the middle of this tail would hold the Empress — spring, growth, what ripens by itself. The couple has the Hanged Man in her place. **A spring forbidden to bloom is exactly 12 in the place of 3**: everything is ready to open, and there is no pollen.

Here the Hanged Man easily mistakes love for its portrait. The king paints Shakuntala on a tablet, weeps over the painting and scolds a bee that has settled on the painted face. The clown reminds him: "It is only a picture, man." The king says of himself: "A traveller I, who scorned the mighty river, And seeks in the mirage to quench his thirst." When a union lives in a pause, it is easy to love in memory and hard to love in life.

The play also shows the way out of the pause. Indra's charioteer Matali stages an attack on the king's friend, and the king snatches up his bow. Matali explains: "I saw that you were overpowered by some inner sorrow, and acted thus to rouse you." This is the push from outside that Lisovskaya writes about. For a couple the push may be a circumstance, a friend, a move, a question that can no longer be answered with "later". There is no reason to resent it: without it the Hanged Man can hang for years.

sections.h2: 21 · Main task: a union with witnesses
paragraphs: The main task of a couple's tail is read mostly through its minus — what the couple fails at and what it has to learn. The minus of the World in a couple shows in two signs. There are agreements, but nobody besides the two of them can acknowledge them. And the two talk but do not hear each other. In Shakuntala both signs meet in one scene — the fifth act, in the palace.

One line of the epic is enough to tell that scene. Shakuntala says to the king, in Ganguli's words: "I am not certainly crying in the wilderness. Dost thou not hear me?" (1.68.34). A union made in the forest does not exist in the capital: there are no witnesses, two people know the agreement, and one of the two does not remember it. Later the king will explain: "this union with you was made out of the world's sight" (1.69.40, our translation). In Sanskrit "out of the world's sight" is loka-paroksha, and loka means "world". Some manuscripts add the line: "and today it has been made again before the world's eyes" — loka-samaksha. **The couple's whole main task fits between two words: "out of sight" and "in sight".**

The two versions of the plot give two kinds of this minus. In the epic the king remembers everything and disowns her because he fears what people will say. Wen describes the World reversed in almost the same terms: the Seeker "is consciously and knowingly in denial", "remaining willfully ignorant", "afraid of change and is hesitating to take the necessary actions". In Kalidasa the king really has forgotten: the world blotted out his memory, and the curse only finished the job.

Finished it — because the king himself had started it. Already in the second act he is afraid his talkative friend will tell the palace ladies about his love, and says to him: "Do not think that I am really in love with the hermit-girl… The light words I uttered were spoken in jest." The friend believes him. In the sixth act he admits: "when you had told the whole story, you said it was a joke and there was nothing in it. And I was fool enough to believe you." The king switched off his only witness himself, long before the curse — for the sake of the secret. **The secret of the entry, carried to its end, becomes forgetting in the main task.**

In that same scene the king describes his own position better than anyone. The capital summons him to a rite, the hermitage asks for protection, and "Two inconsistent duties sever My mind with cruel shock, As when the current of a river Is split upon a rock." A couple with the 9-12-21 tail often lives just like this — in two worlds. In one it exists, in the other it does not. At work, with relatives, among friends, the partner goes unmentioned, and not out of malice: that world is simply arranged without them. It need not be the same person each time. In one part of life one partner "forgets", in another the other does.

The play shows the World in its plus as well. Returning from a battle in heaven, the king descends in Indra's chariot and sees the earth from above: the mountains rise out of the plains, trunks show through the leaves, the small rivers become visible — "It seems as if some being threw The world to me, for clearer view." The World is a view that takes in the forest and the capital at once.

The reunion happens neither in the palace nor in the old hermitage but on Gold Peak, a mountain whose flanks sink into the eastern and the western sea. Shakuntala comes out in a plain dress, her hair in a single braid: so Indian wives went whose husbands had long been away. The king falls at her feet. Then he holds out the recovered ring: "Then let the vine receive her flower." Shakuntala answers: "I do not trust it. I would rather you wore it." (So in Ryder's translation; Monier-Williams has no such line — the manuscripts of the play differ.) **The union no longer needs a token to be recognised by.**

The sage Kashyapa, master of this hermitage, explains what happened: "Reflections are not seen in dusty glass, Which, cleaned, will mirror all the things that pass." The king's line, the play reminds us, has always lived in a circle: palaces in the years of rule, the forest hermitage in old age. Kanva said the same when he let his daughter go: "You are to spend a busy, useful life In the world's eye", and then "Come with your husband to the grove And end your days in peace." The World of this tail is not a departure from the hermitage but a circle that holds both the hermitage and the palace.

Shakuntala's son is named Bharata: in Kashyapa's words, "he will bear the world alone." By one tradition, India's own name for itself, Bharat, comes from his name. A union made in secret ends by giving its name to a whole land. For a couple with this tail the "world" is not necessarily a child. It is everything the two build together and bring into the light: a home, a shared work, a circle of friends, a common life that others can see.

sections.h2: 15 at the centre: a curse at the threshold
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's matrix is its atmosphere — what lies between the partners and is not for show. For every couple with the 9-12-21 tail it is the Devil. In its plus this is a couple where one can show the other one's dark side and not lose them, where desires are spoken aloud and support can be enormously strong. In its minus it is a couple held together by closeness alone, where anyone who enters the house is a cause for jealousy and one's own wishes go unsaid. Lisovskaya's chapter on the Devil ends simply: nobody belongs to anybody.

In the play the Devil stands at the threshold of the hut. Durvasas comes up and calls: "Who will bid me welcome?" Shakuntala sits nearby and does not hear. Her friend says of her: "How could she notice a guest when she has forgotten herself?" The curse, in Monier-Williams's version, runs: "…fix thy thoughts Upon the cherished object of thy love, While I am present? Thus I curse thee, then— He, even he of whom thou thinkest, he Shall think no more of thee… He shall disown thee, even as the sot, Roused from his midnight drunkenness, denies The words he uttered in his revellings." The Sanskrit word here is ananya-manasa — "with a mind for no one else". That is the Devil's attachment: one person blots out the rest of the world.

The curse has a mirror logic. Shakuntala forgot the world for the sake of her beloved — and her beloved, back in the world, forgot her. Two people went blind from two sides. Blindness also stands in Waite's reversed Devil: "Evil fatality, weakness, pettiness, blindness." And in the last act the king himself says, in Monier-Williams's version: "Even though a friend Should wreathe a garland on a blind man's brow, Will he not cast it from him as a serpent?"

The play keeps insisting that nobody is to blame. "This is the work of fate," the clown tells the king. "Ask fate, my child," Shakuntala answers when her son asks who this man is. "Your infatuation was inevitable," Kashyapa tells the king. Wen writes of the Devil almost in Kalidasa's spirit: the card "does not necessarily mean the Seeker is entirely to blame"; "while the Seeker is not entirely innocent and contributed adversely to the situation, the greater culpability rests elsewhere." That is a good compass for a couple. The atmosphere of 15 is not anyone's character: a single person never has such a centre, it is born only between two. Looking for the guilty one in it is useless. What helps is to notice the moment when the two are so taken up with each other that they do not hear life knocking at the door.

A hut for two and an unwelcomed guest at the gate — that is where the Devil lives in this couple. The Hermit at the entry says: "we need nobody." The Devil at the centre makes a chain out of those words. The World in the main task is the very guest nobody heard.

sections.h2: What Waite saw in these cards: the light of the world, a ring and a garland
paragraphs: The cards on the site are drawn in their own way. This section is about the Waite deck and how Waite himself described its pictures.

Waite's Hermit "blends the idea of the Ancient of Days with the Light of the World. It is a star which shines in the lantern." The entry card of this couple already holds "the Light of the World" in its hand — a small one, on a single height. The main task of the tail is to make the whole World out of that small flame. And "the Ancient of Days" unexpectedly echoes the "ancient sage in your heart" with which Shakuntala reproaches the king in the epic.

On the Devil Waite describes a detail that is easy to miss: "There is a ring in front of the altar, from which two chains are carried to the necks of two figures, male and female." The title of Kalidasa's play literally means "Shakuntala recognised by a token", and the token is a ring. The ring is meant to remind, and becomes the chain the whole union hangs on: no ring, no memory. That is why Shakuntala's last gesture weighs so much, when she refuses to put it on again.

The World in Waite's description is surrounded by "an elliptic garland, as if it were a chain of flowers intended to symbolize all sensible things". The two chains — the iron one from the Devil's ring and the flowered one of the World — are this couple's path: from a union held together by a token and a secret to a union that holds itself and takes in the whole visible world. The blind man in the play throws off precisely a garland.

sections.h2: The couple's values: a hermitage, or the moon after an eclipse
paragraphs: The reading has one more sphere — "The couple's values", which Lisovskaya calls the spiritual purpose: what the two walk together for. In two thirds of couples with this tail (66.9%) it holds the Hermit, in a third (33.1%) the Moon. In the example of 05.12.1975 and 14.09.1975 it is the Hermit.

The Hermit at the entry of the tail and the Hermit in the values read differently. At the entry it is the wish to hide; in the values it is what makes going out worthwhile. The play ends not in the palace but in a hermitage — a new one, on a mountain from which the world can be seen. There the king says: "Here is deeper contentment than in heaven." **Quiet for two is a value for such a couple, and there is no need to lose it. What matters is that it does not serve as a refuge from the world.**

Couples with the Moon in their values live by intuition, dreams and a shared night language — and they find it easier than others to take the portrait for the person. Kalidasa has an image for them too. When his memory returns, the king says: "Eclipse flees far; Light follows soon; The loving star Draws to the moon." The moon after an eclipse is the same Moon, only no longer in shadow.

sections.h2: How to break this circle
paragraphs: The play shows not only the breakdown but also what mends it. Its moves translate easily into the language of an ordinary couple.

ul: **Give the union a witness.** At least one person who has been told in earnest. The king himself called his love a joke in front of his only friend — and left the curse very little to do.
**Say the agreement aloud, together with a step.** "Repeat each day one letter of the name" is not a plan but a wait. A deadline without a step turns into the Hanged Man.
**Do not hide a hard truth out of pity.** The friends kept quiet about the curse so as not to scald the jasmine, and sent Shakuntala to the palace defenceless.
**Do not hang the union on a single token.** If the memory of what matters lives in one ring, one date, one ritual, it is easy to drop it in the river on the way.
**Hear the guest at the threshold.** Friends, relatives, invitations, shared affairs — this is the very world knocking at the hut. The Devil's attachment makes a couple deaf to it.
**Accept a push from outside.** If the pause has dragged on, a circumstance that forces a decision works like Matali, not like an enemy.
**Bring the two worlds into one.** The partner exists both where the two are alone and where they are among people: at work, with relatives, in the stories each tells about their life.

paragraphs: The strong version of this tail is a couple that has a hermitage of its own and does not hide in it. Its union is recognised without a ring. It can withdraw into quiet and come back, and the quiet remains a value, not a wall. That is 9 + 12 = 21: quiet for two and a pause endured, added together into a whole world.

ul: **Entry to the task — 9, The Hermit.** What the couple wants together: quiet, a world of their own, a language only the two of them understand, and no hurry to tell anyone anything.

**Middle of the task — 12, The Hanged Man.** How the couple walks the path: the union hangs for a long time between "already" and "not yet". There is an agreement, but no life built on it yet; one waits, the other puts things off.

**Main task — 21, The World.** What the couple has to learn: to make the union visible and whole, so that it exists not only where the two are alone but among other people as well — and so that nobody has to be reminded of it.

intro: Behind the three cards stand two more clues. At the centre of such couples there is always the Devil — attachment, passion and the question of whom the union belongs to. No date of birth ever puts the Devil at the centre of a personal chart: this atmosphere is born only between two people. And the middle of the tail breaks the rule by which a single person's middle is worked out from the two ends. This plot has been written down in full once before — some fifteen hundred years ago, in an Indian play about a king who forgot his wife.

faq.q: What does the 9-12-21 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail: entry to the task — the Hermit (9), middle — the Hanged Man (12), main task — the World (21). The couple wants a quiet union for two, goes through a long pause, and has to learn to make the union visible and whole — so that it exists both in private and among other people.

faq.q: Why is the middle 12 if 9 + 21 = 30 → 3?
faq.a: That is how the middle is worked out only in a personal matrix. In a couple's matrix every point is the sum of the same points of the two partners, and the middle 12 is made of the middles of their personal tails, for example 3 + 9. That is why no single person has the 9-12-21 tail.

faq.q: How does 9-12-21 differ from 9-21-12?
faq.a: The numbers are the same, the roles are not. In 9-21-12 the World stands in the middle and the main task is the Hanged Man: such a couple's path runs through people and changes, and its main trial is pause and sacrifice. In 9-12-21 it is the other way round: the pause is the path, going out into the world is the task. Both tails have the Devil at the centre; 9-21-12 is more common, found in 2.437% of couples.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a relationship?
faq.a: No. The tail does not say whether the union will work out and does not predict events. It shows where the couple's knot lies: in a secret that stays a secret too long, and in a pause that becomes a habit. The play this reading is built on ends with a reunion.

report: Fifteen hundred years ago an Indian king called his love a joke, so that the palace would not find out about it. Then he forgot her in earnest. This is the plot of Kalidasa's Shakuntala, and it follows the 9-12-21 tail almost scene by scene: a union born out of other people's sight, a long pause, and a main task — to bring the union out among people.

The three numbers of the tail add up like a school sum: **9 + 12 = 21**. The couple's main task does not come from outside; it is made of the couple's own entry and middle. The Hermit at the entry is what the couple wants: quiet, a world of their own, a language only the two of them understand. The Hanged Man in the middle is what it goes through: a union that exists and yet seems not to. The World in the main task is what it has to learn: that the union should exist not only where the two are alone.

report.h3: A marriage without witnesses

report: At the gate of a forest hermitage King Dushyanta takes off his jewels and hands his bow to the charioteer: "One should wear modest garments on entering a hermitage." There he meets Shakuntala, the sage's foster daughter, and does not tell her who he is. They marry without a rite and without witnesses. The Mahabharata, from which Kalidasa took the story, calls such a marriage the union "of a desiring woman with a desiring man, without sacred words, in secret". One line holds both the secret and the desire — the Hermit at the entry of the tail and the Devil at the centre of the couple.

Friends of such couples hear about the big events only after the fact. This protects the union, but the entry of the tail stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance: "let nobody know for now" first shields, then locks in. **An agreement known to two people lives exactly as long as their memory does.**

report.h3: A spring forbidden to bloom

report: Leaving for his capital, the king puts a ring on Shakuntala's finger: "Repeat each day one letter of the name Engraven on this gem; ere thou hast reckoned The tale of syllables, my minister Shall come to lead thee to thy husband's palace." The minister never comes. The agreement turns into a countdown — this is the Hanged Man. Two people know about the union, and they will start living by it "later": when work settles down, when there is a good moment to meet the family, when "everything is sorted out". One counts the days, the other is swallowed by outside life.

The pause rests on a silence kept with the best intentions. Shakuntala's friends know trouble hangs over her, but say nothing: "Would any one sprinkle a jasmine-vine with scalding water?" On the way to the palace the ring slips into the river — the token of the union vanishes exactly on the border between the forest and the capital. The king looks at his wife and does not recognise her: like a bee over a jasmine at dawn, he "cannot taste the sweet, and cannot leave it".

When the ring is found and memory returns, the king will punish himself by forbidding the spring festival. Spring will obey: "The mango branches are in bloom, Yet pollen does not form; The cuckoo's song sticks in his throat." Where personal rules would put the Empress — spring and growth — the couple has the Hanged Man. What brings the king out of the pause is a push from outside: the heavenly charioteer stages an attack to rouse him. Sometimes this is exactly what such a couple needs, and there is no reason to resent it.

report.h3: A curse at the threshold

report: The trouble began at the very threshold. While Shakuntala was thinking of her husband, the sage Durvasas came to the hut, and she did not hear the guest. The curse: "He, even he of whom thou thinkest, he Shall think no more of thee." It has a mirror logic. She forgot the world for the sake of her beloved — her beloved, back in the world, forgot her. This is the Devil at the centre of the couple: an attachment in which one person blots out the rest of the world.

The king began the forgetting himself. Even before the curse he told his only friend that the whole thing was a joke — and the only witness believed him. **The secret of the entry, carried to its end, becomes forgetting in the main task.** Yet the play keeps insisting that nobody is to blame. The Devil's atmosphere is not anyone's character: a single person never has such a centre; it is born only between two.

report.h3: Between "out of sight" and "in sight"

report: In the Mahabharata the king forgot nothing: "remembering everything", he said, "I do not remember anything." He explained it this way: the union had been made out of the world's sight. In Sanskrit that is loka-paroksha, "out of the world's sight". Some manuscripts go on to say that now the union has been made again — loka-samaksha, "before the world's eyes". **The couple's whole main task fits between these two words.** The minus of the World is when two people know the agreement and nobody can acknowledge it, and when the two talk but do not hear each other. "I am not certainly crying in the wilderness. Dost thou not hear me?" Shakuntala says in the palace.

In life this looks like two worlds. In one the couple exists, in the other it does not: at work, with relatives, among friends, the partner goes unmentioned, and not out of malice — that world is simply arranged without them. Both can forget, each in their own part of life.

In the play the reunion happens neither in the palace nor in the old hermitage but on a mountain between heaven and earth. The king holds out the recovered ring to his wife, and she refuses to put it on: "I do not trust it," she says, and asks him to wear it himself. **The union no longer needs a token to be recognised by.**

What changes the script is the play's own moves read the other way round: give the union at least one witness who has been told in earnest; name the agreement together with a step, not only with a deadline; do not hide a hard truth out of pity; hear the guest at the threshold — friends, family, shared affairs. The strong version of this tail is a couple with a hermitage of its own that does not hide in it: quiet for two remains a value, not a wall.

unit.title: The hut where the world knocks

captions.M: To want a world for two, away from other eyes
captions.N: To get stuck in "later": together, yet as if not
