seo.title: Karmic tail 9 15 6 compatibility: silence, a bond, a free choice
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 15 6 compatibility: the couple starts in shared quiet, passes through an unspoken bargain and has to learn to choose each other freely.

items.title: Karmic tail 9-15-6 in compatibility: silence, a bond and a free choice
items.short: The Hermit, The Devil and The Lovers look like cards from three different stories: a quiet one, a dark one and a bright one. Yet the two outer numbers of this tail add up to the middle with nothing left over: 9 + 6 = 15. Silence plus desire makes a bond. That is the whole plot of the 9-15-6 tail in a compatibility matrix: the couple begins in careful quiet, on the way binds itself, almost without noticing, with a bargain nobody ever said out loud, and its main task is to choose each other again, of their own free will and in broad daylight.

sections.h2: The play this couple lives in
paragraphs: In 1888 Henrik Ibsen wrote The Lady from the Sea. It is staged less often than A Doll's House, although it reads easily as an answer to it: Nora left and slammed the door, while Ellida Wangel stays — but only after she has been given leave to go. The story of this marriage passes through three states, exactly in the order of our tail. Quotations from the play follow Eleanor Marx-Aveling's translation of 1890; where the Norwegian word matters, it is given.

A small fjord town in northern Norway. Wangel, the town's medical man and a widower with two daughters, married again five or six years ago — Ellida, the lighthouse keeper's daughter. The townspeople call her "the Lady from the Sea": she bathes in the fjord every day in any weather and says the water here is "sick". Ten years earlier, before the marriage, a sailor from an American ship, a man with a dark story, put his own ring and her small ring on a key-ring and threw them into the sea: now, he said, they were wedded to the sea. In the summer when the play begins, this Stranger comes back for her.
The three cards of the tail are three states of this marriage:

ul: **The Hermit:** a house where everyone has a corner and nobody asks anything;
**The Devil:** two agreements nobody truly chose — the vow to the sea and the marriage as a bargain;
**The Lovers:** in the last act the husband cancels the bargain, and the wife chooses him herself for the first time.

paragraphs: The plot looks like a love triangle, but that is not what Ibsen is writing about. In the final scene Wangel himself explains what the Stranger meant to his wife: "Your longing and aching for the sea, your attraction towards this strange man, these were the expression of an awakening and growing desire for freedom; nothing else." The same holds for the couple's tail: The Lovers do not stand for a third person. The "stranger" in a couple can be anything — a city they never lived in, a profession not chosen, an earlier life that still calls.

sections.h2: 9 · The Hermit at the entry: "if we happen to find there is anything to say"
paragraphs: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together and where it begins; the same point is its common language. With The Hermit this language is quiet. Both Wangels came to the marriage out of loneliness: he could no longer bear the emptiness of his house, and she, in her words, was "so helpless and bewildered, and so absolutely alone". Two people wanted a refuge — and got one.

Ibsen shows this house in the very first act. A guest asks where the lady of the house usually sits. She has her own arbour in the garden, the daughters sit on the verandah, and the husband goes to and fro — now to her, now to his children. "I think all parties feel most comfortable in this way," says Ellida. "You know we can talk across to one another — if we happen to find there is anything to say."

This is not coldness. The Hermit has a bright side, and in the play it is real: care. In all these years Wangel has never once asked who her former fiancé was. "You are always so thoughtful for me," Ellida tells him. Respect for boundaries, time and a place of one's own for solitude, an unhurried pace — that is this entry at its best. A couple that does not need to fill the silence with words is rare, and such couples treasure it.

But the entry stands on the line of the task, and the wish for quiet easily becomes resistance. In the Wangel house the silence has long since grown over everything. Every year the daughters secretly keep their late mother's birthday — with flowers and a flag — and claim it is all in honour of a guest; their father knows and says nothing. For three years Ellida has carried a fear her husband learns of only in the second act: "And you have gone about in this state three whole years, bearing for yourself this secret suffering, without confiding in me." The dread came back while she was expecting a child; the little boy died at a few months old, and since then she has not lived with her husband as his wife. That too they both leave unsaid.

Reviewing the old meanings of the cards, Waite recalls that Éliphas Lévi gave The Hermit to Prudence, and offers his own definition: "Prudence is the economy which follows the line of least resistance." Waite means a spiritual thrift, but in daily life the formula works literally. In the fourth act Ellida describes her marriage in just these terms: "I simply left things just as I found them the day I came here." Not one change, not one request, not one argument. Waite's reversed list for The Hermit even has a name for care taken to the limit: "unreasoned caution".

Wen tells two kinds of withdrawal apart. In the Four of Cups "the Seeker may be licking wounds"; in The Hermit the Seeker turns inward "in order to seek enlightenment". From outside they look the same. The Wangels' silence after their son's death seems to be a Four of Cups passing itself off as The Hermit. A couple with this tail does well to ask itself from time to time what it is holding — a lamp or a bandage.

In ordinary life it looks mundane. Two people love quiet evenings and do not pry into each other's souls. He does not ask why she is sad: "she'll tell me when she wants to." She does not say she feels hemmed in: "why worry him." There are no quarrels, because there are no conversations where a quarrel could happen. Among the minuses of The Hermit Lisovskaya names problems that pile up in silence. What goes unsaid does not disappear, and the middle of the tail shows what it turns into.

sections.h2: 15 · The Devil in the middle: a key-ring thrown into the sea
paragraphs: The middle of the task is what the couple goes through on the way from its shared wish to its main task. The Devil stands here, and in Ibsen it appears twice — as two agreements, neither of them truly chosen.

The first is the vow to the sea. The Stranger puts his ring and Ellida's small ring on a key-ring and throws it with all his might into the deep. "Had you no will of your own, then?" Wangel asks. "Not when he was near." Later she wrote to the sailor twice that it was all over, and he answered as if her letters did not exist: wait. This is The Devil without horns or hooves — a tie a person never chose and cannot leave by a single decision. Ellida finds a word for it sharper than any definition: "The terrible is that which repels and attracts."

The second agreement is the marriage itself. In the fourth act Ellida says what both have kept silent through all the years of marriage: "the truth — the pure and simple truth is — that you came out there and bought me." And at once: "Oh! I wasn't a bit better than you. I accepted the bargain. Sold myself to you!" Nobody lied and nobody played the villain: two lonely people made a sensible bargain. The Hermit plus The Lovers — and out came The Devil.

**The strangest thing in this middle is its language. The Devil here speaks in the words of freedom.** The Stranger once called himself Friman, which in Norwegian sounds almost like fri mand, "a free man"; in the fifth act he will say exactly that of himself: "I will live and die a free man." He does not claim Ellida by right: "If Ellida wishes to be with me she must come freely." And again: "Vows bind no one, neither man nor woman. If I hold so steadfastly to you, it is because I cannot do otherwise." A bond that calls itself freedom holds hardest of all: there is nothing to defend against. Yet without meaning to, it also points the way out. The word frivillig, "freely", is first spoken in the play by the Stranger, and Ellida at once repeats it twice to herself. The next day she will turn the word on her own marriage — "It was not freely that I went with you" — and tell her husband: "It all lies in those words. They have enlightened me."

Wangel answers the pull with a ban — and so he too ends up in the middle of the tail. "You have no choice, Ellida. You have no right to choose — no right without my permission." He threatens to have the Stranger arrested and plans to take his wife away to the sea air. And he names his own defeat: "So I have not won you by our living together. Never, never possessed you quite." Ellida answers with words anyone could say about control: "You can indeed keep me here! … But my mind — all my thoughts, all the longings and desires of my soul — these you cannot bind!"

Among the tasks of a couple with The Devil, Lisovskaya lists attempts to hold a partner through intimacy, a child, money or status, silence about one's own wishes, fear and hopelessness. In a 9-15-6 couple this middle grows out of the quiet of the entry. First "let's not talk about it", then unwritten clauses nobody signed: "I provide — you don't ask questions", "I put up with your silence — you don't leave", "we're together because it's too late to change anything", "he'd be lost without me". Each clause is reasonable on its own. Together they are a chain, and both of them hold it. Wen writes that The Devil "does not necessarily mean the Seeker is entirely to blame": a bond always contains more forces than one will. Ibsen has no villain, only two agreements everyone took part in.

To make the point plain, Ibsen sets a second couple beside the first. In the same last act Ellida's stepdaughter Bolette agrees to marry the no-longer-young Arnholm so that she can see the world: she cannot accept help from a friend, but she can accept a marriage. One bargain in the play is cancelled while another is struck before the audience's eyes.

The Devil has a bright side too, and Lisovskaya names it: speaking openly about desires and accepting each other's dark sides. The Wangels' first step out of the middle is the confession in the second act: Ellida tells him everything "just as it is", and her husband listens without passing sentence. Lisovskaya's chapter on The Devil ends with a short thought: nobody belongs to anybody. Ibsen reaches it three acts later.
If control in a relationship reaches threats or violence, it is no longer a matter for reading cards: real help is needed — an emergency number or a crisis line.

sections.h2: 6 · The Lovers: cancel the bargain to make a union
paragraphs: The main task is the couple's chief trial, and it is read mostly through what does not work. With The Lovers it is choice. Not falling in love — the couple either had that at the start or did not — but the decision to be together, made freely and aloud. The difficulty is that such a choice is impossible while the bargain holds: from inside a cage one cannot choose the cage.

Ellida sees this before her husband does. She does not ask for a divorce — "I care nothing for such formalities" — but for both of them, "of our own free will", to release each other. And she explains: "I will not hide behind the fact that I am the wife of another man; nor make the excuse that I have no choice, for then it would be no decision."

Half an hour before the steamer's last bell, Wangel does what neither his wife nor the audience expects: "And so — so I cry off our bargain at once. Now you can choose your own path in perfect — perfect freedom." And he adds the essential thing: "for now you can choose in freedom, and on your own responsibility, Ellida." She repeats it as if tasting the words: **"In freedom, and on my own responsibility! Responsibility, too? That changes everything."**

She stays, and her explanation fits the whole tail: "I could have seen it — gone out into it, if only I myself had willed it. I could have chosen it. And that is why I could also renounce it." The Stranger leaves with the words: "There is something here stronger than my will." Nobody cut the bond — it lost its power the moment there was a choice.
Ibsen adds three last touches, and each answers a card of the tail.

ul: **To The Hermit:** "To think that now we can live wholly for one another —" Wangel begins, and Ellida finishes: "And with common memories. Yours, as well as mine." Two separate pasts become a common language.

**To The Devil:** Ellida calls her stepdaughters "ours" — "They who are not mine yet, but whom I shall win." The Norwegian here uses the same verb eje, "to own", as Wangel's "never possessed you". Owning has given way to winning.

**To The Lovers:** the younger daughter, seeing her father with her stepmother, whispers: "Why, she and father look exactly as if they were a betrothed couple!" After five or six years of marriage they are engaged for real for the first time.

paragraphs: Lisovskaya lists among the tasks of a couple with The Lovers what Ibsen lays out scene by scene. Learning to love oneself inside the couple — and Ellida voices the formula of this task: "Better the meanest work — better the poorest life — after one's own choice." The insecurity that breeds jealousy and control — Wangel, whose first words on learning about the Stranger are: "Only to think that all these three years you have cared for another man… Not for me — but for another!" Dependence on family — Ellida, who for years has lived amid another family's memories and says: "I haven't a key to give up." Idealisation — "I am not what you took me for." And the ability to get through a hard experience together — their son's death, which they could not talk about.

sections.h2: Waite's cards: a ring with two chains and the sun at its zenith
paragraphs: The cards on the site have their own artwork, but Waite's description of his deck (1909) contains details that read like stage directions to The Lady from the Sea.

ul: **The Devil.** "There is a ring in front of the altar, from which two chains are carried to the necks of two figures, male and female." One ring and two chains — the key-ring with two rings thrown into the sea. Ibsen wrote his scene twenty years before the deck, and the coincidence proves nothing, but it makes the mechanism visible: a single knot holds both.

**The Lovers.** "The sun shines in the zenith" — no shadow falls on the couple. Waite calls VI "the card of human love" and, in the same breath, "a mystery of the Covenant". In our reading this is the key to the main task: a covenant in the biblical sense is an agreement made openly and willingly. The Devil binds with a bargain, The Lovers with a covenant.

**The Moon** (the values of a third of these couples). "The path between the towers is the issue into the unknown", and what crawls out of the water "strives to attain manifestation… but as a rule it sinks back whence it came". Ellida takes leave of the Stranger in almost these words: "To me you are as one dead — who has come home from the sea, and who returns to it again."

**The Hanged Man and The World** (the couple's centre). Wen notes that the crossed legs of the hanged man reappear in the figure of The World and concludes that "it is the hanged man who shall attain the fulfillment of the World card". For this tail the centre is always one of these two cards.

sections.h2: Clues in the numbers
paragraphs: The 9-15-6 tail occurs in roughly one couple in 82 (1.217%) and ranks 28th among the 97 couple tails. Going through every date since 1900 shows things about it that three numbers alone do not.

**The middle adds itself up.** In a couple's matrix the middle is not derived from the outer numbers: each point is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. Yet here 9 + 6 = 15 works out with no reduction, just as in a personal tail, where the middle is calculated exactly that way. That is why the order 9-15-6 also occurs for a single person — for 1,559 dates since 1900; that is a different calculation with different roles for the points, and the site has a separate article on it. In a couple it helps to read the equation backwards: 15 − 9 = 6. Take the silence out of the bond and a choice remains. This is our reading, not a rule of the method.

**Nobody brings their own Devil to the middle.** Numbers 13–22 in a couple's point come only from an exact sum, so the 15 in the middle is always the sum of two smaller personal middles. There are three recipes: 6 + 9 (43.9% of couples), 5 + 10 (28.2%) and 7 + 8 (27.9%). In our reading these are three ways of binding oneself: one partner's desire and the other's silence (The Lovers and The Hermit), a rule and circumstances (The Hierophant and The Wheel of Fortune), drive and a contract (The Chariot and Justice). The Wangels' marriage resembles the third recipe — a bargain honestly kept by both sides.

**The Devil is born between two people.** In no such couple do both partners have The Devil in their personal tails; in 44.3% of couples neither has it in the personal tail, and in 17.6% it is absent from all fifteen main points of both personal matrices. A tie that exists in neither person alone appears only in the couple — as in Ibsen, where there is no villain and yet there is a chain.

**The Devil may already be hiding in the entry.** In a third of couples (33%) the Hermit at the entry is made of personal entries 15 and 21 — one partner's Devil and the other's World: 15 + 21 = 36 → 9. The quiet a couple starts from sometimes already contains what it will turn into.

sections.h2: Centre and values: what holds the couple while it travels the tail
paragraphs: The couple's centre is the atmosphere between the two, what is not on show. With the 9-15-6 tail the centre comes in only two kinds.

**The Hanged Man — in 77.8% of couples.** Waite lists among its meanings wisdom, trials, sacrifice and intuition, and warns that in this card "all the significance is veiled". The atmosphere of such a couple is suspension: everything seems in place, but much is unnamed, and one partner carries the union for years. On the bright side Lisovskaya describes tact, attention and the ability to sense each other at a distance; on the dark side, the one who holds the relationship together with all their strength and receives reproaches in return. These are two sides of the same quiet. Wen calls the archetype of The Hanged Man "the wounded healer", and Wangel, a medical man who helps his wife at the cost of his own pain, fits the phrase literally. A centre of 12 is made of personal centres 4 + 8, 5 + 7 or 3 + 9.

**The World — in 22.2% of couples.** No individual ever has 21 at the centre: this atmosphere exists only in a couple. Almost always (in 21.2% of all such couples) it is made of personal centres 9 and 12 — one partner's Hermit and the other's Hanged Man. Waite's list for The World includes "voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place" — everything the Stranger offers with his cabin on the steamer and everything Wangel offers when he plans to take his wife away to the sea. On the bright side The World's atmosphere is full acceptance and a shared philosophy of life; on the dark side, in Lisovskaya, many secrets and illusions about the relationship. The World inside a couple holds as long as it is not mistaken for escape.

**The couple's values — The Hermit (66.7%) or The Moon (33.3%).** Values are what the union exists for, and here the tail comes full circle. In two thirds of couples The Hermit appears twice: at the entry and in the values. What the couple began with as a hiding place has to become its chosen value: time of one's own, a place of one's own, a deep conversation — but as a home, not as a locked arbour. In a third of couples the value is The Moon. Wen recalls that tides are caused by the pull of the moon and writes that under this card "there is an external invisible force pulling on the Seeker", one the Seeker "must understand and work in harmony with". In the final scene Wangel tells his wife: "your mind is like the sea — it has ebb and flow." The value of such a couple is not the absence of a pull towards the unknown, but the ability to live with it together.

sections.h2: Example calculation: 11.02.1976 and 04.07.1975
paragraphs: The partners' personal tails are 9-9-18 and 18-6-6. Neither of the two has The Devil at all — not in the tail, not at any other point of their personal matrices. It appears only in the sum.

The middle here is exactly the first recipe: The Hermit in the middle of one partner's personal tail and The Lovers in the middle of the other's. One partner's silence plus the other's desire. The couple's centre is The World (personal centres 9 and 12), the values are The Moon; this is the rarest pairing of centre and values for this tail, about 9% of couples.

The rest of the matrix repeats the tail. The Hermit also stands at "What to create together", "Home and things" and "Parents together" — four nines in all. The Lovers stand at "What fills", "Path to prosperity" and "What you teach" — four sixes. The Devil, absent from both partners, also stands at "Image of the couple": it is both the hidden middle of the road and what other people see; in Lisovskaya, The Devil in the image on its bright side is a vivid, passionate, unusual couple. Lisovskaya advises adding up repeats: four nines give 36 → 9, three Worlds (the centre, "Way into money", "What connects") give 63 → 9, two Moons ("Where it sparks" and the values) give 36 → 9. Everything comes back to The Hermit. In this couple the quiet sounds from every corner, and the tail shows what it can become.

sections.h2: How a couple lives 9-15-6 and what changes the script
paragraphs: The circle of this tail turns quietly. Two people carefully avoid the sore spot — that is the entry. What goes unsaid takes shape as unwritten terms, and each holds on to the union not because they choose it but because "that's how things are" — that is the middle. The way out is neither a break-up nor a new vow, but what Wangel did: lift the condition and ask again.

ul: **Say the bargain out loud.** Each unwritten clause — "I provide, you don't ask", "I put up with it, you don't leave" — should be talked through by both and decided anew: kept by free will or cancelled.

**Tell solitude from hiding.** Time and a place of one's own are The Hermit's bright side; a shared life where each sits in a separate arbour is its dark side. The test is simple: after the quiet, is there a wish to talk, or to hide further?
**Don't hold on by forbidding.** "I won't allow it" strengthens the pull; the question "are you staying?" weakens it. In Ibsen freedom is not a trick but a risk, and that is why it works.
**Choose the small things together.** Keys, money, a room, summer plans — decisions made by two, not inherited from an earlier life.
**Gather common memories.** "Yours, as well as mine": each one's past is not a hiding place but part of the common language.

paragraphs: The ending of the play is the strong version of the tail. In the first act the painter Ballested says he has settled in the town because he feels "united to the place by the bonds of time and habit". In the last he insists that people, unlike the mermaid, "can acclimatise themselves". Ellida corrects him: "In freedom they can, Mr. Ballested." Wangel adds: "And when they act on their own responsibility, dear Ellida." The same house, the same fjord, the same husband — but what holds them now is not habit but choice.

sections.h2: 9-15-6 and 9-6-15: the same cards in another order
paragraphs: The same numbers form one more couple tail — 9-6-15, the most common of all (4.627%, roughly every 22nd couple). There The Lovers are the middle of the road and The Devil is the main task: the couple travels through choice and learns not to turn love into a bond. With 9-15-6 it is the other way round: the bond is the road, and the choice is where the couple has to arrive.

ul: **9 · The Hermit — entry to the task.** This is where the couple starts and what it wants together: quiet, depth, a corner of its own where nothing needs explaining. It is also their common language — tact, hints, deeds instead of words. When the time comes to talk, the same quiet turns into resistance.

**15 · The Devil — middle of the task.** This is how the couple travels the road: through a bond. What goes unsaid thickens into unwritten terms — "that's how it turned out", "that's how it has to be", "where would we be without each other".
**6 · The Lovers — main task.** To cancel the bargain in order to make a union: to choose each other aloud, freely and on their own responsibility — and to learn to love themselves inside the couple.

intro: A couple's tail does not predict events or pass verdicts: it describes a task two people live through together. The evidence lies in the cards themselves, in the books about them and in the numbers.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 9-15-6 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of a couple's matrix: The Hermit at the entry to the task, The Devil in the middle, The Lovers as the main task. The couple starts from a shared wish for quiet and care, passes through unwritten agreements and attachment, and learns to choose each other freely and openly.

faq.q: Is the 9-15-6 tail a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A tail does not predict events or grade a union; it describes a task. The Devil in the middle is not a verdict but a stretch of the road, and the way out is written into the same three cards: the free choice of The Lovers.

faq.q: How is the 9-15-6 tail calculated in a couple's matrix?
faq.a: Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. For the dates 11.02.1976 and 04.07.1975: entry 9 + 18 = 27 → 9, middle 9 + 6 = 15, main task 18 + 6 = 24 → 6.

faq.q: How is the couple's 9-15-6 tail different from a personal 9-15-6 tail?
faq.a: The numbers are the same, but the calculation and the roles differ. A personal tail is calculated from one date and speaks about the person; a couple's tail is built from two matrices and describes the task of the union. A reading of one cannot be carried over to the other.

faq.q: How rare is the 9-15-6 tail among couples?
faq.a: Roughly one couple in 82 (1.217%), 28th place among the 97 couple tails. The centre of such couples is The Hanged Man (77.8%) or The World (22.2%), the values are The Hermit (66.7%) or The Moon (33.3%).

The 9-15-6 tail tells exactly this story: The Hermit at the entry, The Devil in the middle, The Lovers as the main task. The outer numbers add up to the middle with nothing left over, 9 + 6 = 15: **silence plus desire makes a bond**.

There are no quarrels, because there are no conversations in which a quarrel could happen. What goes unsaid does not disappear — it piles up.

report.h3: The Devil that speaks in the words of freedom

report: In the middle of the tail the unsaid becomes an agreement. Ibsen has two. The first is a vow: ten years earlier a sailor put his ring and Ellida's small ring on a key-ring and threw them into the sea, declaring that now they were wedded to the sea. "Had you no will of your own, then?" — "Not when he was near." The second agreement is the marriage itself, made out of loneliness and need. Neither was truly chosen.

The strangest thing is the language of this middle. The Stranger once called himself Friman, which in Norwegian sounds almost like fri mand, "a free man". He does not claim Ellida by right: "she must come freely". The husband answers with a ban — "You have no right to choose — no right without my permission" — and admits himself: "Never, never possessed you quite." **A bond that calls itself freedom holds hardest of all.** The ban only strengthens the pull: "You can indeed keep me here! … But my mind — all my thoughts, all the longings and desires of my soul — these you cannot bind!"

For a couple with this tail the bargain is usually humbler and quieter. First "let's not talk about it", then clauses nobody signed: "I provide, and no questions are asked", "I put up with the silence, and nobody leaves", "it's too late to change anything". **Each clause is reasonable on its own. Together they are a chain, and both of them hold it.** Wen writes that The Devil "does not necessarily mean the Seeker is entirely to blame". There is no villain in this middle — only an agreement two people take part in.
If control in a relationship reaches threats or violence, it is no longer a matter for reading cards: real help is needed — a local emergency number or crisis line.

report.h3: From inside a cage, nobody can choose the cage

report: The main task is The Lovers, and it is a choice. Not falling in love, but a decision to be together, made freely and aloud. While the bargain holds, no such decision exists. Ellida sees this first: "I will not … make the excuse that I have no choice, for then it would be no decision."

Half an hour before the steamer sails, the husband does what nobody expects of him: "I cry off our bargain at once," and then: "now you can choose in freedom, and on your own responsibility, Ellida." Ellida repeats it as if tasting the words: "Responsibility, too? That changes everything." And she stays. Her explanation fits the whole tail: "I could have chosen it. And that is why I could also renounce it." The Stranger leaves with the words "There is something here stronger than my will." **Nobody cut the bond — it lost its power the moment there was a choice.**

Part of the same task is learning to love oneself inside the couple. Ellida voices its formula: "Better the meanest work — better the poorest life — after one's own choice." Beside it stand the insecurity that breeds jealousy and control, and dependence on another family's ways: after years in her husband's house she says, "I haven't a key to give up."

report.h3: What changes the script

ul: Name the unwritten clauses aloud and decide anew: keep them by free will or cancel them.
Tell solitude from hiding: Wen distinguishes turning inward to seek light from withdrawing to lick wounds. After the quiet there should be a wish to talk, not to hide further.
No holding on by forbidding: "I won't allow it" strengthens the pull, while the question "are you staying?" weakens it.
Make the small choices together — keys, money, plans — instead of inheriting decisions from an earlier life.
Gather common memories. At the end the husband begins, "To think that now we can live wholly for one another —" and Ellida finishes: "And with common memories. Yours, as well as mine."

report: The younger daughter, seeing her father with her stepmother, whispers: "Why, she and father look exactly as if they were a betrothed couple!" After years of marriage they are engaged for real for the first time. In the first act the painter Ballested says he has settled in the town, "united to the place by the bonds of time and habit"; in the last Ellida corrects him: people can settle in — "In freedom they can". The same house, the same fjord, the same husband — but what holds them now is not habit but choice.

seo.title: Karmic tail 9 18 18 compatibility: The Hermit and two Moons
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 18 18 compatibility: what The Hermit and two Moons mean in a couple's tail, a middle no personal chart has, and the key in Pushkin's Snowstorm.

items.title: The 9-18-18 karmic tail in compatibility: one secret shared by two
items.short: Three cards, and two of them are the same: The Hermit, The Moon, The Moon. And the middle is one that a personal chart can never have. In compatibility, the 9-18-18 tail is the story of two people who come together over silence, pass through a fog of guesses and learn one main thing: to say out loud what each of them keeps to themselves. The secret of this tail is that the thing each partner guards as a wall between them often turns out to be shared.

sections.h2: A middle that no personal chart can have
paragraphs: The first clue is arithmetic. In a personal chart nobody chooses the middle of the tail: it is the sum of the two outer numbers. An entry of 9 and a task of 18 would give 9 + 18 = 27 → 9, and the tail would come out as 9-9-18. The couple's middle is different: 18. It is not derived from the outer numbers. Every point of a couple's chart is the sum of the matching points of the two personal charts, so the couple's middle is the sum of the partners' middles. The Moon in the middle is something the two people bring with them.

Most often they bring the same pattern. In 65% of couples with the 9-18-18 tail, both partners have the same personal tail, 18-9-9. Another 23% come from the combination 18-3-12 with 9-15-6, 9% from 18-6-15 with 9-12-3, and 2% each from two rare combinations with no 9s or 18s at all (15-8-11 with 21-10-7, and 21-4-10 with 6-14-8). The tail itself occurs in roughly one couple in 81 (1.228%) and ranks 27th of the 97 couple tails.

In the main case the numbers perform a swap. The personal tail 18-9-9 begins with The Moon and continues with The Hermit. Add two such tails together and the two Moons give The Hermit at the couple's entry (18 + 18 = 36 → 9), while the two Hermits give The Moon in the middle and in the main task (9 + 9 = 18). This is not a reading of the personal tails, which have roles of their own; it is simply how the numbers add up. But the picture is striking: what each partner brings as their own Moon becomes the couple's shared quiet, and what each brings as their own quiet becomes the couple's shared fog.

Hence the first guess about the plot. This couple is often made of two people who carry the same thing. There is a story in which two people carry not just a similar pattern but one and the same secret, and do not know it.

sections.h2: The Snowstorm: a wedding at which nobody saw a face
paragraphs: Pushkin finished The Snowstorm (Metel) on 20 October 1830 at Boldino. He was engaged and cut off from his fiancée by cholera quarantines; in a letter to her he complained, in French, that their marriage seemed always to be fleeing before him. The story he wrote that autumn is about a wedding the bridegroom cannot reach.

The end of 1811. Seventeen-year-old Maria Gavrilovna, who, as Pushkin puts it in T. Keane's 1916 translation, "had been brought up on French novels, and consequently was in love", agrees with Vladimir, a poor sub-lieutenant, to marry him secretly in the church of a nearby village. On the night of the elopement a snowstorm rises. The bride is driven to the church, while the bridegroom circles the fields all night and at dawn finds the church locked.

In the morning Masha comes down to tea as if nothing had happened, and that night she falls into a fever. Her parents decide that fate cannot be escaped and consent to the marriage, but they receive "a half-insane letter" from Vladimir: he joins the army, is badly wounded at Borodino and dies in Moscow. Masha turns down every suitor and keeps his books and drawings. Some years later a wounded colonel of the Hussars, Bourmin, appears in the district: quiet, attentive, silent. They plainly love each other, but he does not propose and she does not hurry him.

The denouement comes by the pond, under a willow. Bourmin declares his love and at once announces "an insurmountable barrier" between them: he has been married for nearly four years and does not know to whom. At the beginning of 1812 a snowstorm led him, an officer passing through, into an unfamiliar village; in the church he was taken for the late bridegroom, and he stood at the altar with a girl he did not know, "impelled by an incomprehensible, unpardonable levity", as he later says. When they were told to kiss, she cried out "Oh! it is not he! it is not he!" and fell senseless. The last words of the story belong to Masha: "My God! my God! <…> then it was you! And you do not recognize me?"
That is the whole secret. For years two people kept one and the same secret from each other. Each believed it was a wall between them, and it was their wedding.

sections.h2: Entry 9: the quiet they meet on
paragraphs: Point M, Entry to the task, is what the couple wants together, what they agree on and what language they speak. The same point also sits in the sphere Relationship and common language. In 9-18-18 it holds The Hermit, and Pushkin portrays it more precisely than any handbook. Suitors circle Maria Gavrilovna, "but she gave not the slightest hope to any of them", and when her mother urged her, she "shook her head and became pensive". Bourmin "seemed to be of a quiet and modest disposition", he had "a spirit of decorum and observation", and "whatever she said or did, his soul and eyes followed her". The noisy suitors withdrew. Two people remained, who had recognised each other by their pensiveness.

This is how the couple's entry looks in life, too. From the first meetings both are comfortable being silent side by side. Nobody asks "what are you thinking about?", each has a corner and a time of their own, and love shows in deeds rather than words: a cup of tea made while the other was working, a blanket laid over someone without a word. The unspoken agreement goes something like this: "no prying into each other's souls". For two careful people this is a gift. At last there is someone close who will not break the door down.

But the entry to the task stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. In Pushkin both are held back by silence, and both honestly. Bourmin does not propose because he is married. Maria Gavrilovna does not expect him to, because, as she will say, "I could never be your wife." In Waite's list of divinatory meanings The Hermit opens with the words "Prudence, circumspection". Here they are at their very best, and it is precisely they that hold the wall up. The quiet the couple came together on is the same quiet that keeps them from saying the main thing.

A couple with The Hermit at the entry usually moves slowly, taking its time from the first kiss to the wedding. In Pushkin this order is turned inside out. The wedding took place nearly four years before the first kiss, and the kiss itself stays beyond the last line: in the church Bourmin "was about to kiss her", and it went no further.

sections.h2: Middle 18: each writes a novel about the other
paragraphs: How does the couple travel from the quiet to the task? Pushkin answers in a single sentence: "the silence of the young Hussar excited her curiosity and imagination". That is the passage from 9 to 18. The Hermit is silent; The Moon makes things up.

Maria Gavrilovna goes through the versions like a fortune-teller through cards: "Was it timidity, inseparable from true love, or pride, or the coquetry of a crafty wooer?" and, "after long reflection", settles on timidity. Wrong. Bourmin, too, knows her secret in advance: "I know <…> I know that you once loved, but death and three years of mourning…." Also wrong. Both "know", and both are mistaken. In Wen, The Hermit reversed describes someone who "thinks he or she knows best" and "prefers to rely on his or her own mistakes and experience than to learn from others". There are no reversed cards in the matrix, but the words "I know" in Bourmin's mouth are an exact portrait of this trap: one's own lamp lights up the guess so well that there seems no point in asking.

For Waite The Moon is "life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit", and from the first page Pushkin keeps his heroine in this light: the French novels, the plan to elope that was "very congenial to the romantic imagination of Maria Gavrilovna", the scene by the pond where she awaits the declaration "with a book in her hands, and in a white dress: a veritable heroine of romance". She even lets the conversation drop on purpose to hasten the denouement; Pushkin calls this her voennye deistviya, her "military operations" (Keane softens it to "stratagem"). Among the reversed meanings of The Hermit, Waite lists "policy". This is not deceit but stage direction. Each writes a novel about the other and waits for the other to play their chapter.

Even the neighbours take part. They "spoke about the marriage as if it were a matter already decided upon", or, in Pushkin's Russian, as of "a thing already done", and they were literally right: the wedding had taken place long before, though they had no idea how right they were. Where The Moon is, rumours follow, and rumours are sometimes more accurate than those who spread them think.

The sharpest scene of the middle is the fever. Maria Gavrilovna "divulged her secret during her delirious ravings", but "her words were so disconnected" that her mother understood from them only what she already believed: her daughter was in love with Vladimir. The truth, spoken in a fog, is heard as a familiar story. Living couples do this all the time. What one finally manages to say in tears, in a quarrel or late at night in hints, the other hears as confirmation of a novel they wrote long ago.

In everyday life the middle of 9-18-18 looks like this. She has been quiet for a week. He runs through the explanations: work, tiredness, himself, someone from the past. To ask would break the agreement about not prying, so he does not ask. She notices his coolness and decides he is tired of her. Both behave reasonably, only on invented data. Resentment arrives from a story that never happened, and a quarrel flares up out of nothing.

There is one more detail. In a personal chart the middle lies on the straight road from entry to task: it is their sum. This couple's middle has left the road. In Pushkin both men lose their way. The snowstorm leads Vladimir into the fields, where "earth and sky became confounded", and Bourmin's driver "drove past the place where we should have come out upon the road". What brings Bourmin out of the storm is a light: "I saw a light in the distance, and I ordered the driver to proceed towards it." The middle 18 is not a wrong turn but the route itself: this couple travels to its task off the road, guided by a small light.

sections.h2: Main task 18: "It is not he!" and "Then it was you!"
paragraphs: Point D is the couple's main task, and it is read mostly through its minus: what the two of them fail at and what they need to learn. The minus of The Moon as a task is an image formed at the start and one day collapsing, feelings hidden as if they were weakness, jealousy and resentment aimed at imaginary people. In Pushkin the image is formed quite literally. Bourmin enters "the church, which was feebly lit up by two or three tapers", the bride sits "in a dark corner of the church", and the witnesses "only occupied themselves with her". She expects one face, sees another and cries: "Oh! it is not he! it is not he!"

Nearly four years later the same woman says of the same man: "then it was you!" Between those two exclamations lies the main task of The Moon. The first is the collapse of an image: this is not the one I imagined. The second is recognition: it is you, the real one. A 9-18-18 couple learns to move from the first to the second: not to run away at the moment the image collapses, but to wait until the person shows through it.

Waite's list of divinatory meanings for The Moon ends with the word "error". The whole plot of The Snowstorm is an error, the wrong bridegroom, that turns out to be right. Pushkin even attaches a proverb to it. Deciding to give Masha to Vladimir, her parents console themselves with the saying that "a woman cannot ride away from the man who is destined to be her husband", and the narrator jabs at once: "Moral proverbs are wonderfully useful in those cases where we can invent little in our own justification." The Russian proverb literally says that you cannot ride round your destined one on horseback, and it comes true word for word, only about another man: the destined one arrived by post-horses through the snowstorm, while Vladimir, with his own horse, never got there. That is how The Moon errs. The feeling is real; its address is invented.

The conversation by the pond shows how this tail works. Bourmin: "there still remains a grave duty for me to perform — to reveal to you a terrible secret which will place between us an insurmountable barrier…." Maria Gavrilovna interrupts: "That barrier has always existed." Both are right. The barrier existed, and it was their wedding. What each hid as a wall was the very thing that bound them.

Wen distinguishes two kinds of secret: "The High Priestess suggests secrets that a person is withholding; The Moon represents secrets of the natural world, the hidden condition of the Seeker's situation that will reveal itself in time." The Snowstorm has both. Each kept quiet about their own story: those are High Priestess secrets. But the main thing, that they were husband and wife, neither of them knew: that is The Moon's secret, and it came to light only when both had told their own. In our reading, this is where the secret of 9-18-18 lies. What each partner in such a couple keeps quiet about, an old guilt, the fear of not being who one seems, a story that would supposedly spoil the image, often concerns them both. Once spoken, it does not drive them apart but brings them together: it becomes clear where the two of them really stand.

And Masha's last line is not a statement but a question: "And you do not recognize me?" They had seen each other every day and did not recognise each other, because each was looking at an image: she at the hero of a novel, he at a nameless wife from a dark church. The main task of The Moon in this couple is recognition. To see the living person where one is used to seeing one's own guess.

sections.h2: A mirror, a candle and two places at the table
paragraphs: Pushkin left the key to The Snowstorm right above its first line: an epigraph from Zhukovsky's Svetlana, a ballad about fortune-telling at Yuletide. A table is laid in the girl's room, and on it stand, in our translation, "a mirror with a candle; / two places laid at the table". At midnight the girl looks into the mirror to see her destined bridegroom: "Dark the glass; and all around / deathly silence lies; / with a trembling flame the candle / barely sheds its light…"

The two objects of the fortune-telling are the two cards of this tail. The candle is The Hermit's light, small and its own. The mirror is The Moon's light, reflected. The two places at the table are the couple. And in Svetlana's dream the bridegroom is silent the whole way: "'Why so silent, love?' / Not half a word in reply: / he gazes at the moonlight, / pale and full of gloom" (our translation). These four lines hold the whole of the 9-18-18 tail: a question asked into silence, and a loved one who looks at the moon instead of answering.

For the epigraph Pushkin took the stanzas about the sledge and the lonely church, and where Zhukovsky has a black coffin standing in the middle of the church and "the friend is silent", he put a row of dots. His church in the snowstorm is for a wedding, not a funeral. The ballad itself ends with a moral that suits the story too: "Here misfortune is a lying dream; / happiness, the waking" (our translation).

Pushkin had used the same ballad for an epigraph before, for the fifth chapter of Eugene Onegin, where Tatiana tells her fortune. There are lines in it that could hang over this tail: "She turns a mirror on the moon; / but in the dark glass all alone / the mournful moon is trembling…" (our translation). You look in the mirror for the face of your destined one, and you see the moon. That is how The Moon works in the middle and the task of this couple: looking into the other, each sees reflected light, that is, their own guesses.

sections.h2: The cost: care that becomes a wall
paragraphs: If the couple stays in the middle, the tail shows itself in its minus, and its cost is a quiet one. Nobody shouts or lies. Two decent people simply spend years shielding each other from their secret. Masha turned down every suitor. Bourmin has been married for years without a wife: "I have no hope of ever discovering the woman upon whom I played such a cruel joke." Both live beside an image rather than a person. Tenderness is held back as if it were weakness. Each is sure the other would not understand, and the very agreement about not prying keeps them from finding out.

In her reading of The Moon reversed, Wen makes a hard observation: "The repressed latent will always surface, and any strong intention to repress will cause a violent surfacing." There is no point in this tail waiting for the secret to dissolve on its own. The only question is whether it comes out as a conversation by the pond or as a fever after which the words are "so disconnected".

One caveat. The tail speaks of the careful silence of two equal people. If someone keeps silent out of fear of their partner, because of threats, control or violence, this is no longer a lesson of the tail but a reason to turn to a psychologist or a crisis service, and in danger to call your local emergency number.

sections.h2: The way out: "Continue: I will relate to you afterwards"
paragraphs: The scene by the pond has a moment that is easy to miss. Bourmin begins, Masha interrupts him with her barrier, and he asks her to stop: "be silent, for God's sake, be silent" (our translation). It seems The Hermit has won, and each will keep their own. And then Masha does what turns the whole plot around: "Continue: I will relate to you afterwards.... But continue, I beg of you." She puts her own secret aside in order to hear his to the end. Only because of this does she recognise her story in his.
From this come a few simple practices for a 9-18-18 couple:

ul: **Say a guess as a guess.** Not "you're tired of me", but "I've told myself you're tired of me. Is that true?".
**Don't answer "I know" to what hasn't been said yet.** Bourmin's costliest mistake fits into two words.
**Hear the other person out.** Put your own "but in my case" off until "afterwards".
**Name at least the outline.** "There's something I find hard to talk about" is no longer a wall but a door.

**Announce the silence out loud.** The right to withdraw remains, but with an explanation: "I need some time alone, it's not about you." For The Moon, withdrawing is a way to recover, not a lack of love, and the partner needs to know that.
**Check the image against the person.** From time to time ask yourself what you know about them and what you have made up.

paragraphs: For the resolution of The Moon's confusion Wen has a formula borrowed from Flannery O'Connor: "everything that rises must converge". Two Hermits climb, each their own mountain, and The Moon promises that the roads will meet. In the strong version of this tail the couple loses neither its quiet nor its mystery. It can still be silent side by side, keeps discovering something new in the other year after year and understands the other without words. But its fog is shared, not dividing: the two of them look out of one window, not each into a mirror of their own.

sections.h2: Worked example: 14.09.1975 and 14.09.1975
paragraphs: The clearest example is two people born on the same day, 14 September 1975. Their personal charts are identical: day 14, month 9, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22, karmic task 14 + 9 + 22 = 45 → 9, centre 14 + 9 + 22 + 9 = 54 → 9. Each has the personal tail 18-9-9: entry 9 + 9 = 18, middle 18 + 9 = 27 → 9, task 9. The couple's points are added pair by pair:

The middle is not recalculated from the outer numbers: 9 + 18 would give 9, while the couple has 18, the sum of the two personal middles. A couple can see its own tail in the compatibility reading from two dates.

In this couple The Moon also stands in the centre (9 + 9 = 18), in the sphere What to create together, and in the couple's values. This is an extreme case: two identical charts double every point. Across all couples with the 9-18-18 tail, the couple's centre is The Moon in two cases out of three (66.8%) and The Hermit in the rest (33.2%). In the couple's values it is the other way round: more often The Hermit (70.3%), less often The Moon (29.7%). No other arcana appear at these two points in such couples. In a typical couple the fog lives in the atmosphere, and the quiet in what the union exists for.

sections.h2: 18-9-18 and 18-18-9: the same numbers in a different order
paragraphs: The 18-9-18 tail (0.963% of couples, centre almost always The Moon, 91.1%) enters through The Moon: the couple is brought together by mystery, enchantment, a story like a novel. The path runs through The Hermit's quiet, and the task is The Moon again. The 18-18-9 tail (0.221% of couples, centre usually The Hermit, 82%) enters and travels through The Moon, and sets The Hermit as the main task: learning not to hide from each other in a shell while still respecting the other's solitude. In 9-18-18 everything begins with quiet, the fog grows out of it, and the task is to bring it into the light.

ul: **M · Entry to the task — 9, The Hermit.** What the couple wants together: a quiet in which nothing has to be explained, an unhurried pace, respect for the other person's closed door. Glances and pauses are also the language in which the two of them come to terms.
**N · Middle of the task — 18, The Moon.** How the couple travels: through guesswork. Each explains the other's silence with a story of their own, and the stories grow faster than words.

**D · Main task — 18, The Moon.** What to learn: to bring what is hidden into the light, to hear the other person out, and to recognise the living person behind the image that has formed in one's head.

intro: What follows is an investigation: what is written in the numbers themselves, what Waite and Wen say about the cards, and why Pushkin's The Snowstorm explains this tail best of all, living it out from the first line to the last.

faq.q: What does the 9-18-18 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail with The Hermit at the entry to the task and The Moon in the middle and in the main task. The couple comes together over quiet and respect for each other's boundaries, passes through guesses and things left unsaid, and learns to bring what is hidden into the light: to talk about feelings, not to second-guess the other, to check the image of the partner against the partner.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a couple?
faq.a: No. The tail shows a task, not a verdict: the method gives no compatibility percentages and predicts no events. The strong version of 9-18-18 is a couple that can both be silent side by side and talk, and whose mystery is shared rather than dividing.

faq.q: Why is the middle of the couple's tail 18 and not 9?
faq.a: The couple's points are not derived from the outer numbers: each is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts. The couple's middle is the sum of the partners' middles, most often 9 + 9 = 18. In a personal chart the middle equals the reduced sum of entry and task, 9 + 18 → 9, which is why there is no personal 9-18-18 tail.

faq.q: Can this tail be read through the partners' personal tails?
faq.a: No: a personal tail has different points and different roles. The personal tails only show what the sum was made of. Most often, in 65% of such couples, both partners have the same personal tail, 18-9-9.

faq.q: How do I find my couple's tail?
faq.a: Enter both birth dates into the compatibility calculator. The three numbers appear in the sphere The couple's karmic tail; read them in the order Entry to the task, Middle of the task, Main task.

report: In Pushkin's The Snowstorm two lovers tell each other of an insurmountable barrier, and both are right: the barrier was their own wedding, which neither of them knew about. The 9-18-18 tail, with The Hermit at the entry, The Moon in the middle and The Moon in the main task, tells exactly this story. **The secret each partner guards as a wall often turns out to be the very thing that binds them.**

The plot fits into a few lines. On the night of a secret elopement a snowstorm drives the bridegroom off the road, and into "the church, which was feebly lit up by two or three tapers", a stranger, an officer passing through, walks in his place and stands at the altar with the bride. When they are told to kiss, she cries "Oh! it is not he! it is not he!" and falls senseless. Some years later Maria Gavrilovna meets Bourmin. They love each other and say nothing: she is sure she can never become his wife, and he is married and does not know to whom. For years the two keep one and the same secret from each other.

report.h3: The quiet they meet on is the quiet that holds the wall

report: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together and the language in which it comes to terms. The Hermit stands here. Maria Gavrilovna turned down every suitor, and when her mother urged her, she "shook her head and became pensive". Both are comfortable being silent side by side, nobody asks "what are you thinking about?", love shows in deeds, and the unspoken agreement goes something like this: "no prying into each other's souls". For two careful people this is a gift. But the same wish turns into resistance. In Pushkin both are held back by an honest silence: he does not propose because he is married, and she does not expect him to, because she is bound by the same thing. In Waite's list The Hermit opens with the words "Prudence, circumspection"; here they are at their very best, and it is precisely they that hold the wall up.

report.h3: The Hermit is silent; The Moon makes things up

report: Pushkin describes the passage from quiet to fog in a single sentence: "the silence of the young Hussar excited her curiosity and imagination". Maria Gavrilovna goes through the versions, "Was it timidity, inseparable from true love, or pride, or the coquetry of a crafty wooer?", and settles on timidity. Wrong. Bourmin, too, knows her secret in advance: "I know <…> I know that you once loved". Also wrong. **Both "know", and both are mistaken.** In Wen, The Hermit reversed is someone who "thinks he or she knows best": one's own lamp lights up the guess so well that there seems no point in asking.

The fever scene is sharper still. In her delirium Masha "divulged her secret", but her mother understood from her words only what she already believed. The truth, spoken in a fog, is heard as a familiar story. In everyday life the middle of this tail looks like this: she has been quiet for a week, he runs through the explanations, work, tiredness, himself, someone from the past, and does not ask, so as not to break the agreement. She notices his coolness and decides he is tired of her. Both behave reasonably, only on invented data.

report.h3: "It is not he!" and "Then it was you!"

report: The main task is The Moon again, and Pushkin fits it into two exclamations by one woman about one man. The first, in the dark church, is the collapse of an image: this is not the one I imagined. The second, nearly four years later by the pond, is recognition: "then it was you!" **A 9-18-18 couple learns to move from the first to the second**: not to run away when the image collapses, but to wait until the person shows through it.

The conversation by the pond shows the whole mechanism. Bourmin is about to place "between us an insurmountable barrier", and Maria Gavrilovna interrupts: "That barrier has always existed." Both are right. Wen distinguishes the secrets of The High Priestess, "secrets that a person is withholding", from those of The Moon, "the hidden condition of the Seeker's situation that will reveal itself in time". Each kept quiet about their own story, but the main thing, that they were husband and wife, neither of them knew, and it came to light only when both had told their own. What such a couple keeps quiet about, an old guilt, the fear of not being who one seems, often concerns them both.

Pushkin left a key to the story: an epigraph from Zhukovsky's Svetlana, a ballad about Yuletide fortune-telling. On the table stand "a mirror with a candle; / two places laid at the table": the candle is The Hermit's light, the mirror The Moon's reflected light, the two places the couple. And in the dream the bridegroom is silent: "'Why so silent, love?' / Not half a word in reply: / he gazes at the moonlight". The last line of The Snowstorm is a question, too: "And you do not recognize me?" They had seen each other every day and did not recognise each other, because each was looking at an image.

report.h3: "Continue: I will relate to you afterwards"

report: The way out is hidden in the same scene. Bourmin asks Masha to be silent, and it seems each will keep their own. Then she says: "Continue: I will relate to you afterwards.... But continue, I beg of you." **She puts her own secret aside in order to hear his to the end**, and only because of this does she recognise her story in his. Hence a few simple practices for such a couple:

ul: saying a guess as a guess: "I've told myself you're tired of me. Is that true?";
not answering "I know" to what has not yet been said;
hearing the other person out and putting one's own "but in my case" off until "afterwards";
naming at least the outline: "there's something I find hard to talk about" is no longer a wall but a door;
announcing the silence out loud: "I need some time alone, it's not about you."

report: The tail speaks of the careful silence of two equal people. If someone keeps silent out of fear of their partner, because of threats, control or violence, this is a reason to turn to a psychologist or a crisis service, and in danger to call a local emergency number or crisis line.

In the strong version a couple with this tail loses neither its quiet nor its mystery. It can still be silent side by side and understands the other without words. But its fog is shared, not dividing: the two of them look out of one window, not each into a mirror of their own.
