seo.title: Karmic tail 9 21 21 compatibility: The Hermit and two Worlds
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 21 21 compatibility: two people become each other's shelter, then a whole world, and their main task is the wider world. Read through John Donne.

items.title: Couple's karmic tail 9-21-21: how two people become each other's hermitage and a whole world
items.short: The Hermit at the entry and The World twice over — an odd set for two people: one card about solitude, two about the whole wide world. In the couple's tail 9-21-21 this is not a contradiction but a plot. First the two become each other's shelter, then a whole world for two, and the main task turns out to be the big world: friends, roads, change, other people's eyes.

sections.h2: The stanza that holds the whole tail
paragraphs: Donne's "The Canonization" is a poem about two people whom the world condemns for their love. The poet's answer: one day they will be made saints, and the lovers of the future will pray to them. The last stanza is that prayer (spelling modernised from Grierson's 1912 edition):

And thus invoke us: "You whom reverend love / Made one another's hermitage; / You, to whom love was peace, that now is rage; / Who did the whole world's soul contract, and drove / Into the glasses of your eyes / (So made such mirrors, and such spies, / That they did all to you epitomize) / Countries, towns, courts: beg from above / A pattern of your love!"
The stanza moves in three steps, in the order of the tail 9-21-21.

First comes "one another's hermitage". A hermitage is a hermit's dwelling, a cell in the wilderness where people went to leave the world; Russian has an exact word for it, pustyn. Love made the two a hermitage **for each other**: they did not retreat to a cell — each became a cell for the other. This is The Hermit at the entry.

Then comes the whole world, shrunk to the size of a pupil. Countries, towns and royal courts fit into the eyes of two people: they learn the world through each other and need nothing more. This is The World in the middle: the couple lives inside a universe of its own.

And finally come those who arrive later, with a request for a pattern. The world again, but someone else's now: people beyond the threshold who might gain something from this love. This is the main task — a World that is not inside the pupil but out there.

In Russian the stanza gains an extra layer: the word mir means both "peace" and "world", so "love was peace" reads at once as calm and as a universe. And the word hermitage has a Russian destiny everyone knows: the Hermitage in St Petersburg. Catherine the Great conceived it as a cosy private retreat for herself, and it grew into a museum filled with art from all over the world. A hermitage that holds a world is not just a figure of speech.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: "For God's sake hold your tongue, and let me love"
paragraphs: "The Canonization" begins not with a prayer but with a shout: "For God's sake hold your tongue, and let me love." The poet goes on to list what the uninvited adviser could do instead: grow rich, study, seek a post, court the great, gaze at the King's face — the real one or the one stamped on a coin. Anything, as long as he lets them love. "Alas, alas, who's injured by my love?" Soldiers still find wars and lawyers still find litigious men, "though she and I do love."

This is how The Hermit sounds at the entry to the couple's tail. The wish is shared: to be left alone. Not out of hostility to people, but because, together, it is finally quiet. In daily life it looks ordinary. Friends hear about the engagement after the rings are bought. The third invitation of the month is politely declined, and both are glad. A conversation that started at dinner ends at three in the morning. Each has a corner and a time of their own, and the other does not barge in. Love is shown in deeds: a fixed tap, a scarf that somehow ended up in the bag, knowing when to fall silent. Every step is taken slowly — from the first kiss to a shared key.
The light in such a hermitage is their own, and they pay for it themselves. Donne has a line for this: "We're tapers too, and at our own cost die."

But the entry point stands on the line of tasks, and Lisovskaya warns that the same wish can turn into resistance. Donne knew this shadow too — in another poem, "The Good-Morrow". The lovers ask themselves what they did before love: "Or snorted we in the seven sleepers' den?" In the old legend, seven young men of Ephesus hid in a cave from persecution and slept there for centuries. When one of them went down to the town for bread, his coins gave him away: they had been struck under a long-dead emperor. The hiding place worked too well. The world moved on, and they were left with money in their pockets that nobody would take. In Donne the cave is life before love, but the image also fits what the hermitage itself can become.

This is the entry on the minus side: a hermitage where the two do not withdraw but hide. Problems pile up in silence, because any hard conversation would break the quiet. Each sits in a shell and calls it respect for boundaries. Being together feels uncomfortable at times, but stepping outside is more frightening.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: one little room becomes an everywhere
paragraphs: In the same "The Good-Morrow" the two wake up from the cave and look at each other:

And now good morrow to our waking souls, / Which watch not one another out of fear; / For love, all love of other sights controls, / And makes one little room an everywhere. / Let sea-discoverers to new worlds have gone, / Let maps to other, worlds on worlds have shown, / Let us possess one world, each hath one, and is one.

Donne lived in the age of the first atlases, when ships came back from the New World with new coastlines for the maps. He answers a whole era: we have no need to sail, everything is here. **One little room becomes an everywhere** — that is The World in the middle of the task, how the couple lives the path from the wish for quiet to the main task.

In life, the room turns into a universe gradually. The two develop a language of their own: pet words, nicknames, jokes there is no one to explain to. Their philosophy — how to spend, how to rest, what to believe — fits so well that there is almost nothing to argue about. Chores are split down the middle. Each accepts the other whole, even on bad days. Often The World is literal: the couple moves to another city or another country, lives between two addresses or through work trips, and misses each other more after every separation.

Next Donne offers an image that maps exactly onto the numbers: "My face in thine eye, thine in mine appears… Where can we find two better hemispheres, / Without sharp north, without declining west?" Two faces in two pupils — two hemispheres of one globe. The tail says the same: The World plus The World, 21 + 21 = 42, which reduces to 6. The Lovers. They stand in the centre of the chart for every single couple with the tail 9-21-21.

The line "each hath one, and is one" is about two universes, not one. The couple holds together as long as it remembers this: its world is made of two wholes, not two halves. Donne adds a formula of the old philosophers: "Whatever dies, was not mixed equally." Mixed equally means that neither has dissolved in the other.

The middle has an oddity that only shows up in the calculation. A personal chart never has such a middle: by the personal tail formula, The Empress would stand between The Hermit and The World — house, garden, household (9 + 21 = 30 → 3). The couple has The World in that place. The two walk the path not through a house but through a universe — through something neither of them has alone.

sections.h2: Main task: "She is all states, and all princes, I; nothing else is"
paragraphs: The main point of the tail is the third, and it is read mainly through the minus: what the couple does not manage and what it needs to learn. For 9-21-21 Donne has a warning poem, funny and arrogant. It is called "The Sun Rising".

The lovers chase away the sun that has looked in at the window: "Busy old fool, unruly Sun, / Why dost thou thus, / Through windows, and through curtains call on us?" Let it go and wake late schoolboys and the King's huntsmen. "Love, all alike, no season knows, nor clime, / Nor hours, days, months, which are the rags of time." And further: "She is all states, and all princes, I, / Nothing else is." The sun is even offered an easier job: since its duty is to warm the world, let it warm the two of them, because they are the world. "This bed thy centre is, these walls, thy sphere."

This is **The World shrunk to four walls** — the main task on the minus side. In Lisovskaya it stands for very down-to-earth things, and a couple recognises them as scenes. Friends drop away one by one: people stopped inviting them, since they would only say no. One partner's hobby — a choir, football, a pottery class — becomes "not ours", first teased, then mocked. One partner patiently re-educates the other into the shared worldview. Evenings repeat like Groundhog Day, and any novelty, from a holiday to moving the furniture, is met as a threat. Agreement does not come: each pulls the blanket to their own side and does not hear the other. And when the closed world gets cramped, someone slams the door — comes back — and slams it again. Together, apart, together.

"The Sun Rising" argues not only with the sun but with the card itself. Waite gives the old names of The World: "The World, the Universe, or Time." The lovers call time rags, yet this couple has that card twice. Two people who stop the clocks in their room are at war with their own tail. In Waite's divinatory list the same card has a reverse side — "Inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence" — and Wen writes of a person who "is afraid of change and is hesitating to take the necessary actions."

Donne knew what makes such a fortress dangerous. In "The Anniversary" the lovers are kings whom nothing can threaten: "Who is so safe as we? where none can do / Treason to us, except one of us two." In a world with nobody else in it, the threat can only come from inside. Most often this is not a loud act but a quiet one: one partner has long wanted out and says nothing, because to speak would be to wreck the universe.

Wen compares The World to the Gaia hypothesis, in which the Earth is a living organism, and writes that to fulfil an ultimate purpose a person "must embrace the spiritual dimension of the Seeker's relationship with his or her environment." For the couple this is the main task: its world has to be in a relationship with the shared one — neither under siege nor in exile.

One boundary. If one partner forbids the other friends and family, checks up on them and will not let them go, this is no longer solitude and no longer the card — it is control. That calls for a counsellor or psychologist, and in danger, a local emergency number.

sections.h2: Donne and Anne More: from "Un-done" to "no man is an island"
paragraphs: Donne was not writing from hearsay. In December 1601 the twenty-nine-year-old secretary to Sir Thomas Egerton, Lord Keeper of the Great Seal, secretly married seventeen-year-old Anne More, the niece of his employer's wife. The bride's father had Donne dismissed, and Donne and the friends who arranged the wedding were sent to prison. Donne's first biographer, Izaak Walton, writes that Donne told his wife of his dismissal by letter and added after his signature: "John Donne, Anne Donne, Un-done."

The court and a career — the world in the most literal sense — closed to them. The years that followed were that very hermitage. First Anne's kinsman, Sir Francis Wolley, took them into his house at Pyrford, where, in Walton's words, they lived "with much freedom to themselves". Then came a cramped house at Mitcham near London, full of children and cares, on very little money.

"The Canonization" and "The Sun Rising" are often read as poems about Donne's own marriage. The grounds are indirect: "The Canonization" has "my five gray hairs, or ruined fortune", and both poems have a king — and King James came to the throne in 1603, a year after the poet lost his post. No document dates these poems: they were printed only in 1633, after the author's death.

What does survive is the letters from Mitcham, and Walton quotes them in his Life. "To be no part of any body, is as to be nothing," Donne writes to a friend, and admits he will judge himself nothing unless he can be "incorporated into a part of the world". The man who declared in verse that beyond the two of them "nothing else is" was, in prose, homesick for the big world. This is the main task of 9-21-21, spoken by the hero himself: a hermitage for two does not cancel the need to be part of a whole.

Walton also describes how the family lived in those years. Wife and children stayed at Mitcham, while Donne took lodgings in London near Whitehall, where friends and business drew him, and often went back — to his family and his books: "to that place and such studies, he could willingly have wedded himself during his life." One leg stands, the other walks. This is no longer a closed room but a pair of compasses.

In 1624 Donne would write a sentence that people know even when they do not know the author: "No man is an island, entire of itself; every man is a piece of the continent, a part of the main." Hemingway took it as the epigraph for "For Whom the Bell Tolls". The road from "nothing else is" to "no man is an island" is the road of the tail 9-21-21 from its middle to its main task.

sections.h2: The compasses: a circle drawn by spreading the legs
paragraphs: Donne's most famous love poem is "A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning". Walton says it was "a copy of verses given by Mr. Donne to his wife at the time he then parted from her", when he left for France with his patron Sir Robert Drury — that was 1611. Anne did not want to let him go and, in Walton's phrase, consented "with an unwilling-willingness".
The poem opens with The Hermit's silence: "So let us melt, and make no noise… 'Twere profanation of our joys / To tell the laity our love." And it ends with a circle:

If they be two, they are two so / As stiff twin compasses are two; / Thy soul, the fixed foot, makes no show / To move, but doth, if the other do. / And though it in the centre sit, / Yet when the other far doth roam, / It leans and hearkens after it, / And grows erect, as that comes home. / Such wilt thou be to me, who must, / Like th' other foot, obliquely run; / Thy firmness makes my circle just, / And makes me end where I begun.

Here is the answer to the main task of 9-21-21. The World is no longer a room or a bed as "centre". It is **a circle that can only be drawn by spreading the legs**. Pressed together, they put a dot on the paper. The circle appears when one leg goes far and the other holds the centre, and the two are joined so that one listens for the other. A leg that runs off without a centre draws not a circle but a line: that is the together-apart pattern.

In Waite, both legs are written into one card. The upright divinatory list of The World reads "voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place"; the reversed list, "fixity… permanence". Taken apart, they mean flight or paralysis. Taken together, they make a pair of compasses: one leg walks, the other stands, and a circle comes out. This is our reading, not Waite's, but it fits a tail in which The World stands twice.

The last line also matches the numbers. "And makes me end where I begun": the main task plus the centre lead back to the entry. 21 + 6 = 27 → 9 — The World plus The Lovers give The Hermit. The couple's circle closes on the very hermitage it began with, only now they return to it rather than hide in it.

In Donne the fixed foot is the wife and the roaming one is himself: that was how things were arranged in 1611. The couple's tail does not care about sex. Either partner can hold the centre or go far, and a strong 9-21-21 couple swaps legs: today one packs for the road, tomorrow the other.

Donne describes parting in words worth remembering: "Our two souls therefore, which are one, / Though I must go, endure not yet / A breach, but an expansion, / Like gold to airy thinness beat." **Not a breach, but an expansion** — that is what the main task teaches the couple.

"The couple's values" matter here as well — the point that answers why the two are together and which path they should take. In couples with the tail 9-21-21 two cards share it almost equally: The Hermit in 51.1% and The Moon in 48.9%.

ul: **If The Hermit is in the values**, the hermitage stands twice — at the entry and at the very heart. For such a couple solitude is not a concession but a value. The task is not to give it up but to make sure each partner also has solitude of their own, so that the shared kind does not become a cage.

**If The Moon is in the values**, a line from the same "Valediction" comes to mind: "Dull sublunary lovers' love / (Whose soul is sense) cannot admit / Absence." Donne is teasing, but he is precise: to the old cosmographers the sublunary world was the world of change, where everything shifts. Wen sees in The Moon "a strong theme of conservation in the card, rather than exploration or expansion", a need to feel protected, "the tough outer shell". Waite writes of "the fears of the natural mind in the presence of that place of exit, when there is only reflected light to guide it." For such a couple one partner's departure stirs up fears and invented stories, and a conversation about the fear before the parting matters more than phone calls during it.

sections.h2: The couple's centre — The Lovers: a pattern, not an icon
paragraphs: Every couple with the tail 9-21-21 has the same centre of the chart, the atmosphere inside the couple: The Lovers, 6. Waite calls the card "The Lovers or Marriage" and writes that in its eighteenth-century form "it is really a card of married life, shewing father and mother, with their child placed between them", and that it "is said to have been entitled Simulacrum fidei, the symbol of conjugal faith". Wen starts elsewhere: "in every traditional interpretation of The Lovers, the card is about a moral choice, about choosing the right path," and only then about romance. And what it means is "partnership with one other person."

For 9-21-21 this means that the air between two worlds is a choice made anew every day. On the plus side it is sincerity, a lot of touch, decisions taken together even in small things, no secrets from each other.

On the minus side The Lovers have traps of their own, and "The Canonization" points straight at one: idealisation. A couple "canonized for love" can no longer be touched: every quarrel looks like sacrilege, every imperfection like betrayal of the pattern. Among the tasks of The Lovers Lisovskaya names perfectionism and idealising the relationship. The pattern asked for in Donne's stanza is alive, not an icon on the wall.

Wen adds one more detail to this arithmetic. For her, The Hermit and The World are both cards of the element of Earth, and in both yin energy is dominant. The Lovers are Air and yang. A quiet, heavy, earthbound tail — and a light centre where a choice is made every day.

sections.h2: Clues in the numbers: what every 9-21-21 couple shares
paragraphs: The tail 9-21-21 occurs in about one couple in 116 (0.864%) — 42nd place among the 97 couple tails. The clues in it are the same for all such couples, whatever their dates.

ul: **Both Worlds are exact sums.** In a couple's chart a number from 13 to 22 can only come from addition without reduction. In these couples the middle always adds up to exactly 21 (4 + 17, 6 + 15, 3 + 18 or 7 + 14), and so does the main task (10 + 11, 15 + 6, 12 + 9 or 13 + 8). The World does not appear "by itself" here; the two assemble it.

**The Hermit at the entry is always 27, reduced to nine.** In almost nine couples out of ten (88%) it is made of The World and The Lovers: one partner has the personal tail 21-4-10, the other 6-17-11, and 21 + 6 give 27. In the rest it is The Moon and The Hermit, 18 + 9: personal tails 18-6-15 and 9-15-6 (10%) or 18-3-12 and 9-18-9 (2%). The very rare pairing 21-7-13 and 6-14-8 again gives The World plus The Lovers. The hermitage for two is made of a world and of love.

**The centre is The Lovers in 100% of such couples.** Lisovskaya advises adding up energies that repeat: if the sum stands in the chart, it sounds in the couple. Two Worlds give 21 + 21 = 42 → 6, and the six is not an echo but the centre. The sum of the whole tail, 9 + 21 + 21 = 51 → 6, is The Lovers again.

**The entry and the centre behave as in a personal chart; the middle does not.** The main task plus the centre give the entry: 21 + 6 = 27 → 9, which is how the entry of a personal tail is always built. But the middle breaks the rule: in a personal chart it would be 9 + 21 → 3. So nobody has 9-21-21 as a personal tail — it is a tail that exists only for two.
**The couple's values are The Hermit (51.1%) or The Moon (48.9%).** Half the couples meet their first card again — where it is decided why they are together.

paragraphs: In passing, Waite is worth recalling: his Hermit "blends the idea of the Ancient of Days with the Light of the World." In the tail 9-21-21 two Worlds stand behind that light, one after the other.

sections.h2: How to calculate the couple's tail 9-21-21: an example
paragraphs: Each point of the couple's chart is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, reduced to 22. The couple's middle is not recalculated from the two outer numbers: it is added up from the partners' middles.
Take the dates 14.10.1975 and 05.11.1975. The first person's personal tail is 21-4-10, the second's is 6-17-11. Add them point by point:

The couple's tail is 9-21-21. The centre is added up from the personal centres 11 and 13, giving 6. This couple's "values" are 18, The Moon. This is the most common pairing of personal tails, 88% of all 9-21-21 couples.

sections.h2: What changes the script for a 9-21-21 couple
paragraphs: The way out is not to tear down the hermitage but to cut a door into it and learn to draw a circle.

ul: **A door on schedule.** One regular evening with guests, relatives, friends in the house. Not a duty but fresh air: a world that comes into the room stops being a threat.

**A road of one's own for each.** Each partner has something outside the couple — a trip, a circle of people, a project — and the other does not treat it as betrayal. The compasses only work when the legs are apart.
**The legs take turns.** It is not always the same person who goes off. Whoever holds the centre today may leave tomorrow.
**A ritual of return.** "And grows erect, as that comes home": the meeting after a parting matters more than the goodbye. Tell what was seen on the road, and listen to how life went at home.
**The other's world is not a province.** Ask about the partner's hobbies and plans the way one asks about an unfamiliar country, instead of reshaping them to the shared philosophy.

**A check against an outside view.** When the couple's judgements about everyone around grow too unanimous, it helps to ask a friend how it looks from outside. Eyes that act as "spies" do not see everything.
**Finishing things.** The World is the card of completion. A renovation, a trip, a joint project is better finished and celebrated than kept for years in a state of "we'll get to it".
**Talking before the trip.** Especially if The Moon is in the values: speak about the fear of separation before it, not in phone calls during it.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail: a hermitage with an open door
paragraphs: In the strong version of 9-21-21 the hermitage remains a hermitage. The two still feel best together, talk late into the night and have no need of crowds. But the room has become an everywhere not because the world was shut outside, but because it has windows and a door, and people pass through them both ways.

Such couples need no persuading to become a pattern. People come to them on their own — to sit in the kitchen, ask advice, see how it can be done. This is the last line of "The Canonization": countries, towns and courts ask the two for a pattern of their love. Waite's Hermit is the card of someone whose light others can see; in a 9-21-21 couple that light is lit for two and can be seen from the big world.
And the circle, as in Donne, ends where it began. After all the roads the couple returns to its quiet — only now this quiet is chosen, not hidden.

intro: The three cards of the tail stand in the sphere "The couple's karmic tail" and are read in order:

ul: **9, The Hermit — entry to the task.** What the couple wants together: quiet, depth, a room of their own, an unhurried pace. Everything starts from this wish, and this is also where it gets stuck: the two close off easily.
**21, The World — middle of the task.** How the couple lives the path: building a universe for two — its own language, its own philosophy, sometimes its own country on the map.

**21, The World — main task.** The main test: connecting their world to the big one. On the minus side the circle shrinks to four walls; on the plus side it widens, and people leave it and come back to it.

intro: This plot is written not only in the cards. Four hundred years ago the English poet John Donne put it into a single stanza — in order, card by card. That is where the investigation begins.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 9-21-21 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail with The Hermit at the entry and The World in both the middle and the main task. The two want quiet and shelter in each other, build a world for two, and the main test is to connect that world with the big one: friends, roads, change. It is a task for self-knowledge, not a forecast.

faq.q: Why does the couple's tail have two Worlds in a row?
faq.a: The middle and the main task are different roles. The first World shows how the couple lives the path: a universe for two. The second is the main task: that universe's relationship with the outside world. In such couples both 21s are always exact sums of the partners' points, and together they give 42 → 6 — The Lovers in the centre.

faq.q: Can 9-21-21 be a personal karmic tail?
faq.a: No. In a personal chart the middle of the tail equals the sum of the entry and the main task, and with 9 and 21 it would be a three, The Empress. A middle of 21 only appears in a couple, when it is added up from the middles of two partners.

faq.q: How can a couple tell that its tail is 9-21-21?
faq.a: Calculate compatibility from the two birth dates. The tail stands in the sphere "The couple's karmic tail": three cards — entry to the task, middle of the task and main task. For example, the dates 14.10.1975 and 05.11.1975 give exactly 9-21-21.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. The calculation gives no other couple tails made of the numbers 9, 21 and 21, so 9-21-21 cannot be confused with anything: it has only one order.

faq.q: Is the tail 9-21-21 a bad sign for a relationship?
faq.a: No. A tail does not predict events and promises nothing. It describes a task: not letting solitude for two turn into a closed circle. On the plus side the same cards make a deep, calm couple that people are drawn to.

report: The two whom love "made one another's hermitage" were promised sainthood by John Donne: the lovers of the future would pray to them. The stanza from "The Canonization" goes on — these two "did the whole world's soul contract" and drove countries, towns and courts into the glasses of their eyes, and now they are asked to beg from above a pattern of their love. Four hundred years ago Donne wrote down the tail 9-21-21 in order, card by card.

First the hermitage — The Hermit at the entry to the task: the two want to be each other's shelter. Then the whole world, shrunk to the size of a pupil — The World in the middle: the couple lives inside a universe of its own. And finally those beyond the threshold asking for a pattern — The World again, the main task: connecting their own universe to the big one.

report.h3: The quiet it all began with

report: "The Canonization" opens with a shout: "For God's sake hold your tongue, and let me love." A couple with this tail starts from the same wish — to be left alone. Friends hear about the engagement after the rings are bought. The third invitation of the month is declined, and both are glad. A conversation at dinner ends at three in the morning. Every step is taken slowly — from the first kiss to a shared key.

But the same wish can turn into resistance. Donne glimpses the seven sleepers' den: in the legend, young men of Ephesus hid there from persecution and slept for centuries, and in the town they were given away by coins of a long-dead emperor. The hiding place worked too well: the world moved on, and the money in their pockets was worthless. This is how a hermitage becomes a burrow — problems pile up in silence, because any hard conversation would break the quiet.

report.h3: One little room, an everywhere

report: In "The Good-Morrow" love "makes one little room an everywhere". Let sea-discoverers chase new worlds: "each hath one, and is one". The two develop a language of their own, a philosophy of their own, chores split down the middle; often a literal world too — a move abroad, a life between two addresses.

Then Donne sees in the eyes of the two the two hemispheres of one globe: "My face in thine eye, thine in mine appears." The numbers say the same: **The World plus The World, 21 + 21 = 42 → 6, The Lovers**. The Lovers stand in the centre for every couple with this tail. A personal chart never has such a middle: The Empress, house and household, would stand there between The Hermit and The World. The couple walks the path not through a house but through a universe that neither of the two has alone.

report.h3: "Nothing else is"

report: The main task is read through what does not work. For it Donne has a funny, arrogant poem, "The Sun Rising". The lovers chase the sun out of the bedroom, call hours and days "the rags of time" and announce: **"She is all states, and all princes, I, / Nothing else is."** "This bed thy centre is, these walls, thy sphere."

This is what The World looks like when it shrinks to four walls. Friends drop away one by one. One partner's hobby becomes "not ours" and gets mocked. One re-educates the other into the shared worldview. Evenings repeat like Groundhog Day, and any novelty is met as a threat. When it gets cramped, someone slams the door, comes back and slams it again. In "The Anniversary" Donne himself names the weak spot of such a fortress: no one can betray it "except one of us two". Most often not by a loud act, but by the silence of the one who has long wanted out.

If, however, one partner forbids the other friends and family and will not let them go, that is no longer solitude but control; it calls for a counsellor or psychologist, and in danger, a local emergency number or crisis line.

report.h3: The man who did not want to be an island

report: Donne was writing about himself. In 1601 he secretly married seventeen-year-old Anne More, lost his post and went to prison, and, as his biographer tells it, signed a letter to his wife: "John Donne, Anne Donne, Un-done." Then came years of an almost hermit's life in a cramped house near London. From there he wrote to a friend: **"to be no part of any body, is as to be nothing."** The man who declared in verse that beyond the two of them "nothing else is" was, in prose, homesick for the big world. And in 1624 he wrote the sentence everyone knows: "No man is an island, entire of itself."

report.h3: A circle drawn by spreading the legs

report: Donne found the way out in "A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning", which, his biographer says, he gave to his wife before leaving for France. There the two are the legs of a pair of compasses. One sits in the centre, the other roams far; the first "leans and hearkens after it, / And grows erect, as that comes home." And the conclusion: "Thy firmness makes my circle just, / And makes me end where I begun."

**A circle only appears when the legs are apart.** Pressed together, they make a dot. A leg that runs off without a centre draws a line. Even the last line matches the numbers: the main task plus the centre lead back to the entry, 21 + 6 = 27 → 9, The World and The Lovers give The Hermit. The circle closes on the same hermitage, only now the two return to it instead of hiding in it.

In Donne the wife stands and he himself roams — that was how things were arranged in 1611. The couple's tail does not care about sex: either partner can hold the centre or take to the road, and a strong couple swaps legs. In practice this means a regular evening with an open door, a road of one's own for each without accusations of betrayal, a ritual of return, asking about the partner's world as about an unfamiliar country instead of reshaping it to the shared philosophy. Parting for such a couple is, in Donne's words, not a breach "but an expansion, / Like gold to airy thinness beat."

There is a trap in the centre too. A couple "canonized for love" is frightening to touch: every quarrel feels like sacrilege. But the pattern asked for in the stanza is alive, not an icon. In the strong version of 9-21-21 the hermitage stays a hermitage — with windows and a door. People come to such a couple on their own, to sit in the kitchen and see how it can be done.

items.title: The 9-21-3 karmic tail in compatibility: a lighthouse above the door
items.short: The 9-21-3 karmic tail in compatibility belongs to a couple who share a lantern but for a long time have no shared home. The entry to the task is The Hermit: the two are happy on their own, with a quiet language of their own and a light only they know about. The middle of the task is The World: the couple carries that light along roads, through moves, across a whole world built for two. The main task is The Empress: to stop and grow something visible — a home, a garden, a shared venture where the light finally puts down roots.

sections.h2: The three cards of the 9-21-3 tail: what each means for a couple

head: Point
Arcanum
How it is derived
rows: 6 + 3: entries of the partners' personal tails
8 + 13 or 7 + 14: middles of the personal tails

paragraphs: The couple's karmic tail is not the personal tail of either partner. Each of its points is the sum of the matching points in two personal matrices. It is read from its main point: **D, the "Main task"** — where the couple stumbles and what it has to learn; this point is read mostly through its minus. **M, the "Entry to the task"** — the couple's shared wish, its agreements and its "common language"; with this wish the couple enters the task, and the same wish can turn into resistance. **N, the "Middle of the task"**, in our reading — how the couple lives the road from the wish to the task.

Put into one sentence: **the couple wants solitude for two, lives it as a road across the whole world, and has to learn home** — a place where its light becomes a visible harvest rather than a secret under a coat.

sections.h2: The first clue: "Have you got your lantern?"
paragraphs: In 1888 Stevenson published an essay, "The Lantern-Bearers", about a boys' game from his childhood in a fishing town on the Scottish coast. Towards the end of September, when the nights were already black, the boys bought tin bull's-eye lanterns, buckled them to their belts and buttoned their top-coats over them. There was one rule: keep the light inside. When two of them met in the dark there would be an anxious "Have you got your lantern?" and a gratified "Yes!"

Then comes about the most precise description of The Hermit to be found outside a deck: "The essence of this bliss was to walk by yourself in the black night; the slide shut, the top-coat buttoned; not a ray escaping, whether to conduct your footsteps or to make your glory public: a mere pillar of darkness in the dark; and all the while, deep down in the privacy of your fool's heart, to know you had a bull's-eye at your belt, and to exult and sing over the knowledge." And the conclusion the essay was written for: **"To one who has not the secret of the lanterns, the scene upon the links is meaningless."** From outside — wet, cold boys. From inside — heaven.

This is the entry to the task for a 9-21-3 couple. Its common language is that password. The two recognise each other by a light that cannot be seen from outside. They need no audience: an evening in one room, each busy with something of their own, is not a quarrel for them but the best kind of closeness. They have their own words, their own jokes, their own pace. They tell others about important things after the fact, once everything is decided.

Stevenson wrote down the wish itself ten years before the essay. In the autumn of 1878 he walked alone for twelve days through the Cévennes with a donkey called Modestine — by most accounts to put distance between himself and a love his friends and family disapproved of: Fanny had gone back to her husband in California. One night he slept under the pines, "between four and five thousand feet towards the stars", and wrote: "And yet even while I was exulting in my solitude I became aware of a strange lack. I wished a companion to lie near me in the starlight, silent and not moving, but ever within touch. For there is a fellowship more quiet even than solitude, and which, rightly understood, is **solitude made perfect**. And to live out of doors with the woman a man loves is of all lives the most complete and free."
That sentence holds the whole entry of the tail: not loneliness but solitude for two. And its last words already show the next card: "complete" — and Wen names the theme of The World as completion.

**Where the entry becomes resistance.** Point M stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish can work against the couple. A lantern under a coat keeps you warm, but it does not shine outward. From outside the couple looks cold and strange, and friends say "you've vanished". Inside, the unsaid piles up: each withdraws into a shell, hurt is lived through in silence, the conversation is put off, because silence counts as normal between them. Twenty years after her husband's death Fanny wrote in the preface to her diary: "Contrary to the general idea, my husband was a man of few intimate friends, and even with these he was reticent to a degree." And she admitted she had cut from the diary things pertaining to the private affairs of other persons, "and, naturally, our own". The lamp stayed under the coat.

sections.h2: The second clue: "voyage, route, emigration"
paragraphs: In Waite's divinatory list, The World carries words that read like this couple's biography: "Assured success, recompense, voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place."

In the summer of 1879 Fanny cabled Stevenson that she was leaving her husband, and in August he set off to join her without telling his parents. He sailed from Glasgow in the second cabin of the steamer Devonia, then crossed the whole of America on an emigrant train. Both parts of his account of that journey — the sea part, "From the Clyde to Sandy Hook", and the land part, "Across the Plains", published together as The Amateur Emigrant — can be read to the end without a single mention of the woman he was travelling to. He explains his choice of cabin by saying he was "anxious to see the worst of emigrant life" and "had some work to finish on the voyage". A whole ocean and a continent crossed — and the lantern still under the coat.

They married in May 1880 in San Francisco: she was forty, he was twenty-nine. They spent the honeymoon in an abandoned bunkhouse of the Silverado mine on the slope of Mount Saint Helena, high above the valley, and Stevenson named all four of them — himself, his wife, her son and the dog — "the King and Queen of Silverado", "the Crown Prince" and "the Grand Duke". Then came Davos, Hyères, Bournemouth and Saranac Lake in America. In June 1888 the family chartered the yacht Casco and sailed out of San Francisco into the Pacific: the Marquesas, Tahiti, Hawaii, then the schooner Equator, then the steamer Janet Nichol. Samoans gave Fanny the name Aolele — "flying cloud". Of the Janet Nichol cruise she would write: "perhaps the happiest period of my life".

This is the middle of the tail — **how the couple lives its road**. For a 9-21-3 couple shared solitude does not stay put: it moves house. Two such people change cities and countries easily, build a life out of different cultures, truly get to know each other on the road, and after time apart miss each other all the more. The World is their joint project: a shared philosophy, a shared map, a shared habit of looking far ahead.

But the card has a reverse side, and Stevenson wrote it down himself. On the schooner Equator he began a poem, "To My Wife", about how long it would be before she saw again a woodland lane with bramble and brier and the wayside smoke over the huts. Here instead, he writes, "from the sea the unfruitful sun shall rise", the allotted hours shall wheel in vain, and the sun shall plunge again "in the unpregnant ocean", while she has to live in the "most unwomanly bower / Of the wild-swerving cabin". The poem remained a fragment and breaks off mid-line. **The World gave this couple breadth, but not what only The Empress can give — fruit.**

The second reverse side is when the world for two closes into a wreath. The couple lives by its own rules and outsiders are not admitted; one quietly remakes the other to fit their own worldview; the days repeat like Groundhog Day; there are more secrets than conversations. Sometimes it is an endless cycle of splitting up and getting back together, where every departure is passed off as freedom. Waite's World reversed reads "Inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence." For a couple whose middle is a road, stopping means risking stagnation. That is why home is the hardest thing for it.

sections.h2: The third clue: "My house, I say"
paragraphs: The house Stevenson called "mine" was a gift. In 1885 the writer's father, Thomas Stevenson, bought a villa in Bournemouth as a wedding present for Fanny. The son had chosen its new name before they moved in. "I am now a beastly householder," he wrote to his friend Edmund Gosse on 12 March 1885. "I shall call my house Skerryvore when I get it." Skerryvore is a lighthouse on a reef off the Scottish island of Tiree, built in 1844 by his uncle Alan. Underwoods contains a poem about the house: "For love of lovely words, and for the sake / Of those, my kinsmen and my countrymen, / Who early and late in the windy ocean toiled / **To plant a star for seamen**, where was then / The surfy haunt of seals and cormorants: / I, on the lintel of this cot, inscribe / The name of a strong tower."

A lighthouse's name above the door of a home is the whole 9-21-3 tail in one gesture. **The Hermit stands at the entrance to The Empress.** The couple still lives under the sign of its lantern, while the house is already waiting for someone to start living in it.

In the same collection, right after the Skerryvore poems, there are twelve lines that hold this card's lesson. "My house, I say. But hark to the sunny doves / That make my roof the arena of their loves… Our house, they say; and mine, the cat declares…" My house and our house — that is the whole difference between The Hermit and The Empress.
The couple's main task is read through what does not work, and here the story offers a scene for every minus.

**A house that was a gift.** The Empress as a task tests whether the couple can stand on its own ground: step out from under the family's wing, live on its own money, make decisions without looking to the elders. Skerryvore was a gift from his father, and until the success of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde in 1886, according to biographers, the household's main income was a paternal allowance of £250 a year. Thomas Stevenson's fortune had been made building lighthouses: the house with a lighthouse's name lived on lighthouse money.

**A house that rests on one person.** In The Silverado Squatters Stevenson describes his day at the mine honestly and almost cheerfully: in the morning he made porridge and coffee, drew water and prepared the kindling — and that ended his domestic duties. "Thenceforth my wife laboured single-handed in the palace, and I lay or wandered on the platform at my own sweet will." A home where comfort is made by one person is also a minus of The Empress, even when it is laughed about.

**A house that eats the work.** In January 1890 the Stevensons bought 314 acres of forest on the slope of Mount Vaea on the island of Upolu and built the islands' first two-storey house there. Fanny managed the estate and worked on it herself. In November 1890 Stevenson wrote to a friend: "Our place is in a deep cleft of Vaea Mountain, some six hundred feet above the sea, embowered in forest, which is our strangling enemy, and which we combat with axes and dollars. I went crazy over outdoor work, and had at last to confine myself to the house, or literature must have gone by the board." And then the formula of the whole conflict: **"If I go out and make sixpence, bossing my labourers and plying the cutlass or the spade, idiot conscience applauds me; if I sit in the house and make twenty pounds, idiot conscience wails over my neglect and the day wasted."** The garden against the writing desk, The Empress against The Hermit — inside one person.

The same letters hold a scene of The Empress at her best. His wife had bread to bake, but between whiles she came down to weed the prickly sensitive plant in the paddock with him. And at night, as soon as he shut his eyes, he saw "endless vivid deeps of grass and weed, each plant particular and distinct" — "a phenomenon to which both Fanny and I are quite accustomed". Two people who see the same garden when they close their eyes — that is "our house". The couple had a harvest of another kind too: Stevenson recalled how he and his wife planned a joint volume of stories, for which she wrote "The Shadow on the Bed"; in 1885 their joint book The Dynamiter came out, and Lloyd, Fanny's son, later wrote three novels with his stepfather.

Wen describes the reversed Empress as effort that yields no result: "There is a sense of emptiness and no production after much work and effort." This is the main risk for a 9-21-3 couple. It invests a great deal — in travel, in conversation, in its own world — but neither the couple nor the people around it can see the fruit. What it has to learn is not love — love sits at its centre — but how to make love bear a harvest.

sections.h2: Lighthouse and house: what Waite wrote about these cards
paragraphs: This section is about the images of the Waite deck and his text; the cards on our site are drawn differently.

**The Hermit.** Waite notes that his card differs from the conventional models in one thing only: "the lamp is not enveloped partially in the mantle of its bearer". "It is a star which shines in the lantern", and The Hermit is "holding up his beacon on an eminence". The boys in Stevenson's essay hid their lanterns completely; Waite uncovered his. For a couple this is a direction of travel: from a light under a coat to a light by which others can see where to go. Stevenson, son and grandson of lighthouse builders, has the same pair of images in his two Skerryvore poems: his kinsmen toiled "to plant a star for seamen", and in "Skerryvore: The Parallel" he sets his sunny house of brick and pine, where "the truant gull / Skims the green level of the lawn, his wing / Dispetals roses", beside a granite tower that stands in the sweep of winds, "Immovable, immortal, eminent." The last word, eminent, shares its root with eminence — the height on which Waite places his Hermit. House and lighthouse are the two halves of one parallel, the M and D of this tail.

**The Empress.** In Waite's description "a field of corn is ripening in front of her, and beyond there is a fall of water", and **"the sceptre which she bears is surmounted by the globe of this world"**. The World the couple travelled through in the middle of the tail becomes, in The Empress's hand, a small globe. A home does not cancel the road — it takes the world into its palm. Waite's divinatory list for The Empress begins "Fruitfulness, action, initiative, length of days". Set beside The World reversed ("Inertia, fixity, stagnation") this answers the couple's main fear: for Waite, home is not immobility but action.

**The World and The Lovers.** For Waite The World is "the perfection and end of the Cosmos, the secret which is within it". The Lovers, the atmosphere of every such couple, read in his list as "Attraction, love, beauty, trials overcome."

Wen has a clue of her own. She assigns all three cards of the tail the same element, Earth, and notes that yin energy is dominant in each. She reads The Hermit's lantern both as light for others and as the sign of "someone who sees the world through his or her own light" — a ready-made bridge from 9 to 21. And of the reversed Empress she writes that "the element of Earth is missing and is the cause of imbalance" and of lack of results. A tail standing wholly on Earth, in a couple that lives on the road, is an exact portrait of the task: come down to earth.

sections.h2: Where the 9-21-3 tail comes from: the numbers as evidence
paragraphs: **Rarity.** This tail occurs in roughly one couple in 4,389 — 95th place out of the 97 possible couple tails.

**Two partners, two doors.** The 9-21-3 tail comes from only two combinations of personal tails: 3-13-10 with 6-8-20 (70% of such couples) or 3-7-22 with 6-14-8 (30%). In both cases one partner's personal tail begins with The Empress (3) and the other's with The Lovers (6). The couple's entry is their sum: 6 + 3 = 9. **This couple's solitude is made of love and home.** There is no point asking which of the two is "responsible" for the home: the couple's points mean something different from personal ones, and the task belongs to both.

**An atmosphere made from the road.** At the centre of the chart every such couple has The Lovers, 6 — in 100% of cases. The same six comes from the middle plus the main task, 21 + 3 = 24 → 6, and from the whole tail, 9 + 21 + 3 = 33 → 6. Our reading: this couple's love is what you get when the road and the home are added together.

**A middle no single person has.** In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is the sum of its ends: 9 + 3 would give 12, The Hanged Man. In a couple the middle is added up from the partners' middles, and it comes out as 21 — the same digits reversed. That is why 9-21-3 never occurs as a personal tail. Where one person with these ends would hang in a pause, the couple goes out into the world.

**The couple's values.** In the sphere "The couple's values", 84.9% of such couples have The Moon and 15.1% The Hermit. The Moon is night, dreams and imagination, and for the Stevensons it too worked for the shared home: in "A Chapter on Dreams" he says the plot of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde came to him in a dream after "one of those financial fluctuations". Lisovskaya advises Moon couples to accept a partner's occasional need to withdraw as a way of recovering, not as a lack of love — and for a tail that begins with The Hermit this is especially apt.

**The tail made of the same numbers.** A couple can also have 9-3-21 — almost 15 times more often (0.339% of couples). There The Empress is in the middle and The World is the main task: first home, then going out into the world. The atmosphere differs too: at the centre 89.6% of those couples have The Devil, and only 10.4% The Lovers.

sections.h2: Worked example: 7 August 1976 and 4 January 1976
paragraphs: Take two people born on 7 August 1976 and 4 January 1976. The first has the personal tail 6-8-20 and a centre of 4. The second has 3-13-10 and a centre of 20. The couple's points are added pairwise, and a sum above 22 is reduced by adding its digits.

In "The couple's values" these two have The Moon, 18 — like most couples with this tail. This is the first of the two combinations: The Empress opens the personal tail of the person born on 4 January 1976, The Lovers open that of the person born on 7 August 1976, and their sum opens the couple's tail.

sections.h2: How the circle closes
paragraphs: The shadow of this tail runs in a circle, and there is no villain in it — only a habit of hiding the light.

First the couple finds a refuge in each other: nobody else is needed, evenings for two beat any company. Then the refuge starts to move: new cities, trips, projects, relocations — or the opposite, a closed world with its own rules. Every movement feels like life, and any stop feels like stagnation. Years pass, and one day it turns out that a great deal has been invested and there is nothing to show: no home that has become "ours", no venture that has grown, no circle of people who know these two. The couple carries its dissatisfaction back into its shell, and the lantern is buttoned under the coat again.
The way out of the circle is not to love solitude less, nor to stop travelling. The way out is The Empress: to give what the couple already has some soil and a harvest.

ul: **Open the lantern at least a hand's width.** Say out loud what exactly makes their "two of us" so precious, and let two or three people into their world.
**Give the road a home port.** Travel from home, not instead of home: a place to come back to is not a defeat of freedom.
**Make "ours" visible.** A garden, a shared venture, a tradition, a book, a house the couple fits out with its own hands — something that grows and can be shown.
**Share the home fairly.** Comfort that rests on one person is a minus of The Empress, even if it is joked about.
**Stand on your own ground.** Your own money, your own decisions, a calling of one's own for each partner — not only a shared one.

sections.h2: "Home is the sailor, home from sea"
paragraphs: Stevenson wrote down the strong version of this tail too — in "Requiem", from the same Underwoods. Its last lines run: "Home is the sailor, home from sea, / And the hunter home from the hill." The hill is The Hermit's height. The sea is The World's road. Home is The Empress. The three cards of the tail stand in two lines, and all three converge on one word.

This couple had two answers to the question of happiness. His, in a letter from Vailima: "I was only happy once; that was at Hyères." The house at Hyères was called La Solitude; that name dates his poem "To a Gardener", in which he asks for onions, artichokes and asparagus to be grown for his supper and promises himself "A book, a taper, and a cup / Of country wine". Hers, about the voyage on the Janet Nichol: "perhaps the happiest period of my life". He was happy in solitude with a garden, she on the road. Vailima became an attempt to fit both kinds of happiness under one roof: a house on a mountain above the sea where two people weed together.

The story has a small rhyme as well. On the night under the pines in the Cévennes Stevenson woke thirsty and drank the water from his tin. The name Vailima means "water in the hand" in Samoan: in an old tale a woman brought water in her hand to a thirsty companion. The popular rendering "five waters" is considered a mistake: the word lima means both "hand" and "five".

And the whole tail once fitted into a single rainy day. In the summer of 1881 at Braemar in Scotland, kept indoors between four walls by the weather, Stevenson was painting in watercolours with a schoolboy, Fanny's son, and drew the map of an island. He labelled it "Treasure Island". Solitude between four walls, a whole world on a sheet of paper, a family in which a book is growing — 9, 21 and 3 at one table. **A couple with this tail is strong when its lantern does not hide from the world and the world does not lead it away from home.**

intro: The riddle of this tail is written into its numbers. In a personal destiny matrix the middle of the tail is the sum of its two ends. Here it is the other way round: the end is made from the road. 9 + 21 = 30, and 3 + 0 = 3. **The Hermit who has travelled through The World adds up to The Empress.** The main task does not fall on the couple from outside — it grows out of the way these two live.

Someone once lived this arithmetic for real. In the spring of 1885 Robert Louis Stevenson, the author of Treasure Island, moved with his wife into a house his father had given to Fanny — and gave it the name of a lighthouse. Behind that gesture lies the whole story of Stevenson and Fanny Osbourne: a night in the mountains when he longed for a companion "ever within touch", an emigrant steamer, a shack in an abandoned mine, three vessels in the Pacific and, at last, Vailima on Samoa — a house, a garden and a large family. None of this proves the Stevensons had this exact tail: their dates are not calculated here. It is a plot in which the three cards read as one story.

faq.q: What does the 9-21-3 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail with three cards: The Hermit at the entry to the task, The World in the middle and The Empress as the main task. The couple wants solitude for two and a quiet language of its own, lives it as a shared road across the world, and has to learn home — to make its union visible and fruitful: a shared household, a venture of its own, its own ground.

faq.q: How is 9-21-3 different from 9-3-21?
faq.a: In the order of the middle and the main task. In 9-21-3 the couple first goes out into the world, and the task is home; in 9-3-21 it first builds a home, and the task is to go out into the world. 9-3-21 occurs almost 15 times more often, and those couples most often have The Devil at the centre, while 9-21-3 couples always have The Lovers.

faq.q: Why does this tail never appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is the sum of its ends: with an entry of 9 and a task of 3 it would be 12. In a couple the middle is added up from the two partners' middles, which gives 21. Such a middle exists only in a couple.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a couple?
faq.a: No. A tail passes no verdicts and predicts nothing: it shows which task the couple will find most interesting and most difficult. In 9-21-3 the atmosphere is always The Lovers, and the main task is learning to turn love and solitude into a home that grows.

faq.q: How can a couple find out whether it has this tail?
faq.a: Calculate compatibility from the two birth dates. The couple's entry to the task is the sum of the entries of the personal tails, the middle is the sum of the middles, and the main task is the sum of the main tasks; if a sum is above 22, its digits are added together. For 9-21-3 one partner's personal tail begins with 3 and the other's with 6.

report: Robert Louis Stevenson wrote the name of a lighthouse above the door of his home. "I, on the lintel of this cot, inscribe / The name of a strong tower," runs his poem about the villa in Bournemouth that his father gave to Fanny in 1885. The house was called Skerryvore, after a lighthouse on a reef built by the writer's uncle. A lighthouse above the door of a home is an exact picture of the 9-21-3 tail: The Hermit at the entry, The Empress as the main task, and between them The World — the whole road a couple travels before it walks through its own front door.

The riddle is written into the numbers too. In a personal tail the middle is made from the ends. Here it is the other way round: 9 + 21 = 30, and 3 + 0 = 3. **The Hermit who has travelled through The World adds up to The Empress.** This couple's main task does not come from outside — it grows out of the way the two of them live.

report.h3: A password between two lanterns

report: In the essay "The Lantern-Bearers" Stevenson recalls a game from his childhood. On autumn nights boys buckled tin lanterns to their belts and buttoned their top-coats over them, so that not a ray escaped. When two of them met in the dark there would be an anxious "Have you got your lantern?" and a gratified "Yes!" From outside — wet, cold boys. From inside — heaven. "To one who has not the secret of the lanterns, the scene upon the links is meaningless."

That is the entry to the task for a 9-21-3 couple. Its common language is that password: the two recognise each other by a light that cannot be seen from outside. They need no audience; an evening in one room, each busy with something of their own, is their best kind of closeness. Stevenson named it back in 1878, sleeping alone in the mountains: there is a fellowship more quiet even than solitude, and which, rightly understood, is **"solitude made perfect"**.

But the entry stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish can work against the couple. A lantern under a coat keeps them warm, but it does not shine outward. From outside such a couple looks cold and strange; inside, the unsaid piles up, because silence counts as normal between these two. Twenty years after her husband's death Fanny admitted she had cut from her diary everything about private affairs — "and, naturally, our own".

report.h3: A road where nothing grows

report: In Waite's divinatory list, The World carries words that sound like this couple's biography: "voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place". In 1879 Stevenson crossed an ocean and the whole of America to reach Fanny without telling his parents — and in his account of that journey never once mentioned whom he was travelling to. Then came the Alps, the south of France, England and three vessels in the Pacific. Fanny would call her voyage on one of them "perhaps the happiest period of my life".

This is the middle of the task: shared solitude does not stay put, it moves house. A 9-21-3 couple changes cities and countries easily and builds a whole world for two. Stevenson recorded the reverse side himself, on the schooner Equator, in a poem to his wife: "from the sea the unfruitful sun shall rise" and plunge again "in the unpregnant ocean". The poem remained a fragment. **The World gives the couple breadth, but not what only The Empress can give — fruit.** And Waite's World reversed reads "Inertia, fixity, stagnation". To a couple whose middle is a road, any stop feels like stagnation, so home is the hardest thing for it.

report.h3: Sixpence against twenty pounds

report: The main task is read through what does not work. In 1890 the Stevensons bought a forested slope on Samoa, fought the forest "with axes and dollars" and built a house. From Vailima Stevenson wrote to a friend: "If I go out and make sixpence, bossing my labourers and plying the cutlass or the spade, idiot conscience applauds me; if I sit in the house and make twenty pounds, idiot conscience wails over my neglect and the day wasted." The garden against the writing desk — The Empress against The Hermit.

The minuses of this card show in their story scene by scene. The house in Bournemouth was a gift from his father, and until the first big success the household lived on his allowance. On the honeymoon in an abandoned mine, by Stevenson's own admission, "my wife laboured single-handed in the palace". In his poem about the house everyone argues: "My house, I say", while the doves on the roof answer: "Our house". The Empress tests whether the couple can stand on its own ground, share the household fairly and say "ours" instead of "mine". Wen describes her reverse side as **"a sense of emptiness and no production after much work and effort"**: a great deal invested, and no harvest visible to the couple or to the people around it.

There is a scene of her at her best too. Between batches of bread Fanny came down to weed the prickly sensitive plant with her husband, and at night, as soon as they shut their eyes, both saw deeps of grass and weed, each plant particular and distinct. Two people who see the same garden — that is already "our house".

report.h3: Home is the sailor, home from sea

report: Waite notes that his Hermit's lamp, unlike on the older cards, is not covered by the mantle, and that his Empress holds a sceptre "surmounted by the globe of this world". The strong version of the tail is both at once: the light no longer hides under a coat, and the world travelled together fits in the hand, at home. Stevenson put it into two lines of "Requiem": **"Home is the sailor, home from sea, / And the hunter home from the hill."** The hill is The Hermit, the sea is The World, home is The Empress.
What changes the pattern for a couple with this tail:

ul: open the lantern at least a hand's width: say out loud what makes this life for two precious, and let two or three people into it;
travel from home, not instead of home;
make "ours" visible: a garden, a venture, a tradition, a book — something that grows;
share the household fairly and leave each partner a calling of their own;
live on their own money and make their own decisions.

report: The name Vailima means "water in the hand" in Samoan. What this couple has to learn is not love — love sits at its centre — but how to make love bear a harvest.
