seo.title: Karmic tail 9 3 3 compatibility: The Hermit and two Empresses
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 3 3 compatibility: The Hermit, two Empresses and The Devil at the couple's centre. Why the middle is 3, not 12, and which garden the couple must grow.

items.title: Karmic tail 9-3-3 in compatibility: a hut for two in someone else's garden
items.short: The couple's tail 9-3-3 looks like a misprint. By the personal formula, 12 would stand between The Hermit and The Empress, yet here the middle is The Empress again. The couple's story hides inside this oddity. Two people enter the union wanting to be alone together (9, The Hermit), live by growing a home and care (3, The Empress), and their main task is the same Empress taken seriously: to grow their own garden on their own ground, not to keep it secretly in someone else's house.

sections.h2: The first clue: a middle that no single person has
paragraphs: In a personal chart the tail is built as a chain: the middle equals the entry plus the main task. 9 and 3 would give 12, The Hanged Man, and a personal tail 9-12-3 does exist. A couple's tail works differently. Each of its points is found by adding the matching points of two personal charts and reducing the sum to 22. The couple's middle is not derived from its ends — it is added up from the partners' middles. So instead of The Hanged Man, who hangs and waits, the couple has The Empress in the middle, who grows.

The 9-3-3 has only one family tree. Running the site's engine through every date shows that this tail appears only in a couple where one partner's personal tail is 21-10-16 (The World, The Wheel of Fortune, The Tower) and the other's is 6-20-14 (The Lovers, Judgement, Temperance). There are no other combinations.

ul: **Entry:** The World 21 + The Lovers 6 = 27 → 2 + 7 = **9, The Hermit**.
**Middle:** The Wheel of Fortune 10 + Judgement 20 = 30 → **3, The Empress**.
**Main task:** The Tower 16 + Temperance 14 = 30 → **3, The Empress**.

paragraphs: Read these sums as sentences and they make a short story. The whole world plus a choice adds up to solitude for two. A turn of fate plus an inner call adds up to growth. Collapse plus measure adds up to growth again. Two different roads give the same sum, 30, and both lead to The Empress.

The tail is rare: it occurs in roughly one couple out of 3,171 (0.032%) and ranks 92nd of the 97 couple tails. It has no permutations: neither 3-9-3 nor 3-3-9 ever appears in a couple, so 9-3-3 is the only order of these numbers.

Every such couple has the same centre — 15, The Devil. The partner with the 21-10-16 tail always has a personal centre of 5 (The Hierophant), the partner with 6-20-14 always has 10 (The Wheel of Fortune), and 5 + 10 = 15. No date ever gives 15 at the centre of a personal chart: this card appears only when two people are added together. "The couple's values" hold The Hermit in 94.2% of cases and The Moon in 5.8%.

There is a subtler clue too. Benebell Wen assigns an element to each card. The partners' personal tails carry all four: for her The World is Earth, The Lovers Air, The Wheel, The Tower and Temperance Fire, and Judgement, by her choice, Water. Yet everything the couple ends up with — The Hermit, both Empresses, The Devil at the centre and The Hermit in the values — is, in Wen's words, a card that "the element of Earth governs". Out of two people's air, fire and water comes solid earth. Keep this in mind: in the story below, everything comes down to ground.

sections.h2: The story: "Six Records of a Floating Life"
paragraphs: In 1877 a manuscript was printed in Shanghai. The brother-in-law of the writer and publisher Wang Tao had found it at a stall selling second-hand books. Its author, Shen Fu of Suzhou, was born in 1763, worked as a private secretary to officials, traded and sold paintings. He was never famous. The manuscript was called "Six Records of a Floating Life" (浮生六記), but only four records survived: of wedded joys, of idle pleasures, of sorrows and of travels. The fifth and sixth are lost, and every "rediscovered" sequel turned out to be a forgery. In English it is available, among other versions, in the translation by Leonard Pratt and Chiang Su-hui (1983); the quotations below are our own translations from the Chinese.

Shen Fu opens by saying he has no intention of inventing anything: he merely records "true feelings and true events". The first record is entirely about his wife, Chen Yun, and their twenty-three years of marriage. For its time this was unusual: a husband writing about his wife as his closest friend, the one he shared books, jokes and outings with.

The title is a clue as well. The words "floating life" come from Li Bai, from his preface to poems about a spring feast in a garden: "Heaven and earth are an inn for the ten thousand things; time is a traveller passing through a hundred generations. And floating life is like a dream — how much joy is in it?" Li Bai was Yun's favourite poet. A book about a couple who spent their whole life in houses that were not theirs took its title from a line about an inn.
We do not know both partners' exact birth dates, and we do not assign the 9-3-3 tail to this couple. But their story can be read by these cards almost word for word.

sections.h2: The Hermit at the entry: porridge hidden for one
paragraphs: Shen Fu was thirteen when he told his mother: "If you are choosing a wife for me, I will have no one but Sister Shu." His mother slipped a gold ring off her finger, and the children were betrothed. That same winter, at the wedding of Yun's cousin, the boy grew hungry late at night. The maids brought him dried jujubes, too sweet. Then Yun secretly tugged at his sleeve and led him to her room. She had warm porridge and little side dishes hidden there. He had barely picked up his chopsticks when her cousin burst in: "I asked you for porridge just now and you said it was all gone. So you were hiding it for your bridegroom!" Yun burned with shame and fled, and the house roared with laughter. After that, whenever Shen Fu visited, he never saw her: she hid.
This is where the 9-3-3 tail begins: **care that is hidden from everyone except one person.** The porridge is The Empress, the hiding of it is The Hermit.

The second scene is the wedding, five years later. At supper the bride eats only meatless food, and Shen Fu realises she has kept a meatless vow for several years. He counts back the years: the vow began when he had smallpox. She had never said a word about it. "Now I am safe and sound — may my sister end her vow?" Yun answered with her eyes and a nod.

This is how the couple's common language worked. For twenty-three years, meeting in a dark room or a narrow passage, they would take each other's hand and ask, "Where are you going?" — hearts pounding as if someone might see. Yun, in her husband's words, could "read my eyes and understand my brows". They had their own jokes. Yun had taught herself to read from Bai Juyi's "Song of the Pipa", and called Li Taibai her favourite poet. Her husband laughed: Bai Juyi is your first teacher, Li Taibai your kindred spirit, and I, Sanbai, your husband — how lucky you are with the character 白, "white"! "I'm afraid I'll be writing nothing but 'white characters' from now on," Yun replied. In Suzhou "white characters" meant slips of the brush. Only the two of them got the joke.

This is no chance resemblance to the card. On the couple's chart, the point of entry to the tail is the very same point as "Common language" on the relationship line. Every 9-3-3 couple has The Hermit as its common language. Lisovskaya describes such a couple as if she had read this book: love here is shown by deeds rather than words, and other people hear about events once everything has already happened.

Today it looks like this. The couple has its own words that nobody else understands. One quietly pays the other's share and never mentions it. At a party they exchange a glance and both know it is time to go. The best weekends are the ones without guests. The family hears about plans once everything has been decided.

In Waite's list of divinatory meanings for The Hermit, "prudence, circumspection" stand beside "dissimulation". It is an uncomfortable word, yet it fits this couple exactly, except that here the pretence is kind. Yun tells her cousin there is no porridge left. She goes with her husband to Lake Tai, telling the household she is visiting her family. She dresses as a young man so she can see the flower festival at the temple with him. These are small screens with which two people fence off their "we" from the big house.
Wen offers another way to read The Hermit's lantern: someone "who sees the world through his or her own light", walks their own path and "is not a traditionalist". So was this marriage.

The entry stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish becomes resistance. When gossip started in the house, Yun forbade her husband to defend her: "Better that my father-in-law scold me than that I lose my mother-in-law's favour." And she never explained herself. **The silence that protected the two of them at first later leaves them without a voice.** Lisovskaya says it plainly in The Hermit's minus: problems pile up in silence.

sections.h2: The Empress in the middle: tea in a lotus flower
paragraphs: Shen Fu's second record is about how the couple lived, and all of it belongs to The Empress. Its last sentence is about tea. In summer, when lotuses are just beginning to bloom, they close at night and open in the morning. Yun would put a pinch of tea into a small silk bag and lower it into the heart of a flower. In the morning she took it out and brewed it with rainwater, and the fragrance was beyond compare.

This is the best image of the tail's middle: what is closed to everyone at night is steeped in fragrance by morning. The Hermit gives silence and closedness, The Empress turns them into fragrance and fruit.

Yun knew how to make plenty out of poverty. Her husband liked a drink with friends but disliked a crowd of side dishes, so Yun made a box in the shape of a plum blossom: six white dishes joined with lacquer into a single flower, "as if a plum blossom painted in ink had settled on the table". She sewed his caps and socks herself. In place of a railing on the veranda she hung an old bamboo blind. Her rule was called "deal with things as they are". Once, so that friends could drink hot tea among the flowering rapeseed, she hired a street seller of wontons together with his portable stove. "Without you none of this would have happened," the guests said.

Together they built a tiny mountain of stones on a tray. Vines grew on it, white water flowers bloomed around it, and the couple decided: "A pavilion over the water here, a thatched hut there. Here one could live, here fish, here gaze into the distance." Shen Fu writes that they talked as if they were about to move in. One night cats knocked the tray over, and both of them wept. The Hermit's hut, built by The Empress's hands, existed only on a tray.

For a 9-3-3 couple today the middle of the road looks much the same. Renovating a rented flat with their own hands, seedlings on the windowsill, Sunday lunches, a shared cat, a shared project. Their home turns warm out of almost nothing, and the two of them are happy in it.

But the same record contains a sentence that is easy to miss. Shen Fu explains why he puts cut chrysanthemums in vases instead of growing them in pots: **"our household had no garden, and I could not grow them myself."** Every garden this couple had belonged to someone else. The room by the Canglang Pavilion was in his father's house. The cottage by Jinmu Bridge was rented for a month. The tower where they were happiest was a friend's house. Then came the village house of Yun's sworn sister and two rented rooms in Yangzhou.

The book's best-known confession was made at Jinmu Bridge. An old woman let them a room in a cottage surrounded by vegetable plots. The neighbours, who lived by their gardens, brought fish and vegetables and refused money, so Yun made them shoes. Chrysanthemums were planted along the fence. And Yun said: "Some day we will build a house here. We'll buy ten mu of vegetable garden around it, the hired hands will grow melons and greens — enough for firewood and rice. You will paint, I will embroider — enough for poetry and wine. Cotton clothes and rice with vegetables — joy for a whole life, and no need to plan distant journeys." Shen Fu adds: "I agreed with all my heart. Now, even if such a place were found, my dearest friend is gone."
The whole tail is in that sentence. Solitude for two with a vegetable garden around it — 9 and 3 as a single wish. And the land that was never bought is the third card, the main task.

In The Empress reversed, Wen sees effort that bears no fruit and names the cause: **"The element of Earth is missing."** To succeed, the person "must commit to harnessing Earth qualities". This is where the solid earth into which this couple's elements add up comes in: it turns out to be the task.

sections.h2: The main task: whose garden is it?
paragraphs: Lisovskaya says the main task of a tail is read through its minus: what the couple fails at and what it has to learn. For The Empress in this role, all the difficulties are earthly — family and money — and the lesson is grown-up practicality. Shen Fu's third record, "of sorrows", shows it in living people.

It opens with a saying: in family life nothing works without money. The couple had no money of its own. At first they pawned things and patched one hole with another, then they stopped making ends meet. The house began to whisper.

Shen Fu's father asked Yun to handle the family's letters. Her mother-in-law suspected her of writing the wrong things and took the letters away from her. The father decided Yun looked down on the job. Yun kept silent.

The father wished to take into service a woman from home, "so that our speech would match" — in effect, a concubine. The son wrote to his wife in secret, and Yun found a girl. While it was still unclear whether the match would work out, the mother-in-law was told that a neighbour's girl had come to play. When the truth came out, the mother-in-law turned against her daughter-in-law.

The brother-in-law borrowed money from a neighbour's wife and asked Yun to stand surety, and when the debt was called in, he claimed to know nothing. Yun wrote to her husband about it and, while she was at it, advised quietly persuading the concubine to say she was homesick. The father opened the letter and read that his wife was called in it "your honoured mother" and he himself "the old man". His verdict: "Your wife borrows behind her husband's back, slanders her brother-in-law, calls her mother-in-law 'your honoured mother' and her father-in-law 'the old man' — what outrage!" The couple was turned out of the house.

Put these stories together and a pattern emerges: **every misfortune in the third record grew out of hidden care.** A quiet note, a kindness done under a pretext, a surety nobody spoke of. There is a bitter detail too. Twelve years earlier Shen Fu had carved two seals with the words "to be husband and wife in life after life" — "for our letters to each other". The disaster came through a letter read by a third person. The language of two, read aloud in the elders' house, sounded like insolence.
Wen warns about this in The Hermit reversed: such a person "can be petulant to elders".

A few years later it happened again from the other side. Shen Fu stood surety for a friend who borrowed fifty taels of silver — it felt awkward to refuse. The friend vanished with the money, the lender shouted at the gate, and the father gave his son three days to move out.

In Lisovskaya's minus of The Hermit there is a line about money: such a couple needs someone to spur its material ambitions. In this couple Yun tried to be that person. When a relative invited Shen Fu to go trading in the south, saying he was "waiting for the dew to cook his rice", Yun backed him: "While your parents are still strong and you are young, better to work hard once than to count firewood and rice for ever." She packed her own embroidery and Suzhou wine-soaked crabs for him to sell.

The second time, they left at the fifth watch, before dawn, in secret, so that the neighbours would not laugh and the lender would not stop them. Before setting out they ate warm porridge. Yun, smiling with an effort, said: **"Once a bowl of porridge brought us together, now a bowl of porridge parts us. If anyone wrote a play about it, they could call it 'The Tale of the Porridge'."** The circle closed: the tail began with porridge hidden for one and ended with porridge eaten in secret before leaving someone else's house.

For a 9-3-3 couple today the main task looks mundane. The two live with one set of parents "until they've saved up", and the years go by. Decisions about the renovation are made by whoever owns the flat. One secretly borrows from a parent to plug a hole in the budget. The other signs as guarantor for a friend because refusing feels awkward. A joke the two of them share sounds rude in front of the family. And each time the couple hides instead of speaking.

The task is not to love less or to grow harder. It is for the garden to get ground of its own: their own budget, their own home, or at least their own rules where they live. Decisions made together and announced, not hidden. Money talked about before it runs short. And each partner with work of their own: Lisovskaya advises a couple with The Empress that each should find fulfilment separately.

sections.h2: The Devil at the centre: two people chained only to each other
paragraphs: The centre of the 9-3-3 tail is 15, and it is always made of 5 and 10: one partner's Hierophant and the other's Wheel of Fortune. The Hierophant is rite and rule, The Wheel a turn of fate. Together they give the card of being bound.

In "Six Records" there is a scene where this sum is all but spoken aloud. In the first months of marriage Yun was comically ceremonious: she thanked him for every trifle and rose to take a fan from his hand. Her husband lost patience: "Do you mean to bind me with ceremony?" She flushed: "Most quarrels in the world begin with jokes." They made peace, and from then on her "forgive me" and "how could I dare" turned into mere filler words between them. Rite tied to fate became a knot only the two of them understood.

Then came the seals. On the night of Qixi, the seventh night of the seventh moon, Shen Fu carved two seals with one inscription — "to be husband and wife in life after life". On his seal the characters were raised and printed red on white. On hers they were cut in and printed white on red. One vow in positive and negative.

Then Yun suggested they pray to Yue Lao, the Old Man under the Moon, the god of marriages. A painter they knew made his portrait: in one hand a red thread, in the other a staff with the book of marriages hanging from it. They hung it in their inner room and burned incense before it at every new and full moon. In the Tang tale that gave rise to this god, the old man reads his book by moonlight and carries a bag of red cords with which he ties the feet of future spouses. "Once this cord is tied, there is no escaping it."

Waite sees in The Devil "the chain and fatality of the material life", and in the divinatory list he adds a qualification: fatality is "that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil". His book also has a detail that is easy to walk past. Describing older decks, he approves of Papus's version, in which the human figures on The Devil card are **"yoked only to each other"**: "The author may be felicitated on this improved symbolism." That is the centre of the 9-3-3 tail. No third party holds the chain; it is stretched between the two. The same goes for the centre 15: neither of the two has it alone, it appears only in the couple.

On the plus side, such a centre means strong attraction and the ability to accept the dark in the other. Shen Fu has a funny scene. Yun loved stinking fermented tofu and melon pickled in shrimp brine — things her husband loathed. He teased her: what are you, a dog or a cicada? Then she pushed a piece of the melon into his mouth with her chopsticks. He chewed holding his nose, then let go of it — and came to love it. Yun invented a sauce from the two pickles called "double freshness". "Where the heart is gathered, even the ugly does not repel," she said.

On the minus side, the same centre becomes a room without windows. That same night of Qixi, Yun looked at the moon and asked: "The universe is so vast, and there is one moon for all. Are there two other people in the world tonight who feel what we feel?" It is beautiful, and it is also the formula of "we need no one else".

In the spring of 1803, in two rented rooms in Yangzhou, shortly before the end, Yun told her husband: "Warm cotton clothes, a full meal of rice and vegetables, harmony in a single room, as at the Canglang Pavilion and in Xiaoshuang Lou — and we would be immortals among the hearth smoke… Strive for it by force, and you draw the Creator's envy and the turmoil of the demon of love." The demon of love (情魔) — that is what she herself called the force that held them and tormented them. Shen Fu drew his conclusion: spouses must not hate each other, but neither must they be too attached, for "loving couples do not last to the end together".

The cards disagree with that conclusion. Numbers say nothing about who will live how long or how long a union will last. Lisovskaya's final thought on The Devil in a couple is different: **nobody belongs to anybody.** There is no need to love less. What is needed is for love not to become a locked room. Shen Fu blames the depth of feeling, while the tail points to two other things — silence (9) and a garden without ground (3).

sections.h2: The strong version: a house with four prohibitions
paragraphs: This couple had a happy example too, and it grew out of a collapse. After the first expulsion, Shen Fu's friend, the painter Lu Banfang, took them into his tower, Xiaoshuang Lou — roughly "the Tower of Clear Coolness". They lived there for a year and a half. Shen Fu would later call them "immortals among the hearth smoke".

This is how they lived. Yun embroidered, the old maidservant spun, the manservant sewed clothes to sell — and that fed them. Friends knew their host was poor and brought "money on a staff". That was the name for chipping in for wine, ever since the poet Ruan Xiu hung a hundred coins on his staff on the way to the tavern. Yun cooked without spending: greens, fish and shrimp took on "an unexpected flavour" in her hands. When the wine ran short, she drew a hairpin from her hair — for wine — and her face did not change. The painters came, in Shen Fu's words, "like swallows under the rafters — flying in and out as they pleased".

The house had rules. Four prohibitions: talk of ranks and promotions, of office affairs, of official examination essays, of cards and dice. The fine for breaking one was five jin of wine. And four qualities that made a guest welcome: generosity, refinement, freedom from convention and **clear quiet**. The Hermit's silence remained — but as a virtue at a shared table, not as a wall.

This is the 9-3-3 tail in its plus, and it agrees with the numbers. The main task is made of The Tower and Temperance, collapse and measure. Here the couple's best home grew right after the expulsion and was held together by "dealing with things as they are". In Waite, The Hermit's lantern says: "where I am, you also may be." In Xiaoshuang Lou the hut for two gained a door.

sections.h2: The couple's values: the old man under the moon
paragraphs: In "The couple's values", 94.2% of 9-3-3 couples have The Hermit and the remaining 5.8% have The Moon. The Old Man under the Moon, to whom Shen Fu and Yun prayed, combines both cards: an old man with a staff and a book — and the moon he reads by. This is our observation, not the teaching of the books, but it shows where this couple looks for meaning: in quiet, in depth, in what not everyone can see.

The Hermit as a value has its shadow too. After his wife's death Shen Fu took the name Meiyi, roughly "plum recluse", in memory of the Song poet Lin Bu. Lin Bu lived alone on an island in a lake and never married, and people said of him: "the plum tree is his wife, the cranes his children". The solitude the two had dreamed of together was left to one.

There is light as well. Shen Fu wrote only "true feelings and true events". Almost seventy years later a stranger found his manuscript at a second-hand book stall, and since then the hidden life of two has become a lantern for strangers. For a 9-3-3 couple the value of The Hermit lies not in hiding the light but in carrying it.

sections.h2: Example calculation: 08.01.1976 and 06.03.1978
paragraphs: A person born on 08.01.1976 has the personal karmic tail 6-20-14 and centre 10. A person born on 06.03.1978 has the tail 21-10-16 and centre 5. Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points, reduced to 22.
The middle is not recalculated from the ends: the personal formula would give 9 + 3 = 12, but the couple's middle is 20 + 10 = 30 → 3. "The couple's values" in this example are 9, The Hermit.

In this couple The Hermit also stands on the entire money line: "Way into money", "Path to prosperity" and "Where it leaks" are 9-9-9. Together with the entry to the tail (which is also "Common language") and the values, that makes five Hermits on one chart. But this belongs to the particular example, not to the tail: by our own count, the money line 9-9-9 occurs in 11.8% of 9-3-3 couples.

sections.h2: What helps a 9-3-3 couple

ul: **Don't hide the porridge.** Say care and sacrifices out loud: "I covered it", "I gave up the trip for us". Unseen kindness piles up in this couple and later turns into resentment.
**Ground of its own.** The couple's own budget, its own home, or at least its own rules where it lives. Decisions are made together and announced to the family, not cleared with the family in secret.
**Loans and sureties — only after talking it through together.** Both of Shen Fu and Yun's disasters had one cause: a signature nobody had agreed on.
**Translate the shared language for others.** A joke for two does not belong in a letter to the mother-in-law. Silence is for resting together, not for conversations about money.
**Open the door.** Invent a house with four prohibitions of its own: where friends come, where people are fed, and where the important things are discussed calmly.
**Nobody belongs to anybody.** Each partner needs work and time of their own. "We need no one else" is a lovely phrase and a poor plan.

**9 — The Hermit, "Entry to the task".** The couple's shared wish and its common language: quiet for two, understanding without words, care that is never put on show. The same wish turns into resistance when the important things go unsaid.

**3 — The Empress, "Middle of the task".** How the couple travels the path: it grows things. A home, comfort, housekeeping, shared projects, warmth for their own — all of it comes out of almost nothing.

**3 — The Empress, "Main task".** What there is to learn: to turn warmth into soil of their own. Their own home, their own money, their own decisions made without glancing at the family — and a garden other people can be invited into.

intro: Beneath the tail, every such couple has The Devil — a centre card that only a couple can have. In "The couple's values" The Hermit returns almost every time (94.2%). What follows is an investigation: clues in the numbers themselves, in Waite and Wen, and in a Chinese book about a marriage written more than two hundred years ago. Its love story begins with a hidden bowl of porridge.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 9-3-3 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's task, not a verdict. At the entry is The Hermit: two people want quiet and solitude together and understand each other without words. In the middle and in the main task is The Empress: the couple grows a home and care, and what it has to learn is to set this garden on its own ground — its own money, its own decisions, its own home — and to keep it open to others.

faq.q: Why is the middle of the tail 3 and not 12?
faq.a: In a personal chart the middle equals the entry plus the main task, and 9 and 3 would give 12. In a couple's chart each point is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts: the middle is the sum of the partners' middles. For 9-3-3 that is always 10 + 20 = 30 → 3. That is why there is no personal 9-3-3 tail, while a couple can have one.

faq.q: Which personal tails add up to 9-3-3?
faq.a: Only one combination: one partner has the personal tail 21-10-16, the other 6-20-14. Running through the dates gives no other variants. This also fixes the couple's centre: personal centres 5 and 10 always add up to 15, The Devil.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a relationship?
faq.a: No. The tail shows where the couple stumbles and what it learns, but it does not predict events or dates. A 9-3-3 couple stumbles over silence and over living on someone else's territory, and grows when care becomes visible and the home becomes its own.

faq.q: Why does such a couple always have The Devil at the centre?
faq.a: Because the personal centres of partners with the tails 21-10-16 and 6-20-14 are always 5 and 10. No date gives 15 at the centre of a personal chart; it appears only in a couple. Its plus is strong attraction and acceptance of each other's dark sides, its lesson is that nobody belongs to anybody.

report: In the winter of 1775, in Suzhou, a girl named Yun hid a bowl of warm porridge in her room — for the boy she had just been betrothed to. Her cousin caught them eating: "I asked you for porridge just now and you said it was all gone. So you were hiding it for your bridegroom!" The house roared with laughter, Yun fled, and for years afterwards she hid from her bridegroom. The bridegroom himself, Shen Fu, wrote the scene down in his book "Six Records of a Floating Life". The whole 9-3-3 tail is already in it: **care that is hidden from everyone except one person.** The porridge is The Empress, the hiding of it is The Hermit.

report.h3: The silence that first protects, then takes away the voice

report: The Hermit at the entry is what the couple wants from the very start: quiet for two and a language only the two of them understand. Five years later, at the wedding, Shen Fu realised that Yun had kept a meatless vow for several years — ever since he had smallpox. She had never said a word about it, and she answered his question with her eyes and a nod. For twenty-three years they would take each other's hand in a dark passage, as if someone might see. Yun, in her husband's words, could "read my eyes and understand my brows".

The point of entry to the tail is the same point as "Common language" on the relationship line. A couple with this tail has The Hermit as its common language: private words nobody else understands, one partner quietly paying the other's share, a glance exchanged at a party, plans told to the family once everything is decided.

But the entry stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish becomes resistance. When gossip started in the house, Yun forbade her husband to defend her and never explained herself. **The silence that protected the two of them at first later leaves them without a voice.**

report.h3: A vegetable garden around a house that never existed

report: In the middle of the tail is The Empress: the couple grows things, and grows them out of almost nothing. In summer Yun would lower a pinch of tea in a silk bag into a lotus flower, which closes at night, and in the morning she brewed that tea with rainwater. What is closed to everyone at night is steeped in fragrance by morning — this is how The Hermit and The Empress work together in this couple.

Having rented a room for a month in a cottage among vegetable plots, Yun said: "Some day we will build a house here. We'll buy ten mu of vegetable garden around it… You will paint, I will embroider… Cotton clothes and rice with vegetables — joy for a whole life." Solitude and a vegetable garden, 9 and 3, are a single wish. Yet elsewhere in the same book Shen Fu lets slip: **"our household had no garden"**. Every garden this couple had belonged to someone else: his father's house, a rented room, a friend's tower.

So the main task is the same Empress read through its minus: family and money. The couple had no money of its own. Yun quietly handled things for others: she found her father-in-law a woman to serve him, telling her mother-in-law that a neighbour's girl had come to play; she stood surety for her brother-in-law. Her letter to her husband was opened by her father-in-law, who read in it "your honoured mother" and "the old man". The couple was turned out of the house. And twelve years earlier Shen Fu had carved two seals with the words "to be husband and wife in life after life" — "for our letters to each other". **Every misfortune grew out of hidden care**, and the language of two, read by the elders, sounded like insolence. A few years later Shen Fu, out of awkwardness, stood surety for a friend, the friend vanished with the money — and the couple was turned out again.

They left in secret, before dawn, and ate warm porridge before setting out. Yun, smiling with an effort, said: "Once a bowl of porridge brought us together, now a bowl of porridge parts us." The circle closed.

Today this task looks mundane. Two people live with parents for years, "until they've saved up". One secretly borrows from a parent, the other signs as guarantor because refusing feels awkward. There is one thing to learn: to give the garden ground of its own — its own budget, its own home, or at least its own rules where it lives, and decisions made together that are announced, not hidden.

report.h3: A chain stretched between two

report: Beneath the tail, such a couple has The Devil — a centre card that neither of the two has alone: it appears only when two people are added together. Waite, describing older decks, praises a version in which the human figures on The Devil card are **"yoked only to each other"**. Shen Fu and Yun prayed to the Old Man under the Moon, the god of marriages, who ties spouses together with a red thread: "Once this cord is tied, there is no escaping it."

On the plus side, such a chain means attraction and the ability to accept in the other even what one dislikes: Yun once pushed into her husband's mouth a pickle he loathed, and he came to love it. On the minus side, it is a room without windows: "Are there two other people in the world tonight who feel what we feel?"

Near the end, Yun herself called this force "the demon of love", and Shen Fu decided that the trouble lay in too strong an attachment. The cards disagree with that conclusion. The Devil's lesson in a couple is different: nobody belongs to anybody. There is no need to love less — what is needed is for love not to become a locked room.

report.h3: A hut that gained a door

report: This couple spent its best year and a half right after the first expulsion, in a friend's tower. Yun embroidered, guests chipped in for wine and came "like swallows under the rafters — flying in and out as they pleased". The house had four prohibitions — talk of ranks, of office affairs, of examinations and of cards and dice — and four qualities that made a guest welcome. The last of them was **clear quiet**. The Hermit's silence remained, but it became a virtue at a shared table rather than a wall.

The couple's best home grew out of a collapse and was held together by measure. In Waite, The Hermit's lantern promises that others can reach the place where he stands. The strong version of the 9-3-3 tail is a hut for two that has a door.

seo.title: Karmic tail 9 6 15 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 6 15 compatibility in the destiny matrix: the Hermit at the entry, the Lovers in the middle and the Devil as the main task, with a worked example.

items.title: Karmic tail 9-6-15 in compatibility: the Hermit, the Lovers and the Devil
items.short: The most common couple tail has strange arithmetic: the Hermit plus the Lovers make exactly the Devil, 9 + 6 = 15, with no reduction at all. Solitude for two, added to love, turns into attachment, and that is the whole plot of the 9-6-15 tail. The couple enters the task with a shared wish to shut the world out together, goes through it by love and by choosing each other day after day, and the main task is the Devil: not to let care, habit and the fear of loss become a chain that binds the two only to each other.

sections.h2: How the 9-6-15 tail is worked out in compatibility: an example with two dates
paragraphs: Each point of a couple’s matrix is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The couple’s tail is not taken from one date or guessed from the partners’ numbers: point is added to point.
An example: 05.07.1975 and 14.08.1975. The first date has the personal tail 12-19-7, the second 15-5-8. Add them point by point:

The couple’s middle is added up too, not derived from the ends: 19 + 5. But in this triple it also agrees with the ends: 9 + 15 = 24 → 6. And the first two cards add up to the third: 9 + 6 = 15. In the 9-6-15 tail each number comes out of the other two.

This couple’s centre is 5 + 7 = 12, the Hanged Man, and “The couple’s values” holds 9: the Hermit a second time. And one more detail we will come back to: on the “What to create together” point the couple has 7 + 8 = 15, the same Devil.

The 9-6-15 tail is the most frequent of the 97 couple tails: it falls to 4.627% of couples, about one in 22. It is built from only six combinations of personal tails. The three most common are 15-20-5 with 21-4-10 (37% of such couples), 12-19-7 with 15-5-8, as in the example (37%), and 18-9-9 with 9-15-6 (13%).

As a personal tail 9-6-15 never occurs: this triple is not among the 26 personal tails. In one person’s chart the Devil in the karmic task always comes with the Empress in the centre and the Moon at the entry — that is the tail 18-6-15. The sequence “Hermit, Lovers, Devil” exists only in a couple.

sections.h2: Old World Landowners: the couple who had no evil spirit
paragraphs: In 1835 Gogol opened his collection Mirgorod with a story about two old people, Afanasy Ivanovich and Pulkheria Ivanovna Tovstogub. The narrator himself tells us which myth to hold it against: “If I were a painter and wished to put Philemon and Baucis on canvas, I would never choose any other model but them” (here and below, Gogol’s words are in our translation).

The story’s first paragraph reads almost like a description of this tail’s entry. The narrator likes “to step down for a minute into the sphere of that uncommonly secluded life, where not a single wish flies over the palisade that surrounds the little yard”. And further: the owners’ life is “so quiet, so quiet, that for a minute one forgets oneself and thinks that passions, desires and the restless offspring of the evil spirit that trouble the world do not exist at all”.

That sentence holds the whole riddle of the 9-6-15 tail. The couple builds its world so that there is no evil spirit in it, and the couple’s main task turns out to be the Devil himself. Gogol shows how this comes about. Between the two old people there are no betrayals and no scenes; nobody slams a door. The Devil here does not break down the gate — he grows inside the palisade, out of tenderness, care and habit.
Read beside the three cards, the story falls into the points of the tail.

sections.h2: The Hermit at the entry: keeping the world beyond the palisade
paragraphs: “Entry to the task” is what the couple wants together: its shared wishes and agreements. Lisovskaya also calls this point the point of common language, and with it the point of resistance: a wish may not match reality, and then the couple runs up against its own dream.

The common language of the old-world landowners can be heard from the first page. They speak to each other only in the formal “you”, the Russian vy: “Was it you who pushed the seat of the chair through, Afanasy Ivanovich?” — “Never mind, don’t be cross, Pulkheria Ivanovna: it was me.” Their day is marked out by one and the same question: “Well, Pulkheria Ivanovna, perhaps it’s time for a little bite of something?” It is the language of two people who hardly need a third. Even in the closest intimacy they keep that small formal vy — a distance nobody ever breaks.

In a couple today with this entry everything looks different, yet it is recognisable at once. The two leave a noisy party first, and in the taxi they feel better than they did all evening. They talk about plans once everything is already decided. A Friday evening without guests is not boredom but a reward. The Hermit at the entry is a wish they have shared since their first meetings: a corner of their own, a pace of their own, words of their own.

The resistance grows from the same place. Everything that comes from outside — friends, family, one partner’s new interest, an offer to move — is first tested for one thing: will it disturb the quiet? The wish “let them leave us alone” quietly becomes a rule, and the rule becomes a fence that no wish flies over. Not even their own.

The numbers add a detail. In 86% of couples with the 9-6-15 tail neither partner has the Hermit in their personal tail. On their own they do not carry this card in the tail: the Hermit appears only when the two are added together. The same point M is also the end of the couple’s relationship line, “Common language”. And in “The couple’s values” the Hermit stands for 63.9% of such couples: a quiet world for two is for them not only the entry but also what the union exists for.

Wen writes of the Hermit: “He is neutral in the war between good and evil. He has transcended that war and has found peace.” In Gogol peace is arranged differently. Nobody transcended the war; it was left beyond the palisade. Hence the tail’s task: what was not let in at the gate does not vanish, it looks for a way inside.

sections.h2: The Lovers in the middle: a choice that was forgotten
paragraphs: For Lisovskaya the “Middle of the task” has no meaning of its own — it adds to the main task. In our reading the middle shows how the couple travels from the wish to the task: what it does and what it goes through. In the 9-6-15 tail this road is laid by love.

Gogol mentions in passing how the quiet house began. Afanasy Ivanovich married at thirty, “when he was a fine young fellow and wore an embroidered waistcoat; he even carried off, quite deftly, Pulkheria Ivanovna, whom her relatives did not want to give him”. There they are, the Lovers: a choice against the family’s will, an elopement, a decision of two. And right after: “but even of this he remembered very little now, at least he never spoke of it”.

That is the whole middle of the tail. Love in such a couple is not a feeling to be talked about but a thing to be done: someone has saved “dumplings with berries” for the other on purpose, someone remembers which pies the other likes. “One could not look without sympathy at their mutual love,” writes Gogol. But the choice where it all began has long since become a given. Nobody repeats it — it is simply there, like the walls of the house.

Wen notes of the Lovers: “Overall, there is a strong feeling of paradise, at least in the beginning.” The middle of the 9-6-15 tail decides what becomes of that paradise later. The Lovers stand here between the Hermit and the Devil and are made of them: 9 + 15 = 24 → 6. This couple’s love is made of two substances — solitude and attachment. While the choice of each other is made again, love keeps the solitude open. When the choice is forgotten, only attachment is left.

In a couple today the middle shows in small things. One partner makes decisions “for both of us” because it is quicker. The other stops asking whether the first wants the same — it is obvious anyway. The relationship is gradually measured against the picture of “how it used to be with us”, and any difference from it is frightening. Among the Lovers’ tasks in a couple Lisovskaya names perfectionism and idealising the relationship, and insecurity that breeds jealousy and control. In the 9-6-15 tail none of this sounds like a scene; it sounds like a quiet wish that nothing should change.

sections.h2: The Devil as the main task: “grew attached through habit”
paragraphs: The “Main task” is the couple’s chief problem and trial, and it is read mostly through the minus: what does not work and what has to be learned. For Lisovskaya the Devil in this place means dependence and the wish to possess, attempts to hold on to the partner, silence about one’s own wishes, fear and hopelessness. Her final thought on the fifteenth energy in a couple: nobody belongs to anybody.

Gogol gives this Devil an exact definition — about a cat, as it happens: “One cannot say that Pulkheria Ivanovna loved her too much; she had simply grown attached to her, having grown used to always seeing her.” Grown attached through habit: not passion and not vice, but the habit of seeing someone nearby. And of the old couple themselves we are told that “all their attachment was concentrated on themselves”. Attachment has nowhere to flow beyond the palisade, and all of it goes into each other.
Then the story shows how this attachment works, in scenes almost any couple will recognise.

At night Afanasy Ivanovich groans. “Why are you groaning?” — “Oh, as if my belly aches a little.” — “Wouldn’t it be better to eat something?” He eats a small plateful and says: “Now it’s as if it has become easier.” The remedy for unease is a little more of what causes the unease. Wen describes the Devil as a “preference for instant gratification over delayed gratification”. In a couple it looks like this: dinner instead of a conversation, a present instead of the question “what’s wrong?”, one more cosy evening instead of a change.

A guest at their house “was on no account let go the same day: he absolutely had to stay the night”. The hospitality is real and warm, and still the guest is not let go. Care inside such a couple is built the same way: it is sincere, but it has no door to the outside.

And when Afanasy Ivanovich feels like joking, he asks: “Well, Pulkheria Ivanovna, what if our house suddenly caught fire, where would we go?” Or he announces that he is off to the war. She gets cross: “I know he’s joking, and yet it’s unpleasant to hear… sometimes you listen and listen, and you get frightened.” This couple’s merriest game is to imagine that the shelter is gone or that one of them leaves. Their fear of loss lives not in quarrels but in jokes.

And the strongest scene. Pulkheria Ivanovna, sure that she will soon die, regrets only one thing: “I regret that I don’t know whom to leave you to, who will look after you when I die. You are like a little child.” She arranges everything so “that after her Afanasy Ivanovich should not notice her absence”. This is love — and it is also a chain: the care was so complete that the other forgot how to live on his own. Lisovskaya has a formula for such a union: one partner leads the other from the plus into the minus. In Gogol nobody leads anyone anywhere. The two simply did everything for each other for many years.
That is why the Devil of the 9-6-15 tail is so hard to recognise. He does not look like evil. He looks like a home that is warm and well fed, where someone is always close by.

sections.h2: The evidence in the numbers: the Devil is added up by the two
paragraphs: The numbers of this tail say the same thing as Gogol, only more briefly.

The first piece of evidence is already familiar: 9 + 6 = 15. The Hermit and the Lovers give the Devil without any reduction. A quiet world for two plus love equals attachment. This is not mysticism but the structure of the triple: the main task in it literally adds up from the entry and the middle.

The second piece of evidence is where the fifteen in the main task comes from. The couple’s main task is the sum of the two personal karmic tasks. In couples with the 9-6-15 tail these are always two small numbers that make 15 directly: 7 + 8, 5 + 10, 4 + 11 or 6 + 9. Neither partner has the Devil in their karmic task — he appears only in the sum. And in 13.5% of such couples the personal tasks are 6 and 9: one has the Lovers, the other the Hermit, and together they make the Devil again.

The third piece of evidence is where the Devil does appear. In 99.4% of couples with the 9-6-15 tail the fifteen stands in the personal tail of exactly one partner and never in both: almost always at the personal entry of the tail (86%), less often in its middle. This does not make him or her the “carrier” of the Devil. The fifteen reaches the couple’s main task not from there, but from the sum of two tasks in which neither has a fifteen.

The fourth is what the partners lack. In 86% of couples neither of the two has a nine or a six in their personal tail. The Hermit and the Lovers belong to the couple itself: they are not in the partners’ tails taken one by one.

Together the clues add up to one thought. Neither of the two brought this tail ready-made. The Hermit and the Lovers appear only in the sum of two charts, and the Devil comes from adding two tasks. Nobody forged this couple’s chain in advance — the two weave it themselves, day after day.

sections.h2: Waite and Papus: the Devil under whom two are bound only to each other
paragraphs: Waite describes his Devil card like this: in front of the altar there is a ring, and from it two chains run to the necks of a male and a female figure. “Hereof is the chain and fatality of the material life,” he writes. And he adds at once that “he who is exalted above them is not to be their master for ever. Even now, he is also a bondsman”.

Another passage matters more — in the first part of the book, where Waite goes through old designs of the card. On eighteenth-century decks two small demons are tied to the pedestal. In Papus’s book Le Tarot divinatoire, Waite writes, the demons were replaced by “naked human beings, male and female, who are yoked only to each other”. And he adds: “The author may be felicitated on this improved symbolism.”

For the 9-6-15 tail this is the key line. Two people are bound not to a master and not to an altar, but only to each other — that is this couple’s Devil. There is no master: no one to overthrow and no one to run from. The two hold the chain themselves, and only they can take it off.

Yoked means “under one yoke, in one harness”, and in Waite the word sounds almost domestic. Max Vasmer writes of the Russian word for spouse, suprug: in Old Russian suprug meant “spouse”, “married couple, husband and wife” and “team of harnessed animals”; the word comes from prjagu, “I harness”, and is built the same way as Latin coniux (hence English “conjugal”) and Greek σύζυγος. Spouses are literally those harnessed together. Papus’s Devil is the shadow of the word “spouses” itself: the same harness, only with no cart and no road.

Waite even refuses to see the Hermit as a recluse. The card, he says, “is understood quite incorrectly when it is connected with the idea of occult isolation, as the protection of personal magnetism against admixture”, and he calls this one of the “frivolous renderings”. A couple at the 9-6-15 entry risks reading its Hermit in exactly that way — as a fence against strangers. In Waite the Hermit holds up his lantern on a height, like a beacon that says: “where I am, you also may be.”

sections.h2: The cat who chose love
paragraphs: Gogol opens the turning point by saying that the event “came from the most trifling occasion”. Beyond the garden, in a dense wood, live wild cats. For a long time they sniff at Pulkheria Ivanovna’s little cat through a hole under the barn and “at last lured her away, as a detachment of soldiers lures a silly peasant girl”. A few days later the cat comes back thin, eats greedily — and leaves again. “The ungrateful creature had evidently grown too used to the predatory cats, or had picked up the romantic rule that poverty with love is better than a palace, and the cats were as poor as church mice; be that as it may, she jumped out of the window.”

Gogol is mocking here, but the scene is precisely built. The cat repeats what Afanasy Ivanovich once did himself: she leaves a well-fed house for love. The household had grown attached to the cat, but the cat herself was not attached — and she left when she wished. And the mistress reads it like this: “That was my death that came for me!”

In a closed world any departure sounds like the end of the world. In his list of divinatory meanings for the Devil Waite names “fatality; that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil”, and among the reversed ones “evil fatality, weakness, pettiness, blindness”. Pulkheria Ivanovna submits to the sign. A few years later Afanasy Ivanovich will submit in the same way, when in the quiet garden he seems to hear a voice calling his name: “he submitted with the will of an obedient child”.

The 9-6-15 tail says nothing about death — anyone’s. The cat scene matters for something else: this is how a closed world reads another’s freedom. If one of the two goes out for an evening with friends, to a course, into a venture of their own, a couple in the minus of this tail may feel it as a small end of the world. The task is to see in leaving not a verdict but freedom, without which coming back means nothing.

sections.h2: “Passion or habit?”: Gogol’s question and the tail’s answer
paragraphs: After Pulkheria Ivanovna’s death the narrator recalls a young man who was in love “tenderly, passionately, madly”. His beloved died, his despair was such that his family never let him out of their sight, and a year later the narrator sees him in a crowded hall playing cards, with a pretty young wife standing behind his chair. Five years on, Afanasy Ivanovich weeps “like a stream” over a dish that reminded him of the dead woman. Gogol asks: “Which then is stronger over us: passion or habit?” And he answers: “all our passions seemed childish” to him “against this long, slow, almost insensible habit”.
A few years earlier Pushkin had said of another landowning couple: “Habit is given us from above: it is a substitute for happiness.”

The 9-6-15 tail has its own answer to Gogol’s question. Passion and choice are the Lovers in the middle. Habit and attachment are the Devil in the main task. Gogol sets them against each other, while the tail puts them on one line: the Lovers are the road, the Devil is the task. The couple does not need to choose between them. It needs habit to remain a choice. Attachment that two people choose anew each day is no longer a chain but a harness: it pulls them both the same way.

sections.h2: The centre of a 9-6-15 couple: the Hanged Man, or a World no single person has
paragraphs: The centre of a couple’s matrix is its atmosphere, what is between the two and not on show. In couples with the 9-6-15 tail the centre is almost always one of two cards: 12, the Hanged Man, in 62.2%, and 21, the World, in 37.2%. The remaining 0.6% have the Empress.

Waite’s Hanged Man is “life in suspension, but life and not death”, and his face “expresses deep entrancement, not suffering”. This is exactly Gogol’s atmosphere, where all the old adventures “gave way to a quiet and secluded life, to those dozing and yet somehow harmonious reveries”. In the plus: depth, slow time, the ability to look at the world from a point of one’s own. In the minus: life on pause, where everything important is put off till later. Wen sees in the Hanged Man’s crossed legs “the balance between dominion and slavery” — the very line along which this couple’s Devil runs.

The World in the centre is a finding of a special kind. In the centre of a personal matrix 21 never occurs, for any date: such an atmosphere exists only in a couple. In these couples the personal centres are 10 and 11, the Wheel of Fortune and Strength, and a whole world appears only in their sum. The World is completion and fullness, and in Waite’s reversed list it is “inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence”. For a 9-6-15 couple these are two faces of one home: a world that has everything, and a world in which nothing moves any more.

In “The couple’s values” such couples have either the Hermit (63.9%) or the Moon (36.1%). Waite’s Moon is “life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit” and “the fears of the natural mind”. In our reading, for couples with the Moon in their values the shared world also rests on imagination: on forebodings, signs and private meanings of their own. In Gogol these are the cat taken for a messenger and the voice in the garden.

sections.h2: What the 9-6-15 tail looks like in a couple’s life
paragraphs: In the plus this is a couple whose company is calming. It is good to be silent with them; people come to them to rest, like Gogol’s narrator, whose “soul took on a wonderfully pleasant and calm state” at their porch. The two understand each other from half a word, talk deep into the night, keep their word and keep their quarrels at home. Their love shows not in declarations but in deeds.
In the minus the same tail can be recognised by its scenes:

ul: **The evening that cannot be cancelled.** The couple has its ritual, and any invitation from outside is felt as an attack on it. One partner sometimes wants to go but does not: the other will say “of course, go” — and fall silent for the evening.
**Care instead of a conversation.** One feels bad; the other cooks, buys, arranges. The question “what happened?” never gets asked, because dinner is already on the table.

**The joke about leaving.** “One of these days I’ll leave you and join a monastery” — both laugh, and then the whole evening is heavy. The fear of loss hides in play, as with Afanasy Ivanovich’s fire and war.
**The wish that goes unspoken.** One wants to change jobs, to study, to go away for a month — and stays silent, because it threatens the quiet. The wish does not disappear; it piles up.

**Indispensability.** One does everything for the other: papers, phone calls, food, dealings with relatives. This is love, but after a few years the other can no longer manage without it — “you are like a little child”.

paragraphs: These scenes show how the tail’s cards work together. The Hermit and the Devil give silence: problems and wishes pile up without words. The Lovers and the Devil give a love that wants to hold on. The Hermit and the Lovers give a world for two, and all three together give a world that is hard to leave even for an evening.

sections.h2: What changes the story: a gate in the palisade
paragraphs: The task of the 9-6-15 tail is not to destroy the shared world. This couple needs its palisade: without a corner of its own it suffers. The task is to put a gate in it.

ul: **Each has a time and place of their own.** Among the Hermit’s pluses in a couple Lisovskaya names exactly this: each partner has a time for solitude. Solitude apart does not threaten what is shared; it airs it.

**A wish said aloud, and before it turns into a grievance.** Her own advice for the fifteenth energy: admit one’s secret wishes and talk about them. The rule is simple: if one wants something that will “disturb the quiet”, say so first.
**Make the choice again.** Not “but we’re together” but “I choose you” — in words, in questions, in small decisions. Ask rather than guess for the other.

**Care in a way that keeps the other capable.** Do not do for the other what they can do themselves; show where the keys are. The phrase “you are like a little child” is a good marker: once it starts to fit, care has become a chain.
**Turn the joke about loss into a conversation.** Say plainly what each is really afraid of, without fires and wars.

**Let go.** The guest when he wants to leave; each other for an evening, a course, a venture of one’s own. Pulkheria Ivanovna’s cat is the test: in this couple’s home freedom should not sound like disaster.

paragraphs: Waite leaves this card a way out right in its description: the one who holds the chain “is not to be their master for ever”. Wen writes that the reversed Devil means “the removal of bondage”. For a 9-6-15 couple the chains and the master are the two of them, and so they remove them themselves.
If attachment in a couple turns into control, prohibitions and fear, this is no longer a task for reading cards but a reason to see a family psychologist.

sections.h2: The strong version of the 9-6-15 tail: Philemon and Baucis
paragraphs: Gogol called his old couple Philemon and Baucis, and it is worth opening Ovid to see how the two couples differ. In the eighth book of the Metamorphoses Jupiter and Mercury, disguised as travellers, knock at doors: “a thousand homes they approached, asking for rest; a thousand homes were shut against them by bolts; one took them in” (mille domos clausere serae; tamen una recepit — here and below our translation). The one that took them in was the house of a poor old couple.

Of the owners it is said: “it makes no difference whether you look there for masters or for servants: the whole household is two, and the same two give orders and obey” (tota domus duo sunt, idem parentque iubentque). This is what the Devil lacks: master and slave. In the house of Philemon and Baucis nobody is master over the other.

The two couples share the same Hermit — a small house far from everyone. The same Lovers — love for a whole life. Only the Devil differs. In Ovid the door opens to strangers when a thousand others are locked; in Gogol the guest is not let go. In Ovid nobody is anybody’s master; in Gogol one becomes the other’s nanny. At the end Philemon asks: “let the same hour take us both” (auferat hora duos eadem). The gods turn the old couple into two trees, and the local people still point out “neighbouring trunks from a twin body” (de gemino vicinos corpore truncos). Two trunks side by side, not one.

This is the strong version of the 9-6-15 tail. Not less closeness, but a door in it. Not one body for two, but two trunks growing side by side. Lisovskaya describes the Devil in a couple in the plus as well: passion, accepting each other’s dark sides and forgiving mistakes, open talk about desires, powerful support, attachment in the good sense; sometimes the union helps one leave earlier destructive relationships. In the example of 05.07.1975 and 14.08.1975 the Devil also stands on the “What to create together” point, which is read only in the plus. On this point, Lisovskaya says, fifteen very often means breaking free of dependence. In our reading this is the tail’s best answer: the Devil the couple wove itself, it also turns into freedom.

sections.h2: 9-6-15 and 9-15-6: the same numbers in another order
paragraphs: The same numbers give one more couple tail, 9-15-6, in 1.217% of couples; their centre is the Hanged Man in 77.8% and the World in 22.2%. There the Devil stands in the middle and the Lovers in the main task: the couple travels through attachment, and what it has to learn is love and choice themselves. In 9-6-15 it is the other way round: love is the road, and freedom within attachment is the task.

ul: **9 · The Hermit — “Entry to the task”.** What the couple wants together: quiet, a world of its own behind a fence, an unhurried pace, low-voiced talk. This wish is both the way into the task and the resistance to it: whatever comes from outside first looks like a nuisance.
**6 · The Lovers — “Middle of the task”.** What the couple goes through: love shown in deeds every day, and the choice of each other — made once, or made again and again.

**15 · The Devil — “Main task”.** What the couple has to learn: to tell closeness from ownership. Attachment with nowhere to flow but into each other becomes a chain, and only the two of them can take it off.

intro: A couple’s tail is not a forecast and not a verdict: it describes how the task is built, not what will happen. What follows is an investigation: what is written in the numbers themselves, what Waite and Benebell Wen saw in these cards, and why the best book about this tail was written by Gogol in 1835.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 9-6-15 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a tail of the couple’s matrix with the Hermit on the “Entry to the task”, the Lovers on the “Middle of the task” and the Devil on the “Main task”. The couple wants a quiet world for two, goes along the road through love and the choice of each other, and has to learn to tell closeness from ownership: not to let care and habit become a chain.

faq.q: Does 9-6-15 occur in a personal destiny matrix?
faq.a: Not as a karmic tail: this triple never occurs in a personal chart, and a person with the Devil in the karmic task always gets the tail 18-6-15. But the same three numbers do occur in a personal matrix as lines. As the relationship line (entry of relationships 9, under the heart 6, crossing of the lines 15) in 0.59% of dates, and as the money line (entry 9, middle 6, crossing 15) in 0.71% of dates. These are other points with other roles; a search for a “9 6 15 channel” may be about them.

faq.q: How can one check that a couple has the 9-6-15 tail?
faq.a: Work out both personal matrices and add the matching points of the tail, reducing sums over 22. For example, 05.07.1975 gives the personal tail 12-19-7 and 14.08.1975 gives 15-5-8; point by point that is 12 + 15 = 27 → 9, 19 + 5 = 24 → 6 and 7 + 8 = 15. The compatibility calculator does it automatically.

faq.q: Does the Devil in a couple’s tail mean infidelity or addiction?
faq.a: No. A card does not establish facts about people: infidelity, addiction, debts, anyone’s guilt. The Devil in the main task names a theme the couple has to learn on — attachment and ownership — and in the 9-6-15 tail this theme is usually a quiet one: care, habit, the fear of letting go.

faq.q: Whose Devil is it — his or hers?
faq.a: Nobody’s on their own. The couple’s main task is the sum of two personal karmic tasks, and in couples with the 9-6-15 tail neither partner has fifteen in the karmic task: 15 comes only from the addition, for example 7 + 8. The Devil does occur in one partner’s personal tail, but it does not reach the couple’s task from there.

faq.q: Why can a couple’s centre be 21 when no person has such a centre?
faq.a: A couple’s centre is the sum of two personal centres. A person never has 21 in the centre, but a couple can: in 37.2% of couples with the 9-6-15 tail the centre is the World, and it is made of the personal centres 10 and 11. It is an atmosphere neither of the two can bring alone: only the union creates it.

report: The Hermit plus the Lovers make exactly the Devil: 9 + 6 = 15, with no reduction. In the 9-6-15 tail this is not a coincidence but a plot. The couple enters the task with a shared wish for quiet and a world of its own, goes through it by love and by choosing each other, and the main task is the Devil: **not to let care, habit and the fear of loss become a chain** that binds the two only to each other.

report.h3: A house where the evil spirit seems not to exist

report: Gogol wrote the best description of this tail in 1835. Old World Landowners opens on an estate “where not a single wish flies over the palisade that surrounds the little yard”, and the owners’ life is “so quiet, so quiet, that for a minute one forgets oneself and thinks that passions, desires and the restless offspring of the evil spirit that trouble the world do not exist at all”. The couple builds a world with no evil spirit in it — and the Devil himself turns out to be its main task.

The Hermit on the “Entry to the task” is a wish shared since their first meetings: a corner of their own, a pace of their own, words of their own. Even in the closest intimacy Afanasy Ivanovich and Pulkheria Ivanovna never drop the formal form of address, and their day is marked out by one question — isn’t it time for a bite? It is the language of two who hardly need a third. But on this point the wish also turns into resistance: everything that comes from outside — friends, family, one partner’s new interest — is first tested for one thing: will it disturb the quiet?

The Lovers on the “Middle of the task” are a road laid by love. Long ago Afanasy Ivanovich “carried off, quite deftly” a bride whom her relatives did not want to give him, “but even of this he remembered very little now”. Love in such a couple is not words but deeds: “dumplings with berries” saved on purpose, the pies the other likes. But the choice that began it all has long become a given. While it is made again, love keeps the solitude open. When it is forgotten, only attachment is left.

report.h3: Grown attached through habit

report: Gogol gives this Devil an exact definition — about a cat, as it happens: “One cannot say that Pulkheria Ivanovna loved her too much; she had simply grown attached to her, having grown used to always seeing her.” Not passion and not vice, but the habit of seeing someone nearby. Of the old couple themselves we are told that “all their attachment was concentrated on themselves”. Attachment has nowhere to flow beyond the palisade.

Then the story shows how this works. At night Afanasy Ivanovich groans, and there is one remedy — to eat another small plateful: “Now it’s as if it has become easier.” The remedy for unease is a little more of what causes it. A guest at their house “was on no account let go the same day”. The husband’s merriest joke is to ask where they would go if the house burned down, or to announce that he is off to the war: their fear of loss lives not in quarrels but in jokes. And Pulkheria Ivanovna, sure she will soon die, regrets only that she does not know whom to leave him to: he is “like a little child”. **The care was so complete that the other forgot how to live on his own.**

That is why this Devil is so hard to recognise: he looks like a warm, well-fed home where someone is always close by. In a couple today he looks like this: dinner instead of a conversation, a present instead of the question “what’s wrong?”, and the wish to go away for a month stays unspoken because it threatens the quiet.

report.h3: A chain without a master

report: Waite writes of the two chained to the Devil and adds that the one above them “is not to be their master for ever”. But this tail is caught most precisely elsewhere in his book. Waite notes that in Papus the man and the woman on this card are “yoked only to each other”, and congratulates the author on this improved symbolism. There is no master. No one to overthrow and no one to run from: the two hold the chain themselves.

Yoked means “in one harness”. In Max Vasmer’s dictionary the Old Russian suprug, the word for spouse, meant “spouse”, “married couple, husband and wife” and “team of harnessed animals”: it comes from prjagu, “I harness”, like Latin coniux and Greek σύζυγος. Spouses are literally those harnessed together. **This couple’s Devil is the shadow of the word “spouses” itself**: the same harness, only with no cart and no road.

The numbers say the same. The couple’s main task is the sum of two personal karmic tasks, and in couples with this tail neither partner has fifteen in the karmic task: the Devil appears only in the addition. Nobody brought him ready-made — the two weave him themselves, day after day.

report.h3: A gate in the palisade

report: In Gogol the turning point begins with the cat. Wild cats from the wood lured her away; she came back thin, ate her fill and jumped out of the window again, as if she had “picked up the romantic rule that poverty with love is better than a palace”. The cat repeated what Afanasy Ivanovich had once done himself: she left a well-fed house for love. And the mistress read it as a verdict: “That was my death that came for me!” **In a closed world any departure sounds like the end of the world.** The tail says nothing about death; the scene is about something else — how a closed world reads another’s freedom. An evening one of the two spends with friends, a course, a venture of their own may feel like a small catastrophe to a couple in the minus of this tail.
The task is not to destroy the shared world: without a corner of its own this couple suffers. The task is to put a gate in the palisade:

ul: each has a time and place for solitude;
a wish said aloud, and before it turns into a grievance;
the choice of each other made again: asking rather than guessing for the other;
care that keeps the other able to live on their own;
the joke about loss turned into a conversation about what each is really afraid of;
letting go — of the guest when he wants to leave, and of each other.

report: If attachment turns into control, prohibitions and fear, it is no longer a task for reading cards but a reason to see a family psychologist.

Gogol himself named the strong version of this tail — Philemon and Baucis. In Ovid it is said of their hut: “the whole household is two, and the same two give orders and obey”. No master, no slave. Their door opened to travellers when a thousand others were locked, and at the end the old couple became two trees — “neighbouring trunks from a twin body”. Not one body for two, but two trunks growing side by side. Attachment that two people choose anew each day is no longer a chain but a harness: it pulls them both the same way.

unit.title: A gate in the palisade

captions.M: Wanting quiet and a world of your own
captions.N: Loving in deeds and choosing each other again

seo.title: Karmic tail 9 6 6 compatibility: the Hermit and the Lovers twice
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 6 6 compatibility in the destiny matrix: the Hermit at the entry, the Lovers in the middle and the main task. Why the couple hides its love.

items.title: Karmic tail 9-6-6 in compatibility: love under the Hermit's cloak
items.short: The karmic tail 9-6-6 in destiny matrix compatibility is the Hermit at the entry and the Lovers twice in a row, in the middle and in the main task. The couple comes together through quiet, depth and a language of its own, and it has one thing to learn: not to hide its love from each other as carefully as it hides it from the world.

sections.h2: Why no single person has the tail 9-6-6
paragraphs: Every point of the couple's matrix is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The middle of the couple is not derived from its outer numbers; it is added up from the partners' own middles. That makes 9-6-6 a tail born only between two people. It occurs in roughly one couple in 97 (1.026%) and ranks 36th of the 97 couple tails.

The site's engine finds nine combinations of personal tails that produce 9-6-6. The most common are 3-7-22 + 6-17-11 (25% of such couples), 18-3-12 + 9-3-21 (22%) and 21-4-10 + 6-20-14 (17%). The couple's middle is assembled from other people's middles: the Chariot and the Star (7 + 17 = 24 → 6), two Empresses (3 + 3), the Emperor and Judgement (4 + 20 = 24 → 6).
Three clues are hidden in these nine combinations.

**First: neither partner has the Lovers as a main task.** The partners' personal main tasks in these combinations are 22 and 11, 12 and 21, 10 and 14, 12 and 12, 13 and 11, 19 and 14, 15 and 9, 16 and 8. A six never appears. The couple's task exists only once the two are side by side.

**Second: one partner's love becomes the couple's quiet.** In about three couples out of five (61% across the combinations) one partner enters their own personal tail through the Lovers: 6-17-11, 6-20-14, 6-14-8. Yet the couple enters through the Hermit: 6 + 3 = 9, or 6 + 21 = 27 → 9. Our reading: someone who starts with love when alone starts with quiet next to this partner. The Lovers come back to the couple later, as the road and as the test.

**Third: the Hermit is not there to be defeated.** In the couple's values, such unions have the Hermit in 70.2% of cases and the Moon in 29.8%. For seven couples out of ten, the card of quiet is not only the entry but what the union exists for. So the task is not to stop being hermits.

In the atmosphere inside the couple, 56.7% of such unions have the World, 38.7% the Hanged Man and 4.6% the Empress. No date of birth puts the World in the centre of a personal chart: this card reaches the centre only for two. Waite's divinatory list for the World reads "voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place". For a couple this is no forecast of a move; it is the air between two people, the feeling that together they have a whole world.

paragraphs.h3: Example: two people born on the same day

paragraphs: The example uses the dates 05.12.1975 and 05.12.1975, a couple who share a birthday. Each has the personal tail 18-3-12, the Lovers (6) in the centre of the chart and the Hermit (9) in the spiritual purpose.
