paragraphs: Look where the cards have moved. For each of the two, the Lovers sit in the centre of the personal matrix, deep inside, and the Hermit sits in the spiritual purpose. In the couple the same two cards come out into the tail and become a task. What each of them keeps inside, the two of them will have to do.

sections.h2: The room in Wimpole Street: entering through the Hermit
paragraphs: On 10 January 1845, Robert Browning, aged thirty-two, writes a letter to Elizabeth Barrett. She is thirty-eight, one of the best-known poets in England, and for years she has hardly left her room at 50 Wimpole Street. The letter opens: "I love your verses with all my heart, dear Miss Barrett", and in the middle stands: "and I love you too."

He goes on to recall how he once nearly saw her: a mutual friend went up to announce him, but she was too unwell. "As if I had been close, so close, to some world's-wonder in chapel or crypt, only a screen to push and I might have entered… and the half-opened door shut." She answers the next day and takes up his word: had he entered the "crypt", he "might have caught cold". "Winters shut me up as they do dormouse's eyes; in the spring, we shall see."

In spring she writes: "You are Paracelsus, and I am a recluse." And explains: "I have lived only inwardly." Before his first visit she prepares him for disappointment: "There is nothing to see in me; nor to hear in me… If my poetry is worth anything to any eye, it is the flower of me… the rest of me is nothing but a root, fit for the ground and the dark." And at once she sets a condition: "You will not talk of having come afterwards I know."
The first meeting is on Tuesday, 20 May 1845. On the envelope of her letter Robert writes: "Tuesday, May 20, 1845, 3-4½ p.m." He marked every meeting this way, to the last.

This is the Hermit at the entry to the task. Point M is what the couple wants together, its common language. Two people with the tail 9-6-6 want not a noisy crowd but a conversation where the important things can be said. They take every step slowly and show love by deeds before words. Benebell Wen notes that the Hermit's lantern can be read as light for others, or as the sign of "someone who sees the world through his or her own light". Two people with this entry recognise each other by that kind of light.

But point M stands on the line of tasks, so here the wish turns into resistance. The very letter that invites him says "there is nothing to see in me" and asks him to keep the visit quiet. The Hermit lets people in only by appointment: "any day after two, or before six". In a couple today it looks like this: two people text each other until three in the morning and know more about each other than friends of ten years, yet when one asks "how are you?", each answers "fine".

sections.h2: The missing letter: the middle of the task
paragraphs: The correspondence survives almost entire, 573 letters. The poets' son published it in 1899 and described how it was kept: Robert held the letters in an inlaid box into which they exactly fitted, "letter beside letter, each in its consecutive order and numbered on the envelope by his own hand". One letter is missing from that box.

After the first meeting Robert wrote something she did not expect, most likely a declaration. Three days later she replies: "You have said some intemperate things… which you will not say over again, nor unsay, but forget at once, and for ever, having said at all; and which (so) will die out between you and me alone, like a misprint between you and the printer." And she adds that if one word of answer is attempted, "I will not see you again." Robert asked for the letter back and destroyed it. Half a year later she asks for it herself. He replies: "Could you think that that untoward letter lived one moment after it returned to me? I burned it and cried 'serve it right'!"

Here are the first Lovers of this tail. The middle of the task is where the word of love finally sounds, and at once the Hermit asks for it to be treated as a misprint. Wen writes that the Lovers are the beginnings of romance, and that the feeling of paradise on this card "may be evanescent if caution is not observed". In a 9-6-6 couple caution is built into the entry itself. It guards love and nearly smothers it. The couple passes the middle when it learns not to burn the first letter.

paragraphs.h3: The ninety-first meeting

paragraphs: The second half of the middle is a choice. For Wen the Lovers are above all a card of choice, and this choice cannot be made halfway. Elizabeth's father disinherited each of his children who married without his permission, and he never gave permission to anyone. So the choice is made in secret.

Saturday, 12 September 1846, St Marylebone Church, two witnesses. On the envelope Robert writes as before: "Saturday, Septr. 12, 1846, ¼11—11¼ A.M. (91)." The wedding entered his count as their ninety-first meeting. After the church Elizabeth goes not with her husband but home. Next day the room is full of visitors, and suddenly bells ring. "'Marylebone Church bells' said Henrietta, standing behind my chair." A friend of the family drops in, and one of his first words is: "When did you see Browning?"

A week later she leaves the house with her maid and her spaniel. In his last letter the day before, Robert asks: "Write to me one word more." She writes: "Is this my last letter to you, ever dearest?" She admits how dreadful it is "to have to give pain here by a voluntary act—for the first time in my life." And adds: "none are so bold as the timid, when they are fairly roused."

For a 9-6-6 couple this scene holds the whole mechanism of the middle. The Hermit says "not now" and waits sixteen months; the Lovers say "now or never", and the whole ending, the wedding and the departure, fits into a single week. In ordinary life the door is seldom locked by a father in Wimpole Street. More often it is closed by the two people's own caution: "let's not tell anyone yet", "let's talk about it later". Sometimes by a parent's voice that speaks in an argument before one's own. The middle is passed when the choice is spoken, at least to each other.

sections.h2: Sonnets handed over from behind: the main task
paragraphs: The two poets discussed their work in letters all the time, but Elizabeth did not show him her poems about him. On 22 July 1846 she writes: "You shall see some day at Pisa what I will not show you now. Does not Solomon say that 'there is a time to read what is written.' If he doesn't, he ought." Solomon said no such thing. Ecclesiastes has "a time to keep silence, and a time to speak". She rewrote the verse to suit herself.

What happened next was told by the critic Edmund Gosse in a book of 1896, from a statement Browning had made to a friend eight years before his death. The couple had a rule: to write alone and not show each other what they had written. Robert sometimes broke it; she never did. One morning after breakfast he stood at the window and became aware of someone behind him. It was Elizabeth. She **held him by the shoulder to prevent his turning to look at her**, and pushed a packet of papers into the pocket of his coat. She told him to read it and to tear it up if he did not like it, and fled to her room upstairs. The papers were sonnets about the two of them; the book has forty-four. He read them, ran upstairs and, in Gosse's words, "stormed that guarded citadel". Later he would say: "I dared not reserve to myself the finest sonnets written in any language since Shakespeare's."

This scene should be read as a family legend, not a record. Gosse placed it in Pisa in 1847 and cited a slim first edition, "Reading, 1847". In 1934 the bibliographers John Carter and Graham Pollard proved that edition a forgery by Thomas Wise, and biographers now date the day of the sonnets later. The only document is the July letter: "what I will not show you now".

When the sonnets were to be printed, they needed a title. Elizabeth proposed "Sonnets translated from the Bosnian". Robert replied: "No, not Bosnian—that means nothing—but from the Portuguese! They are Catarina's sonnets!" He had long called her his "own little Portuguese", and she had written a poem, "Catarina to Camoens", about a love just like this. Gosse calls the title **an ingenious device to veil the true authorship**. One of the most open books of English love poetry came out in 1850 in the mask of a translation.

The couple's main task is point D, and it is read mostly through the minus: what does not work and what there is to learn. The scene at the window shows it in one gesture. Elizabeth hands over the most open text of her life — that is the Lovers. But she does not let him see her face — that is the Hermit. The task of 9-6-6 is to turn around.
What stops people turning around is written in the same sonnets.

ul: **"Hard to love".** Sonnet XXXV: "Alas, I have grieved so I am hard to love. / Yet love me—wilt thou? Open thy heart wide". The Lovers in the task teach self-love inside the couple, and sometimes the other partner is the teacher.

**The fear of being loved as someone imagined.** As early as May 1845 she writes to Robert of his "mistakes in me", which "have humbled me by too much honouring". Sonnet XIV asks: "If thou must love me, let it be for nought / Except for love's sake only. Do not say / 'I love her for her smile—her look—her way / Of speaking gently'". These things "may be changed", and love so wrought "may be unwrought so". An ideal image of the partner is a burden here, not a gift.
**The need to hear it again.** Insecurity that is given no words looks for proof and easily turns into jealousy and control. Sonnet XXI turns it into a request said out loud.

paragraphs.h3: Why the Lovers appear twice

paragraphs: Sonnet XXI begins: "Say over again, and yet once over again, / That thou dost love me." And it ends: "Say thou dost love me, love me, love me—toll / The silver iterance!—only minding, Dear, / To love me also in silence with thy soul."

These lines hold the answer to why the six repeats in this tail. The repeat does not mean twice as much love. It is one word in two roles. In the middle it is said for the first time, and what matters is not to burn it. In the main task it has to be said again and once over again, and silence is not driven out but invited in: "also in silence". In this tail the Hermit is not the enemy of the Lovers. He asks for a place beside them.

sections.h2: Two soul-sides: Browning's answer
paragraphs: In 1855 Browning publishes the collection Men and Women, fifty poems in which, as usual, he speaks in other people's voices: a painter-monk, a knight, a painter. The last poem is called "One Word More" and is dedicated "To E. B. B.". It is what he asked of her in his last letter before the flight: "Write to me one word more." The echo is our observation, but it speaks for itself.
Only here does Browning speak without a mask: "Let me speak this once in my true person, / Not as Lippo, Roland or Andrea". And then come the lines that hold the whole 9-6-6 tail:
"God be thanked, the meanest of his creatures / Boasts **two soul-sides, one to face the world with, / One to show a woman when he loves her!**"

He calls her "my moon of poets". The moon, if she loved a mortal, would turn to him a side no one had seen, not Homer, not Galileo. The world sees her poems and praises them; he praises them along with everyone. "But the best is when I glide from out them… / Come out on the other side… / Where I hush and bless myself with silence."

The second mask shows here too. She hid her love behind a "translation from the Portuguese"; he was used to hiding behind other people's voices. Both took off their masks only for each other. This is the strong version of the tail: **the Hermit faces the world, the Lovers face each other**. Trouble starts when the cloak is turned inward and the two hide from each other what they keep from strangers. The Moon in the couple's values, found in three such couples out of ten, sounds especially close to these lines: the far side, shown to one person. This is our reading, not a rule of the method.

sections.h2: Lamp and cloak: the Hermit and the Lovers in Waite
paragraphs: Waite's drawing is not the card on the site, but two of its details hold this tail together.

Waite changed the old Hermit with a single stroke and said so himself: "The variation from the conventional models in this card is only that the lamp is not enveloped partially in the mantle of its bearer." "It is a star which shines in the lantern", and Waite calls this "a card of attainment". Half a century before his book, Browning had used the same word about himself in "One Word More": "I stand on my attainment."

The Lovers, as Waite describes them, are a man and a woman "unveiled before each other". Not before the world, but before each other. The whole tail fits between the two cards: from a lamp under a cloak to two people without veils.

Waite's divinatory lists read like a commentary on the story. For the Hermit: "Prudence, circumspection", and reversed: "Concealment, disguise, policy, fear, unreasoned caution." The title Sonnets from the Portuguese is a disguise in the most literal sense. For the Lovers: "Attraction, love, beauty, trials overcome", and reversed: "marriage frustrated and contrarieties of all kinds."

Elizabeth has a sonnet that reads like this card. In Sonnet XXII two souls stand "Face to face, silent, drawing nigh and nigher, / Until the lengthening wings break into fire". The angels would press on them, aspiring "To drop some golden orb of perfect song / Into our deep, dear silence." She asks instead to stay on earth, where "the unfit / Contrarious moods of men recoil away / And isolate pure spirits", and to have "A place to stand and love in for a day". The silence in this sonnet is not a wall between two people; it is what they share.

sections.h2: How the 9-6-6 circle turns in a couple's life
paragraphs: The beginning is nearly always quiet. The two prefer an evening under a lamp to a party, talk late into the night and understand each other from half a phrase. One silently fixes the other's bicycle; the other leaves the hall light on when the first comes home late. A year passes before they share a flat, and friends learn about the wedding from a photo. From outside they are a calm, slightly closed couple, and they like it that way.

The first crack appears where it did for the Brownings. One says something important too early: "I'm frighteningly happy with you", or "let's live together". The other goes silent, and the next day jokes: "let's forget it, that was the night talking". The word is filed under misprints, and both pretend it was never said.

Then a rule takes hold that nobody announced: write alone and don't show. Hurts wait in a drawer until some "Pisa", proposals go unspoken, drafts stay hidden. From outside the couple is as calm as ever; inside there are two rooms on different floors. In Pisa it was exactly so for the Brownings: he worked downstairs, she upstairs.

Then comes the minus of the Lovers. Insecurity grows in silence. One asks "do you still love me?", the other answers "I'm here, aren't I?" — for the Hermit, the deed is the answer. The first wants more, starts looking for proof, and the second feels examined. From there it is not far to checking and jealousy. Or to the other extreme: one sees the partner as an ideal, and the partner dares not step out of that image and hides whatever does not fit it.
The price of the circle is years of love that exists but is not said. Two hermits under one roof, each with a lantern, each sure the other knows anyway.

sections.h2: What changes the script
paragraphs: The way out is built into the cards. The Hermit does not need to be driven away, and the Lovers do not need to be proved. The cloak needs to be turned outward.

ul: **Say in words what has already been done in deeds.** The Lovers ask for the word; the Hermit thinks the deed is enough. Sonnet XXI asks for both.
**Don't ask for what was said to be forgotten.** If a partner said too much too soon, "I need time" is more honest than "let's pretend this never happened".
**Show the draft.** Not only the finished decision, but the doubt, the fear, the unfinished thought. In this couple the most important things often lie in a drawer.
**Decide out loud, to each other.** The world can be told afterwards, as the Hermit likes. Each other — at once.
**Turn around.** Hand over important things face to face, not from behind, and hold the look that comes back.
**Keep room for shared silence.** Silence chosen by two holds a union together. Silence in which each one hides pulls it apart.

sections.h2: The strong version of the 9-6-6 tail
paragraphs: In its strong version this couple stays quiet to the world and open inside. Its silence is the "deep, dear silence" of the sonnet, not a wall. The Hermit's lantern shines first for the two and then for others: such a couple can give sound advice, because it knows how to listen.

In the preface to the correspondence, the Brownings' son explained why there are exactly 573 letters and will be no more: they are "all that ever passed between my father and mother, for after their marriage they were never separated". The Hermit's language, the letter, ends where life face to face begins. Elizabeth's last letter asks: "Is this my last letter to you, ever dearest?" The tail 9-6-6 puts the same question to the couple: when will the two stop talking through a box of letters and start speaking to each other face to face?

intro: The riddle is in the numbers themselves. A card of solitude opens the road, and then one and the same card stands twice, halfway along and at the end. No single person has this tail: in a personal matrix the middle is the sum of the two outer numbers, and between the Hermit and the Lovers it would hold the Devil (9 + 6 = 15). In a couple the middle is brought by two people, and it turns out to be love again.

ul: **M — "Entry to the task", 9, the Hermit.** What the two want together: quiet, depth, a conversation where half a word is enough. The couple enters its task through this wish, and the same wish is where it gets stuck.
**N — "Middle of the task", 6, the Lovers.** How the couple travels the road: through a word of love said out loud, and through a choice that cannot be made halfway.
**D — "Main task", 6, the Lovers.** What there is to learn: to love openly, to let yourself be seen and to believe you were chosen.

intro: The plot shows best in the story of two English poets, Elizabeth Barrett and Robert Browning. For twenty months they wrote each other letters, they married in secret, and she passed off her most open poems as a translation from the Portuguese. Nobody here calculates their matrix: the story is not proof but a mirror that shows how these three cards work.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 9-6-6 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail where the entry to the task is the Hermit (9), and the middle and the main task are the Lovers (6). The couple comes together through depth, quiet and a common language, travels the road through a word of love said aloud and a choice, and its main task is to love openly and let itself be seen, without hiding from each other what it hides from the world.

faq.q: Why is there no 9-6-6 tail in a personal matrix?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail equals the sum of the entry and the main task: 9 + 6 would give 15, the Devil. In a couple's matrix every point is the sum of the same points of two people, and the middle is added up from the partners' middles, most often 7 + 17, 3 + 3 or 4 + 20. So 9-6-6 appears only in a couple.

faq.q: The Lovers appear twice — does that mean twice as much love?
faq.a: No. A repeated card does not double a quality; each six has its own role. In the middle the Lovers describe how the couple travels the road: through the first word of love and a choice. In the main task they describe what to learn: to repeat that word, to believe you were chosen, and not to hide what is imperfect from the partner.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers?
faq.a: No. The site's engine produces no other couple tail from a nine and two sixes, so 9-6-6 cannot be confused with a permutation: the order "entry — middle — main task" is the only one here.

faq.q: Is the tail 9-6-6 a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not predict events or pass verdicts; it describes a task. For these couples the Hermit is both the entry and, in seven couples out of ten, the value of the union. The difficulty is not the quiet itself, but the moment the quiet starts being kept from each other.

faq.q: How common is the tail 9-6-6?
faq.a: It occurs in roughly one couple in 97 (1.026%) and ranks 36th of the 97 couple tails. It is formed by nine combinations of the partners' personal tails; the most common are 3-7-22 + 6-17-11, 18-3-12 + 9-3-21 and 21-4-10 + 6-20-14.

seo.title: Karmic tail 9 9 18 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 9 18 compatibility: two Hermits and the Moon. Why a couple that guards its quiet gets doubt as its task, read through the Odyssey and the cards.

items.title: The 9-9-18 karmic tail in compatibility: two cautious people and the Moon between them
items.short: The 9-9-18 tail in compatibility poses a riddle. The couple wants quiet and trust — The Hermit stands at the entry and again in the middle — yet the main task belongs to The Moon, the card of fear, guesswork and deception. The answer is this: nobody brings the Moon in. It grows out of the very quiet the two of them guard so carefully — in the dark between two lamps, each one fills in the other alone.

sections.h2: The Odyssey: the most cautious couple in world literature
paragraphs: Odysseus comes home disguised as a beggar and says nothing about who he is. Penelope talks with him by the fire at night as with a stranger. When it is all over and her husband stands before her without the mask, she sits down opposite him — and falls silent again. The subtlest trial of the poem is not the bow and not the suitors, but the question of who moved the bed.

Homer makes this couple equals in one quality: caution. Penelope's standing epithet is περίφρων — dictionaries give "very thoughtful, prudent"; Murray's English, as a rule, renders it "wise Penelope". The old nurse says Odysseus silenced her "in the great wisdom of his heart" (Zhukovsky's Russian makes him "cautiously wise"). In this couple both the husband and the wife are crafty, and the roles are not split by sex.

Set Waite's divinatory list for The Hermit beside them and it reads like a portrait of the pair. Upright it includes "Prudence, circumspection" and "dissimulation, roguery"; reversed, "Concealment, disguise, policy, fear, unreasoned caution". Dissimulation is Odysseus, who, in Homer's words, "made the many falsehoods of his tale seem like the truth". Concealment is Penelope, who for three years wove a shroud by day and unravelled it by night. Disguise is the beggar's rags. Fear and unreasoned caution are Penelope at the hearth in Book 23.

Two Hermits in a couple's tail are not two lonely people. They are two people equally good at keeping their light to themselves. That is what makes them kin — and out of that same kinship grows their Moon.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: a happiness only the two of them know (M = 9)
paragraphs: Cast up by the sea on a foreign shore, naked and with nothing, Odysseus wishes young Nausicaa the best thing he knows:
"For nothing is greater or better than this, when man and wife dwell in a home in one accord, a great grief to their foes and a joy to their friends; but they know it best themselves."

Homer's word here is ὁμοφροσύνη, oneness of mind. The Greek of the last clause can also be read as "great fame for themselves", which is how Zhukovsky put it in Russian; Murray reads it as "they know it best themselves".

This is The Hermit at the entry to the task. The couple enters its task wanting a world that makes sense without explanations and needs no witnesses. Odysseus and Penelope have literally built such a world: a bedroom the husband raised in stone around a living olive tree, and a bed that, apart from the two of them, only one maid knows.

In everyday life it looks quiet. Friends hear about the engagement when the rings are already bought. A holiday means a cabin with no signal. An evening when each sits in their own armchair with their own book is not boredom for them but happiness. They love through deeds: they fix things, fetch things, remember that the other won't eat onions. Nothing is done in a rush — so much time passes between the first date and a shared flat that acquaintances stop asking.

In the couple's reading the same point also appears in the sphere "Relationship and common language": The Hermit is their common language. The two understand each other from half a word, and that is their gift. But in Lisovskaya's scheme the entry to the task lies on the line of tasks and can turn into resistance. Here the resistance is quiet: half a word starts to be enough every time, and each fills in the other half alone. A door closed to strangers one day turns out to be closed to each other's questions as well.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: twenty years, two fires (N = 9)
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya's book the middle of the tail has no meaning of its own — it is an addition to the main task; we read it as the path the couple takes from the wish to the task. Here again stands The Hermit, which means the path is walked alone, each with their own fire.
For twenty years Odysseus and Penelope live apart, and both survive by keeping secrets. He tells everyone he meets plausible stories about himself. She strings the suitors along with her loom:
"Then day by day I would weave at the great web, but by night would unravel it, when I had let place torches by me."

The most exact scene of the middle is the night in Book 19. Odysseus and his son carry the weapons out of the hall, and Athena goes ahead of them, unseen, "bearing a golden lamp". The son is amazed by the light, and the father cuts him short: "Hush, check thy thought, and ask no question". There is light, but you may not ask about it — the Hermit of the middle in a single line.

Then Penelope comes down into the empty hall and talks with the beggar by the fire deep into the night. She tells the stranger about her great ruse, the loom. He answers with fiction; Homer says he "made the many falsehoods of his tale seem like the truth". She weeps for the husband who is sitting beside her; he pities her, yet "his eyes stood fixed between his lids as though they were horn or iron, and with guile he hid his tears." Two people in one circle of light — and each alone with their grief.

Benebell Wen offers two readings of The Hermit's light. The first is a light in the darkness for others. The second is a person "who sees the world through his or her own light", who "walks in the direction of his own thoughts only". When there are two Hermits, the second reading becomes the couple's plot: each sees the partner in their own light — and partly sees themselves.

Today this middle shows up in small things. One partner mentions being made redundant once the new job is already found: "I didn't want to load you with it." The other sorts out a hard conversation with their parents and reports it once it is settled. There are no loud rows — problems, as Lisovskaya writes of the Nine in its minus, pile up in silence. This is not coldness but care in The Hermit's language: you weather your storm yourself so as not to worry the other. The price is that the other learns of the storm only after it has passed — and starts wondering how many more there were. That thought is where the Moon begins.

sections.h2: Main task: recognising the person sitting opposite (D = 18)
paragraphs: The suitors are gone from the house, the nurse cries that the husband has returned, and Penelope comes down and sits facing him by the fire:

"Howbeit she sat long in silence, and amazement came upon her soul; and now with her eyes she would look full upon his face, and now again she would fail to know him, for that he had upon him mean raiment."

That flicker of "it's him — it's not him" is moonlight itself: now visible, now gone. Her son cannot bear it: "thy heart is ever harder than stone". Nor can Odysseus: "Strange lady! to thee beyond all women have the dwellers on Olympus given a heart that cannot be softened" — and he asks for a bed of his own: "that all alone I may lay me down, for verily the heart in her breast is of iron". Penelope replies: "Strange sir... right well do I know what manner of man thou wast, when thou wentest forth from Ithaca on thy long-oared ship."

Husband and wife address each other with one and the same word — in Homer it is δαιμονίη and δαιμόνιε, "strange one, past understanding". Each sees the other's coldness and not their own. And Penelope says the key thing about this couple's Moon task: **she is checking a living man against an image twenty years old**.

Lisovskaya, describing The Moon among a couple's tasks, names this too: an image created at the start that later collapses; feelings hidden because tenderness is taken for weakness. For a 9-9-18 couple the image is usually not false but out of date. The two change quietly, each on their own, and remember each other as they were. Years on, you can sit across from a person and measure them against who they once were.

In Waite there is a bridge between these cards. The reversed Hermit has "fear, unreasoned caution", and the reversed Moon has "Instability, inconstancy, **silence**". The silence two Hermits choose as peace already belongs, in Waite's list, to the Moon.
Where does the fear come from? Strangely, not from the partner. Before his homecoming Odysseus hears, in the land of the dead, the advice of Agamemnon, whose own return home ended in his death:
"Wherefore in thine own case be thou never gentle even to thy wife. Declare not to her all the thoughts of thy heart, but tell her somewhat, and let somewhat also be hidden."

And again: "for no longer is there faith in women." Penelope, explaining her coldness later, calls up Helen. Other people's marriages end up in this couple's bedroom. The Moon works the same way today: a friend's divorce, the parents' story, past relationships suggest the plot, and the partner answers for things they never did. Lisovskaya writes of jealousy and grievances spun from invented stories — here you can see where they are invented.

paragraphs.h3: Truth sent out through the gate of ivory

paragraphs: The subtlest clue is Penelope's dream. She dreams of an eagle that kills her geese and speaks with a human voice: "I, that before was the eagle, am now again come back as thy husband". She tells the dream to the beggar — that is, to Odysseus himself — and he confirms it: "in no wise is it possible to wrest this dream aside and give it another meaning". Penelope answers with a speech on the two gates of dreams: "one is fashioned of horn and one of ivory". Dreams through ivory "deceive men, bringing words that find no fulfillment"; those through horn "bring true issues to pass". And she decides her dream did not come through the gate of horn.

The truth has been said twice, plainly and aloud — and it is filed among the deceptions. Homer plays on words here: "ivory" (elephas) echoes the verb "to deceive" (elephairomai), "horn" (keras) echoes "to fulfil" (krainō). **This couple's Moon task is not only to stop believing phantoms but to recognise the truth when it is spoken simply.**

A detail that is easy to miss: in the same book Odysseus's eyes, holding back tears, are "as though they were horn or iron". The truth sits by the fire with eyes of horn and keeps silent. This is our observation, not Homer's gloss, but for the tail it fits: in a 9-9-18 couple the truth is more often not hidden but held behind a motionless face.

paragraphs.h3: A test is fear in disguise

paragraphs: The Moon also breeds a habit of testing. In the last book Odysseus comes to his old father in the orchard and hesitates "whether to kiss and embrace his father, and tell him all... or whether he should first question him, and prove him in each thing". He chooses the test, "to prove him first with mocking words". Just before, he had said outright what he feared: "see whether he will recognize me and know me by sight, or whether he will fail to know me, since I have been gone so long a time."

The one who tests is afraid of not being recognised. In a 9-9-18 couple the tests are small: will they notice I've been gone all evening; will they ask without prompting; will they remember without a hint. Each looks like caution, but at heart it is the question "am I still here for you?", asked in a way that makes it impossible to answer.

sections.h2: Clues in the numbers: a room built around one trunk
paragraphs: The 9-9-18 tail occurs in roughly one couple in 31 — 3.26% of all date combinations, seventh of the 97 couple's tails. What stands next to it is more interesting.

The centre of the couple's matrix — the atmosphere inside the union — comes in only two kinds for these couples: The Moon in 74%, The Hermit in 26%. "The couple's values" are also only these two cards: The Hermit in 76.3%, The Moon in 23.7%. A third card never appears, and that is no coincidence. Adding and reducing numbers preserves the remainder on division by nine, and in any matrix the entry to the tail, by that remainder, equals the main task plus the centre. In this couple both the entry (9) and the task (18) divide by nine — so the centre must too, and among numbers up to 22 that leaves only 9 and 18. By the same arithmetic the couple's values must divide by nine as well.

**Five key points of this couple — the three cards of the tail, the atmosphere and the values — are written with two cards.** Like Odysseus's bedroom, built around one trunk: everything inward in this couple grows from the same olive. The Moon in the atmosphere of three couples out of four is the gift hidden in the task. According to Lisovskaya, in its plus such a couple understands each other by intuition and every year discovers something new in the partner. A partner who can never be known to the end is both an anxiety and the thing people hold on to for years.

A couple's tail is made from the partners' personal tails, and here there are only seven combinations. The most frequent are 15-5-8 + 21-4-10 (48% of these couples), 12-19-7 + 15-8-11 (24%) and 18-3-12 + 18-6-6 (17%). Our own run over the same dates adds a detail: in 82.3% of couples neither partner has The Hermit or The Moon in their personal tail, and in the remaining 17.7% both partners have these cards in their personal tails. It never happens that only one of them brings them.
In this couple there is no "hermit" and no "dreamer", no one who "shut down first". The quiet is made by two — as in Homer, where caution is shared equally.
The same 9-9-18 order also exists as a personal tail — for 924 dates since 1900. That is a different calculation with different roles for the points; the personal tail has an article of its own.

sections.h2: The bed of living olive: what disperses the Moon
paragraphs: Recognition does not come through evidence. The nurse has already seen the scar on her husband's leg — Penelope did not believe her. In Book 19 the beggar described Odysseus's cloak and golden brooch exactly — she believed he had seen her husband, not that he was her husband. Something else works. "So she spoke, and made trial of her husband": Penelope orders his bed to be carried out of the bedroom for him.
And the man with the motionless eyes flares up:
"Woman, truly this is a bitter word that thou hast spoken. Who has set my bed elsewhere?"

The bed cannot be moved: its base is the stump of a living olive around which he himself built the bedroom. In Murray's words, "a great token is wrought in the fashioned bed, and it was I that built it and none other." And at once Odysseus imagines the worst: "whether by now some man has cut from beneath the olive stump, and set the bedstead elsewhere."

This is a flash of jealous Moon — a story made up in a second. And it is exactly what proves to Penelope that her husband is before her: a stranger would not have flared up. Wen draws a precise line: "Key 2 is about disguise. Key 18 is about revelation of the inner self". Disguise belongs to another card; the Moon is the minute when the inner self comes out. **In a 9-9-18 couple the Moon gives way not when the evidence is in, but when someone stops holding their face still.**
Penelope answers in kind. "Be not vexed with me, Odysseus" — and for the first time she names her fear aloud:
"For always the heart in my breast was full of dread, lest some man should come and beguile me with his words; for there are many that plan devices of evil."
A fear said aloud stops being the Moon and becomes simply a fear, something two people can deal with together. "Lo, thou dost convince my heart, unbending as it is."

Then Homer gives a simile that seems to be the wrong way round. As shipwrecked men who swim to land are glad of the shore, "even so welcome to her was her husband, as she gazed upon him". It is not Odysseus who is compared to the shipwrecked, but the one who sat at home for twenty years. In a couple of two Hermits there is no "one who left" and no "one who waited": each went through their own shipwreck alone, and both need the shore.

And then "the long night she held back at the end of its course" — Athena delays the dawn. The Moon's time becomes a time for telling. Penelope speaks of the years in a house full of strangers. Odysseus tells of himself — and not only of what he endured: he "recounted all the woes that he had brought on men, and all the toil that in his sorrow he had himself endured". Earlier still, when he mentions a new and heavy prophecy, she asks him not to put it off: "come, tell me of this trial, for in time to come, methinks, I shall learn of it, and to know it at once is no whit worse." And he, the master of half-said things, answers: "Yet I will declare it, and will hide nothing. Verily thy heart shall have no joy of it". Two Hermits turn their light towards each other.

sections.h2: What changes the script: five habits instead of tests
paragraphs: Leaving the tail's script does not require becoming loud and sociable. Hermits stay Hermits; what changes is where they shine their light.

ul: **A sign instead of an exam.** A 9-9-18 couple shares much that nobody else knows: pet words, places, the story of how they met. That is their olive. Among the Moon's minuses Lisovskaya names a partner's secrets turned into weapons; the strong version of the tail makes shared secrets a root, not a weapon.
**Name the fear instead of testing.** Instead of "let's see if they notice" — "I'm afraid that…". A test is fear in disguise; said aloud, it loses its force.

**Tell before, not after the fact.** The storm need not be shared, but its coming can be announced: "I'm having a hard week, I'm coping, I'll tell you later." That is enough for the other not to fill in the rest.
**Check against the living person, not the image.** Now and then ask each other what has changed. Two Hermits change in silence, and the memory of the earlier partner ages faster than it seems.

**Distinguish withdrawing into yourself from withdrawing from the other.** Lisovskaya advises a couple with The Moon to accept that a partner's need to withdraw is a way to recover, not a lack of love. For two Hermits this is the main rule of quiet: silence frightens no one once it has been agreed on.

paragraphs: The strong version of the tail is Odysseus and Penelope at the end of Book 23: two people who went through everything alone and now stay awake until dawn because they are telling each other. "Nor did sweet sleep fall upon her eyelids, till he had told all the tale."

paragraphs: Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. A person born on 14.08.1975 has the personal tail 15-5-8 and centre 7. A person born on 14.10.1975 has the tail 21-4-10 and centre 11.

paragraphs: The couple's middle is not derived from the two outer numbers: it is added up from the personal middles, 5 + 4. In this example The Moon also stands in "The couple's values" and in the point "What to create together" (8 + 10 = 18), while The Hermit also sits in "Common language". The couple's tail is read by its own roles: the partners' personal tails are not retold in it.

sections.h2: 18-9-9 and 9-18-9: the same cards in a different order
paragraphs: The same numbers make two more couple's tails. In 18-9-9 (1.754% of couples; The Moon in the centre for 57.1%, The Hermit for 42.9%) The Moon stands at the entry: the couple enters its task through enchantment, mystery and a shared fantasy, and the main task becomes The Hermit — not to drift into two separate cells and not to go cold.

In 9-18-9 (1.136% of couples; The Moon in the centre for 81.3%, The Hermit for 18.7%) The Hermit stands both at the entry and in the task, and The Moon in the middle: the path runs through a fog of misunderstandings, and the lesson is not to hide in one's shell. In 9-9-18 the order is the least noticeable: first comes the quiet, and the fog arrives at the end as its direct consequence.

**M · 9 The Hermit — "Entry to the task".** What the couple wants together: a world of their own with no audience, understanding without spare words, an unhurried pace. This is also their common language.
**N · 9 The Hermit — "Middle of the task".** How the couple walks towards the task: each with their own light, settling much alone and telling the other after the fact.

**D · 18 The Moon — "Main task".** What grows in that quiet: guesses, tests, the fear of being deceived, a memory of the partner in place of the partner. The lesson is to get to know each other again and again, and to say aloud what usually gets filled in by imagination.

intro: A couple's tail predicts nothing and passes no verdict on the union: it shows where the same difficulty keeps returning for the two of them. That difficulty has a great literary double. It is not a story of love at first sight but of a husband and wife who kept faith with each other for twenty years — and when they met again, could not open up.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 9-9-18 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's task, made of three cards. The Hermit at the entry: the couple wants quiet and a world of its own. The Hermit in the middle: the path is walked in silence, each with their own light. The Moon in the main task: guesses, tests and fears grow out of the quiet. The lesson is to get to know each other again and again, and to say aloud what usually gets filled in by imagination.

faq.q: Are the couple's tail 9-9-18 and the personal tail 9-9-18 the same thing?
faq.a: No. The couple's tail comes from adding up the points of two personal matrices, and its points mean the couple's entry, middle and main task. A personal tail with the same numbers occurs for 924 dates since 1900; it is a different calculation with different roles for the points.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a relationship?
faq.a: A couple's tail does not grade the union and predicts nothing. It shows where a difficulty keeps returning for the couple: here, in the silence from which guesses grow. The same two cards also give strength: deep conversations, respect for boundaries, the ability to keep discovering each other for years.

faq.q: Why does such a couple only ever have The Moon or The Hermit in the centre?
faq.a: It is the arithmetic of the matrix: reduction preserves the remainder on division by nine, and by that remainder the entry to the tail equals the main task plus the centre. With an entry of 9 and a task of 18 the centre can only be 9 or 18: The Moon in 74% of these couples, The Hermit in 26%.

faq.q: How can a couple find its own tail?
faq.a: Enter two dates of birth in the compatibility calculator: the reading shows the three cards of the tail in the sphere "The couple's karmic tail". By hand, add up the matching points of the two personal tails and reduce any sum above 22, as in the example above.

report: The subtlest trial of the Odyssey is not the Cyclops and not the suitors, but the question of who moved the bed. The husband is back after twenty years, the house is quiet at last, and the wife sits down opposite him by the fire and says nothing. The couple's tail 9-9-18 — two Hermits and The Moon — is built like that scene. The couple enters its task through quiet, walks it in silence and gets The Moon as its main task: guesses, tests, the fear of being deceived. **Nobody brings the Moon in — it grows out of the very quiet the two of them guard so carefully.**

His bedroom is built around a living olive tree, and apart from the two of them only one maid knows the bed. Half a word is enough, and that is the couple's gift. The trouble begins when half a word is always enough and each fills in the other half alone.

report.h3: Truth sent out through the gate of ivory

The fear does not come from the partner. Before his homecoming Odysseus is coached by Agamemnon, whose own return home ended in his death: "tell her somewhat, and let somewhat also be hidden". report.h3: A test is fear in disguise

report: Even his old father Odysseus tests before he embraces. And Homer names what he fears: whether his father will know him, "or whether he will fail to know me, since I have been gone so long a time." The one who tests is afraid of staying unrecognised. In a 9-9-18 couple the tests are small: will the other notice I've been gone all evening; will they ask without prompting; will they remember without a hint. Each looks like caution, but at heart it asks "do I still matter here?" in a way that cannot be answered.

report.h3: A bed that cannot be moved

report: Recognition does not come through evidence: the nurse told of the scar, the beggar described the cloak and brooch — Penelope did not believe. So she orders his bed carried out of the bedroom, and the man with the motionless eyes flares up: "Who has set my bed elsewhere?" The bed's base is the stump of a living olive; "a great token is wrought in the fashioned bed". At once he imagines the worst: the root has been cut. Penelope answers in kind and for the first time names her fear aloud: she was afraid a stranger would deceive her with fine words. A fear said aloud stops being the Moon. Homer compares her joy to that of swimmers reaching the shore after a shipwreck: the one who waited at home was shipwrecked too. Then Athena holds back the night, and the Moon's time becomes a time for telling. Odysseus speaks not only of what he endured but of "all the woes that he had brought on men".

The whole matrix of such a couple is built around this plot: its atmosphere and its values also hold The Moon or The Hermit, and the arithmetic of addition rules out a third card. And in no such couple are these cards brought by one partner alone — the quiet is made by two. **So the way out is shared as well:** a sign instead of an exam, so that shared secrets become a root and not a weapon; a fear named aloud instead of a test; telling before, not after the fact; checking against the living person, not the image. The strong version of the tail is two people who went through everything alone and now stay awake until dawn because they are telling each other.
